_childDocuments_.review: - Primarily black-and-white noir stylings all around, with rare pops of color- The character designs are unique, to say the least- The music is pretty great. Given the noir veneer, you'll hear a lot of swingy jazz and the occasional bluesy track- The most impressive part of the entire presentation is the voice acting, in my opinion. Sonny's VA is the clear stand-out, but all of the voices are really well done- It's like Dragnet, but with animals- The characters are all pretty great, even if they are just film noir parodies and archetypes- The promotional content should have clued you in, but the game is quite funny- The story is quite good, even if the twist is a little predictable. Still a good mystery- It's a point-and-click detective game, so you'll be skulking around town to find clues, track down leads, and interrogate animals of interest- The interrogation scenes are pretty fun. I appreciate the ability to retry each one for a perfect score- The "putting it together" minigame is a bit more confusing. The solutions make sense, but it feels like I was mostly just trying things until it worked- There's other minigames and events to spice things up as well- I don't think I'll be replaying, even though I wish I would have been thorough enough to 100% the game- With the humor and good story, this is an easy game to like- I played through the whole game on the Steam Deck, and it ran flawlessly- . The story and gameplay won't blow you away, but it's still a very enjoyable experience

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:1. the voice acting deserves marvelous thumbs up.2. nice music for the noir style.3. recommended for those who love noir ambiance and point and click novel. Better buy it at discount price.Cons:1. Despite the great voice acting, sometimes it's just too lengthy and trivial like they never end, which slow down the whole story pace.2. For the above reason, the whole game is just not exciting at all...nor make you immerse in it. You don't feel the impulse that drives you to continue the story. You don't feel like it's a game but an interactive script.3. The story is flat and doesn't build well.The story tries to make it mysterious in the beginning, but not convincing, some plots lack of logic.In the middle of the story, things become clear, but also start to get boring, (not to mention it isn't very exciting in the very beginning) Players may expect there would be more twisting, but that's all. No any other surprise.4. The protagonist is lacking charisma.The chicken police. The one that players act is an old rooster which is just so pessimistic, wait for retirement all the time, and view the world grey on almost everything from the beginning to the end of the story. Although his partner tries to compromise this dragging style, and be young and intrepid, you just don't feel the joy or the hard-boiled spirit to be these chicken police. (I know it's a noir style story, but the protagonist is just so phlegmy and lack of energy to be a detective or a police officer)It's interesting to watch these two roosters voice acting in the beginning, but they just disputing on irrelevant things soooo much with each other. In the end it's like hearing two old men (especially the protagonist) quarreling over trivial things, which is not appealing at all.5. The questioning system kind of lack of logic, maybe I didn't get it. It doesn't influence the story process though, if you are not obsessed with the Steam achievements.6. Not a very convincing background conceptThe story uses animals to represent different race, but not very convincing. They behave like humans with animal-features but at the same time you can hear "I am glad she didn't eat me" this kind of dialog all the time. If they were already humanized, why "eating" each other? This concept just so disturbing and unreal. Overall: You could see the ambition in the game, the voice acting is absolutely great and worthy. But it's not an interesting game nor a juicy novel. (It's not even a mysterious novel, just a noir story if you must say.)For the similar games, Blacksad does better in the story telling or pacing with a more realistic world concept built. L.A. Noire allows players to experience as a righteous detective. For Chicken Police, you may be disappointed if you have high expectations due to its "overwhelming  positive" comments or awards. It just has a long way to go in so many perspectives.

_childDocuments_.review: By the Wild Ones, Chicken Police is a cluckin' masterpiece of noir storytelling - albeit in an animal world. It takes place in Clawville, a once glorious city-state where animals of all species supposedly live in "peace everlasting."Sonny Featherland, the main character, is the grizzled, booze-soaked veteran on the edge of retirement, who pairs with Marty MacChicken, his longtime partner. Together, they embody every classic detective trope, from dimly lit offices to smoky jazz lounges.Really enjoyed every bit of this game – the art, the music, the secrets, the humor. Definitely recommend it for anyone interested in diving into this world with no hurry.

_childDocuments_.review: I found myself buying this game because of the style and Noir Detective theme but enjoying it on its own merits. The characters and story within are great. The hidden and untold stories, even more fascinating. There's a lot that gets said and unsaid. The story leaves a few good plot threads dangling but also satisfies in all the right ways. It's a point and click where I only felt lost once or twice and that led to me having to look up the answer but that was because I had missed an interaction in a subscreen. Otherwise, the game never throws any curve balls at you that I have had as criticisms of other point and clicks and why I generally avoid the genre except for a few games here or there.I don't think I can say enough good things about this game. The voice acting is superb, the writing amazing, the art, very stylistic and appropriate. The black and white with splashes of color really highlight those moments but the art in the art gallery, which contains a lot of full color, shows how talented the artists actually are. The puns and clever use of the animal people setting is great, both in how it plays into the dialogue and how it plays into the setting in general. This feels like a fully realized world and we're only getting glimpses of it.The game plays very heavily into the Noir theme and you can kind of guess some of the twists before they happen. If you are familiar with Noir Stories, I can't recommend this enough, especially with ALL of the references that just make me want to laugh harder and harder. If you don't mind playing a point and click adventure, I highly recommend this game. It's a great story from beginning to end.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, couldn't put it down until I've finished it.Really hope there's another one in the pipeline, I'll definitely get it.If you like detective games, and/or noir then it definitely will worth your while.The concept of using animals in the art while weird at first glance, really grew on me, especially when I heard them talk.There's just so much effort put in the art and voices it's hard to overstate.I'm actually super interested in some unexplored areas, like the hive and Roachtown.If you explore the game deeply, the lore goes fairly deep, it's a really well put together world.While I definitely recommend the game, there are some feedback / caveats I'd like to mention:- When learning about new things that appeared in the codex or as new pieces of information of a person I found it confusing to find what was new in my notebook. There's essentially no differentiation between notes that I've read / seen and ones that I have not. This is quite annoying, when I have a lengthy discussion with a person, and I have multiple notifications about new entries. Because of this I had this lingering thought while playing that I may have missed something from my notes. (This was even more annoying as I got more entries in my "codex" page, and it takes ages to get to the end of it just to find out there's nothing new there.)- It would've been helpful to show some sort of indication that I've exhausted a type of interaction (like talk/ask/see), instead of having to experience a certain discussion twice just to realise I've done so.- About midway subtitles started to differ from the voice over. Just a pet peeve of mine.- Investigations didn't seem to have any weight, and there's no way to do them wrong. It also seemed a bit inconsistent and hard to figure out the logic behind it at times, so once or twice I resorted to just trying whatever the game told me to put where.- Another pet peeve, but a couple times "seeing" someone actually started conversations instead.- I have a 13" laptop screen, and maybe this is better on bigger screens, but it was quite annoying having to click on all note entries to be able to read them.In any case, the story was great, got me hooked and didn't let go until the very end.Apart from some minor annoyances mentioned above, I have no complaints, and I can wholeheartedly recommend the game to anyone who has the time.You can easily get 16h of fun out of it if you visit all the temporary locations, which is what I did, and I'm sure there's a couple more hours you can squeeze out of it, especially if you listed to dialogues to the end, instead of clicking through as soon as you've read the text. (Again, which is what I did.)

_childDocuments_.review: This is very nice game.It is classic noire story about veteran detective with just few days until retirement who got dragged into horrible mess by pretty lady.In this game humans has been replaced by animals. Animals of course serve as allegory for humans. The world setting gives space for lot of animal puns and humor ... and the quality of humor is pretty high.The quality of writing in this game is pretty high in general, it is fully voiced and I enjoyed very much listening to the conversations.The gameplay itself is half adventure game, half visual novel. You click on stuff and the hero chicken gives you commentary, you click on characters and you talk to them. There is interrogation minigame where protagonist says that he should focus on certain behaviour feature of target and you need to chose your questions based on that. It's not easy but at least the protagonist leads the conversation in direction you selected and doesn't go crazy like in L.A.Noire. Plus you can repeat the minigame if you are not satisfied with your performance.The game is not very long, but it's time well spend.I can only recommend this game, it has been long time since I was so satisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicken Police: Paint it Red is a point & click adventure game which has a unique premise and art-style: the city of Clawville (where the game takes place) is populated by humanoids with animal heads!This premise allows the telling of a suitably noir story, complete with sizzling inter-species tension, dames with legs that just won't quit, gangsters, and sleaze up the wazoo (where else would you find it, to be fair?).It's all off the record, on the QT, and very Hush Hush!Chicken Police features fully voiced dialogue, and the writing is top-notch leading to many laugh out loud moments, as well as the odd snicker at just how absurd the photographed visuals continue to be.This is a solid and enjoyable experience for anybody who enjoys point & click, adventure games, or visual novels... or even if the player enjoys noir fiction in books or movies... the world of Chicken Police is both familiar to us, and can still surprise with it's inventiveness.I made a video which goes into more detail and serves as a good jumping off point if you are considering buying Chicken Police: Paint it Red for yourself:I'm going to play more on camera if you enjoy the video, I'll be recording a short series. _childDocuments_.review: I received press code for this from HandyGames to stream some of it but finished most of it on my own.I'm not going to lie, I didn't really know what to think when I first saw this game but I'd heard good buzz and decided to give it a go. I'm very glad I did. Don't let the anthropomorphic animal characters put you off, this is an awesome experience and the animal characters have such personality and are so well designed, I think you'll be impressed.Chicken Police is about 80% visual novel and about 20% basic detective adventure game. As someone who normally doesn't like visual novels, this one got my attention because it was a noir detective story which we don't get a lot of these days and also because it was fully voice acted. The writing's sharp and often funny and the voice acting is pretty much stellar all around. Without it, I don't think this would have been as good to me as it was. Most of the investigation elements are pretty basic, consisting mostly of clicking around the environment, talking to people, doing some interrogations that are pretty hard to fail and then connecting clues in a way that you literally can't fail and which you're pretty much handheld through. I will admit, I do wish this was fleshed out more and had more depth to it but it still got the job done.It's not a short story and unlike most visual novels, it only has one conclusion so once you've finished it, that's basically it, unless you want to go back for achievements and collectibles, of which there are plenty. I was quite satisfied with the story I got though and despite the game being more verbose than it needs to be at times, I was compelled to see it through to the end and was never bored.The art style is very striking and the soundtrack is absolute perfection for a game like this. I bought it on Bandcamp after my first play session. Games like Hatoful Boyfriend I have no interest in at all and when I saw the animal characters, I was initially turned off too but they're so well drawn and each has their own unique, memorable personality. The lore of the game world also takes into account that it's all animals and has unique societal conflicts and strife that are related to that. If anything, I would have liked to see this expanded upon more.Chicken Police was one of my biggest indie surprises of 2020. If you like good stories and especially noire stories, definitely don't pass this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the most fun and refreshing visual novels I've played in a while. Takes a really straightforward genre (detective noir/whodunnit) and sets it in a unique and interesting world, but the familiarity of the genre makes it a lot easier to digest what is some surprisingly complex world building. It's not flawless, the gameplay doesn't always flow that smoothly and it can be pretty difficult to deduce the right way to interrogate/search for clues unintentionally, but I only encountered that a couple times in a ten hour playthrough. I've come to love the characters and am very excited to see them in the upcoming HIVE sequel. I imagine a lot of the gameplay issues will be streamlined in the next game, but I still highly recommend it for the strong character writing and storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: If I pitched you a noir detective video game in writing, saying it stars "people" with human bodies and animal heads, what would you say (beside that I'm gone out of my head)? Luckily, Chicken Police doesn't have to rely on dry words alone, and the moment you see the beautifully composed black-and-white images with our suit-and-tie-and-rooster-head protagonist, you'll probably feel that the creators tapped into something really exciting, instead of being simply crazy. Please note that I'm not saying that they are -not- crazy :)Still, having an insane-ish idea and translating it into beautiful imagery is far from enough for success. The real interesting thing about Chicken Police that it weaves a somewhat ordinary but still decently written crime story, it creates a pretty standard background city, and makes the whole thing work by crafting some very good characters from the human-animal hybrids, using but not overusing the animal stereotypes to very good effect. Add in the superb soundtrack, and Chicken Police becomes as good as a noir visual novel can ever hope to be.While the game is admittedly part visual novel, the creators wanted to add in some adventure gaming elements, which, for the most part, don't work too well. There are some rather forlorn attempts at skill minigames, there's a clue-analysis type of game that is decent but way too obvious, and there's the interrogation, which is supposed to be a key gameplay mechanic, but it's not used very much, and more often than not, I ended up totally confused by how the game evaluated my efforts. On the positive side, the game bombards us with character and case information, but instead of overtaxing out memory, it puts them in a surprisingly neat and handy information filing system.Chicken Police is a game not to be missed if you're a fan of noir detective stories, if you love stylish black-and-white visuals, or if you're into weird ideas well executed. It's far from flawless, but it's unique and its depiction of its characters and its world is really noteworthy.

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly, I haven't played this long enough to write a review. This really is more of an opinion.There is much to love about Chicken Police. The visuals are very well done, the voice acting is superb and the soundtrack spot on. As a VN, gameplay isn't really the main attraction here. It's alright but sadly a bit fiddly. Especially the questionings feel pretty random. You get some questions to chose from and need to find the ones that best work on the person you're talking to. But I never really felt in control of that part of the game though I did reasonably well. The writing is hit and miss and all over the place. Some parts are very atmospheric, a great addition to the visual experience. But then the game often forgets what it wants to be. A moody noir story? A comedy? A persiflage? Of course it can be all at once and still work but for me it did not. I just couldn't buy into the cliched narration that felt like a best of noir quotes followed by poorly executed jokes. Both got into the way of the story itself and both did not work on their own. The best example for the overly ambitious writing that screams "I'm new to this, I don't trust myself to get my point across subtly" is the way the game portraits racism. It's a theme that this game just had to implement and I was very much looking forward to it. But it was so shallow in its approach. Being racist to an entirely different species just doesn't feel like a good commentary on the topic. I expected a more nuanced approach to it but sadly it was using racism mostly as a joke. Let's stick to the issue of how the game implements racism a bit. One of my main criticisms of the writing would be that the main characters are constantly talking about the species of each person you come across. This really breaks the immersion for me. I don't believe that these characters who never experienced a world that is not like theirs can't approach a single person without making remarks about their appearance. Just think about it. If you'd talk to a stranger, would you constantly bring up the color of their hair, skin, eyes or whatnot? And while they are constantly doing this, constantly making jokes about other people based on their species, they also get all whiny when somebody mentions their own species. Suddenly it's portrayed as racism. It just doesn't make sense and is not well thought out. The writing is just inconsistient (notice how I'm not even touching the topic of racism itself here nor am I saying the game is racist or I dislike the game for implementing racism).Another thing that did strike me as odd was the way women were talked about. And this goes back to my initial point of the game not knowing if it is a noir game, a comedy or persiflage. The game just mimics the way women were portraited in some of those old noir movies. They are overly sexualized Femme Fatales. Fine, but then the game goes on and makes very modern jokes and has an opinion on racism, however shallow it may be. So you really gotta ask the question why point out that old school racism was uncalled for by using it as a source of humor but then mimic good old sexism without much comment on it? To me it all boils down to the writers not having a lot of confidence about their vision or maybe it was not thought out well enough. Maybe they weren't discussing it on such a meta level which they should have. But this is just guessing. In the end I can only tell you what I think of the game. And I think it's a tiny bit too average in terms of writing to be worth my time. But I see how good some of it is. And if you can enjoy a story even if it feels constructed and messy and jokes are clearly tagged on then this game can be a wild ride. There is much potential here. And if I were to come across this game 10 or 15 years ago I might have loved it. Sadly I was playing it as an old fart who refuses to be entertained.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicken Police is a nice little Visual Novel that I can recommend in general. Maybe not for the full price of 20€, but If the game is on sale for 15€ or less, I would recommend it. The biggest strengh of the game are the visuals and the good voice acting and of course the fact that every character is a anthropomorphic animal. You play as a Cop and you are trying to solve some vague threats that quickly turns into a murder case. The game and story obviously takes heavy influence from the genre of noir. While serious things happen in the story, the game always knows that it is a bit silly and is using the frame of the setting for some gags. This is not a "comedy" game, but one that is self aware and usually winks a bit at the player.The story is "alright" but gets a bit silly in the end. A lot of story points and characters become a bit meaningless and sometimes even pointless in the end. It feels like the developers may had bigger plans for the game, or maybe they are planning to expand on certain aspects of the world and some characters in a sequel. While the game features some "detective" elements like questioning characters and doing "case work". Do not expect anything deep here. This is actually one of the flaws of the game, but some of these aspects do not make a lot of sense and some of the questioning situations are a bit trial and error and not really based on observation of behavior, clues, evidence and putting this together.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a classic noir detective movie played completely straight, made with love and charm. I can't pitch it better than to just tell you to go watch the trailer and listen to the protagonist's phenomenal voice acting. If that doesn't sell it to you, I don't know why you are even bothering with reviews. The game itself is a VN. There are brief minigames here and there and a few interrogations where your conversation tree choices are scored but you're not here for the gameplay. You're here for the writing and presentation which is phenomenal on every level. The world building is packed with little bits of lore that just did not need to be there but these guys went the extra mile. Every single conversation tree is a delight, whether you're meeting some dude doing an old movie character actor routine for exposition or your ***hole protags are volleying banter with someone else who is equally an ***hole. The game is packed to the gills charm and an absolute delight. And unlike a lot of stories of this sort, the core mystery fits the story pretty well and doesn't feel like a copout that you have to say "Well, it's more of a character study..." to cope as the credits roll. _childDocuments_.review: Finished the game in 11 hours, 100% complete on PC in about 2-3 playthroughs for achievements. What is it?- Think LA Noire / LA confidential, but with an animal protagonist. Completely voice acted visual novel. Takes most of the cues from that era of "Noir"-esque writing, which can be good/bad depending on how well you like the genre. A point-and-click adventure style format light detective game but really, you're here for a story more than anything else.RATING: 7/10GOOD: A. Top notch voice acting, including distinct characters. Animal characters have both stereotypical accents from various earth-like "regions/countries" alongside quirky animal "ticks". I believe every line (or close to) is fully voice acted to an AAA degree, which elevates this above a simple text adventure Noir tale.B. Good worldbuilding - As you spend time in basically furry LA, alot of the world building goes on around you in tabloid snippets and character dialogue. Makes it feel like a lived in universe.C. Good writing - Again, this can be good/bad depending on your familiarity with Noir-esque work/film so I would say it matches what you'd expect from a gumshoe detective novel. Relatively decent villain though I consider it more black and white in terms of motivation and goals. MIDDLEA. Story length, replayability - While I got 11 hours of content from the game, I was expecting a 20-30 hour game with more subplots and story elements, or a padded out detective element to the game as mentioned in the "Needs improvement" part of my review. As a pure story and visual novel it does just enough to give enough screentime to characters making up the world, but not enough to truly make you remember them. B. Visuals / Soundtrack - Visuals are unique, certainly not your average anime type or overtly western comic drawn game. May not be for everyone, but the tone and atmosphere reflects correctly to the 1920s they try to represent. They also have a locale reminiscent of Edward Hopper's Nighthawk painting, something that vibes with the era. Soundtrack is as you'd expect jazz, but nothing too memorable comes to mind.NEEDS IMPROVEMENTA. Being a detective - While it may not be the intention of the game, a rework to the interrogation gameplay for the next story might elevate this game from a pure visual novel, to a true crime game. The gameplay format used is adequate, but doesn't punish nor really reward the player for truly being a detective. IE: Interrogations use a multiple choice format to get the player through to a true confession, but doesn't quite give the player enough pathways to truly mess up. You basically have to not pay attention to fail the interrogation, and you don't really get a huge advantage if you 100% it. - 1. Potential improvement: Write more options in, or have suspects throw you red herrings, or even have some suspects be a red herring themselves. Referencing board games like "sherlock holmes consulting detective", you can design it in a way where players have to read the tidbits/tabloids and the world around them to ask smart questions to get around an investigation. - 2. Potential improvement: Blank out the "replay" option for the interrogation first playthrough. Sure it adds frustration, but if you have enough endings/dialogues, I don't think it'd be an issue.- 3. Potential improvement: Time sensitive suspects. I don't mean a countdown clock. It could be that during each chapter where you interrogate key suspects, you can only select 1 out of the X suspects for the interrogation. Doing the wrong or red herring suspect will leave you with a different ending/outcome as each chapter goes by. This is where your writing gets to shine if you manage to give very plausible motivations for each character. The goal here is for players to separate coincidence from root cause.- 4. Potential improvement: Case file examination could use a more hands off approach. Similar to the earlier recommendation, I think you should just let the player come up with his/her own motivations with the case board, but they have to present it to the captain at the end. As with everything else, a player who pays attention to the world should be able to succeed, while half-hearted detective-ing will have half-hearted results. Going the extra mile working with retired inspectors could bring some truly unique insights to a game like this.B. Puzzles and flash type elements - Puzzles were ok, nothing too daunting, but the flash type elements didn't really add anything to the tension of the game. I understand trying to vary content here and there, but overall, it could just be replaced by a cutscene/dramatic writing, and more manpower directed to establishing great detective gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Video: Written: Chicken Police, ladies and gentlemen. Now, you might think, why? That’s an excellent question, and I don’t really know either, but I stumbled on the trailer half a year ago, I was actually very intrigued by it, I got a review key from the devs, and I played throughout the entire game. And I loved every minute of it, every minute of the 10 hours I spent in Clawville. Hey everyone this is Thyworm and today, I want to inform you about Chicken Police, easily one of the best indie games of the year. Enjoying this video? Consider subscribing.So, what sort of game is Chicken Police? Well, it has chickens. And a lot of other animals. It’s a buddy-cop noir, cinematic experience, in which you need to solve a murder. But it’s so much more as well. Chicken Police was inspired by 40’s grim-noir movies, games like Grim Fandango and L.A. Noire, and animated films like Fantastic Mr. Fox. There are plenty of references in the game as well, such as the horse bartender who is referred to as BoJack. I thought about Sin City a lot, while playing this, and I’m sure other IPs come to mind as well, like HBOs True Detective. What immediately struck me was the music and tone of the game. Old-fashioned, smooth jazz sounds play in the menu. Rain is falling in the background, a storm rises, and inside you see the smoky office of detective Santino Featherwind, a smoking, drinking, old chicken with only 121 days left to his retirement. This scene just looks so authentic, and a lot of work went into crafting the set pieces. It’s like you’re in an interactive movie, and you sort of are, as this isn’t really a game in the traditional sense. It’s more of a thrilling ride, with some minor puzzle elements, but despite that, despite this not really being something you’d normally play, it still comes highly recommended.I’ll introduce the story a little bit, for some context, without spoiling anything that you don’t discover yourself in the first 30 minutes. Detective Featherwind, Sonny, receives a mysterious note from a famous singer and club owner, Natasha Catzenko, in which she asks for help. Someone has been threatening her and she wants it to stop. You pick up your old partner-in-crime, Marty MacChicken, with which you once formed the infamous duo the Chicken Police, until a buckshot from up close abruptly ended that relationship. Together, Sonny and Marty attempt to unravel the mystery behind this intriguing woman, and it takes them all across the city Clawville. They meet and investigate many other animals, visit tons of locations, search for clues, evidence, witnesses and do all that good old-fashioned police work.Part of the game is about finding those clues, and if you’re paying attention like you should, since you’re a detective, most clues aren’t that hard to find. Interrogating suspects or victims is another small gameplay element which drives the plot forward, but I don’t want to overstate the interaction you’ll be having with the game and its characters. Because it’s not primarily about that. While the gameplay elements serve its purpose, which is involving you in key decision, Chicken Police relies heavily on the story. There are story-driven games, and then there’s Chicken Police, which is a game-driven story. The script is excellent and smart, not making the many obvious animal jokes you could think of, but much rather being subtle about most of it. Apart from you playing it, perhaps, no one in the game is at all surprised everybody is an animal, living in a city, and they all can understand each other as well, for the most part. Insects, which in Chicken Police are roughly the same size as a bear, do exist, but apparently speak a different language. Those insects also live in a separate part of the city, the Hive, and they’re considered lesser civilians. Not all animals are created equal, it seems. It reminded me of District 9, which introduced a similar restricted zone for outsiders, in a very natural and believable way.As a matter of fact, the writer and director of the game has cleverly put in many other concepts, not avoiding racism, separatism, mixed marriage and the monarchy. Without really going in-depth, the game does explore several of these topics, often on the side, and never in spite of the actual story, which is still just a great detective story. By flawlessly weaving in some other, more sensitive and more political topics, the game gains some gravitas and the world of Chicken Police becomes more authentic. The centre piece of the game revolves around crime and the detectives solving it, but by exploring the city and its inhabitants, you discover so much more about its history, its foundation and its flaws. There is some excellent world-building going on here.Authenticity is a proper way to describe this experience, I would say. Almost the entire game is in black and white, apart from certain elements that have to do with love and hate, as the antagonist so eloquently put it. The original sound track, is, well, 100% original and written for this game. Every scene and set piece are full of details to explore and enjoy. All the characters, about 30 of them, have their own past, their own story and their own voice lines. As a matter of fact, the entire game is voice-acted by a cast of amazing voice actors. It makes the scenes come alive. In fact, let me just play you a scene from Santino, who meets Natasha for the first time in her own club.The protagonist has this really worn-down voice, while almost drowning in self-pity, claiming to be an old drunk, close to retiring. It’s a cliché really, but very convincing nonetheless. Not so cliché is Natasha, who cleverly counters his pessimism, displaying her wits, her knowledge of people and also her mysteriousness. This depth of character is found in every animal you meet, and it doesn’t take you long to appreciate and connect with some of the main characters in the story. And without spoiling anything, the story is gripping and well worth your time. It’s a classic detective, in so many ways. It should be clear; I’m heartily recommending this one. As some outlets would say, it’s got a little bit for everyone. Chicken Police is a fantastic game, in every sense of the word, and if you give it a shot, you’ll discover many more layers below the surface. While unravelling the plot, you’ll appreciate all the small and subtle hints, the amazing conversations and the clever gameplay elements even more. This is surely a game you will remember. 98% of the users on Steam like it as well. It’s available on Steam, for 20 euros.

_childDocuments_.review: I was surprised at how little I ended up enjoying this game and how sick of it I was by the last parts and eager to just get it over and done with.  Considering that it really turned out to be more of a visual novel than a game, the critical flaw is how poor the writing is.  I would be quite surprised if the writers have ever read any of the classic noir they are supposedly inspired by and trying to imitate (like The Big Sleep or The Long Goodbye or the Maltese Falcon).  I have, so it was apparent to me that if the writers of this game ever did actually read those classics, they did a bad job imitating them.  The biggest issue with the writing that makes the game an increasing slog to play through is how unnecessarily long and largely pointless every single conversation is.  They all go on, no exaggeration, 4 or 5 times longer than they should.  There's never been a noir detective with such uncontrolled diarrhea of the mouth.Amplifying the poor writing is the annoying voice acting used to perform it.  Most of the voice actors are technically competent and could probably be quite good with the right direction (the big exception is the sidekick who has the second most dialogue; Marty's VA is just a straight up bad performer).  But all of them take things so over the top that it quickly gets annoying.  I mean, there's a sailor character who says "Arrrr" in EVERY SINGLE ONE of the way too many sentences he speaks.  That gives a pretty good summary of how silly the acting gets by most characters, including the annoyingly affected performance of the lead character.Otherwise, the actual game parts of this that occasionally break up the visual novel are pretty broken.  There are two mingames, interrogations and story board 'investigations.'  In both cases there's never any apparent logic to the correct choices.  It doesn't matter for the dialogues except for a few achievements, since the game continues the same whether you pile up positive or negative points for the questions you choose to ask, but the randomness of what's considered 'right' and 'wrong' by the game is still annoying.  As for the story board investigations, nothing's ever clearly explained, and it's never really clear what you are trying to do or what the game expects of you.  Again, there's no consequence for failure, so in most cases I ended up just putting clues together almost randomly until I got the right obscure combination the developers wanted me to pick.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun film noir detective point-and-click game with anthropomorphic characters.This is definitely a strange one.  The animal heads on human bodies motif is very, very weird, but the visuals are beautiful and the detective story is engaging.  And the interview system, while I didn't really master it, is one of the best of this genre of video games I've seen.The Positives-This game is gorgeous.  The black-and-white aesthetic with the color for the characters or for artistic moments is great, and many of the animals' visuals are just perfect.  I would mostly stare at the heads because the human bodies freaked me out, but the character visuals and the settings were beautiful.-The detective part of the game is surprisingly superior than other games I've played.  Most of these games are just click on everything, try to find clues, and then ask every question to get the information you need to later solve the puzzle.  You do need to click on almost everything in this game, too, but the interrogation system is fantastic in that it gives you the detective's read on the kind of person you're dealing with and you use that to determine how to approach the interview.  I got it down well where I could get 90% most of the time, but it had some curve balls to keep me guessing.  A couple I couldn't understand even when I looked up or retried until I got the right answer, but otherwise the logic matched the questions you could ask that were what the game considered to be correct.-The story got pretty wild, but I liked it.  I enjoyed the twists and turns and the big reveals.  I have to say that I surprisingly guessed a couple of them, but because it was getting wild like a Soap Opera, I have a few wild guesses and so it made me wonder where'd they go with the plot until the end.-The humor was fantastic.  The main character has abrasive relationships with many of the other characters, and so you're trading barbs with half the characters in the game.  And you even have fans, so you're really a love-him-or-hate-him kind of guy, apparently.  I liked most of the characters and most of the dialogue.-The ending put everything together: the visuals, the gameplay, and the story and humor all showed up at the end.  Everything that the game was trying to build toward paid off.-Oh, special props to the game for letting you speedrun through a subsequent run by clicking through all dialogue, etc. to get all the achievements or to see other options you missed.The Negatives-You might like weird-looking things, but I could never get used to the anthropomorphism.  At least the chickens wore long-sleeved clothing and gloves; the bare skin is what got me.  But it was too much fun for that to be too much of a bother.  Note that sometimes the anthropomorphism was inconsistent: some animals had the head of one animal and the body of a human, whereas others had the head of one animal, the body of a human, but then had hooves.  Others had human hands but animal nails.  Artistic license.-The dialogue changed a lot every time you clicked on anything when a plot event happened, so you had to reclick on everything a few times throughout the game to make sure that you didn't miss anything.  On one hand, that's a great feature so it doesn't give you the same text every time; on the other, it makes you click obsessively on everything so you don't miss anything.  And, strangely, it would kick you out of dialogue only for you to have to reopen the dialogue to continue the game.  So you always had to click one more time to get repeat text to know for sure that you were done talking to the character.  So that was slightly annoying.-If you like to collect things, you're going to hate that previous point.  You can go to the police station, for example, click on everything, leave, and then a couple of events later, you have to go back there and into the shooting range where you will have no business for the rest of the game and chat to get some hidden dialogue options to unlock everything.  It's stuff like that where it's both cool (because the dialogue is not repetitive) and annoying (because you have to be repetitive by revisiting everything just to make sure you didn't miss something).-If you're a completionist, note that you'll run into issues like optimal interviewing causing you to miss collectibles.  Interesting choice for the game, but it's not that big of a deal.  Just know that it'll be difficult to 100%--just look up whatever you miss or you'll be clicking yourself insane (in-game reference intended).Overall, I really enjoyed this game when I didn't expect to.  Other than the anthropomorphism freaking me out, the art was gorgeous.  The plot was fun.  The voice acting and music were fantastic.  The gameplay was engaging as long as I wasn't driving myself nuts clicking to see if there was any more dialogue to trigger.  And the interviewing was a lot of fun and not just random guessing or completely obvious.  I highly recommend this if you like film noir or point-and-click story games.  Only if you hate those kinds of games would I say that it's just not for you; anyone else, give it a try.  It's a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicken Police is a wonderful visual novel that managed to impress me with its surprising quality. The artstyle, which can have its highs and lows, is definitely the first thing one notices, with its simple yet effective fusions of animals and humans being used to (sometimes more subtly, sometimes less) portray interesting details about each character's personality, and the animations, albeit simple, actually support this stle rather well, and sometimes in their simplicity become even more charming.The gameplay is, of course, rather simple, but it manages to not become boring by breaking up the dialogue with pleasant minigames that don't overstay their welcome and actually keep a good amount of variety, although there was one puzzle in the first part of the game that I did find a bit confusing. The last and most important piece of this game is of course the story. While not being the literary revelation of the century it doesn't aim to be, nor does it need to, as it is a very charming and well written hard boiled noir story that perfectly stands on its own two legs and delivers a very palatable mystery with an engaging plot and fun twists and turns. This is complemented by the characters, all of them playing classic detective story roles: The rugged veteran detective, the meathead sidekick with a big heart, the hardass boss, the femme fatale, the list goes on, but each one is written perfectly to fit the story and setting, and the voice acting is extremely well done, enriching each scene greatly and helping immerse the player.I did encounter a small handful of bugs while playing but it was nothing major and it was easily ignored. There is a collectible system but it doesn't change the experience at all, it's just a bit of extra fun for those who enjoy collecting things and being completionists.Overall a very solid experience and I would even say that this game's quality is above average.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 I thouroughly enjoyed every minute of this game, except for one short but unnecessarily difficult minigame (the burning ship) that almost made me ragequit. Extra points for lovingly crafted game with lots and lots of optional content. Talking to the same character again and again just to get that last bit of dialogue became a habit for me. _childDocuments_.review: Never in my life I have been this torn on whether to recommend or not recommend a game, just to finally let my bias decide and make the good stuff weight more than the bad. Chicken Police is a visual novel with heavy emphasis on conversations, and one that has an unexpected amount of quality put into its world building, aesthetics, music and characters. It does them so well that I am looking forward to the sequel and how it's going to improve. But unfortunately, the storytelling and story progression are where the game is lacking in.The very first thing that someone notices after taking a glance at the game's images is surely the character design. Chicken Police is another piece of media that goes for an all-animal setting, but the way it represents the characters is wildly different. The characters in this game are all just real animal heads attached to digitized human bodies in a seamless manner, and aside from the second chapter when you see some truly weird and uncanny imagery, the overall character design looks acceptable and well-done.And it's not just the looks of the characters that is well-done. Every character not only has a distinct look, but also a distinct personality. Nearly each of the characters have a believeable personality of their own, with their voice actors managing to relay those personalities through the way they talk. Chicken Police has a stellar cast of professional voice actors that have done their job incredibly well, with the main character, Sonny Featherland, being the highlight of the bunch. How stellar you ask? Well... one of the voice actors has also voiced the oldest living witcher in a game called The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. Got your attention now, huh?If there's one thing that Chicken Police absolutely nails, it's the presentation; both in terms of how it looks and how it sounds. All of the environments are well-detailed and in tone with the atmosphere and noir theme of the game. And the jazzy music that accompanies you in each of the locations is superbly composed. You bet "My City Is On Fire" and "Have You Been With A Predator Before" are now on my music playlist.But... well... while all of these aspects of the game have ended up looking incredible, there is one aspect that its quality really isn't up to par with the rest, and that's the story.Believe it or not, Chicken Police's biggest problem is ultimately the story and its progression.Make no mistake, the game starts really well in terms of the story and even has some positive points. There's a whole bunch of lore prepared for the world that the game's events happen in, the writers have included witty references to classic stories such as the tortoise and the hare, some of the jokes actually managed to get a chuckle out of me, the banter between the main characters is enjoyable as a whole and the mystery surrounding the plot seems compelling at first. But when it comes to the game moving forward with the plot, it really cannot keep the same amount of quality throughout it.The story starts with an interesting premise that can go anywhere in terms of how it can end. But the game ends with a completely predictable and rather unsatisfying ending. By the time you find out about the story's "twist", you can immediately put the piceces together and find out how it's going to end. The reveal and the ending are so cliché and disappointing that not only all of the mystery established in the first chapter comes crashing down, but they also raise questions about various events throughout the game with no way to answer them.Then there's the issue of dialogue fatigue kicking in after a few hours. As established before, Chicken Police is a narrative-driven visual novel with a huge number of conversations. A normal playthrough of the game takes about 6.5 hours on average, and a completionist playthrough (which involves talking to everyone and interacting with every item multiple times at various points in the game) takes about 9.5 hours. That basically means you are dealing with nearly 6-10 hours of almost non-stop dialogue. And unfortunately, the game doesn't offer much to keep the fatigue from kicking in.Chicken Police is a noir, detective themed game. It doesn't have the freedom of other visual novels in terms of events it can use to break the staleness. So basically, all it can offer are minigames and puzzles, and there's not much of them. In terms of minigames, you only encounter 4 of them in the whole game, with each chapter's epilogue containing a simple "connect the dots" type of minigame just to summarize your findings. As for the puzzles, you only encounter two. This means most of your time will be spent watching conversations, some of them feeling unnecessary.In the story, the main characters go through various situations and sometimes, the tone of the conversations either doesn't fit the situation or they feel completely worthless; especially when it comes to optional locations you can visit. At first, these optional locations seem to add interesting tidbits. But as you progress further, you'll notice some of them (like Mullen's Newsstand) feel incredibly redundant; So much so that you could remove them from the game and nothing would change.The game also does something that can really sour the experience: Not telling you whether or not doing a specific action is required for progression. There are multiple sections in the game, one of them being the ending, where doing a specific action is needed to unlock the ability to progress but the game neither tells nor hints you about it. On the other hand, there are two specific sections in chapters 1 and 4 where doing a specific action immediately kicks you out of the scene you were in. For one of them (chapter 1) the game allows you to go back to the scene later on, but the other has no warnings attached to it and you can never go back to it. This especially becomes a problem when you realise the scenes you cannot return to, are actually the ones that host some of the collectibles.The next problem with the gameplay presents itself in the form of questioning sections, where you have to basically interrogate a person for information.The questioning phase in Chicken Police is incredibly weird. You are supposed to take the main characters's personal remarks about a character into account and study the personality traits of the character in front of you, and then choose one of the questions that appear on the screen to get information out of them. The game then rates your performance at the end of questioning, telling you how many questions you asked and how well you did. However, the questioning process makes little sense.It seems like every question that feels like the right choice to the player is actually wrong. There are numerous instances in the questioning parts where you might choose a question that you think will work well, but instead it does the opposite, forcing you towards trial and error. This was a HUGE issue back when the game launched, as the game didn't offer you any chance to retry the questionings. Nowadays, and with the introduction of a retry button, it's not as bad as before. But still, this doesn't really fix the issue.Its unique art style, great soundtrack, likable characters and superb voice acting make it incredibly charming. But story progression & the clichéd ending make it really tough to recommend to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicken Police is a hybrid of visual novel and point-and-click adventure game that tells a grim film noir tale with anthropomorphized animal characters that inhabit the city of Clawville.  If that doesn't sound awesome to you, look elsewhere.  If it does, buy this immediately.The writing is great and the English voice acting is some of the best I've ever heard in a game, which is shocking considering this was made by a small Hungarian studio that couldn't have had a very big budget.  A surprising amount of attention has gone into world-building here, with the game often referring to a larger world beyond Clawville and its famed chicken detectives, with unique politics and history.The gameplay largely revolves around dialogue, with some investigation and interrogation minigames and light puzzling.  It all works extremely well.  There were a couple of instances where I was unsure of what action I needed to trigger to progress, but that sort of thing is part and parcel to the genre.  Strong recommendation for fans of offbeat, story-rich indie titles.

_childDocuments_.review: An alcoholic detective who has simply had enough and sees the world for what it really is... just black and white; his loyal, gun-loving, hit-first-ask-questions-later partner; a mysterious case which starts off innocently then goes deep into organized crime and the mob in the city... what could go wrong really?Chicken Police takes all the clichéd tropes (and some new ones) that have been used before many times and combines them all together. The strong script, professional voice acting, clever humor, interesting art style, well-suited soundtracks, deep lore into the in-game world and its characters, three-dimensional and well-written characters all try to make you forget about its clichéd tropes... and somehow it works! I can safely say this is the best point-and-click game I have ever played without any doubt.The final twist of the story becomes rather predictable in Act 3 of the game, but they don't try to hide its predictability. It's rather used to make the story more realistic.You might not even be a fan of the genre, but play this and in the end, you will be. I know I was.

_childDocuments_.review: Buy this.This is more or less a visual novel, with gameplay consisting of looking at things and talking to people. And fortunately the things, people, and dialogue are all extremely well done. In particular, the rapport between the two titular bird cops is perfect and often laugh-out-loud hilarious. Marty is the eager, personable, and gun-happy supercop while Sonny is your traditional grumpy noir protagonist complete with Bogart impersonation, alcohol addiction, broken marriage, and crippling male stubbornness.There are a few mini-games to add some variety, but I found the Questioning and Investigation ones to be unintuitive. If I'm questioning someone that the game tells me is "scared", does that mean I should be reassuring or that I should be amplifying their fears to break them? The Investigation is meant to be like creating a 'conspiracy board' to get your ducks in a row, but really fails to be interesting and is more of a guessing game. However, you can repeat Questioning as many times as you wish, and Investigation has no negative outcomes, so they aren't really a hindrance to solving the mystery.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicken Police is an absolute triumph that seamlessly blends the quirkiness of an animal-based world with the gritty allure of a classic film noir. From the moment I stepped into the captivating world of Clawville, I was hooked by its intriguing characters, gripping storyline, and unique visual style.The game's protagonist, Sonny Featherland, is a standout character with his snappy one-liners and world-weary demeanor. Teamed up with his partner, Marty MacChicken, they form an unlikely yet utterly compelling duo. The voice acting is top-notch, breathing life into every character and enhancing the immersive experience.The attention to detail is astounding. From the dimly lit, smoky interiors of bars to the rain-soaked streets, each environment exudes an atmosphere that's a perfect match for the noir genre. The developers have truly outdone themselves in creating a world that feels both nostalgic and fresh.What truly sets Chicken Police apart is its writing. The dialogue is sharp, witty, and often surprisingly poignant. It seamlessly weaves humor, drama, and suspense, keeping you engaged in every conversation and interaction. The story unfolds in a gripping manner, gradually revealing layers of intrigue that kept me on the edge of my seat throughout my playthrough.The gameplay mechanics, a mix of point-and-click investigation and visual novel elements, are well-executed and intuitive. Unraveling the mysteries of Clawville is a delight, as you gather clues, interrogate suspects, and put together the pieces of a complex puzzle.In a gaming landscape often dominated by big-budget titles, Chicken Police stands out as a testament to the power of indie creativity. It's a rare gem that not only captivates with its storytelling but also leaves a lasting impact. If you're a fan of noir, mystery, or simply appreciate a well-crafted narrative, Chicken Police is an absolute must-play that will keep you clucking for more.

It is a point and click game where you can explore a film noir detective story. It's a funny and quick game to beat.Some things that I thought could have been done better were UI improvements. You spend a lot of time talking to other characters and of course that gets exhausting especially after slowly realizing that all conversation options have been exhausted. It would help if the UI made it a lot more clear when all conversation options have been exhausted. It would also be nice to know or have a stronger ability to backtrack. Be aware that after you trigger certain events or move on to new scenes, there may be progress items that you won't be able to retrieve again without doing a whole new replay of the game.The game play in general is strange but it works. A big part of the game is the interrogation interview -- I have no idea how to do this right, I used online guides to find the right responses I was looking for. Without the guidance, I was getting average detective scores. You can retry as many times as you'd like but hearing the same dialogue over and over again is exhausting (yes, thankfully there is a skip button). I was interested in the game for the humor. Because of the easy to miss stuff, this game can get frustrating for 100% completionists -- BUT, it does not take long to 100% the game. The game could probably be 100% in about 16 hours if you have a really good guide and you're able to do everything without requiring a second play through.

_childDocuments_.review: Manometer: 7/10The good- Beautiful visually. Elegant black and white aesthetics with some colors to stand out here and there.- Deep lore. They have built a solid imaginary world of animals with history, past events and territories that you learn about them as you play the game. The codex information about the world are very interesting.- Cool mysterious noir atmosphere that gets you immersed right from the beginning.- Nice direction and artistic cut scenes. It resembles old noir movies in a great way.- Well designed characters with vivid personalities and backstories. They have combined cleverly human bodies and animals' heads to match each profession and behavior.- Top notch voice acting performances. They're very convincing and add to the characters' personalities.- Good crime story full of conspiracies. Even better storytelling with great rhythm that takes you smoothly from each event to the next one.- Well written. Exceptional dialogues. You never get bored to explore them all and talk to every possible character available. Info in the notebook are well written too.- Cool sense of humor with lots of funny puns about animals' temperament and physique, although sometimes it gets a bit tiring.- Great music that fits perfectly the noir, grayscale aesthetics.- Interrogation is an interesting procedure despite its problems. The outcome doesn't affect the story as much as you'd expect, but they are mini challenges that add to the atmosphere and the investigator's profile.- The world, the characters, some events reflect many sides of the real world. This way, it puts on the table various social/political issues like racism, inequality, social rights, corruption.The bad- Despite their chicken nature, the protagonists are the stereotypical tough guys that are always cool. Although the continuous teasing between Sonny and Marty seems funny initially , after a while it gets monotonous and tiring. No matter how deep into the case they are and how deadly the situation is, they continue in the same mood. All this feels unrealistic and kills the vibe of agony and mystery.- During interrogations, the conversation continues far too long after you make a question with a result of taking paths you don't want or you couldn't imagine initially. You should have the option to choose your replies more often in order to manipulate better the conversation and plan your strategy. Now you just press a fitting question and you just hope that Sonny won't mess it up in the process.- Mini games like shooting are clunky, uninspiring and for sure they don't fit the rest of the game's aesthetics and gameplay.- The few puzzles it has are too simplistic and not so creative.- The whole mystery's solution is too obvious since about the middle of the game (after a certain discovery). This is never a good thing for a police/crime story. I found it a little bit cliché too.

_childDocuments_.review: I was torn between recommending and not recommending the game, but decided not to.Tl;dr: "Chicken Police - Paint it Red" is a great and unique looking and sounding visual novel, but lacks gameplay and has a storyline that's OK at best.There is no investigative gameplay - the one thing that investigation games should have. The game holds your hand throughout the whole experience, pretty much disallowing you to fail. It tells you the story without requiring you to pay attention.As many other reviewers have already stated: 95% of the game is nothing but dialogue. There are a couple of simple puzzles and point-and-click -shootouts but mainly you just click everything and everyone as many times as you can until they start repeating the same lines. This way you'll gain information - information that's barely even needed. All the notes are irrelevant as the player never needs to go read them through in order to be able to do some investigation work. Neither do you need to be a good negotiator as you can always give each interrogation another shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicken Police is a visual novel that plays out most of the noir detective clichés and turns it into an enjoyable experience.It has stunning visuals and atmosphere. The writing is great and all the characters are charming and filled with personality. All the lines are also voice acted which is a massive plus.It is interactive and has gameplay elements here and there but it is around %95 percent reading so if that's not your cup of tea, look elsewhere.Now for the most crucial part, the story. It hooked me from the beginning and i had to finish it as soon as possible. The mystery surrounding the case made it really intriguing. Though it was predictable, the story unfolded quite nicely but unfortunately i feel like the ending was either rushed or the writers just ran out of ideas which made the game much less impactful than it could've been. Apart from the ending, the journey to get there was great and i would still suggest it because of that. I would recommend you to buy it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely oozing with charm and style, Chicken Police: Paint it RED! is a feast for the eyes and ears! I recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind a visual novel, or to anyone who is curious about the genre. Play the demo, and if you like it, buy it. It's as simple as that. Read on if you'd like some more detail!Placing you in a world populated with half-human animal creatures, Chicken Police has you play as a hard-boiled detective named Sonny Featherland trying to solve one last case before retirement. He'll need all the help he can get, leading you to meet a cast of colorful characters to interact with. It's a fantastical world, but it's very much —one you can believe exists and get a feel for. The whole game is voice-acted, and you'll need to make sure to repeatedly interact with every object and character until the dialogue repeats if you want to find out everything there is. Be prepared to click a lot! Now, the few things that fell flat for me—the interrogation parts where you question individuals didn't completely jive with me. It seems a bit too tough to tell what the correct question is, and I often felt clueless. However, after each interrogation, there was a provided redo button if I wanted to shoot for a 100% score, something I very much appreciated. The last plot twist I saw coming from a mile away, which isn't necessarily a bad thing—an ending should never come completely out of the blue! However, it's very much a cliche, and I was a little disappointed it was not something more imaginative. The ending itself was a bit anti-climatic, but as the rest of the game was an A, a C+ ending didn't bother me too much.Overall, I can say I happily recommend this game to anything who thinks it looks interesting! You're in for a delightful treat.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have ever liked any detective novel, show, movie, or game, stop reading this review and buy this game right now.Chicken Police is a beautiful, intricate world of animals steeped in noir, both in style and story. A 5-ish hour adventure, you'll love being taken along for the ride with Sonny and Marty. This game isn't as much of a detective game as it is a point and click adventure with a detective theme, but the interrogation system is a unique experience - more about asking the right questions as opposed to asking them all. With unique and memorable characters - who are beautifully voiced, breathe life into Clawville as if it's always been there. You never feel like a fish out of water, you're with Sonny as much as he's with you.  I wish I could play it for the first time again.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as writing goes this was serviceable and the plot came through with a great twist. Anyone more than familiar with these tropes will recognize many of the story-beats here and rarely are they subverted. The writers, somewhat understandably, blunder on metaphorically handling racism in much the same way that solid prejudices within a world made up of anthropomorphized animals usually does; but they also used so-called racism as a punchline–. This makes for awkward humor. But as I said, the world is an interesting one and I hope that any potential sequel continues to build on that first and foremost. It was fun to play and the art direction really worked for the week or so that it took to complete it. That earns it a recommendation, all things considered.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so clucking good, I know so original, haha, but still, I stand by my point 100%.Who would have known cropping out animals' faces and sticking them on a human body, using every detective/cop cliche imaginable, and removing all the colours for a noir vibe, would turn out to be a brilliant game, whoever came up with the started this idea is genuine. There are plenty of corny and quirky dialogues, along with animal puns and some charismatic characters all with their own personality trait reality to their species to banter back and forth. All of it is fully voice acted by the way, and the music is so soothing it gets my heart pumping.The funniest thing about this game is that it takes itself seriously I can't help but laugh a bit every time I come to realize how bizarre it is in nature. The story, as well as nicely pace and the mystery surrounding the murder, makes sense, it only took me 20 minutes before the corporate of the crime 20 was revealed for me to figure it out from the notes taken throughout the game. It takes a more grounded approach and doesn't do what other games mistakenly do and make the crime taken overtop and complex.  Much like in Zootopia, there are a lot of social commentaries to do with privilege, class, and predator vs prey, for example . I love how like stuff is included in the game, making it more reality base as well as advancing the world-building by discussing how the cities were divided, how specific animals are treated, or who is the God or Goddess in this universe .I've got nothing but high praise and hype for this game, I could tell the developers poured a lot of love into making this game, , I'm not even going to discuss the nitpick because they're minor.

_childDocuments_.review: The production value of this game is pretty insane. All the dialogue is dubbed (even monologues), the artstyle is gorgeous, cutscenes are well-animated, and the soundtrack is very climatic. The game has many jokes, most of which I found to be very funny, and the whole premise of "noir but animals" is executed extremely well.The story however isn't anything to write home about. It's pretty much exactly what you would expect from an average noir detective movie, including all the character types, clichés and dumb plot twists. But again, the animal aspect saves it a little bit.On the gameplay end it's pretty much an average point and click, except it relies more on dialogue, interrogations and asking questinos, than on puzzles. Pretty much evey character and every piece of information on them or the case are accessible in your notebook, which is very well-thought. The way you gather it is not as good though. Oftentimes I wasn't sure where to go, or who to talk to, because once I stopped talking to somebody nothing happened, and I got lost for a short while. I also had some issue with choosing the right question to ask during interrogations, because many of them sounded pretty much the same.Overall I would recommend this game if you're looking for something easy to realx to for ~two evenings. It's not bad, but it could've been better, or in other words, it does its job, but not much besides that.

_childDocuments_.review: That game is amazing. While adapting the detective genre in video game is probably really hard, it's a frank success ! When you think about it, it's really hard to build a video game entirely on its story, because the player interacting in true dialogues causes branching, which leads to a massive increase of the narrative content to put in the game. Here I'm not sure how the devs managed it, I don't believe there is significant narrative branching, yet you don't feel that the dialogues are vain, quite the contrary actually. The dialogues are amazingly written, it's true big muscles literary work here, with perfect voice acting. Chicken Police is the game that made me laugh the most in my entire video games player career, much more than all the fun games that don't use narrative, like let's say Getting Over It, QWOP, Gang Beast... These games are fun at first but quickly repeat the same situational comedy tricks and reveal their empty shell. In Chicken Police the comedy comes from the dialogues so it's always different jokes, just like a comic show. But the fun is not even the purpose of the game, there is no empty shell, instead a great detective story with a real plot. Without overstating, one of the best recreational experience of my life, I hope the devs will release a new project soon and I hope others will get inspired do make similar stuff. The only little negative thing I would mention just to prove I'm doing a honest review, is that the musics get repetitive. You spend quite some time in the same scenes going through the narrative content, and the background music gets annoying at some point. Great work devs if you read me, and thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: So many perfectly executed elements go in to making this one of the best hard-boiled detective noir games available, but none more so than the voice acting. Kerry Shale's whisky-soaked delivery of the wonderfully written lines is beyond superb, but every VA in this title delivers their lines pitch-perfect. Then there are the gorgeous backgrounds and artworks to immerse you in this rainy, downward-spiral of a city that is Clawville. And a surprising amount of world-building is included - none of it truly necessary, all of it very welcome. Chicken Police is a must-play for anyone who loves the a good noir story.

_childDocuments_.review: A noir detective visual novel with antropomorphic animals.  The presentation is breathtakingly good. Everything is black and white, with a rare and shocking splash of color. Backgrounds are rendered in high resolution, the characters are a collage of modified animal pictures and photos of actors. The animation is limited, mostly static. The end result is heavy noir atmosphere mixed with surrealism. The music fits the genre well and really underscores the atmosphere. Special mention goes to voice acting: Every line is voiced, including the heroe's inner dialogue, and the quality of voice acting is superb. Apart from different accents, some characters have speech mannerism befitting the animal they are.  Writing is excellent too. The world is built with its own history and culture, all tied to its people being different kind of animals, and with problems such co-habitation brings. This is reminiscent of movie Zootopia. The story and characters drive inspiration primarily from noir genre, but with more fable-like and absurd elements and it is lightened with a dose of humor. Part of it comes from jibes main heroes trade between themselves and other characters, part of it is outright parody of the noir genre and its tropes. Despite its setting, it is certainly not depressing.  Gameplay is based on dialogues, exploring limited set of locations and a questioning minigame. The minigame requires navigating a dialogue tree using hints about the chracter and mood of the questioned character. My ability to solve it was a bit of hit-or-miss, but it can be freely retried. There is also a mingame with connecting clues, usually at the end of a chapter, that can be solved using logic and some intuition (and it cannot be failed anyway).  Be prepared that this game is  verbose, on the level of Ace Attorney. It also only autosaves after major events or location change, so take that in mind or risk losing your progression. This brings my only gripe: sometimes I triggered an event before I fully explored a location and I was not able to return to it, becase the save was overwritten. It did not happen often, since I tend to leave the most significant clue/character for the last, but it was annoying.  Overall, this is an excellent game and tongue-in-the-cheek love letter to noir. The closest equivalent experience I had was Aviary Attorney. Bonus points for quoting Cowboy Bebop.

_childDocuments_.review: Very very solid experience. Chicken Police is basically a visual novel, but its production value in the 'visual' department is a lot higher than most. It is hard to believe this game has so little attention-- perhaps that's due to its niche nature or odd premise, but I think ultimately the animal characters and bizarre world are to its benefit-- it keeps the story from taking itself too seriously but it's never presented in a way that's outright comedic.I love the presentation. The noir theme was captured elegantly, and the voice acting is for the most part excellent-- different animals have different accents or inflections with how they speak, and the voice acting cast does a great job. Sonny in particular is really good and probably the best overall. The soundtrack itself is alright, but it becomes repetitive especially on repeat visits to locations, but it's never out of place or bizarre or anything like that.The story itself is a good one. It's very much a noir story, so you can expect some obvious high and low notes on account of it. The premise itself, a buddy-cop detective thriller, isn't anything new, but the characters and the world lend themselves to making it not feel like a complete retread of the noir films of old. There is a surprising amount of world building to behold-- everything is 'original,' as in it's not as if it's just Chicago with animals-- I mean, it looks like that for sure, but the town itself and other countries that are mentioned have histories and events that people discuss.I do think that the story did open up some threads that never really got properly closed. I won't spoil anything, but there are times when the game seems to act like the picture is a lot bigger than it really is. The twist itself is very, very easy to guess as soon as you stumble upon the first hint. From there, nothing too out of the ordinary happens but I don't think the game ended on a bad note or anything. It's just, once you've figured it out, that's about all there is to it. The last interrogation you have you don't really learn much of anything other than insight into the person being interrogated. I think the first two chapters and some of chapter three were the best parts of the game, but the last half doesn't really plummet in quality or anything.I also like how there is clearly an 'existent' world in the game. To refer back to the worldbuilding, you frequently hear about places like "the Hive", an insect-only ghetto ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and other places which you never actually go to. Which from a game standpoint seems irritating or even lazy, but from a realistic perspective it's a very natural thing to discuss segments of town or events that have nothing to do with the story at large. A very nice touch.Also, there is a secret ending if you get all 10 of the dime store novels in one play through.

_childDocuments_.review: Chickens are one of my favourite animals. They’re relaxing to watch as they roam around, hens pay rent with eggs, and ultimately, they’re delicious. One thing I’d never asked myself was “how well would chickens function as hard-boiled detectives?” Thankfully Chicken Police: Paint it Red answers that unasked question!The setting is delightfully creative, and well fleshed out. The art style is great, not a fan of jazz but the soundtrack fits perfectly with the noir setting. The game is well written both in terms of the humour (beware of the puns) and the mystery which is more than credible enough (humanoid animals not withstanding) to stand alongside more serious examples of the genre. The mini-game elements of piecing puzzles together work really well, as do the interrogations. The only negative thing I can think of in the game is the reliance on the auto-save and the lack of a manual save function. Which is far from a deal breaker.I read on the forums that they’re looking at a sequel, and on the strength of this game they’ve earned a day one purchase for it.
