_childDocuments_.review: There's a great game in here, and I'm sure that when it launches in a year or so, it'll be fantastic. Larian has done pretty good in the past with Div1/2 and the free post-launch support. That said, I can't recommend the game right now, and I wish there was an option of "Wait" instead of an incredibly unnuanced "Yes, game good" and "No, game bad." I'll recommend it solely because it WILL be worth getting, since the fundamentals seem great and that's more important than any current bug, gamebreaking or otherwise, but I can't recommend it NOW.Bugs include:- Characters dying and phasing into the floor, the bugging out and stretching across the screen- Progression bugs where the triggered cutscenes don't work- Character locking, where I suddenly can't move and can't unstick myself intentionally (I was trying to jump to a ledge off in the distance, but I guess it wasn't meant to be)- Game thinks you're in a convo, but you aren't. Interacting with the NPC again doesn't work, etc. - A general lack of polish in cutscenes. Lips not moving, janky animations and a lack of fluidity.Also, I'm not sure if I just missed it, but an option for difficulty would be nice. Whether a generic slider or more detailed tinkering of difficulty, like being able to turn off perma-death, etc.On the plus side, the visuals look fantastic, from art design to character designs. I wish there would be more options for character customization (especially in the hair department because of these whack ass hairdos). Female characters have it pretty good, but male characters. Oof. Faces are all over the place, from a few decent ones, one good one and the rest being bad for Male!Humans and the hair is god awful, again for M!Humans, imo. But, hopefully, these are all Early Access pains, like all my other "issues" with the game that lead to my refund.EDIT: Act 3 and the ending feels unfinished af, and the performance as of Patch 1 is doo doo, but the rest of the game is an easy 9 or 10/10. I'm sure Larian will put out a Definitive/Director's Edition a year from now that'll patch out most of the issues and revamp Act 3 to a state where it feels really good. As it is rn, I'd still buy it.Also, ♥♥♥♥ fights w/ 10+ enemies. It takes like a year for the turns to get back to you and friendly AI is as dumb as rocks. I had a mfer Misty Step away from 2 dudes, then proceed to run back to said two dudes, then past them, triggering an opportunity attack that absolutely merked the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ before they ended turn RIGHT NEXT TO THEM.

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't have the following:* A Ingame Store filled with Macrotransactions* A Battlepass* Lootboxes* Always Online* DRM!This game does have the following:* A beautiful world to explore filled with lots and lots of loot* Fully voiced, all the way from the NPC you meet along the way to the animals you can talk to* A good story* Is Feature Complete* Flying SquirrelsLarian Studios not only shows that you can still make awesome games without the need to nickel & dime people for the last penny they have, but they have caused many dev studios to go into defense mode to try and justify their predatory systems they have been using for the last decade. Baldur's Gate 3 doesn't have a in game store filled with cosmetics that cost you $25 a piece, nor does it have a battlepass that only exists to siphon more money from the players bank accounts. You just buy the game and enjoy it... and damn, is this game enjoyable.This is my GOTY. So thank you Larian Studios... for being a source of light in these dark times. You guy's are awesome!

_childDocuments_.review: So the game's finally out and I feel like I can update the review. Unfortunately, this is still a "thumbs down" from me. I'm sure that many people will enjoy it, and Larian is certainly not trying to rip you off or anything, but in MY OPINION, while the art is great and the combat is generally good, the game overall is immature, the world-building is mediocre, and BG 3 is not a worthy successor of Baldur's Gate 1 and 2. So lets break down things a bit:1. The music. It's phenomenal. Just great.2. The art/map artwork is outstanding. Some of the maps are just breathtakingly beautiful (Temple of Lathander is my favorite so far). Note, I don't like the "map design" so much, where everything is jammed together, but aesthetically they are top notch.3. The combat is pretty good, with two notable exeptions. 5E is a pretty good combat system and Larian has stayed largely faithful. Their addition of weapon-specfic special attacks works well. Where it really breaks down is shoving. In BG3, shoving is king, and it often breaks the combat. There are three interlocking problems: BG3 makes shoving a bonus action (so you can attack AND shove), it increased the shove distance (from 5 feet to A LOT), and it made big fights very vertical - with lots of ledges and bottomless pits. This introduces a lot of save-or-die Athletics checks (either when you are shoving an enemy or the enemy is shoving you) that just break the system. They're especially prevalent in "big battles" - for example, of the six big battles in Act I, 4 have save-or-die shove mechanics, either from bottomless pits, high heights, or pits with monsters. The second major issue is surfaces and grenades, which make armor and concentration spells less valuable. I know Larian loves shoving and surfaces, but it's too much.4. The potential party members are good in some ways and terrible in others. Honestly, the writing and quips are mostly fine. The "romances" seem like they were written by and for teenagers with no idea what real romance actually is (I mean, these NPCs are throwing themselves at me just because I'm not a jerk - it's ... off-putting). By far the worst though are the origins of your companions - they're all super special snowflakes, the "Coolest Adventurers That Ever Cooled", who just went down to level one because of the tadpole. They honestly outshine the player character, and that's REALLY BAD. The PC should be the hero of the story, but the other party members are just written to be so much better than you. Larian did this in DOS2 as well and I hated it. It's like playing with a DM who made a bunch of super-cool NPCs that are just better than the players. Very lame.5. The world building is where this game really fails for me. BG1 and BG2 felt like real, lived-in places, with politics, economies (BG1's whole plot was economic intrigue), and towns where people live. BG3 feels like a series of disconnected set pieces and "the world" breaks down as soon as you think about it. "Worldbuilding" doesn't mean putting a few books in and referencing place names, but that's the Larian approach. The problem is that there's no deeper thought into making sure things "make sense". There are tons of examples of this: from two brothers walking 10 days "from Baldur's Gate" to find their sister, to the merchants constantly refreshing their supplies, etc. Honestly, I think this is less Larian and more "modern D+D" - which has moved away from "realistic fantasy worlds" to "exciting fantasy fights". I hate Critical Role, for instance (I find it shallow and splashy - the Michael Bay of fantasy). If you like Critical Role, you'll probably like the "world" that BG3 builds for you. Just be aware that it doesn't compare favorably to BG 1+2. This lack of "consistency/internal realism" is a big turn-off for me (and if you're about to say "why are you looking for realism in a game with dragons?" just realize that this statement isn't the burn you think it is, but rather says a lot about the low-brow fantasy you obviously enjoy).6. UI/Itemization/inventory management. It's really bad. It's the same system as DOS2 - it was bad then and it's bad now: a clogged action bar (Solasta does the 5E UI just so MUCH better, even if the game is much rougher than BG3 overall), too many magic items/different items to track in inventory, no good way to sort things, and merchants with better items than what you find after epic quests (the only +2 item I saw in Act 1 was in the Zhent merchant at the Goblin Camp. This isn't a key point for me, but yeah, it's certainly bad.7. They really treated the original voice actor for Minsc poorly by refusing to bring him back to voice the character that HE made so iconic (yes, Jim Cummings wanted to reprise his role). Instead they went with Matt Mercer because Matt is popular and Minsc is popular. By all means, write another character for Matt (I think he's very talented), but writing Jim out of BG3 really reflects poorly on Larian (and honestly on Matt for taking the gig).Anyways, buy it if you like. I'm disappointed in it: given the resources, time (remember, they originally said 2021), and source material they had to work with I feel like it's come up short.

_childDocuments_.review: It is early access, I grant that. But it is most certainly not anything like Baldur's Gate or any other DnD game I have played. I don't even feel like I am playing a DnD game. Maybe it will get better. Who knows? I will certainly try again after release, but for now, I would say to stay away if you are looking for a follow up to the original series.Certainly not going to touch it again until release, maybe they can fix it. It lacks races and classes galore just to start with. You would think it would have more, but not even close to what you used to be able to pick with something like NWN. Classes feel lifeless. Seriously, you can only pick fighter, thief, ranger, cleric?, warlock, and mage. Not even going to start with the lackluster NPC's. You want to be a  white knight, hang it up, most shelfish bunch of NPC's I have ever seen. Not a Kelgore or even a Neeshka among. Lifeless.Maybe I am to old and expect to much from a game that is trying to bear the title of one of the most successful games of all time. Baldurs Gate brought DnD games to life. Follow that with Icewind Dale, NwN, and their successors. This is a big step backwards from those. This feels like a nail in the coffin.

_childDocuments_.review: Alrighty. I'm changing my review. I originally left a negative review because this game didn't feel like dungeons and dragons at all, but after almost 2 years it feels much closer. There's some adjustments here and there for balancing (which are welcome improvements), and there are still some ground effects (but they aren't nearly as intrusive), but overall it finally feels like D&D. So yeah, I'd recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: Baldur's Gate 3

_childDocuments_.review: I am not one that usually replays long games but this is for sure an exception. It really feels like you are a part of the world and each playthrough it is so fun to roleplay as new characters and even more fun when you do it with friends. At first I was worried I would not like the combat or the way the map was setup but the combat began to become second nature and was a big highlight of the game. I also played on the steam deck which was great since I was able to use the joystick to walk around like it was an open world game. The story is fantastic and the game gives you so much customization when it comes to combat that you really feel in control and can set the game up to be played however you feel is the most comfortable to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Baldur's Gate 3

_childDocuments_.review: Larian Studios, I hope there never comes a day when you end up like Bethesda, Blizzard/Activision, EA, or any of the other AAA game studios that crank out overpriced garbage. So, what do you get with this game?"Baldur's Gate 3" is basically a game that allows you to go and do what you want, how you want. It doesn't hold your hand and can be difficult for plebs like myself. You are free to complete most objectives in any way you see fit. The game was designed to give you the freedom and feel as if you were doing a D&D campaign with your friends. Most, if not all, of the characters in the game seem like living people. The voice acting is superb, and character backstories don't feel forced. To top it off, the game is beautiful. "Baldur's Gate 3" is a gem if there ever was one. I recommend this wholeheartedly; it's worth the price, even better with friends (chaos!).I guess the only real downside I found was the learning curve. I don't do D&D; it's not for lack of experience; it's just not my cup of tea. As such, character builds and tailoring your character to fit your play style and be effective at it are beyond me. It took me quite a while to not only figure out which class was most enjoyable for me but also the insane number of builds, which were overwhelming in number.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with amazing characters and beautiful graphics. Mechanics are quite good and the variety between different classes is enjoyable. Really liked the story so far with all of it's depth and nuances which feel like player choices matter for the world.The weakest part currently felt like the combat. This included bugs where combat would not start properly and an enemy would act as if out of combat while being attacked for multiple turns and bugged out textures where the guardian of the forge was invisible at the start of the combat. At times opportunity attack marker was hard or impossible to see especially with other elements such as lava on the ground. Took some unintended damages from multiple fights due to opportunity attacks that could have easily been avoided by disengage had I seen that this was necessary.Party AI seems quite good in general, but infuriating in places near traps or damaging surface where I had to split the party grouping and move each character manually which felt like holding the hand of a toddler and telling them please don't jump in the fire.Overall exploring the world felt enjoyable and rewarding so if you love discovering secrets and side stories then this is definitely the game for you and considering that this is an early access I trust that the developers will fix the previously mentioned bugs and problems and the final release will be a true gem that it seems to be forming into.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really good for 2/3rds of the game, and it gave me the illusion that I was playing a game of a lifetime. Once you start the last act of the game though, you quickly realize it is not a "feature complete" game. The game culminates in a rushed and unfinished final act that left a sour taste in my mouth. If you try and start over to explore what you thought were massively branching paths, you'd realize those too are incomplete and not nearly as impactful as you are led on to believe. The game really feels broader in your imagination than it is in reality.Having said all this, I will say that it is a worthwhile game to play, and you'll get at least 60-70 hours of what was building up to be the game of a lifetime.I'd recommend waiting on a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Baldur's Gate 3

_childDocuments_.review: The game has grate story, it's one of the most repayable RPG I have ever played.Not to mention the freedom and the options you have to approach any situation is amazing.If you can think of it you can do it in the game, I have no idea how Larian Studios managed to pull that off but man, the freedom in this game is amazing.If you want to kill every single thing you meet across your journey you can, and somehow it still end in a logical conclusion like its what supposed to happen. All the hype and prizes the game have not giving it justice!If you remotely interested in gaming playing Baldur's Gate 3 is a must.But be wary, finding a new game to play after this will be hard.

_childDocuments_.review: Edt: Obviously all the support its getting is great, they added some evil path options, which might fix some of the issues I was having, I do not know.TL;DR: In its current state I really cant recommend this game for anyone planning a serious playthrough. This will hopefully change after some patches, but that doesnt excuse the current situation. Larian seems to have a history with delivering games with seriously ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and unfinished last acts and it sucks they apparently dont change.First things first: There is a huge discrepancy the perception of the game between people who are still in act 1or 2, people who finished the game and people who finished the game multiple times. Depending on your choices (more on that later), Act 1 and 2 are really good, especially for a first playthrough. Starting from Act 3 it mostly goes downhill and takes a nose dive with the ending. On subsequent playthroughs you start to notice more and more cracks, since you try out different things and will see more and more broken stuff in the game. If you want to have fun, play good (or goodish), , use the tadpoles and have fun. You will probably have a good time. But deviate from that path and stuff starts to falter.  Some of the companions have straight up broken and or unfinished questlines. Especially towards act 3 a lot feels like there are only disappointing resolutions to setups and no proper closure. Want to play with Minthara and for that lost three other companions? Well, sucks to be you, her dialogue is broken at the moment for act 2 and 3 and wont trigger or only trigger at unfitting moments. Having fun with kerlach? Well, her quest doesnt really have a solution, so have fun with that. Excited for Halsin? He is just horny as soon as he joins your camp, but wont join your party until some 20-40 hours later (depending on how long you take and what you do) and wont really have any interactions in act 3 anymore. After my second playthrough i started to realize that dialogue options with other companions were also already broken in act 1, which is extremely disappointing.Over the course of act 1 and 2 a great buildup happens, only to be smashed by act 3. Most of the setups (also the new ones in act 3) receive either no closure or disappointing closure. Major choices like the tadpoles have no effect whatsoever on the endings. I dont mark that as a spoiler because you literally only miss out on content if you dont use them, because they have fun and interesting abilities and you literally have no benefit whatsoever from not using them. It feels like act 3 just wasnt finished and they just cut parts and somehow cobbled everything in the end together in the last minute. Of course there are a few highlights in the last act, but also major ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ moments with quests that you can only succeed with some luck and hasting everybody or giving them other fast movement abilities or battles that dont trigger because the boss has only zero HP because you fought them already once in act 1 and their health didnt get reset. When you explore Baldurs gate, you slowly uncover what is going on in the city, but instead of being able to act on it and doing something about it, there is no benefit to finding that out, you are still only able to act in the same way as you were if you didnt know anything about it.The romances are also hit and miss and for some reason no companion is a fan of the idea of just being friends, if you want to do stuff like have a drink with a companion you better also be ready to go all in and have sex.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say? I have played over 280 hours of this game and I havnt even reached Act 3. I restart so many times to see all the variety of outcomes and choices. Im still finding new things, and love this game. The game play is turned base, so if you dont like that you may not like this game, but the amount of variety in this game is astounding. You can avoid enemies completely, or even talk your way out of most fights. There are also a ton of unique builds and multi-classing elements where you can just ignore almost all combat completely. There's a reason this game has won so many rewards. The voice acting alone is enough to make you melt. Your decisions matter and progress where you go. If you see someone in Act 1 odds are you will see them again, unless of course their fate is tied to death base on a decision you made. I will eventually beat this game and enter Act 3 but I have way too much fun creating new characters and picking a path of where that said character would do x thing, and for the most part my adventures almost always different than what I picked on another character. Rating: 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: It is easy to see why most of the reviews of Baldur's Gate 3 are positive when looking at the story, music, and environments of the game, which are all very good. However, I regretted getting the game until around the 50 hour playtime mark, and still have a love/hate relationship with the game. This review focuses on why you may want to think twice about getting it.Using the camera and moving around the environment always feels terrible. It is way too easy to misclick when trying to interact with people/items/bodies, and it is really annoying to accidentally start a conversation when I was trying to search an area, or worse attacking an ally when trying to attack an enemy. I misclicked on things hundreds of times in my playthroughs due to the awkward controls of the camera combined with point and click movement.Holding a key down to show interactables in an area is annoying. This should have a toggle option.Searching bodies is a tedious task after combat. It is made worse by having dead bodies show an * to signify they haven't been looted yet, and then being completely empty upon searching them.Inventory management is a constant problem. You can place items into bags to keep similar items together, like scrolls bag, potions bag, etc. However, there is no way to automate this, so you have to drag every item you acquire manually into a bag or leave your inventory as a giant mess.Combat where the enemy outnumbers your party, or combat that includes a bunch of allies with the party takes way too long for the ai to take its turn. You can be sitting around for 60 seconds or longer just waiting to get control back for your characters. There is not any option in game to fast forward through the ai turn.Game can be buggy at times. One instance my party was permanently frightened after combat ended, leaving them unable to move, and I had to reload a save to fix it. Doors are very weird. Sometimes the game refuses to let my party through an open doorway, so I have to get a character to close the door and reopen it to pass through. This happened to me dozens of times. A few times the game let enemies attack through an open door, but when I tried to attack back the game stated the enemy couldn't be reached with either ranged attacks or melee. Companions also constantly got left behind, forcing me to separate them from the party, switch control to them, and then make my way back to the rest of the group. The game is designed with Dungeons and Dragons in mind, which is a good thing for players that enjoy that setting. However, in D&D, the dungeonmaster and the players create a story together, and having poor dice rolls at times is part of that story they create. With BG3, on the other hand, the story is already set (though quite complex), and if you roll poorly on key rolls, you end up missing out on parts of the story. This feels terrible as a player, and incentivizes save scumming (saving before an important roll and reloading every time it gets a bad result), which is not fun. It would be far more enjoyable if the story did not have randomness to it, and was solely based on the player's decisions, with some decisions availability being locked behind being a certain race or being proficient in a certain skill.If the above issues do not bother you, or if you use mods to correct them, then it may be worth picking up Baldur's Gate 3. However, in the current state of the core game, I can not recommend it at this time.
_childDocuments_.name: Baldur's Gate 3

_childDocuments_.review: 42 hours in, a good bit of which was idle, and I believe I completed all the early access content so here's my take so far. The game in its current state is only worth buying if you're a fan of turn-based RPGs, Larian Studios, or both. Throughout your play through you will consistently encounter visual and combat bugs, soft locks that require reloading, and spots which will drop your frame rate so low that you'll need to restart.That being said, I still really enjoyed my experience playing through this game. There's nothing like that sense of exploration in a new world, mysterious companions, and optimizing your build and strategy for each unique fight. The game mostly allows you to play how you'd like to, but isn't afraid to punish you severely for missteps . This world is supposed to feel like a treacherous place and the game expects you to save scum.Overall my experience was very positive but if you have little experience in these types of games, or little patience for an unpolished and unfinished product, I would wait for the full release before trying it out. I myself really enjoyed this test run so that I could figure out how I wanted to approach the game on my actual play through on release. Happy adventuring and may the dice rolls be in your favor.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first Baldur's Gate game that I've ever played. I wasn't that interested in the story of this game or previous Baldur's Gate games, so I skipped them and went straight to this. I personally wanted to play this game to experience what everyone was speaking about; the way you can approach each quest and shape the world. And for sure, it met my expectations.The story of this game is pretty average, but no offense, to me personally all these RPGs have similar generic stories (gather the allies and beat the evil). And that is fine, it's just not for me. However this game does add some "unique" stuff to these classic stories, but the characters are mostly bland till the third act, and I didn't care much what would happen to me or my companions. In Act 3 (the final act of the game) they became more interesting because this is where all these companion quests end. The funny thing is that most people seem to hate the ending, and I personally found it interesting. It's different, the bitter-sweet as my friend Dean said. Could be improved of course.Now let's talk about the most important stuff regarding this game. There are many games where you can make choices, and where you can attack friendly NPCs, but what this game offers is that you can kill NPCs and they will literally stop existing. All quests related to them will disappear. I for example had an issue with one boss, cause he was killing my companion in the dialogue as soon as I approached it. I had no way to save him, so what I did is that I attacked him with a bow from a distance which triggered the boss fight. Killed the boss and my companion stayed alive. Some guy even managed to kill one of the main villains literally 10-15 hours before the final duel teleporting the enemy somewhere else and pushing them off the cliff, which caused the mission to be successful. And it's not just about killings. It's hard to even explain it, you need to experience it yourself.There are many ways to approach the quest like I said, but there are also issues. For example, in Act 1, SLIGHT SPOILER AHEAD there are 3 goblin leaders, whom you need to kill to save some people in the camp led by Zevlor, and the first time I played the game I killed them after speaking with Zevlor, and getting quests from them. This time I decided to kill them first. This is good right, you can do it whenever you want. However, my issue was that after killing them and then talking with Zevlor for the first time, he didn't seem really excited. He just said hey I heard that goblin leaders are gone, here are coins for you. There was barely any dialogue. After I met him in the camp, he was just standing there, without any option for me to talk with him. My point is, if I finish the game again, I am not sure if there will be too much variety since I will probably do the quests a similar way, or in a lot of cases the same. It's mostly if you want to be a good or a bad guy, rare are choices where you actually have to think; one of the exceptions is the ending of one of the companion's quests. That choice really made me think, probably one of the best choices I saw in gaming. But for the first playthrough, this variety is amazing.As for companions. I may get some hate for this, I personally don't have anything against people who are attracted to the opposite gender, however, please don't rub it in my face. In the beginning, I was scared I would select the wrong dialogue option because every male companion was hitting on me. Mage told me "Hey come here to see some magic", and I was like sure, he is a mage, he probably wants to show me real magic. But oh boy, I was wrong. I immediately reloaded the game. However, after you reject them a few times, they stop trying. But the beginning was a bit annoying. Especially the Astarion, the gay vampire who is constantly trying to suck you. I mean your blood.The gameplay-wise, this game follows the 5e dnd ruleset. Every time you attack game will toss dice in the background (you can't see it), and based on what number it lands you may land an attack or miss. However, when you make some choices in the dialogue you will be asked to toss the dice, and the rolling of the dice will be shown on the screen, which is pretty cool. If you get a high enough number you will perform what you chose in dialogue. Otherwise, it will fail. This way you can talk yourself out of some fights, by getting good numbers. Combat is turn-based, which I personally found pretty fun, having never played a turn-based game before. The game wasn't that hard, but wasn't easy either for a turn-based noob like me.It took me around 100 hours to beat the game, and clear most quests that the game has to offer. Performance was fine until Act 3, where it started dropping a bit more, however, I can't say that I cared too much, because it seemed optimized enough. The atmosphere and music are really average.- Amazing way in which you can approach the quests and shape the world- Companion quests are pretty good- Fun gameplay and the combat itself- Interesting ending- Story is average- Companions are okay, but a bit bland at first- Performance is mostly fine- There are some bugs, but it wasn't that bad in my experience- While the ending was interesting, it could have been done a bit better- Variety could be even better regarding choices, in most cases the choice is if you want to be a good or a bad guy, however, there are some "hard" choices which I enjoyed- The main villains of Act 3 are cringe In my opinion mechanic-wise this is the best RPG I've ever played. There is nothing like it on the market at the moment. The way you can play the game and shape the world is just amazing. For this reason, I would recommend this game. Sure, some stuff could have been done better, but in the sea of generic games coming out every month, this game is amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: T.L. D.R. this is one of the best games ever created and deserve every single award it won.My first playthrough of Baldur's Gate III took over 250 hours to complete, just by walking around, interacting with party members, NPCs, trying to complete every quest, testing different builds. Yet the game never felt like it was padding.It's no wonder a lot of AAA devs complained that this game overdelivers, because it does in all aspects. You can truly see the passion and dedication of Swen and his team with this title because it's just so freaking massive; yet by the end of final Act you're still left craving for more, wanting to explore more of this beautifully crafted world and characters.✅ This game provides a fantastic, almost accurate experience of 5th Edition Dungeons & Dragons. The devs had to adapt a lot of the rules to fit the game format but if you've played DnD before then this will be easy to grasp.✅ I think the best part of this game is how much freedom you have to tackle on challenges and fights. For example, I play a lot of Stealth Strategy games (like Commandos, Desperados and Shadow Tactics), so I really enjoy setting up my party members to dispatch bosses with few actions as possible while striking with one character after the other while hiding. There is a lot of player expression you don't see in any other game.✅ The character writing of this game reminds me a lot of BioWare's, which is poetic considering that Baldur's Gate I & II were made by them. Nearly all character arcs feel satisfying. I've been craving for a game like this since the Mass Effect Trilogy. Also, if you've played the original Baldur's Gate games, prepare for some nice surprises.✅ The replay value of this game is absolutely gargantuan, because there are different routes, quest outcomes and small details that carry changes through the rest of the game. Not to mention different classes to experience. You'll often find yourself tempted to start fresh new save files to restart your journey with different classes, and I don't blame you.✅ The fact this game has, on top of all that, FULLY FUNCTIONAL ONLINE MULTIPLAYER WITH UP TO FOUR PEOPLE, is the cherry on top. Being able to play this game with friends (and struggling to align the schedules) is ridiculously fun and further adds replay value.✅ The modding community is very active and Patch 7 (September 3rd, 2024) even added an official mod  manager and support in-game.❌ Even on the lowest settings performance can sometimes tank a bit in large populated areas. You may see a significant drop in FPS. But overall this game is very well optimized.❌ I feel this game could've done a better job with some of the tutorials. For instance, you can fail or even downright miss quests if you long rest too much depending on which part of the game you are.❌ The game rewards "murder hobo'ing" a bit too much. You still get experience for milestones (discovering new locations, completing quests without killing, etc.), but if you want to maximize experience gained it's easier to just slaughter everything.❌ The final Act feels a bit lackluster in some aspects, not to mention the gauntlet of fights leading to the final battle being a bit disappointing. No spoilers but I was expecting something more way more flashy and bombastic.Baldur's Gate III winning Game of the Year in 2023 is a testament that gamers just want fun, complete experiences that respect their time and don't try to exploit their wallets with lootboxes, season passes and cashgrab microtransactions. Crazy, huh?It's a shame we won't get an expansion or DLC for this game, but I frankly can't wait to see what Larian is cooking; whether it's Divinity: Original Sin 3 or a brand new IP. I'm sure they'll apply everything they learned with Baldur's Gate III and blow our minds once again.

_childDocuments_.review: Update after completing the game: Others will say it, still others will debate it, numbers will show it, this is the BEST CRPG of the decade! Without spoiling contents, I will simply state that this game has given me back a feeling I haven't had since Baldurs Gate II. Feeling for my character, feeling for the npcs, feeling for the inhabitants of Baldurs Gate (& environs). The game works, sure there a few kinks, but we're at hotfix 3 within the first week of release, remembr that Larian released one month ahead of schedule - incidentally timed with a cold and wet summer period in northern Europe. So Hooray for Larian for making a fantastic game. Hooray for a NEW INDUSTRY STANDARD - no pointless microtransactions, musthave skins or DLCs - though everyone is hoping for more Baldurs Gate, or at the very least more D&D games. D&D is intellectual property though, and Wizard of the Coast took a chance with Larian, and the IP of Baldurs Gate, and I believe they feel it has paid off enough that more games in this genre is on the way. We can only hope that Swen and Larian aren't too exhausted and fed up with BG3. For now though, there is a good 300 more hours in this game I imagine, like BG1 & BG2 it will one those games you just always have installed and always think of giving another go.I cannot stress enough that if you like RPGs, if you like D&D, if you enjoy choices matter and very diverse encounters and quests, then this masterpiece must be yours.Previous review from early access (pre-Grymforge mind you)Absolutely marvelous for an alpha, with enourmous potential and a very clear message of just how awesome the full game will be. Very few glitches, awesome graphics and a very true adaptation of 5e rules and lore, mixed with an intricate lace of humor. Group social dynamics seem quite realistic, and while some have already deemed this as 'hostile' who would not believe themselves hostile while threatened with imminent death and amongst strangers whom you must entrust your life. Others have pointed out that the somewhat static action dynamics of early levels - where fighters hit stuff, and mages get to have all the fun, is a somewhat lackluster experience, while I concur, it is to be said that this is the very nature of D&D 5e. At the time of writing this, my party has reached level 3 and each class (Rogue, Fighter, Cleric, Mage) is starting to show the diversity everyone's probably already used to from pen and paper campaigns or other CRPGs. The fact that 8 hours has yielded 3 levels tells to the scope of this pre-release, as max level is 4. (Edit: I was mistaken, max level is 10+ in the final game, xp is capped in the pre-release. Feeling plenty powerful though). As a side note, you can probably do a playthrough of BG2 faster than you can do a playthrough of this pre-release of BG3.Were it not for the 0.4.1xxxx at the top right of the screen, I would be so immersed as to probably not notice that this is indeed an alpha, before I reached the end of the content.Get it now, or get it when its complete, either way just get it - this game is born a classic, and will likely become a legend, something not many games achieve these days.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is going to put aside all the controversy as well as some of the push-back from other studios etc. This is about BG3 itself, not involving politics, social acceptances/unacceptances and social norms, etc. So if you are interested in that type of review that doesn't include all that stuff, keep reading. If you are looking for instant gratification, you won't get it, actually you may not even want to read the rest of this review because it is long and detailed as this game truly deserves it.Some bugs exist particularly later in the game, you may notice slower dialogue, or scenes that just appear to stop or have awkward pauses in them. It is not unexpected with a game of this scope. With that being said, do yourself a favor and actually read the patch notes. They are actively being worked on and fixed. I myself came across a few particular bugs on I think it was August 6th or 7th and quite literally in the August 8th Hotfix the bugs I came across were fixed.There are some quests that appear to be broke or contain some misinformation. They are not  quests or won't result in full on blocks to the story but they are noticeable. Most of the time they appear to sort themselves out but can potentially confuse a player. My suggestion is to use the report feature but don't let it stop you from continuing forward.Dice rolls, honestly there are times where I feel like the Dice are weighted against the players. I mean 95% chance of success on an attack and you get a Critical Miss (which means you rolled a Nat 1) when that single attack would have ended the encounter if it hit. But now the enemy gets one more turn and manages to take out 2 of your best teammates? Huh?Skill checks, there seem to be a lot of skill checks that you can outright fail and then have no way of knowing what it was you missed and no way to go on and discover it. This may upset some people as they cannot get the satisfaction of knowing what was there, only knowing that something was there since it was clearly a failed check.No True Guidance - Take this as a negative if you will. I am posting it here because often times people are always looking for guidance for something. This game does not hold your hand. It provides you with objectives and marks spot on the map for you. It is up to you to decide when you will do it, how you will do it or even if you will do it. With that being said it is certainly possible to lock yourself out of other quests and encounters or parts of the game entirely because of decisions you made. (To my fellow Dark Urge players, you understand.)Clunky - there are parts of the game that seem to be incredibly sluggish at times, especially if playing for long sessions. I imagine this is being actively worked on but really only starts showing itself in like the middle to later part of Act 3. I have made reports about it myself, but for you performance lovers out there, you may see some performance dips especially later in the game or during long play sessions. Steam Deck performance - Performance on the Steam Deck is good, however the controls seem to be a little bit clunky. The game runs fine but the controls require some getting used to especially if you are like me and play actively on both the Steam Deck and the PC. BG3 is an excellent game that even with 306 hours I still have so much more to do. This game is a  product. You pay your money and you get a  experience. No battle-pass, season-pass, yearly-pass, whatever-pass. No content locked behind a Pay-Wall. Nothing. Just a genuine full and complete game like back in the old days when I started gaming almost 25+ years ago.The amount of work that was put into this game is 100% apparent. The sheer amount of details that the Developers took into consideration when making this game is astonishing. I can't begin to say how many times I have done something out of the box and the game "anticipated" it. The atmosphere in this game truly exhibits a notion of "This is your character, you do what it is you want," and the game acts accordingly. It is not the reverse where you act according to the game. There is something to be said about the attention to detail that the developers put into Baldur's Gate 3. You can tell it was a labor of love and dedication to a project. Not just some new Title that needed to be released to satisfy a deadline and bring income. The Development Team truly loved creating this and loves continuing work on this project. Just look at the Hotfixes. You can see it if you step back and just think about what must have gone into creating this masterpiece. The mechanics and gameplay itself are excellent. It isn't "handed" to you, especially in the later acts. You need to think, you need to utilize your brain and take into account all that is going on, who you are up against, etc. etc. You need to author your story. The satisfaction one gets from completing a difficult fight is next level. There is one particular battle that involves a particular soundtrack, that I KNOW will stay with me forever, and that says a lot.Moving to the next point. The Soundtrack of this game. It is another masterpiece within a masterpiece. The atmospheric scenes created with the sound, the battle music. It is all next level and truly is something so underrated. There have been a number of times where I just stopped, just to listen to the music. Even side-missions like with a particular Bard in a particular grove has an entire cinematic scene dedicated to the music and it is just awe-inspiring. Just stop for a moment and think just how much went into making that one scene. That is the type of love and dedication that the studio put into this game and you just don't often see that anymore. The World feels alive. You go into a Grove, or you go into a town, and it is bustling with NPCs carrying on their routines, having an argument, fighting, training,  and are having this conversation . Just step back an appreciate that and think about how much effort was made for the game to adjust itself to one of the tons of different ways you could have done/accomplished/failed something.Combat - combat also is rewarding. There are so many different options, use your environment, perhaps you picked up some barrels from the tutorial zone and have been holding onto them since the beginning of the game and decide you want to toss them into the battlefield and detonate them, or maybe you been lugging around some barrels of alcohol that you now want to utilize on the field. Go for it. Maybe you bit off more than you can chew and need to make a tactical retreat. Combat is so dynamic, there is no "set-way" to do something. Your options are numerous. Maybe you do want to just truck through everyone and don't want to think tactically. Sure go right ahead. The mechanics themselves are intricate, with the different damage types, resistances, buffs, debuffs, etc. All within the nature of Dungeon and Dragons. The Story - it is yours to craft and how you get to the end is up to you. It is detailed, it is interesting, it has its twists and turns that will make you say "no way," "are you serious," "I knew it," and the list goes on and on but you are the one who creates the story.If you are looking for a full and complete game with wonderful music, a studio that cares about their community base and product, great mechanics and an outstanding story that you create with your decisions and you can look past some minor over-sights in a game of this magnitude and slight performance issues that are actively being worked on then Baldur's Gate 3 is for you and you will get your money's worth, with or without any DnD experience.

There hasn't been such an great RPG with various possibilities for a long time, and it probably won't be. The audiovisual within the genre is excellent, the game is completely voiced even with its huge content.We control a group of a maximum of 4 members in a RPG world full of quests with variable solutions. In the framework of the world, there is typical Larian creativity in the game, in addition to the classic use of the abilities of the heroes  and items, there is also an interactive environment, elements, stealth, branching dialogues, jokes, very interesting NPCs with their own stories. _childDocuments_.review: I uninstalled today after playing 18 hours total. There are just so many bad decisions and sloppy implementations that I won't even bother until they do a lot of work.If any dev happens to read this FIX THE ENCOUNTER DESIGN and game balance. - You should not be giving every goblin and other humanoid monster class levels. They should *not* all be spellcasters an/or carry alchemical items and magic arrows. 5th ed is simply not balanced around that idea. The goblins in this game are all *individually* as strong as a single PC, and there are WAY too many of them in the combat encounters. That shows complete lack of understanding of how this system works. Look at the challenge ratings and stats in the monster manual and realize that you are no where close to how 5th edition should feel and balance.- Make escape routes and alternate approaches to fights. There are basically no ways to approach many of the combats other than charging head on. Sure you can sneak up and get a surprise round pretty easily most of the time but that's about it. There are no ways to easily end combat/run away once a fight starts. That is horribly frustrating and makes any kind of non-save scum based play impossible.- Ranged weapons should have disadvantage to hit beyond their short range. Goblins with shortbows should not be able to snipe you across the map. Likewise, cover and line of sight seem almost meaningless in this game; partial and 3/4 cover bonuses need to be implemented in some form to make melee characters have half a chance to get in close. The combat feels far too ranged focused on both sides; I found myself using bows and ranged cantrips constantly even on my melee focused characters.- Get rid of all the Divinity holdovers. Eating food in combat to restore HP is not a D&D mechanic; a piece of cheese should not be superior to a healing potion. The persistent burning effects from fire spells, and persistent acid and fire aoes all over the place are not generally an effect of the items and spells that currently produce them in the game. You copy pasted way too much from another system and it's screwing up the game balance.- Your spellcasting rules are quite simply, wrong. Casters should be able to cast lower level spells with a higher level slot, that is pretty key to 5th ed resource management. Several of the spells take the wrong kind of action or don't work correctly. original review below, sorry this post is so huge.I really want to like this, but so far, I'm not impressed. Maybe I'll warm up to it once the full build releases but as is, can't recommend.Positives:- Art and cutscenes are lovely so far, even unfinished.- The combat does actually feel like playing 5th ed D&D, which is what I've been wanting out of a game for 8 years now.- Forgotten Realms is not my favorite setting but the references and atmosphere are there. You are definitely in Faerun.Negatives:-The game is in rough shape technically still, that's to be expected with early access. The lack of integrated bug reporting/feedback is not encouraging. Like, if you're gonna release what's basically an alpha (I won't call this a beta build even when half the classes aren't implemented), keep the ability for players to report.- The controls are exactly like D:OS 1 and 2. I found that series a bit overly fiddly and the same applies here. It seems almost designed to make you misclick. There are so many clickable and loot-able object that do absolutely nothing besides crowd your screen with interactables. It is possible to aim an attack or spell at *nothing* and activate it and there's no confirmation if you do. The cursor doesn't even snap to enemies in combat at all that I can tell, so you better make damn sure you see the hit percentage and don't wiggle your mouse again before you click. The camera is all over the place, particularly the zoom level and vertical angle.There are also different buttons to access your bags vs. your paper doll, which is very strange. The menus in general are a bit of a mess.- Related, the amount of vendor trash/useless items is absurd. Not quite Skyrim level, but up there. I know it's traditional but please make it so that the "wares" flag removes items from the general inventory and makes it less crowded. - You can't change party except during camp/long rests, even when you recruit a new party member. This is not explained well and thoroughly frustrating if you camp and forget to swap *before* you go to sleep. Why the hell don't you pick your party when leaving camp or a city, like, every RPG ever?- The party members are a bunch of unlikeable edgelords all hiding some dark secret and all seemingly evil or neutral at best. I don't generally RP lawful good but if I wanted to, I can't imagine how you would get through this game without pissing them off. Two of them get mad at you for rescuing a child at one point. Wynn shows some good tendencies but also acts very bloodthirsty and a little racist so, yeah, can't really say I like him much either.- The quests are structured so that if you are playing a low int/low cha character you are generally locked into the worst possible outcomes. Again, this is similar to a lot of previous CPRG's but could easily be addressed to at least some degree by integrating more types of skill checks.- Autosave feature does not function well at all. It seems to quit working as soon as you start picking up party members.Anyways, I expected more from the return of *the* D&D video game franchise. Hoping it improves significantly.Edit: Thanks to those who pointed out quicksave is F5,To those saying I don't get Baldur's Gate or D&D...yes, I have played the previous games, and many other CRPG's, and I've been playing D&D for 27 years. So...sorry my interpretation differs from yours I guess? My problem isn't that the NPC's are all evil, it's that they are not FUN to interact with. They're just boring ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who ♥♥♥♥♥ about everything you do. And Wynn's comments about goblins *are* racist, like I'm not saying that as some kind of value judgement on the game, just pointing out an aspect of the character that made me dislike him and think he's probably not good-aligned.Finally, for those saying "good characters will come later" - ok, again, I get this is early access but the way the party is introduced sure makes it seem like they are the default starting group. Seems kinda weird you would have to play through 8+ hours just to put together a group who doesn't get mad at you for not letting a kid die.Day 2 edit:Unfortunately have to retract my comment that the combat feels like 5e. The encounter design becomes horrendous rather quickly. Enemies all have spells or alchemical items that make fights miserable slogs requiring multiple reloads/long rests. They are clearly not designed off of 5e monsters as they use multiple class abilities that they normally would not. To top it off the boss monsters all have multiple actions a turn on top of a large horde of minions. With a party of only 4 your action economy deficit is way too high to be efficient with your own attacks, and with Larians' raging hard on for persistent acid/fire effects on every inch of the map, it's really tough to position well either.Also, giving everyone the ability to disengage as a bonus action seemed ok at first, but in larger fights it completely negates the ability of melee characters to lock anyone down. This needs a lot of tuning and they need to start by reading the damn monster manual. If you're gonna use 5e math for the players, you gotta use it for the monsters too.The monsters have infinite aggro radius and combat never ends even if your entire party is hidden or miles away. So...once you are in combat, no way out til all the monsters are dead or you are.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I'm hooked to the game, feels like a throwback to good old D&D games. Personally I think the turn-based style from Divinity works very well with the D&D rules on top of it. I'm liking the story so far and the dialogue is good. It starts off immediately interesting without wasting much time setting the pace, and the characters have believable motivations to stick with you plus they don't necessarily like you, everyone definitely has some personality.Early access does have some missing features though like planned classes etc (for instance at the time of writing you can't make Druids or Bards). I noticed some missing lipsync and animations in cutscenes sometimes, but it hasn't bothered me enough to break immersion much most of the time. Character creation was also a little bit limited with face options at least (I would've liked to see some sliders), also there were only 2 voices per gender to choose from. But otherwise it was pretty solid and seems to stick with actual D&D rules for the most part and your character progression is very much the same. I myself went with a Human Rogue/Arcane Trickster and am enjoying it so far, there's LOTS of playstyles and party customization.Visually the game looks great, and I think the facial expressions are some of the best I've seen. All of the playable races also look amazing and I don't really have any complaints with their design (first thought was "wow female dwarves actually look pretty" :p). I'm running it at 'high' preset settings @ 1440p on a 1070 GTX coupled with a Ryzen 5 1600, and I get 45-60 FPS most of the time, which is fine for me personally. Though I might need to move the game to an SSD because sometimes I noticed the textures loading pretty slowly from HDD. Also the soundtrack so far has been nice, especially the main themes.I'm sure the game will get better over time but if you can deal with limited content at the moment and aren't going for a very specific character that you cannot make yet, I'd recommend it. Also there's some technical hiccups to be expected, but they haven't distracted me from enjoying the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Before writing my review I have to say that I have no history with any DnD-like Videogames like BG.I never even liked these these turn-based style games, but after reading some reviews I changed my mind and gave BG3 a try.I am playing this game with 3 friends and so far it's been a blast.We try to stay in character for most of the dialogue options and also try to handle things the "ethically correct" way, but sometimes things got a little to heated.So let me introduce you to my group:Gwyndolyn Bloodeye - a DROW ROGUE from whom no loot is safe, every door is "unlocked", there has to be a reward for every quest, right.. right?Flump Blipp - a GNOME SORCERER (even if often disguised) that will handle things with finesse until there is an opportunity for.. Fireballs maybe? So to say, he could be a little more athletic so our Dwarf doesn't always have to throw him up obstacles.Ceilaya Teilyar - a ELVEN CLERIC - the heart of the party, often saved our asses with massive healing spells - yet a little on the naive side when it comes to speaking. Oh and.. Scratch must be cuddled everytime at camp, period.Rabogard Eisenkittel - a DWARF BARBARIAN who is often not going to mince matters but falls a little short before every encounter - he guards the door so the others can go first. He even throws every spear, chair, goblin on on everyone making fun of his height - and his hair (which is fabulous)The storytelling is one of a kind and the voice-acting is one of the best I've ever seen in a videogame.We are 120 hours in and are halfway through Baldur's Gate, we never felt the need to rush things and tried to avoid leaving any quest unsolved.I think there are nevertheless some quests we might have missed in the first two acts. So maybe there is room for another play-through with another concept.If you got some friends to play this game with I'd highly recommend you give it a try.There are a lot of publishers out there that should take a leaf out of Larian's book. For me an easy contender for GOTY.(I am the dwarf and my hair looks fabulous.)

_childDocuments_.review: The scope of this game is staggering and thus I can forgive it for the bugs, but some of the bugs I've encountered are game-breaking at worst and extremely disappointing at best. I have had to use reddit on multiple occasions to determine if I am the only one who has experienced certain bugs, and although the issues I encountered are apparently rare, they are still enough of a problem to reveal that BG3 still needs several more months- or even a year- before it is completely polished and in a state that is fully worthy of release. While people are rightfully singing its praises, I am finding it harder to overlook the bugs than most, as its flashy veneer and gripping story don't distract me from just how devastating some of the bugs have been.Here are some examples.1. act1 character spoiler: This wasn't a game-breaking bug, but heartbreaking, because for a moment I thought something important bugged out of existence and I needed reddit to tell me how to fix it.2. Generic romance spoiler:  Again, I needed Reddit to tell me how to advance. I genuinely thought I would never be able to speak to this character ever again without softlocking my game.3. A few odd dialogue triggers occurred, in particular involving companion romance. Companions assumed I was romancing Gale when I had no idea I had already begun a romance with him. Fortunately for Gale, I was already planning on starting his romance subplot, but I was thrust into it without my character having any sort of say-so. 4. Minor stuff: I've had instances of lines of dialogue being skipped entirely, making my character say things I did not intend. NPCs blipped out of existence (handing over a Special Torch to an NPC who then proceeded to tell me to follow them just disappeared and left me stranded), combat triggered when dialogue should have been triggered (I did not even know this because I died in a combat, reloaded my save, and doing the same actions resulted in something completely different: allowing me to talk to an NPC that previously immediately attacked. I would have completely missed this had I not reloaded my save.)(All this occurred after Patch 4/Hotfix 10.) These are just the most recent examples of the multitude of bugs I encountered thus far. A cursory search of google and reddit and the steam forums will reveal that I am not the only one still suffering from the game's unpolished state- but kudos to the dev team for continuing to patch the game and give it the love it deserves. I just wish they could have held off just a little longer before release, but I get it. The pressure was on to put this game out in the world, even if it wasn't quite 100% ready. I want to keep playing because the story has me invested, but I really wish I could have played it some time in the future after another set of hotfixes and patches have been applied. Reloading my game and waiting on loading screens when a glitch occurs eats away a lot of time I could otherwise spend playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am only thru Act 1 and I can already say with confidence that this one is something special.  If you enjoyed the divinity Original sin games and/or are a fan of DnD you will love this.  The turn based combat is good.  It plays almost exactly like the divinity titles that this studio worked on before.  The story is rich and accessible as are all of the NPC characters.  The graphics are top notch and you do get to choose how you handle almost every situation and encounter. You can completely customize your character or you can play a pre-crafted one if you are new to the DnD world and its rules.  The game gives you good quest guidance in the form of mini map markers for the main quests, but allows you to discover the world for yourself as well.   I would say that this studio is punching above their weight class on this title and they really delivered a wonderful experience in Balder's Gate III.  It is definitely challenging, but not oppressively so.  The balance is great.  There are a few small bugs, but nothing that auto-saves and manual saves can't manage.  Nothing crippling.  Its fresh and there is not a battle pass or micro transaction in sight.  I'd give it a solid 8.5/10 so far and if they iron out the bugs my rating goes up to a 9.5/10.  If I were to pick one small thing about the game that really surprised me it would be actually be two things.  I loved that I was able to pick feats instead of just the standard ASI and I love the cut scenes and cinematic.  They set the game apart from other similar DnD titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Baldur's Gate 3 is fan-f**king-tastic perfection. The original Baldur's Gate was the second PC game I ever played (we got our first PC in '97, so had just played Commodore games before then). It was perfection to me, a kid who loved D&D but had barely ever gotten to play it IRL, suddenly I could play as much as I wanted in a game that encouraged my obsessive need to explore every corner, read every book, and talk to every single NPC. All the following Sword Coast games were similar faves. Even though I eventually explored outside the single-player-RPG genre, (begrudgingly at first, with the multiplayer/social aspect of WoW being a big scary hurdle to overcome for my socially anxious self), these games will always be my first loves, they were fascinating, exciting and comforting all at the same time.So, I'd say my expectations for a new BG game were as high as they could get. I was over-the-moon when I learned that Larian Studios would be making it, as I was certain they were THE only choice to be able to live up to those expectations. I had previously participated in the Kickstarter campaigns for both Divinity Original Sin 1 & 2, and I fell in love with the passion these guys showed for their games. Their attention to every detail, bard-level storytelling skills, great sense of visual and musical style, their wonderful sense of humour and ability to create beautiful loveable AND horrifyingly heinous characters with rich backstories... All this came through in Baldur's Gate 3 in a way that couldn't be more perfect if I had dreamed it up myself. I'm playing as slowly as I can to make it last as long as possible, because I don't want this adventure to end (though at the same time, I'm already thinking of future playthroughs and new things I want to try!). I'm enjoying finding all the hidden secrets and details, replaying some fights because they were so hard but so fun that I just have to try them again, I'm loving chatting with all my companions and listening to their stories (and romancing them because omg they are so amazing and I want them all to love me as much as I love them hahaha). Oh and speaking of the amazing companions and NPCs, major props to the voice actors! The acting is top-notch, and a huge portion of my enjoyment of the game is because of the quality of the interactions and conversations I'm having with my adventuring buddies. I could go on for hours and pages, but I think I'll wrap it up and just say that I'm always looking forward to getting back in the game, and I hope I get to experience all the thousands of permutations of this story for many years to come!Oh and I forgot to mention, but I'm barely above the minimum hardware requirements (my video card is pretty much the minimum) and I have no issues running the game with settings on high/ultra with all graphic effects turned on. Might run into performance issues in Act 3, but so far in Act 1 I run it no problems even with two browsers open at the same time with a dozen-ish tabs open in Chrome and 6 in Brave.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful graphics, beautiful cut scenes, amazing music, fantastic voice actors, and great story.  There's nothing about this game that I don't love. Absolutely love that this is a game that can make you second-guess almost every decision and so many decisions have ramifications later in the game. Dilemmas with no obvious good answer and great role play. I've played at least 5 full games so far with different races, classes, and subclasses and have yet to have a game that felt like a replay of another. Add in the Dark Urge story and you'll never have the same experience twice.If you're on the fence...just buy it. You won't regret it. If you're worried about getting your money's worth, I got over 100 hours of play out of one game and missed a ton of content.If you're just mildly curious about this game and aren't sure you'll do well because you're unfamiliar with D&D, this game will guide you and when it's important, you can always turn on the turn-based mode and take your time to make sure you are doing what you're meaning to do. _childDocuments_.review: Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just a worthy successor to its legendary namesake; it's a sprawling, character-driven RPG that sets a new standard for the genre. Larian Studios has crafted a world that's both familiar and refreshingly unique, brimming with danger, intrigue, and the potential for an epic adventure. Fasten your helm, adjust your moral compass (or ditch it entirely), because Baldur's Gate 3 is a wild ride you won't want to miss.Baldur's Gate 3 throws you headfirst into a narrative that's both personal and world-shattering. You awaken filled with a mysterious tadpole lodged in your brain, granting you otherworldly abilities – and a slow march towards an explosive demise. The quest? Unveil the secrets of these tadpoles and potentially avoid a gruesome fate (or maybe even turn it to your advantage). But Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just about tadpoles. It's about the characters you meet along the way – a motley crew with their own agendas, secrets, and deep-seated motivations. From the snarky tiefling warlock Shadowheart to the delightfully chaotic tiefling bard Astarion, these companions feel real, flawed, and utterly captivating.The world itself is rich with history and lore. Fans of Dungeons & Dragons will feel right at home, encountering familiar races, classes, and locations. But Larian Studios doesn't just rely on nostalgia. They weave a new tale that feels both respectful of the source material and daringly original. The story is full of twists and turns, with choices that genuinely feel like they matter.  Will you embrace your inner hero or succumb to the seductive whispers of power? The answer is entirely up to you.Here's the beauty of Baldur's Gate 3: there are no truly "wrong" choices. You can be a paragon of virtue, a ruthless tyrant, or something gloriously in between. The game reacts to your decisions in meaningful ways, shaping the narrative and your relationships with your companions. With multiple endings and a high replay value, Baldur's Gate 3 encourages you to experiment and see where your choices lead.If you're familiar with Larian Studios' previous title Divinity: Original Sin 2, the core gameplay of Baldur's Gate 3 will feel instantly familiar. It's a turn-based tactical RPG that rewards clever positioning, smart ability usage, and a sprinkle of dice-rolling luck.  The combat is challenging but satisfying, with a focus on environmental manipulation and creative spell combinations.One minute you might be hurling an unsuspecting goblin off a cliff with a well-placed shove, the next you're raining down fire with a strategically placed fireball.  The addition of D&D's action economy adds another layer of depth,  letting you use your cunning to your advantage during each turn.Outside of combat, BG3 shines with its exploration and dialogue options. The world is a joy to delve into, filled with secrets to uncover and hidden paths to explore.  Whether you're bartering with a wisecracking tiefling merchant or navigating a conversation fraught with tension, your choices hold weight.  The dialogue is witty, engaging, and often laugh-out-loud funny,  perfectly capturing the spirit of D&D. BG3 is a visual stunner. The developers haven't skimped on graphical fidelity, crafting a world that feels alive and vibrant. Lush forests teem with life, while towering mountains inspire awe with their craggy peaks. Bustling cityscapes overflow with detail, from the bustling marketplaces to the towering structures. Even the dankest dungeons feel oppressive and atmospheric, thanks to the use of lighting effects.Character models are a particular highlight. They're expressive and detailed, bringing your companions and the world's denizens to life. You'll see the worry etched on a character's face during a tense negotiation or the glint of determination in their eyes before a pivotal battle.  Lighting effects play a huge role in setting the mood, with dynamic shadows and soft lighting creating a believable and immersive world.  Whether you're exploring a sun-drenched meadow or navigating a torch-lit cavern, the graphics consistently impress.The sound design of Baldur's Gate 3 is equally impressive. The soundtrack is both atmospheric and evocative, perfectly capturing the mood of the narrative. From the triumphant orchestral swells during epic battles to the haunting melodies that underscore quieter moments, the music enhances the experience without being overbearing.The sound effects are equally top-notch. Spells crackle with power, swords clash with a satisfying thud, and the world itself is alive with ambient sounds.  You'll hear the wind whipping through the trees, the crunch of footsteps on snow, and the murmurs of conversation in crowded taverns. The voice acting is superb, with each character boasting their own unique voice and mannerisms. Minsc's manic pronouncements and Shadowheart's sardonic barbs come to life with perfect delivery, further immersing you in the world.Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just a great RPG; it's a landmark achievement. Larian Studios has taken everything that made the Baldur's Gate series great and infused it with their own unique brand of storytelling and world-building. The result is a game that's both nostalgic and innovative, challenging and rewarding.Whether you're a seasoned adventurer or a newcomer to the series, Baldur's Gate 3 has something to offer. With its engaging story, memorable characters, and deep tactical combat, it's a game that will stay with you long after the credits roll. So grab your dice, gather your party, and prepare to embark on an unforgettable adventure. You won't regret it.

Larger studios wariness over the game's success is totally unfounded, because I don't immediately compare this game to all the others and find them lacking, it just makes me want to play more games in this genre.The sheer potential within the world and the combat is staggering, and navigating through the world and being rewarded for craftiness and creativity is refreshing. Very few games actually reward unique gameplay styles and exploration is actually fun and exciting.Uncovering the story and growing with the cast of characters is excellent, and I'm glad that they don't shy away from turbulent themes and the character growth feels unique and realistic.Balance is extremely important in these types of games and I believe it has been struck perfectly in Baldur's Gate 3.If you are on the fence about this game at all, there is no doubt in my mind that you'll enjoy it immensely.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: After a few months, I came back with mods to address some of the gameplay issues I was having, specifically a camera mod and an auto-junk seller for inventory management, and this really helped me overcome some of the hurdles barring my path to fun. I also changed the class I was playing, so the combat didn't feel quite so dull to start. With these changes, I was able to start getting into the story and found Act 1 to be absolutely spectacular. I thought the game's main narrative took a dive in Act 2 and Act 3 was ridiculous (I also took offense to the butchering of some BG2 guest stars, but that's probably WOTC's fault, not Larian's), but the companion stories and certain side quests were among the best of the best. And it was the companions and these side quests that stuck out the most and made me actually like this game. I'll also begrudgingly admit I started to enjoy the combat at about the halfway point. Though I still have some issues here or there and need mods to really be able to enjoy it, I definitely loved my overall experience and so I'm changing my review to recommended!Orignal Review:To be honest, I didn’t think I’d like this game. I’m a huge fan of BG1&2 but I did not enjoy DOS1&2, and I felt like BG3 was going to be another DOS2 with a D&D paint job. But it began to take such a beautiful shape, everyone was praising it so highly, and so many people were saying that if you didn’t like turn-based combat that you still might like this game, so I started to think I might be wrong and that the most disappointing thing about BG3 would be the way I would have to admit to putting my foot in my mouth for how much fun I actually had playing it but...I really did not have fun playing it.There are a ton of tiny issues that bar my path to fun. 1) The camera drives me crazy. It's too close, and having to rotate it constantly, phase through the environment, and struggle with the leash is so frustrating and I haven’t once enjoyed exploring because of it. 2) The number of containers I feel compelled to open to find junk at best, nothing at worst is tedious to the extreme. Looting should be exciting and fun, but in BG3, it's a chore. I stumbled into a vault the other day and groaned because I knew I would have to open every dumb crate, barrel, and vase because gaming for 20 years has trained me to do that, and it would take forever, in part due to the obnoxious pathing issues that cause characters to walk 10 ft back and forth to open a container right next to one they just opened. 3) I have to hold down alt to click on stuff because there’s so much crap and the mouse highlights all of it except the one thing worth clicking on, but then the game doesn’t seem to register more than one click at a time so if you click to pick up one item and then click to pick up another before the character is finished interacting with the first, they just stand there and you have to reissue the order. 4) Because the alt-viewed item labels shift when one thing gets picked up, you often accidentally pick up stuff you don’t want when you’re trying to move through the process quickly, and then you have to dig through your inventory to ditch the unwanted item because inventory clutter is REAL in this game. 5) Selling is annoying. You can quickly mark things as wares, but almost never sell them with the sell all button because the NPCs never seem to have enough money. So you're back to selling or bartering bit by bit. 6) The fact that there's no option to automate some of the tedious dice rolls is just outrageous. The novelty of clicking the dice wore off after the first 10 times, so disarming all the traps becomes a slog. 7) The fact that there's no settings option to hide failed passive rolls is beyond irritating. Quite frankly, I don't want to know when I'm failing something I didn't know existed until I failed it. I could argue it’s unimmersive, but it’s mostly because when I KNOW, my curiosity demands I reload, which is its own nightmare.These issues account for about 70% of the game as I've experienced it so far.The rest is combat. I don't like turn-based combat so I expected I wouldn't enjoy BG3s combat, but everyone was like, "Don’t worry, it feels so good!" No. No, it doesn't. It's as boring and tedious as I've always found it to be. But I feel like I could tolerate it and find some enjoyment in the game if the rest of it wasn't such a frustrating slog. I tell myself to just keep playing and maybe I’ll get past it, but after 45 hours, I’m still aggravated and will often let days go by before I boot it up again. I have to dig deep for the motivation to play, because all I can think about is how I'll spend 2 hours on 15 minutes of gameplay I didn't even enjoy.I won’t comment on the story or characters because I’m too biased by the frustrating gameplay to be fair right now. The voice acting is well done. That’s all I’ll say.Listen, most people love this game, and that's great. I'm not saying it's a bad game. I'm merely saying that I don't have fun playing it. I’m not giving up entirely, but I am going to put it down for now and wait for Larian to finish updating and patching it. Hopefully they will address some of these QoL issues, and then maybe there will be mods that cover the rest so that I can finally play this without feeling like I'm struggling to have fun. And maybe this game will never be a game for me, who knows. I’m clearly on the outside here, so take this review with a grain of salt.
