_childDocuments_.review: The game rarely falters in quality through out its 3 ACTs, perhaps in the final ACT some rough edges can be spotted such as them   , but it's still a spectacular final note in the game's story I'd say, far better than what Divinity Original Sin 2 did with its last act. However, upon replaying it a 2nd time already with an evil run as dark urge, i have notice some more shortcomings with the game's story at times and experienced some more frequent bugs in some scenarios with the most notable being how buggy Minthara is, though it was not enough really to shatter my rather overwhelmingly positive view on this game but enough to point it out and say that they do need to do a fair bit more patching for this game in some areas. My first run that took 150 hours was rather smooth in terms of issues but this 2nd run did show a fair bit more problems.Visually game looks absolutely gorgeous due to fantastic art design,assets and just excellent use of lighting , shadows and colour while the music is beautiful and memorable as hell. Performance wise it was really good in the first two acts but sadly 3rd act starts getting performance problems as you get in the extremely NPC populated city and can require restarting the game after prolonged play to reduce fps and stutter issues that get worse the longer you stay in a session while in ACT3, it was an annoyance for sure and hopefully we'll see it get improved.If you never played any CRPG, this is an excellent way to finally dip into this genre that started re-emerging a couple years ago with Pillars, Pathfinder and Divinity and now with this game, it has exploded into the main stream even , people who never knew about CRPGs or never wanted to touch them are flocking to jump into this, it did what seemed the impossible, make a CRPG that managed to grab the attention of the average shmuck that probably only plays Blizzard games or CoD or CS:GO or something, that is damn right impressive.I cannot wait to drown a further hundred some hours in future solo or co-op runs.Even with some of the technical issues such as bugs and optimisation problems in ACT 3, it wasn't enough really to hinder me loving this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm old enough to have played the isometric RPGs of the 1990's and early 2000's. I like these types of games, and I was quite hyped about something that scratched that itch. However, this aint it. I know I'm in the minority here, but I genuinely think there are parts of the design of this game that are just flawed.The mechanic where abilities have a set number of uses before you have to rest, rather than having a cool down, is something brought over from the tabletop RPG. And it works in a tabletop context because the focus is on doing scenes, you usually don't put that much time into role playing walking from one scene to another. But in a computer game, where you play the uneventful parts as well, it just becomes another resource management chore. I get that they want you to have conversations with the companions in camp, but it feels very contrived and kind of breaks the flow of the game. Having dice rolls determine the outcome of situations is great when done right, like in . But for this to work, the result of failure has to be interesting in some way – it has to lead to character development, or progress the story in another direction than the one you expected. In a tabletop RPG, this is what a good GM does since save scumming isn't an option. But in BG3, failure mostly just leads to getting stuck or having to fight lots of enemies. Not once have I encountered a situation where a failure led to something interesting, funny, or story progressing. The companions suck for the most part. They're all rather one-note, and half of them are just grumpy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don't care about any of these characters, I have zero investment in them. Overall, the writing is pretty weak. The setup is rather rote and heavy handed, there's no sense of intrigue or mystery here. Why even have the big fight playing out in a cut scene, why not just have my character wake up in a broken pod with memory loss and then having to puzzle together what has happened (kind of like in )? The quests mostly boil down to "kill this guy", at times using persuasion or stealth to kill them without having to fight quite as many minions. In act one, you have a situation where there are three leaders you have to get rid of. There is no way to play them out against each other, no way to poison them, no way to convince them their cause is doomed, no way to turn their underlings against them by framing them for something bad… In the end, you more or less have to fight and kill every minion in that location. And it's simply not interesting. As far as I can tell, my character has zero friends and zero attachments to the rest of the world – there are no old friends, they haven't been to any places before, they didn't have a job or a family or anything really before they ended up on that ship. Your only motivation is to get the parasite out of your brain, but because we haven't really seen anyone turn into a mind flayer it doesn't really feel like a pressing issue. The whole ilithid powers thing could have been interesting had they done something like what  does, where giving in to the urges will make the game easier but also makes you lose more and more of your humanity. But there's none of that here, it's just a random super power that your character has because plot.

_childDocuments_.review: I have spent 20+ hours in early access and then 200+ hours on release. It is a good game. Not a great game as there are some choices and mechanics I do not personally like but it is still a good game. In the end I was in it for the story, though, I think I would struggle with a second play through. I played a solo game with a custom character. I tried to play the same character I had done in previous Baldur's Gate. A high elf sorcerer with Dragon Heritage. It fit but a lot of the character mechanics I loved in previous titles were not there. That's not to say the game isn't fun. I was. I enjoyed but I just don't see myself putting another 200+ hours into a second play through. Speaking with friends, they have similar experiences, meaning the game doesn't offer a great change of variety in the story. I managed to gather 9 of 10 companions and complete their stories to the best of my ability. I would give this game a 9/10 score for gameplay, story and overall experience. Think of it in value. You go to the cinema and pay £20 for a 3 hour experience worth of content. You spend £50 on this game and you have close to 200 hours of content. Its full of value that said I don't think these enough content for a second play through. I chose what I consider after playing the selfless good path, despite my choices to be a ♥♥♥♥ 90% of the time. Yet I was still the hero, regardless of my methods and less than heroic actions (murdering an entire village), everyone still liked me and the genocide ignored. I considered playing a more evil character, killing companions and the like but after reading up on it, I don't see the point. The companions and related stories are part of the content, killing them off is robbing yourself of the game.  So, overall this game is worth your time but I don't see any re-playability unless your some sort of completionist achievement seeker or are playing for a muck around with friends. [Spoilers ahead]One of the highlights of the game was at the end. All the allies and people I have helped during my goody play through granted me a number of NPCs at the end. I was a little choked up seeing those I have helped and wonder if I hadn't off helped them, who would have turned up. It made the end very fun, very simple and entertaining as I could call upon dozens of NPCs to join my in battle and it was glorious. There's nothing like an Angel and a Devil fighting side by side or the City Watch fighting alongside criminal thugs. It was like a proper DnD Session with dozens of characters taking their turn as I waited for my characters to take their turns. Pretty epic and a strong sense of achievement as the efforts you made in game pay off. I don't know if everyone had the same experience as I am pretty sure they would have had the same ending fighting the bad guys on the Elder Brain.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid story line, great mechanics, lovable characters, and meaningful choices. It took me 130 hours to complete my first play through doing pretty much everything I could get my grubby little hands on, and I know I still missed so much. If you buy a game for sheer volume of content, then this game has you covered. If you buy a game for a good story and characters, the ending bits with certain characters had me crying. If you want to support a studio that legitimately cares for its creators and its games, then this is a game made by an amazing studio that deserves your support. Worth every penny, and every hour. 9001/10 would recommend again.

_childDocuments_.review: Role-playing in an RPG? I loved DOS2, but BG3 is next level. Just enough of a deviation from D&D 5e to make a great video game. The fights are turn-based. Depending on the difficulty level, it takes a bit of strategy. The team at Larian have done an amazing job of making sure that you can approach an encounter how you want. Even on Explorer Difficulty (easy) you're going to have fun just taking different paths with your character. If you want to play on Tactician Mode and scum save or cheese fights, go for it. It's your game. Play it how you want. (Drop in couch co-op is also very welcome.)

_childDocuments_.review: Honest review: Game goes down hill after Act 1.Finished two runs of the game so far, but it feels like the quality of the characters and writing falls flat in act 3. Act 2 is already a lot less substantial than Act 1 was, but 3 just feels unfinished.The character design and writing feels like the strongest and most interesting part of the game, with combat also being very dynamic and well put together. With this, Act 1 was full of interesting dialogue and choices for even minor interactions with non-essential characters. Act 2 has some awesome high points and some incredible moments. Act 3 has neither of these strengths and I felt almost badgered by a few specific NPCs.Heavy Act 3 spoiler, do not click this if you haven't finished the game, you have been warned:There are a lot of good parts of the game and a tremendous amount of detail put into small and often overlooked parts of the game, but I still think the aspect of the game that carries it the most is the story and the writing. For that to fall apart in Act 3 has left me with mixed feelings about the game overall.Act 1 is a 9.5 / 10.Act 2 is a 9 / 10.Act 3 is 6.5 / 10.Hopefully either more content updates or DLC will expand upon Act 3, but ultimately the game still feels like it was released 3 to 6 months too soon.Also, I've avoided mentioning the plethora of bugged quests or interactions that are most prevalent in Act 3. There were 2 broken interactions we encountered in Act 1/2, but in Act 3 we had countless. Even as far as a quest that "completed" after we accepted it, giving us the reward and completing it in the journal but the quest giver continued to give us dialogue as if we only just accepted the quest and the actionable objectives were removed from our world.Bugs both can and are being fixed. In a game this size, I think it's reasonable to assume there would be bugs. Poor narrative and writing in Act 3 is substantially more time consuming issue and I'm not sure it will improve anytime soon.Overall, the game is a 8.5/10. It gives the same vibes as a great TV series that runs out of gas in season 5 or 6.

_childDocuments_.review: as someone that has been playing dnd for ~3 years now, this is quite literally the best video-game-ification of the 5e rule system. It feels this way in the mechanical sense of the rules and the actual imaginative play of dnd. My personal choices actually feel like they have GENUINE impact on the world. This is reinforced by characters saying "hey you saved these people like 10 quests ago and I still think about the impact of it.", or something like that. As someone that likes to play righteous paladins, being a vengeance paladin sworn to vanquish evil has been SO fun and the class fantasy is almost perfect. Because I am this kind of paladin I get to tell monsters I will have their head and then get to tell actual people I have no issue with them as they are innocent in my eyes. There have even been moments where I had to switch my playstyle juuuust so I don't break my oath.I also build 5e PCs a LOT, and it is sooooo awesome I can translate my real 5e character builds to a video game and play them the same way I play them on tabletop. This game is truly awesome and I know I am at minimum going to play 5 playthroughs lol. Can not recommend enough

_childDocuments_.review: Finally finished my single player campaign and it took about 99 hours on record. But its more realistically at 110-115 with the retries. The rest of the time is a bunch of other campaigns started with friends. My only gripe is that cutscenes won't load the assets in time, so the cutscene would be playing even though there are floating items around and empty scenery. But its a minor thing that I would expect to be fixed in the next coming months. The story is amazing. The choices actually matter. The ending is epic. Every single character has a crazy amount of work into them. I really loved every single second of it. The Balanced difficulty is a good challenge but lenient enough to be satisfying. I definitely want to replay it, probably as the Dark Urge.Just in love with this game. I thought TOTK would be the obvious game of the year, but I think this takes the cake.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review:I am both a D&D players since 3rd edition, and currently a DM in 5e, also a veteran player of classic rpg on computer (Planescape, BG1/2, NWN, Kotor, DoA etc etc). All I can say is that this is a worthy succesor to BG1/2. For 60 euro I have gotten 150+ hours of entertainment. I've done a full singleplayer good bard playthrough (where I could roleplay my way out of most combat encounters with some insanely good and sometimes very funny writing). Now I am running an evil multiplayer campaign as dark urge together with my younger brother, and it's like a completely different game, that would have been worth paying 60 euro again for another 100 hours of excellence. As a DM I can say, this is as close you will get to the "true" D&D experience in a virtual enviroment with the computer as DM. 10/10.What can change the nature of a man? A great game like this might!Played for 2.5 hours. Old BG1 and 2 veteran. This feels like Baldurs Gate, and I am very pleasently suprised. A lot of haters here, who are whining about everything, but from my play experience, and since its day 1 of EA, meaning the game is a full year from full release, this is amazing. Truly amazing. I've already had some really great combat, and great role playing experiences. I've waited 20 years for this, and looks like Larian won't let me down.

_childDocuments_.review: I never do reviews but after near 200 hours I must say I am just absolutely impressed with this game.  While it is in Early Access Larian Studios in my opinion have obtained a near perfect balance.  BG3 holds great meaningful story telling with excellent immersion and clear evidence time and again that your decisions, actions and lack there of really impact the characters and the world around you.  This is not just for a few key decisions that act as goal posts but for me feels reinforced again and again and I still haven't really unlocked all the stories/depth to the core companions yet.  After two full plays through the content and at least a half dozen restarts across differing races and classes I am still amazed to find a mix of new in game cutscenes, dialogue and ways to do things as I watch how the game remains flexible when I attempt a unique path that's really out of left field so to speak.  Game play for combat is simple enough but holds complexity and creativity across classes with fairly good balance and it really feels like DND5e.  A little more creativity at character creation would be great and I can't wait for full release and can't wait to see what the modding community does when its fully unleashed.  The narrative is engaging (creating a sense of urgency) I do really hope at some point the world opens up sandbox style and lets you come and go as you please.  Its clear the system will allow for future scenarios as DLC but if Larian Studios are smart enough to release some kind of creator/editor that will allow people to create their own 'space/home' or dare I say dnd/adventure 'stories' to share with their friends it will totally be played Skyrim-style for well in excess of 10-15 years acting as an open sandbox platform with high quality graphics, good gameplay, unrestricted immersive exploration and unmatched creativity.  In my opinion that would effectively become DND5e online giving it endless replayability.  Even if none of that action is taken I do believe the game will still go down as one of the greatest RPGs ever.  The only thing bugging me is the limited ability to edit/impact the camera angle.  Totally get 'top down' is the Baldurs Gate way, but you just need that 20% more rotation at times to really feel 'in' the gameworld rather than trying to peer though the top of my monitor.  Well done Larian Studios!

_childDocuments_.review: This is One of if not the greatest game that has come out as of these last few years.The story is great jam packed with choices that actually matter and affect the world around you.The characters are stellar, the sole ammount of work that went into making so many dialogue options, that are completely unique, and fun, The character specific quests are a awesome way to get to know your favourite characters better and help them overcome their problems.The voice acting is also perfectly on point, you can really feel what the characters are feeling at a set moment.The combat is great, the possibilities of going about encounters are as limited as is human creativity, in most cases if you want to try something, you can probably do it.Graphics are also great, the visual effects are awesome.In my time of playing so far, I have not encountered any glitches, like really, any glitches, which is obviously good and shows that a Giant game can release without crashing/glitching out of control. _childDocuments_.review: What's left to say, it feels like there hasn't been as much of a buzz about a fantasy RPG since Skyrim and to some extent the Witcher 3, though this game is better than both. I didn't look at or played act 1 in early access, so had no expectations beyond the game probably being like Original Sin 2, except in a DnD coat, and hopefully with better writing since that has been a bit of a Larian weak point. Yet every hour of (co-op) Baldurs Gate 3 we played, we realised more and more this is something much bigger than the Original Sin games are, even if they are great games in their own right.Larian has taken the best of old Bioware here, crafting great stories and characters with interesting backgrounds and plot developments during the game. This is wrapped up in a gorgeous coat and presented in a cinematic way, like Bioware did in their Dragon Age games. The game feels like the closest successor to Dragon Age: Origins in these regards, one of my favourite games, especially considering it doesn't waste any of your time with mindless bloat quests or open world emptiness. Every house and street you can access is there for some purpose, to draw you into a quest or story, or to be the background for cool battles, cutscenes, or shops. The incredible variety of characters both with you and against you are wonderfully realised and superbly voice acted, and everybody will be able to pick out their own cast of favourites. The gameplay is as close to DnD as a game has been able to come. The spells are vividly transported to video game form, and you have seemingly a hundred ways to deal with any given encounter, be it talking your way out of it, or getting into the fantastic combat system that will keep the game very replayable. There are so many builds to try, so many stories to see different outcomes of, and so many ways to replay encounters in completely different ways. The fact that i just spent 130 hours getting through our first run and wanting to dive right back in for another go, should give you enough info on how much i enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel... Electrified. HYPED as in 2011 when TES: Skyrim was about to launch. Or when I first opened and played Kingdom Come: Deliverance, discovering how astonishing it actually was despite initial bugs and mixed reviews...Baldur's Gate 3 is, in my view, another "gaming messiah" that will mark our minds, hearts and souls forever. The developers have done a truly wonderful job with the characters, humor, the atmosphere of the plot(s), the thrill of adveture that awaits you... and the soundtrack (gods, that soundtrack!). I have never felt the need to stay in the character creation screen purely because of music :) Well done, Mr. Slavov, well played.All in all, it's like the old Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Icewind Dale or the Temple of Elemental Evil games, but at the same time - it feels fresh. A new home for the tired wanderers seeking that ultimate RPG once again.It also needs to be highlighted that the producers have provided us with an uncensored game in an old-school fashion - something very rare these days, when violence and gore are fine, but the most common and natural thing in the world that we face every single day of our lives - the very image of the human body - is not.All in all - this is exactly how games used to be made in the days of old and it serves as a proof that such productions are still relevant and can be appreciated today. Here's hoping we'll get more of them in the future.Larian Studios - I thank you so very much and am looking forward to playing your other games, both past and upcoming.

_childDocuments_.review: Mall Brawl is a really fun, true to its roots beat 'em up with great reverence for the View Askewniverse. It completely nailed the feel of an NES beat 'em up while never feeling unfair, and was very satisfying to learn the simple combat system and how to fight each new enemy type. We were also surprised by the great soundtrack. Definitely comes highly recommended for Kevin Smith fans, though it may be a little too basic (and maybe a smidge too expensive) for fans only of the beat 'em up genre, despite how high quality it is.Minor complaints:- It's kind of disappointing that weapons disappear after each encounter.- I wish there were another use for the stars. AFAIK it's currently just an alternate combo finisher, would be cool if you could hold the attack button to pull the finisher out early since it's hard to get a full combo in on some bosses.- The _ knocker boss fights are annoying. Wait, attack, run around, rinse and repeat.- If you die on Chapter 9, you get taken back to Chapter 8. _childDocuments_.review: Jay and Silent Bob: Mall Brawl is a side-scrolling beat 'em up that would have been well at home in the 1980s. Mall Brawl is a solid, if not quite spectacular, Double Dragon clone, with detailed 8-bit graphics, a decent variety of bosses and opponents, and nine levels of outrageous punches. Reckless women with baby strollers, and even a poop monster are there for you to defeat. You read that correctly: a "♥♥♥♥" monster. Mall Brawl features the duo's trademark potty humor.While enemies are essentially cut and pasted with different color ensembles or costumes, boss fights are where Mall Brawl shines. Each boss battle is unique and memorable. You'll face a crazed man riding a unicorn, a brawl on a gigantic air hockey table, a Mega Man-inspired duel, and even a poop monster hidden in the mall's restrooms. Boss fights are both tough and enjoyable, especially since you know you'll have to retry the entire level if you fail.In Mall Brawl, you only have one life, but you can control both Jay and Silent Bob (or one of them if you play in co-op), who each have their own health meter. While playing alone, you can freely swap between the two. While you are actively playing, the character that is not being used will gradually replenish their health - but be advised, you cannot stand still and expect health to regenerate. You must be actively progressing or fighting. This strategy, possibly the finest way to play Mall Brawl, requires players to stay active and switch between characters frequently.When playing co-op, each player controls one of the characters, each with their own health meter that does not refill on its own. However, if one player dies and the other survives long enough, the other character will gradually restore their health and allow them to rejoin the game once their health meter is around half full. It adds a good level of tension to survival when you're up against a boss or numerous enemies and running low on health.The only downside: While I appreciate a good challenge, I believe Mall Brawl lands on the side of difficulty and more in the playable but too stressful to be pleasant pile. This is due to the long stages, only having one life, no difficulty options, being forced to restart from the beginning of the level upon death, aggressive adversaries with unusually big health reserves, wacky controls (Turning while attacking / spamming is not possible), and just too much being thrown at you, especially towards the finish. Casual players beware, but everyone else can buy this without any hestitation!

_childDocuments_.review: Jay and Silent Bob: Mall Brawl was conceived as a free digital bonus game for backers who wanted to pre-order the Deluxe Edition of , a game that still hasn't released since it was funded in 2016.A limited physical NES Game Pak was made available through Limited Run Games and is playable on the original NES as well as other compatible clone systems. Afterwards it was also released digitally on current platforms.As a physical NES Game Pak it may have made a nice novelty for hardcore fans, but the actual product is not worth playing. The game is really bland and subpar. Don't bother. Character movement is slow, combat is clunky, shallow and unsatisfying, enemies have way too much health, and there's no variety in anything. Even the stages are basically pointless with no interaction or even anything interesting to look at.There's a decent attempt at some borders and a CRT filter. You can remap the controls, but there doesn't seem to be any actual native support for various controllers. The default controls aren't intuitive. Game has Steam Cloud and Achievements.Even if you like retro games or have a buddy you want to play with, this game is outrageous in its full asking price of $15. You could get the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle games instead that are a lot more fun. The Cowabunga Collection and Shredder's Revenge are both on Steam. Even with the price being higher and some questionable rights issues, the choice is a no-brainer.I don't have much experience with Kevin Smith or his films outside of the original Clerks, but I don't see anything in this that screams that a fan of his work would enjoy this. If you changed out the characters, no one would know this was connected to Jay and Silent Bob.

_childDocuments_.review: Jay and Silent Bob: Mall Brawl is a 2D retro pixel console ported arcade brawler, like Golden Axe or Double Dragon, only not as good.  The only single selling point for the game is the licensed characters from Kevin Smith's View Askew film universe.  Gameplay, like all of these kinds of games, involves very simplistic arcade brawling with a limited number of moves.  The game is also relatively short as you recreate Jay and Silent Bob's escapades against mall security depicted far better in the film, Mallrats. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.PC gamers will be insulted by the presence of console peasant children's toy controller prompts, despite this being on PC.  Developers should try to be aware which platform they're developing for.Because this is a console game, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.SteamDB shows the game only ever peaked at 21 players concurrently, just once, close to launch.  This might be okay for indie shovelware, but this is a licensed product from a multimillion dollar film franchise... that's a completely pathetic outcome. Jay and Silent Bob: Mall Brawl has the preposterous price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games, let alone the sheer number of free games available on Steam.  The pricing here compared to the woeful quality of this sloppy console port is completely disproportional, as the game relies solely on the license from View Askew for sales.  Jay and Silent Bob can't make this crap game any better, but this game certainly has made the View Askew franchise worse.

Jay and Silent Bob Mall Brawl, an all new side-scrolling brawler set in the world famous and beloved View Askewniverse, is now available as a fully functional cartridge compatible with the original NES. This cartridge is a full game playable by either one or two players! There are three color variants available - Silent Bob Green, Jay Yellow, and NES Grey.

Each copy of Jay and Silent Bob Mall Brawl comes in a retro box that has been painstakingly crafted to be as authentic as possible. The box is printed on the same material as original retro boxes and matches the same flap design at the top. The metallic gold ink on the "Limited Run" seal has also been matched to the original seal's ink.

Included in the box is a retro manual, dust sleeve, and of course, a styrofoam block to hold the cartridge up inside the box. Each copy of the game will arrive shrinkwrapped.

The game itself was programmed by Tomas Guinan from Spoony Bard Productions.

This game is region free!

Corruption & Regrowth: Eradicate the gunk, restore nature, and transform the world around you. Employ the revived plant life to delve deeper into this strange and wondrous ecosystem. Intimate Narrative: The narrative is intrinsically linked with the exploration, where our two main characters keep in tight radio contact throughout the game. Fiona Nova lends her voice in a stellar performance as main character Rani. Music & Atmosphere: The Gunk invites you to take the time and listen to its soothing tunes. An explorative atmosphere conveyed through an evocative art style. Kick your feet back and enjoy an adventure like no other!

_childDocuments_.review: A duo of space-faring adventurers, Rani and her friend Tara (?) (forgot her name already, that’s how unremarkable she was…), happened upon a seemingly untouched planet, ripe for exploration and all kinds of novel discoveries. Soon enough Rani, in charge of on–site operations, finds out about a strange substance quickly dubbed The Gunk, which seems to be siphoning energy from the planet’s ecosystem. With a half-wrecked ship in need of repairs and a mystery to solve, the duo, alongside the ship’s robotic cook, delves deeper into a planet that may not be so uninhabited… after all.Despite verdant landscapes that contrast well with the poisoned, gray-scaled areas infested by the Gunk and competent art direction, this title falls flat on both narrative and character development. On one side you have a run-of-the-mill, stereotyped sci-fi trope recycled a million times before, one the other a main duo that never really stands out for neither personality nor charisma. The other characters found along the adventure are sideshows at best, even more unremarkable, with forgettable and uninspired dialogues. The story events, despite involving planet-wide consequences, never feel grandiose or epic at any point due to boring narration - it does the job, but nothing more than that.Even if it’s a game that tries hard on story focus, that proves to be one of its weakest components: so much more could’ve been accomplished with the setting at hand.Playing as Rani, you’ll be tasked with exploring the planet to find out more about The Gunk’s origin, while also studying the ecology and properties of various locations. Mainly, you’ll be going through platforming sections that feature fixed or moving obstacles, simple jumping puzzles and of course, Gunk infestations that need clearing out, harmful to the touch and sometimes featuring hostile creatures (more on that later). For that purpose the Vacuum Glove is paramount, enabling you to absorb the foul substance, restoring each self-contained area’s ecology once all of the waste is gone. This enables plants to regrow, unlocking both resources to acquire, that translate into upgrades for your hardware using the ship’s workbench, and research material that is used to unlock the upgrades themselves; the more new stuff you scan, the more craftable modules you’ll unlock. These range from utilities such as better vacuum range, to all-new tools like the Decoy used to distract enemies, or various upgrades to make your life easier in combat.While each area contains some small side-areas with extra crafting materials or the odd “out of the beaten path” research article, the game’s level design is largely linear, subdivided in zones you can return to at any time via a convenient fast-travel system unlocked not too far into the story. There are no major secrets, side areas, worthwhile backtracking or anything else to discover: exploration proves limited in scope. From time to time you’ll be able to return to the ship, and engage in brief dialogues with the NPCs present there, that however provide nothing more than listless exchanges.The main issue of the general gameplay loop, is that it never really evolves significantly from start to end: some variations happen and are welcome, however they never feel critical turning points. Also in this case, The Gunk feels unambitious, premature, not elaborated enough upon.The Gunk itself is an enemy on its own, at first stationary, then floating around and even actively trying to inglobate Rani and kill her. In addition, the mysterious phlegm also generates creatures hostile to you, ranging from small but still dangerous spawns, to massive, charging hulks that require a bit more strategy to defeat. Also here, the glove will be your primary weapon, enabling you to throw enemies into one another, eradicate fixed turrets and use environmental opportunities like explosive melons (yep, that’s a thing) to obliterate foes. Enemy variety proves rather low, with just three foes, in addition to the Gunk itself, throughout the game - exceptions made for the final boss. Generally combat difficulty is on the lower side, same goes for exploration mishaps: death is inconsequential, respawning Rani near where she fell or at worst, at a close checkpoint from either a manual or auto-save. Later on the Glove may be upgraded with more tools like a distracting Decoy or a lethal plasma cannon that stuns and kills, however these don’t really feel needed: you’re already powerful enough as it is, nevermind with most upgrades done. Those seeking even a moderate amount of challenge won’t find it in this game.Mostly entail using environmental elements to unlock pathways. For instance, seeds can be thrown in special “energy pools” to make plants grow, then acting as platforms, or explosive plants thrown onto debris to clear a path. Some machinery like elevators, rotating platforms and energy conduits will also be present later on, but generally nothing complex, following an “activate once or twice” pattern at most. Even if you’re new to puzzles, you'll find the proposed enigmas simple enough - challenge and this game aren’t concepts that go along.

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Great visuals and lush vegetation✅Music➖Dialog can get annoying➖Fairly predictable Game World: Gunk takes place on an alien planet in the seemingly nearish future. No specific times have been mentioned, but it's fair to say within the next ~100 years. On this planet you encounter a type of goo that inhibits natural growth. As you clear the goo out, vegetation springs to life and fills the bland world with lush greenery. I found the game world to be a great positive. The levels were designed in a way that I never questioned where to go. Furthermore, it was satisfying to clean up gunk and watch the world come to life. Narrative: The narrative is pretty simple. You play as Rani, a spunky mechanic and half of the duo of the Dust Bunny ship which consists of Becks. There’s also a robot named Curt who’s kinda like Hodor, mostly useless. The trio are broke and down on their luck, they stumble upon this planet with the hopes of making some money but find out there is something deeper going on. I felt the narrative was just okay. It could almost be a Saturday morning cartoon. Perhaps that is too harsh, but really, the writing is incredibly straightforward, just like the game world. There is a clear enemy and a clear goal. Length: I finished the game in about 4.5 hours. Controls: Good. Normally I play platformers with a controller, but the aiming made me first try with the KBM and I stuck with it the whole time. There’s really only 4ish keys aside from movement, so again, simple. Mechanics: There is one major mechanic of the game and that is your vacuum. You embody Luigi from his mansion in that you have a hundred questions and only a single answer for them all - suck harder. There are some smaller mechanics like lures and puzzle mechanics like explosive orbs, but generally, you’ll be sucking 90% of the game. Difficulty: Easy. I don’t believe I died once. Quality: Good. Game looks good. I like the way the environments look - vegetation, distance, everything is good. UI: Minimal. There is nothing to display, not even health. Performance: I ran into only a single part of the game that had obvious performance issues on an elevator near the end, but other than that, game ran flawless at 60 fps on my desktopi9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDI did run into multiple bugs, including one nearly game-braking where I was stuck in an environment. Another was an elevator that was invisible. Thankfully, the Gunk saves often enough to where none of these were a big issue. Sound Effects: good. Voice acting is of good quality, but the writing was a bit annoying. I was really starting to get annoyed by Becks who was acting like a mother asking if I was safe every 5 minutes. Music: Again, good. Nothing I will remember, but it was very pleasing in the time and set the tone of the game well. Only achievements, that's it. I generally don’t like platformers, so I was surprised at the start when I was really enjoying this. The Gunk does nothing great or even amazing, but everything it does is done well. Except for the name. I hate that. Call it something like “Space Lesbians Clean Up Coronavirus”, I don’t know, anything but GUNK.  but $24 is way too much for this short of a game with no replay value. Get it on sale or in a bundle. Pretty sure I got it off Humble or Fanatical bundle. You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game by any stretch but it's quite basic.From previous reviews I can see people have been comparing this to Journey to the savage planet. However, this really isn't true. They may share a similar theme but the gameplay is quite different. This is a simple, on rails platformer with mild puzzle elements.The animations and some of the models are not the best. Strangely, the main character is poorly animated in cutscenes and their model looks like an unfinished playdough figure with sausage fingers and stick legs (I honestly thought she had prosthetic limbs for half the game). The puzzles are rather simple and basic. I can't say there was any real complexity till possibly the end level. A lot of the puzzles just end up being; suck up the gunk and put the plant that springs up in the green puddle to get up that step you can't reach. Combat, can't really say it exists. What few combat encounters exist are nothing more than a minor inconvenience. There are 3 enemies. Little critters that you just punt away, stationary plants that shoot fireballs at you but they serve more as a puzzle element than an enemy to be honest (you just navigate around them till you can reach and kill them to continue the level) and what i think was meant to be a mini boss (you're meant to lead it into rocks to stun it then attack its back. I literally just stood by a rock and it repeatedly headbutt the rock stunning it.Platforming. Very basic, move and jump. Sometimes there's spinning platforms. The game very much railroads you as you can only jump very slightly. You can also only really jump in pre-designated spots (yellow markers). you'll come across a step for instance and despite it being perfectly level, you can only jump on the yellow section. You can also only stand on designated platform plants. while other things may look like you could land on them, you'll clip right through.Exploration. You can scan some stuff but a majority of things you can't. The only point to scanning is to progress your upgrades.  Not really any secret areas, every now and then there will be a slight fork in the path that immediately ends, that's your secret. There's no collectables or things like that in this game. You gather 4 resources from plants and rocks. Upgrades require you scanning things to slowly unlock them in a linear progression and then use the resources to buy them. There are 6 teleport points in the game. You can only upgrade your tool at the base camp. There's no reason really at all to ever back track. You don't unlock new tools that let you open new areas or find new secrets. This makes having to travel to basecamp every time you want to upgrade just an annoyance. Honestly the upgrades are just minor quality of life upgrades and you really don't need them. The upgrades that make you go faster are probably all you'll use. I'd like to say the combat upgrades are useful but combat is small, rare and over quickly. I 100% complete the game in 4 hours. That's with no back tracking. When I thought I'd finally made it to mid game, it turned out I was more or less at the end. Story is a cool concept but not really fleshed out. I get the strong feeling more was planned but the devs ran out of time or money and rushed this game out. After rescuing a guy he mentions a north, east, south and west tower but you then just proceed right to the end game location.While this may look like an adventure, open world exploration game where you collect resources and find upgrades to help you progress, it is not. It is a simple platformer with simple puzzles that you can finish in a few hours. I can't say it's got combat because it really doesn't exist enough for that.At £20 and the effort it takes to make games these days, you can't really fault the devs on the price vs content. It's not always about play time. That said, I'd recommend you get this game on sale, at least 50% off, if you plan on playing it. It's something you'll likely 100% during casual play, there's no real replayability.  It's a big step up for the developer whose previous games have been essentially old flash games. You can see a lot of effort went into this. Unfortunately at the end of the day, the game just falls a little bit flat. If you removed the language that occasionally happens, it could be a nice game to introduce younger gamers to the world of platforming.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 5/10Story: First things first, I love narrative-driven indie games and went into this completely blind, with zero expectations. I think you can find a lot of hidden gems within indie games, but this is unfortunately not the case here. The Gunk is a story-driven puzzle/platformer game where you control a space scavenger named Rani who has arrived on an alien planet with her partner Becks in search of valuable resources. The planet is full of various biomes such as canyons, jungles and caves, but the terrains have been corrupted by a black/pink-ish goop called 'the Gunk', which is actively draining the environment's color, energy, and general life. Through the story, you are equipped with a power glove that can be used to suck up the gunk and effectively restore the original environment. This is basically the goal of the game: clear out all the Gunk and figure out what happened on this strange planet. Unfortunately, the narrative being told is simply not that good. The story felt predictable and simplistic, following a standard sci-fi adventure template without much depth or surprising twists. While the voice acting is above average (I'd certainly say good, not great), the characters also felt extremely underdeveloped, which made it difficult to really feel for them or see significant growth. Additionally, the game just tip-toed around various deeper themes such as environmentalism, isolation and connection, etc. instead of exploring them or expanding on its world-building, which lead to a feeling of unfulfilled potential. I would say that The Gunk could potentially target itself more towards kids, but the mature language within the dialogue makes that a hard sell, leaving it in a kind of limbo where as an adult, it doesn't really do it for you (due to the lack of depth), but it could be deemed too inappropriate for some children.Visuals:Visually, The Gunk is beautiful. All the art style, graphics, and color scheme make the game very pleasant to look at, especially when you clear the Gunk from an area and get to watch the life and vibrant color restore before your eyes. The visuals as well as the music are definitely shining points.Music/Sound Design: Speaking of the music/sound design, they both compliment the world excellently. The soundtrack really gives the world another layer of life through expertly composed soundtracks that convey the calm, mysterious (and intense when needed) vibes that are presented to you. The sound design stands in this corner as well. The noises and sounds you hear are impressively immersive and unique, especially those involving the Gunk, such as when it is moving, being sucked up, or just dropping from the ceiling. these are just a few examples, but the sound design is great from top to bottom.Gameplay:The gameplay, however, is another very weak area, in my opinion. To put it bluntly, it's just not interesting or compelling. It's not a very long game, but the simplicity and repetitive mechanics led to me finding the experience monotonous over time. The lack of challenge, coupled with the game's short length, certainly left me feeling, ironically, overwhelmingly underwhelmed. This is especially true since the story and world building doesn't do enough to captivate you.World:As a setting, the alien planet appears very interesting, and admittedly does retain its charm throughout the story, but this is just visually. As mentioned earlier, the world building overall is on the most basic surface level. The disappointment here is amplified for me personally because I felt like there was so much unfulfilled potential here too, just as there is in the story. The core is there, but it's not fleshed out in a way that feels good to experience.TL;DR:Despite the beautifully unique music, and eccentric and interesting visual design of the characters, environments, and atmosphere, The Gunk Doesn't offer enough in terms of gameplay or narrative experience to stand on its own two feet as a must play experience. I unfortunately can't recommend it, especially not for the price point of $25.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Gunk" is a relatively short (7h for a thorough playthrough), decent puzzle platformer in third-person 3D with a bit of combat thrown in.You play the adventurous half of a two-woman team of space scavengers who are down on their luck. You follow a signal to an apparently uninteresting planet, which turns out to harbor secrets that may change your lives - but they are hidden beneath layers of a malicious substance that you call "the Gunk". As you explore the planet, you clean it from Gunk and discover its tragic history.I found the story interesting and engaging. While it isn't particularly original, the characters are well-designed and their banter at the beginning of the game is very enjoyable. Midway through there is a change in their relationship that might feel sudden and insufficiently explained to some players, but it gets explained in the end (and you can guess the reason fairly easily if you pay attention to the dialog). The story develops in a completely linear way and you do not have any choices.In the beginning, the game gives players the impression that they are exploring an intricate ecosystem - you can scan plants and minerals, and each will get an entry with a short text in your encyclopedia, which is nice. But after two chapters (out of eight) you's seen almost all of the plants and minerals that the game has to offer, and you realize that they all serve only one single purpose: each plant can be harvested once for one of four resources, which you need to upgrade your abilities. This made the setting far less interesting than it could have been.You'll spend most of your time platforming, puzzle-solving, and occasionally fighting. The gunk removal feels a bit like a cleaning sim. There is very little room for exploration as the maps are fairly linear, though thorough investigation of small side areas rewards you with more resources.The platforming is pretty easy. Potential paths are indicated by yellow paint, and your character responds quickly to mid-air direction changes. There are lots of bottomless pits in the game, but if you fall into one, you simply respawn at the last point where you had a safe footing.The puzzles are very simple. Most of the time, you just have to figure out how to remove gunk that you can't immediately reach, how to bring a seed to a planting spot, or where some switches are. There aren't any complex mechanics, you cannot get stuck, and a simple "plant every seed and flick every switch" approach will get you through the entire game.Combat consists mostly of fighting off small critters while removing gunk, though there is one bigger enemy type, as well as a boss fight at the end with several phases and slightly more elaborate mechanics (but it's still very easy).Technically, the game has a crafting mechanic, but you just harvest 4 different resources in order to craft upgrades that aren't very impactful.The graphics look adorable, but I the lighting does them a disservice. I couldn't find a setting where the colors would shine, they looked either washed-out or the scenes got way too dark. Viewing distance is very short for a modern game, everything in the distance is hidden in a white-ish fog. There was also a blurriness that I couldn't get rid off. I think that this game could have looked great with crisp, colorful graphics, but I just didn't manage to get it there.Sound and music get the job done, but I didn't notice anything especially good or bad. The voice-acting for the two main characters is very good, but other characters just talk gibberish and you have to read the subtitles if you actually want to follow the conversation.The game provides a resolution selector, an unspecified upscaling option, a frame cap selection can't go higher than 120 Hz, and a vsync toggle. There are 4 presets for graphics quality, but you can't control any details except for a "motion blur" on/off toggle. Four separate volume sliders let you finetune the acoustic experience. Action keys can be rebound, but the movement keys are fixed to WASD, which makes that feature almost worthless. Arrow keys can't be used for movement either, they control the camera.There is a camera sensitivity slider as well as separate inversion toggles for both axes, you can also switch between manual o automatic camera control. Aim mode can be set to "toggle" or "hold" and/or "automatic". There is no FOV slider.You can change the subtitle size, color, and background (or switch them off completely), but you can't set them to a different language than the audio. Other accessibility settings do not exist. Colorblind players may run into minor problems as the game uses red/green coding in some parts of the UI, but it should be manageable. Deaf players should be fine.You can manually save at any point and I didn't notice a limit to the number of save files. The game also autosaves frequently. I didn't run into any bugs - a few times a though I might be stuck in the geometry, but I could always wiggle free.Generally, the user experience feels a bit half-baked. While some features can be controlled to good detail, others are sorely lacking.I mostly enjoyed my time with "The Gunk", though I did get a bit bored on the way and only finished it because I was already almost at the end of the story. I feel that I can still recommend it to fans of 3D platformers and casual gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of negative reviews about the game being too short.  The game being a  walking sim.  (From people who don't know a platform puzzler when they see one).  The characters being ugly, etc, etc...I loved it.  I'm still not through because I'm not a great lateral thinker especially at my advanced age.  It is one of the most enjoyable games I've played for a long time.  Why?1. The graphics are wonderful and immersive. 2.  I can use a controller or my trusty keyboard and both work well.3.  Gunk may  not be the shortest game I've played; but for me it is the most engaging game I've played in a while, 4. The characters have their own charm.  The characters are regular human beings.  I like that.  They aren't good looking, they aren't endowed with super abilities, and the  art style used to portray them is cute.  5. The  controls are simple and I don't have to be a gaming god to play it.6. Movement is intuitive and smooth and the puzzles while not challenging for some are a nice middle ground for me.  I do NOT like being overly frustrated by games.7. Games are meant to be fun, and this game for me, is FUN!Remember, it's not the amount of game you get, it's the amount of enjoyment you get out of playing that counts. Hard games and long games aren't the be all and end all of life:  I'm pretty sure there are more average players out there than gaming aces, so don't let reviews that say it's not worth the money put you off. _childDocuments_.review: I happened across this game by accident while scrolling through the upcoming releases. It immediately piqued my interest because the production value looked pretty high. I thought it was fun, engaging and the story was decent - a well done hero's journey. I was surprised by the good level designs. It seemed to have just enough challenge to be fun and interesting without leaving you bored or over challenged. Some things I noticed;- the attention to detail was really impressive. The interior of the ship was so incredibly well done it is really a shame that you don't get to do more in there. The calendar, t-shirts, posters, it looked lived in. - I enjoyed the characters who seemed believable if not just a little stiff with the dialog sometimes but over all really good. - I thought the character design was excellent and very detailed. - You got served! Things I wish they would have done;- I wish you could scan more items even though it would have been all flavor text. it would have made exploration more enjoyable. Since there were only some things you could scan you quickly figured that out and kind of just ran along without bothering to explore much. - More area's for exploration and discovery - I can see how too much of this might have resulted in players getting lost but - I'm an explorer so it's what I'm looking for. - It would have been nice to have more fauna even if you didn't get to interact with them. - I don't know if I found all the upgrades but - I wish there were more. - Too short? I hate to sound cliche as I do see this complaint often but I only say it because I enjoyed the world I was exploring and wish there was a bit more to discover even if it was meaningless to the overall story.- Just for fun I lowered all the graphics settings to minimum and it looks almost pixelated. Might have been a missed opportunity to toss in a retro pixel filter just for fun.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like someone played Luigi's Mansion and was really upset when they realized they couldn't vacuum all the dust!I was really surprised by this game! It wasn't the best game l've ever played, but it had beautiful environments, satisfying gameplay, and good pacing. It’s one of those games that’s perfect for when you aren't trying to play something too serious, and just wanna kick back and have a good time. Game gets a bad rep since the characters aren’t “straight“ sexually and apparently per the sheep, that goes along with the “woke” culture, whatever the hell that means.There is something extremely cathartic and satisfying about cleaning up the gunk and once you get it all in an area, the color comes back and plants regrow in front of your eyes. I really liked this game. It’s nice and relaxing, lovely tinkly music with a gameplay mechanism like a lot of the "work simulator" games like House Flipper etc. Coming into this directly after Halo Infinite, and competitive racing on FH5, it's a lovely, quaint game. For those who expect a challenge from this game, it would definitely be a huge disappointment. It’s more of a relaxed game with almost nothing except exploring and enjoying the colorful world unfold from cleaning out the gunk. I personally liked it as I play it to relax from other violent games I play. Doom eternal, I’m talking about you.It offers a solid game with beautiful graphics and a simple gameplay with a duration ideal for a Saturday evening, it's not a hard game at all which makes it ideal for kids too. it also gives a simple exploration experience which is somewhat optional. This isnt a combat driven game, so don't expect major fights or action, and it has maybe 2-3 instances of tension, but the rest is a really chill experience. It's not GOTY, but a lovable game to spend an evening.This game has a lot of potential for a more complex, longer sequel. The core of the game is fantastic. Intuitive controls, beautiful art style, and interesting landscapes. It’s simple. But there’s nothing wrong with a fun simple game every now and then.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: With over 4000 space games on Steam, we sure get to see the farthest-flung corners of the galaxy as travelers and assh*les: invading, conquering, and harvesting planets of resources. , however, takes a more humane approach, the kind that we get to leave the place in a better state than when we arrived.At the heart of  is a neat eco-friendly fable, so it has a sort of moral and ethical sweetness from the off. Crucially, though, it is also a game about tidying up, so that moral and ethical sweetness is knotted to something else that borders on compulsion. Maybe gamifying burdensome housework is enough, or perhaps it boils down to the fact that these games can make you feel productive even when you're procrastinating. Either way, this one is about reveling in the satisfaction of suction, even though it isn't working on high Watts.As broke and fractious space scavengers, Rani and her (more than just business?) partner, Becks, stumble upon an alien planet in search of their fortune, on the trail of a mysterious signal pointing to a potential energy source. What they find instead is a planet where the life around them is being strangled by dark blobs of some zero-G snot. A combination of determination and desperation leads them to uncover the face of this rock off its mysterious goopy veil. Luckily, Rani comes equipped with a bionic vacuum arm and an infinity of space to hoover up all that mess.It sounds fairly interesting but moving past the first hour, the narrative features a bit too many overused story beats and clichés to be considered engaging, let alone original. It's the type of story that begins to dissipate from memory the moment you walk away from your PC. Having two strong-willed women trying to "make it" in the space and pushing back against each other is welcome, but I was bothered to no end by the game's refusal to define their relationship. Was Becks a prudent and pragmatic friend, an over-protective mother figure, or a  concerned and caring lover? It is left to your imagination, unfortunately. The vocal performance goes a long way to make the duo likable, but disconnected backstories and forgettable dialogue drag them both through the gunk. On top of all, during dialogue-heavy sections, the characters' lips flap like lifeless puppets, resulting in cutscenes that are fine to listen to but awkward to watch.When Rani gets a moment to herself, she has to suck up the black ooze. Then, the grey fades and foliage bursts out of the ground with all manners of strange, characterful fronds. New paths open up—there's a bit of casual platforming to be had in here as you make your way through the world—and certain kinds of plants offer resources or items used in puzzles. The resources tie into some insignificant upgrades, ranging from increased vacuum speed to more potent powers like a lure that'll briefly distract enemies—an ability that could be helpful was combat not so trivial that it never felt like something I needed any help with anyway. This isn't a challenging game in the slightest. Instead, it's one in which most activities are fairly simple and have a lovely zip to them, barring Becks' constant bickering in your earpiece. You might climb higher by finding the right kind of seed to chuck into a glowing pool so it sprouts huge bouncy platforms for you to use. Wreckage blocking your way might require an exotic and explosive fruit-like sticky bomb.Thing is, neither the platforming nor its puzzles go beyond their humble beginnings. This laid-back design is relaxing at times, though the low stakes make it difficult to feel engaged. Rani is a scavenger, not a fighter, so the vacuum glove is utilized to defeat the aggressive gooey critters in much the same way as you'd clean up the Gunk. Smaller enemies can be sucked into the vacuum before being tossed into each other, and projectile-spewing turrets can be pulled from their roots. While this approach makes sense, it means that the combat doesn't stand out, acting as a diversion more than anything else.To some, the simplicity may be an issue; to me, it created what I sought with , a serene adventure. Its vision of an alien world is day-glow colorful, filled with flora and fauna that should otherwise grow in deep waters. Navigating the planet's gloomy caves and abnormal jungles is a beautiful and calming experience, considering that you're willing to jump through a couple of hoops to get rid of some excessive effects by hand, such as blur, film grain, TAA, and so on. The musical score, too, needs a mention for how good it is at immersing you in this reverse ocean bed. It is strangely relaxing when paired with the act of cleaning up the Gunk, and you'll only ever notice how melancholy it is when you get a moment to stand around doing nothing but listening to somber violin tunes.On a technical note, my  run this space beater on 1080p at 60 FPS, but there's a bit of grime and gunk clogging up the engine. Framerates dipped to 40s in certain areas back when I played the game on release—eons ago, my bad! A couple of patches have been dropped since that probably have fixed the performance hiccups.You say "middle-of-the-road, milquetoast, mediocre". I say "unambitious, unassuming, uninsulting". A peaceful space janitor simulator that, at the very least, respects your time and intelligence by keeping things short and simple.

_childDocuments_.review: At an overall 5-7 hour experience that is easily forgettable, this is a $5 purchase at best. Pretty graphics do not make up for boring, linear gameplay, horrible writing, and abysmal storytelling.The story starts off with the premise of you playing as a teenage(?) girl with her captain....another teenage girl (again, not sure on age as it's not inherently stated anywhere) and a robot landing on a planet looking for resources. You are given zero context as to who these three are and are never given any character development beyond sentences like "we found the robot on that planet". This is done repeatedly throughout the game and is just poor storytelling. Want to know why the main character has a vacuum attachment for a hand? Refer to the one-liner of "Glad you were able to replace my arm with Pumpkin (the name of the vacuum-like attachment) after you found me on that planet!" That's it. That's a really big plot point to leave to a single sentence since it's the premise of the whole game. Yet, you continually just keep getting one-liners that are supposed to cover everything going on and it's flat out lazy storytelling. The voice acting is bad. The script doesn't help, but the VA goes from kid-friendly to teenage angst and back so many times that I wanted to mute the main characters whiny heroism 10 minutes into playing.The gameplay starts out as intriguing and never goes anywhere. You vacuum up gunk in a linear fashion to progress the paper-thin story. There are resources to collect for upgrades, but none of those upgrades matter as you will never use them because there isn't any situation in the games linear gameplay where you would need to use them. There are many, many spots in the games platforming where if you didn't jump at the exact spot that it was designed for, you won't make the jump. Seriously. There are pillars that you need to jump onto and can easily jump onto at any angle but you will not jump onto it unless you jump onto the side that has a clearly marked yellow side....even though you can jump higher than the pillar. There are also several places where your character can get stuck in free fall in the environment. These aren't bugs per se, but players shouldn't be able to jump into pockets of nothing, or only able to complete platforming that can be clearly reached but from the one side deemed interactable by whoever programmed it. It's bad design. The full game feels like it should have been the first part of a much larger game or experience. The final boss fight is the only boss fight in the whole game, so there is no build up. The ranged enemy (there's only one) could have had an entire arc. Introduction to a new enemy and you need to simply figure out how to survive, then you figure out how to kill it, then, through an upgrade, you can repel it's ranged attacks. Along the way you would learn about how the gunk transformed this natural inhabitant and the MC saves it. Nope. nothing of the sort. Just a single bland ranged enemy over and over. I believe there are 5 enemies in the entire game. That's it. No variation, just 4 enemies and the final boss. Overall, the graphics can only carry you so far. And that's the only good thing going for The Gunk. It's a pretty game. The second you focus your attention on anything other than the pretty visuals, is when it all falls apart.

_childDocuments_.review: A reasonable short game about two scavengers who land on an alien planet, discovering some weird gunk that needs to be cleaned up, but by staying longer and exploring they discover the planet isn't what it seems to be. A great simple storyline, game mechanics that just do work (albeit some bugs and due to auto-save it requires to reload the game at specific buggy points), all in all it was a nice adventure game with "relaxing" cleaning up gameplay and fun interaction between the two main characters. A bit too easy, perhaps, a bit too cliché, that may be, but it is a charming and (relaxing in the beginning) story and it was fun to finish it. It has solid gameplay and puzzle mechanics and great music & voice acting. Although I finished the game in less than 5 hours, I wouldn't recommend it full price. 25 euros for a 5-hour game that doesn't have replayability... I don't know. But on sale, definitely worth checking this out.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed in under 5 hours. Quickly realized this wasn't quite the game i thought it was going to be and thought about getting a refund after watching the trailer on youtube. However the graphics, sound and mechanics were enough to override that feeling.I feel that this game is more of a walking simulator akin to Death Stranding and the like, an atmospheric storytelling engine where you uncover the truth of the planet you've landed on. The upgrades are useful, but there's only one i think you need, and the story forces you to get it. the scanning is more for a completionist vibe, the puzzles are the right level of difficulty for a game like this - nothing that will cause major issues, but the execution of them is quite nice.All in all the pricing seems fair for the content provided, unfortunately there's no real replay-ability due to the linear nature of the story, but for a nice calm sojourn into a breathtaking environment with a solid story I'm glad i stuck with it. sad to see it end so soon.No bugs found, only one area my PC struggled with (the long elevator) all in all a very smooth experience.Buy it if you'd like to explore a beautiful planet and clean up all the Gunk™

_childDocuments_.review: The characters really need to stop talking. If there was half the amount of dialogue there'd still be way too much. I'm also not a fan when games tell me how beautiful they are (especially over and over in this case.)I really hate sounding so negative, but I really can't see how anyone can enjoy this game. Maybe if they don't play many games, so they just want a movie experience (but without a good story), and they enjoy eavesdropping on strangers small talking.I'm really disappointed because me and my gf were looking forward to playing it together, but neither of us could stomach the dialogue. _childDocuments_.review: Bought the game based on the developer's name alone, but this game is very different than Steamworld. Instead of a quirky, yet interesting indie game, The Gunk is a flashy, linear game with unimaginative game mechanics. The game has you walking along a straight, predetermined path, sometimes literally a yellow line on the ground. There are trappings of crafting and exploration, but that is all window-dressing for a game that constantly leads you by the hand. There is always just one way to go, unless there is a side room with a couple unnecessary resources. And while the "sucking gunk" mechanism feels good, especially with controller vibration, it gets boring. There are no interesting choices. The lack of puzzles, combat, or other challenges makes it hard to stay engaged. Just look at the steam achievements, where 95% of owners got the achievement of starting the game, but only half of those kept playing for the "Cleared the Gunk Tower" story-based achievement which is unlocked after only an hour or two.I hate giving this game a negative review, because the graphic artists did a lot of work here. The art style is amazing, with really nice, detailed character models. The story, characters, and voice acting is not bad either. It's just that all while playing, I could not forgive all the ways The Gunk was made to seem like a deeper game than what it is. What we have here is just a walk forward, have very simple game interactions, and advance the story. It's like the game designers just could not be bothered making interesting game mechanics, but still wanted to get all the boxes checked for the marketing department. I don't know what happened, but it is a real shame that no one could find a compelling reason for clearing levels of the gunk and finishing the game. That's a disservice to the story's enjoyable female duo (and "kurt").My Gunk Vacuum ran on an Ubuntu Linux desktop, thanks to the amazing Steam Proton compatibility software. The software ran without any technical issues, despite the developers not offering support to Linux gamers, as they did with previous game releases. Not sure what happened at Image & Form but they lost a loyal customer to The Gunk.

_childDocuments_.review: The Gunk is a 3D platform game where you have to suck up the black slime to recreate the once colorful game world.You suck up the black gunk by using Rani's transforming power gauntlet.Watch my first gameplay here: In The Gunk, you take on the role of Rani, a space scavenger who, along with her partner Becks, searches for new energy sources on planets.When both characters discover an interesting planet, they soon find out that it is infested with a slimy parasite they quickly call Gunk.This gunk suffocates plant life and mutates creatures into aggressive monsters.Although the plot of The Gunk is very basic, the relationship between Rani and Becks is very interesting.The two will therefore argue more and more about what to do during this adventure and whether the Gunk is really their concern.There is also a kind of crafting system that has been kept nice and simple.In the game world you can collect four types of resources, and if you have enough of them you can upgrade your handy glove.Visually, The Gunk can be quite impressive at times, with a more realistic style than some other 3D games, and has a clear visual line. The bright colors splash off your screen when you free it from the gunk and next to it are the character animations.The game also have great support for ultrawide resolutions, check a gameplay at 3840*1080 here:

_childDocuments_.review: The Gunk made me remember how much I love games that have a beautification mechanic - as in, clean up corruption or dirt to make an area look great again. Okami awakened that desire many years back, and since then, I've been hard-pressed to find games that do something similar. The Gunk does it, and I am glad, because it kept me playing through the whole game.(Literally) armed with a vacuum, you go around and suck up gunk on a distant planet that you and your girlfriend land on, in the search for energy. Once a given area is cleaned, it transforms back into its lush self, allowing you to progress. You also suck up materials to unlock improvements, and scan plants and environmental objects to get new improvements you can unlock. It's a pretty satisfying gameplay loop. There is even a bit of combat as the game progresses, but it never gets out of hand.The game is only about 5 hours long, so not too bad, which is good as it falls off pretty hard in the last third. The environments aren't as interesting, there is more walking back and forth (even traversing one area twice) and the story, while not that interesting before, takes a nosedive - At least the ending is somewhat satisfying, though the final boss fight is very buggy - I got stuck in a wall twice, which meant I had to restart the fight twice as well. The soundtrack is also hauntingly beautiful and the game runs well, with only a few weird FPS drops in the last area.Overall, The Gunk doesn't overstay it's welcome and I would say it's definitely worth a playthrough. It scratches a very specific "cleanup" itch that only few games do, and the environments are often very pretty, even if it falls off a bit later on.

Nothing feels forced or out of place.  The game doesn't feel underbaked or unfinished. Easy recommend. Price seems fair.

_childDocuments_.review: The game could have been salvaged if only one of its core elements was good, but not a single worthwhile or even interesting quality is present - writing, level design, character handling are all so very powerfully boring. Note that almost none of it is , per se, just blatantly pedestrian and without any notable features. Even the specific way in which this game sucks is boring which is honestly kinda uniquely hilarious. A weak narrative constantly underpinned with gratingly poor writing. The puzzles are far too spread out and easy for this to be a puzzle game. Level design is entirely on rails so I couldn't call it an exploration game and neither is it in any way made to facilitate platforming. (which was my main expectation, personally) Might as well because the movement set is barebones. Combat is basic to the point where I'm not even sure if combat is an appropriate word for it; it's more of a side diversion or afterthought.Who is this game for exactly? What was the creative vision behind it, if any?If you want a fun platformer, play . If you want an interesting setting get . For platforming and combat shenanigans that new  is crazy good. You want a whimsical puzzle game?  has you covered. For that oddball scifi vibe check out . The Gunk? I wouldn't recommend it to literally anyone for any reason whatsoever, except for maybe game developers as a case study in how not to make boring games. It is completely uninspired and provides no value to its players.The art direction is neat, which is really the only positive that I can report on. Even that is marred though with an aggressively unattractive protagonist that really got on my nerves whenever she was on camera.For me The Gunk is a lot like all that immediately forgettable ♥♥♥♥ that Netflix has been pumping out recently like that movie with Ana de Armas and Captain America. I can't even remember the title of that movie and I only just recently saw it. It didn't do anything bad. It was a movie, and I watched it. Like The Gunk, it was manufactured to be flavourless and inoffensive content that you consume without any thought or feeling.
