_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered: The "bad" Yakuza game.Coming as one of the millions of newbie Yakuza fans, I always was confused by why everyone immediately singled out Yakuza 3 as the bad one. I mean the franchise on the whole maintains some semblance of quality, but none of the spinoffs hold as much disdain as 3. Not Kenzan, Ishin, RGG Online, Dead Souls is liked more than this game. So I wanted to know why.Tamashiro's bossfight told me everything I needed to know.Yakuza 3 is not a bad game, but by god does it have some flaws. For the most part, the game is standard if clunky Yakuza fun. Same open world, same weird substories, same everything you've come to know from Yakuza, but now in the neat setting of Okinawa. However there are TWO things you need to know about this game before going into it.1: The combat system is busted. This game will remind you that Yakuza Kiwami and Kiwami 2's biggest improvement was using the later game's combat systems because this game's system is jank. Enemies will either bum rush you like a horde of terribly dressed piranhas or stand in the corner of the arena in a permanent block. And it's a block you can't break. Some bossfights are now seared into my memory just from having their block on constantly and without being broken. Tamashiro especially. 2: The game's pacing is constantly chin checking you. Yakuza 3's not particularly long for a Yakuza game, but it's plot is rather kooky and the game's way of pacing itself doesn't help. You go from a slow burn in the first few chapters to wacky shenanigans with Kanda, then the Snake Flower Triad, then the frickin' CIA and THEN the actual main antagonist. And intercut with slice of life bits where Kiryu manages his orphanage of kids and helps them with day-to-day issues. In-between gang fights. It's not a bad plot, made up for by the power of characters like Rikiya, Mine and others, but the pacing will keep messing with you.If you can stomach those issues, then Yakuza 3 Remastered is fine. It's the end of the original "trilogy" of Yakuza games and it's the push we needed to move on from it being just about Kiryu. If you can stomach the painful combat and endure the rubberbanding pacing, you'll be able to enjoy this game for what it is. Plus tuna. Don't forget the tuna. Real men get that FRICKIN' TUNA.

_childDocuments_.review: Another chapter in the story of the Dragon of Dojima, now he being a parent!Yakuza 3... Oh man... Look, just like Kiwami, this is a good game and a very worth play, specially if you played the previous ones as this is the start of one of the most important arcs in the life of Kiryu. However as you might have noticed, unlike the first two games which got a Kiwami remake that modernized the original games, Y3 recieved the Remaster treatment, so the game is pretty much the same gameplay wise than the original PS3 release with a few touches regarding censoring and cut content that happened in its original release in America. _childDocuments_.review: Even when it was released on the PlayStation 3, Yakuza 3 was seen as a black sheep. Not because of (at least for the western release) cut content but due to the mechanics, the change in location and how the game feels somewhat stiff at times. This is not to say that Yakuza 3 was seen as a terrible game or a misstep. Far from it. It was just that it was something that felt different and took a while getting use to but also paradoxicality not feeling like much has changed in the formula (this was felt even more in the West, due to how long it took for us to get it and again cut content.)Which is what puts Yakuza 3 Remastered in a weird spot. 1 and 2 got revamped with Kiwami, but Yakuza 3 Enhanced is basically just updated graphics with all content from the Japanese version. But the gameplay remains unchanged from the PlayStation 3 version. No revamp to the awkward combat, the experience and many of the mini-games are a shell of what you’d come to expect from Yakuza Zero, 1 and 2 Kiwami and the visuals don’t leap out like before. And if you’ve come from those games, it’s going to be an even rougher experience. There’s the level up system which feels very restrictive. It may have been done to prevent grinding to make Kiryu into a near-overpowered badass early into the game but it also feels gated. The same feeling goes for getting heat actions, weapons and armour, with the game’s modding system not being noteworthy until very late into the game and even then the available options still feel limited. It’s justifiable to not have Kiryu once again become overpowered early/midway into the game, but it’d be nice if Yakuza 3 Remastered was more generous in what you could unlock. The combat feels off. It feels like they had to nerf Kiryu and so you don’t feel as badass as before. Some heat actions don’t feel as epic and it does have an awkward feel. This is especially noticeable against bosses and tough opponents (e.g. the ones you face in the Coliseum activity), where it seems you have to cheese them more than use what you’ve learned up to that point.  It’s not a total disaster, as its still solid enough to be enjoyable but you do feel like a handicapped badass. Visually, even considering the time frame and how this is only a remastered and not a remake/overhaul like the Kiwami games are, it’s still a let down to an extent. This wasn’t a huge leap back in the PS3 and you can see the age and rough edges still present, such as sudden pop-up and sometimes NPC’s having derpy or dead-eyes look. And of course, it has its own set of Yakuza restrictiveness: Save points are really far apart, you can’t accept more than one hitman mission, can’t buy more than one food at a time, item inventory is always a pain and other, somewhat archaic game design choices.  Again though, this must be stressed that DESPITE these issues Yakuza 3 Enhanced is still overall a fun game. When it hits its stride, the dopamine hits hard and you remember why you love the series; Kamurocho feels like an old friend, vibrant, looking different but also similar and hiding its share of secrets underneath all the glitz and glamour and while Ryukyu isn’t Sotenbori (Osaka), it still has its character and charm, feeling like a place to visit and absorb a different aspect of Japan. While the visuals might not pop out, its still an impressive showcase of packing cities with details and small touches that still make it fun to explore and just run around. The music is banging, as expected with the Ryu Ga Gotoku library (and this being Sega, who rarely drop the ball when it comes to music,) with a mix that ranges from techno to J-pop (and that’s not getting into the Karaoke songs.) There is always moments that are dramatic or comedic (sometimes swinging around in the same scene) that make one actually care what is taking place and invest in characters, even those who just appear in a small substory. Speaking of those, the substories once again reveal the soul of Yakuza/Ryu Ga Gotoku series, with some amusing (and even downright heart-warming) scenes. And yes, some of the activities aren’t that engaging or fully fleshed out (hostess ones spring to mind) but Yakuza 3 still has a lot of content that it hits more than it misses and just when you begin to flag or tire of one thing it throws something else to keep you hooked. Yakuza 3 Enhanced is often seen as the “worst” of the games in the franchise and it is justifiable line of opinion. But it also hides a truth about it; That even the “worst” games in the Ryu Ga Gotoku franchise are still solid b-tier fun. This is enhanced (ahem) by the fact that the price of the game is dead-cheap (it’s also part of the Yakuza Remastered Collection, again a fantastic bundle). It is best to come to Yakuza 3 Enhanced with expectation in check but also the fact that you’re still going to have a lot of enjoyment pounding solutions into people’s faces. (*More towards a 6 than an 8)

_childDocuments_.review: Leaving a review mostly for newcomers to the franchise coming off of 0 -> K1 -> K2. This, along with 4 and 5, are *remasters*, not remakes like K1 and K2 were. They all look and feel VERY dated. Textures have been updated since the PS3 days, and translation errors/consistency fixed here and there, but that's about it.3 in particular is a very mixed bag. The story is by far one of the best in the franchise, even if it can be slow-going at points. The substories have their usual charm you've come to expect from these games. But all that being said, the combat is some of the *worst* in the series. Whatever difficulty you're most comfortable on in other games, drop it down a level or two (and if you plan on doing a Legend run, do it off a 100% NG+ save for the golden gun and other endgame gear). Enemies CONSTANTLY block, even mid-combo, quickstep is bugged compared to the original PS3 release (though there's a mod for that on PC to kind of fix it), and damage output is ridiculously low.The game shows its age. It's absolutely worth playing for the story, but just be aware the gameplay is VERY dated, and a bit of a blemish on the franchise as a whole. And if you're a masochist completionist like me, good luck.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza has always been a hard boiled drama with extra fun moments and a bunch of mini-games, but the way 3 sets things up, messes a lot of the pacing on what could have been a rather impactful story to tell.3 starts off has a flash forward of events to come right after the second game. While that would have been fine; the fact we go back in time to the exact events that happen right after Yakuza 2, isn't. And this isn't the only time Yakuza 3 chooses to have awkward pacing either, often the game will tell you have a day to get ready, but then you'll see 3 days pass before you actually go anywhere. On top of all this, you are constantly shown things in a slightly odd order, in what appears to be an attempt to keep the player entertained while establishing a relationship with your kids in the orphanage. Oh, did you not know about the kids at the orphanage? WELL, tough luck, because you only get the after effects of Kiryu getting the orphanage and having an already established relationship with them. Honestly I really wouldn't mind Yakuza 3 focusing fully on the orphanage thing in the first half if it JUST DID, but it constantly doesn't. You help a kid, fight some thugs, help your kids some more, fight some thugs, fast forward, more story beats, help your kids before leaving to Tokyo. It's really exhausting going through this game because it just can't make up it's mind at the beginning of what it wants to **** sad truth too? All the kid stuff is genuinely really good and helps establish Kiryu's character in a way the rest of the series didn't while still maintaining some Yakuza gameplay. Would have Yakuza 3 had a slower start? YES, but that was kinda needed for this game, and the fact they didn't do that and instead made a really complex plot point for no reason is frustrating because you can see the writers making it up as they go along. There are clear ideas that Yakuza 3 has, but it's never able to settle on one, and makes a lot of moments less impactful or worse, **** there better Yakuza games out there? Ya, pretty much any other Yakuza game could beat this one, but there isn't a lot of them that show Kiryu being a parent to a bunch of kids, and that's what upsets me the most about this game. They had a chance to slightly step out of the usual Mafioso tale and didn't stick to it. There is still plenty of shine and glimmer of what Yakuza 3 could have been, but with an outdated system, odd pacing, and a mess of a story; the bad still outweighs it. Yakuza 3 is a good game, but a bad Yakuza game.

_childDocuments_.review: The first true Yakuza game that was released in HD. If this is your first time going into 3. It is very rough around the edges when compared to the Kiwami titles and Yakuza 0 in terms of its combat. You don't get the same crazy level of customization with your fighting styles as you only stick to one portion with Kiryu. So for some newer fans, that might make the combat in the game more tiresome and tedious. However, if there's one thing that Yakuza always gets down really well, it is the modes within the world. The amount of exploration you can do within the returning district of Kamurocho and the new Ryukyu area are fun places to get distracted in. Plenty of side stories to keep you coming back for more exploration within in each town. A huge amount of returning minigames like Baseball, Fishing, Bowling and Golf all great distractions from the combat.  The story is incredibly deep in Yakuza 3, with plenty of unexpected jaw dropping moments. Lots of characters both good and bad have plenty of screen time throughout. It almost feels like you're watching a movie sometimes when playing these games and that's what I love about this series. The story can be one part ridiculous and then it can be super serious at another turn. Yakuza 3 is able to blend these moments extremely well and it'll keep you interested until the ending hits.Overall, Yakuza 3 is a bit rough in terms of its combat system. But for those who are looking to get deeper into the story of Kiryu Kazama's power struggle should not miss out on this game at all. Plus, the distractions that are scattered throughout the game are really fun experiences! Since this game is bundled with the Remastered collection as well, you're getting plenty of action if you decide to buy all three games in the collection!

_childDocuments_.review: I've been going through this series for the first time, never played the games before. So naturally, doing so on Steam, I started with Yakuza 1 Kiwami, Yakuza 2 Kiwami, then Yakuza 0. The plan was to then move on to Like a Dragon, but then the remasters for 3, 4, and 5 all dropped on the same day! My friend and I were excited, as less time in between 2 and 3 meant we could continue essentially the next episode of the story. Great!Unfortunately, there's a clear reason why the previous games were remade and the trend not continuing was seriously painful. For one thing, the character models are immediately jarring, the drop in quality between 2 Kiwami and 3 Remastered is absolutely devastating, with Haruka being a massive example who is present for most of the opening. That said, while not a great start, I can look past that. I forgave Persona 4's art quality drop from Persona 5, I'm not all about graphics.Unfortunately, the moment I got control of Kiryu in the city of Kamurocho I was now so familiar with, the problems with the port were made sorely evident. There are clearly massive memory leaks in the game regarding the large crowds of NPC that are present throughout the city, leading to the game to slow down like the world flooded and everyone just learned to breath underwater but not swim. Every aspect was now plagued with permanent slowdown, movement, combat, you name it. While this was absolutely hilarious, it was also insufferably unplayable. On top of that, the combat is, unfortunately, the blandest of the games I'd played. Yakuza 1 Kiwami and 0 had their adaptable multi-styled combat, while 2 Kiwami brought in the joys of ragdoll, making everything feel much more impactful. There was none of this here, just comparatively generic gameplay and a lack of the usual excitement I felt during it in the past.I'm certain this is a nice nostalgia trip for the folks who'd played the game in the past (performance aside), but I'm not part of that gang and, while I can normally overlook downgrades for older games (Red Faction, Saints Row, Just Cause), without the benefit of the iteration gained by the time of the remakes, playing these in chronological order is just too tough of a pill to swallow.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A mediocre game in an amazing franchise.Graphics:While I was not a fan of how shiny everything in Kiwami 2 was, this game looks much worse. This is because Kiwami and Kiwami 2 were full remakes, while this game just remasters an older title.Storyline:Incredibly boring until the final 2 chapters. Mostly just fetch quests and hunting down people - but the ending was extremely emotional and very well made.Price:If possible, I'd wait for a sale. If there isn't a sale, it's not a bad purchase if you're just hoping to keep up with the storyline.Difficulty:Not difficult, just annoying at times.AI:The enemies LOVE to block. Interestingly, most can also stun you out of a block. Not a fun combo.Cutscenes:When they're used, they're really well made. This game, however, primarily uses text screens... and there are A LOT.Fun:While not as fun as prior titles in the series, I had a lot of fun! The substories and controls are noticeably worse than in prior titles, but it's still a fun game. It just doesn't live up to the standards of prior entries.Sounds/Music:Not memorable, but generally nice.Launcher:NoneAchievements:Story progression and tedious minigame grinding.Replayability:I'd likely pick Kiwami or Zero to replay, not this one. It doesn't have much to keep playing, missing things like Cabaret Club or the construction company minigame.Controls:Noticeably worse than prior entries. _childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 is the definition of an HD PS2 game with a remaster that doesn't really do anything to improve the experience.  The only way that this can be considered a good remaster is if it put up against the original English release which had a worse script and several missing features, although the boost to 60 fps is nice it seems to have broken some QTEs.  Those missing features being all of the extremely Japanese minigames which aren't even that good but it is good that they're here regardless, most of the minigames this time around are actually kind of mediocre.  The best example of this is the cabaret minigame which was the first in the series and you can tell as it doesn't resemble it's 0/Kiwami 2 counterpart but you can clearly see the foundation that those game use in this one.  It's like that for the combat, quest, and design of Kamurocho as well, they are all the most basic forms of what can be seen in the later game and the game kind of suffers for it through no fault of it's own (except only having 3 taxi's that is entirely this games fault).  The combat doesn't have styles yet and isn't that fun until you do Mack and Komaki's training, following these tutors are so important to the games combat that it makes no sense that they are optional.  Although it is still fun once you get trained up and the boss fights here are great except the boss of chapter of 8 who is easily the worst boss in the series so far and really exempliefies this games issue of having enemies block all of your attacks.  Substories are beginning to tell there own stories but not many manage to leave an impression and this isn't helped by the game's main story.  Lastly, Kamurocho feels barren as the map isn't that populated with the stores yet, which kind of makes the city seems like a bunch of connected hall ways and weirdly some regions of the map just simply don't have enough in them.  The story of the game is good but not great, it's nice to see Kiryu being a father but when the game pauses the story so you can help there problems so late in the game, it just feels like filler instead of how it felt at the start of the game, making you wonder why these weren't just substories.  The new characters are cool but they're all wasted on weak writing that doesn't spend enough time with them to leave a lasting impression, except Mikiya but most of his stuff is confusingly optional, but it is weird that important characters like Kashiwagi and the Kazama look-a-like are moved on from so quickly.  The game is still good but it could be so much better, it leaves you weirdly wanting more even though the game has some sections that feel like filler, although the fact that this seems to be the series low point should be a testament to Yakuza's quality as a franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: I have many mixed emotions playing this game. This is my first time playing Yakuza 3, while reading more about the development and challenges about the development of the game. I see why there are some story beats that doesn't seem to be pacing itself appropriately.I would like to begin this personal review with the story.I feel like the story is "Meh", best describes it for me. I personally, initially, dislike the orphanage part of the story. I understand that we are meant to connect to them, but as a parent myself, I really don't want to play a game that reminds me with taking care of my kids. I can do that on my own time and don't need a game that reminds me of reality. Second is the main protagonist, or I would say End game boss. The motive is very bad to say the least.  Like many Yakuza games, I was hoping for this grand reveal, the intricacy of decisions made they made and act this way. Yet, there was no build up, there was no slow reveal who it is. Everything was laid out AT THE END of the game. It was a very disappointing story for me. Gameplay wise, I feel that this has aged poorly. Maybe because later Yakuza entries focuses more on attack based combat instead of properly balancing it between offense and defense. I really am not a fan of the combat here, the early game section is so difficult it wasn't fun at all. Later makes the combat bearable.The substories for me are the weakest of the series. I still recommend this game for Yakuza fans. Just don't expect a blast playing this. I have 40 hours playing this game and I feel that 40 hours is enough for me. I won't be looking back at this game any time soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered may be the oldest and dated Yakuza game compared to other entries as it was first released in 2009. Yet, its characters and story revolving around empathy, selflessness and orphans are such breath of fresh air with many incredible instances throughout its main campaign.The first arc focuses solely on Morning Glory Orphanage and the children do wonders for Kiryu's character development and its commentary on orphans. Smaller scale stories about the children struggling with loneliness, bully and coming to terms with oneself are exactly what Yakuza 3 needed. Later on when the plot gets intriguing with politics, it still does well mainly due to its compelling villains and characters. Yakuza 3's story plays a very integral part for Kiryu and years later, it's still a very compelling one.What drags the game down is its dated gameplay, visual, sound design and Heat actions lacking weight. But those are all minor issues if you are already aware that this is a 2009 game. It is still filled with enjoyable substories, minigames and Ryukyu as a new setting really stand out.Even with its dated flaws, it is still a must play for anyone interested in Yakuza and others looking for compelling video game narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: Although it'll be quite the adjustment going to this from Kiwami 2 and the chronologically earlier entries, it's still a fantastic Yakuza game that hits all the high notes you'll have come to love about the series so far -- dramatic shirt removals, crying men, heartfelt drama, positive vibes, Kiryu being a goof, and so on. Personally speaking, I found the clunky animations and PS3 era character designs charming and quaint. Just make sure to install the SilentPatch and the Quickstep Fix, remember to use your grabs very (!) liberally, and enjoy the ride, aniki. It's one of my favorite in this series so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 remastered is fine but not as good as the earlier re-releases. The remaster has given it a face lift but the underlying game play feels a bit long in tooth. It shares similar systems with the previous kiwami and yakuza zero but in certain aspects make it feel slower. Kiryu's running speed, for example, is variable sometimes its fine, other times its like watching a man run with weights under water. Chapters can be ridiculously short (eg go here beat up this guy) or padded in length (eg you need to track this person down and time is crucial, oh hey boss, I'm new to this town can you show me around?). In fact the game starts in media res then flashbacks but by the time I get to the section leading to this point I was confused because I had forgotten how it started. Side quests attempt to liven up the world but creates a somewhat limited world experience as outside of side quests the npcs are pretty wooden. While I was heavily engaged in the kiwami and zero, yakuza 3 doesn't pull me in the same way. Several of the early chapters are rather mundane. The focus is on the day to day life at the orphanage which is meant to create an affectionate air around the children but feels slow and bloated. It tries to spice up the average day of an orphanage director with mystery and story twists that rather feel like a soap opera. The main character runs the orphanage and takes care of the kids - sort of. Interaction with them can be a little inconsistent. I was asked to buy a copy of the in-game version of Shonen Jump by one kid and when I returned home he never asked for it and my character never gave it to him. It felt like I should have taken an extra trip just to hand him the comic magazine if I wanted that task resolved which is bizarre because the trip only took a few days and the magazine wouldn't be out for weeks which is why it was requested in the first place.Combat is serviceable but not quite as fun as the revamped earlier editions. It feels basic with a lot of later enemies blocking - a lot. There are mods that improve it but playing stock port is less fun compared to zero, kiwami 1 or 2. My advice hit the weapon store before the final chapters and buy guns. Lots and lots of guns. On the flip side, you can still pull off a decent amount of sidestepping counters and power attacks with a bit of timing on bosses. Skill gain appears to be a one way street. You gain skills as you upgrade for experience and choose which skill as you go up. However once picked there doesn't appear to be an option to get the other skill.  Inventory management is less forgiving and it's still ok but it's not as good as the others that were re-done before it. There are still quick time combat events which did happen in previous fights but feel so much more pervasive in this one. Some of the button mashing events being the most annoying.Another annoying part of the game is the psuedo option. It pretends to give you a choice but it either forcibly tells you to pick the other one or events make the choice moot. Its a waste of time for no reason other than making sure you don't fall asleep. Lastly its short. There are a number of side quests I could have taken to expand the length but I just didn't find them interesting. To get the full view of the Yakuza timeline, I would encourage playing through the game at least once,

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 is a strange one. It’s commonly called the worst game in the series while also having tons of diehard fans for it. I at first skipped it and played 4&5, but I caved and bought it, and what do you know, I nearly completed this game in less than a week, not because it was short, but because I couldn’t put down the controller. With most of the series in mind, Yakuza 3 is overall the worst game in the series, in both gameplay and story structure, but by no means does that make it not worth playing. It’s still pretty good, if not, great at times and its major flaws can be easily avoided. So if you like Yakuza, get this game!GAMEPLAYYakuza 3 is most hated for its combat, mostly because enemies blocked too much and had too much health, making boss fights and normal encounters last way too long. Strangely, this can be easily remedied by playing the game in easy mode. It pretty much makes combat feel totally normal, aside from it being easier. Though the combat is by no means perfect. Compared to the games that came after, it’s not quite as involved. I can now see why Y4 took the multiple protagonists approach since Kiryu’s gameplay was growing bland on its own. The combat ain’t all bad though, I found the Komaki training rewards pretty entertaining, especially the final heat move which is pretty difficult to pull off. All in all, the combat feels mostly normal, the only issue is that it outstays its welcome. But there are other parts of this game, like the side content, I actually think this is the real black sheep in Yakuza 3. Most of the substories, while straightforward and easy, just don’t need to exist. I did most of the side quests because I previously made it my mission to defeat every iteration of Amon in the series. In a way, adding other requirements (like hitmen missions and IF7 fights) to fight Amon made the substories less valuable to me. None of them are bad, just not worth the time I spent on them. Overall, the greatest problem with Yakuza’s gameplay is that it tries to squeeze so much of it in where it isn’t necessary. If the game was just a bit lighter in content, or if its requirements to fight Amon were the same as the rest of the series, I think I’d have a lot fewer problems with it.STORYNow, this is what makes Yakuza 3 truly worth experiencing. Its story is the most intimate and wholesome in the series and Kiryu smiles here more than he probably does in the rest of the series combined. Parenting and getting to know these orphanage kids was a real treat and it gave me something to lose later in the story. Plus, there’s Rikiya and the rest of his family, he was a pretty likable guy even though I knew he was going to die at some point. Kiryu’s relationship with Haruka is interesting too. Just as a 6th grader, she’s pretty much in charge of everyone and she reminds Kiryu of chores and such. If they are met with a big story-related problem, they just look at each other and nod. I really like this silent trust that crescendos by the end of the game. Like most of the Yakuza games, their relationship is one of the best parts of the game, only being outshined by Yakuza 5&6. I’ve seen complaints about the first few hours of the game, saying that it’s “boring” and “goes nowhere” but it is actually the most valuable part of the game. If you get invested in these characters as I did, you will be pissed, sad, and glad like I was as ♥♥♥♥ happens in the story. Ironically, the political side of this game is my least favorite in the series. Yakuza is normally the best in the industry at tonal dissonance, Y0 especially, but Yakuza politics really don’t mesh well with the intimate Morning Glory part of the story. The story could have been much simpler while possibly being even better. Just like the gameplay, they just shoved too much unnecessary stuff in the story. But those are my only gripes with the game. Since I’m not a fan of the Yakuza politics, I’m just going to highlight moments I really liked. Majima was GOATed in this game. For the first time in the series, he and Kiryu treated each other as friends. They speak out of understanding, which is absent in the rest of the series. Unlike Yakuza 2, their fight in the Coliseum was entirely consensual, Kiryu was actually excited to fight Majima here. Majima’s dialogue is hilarious and him saving Kiryu in that massive pink truck was funny as hell. Not much else interesting happens until the third act of the game. Mine, the main antagonist who before this point seemed cool and brutal, brought a whole Yakuza family over with a bulldozer to trash the Morning Glory. At this point in the game, after connecting with all of the characters and enjoying Kiryu’s new home, this is probably the most anger-inducing scene in the game, if not the series. In a flash, I went from thinking Mine was cool as hell to realizing he was a heartless bastard. Afterward, Kiryu goes to the bullfighting area to save Rikiya’s boss Nakahara, who was already in recovery from a gunshot wound. A Yakuza boss that we fought near the beginning of the game threatens Nakahara’s life by putting him in the middle of four bulls. Up until this point, Nakahara seemed pretty sickly, but when his surrogate daughter, who has been mute for the whole game, yells for him, he flips a bull by its horns and achieves a new purpose in life. Kiryu flips a bull, fights the boss, and Rikiya comes to his side. That’s when the Yakuza boss tries to shoot Kiryu in the back, which Rikiya prevents with his own body. As Rikiya lies dying, asking Kiryu to show Mine what for, Kiryu can do nothing but wail and beg for him to stay. This is the most emotional he has gotten in the series and it really sends home Kiryu’s fear of being involved with the Yakuza. Even when he’s many miles away from Tokyo, the people he’s close to still get hurt. I felt something in my eyes when I watched this even though I knew of Rikiya’s fate beforehand. I think Kiryu’s reaction is what truly got me, not Rikia’s death. Now, Kiryu is on what he thinks is a suicide mission to save Daigo from Mine. So in what he thinks is his last time to wander with Haruka in Kamurocho, he selfishly takes her with him. Haruka understands this though and encourages him by hugging him in the middle of the street. Kiryu leaves her at New Serena and fights his way up the hospital to Daigo’s room, he finds out Daigo was taken up to the roof by Mine and reaches them. Mine threatens Daigo’s life, saying Daigo doesn’t have to struggle anymore. This gave me Y0 Nishiki flashbacks and Kiryu diverts Mine’s attention to himself. They have a cool shirtless battle on the rooftop and Mine finally sees that money isn’t everything. In a moment very reminiscent of Like A Dragon, he calls his secretary and refuses a billion yen deal. The Black Angels attempt to kill them, Daigo deadeyes all of them, and Mine sacrifices himself thinking he doesn’t deserve a second chance, despite him already making progress moments ago. As Kiryu’s about to leave Kamurocho with Haruka, one of the Yakuza patriarchs, Hamazaki, comes to him and sabs him as revenge for ruining his life. In a moment that feels a lot like Yakuza 5’s ending, Haruka leans over Kiryu yelling for him to stay with her. Hamazaki really could have gotten more screen time. I wanted to fight him but we never got the chance. At least we get that chance in Yakuza 4. The credits roll with what’s probably the best song in the game, and we see Kiryu living peacefully at Morning Glory with his orphans again. Although the game is riddled with flaws, Yakuza 3 has one of the best stories in the series. The gameplay is dated, but it has its high points and it deserves credit for paving the way for the games that came after. This game may be disregarded as filler to many, but like ATLA’s filler episode, The Tales In Ba Sing Se, it is still a highlight in the series nonetheless. Yakuza Kiwami 3, please!

_childDocuments_.review: this game is very frustrating to play in 2021, especially after playing Kiwami 2, which is contender for the best one in my book. the combat is very stiff and there are dozens of QOL issues that I feel like they could have fixed with this remaster. the 'intro' is about eight hours long, it takes a very long time for this game to get going, and once it does, the story is only really about 6 or 7 hours long. The enemies block SO MUCH and heavy attacks dont usually break their guard. Bosses have crazy true combos that make you wonder if it was designed to be a battle of attrition as far as using healing items go. It felt like I had to cheese most bosses, and in the end I was rushing through, trying to finish the story ASAP to know what happens next. I also felt like the pacing of the game was very slow, the story seems like it could have been wrapped up faster, and that's saying a lot, because the game's super short for a Yakuza title.The story I actually enjoyed, but I felt like it was really drawn out, even though it was the shortest one so far. I finished it at 15 steam hours (12 in game hours) and it felt a lot longer, mostly because all of the slice-of-life fluff and the clunky combat. It definitely hasn't aged well, and i'm only about an hour into Yakuza 4, but I can tell that's where they really hit their niche as far as developing on the PS3 goes.It's a rough game to play today IMO, the remaster doesnt do it many favors, but i'm still glad it's here and that Sega is supporting PC, so it gets a thumbs up for that. I'm glad I played it, but it's definitely the worst Yakuza i've played so far. For anyone playing them in order, Y4 is pretty fun so far, the combat is more fluent and I actually enjoy the combat more.I'd say you more than likely can skip this one, since it basically just explains where Kiryu went after Y2, who Kazama's brother is, and what happened to Daigo after he was injured. Other than that, i'd say this game definitely isn't mandatory to play. Again, I love these games, but this one was a chore to play through. It just hasn't aged well and was kind of sandwiched between a more modern game, and a really great remake.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll admit, when I started *Yakuza 3 Remastered*, I underestimated it. The game begins with Kiryu running an orphanage, and at first, I thought, "Wait, how can this lead into the intense, action-packed Yakuza stories I've come to love?" Boy, was I wrong. The orphanage plot isn't just filler—it's the heart of the game. It humanizes Kiryu in ways I never expected, and the bond he shares with the children adds emotional depth that complements the larger, high-stakes Yakuza drama.The story is masterfully written, weaving together themes of family, loyalty, and sacrifice. It’s not just about gang wars or criminal underworlds—it’s about Kiryu protecting what matters most to him, whether it's his orphaned kids or his values. The slow build-up is worth it, and as the game progresses, it hits you with some truly emotional and action-packed moments.If you’ve been a fan of the series, or if you’re new and curious about this game, *Yakuza 3* delivers on every level. Don't underestimate the quiet beginning—it's all part of an unforgettable journey.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr, it's not a bad game, but it's not the best the franchise has to offer. A mediocre Yakuza game is still a good game relative to what else is on the market.John Yakuza just wanted to retire to an island and foster a clutch of orphans, but then, as always, the reprobates of Kamurocho drag him back into a messy fight for something it's not clear he actually believes in but feels forever obligated towards. The story is fine, but follows the same main beats as all the other Yakuza titles. This time the villain is less compelling and we spend less time growing to dislike him. I went into the final battle not even aware it was the climax of the game. Story isn't the only aspect of this entry that's notably weaker than the others, though it's less forgivable since it doesn't have the limitations of an older game engine as an excuse. Combat is button-mashy and the visuals are PS3 era (but not bad - in parts even quite beautiful). This time around the side content is especially weak. Playing through the games numerically, I typically have a completion percentage in the high seventies to mid eighties. I finished this one at thirty-six percent and will not be going back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was pretty good in spite of what some of the other reviews might say. Sure- coming to this game from Kimwami 2 was a pretty big step, as this game is missing a lot of the creature comforts you would be accustomed to after playing through Yakuzas story thus far but it absolutely has its shining moments just as 0, k1 and k2 do.The combat is not the greatest as any enemy you encounter has the unbreakable blocking skills of god himself. The best way to get around this weird mechanic though is to just play through the game on easy mode. The story is pretty slow at the start of the game, but if you can muster enough gamer strength to push through something a little bit boring, do it, because the meaty story of this game after the start is surprisingly good.If you've been playing the Yakuza series this far, and have fallen for all the characters like I have, buy the game (on sale maybe) play on easy mode and muster enough focus from ur ADHD brain and get through the slow-ish start of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: While I'm giving this the thumbs up, I'd say it's not nearly as strong a recommend as Yakuza 0 or Yakuza Kiwami 2. The combat system is a bit different, where you'll almost all enemies block the majority of your attacks and combos, resulting in throws being a huge friend throughout the game and a constant need to get behind or to the side of your enemy no matter how trivial the thug should be. The music's still great, the minigames are less refined compared to their counterparts in 0/1/2, and the story has some real strong points offset with some real bad segments. The characters seem to fall in one of two categories, either you'll absolutely hate them, or they start off meh and gradually build up to a pretty great character with development.I would say not to skip this game if you're playing through all of the Yakuza titles, but at the same time, don't go out of your way to do content you don't care about. The main story is solid barring a couple spots, but the side stories vary so wildly you may not even realize you did one until you get a random burst of exp after a dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: Just to preface this review: This game is widely regarded as the weakest Yakuza game. As we all know, though, weakest doesn't necessarily mean it's a bad game.Everyone says the combat is bad and that dissuaded me from playing the game initially. But so far it's nothing crazy judging from the first two bosses on normal. And anyway, whether or not I believe this game's combat to be good or bad by the time I finish it, can we really make this criticism about Yakuza 3 ALONE? Because Yakuza 0, Kiwami, and Kiwami 2, the only games I've completed so far, definitely all have their fair share of unfun combat. Yakuza 3 is, just off of hearsay, unique in that enemies spam block... but why are we ignoring the fact that so many bosses in Kiwami 1 and 2 just spam quicksteps and counters, making it impossible for the player of a BEAT-EM-UP GAME to confidently attack without worrying about being punished? Like some of them pretty much had their own Tiger Drop... some, LITERALLY. Notably the damn "Man in Black" from Kiwami 2 that you fight MULTIPLE TIMES. In Yakuza 0, this was Sera and Shibusawa. In Kiwami 1, pretty much half of the bosses. And don't get me started about the evasiveness of Kiwami 1's finale enemies... who designed the MIA colonels? If you decide to look up No Damage boss runs, most people rely on quickstepping and countering to initiate their combos because so many bosses have their own counters that make throwing EVEN ONE attack risky. And... in a beat-em-up game? Why? It doesn't help that they're random either; thank god there are some bosses in all these games that do some stance or something that shows they're gonna counter you if you attack.On to the story... I've pretty much spoiled myself for the story and am pretty much playing to experience it myself. If I had to comment on the story, it's actually very good. It's definitely better than Yakuza 4 and 5 (I also spoiled myself for these games as well... got no clue what happens in 6 yet tho). The end got me feeling some type of way... Something really stuck out to me about 3 coming from Kiwami 1 and 2 in terms of its writing: it is so, so, SO MUCH LESS CHEESY. For Kiwami 2, "the cheese" stuck out so much because the main plot without it was actually interesting. Spoilers on Koji Shindo: So yeah, unlike Kiwami 2 and 1, Yakuza 3 actually manages to have an interesting main plot and not have it play out with Romeo and Juliet levels of cheese. That makes it in terms of the story an 8/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've given this a thumbs up because Yakuza is an amazing series.But Yakuza 3 is a little hard to go through.I only pushed on because the broader story was somewhat interesting, and, well... I'm a big Yakuza fan.I got really impatient at times because the pacing could be very excruciating. This mostly happened during the chapters related to the Morning Glory orphanage, Kyriu's little baby project in this "episode".Running back and forth, sometimes without any indications whatsoever, just isn't fun (big f.u to the chase missions, which have some of the worst gameplay).Most of these story missions felt like padding. But despite these glaring issues, they paint a pretty picture as the story itself is very endearing.It would've been fine if the game lined the missions better. Instead, you're told you have to do X big task, but before then, you have to complete dozens of little errands and just all around annoying tasks. I felt overwhelmed and just wanted to get it over with...Another thing that greatly tested my patience was combat. It's a real chore.There's a clear lack of variety when compared to other entries, which isn't a problem really.But the combat AI is rubbish. Enemies guard 4 times out of 5, so it mostly becomes a patience game. And don't get me started on the Boss fights.It takes the fun out of it completely.All in all, the story is captivating enough to keep you going. But seriously, be patient with it, and DON'T bother playing in hard on your first run. Especially if you just want to breeze through it.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Yakuza 0, 1 Kiwami, 2 Kiwami and 7 before going into Yakuza 3, and it was really hard getting used to the older graphics and gameplay. However, after giving it a chance, I grew to love this installment too.The fighting is probably the worst I've experienced until now, with the enemies blocking almost everything you throw at them. Even the blunt weapons seem super ineffective. I tried playing in hard mode, but this aspect was so frustrating that I had to change to normal mode. But as you level up and get better equipment, it becomes a lot more manageable. The real strong point of this game is the story. The orphanage setting is very easy to relate too, and is much more personal than a purely political story. It still has a fair amount of politics, but the main goal is clear and simple: protect the orphanage. In conclusion, I recommend the game, but be aware that if you're playing this after playing the remakes or the newer installments, there'll be a lot of outdated stuff  you will  have to get used to.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr I found the combat boring and the title of "remaster" questionable. Story dragged often, but I didn't necessarily dislike it. Also, this game suffers from a critical shortage of Majima.GAMEPLAY: What you've likely read before (either now or back in 2009) is correct; enemies block like absolute champions for 80% of each fight. It is relatively simple to get around this, but I hope you find the idea of constantly grabbing and throwing each enemy in an encounter over and over until their health bar depletes entertaining, because that's one of the only reliable methods of doing so for a considerable chunk of the game. Perhaps it's more bearable on lower difficulties, but there's no way I'm bothering to test that.Yes, you can also do the good ol' Yakuza shuffle and quickstep around behind them while they're attacking you, or parry them, or Tiger Drop them if you're feeling SPICY... if you can get them to attack at all. Even in large groups of 5-6 enemies, it was not uncommon for them to circle around me, turtle up, then do nothing for 20+ seconds, even if I provoked them. Hell, even some bosses did this during their fights, which is just absurd. Those fights devolved into sitting around and Tiger Dropping them when they deigned to attack me once every 30 seconds until done. And if you can't get them to attack, what do you do? Throw them. Kiryu should really follow Taichi into professional wrestling.By far the worst part of combat are all the Yakuza 3 zombies that show up and start chanting "lol skill issue" whenever someone just points out that combat that relies entirely on exploiting broken game mechanics and INTENTIONALLY WHIFFING 90% OF A COMBO SO YOU CAN LAND A HIT is objectively bad. Nobody said it couldn't be beaten, it's just annoying to do it.REMASTER(?): I also have some issues with the "remaster" itself. Namely some half-assed censorship, removal of licensed songs (sasuga SEGA), and pre-rendered cinematics of LOWER QUALITY THAN THE ORIGINAL PS3 VERSION FROM 2009. Most of that can be "fixed" by replacing relevant game files, but that only makes me wonder what part of this "remaster" I paid for is actually remastered.STORY: I liked the bits involving the orphanage and Okinawa in general, but they often overstayed their welcome and started dragging on. Beyond that, it's Yakuza.MAJIMA: I'm 100% serious about the Majima shortage. That is all.This is a 2009 PS3 title. Some of this was to be expected. But I'm not touching this one again on future replays of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered breathes new life into the original game, offering an emotionally resonant story as Kazuma Kiryu balances his role as an orphanage director with the complexities of the Yakuza world. The remaster features improved graphics and gameplay mechanics, enhancing the experience while retaining the engaging combat and rich side content that fans love. Set against the picturesque backdrop of Okinawa, the game introduces a refreshing atmosphere compared to Kamurocho. However, pacing issues and some dated mechanics can detract from the experience, making certain segments feel drawn out or repetitive. Despite these flaws, Yakuza 3 Remastered is a worthwhile experience for fans and newcomers alike, showcasing the series' signature storytelling and character development.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get the deal of this part being "bad". The only reason why you would consider this bad is because it is between remakes and newer, refined parts of the series. Story - Awesome. Honestly, it felt much more emotional than even story of first Yakuza, especially near the end. The drive to get to the end was superb.Music - It's still great. Of course, it's not as varied as in newer parts, but it is still great.Combat - This is a bit divisive, but once i got a hang of it, i did enjoy the combat greatly, because it was actually quite interactive. Spamming moves got you nowhere, and concepts of fighting games like wiffing, punishing, spacing - everything worked here. And it was great, once everything clicked.Also heat actions were great, and even though they aren't varied, i did enjoy repeatedly inserting thugs faces into cement.The only thing i can warn about this... Are technical issues. For like 3/4 of the game i played it perfectly normal, and after that, all hell broke lose. From frame drops, through freezing, until actual crashing. It took several tries of fine-tinkering settings just to actually pass through the game without pulling my hair out. i still got occasional freezes, sadly.In the end though, once technical problems are through and done, i can recommend it to anyone who played earlier parts of Yakuza. It's great. As for people who don't...What are you doing here? Back to Yakuza 0, Yakuza Kiwami and Yakuza Kiwami 2 with you!

_childDocuments_.review: In short:If you are here because you are playing through the series. Yeah, play this game.If you are here for any other reason. Do not play this game.I started playing the series from Zero onwards and 3 was a definite low point. Even on easy the game is sometimes obnoxious combat wise. The story itself is frankly really bad compared to the others. Even Yakuza Kiwami 1 beats out 3 in my opinion and Kiwami 1 is honestly a rather sloppy story. There are multiple extremely long diversions with the various children in the story which serves great to characterize them, but it destroys the pacing. Not to mention the fact that the game LOVES to make story quests not have markers so you have to comb the city for the location of the kid before you can continue. Completion list doesn't provide in game benefits which really destroys motivation to do it when the minigames are about the same as they were the last 3 titles (though I bet back in the day they were a step up from Yakuza 2).There are a few good story moments. The finale is not terribly good in my opinion. Highlight of the game is the hilarious american voice actor for Andre and the random adjectives the game puts on everything you get from a street fight.I recommend throwing it on easy and blasting through it as fast as possible, stopping only to do the karaoke songs once. 4 is much better so far.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Yakuza after playing the previous games, this one is a no brainer. However, it'd old and you'll notice that. This game has issues, and pretty bad and annoying ones. This game's combat and random encounters are some of the most annoying in Yakuza. Enemies block constantly and early boss battles can drag on for what feels like forever, and it really gets boring. However, in Chapter 5 you can finally do Komaki's training, if you find it that is. It's not obvious to unlock, and can be easily missed if you don't do substories. I found it at chapter 6, which was after a boss battle that almost made me quit the game. I mean it when I say Komaki's training is necessary to even being able to enjoy the game.The story really carries this game, it has some of the most interesting characters so far in Yakuza, and with that a lot of wasted potential. I'd probably rank it below 0 and Kiwami, but definitely better than 2.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the Yakuza series, and this game isn't terrible, but it is a let down from Kiwami 2. Kiwami 2 has beautiful graphics, fighting was great, storyline was good. But in this one, the graphics and lighting are flat and dull and the mechanics are all weird - meaning the fighting is bad (the enemies just block practically all the time and your hits barely make a dent, even with heat), the way you walk and especially the way Haruka (+ people in gen) walks looks silly, loading screens for fights and entering and leaving a building, not to mention it always looks you're moving in slow motion or running the way you do when you're in a dream. The game starts off super slow too. It's a nice change of scenery being in Okinawa, almost like a slice-of life game which I wouldn't mind if it were at the end, but it's almost a pain to get through the beginning. And the cut-scenes are also SO LONG. It'll be a cutscene, then the cutscene will end but it'll just be a tap-though conversation, and then ANOTHER cutscene. I easily sat through like a 20 minute scene in chapter 5 or 6. I'm going to play through for the sake of the story and it being a part of the series, but it doesn't feel like it has the same intensity as the previous 3 games.

_childDocuments_.review: 🗾Yakuza 3 is the only entry in the series so far which definitely doesn't deserve the 😍 rating. It wouldn't be fair to call this game  or  or what have you – it still delivers a unique Yakuza experience and it's really good in its own way, but it falls short in just  crucial areas which are way too important to be overlooked. Since I'd like to end this review on a positive note, let's get all the bad stuff out of the way first – we don't really have a lot to talk about here, just the  and .You can also read what I had to say about , , and  here.🀄Since you've played at least 2 Yakuza games before this one, you know very well how important minigames are in this fictional universe. They offer a welcome distraction from a hectic pace of an intricate criminal drama, a much-needed comic relief among a three-ring circus of neverending schemes, murders and betrayals. Unfortunately, in this iteration of the franchise, they sucked most minigames completely dry of all the fun that made them so great and memorable.🀄Bowling has messed up pin physics; they feel like they're made of paper and constantly clip through each other and never fall when they're supposed to. Darts is still broken, much like in 0 and Kiwami, but also has absolutely insane completion requirements. Karaoke, my favourite minigame of all time, has such substandard interface and unsatisfying mechanics that I didn't enjoy it at all; Kiryu also sings literally 1 short song and that's it. Balls in pool feel weird and change trajectory seemingly at random. Batting seems ridiculously unfair with extremely short reaction times required from the player. UFO Catcher is the worst one yet. And they even ruined the most sacred minigame of all – Hostess Maker. It went from one of the most engaging side activities to a dreadful snoozefest. I mean, should I even continue? You get the gist.🀄One could argue that of course Yakuza 3 is gonna have worse physics – it's a much older game than Kiwami 2, so what am I talking about? True, but many issues that I've listed above have nothing to do with when the game came out. It's just bad design choices. 🀄You can still have fun with fishing, gambling, and maybe even mahjong if you're a masochist like me, but the overall impression is tarnished nonetheless. So, minigames suck, okay, but the main plot has to be good then, right?Right, but sadly, 🎭What if I told you that at the very beginning of the game, when things just start to get interesting and you're ready to be immersed in a typical yakuza storyline, the game's pacing is brought to a screeching halt, and for several hours you're forced to deal with boring kid problems – this boy gets bullied at school, this one is allergic to buckwheat, someone had their pocket money stolen, yadda yadda yadda. So, when in previous games you've already done 10 years in prison, foiled several assassination attempts and are now in the middle of a clan war, here you've taught some kids how to say sorry and be brave. I mean, it's not bad per se and I welcome this change as it shows us how Kiryu is developing as a person, but good Lord above, this thing is sooo... looong... and tedious...  when you need to complete the game several times to unlock the Legend difficulty. 🎭Moreover, imagine that you have a 30-minute cutscene in your game (I'm not even kidding) with some guy telling you about all important plot details, who is who and what everyone's motivation is. This is so unbelievably lazy; it's creative writing at its worst. Don't just  me what kind of person everyone is and what they want –  me! You might not actually  as much as you can , but there's no need to lay all cards on the table – stop chewing my food for me, I can arrive at my own conclusions and I don't need anyone sitting me down and going,  I love Yakuza cutscenes and I think many of them are brilliant, but this 30-minute slog had me yawning and begging for the torture to end.  ⭐To be honest, if you start playing right after completing Kiwami 2, you'll have a hard time getting used to how old this game looks and feels. Gone are the glorious ragdoll physics and K textures; despite that, Yakuza 3 can still be gorgeous in its own ways – there was neither a sandy beach in previous games nor a breathtaking view of the night sky full of bright stars – and it still has a solid gameplay foundation that will keep you from getting bored. Unless you're stuck in the middle of a neverending cutscene, that is...⭐There are a whopping  (!) substories – almost twice as many as in other games, and they are really –  – riveting and imaginative. At some point you even solve a murder case, Agatha Christie style. Just be careful not to start too many substories at the same time – this may prevent other side activities from working properly, and you'll be stuck in what I call a Vicious Substory Loop of Death. While researching how to get out of this, I accidentally saw some pretty heavy spoilers. So, just finish any substory that you start and then move to another one if you wanna be safe.⭐The music is as great as ever – that's definitely something this franchise will seemingly never stop delivering on. Isn't it just  you've ever heard? Simple, yet elegant and melancholic. It gave the Agatha Christie substory that special push to make it even more emotional.⭐Have I mentioned that there's finally a new city to get lost in? Since we already know both Kamurocho and Sotenbori inside and out, having a new place to explore was a much-needed breath of fresh Okinawan air. It's kinda small though, maybe half the size of Kamurocho, but I don't think it matters that much. You'll be learning a lot about people living in Okinawa, their language, customs and outlook on life in general. ⭐There are many other things I could cover here, like Revelations, chases, levelling and combat systems, Ultimate Matches, et cetera; however, I don't want you to know absolutely everything before you start. It's always good to go in somewhat blind and let yourself be shocked (in a good way) – Yakuza is the perfect franchise to have your jaw dropped or your thighs slapped in an uncontrollable fit of laughter. Have fun!P.S. A completionist would naturally find that it's too late to stop now, having already perfected three games before this one, but I feel obliged to say it anyway – Yakuza 3 will be absolutely  to anyone who strives to achieve 100% completion. It's head and shoulders above all other entries in the series simply because of all the broken minigames. However, take heart – if I did it, you can, too!

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered is the remastered version of the original Yakuza 3 (2009 in Japan and 2010 for North America), which was originally released to PlayStation 3. The PC version was released in January 2021 as part of the Yakuza 3-5 Remastered Trilogy pack. The story takes place in 2007 and 2009, after the events of Yakuza Kiwami 2 (or Yakuza 2) of which the Tojo Clan held out from collapsing and survived an all-out gang warfare against the Omi Alliance. Daigo Dojima became chairman of the Tojo Clan, but an internal conflict started to brew. Yakuza 3 takes a stark contrast than its predecessors, leaning on heavy character developments and interactions, extending to cinematic story structures, cutscenes, and different environments. Is Yakuza 3 worth playing?Yakuza 3 and the remastered version aged the worst of all the titles releases so far. It’s not a negative, but in comparison to other titles, the game engine didn’t age well. The graphics were only upscaled from the PS3-era graphics to its modern standards. There shouldn’t be an issue for anyone to max out the PC settings. However, the environment, audio immersion, and game soundtrack are great and outstanding. Notable examples are the soundtrack like Fly, Aqua Sky, Clay Doll on the Cradle, and among others are top notch and notable. The composer, Hidenori Shoji (and the RGG audio team), has done an outstanding job. As mentioned in the introduction, the environment is different than its predecessors. Most of the story takes place in Okinawa, where the main character, Kiryu Kazuma, runs the Morning Glory Orphanage with his adoptive daughter, Haruka Sawamura. Many found the story pacing in Yakuza 3 as slow, boring, and/or unnecessary. However, I found it impressive, because the Okinawa setting gives deeper character development for Kiryu as a father figure for not just Haruka, but other orphans. A true, ideal masculine figure not just on responsibilities of being like a father figure, but also for selfless reasons in various situations. Additionally, I like Haruka Sawamura’s character growth in Yakuza 3 as she becomes mature and became the eldest sister figure to the other orphans. Those are the strengths in Yakuza 3. Yakuza 3 does have good and underappreciated strengths, but there are disadvantages, and few negative attributes need to be considered. The substories in Yakuza 3 are the most in all the series, but most of these were fetch quests and tends to drag. As much as I like the story in the game, I do find some plot elements a bit out of place when it involves an outside party. I won’t spoil it any further. The combat in Yakuza 3 is stiff and janky. There were arguments from the community, stating Yakuza 3 should get an “Kiwami” treatment. I agree. If Yakuza 3 gets a “Kiwami” remake with revamped combat and enhanced graphical environments, especially for Okinawa, that’ll be perfect. Yakuza 3 Remastered is certainly an anomaly compared to the other titles in the series because of the story pacing, different approach on the story – character development heavy, and extensive cinematic cutscenes. Most of the community didn’t like Yakuza 3 for a variety of reasons, and it’s fair. Yakuza 3 is a diamond in the rough. The combat gameplay and story can feel draggy at times, but Kiryu Kazuma’s character development growth, Okinawa setting and orphanage storyline, and overall plot blossomed. An underappreciated title to the series. Recommended but reservations on the negatives.

_childDocuments_.review: Stunlocked for almost 3 years. I played the 2nd worst game of their series (Infinite Wealth 1) and thought I needed a refresher and came back to the game yesterday and while this is by far, the most annoying downgrade (especially after Kiwami 2 which had fixed some of the issues of Kiwami).If you look around all across the series, why does Yakuza 3 sucks so much? Graphic wise, it's poorly remastered, it's also a hit in the face to go from a fighting system where there was a fluidity to this rigid fighting style. Weapons are very important but also very boring. They tend to make the fighting extremely easy. They are also extremely expensive to repair. But in this game, there's a early stage of what the weapon system of Like a Dragon is. The inventory is the most realistic to its own demise. Going to a M Convenient store would normally be: I buy and max everything including tissues by the time you're mid game. Now you have to be super careful with the balance of your gear taking a spot, your weapons, also taking a spot and finally your potion/food/booze where you're basically left with roughly 12 spots total The Levelling is kind of annoying; without leaving previous methodology (Body, Soul, Heat, Tech), it's gotten to the point where you have a limited choice blocked by the leveling you get. You're also limited to the fights you get in the street. They are scattered around and respawn once in a  while; no hard grinding of that way. The Carabet game is a very diluted version of their previous iterations. No Easy money, no easy grind for Items or Weapons. You need to be careful with your spending and how you waste your item otherwise the grind is insufferable. The games are also different. Dart which is usually super fun is awful on this one. The fishing is very hard and extremely annoying. There's some solid points though; it feels like a lot of themes are touched which are pretty taboo (in the classic style of Yakuza being one of the most progressive Japanese game), the substories have substance, decent writing and overall feels right at home. Some are however extremely subpart but from from the LaD IW, it's not as bad! In fact, I would say that it's a strong counterpart after naming all the negatives. There's a turning point in all Yakuza game; If you grind enough, you'll be able to reach a point - regardless where you're at in the game - where things runs smoothly. There's mainly due to the training master + doing all sub stories, abusing the coliseum fights. Not here. You need to be in perma heat otherwise you're incredibly weak. You're stuck blocking as the avoiding moves are very clunky and rigid. You're only able to cheese boss fight with weapons because they lost NO fluidity and you're sometime better running away rather than avoiding while locked on the enemy. As a result this game is an easy skip for the game play but not for the story which - compare to some other hater - I feel held on pretty well.It's at this spot in Kazuma's life where he's in his early 40's and he's as out of the Yakuza and he'll be until - of course - getting back in to protect/avenge somebody. Those moment throughout the series is the sole reason I've resolved to continuing and finishing the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Another day, another Yakuza game.I was actually pretty nervous about this one given the fact it has the lowest steam score and videos online give the impression that this is the weakest game in the series.After playing it all the way through per usual, I can confirm this as true, however its not a bad game. It's a perfectly serviceable Yakuza title, but its one that suffers from feeling like a filler episode with its awkward pacing and piss-poor gameplay changes.It's the shortest Yakuza game yet, taking me around 15 hours to finish even with side content added into the mix. The actual plot of the game doesn't really kick off until you're about halfway through and because of this, the actual plot feels like it goes by at a lightning pace compared to previous titles.At this point the formula is feeling pretty predictable and nothing happens that you aren't already expecting to. It has its moments, but this mostly felt like a filler story that could've been cut out entirely and not much would've changed.As for the gameplay changes, it basically feels like the worst parts of Kiwami amplified. The regular fights feel like for the most part, but the bosses can take way longer than they should due to overly large health bars and the fact that they block almost every single attack type in the game. Heat takes a stupid amount of time to build up unless you're under the alcohol buff, so you need to become a straight up alcoholic if you want to use your heat consistently. The progression system feels weak and restrictive, leading to a very stop-start style of progression rather than natural growth. It's probably the easiest Yakuza game, but the fights are also probably the most tedious. Not to mention that they halved the evade's effective distance, making it basically useless in all combat.The substories this time around are mostly incredibly short check-list quests that don't offer much additional meaningful gameplay this time around.I could go on for a while, but truth be told, its just a very weak entry. My stance is that I would recommend playing it through one time if you're a fan of the series, but its definitely not an entry I would be revisiting.It just barely gets a positive rating out of me simply because I never felt like putting it down during my playtime, but at the same time, its the least special of the Yakuza games so far.

_childDocuments_.review: For context, I'm writing this review from the perspective of someone starting with Yakuza 0 and playing through the series chronologically. I've played 0, Kiwami, Kiwami 2, and now, 3 Remastered. This is the most dated game out of the Yakuza PC ports, and it shows. The graphics are a little jarring at first, however they will grow on you, especially if you've played other PS3 era games.The levelling system is very linear and the combat feels very restricting. Enemies block way too many attacks, which makes a lot of fights feel frustrating. Admittedly, I can't speak for how the Komaki moves affect combat because I completely missed him, however, I blame this on another flaw of the game. Unlike the more modern games/remakes, Yakuza 3 is lacking in incentives to engage with optional content. In the other games mentioned above, various events will interrupt your flow to entice you to do substories, play minigames, etc. Additionally, Yakuza 0's dual protagonists system creates a mild sense of FOMO for progressing the main story without doing side content while you have the chance (without making it too punishing). Yakuza 3 has nothing of the sort, and some of the side content is pretty well hidden in areas you mightn't think to check as you've already fully explored Kamurocho in 2-3 games by this point.This game's biggest redeeming quality is it's story. While the story isn't the best, the contents of the story are brilliant and it is a vital part of Kiryu's character growth. There are also some legendary moments, including one of the most emotional scenes in the series so far.My review may seem quite negative, but I'm reccomending it because, despite its flaws I still enjoyed it, and it is essential for anyone who wants the experience of playing through the whole series chronologically. If you decide not to play it, you should at least watch the cutscenes on Youtube.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're getting into this game in particular, chances are you came straight from Kiwami 2. Unfortunately, this is a huge downgrade in comparison on loads of levels.For this "Remaster", the game can now run at 60 FPS compared to the original PS3's 30, they restored some content, and removed & censored some other things because of dumb social norms. There's also the case of NPC & music changes, but that's more a licensing issue.Because the game can now run at 60 FPS, supposedly some gameplay aspects have been affected. The only one I've noticed is that Kiryu's basic quickstep dodging's become less effective as a result, and you need a patch to restore its usefulness, or set the game to 30 FPS.This game takes place directly after the events of the second game, as the game starts off with reminiscing about the ending of the last game, and even the first game before it.The story is that Kiryu's running an orphanage all the way out in the countryside, but is being told to move out and then gets threatened because he doesn't want to. It's a story that's full of "this is why all this is actually happening" that keeps proving previous answers wrong.The plot itself is fine, but its pacing is pretty bad. One minute you're progressing the main plot, but then all of a sudden you have to spend 10-30 minutes with the kids you're taking care of, which almost never have actually anything to do with the main plot itself. Getting to know each of the orphans in the home is fine and all, but these moments keep breaking the pace of the actual story.They did some "re-translating" for this game, as in really "localized" it as opposed to direct translations for loads of places. It's one thing to completely change a joke or phrase due to not translating well to another language, or giving a group of people a familiar-to-westerners dialect in English because it'd be the best way to show how Japan's countryside people talk, but when you can clearly hear them say "オラ" (ora) or "そ" (so) and then the subtitles show something completely different like whole sentences for those single sounds, that's going really hard on the liberty-taking. One of the worst examples I found is when someone is supposed to say "are they okay?" (大丈夫なのか...?) (daijobuna no ka), but instead the subtitles say "love is a magical thing..." Because of this, during the text-based cutscenes namely, I can't tell when characters are being obnoxious in how they talk or if the "translators" are just having too much fun seemingly rewriting the script.Supposedly this kind of thing is present in all the """Remasters""".The combat in this game is broken.Enemies have loads of animations where they just outright become immune to grabs and basic attacks to the point where they only have so many safe moments for you to be able to land any actual attack, making you constantly wait for certain enemy animations to start or end just so an attack of yours can register properly.Half of the Heat Action trigger requirements are way too strict, and this port being un-optimized forces you to press buttons for QTE moments twice because the first press won't always register.Don't play on Hard mode or later, because there, all enemies block almost all the time the moment you press a second attack, and you have to resort to AI exploitation  just so you can hurt them at all, as opposed to proper skillful play or having fun in general. Playing on Normal or lower doesn't have these have these specific annoyances, but the lower difficulties become way too easy due to the enemies not being as aggressive or even mildly defensive.In addition to all that, this port in general is busted, and there's supposedly no Denuvo to blame for it either.There are loads of frame skipping when there are too many movable objects on the field.The game frequently crashes upon finishing a fight with a Heat Action, which is supposed to have been fixed via an official patch but it still occurred frequently until I used a fan-patch that  mitigated it.Despite the pacing issue, its story is actually relatively short, but still pretty interesting if you were into the previous games' plots.The substories are mostly short themselves, but they're still charming.If you just absolutely feel like you have to experience the series first-hand, then go play it I guess, but this port & "remaster" kind of sucks as well as the game itself not being as great.

_childDocuments_.review: Y3 does a poor job of balancing the serious Yakuza drama with the Daddy-Kiryu narrative. The conflict behind the serious-Yakuza drama is very weak, with a main baddy who is more confused than malicious. Poor major conflict aside, the supporting cast that round out the Okinawa location are fantastic. Rikiya is a fantastic alt-take on Nishiki and the kids are a lovable bunch that often lead to funny story threads. Combat is fine. There's only one fighting style, the skill tree is frustratingly spoon fed to you in such a way that you can't quite tell how each thread branches out. I felt the random combat encounters were more prevalent this time around. You'll still get frustrating by the enemies blocking your attacks, or how they magically track your dodges. TLDR: Daddy-Kiryu is fantastic, the serious-Yakuza drama that pulls him back to Kamurocho is half-baked. The heart and charm you expect from the series is fully intact. A solid entry in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried so hard to enjoy this game, and went into it with an open mind, despite all the hate it gets recently. While the writing is admirably subtle at some points and staples of the franchise are introduced in this game, I cannot recommend it to fans of the franchise. This game deserves a complete overhaul and remaster. Game design and objectives are poorly conveyed, the minimap experiences glitches, frame drops during sidestep, but don't even get me started on the combat... This game breaks the mold of the action genre in the worst way possible, practically punishing the player for trying to execute basic three step combos, or even more advanced ones. Kiryu's progression system is dramatically downgraded in all sorts of ways from previous chronological entries, which would be forgivable if other jrpgs such as Final Fantasy 10 hadn't already figured out more nuanced systems 7-8 years prior. Character models are ugly, substories are basic, pacing is conducted poorly, and the mandatory minigames are extremely unfun. Going back to story, the events of Y1, Y2, alongside their Kiwami counterparts are almost disgracefully disregarded, completely removing important characters the moment the game starts, a huge disrespect to the more nuanced writing of previous titles, might has well have taken the three out. This game made me put it down only 5 hours in, and if you ever wanna try it, wait for a Kiwami 3. Overall: 2.5/10
