_childDocuments_.review: [Spoiler-free review]Above anything else, the biggest thing to know about Yakuza 3 Remastered is that, unlike the previous Yakuza games available on Steam; Yakuza Kiwami and Yakuza Kiwami 2, which are remakes of the original Yakuza 1 and 2, Yakuza 3 Remastered is effectively a direct port of the PlayStation 3 version with minor graphical upgrades. If somebody was coming from the original PlayStation 2 versions of Yakuza 1 and Yakuza 2, this game would be considered a significant upgrade in nearly every way, but obviously the vast majority of people these days will be coming to Yakuza 3 directly from Kiwami and Kiwami 2 as I did. This means that the consistency is quite off; you're playing a much older game, and it shows.I went into Yakuza 3 Remastered knowing this ahead of time, and it rightfully feels like a significant downgrade coming directly from the much more modern Kiwami 2 engine. The combat controls feel quite stiff and not as free-form, which tends to make fights a bit frustrating and more difficult than they need to be, especially in the early game when you are weaker and don't have access to many Heat actions, recovery items, weapons, or upgrades.The graphics themselves have clearly been cleaned up and remastered for the PC release, and are decent enough given the origin is a PlayStation 3 game from 2009. The environments are nice and bright, and lighting effects, especially with neon signs at nighttime, are as pretty as they always are in Yakuza games. One small complaint I have regarding the remastered visuals is that, while it appears some of the story cutscenes were quite well-remastered for this release and look amazing, others appear to have been left completely untouched from the PS3 version, with somewhat-grainy and low-quality video. I'm not sure why this was done, but it seemed to only be like that for cutscenes with many things going on at once or very large environments. Given this is the most modern way to experience Yakuza 3 right now, it would have been nice if all the cutscenes in the game received the same remastered treatment.I don't go into specific story details in my reviews for the sake of avoiding spoilers for those that are interested in the game, but I will say that the story is very enjoyable. I can't say it is quite as good as the previous chronological games, Yakuza 0, 1, and 2, but it is still very good and beyond a worthy addition to the Kiryu saga of Yakuza games.As far as the PC port and optimization goes, I never noticed any issues. Just like Kiwami 1 and 2, the game is very well optimized and ran perfectly on my system. As always, I give Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio a massive thumbs up for adding PlayStation button prompts for DualShock 4 controllers through Steam, even in this release of an older game. It's a small thing but it's really nice for many parts of the games to have proper PlayStation button prompts, rather than the generic Xbox-style button prompts most games display.Unlike the previous games, I admit I didn't really get invested in a lot of the sidegames in this release, as I didn't find them as engaging. But even so I very much enjoyed Yakuza 3 Remastered, and having got it on a very good sale for less than $10 CAD, I will say it was more than worth the purchase price.That said, in the future, I'd like to see Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio give the proper Kiwami remake treatment to Yakuza 3 and 4, as out of the entire Yakuza series, 3 and 4 are the only ones with very dated PC ports originating from the PlayStation 3 versions. I think it would really breathe new life into these games and complete the entire Kiryu saga experience in a more consistent, modern feel for players.

_childDocuments_.review: Four? Yes, four. Fourth Yakuza game in the franchise that I managed to 100% and lord, was this game a doozy. It took me almost 66 hours to fully 100% this game, which from what I've heard and seen from other people, is still quite quickly in terms of getting all the achievements and all the completion points in this game. How was the game however? Let's find out.The game begins right where Yakuza 2/Kiwami 2 left off. Kazuma Kiryu had defeated the Jingweon Mafia and survived the supposed bombing that the Mafia had placed at the end of the game. Where the game starts is the same as Yakuza Kiwami 2, with a recap in text at the graveyard. Now with gravestone of Yukio Terada as well. Explaining to Kaoru Sayama Kazuma Kiryu has decided to go to Okinawa to care for the Morning Glory Orphanage. Two years went by when the story picks up, with a new resort and military base wanting to claim parts of Okinawa, under which Kiryu's orphanage is part of. Once more Kazuma Kiryu is forced to take to action, in order to protect what he holds dear. His children and the orphanage.One of the biggest pros that Yakuza 3 has to me, is the more slice of life feel that you have in between gripping, dark and gritty story beats within the franchise. Caring for the children, of which there are nine in total, each with their own personality. Not to mention some minigames that, in my opinion are better in these games. The fishing mini-game in Yakuza 0 was okay, but I enjoyed the sea fishing in Yakuza 3 a lot more. I enjoyed the actual more realistic approach of fishing, with tension, slack, etc. I also liked the addition of the Golf Course. It was a lot of fun to play Golf, and wish it was brought back in Yakuza 0 and Yakuza Kiwami. And wish it was the same way in Yakuza Kiwami 2. And lastly the Heat moves. Oh gosh, some of the heat moves were so much fun to see and perform. My personal favorite in this game has to be the Essence of Smoking. I wish that they had this Heat move in all of the Yakuza games, past and coming to be, because it's to me one of the biggest 'badass' moment in there.Let's start with the obvious con here for Yakuza 3. It's combat. Coming from previous games like Yakuza 0 and Kiwami/Kiwami 2 you can tell that this game feels aged in terms of its combat. The controls are clunky at times, and don't feel as fluid as it did in the previous games. And of course the amount the enemy blocks in this game is tremendously bad. It's why people have made mods such as the Quickstep Restoration and No More Blockuza 3 to make the combat feel better and less annoying. And I played the game fully with the No More Blockuza 3 after playing it for the first four chapters. And I'll admit with the mod, the game was more fun to me. Another big issue I have is what a certain achievement that almost made me unable to 100% this game. Which is the Exposed Dragon achievement. Now, I'm not a master at Mahjong, but I can get most of the completion points. Did so in Yakuza 0 too. But why make an achievement that's based a lot on luck? I got it, with some help, but it was an annoying achievement to get.When looking at what score to give Yakuza 3 I looked at the story elements, the gameplay and the minigames. And all in all, I don't see this game as a bad game. Yes, there are flaws, but in terms of when it was released as a sequel to Yakuza 2. Overall I'd give this a solid 7.5/10. It's not as great as Yakuza 0 or Yakuza Kiwami 2, but I would say this is on equal footing as Yakuza Kiwami at least. Some of the new Heat moves are great. And I thoroughly enjoyed some of the minigames that Yakuza 3 had introduced to the franchise. And most of the completion list stuff wasn't very difficult to get in my opinion. The only achievement that was a pain was the Exposed Dragon one, but they learned from it when it came to Yakuza 4.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered is the third installment in the series with a nice number of updates and additional content. This is the first of the 3 games that has received fairly minor changes in contrast to 1 and 2 which got the full remake treatment. There are definitely flaws that make this hard to recommend as “My First Yakuza” game, but for fans of the series, it is a nice entry worth playing.    The Tojo clan is still reeling from its losses from its war with the Go-Ryu clan and Omi Alliance. The game opens up with Kiryu running an orphanage when he learns that his aniki Rikiya’s boss after he has been shot. Cut to Chairman Dojima Daigo, driving to a meeting to discuss “the Okinawa deal.” He calls it off despite the caller’s payments being the only thing keeping the Tojo clan running. He cites that the land acquisition of Kiryu’s orphanage is wrong as it is the only place where Kiryu belongs after all he has done for the clan. Daigo returns to Tojo HQ but is faced with the assumed-dead Kazama Shintaro and an unknown foreigner. Kazama urges him to go through with the plan, but Daigo stands resolute- Kazama shoots him. Kiryu, learns the identity of the man who shot Rikiya’s boss via witness sketch. It is none other than his deceased father, Kazama Shintaro. The rest of the game follows Kiryu’s life as a father figure in Okinawa and a former Tojo clan member seeking the truth. Overall, playing as the Dragon of Dad-jima is really wholesome, but the first 4 chapters are almost entirely about being a dad and having to deal with your 9 orphans. There are certainly sweet moments, like comforting a girl who is insecure and sad about not having a family.Overall, the beginning is VERY slow as a result; being shown the intense mystery as the opening cutscene then having to be a dad for a while is definitely strange pacing. Likewise, you will continue having to deal with dad stuff throughout the story, some arcs dragging on longer than they should and being obvious filler until the next plot point can drop.The actual Yakuza plot is pretty good, focusing on stopping an internal coup d'etat as Daigo is in critical condition, figuring out how Kiryu’s orphanage is wrapped up in all of this, how Kazama is still living, and more. Overall, I was satisfied with the story in its 12 playable chapters. However, I feel that the main story could’ve been stronger if the dad stuff were trimmed a bit. As a Japanese crime drama, expect a lot of exposition, trope-y monologues, fights and cutscenes.    The Remastered edition has added back some cut substories. I do not know which ones were added back, but there are definitely ones that are more involved with greater story elements and player involvement. Others are pretty standard sidequest fare and can be completed easily. Overall, the fairly low ratio of engaging ones to typical ones made me start skipping them around chapter 8-ish despite the good rewards. Combat is largely the same as the original 1 and 2. New to this game are “Revelations” which are flashes of insight Kiryu gains from finding specified NPCs, passing a brief QTE segment and coming to a correct conclusion via multiple-choice to learn a new move. These are really useful and quite powerful, further rounding out Kiryu’s abilities. One major annoyance in fights is that enemies, including bosses, LOVE to block. You can break guards with upgraded combos, spamming grab attacks and striking them from behind. However, the issue is that the passive AI slows the game's flow conisderably. Likewise, Kiryu has counters but passive enemies means you will have to either continuously bait an attack or wait for them to attack. The end result is a rather clunky and annoying combat system that functions but doesn’t feel as gratifying as other entries. Bosses are much more aggressive but them blocking makes encounters much more tense and the fights feel more realistic, as it should be. Purportedly, this issue is due to the jump from the PS2 to PS3. The game also has chase scenes where you are forced to follow/ catch/ run away from an NPC. You and your target have a stamina gauge that depletes over time; slamming into objects or people causes you to lose stamina and speed. If your target gets too far away, you fail. This is used pretty often but I didn’t particularly care for them. The game got an upgrade to its resolution and framerate. Overall, things definitely look nice but some textures easily show their age and look low-res or weird. The game goes for a realistic take on locations and does an excellent job recreating their real-life counterparts. Kamurocho is a dense, bustling nightlife city and Okinawa is a peaceful, small island city with a beautiful beachfront.  Overall, character models are good for the main cast. Animations are overall pretty good. Fights feel great when the enemy actually fight back and Kiryu definitely has weight behind his moves. There are a few weird animations that stick out and some clipping, but it doesn’t majorly detract from the experience.     The only real issue are the pre-rendered cutscenes which were directly copied from the PS3 version. They have a lot of compression artifacting and jaggies. Some also seem to dip in FPS sometimes despite setting the game to 60fps.   Overall, the soundtrack for the game is great. The mix of rock and some pop for encounters gets you feeling ready to tussle against thugs. Boss encounters are super tense and energetic with bombastic tracks. Slower and tender moments are impactful with softer instrumentals and tense situations more serious. Sound effects were pretty good. Combat sounded fantastic with meaty blows. General SFX were good.   As a Remaster, the game performed well with no significant issues. However, there is definitely a lot of pop-in and some z-fighting. Likewise, 60 FPS hurts sometimes. In cutscenes, clothing sometimes begins vibrating at a fast rate or an object may start vibrating in the background. Certain objects start to continuously bounce in the background of fights as well, making the associated SFX play each item it does. These were mostly nuisances and I was able to overlook them. As mentioned before, the higher-res textures and framerate feel really good. The additional substories are nice and the more involved ones have nice story beats. Side quests are now marked on the map like with modern entries. The quiz on Japanese history was removed from international releases and some translation issues were smoothed over as well. Yakuza 3 is a nice follow-up to 2 but doesn’t hit the same highs story-wise due to an emphasis on being a dad and all the mundane busywork that comes with it. The crime plot is much more interesting but has to fight for screentime with the orphans, leading to some weird pacing issues. Nonetheless, the overall story is interesting. Gameplay is good but the passive enemies leads to frustration at times. The HD treatment looks good despite some age still showing, especially at a higher framerate. Music is great as expected from the series. The remaster tweaks are also really nice. Overall, I definitely think this is an entry that is worth playing but please temper your expectations going in.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR;If you're interested in the story, just watch a youtube video. If you're deadset on playing it for yourself, put it on easy mode and just burn through the mainstory. DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME ON HARD MODE. You cannot change the difficulty once the game has started, and this game's combat is unbelievably bad. It is hard to fathom just how bad it is if you are coming from 0, Kiwami 1 and 2. I refuse to believe there was any kind of a QA process with the combat. There is no way human beings were sat down to test this game and would have had anything positive to say about it.As a port, it's mostly fine, I've only had the game crash once. As a game, Yakuza 3 is absolutely terrible. I can't even give it a pass for being an old game because it's just that bad. Enemies block constantly, they become immune to grabs (and some enemies are just permanently immune to grabs), when they're not blocking many of their attacks are fully invincible, bosses literally cheat the system with no recovery on their attacks, infinite dodges, they whiff moves and then go invincible so you can't hit them and even if you do hit them, they either block immediately so you only get one hit or they just armor through and hit you back. The only way to make combat tolerable is to bring weapons and try to spam heat actions to cheese it. I really can't say enough bad things about just how bad the combat is in this game. It sours the entire game for me, by the time I'm done slogging through the awful combat I don't even really care what happens in the cutscene.The revelation system for learning new moves is awful, it's a QTE where if you miss any of the QTE's, you still have to watch the whole cutscene (which is unskippable) so that you fail and then have to go find a place to enter and exit so you reload the area to try again. If you succeed at the QTE, you have to guess between 3 dialogue options and if you choose wrong, you fail and have to reload the area and watch the entire cutscene and do the QTE again and god help you if you choose wrong a second time.Seriously, just watch someone else do a playthrough or find a youtube video that just has all the cutscenes because this game is complete trash.

_childDocuments_.review: Come on, Kiryu! The Tojo clan needs your help once again. But wait! Don't get too excited. All in mandatory story scenes.It's like they took some amusing substories and made them part of the main plot. I'm referring to chapter 4 in a 12 chapter game meaning about a third of the entire thing is dedicated to what is essentially a very long introduction.The extremely slowly paced intro wouldn't be too bad by itself, but combined with the severe drop in visuals, and quality of life features makes it all feel very tedious and clunky. Technically the oldest Yakuza game available on modern systems and it shows. Combat is slow, minigames are made up of too many menu screens, and you're often given objectives with no hints or sense of direction. They don't call it Blockuza 3 for nothing as boss fights feel like they take 10 minutes at times. If you do manage to break their guard it's up again instantly and most of them resist grabs. It's very tedious.If you play this one I'd recommend you go for a story only run on easy mode; just get it done and move on.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be blunt so please bear with me here- at first, I HATED Yakuza 3. As a new fan of the RGG series, jumping into Yakuza 3 was a REAL shock to the system. After playing through Yakuza 0, Kiwami, and Kiwami 2, I had gotten used to the more modern remasters; polished graphics, smooth gameplay, refined combat, and immersive minigames. So when I fired up Yakuza 3, I felt like I had stepped back in time... 8 years back to be exact. The jump from the remastered brilliance of the previous games to the much older and less polished look of Yakuza 3 was jarring to say the least. I couldn’t believe how much of a downgrade everything felt.The graphics were rough, the combat clunky, and the controls felt stiff compared to the fluidity of the more modern games. Even the minigames, which I usually enjoy, felt lacking in comparison. I couldn't play them at all aside for the fishing. And honestly? At first, I hated it. It felt like I was forcing myself through a relic of the past, and I kept wondering if it was worth it. I wasn’t sure if I could power through, but I’m so glad I did because once the story started to unfold... everything changed.What Yakuza 3 lacks in modern polish, it more than makes up for with its heart. The story had me hooked and I ended up growing to love the game because of it. In a way, it felt like the game forced me to love it. As rough as the gameplay is, the depth and emotional weight of the narrative grabbed me in a way I wasn’t expecting.This game focuses on Kiryu in a new way. We get to see him in a more mature light, stepping away from the chaos of Kamurocho (though not entirely) and trying to build a life of peace. Watching Kiryu grow into this more reflective version of himself, someone who finally sees the value in leaning on others and embracing relationships, was honestly beautiful. The emotional weight of his journey felt so real, and for the second time in the series, I found myself crying my eyes out. The game touches on themes of family, loyalty, and personal growth in ways that feel so... genuine. I could feel Kiryu’s emotions, his struggles, his hopes, and his quiet strength- and that’s what makes the game unforgettable.Beyond Kiryu, the cast of characters in Yakuza 3 is what truly elevates this game. Rikiya and Mikio are two of the most lovable characters I’ve come across in the series, and brought so much heart and charm to it. Rikiya, especially, is such a shining presence... a tough but warm-hearted guy who looks up to Kiryu like a brother-- sorry, ANIKI. His bond with Kiryu is incredibly touching, and I found myself rooting for him every step of the way. These characters TRULY make Okinawa feel like more than just a setting; it’s a living, breathing place full of people you grow to care about. And then there’s the Morning Glory Orphanage. The kids at the orphanage, each with their own little personalities, are impossible not to love. Watching Kiryu take on this father figure role is heartwarming, and the way the game emphasizes the importance of family, both blood-related and chosen, is one of its greatest strengths. Every interaction with these kids feels meaningful, and it's reminding you why Kiryu is such a compelling and multi-dimensional character. He's a fighter, sure, but he's also a man with a heart full of love and responsibility.Even returning characters like Date, Majima, and Daigo have their moments. Date’s loyalty and friendship with Kiryu remain as steadfast as ever. He’s a character I ALWAYS love seeing, and his role in this game feels like a natural continuation of the bond he’s built with Kiryu over the years. Majima, with his wild unpredictability, shows a different side here too- but I won't go into detail as to not spoil the game for you. And Daigo, well... without spoiling anything, let’s just say his presence is important and adds more layers to the story.The game also does an AMAZING job of making you care about the smaller stories. The sub-stories, while sometimes quirky and offbeat, feel super grounded in the world of Yakuza 3. You find yourself invested not just in the main plot, but in the lives of the people around you- helping a hopeless couple (yet again), resolving disputes between friends, or taking random pictures for Kiryu's silly internet blog. Yes, that is a thing.Now, I have to be super honest- the gameplay itself never really grew on me. The combat remains clunky throughout the game, and the controls feel stiff, especially coming off of the later games. The lack of polish in those areas makes it hard to recommend Yakuza 3 purely for the gameplay, but I would recommend it without hesitation for the story alone. The narrative is what truly carries this game, and if you can look past the dated mechanics, you’ll find a story full of heart, growth, and incredible character moments.Would I recommend it?... Absolutely. If you started the series, you absolutely have to play it. Even though I struggled with the gameplay, the story is unforgettable, and the characters will stay with me for a long time. Will I come back to it? Probably not, but I heard that many people did, and that's great for them. So, in conclusion... Yakuza 3 is a flawed gem, but if you give it the time, it will show you a side of Kiryu- and the world around him- that is incredibly touching and real. It’s not perfect... but it’s beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: A begrudging upvote from me since I love the Yakuza series. I have only played 0, Kiwami 1 and 2 and this one is the worst.The story is ok, but the pacing is very slow since you need to do many quests for your kids (ie, the dad simulator jokes). They are typically boring comprising of 'finding a person/thing' or fetch quests. More plot holes in the main story than in the prior titles, but overall interesting.Combat is uninspiring as you only have one style so you are basically doing the same combo the entire game. As you level up you'll get some quick time event triggers that add in an additional attack but generally still the same thing. The counter attacks are back and still quite powerful, but the timing windows are much shorter and too unreliable to use consistently. Most of the boss battles are just dodging/blocking their attacks and trying to get behind them to punch them with your single combo.Achievement hunters should skip this game since they have made them very mini-game centric. You have always needed to do them for 100%, but over a quarter of the achievements are directly linked to games in this one. The menus are sluggish so you waste a ton of time waiting for the AI to roll dice, or whatever else. To compound the issue, the port has some issues so some games are super speed (ie, fishing) and others have messed up physics. Overall a huge test of patience. It seems like if you are really dedicated it you could 100% in 70-80 hours, but over half of your time would be doing mini-games and mundane repetitive tasks.I'm glad I played Yakuza 0 first since that is a masterpiece and got me sucked into the series. If I started with 3 I would have skipped the rest of the series since it is only an 'ok' game. Still has Kiyru so I'll give it a 6.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: I only played as far as chapter 5 and my experience is based on hard mode Yakuza 3 is a truly miserable experience. Every single review talking about how each and every enemy in the game blocks every single one of your attacks from the front is true. And their blocking ability is pretty much absolute. Can't break that. But Yakuza fans will probably tell you to just get good and quickstep around enemies so that you can attack their backs. Too bad that the quickstep in this game moves you about a millimeter to the side while locking you into its animation for about a second and thus is incredibly ineffective. And even if you manage to hit a boss in the back in this game, Kiryus damage output is pathetic. His attacks truly just tickle bosses in this game and he has never felt this weak."But have you tried grabbing the enemies?" Sure, while that is a way to deal with the constant blocking, it doesn't improve the gameplay. If the optimal way to play a game is to staple a dipping bird toy to a specific button on my controller, I'd rather not play the game at all.Okay, so the combat is terrible but if you are playing the Yakuza series, chances are, you are probably here to experience the story. Well, I've got bad news. Even that isn't very exciting. Some new and likeable characters get introduced in this part of the series but if they only get used to retread the same old plot threads from previous games, meshed together in a very slightly different way than the last time around, then their potential as characters is just getting wasted.I really liked the Yakuza series up until now and even learned Mahjong to be able to deal with its minigames, but this game made me want to stop playing the series and maybe return to it at a later point since it just does not feel good to play and experience at all. Sure it is old. Sure the newer parts are better. But I am an old guy who has played a lot of old games and enjoyed them. I just really don't enjoy playing this one.

The game is a bit old, animations are ankward sometimes and the textures of some faces are low quality but the story and quests are still as good as previous games and its worth to do this game if you're a fan of the series.Score : 7/10Pros :-Good story with a lot of great characters. The start is a bit slow but the story ramps up fast.-A lot of interesting quests and some of them are very funny like always in a yakuza game. The new hitman missions got a bit of a story behind them and are entertaining.I didnt touch any minigames except if i need to do them for some sidequests. You can easily counter the "block moves" bosses and bigger ennemies do by going behind them or Tiger drop with the right timing like the previous games.Negatives :-The textures in cinematics (not the pre-rendered ones) are better than during gameplay for no reason.-It's slower to travel in general : Kiryu run slower than in previous yakuza games and there are only 3 taxis stop in Kamurocho.-Inventory is very limited : you cant stack items.-Its hard to avoid combat in the streets compared to others games.- The "hotess maker minigame" is a letdown compared to 0 and K2 and the cabaret minigame is a bit too long.

_childDocuments_.review: Prior to the game being released on PC, I heard negative things about Yakuza 3. After playing it myself I can confirm that the game is indeed the weakest Main Yakuza title out of them all. Is it a bad game though and should you just skip it? Its still a damn Yakuza game! You get to kick ass, sing karaoke, enjoy a great story and listen to amazing music tracks! The main problem with Yakuza 3 is its weak first chapters where the game drags on and on with the story and makes you bored outta your mind. I'm pretty tolerant when it comes to Yakuza games and still I found myself rushing and skimming through the story quickly during the starting chapters, particularly in Okinawa. The substories are also a letdown and the side content is not as interesting as you'd expect. Side stuff is a lot more grindy here. They're not bad, they're just average compared to other Yakuza games.However, after a couple of chapters, the story definitely picks up and makes you interested again. You get great twists n' turns and characters become a lot more interesting. The game is also tough as nails which I really liked, especially after playing Yakuza Kiwami 2 where the difficulty, even on highest is a joke and even an autistic infant with severe brain injury can beat that game.

Thank god I did, those games are great!But yeah... if this game is becoming a slog for you, just skip it.Try to play it if you like, but if it's becoming too painful, don't be afraid to quit.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the weakest installments in the Yakuza franchise, but it holds up decently today. While the story was hard to wrap my head around at times, I loved it overall. The combat is very underwhelming though. It doesn't try anything new, and the age of the game makes it a clunky mess. I also found 100%ing this game to be extremely unfun. For context I've 100% all the previous installments, and while being slightly tedious I didn't hate doing it. Yakuza 3 was a pain to 100% for many reasons, but the biggest reason being the repetition of the same task over and over again (ex: the environmentalist achievement and the cabaret minigame).6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Admittedly Yakuza 3 isn't the greatest game in the series, especially if we compare it to 0 (which I try not too)  but I still enjoyed a large percentage of it -the orphanage stuff is ok, and I know it's part of Kiryu's life, I'm just not a kid person so I found that aspect of it a bit boring, although it is sweet seeing the big 'scary' Dragon of Dojima interact with his kids!Despite it looking and feeling a tad dated, (those graphics are a little funky, and the fighting/controls feels off for most of it), it's still a fun game to play and the side quests and mini games really help to flesh it out nicely, along with giving it that wacky charm we know and love from the series. I've completed the main story (and hoo boy did I cry at that ending) and I still have a lot left to complete, so it's definitely got plenty of hours worth of game time to it.I'd say if anyone is considering playing number 3, go for it if you can get it when it's on sale (or in the bundle like I did) but it's not really necessary to play it in order to understand the series as a whole, it's just nice to add it to the collection I guess!I mean seeing Majima is a big plus so, you could buy it just for that <3

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered. You will notice the graphics is out dated compared to the other series from Yakuza 0 , Kiwami 1, 2 and so forth from 4, 5 and 6.  Its gameplay is not as good either.  So now that I've gotten the negative out of the way, the story however is the reason to play through this game. _childDocuments_.review: I can see why this wasn't received well when it first released on the PS3, it's like you're playing two different games, one is about a guy running an orphanage and helping the kids out who live there with their daily problems, and the other is a Yakuza game where you beat the f*ck out of everyone to get what you want.There is a new city in this, Okinawa which i appreciated after being stuck mostly in Kamurocho in the previous games, which is still in the game also. The two locations add to the tonal imbalance in the story, with the babysitting gameplay kept to Okinawa where your orphanage is located, and most of the super serious traditional Yakuza story is kept in Kamurocho, so it has you flying between the two as the story progresses.Is this the worst Yakuza game? so far from the one's i've played it is, the combat is really boring with all the enemies you encounter blocking your moves which makes the fights tedious. I played it on easy mode because i heard about how bad it was, once you level up your character and unlock new moves it becomes better, but i'd recommend playing the game on easy like i did so you don't get frustrated by it.Also all the mini games are either bad or broken in this, i hated them all, with pool and darts being the worst i tried. This seems to have something to do with running the game at 60fps, if you lock it to 30fps you might have more luck with them, but the game is 12 years old now so don't expect much from any of them.All that said... the game is actually better than i thought it would be lol i heard it was really bad, if you just focus on the main story and sub stories it's ok, just don't mess around with the mini games.

_childDocuments_.review: Had lots of fun with this one. Dated combat and infamous exposition dump scene aside, I had fun with the story and gameplay. Gameplay-wise, I'd argue the combat in 3 is better than Kiwami 2 because at least Kiryu doesn't feel sluggish and awkward.  Kiryu's movements feel fluid and powerful. The people who complain about blocking forget that the grab and evade buttons exist. The bigger issue was how little damage you do against certain bosses, which made those fights last longer than necessary.Story-wise, 3 is easily the most emotionally impactful up to that point, I cried multiple times. I will admit, yes, as a crime drama it is far from perfect. It's clear that the writer for this game knew nothing about Yakuza, or at least not as much as the writer for 0, 1, and 2. But many of the characters have a great emotional core. I'd say this game absolutely shines when it focuses on what I believe to be its core theme: found family. People say if you were to skip any game it'd be this one, and I disagree. Even as someone who doesn't really LOVE children, the kids in this game are really well-written and, to me, are what make the whole experience so special. All of the emotions flood back to me whenever Morning Glory is mentioned or shown in later entries, which speaks to how much this game got me invested into it.This game deserves better than to be known as "the game where enemies block a lot." Real Yakuza use a gamepad and play Yakuza 3.

_childDocuments_.review: So many people call this the worst one of the series, and in my opinion if this game is the worst that the Yakuza series has to offer, then it's actually a good thing. So first off, let me just say that this game is definitely not as bad as a lot of people may lead you to believe. I do agree that it's the worst one, and I'll get into the flaws later. But no way in hell is this game a skip.One thing is for sure, I really do wish this was Yakuza Kiwami 3. The main problem with this game is that it suffers from being the "revolutionary" game in the series. It was the first game making the jump to the PS3, and it did a whole lot of stuff for the first time ever. The minigames that are one of the most iconic parts of the series? Yep, started in this game. The problem is that you can tell that these are very early, unpolished minigames. Honestly I was pretty disappointed when I saw like 8 karaoke songs, and only 1 you sing yourself. I've heard all sorts of complaints about the mechanics in other games such as pool, I didn't try them myself but keep that in mind. Long story short, remaking this game and modernizing all of its side game mechanics would've helped a lot.Now about the most controversial part of the game, the combat. It doesn't seem all that bad, up until you get to boss fights. At that point it's such a slog, you hit for no damage, the boss doesn't even hit that hard either. Yeah there will be a lot of blocking from the enemies. Regular/non boss fights are still the same fun as before, but maybe avoid the coliseum as they follow the same boss fight damage properties. The upgrade system is bang average, not bad but I think that it lacks the efficient/not totally unbearable exp grind that Kiwami had in Majima Everywhere. Honestly revelations are pretty cool and a funny way to get surprisingly useful moves. Onto the story. One of the issues I had with this game was how long the filler orphanage sections were. The first 4 (!) chapters are almost entirely spent doing mindless chores in Okinawa. Then, when the plot and conflict start to heat up, you get smacked in the face with another random filler section. Ignore those parts and I actually really enjoyed this story. The new characters introduced such as the Ryudo people are great. Yoshitaka Mine is probably my favorite villain of the series so far, his character is just really dope and I like the integrity and respect that makes him stand out from some of the other bad guys in this series. One thing though, without getting too spoilery, the last scene makes absolutely no sense. At all. It's like the writers wanted to have some shock value in the story but realized that the conflict is supposed to be over, so they took some shots and then wrote whatever came to mind. Serves no purpose to the story, just leave you incredibly confused as the credits roll.Anyways, I'd still recommend this game to those of you playing along through the series like I am. It's alright to play it like how I did, speeding through and skipping almost everything besides the main story. Usually I like to go through at least maybe 50-70% of the substories but knowing that this is the worst game I didn't. For one last note, get tiger drop as fast as you can. This is the game where it's easiest to land, you can get it relatively quick, and overall just makes the boss fights a lot more bearable. Don't let other people convince you this game is unplayable, it's honestly really overhated.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 is good, but has flaws.The combat is just infuriating with very little variation at this stage of the game (around 10 hours in despite what play time states mostly due to afk'ing a little and also losing a save file)The lack of styles or moves and slow progression to unlock more makes combat a task. Enemies block 95% of your hits before finally letting their guard down for a light attack. Normal enemies can just be throw around as a way around this but bosses and even just heavy thugs are a chore. The only difficulty in this game is remembering to stock up on healing items a after any mini-boss.That being said I still recommend this game as the story is pretty good (definitely a Dad simulator but shows a softer side to Kiryu which makes sense within the story) and it has the classic Yakuza humour and dumb side-quests which are typically the highlights of the series. As suggested by others, play through this on a lower difficulty to absorb the story and move onto 4.EDIT: Finished the game and wow did that feel like chore. Combat never gets better and the only difficulty in fights is trying to escape attacks that seek onto you and combo you down to the floor. Awful combat but story is good.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 is a weird game to recommend, not because its bad, but becaise its tecnically the oldest of the franchise available to play.If you played this right after finishing 0 to Kiwami 2, you will notice how mechanically dated the gameplay feels, since most of the quality of life improvements still have to happen and the gameplay feels stiff and simple.Kiryu moveset is very basic and pretty much every goon can be dealt with button mashing. The combat lacks the stance system from 0 and Kiwami and lacks the dynamic system from Kiwami 2 to become interesting.Punches lack weight and you are mostly repeating the same 4 combos over and over and over.It can still have a few satisfying moments, but you will want to go back to the other games.Bosses on the other hand are annoying since they mostly play the same: block every attack, immunity to throws, can attack immediately after blocking and usually have a counter attack that always hits you before you can dodge or counter.As soon you get Tiger Drop, most bosses turn into a joke. Punch them twice so they counter, then Tiger Drop.There is still a bunch of minigames scattered, but there is little to no reason to do them. Kiryu also moves at a fast walk at most, so getting around gets a bit annoying, even worse that enemies can't be seen on the minimap and instead stay still on several spots around the map, so avoiding fights is a pain since you have to go into other streets since most places are far too tight for you to maneuver.The Hostess minigame makes a return, or better yet, its debut. Its very rough, boring and takes a lot of time for almost no payoff.All you do is go back and forth two rooms about three times, just paying attention on 3 lines of dialogue and then changing the hostess clothes a bit. It gets boring really fast.Talking about the minimap, some substories don't show at all until you stumble upon them. I have found a few of them during the last chapter because I never had to enter most buildings.The story is ok. Not bad, but nothing to write about, there is some plot and twists to keep you invested, but overall it feels rather weak after 2.Characters come and go, deaths seem to happen only so there is some drama and eventually the plot barely matters at the end. Even the twist they do right at the end gets resolved post credits, so there was no point.The story feels pretty short, since half of it is Kiryu taking care of his kids.The 60fps improvement of the remaster also brought a few problems, since a few things were tied to frame rate, the quickstep distance is halved and button prompts require you to mash way too fast, causing some counters to be basically impossible and the "Feel the heat" moments not charging fast enough.Some mods are available to fix the quickstep problem at least.Music is still very good, "D 2 A" was so out of place that it became one of my favorite songs of the franchise. There is no song at "Receive you the madtype" levels, but that one is on a tier of its own.Overall, not a bad game like I said, but the wrinkles of time are very apparent on this game and unless you keep in mind that this is basically the mecanically oldest game in Steam, it will feel like a letdown.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 Remastered : By Triple F“Yakuza 3 Remastered” is a definitive version of the third installment in the beloved Yakuza series, which follows Kazuma Kiryu, a former yakuza turned orphanage owner, as he navigates both family life and his violent past. Originally released in 2009 for the PlayStation 3, Yakuza 3 marked a shift in tone for the series, bringing more personal stakes to Kiryu’s life as he tried to leave behind the world of crime. The remastered version retains the story’s emotional depth while improving visual fidelity and performance, offering fans of the series a polished look at Kiryu’s quieter yet deeply impactful journey. While it shows its age in some design aspects, “Yakuza 3 Remastered” remains a compelling chapter in the saga.The story of “Yakuza 3 Remastered” picks up with Kazuma Kiryu running the Morning Glory Orphanage in Okinawa, far from the crime-ridden streets of Kamurocho. For the first time, players see Kiryu in a parental role, responsible for raising the children in his care while managing the orphanage’s financial struggles. However, his quiet life is disrupted by political conflicts involving the Japanese government, real estate developers, and yakuza factions, all seeking control over Okinawa for their own agendas. Kiryu is forced to protect his new family, fighting against powerful enemies who threaten the lives of those he loves. This duality of peaceful family life and intense yakuza drama makes the narrative uniquely compelling, showcasing Kiryu’s softer side while emphasizing the sacrifices he must make to protect those he cares about.The game’s setting is split between Okinawa and Kamurocho, both of which are meticulously crafted and distinct in atmosphere. Okinawa, with its sunny beaches and rural charm, contrasts sharply with the neon-lit, chaotic Kamurocho, reflecting Kiryu’s conflicting lives as a family man and former yakuza. The remaster has enhanced these environments with improved textures and resolution, making them feel more vibrant and detailed. Although the visuals aren’t as polished as recent Yakuza entries like Yakuza Kiwami 2, the remaster’s graphical improvements make the cities visually pleasing, with character models and animations that feel smoother than in the original.Combat in “Yakuza 3 Remastered” retains the series’ signature beat-‘em-up style, with Kiryu using an array of punches, kicks, grabs, and environmental attacks. While combat may feel clunky by modern standards, it is still satisfying and challenging. Kiryu’s moveset includes his signature Heat Actions, powerful finishers that are flashy and brutal, allowing players to use objects in the environment to deal devastating damage to foes. Although the combat lacks some of the fluidity introduced in later titles, it maintains a visceral appeal that rewards players for mastering Kiryu’s fighting style. However, some players may find the random encounter rate high, which can become repetitive during exploration.One of the game’s standout features is the depth of side activities and mini-games, a hallmark of the Yakuza series. In Okinawa, players can spend time with the orphans, each of whom has unique challenges and personal quests that Kiryu can help resolve, adding a layer of warmth to the game. Kamurocho offers a wide variety of mini-games, from golf and karaoke to arcade games and host club management. These side activities provide a fun diversion from the main story and flesh out the world, giving players the freedom to immerse themselves in the life of a retired yakuza. While some mini-games feel dated, they add to the charm and depth of the experience.The remaster also includes previously cut content from the original Western release, such as certain side missions and mini-games that were omitted due to localization constraints. This version restores these elements, giving players a more complete experience of Yakuza 3. Although these additions may seem small, they contribute to the game’s authenticity and help build a fuller world, making it more comparable to the original Japanese release. Fans of the series will appreciate these details, as they add to the nostalgia of revisiting Kiryu’s story with minimal content loss.“Yakuza 3 Remastered” delivers a memorable and fitting soundtrack that enhances the game’s emotional and action-packed moments. From the serene, gentle music that plays in Okinawa to the intense, rock-driven tracks that underscore battles, the soundtrack adds depth to every scene. The voice acting, delivered in Japanese with English subtitles, brings life to each character, with Kiryu’s calm and stoic demeanor contrasting against the flamboyant personalities of the supporting cast. This commitment to strong audio production creates a rich atmosphere and helps players feel invested in Kiryu’s journey.Ultimately, “Yakuza 3 Remastered” is a heartfelt and intense entry in the Yakuza series that explores Kiryu’s struggle to balance family life with his yakuza past. While it may not have the mechanical polish or visual quality of newer installments, it shines in its storytelling, character development, and immersive world. The restored content, detailed environments, and wide variety of activities make it a worthwhile experience for fans and newcomers alike. For those willing to embrace some of its dated mechanics, “Yakuza 3 Remastered” offers a touching, complex story that captures the essence of the series and further develops Kiryu as one of gaming’s most beloved protagonists.

_childDocuments_.review: This entry should be a nobrainer if you like the Yakuza storyline. However, this being a faithful remaster, it does pose a different kind of experience to the more modern experience that was present in Yakuza 0, Kiwami 1 & 2. While I haven't played 4 & 5 as of writing this review, I have the suspicion that 3 is the low point of the series overall. Even with that said, it's worth playing if you're into these games. My main gripe is definitely the combat - enemies are way too efficient when it comes to blocking (and dodging, in some cases). The combat itself isn't all that varied, but in a true Yakuza fashion, heat actions and comboing enemies to oblivion (when they don't parry everything) feels satisfying as it should. I found the story to be serviceable, but not the most memorable around. Activities and substories are good fun overall.Overall, it's definitely a product of it's time, just like a true remasters are - but with fresh paint on top. All the issues can be circumvented in a way or another. You can learn to accept, maybe even love the game's flaws as they are.... Except the hostess maker minigame, which boring AF. If you're not doing a completionist run, avoid it. The rewards and the gameplay loop are trash.

_childDocuments_.review: As a  of the Yakuza series, I was thrilled to dive into Yakuza 3 Remastered and relive the adventures of Kiryu Kazuma once again. However, while the game certainly had its strengths, it also had some noticeable weaknesses that dampened the overall experience.Let's start with the positives. Yakuza 3 Remastered delivers an engrossing narrative, packed with compelling characters and intense moments. The story takes players on an emotional rollercoaster, exploring the depths of Kiryu's past and his struggles with the Yakuza lifestyle. The remastered visuals breathe new life into the game, making Kamurocho and Okinawa vibrant and immersive. The attention to detail is commendable, and the world feels alive with its bustling streets and intricate shops.However, the game falls short in certain aspects, particularly the combat system. While Yakuza titles are known for their brawling action, Yakuza 3 Remastered's combat can be . The enemies seem to have an unfair advantage, often blocking your attacks indefinitely, leading to a repetitive and dull experience. It's disappointing when you want to unleash Kiryu's full power but are met with relentless blocking.Another drawback that impacted my enjoyment was the abundance of filler content. While side activities have always been a part of the Yakuza games, Yakuza 3 Remastered takes it to another level. There were numerous times when I felt these filler moments dragged on for too long, disrupting the pacing of the main story. As a fan, I felt compelled to push through, but it did detract from the overall experience.That said, despite its flaws, I would still recommend Yakuza 3 Remastered, but with a specific audience in mind: . If you're a fan of the series and eager to delve deeper into the lore, Yakuza 3 Remastered provides valuable insights into Kiryu's past and the world of Yakuza. However, I wouldn't recommend playing this game casually or as an introduction to the series.In conclusion, Yakuza 3 Remastered is a mixed bag for fans. It excels in storytelling and visual enhancements, but falters in its combat system and the excessive filler content. If you're a devoted fan seeking more Yakuza goodness, this remastered version is worth exploring, but be prepared to endure some frustrations along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 is finally on PC, and it’s the fourth game in the Yakuza franchise chronologically.  However, it is now the most dated for the franchise.  Where Yakuza 0 was released in 2015 for the Playstation 4, and Yakuza Kiwami and Kiwami 2 were remade in 2016, and 2017 and also released for the Playstation 4, Yakuza 3 was originally released in 2009 and for the Playstation 3. The version on PC, Ps4, and Xbox One is the remastered version, which has all sorts of bells and whistles fans would expect.  There is a higher graphic fidelity and more standardized 1080p resolution. There is also content that was cut from the original English version that has been restored, and a retranslation that removes important mistranslations. I bring this up not to just enumerate the changes, but to dive into the big issue with Yakuza 3.  Yakuza 3 is a remaster.  While it has a large amount of additional content and gameplay, this is ultimately a PS3 game with a slight graphical upgrade.  Where the previous Yakuza games are beautiful, Yakuza 3 is dated by the simple fact that this game originally was made for the PS3.  While the graphics have been rescaled for larger resolutions, they still look weak.  There’s something off with how the scaling happened, which can make the main character, Kiryu, a little wider than he should be, and it’s become a noticeable issue, to the point memes have been made out of it. Having the original game based on the Ps3 version of the game also makes the character models noticeably weaker.  That’s not to say Yakuza 3 is a horrible game, as the PS3 still had a lot of graphical prowess, but while I normally skip talking about graphics this is particularly jarring when coming from the previous three games in the series.At the same time, Yakuza games are packed with content to the point that graphics don’t matter as much and the core of the Yakuza story will always be what matters.  If someone was to make Yakuza 2’s amazing story and couple it with these graphics it would be almost as enjoyable.Yakuza 3’s story on the other hand is more of a struggle.  Yakuza 3 starts with a flash-forward showing two major shootings, and then without telling players what is up, the game jumps back a year.  This is the same issue that happened in Yakuza Kiwami, and while there’s only one major time jump in Yakuza 3 it’s a jarring one, though perhaps it was to alert fans to expect that  Yakuza 3’s story will eventually include the Tojo Clan, along with the current chairman, Daigo Dojima.In practice, this is a strange moment that doesn’t fit with the game, though its need is clear when the opening chapters of Yakuza 3 deal with the life of the retired Kiryu Kazuma.  After the events of Yakuza Kiwami 2, Kiryu is now running an orphanage in Okinawa and takes care of a large group of kids, including Haruka, from both of the previous Kiwami titles. The orphanage is a central part of Kiryu’s story, and the game takes a long time to develop the new character and laidback lifestyle.  Kiryu is no longer the big bad Yakuza, but rather just trying to live a civilian life, and while fighting random people is never that far away, it’s a very different opening and story. Some fans will dislike this, as the previous games were all about the seedy underbelly of life in a big city, and while Yakuza 3 does eventually reach that point, it takes a significant amount of time to reach it. Yet this is a strong way to develop a sequel that takes some risks with the already established characters.  Yakuza 3 shows the player a different life for Kiryu, and that experience is well developed and defined.  It’s clear how Kiryu has changed as a person. Eventually, those opening scenes catch up with the story about five hours in, and Kiryu is off to Tokyo… Except he’s not.   Yakuza 3 has serious pacing issues, and when Kiryu is planning to leave for Tokyo is a perfect example.  There is a critical and important reason Kiryu needs to leave immediately.  However, Kiryu will play baseball with his children, start to teach a dog a few tricks, and can go on an elongated side mission involving characters from the previous game.  All of this feels like a waste of time.  There was perhaps an hour or two between when Kiryu said he had to travel to Toyko and before the game would allow the player to go. While Yakuza games have the issue where players can wander off the main path to do side content, it’s Yakuza 3’s main story that has these issues with pacing.This becomes a common theme.  Major events are happening, yet Yakuza 3 decides some minor situation is more important.  Rushing to save someone’s life is delayed because spending time with Haruka is more important to the story.While the story in Yakuza 3 is poorly told, some concepts are interesting.  Many major story points in Yakuza 3 work.  The concept of life after being in a Yakuza family is interesting, and not only does Kiryu explore that but another group inside the game does as well.  The problem is Yakuza 3’s story isn’t as good as the core concepts are.  There are numerous jumps in logic, or outlandish actions, that just don’t make sense, and there’s a major mystery that is explained by logic that would better fit in with a soap opera, than a serious crime drama. I also have a slight issue with the ending of Yakuza 3, but without wishing to dive into spoilers, it’s not only terrible in hindsight but also terrible in execution. Yakuza 3 still contains the side content that the series is known for, and has multiple different mini-games, including fishing, an arcade shooter, golf, cabaret club,  and more.  There are over 100 side stories and a ton of content.   Many of the mini-games in Yakuza 3 are significantly harder than they should be or require multiple plays due to random number issues instead of an actual challenge. However the amount of content is still at the levels that will draw in fans of the series, and the side stories are often interesting, hilarious, and entertaining.  I found myself wandering off to tackle side stories whenever they appeared as they continued to be the most entertaining piece of Yakuza 3.But like always hiding behind everything else is the combat, as Yakuza 3 will eventually have a reason for Kiryu to fight enemies.  Whether it be in the main story, random encounter, or the resolution of a side story, there’s always someone who needs a beatdown.  There are two types of enemies in Yakuza 3.  The random thugs that players will find throughout the game are the typical fare for the Yakuza series.  A few swift attacks, and maybe a special move will knock them down in seconds and while players can be swarmed, a good solid strategy will win out most of the time. On the other hand, there are the “bosses” and I use that term to generally collect anyone who is given a similar style and a hard fight.  Yakuza 3’s style is to allow the “boss” enemies to block almost every attack.  The most egregious problem with the system is that “bosses” are allowed to block in the middle of a normal combo for Kiryu.  If Kiryu lands the first hit, there’s no guaranteed combo and the send hit will usually be blocked.The full review is available at  If you enjoyed this and want to see more from me, you can check out my youtube channel at

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who adores this series, I'll be honest, after the first few hours I eventually had to take a break from the game. The intro is nice and it all definitely has it's appeal/charm, but eventually I found it just got a bit tedious. Also, to address the elephant in the room, this is probably the worst that combat gets in the series.With all of that out of the way though, I would still absolutely recommend the game.While the combat may be a bit iffy — especially if you have just come from playing 0 or the Kiwami games — it doesn't take too long to get used too, and once you start to build up your collection of special moves and combos through levelling I'd argue it's not even an issue (and you can get to that point pretty early game trust me). For what it's worth I actually found myself really enjoying the combat as per usual once I had a few good moves in my arsenal.Also, if you happen to play this game and find yourself getting tired of running around doing errands in Okinawa, I heavily advise you to see it through a bit longer, as I myself happened to put the game down for almost a year just before finishing the intro section because I had gotten bored, but once I returned to it I felt like I was playing a whole new game. If you dislike the intro then don't worry, the game immediately increases in quality once it's done (and I mean immediately).In summary:- Please do play game, and while it may be a bit slower at first, it gets incredible pretty abruptly and early on.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: While it is the weaker game, I personally enjoyed Y3 more than Y0, YK, and YK2 for the following reasons; (ON HARD DIFFICULTY)+ Sound design and music is great and builds a nice grunge atmosphere  -> I have to give special props to the combat sounds, like the knuckle CRUNCH and the voice lines+ Combat is fun once you learn how to approach enemies+ Heat actions look and sound powerful (but aren't always actually impactful...)+ Story is intriguing and develops the main characters well+ No, the orphanage sections aren't horrible and are thematically appropriate for Kiryu+ Substories are plentiful and mostly involving and intriguing+ Enough fun side activities to lose yourself in+ Boss fights are (usually) great fun and a decent challenge+ Gameplay is shaken up every once in a while as to not become repetitive + Possibly the best final boss in the series next to Y2 and Y5+/- Story begins slowly and doesn't really pick up for a while (although I enjoyed the orphanage stuff above the crime)+/- Humor is sort of hit or miss and won't always land the joke well+/- Chase sequences - They can either be really fun or punishingly difficult (Especially without the comfy soles)+/- Game starts out pretty hard if you don't know what you're doing or used to the combat of newer entries- Performance is actually very intensive for some reason and may cause severe framedrops   -> SilentPatch will be very useful- Enemies are very aggressive, especially those with weapons and will cause a great many stunlocks- Blocking is not as bad as everyone says, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is it annoying  -> Komaki's many techniques are a lifesaver and will admittedly be the main ways to get through battles- Most heat actions are next to useless when used on bosses as they deal very little damage- I really f*cking hate the chapter 3 and chapter 8 bosses on NG. They just suck Overall, Yakuza 3 is a great game with some hard to ignore problems, but whatever they detract from the game is more than made up with its many positives. Arbitrary rating:★★★★★★★★★☆  - 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Although this is the weakest of the Yakuza games that I've played (Yakuza 0, Kiwami 1-2 and 6 on PS4 and Y:LAD on PC), it was still a great time, despite the rough edges. Even the weakest Yakuza game is still more worthy of your time than most games.When I finished Kiwami 2 over 2 years ago on PS4, I was very excited to play the next game in the series. So with the absence of any concrete news of a remake or even a remaster for Yakuza 3, I inevitably looked up some info on it out of curiosity. The point of this is, I knew what I was in for if I was going to play Yakuza 3. I knew it was going to be more rough than the Yakuza games I've experienced, considering it's way older and predates many quality of life improvements that were introduced over the series and eventually made it to Y0 and beyond.That said, I was pleasantly surprised with how it plays in a few key areas, while still acknowledging that it's really inferior in others. Something which felt incredibly natural to me was the combat. Although it's very restrictive and lacking options that would later make it to the future games, at its core it played in a very familiar way coming from 0 and K1, and I did not find any particular difficulty with it other than having to be more strict with your blocking\dodges. One tip I can give you to counter the enemies constantly blocking - the throw move is very powerful here, use it often.I played on Normal, of course, so I'm sure Hard mode brings its own issues, however what I wanted was to experience the story, and what's there was definitely playable and enjoyable.What makes this the weakest Yakuza to me though is substories and how they're managed. Substories is something I value no less than the main story in a Yakuza game and that's about the main thing to drag Y3 down for me.Substories are far less memorable, enjoyable, and engaging than they are in Y0 and the remakes of Y1 and 2. And sadly they're also very clumsy to keep track of. Where in Y0+ once you find a substory, you'll always have its objective markers showing on the map. In Y3 on the other hand, you'll have their starting point on the map, but once you discover them, you won't have any objective markers, and you'll need to scroll through your many completed\in-progress substories list in order to read their objectives and be reminded where you need to go and what you need to do, which makes completing them in bulk incredibly tedious.Speaking of tedium, traversal can get a touch exhausting as well, as there are way less taxies than what you'll come to expect if you're coming from Y0+. Less saving points too (Saving is handled like in Y0, only phonebooths and chapter endings)As for the story, which is often criticized for its notoriously slow intro - while I recognize that Y3's story has severe pacing issues, I still found it incredibly enjoyable, even the slow bits of it in the orphanage. I personally got invested in seeing more of this side of Kiryu as a father figure. And granted, yes, the story gets pretty crazy and stupid, even by Yakuza standards - it's the fun type of ridiculous, and that's a big part of the Yakuza experience.Now, as for the port itself. Something to keep in mind is that this is locked to 60fps. While it's a step down from the unlocked framerates of the other Yakuza ports, do keep in mind that this was a PS3 game which was locked to 30fps, and pushing the framerate beyond 60fps would introduce many issues. Even at 60fps, you can tell that some minigames are playing faster than they should, as they were originally made with 30fps in mind. Because of that I understand and have no issue with this being locked to 60, considering the game's age and the potential issues that would arise if gone further.That and 60fps is more than just "acceptable" for a Yakuza game, as it's not an intense first person shooter or anything like that.I noticed many people complain about massive slowdowns\framerate drops, which is something to keep in mind and test out before your 2 hour playtime mark - although I personally experienced no performance issues with the port whatsoever.I had no dips in framerates, no crashes, or any technical issue of note. You can choose between Playstation and Xbox controller prompts, no matter which controller you're using, which is handy. KBM prompts are also present, although it's not an ideal option for a Yakuza game, but that option's there if you want it.If you played Y0 and K1-2 and enjoyed them, give Y3 a go. Just keep in mind and mentally prepare yourself that this is a more rough version of what you've played.Adjust your expectations for something older than Y0, because that's what it is. Yakuza 3 is 6 years older than Y0 (JP releases).If you think you can handle that, you won't regret playing this, even if just for the main story. I haven't experienced any Yakuza game so far that I'd recommend skipping, and despite many undeniable flaws, Yakuza 3 is no exception.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam had a neutral review option because so much of Yakuza 3 leaves me asking..."why?".Combat is probably the worst iteration sans the PS2-era entries; punch, punch, kick is still the standard winning combo but this time around, enemies block EVERYTHING. Fights turn into slow, tedious meandering waiting to exploit an enemy whiffing their strike to get maybe one or two punches in before they default to a block again. This game is paced abysmally, probably the worst offender in the series. The actual game does not truly begin until Chapter 5; prior to that, you're playing the role of Dad Kiryu to the kids of the Sunshine orphanage with a few fights sprinkled in-between to keep you invested just enough to not put the game down.  From chapter 6 thereafter, the game picks up speed and pacing gets a lot better, only to slow to a crawl again in Chapter 10.  However, with that being said, chapters 11 and 12 are actually some of the best in the entire series and why I'm not giving this game a negative review outright: the final boss is one of the best of all the RGG Studio games (theme, gameplay, performance, barely blocks your attacks and actually fights you like a man) and the gauntlet of enemies you fight leading up to him is one of the more impressive out of all the games - even 0 which did them the best. A nitpick and sign of the times it released, but I hate having to pause the game to access the menu just to open the map. I'm spoiled by having the back button do that in 0, K1 and K2. Soundtrack is awesome, Sega Sound Team never really miss. If you play this, stick with it past those boring first few chapters because it does get much better. They serve their purpose to get you invested emotionally, but from a gameplay perspective they're the worst parts of the entire series for me and caused me to drop the game for four whole months before I came back to finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, Yakuza 3. The title that sparks debate amongst every Yakuza fan who has played the entire series. The title that first introduced the mold of the modern Yakuza game by adding karaoke among other extra minigames, the game that gave us the first dynamic intro in the history of Yakuza games, and the title that first employed the use of face capture to give us the iconic faces of Kiryu and Majima that we know of today. I'll start with the story. Story is overall really good or really bad depending on how you see the orphanage sections of the story. For context, you will spend entire chapters purely on taking care of the kids in Morning Glory and being a proper father figure to them. A lot of people have been complaining about how these specific parts of the story are dragging and completely uninteresting, but personally I actually love these parts. It shows us another part of Kiryu that's usually not too noticeable in the other games, his compassion. It's hard to imagine the same guy who was roughing up delinquents in the streets of Kamurocho cry over cut onions in a dish he's making for his kids. But the game gives us exactly that and further emphasizes that underneath that big, burly structure with a dragon tattoo, he's human and has emotions (ignoring his physical capabilities at least). Whether those sections are a big turn off for you or not, they did a pretty good job at delving deeper into the character that is Kazuma Kiryu. The characters that are introduced here are really fleshed out and the villains have a menacing aura that's unique to each one of them. The final boss is a very well done antithesis to Kiryu this time around (they even have opposing tattoos!).  is a work of art in terms of video game villains. My nitpicks about this would probably be how one villain was underutilized considering his introduction cutscene and another character that could have made Kiryu and Haruka grow even more was completely written off within the first chapter and shipped off to the Land of the Free. Other than that, story's as solid as the rest of the series.Now onto the most controversial part of the game, the combat. Now this is something that's undeniably a flaw in the game and it alone could and should warrant a Kiwami 3. I'm not sure about the lower difficulties but on Hard, everyone (AND I MEAN EVERYONE) has the reaction speed of a fly when it comes to blocking your moves. You quite literally cannot start an offensive against any enemy, even the common street thug, coz of that sole reason. To top it all off, they actually had to nerf the quickstep distance in order to keep up with the increased frame rates the Remastered collection gives (. Heat actions deal a lot less damage than it's supposed to. There's this one fight with budget Majima where he quicksteps 24/7, only stopping to attack you (real big pain tbh, I decided to give up the fight midway coz of that). Early game combat becomes a real bore real quick not gonna lie, thankfully once you unlock the 3 Komaki moves combat actually becomes decent enough to play through. There's also the underlying problem of the chase mechanic which is just as much of a sucker punch till you get the upgrades. Later titles at least made it a lot more enticing. Overall combat is pretty bad till you unlock the Komaki Parry, after that it becomes decent.Minigames and Substories can be pretty unpolished at times. This was where Karaoke was first introduced and frankly the songs are pretty forgettable. Fishing is a lot harder compared to later titles. Some of the substories aren't exactly worth doing at times and a lot of them are tied behind the minigames. There isn't exactly a "Be My Baby" one in terms of how much it stands out from the rest. They might have been eye catching back in 2009 when the game was first released, but now they pretty much pale in comparison to the rest of the series' substories. Graphics will be a major problem if you played Kiwami 2 before this, but you'll get used to it as it isn't that bad. Soundtrack is one of it's stronger points in terms of the experience. Still has traces of that grungeness that was prominent in the first 2 games so if you're not into distortioned guitars it will be a con for you (I'm loving it tho). Bottom line, they haven't exactly aged well but the music slaps. That's pretty much my take on the game known as Blocku- I mean, Yakuza 3. Sluggish combat paired with a very rich character-building story with a dash of outdated substories and karaoke. Some continuity errors will persist if you played Y:LAD first, but the experience can be slightly enjoyable once you get the hang of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 has a poor reputation, with many people saying to even skip the entry altogether. I think that while Yakuza 3 is dated, it is by no means bad, and should not be skipped. This entry is still solid despite its flaws, and I enjoyed it a lot even playing on Hard (which people apparently recommend not doing).I loved this game's story, and the characters are extremely well done. A really strong plot entry and I would say that I personally enjoyed this story more than Kiwami's. I adored the slice of life change of pace in the chapters before you really get thrown back into the Yakuza action. I really grew unexpectedly attached to the characters introduced in Okinawa, especially the Ryudo Family . Seeing Kiryu raise the children so gently and so kindly seriously just warmed my heart; I think it was a great segment through and through and not at all boring to play.The combat in this game is janky and dated. But even on Hard I didn't feel that there was too much difficulty getting through the game. Certain fights  were terrible, but generally nothing really walled me off. The combat is mostly difficult until you realize how to deal with the blocking. Utilize grabs liberally, install the Quickstep Mod to fix the broken quickstep in the remaster. When enemies start to get up from the ground and are on their knees, use square triangle triangle to combo them to the ground. And use Komaki Parry as much as you can as soon as you can get it. It's much better than Tiger Drop in this game, since Tiger Drop has a less generous window in my opinion. If you use everything in your arsenal, you can get through with relatively minor annoyances.Anyways, this game is really good in the story department, kind of jank in the combat department, but 100% worth playing. Seriously, DO NOT SKIP THIS GAME!
