_childDocuments_.review: Wow, really where do I begin, the story in this game is outstanding, as soon as you think you know what's going on this game chucks a twist right into the story line. The visuals in this game are like no other i've ever seen, And the gameplay just doesn't get boring at all! The 3 different chapters in this game were all incredible and the map usage in this game was so fun, getting to choose where to go to make a strategy work or to get better cards made Inscryption never feel old. The puzzles in this game were unique and having to play the game more just to get them really did rope me in, and gave me a feeling that I haven't felt from a game in a long time. All I can say is wow, this game is definitely going down as game of the year for me and is worth every cent you spend on it, do yourself a favour and buy this game while going in blind.

_childDocuments_.review: Non spoiler review: It's good, it's everything I could ever want from a game. go in blind and experience it as how it should be experienced. Ik it is usually advertised under the guise of "roguelike deck building game" which is true, but that's not what it's about. This isn't just a card game, this is a Dan Mullins game, and that means you can expect whatever the mechanic of the game is, whether it be a deck building or a 2D scroller, is only the medium to carry out the story. Not saying that gameplay isn't important, (it really is and it was fun for me) but I'm saying that you shouldn't come in a game expecting something super specific, I've read a lot of feedbacks (not that significant proportion) that they're disappointed bc it was not what they thought it was, so uh... that's a possibility if you do set your expectations up.ANYHOWSpoilers ahead but not too much!!Oh god where do I even begin, I guess I should review  separately but I am not that organized, so here's a whole chunk of my thoughts.All in all, I really love how the game's got something for ppl of different crowds to enjoy, I'm sure you'd find something you love, and the story is not one to disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% would recommend for anyone interested in an immersive and addictive, card based game. Played the game for 10 hours straight and I don't regret doing so at all. This game uses not only interesting and new abilities on cards, to give yourself an edge against your opponent, but also incorporates an interactive environment to help the player out. If you're thinking about getting this game, do it, this was hands down one of my favorite games that I've played in a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: Inscryption

_childDocuments_.review: Words cannot describe how much I ADORE Inscryption.I'm not much for card games, so I didn't pay as much attention to it initially when it came out.But then - I encountered a video in my youtube feed of someone playing it. I literally had to force myself from not continuing the video when I realised that I NEED TO BUY THIS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ GAME.Inscryption is the perfect balance of failure, repeat & continue onward without making it feel cheap when you lose everything you gained thus far. Similarly to Hades, it progresses the story further and also strengthens you, making you feel as if dying is meant to be a part of the gameplay loop rather than an annoying hinder.Admittedly I was initially so bad at the game that I never even got the "too fast, too soon" encounter that I know others have gotten, lol.As for the acts, I would say act 1 is a clear winner in terms of how good it is. The mystery, the horror themes, the strategies behind each card you obtain and upgrade, and the choices you make along your path toward the cabin. The lore is also perfectly balanced to where it's not overbearingly in-your-face and unskippable, but also stays subtle and leaves you wondering what certain things actually mean.Also the music. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ music. I'm in love.Act 2 is the weakest out of the bunch for me - I treated it more as a trainng ground for my Ouroboros using my amazing undefeatable super-deck (feel free to copy):1 ouroboros3 black cats7 squirrels9 burrowsAs for act 3, it really picks it up again. The eeriness returns, and leaves you with a feeling of that something bad is creeping closer constantly.Inscryption is, to me, a 10/10 game.One of the best games I have ever played - in any category.
_childDocuments_.name: Inscryption

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game from start to finish.  Seriously one of the most unique experiences I've ever had in a video game in over 25 years of gaming. If you're a fan of RPGs or Card-game style mechanics this is definitely for you.  I can't say enough about this game, truly a masterpiece!

_childDocuments_.review: Inscryption is one of the most unique games that I've played this year. It is very difficult to describe without spoilers but in its most basic form it is a card game with a great atmosphere and a great story. The actual card game mechanics are fun and make you think about what move you need to make without being too difficult and hard to understand. The game is split up into three distinct acts as well a finale. The first act is probably my favourite and while the third act probably goes for a bit too long that doesn't make it bad by any means. I won't say anything on the finale or ending although they were both really good, even if the ending happened a bit quickly. I'm sure this game has many secrets,  and although I was left with more questions than answers, telling the player everything would definitely detract from the experience. If you want to buy this game, go in completely blind, because knowing just about anything about it could spoil the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Inscryption presents itself as a deck building turn based strategy game, and that part alone has enough challenge and variation to make it fun to replay. It's full of surprises right up to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Put simply, Inscryption is a masterpiece unlike anything else I’ve ever played. If you’re even remotely interested in any of the genres or subgenres Inscryption is listed to have, I strongly recommend you play it. I’m honestly not even sure where to begin talking about Inscryption and why it’s so good. I could write paragraphs and paragraphs about its masterful blending of a deck-builder with an escape room, all built on the underpinning of a mysterious almost horror-like story and lore. I could write about how the game is really fun to “break”, with many unique and interesting card combinations that are fun to discover. I could write about the narrative and how it kept me glued to this game from start to finish. I could write about any number of things, and I cannot stress enough, that in every corner and crevice of Inscryption, you find nothing but an incredibly fun and well designed game coupled with a unique twisty mystery of a story. Now, I’m the type of person who enjoys writing long and drawn out multi-paragraph extended novels of near nonsense for my game reviews. But I loved going in blind with this game, I feel like that’s a core part of the experience. So I just can’t bring myself to write in detail about anything else. Consider that a MASSIVE recommendation from me! I really think this game has something to offer the vast majority of players out there, and I really think the experience is worth the price and the trip. If you are curious, and this review didn't quite sell you on it, I am doing a DEEP DIVE spoiler riddled podcast episode on it in the near future. Search for VOID ARCADE anywhere you listen to podcasts to see if it’s out yet (will try to retroactively update this review with a link). But more importantly, PLEASE don’t pass this one up! It’s a Masterpiece! NameBrand.

_childDocuments_.review: I am really disappointed with this game. I really don't like saying this because I have enjoyed Daniel Mullins's previous works a lot, but this game is deceptively bad, which I'm going to try and explain without spoilers and focus on the mechanics.Quite shortly into the game, around the 2nd or 3rd hour of play, the fundamental rules of the card game change in very minor ways, but ways that completely ruin its balancing as it becomes a lot more at the whim of RNG. Instead of being able to choose between 2 decks, your monster cards and squirrel cards (for those unfamiliar, the former cards usually require sacrifices to play, but squirrels don't and act as a free sacrifice to play on the board), from now on you get a completely random card. This means it is now common to get turns where you cannot play a card, and it has even often happened where I lose a match just by being unable to play any round until I lose. From what I understand, with this change in the rules the best way to play is the most boring way to play, i.e. play your strongest monsters as much as you can, rather than monsters with interesting additional mechanics, just boof your opponent hard and fast.Basically, after a fantastic first couple hours, this game careens downhill in fun, in how interesting it is, how tactically diverse you can play the game. It really feels like I was sold a game most of which I find unenjoyable by the advertising and demo only showing parts from the first couple of hours.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a long time to write this review, wanting to include all aspects of a game with so many faces. I also wanted to complete all the achievements, which I did after about 90 hours of free play, completing the main story three times. Exact time depends on the person and their individual speed of play.You start playing Inscryption as a card game, combined with the theme of an escape room. Your goal is to solve all of the puzzles, battle with the mysterious being on the other side of the table and win. Apart from your opponent, you face the questionable morals of the rules of the game itself — the game you  play to get away from the stranger’s cabin. Although this may be a subjective opinion, I believe that the card part of the gameplay is varied enough that the player does not get bored and has fun giving their cards different sigils or coming up with tactics. (Speaking of which, Kaycee mod is a nice addition for people who, just like me, particularly liked the game mechanics.)As the story progresses at a steady pace, Inscryption keeps surprising you. Until it violently breaks through the fourth wall. And again, and again. While you still have many questions and their number is growing, the place you are in is slowly starting to feel more… familiar to you, the player.I won't talk about the visuals in the non-spoiler part of my review for a reason, but I will mention the music. The soundtrack fits perfectly into the disturbing atmosphere of the game, fully exploiting the potential of background sound effects. It’s amazingly climatic and startling, slowly begins to combine various themes, which, however, connects very well to the whole. The first track you hear is, I believe, the most complex one, well-planned and well-thought-out, and you will learn its full meaning only after finishing the game.And the most fun you get from Inscryption is when you play blindly, knowing as little as possible about it.Anyone who has played Mullins' previous games will understand that the main plot still revolves around the same matter and everything happening in Inscryption goes beyond normal understanding. It dances around meta themes, slips through tiny lines of enigmatic dialogue and breaks the fourth wall. It's an extremely satisfying experience, rewarding your patience and time spent building the deck and solving the puzzles. The Inscryption ARG was also neatly constructed and I enjoyed reading through what had already been solved by others.It’s not only about the brilliant story itself, but the characters — and each of them is somehow flawed, yet in the end you can find yourself care about them. Even if a side character has only a few lines of dialogue, they are so easily remembered and characteristic.The artstyle is simple, yet spine-chilling. In the later stages of the game the graphics become more retro, which fits so well into the overall story. (Also, can we talk about how cool the physics of the little bone tokens are?) Designs of the main characters are so… weirdly creative and unsettling in their bizarre way.I can't go too far in my thoughts on Inscryption. Not too far, not too soon. I don't want to take away from new players the experience of exploring everything on their own — at the same time, I think most can be said about the plot itself, which is something I tried to avoid, wanting to focus on many aspects of this game. I hope that many people enjoyed this game as much as I did and are equally looking forward to the next games from the same publisher.

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't want to leave a negative review for Inscryption, it has so many good things going for it.Though the bad parts have made me decide to stop playing and uninstall the game. The worst part, the part that GALLS the F&*K out of me is that at the end of every act, you lose EVERYTHING. All the cards you spent time building and learning how to play will be replaced by a new useless starter pack with another unnecessary set of mechanics that you have to adapt around. This is the main reason why I am not interested in finishing the title. The next worse part is that RNG dictates your deck due to such a tiny handful of fights and booster packs in the world. It is entirely too easy to just never get that lynchpin combo that you are planning. Granted this isn't unique to Inscryption and seems to be a persistent issue that infects every single card battler roguelike on the entire Steam market. The least worse thing is just how disrespectful this game is of your time. For example in act 1 (spoilers because Idgaf anymore) YOU CANNOT PROGRESS until you LOSE at least one round past a specific point. There is zero clue to this anywhere in the game. 20 of the 25 hours of my current game time was on doing act 1 again and again and again trying to figure out why everyone was talking about GBA graphics and power and mox for cards. I'm pretty sure Mullins put this in specifically to piss the hell out of people like me.

_childDocuments_.review: This really starts off strong but goes on to stumble and fall flat on it's face. I have not played the Acts after I (I didn't even know there was enything else), but from the reviews, it only gets worse.The Beginning is very good. If you're interested in the atmosphere from the trailers or like card games in general, I can reccomend you give it a try at least, because it's executed very well.However, the first issues cropped up about 4 hours in, when RNG would screw me repeatedly, making entire runs doomed from the start. This is a roguelike game, so apart from the first few scripted deaths you may die over and over and have to repeat the first few stages over and over, because the game gave you garbage loot. While the maps and encounters change each time, eventually you will get bored. Or the game shoves amazing cards down your throat the first time and you can oneshot the entire game.Unlike most roguelikes, there's almost nothing you gain from restarting. You may have some more knowledge of mechanics, but the main death-boon has an extremely low chance of actually appearing in your next run. Or ever.After the first Act Boss, the game reveales the biggest let-down imaginableI'm glad I've tried this game, but I'm also glad I've stopped.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game should win GOTY!  It has everything a gamer could ask for even though it "just a card game"!  There is so much to this game that it is hard to know where to start.  The game design is a mixture of Hands of Fate (an outstanding deck building game) and Slay the Spire.  Instead of being your character up, your build your deck and upgrade the cards to help progress through the card.  Without spoiling the game, the type of cards you get to add to your deck and the ways some are created are the most unique designs I have seen that are enjoyable and actually add to the immersion of the game.  The map is the same as in Slay the Spire: a road with branches that lead to different events.  The card battle is much like Hands of Fate with the items, currency, and buff mechanics.  The difference being the cards do the battling instead of a third-person slash and dash mini game.  Difficulty is hard to determine due to the rogue-like genre.  I enjoyed the learning curve and was punished for some mistakes but some players may find the difficulty plateaus at some point.  Sound Design is unmatched.  There are a few moments where you will pull your headphones off your ears to stop the bleeding due to sudden screeches unfortunately.  Aside from those few moments, the music and SFX create a very immersive atmosphere with some bangers hidden in there!  Aesthetically, everything from the cards to the map to the rooms to the bosses are fit perfectly together to create whatever immersive theme presented by the level.  Although, you spend most of you time looking at a map or a boss character who controls the map, the visuals are never stale!  The bosses change themselves into characters you meet along your journey as though they are performing a One Person Show. ().  The backgrounds change like different sets in a play.  If the design was meant to be like a Broadway production, they nailed it!There more to the game than just collecting cards and beating bosses.  It's hard to go into these aspects without spoiling the game but there are tons of hidden puzzles with great rewards, clues to puzzles cleverly hidden during gameplay, and cut-scenes to tie everything together into one pretty good story.  It's a Daniel Mullins game so it can get a little dark (not just in brightness!) but the pull no punches approach makes the game that much more enjoyable and satisfying to complete.  It is also a bit META for those that don't like that type of game interaction.  I think the only problem would be replayability.  Then again, it's only $20 so I think you get more than enough game play for that amount of money.  The game does seem to have multiple endings so I am excited to see what happens on a second playthrough.  I actually haven't beaten the game yet myself but I watched a streamer beat the game and I REFUSE to believe that is the only ending.  Especially in this game!Overall, I am very impressed by this game!  It has been a while since I have purchased a game and thoroughly enjoyed playing it.  This game has so much character it makes you want to keep playing it even after your 10th death!

_childDocuments_.review: Scroll to the bottom for my tickbox review.A great card game with actual plot. I'm going to try be spoiler free here (which is important to your experience). It's a Slay the Spire like game, but with no action cards. You use an energy based sacrifice system to play cards, and a fun shared-HP system (using a scale) in matches. Cards can have traits, traits can be transferred, and different traits can stack. You can carry up to 3 consumable items, which persist throughout runs. Each boss brings a twist, a new rule (for that fight) that changes gameplay, which adds to the fun. It's important to note that beating the final boss does not finish the game; you must complete some puzzles to progress the game (and plot) - this confused me. I also recommend collecting all achievements before defeating the final boss, as you may have to restart the run.I'll start with the game board, or map. You have multiple paths to pick, which can branch our 2-3 times and then merge. Nodes are balanced, so there's always an available node regardless of which path you take. Nodes are same type horizontally, so you will an event node or combat node in the same row. At the end of every region is a single boss node, where all paths will merge together. You can "step away" from the board and explore the room you're in, solving puzzles and pressing random things to gain bonuses.Cards have multiple properties marked on them, such as the name and picture, which serves no functional purpose. There is a sacrifice cost (with the blood icon) in the upper right corner, an attack and HP value, a "family" (e.g. wolf, insect) and optional traits. You can have up to 3 (maybe 4) unique traits, which can affect the way the card interacts with other cards. Traits can be transferred to another card (assuming there's space on the target card) by "sacrificing" it at an altar, which is one of the random event nodes you can encounter. Sacrificing it in this way will permanently lose the card. However, this is useful for various reasons, including thinning our your deck - it's very hard to find card removal, as you cannot "build" your deck. You can combo multiple traits together to get nice combos like counting as 3 sacrifice, undying (returns to hand when it dies), and gain a copy of this card when played. The best and most important card in the game is the Ouroboros card. Each time it dies, it permanently gains +1/1 to its stats, which carries through runs! Once you're familiar enough with the game, you can easily farm and raise the card's stats. Once you're happy and farmed enough, you can 1-shot battles with the card and gain insane amounts of currency.Each turn in a match consists of 3 stages: the draw phase, summon phase, and battle phase (in that order). There are no limits to how many cards you can draw, hold, or play. It's possible to draw, play, hold, and summon your whole deck in one turn (with the combo). The board has 4 slots to play cards, with potential obstacles (0/x cards) scattering when the match starts. Additionally, there is a 2nd row, on your opponent's side that shows you the cards they'll play on their next turn.At the start of your turn you are required to draw a card. You have 2 decks to draw from: one is your actual deck, and the other is a squirrel deck. Squirrels are 0 cost 0/1 fodder cards, which can be used as a wall to block 1 card's attack for one turn, or to count as a sacrifice to summon another card. During the summon phase, you select the required sacrifices, which will disappear from the board, and then you can choose which slot to place your new card into. It's during this phase, and the next, that showcases how important positioning is. In the final phase, the battle phase, the turn player's cards will attack the card opposite it. 0 attack cards won't attack, and once a card reaches 0 HP it dies and gets removed from the board. If there is no card opposite, that card will deal damage to the character, which will be indicated on the HP scale. When your opponent's card dies, overkill damage is applied to any cards. Overkill damage to your opponent's HP will great Golden Teeth. Some cards will have a flying trait, which will ignore the opposing side, and directly deal damage to the character. There is also a water (submerge) trait, which hides the card during the opponent's turn, and lets them deal direct damage. Against opponents with those decks, you will want to deal high damage fast, or you may lose.Most cards require sacrifices, which is an energy system. Sacrificing (and losing) a card will grant 1 sacrifice (1 blood) towards playing a new card. A card could require 4 sacrifices, which means sacrificing up to 4 cards (there is a maximum of 4 cards on the field). Some special cards (like the goat) coat as 3 sacrifices, so you only need to sacrifice that one card. You can only sacrifice 1 card to summon 1 card, so a goat cannot be used to summon 3 cards.Each card battle, you a presented with a scale on the left hand side of the screen, which indicates the combined HP of your player and your opponent for this match. The scale has 11 values, with the middle value being full lives for both players. I will refer to these values as -5 to 5 to simplify things. Each damage you take from an opponent's card will deduct one life from the scale, and once you reach -5, you lose the match. As this is a shared HP system, the value of the scale can move all the way from -4 to 5 (9 damage), so it's possible for you to be on the brink of death and clutch a victory from a topdeck. Conversely, this can drag out a battle if you're at a standstill, and it can also mean you lose in one turn too (although this is very unlikely).The full review is in the forums, due to reaching the max character limit: ---{ Rating }---9 / 10---{ PC Requirements }---☑ Potato☐ Decent☐ Fast☐ Rich boi☐ Ask NASA if they have a spare computer---{ Audience }---☐ Beginner☐ Casual Gamer☑ Normal Gamer☐ Expert---{ Graphics }---☐ You forget what reality is☐ Beautiful☐ Good☑ Decent☐ Bad---{ Audio }---☐ Eargasm☐ Great☑ Good☐ Okay☐ Bad---{ Gameplay }---☐ Great☑ Fun☑ Challenging☐ Generic☐ Frustrating---{ Difficulty }---☐ Just press 'W'☐ Easy☑ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Difficult☐ Dark Souls---{ Grind }---☐ Nothing to grind☐ Only if you care about leaderboards☑ Isn't necessary to progress☐ Normal☐ Too much grind---{ Story }---☐ No Story☐ Bad / Generic☐ Some lore☑ Good☐ Fantastic---{ Game Time }---☐ Really short (0 - 3 hours)☐ Short (4 - 8 hours)☐ Few hours (10 - 20 hours) [if you focus on the main story]☑ Many hours (20 - 40)☐ Long (40 - 60 hours) [if you complete everything]☐ Very Long (61 - 100 hours)☐ Extremely Long (101+ hours)---{ Replayability }---☐ It's a one-time experience☐ Only for achievements☐ If you wait a few months / years☑ Definitely☐ Infinitely replayable---{ Bugs }---☑ Never heard of☐ Minor bugs☐ Can get annoying☐ Lots of bugs☐ Bugs destroy the game---{ Price }---☑ Full price☐ Wait for Sale☐ If u have some spare money left☐ You could also just burn your money

_childDocuments_.review: To start off, this isn't a horrible game but I don't think it's a great one either. The RNG is beyond infuriating how random it is and how many times you get a huge disadvantage compared to the AI just because you had an unlucky roll. Every time you die you start from the beginning with basically the same starter deck you initially started out with. After you die you can craft a "death card", they are special cards you can make as a combination of the cards you collected through your run but it's also based on their ridiculous random luck generator so you can almost guarantee it's going to be a garbage card.I do really like the concept, music, sounds and style of the game but the gameplay drawbacks are too much for me to endure playing for more than a few hours in a row.If this game had some way to improve your luck or overall strength and quality of cards over multiple runs I would probably enjoy it a lot more but I feel that the way this game is supposed to be played is incredibly boring and repetitive. The maps are sort of randomised each run but still comes down to the same bosses, same cards, same unlucky rng, overpowered AI etc.After getting the hang of the game a bit I even tried bringing a good deck on the first boss after fully wiping my save and restarting the game and when you are actually about to defeat the first boss he goes "berserk" and spawns in 8x super OP cards so you have no chance of winning because you HAVE to die and you HAVE to lose. I hate games that force death on you to continue the story or to make you "learn" the game. That's fine for people that enjoy that kind of game but it's absolutely not something I enjoy. I will give it a few more tries but it's not a game I would recommend if you're just into regular card battle games.It just gets worse, all the screenshots you see in the Steam Store are just the 1st part of the game and even though it's frustrating, that was the most fun part of the game. The 2nd act turns into some kind of Super Mario map-style RPG where you have to defeat bosses with a way to complex card system, you get several additional types of cards that make it very complicated to figure out how to build a good deck. The bosses are all very tedious, every single one just has the "defeat my 3 minions before you can face me" style and then the combat itself was sort of underwhelming. I expected something like the final battle in the 1st act. The "voice overs" from the guy who is supposedly playing Inscryption are very unnecessary, boring and annoying and, to me, add nothing of value. The videos of him talking about the game are just dumb and could've been left out of the game completely and probably make the game more enjoyable as a whole. You can easily skip/avoid these so that's a good thing at least.The worst part comes after the already bad 2nd Act and this is where I stopped playing after like 15-20 minutes, Act 3. The 2D-ish game you were playing now turns into a 3D world with boring gameplay, boring puzzles, boring maps, boring interactions and so on. Very disappointed at the game because the 1st Act art style is one I really enjoyed, the 2nd I didn't really care for and the 3rd is just horrible. It's not what was promised, none of the screenshots in the store show the 2nd or 3rd Act art styles. If I would've known about the 2nd and 3rd Act I would've held off buying the game completely. I feel cheated because it's a completely different game you're playing and it's not something I would've bought if I knew beforehand.The game would've been like a 6/10 before the 2nd/3rd Act but because of above mentioned issues, this drops to a 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Inscryption is one of the best indie games released this year. This game feels like the capstone of Daniel Mullins Games. Amazing visual styles, great story, awesome gameplay, and a genuinely creepy meta-story (as always).This game is a deckbuilder. A game where the main appeal is to build your deck of cards as if it were a trading card game without the trading. The actual card game itself is very fun, but also incredibly broken and unbalanced in a way that favors the player by a huge margin. And that is perfectly fine, in fact I love it. Also, I have been asking for YEARS for games similar to Magic: The Gathering Shandalar, or Pokemon TCG for the Gameboy. Now this game is more so multiple games in one, much in the style of The Hex, however I will not go into detail.Graphics: 9/10, the art style(s) are perfect and set up for the feeling that the game wants to get to you. The dark of the cabin, with a creepy art style sets the mood for Inscryption. And just watch the trailer.Sound: 6/10, I couldn't point out any specific thing about the soundtrack, but it wasn't offensive at any point and it did add to the experience.Gameplay: 8.5/10, The gameplay is good, but I feel like it is too simplistic. The fact that you win the game by putting weights on your opponents side of the scale until that side reaches the bottom is a cool way to make it so that you have to have dealt at least 5 more damage than your opponent has. However, the low amount of 5 makes the game very quick and defensive strategies impossible.Difficulty: 4/10, the game isn't difficult, especially if you have played other deckbuilders before, but there is a level of artificial difficulty you will need to account for. Also it is easy to be TOO good for the game and in this scenario the game forces you to lose for the sake of the story.All in all: a solid 8.5/10 in my opinion, however I understand that there are some people you will LOVE this game and others who won't care for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Inscryption

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Undertale but in reverse.Undertale takes bullet hells and makes them easy and pretty relaxing. Inscryption takes deck builders, a genre that's usually meditative, and turns them into nail-bitingly brutal crucibles. Undertale uses retro art styles to draw you into an inviting and colorful world. Inscryption uses a retro art style to make its grotesque and inhumane world even more alienating.Undertale is a story about learning to see the best in fundamentally good people who sometimes make mistakes. Inscryption is a story about learning to acknowledge that you're surrounded by fundamentally bad people and how even their acts of kindness are ultimately motivated by selfishness.And when the game makes these misanthropic bastards suffer, it breaks your heart to see it. Because like Undertale, Inscryption has the balls to ask you to be their friend in spite of everything.

_childDocuments_.review: What a game.Like many reviews before me, play this game blind! Avoid the spoilers! This is an experience that is best enjoyed at your own pace on your own terms. There are settings in the options to turn off several of the filters if the visual noise or CRT lines hurt your eyes. There's also an option to turn off certain flickering if you're photosensitive. I love seeing these options in the game because although it really adds to the aesthetic, there are those who aren't me whose eyes can get tired from looking at such effects. I won't go into details about any of the story beats. My review doesn't need it. This game roped me in and enthralled me for the entire duration it took for me to beat it. The game knows what it is, and confidently rocks it. The aesthetic is tight and cohesive. The sound design is amazing and immersive. The gameplay itself is smooth and easy to play quickly once you know what you're doing. The story itself made me cry at points, in a way that were I to play the story again from start to finish, it would hurt just a little. Every single card element across the entire game is lovingly thought out and iterates on itself incredibly. But this is not Slay the Spire. This is not your next roguelite, though it does give you the option at the end to play it as such. It's unfair to the game, however, to act like it not being a game with infinite depth of replayability is a flaw. That's not what this game is. I can understand wanting more depth because parts of the game are incredibly fun! The card game is so thoughtfully woven together with the rest of the game's stories that there were little things that made me go "oh crap" with realization at multiple turns.tl;dr: An amazing game that was compelling and enjoyable at every turn. It has insane polish. Buy it, play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying that when I heard of this game, I could NOT have been more hyped. A horror esque escape room card game? SOLD!But, you know what makes a rogue-lite? What really makes them fun? Being told odds can only be AGAINST your favor. Whenever that became the norm I'll never know.Can't have someone doing TOO well and NOT padding the gameplay now can we?Every ounce of tension and intrigue is sucked dry after the 2nd, or even 3rd time I was slammed to the start because literally, not paraphrased "Too fast, too soon" and was hit with a wall of cards noone could ever win against. This was almost thematic until the 4th time it happened and I wrote this review.  I'll also say, the 2 minute death sequence DEFINITELY contributed to me wishing I'd spent the $15 on a decent burger. Just as well considering the game is a bait and switch where this is the BEST segment. Or that I'd spent less time trying to make excuses for the game and been in my refund window. Amazing, truly fantastic idea, terrible execution and even worse implementation.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I like this game, I cannot in good conscience recommend it. One of the later bosses - well over two hours into the game - demands access to your hard-drive as part of the boss's gimmick. The player has no ability to decline and Inscryption will even in certain circumstances delete a file from your computer. There is no warning prior to this boss that this is a mechanic in the game and until the developer removes this 'feature' I will strongly recommend that nobody purchase this game.EDIT: It has been pointed out to me that it doesn't actually delete your file, because I didn't trust the game enough to actually offer a file for deletion. However, I maintain that the game should have offered forewarning before forcing the player to give it access to the file directory.

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game this was to play. The story was very interesting and the game play was really fun. _childDocuments_.review: To cut a long story short, if you're undecided on whether or not you should buy this game, do it.I'm not really an avid fan of card games, but the mysterious shroud surrounding this game along with the resounding support that you see in reviews tempted me to to buy it. And boy-oh-boy am I glad I did. I can't really talk much about the things that make this game so great without going into great detail, but just like every other review you see for this game, I can agree that you should go into it as blind as possible. If you like card games, this is very much so worth the full $20 dollars, especially more-so if you can catch it on sale.If you like games that have an atmosphere that enhances the experience, this game does it better than any I've ever seen; the soundtrack, the sounds, the animations, the artstyle, everything coalesces into a wonderful game that will leave you coming back for more. If you are a fan of the gameplay, there is a mod released by the developers that expands upon the gameplay which I highly recommend checking out after you've beaten the game. All in all, one of my new favorite games of all time, and a must-play for anyone who likes card games, or anyone who wants a truly unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So I didn't know too much about Inscryption other than it was a horror, deck building game when I got into it. I have to say the story was a real trip, and I deeply enjoyed it. The card system is great, and has some unique mechanics you might be familiar with in games like MTG, but others that are unique to it alone. My only honest complaint about this game is the length. You'll get about 13-16 hours on it depending on how much of a of a 100% clear you want, and how long it takes you to do puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Go for it, buy it, play it, even if it's annoying and feels rigged - it is, there's a reason for that, keep playing! Great game and you basically get 3 games for the price of 1 - even though, somewhat short (playthrough was 15-ish hours to me).Details (no spoilers!)I bought the game when it came out & refunded as I found it annoying it's far too random and often was not possible to win with a hand, and "back then" bumped into far too many games of the kind (i.e. too random-heavy, less about playing smart).But something in the back of my head told me this game really is different and I should give it a try again. This was a good decision!Yes, the "early game" is rigged, but that's part of the story. Without spoilers, all I can say is, play on, yes it's difficult, but keep playing, it will be rewarding!There are 3 "acts" in the game, but for me it feels there's a 4th as well, the end game, all acts are different and all have a twist to it.The only, and for me, big negative I can mention is, nothing is explained on any level and there's far too much "trial and error" moments figuring out the mechanics. So IMO there should be tutorial plays for all game types, one round in which the "playing partner" explains all the mechanics - especially (if not exclusively) in act 2 where all those new things are introduced.Hm. I think this is it. Go for it.I hope to see Inscryption 2 very, very soon![NOTE: Kaycee's mod is nice in the beginning, but after the a few wins it turns into a dumb grindfest, i.e. only the best hands and most lucky calls allow a win, so I abandoned that. Shame as it could have been more fun, as well as I miss Act2 play in Kaycee's mode style]

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a massive bait and switch. Without too many spoilers, what you are seeing in the steam trailers is not at all what you are getting long-term. If you read any of the other negative reviews, any and all of them will tell you all about this.What other reviews don't generally mention is what the community will generally say as a counter to this; "keep playing and eventually you'll get to 'kaycee's mod', it's made for people like you who just wanted what was on the steam page, trust me it's just more of act 1 it's great!".Kaycee's mod is in itself kind of another bait and switch. It's a very hardcore roguelike that ditches any story or atmosphere. The puzzles are essentially completely removed, there is almost no reason to ever stand up from the table again, and there is no new content to discover (in terms of new boss battles, new maps, new interactions with any NPCs, etc. You do unlock a small handful of new cards). Instead the difficulty is bumped way the ♥♥♥♥ up as you are served the same old reheated stale leftovers from yesterday over and over again, but doused in a bucket load of sriracha sauce. The joy of discovery is gone, the tension is gone, the atmosphere is gone, all that's left is pure punishment.Kaycee's mod is designed and aimed at people who are into the hardcore card game deckbuilding experience, who've come at this from a background of already having mastered slay the spire or hearthstone or etc. People who get their rocks off on refining their deck and micromanaging odds and exploiting loopholes mercilessly, because the game will now punish you if you are not exploiting every loophole as it expects that you are stacking your deck as hard as possible. And that's fine, I can understand why that might be appealing for some people. But the community will hype it up as being a replacement to act 1 and it really is not, it's a completely different type of game meant for a different type of gamer. It's nothing like the the intense, moody, horror/escape room/puzzle solving/deckbuilding hybrid that you think you've signed up for based on the store trailers and anything you've seen about this game and the first few hours. That stuff is gone, long gone. You think you're buying one thing, but it will hard swerve into something else pretty quickly and in the end you will only ever end up getting maybe 3 hours of what you thought you'd bought.(Also, please note that if the above sounds really appealing to you, to get at kaycee's mod you're going to have to slog through about 10 hours of yet another different kind of game targeted at a different kind of player first. At least part of the 'real' game sandwiched in between act 1 and kaycee's mod seems to be targeted at meta/ARG fans who want to spend all day watching theorycrafting deep lore videos on youtube. The game just cannot stick to a target audience.)

Do note that it is essentially impossible to describe this game in any aspect without spoiling it, and spoil it I do not wish to do, but I must give at least some small spoilers ahead to discuss the game in any detail.This game is not what it appears on the tin - and in my opinion, I think it's all the better for it. But, do not expect the game to end in the infamous cabin where you begin. The gameplay changes up heavily throughout the game's different acts. There's dozens of secrets to find and while not essential to complete the game it very much rewards the curious explorer for their pursuits. The game is also peppered with plentiful humor that never gets in the way, and a truly climactic ending that touches off the whole journey I'd say rather spectacularly.Excellent game, very few if any issues with it. Very polished, very fun, although not terribly challenging really. Perhaps my favorite game of 2021.(Also worth noting there's a free expansion that as of the time of this review is in open beta that transforms the opening act in the cabin into a proper roguelike experience, which is also quite nice to see and I look forward to spending even more time with that)

The deck-building, roguelike and escape room genres are there, yes, but none of those areas are perfect or revolutionary in any way. I will say that I did really like a lot of the card mechanics that were implemented and enjoyed making different decks focused on the different mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: This game is great! It starts looking like an interesting card game only to quickly evolve into an intriguing and eerie story. The greatest aspects of the game only become apparent once you've completed what I'd call Act I. It leads you to believe that the game will reach its climax, but instead greets you with a new challenge as you struggle to balance new mechanics and build an effective deck. By the end of Act II you'll find yourself piecing together a greater story that is continued in Act III. Act III starts by looking like just another round of the game you'd find at the beginning of Act I (with a couple small twists). You will quickly find that this is not the case, as the developers ensure that you do not feel as though your time was wasted by making you rebuild yet another new deck. You will feel that the momentum continues to build through Act III and by the end it leaves you empathetic to those you initially blamed for your predicament. Ultimately, this is a great game that will keep you entertained for hours and gives you a story worth embracing!

_childDocuments_.review: Inscryption was such an interesting game. The story it had was definitely not what I expected, but as you progressed through it you just wanted to know more. The less you know about it, the more you are likely to enjoy it. On face value Inscryption is a deck-based game where your decks evolve as you progress through the story. The way your deck changes over the course of a game feels very unique and you are rewarded for understanding the mechanics early on. Oddly enough, there are a ton of mechanics, both explained in the rule book and just explained by the main antagonist. I highly recommend you do not skip text if you can help it, a lot of people fat finger their mouse and miss some important detailed that don't get recalled. Surprisingly, it is easy to comprehend and never felt overwhelming in the slightest. The atmosphere is unsettling and feels appropriate for a horror setting. The music design is just as unsettling and ties everything together. There is quite a shortage of creepy deck-builders out there!Post-story you get an option to hop into a rogue-like version of the game called Kaycee's Mod. It was free DLC added back in March and offers some more lore and challenges for people looking to get more out of the game. Some of the challenges are pretty rough and will depend heavily on RNG with only one real viable deck (that is consistent, at least). While most challenges are easy enough, you eventually have to stack some and it gets to a point where you cannot play the game organically and you have to hope you get the run you need.You can replay the story after finishing it, which devolves into a chapter select. If you are just looking for some extra gameplay, Kaycee's Mod post-game offers a roguelite experience to take advantage of. The base game maybe took me 15 hours, but Kaycee's Mod can easily add in dozens of hours with it's challenges alone. Replaying the story, with some knowledge of various puzzles, can lead to some interesting discoveries for a second playthrough. The base game achievements are very easy to miss and are naturally hidden in steam. Unless you have prior knowledge of what to look for, you will end up doing a second playthrough. Some of them are extremely specific, so it's impossible to get them all naturally. Once you know, collecting them is not an issue at all. Kaycee's Mod added new achievements and are mechanically the hardest to achieve. Most of them just require natural progression, but the final achievement to have every single challenge on is hot garbage. Because it's all RNG, you will probably spend more time trying to get a perfect run going for the Storm achievement compared to all the achievements combined. While it never crashed, my bootup into the game and into my save file both stalled on loading. I never had to close it and it naturally loaded anyway. It was more odd than anything. Clicking too much during loads resulted in Windows asking if I wanted to close the program. Again, just letting it load was fine, and it was a very short load time. Once in the game, the issue never showed up for anything else.  The base game took me maybe 15 hours, and Kaycee's Mod challenges left me a little over 30 hours. I think it's pretty great at $20, and it often goes on sale for less than $15. Definitely worth it at any price, it has easily become one of my favorite deck builders.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gives a new definition to the word "roguelike." Yet it's also a continuation of an ever deepening story of mystery, horror, and video gaming itself. Right when you boot up the main menu and press "continue" in lieu of starting a new game (the option being denied to you... at first), you are immediately introduced to the nature of Inscryption as a subversion of even your most basic expectations. A game where the questions you'd normally ask no longer apply, where the story can only be deciphered by actively searching for it, where your perspective as a player (and perhaps YouTuber) is directly integrated into the character you play as and the gameplay you experience. Few games have the balance between showing you the ropes and refusing to hold your hand, and fewer still successfully make that a rewarding experience throughout the entirety of its content. This is also the first time I've ever encountered a game where I was invested in the story, couldn't fully make it out, then realized that that was because I was meant to play other games from the same developer without ever being told or clued in directly by the game itself; subtle hints and references to Pony Island and The Hex are included in such a way that both longtime fans and discovering newcomers can be pleasantly satisfied. Thank you to Daniel Mullins Games for absolutely sticking to the road less traveled by, and sharing a truly one of a kind game for all to enjoy. Can't wait for Pony Island 2: Panda Circus!
_childDocuments_.name: Inscryption

_childDocuments_.review: "Inscryption" combines everything that I love from a number of genres. It has rogue-like elements combined with a grim table-top card game setting. The learning curve is high and it's easy to get into as soon as you start, as long as you're familiar with the genre. Think "Darkest Dungeon" if it was a low-res, claustrophobic romp in a train car with a mysterious dark figure dead-set on your self-mutilation and destruction. The horror elements add great flavor. Also, the ability to continuously mint new cards - upon your inevitable death - to build a more powerful deck - makes it endlessly enjoyable and addictive.
_childDocuments_.name: Inscryption

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible deck building rogue-lite. _childDocuments_.review: I implore you. If you think you might be interested in this game at all, be careful. I went in blind and that is most certainly the way to go. If you carelessly search around, watch someone play too far into the gameplay loop, or read much about it you will totally spoil what I can only call an  that you can't get back.With that out of the way, I'm afraid I can only say that my review must be vague and shallow for the same reasons. Inscryption is creepy as hell, deeply stylized, dripping with atmosphere and charm, and continues to draw me in further the more I play it. Its quite a clever premise, and I suspect this 'style' might be one of the next big things that other devs attempt to copy or capture the magic of.At its core, it certainly is a deck based card battle game with roguelike elements exactly as described on the tin. It might seem really difficult at times during the early stages but once you're familiar with the mechanics and make progress, the core gameplay loop is so very satisfying to play through. But Inscryption is so much  and that's the essence of why knowing as little as possible beyond the main points is vital to enjoy it to the fullest. The game has already thrown quite a few surprises at me and the deeper in I go, the weirder it gets and I love that.Its phenomenal.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to check this game out because you're curious and haven't seen more than people's praise of it, I would recommend you stop reading reviews now and go play it.That's what I did and It really did surprise me, all around quite fun and kept me entertained for the time I gave it. As a player of irl card games it really did tug on a few heart strings in certain places, especially towards the end. The gameplay was interesting and brought several unique aspects unique to a digital card game that I hadn't seen before. The characters you meet along the way were great fun, and seeing their secrets and their interactions was sweet. The deckbuilding felt quite sleek, a lot of the time you could keep your decklist quite short and it would still pack a punch.I do reserve a few criticisms however. As much as I can understand that the game features digital horror and pays homage to the classic 'haunted cartridge' creepy pastas - I feel like some of the choices they made were a little cheap: often times there would be harsh static and glitch sounds, as well as lots of visual stuff that comes at you very suddenly which I understand is the point of it, but a lot of the time it went on for way too long and at some points I had to take my headphones off and look away, even with the volume set to the lowest.The video sections that centre around Luke were not to my taste at all, the first few were good and set the scene, but by the end I was just clicking them to get through them in case there was a secret or something that I ought to see. And Act 3 of the game lost my attention a little bit, it dragged on a little too long for me.All in all I had a great time with this game, but seeing how many achievements I had missed I would normally feel compelled to go back and hunt them out, especially with roguelikes and card games like this. However, for this game I can't quite put my finger on it but I have no ambition to do that here - make of that what you will.- Leshy stan forever.

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Fantastic concept. It uses its narrative means by such an imaginative ways that they transform a simplistic card game into a really unique experience. It's a lot more than what you're initially expecting.- Amazing, weird story with tons of mystery and twists. Also, it has great pace and the way it evolves will surprise you.- Simple but very immersive gameplay during the card battles. You will always want to play one more match. By time it evolves and some new mechanics enter the game so it never becomes boring or repetitive.- Great atmosphere and awesome direction. It gets you immersed right from the beginning inside its mysticistic, dark world and it makes you wonder what's going on there, where are you and who is this guy at the other side of the table.- Well written dialogues. Talking cards is a nice addition and actually they are more of npcs. To get you sympathize or attach emotionally with your cards is really clever.- Some interesting boss fights that force you try different tactics and tricks in order to beat them.- Wonderful music that enhances the atmosphere and gives the tone during battles.- Aside of the card part the game has a lot of hidden secrets and small, clever puzzles that give it extra depth and put you in a total different process of exploring and discovering the world around you.- Some insanely crazy hidden secrets connected through Mullins' games' universe that you'll never actually find by yourself but it's really fun to search for them on the internet.The bad- The gameplay of the card part is very immersive, but you'll master it pretty quickly and although it evolves, it never gets really deep. Soon, it feel less challenging and after the ending it has little replayability value.- Although it has fantastic atmosphere and you don't really need better graphics for this kind of a game, some 3d images look low res and have a lot of noise.

_childDocuments_.review: The base game is fantastic. Honestly only complaint for the story is that it wasn't longer. Just a ton of fun filled with surprises and great gameplay mechanics. However, I have to say, Kaycee's Mod needs a lot of work. Before anyone starts saying "Roguelikes are supposed to be based on RNG" and all that hemming and hawing to defend Kaycee's Mod, the game mode is just completely unbalanced. Sure, RNG plays a part in many rogue likes. "Slay The Spire" can rely heavily on RNG. However, there is also a fair amount of skill involved. And even in losses in STS, I always felt like I learned something, or got closer to winning the game.Kaycee's Mod does not feel that way at all. There are certain rounds where you are just going to lose. From the get go that match will be a loss because of the cards you draw and what Leshy is going to play. Relying so heavily on card draw luck is not fun. And also the fact that to unlock more content, you have to keep making the game harder on yourself is infuriating. I have played Kaycee's Mod for nearly ten hours now, and I have only won once. And so many of my losses feel like utter BS because there was no way I was going to win because of RNG. Skill takes almost no part in the mod. It is just purely RNG luck. That isn't fun to play.It is just sad that the fun of the story mode is sucked away from Kaycee's Mod. When really, Kaycee's Mod should be about making that fun last as long as possible. Kaycee's Mod needs heavy balancing work. Until then, I don't think I will be playing it anymore. Which is unfortunate because of how much I loved the story. And the story is worth the price of the game alone. Just don't expect Kaycee's Mod to give you that same fun. Instead expect more frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: this is an incredibly immersive, beautiful, atmospheric art piece that I just didn't enjoy.  The dialogue, character design, sound design, and environmental storytelling are amazing!  The card battle mechanics, though, aren't really that engaging.  I have played a TON of deckbuilders from monster train to slay the spire to monster slayers to trials of fire etc, but the actual gameplay mechanics here didn't grab me.  If you are really good at deckbuilders (I love them but I'm no savant), and you can play through this game with no deaths and enjoy it as a story, you are going to LOVE this game.  If you are like me and you die a lot in every game, this game will get stale the fifth time you face the prospector, and all the art design in the world can't keep that from being tiresome.  There's a demo you can play to give you some idea if you'll like it; I played the demo and loved it so much I bought the game!  But still, two hours later, I realized I just wasn't having fun any more.  I get the impression they were going for a Hades-esque "the story doesn't stop when you die" sort of thing, but in Hades at least there was some metaprogression so you felt your deaths contributed to the story and next time you'll probably get farther: here, your death just means you're going to fight the prospector and fisherman again and hope you get better cards.Again: this is a GREAT GAME that just wasn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is probably one of the best deck building games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. What makes it great isn't just the deck building aspect but the amazingly deep story that goes along with it. Truly a masterpiece. There were some moments where I felt like it might become grindy, but it honestly never overstayed its welcome. The moment it felt like it could become grindy, they introduced a mechanic that sped the game up significantly. Mainly, introducing new abilities for cards that suddenly turned something weak into something fairly overpowered. I think that's what this game does best is introduce mechanics in a smart and methodical way so you feel yourself becoming more powerful over the course of each act of the game through just the acquisition of more knowledge. I would actually sort of compare this game to The Witness in a way. Each card battle was its own puzzle and as you play, you learn more about the inscriptions on the cards and what they mean and how they interact with other cards. You quickly discover what is really good and what is really bad. Much like The Witness, you have the ability to know the answers from the start if you look up mechanics online, but part of the joy of this game is learning about it yourself and making discoveries as those discoveries directly correlate to the story beats of the game.Highly recommend this game, and I believe its probably my game of the year easily.

_childDocuments_.review: A deranged Dungeon Master keeps you hostage in his cabin and forces you to play his deck builder campaign while he narrates.Takes elements from  (deck building, choosing a path, items, etc.) while also adding a meta point-and-click-adventure whose choices affect your future runs in a story-driven format.Instantly my favorite rogue because of the story-driven nature. Other roguelite deck builders can have great card mechanics, but typically have little to no story progression.It is worth mentioning that the card mechanics in this game are more like a puzzle game. Like most deck builders, you can see your opponent's upcoming moves and plan around it. But due to the health system, each card battle is typically over in less than ten turns, rarely going over five turns.The health system is a breath of fresh air: it's a weight scale. Each time you deal or receive damage, a weight is placed on that player's side. When the scale is tipped over (requiring five damage from a neutral position), the player who tipped it wins. This system can lead to back-and-forth turns. You can calculate the incoming damage and output enough damage to keep yourself alive for the next turn.If you like story-driven roguelites this is a great game to pick up. Due to the short battle length, it also plays more like a math puzzle game than a traditional TCG.

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. The concept is stellar, the graphics are lovely, the systems for deck-building are fun, and I love going back for more bell-ringing. The escape room aspect of the game is utilized incredibly creatively, and you're greatly rewarded for solving the puzzles the room contains, not to mention the underlying plot of the stoat card. If you like puzzles, duels, D&D, deck-building, and fighting extremely tough odds and don't mind setbacks, this game would likely be a great fit for you! Disclaimer: If you're easily frustrated or are at a low-to-moderate skill level for deck-building games (no judgement!), you probably won't have a great time with this game. It's designed to be difficult and very punishing for mistakes; you are not supposed to win easily. The game will even purposefully throw extremely strong creatures at you if you progress too quickly without dying enough (you unlock more mechanics whenever you die). Additional disclaimer (very minor spoilers): Some items in game meant to help tip the scales (literally) are... bloody. One is a  pair of pliers that rips out the player's tooth, and one is a knife that takes out the player's eye. The visuals aren't viscerally graphic (a momentary red screen and a reddened eye, as well as a partial loss in vision), but if you need to, brace accordingly.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING!THIS IS NOT A PURE DECKBUILDER OR CARD GAME (NOR A ROGUELIKE).This is a trippy horror-adventure game that uses cards as a base to move the plot forward.That is for informational purposes only. Still,  it is a very interesting, original, and unique game in many aspects, but there are just too many positive reviews, so I will focus on what is bad:1. act 32. Card gameplay3. confusing, never explained, and purposely too enigmatic plotad 1. The best part of the game is Act 1—best graphically, most engaging, and most interesting. Even the story could have been fully told there.Act 2 is different in both good and bad ways.Act 3 is a chore with too many filler fights with non-existing deck building (you have only one run and one try for your deck, so where is Roguelike there?) just to get to a linear ending.ad 2.I heard that gameplay was purposely made "easy," so almost anybody can beat the game. The problem is (as you can see from reviews from other people) that this is not true. The game is not easy if you are not good at card games; it is very random (especially act 1) and hard initially (all acts), where you have a weak start.The game gets easy when You get powerful cards that can, in 1-2 turns, just win you a game (like a mantis god with a +1 or more power bonus) or some flyers with a lot of attack. It gets even absurdly easy then: draw a card, play it, and win—every time. Works on all bosses in Acts 2 and 3. To be honest, it is even hard to call them bosses—just another random easy fight.There are a very limited number of cards, and most of them are useless or just very weak. It feels like playing Magic the Gathering with only common creatures from one specific set.You get reset on your deck in every act, which could be refreshing but is just boring, and you can't really build a good deck here (like in Slay of the Spire)—you only need 2 good cards. Synergy doesn't matter if you don't have the time, possibility, or need to try or make it.In conclusion, an average or even below-average deckbuilding gamead 3.I do not know this game maker. Some people call him genius, but I know one thing: if you can't understand the plot unless you play his other games, then F... this.SPOILER ALERT:I really like mysteries and Dark Souls' storytelling with minimal information, but this is different. This seems so dark, mysterious, and convoluted just for its purpose. Why is there "old data" in the first place? Why couldn't it be just a magic-evil game as simple as that? Questions above: even after watching YouTube videos explaining the story, there is still no information at all, and everything is a guess and not in good sense (good sense would be a protagonist walking toward the sunset).On the plus side, this left me with some uneasy feelings and questions. Made me feel something, which is always good in the game.TLDR:This game is medium-core in terms of mechanics. Do not play this if you want a roguelike or deckbuilding game.This is more of a quiz/adventure/horror game, a strange experience with vibes similar to Doki Doki literature club but with card game filler.

_childDocuments_.review: [SLIGHT SPOILERS]I cannot believe I am saying this about a deck building rouge-lite game (my favorite video game genre, bar none), yet alone one developed by Daniel Mullins, an excellent game developer but this... THIS... was almost certainly the most disappointing video game experience I have ever had. Mind the wording, DISAPPOINTING, not bad, or awful, or terrible. I can absolutely see how someone might get a kick out of this game. As much as I hate to be a broken record, as this has been said time and time again about this game, and I am most certainly very late to the party, but it is all about Act II and Act III, which are not, and fairly so, advertised at all for this game.Everything after Act I is an utterly unenjoyable slog. I cannot believe the ennui I experienced after Act I. For the record, I could not force myself to finish the game after halfway through Act III. It sat installed on my computer for a month before I finally uninstalled it knowing I would never go back. I completely understand why Act II and Act III are completely hidden away and not advertised. Its for the story and """twist""" of the game. Mullins is known for this, it does not surprise me. I do not blame Mullins at all and it does not upset me in the least. However, Act II and Act III combined are a much larger portion of the game than Act I and I purchased Act I. I would never have purchased the game that is composed of Act II and Act III. And no, I do not find Act III to be "exactly the same" as Act I. However, I admit my issues with Act III stem more from a certain robot than the gameplay but only barely. I've been lucky and probably pretty permissive when it has come to video game experiences over the years so I can say with confidence that I have never experienced a greater and sharper letdown than this game. Shows me for having such high expectations, but Act II genuinely took my breath away with how far and fast my enjoyment fell off a sheer cliff. Act III was more of the same.The genuinely incredible atmosphere of Act I is completely gone by Act II as well as the thoroughly enjoyable antagonist. Replaced by far less interesting adversaries. The least interesting of which is made the focus of Act III. The art style of Act I is some of the best I have seen, while Act II's is a letdown to say the least, but I suppose its fine if you enjoy pixel art, but I feel Pony Island did a much better job with the medium. Act III's art is just off putting but not horrible or anything. What Act II adds to the gameplay is shallow and frustrating at best while Act III seems to (purposefully for story reasons) mock and spit on the excellent gameplay of the first Act. Not to mention (especially in Act II), the game throws so many new mechanics at you so fast and it does not feel like you are given any time to get used to any of them before another is thrown at you or the Act ends.I've had many a personal friend of mine give me grief over how critical I am of Act III (and the fact I've had no one personally challenge me on my disappointment in Act II compared to Act I has not escaped my notice). I admit I don't have a complete and coherent answer as to why Act III bothers me so much. I guess it was just the gutpunch of the sheer cliff fall from Act I to Act II, then taking the worst story bits and characters from Act II and making them the focus of Act III while spitting on the mechanics and theming that made Act I so great (again, on purpose, for story reasons). I was genuinely tired by the time I got to Act III. Genuine ennui. Like the joy got sucked out of me. I'm not trying to say that Act III is the "WuRst g4Me 3VeRRR!" But it did happen to be a part of my most disappointing game experience ever.It is frustrating because it feels like someone took all the parts to what should be one of the best game experiences I could have and threw them in a woodchipper and Elmer's glued the pieces back together in an effort to make some sort of "modern art" piece that doesn't look like anything and is just a pile of trash. This story does not justify what Mullins did with the quality of this three act structured game.I do, however, want to clarify Act II and Act III are nowhere near the worst games I have ever played.  Act II and III  are below average gameplay quality at worst. My feelings about this game have just as much to do with the quality the later two acts compared to the first and how the game flows and is composed. It is disappointment and ennui slightly more than it is "2/3 of game bad."Kaycee's Mod  doesn't make up for it, either. It's just not worth the money. Act I done better with the endless mode and new content is still not worth the price of admission. I was expecting more, and, more importantly, much different. No developer is "obligated" to meet a customer's expectations, I suppose. Certainly not a game like this. However, if you are pulled in by what you've seen in video thumbnails and official advertisements, know you are in for a completely different game after 1/3 in, and I happen to not enjoy that 2nd and 3rd third whatsoever.Also it is overwhelmingly unlikely for someone to come across Act II and the severe whiplash of a game changer that it is before the two hour mark. I don't think that was by design or anything, it is just rather frustrating so buyer beware.

_childDocuments_.review: The less you know going in, the better. Get it and play noww!!I personally went in completely blind, and fell in love with this game.If you enjoy rogue-like deck building/card games, escape rooms/puzzles, and mystery/spooky stories this is THE GAME for you. There are some moments that feel a bit cliche, but I think the general love and joy this game emits overpowers or nullifies any of those gripes I had. I really don't want to spoil anything because again, I think the less you know, the better. It feels like a love letter to game-lovers and developers. I think the game overall does a great job of empowering the player and keeping a level of RNG but also certainty. It manages to provide some challenge, keep interest and continue to introduce new mechanics that keep you hooked. My only real gripe is that I played it on my laptop with no mouse, and there wasn't really a way for me to right-click. This didn't really affect the gameplay, but just made it a bit harder to check what certain cards did at times. There's also a lot of elements to remember and the fact that you couldn't opt-out of certain "buffs" felt annoying at times, but not a huge deal and ultimately made the path choices you made that much more important.I do think it's worth mentioning that with both the first and second major shift in the game, I had to overcome a slight frustration with having to learn what felt like a whole new game and that everything I had built up was gone. I'm mentioning this because I saw someone mention this in their negative review of the game and I believe it was their reason for not continuing the game. I think if you can stick with what the game ends up throwing at you, overcoming and letting go of that feeling of loss, the pay-off is worth it.It's one of those games that you will wish to play again with your memory wiped, so you can experience it again, akin to Outer Wilds and Obra Dinn. The main story has some replayability value for me in terms of being able to play with the cards more and taking my time with it, like re-watching a movie you enjoyed that has a twist ending. It won't be the same, but I do see the value in doing it at least once more. Also the introduction of Kaycee's mod will provide what I think I was hoping for in terms of being able to just keep playing the core card game, and I'm planning on dunking hours into that now. So, the general value of this game is also through the roof IMO.

One is that I love card games, but I often feel they lack the presentation and storytelling that card games could excel at. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DRIn the beginning you start in a murky cabin and a creepy figure introduces you to the card game.It lays down an interactive map and you start playing.During your time playing you will stumble upon events that force you to make tough choices and the creepy figure wears uncanny masks to act like characters and narrates the story.- Some animal cards are alive and talk to the player- The player can leave the table and explore the cabin- Whenever the creepy figure switches to a character, the music changes too.- One wrong move could be fatalAfter beating the creepy figure, everything changes for the worse.The plot, the music, the entire game turns from 3D to 2D, changes which nobody asked or paid for.All your expectation, excitement and imagination how you could possibly escape the cabin goes down the drain and you get introduced to new rules and new plots that are terrible than the one you experienced in the beginning. The whole concept of the cabin has been thrown into the trash.The reason why it's misleading and false advertising is not only because that they didn't show the second and third arc, it's because 1. Arc 2 added more creatures that aren't "woodland creatures" and there's no violence, events, let alone self mutilation which made the game dark and interesting to begin with. Everything they advertised was a sham!2 "Secrets lurking behind the walls of Leshy's cabin" There was no secret, they just made you play a different game than what they advertised. They completely dropped the whole concept of the cabin.That alone was a huge disappointment and I felt like I had to sit through while playing arc 2&33. "Embark on an unexpected and deeply disturbing odyssey." I really did not expect that they would make me play a completely different game that nobody asked for but what's worse is that the second and third arc wasn't even mildly disturbing at all.The things I liked are gone:- Animal cards that talk to the player are gone- The player can't leave the table in arc 2 since the whole cabin concept is gone.- No creepy figure, no horror, no events, no cabin- If you lose, nothing happens and you can just talk them again until you win. No more dying, no horror and completely lackluster plot than what happens in the first arc.Once again the player gets introduce to a new plot, rules and cards but they are awful, lackluster and there's no horror, creepy figure, self mutilation etc. Every screenshot, video and trailer was just arc 1. The third arc's game mechanic was ridiculously boring and repetitive unlike the first arc.It could have been a good game if they kept it simple. If they had only advertised it what it really was instead of lying to us and give us the false expectation that it was all about being trapped in a cabin, playing cards against our captor and that we could escape somehow.But instead we have a game that started good, but then suddenly changed completely just to tell a pretentious plot that sounded as if an obnoxious kid tried retell it, who also kept adding new rules, unnecessary cards and removed interesting mechanics which made the first arc interesting in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: Creepy, eerie, but most of all... INTRIGUING comes a horror rogue-like card game. As a fan of rogue-like card games and this studio's previous work, I knew I had to try this game out!I'm still going through it, but overall I'm very happy with the complexity of the card game. Despite the horror genre (which often leads to simplified gameplay), there's enough in the card games where there's always a new mechanic to learn. Be warned; although it is a horror game, there's a lot of card-related gameplay. You better be ready to throwdown a lot! I also believe your skill in card games can dramatically affect the length of the game.The storytelling and environmental effects are incredibly immersive; the overall theme has me returning for more. As for the horror aspect, I don't play too many horror games since I am very bad with jumpscares. This game focuses more on environment and themes in order to invoke uneasiness; which is right up my alley!Conclusion:- Moderate complexity in card gameplay- Great storytelling and visuals- No jumpscares (yet!), but still very horror-esque- Super worth it for a horror-loving, card-slinging nerd like me
