_childDocuments_.review: Mount and Blade with ARPG combat. All right. That's it. That's the review.Just kidding. Let's start with the good, because this game does do some things quite well, and then we'll move on to the bad and the ugly. I would like to preface all of this with a preword. At the time of writing, this game was freshly translated to my native language, English, and as such I've decided not to touch too heavily on the story. Now it's there, but the English is quite broken. Even so, things like pacing, introduction of character and building of tension and stakes are severely limited. Does that matter in a sandbox game? Probably not. That's why my section on story is here and not in Good, bad or ugly.The Good. The game's honestly quite fun. If you enjoyed any of the army management or kingdom management stuff from Mount and Blade, you'll probably like this game. The different armies are varied and interesting and the tiered troops feel stronger and stronger, gaining ARPG abilities as they level up to accomodate their style and not just flat statistical improvements. Hero characters can have their own, unqiue skills that change the way they fight and it's all quite interesting to explore. The maps are presented as wonderfully hand-drawn almost woodblock looking maps and everything is easy to read and identify. There's nothing really new, but the Action RPG skills and customization is an interesting approach. The game features a system called "Prestige" which allows you to bank points for consequent playthroughs. These are awarded as Legacy points to your character on character creation, incentivizing repeated playthroughs. With these legacy points, you can also scale the difficulty, and in-game it claims there is no limit to the difficulty scaling coded, so the game has a lot of replayable value besides just the classes themselves. Speaking of the classes, the design and theme of the game are great, being primarily influenced by Chinese culture but also having many aspects of middle eastern culture such as Sultans, Hashashin, Camels and desert culture in general, but overall there isn't a lot added to the classes. We've seen them all in other ARPGs, with perhaps the exception of the "Errant Knight" who's class would probably make more sense if it was called "Ronin Samurai", because that's what he is. English speaking players expecting a "Knight" might be a little confused for a moment. Using this system, you can even later create your own class who can take legacy bonuses of having the abilties of the other classes, allowing you to fully customize your character.The bad. The A.I. is abysmal. Now, if you're used to Mount and Blade, none of this is going to sound too new to you, but the game is fraught with A.I. making the dumbest decisions. I'm not expecting every fight to be a match of wits against Zhuge Liang, but so many aspects of the A.I. are just broken. Enemies who are designed to Skirmish like cavalry or archers will flee into walls and get stuck. Your character rigs to the ground to play a swing animation with no chase, so if anything moves slightly, you miss. The extent of the military strategy is just big, ugly murderballs and your A.I. allies will gladly fight them or engage in battles with no chance of winning on the offensive. Nearly no aspect of the A.I. is really good to look at.The game is also horrifically imbalanced from almost every angle or approach, with some classes being clearly far superior to others. This is marginally mitigated by the option to take Legacy Skills so you're able to fill in the gap on your character class, but there are also classes with no gaps so they use those same points just getting and remaining outright stronger with, for example, a stat boost legacy. Part of this imbalance arises from a system which I think is pretty neat, which is a shame. A lot of the encounters and events in the game are split up into "Squad" and "Company" battles. Squad battles are essentially small encounters with you and your bodyguards similar to an ambush in Mount and Blade but much more prevalent. Company encounters use your entire force. Certain classes, such as the Shaman (Beastmaster) and Sentinel excel at fighting in Company and others, Such as the Hashashin and Jackal (Bounty Hunter) excel more at smaller encounters and duels. Then there are the wild boiz who can do anything, such as the Spiritmancer and the Knight Errant. The problem is that as the game progresses, you're invariably going to fight wars against other Kingdoms. There's no way to honour duel or use your single-target character's abilities to reduce the enemy's forces effectively, and even worse it's a much more painful crawl to get to the point where you're strong enough to be sufficient either way. They don't even have an advantage in the early game to counteract. So you're just going to have a MUCH easier and easily noticed time playing different classes.The UI could definitely use some work and specifically, the player should be alerted of friendly armies on the march and their destination as well as easier options to collaborate with your allies, perhaps through a Marshall or messenger, but a lot of it's functional at bare minimum.The ugly. The elephant in the room for this category is the character portraits, but i'll also put down some other minor gripes. The character portraits look like something out of an anime fanpage on deviant art. And not one of those amazing artists, but someone who's just getting started and has no talent. I appreciate the customization within the confines of the system and some of the art genuinely looks good, but the whole procedure feels cheap and reminds me of a mobile game or one of those facebook gimmick "meme" generators. I would rather have the limited choice between a bunch of those crazy eyed Japanese woodblock characters or some traditional chinese inspired art than a build your own chinese anime husbando or waifu, but with the interactions playing out like a visual novel, it's hard to imagine another system working.I would love to see at least double the number of legacy skills and perhaps a skill builder that allows you to add effects like "Dash" and set variables for range, then chain it into something like "AoE", "Knockback" "Draw in", ect, because the current skills just feel like they're (perhaps purposely) lacking some punch, and this system would allow you to comprehensively fill gaps in character design, but I can also understand why the systems might be the way they are. Still, if it's buried deep enough in the legacy system, new players wouldn't miss the original vision.Ultimately, I think if you like both Mount and Blade and Diablo you'll be able to extract the asking price's value worth of enjoyment out of this game. I've already sank around 20 hours into just playing a few classes and I still have plenty of things to learn and explore. Wiki pages are limited in English at the moment so it might be a bit difficult if you're not used to wading into the game with reckless abandon, but with a very minor roguelite element that allows for persistence in the form of prestige and legacy, even your first few failed attempts will be worthwhile down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: The Chinese version of Warband, except it adds A TON of good ideas from many, many other games. The influences of High-Fantasy Asian MMORPGs is quite evident too, but the story has a lot of less filler. The arabic setting feels fresh. The controls are frustrating until you learn that shift lets you aim the shots. The music is good, but the same tune gets played way too often so you'll probably turn it off after a while. Everything else ranges from acceptable to really good.It's also a bit like Kenshi, in that it tries to do everything at the same time. However, it ends up going a lot deeper in many areas while managing to stay more polished and streamlined.After 2 hours of playing I thought it was ok, and wasn't thinking on recommending... But then I found a mod that re-enables the chinese voice-over. WHAT? For the price tag, absolutely recommended! Do grab the mod, though!

_childDocuments_.review: Note: if "meh" was an option I'd have used it.Good:- Conceptually this game is great. It's got party building and dude upgrading, very reminiscent of M&B, but seen from a perspective where it's actually reasonable to control your party to some extent. - The setting is really cool. Lots of mythological things flitting around trying to murder you or joining your party.- Battles are reasonably fun.- Lots to do in the world. There's a lot to discover, tons of different troop types and factions and quests.Bad:- The whole game felt like a gigantic QOL issue. Inventory management is kinda bad. Troop management is kinda bad. Control in combat is kinda bad. Dialog is kinda bad. Quest management is kinda bad. Basically, the UI needs to be overhauled by a professional.- Fiddly, without much explanation. I didn't play that long, but there were numerous systems where I had no idea what in the world was going on. My guys died. I guess I can bring them back? But I need potions? Unless they're not all dead? Where do I get potions? Stuff like that. A lot's going on and the game figures you'll figure it out eventually.- Too sandboxy. This is probably a personal preference, but I like to be guided a little bit. I like M&B, so I clearly like a good sandbox, but I didn't feel like I had a goal that I cared about so I was mostly wandering and fighting. The quests I did do were often frustrating - find this dude, or fetch this thing. I started to feel like I could either do the fun parts of the game or do the story parts of the game, since all the quests were boring.

_childDocuments_.review: Action RPG with pretty optional plotlines, recruiting units to battle alongside you and chance to conquer cities (and NPC nationalities that battle with each other and also you if you choose to establish your own state) in a fantasy setting. Roaming bandits (and other threats) are early game foes as you most likely fulfill simple missions for village chiefs while recruiting and leveling up locals. Plot gives something to work towards as you most likely wander around different maps looking for next brawl you could win while trying to avoid too many permanent casualties among recruits (as you need either promote or use special potions to bring back the dead). Battles are pretty fast paced and very early you learn to keep fast-forward button pressed as you travel around map from one village to next so that it doesn't take ages to get everywhere. Having a good AOE effect simplifies most fights between regiments and being able summon monsters makes solo fights a lot easier - characters differ somewhat how easy they are to play, but personally game seems to disagree with me somewhat how easy or difficult characters are in starting screen. Nameless is difficult to play, though.

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of people trashing this game because of the translation or other small issues, completely disregarding the price-point ($15) and existing contentThere are fan made workshop mods that tighten up the English translation.At time, to be fair, it does feel more like an 85% complete game that should still be in early access but even if they stopped adding content TODAY there is enough in this game at the price point to make it worth it (especially if it's on sale)I wish the Faction creation system and town creation system were more robust with more building options (but the same amount of plots to stimulate specialization).I wish there was a layout section prior to entering combat where you can position your units for the initial chargeI wish the interpersonal system for unlocking army passives and follower backstories was more nuanced with more attention to each follower, especially with more unique dialogues between followers (they seem to be archetyped and similar archetypes share dialogue pools)But these would all just be enchancements, tbh. The game is fun as is and, again, if I stopped playing tomorrow I'd have gotten more than my money's worth of entertainment

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty fun game, It's an auto battler but gives the player agency as an in game unit that is controllable by the player. It reminds me of DOTA in some ways. Although, the game isn't fully translated to English yet it's still quite playable and enjoyable, and the translation that has been done so far is easy to read and understand. _childDocuments_.review: How many games are there where your character can travel around an open world with a big party of heroes, their lover, and a huge army that can have warriors, wizards, and monsters in it? You level them all up, do quests around the land, build reputation with different factions, and can recruit practically anyone you meet. You can just explore dungeons or trade goods too. Then there's a whole strategy/war element where you conquer towns, build them up, appoint sultans from your recruited heroes, rally multiple armies, and so on.Now mind you this game is VERY rough around the edges, a lot of things are poorly written/translated, and not very fleshed out. But there's just so much to enjoy in it, if you don't mind a little jankiness in your sandbox, you'll get hooked.The new game plus system is a real treat, being able to pick more starting companions/bonuses based on how far you got in your best previous character (like a high score). The main story was an almost incomprehensible, elaborate fetch quest with some interesting ideas, which even on story mode you can just ignore for in-game years while you do your own thing, and doing your own thing is what this game is all about.Most important tip for the prospective player: Open your map and right click any location/town, even on different maps, and click "move here". When you close the menu, your party will autotravel to it in real time. Your wrist will thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to try this out.  The main interface is as a point-and-click RPG, which is pretty much the least engaging or immersive type of game possible.  Sands of Salzaar, however, is much more than a point-and-click.  An initial level cap of 20 was a Big No for me, too; but SoS has an enjoyable replay value that increases the level cap each time you start a new character (which is a new part of an overall RPG story - the way multiple characters  be done) .With multiple options in HOW to play and your choice of side characters not to mention how to modify, outfit, and level those characters up SoS is the framework for what the future of the RPG genre should be.  If I had the funds to invest heavily in this title I would do so; a first person interface and freedom of movement in a swichable game mode, and of course the interface to go along with it (not point-and-click) would make this the top RPG of the 2020s.  As someone who hand-down hates RTS and point-and-click games, Sands of Salzaar has become a shining exception in my book.  Checks all the boxes for your rpg itch without letting you down gives it a 10/10, but the fact that they're still improving and adding to the game brings it a full 'nother 5 points, and the additional joy of having developers appropriately combine sandbox features into a fully enjoyable experience places this game a 19/10 on my scale, breaking expectations and going the extra mile to add something to the gaming Industry as a whole.

There are static pictures of your character like in old RPGs but there isn't a sprite that matches every character, on top of that the sprites are very low definition and just generally look bad. Ah, I just realized why people would say it's like Mount and Blade, the units you hire level up over time and some units have different upgrade paths, that's the only similarity. I can not stress enough how bad the combat is, it's so bland, boring, clunky and the ai pathing is horrendous, they go in a straight line and will get stuck on literally anything in their way. _childDocuments_.review: Before we delve into the bulk of the review, I would like to utter a confession. I bought this game with only minor prior knowledge, having minimal information for the developer or the story itself. I bought this game for the aesthetics and frankly, because of my heartfelt desire to pollinate with that seductive, blue eyed vixen featured on the front cover. Now that my confession has been revealed, allow the genuine review to commence.Upon loading into the game, I was greeted with personally engraved Chinese messages. Using my knowledge of basic Mandarin, I was able to decipher the true meaning of these messages. It appeared that an entire barrage of threats, perpetuated by the Chinese government was being sent to my person. An onslaught of demands, ‘requested’ my assistance, with refusal to do so resulting in imprisonment in one of their ‘training’ centres. Naturally, I refused to comply with these unfeasible demands, promptly changing the translation to English. Note, the ability to change the language wasn’t exactly concealed and as such it took 10 minutes to locate. You’d presume that you’d be able to alter the default language before you loaded up the game, but alas no, these developers want you to suffer for not speaking fluent Mandarin. After, changing the language, I briskly began to play the game, entering the customization section. Quickly, I realised that the options were relatively limited, with the hair and eye colour unable to become modified. As a result, I used what tools were available to my person and set about creating a bug eyed, wilderbeast, wearing the mask of a feline. Truly the epitome of masculinity. After creating my elite Chinese soldier, I delved into the realm of this already peculiar game. Upon loading, I found myself venturing in the barren depths of the Chinese desert, scavenging for supplies like a lowly peon. Due to the lacking tutorial and complete disappearance of any quest markers, I was at a loss. I decided the most logical course of action would be to accumulate an army and fortunately there was an encampment nearby. My cursor revealed that in said encampment there were mistreated prisoners, with the hastily made translation insinuating that the prisoners would fling to my banner if I saved them. Naturally I attempted to free the prisoners, albeit it all went awry. After attempting to assassinate 15 guards, inflicting minor wounds, my skull was cracked open like a coconut crab and I was promptly released with a stern warning.  I was astounded by this utterly idiotic dialogue, these guards who were supposed sadists, torturing defenceless prisoners just allowed an attempted murderer to leave, virtually unscathed. Astoundingly, these guards are a tolerant bunch. After my stern warning I learnt my lesson and began to wander the desolate, bleak plains of Feudal China. Everywhere I went, I was harassed by wolves and insecure bandits, facing animosity in every direction. All the while, I was stuck in this God forsaken desert, surrounded by the same surroundings. Truly an extraordinary start. After fighting numerous adversaries, I realised with dismay that the combat was repetitive drivel, with the auto combat rivalling that of even Raid Shadow Legends. From my experience, the combat appears to be occasionally clicking space to dodge, left clicking enemies to attack and sparsely using special abilities, all the while allowing the character to auto manage the majority of the combat. Truly, I would rather have Dwarven harlots come to my house daily, with Jehovah’s witness ham fisting a Bible down my throat then endure this disgraceful combat system. Anyhow, even after all seemed bleak, I persevered, determined to try to extract a tinge of enjoyment. Shortly, in my campaign I encountered a bandit leader camp, and promptly decided to “Make Trouble” for them. While I originally envisioned a mass assault, resulting in a massacre, the reality was relatively underwhelming. Apparently the hastily constructed translation meant 1v1 duel the bandit leader with flimsy practice weapons and afterwards shake hands. After my initial triumph, I attempted to fight the bandit leader again, however, the bandit with a gesture of chivalry deigned not to. It is truly astounding, how such courtesy exists in a world rife with violence and bloodshed. At this moment I gleaned some significant information, the story, narrative and translation was immensely shoddy. Barely any consistency exists, characters change allegiances on a whim, quests don’t have markers and it all erupts into a confusing mess. The characters motivations if utterly devoid of logic and is frankly ludicrous, I recall witnessing the justification for a quest being, “He seems serious we should do something.” This ties in well with the locations for quests. When compared to a game such as Mount and Blade, although no quest markers existed, the description detailed the location of the village the quest was nearby, allowing the missions to be completely with convenience and administrative efficiency. In this game on most occasions you are told, “Please save and ransom my friend, he is nearby.” GREAT, THANKS. Furthermore, since I am not a Chinese farmer toiling away at my rice fields ,describing a characters appearance as, “He is as a dried vegetable on the first day of the rainy season” makes little sense. Overall, the dialogue is more perplexing than all the solar systems combined, it is a genuine enigma. I have witnessed those with Stockholm syndrome, attempting to justify a positive review for this game. They describe this game as a ‘Good alternative to strategy games.’ To call this game a good alternative to other strategies, is equivalent to saying, ‘This toaster is a suitable alternative to bath soap’, it is utterly ridiculous. Those suffering from Stockholm syndrome, furthermore, call the game a ‘Good game with flaws’, which is identical to saying, ‘Ted Bundy is a wholesome man with slight personality flaws.’ It becomes apparent that the undying fans, of this shrivelled, decayed game are severely downplaying the downsides in order to convince themselves that this game in it’s current state is a worthwhile investment. Overall, this game is as though I am bound to a chair, being slapped and beaten within an inch of my life by an old man. Every time, I recuperate, he then forces me, under threat of assaulting my wife and children, to play this game, essentially perpetuating me to endure this game. Eventually, after such a prolonged period of playing this game, I scream, I bellow and I shout and eventually the neighbours hear and alert the police, who siege my captors house and eventually save me. Afterwards, I then suffer from trauma and resort to alcoholism in an attempt to purge the memories of my experience playing this, temporarily it succeeds, however, eventually the embodiment of mediocrity returns to haunt my computer. Fortunately, shortly afterwards, I write this review and with the power of venting, all of my inner demons are expelled and once again I am a pure individual, able to escape the wrath of this game and their squirrel developers. It is not often that I play a game of this calibre. I would like to conclude that my enjoyment level while playing peaked at 2/10, that our overlords have flawlessly translated this game and soon it will be ready for cyber warfare.

_childDocuments_.review: To put it simply, I love this game. However, this game is not for everyone and certainly has some issues that may be too difficult for some players to overlook. This game is not originally in English. The translation is fine but nowhere near what you'd expect from a AAA title; some lines read poorly and quest locations can become difficult to find without a guide. Also some mechanics are poorly explained due to translation issues as well resulting in many mistakes in your first play-through. Nonetheless this game has an amazingly fun loop. Rally troops, earn favor, gain territory, and fight war; it gives you a great Mount & Blade experience that I personally enjoy more than Mount & Blade. The game has a lot of troop variety and some choices when it comes to base design. Want to be an independent Knight Errant who is wanted by all factions, you can do that; want to be a Dakn loyalist eventually being made general under Queen Rebiya, you can; want to say screw it and take a foothold in the Ifrit lands and declare war on everyone as the new big bad, you can. This game gives you the freedom to play how you want and rarely limits your decisions no matter the consequences. One game I played had ten factions running around the map and none of them were the original starting factions. The main story is serviceable but the game truly shines in Sandbox mode where you're free to play how you want; be a trader, a merc, a soldier, etc. All in all, I love this game and if you want another Mount & Blade with an Arabian Nights feel, then give this game a shot. The price is very fair for this title and I was even able to pick it up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to start by saying that I hate this game. I did not find the game play fun. It's kind of like Mount and Blade but Mount and blade is far more tactical and the combat in this game is akin to watching a toddler smashing two cars together. Whoever has the bigger stronger army is going to win. That being said I can see how someone might find the game play to be mindless fun and might not want a complicated tactical rpg. The real problem with Sands of Salzaar is the story. The story for Sands of Salzaar is bad. The majority of the game doesn't have much of a story you complete random quest and get stronger and some of your starting heroes have character specific quests but not all of them. I would prefer it if the game had no story (Mount and blade doesn't have one) but the last quest of the game dumps the story on the player giving long unskippable flashback sequences and hitting the player with lore at the very end of the game. The story goes like this; you bring peace to Salzaar and then you are betrayed and war starts up again, you confront the betrayer and beat them but the game tells you that you lost and teleports you to the other side of the game world and you have to go back and fight them again. You beat them again but the game tells you that you lost again and teleports you through time where you get a lore dump. In the past you are betrayed once again by someone that you have been told the whole game is the savior of humanity then are dropped into the present where you are betrayed by one of your companions before fighting the final boss. After playing through the last mission of the game I feel like I got whiplash from all of the plot twists that the game just drops on you. I would tell you that the game is trash and that you should stay away from it, except I bought it for 5 dollars, and if you don't like the story then you can bypass it entirely by choosing sandbox mode. Alright, fair enough game; you win this time.

_childDocuments_.review: Sands of Salzaar is an attempt to reverse engineer the out-of-combat systems Mount & Blade Warband from over a decade ago, replace combat with a simple top-down point and click experience, with some semblance of a story and quests, and the New Game +++ score/grade shop system from JRPGs like the Tales series games.Anyone who has played M&B Warband will feel right at home just an hour or two into the game, perhaps too much so. It is astounding and impressive how the developers managed to reverse engineer M&B Warband and make a copy of its systems, going so far as to replicate not only its good points, but also all its ugly flaws from a decade ago. Obtuse conversation options, faction members calling for a siege and then never doing anything, not being able to join parties although AI members can are just some of the quirks that they have maintained from copying M&B Warband.I had a lot of time with Warband when I played it, but I wouldn't play Warband today because I cannot tolerate the flaws that I've uncovered. When another game comes along 10 years later and replicates these very same flaws to a fault, I am really speechless. The new game plus score system is exciting, but if the base game itself is so janky to play, how would I even make it to NG+?Still, leaving a recommend for such an impressive feat by an indie developer.

_childDocuments_.review: I gotta say.. I used to love this game. It had it's bugs, sure. But the core was good. I recently went ahead and bought all the DLC's only to find that the bugs are getting progressively worse. The lack of translation in MANY parts of the game (Including a four-part quest that you get but cannot read because it is not in English) and many dialogue options. The things that ARE in English are often hard to understand.The AI is pretty horrendous. On the map, you never know what anyone is doing. "Meet here to siege this" but it never happens. Wasted your time. In the battles, there will be terrain features that the AI (which can be most of your army) gets stuck and cannot figure out how to get around.A lot of the items that are in the dungeons just flat out do not drop. They are listed as possible loot but, even after google searching, they just.. don't.A lot of the quests give zero indication of how to complete them. There is one to "Find the missing children" but it is timed and there are no markers on the map or anything. There are many that fall into this category. If you fail it, there are no do-overs. In fact, one of the very first quests you  get puts you in negative standing with one of two factions based on who's side you choose. It's not hard to recover standing but you shouldn't have to worry about an entire faction seeking you out in the first five minutes of the game.Sieges are terrible. The commands for your troops are so basic that more often than not, issuing them will just amount to higher casualties. Oh, and sneaking into towns? Don't even think about it until you are strong enough to kill the guards. lol.There also needs to be an auto-attack feature that your character will attack the nearest unit and move onto the next. This game makes your wrists hurt and the battles get so large that having to click on a new unit to attack them just becomes tedious. On this note, the color of the cursor- it matches the color of the sand in the desert. It is SO easy to lose track of it during battle, causing skills to go off in random places rather than where you intended. Not sure who's great idea that was.tldr: Don't buy the game. Get Bannerlord 2 or something instead. Though also not great, it is much better than this. It seems like the Dev's just no longer care. Unfortunate. This could have been great.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely fantastic game. It has a lot of problems.If you have ever been obsessed with the flash games Feudalism and Feudalism 2 like i was back in the day, this game will scratch that itch perfectly. There's a very natural progression from being this weakling loner with one follower to the leader of a powerful rampaging army, and it's fun at every stage. There are a ton of characters to play as, each with different play styles, there's so much to get lost in, like I'd say maybe 40 hours out of the 50 I've played are me not even acknowledging the main story and just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around on my own.You can join a faction, and enjoy the benefits that come with that, like built in allies and allied cities that offer security and plenty of money, or you can start your own faction, which is super fun, but seriously dangerous and hard. There are so many heroes you can fight and recruit and poach from other factions to join your own, or to not join your party but reinforce a siege on a city that you want. Only some of them have special stories, and some don't even have character blurbs, which sucks, but they all look pretty cool and seem like intimidating, competent fighters.No matter what I'm about to say about the negatives, this game is fun, and I'm having a ton of fun playing with it. HOWEVERAs with almost all games written in a different language and then translated into english, if you speak english, this game is going to be a little confusing at times. You can tell when things don't translate perfectly, which happens a lot, and sometimes things straight up don't make sense, or a character is saying they hate you, with language that doesn't accurately portray that. So there's that. But the confusion is not just relegated to the dialogue, a lot of game mechanics themselves are a bit confusing, or feel unfinished, or are straight up not explained. So for example, combining troops. Inn this game, you can take squads of the same type of soldier and combine them with an identical squad (levels don't matter for combining them, but the class and amount of soldiers in it do). This is basically essential to progress in the game, because it effectively doubles the size of your army once you figure it out. However, it never says you can do this, and unless you dig around in the management tab, you'll never know about it. An example of it feeling unfinished is no matter what, every character will say the same dialogue if you ask them something. If you ask a character about another character they have max relationship points with, they'll just tell you who they're allied with and where to find them. If you ask a character about someone they hate, max negative points, they'll tell you who they're allied with and where to find them. If you ask anyone in your faction the prompt "What's the plan?" at any stage, whether you have one city, or every city except one conquered, they'll say "We're developing and strengthening our forces" and if you ask "What do you think of our current situation?" anyone, from someone just recruited to the leader of the faction will say "We should launch more violent attacks on our enemies!" It kind of takes you out of the game, because it makes it feel like these political figures in the world aren't complex characters with different personalities, they're all the same people with different appearances.At a certain point in the story there's a massive spike in difficulty, and it kind of seems impossible from where I'm at 50 hours in.Side quests can either give you a super powerful piece of equipment, or give you 300 coins and be a complete waste of your time and there's no telling which is which.Those are all my major complaints. This is a flawed but beautiful game. My genuine advice is to buy this game and play it for 1 hour and 59 minutes, and then make a choice whether or not you want to refund it. I absolutely adore this game and probably will eventually sink 100 hours into it, but it's very clearly not for everyone, and I recognize that this game does have a lot of flaws that might be deal breakers for some. But truly, give this game a chance. Set a timer, and worst case scenario, you hate it and have wasted an hour. It might just hook you in like it hooked me though. 8/10, definitely give it a shot

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR : Game's janky as hell, but hey, wuxia mount&blade.+ It does what you'd expect from a mount&blade game : run errands, hire companions & troops, conquer cities and build improvements, talk with big shots and perform percussive diplomacy+ Actual variety of combat playstyle across classes, good variety of skills and spells+ Surprisingly good variety in NPC and companion character design, one of the strongest points imo+ Some wiggle room for builds as most equipment is viable and comes with both fixed & random passives/actives+ Decent replayability (NG+ shop for which you get points through achievements, different stories for each class)- Combat is clunky as all hell, you can't hide from it :-- Movement is only possible if you find an empty area to click, and that *will* become challenging later on-- Untargeted attacks require you to hold shift, and some weapons (smite-type) don't work with that at all and you end up hitting yourself instead of your cursor position-- Skill animation duration and general readability is unclear, some skills vfx feel hastily put together and offer poor if not no impact feedback-- Rolling out of telegraphs to dodge attacks works when RNJesus says it does. Spinning in circles very close to the boss / enemy pack has proven more effective than any attempt at arena-game style combat.-- Getting CC-locked (stunlocked, frozen on repeat or juggled) is a thing and will mess you up. Thankfully you have items to reduce CC duration below 0% and passives to render you immune to freeze and the like. You'll get frozen anyway.-- Squad orders limited to "attack/defend/follow", no tactical positioning options, you have to drag the actual squad behind you with "follow" and sit them down with a "defend" order. Not that it matters as both armies clash within the first 10 seconds of every fight anyway. Enemy only knows "charge".- Exploration is a bit limited (there will be 30 landmarks per map which are just repeat copies of some 4-5 biome-appropriate landmarks) and environments are cliché (Plains, Swamp, Tundra, Desert)- Bad pathfinding unless you're traveling from city to city- Story missions, dialogue, cutscenes, scene transitions, etc feel *very* amateurish and will leave you wanting for better moodsetting. Actual plot is good though.- The main modding scene is chinese, and unless you're able to read it you'll be limited to the crumbs translators had the patience to port to english (often outdated and unmaintained)All in all, it's a game with great ambition and a very solid amount of enjoyable content, but it brutally lacks polish and is less enjoyable for the english audience. Would still recommend if you can deal with and look past all the clunk.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with a lot of invested effort. But all of said effort has been thrown into a trash can on the last stretch.In spite of being out of early access, i'd discribe the state it is in as "open beta". The content is all there, it runs smoothly and mostly bug or lagfree, the writing's there, replayability etc. And it is great , but...- feels like localization has been screwed up at about 20% of the time, you'll feel it. Nonsensical dialogues, typoes, characters adressing the wrong genders and/or wrong names all the time etc. The actions of an outsider are sometimes adressed as your actions. (You nod)- The ending quest seems to have been tossed out hastily, seen by the multiple mentions of a third npc that supposedly traveled with you. They exist in the game, but never were part of the main story quest line at any point.- the music is not fitting the surroundings a fourth of the time. it's getting there, but feels like someone just decided to not finish their work. Maybe the project ran out of budget, i don't know.- because the story is dark and written to be immersive, such shortcommings hurt the experience a lot more, than they would with a title, that doesn't take itself seriously.I'd love to recommend it, and it is enjoyable - but at the same time, it doesn't sit well with me to encourage others to have a bite of an unfinished dish. Decide for yourself, if you are willing to overlook it's current flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr:Not ready for full release, but a gem in the rough. Translations need a bit of refinement but don't obstruct game play so far. Map and questing system needs a bit of review and refinement. Had to hand-write down all the quests because it's hard to tell when you will or wont get all the information needed in your quests journal. Enjoyable soundtrack. I'd like to see more of the characters art flushed out. Not all characters (heroes that can join your party) have custom art. character creation needs some work and cleaning. I don't think the game was ready for a full release and should've stayed in early access for a bit longer. Despite that, I think it is worth the price (on sale $8). Some people have said they've had issues because of the translations, but imo, they just need a bit of refinement and review. A bad translation has yet to cause me to not understand something, but I have noticed quite a few things that need a bit of review or change in wording. The other thing a lot of reviews I saw mentioned, was the quests. Indeed, the quest markers have honestly been the biggest issue for me. I started writing quests down by hand because they don't always tell you everything you need to know in your quest manager/journal. The map I think could also use some work, it is often hard to tell were things are and zooming in and out on the map is quite disorientating/ hard to follow.Last notes, many of the side quests were quite repetitive, but I have yet to really get bored of them. I'd really love to see them improve their character customization and add more character specific (as in heroes) art. _childDocuments_.review: Fun game, a little grindy but the progression is very satisfying early on. Sadly it suffers from the same issue as bannerlord (imo) where it becomes less fun the more cities you have to manage. I think the progression becomes less and less satisfying the deeper you get in the game. It's a very deep game, but the end game doesnt feel very complete. It also suffers balancing issues like bannerlord, like how you can just spam craft spears and sell them to every city for excessive money then proceed to win the game with your unlimited gold in banner, in salzaar you can just spam buy thur rams and watch them bulldoze everything without even costing jade (a rare currency commonly used to upgrade rare or high tier units).I'll give an example, let's say you find a weapon you really like, because of a unique effect that you can make entire really neat build around. Guess what? If that effect is unique to the weapon you wont ever see it again in a higher level version. Maybe it's like that for balancing reasons but it doesnt feel like there are too many choices for gear. You just run the highest lvl dungeons and make your character around whatever is available, which means you're limited to one to two unique effects per weapon type (aside from the random stats/effects you get).  Here's an example of one the things that start to feel not so satisfying. In the beginning after you realize you want to recruit the strong heroes as soon as possible, its fun going town to town seeing who's there and running errands for the first few heroes you like cause its super satisfying once you have them in your party. Missed one or two heroes you really wanted? Thats okay after you've done enough dungeons youll probably have more then enough gifts to have at least one or two that they will like, then combined with an errand or two you can poach them from their faction. Now here's where it gets lame, once you start your own force you need to start recruiting as many heroes as you can cause youll need to leave them in towns to manage and defend them, or do things for your force. This means they wont even be in your party, which is fine, but you'll also have to go around gifting and running errands for whoever you can. In fact it's recommended that you get your favor/reputation up with as many heroes as you can before you even start your own force since it makes you declare war on everyone. Endgame seems to be just doing NG+ on a higher difficulty, and I love the NG+ concept, especially with the legacy points system since it encourages you to just do whatever on your first run to figure stuff out while you grind legacy points for your next run. End game on your new save will probably just be picking a class(es) and arcana you like, then grinding wisdom crystals. This would be more fun if there was content that required you being that strong. I actually enjoyed the stories and side quests. Im not a story type of guy, I always skip rpg dialogue and story, but even the side stories were really interesting and fun, lots of plot twists and surprises. It reminded me of the old final fantasy games, final fantasy 1 specifically, where you find quests randomly just from exploring around and there's no hand holding to progress it, but youll probably progress your quests on your own anyways just playing the game. It's a more natural flow that I enjoy, rather than a linear experience where youre just trying to brute force your way to the next part in a railroad of events. That said there are a lot of things that will frustrate you to no end.. like trying to find people, and some quests will completely stump you. Honestly most of the game issues can be fixed with mods. Like the issue of jade farming being really hard, theres a mod for that makes it just slightly easier without making you feel like youre cheaing, etc. Overall this game is a very solid 8.5/10. I was not expecting much tbh, it was way better than I thought. Easily worth the full price. I hope it keeps improving. Game is still getting frequent updates which is really cool to see too.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, and if the devs keep building on it, it will become incredible, but it gives you virtually no help/guidance, so I've decided to share some of the key things I've learned since starting the game last week. Hopefully these tips can prove useful to new players:1) The start is going to be ROUGH. You're going to want to explore and get drawn off into the vast world on offer, but you'll find yourself out of your depth and failing quests pretty quickly if you're not careful. Stick with your main character quests and the Redstone keep area whilst you level up, otherwise you'll end up with a dead squad and lost reputation with factions. Don't worry, once you level up, you'll feel more powerful and it's a pretty decent power curve depending on your character class.2) Don't be afraid to take on basic units for 150Utar - they will grow with you and can be levelled up into very powerful units. 3) Keep hold of anything you receive as a 'gift' when raiding/questing - they are usually items of interest that you can give to potential party members to win them over. One example is the combat gloves/helmet etc. - you can gift those to a female character in the Eastern Umbra Cliffs with red hair (I forget her name) and she will join you.4) Don't go seeking out any quest and hoarding quests as many have timers (it will tell you, but only AFTER you accept the quest) - many will be beyond your capabilities for a while, so better to come back later once you're Lvl 15+5) In Umbra Cliffs you can find Ultimate Forge Hammers easily which will repair any equipment, so if you find yourself with a decent piece of gear with low durability, head down there and stock up.6) Utar is tight at first, a great way to get more is to ask town Chiefs for quests and sometimes they will give you a quest about a kidnapped noble with a 1,000 Utar reward. They will give you 1,000 Utar (which you can spend if you want and go rogue) which if you then deliver to the Bandits who kidnapped the noble, will net you a 1,000 Utar reward with no fights and minimal work. Easy 1,000 Utar, plus reputation gain. 7) Another easy early quest to look out for are ones about groups of teenagers that have run away, they will usually be easy to find (one set to the right of town, left of town and below the town). You get an easy fight for XP, then nice XP, Utar and reputation gain upon completion which is pretty quick.8) Trading is the best way to boost your Utar - from Redstone buying the pepper is an affordable investment, then head north and you can sell it for a significant profit at the Golden Bazaar or another town near the top of the map. Similarly, taking something from the far South towns up North is easy money too.9) You can fast travel. Press M to open the map, then right click on a location and select 'Move Here' then press 'T' and it will massively fast forward time so you get there v fast.10) If you have a dead unit, you can revive them with a White Rose potion - I'd recommend getting early talents in the healing tree which will give you 2 potions every week, so that you can revive units if you find yourself regularly getting into tough fights.11) Look out for Bandits attacking trade caravans - you can join the fight to assist the caravan for nice XP and loot - they are usually quite easy fights as you get help from the trader's party.12) Once you're lvl 5+ attacking the Prisons to free captives is a good way to get free new units for your army.13) If you come across a villager wanting wood in the Umbra Cliffs, don't give them any until you have a HUGE amount as I have almost 1,000 wood with no result.14) To capture a camp you will see several control points once you attack it - simply go and hold each one until it turns green (Domination style) - if your units aren't doing what they want or you want them to push to take a point, select 'All Units' then 'Attack' to get them moving as sometimes they will just stand there.15) Don't worry too much about Talent Point allocation as you get a seemingly endless supply regardless of level cap. They are all strong trees and there's no 'best starting tree' as it depends what you'll be focusing on first (trade vs more characters in party vs large army etc.)There's still a way to go and the combat could certainly be improved with units running endlessly into walls etc. but it's well worth your time and money - plenty of replayability and quest galore. I haven't tried taking over a town for myself yet but will be giving that a go soon too. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun, it's like a moba fight style mount and blade. A lot of aspects are more or less copied directly from M&B. If you enjoy the game play loop of M&B this is enjoyable. But it's unfinished. I bought this a year ago when it was still in EA to find that half of it was in Chinese. I refunded it, and saw recently it was on sale with DLC out. I figured I'd give it another shot, and yeah still unfinished. More is translated but there's still quite a bit that's in Chinese. There's frequent stuttering and game breaking bugs. 6 dollars still isn't bad if you're a fan of the genre but I hope this helps people make an informed decision.Edit: Google Translate app is very useful in some situations if you do want to try this game. There is a little pen next to the mic which will allow you to draw hanzi. As long as you're kind of close, the app will give you a handful of similar hanzi in the little autocorrect barAlso the workshop is overflowing with adult NSFW mods. I mean that's cool and all, you do you, but some regular mods would be cool too. (Mouse cursor is hard as ♥♥♥♥ to see in big battles.)Another added note. I've now reached end game on three different saves and it's just broken. Defeated heroes/leaders recover near instantly. The game still continues when you're in a battle, but at a ridiculous rate. By the time I run to another village and take it, my original village is gone. The leaders from every other faction, despite being at war, team up constantly to attack my one village. Pretty ridiculous since if their caravans are attacked by bandits my only option is to help out the bandits. I was set on 100% completing the game but the inconsistencies and balance issues outweigh the fun now because of how broken the end game is. I can solo entire armies but it doesn't matter, because of everything that happens simultaneously outside of the battle.

_childDocuments_.review: i've only just started the game, but my first playthrough went from picking it up at around 9 pm and playing until 4 am. Can't really speak much on the story since I got side tracked from that, however I'm sure its cool enough.Pros:- The in game faction politics are very fun, and immediately change how you get through the game. ♥♥♥♥ over any faction and you can get hunted down, and you'll have a harder time being able to do other side quests-The scope of combat can get quite large, and there is a good balancing between skill of the player and how squishy he is against dozens of mobs. The 2d overhead view also helps manage the battle.-Combat has loads of way you can spruce things up with abilities and items and can help turn the tide of battle.-There are various kinds of quests in this game, some flashbacks, some basic fetch quests, some centered around slaying enemies, recovering farmers etc. Most village quests coming from unnamed npcs will have this randomized ai feel to it but that's ok, I just hope the story is good.Now here are my cons/areas to improve:-Npcs leftover from quests you failed to finish with just walk around the map and can't even be interacted with anymore. I say that at least in single player mode there should be a way to get rid of them-Nothing wrong with a lot of these quests having a timer, the main issue is though that we don't have any reliable ways to get to any where or know where things are. Not saying we need some massive arrows leading us everywhere but maybe some interactable sign posts being put up can help us a bit? These are my current thoughts and I'd like to update them as time goes on. This is my first alpha testing and I have high hopes for this game, especially since I haven't enjoyed many games in months

Thats it. Wow. I cant finish my previous quest. BUT YOU CAN TRACK THE QUEST AND IT EVEN HAS A MARKER THAT LEADS RIGHT...to the questgiver and almost no quest has those anyway.Wow. How in the world did this got released? I got fooled by the good reviews, absolute SHAME on you. Time to refundEdit2 from comments: Someone said you can actually talk to people to know more about your quests, its a little unusual and I personally did not found it but at least its something that kind of helps but they should really make a tooltip about this.Edit3 from comments: I turned them off now because people obviously couldn't read properly but kept coming with accusations.I'll give an example with two quest I've had now. One was bugged and the other one shows exactly how this games quest design is simply not "oldschool" but instead just absolutely awful.1) Debt CollectionAsgrid (A hero from a tavern that I can possible recruit) asks me to collect debt from Latif. She tells me in what region Latif is but not the village. You can ask a waitress at a tavern for the exact location. I went there and found Latif, even the waitress confirmed me its the exact location of the guy - however Latif only had another quest for me and after that I couldn't engage in dialogue with him again or do my quest and collect the debt.The new quest I got from him is entirely unrelated to the previous and is its own seperate quest.2) Rescuing NoblesWe all know this quest from Mount and Blade - rescue the brother of a family or whoever from bandits. _childDocuments_.review: The unfortunate thing here is that Sands of Salzaar is a good game, but I can't recommend it in it's current state.The game is basically mount and blade but isometric and with fantasy elements. If you enjoyed mount and blade, you'll enjoy this. Only problem is that the game feels unfinished. There's bugs/typos/glitches everywhere. I got quite close to the end of the game but was unable to complete it because of a progression-halting bug. There's also plenty of chinese characters where I guess they hadn't yet implemented the english translation.There's also an extremely limited amount of battle maps, so you're going to be fighting on the same terrain over and over. Doesn't seem like a big deal until your 50th battle on the same map.The story/dialogue is very anime-esque (ultra dramatic and ultimately nonsensical) so if you're into anime, you'll probably like it.The game has lots of items/characters that do feel relatively unique.. so they did a nice job in that regard. The combat it'self is also quite good, though as your party grows in size, massive battles are over in seconds.. which feels... weird. Maybe some adjustment to TTK is needed.TL;DR - this is a fun game. It really is. But it doesn't feel finished and I have no idea how active the developers are at the moment. My recommendation would be to keep this game on your wish list and check in on it in a year or so.

_childDocuments_.review: * Sands of Salzaar plays like a 'RPG meets Mount and blade' game. The gameplay loop is as follow : - Start as a lone wanderer and travel the world to meet gain some experience and artefacts,- Help the world's inhabitants with their quests, meet the mighty lords and heroes, accomplish tasks to gain their favor and reputation with their factions. - Recruit those heroes or lords into your inner circle. Recruit generic troops from merchants or towns, hire deserters or release prisoners.- Gather resources to improve your troops.- Purge the world of bandits, hunt and be hunted, slay the evils that lurk in the wild. - Once you're strong enough, besiege villages or cities to rule over them, join a faction or create your own kingdom. * The game is currently 99.3% playable in English. I have seen only two texts not translated and they were on very minor dialogs with no consequences. * The graphics, though simple, are consistent between maps, faithful to this desertic athmosphere that the name of the game hints at.* I haven't met any technical issue or bug. * The game is highly replayable. Each playthrough will give you legacy points to use at a new start and unlock different advantages or companions.

_childDocuments_.review: Sands of Salzaar is one those games I wish I could give a mixed review, so I'm going to lean into it being negative.I didn't play Salzaar early in its development cycle, so in its current state, the English reads fine. There's still something in the talent tree left untranslated, and some story text needs an extra quality pass, but thankfully none of it is machine translated, there's rarely any Chinese, and based on past reviews I could tell the game's had several patches. Overall, the English translation is solid, so don't let any of the older reviews concern you.The main concern left unaddressed is it tries to imitate Diablo's combat... poorly. First, the combat is too quick, so set the in-game speed slower (yea, that's a thing). Second, it's hard to click with any degree of precision, especially if you don't voluntarily slow the game down, so I recommend playing a spell-caster for area of effect tactics. There also doesn't appear to be auto-attack, so if you're not clicking, your character will just stand around. Regardless, combat gets repetitive; there's a lack of battle map variety, with each area sharing only 1-2 maps, depending on if it's a siege. The AI's fairly bad and can be manipulated thru clever tactics. You'll typically only lose when massively outnumbered, even near max difficulty on just your first new game attempt. Salzaar only gets easier the more you play by rewarding Legacy points for completing in-game achievements. Legacy points are used for bonuses at the beginning of your next new game. You can also artificially make the game harder with these bonuses, but why someone would subject themselves to more of this game's torturous combat is beyond me.Salzaar's defining feature is it's campaign world map. It borrows a system nearly identical to the game Mount and Blade (PC). Unlike Mount and Blade however, Salzaar does a better job making the player invested in the story and characters. Mod support further personalizes the player's experience, allowing them to import their own portraits and other tweaks, although most of the mods are in Chinese.Overall, I wish I could have the world map and characters of Salzaar, but with the combat system of either Diablo or Mount and Blade. Salzaar's combat is holding it back and needs an overhaul. I tried forcing my way thru the combat, but it's a grind that will make you question if the combat is worth investing dozens of hours. If you want a Diablo clone, there's better ones out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to give this game a shoot because of the mixed reviews.This game feels stressful because of the constant time pushing mecanic that is pressuring you to accomplish missions or stuff to do in the enormous map with too many cities that is almost impossible to memorize.The UI/UX experience for quest tracking is painful, when you "track" quests, you don't receive a pin in your map, just text in the corner of the screen that tells you what to do (in a time frame), then you need to open the world map and figure out where you are and where is the destination, make a mental map of where you need to go and keep manually tracking, none of the mechanics are explained, so you need to figure out everything, i have spent too much time in worthless mechanics that don't reward anything helpful for the story.Is it a City Builder? No. Is a combat extensive game? No. Is a lore focused, story based game? No. After 12 hours of gameplay i don't know what i'm doing, just travelling in the game doing pointless quests and fighting worthless enemies in the map, there's almost no strategic focus in raids, just mobbing.It seems other players have found how to tame fantastic monster, after 12 hours of gameplay and having all my heroes and armies in Max Level (20, too easy to reach max level, after that it feels worthless to just keep fighting to lvl up) i haven't found that mechanic.Another mechanic, Brawling feel pointless, what's the point of this? Feels clunky as hell, there's tournaments but is just a bunch of enemies rushing tru'you stunning or knocking you, there's nothing there for the other mechanics in the game, game doesn't explaint why you should do this, other than completing more "side quests" to get favor points from heroes.That brings me to Solo Hero Fighting, there are some combats where you will found you fighting other heroes in 1v1, but the combat mechanic is sooo unresponsive, super clunky, dodge/roll doesn't seem to help at all, you click enemies and your hero just make an unresponsive attack after X seconds, and thats it, there are some enemies that EVERY attack knocks you up and is unavoidable, and they also heal, with a maxed melee champion can't do ♥♥♥♥ about that, because everytime you have an opportunity to hit, they knock you and if you are lucky enough to hit them they heal that up, making it an endless fight, and you cannot leave the fights, forcing you to quit to menu and reload the last save/checkpoint you did.There's no real politics in the game, just gaining favor points tru' quests and helping other heroes in the same faction.Economics isn't a real thing also, when you found a route to trade a 400 item to sell it to another city in 1200 thats it, cities don't grow in resource production, so you are always capped by the amount of resources you can find after the spawn time frame is reset, the max amount of "wood" or "iron" has been 100 in a CAPITAL city, and you need 6,000 of EACH to upgrade some buildings in your "cities", another mechanic that isn't explained, you receive a City after having favor with your faction and they give it to you without hesitation or doing anything, just there, existing, and you receive passive income after every week.With an Overclocked Ryzen 9 5900X, 6700XT gpu, 32 gb 4000mhz ram, PCIe4 m2, the game have long loadings every before and after you enter another scene/combat/map, the game 'stucks' and weird noises happen for like 5 seconds, it's a 2D non-intensive resourse game, that should happend every 30 seconds or 1 minute when you try to do an action in the game, gets you out of immersion.I have too much negative points of view for this game, at this stage the game feels pointless nor rewarding to play, just capped grindy with empty mechanics that could have potential.

_childDocuments_.review: At first, it appears fine. But even for a low budget game, it's bad.First, the looks. It's dated as hell. I played better and more pleasing looking games 25 years ago. I played better looking low budget games in the meantime. Even tiny one man studios delivered better.Second, the engine. Microstuttering all the time, it's just physically tiring to play it.Third, music. It's also tiring all the time, and the battle music don't fit so much it's laughable.Fourth, the strategical map. It's ok, but again it looks bad, and it's incredibly monotonous, even though there is few variations of it. It's not even 1990's look, it's bad 1990's look.Five, the battles. Give me a break. Orders? Gameplay? Nonsense. It's fast paced chaos you won't be ever able to control, so better bring a bigger and better army than opponent.Six, mods. I love mods, moddability is usually one of the big factor in buying the games for me. This game has potential, there are even tons of mods for it. But nearly all are in Chinese. I mean, it's a chinese game so it is to be kinda expected, but still, a reminder.Overall: It's a trip bak to 1997, but a bad trip. For the full price, it's heinous rip-off. Even for the current -40% you would better go and buy Mount & Blade Warband - it's similar game but way way better in ever aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: Dec 18, 2021 after 37 hours in:Pros outweighed the cons for me, so thumbs up for this one.There are my opinions and not necessarily right or wrong.Very fun to play.Some bugs encountered and head-scratching on quests,  but nothing game breaking that I couldn't work around.Sure, there are things to be tweaked, but I think the skeleton/backbone/main-structure/heart/core of the game is pretty good.Games I like which this game reminds me of in one way or another:Mount and Blade (M&B)KenshiBattle BrothersCompared to Mount and Blade, I wouldn't way combat is necessarily better/worse; rather, different.Different in a good way.As with M&B, you do 'zoom-in' to a battle zone whenever combat happens.You start as a main hero from several class types, some relying more heavily on melee, magic, AOE, animals, etc.As with M&B, you can recruit heroes(after doing quests for them) and regular troops.Some folks want more punishment for losing battles; I'm fine with the current implementation.I mean, if they want to add a 'toughness' stat that you get from getting beat us (as in Kenshi), that would be nice though.Depending on who defeats you, you sometimes have to pay a small ransom to get your troops back.I like how you start with full HP(hit points/health) at the beginning of every battle; there is a chance your troops will go from 4/4 to 3/4 or lower though.... where you have to use a certain potion to raise the squad count to full.You can spec into reducing the chances troops will get injured (which helps)There are multiple game saves allowed. "F5" quick save works too.Map is static, not procedurally/randomly generated, but is pretty big and decent.I'd rather a static map than a procedurally generated one that is essentially the same thing with different colors and in No Mans Sky.There are about 5 or 6 kingdoms with unique units, strengths/weaknesses.AOE is king in this game, which seems to make single-target damage classes kinda weak.Though, as you get bigger armies, that evens out a bit more.Some quests make it so that only your hero units (you start with one) can do certain missions.There is probably some balancing to be done in the future.English translation quality? I'd give it a 8/10.Graphics:pretty good in my opinion; have not disappointed. Consistent for the most part for the style of the game.My biggest gripe would be losing track of where my mouse cursor is in a battle because of all the 'firework'-like action going on in a given battle.Quests:Others are right about quest givers.It is often unclear where you have to go to complete some quests depending on the type, which makes that part of the game feel unfinished. The workaround is to only accept quest types that you know are straightforward, which I hope will be patched/updated later.Pet Peeve:I do not like how we have to complete the main story before going into sandbox mode.Am not exactly sure if sandbox mode is different from story mode or not, but having to run through story mode with numerous new class builds is a bit annoying, but not game breaking.Have not finished story mode, but I like the plots and story twists in what I came across so far.Buffs/Debuffs:It is not clear when your character has a buff/debuff on them.It would seem that would have to be a future game area of enhancement.No game crashes so far.I did find that restarting the game made loading screens go faster, so maybe there is a slight memory leak that will be fixed in the future for that.Enemies scale up in level and quantity as you progress, but it is not clear to me what the algorithm is.Number of squads I have?My hero level?not sure...For the most part, I think they did a decent job of having a game where you can free-roam to all kinds of regions but not constantly get one-shot by super high level enemies without warning. There are points of interest which give you a recommended level number ( good idea).You can conquer towns in the game, but I haven't done a whole lot yet.I read that you have to be a Sultan class in order to build extra buildings in a conquered town/city; haven't tried yet.From what I saw so far, it does not appear there is any deeply complex empire management simulation.I did eventually find myself spam clicking the mouse through dialogues that I already read a few dozen times already.There are mechanics in the game such a 'prestige', which seem to be undocumented so much so that I stopped the beastmaster class(or whatever its called) because I couldn't figure out how to get enough 'prestige' to continue in the hero's quest chain so that I could learn how to morph in to more powerful animals.As other mentioned, some quests are mostly undoable because it's unclear where to go or what to do.The workaround is to do the kinds you can understand.Things I noticed fixed since release:There were a few buildings that were unable to be interacted with that I saw were patched in 2 days since release; not bad.Looks like some balancing with scaling was fixed with some bandit mobs as well.Much of my guidance in the game literally came from web searches about the game.There seems to be no well defined English wiki for figuring out game mechanics.Crafting systems in games are hard to do right. Can't say I noticed much in the way of crafting in this game, but I'd rather no crafting system than a crappy one. (my opinion)I really didn't find interest in utilizing consumables in the game for temporary buffs, mana/health restoration.Maybe I should, but that's just me. So game allowed me to keep it simple if i wanted to; I didn't feel forced to.Game did NOT feel overly grindy to me (every game needs some, but not too much).Attack animations felt 'weighty' so that a weapon swing looks more like attacking with a weapon than a paper plate, if you know what i mean. Good animation work.You can pay (a reasonable amount of) money to get neutral with a faction if you totally got them pissed.So no need to do senseless game re-rolls over that.I read somewhere that there might be a game enhancement to allow respec'ing of hero talents/skills. (not necessary, but nice to have)Gratifying to see units follow your main hero around the game map, accurate to which troops you have.Lots of points of interest to go to, but I wouldn't complain if more were added. (maybe an option to choose how many in game start mode?)Pleased with a number of game design decisions.Here is one:Some things you do in-game set you up for bonuses for future game playthroughs, which seems to be a feature often seen in rogue-like games, although this game has game saves so that it is not a rogue-like genre.(good since it rewards you for finding those little treasures in the game for yourself; gives reasons to explore and do random quests)Overall, I think Sands of Salzaar is a welcome addition to my Steam library.I don't regret picking it up.I haven't looked into anything about the history of the dev team for this game with regards to fixing content after releasing a game, so I cannot comment on that. I did see there was a Discord channel for reporting stuff, but I didn't go to it. If I had an in-game bug reporter, I would use it though. (Osiris New Dawn has a decent one implemented)

_childDocuments_.review: In short, the game is like a 2D version of Mount & Blade, except it put much more emphasis on main character customization. Since it is in many way similar to Mount and Blade, I will use it as comparison in this review.You are been thrown to no where and are expected to figure how the game goes by playing it. Fighting small battle, gaining fame and money until you are strong enough to take on a nation. If a RPG-like army building sandbox game is your thing, then the game is for you!Because it has more RPG element than Mount and Blade, your main character often, if not always, will decide the outcome of battle, since many of the skills the PC has can take down scores of enemies while your actual army take out a handful of fleeing enemies that you are will likely not bother to chase in order to finish the battle. Though the combat system is simple and easy to get proficient at, honestly the game  seems to be model after many Chinese mobile phone game,  more focus on clicking bottoms. There is very little technique you can master to win the combat other than skill CD management and how fast you train your army. Because of this, the combat will become  a chore rather than an actual challenge in later game. To me, currently build, the combat is the only weak link of the game, other part of the game such as city management, party building, story, or even art style are well designed.

_childDocuments_.review: Sands of Salazaar has a solid foundation and I've enjoyed my time with it so far. If you've played Mount and Blade you'll recognize it's combination of RPG elements with light army, settlement, and diplomatic management.You've got your rank and file troops that take part in battles and sieges, which are the bulk of the game play; then there are the hero/officer types that can take part in the former but can also join you in dungeon exploration sections, which are mostly text basted except for the combat and a usually a small map to explore at the end; and then there's your personal character that takes part in all parts of the game play, of note there being one on one duels and showdowns against another - a good number of them being special challenge or boss type fights.As of writing this review the game world has all your basic when it comes to things to do and interact with. You got your main campaign as well as NPCs on the map that offer one-shot story side quests. Most raid spots and dungeons are repeatable and farmable after a reasonable cool down period. The other major characters and settlement chiefs offer randomized missions or "errands" as they're often referred to in the game. There are some map spots which are one shot, usually (to my knowledge) the more exotic units only obtainable by these, which is a shame as the human units can be kinda samely and basic - but also understandable for rarity's sake. Overall the core game play loop works and is enjoyable, and same could said for the game's aesthetics.There's is a bit of a ticking clock to do some things, such as completing story missions or defeating special opponents found in the map, in a certain amount of time to gain legacy points that can be spent to get bonuses on your next play through. This does add a fun bit of pressure to the game play, but can be annoying when you get missions to track down a mobile NPCs that are running around a large region not much to go on to figure out where they are other such inconveniences.Other little nitpicks are that the controls are little clunky and ability cool downs a little long. Would rather have some less power but more repeatable abilities added in, as most of the abilities are the powerful kinds that leave you stuck relying on your basic attack waiting for them become available again. Even your basic roll out of the way dodge type skill has a recharge time, although you can store up a few usages. I can understand this from a balance perspective, but from a game play perspective it makes the game play revolve too much around cool down management for my tastes. In my playthroughs, I acquired various different versions of ranged magic attacks that did roughly the same thing so I could make sure to have at least one available even though it took up a number of hotkeys. Most games the limiting resource for basic skills would just be mana or energy (which this game uses too) and cool downs would be reserved for the more powerful abilities. And also right now there's only a single way or a limited number of ways to do certain essential actions, such as repair equipment or restore damaged squads to full strength (both done by using hammer and potion inventory consumables respectively). I'm sure they'll probably add more options and they flesh out the various game systems in time, but as it stands the lack of say NPCs in settlements to do these kinds of things as a plain and simple paid service does feel sorely lacking. Especially since the current system for repair and squad restoration does get a little tedious.Overall despite the nitpicks, I think the game Sands of Salzaar is enjoyable as it is though a little rough around the edges still. But looking at it's update history, I do feel optimistic and look forward to how they further develop the game.

Quest reward : 200 coins.Town mayors keep trying to force you to take the 1000 coin ransom quest at end game, and I dont want to click 4 times just to reject this. Should give a toggle to auto reject particular town quests or give option to pick whichever quest you want.Main story quest forces you to peacefully negotiate with all 5 tribes, but if you have joined a tribe then the other tribes treat you as a criminal and dont let you enter their city or meet their members. Tribe leaders once they see you on map either fight you on sight or just run off to nearby city and there is no further way to talk with them to progress on quest other than to siege their city and force them out.Thur - Ludo Khan kept fighting me on sight any time I tried to talk to him, so I sieged every city he had in Umbra Cliff, when the last one was left he let me progress on main quest.Dakn - Rebiya first game me the quest, I finished it but I couldnt submit because she kept attacking me on sight or camp in some city. Just like Thur, I sieged every city but still wouldnt let me submit quest. So, I finally wiped this faction off map.
