_childDocuments_.review: For most of a time I thought it is a decent game. Sure it's tidious, you got to fight the same enemies in the same locations over and over. Sure the fight system is too complicated to the point where you don't have to care much about most of mechanics. Sure the world is empty and all of the districts look the same. But this game is competent, it's easy to get the story, the atmosphere is engaging, voice acting is very good and dialogues are well written. There is a lot of character classes, a lot of different weapons, different armours, progress system is kinda cool and you feel that power rising.  And then comes the ending -there is none. Throughout whole game there were no cutscenes that we could see in a trailer (that's just different camera angle!!) and it reached lazyness level highest in a finale, where I don't even know what has happened - there is no dialogue, no information about anything, just one question - would you like to go back to menu or start new game plus - I have never seen ending that lazy. If this was early acces I would just get that ending hasn't been added yet, but no - it's full version and the thing that happened in a last two fights are ridiculous.

_childDocuments_.review: ► The strategy associated with classes and party building was actually very interesting and engaging. However, a lack of clear and detailed explanation led to some confusion in understanding just how everything works. Should be easier for others.► A good mix of 15x classes form the base element of tactical strategy. Some are unique, others overlap thus providing an idea of which ones should blend well together. This allows for a wide range of possible party configurations that provide many possible combinations of tactical synergies.► The flexibility afforded through the open class customisation is strong. All done by just equipping the requisite equipment. The need for finding equipment is an additional foil to exploring the city.► Learning class abilities is easy, by delivering enough attacks using the appropriate weapon. A lot of needless repetition is avoided as it becomes available to any character in the party who subsequently adopts the class. As an added benefit the weapon does not even need to be equipped.► The way "advanced" or rare weapons are introduced into the latter stages prolongs the opportunity to change or add new skills to a particular class.► At its core turn-based tactical combat feels calculating and retains a puzzle-solving feel.► It saunters between being a maddening experience and a engaging one, depending on game progression and party level.► Forming the bulk of gameplay it eventually becoming very repetitive, as the party make they way through 100+ fights by the end of a single playthrough.► Tactical depth comes from the many layers: character stats, weapons and armour, flanking attacks, buffs and debuffs, critical hits, elevation, bonuses from trinkets and throwables. Class abilities that inflict damage and most important, the use of 4x humours that require catalysation.► Begins to feel formulaic, with only the abilities from newly unlocked classes or from those unlocked with newly acquired weapons prompting the player to change established and winning strategies, tactics and/or synergies.► A generous amount of action points allow for multiple phases of movement and attacks, providing the party with the chance to deal with enemies when outnumbered. Particularly so after the first act of the game and the party grows in strength.► The game ran at 60fps for the most part. Only on a few occasions did I notice any stutter in motion and this was specifically when traversing the city in exploration mode after a few hours in session.► A few crashes were experienced. Thankfully the save system uses several autosaves to minimise loss of progress. Additional crashes have been reported by other players. Unclear if these have been fixed since.► Bugs experienced: access to Main Menu ceased after visiting the hub or leaving the sewers. A few slain enemies would remain animated. Lights of "friendly" buildings were on all the time. NPC recruits in some locations were duplicated.► Possible QoL issues: The side-quest for finding a certain type of enemy that rarely spawned. Another side-quest did not materialise. Unsure if this was just missed, but its required for an achievement. The finale seemed rushed and did not have a cutscene.Black Legend is easy to overlook. At times it feels frustrating, with an early game that is difficult and unbalanced. Eventually it becomes formulaic and repetitive, with a seemingly unfinished finale.Looking past this, combat has surprising depth due to the class system and inventory. This is a joy to use as freedom and flexibility allow for a good amount of experimentation with party building. The introduction of rare weapons late game, keep this relevant.I enjoyed BL more than I perhaps should have. However, given the overall picture Black Legend is firmly in the  category, but what could have been...

_childDocuments_.review: Short, Short Version: Broken and repetitive. Short Version:Black Legends is fundamentally unbalanced with an inconsistent UI and clarity. These things are fixable and hopefully will be in these last few days before release. However, the boring, extremely repetitive battles probably are not, barring some sort of fundamental redesigns that will almost certainly not be happening. For me, if the UI and balance are fixed up I could find fun over the course of the ~20-25 hours of gameplay, but the repetitive battles will leave it as a toy rather than a truly great and engaging game. I would generally recommend holding off on it for now to see how the launch and post-launch support go. However, the flexible class system and unique builds are engaging and those looking for that in a tactics game may enjoy the game as is and find it worth looking past the flaws. _childDocuments_.review: Black Legend is almost a good game.  Graphics are pretty decent, if not a little drab.  And, the engine is smooth.  I don't mind the high learning curve.  Whether that's changing your class, adding cross class abilities, equipping /changing items, or even moving during combat.  And, speaking of combat, it's not too bad, but definitely needs improvements.  However, there are some design decisions that are just poorly thought out.  The first is the healing; you can first aid bandage yourself for a few HP  (which is a joke) and items only self heal (also, there's no confirmation so you may (will) inadvertently use a potion).  The second is enemies (and players) can roam around the battles with no recourse; meaning you have no fear of attack of opportunities (because they don't exist!).  This is obviously annoying when you have an enemy 3/4 boxed in and he just happily moves out of this and behind one of your characters to backstab them himself.  Backstabbing, which btw, can be performed on the side (which makes zero sense).  Additionally, bows cannot backstab (another weird decision).  Finally, the thing that bothers me most is the respawning of enemies if you transition to an area.  Going back to an area you just cleared only to be filled again is quite aggravating; considering you've probably lost units and used items.  Replenishing them is not so easy.I do believe there's a good base here.  There's potential for this to be a really good game.  But, I doubt anything is being done insofar as QoL fixes.  At $10, it's still hard for me to recommend in its current state.  Sad though, because this had a chance to be a black sheep.

_childDocuments_.review: is a highly climatic turn based RPG set in XVII century Europe. It is perfect for fans of hardcore combat and, thanks to custom difficulty, it's suitable for more relaxed and story focused gamers as well.✓ Art, soundtrack and voice acting are very good.✓ Flexible custom difficulty makes the game accessible to everyone.✓ A large variety of weapons, abilities and classes makes for an interesting gameplay.✓ A well narrated story that tickles player’s curiosity.✗ Premade difficulty levels feel somewhat unbalanced.✗ No minimap in a game that has the player run errands and a lot of backtracking in a complex environment.✗ All the enemies respawn each time a zone is left.The city state of Grant was once an opulent place. However its wealth was also a tragedy in the making. When bandit raids have begun, the city asked the legendary alchemist Mephisto for help. And so he created a deadly fog that engulfed the streets, distributing the antidote to the citizens, to soon leave the helpless city behind.The King wants to regain the control and the former glory of Grant. He promises the protagonist, a mercenary, to forgive them for their crimes if they’re able to help him achieve his goal.And so they will see with their own eyes how far has the corruption rooted itself in the town and what devious plots are being unraveled by the cultists amidst the fog.As they’re tasked with the activation of mechanisms around the huge city they encounter some survivors willing to collaborate. But there is no way around multitudes of adversaries, some of which wear faces of former allies. Side quests follow main objectives, often requiring to fetch an item or talk with someone in the next zone to be explored. They will help the player to obtain very useful items.During exploration some paths are blocked by the enemies who patrol their paths. Sometimes it’s possible to avoid the fight by following a path which is out of their field of view. However, once a false step is taken, the battle is inevitable. It is possible to rearrange the party on a limited section of the front before the combat beginsPlayer’s team consists of four mercenaries. Each character has a pool of action points and independent from those, the movement points. Action points seem to be fixed at the value of three. There are also two consumable slots on a character and using them has no cost.There is a lot of freedom in the movement, including climbing up on crates and surfaces to improve ranged view angle. However it is impossible to move diagonally. In a similar way there are very few (polearm) melee skills that allow for such an attack. A fighter is more susceptible to damage if they’re hit in their side or back. If a fog grenade has been used the enemies within the area of effect can’t be attacked with a ranged attack nor some of the melee ones.There are also some abilities and items that grant statuses such as “Burning”, “Blinded” or “Inspired”.Nothing is really set in stone when it comes to characters and their builds. Outside of the battlefield the classes of each character can be changed freely. There are fifteen of them in total and each can only equip a few selected weapon and armor types. Different classes are unlocked only after those requirements can be met.Additionally every class influences differently the growth of a character as it levels up. This should be considered when choosing the set of skills the character should use, since their strength scales from a specific statistic.Initially a skill can only be used by the class it’s tied to, using a specific weapon type. When used in combat multiple times the skill is learned and can be used by that character even when they change class and weapon. But even when they have been mastered not all the weapons will be able to perform all skills. Passives can be learnt in the same way, however they are restricted to their classes.Attack skills have a modifier on them, which allows them to apply a single or multiple stacks of humor on the enemies. These are Rubedo - Red, Albedo - White, Nigredo - Black and Citrinitas - Yellow. Those can stack up to three times for a color and some of them react together. A catalyst attack will consume all the reactive stacks and deal a large amount of damage. It is possible with some abilities or consumables to cleanse the humors on a character as they’re very dangerous.It can be melee or ranged, depending on the type of weapon used. Some classes allow for both types of armaments to be equipped at the same time.Two trinkets can be equipped on a character. They usually grant bonuses regarding application of humors on the enemies.I suggest to whoever decides to play the game to make a first run in which they will try their hand at the mechanics and see what difficulty will better suit them. This game is challenging even at “easy”. The encounter difficulty grows progressively and the player will be always at edge, even if they make they explore entire maps and skip no encounters. Higher difficulty levels add further challenges such as less health recovery after battle and make the game extremely hard.The variety created by different weapons and classes is both fun and overwhelming. While it’s quite an original process it adds a lot of complexity and makes the learning curve steeper.All the enemies respawn every single time the player leaves a zone and this can become very frustrating as there is no minimap and navigation through the town can be confusing even with directional signs and shortcuts. Worth mentioning is a very unique choice. The player has the freedom to choose from a number of places where they want to fight the second boss.The graphics are quite detailed and moody. The town looks like it was once alive and now is an aching shadow of what was. The artists captured perfectly the grim fall of a once great and active centre.The class icon design is very ingenious and noteworthy. It takes shapes from alchemical symbols and recomposes them into visual representations of each class.The dialogues are intriguing and read by skilled voice actors. In the beginning it might seem like they lack that little spark of emotion, but as the story goes on the narration becomes more compelling as well. The soundtrack ties everything together beautifully allowing the player to immerse themself in the world that is being created in front of them.While using “Hotshot” ability which allows two indipendent shots from a firearm, if the player tries to perform a different action after the first shot, the game will freeze.The camera might be hard to move sometimes during battle, but in that case rotating the view will allow to conclude a turn with no issues.I also find it very hard to climb on objects while exploring and as a result couldn’t reach a loot cache I found. Aside from the preset difficulty levels, the "custom difficulty" option makes the experience fully personalized. And so it can be enjoyable by those who seek hardcore turn based combat and for those who just want to follow an engaging story.The game is set in the XVII century in a world with just a sprinkle of dark fantasy. It also features a huge array of weapons mostly from modern Europe, as well as some gems like the Labrys, a gorgeous Greek war axe. The art is highly convincing and the environments carefully constructed. The town feels real and is very immersive. There is a fair share of death imagery however.The time required to complete this game is subjective, but it requires 15+ hours.

_childDocuments_.review: ✔️ Interesting and intricate turn-based tactical combat.✔️ Engaging and deep progression mechanics.✔️ Very cool costume design.✔️ The narration is actually pretty okay, even though a bit on-the-nose.❌ The onboarding is awful - the game just showers you with all the game mechanics right from the start, which makes them a bit difficult to appreciate.❌ Some annoying bugs. They aren't too frequent, but when they happen boooy they suck.❌ The environments are pretty monotonous and the enemies really lack variety.Overall, I recommend Black Legend because I find that it is a pretty nicely done turn-based tactical RPG that I personally had a lot of fun tinkering with. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a rare gem, even though there are others like it. It's true that it has gone through some rough stages, but if you like turn based tactics, this is a challenging title. Especially on higher difficulty, but unlike in the other similar games, the Ironman rules are not about the save scumming. You will die if you turn up that dial. That is certain.You will only have one save and one goal, to survive. Luckily they don't throw you in the deep end straight from the beginning, but you won't be able to feel the bottom under your feet either. The encounters will start to come in fast, but if you're into speedrunning, there is a sprint and you can find a way around the encounters. So anything is possible, but towards the end of the game, you will have to do some clashes.The game itself is a Bloodbornish tale set in medieval  city and the game follows Souls kind of style, with mobs respawning and becoming harder after each encounter. The narrative side of the game is a bit lacking, but it's not a really bad. I've seen worse stories.Some of the people claim that the game is short. The answer is, anything is short if you run it on Easy. At the moment of writing I haven't finished the story. So in that sense, if you're looking a challenging game that can take you up to hundred hours to finish, check it out. You should note that even though it has gone gold, the story is still evolving and the devs are actually doing some work, plus answering questions in the forums.I am my hardest trying to give a harsh review and yes there are things that could have been done differently. The biggest strategy challenge in this game is finding yourself at the end game, because it can be a challenging to get right roles and keep your people alive. Do this poorly and you'll end up restarting the game or writing a bad review, when there is nothing really to give a bad reputation. This game isn't Fo76.  Check it out, it might be worth of your time. And money.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The bare bones of a team based RPG, with a nice class and combat system that will keep you entertained for a while if you can look past the lack of polish. As it stands, it would be more at home on a PS Vita than a PC, but it's not a bad game. I confess to being a little disappointed with this game off the bat. The sample videos and pictures do a great job of painting it in the best possible light (obviously) and the actual experience is somewhat different. However, the few hours I have played have been engaging, and I do find myself wondering when I will have the time to play a bit more. It has that addictive quality that makes you want to dump another ten minutes into it, take out one extra group of cultists, or search one more little nook. Graphics:A bit on the basic side. Wandering around the city isn't so bad, and the colour scheme and lighting provide decent enough ambiance that you tend not to notice the outdated graphics. Where things can get a bit jarring is when you open the character screen. Character models look a bit clunky, and the pasted on hair reminds me of the original Mount and Blade. Seeing as this is a character focused game, I would have liked a bit more polish there.Customisation:A bit of a follow on from my previous comment, but all of the characters look basically the same. All units are the same build and stature, and once you start to equip armour with helmets, they're really only distinguishable from one another by their moustache colour. It's nice that equipped armour shows on the character models, but there is no distinction between armour of the same type. This seems like a bit of an oversight in my opinion. Classes:The classes are varied and interesting, and the ability transfer between classes is great. Basically, you use an ability 3-4 times and then your character is able to equip that ability when they switch to a new class. Great system! But...The Team part of the Team RPG:What's the point of having a company roster! You can only have a piddly 4 characters in play at any one time, even though you can unlock several more as you wander around the city. If you can change classes at will,  why on earth would you ever switch out characters? Just pick the ones that have the moustache you like and cycle them through different classes until you have the abilities you want. Without any class specialisation, there's really no need to give you more than the starting four plebs. Unless of course you play with perma-death, which I wish I had done. It's not even like the guys back at base regain health, which would make alternating worthwhile. This was a big let down for me, as I love a team-based RPG.Gameplay:You wander around the city as your MC and then enter turn based combat when you come across a group of enemies, which is often. The wandering around is alright. There are a few chests to be found and some nice assets to check out, but nothing ground breaking. If you could find items in sacks and crates, rather than just copy/pasted chests, it might make exploration a bit more enticing. Combat:As above, it's turn based. My first impression was that it was going to be like Mordheim or Valkyria Chronicles, but it's standard tile based battles (don't be fooled by the vids). The combat is also not in the style of XCom or Phantom Doctrine, as many people were expecting, based on the reviews. No, the combat here is much more akin to your handheld console games, such as Final Fantasy Tactics, or Fell Seal (for a PC comparison). Know what you are getting in to!So now that we have established what kind of combat we are looking at, is it fun? Absolutely. I honestly think the game shines here. It doesn't lean on RNG, and  there's not a cover system to rely on. No, this is good old fashioned stand next to the enemy and whack them with a stick. Flanking plays a part, but really the excitement, and the challenge, comes in the form of applying debuffs, in the form of humours, which you then remove with an attack for drastically increased damage. If the enemy has 3 stacks of red and 3 stacks of black, say, you hit them for roughly four times the damage that you would have normally. It's quirky, and it keeps the battles fairly dynamic. It also forces frequent class changes, to make sure you have the abilities you need to build up the stack combinations required for the best damage output. Challenge:One thing I like about the combat is that you and the enemy are basically toe to toe specs wise. This means that you do and will take damage, and quite a bit of it. The best side effect of this is that you will actually use consumables. I have played many RPGs over the decades, and have used maybe five potions in my entire gaming career. Black Legend has actually forced me to go back to the shop to buy healing items! The otehr consumables are actually useful as well, as they often add stacks of humours to the enemy, and you get use out of them because they don't cost AP to apply. Huge plus in my eyes. On a less positive note, the challenge is also maintained through enemy level scaling. Yes, it makes the figths consistently semi-tough, but, eish, I don't like it. There's pretty much no reason to grind and level up your characters, because the next enemy to spawn will be the same level as you anyway. As someone who likes to be rewarded for pouring time into character development, this one bugs me a lot. I mean, this was ultimately the reason why I stopped playing Assassins Creed: Odyssey. Story:It's there. It's alright. Did anyone come for the story?Voice Acting:Should probably go to hell and die. Conclusion:A pretty good little time sink with some fairly compelling combat. Gathering equipment and optimising classes is fun, but a lack-luster character and team customisation system leaves the whole experience feeling a little hollow. It didn't reach it's potential, which is frustrating, but I will get some fun out of it before probably forgetting all about it.       Like my rambling? Check out other reviews from myself and my brother on our curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: Turn-based battles in the style of XCOM, but not in a science fiction scenario but in the early modern era of the 17th century? Not a very often chosen scenario for a computer game. However, Black Legend is a gritty turn-based tactical role-playing game, set in the 17th century in a world full of alchemy and religious fanatics. Not to mention a few monsters from the fairytale realm. It takes place in Grant, a formerly wealthy seaside trading town now ruled by cultists and engulfed by a slowly spreading fog that drives anyone insane who has not ingested an antidote. Fans of John Carpenter's The Fog will love the story.We play a group of four mercenaries and enter the city (after taking the antidote?). There we immediately encounter the resistance - apparently not the entire city is in the hands of the cultists after all. At the beginning of the game you create a character. However, the creation is limited to a few visual things such as face, hair or gender and the name. Your three other party members are predefined. The abilities of your heroes are determined by the equipment you wear. In the course of the game, we can add new members to our party if we remove someone else in return.There are 15 classes (thief, sniper, mercenary,...) with unique abilities. To unlock these classes, you need the necessary equipment for them. A very interesting approach, after 40 years of role-playing games annoying me with finding things that my hero can't use. So in Black Legend you have to find or buy equipment to unlock new classes. If you then choose that class for your character, he automatically uses the most appropriate equipment for that class. Very convenient.Weapons increase combat power, but can also give your hero new (active) abilities. If you use them often enough in battle, your character learns them and can eventually use them without the weapon. Passive abilities are learned simply by using the corresponding weapon in combat. This is also a completely new approach in the role-playing genre.Once an active skill is learned, it can be used "across classes". Each unit can use up to 3 abilities learned from another class in addition to the abilities of their current class. This allows you to either augment the strengths of your current class with abilities from other classes or cover weaknesses. However, passive abilities cannot be used across classes and are only available if the character is playing the associated class. Apart from the armour, the weapon and two items (throwing knife, healing potions,...), each character can also wear two small trinkets that enhance certain abilities.You move your group (as actually only your hero, who symbolises the whole group... while the rest of the party stands around at the place of your last fight) through the city in real time and 3D. Here you can examine objects, talk to inhabitants and thus get an idea of what is happening in the city. A compass is permanently displayed, as is a list of open quests. Houses with inhabitants who are willing to talk are marked by a glowing lantern. Strange, firstly because most people don't really talk much anyway and have barricaded themselves away, secondly because I tend to associate the glowing lanterns with other services. Well, anyway, it's very strange that someone who has hidden from the cultists and barricaded himself in his house has a glowing lantern hanging over the door.You can usually see enemies at a distance and can sometimes sneak past them. However, if enemies discover you, a fight will ensue. The core of the game are the turn-based battles. At the beginning, you position your heroes in the starting area. The units can then be moved and perform actions in turn. The calculated turn order is displayed at the top of the screen. Movement and actions consume movement and action points respectively. Each unit has (usually) three action points to perform attacks or special actions. Actions and movements can be used interchangeably, there is no fixed order. This means you can move, attack a target, move again and then perform an action in any order. Your characters cannot attack diagonally, which is strange. Using consumable items (such as potions) does not require action points, but can only be used once per battle. Disengaging from the enemy is possible without the enemy stabbing you in the back. This means that you can regularly attack enemies from behind, as long as there is no one in your way. You cannot move through your own heroes, they often stand in your way. An Overwatch function to automatically attack outside the turn order is not available.If you end a turn without spending all of your action points, the character will have a higher initiative value in the next turn (and will therefore get to move again more quickly). The battlefield can be viewed from all sides at any time. There is no undoing of a move if you have clicked the wrong way. The AI is not overly clever, enemies prefer to throw stones at units far away instead of attacking your unit next door with a sword.Ranged weapons such as pistols, rifles and crossbows require a clear view of the target, but this is often blocked by allies, obstacles or other enemies. A certain minimum distance is also necessary. With melee weapons you achieve particularly high damage if you attack from the flank or even from behind. You should be careful with the Espingole, which is a kind of pump gun from the early modern era. With this short shotgun with a funnel-shaped flared muzzle you can hit several targets at once, but you can also unintentionally shoot your comrades.Adrenaline builds up in battle when units deal or take damage. The higher your adrenaline level, the greater the chance of landing a critical hit that deals significantly more damage. As soon as a unit lands a critical hit, your adrenaline level drops back to 0. It is simply reassuring to have eliminated an enemy. There is no classic magic as in most fantasy RPGs, but a strange alchemy system.Black Legend is a turn-based tactical role-playing game set in a 17th century Flemish city shrouded in a toxic fog. With a party of four heroes, you explore the town and fight in turn-based battles with sword, axe and crossbow against the ruling cultists who worship the poisonous mist and use the blood of the inhabitants for a healing potion. Support the resistance to drive the cultists (and some other monsters) out of the city and dispel the mist. Black Legend doesn't reach the quality of genre greats like XCOM 2 or Banner Saga, but the unused scenario is quite fun and plays refreshingly - even though it has some serious flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: The goodTurn-based combat that's satisfying to masterI love the atmosphere: set in a dark and brooding city, whose regions/districts offer enough variety to make exploring a new area interesting and uniqueGreat array of weapons and armour, each with its own descriptionLots of classes to exploreArmour worn and weapons wielded make cosmetic changes to charactersBosses are unique and memorable, although this might also be because they are very rareThe neutralCombat gives you the info you need, but only if you are paying attention. The skills used by the enemies will flash onscreen, and then the damage done, buffs/debuffs, and the various humour stacks in rapid succession. There's no battle logYou can see if you'll be close enough to target an enemy before you commit to moving, but there's no way of undoing a move if you misclickThere are a few classes that greatly outperform the others. Because you get stats allocated based on your current class when you level up, and because you can level up several times in a single encounter, it sort of discourages too much experimentationCompanions are very generic and forgetable, even the occasional "special" ones that joinMinimap is serviceable, but larger overhead map doesn't have a "you are here" indicator, making navigation a bit cumbersomeYou get lots of money throughout the game, but there's nothing to spend it on. Equipment you find is far superior at every stage of the gameThe badLots of walking/fetch and return/revisit areas. Enemies respawn, so it feels like it's just padding the length of the gameVoiceover is inconsistent, not just in terms of the quality of the actors, but the volume as wellCaptions display onscreen for dialogue, but without naming the character that's speakingInventory management is poor. No sort function, just a "view by type" toggle. Can't see which classes can equip a given weapon, unless it grants an ability to a specific classElevation changes are possible, by standing on boxes. As other commenters have noted, it's a bit strange to see your characters scrambling over multiple boxes in order to get behind an enemy during their turn. If your character climbs too high, the aiming reticle snaps up to their level and you have to sort of trick it navigate back to a ground level enemy (on gamepad at least)Summary: I feel I got my money's worth. I enjoyed it for the first 60% of the game, when you are unlocking new areas and classes. The visuals are great, and I like how your characters actually wear and wield the armour/weapons. After most areas are unlocked, it's a bit of a chore due to limited fast travel options and having to fight several groups of trash mobs to backtrack from one already explored area to another. With a bit of polish and a more linear quest path, it could've been great (the quest arc is very linear, this was just referring to having to go back and forth to various regions). I played it, and will beat it, but probably won't replay it unless it gets some needed QOL improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: is a tactical game with turn-based combat. The story is linear with 1 choice at the end. There are side quests with different objectives, which do not offer any choice story-wise, but include a lot of backtracking. The character development system is class-based and classes are unlocked with equipment. In turn, equipment provides active abilities (they can be used with another class) and passive ones (only for their class). Stat growth depends on the class chosen. Equipment includes weapons (possible to dual-wield), armour, trinkets (various bonuses), and consumables (from healing potions to grenades). It is possible to customize the appearance and the name of the player’s (main) character (but they can't be a person of colour or left-handed for reasons unknown - the PC's appearance is never referenced and animations are independent). There are two unique companions, other mercenaries are random.  The combat system is focused on Humours. Humours are passive status effects, they do not do anything by themselves, but can be Catalysed, causing damage. There are also more typical status effects, such as Bleeding and Poison, buffs and debuffs. The areas become available as the story progresses. Combat encounters respawn, sometimes with different enemy types and numbers. Some of them are possible to avoid. There are shortcuts within areas and a fast travel system between them. The latter becomes available only by the end-game, thus it is recommended to do side quests after unlocking it. The equipment did not seem random as the most powerful items were located in the second-to-last area.The controls are comfortable and customizable. The saving system supports manual, quick- and auto-saves (possible to set the number before rewriting) and it is possible to save the game mid-combat (on Normal difficulty; blocked on Hard). Combat animations can be sped up. The artstyle is consistent and fits the narrative, units and interactive objects are easy to see. The game has one of the best armour and weapon models I have ever seen in games. The voice acting and music are adequate. There were minor bugs, mostly graphical and harmless. Once a boss’ loot did not drop.

_childDocuments_.review: Black Legend is a nice game with a creepy atmosphere (both sound and visual). It's a turn-based strategy game with its share of originality in its gameplay, namely alchemy. Hard to pick up, alchemy is very satisfying when it is well executed. I just died after an hour of playing on maximum difficulty. The AIs are therefore quite tough, and even if their behaviour may seem rather basic, you will still have to be strategic to defeat them.A few small negative points however, the battle locations are sometimes a little too narrow, which makes moving around complex. The price is also a bit too high imo, so take advantage of it while it's on sale, it's worth a look!

_childDocuments_.review: A great, simple but not simplistic squad based tactical game with some fun ideas around cross-class abilities. The setting and story are surprisingly deep and well thought out if not especially complex, and there's enough content here to keep you engaged for the 15-25 hours the main campaign takes (there are a decent number of side objectives that can really expand your playtime).Bugs are the only major issue, I've had a few crashes and party members getting stuck in combat, nothing game breaking but more than enough to be an irritant. Overall it's worth a buy if you enjoy squad based combat games, though be advised it's more like XCOM: EO or W40K Machinicus than a more complicated experience like Mordheim: COTD .

_childDocuments_.review: So, is the game good? Yes.  Why?  Well I may be biased cause I'm a fan of Mordhiem and Xcom and this is like a child of the two.  Essentially, it's an RPG where you explore the city and when you fight, go to XCOM-style arenas.  The game looks like Bloodborne, plays like XCOM, and is fun.  I think the class system is neat being able to swap classes like Dragon's Dogma to build truly custom characters in terms of skills and abilities.  The story is simple but fun and the lore is surprisingly engaging.The game is hard on Normal and you need to learn to balance the games combat, which is fun and thoughtful with it's 'HUMORS' system where you need to align the abilities you use to build up the debuffs on a target to do massive damage. You cannot win without this juggling act and any reviews that say the combat is simple or too hard is clearly people that don't understand this system. It's engauging and fun. But beware, the enemy will be doing the same de-buff dance for max damage on you and can one shot your chars if you arent careful if you let the de-buffs build.Look its good. It's clearly a passion project, and I enjoy it. If you at all enjoy XCOM or Mordhiem, you will enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: Great idea with class/skill system and good climate. Other then that it's not very well done - story starts off interesting but then it's pretty meh, alchemy system is a nice idea but very poorly executed. The worst thing in the game is probably combat - constant "move behind enemy, click attack", no strategy, no opportunity attacks etc. And you have to fight a lot in the game, since enemies respawn. RPG with turn based combat should have a lot more when it comes to actual combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it. Will update (gradually) till I finish.First update: I am really enjoying the atmosphere and the whole feel of the game. The areas are dreary and you actually feel like you're fighting in the fog. But the best part is: THE EQUIPMENT! I'm a big fan of realistic looking armour and weapons and this game is just what I was looking for. Normal sized weapons, an insane variety of them, great designs, armour that fits the setting, great metallic textures. Its not always pretty -and personally I'm glad its not pretty and shiny- but it makes you feel like you're living in times past, not in a fantasy world of elves hoping from branch to branch in magical polished completely fake armour. I find the areas, weapon and armour design to be the best part of the game. I'd buy it just for that.I'll get into more details later but not to leave the review one sided: the combat is good and enjoyable, the story has issues, mainly I'd want much, much more story.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game so far! It's a lot like Mordheim but also a lot better, as the AI/computer doesn't cheat. I'm having a lot of fun exploring, finding new gear, and leveling up my crew. There are a few hiccups here and there (UI typos, multiple instances of one character appearing on screen, speech volume inconsistencies), but no game-breaking bugs as yet. The tactical combat is fun, the alchemy system is a cool mechanic, and I like having a lot of control over how my characters develop. I'm still unsure what triggers/unlocks new classes though, and as it's my first playthrough, I'm kind of just making all my characters unlock everything because I'm not sure what's effective. For a small indie-game, it's worth the money for me, and I'm excited to see it develop over time and get some more polish.

_childDocuments_.review: Points of consideration: - This is an indie studio.- I judge games for what they are, not for what I want them to be.In this game you go into different districts of a city overrun by a crazy cult, set in a pseudo 17th century. Your mercenaries will engage in quests that will take them around the city and will enter in fights in a turn-based, strategy style. A little similar to XCOM, but the mechanics are different, no cover, no misses.Let's start with the areas of improvement first:- The camera is a bit wonky in certain areas, and it doesn't let you zoom in as much as I would like.- The tutorial lacks visual examples, and some people may find some mechanics difficult to understand as a result of this. (Update: Devs have alread ymade improvements in it)- The class/skill system is complex, and this will definitely confuse you, until you get it and then it is awesome. Some UI improvements during the setting of a class/weapon could help make this more clear. (UPDATE: Devs already added multiple UI improvements to make it easier to understand).- There is no map. I can live without it, and a lot of the point of the game is to make the player explore but I can see some people having issue with this. (UPDATE: Map has already announced to be introduced in upcoming patch)- I am playing on PC and haven't encountered any actual bugs.Now, the things I really liked:- The models are pretty nice, both characters and equipment, sticking to mainly realistic stuff. Some have complained that the characters are not attractive, and my response to that is: this is not about being sexy.- The dark atmosphere is great, with sounds and noises in the background, letting you know the horrors that are coming.- The combat mechanics are deep: you can have multiple characters that level up independently, skills come from classes and are unlocked progressively the more weapons you find, eventually you need to level up multiple classes in a character and combine the skills, allowing you to make super custom characters (think Final fantasy Tactics advance). There is also a "humours" system, where some skills give stacks of certain elements and mixing some elements allow triggering damage multipliers, pretty cool stuff.- The enemies have different sexes and outfits, even among the same classes, which is really cool (some are even half naked!)- The game really rewards your exploration, and finding new equipment and weapons feels awesome!- It is deliciously dark in tone and brutal in presentation.- The progression is fast and allows you to experiment a lot. - There is an interesting story which I won't spoil but it is related to a crazy cult.

It does not even look finished and controls are clumsy. Combat mechanics are lame in best words and there is no tactic except hitting enemy. Graphics look like a 2000 game and I do not recommend it to anyone to buy it except from a huge sale or get updated from this alpha look state. _childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

_childDocuments_.review: If you like "XCOM-likes," then this is right up your alley. While flawed, Black Legend is incredibly impressive for something done by such a small team. The world is interesting, the atmosphere and music are on point, and the characters are fun.Choice matters, playing it cautious matters, auto save keeps people like me who like to save often and reload when making mistakes actually sit and think about tactics as opposed to loading last save and trying again.You get attached to your Mercenaries and although they all look the same with only slight variations, there is an odd sense of personality with them that is hard to put to words.Really unique game with thoughtful mechanics and an amazing presentation and feel that I'm enjoying immensely atm.Definitely worth a play through.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

_childDocuments_.review: So far a very enjoyable game. It lacks the depth of story of most RPG's but makes up for it in other ways. The game is challenging, the weapons are fun to use, the tactical combat is also fun and engaging. The notes you find throughout the game can be quite humorous and the enemies are interesting and unique.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely rich and engaging tactical gameplay. The way the skill system is designed makes finding new weapons an addictive treat and the battle system is fun and rewarding. There is a lack of polish, especially in the beginning, where it just throws you into a city with little exposition, however, this game has a ton going for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review: Play as a mercenary who has be given a chance of redemption from the crown. The city of Grant, blanketed in a deadly fog plunged into chaos with various groups running the town. The Crown sends you to the city to liberate and return this once vibrant city back to the flag of its previous rulers. A task that seems like a death sentence but a chance to escape the gallows none the less. Along your journey you will talk to the inhabitants and learn the fears and hopes of the civilians, and learn the sad fates of the leaders of this crumbling city.Black legend is a turn-based strategy game with a few twists to the mechanics. One being the roles your team can choose. From mercenaries, to captains, or rogues to plague bringers, all with their own unique special ability's, and weapon and armor limitations. The big factor is the way you can unlock special abilities on each role and can be used when you change the characters' role. So, it encourages you to try different roles and find a good combination. I was hell bent on having every character be the alchemist till they unlocked the ability panacea, which was a great healing ability that could be used on that character and others. This multirole development system is great to give a lot of freedom on how each playthrough could be ran. If they just kept the roles locked and you could only select one this would have been a far blander feature, and in my opinion was a smart choice.Now for the combat portion we need to take a small 17th century medical lesson. The 4 humours, some that are fans of medical history may already know this, but it use to be believed that the body had 4 different humours that once in balanced you were healthy, if you were sick one of the humors where out of balance and need to be fixed. The humours where given colors, Yellow bile, Red Blood, Black Bile, and white for phlem. Your special attacks apply imbalances to the humours indicated in the attacks icon. Each color can be stacked 3 times and if you imbalance correctly like 1 black and 1 white humour you can catalyze them to deal heavy damage to the enemies. This is a stratagy you will need to become proficient in because this is the best way to quickly end fights and prevent your team from taking to much damage. This is also the biggest reason for you to keep switching classes with your team to have a wide variety of specials to cover all the humours. It's a wild concept but makes the combat a lot more intuitive and strategy heavy other than swapping blows till one dies.  When not in combat you can travel around the town talk to the locals and pick up new recruits and find cultist item boxes scattered around. The cultist boxes can provide you with helpful items and can store new roles for you to use. You need to keep a sharp eye out as for the boxes can be missed and blend in to the environment, best advice keep an eye out for little nooks and check the corners to find the boxes. The recruits you can find on the city streets are easily acquired just talk to them and agree for them to join you. You can only have 4 to the squad and to be honest once I had my first squad built up, I just sent the new recruits to the barracks and never bothered pulling them out because I had already had my team set up. But this was on normal difficulty. You can select from easy with high exp gain, full health recovery and more for people who are here for the story to normal and hard difficulty with progressively harsher penalty's like far few exp gains, no auto health recovery and perma death of team mates to feel the true brutality this city can deliver.Black legend graphicly is on the mid range when it comes to details. I played a pre-released copy of the game and small things could be changed upon release but looking at design and character models they are not going to be your high fidelity, high detailed characters but this is fine due to the camera angle and distance you will most likely have it at. I will say the bosses and your teammates armor and weapons on the other hand are the exception, with beautiful sets of armor and clothing with various tiers adding more to the outfit and weapons with unique designs and patterns. The bosses feel unique and are highly stylized that fit the background of what happened to them. Its not the most beautiful game with a color scheme of gray and most normal enemies you will fight all look generic and not much variety the group. But the landscape has wonderful story telling throughout. One section you are sent to the Church district to investigate what happened to the scouts and find out cultist are not the culprits of the disappearance. With large barricades set up with cannons pointed towards them it paints this picture of dread and fear knowing what of conspired here was grewsome and the fear these men had to have felt must have been immeasurable. You can find sections like this all across the town if keep your eyes open but like all things in this game it blends into the city and can be missed very easily.Music in this game is what you would except from looking at the visuals, dark and foreboding music while exploring and only picking up slightly when in combat. Almost giving you the feeling that wither in combat or exploring the town you are never truly safe or at ease.  Sound effects and voice overs are crisp and have good punch to them. The combat sound effects are repeatedly used but at least while I was playing this was never annoying nor did I find any sound that drove me crazy along the playthrough.Overall Black Legend is an interesting, fun, and sometimes difficult turn-based game. I loved the story setup and the backstory to the town, its people and the bosses in the game. The combat felt familiar but with enough unique mechanics to make it stand out from the crowd. I think if you are in the hunt for a fun turn-based game with somewhat souls like look and feel to the environment you should look anywhere else. I haven’t beat the game but with 9 and a half hours and many side quests left to do and how ever many more bosses I need to slay, there is a lot of game here, and a rerun of the game with perma death is in my future, to test the full punishment this game has to offer and to push my strategies to the limit.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice slow paced game. The possibilities of the tactics which can be played are not too massive and not too complex. I like this as it doesn't need too much thinking and is perfect for casual players. There need to be some minor improvements when it comes to some camera bugs etc. and some combat bugs like clicking on the wrong field when a mercenary is on the high ground and you then "click through" this field and select a field on the low ground. All in all it's a very nice game for the casual player.

_childDocuments_.review: Bumbling in the grey ...so much promise - Mercenaries fighting in XCom Style in a fantasy setting. So dissapointing the result.Cheap graphics, cheap execution, cheapest Battle system (you can´t even attack diagonally.. the enemy is beside you and you can´t attack... really?), and even cheaper UI.It has some interesting ideas (able to changing classes throughout the game) but in the end is just way to lackluster for the price.Score 3/10
_childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting little game. I like the core mechanic to get better by learning new skills based on the weapons you are using. I'm also a fan of the game not holding my hand. The map is practical to find your way, but nothing more. There are no question marks or other markers, you'll have to find everything yourself, which I like.The story is pretty bland and the end is too abrupt and disappointing, but I still enjoyed the atmosphere and premise. I hope there'll be a Black Legend 2 eventually
_childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very unusual game, it is very different than many other games of its type. I think the alchemical humours system really adds a lot to the game, the combat is fun, the map is rather interesting and the story is decent, I quite like the wide variety of equipment. However there are a few downsides, the tutorial isnt very good at explaining how skills work, the npcs at the main base are rather lacking, there being only really four, (and a dog) and some classes just feel better than others. However it is a good game, and you should buy it, but just give it some time for it to really get rolling, as the first hour is a bit slow.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of the turn-based strategy genre, this game will be right up your alley. It’s a very fun game with a unique take on turn based. First of all, there is no such thing as missing your attack through RNG (thank God!), so the chances of survival are purely based on your decisions. Secondly there is the alchemy system, which is a good, refreshing feature. It could need some polishing and visibility upgrades, but generally it is a great feature and adds another layer of complexity to the battles. You’ll actually have to plan ahead on which humors you want to apply and when to catalyze them to maximize damage. Speaking about the world itself, I truly love the vibes. The city is great looking, and the ambient music adds another layer of intensity. I don’t mind (sometimes) getting lost in the city at all.I know there are some bugs in the game but, to be fair, no game releases in perfect state, there are always some bugs or flaws, which I’m sure the developer will fix over time. And after these fixes have gone through, the game will be in a fantastic place. I would say this game is worth getting into and could really be a hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Legend

name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy
detailed_description: RPG? Adventure? Strategy? Unexplored is a genre-bending adventure. A procedurally generated open-world RPG where you will explore worlds beautiful and strange. Fantasy fans will find it subtly familiar yet entirely new - a wild world of elemental spirits, bright colors, and layered history of politics, magic, and legends. With its unique blend of challenging, strategic, and slow-paced gameplay, the emphasis here is not on combat, but on the path you carve through your actions and decisions. As you delve into the richly woven narrative and master the intricacies of the game, you'll be treated to an award-winning soundtrack and an impressive visual style, both designed to enhance your gaming experience. And the journey doesn't stop there – Unexplored 2 continues to grow and evolve, thanks to our dedicated team's regular updates. This ongoing development is our commitment to refine, expand, and perfect your adventure. A Procedural RPG in a Boundless World Unexplored 2 offers a vast, rich fantasy world that unravels over several journeys. Our game breaks away from traditional RPG norms, eliminating grind, XP, or gold, and instead, focusing on your choices and their far-reaching consequences. From the safety of Temple in Haven, you will select a wayfarer, a quest, and prepare for the journey ahead. Each journey will see you traversing varied landscapes, interacting with diverse peoples, encountering mystical creatures, and unearthing ancient ruins. Each discovery brings you closer to the ultimate goal of taking the Staff of Yendor to the Prime Elemental Forge in the First Valley and to destroy it once and for all. A World Finite Yet Infinite In Unexplored 2, life and death have profound implications. Each wayfarer that sets out from Haven might not return. You will have to manage your roster of wayfarers carefully. Choose the quests that you think are achievable with your current wayfarer’s skills and resources. While traveling keep an eye out for new characters that might be recruited to join your cause. Should you die, rest assured that there is always a new wayfarer ready to bear the burden. However, only try the final mission to destroy the Staff of Yendor when you think you are fully prepared to face the dangers of that quest. For if you fail then, that world will be lost. Forever. Key Features Dynamic Content Generation : Ludomotion's groundbreaking approach to content generation layers unique elements every time a new world comes into being. Generative Storytelling : Though the ultimate goal remains the same, each journey will have its unique set of locations, events, and encounters. Systemic Depth : Numerous game systems ensure fresh discoveries even after hundreds of hours of gameplay. Legacy System : No journey will leave the world or the wayfarer unchanged. Pass on gear, resources and even skills to new heroes in order to bolster their chance of success. Distinctive Presentation : Unexplored 2 surprises with its beautiful art style, a rarity among generative games. A versatile lighting system adapts to the day and weather, setting the perfect mood for your adventure. Adaptive Orchestral Soundtrack : Our award-winning original score reacts to your actions and decisions, wrapping your adventure in a cloak of immersive sound.

Endless replayability with a huge set of difficulty modifiers. Boasting an award-winning soundtrack, a beautiful art style, and regular updates.

_childDocuments_.review: It looks really neat. The procedural generation sounds cool, and the story even sounds kind of interesting.However, when I sit down and play it, it's quite slow, pretty obtuse (a little too random for my tastes), and nothing really stuck out to me as actually interesting.The game clearly isn't a game focused on combat; in the tutorial it straight-up tells you to avoid combat almost always. Ok, so combat isn't fun, and it also isn't supposed to be rewarding. So, that means that the story would be good, then? Well, judging by the story that was revealed to me during my time playing, it clearly isn't trying to tell me a masterpiece. The random elements in the game basically reduce anything interesting to encounters, but more often than not, it just seems like empty towns. Loot, then. Well, what's the point of loot if the combat is trash and should be avoided?Ok, so the the procedural world, then? That's the core thing in this game, right? I mean, it sounds interesting, but like most procedural games, the feeling of "anything is possible" wears off really fast once you learn a few of the layouts and have seen a few things. Things like randomizing dungeons are great for replayability, but unfortunately the dungeons felt so empty and pointless that I really didn't even feel like going through the current dungeon, much less coming back later. Random things, like "why is there a burg-style well in the middle of this ancient underground temple?" not only does it not make sense, but it's that kind of procedural flavor that kind of insults your intelligence. "Why are 3/4 of the paths in this encounter dead-ends?" It's just pointless; random for the sake of being random, and about as fun as flipping a coin over and over.On almost all random encounters, I just walk through them, ignoring the enemy because the game straight-up tells you enemies will almost never drop anything, and just act as a drain on your resources. Once I get to an area with a quest event in it, I just wander around because it's supposed to be random, and if I'm lucky I'll be able to find what I was supposed to trek all the way over there for. Sometimes, I just can't find anything, or it seems like I was supposed to go somewhere else first.As it stands, I can't tell why this game is supposed to actually be fun; it's a neat idea, but it really comes off as a procedural storytelling engine like Wildermyth or RimWorld. However, unlike those games, it doesn't really seem to have anything in it, and there isn't really enough going on to make you care about the character you have. Feels more like a tech demo more than anything else.I've also encountered a number of bugs and very consistent frame drops in this game so far.I know this game is called "unexplored", but I didn't expect that to be the goal.---really appreciate your comment, and yeah I can see why the game would lend itself to more of a storybook, history-style procedural narrative game, like Wildermyth.I'm sure there's plenty to see later on as it pertains to story later in the game. I hope others find a way to explain what this game offers and what to come here for.I think the disconnect for me came from the sense of what entity this story is being applied to. In most games, this is effectively 1st person; "I did this, I did that". The goal in these games is mostly to observe a world firsthand and gain mastery and all that. Self-actualization in a short time.Then there's what I'll call "2nd person", Hades for example. Zagreus did this, this character did that. Feels more like listening to conversations over the shoulder of a good friend than doing it yourself. The story in this way is interesting because the characters are effectively not procedural, however the situations are. This makes you want to play over and over to see the weird setups and ways those might shake out.As for third person, we have RimWorld and Wildermyth. With these, the technique seems to be to give the player a team of ragtag adventurers, all with their own personalities. Wildermyth has a story and a decent-sized sandbox, RimWorld effectively has no story and a huge sandbox. This fun is mostly as an ant farm, peering in, imagining a complex personality in a complex world, and not telling stories so much as recording them.All of these strategies are great ways to build engagement by applying player agency in the right places, teasing out specific types of fun to act as the lubricant along the player's journey.I think the issue for me was that this game did none of these for me; I had no desire to step into the shoes of this character, but the character themselves had no actual personality or seemingly unique story to tell. Random is as random does, so if all I see is a bunch of stats, this isn't a character, it's an avatar. As a result, I didn't get hooked into 1st, 2nd, or 3rd person engagement. I am not the character, the character isn't interesting enough on their own, and what is around them might be interesting, but being shackled to the character is where engagement fails. The character isn't fun to explore with.I think this game would benefit from outright removing combat and direct player character control, focusing on procedural storytelling through vignettes, where the player doesn't actually have control over anything but the thread of the story directly. The player character then acts as an ant, being strung along by grains of sugar that the player chooses to leave for them. Similar to Wildermyth, but a little farther back, not as focused on tactics so much as interesting choices and outcomes. Whether or not the character themselves has the ability to override player choice is a design decision that sounds interesting.The game has a fantastic art style and a very interesting promise of worldbuilding. However, mechanically it didn't hook me, and personally I think this game's flavor of direct player control gets in the way more often than not.

_childDocuments_.review: Unexplored 2 is something I've been following closely for a long time, ever since the early access period (which wasnt on Steam) started.  On top of that, I am also a huge fan of the original Unexplored, and even helped a bit with testing and such.  So, I've got quite a connection to this one.And one thing I'm noticing when I see people talking about the game, or see reviews, is a lot of misconceptions, or outright thinking that the game is one thing when it is in fact something else entirely.  And also, a LOT of "it's too obtuse" comments.So, let's talk about these things in the hopes of helping you, dear reader, make an informed purchasing decision.  Know before going into this though that yes, I think this is a spectacular game.  So I sure as bloody heck am not trying to convince you NOT to buy it.  Moreso, I want to help you figure out if this is the sort of thing you might enjoy. So what IS this game?  Well, I think it's better to explain what it ISNT.  Though this is a real-time game (instead of a turn-based one) this is NOT going to be like Binding of Isaac or Gungeon or one of those.  At the same time, it is also NOT Nethack or any of the "core" roguelikes.  It is also not the original Unexplored... or much like it at all.The original game was inspired by things like Brogue or DCSS, and was meant to take that type of experience and translate it into a real time action game, with all of the depth and complexity that this implies.  It did this well... combat was extremely frequent (just like in the core roguelikes), and you were frequently finding magical swords and such and using potions and scrolls that did who knows what.  It was a traditional roguelike turned into an action game.This is NOT that.  Oh dont get me wrong:  some concepts translate over to here anyway.  But overall gameplay?  No.  Similarly, this is not like Isaac or other action-roguelikes.  You're not going to have constant bullet-hell wackiness or crazy OP builds or short runs.  That's not what this is.In fact, if I had to compare the overall nature of the game to any existing roguelike, I would actually compare it to CDDA.  Both games are slow paced and very DELIBERATE games, if that makes sense.  You arent chopping through waves of orcs and such with your magical umbrella of poking +1.  Like CDDA, your primary goal is SURVIVAL.  Combat is secondary to that goal, and only to be attempted in pursuit of that.  You'll be exploring a lot, while also trying to keep stealthy, avoid aggravating monsters, and talking your way out of dangerous encounters with NPCs.  You cant take much damage, and healing is very difficult.Similarly, a lot of the items you'll find are also survival-based.  Again, you're not constantly finding wild enchanted gizmos, nor are you going to spend time identifying and throwing potions of monkey farts or whatever.  Rather, you're going to be dealing with items like cloaks that can specifically protect you against cold, or maybe things like bedrolls to allow you to rest in areas where you cannot use a campfire.It's not that more traditional roguelike items dont exist... they do.  But they are absolutely not the focus here, and are often hard to come by.This all means that you cannot approach the game like a traditional roguelike.  Try to fight everything and you will get smeared all over the wall. You dont need to anyway. Combat isnt what gets you skills and upgrades and items.  Rather, you fight when the situation requires it in order to either proceed (such as in a dungeon) or escape bad situations.   I keep seeing people going into this and complaining that "combat isnt rewarding", but again... it's not MEANT to be.  It is a means to an end.  A necessity at times.On top of that though, let's talk about game length.   This is not Isaac or Gungeon.  I know a lot of action roguelikes tend to have runs that last right around an hour.  But THIS game is more like oldschool roguelikes.  Games like CDDA or any of the core roguelikes are LONG.  Really, really long.  And, in fact, the original Unexplored was like that too.  A run in a game like this is a marathon... and it's intentional.  It's not a bad thing at all... like most aspects of this game, it's about personal preference.  Some people really like games with long epic runs.  Others do not.There's one other major thing I keep hearing about though, which is that the game is "obtuse".  No... it really isnt.  But you have to approach it in the right way.  The game really does a great job of teaching you everything you need to know but you have to be paying attention.  LISTEN to the NPCs.  READ the inscriptions on monoliths you find in dungeons.  That puzzle you're so confused by?  You are NOT meant to figure it out by staring at it.  You're meant to go find the clues... which are almost always in actual text... and then solve it THAT way.  The first game did this too.The game ABSOLUTELY gives you the info to learn everything.  But I see people going into this thinking that prior roguelike experience will take them through it, and... yeah, no.  It doesnt work that way.  Pay attention, experiment, and read the bloody text.  That's the right approach.It's not JUST that it is unlike traditional games.  It's also that this one does some very unique things of its own!  The proc gen for instance is *amazing*, a trait the original had too.  But it's divided into both the action scenes and the world map, and understanding BOTH is important.  You cant just think of the action scenes only.On top of that there are mechanics such as the "fortune" tests... these are similar to skill checks in D&D, sort of.  Just because you read that inscription doesnt mean your character immediately can understand it... gotta pass a check first.  And dont get discouraged when you fail.  Like Unexplored 1 you are NOT meant to pass everything.  There will be things you just cant get because you dont pass a test (and in many cases, once you fail at a test, well... that was your only chance).  The first game did this too, and it actually worked wonderfully.  Instead of getting irked that you couldnt get through the door to get a particular treasure, stop and think to yourself... okay, what now?  What is my backup plan, what is my next step for when this bit failed?  Where do I go next?  You are meant to figure stuff like that out, and truly EXPLORE the world, knowing full well that you cannot get everything.  And believe me:  This absolutely works.  But it takes some getting used to.On top of that, this is also a game about making very careful decisions, and taking calculated risks.  Always always always consider your currently available skills and equipment when moving along map nodes, for instance.  The game outright tells you what kind of hazards/effects/encounters are present along any given path... it aint hidden information.  And as long as you've been listening to NPCs and things like that, you will often know things about a given destination before you even head towards it.  You arent heading towards that tower because it MIGHT have something useful in it... you're heading there because someone TOLD YOU that it has a particular bit of content there, and because you decided that this was the correct move at the current time.There is so much more I could say about this game... almost all of it positive.  But Steam doesnt like words, so this will have to do.It really is a brilliant game... it just isnt for everyone.  All depends on what you like in games like this.  And if it IS for you... you're gonna have an absolute blast in a game with LOTS of replay value and content.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, TLDR at the bottom. Also, this was post-release with some patches. Need to revisit.Secondly, what is the game? Unexplored 2 is an adventure-style, roguelite game where you are trying to destroy the one rin-, I mean the Staff of Yendor so you can save the world. In order to destroy the staff, you have to figure out where to go, who can help you, and what dangers await ahead. The best part is there is no one solution, but you won't know that until you... explore. The roguelite element is the world you are trying to save. You get multiple chances, and time progresses after each death with the world adjusting accordingly. You can grow stronger each death, until you succeed or the world is truly doomed. Succeed or fail the quest, the world's story is wrapped up.  Afterwards, you can start up a new world and try again. You CAN have multiple worlds.Managing exploration and survival is the entire focus of the game, and notice I said survival and not combat. Exploration is traveling between locations on the map, represented by nodes, and discovering their secrets. The game WILL NOT directly tell you where most secrets, special treasures, or special locations are located. You can learn rumors by talking to NPCs and exploring ruins, and then your map/quest journal will update accordingly. For example, you may travel to a trade post, only to discover it is abandoned and overrun with undead. It Is possible to learn that before traveling to the node. There are also hazards when you travel, like bad weather or rough terrain, which will eventually lead to defeat if you ignore them. Survival, then, is carrying the correct equipment with you to help you solve problems or avoid trouble. Whether that is cold weather, bandits, or a temple you are going to plunder. With the undead example, a trusty hammer and shield may be the solution... or just running away. Proper equipment DOES matter.So a quick rundown on the Good, Iffy, and Bad.Unexplored is an enjoyable game that captures the spirit of adventure, has good progression, and an interesting world. I give a positive rating, with some concerns. The core systems are there, including the gameplay loop, but it could use more polish. If you play well, you can win your first try, but the interesting meta-progression ('world-progression') can give you the needed push on your next attempt. Load times between level transitions needs to be mentioned and have been addressed a bit recently, and while not my only complaint, is the most major.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not for everyone.I can't say how many times I debated in my mind to refund the purchase. And while I eventually came to like the game after going through its steep learning curve. I wouldn't recommended the experience to anyone looking for an adventure-exploration experience. The game is tagged as an "rpg"when it's not quite an rpg as you are railroaded into some specific playstyles just to progress. Some load-outs are just more superior than others (due to encumbrance mechanics). . Edit for Update: There is a save feature implemented in game (save while in camp). This does alleviate some frustrations for character loss (especially when said loss is by reason of bugs). However, it also eliminates the reason to create your next character as rare buffs can only be acquired once per world (a subsequent character will be weaker compared to the first character who acquired those buffs - unlike how other roguelikes work)Another issue with the game is it still has loads of bugs. While there is a "prayer" system that helps you get out of stuck situations. There are instances where this mechanic can only do so much and then you have to go ask the devs in discord to help you with the problem. Though I appreciate the quick and responsive support of the devs, the problem shouldn't have existed in the first place, being that the game is already out of early access. I personally experienced this as I can't get into the endgame area since a mountain generated in front of the path and I can't back-out since I already unlocked the final gate.Another problem with the game is that you can't just experience the entirety of the story in one world, there are elementals/masks that are not unlockable due to the world generation limits. It wouldn't be a problem if the game session per run was a short and repeatable experience (e.g binding of isaac), but it's not. Playing the game is a slow, deliberate and careful effort that starting a new game just to experience the same slow yet now more repetitive thing (since you've experienced it already) is no longer that fun.Edit: I finished the game, however, there is another aspect of the game that is quite weak - its Story. There is indeed lore scattered about in the game, however, such lore are a bit scarce considering the number of ruins scattered about. Furthermore, the world seems to despise your character or don't really care about them. For a person who is working to save the world, it doesn't really seem motivating when people (even ordinary vagrants) attack you. You need to work a lot to turn other clans to allies (as if these clans don't care if the world ends) and there is no lore explanation why one clan has "angry" relations with you to begin with. The ending is also a bit empty (no post-ending or epilogue) and the world doesn't mourn for the death of your character (no tombstone, memorial, or even a passing mention).While I really liked what the game was going for (music, world-building, artstyle, LOTR influence), ultimately like other reviewers said, the game just doesn't respect your time. So with a heavy heart, I just can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Unexplored 1 and it was by far one of my favourite games. Intense combat, interesting map generation, stealth and funny interactions - the game had it all! So I came into this game expecting a similar type of feel with the same level of fun but... the game just isn't fun for me. Don't get me wrong I love what they did visually to it but the raw gameplay just feels missing. Combat feels less impactful and watered down from the previous game where you had to manually control your thrust forward and worry about where enemy weapons would be facing - it was iconic, unique and FUN. What makes the second game even worse is the fact that the game tries to make you avoid combat given that most things won't drop anything. This makes the game feel extremely unrewarding - is there a tough enemy that you managed to beat? Great you get absolutely nothing for it! This would be ok if there were rewards to be earned elsewhere to compensate for this change but in general there's very little in this aspect. This makes the game feel less of a game and more of a chore where your will to continue playing exponentially subsides. Even the procedural mystery elements don't feel right in this game, its unnecessarily convoluted and very confusing. TLDR: Overall I'd say the game looks really good but just doesn't have any of the same charm the first game did and just straight up isn't fun.EDIT: Just to make it clear so that my playtime isn't misleading - I've been following this game since early access (Epic Games) as an avid fan of Unexplored 1. However in saying that - this game does have some good explorative elements that I know some people enjoy so please don't let my review put you off if good combat isn't a must for you!
