_childDocuments_.review: Unexplored 2 is not a fighting game. It's not about getting geared up and skilled up in order to beat harder and harder foes. Play that way and you WILL lose. Instead, the game is about learning to survive, about making the right choices with what limited resources you have in order to make enough of an impact on the world before you die. Most conflicts need to be avoided, which admittedly is a play style I found challenging at first. There are all these juicy targets running around and I'm supposed to just ignore them? But the title of the game IS Unexplored, and your success will be measured by the quests you uncompleted, the bosses you undefeated, and factions you unimpeded. Everything is so difficult and dangerous that really have to choose your objectives wisely. You'll be given far more to do in a run than you're likely to complete, so the learning process boils down to understanding how to prioritize your power growth and leave important things for future generations.The persistent world in this game is pretty cool. Your reputation, exploration, quest completion, and items are left for future generations to pick up, though with each incarnation the sinister Empire consumes more and more of the world map. Graphics: 6/10 - Risk of Rain 2 styleAudio: 7/10 - nothing specialGameplay: 8/10 - fun, lots to masterDifficulty: 9/10 - even on easy modeBugs: 8/10 - frequent but not game breaking

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I would really enjoy this game... and for a while I did. But then I began to see how the game design was really flawed. The best way to describe it is "RNG to a fault". I went to a story dungeon and attempted to clear it, however the RNG put the goal behind a wall that was behind some stairs and I could not access it. I searched the whole thing over and over, no door to get in, no portal to activate, no teleport spell to invoke. Another example of this would be a huge tower dungeon that I spent over an hour in. I slowly clear mobs and dodge traps and get all the way to the top. Summon the chest through an invoke spell after clearing the trap mobs and open it to find that the chest is... empty. RNG rolled that there would be no reward at the end of this huge dungeon.The BAD:- It is way too hard to get around the map. The constant stops while traveling make this game a huge time sink with no payoff. - "Hope" is a finite resource, as you lose hope (from seemingly any source) you will lose skills making your character less powerful. The only item that can replenish one hope MUST be cooked with fresh food and it spoils quickly if not used.  Also, trying to close the rifts will drain your hope so quickly that one attempt will take away two skills if you are not careful.- Glitches, so many glitches. Spirit keys do not open spirit doors. Attempting to loot quest items and they never move to your inventory, try and close and reopen and the item is gone from the container. Talk to a vendor once, go into a building and come back out and you can't talk to the vendor again. Look at a pouch to decide if you want to steal and you cannot close the menu.- No rhyme or reason to the upgrades you can buy from a vendor. Some weapons and gear will show and others will not.- All the damn space that support gear takes up in your inventory. everything takes up space and you cannot reasonably carry anything around while also hoping to find good loot. Also, worn items and gear for some reason also take up bag slots.- there are gear slots on the character screen that are not even used... just why? No headgear anywhere to be found. I found a crown once that had a sigil slot so I put a sigil in it... and it did nothing.All in all, after playing this game it just feels so unfinished and the game design is just so user unfriendly. -

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty sure that Ludomotion is going to end up making my favorite game eventually because I love procedural generation, and they are the best at it. Unfortunately, this isn't it. I feel like its against my best interest to leave a negative review if I want this goal, but I started writing this with "yes" checked and that felt dishonest.I loved Unexplored 1, but my biggest issue with the game was that it was too long. The highlights of the game were finding gear and consumables and discovering that the game was giving you exactly what you needed to overcome challenges (which were sometimes entire floors) that looked impossible... but not if you have potions of fire protection, and the game just gave me 3 of them! Moments like that happened regularly, but a single session of the game still felt like it overstayed its welcome because most of the floors didn't have this excitement, the game advertised itself as a gear based RPG, and you would find truly exciting gear maybe like 2-3 times in the 4(!) hour run. A game like this needs to have EVERY floor feel meaningful, so they all need to have bosses or legendary loot, or key items, or multiple of these things hidden behind puzzles and secret areas.Unexplored 2 is a much prettier game, but amplifies this problem times like 100. I've played it for probably a total of like 12 hours across Epic through early access and Steam, and it is shocking how little progress I've made in any given run during that time. There is certainly loot to be found, but the majority of your real world time in actual gameplay will be sneaking around enemies (which the prologue warns you to not bother fighting) as you move to the destinations you care about. Also, "fun" gameplay elements such as needing to camp because you are fatigued, or needing to camp because you are wet. In my current run, I've been playing for 3.5 hours. I just barely got to the first major point of interest (which still isn't the first quest yet), and I got through a large area, through a major dungeon to discover an important looking machine that I can steal sigils from to power it down, but I don't know what the consequences of that are. If my entire run up until that point was 30 minutes, I would feel like experimenting, but its been 3.5 hours, and I'm probably like 1/20th? of the way through the game, so I didn't want to mess it up that early, so I guess no reward for me... Unexplored 2 takes a big step back in terms of fun compared to unexplored 1 for me. In my time playing, I've never had the experience that the level generator did something cool which was the major selling point of unexplored 1, and I know the response is going to be to sink more time into it, but compared to other video games, the moment to moment time spent in this game is way less valuable.My personal ideal unexplored game would be the metaprogression/overworld of desktop dungeons with the art style of Unexplored 2. On the overworld for that map, all of the nodes would be self-contained missions that take an hour to beat that have a similar vibe to Moryonder in Unexplored 1 where there's a fixed goal and unique biome and the generated level is densely packed, and beating those levels unlocks new content to play with as opposed to permanent power ups for your character that increases the diversity of what you will see on that given level, but also unlocks new levels to explore. A complete game in this style would probably have been 1/3 of the work compared to UE2, but I'm already feeling like I don't want to spend more time in this game, so the impressive amounts of content that it has will continue to be unexplored :(

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished the game, and I absolutely love it. This is my first review ever: I had to write because I feel this game deserves much better than the current 75% recommended. The game is constantly improved, so I guess some of the older negative reviews complaining about bugs don't hold up (that much) today.My first run was frustratingly hard, I abandoned it after a few hours. Then I lowered the difficulty for the second: with easier combat the exploration aspect could shine. There are quite a few options to make the game easier (or harder if that's what you are into), even perma-death is not mandatory: by default you can always restore to the last time your character rested.I don't think this is an RPG. Your character won't really improve, your gear determines what you can do. And the interaction with NPC-s is also limited. I would rather say this is an adventure game where the main point is exploring this wonderous world.I played on Steam Deck, and my related experiences:* I had to lower the graphics settings to have 2-3 hours of battery life.* The description of overpowered items is hard to read.* The D-pad right doesn't activate the right quick slot, I remapped it to Keyboard - X to work.There were some bugs: in a ~60 hours playthrough I'd say five locations out of hundred* Usually I could move on using the "pray for help" feature* I had to use the "restore save" in one dungeon which was so badly generated that I couldn't even go out.* Loading one location in the main quest seemed to be frozen, I had to reload the game six times until it succeeded.P.S.: douse your campfires before you move on.

_childDocuments_.review: Borderline recommend. This is an amazing game if you're after how No Man's Sky used to be, a pure journey simulator without all the silly crafting grind Hello Games added later. Unfortunately Unexplored 2 still has lots of weird issues which will make you want to quit every couple hours. _childDocuments_.review: The game is quite nice, and there's a lot of organic stories and moments that pop up thanks to the free-form exploration, the procedural generation and the different systems that interact to give meaning to your character creation choices. However, the game is surprisingly unstable and crashes ALL THE TIME.Just earlier today, I booted up the game and had a crash after 10-15 minutes after which I opened up Steam to write a review mentioning that the game was crashing too frequently, as it has every 20-30 minutes in the past 10 hours or so that I'd played the game for. Then I decided to give it another chance and erased the review, booting up the game again. 5-10 minutes later, the game froze on a loading screen. I could not be patient any longer.In principle, I wouldn't even mind. However, for a game with an immersive world, where the journey is most important, where every moment is full of some kind of exploration and wonder, such frequent crashes really do not help the experience at all. Underneath the poor performance is a FANTASTIC game, genuinely - but the performance is really unbelievable. Add to that the fact that every time you explore an area from the overworld map, it "Generates" the area and "Builds" it, a process that takes close to a minute easily, and it's easy to see why I'm spending more time in loading screens than actual gameplay between crashes. I'm writing this while playing on an Intel i7-7490K, GTX 1080 card and 32 GB RAM system, which isn't modern but easily above the spec. The sad part is, it may be entirely possible that it is some esoteric setting which I have not activated or some update which I haven't gotten on my system which aggravates performance, so your mileage may vary. But for that reason I would recommend playing the demo before purchasing.On the objective side, here are the best reason to give the demo a try:1) The graphics are legitimately gorgeous. There's no other way to put it, this is a beautifully realized terrain and world generation system which at least so far has not given me any problems (in terms of spawning impossible puzzles or objectives, etc.)2) The RPG aspects, for me, are stellar. In terms of the skill checks/dice rolls that the game tries to emulate with the "Fortunes" system, it nails a big part of the experience at least for me. It really does feel like my character build is relevant. 3) Internal systems also work very well - I was in a dialogue check to avoid combat with some threatening bandits, when I realized that I had lost my bonus of being a smooth-talker because I had entered the conversation with my weapon drawn! There's a lot of nifty little details like this in the world.4) The legacy system is pretty fascinating - seeing familiar locations evolve and change over time really puts the journey that you are on in perspective, and it's real fun seeing if there is any way we can be part of that.There are many more, but in short - this game is packed to the brim with fantastic systems, ideas and possibilities. The fact that it crashes so frequently even on hardware well above the recommended spec is offputting to me, and if it might be for you as well, then try out the demo first. I really hope this situation improves at some point or the other, since there are patches being released, and when that happens I will gladly change my review, since the game very much deserves applause for what it's trying to do and how well it does it (aside from the crashes).

_childDocuments_.review: 21 hours in and instead of enjoying my weekend I am extremely irritated by the game.The artstyle and gameplay looked so chill I forced myself to learn the game (I don't like that process) to at some point understand the way it's supposed to be played and start enjoying it.I don't know what to say, that it's not for me or it's just a mess?Whole idea of exploring feels so irritating. Even after I created new world with ease modifiers, traveling is so punishing I don't have the will to go anywhere anymore. Every traveled dot on the map uses your items or inflict negative statuses on you. To repair/ recharge the traveling equipment you need: a repair kit, set up camp, light source, ingame time. Repiar kit of course takes a precious place in the inventory and is a diminishing resource that can be bought. And to earn goods for trade you have to loot. Looting items or being well equiped seems extremely limited because of "encumbrance". Both these elements make the core game mechanic frustrating instead of fun. There's just no way you can travel with half the crucial items (pan, bed roll, rope, cloak, armor, weapon, shield, boots, pickaxe, torch/lanthern, anti spoling bag, cold/hot anti-weather item, repair kit, wood and whatever I forgot) and have space left for any loot. Every mechanic of this game is bothersome keeping me in state of worry constantly. (I found out that reducing encounters on the road makes game harder, not easier. Because you miss opportunities to collect wood and extra sparks)Some paths (inside a location) are the only available route to your destination and for example you have to climb it. So you either go back to base for rope and waste another (realtime) half an hour and resources or force yourself with these lottery events. Which are often without a chance to succed in the pool at the start(?). So you use a fckton of 'sparks' or 'hope' or lose health and gain negative stats. There is no alternative way. Remember you have to also come down later, and if you gained some negative statuses that will obvioulsy hinder your lottery chances, believe me, you will die there or on the way back to the city. Because of these stacked negative debuffs that punishes you on every dot on the map. If you somehow manage to crawl back you lose so much 'hope' that it's hard to proceed anywhere further into the world later).Then there are also glitches and bugs. I spent an hour trying to open some door looking for a key. Not sure if just procedural generation failed me again or am I missing something. The ingame hints are so vauge, you can waste even more time trying to follow them. Decided to finally use "pray" to open the door. There were turrets behind so I backed off to get hide status and then doors just closed. I used "pray" again and got instantly punished by a game with a rift. All this happened because I wanted to find a key for some other gate in the first place. And after carefully inspecting whole dungeon and outskirts  (you guessed it right) I didn't spot it anywhere. And I will never be sure if I just couldn't find it or if it was never there at all. I can't search for help throught disscussions/google because it's procedualy generated content.Another gaming session with new world I managed to talk to some kobolt leader to join my cause and defend against empire. I travel to the adjoining "Keep" where I'm supposed to clear it out of spider like creatures. I wipe them out, get a notification in the corner screen to prove it but still can't offer the keep to a clan because info message states that I haven't cleared the location out of enemy force. Sucks. I travell back to the kobolt cave to trade some loot and I notice there is no more a kobolt mark on the map. They vanished, whole generated location looks empty. No messeage, no info, they just vanished. I go back to that Keep nextdoor and it's filled with these tree turrets now and some Empire travelers. Corner screen status informs me I can misslead the empire If I talk to them. So I sprint throught all the previously cleared corridor paths to reach them. But to my surprise I can't talk to them, they just nod to me. Checked and still can't offer the Keep to a clan. Enough for this gaming session. I'm out.Who is willing to throw away so much of his time because of bugs? I have more or less 5 hours of free time a day. Would prefer to actually relax and feel some sort of accomplishement instead of irritation because of flawed game.On the performance side: I've got myself some high end gaming pc and the game doesn't give a damn about that. Making me wait for loading&building levels 1-5 minutes, even tho I've visited them before. I would consider them small. Loading even crashes sometimes. It's so time consuming. I checked ingamie options like 'loading in the background' or 'remembering last locations' but it didn't have any noticable impact.

_childDocuments_.review: Astronomical potential, but it's just not there yet.The bugs are pretty fixable with the "Prayer" mechanic, so nbd. Still, it seems like there's a lot of tweaks to enemies becoming invulnerable, misaligned terrain, etc. Good, just not quite there.The customization and interactivity with other cultures makes it a very immersive experience. There's lots to learn, the barter system is great (albeit lacking in content, as you mostly just trade the same things around) and the environmental/provisioning system is pretty demanding without feeling too oppressive. It's just enough of a struggle that poor planning will ruin you, but planning ahead feels like you beat the game.Big complaints are the painful lack of diversity in gear, the ambiguous magic system (including that the staff use at specific locations is both useless and infuriating) and the limited array of tools to overcome problems. This is like the roguelite RPG version of "No Man's Sky" - gigantic, ever-changing world full of beauty and mystery, but the only content so far is a storyline that's so basic and gruelingly long that it's basically just a travel simulator at this point. Buy on a really cheap sale, but supporting the devs at this stage of development shouldn't be $20.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of games like Dwarf Fortress that generate a fantasy world for you to play in, this is one of the better ones. It's a roguelite action RPG.The randomly generated world map is small enough to keep in your head, but large enough to feel big and with a varied composition of different terrains. I've generated two different worlds and they felt really different from the other, and had different features and layouts.The world is dynamic - there are a number of factions from a globe spanning conquering empire, to various clans defying them down to individual bands of mercenaries, refuges or monsters. All these factions take actions and the map changes as time goes on. Magic can become drained, or empowered, sites can become conquered or lost to monsters. It's really neat, and everything is a big deal for your plans. Nothing is just some words for you to read, everything changes the game world in a way that matters to you, the player.Time will go on - both while you journey from place to place, during, and after. It takes at least a day to move from one site to another. You also may need to camp, which passes time. Your player character can die or retire, and you can continue the game with a new character, but with all your old equipment (assuming you made it back to Haven)... Time will pass between one adventurer and another as well.Even the seasons and weather changes, and the different regions have different seasonal weather.I have run into a number of bugs, but nothing game breaking so far. The world map I love so much is a new, big change to the game - and I understand it broke a lot of things when it came out.It seems like the devs are actively fixing the bugs, and besides I've been having a lot of fun, so I do recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: 4/10. It's not what it could be. Unexplored 2 has incredible charm, but the flaws are simply too glaring, the biggest of which is that it just doesn't respect your time.Most of the game consists of hours of incredibly inane, trivial, yet time-consuming activities. Like waiting for a map to generate so you can run around some dangerous plants, a few seconds loadtime after each node of uneventful travel, entering a level to rest after travel(why can't your character do that on its own?), killing 20 rats/spiders/bats that spawn when you trigger a trap, talking to a dozen different NPCs to gather rumors about which places might be worth going to......and then you get ambushed by an imperial battle squadron or run into a weird enemy, and they kill you before you even realize what you've done wrong, which is the main way you will die as other enemies are mostly boring and easy.What this game needs is to abstract away the tedium, replace random spikes in difficulty with more consistently enjoyable encounters, and to recognize that long-term progression and permadeath just don't mix- making a new character is cool and great, but you just do the same things over and over, except without the loot you've already looted and the leveling opportunities you've already used up.I wanted to like it, but I can't. The payoffs aren't worth the time and tedium.

_childDocuments_.review: A highly recommended diamond, with some edges still being polished! Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy is a rouge-like-rpg-fantasy-world-adventure game which tries, and I would argue, succeeds at doing something quite interesting. You play as a single character in a randomly generated fantasy world (well, almost randomly, there are a few givens, such as the general geography, and the presence of the evil Empire that you're supposed to halt in its tracks). In this world, you start out with carrying a McGuffin called The Staff of Yendor, which you eventually must destroy in The Elemental Forge in The First Valley. All pretty epic stuff. Now, you get there by way of adventuring, securing better and better equipment and skills for your character, and interacting with the denizens of the world you're chosen to protect. When your current Wayfarer gets worn out and loses his Hope (a game mechanic that pertains to the stats and skills of your character), you can retire it and proceed with a new character in the same world, carrying on the task. This is the roguelike element to it, and retiring a worn-down character is eventually desirable, since by finishing quests and affecting the world, you unlock new starts, character skills and so on and so forth. Alternatively, you die at some point, and if you're not carrying the Staff just then, you get to create another character, and explore new regions.All this is done within a very pretty and imaginative cell-shaded-kind of graphics environment, somewhat reminiscent of the open-world game Sable, or the comic artist Moebius. The randomly generated environments have a good mix of fighting and puzzle mini-games, and are pretty to look at. The sound and music design fit in well enough.Now, this game does something quite interesting in that the dungeons and environments and the engire game world are randomly generated each time, with some pre-built set-pieces here and there. This can get troublesome at times, and there's a game mechanic that lets you work around unsolvable puzzles, should they arise, but generally they work out just fine, and its up to the player to experiment with different weapons, armour and magics to reach their goals. This is done in a reactive, persistent world that feels surprisingly engaging and alive, in some respects pulling off the a similar trick that RimWorld does, and I would love to see other developers try to create something similar, generating RPG-worlds that actually are distinct, interesting and engaging.This is a game long in the making, as I understand it, and the indie developers behind it are very helpful and seem to genuinely care for it, and are quite active and helpful on their Discord server, and are as of this date still actively working on the title, with some interesting plans in mind. I think it's worth buying!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but it is so amazingly frustrating.I've played a bunch of campaigns but never finished it; every single run has had a game-breaking bug. _childDocuments_.review: Update:Each update, while supposedly bringing the game closer to the vision of the team, only seems to break necessary systems further and further. This isn't a game, it's an experiment in design. It's not playable, and is not currently a product capable of standing on its own merits.If you want to support a team working to try and hammer procedural generation into the shape of a game, that's definitely viable. But if you're looking for something to play, look elsewhere.Original review below:-----I actually had to go back and check to make sure this wasn't early access. Bugs aren't exactly rampant, but they can and will *strongly* interfere with your ability to progress and just..function through the game.There is some relief via a prayer-system for map-generated issues that occur with some regularity, but they won't resolve bosses that don't spawn, enemies that are seemingly immune to any and all attacks that you throw at them, or getting locked into menus or interactions trying to rest/repair/whatever and having to force close out or jank your way into some kind of solution. Losing an immense amount of progress even with constant rests and saves each time this happens kills the interest in playing this further.I would estimate that I've hit a game-interrupting bug that wasn't fixable via the prayer system every 2-3 hours. Keep in mind that for about 30% of those, the solution was either to force close the game or reload from a save and lose a fair amount of progress.There are some neat ideas here. The legacy system is cool, and the path to finding and building your toolkit is pretty neat. I just wish I could, you know, play towards those goals consistently rather than fighting the bugs the game throws at you.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game so far. Really makes you feel like your exploring. Magic items and loot are rare and meaningful to the point where you will quest for them and be greatful for each item you find.The combat seems to be a sticking point for alot of people but I quite like it. Its risky and best avoided which makes sense to me.Its generated an interesting story for me - I proceeded south on an expedition to a temple I needed to explore for information on how to fufil my task of destroying the Staff of Yendor - when I got there I found I needed something to get in and couldnt proceed. Dejected I decided to investigate a nearby ruin whereby after defeating a giant spider I found a magic mask. The mask didnt do anything but it did have 3 sigil slots. Proceeding back to Haven I stumbled upon another ruin - after solving a puzzle I found a legendary and balanced sword to compliment my short sword that I decide to dual wield. Up until this point I had been sword and boarding with my good but not excellent legacy shortsword (legacy items are bound to you and remain with you when you die).Arriving back at Haven with a backpack full of loot I forged the mask using the sigils I had found. This mask now grants me additional damage on each hit and makes attacking much faster. Additionally I forged my short sword to invoke lightening damage on hit every 10 seconds. With the items I hunted and scavaged I traded with the smithy to add balanced to my shortsword and sword which reduces attack cooldowns by 20%. Now I am a whirling dervish of dual wielding destruction . I head off to a nearby clan hoping to cement a friendship between Haven and myself. They want my legendary sword as a gift - and I cannot bring myself to part with it. I decide to push my adventure onwards towards a magic site hoping to find something that will bring the clan and Haven closer together without sacrifice my new found dual wielding build of rapid evisciration. So I proceed to the magic site whereby a explore a Temple on the top of a mountain. Several climbing challenges exhaust my sparks (currency used to aid in skill checks / challenges). I get to the top of the mountain and find a curious machine locked behind a pickable door. I attempt to pick the door but without agility skills and any sparks I snap my second last lockpick. No good - I decide to explore hoping to find a key which I do. Coming back to the machinery I have a choice - take 4 sigils or take a new hope trait. I choose the hope trait and decide to try to pick the lock of a door in the temple. I succeed and come across a very interesting item - the Skyforge. The only issue is that it is extremely heavy so I am faced with yet another choice - ditch items such as my bedroll, sturdy boots and cold weather gear or leave the skyforge behind. I choose the skyforge and eagerly anticipate what it might do for me when I bring it back to town.From there I went and fought an Imperial boss - beat him and got a wicked artifact albiet in a massive cost to my life. I stepped outside the portal I teleported through to fight him and stepped on a trap. RIP Grunbald, mighty warrior, intrepid explorer and blademaster unrivalled. Its riveting stuff.  There are so many inspired design elements that force decision making and tough choices; the inventory system, the bartering, which items to sigil up and/or improve via the smiths and even which regions to head towards. It all condenses into a rich tapestry of systems that keep gameplay fresh no matter where you are in your run. Furthermore the legacy system and a huge amount of unlockables based on actions you take in the game really takes the sting out of dying as usually there is something new to try on the next run. Patches are coming thick and fast - the game is already heaps better after a week of patching and many issues have been fixed already - if you read the PC gamer review and were turned off things are already heaps better.This game is a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish I could give it a better recommendation, but I don't feel as if I can. The art and music is great, as well as the general atmosphere. (When I saw the game at first I kind of got Outward / Caves of Qud vibes for whatever reason) But...that's about all the praise I can give it.The game systems feel...incongruous? I'm not sure what the best way to describe it is. Others have said similar, but my biggest gripe is combat. I don't even mean the feel of it, though it's not great. It's how much combat I've run into despite the game very clearly trying to steer you away from it. (There is completely no benefit to getting in a fight ever) There's even pop-ups which blatantly tell you that there is barely any benefit to combat, which is a bit concerning because running into enemies has been most of my experience so far.Besides combat, there really only seems to be three major things I found to do: Talk to NPCs. Perform skill checks through an RNG mini-game and finally, what seems to be the brunt of the content, sneaking through dungeons and avoiding enemies/traps, as well as solving puzzles. For me, the problem is sneaking around and solving those puzzles isn't fun in the slightest. The stealth system is not engaging at all, and most of the puzzles (at least at the start) seem to revolve around finding levers and getting keys. Considering the procedural nature of the game, I can see where this is going 5+ hours in and I'm noping out now.I won't act like I'm an authority or speaking gospel, but it feels as if there may have been some troubled development. Why have all these weapons, armor, enemies and isometric movement akin to Diablo to make a game that doesn't take advantage of the combat it has in place? I could see this style of game being amazing as a text-based game, but as is, it just doesn't vibe with me.Maybe there was a change in vision half-way through, or maybe it was a pivot due to the inability to make appealing combat, I don't know, but the game's foundation feels at odds with how I'm being told to play it. I'm fine with bad combat, or even no combat, but with the way things are designed it turns into a mediocre stealth game with what appears to be boilerplate puzzles from procgen. Maybe I would enjoy it more if I just turned it down to the easiest difficulty, but If the "intended" difficulty wasn't something I found fun, I doubt it being "easier" would help.If a pop-up box is required to prompt players how to play your game, that should be an indication that you need to re-asses your design. I could only recommend you try the game if you REALLY like exploration and crank the combat frequency down. As for myself, the exploration elements aren't enough to prop up the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Unexplored 2 is difficult, not difficult as in hard to play. Game's aren't actually difficult. No, Unexplored 2 is difficult the same way life is difficult. Much like how; if you can't carpool on your timeshare moped consistently to work every day, you might starve until you find another job. Unexplored 2 is the same way. Where a lack of wisdom can cause the minor difficulties of life to accrue and eventually kill you. And although you can pray to God for help, God also likes to punish you too.Unexplored 2 is a fantastic simulator of what it's like to be homeless. It has helped me gain perspective on what it's like to be hunted by the authorities, lose hope for the future because of a rainy day, communicate with the spirit world, and trespass on private property -and then murder the occupants. You won't have a funner time fighting to the death over squatter's rights disputes, than through Unexplored 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Unexplored 2 is like if you mixed Caves of Qud and MorrowindOkay with the comparisons out of the way, I've fallen in love with this game.I hardly ever write reviews (i should get better about that) but this game deserves it. It's such a fascinating, charming experience unlike anything else I've really ever played. I'm a huge fan of ttrpgs and this scratches that itch really well with the fortune system and the fun lore and roleplaying opportunities. I also end up becoming REALLY attached to my little guy by the end of the run (usually their very sad death)The roguelike system in this game feels, to me, like a great middleground between the very tough and brutal old school, "no progression, just skill" style and the new school "each death makes you a bit stronger" because you as the player can determine what you will bring into your next character and even completely start over if you feel like this world isnt working out.I adore this game, but you have to go into it willing to get lost, be confused, die, and learn a lot. It's a bit janky, but in the most charming way possible.

_childDocuments_.review: LOVE IT!!! This game is criminally under represented online. No wiki, 13 people playing at time of writing. I am genuinely shocked that people have not jumped onto this gem. Sure it's still a little buggy but each regular updates add both content and polish that have made this one of my all time favourites after only 40 odd hours game play. Obligatory Pros and Cons list;Pros*God tier procedural generation for the dungeons and over world map. Each location feels hand crafted, even the throw away encounter maps are stuffed with character and interesting puzzles, id rather run one of these dungeons then almost any of the throwaway dungeons in skyrim for example*Unique permadeath system, your characters past progress will unlock new cultures, classes and races for future playthroughs. Weapons and equipment with the "legacy" modifier will be passed onto future characters, softening the blow of losing a character (sometimes encouraging suicide to try out new unlocks). Each death also changes the world map, in logical ways, as years pass biomes change, factions take and lose ground against the big bad corruption element*Art style slaps*Lore slaps*High difficulty customisation allows you to tweak game to your liking*Consistent updates breath new life into the game every week or so*Intuitive mage/upgrade system. Magic runes are used for both puzzle solving and equipment upgrades AND once applied can be removed Cons*Buggy but not game breaking (most of the time anyway) *Some areas will feel unsolvable only to find out after hours of play you have had to search an obscure corner of a cave to dig up the only key available to finish a quest*Combat is a tad clunky, satisfying but clunky, could use a dodge roll mechanic (or something else) as to not force players to rely on shieldsIm not one to review games on steam but i feel this game needs way more attention. I want the devs to keep polishing this gem but that wont happen unless some more people buy this game. If you like proc generated dungeon crawlers but want something more then level after level of 9 interconnected rooms filled with random fantasy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this could be the game for you

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a reviewer, but I had to share this. I stumbled across this game recently and wound up having a lot of fun with it. I especially appreciate the custom difficulty settings which allowed me to play one world for several hours, then with the benefit of game knowledge, tailor my second world to a difficulty that I enjoyed without nerfing things that I didn't want to adjust. After clearing that world I am inclined to go back and ramp things up even further in a new world save.This is the part I really wanted to share. It starts out like a gripe but it's actually the reason I came here to write a positive review. At one point I encountered a bug and became stuck in the spirit world unable to exit. I assumed my game was toast and it made me very sad, I had made quite a bit of world progress on my first character. Not knowing what to do I came across the bug reporting function. With one key press I had a zip file of my save game and an email address to send it to.I very nonchalantly typed 'stuck in spirit world at Doorn, can not exit' and sent it off, expecting nothing.In the meantime I started screwing around with my save file in an effort to cheat my character out of the area so I could continue the game. To my absolute amazement I managed to succeed, changing my saved location and (I think) confusing the game and making it reset my position. No clue, but it worked, and I continued my play and even ended up clearing that world. It felt awesome, only mired a bit by that hangup that almost destroyed my progress.A few days passed and I actually received a response email from one of the developers about my bug report. I was totally shocked. Not only was the response not some automated nonsense 'thanks for your feedback etc' but it was specific to my bug report and contained an apology for taking a few days to fix, and a fixed save file for me to load back up and continue my save game. I can't overstate how much I appreciate that email!A few days later I saw the game had been patched, and behold one tiny line of text in the notes:- Resolving an issue with returning from Doorn’s spirit world.Was I the only one who encountered this bug? Probably not, but it made me smile, and it made me want to come here and tell everyone about it. Thanks for reading!As I said at the top I'm not a reviewer, but I will say this much: If this game looks even a little interesting to you, I recommend you give it a fair shot, I don't think you'll be disappointed. Good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first Unexplored. It scratched that real-time RL itch that comes up sometimes that only a handful of games have done right (Barony is another). There's even an option to play the game as the Roguelite that the devs envisioned before the project changed-though I haven't tried this yet.What made me write this review is the fact that the devs are still pushing regular updates a few years later. _childDocuments_.review: Just discovered this game it very much is my cup of tea! The feeling of playing it reminds me of games like Gothic or Risen (except procedural!) where you just feel like a small part of a larger, dangerous world and getting to the end is no easy feat. You are allowed (and expected) to fail. However, this also means that progressing and succeeding feels real and meaningful.The good:- Meaningful progression- A large world to explore and learn about- Faction system is great, makes the world really feel alive- Just as much of an emphasis on preparing for a journey as there is on the journey itself- Tense combat meaning you have to carefully pick your battles- It offers a ton of options to help you (though learning the game will still take effort)The bad:- I do think the game could do a better job at teaching some fundamentals (I still don't fully understand parrying, the game says it will happen automatically but it just doesn't seem reliable)- Its very easy to accidentally steal something from somebody, it really should tell you when a container's content is owned like it does for smaller containers (or at least make it so that if you take stuff when the owner isn't around then they don't immediately become aware of it)- Bugs! _childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give this game a "not recommended", as I think both the core idea and the visuals of this game are excellent, but the gameplay didn't feel as fun as in the first game.Let's start with the positives:- beautiful, vast world to explore, with a lot of unique structures, creatures and events- the world moving forward in time and changing after your character dies is something that is great and more games should try doing (looking at you Weird West)- the way encounters/skill checks are done is pretty unique and a good blend between risk and reward- the way you can tailor the difficulty to your liking is pretty robustHowever a lot of this is sadly held back by its gameplay and lack of polish.The game tells you in the beginning that combat is not the focus and that rewards from combat are not good ... which would be fine if most encounters you find weren't combat related.I've also encountered a lot of bugs, such as:- NPC's being stuck in walls- Quest items disappearing when dropping an unrelated item from inventory- Player model disappearing (game reload fixed this one)One thing I'm not 100% sure if it's a bug or intended - went into some portal hole, got stuck as everything in there required me to be "awakened", and there was no way back.Also, by default (maybe there are upgrades later) the player inventory is waaaay too limited.Overall, this game holds a lot of potential, but I would not recommend getting it right now.Maybe in a few months?

_childDocuments_.review: "WARNING: the gameplay has a great systemic depth, but be warned: there's a bit of a learning curve. It WILL take some time to get the most enjoyment out of the game."This is part of the games description, and i suppose I should have really heeded it. Unexplored 2, is a unique, ambitious game in an oversaturated market full of procedural generation or roguelikes. It can be said, that this is a hidden gem. What i HAVE been able to play (I will get to this) is good. The procedural generation is interesting, the biomes and settings are good, there are multiple clans, dozens of items, events, good item generation with numerous stats. The biome to biome travel is interesting and atmosphere is great. Art style is also fun  and cool, in my opinion of course. Combat is fun, and tricky, but not the best i have seen obviously. Unexplored 2, is a great game, that i cannot suggest to you in good faith to purchase UNLESS you understand the RIDICULOUS amount of near gamebreaking bugs in the game, and in my case, a strange optimization issue that i have that the dev team, which i imagine is horribly busy, for the love of Raaf, cannot help me resolve. The game runs, at a horrible 30fps at most times on my 4060, And it doesnt matter what settings i tweak. It lags horribly. The game also has had instances where it locks me inside rooms or biomes and i cannot progress any further. For in-biome technical issues, you could "pray to Raaf" to teleport you to another location - its a way of the devs saying "we know this game has issues so here you go: its a tool you can use to solve them in a bandaid way." I have had to abandon my world due to this issue.I am leaving a positive review, because this game is a hidden gem, but it shouldnt be. at worst it should be an EARLY ACCESS hidden gem, and at best it should be acknowledged as a game with passion and incredible potential. This game really did need to be in early access - it isnt really presentable in a flattering way, right now.This is a hesitant, HESITANT recommendation. This is a buggy, messy game. And its also a good one, with a lot of potential. Thank you for one of the devs in trying to resolve my issues. Do not be discouraged.

_childDocuments_.review: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~New Review One year Later~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~A Lot of what I said before in my Original review remains still true so i'll keep it at the end of this review for the sake of clarity.Before i continue any further i wanted to clarify some points  for any potential buyersIf you have played Unexplored 1, loved it and are now considering getting this game because of that then i would advise caution This game is entertaining however lacks so much of the polish and precision in its current state that made the previous title a gem,If you come into this currently with the expectation of a an experience that feels almost hand crafted like the original then you will be sorely disappointed A big reason for the current lack of polish and refinement comes in two parts, The first part being a much larger scope than the first game Unexplored 1 is heavily inspired by Brogue and other OG roguelikes. All it needs to generate and maintain is a  Singular Dungeon and the Vast quantities of monsters , puzzles and traps that lay within {if you haven't played it and even remotely like Roguelikes then 100% stop reading this and go check it out because it is in my opinion one of the greatest roguelikes ever made)Unexplored 2 has to do a similar job but for an entire world that also deals with Factions, Stories, An actual active threat. Where in the original your goal is to retrieve something at the bottom of a dungeon and make it back and that's it, this game you have to explore a world to find passage to a secret valley where you will bring a magic staff that was given to you at the very start of the world to defeat the evil empire which i might want to add isn't sitting by twiddling their thumbs but instead actively conquering the entire world, armies marching through subjugating tribes and leaving devastation in their wake twisting the very land it self Not only is your goal larger but your timeframe larger as well. In Unexplored 1 when you die, you die that dungeon is gone and all your impact in it is also erased. In Unexplored 2 when your character dies that marks the end of his journey but not yours or the worlds. in fact you make a new character to continue in the world that the previous one left behind with all the impact that they had shaping the world. Clans are now allied , treasures are now stored in your possession, passageways that you had to quest to open are now open from the start and the empire is closer to conquering the world Each character is a Roguelite where their progress can improve and assist each subsequent characters adventure But each World is Roguelike where the journey the world has gone through will never be exactly the same as any other world. In every world you will eventually end up forced into a final run by the empire reaching your haven or you deciding to take up the staff. If you lose the final run then that world is lost forever with all the history and stories in that world gone. This game is more ambitious than the first one ever could have beenThe second part which is more subjective and absolutely some people will disagree with me is that:This game is absolutely still Early Access Yes it says its full release Yes it had an Early Access period which it now left It doesn't matter it's still 100% an Early Access title in my eyesThe Devs are still actively implementing and reworking major game features and core mechanics consistently and the game is nowhere close to the fully realized vision that the Devs and the Community has for it.Of course it's going to still be in development, with a scope that massive there is no way it couldn't be.The Devs basically had no choice and had to fully release it in the state it was mostly due to pressure from the publisher that they were working with at the time so i don't blame or fault them at all for doing it. The fact is they have not given up or abandoned this game and are continuing to constantly work on it I personally don't regret buying this game at all because I have loved seeing the progress the devs have made and by joining their discord have actively been a part of their development process. They are surprisingly active on discord and encourage fans to give feedback,opinions and suggestions and actively take it on when continuing forward and i have full confidence in themWhile i don't regret it for the reasons i listed i know that won't be the case for a lot of people that doesn't matter to them so here's my final opinion on whether you should get it or notIf you are interested because you want the same level of polish and feeling of hardheartedness that the first one had then I would recommend you give it around 2 years and then come back to see what it's like then. If you are buying this game you must come into this game with the mindset that it is an early access title and if not then i encourage you to waitI'll try to update this review again once (not if) the game begins to reach that the state where the  gameplay lives up to its incredibly innovative and ambitious design which the devs are currently and constantly working tirelessly to make a reality~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~OG Review (Jan 2023)~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Honestly this game is a weird one its feel like this should be an early access gameI'm half inclined to recommend you wait like another year from this point before buying it because it doesn't feel as fleshed out as it will be. The base concept of the game is there however the world feels much emptier and hollower in that there isn't nearly enough mechanics and just things going on in the world and several mechanics aren't as deep as they really should be:like for example clans don't feel that good and the empires presence isn't nearly as impactful as it should be, its feel less like a world ending threat and more like a mild inconvenience especially given how the people of the world don't really seem to be that bothered or care about fighting/defending against ithowever i don't really regret purchasing this game because from what i've seen interacting with the developer on the discord server and the regular updates they post to try and improve the game, i have full confidence that this game will be exactly as good as the trailers and store page makes it out to be. it has all the necessary building blocks for it and a developer that i have faith inThis is why i say it should have been early access. Its not ready yet and having it be sold like a complete game really gives people the wrong impression of what its state currently is

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a lovely indie gem that deserves more attention. It's a (real-time) roguelike/lite focused on exploration and procedural generation. The first Unexplored game was set in a multi-floor random-generated dungeon, now your playing ground is this fantasy continent (with lots of random-generated dungeons). This time the focus is not just on fighting, but travelling and surviving the harsh conditions on the road. Diplomacy and stealth can be really useful.Your quest is to take this powerful artifact to the other end of the world to destroy it properly before the evil forces get their hands on it. (It's an obscure fantasy novel, you probably haven't heard of it.) It's not going to be an easy job and when (not if) your adventurer dies, the next chosen one inherits the job. The world stays in whatever state you left it in, the quests continue from where the previous adventurer stopped, your most important resource is whatever facts you have learned about this world. There's metaprogression in that if you befriend new clans and help them learn new skills with lost relics, those become options for future adventurers to start with. Your biggest magical treasures also somehow find their way to the next hero to be inherited.My first character took close to 20 hours of playing to pass the torch. I've yet to finish the main quest, but it's going to take tens of hours more of exploration. Don't expect to finish a run on your coffee break, it plays more like a huge, sprawling cRPG. I'd keep notes, but the quest log and the world map already do quite a good job of it. It's also quite a slow game that rewards paying attention to details and soaking in the immersion, even though it controls like a twin-stick shooter. It's also got that nice tabletop RPG feel that there's other ways to succeed than just combat.It's got that roguelite itch though, when a run has ended you're shown a little montage of what changes in the world, some factions gain more ground and powerful monsters claim territory. At that point I just can't resist to click "play again" and roll another, completely different character and see what's changed this time.In a way, it reminds me a lot of Dwarf Fortress's world generation, although this is not as insanely detailed and there's bound to be building blocks that start repeating after extensive playing. Part of me wants to generate another worldfile and see what the world turns out like there, but at the same time I'm really invested in my current generated world, more than in many other games' hand-made fantasy realms.I don't know what it is with these backpacker games, but I really enjoy it when there's a game where you are PLANNING and preparing your future route on the (unreliable) map and then pick what you think are the essential things to carry in your limited backpack. Your quest details might be obscure or even false, you might just have vague rumours about what region you should be heading to. You've got to be prepared for anything, but you don't have the room for it. Perhaps you don't need extra water if you're headed to the mountains? Is the cool magical sword worth freezing without your trusty sleeping bag?The major downside to this game right now is that it's still got quite a lot of bugs. A lot of them are just small issues that can be ignored and sometimes you can bypass the bugs even with in-game mechanics, the unstuck prayer and the scroll that forces open puzzle doors helped me a lot. But now and again, you might run into a major bug and that can really stop your progress and kill the mood.Since a lot of the game is procedurally generated, like puzzles in dungeons, I'm not always sure if I'm facing a bug issue or if there was some well-hidden key I missed, or in one case, I didn't pay enough attention to the local village storyteller. The developers are squashing bugs constantly, so it is getting better every day. I recall the proc-gen being excellent in Unexplored 1, so I have faith that this'll get there too, but if you have a low tolerance to bugs it might be better to wait. This game has brought me such delight that I'll just head in for more, even with the occasional bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique game, certainly not for everyone, but if you like games with a story where you feel your choices have significant impact, and you really do not know what will come next, this game is a treat.It takes you through a deep story, that is not easy but rewards those who play, lose, and learn. _childDocuments_.review: Most of the recent poor reviews come from a certain demographic who tend to feel that if there's a convenience feature that can be added to a game, it should be added. This way of thinking ends up making all games the eventually the same. If you get angry when games make you think or make you choose, if you can't accept a loss of progress or a bad roll of the dice, then this game is not for you. Otherwise, keep reading:Unexplored 2 is doing things that no other game has successfully done and manages (in theory) to deliver on an incredibly ambitious premise: to give the player a procedurally generated, open, engaging, and complex world to explore and interact with. It's got everything. Travel, dungeons, combat, puzzles, unique flora and fauna, crafting, artifacts, a mysterious history, unique cultures, factions, 4x-style overworld events, and even a legacy system. It's genuinely amazing.If that sounds good to you, you'll want to buy Unexplored 2 when it leaves early access. Because right now - and for years - the game has been riddled with bugs. Bugs that crash your game, bugs that corrupt your world, bugs that leave one critical item out of an oblique puzzle, leaving you confused and frustrated. Totally game-destroying, joy-destroying bugs that seem to exist in infinite number.Some day, perhaps these bugs will be fixed. When that happens, I will recommend this game to basically everyone who has good taste in games. Currently, I would only recommend it to hardcore gaming nerds who are willing to accept some serious playability and stability issues.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my new addiction. It has some really great mechanics that offer up hard choices in field. In my current play through I've lost my main character twice. Once because I was thoroughly unprepared for the task I was hoping to tackle due to my novice, and the second I actively retired.I really like the Perma-death mechanic tied with the idea that some items can be stored up for your future characters. The mechanic forces you to plan for your future character when things start to get dire and to stow things you know are risky to take with you into the field on a dicey quest.In most RPGs the primary focus is about health and equipment maintenance. Unexplored 2 adds a higher level stat that almost works like a doom countdown: Hope. Your hope meter is not something you can (easily) boost back up, and when certain levels of hope are lost, you cannot regain them. If you lose all hope, it's not long until your character is done for. The character I had to retire had lost the will to eat and so I prepped him for his journey into the unknown by stashing things for my next, making difficult trades to consolidate items, etc.It's an interesting approach, and it really adds a level of tension you can only understand when you experience your hope suddenly drop from an enemy you've never encountered.Definitely worth the buy.

_childDocuments_.review: It's extremely original, has an immersive setting, and tries for some interesting unique mechanics that it mostly pulls off. I recommend it, but for gamers with A LOT of patience, both to learn its idiosyncratic & challenging systems and also deal with glitches that stem from its ambitious procedural structure.When I first started playing about a year ago, I would have given it a reluctant Thumbs Down review due to the constant uncertainty around bugs - it was often hard to tell whether I just couldn't figure out a puzzle or whether it had generated in an unsolvable state (which did happen more than it should), or whether some major negative development (a faction suddenly hating me for example) happened to due a real mistake or some mechanic short-circuiting.But I give the devs tons of credit - this is clearly a labor of love for them, and when I recently revisited the game it is MUCH more stable and many of the more janky mechanics have been streamlined & improved. They still regularly update and it's gotten much more accessible. I'm really impressed.One of my favorite aspects (besides the very singular visual style) is that it is a genuinely dynamic world that changes both due to your actions & also independent of them. Your actions have both big & small ripple effects that aren't just determined by some "Do you save the Elven Village or the Dwarf Fort?" obvious dialogue choice common to most CRPGS - in Unexplored 2 even some of the ways you interact with the environment or items will systemically alter the world, how magic works in different areas, etc.Time passing is also a factor that adds urgency to your quest - the evil Empire is marshaling its forces and you watch them gradually expand on the map, occupying locations, assaulting settlements. It has a LOTR feel in that respect, yet you also feel like you do have time & freedom to explore.Exploration is also rewarding, as there are many corners of the world, strange devices or structures, odd environments, etc. Sometimes you will understand them, other times they will be a mystery to solve. Others you will remain a mystery at least on your first playthru, but there's so much else to do it just makes the world feel more lived-in and mysterious.Definitely a buy for folks who enjoy original RPGs and learning new mechanics without hand-holding.

_childDocuments_.review: After a couple of hours, Unexplored 2 seems like a game with the potential to have a place among the great roguelites of recent memory. It evokes the same great gameplay elements that roguelites do better than any other genre: challenge, risk, build-theorizing, and exploration - while having created a world that feels lived-in, reactive, and beautiful.What stands out the most to me about Unexplored 2 is the developers' care for building an ambience - which I think sets this game apart from any other in the genre. I love hearing the sounds of rustling bushes and scurrying mice while shadows stretch across the landscape in the evening sun. I love it. And I think the developers do well by pulling you back into those environments at every opportunity while traveling through the overworld. Unfortunately, there are some persistent performance hiccups while traveling on the overworld, and loading into those levels, and can make that experience feel disjointed and awkward. And that's frustrating to feel because when everything *does* come together it does so *so* well. Obviously it's early in the the life of this release, so it's easy to forgive issues along those lines. However, I think if they aren't resolved - or at least lessened to some degree - it could really come to hurt the game moving forward. That said, I'm staying optimistic that the Ludomotion team can find ways to smooth out these technical bumps and deliver a truly incredible game.

_childDocuments_.review: *** Update ***Every single point has been addressed. All of the flaws that I had originally pointed out, I thought would be too big a lift for the developer to change. I am stunned that a developer would put this much effort to care for a game after release, and I'm sad I didn't change this review earlier. Thanks for making a great game. *** Original Review ***This game has some stellar ideas. The mechanic for skill checks is one of my favorite in any game, and I hope it's adopted in other areas. The graphics are great, and the IDEA for the game just spoke to me. I was really excited to play it only to find that for me, it's just not... fun. What it felt like was the developers had some great concepts, and brought them to life using some clever procedural generation of lore, maps, and encounters. They even had workarounds for most cases where the procedural generation didn't leave you with an accessible end to the level, but left out a fix for having an impossible task. If there was a quest to enter the spirit world, but then no spirit portal formed, you just ran around for 10 minutes trying to figure out what to do. That happens pretty often, so you're met with this feeling of  for the first few hours. While there is a combat system, the tutorial tells you outright to avoid it at all costs - and they're right. There is no reward for combat of any kind, so the only rewards are for expending your resources to explore further into the nodes on the map. However, this means that the best course of action is just to sprint through every encounter, turning every travel between nodes to just be a waste of time after the 10th time you've done it. Despite the procedural generation creating a new encounter, it becomes a grind, and that feeling of progress starts to fade quickly. If you find that you enjoy very slow paced games, and want the TTRPG experience, this game might be for you. Just go in knowing that there is no crafted storyline, progression happens slowly within a run, and the progression of unlockables in the overworld is just as slow. My goal is to try again later to dial in the expansive options for tweaking gameplay, but I'm afraid that some of the critical systems are flawed in a way that will never give this game that excitement of thinking about it while I'm at work, then rushing home to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an extraordinarly unique game. It takes the roguelite concept and expands it from one mega dungeon to an entire world. The Second Wayfarer then gets revenge on the bandits and passes the powerful weapon onto their descendants so they can travel to a far flung city that hates him. And this kind of story telling is constant and rises completely diagenically.Edit: They dded a memorial, so I guess christmas is on the 20th this year!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game - If you can get through first few hours there is a true gem of a game waiting for you. The time element is crucial as the game only properly opens up and reveals its true potential 10-20 hours in depending how good you are. The early game can be really tough for new players - as it takes time to get used to the multiple mechanics at play (resources, seasons, equipment, combat). This is where I believe a good chunk of players stop - as the effort/reward dopamine hit is rather sparse at in the early game (for brand new players at least) To be honest the only thing that kept me going initially was the incredibly beautiful visual style/soundtrack and my hard headed resolve not to be defeated so easily.    I actually had a quite nice/lucky 3 hour run with my first character before dying in the spirit realm. My next two characters did not last even an hour. So I went on YouTube and watched a couple of episodes of Tonehack's playthrough series. Then went back to the game and took advantage of the combat practice arena (accessible from menu) to improve my combat skills. Only then I went back to the game - this time selected the Story (easy difficulty) ready to experience the game at a less punishing pace. Despite that I managed to die three times within an hour - and was tethering on the edge of quitting before giving the game one last chance. However, this time I hit a real stride - and 15 hours in with my new explorer managed to get deeper into the game - I finally got comfortable with the key mechanics and at the same time the fabulously magical secrets started to reveal themselves one by one. Leaving me in awe time and time again - giving me my dopamine hit. Seriously there are some fantastic looking surprises/experiences for the explorers who manage to persevere. This game reminds me of the original Subnautica - where I put that game down after few hours and only when I returned to it few months later I really fell in love with the game. Unexplored 2 shares the exploration, resource gathering, survival DNA with Subnautica. However, more importantly than that, both games share the essence of true exploration, with unique, rewarding and exciting world where one wrong step can alter the fate of the explorer's journey for ever.  The Wayfarer's Legacy has become my favorite game of the year (I do not normally play these type of games - and prefer much faster titles) However, this game really cast its spell over me - and I can't wait to spend some more time exploring its world.Positives- Fascinating world- A lot to discover (you will be in awe if you can persevere)- Incredible visual style- Fantastic soundtrack - Exciting game loop (discovery, one never knows what lurks under the next journey node)- Pray for help system (when you are at your wits end)Neutral / Negatives- The game would really benefit from reference guide - where the mechanics could be better explained to novices. - Clunky combat (stealth approach is promoted over combat)- Controller mapping still feels weird to me even after more than 30 hours- Game requires certain mindset/resolve to be truly enjoyed (but so does real world exploration)- The game loop is based on a fact that your explorer should die again and again and learn what to do through death. I find no satisfaction in this approach.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. The sense of discovery and exploration is amazing. Although the main quest is the same (destroy the staff of yendor), each world and all areas are randomly generated, so each world will feel different and unique. So there is replay value even if you finish the game once.Unfortunately you will definitely encounter some bugs and the randomly generated nature of the game can lead to unsolvable puzzles (eg. lever to open door inside the room you want to open). Luckily the developers acknowledged this and added a "pray for help" machanic which can help you out in a situation where you can not progress or are trapped/stuck.Also dying in this game can be very frustrating. You can grow very attached to your wayfarers, and if they die, they are gone forever.I still highly recommend the game. Give this hidden gem of a game a chance and the recognition it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: ORIGINAL POSITIVE REVIEW 12/2022:Very strong procedural generation. In this game, not only the dungeon levels are generated - the whole region, encounters between different places and some kind of story interactions are also generated. The game still needs some polish but is updated frequently. It is really unique.EDIT TO NEGATIVE 05/2024:Recent updates heavily change the game at it's core. Fixed quests, that you HAVE to take from a central questgiver, making questsites inaccessable unless you singularily follow this one quest, automatic healing, restocking, restricting camping to fixed campsites, automatic transfer of items to new wayfarer, securing of important NPCs to not accidentally kill them, removal of skill points, removal of character creation and many more of these kind of changes.This is the complete opposite if what Unexplored 2 was for me and it is the opposite of what i wanted when i bought the game. I wanted a hardcore, open world RL with simulation aspects where i can freely journey around and where i have to plan and think to survive. I wanted a real roguelike, just in realtime.Now it feels like it is turning into an MMO or mobile game. Why? I am really sad about this new direction. I dont want to play this new Unexplored 2 anymore and i would never have bought a game that would have been advertised like that. If i could still have my money back and refund the title, i would gladly do it and be done with it forever.

_childDocuments_.review: Unexplored 2, it's like the rebellious teenager of the roguelike world. It's not your typical turn-based dungeon crawler, nor is it the fast-paced, bullet-hell madness of games like Binding of Isaac. Nope, it's carving out its own path, strutting its stuff like it's on a red carpet.Think of it more like the indie film of roguelikes. It's not about flashy combat or epic loot drops every five minutes. Nah, it's more about survival. You gotta tiptoe around, negotiate with NPCs, and sometimes just leg it when things get hairy. Combat's there, sure, but it's more of a last resort than your go-to move.And speaking of time, forget those quick runs you're used to in other roguelikes. This game's a marathon, not a sprint. It's like settling in for a Lord of the Rings marathon, but instead of popcorn, you've got your controller in hand.But here's the kicker: this game's got brains, too. It's not just hack and slash. You gotta pay attention, read the signs (literally), and use your noggin to figure stuff out. It's like being in a puzzle where the pieces change every time you blink.Sure, it's got its quirks. Bugs and glitches? Yeah, they're like the annoying relatives crashing your party. But hey, every family's got 'em, right?So, if you're up for a challenge and don't mind taking the scenic route through a roguelike, give Unexplored 2 a whirl. Just don't expect it to hold your hand. It's more like that eccentric uncle who throws you in the deep end and expects you to swim.
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Game exposes you to too much stuff to do from the get go and leaves you alone without further guidance on "how to win", or even "how to play [efficiently]". On the bright side -- it encourages you to find your own way to win the game -- if you feel adventurous.On not so bright side -- it paralyses your mind, especially if you are a cautios guy and like accomplishments.Mental stance which helps immeasurably with this blockage is: "OK, lets die and ruin a couple dozen of runs simply to try different things and understand the rules -- and then *finally* start playing the game".It makes all your decisions in game *much lighter* and helps you to start enjoying the game itself already.
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: It has yet to hit the highs the first game did for me, but with ongoing weekly updates and more and more legacy features making their way back in I feel comfortable recommending this.The overworld and node system is a fun foundation for when the dungeons and combat gets fleshed out and in turn makes the broad stroke events feel more meaningful and believable.There's still an odd disconnect with what a journey should be and what is rogue-lite about it. The modifier system is a good quick fix, but requires a lot of knowledge beforehand of what turning the gears really means for your playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty torn on whether I recommend this or not, there were a lot of frustrating things. The worst was there was a whole quest branch for waking the fire elemental, I got the special (excessively heavy and so annoying to travel with) weapon, and absorbed all the fires in the area which I assume is what I was supposed to do for that quest, and nothing happened. I ran around the area for like 45 minutes looking for anything else I could do, stabbing veins that make more monsters appear in case that would do something, etc. then finally I gave up and asked the internet and all the references I could find to this quest were from 2022 saying it wasn't implemented yet. Looks like in 2024 it's *still* not implemented, based on the achievement lookup thing saying 0 people have that achievement.I got stuck in badly generated scenery a couple of times, but the "escape to entrance" option to break out of that makes it not too annoying (but still a bit annoying).The crafting stuff is super weird because it's like "you need 5 fur to make an item fur-lined" and throughout my entire playthrough to victory I saw a total of 8 fur. All the ingredients seem that way. I discovered late in the game that you can revisit a place you've already been and all the stuff regenerates, so I guess you can just *farm* sigils from a location that says "there's a sigil here", though I didn't try it. (I make the assumption based on taking the key-forging plate out of the forge while I went to fetch a fire sigil, and when I went back still carrying it there was another key-forging plate in there.)Inventory management is annoying, as the home base keeps slowly filling up with trash items so you run out of space to store the items you actually want to keep.But despite all these annoyances, I enjoyed playing the game to completion, on the easy "adventure" mode. I'm pretty sure I would absolutely hate it on a harder mode, because most of the danger is from things you have little control over (like a path near the end with 5 "cold" events on it - even if you're somehow wearing the maximum amount of cold-resistant equipment and none of it has been drained that's still gonna hit you, and it's pretty much not possible to be in that state since you can't recharge your cold-resistant equipment during that whole trip.)All of the equipment for resisting the elements being encumbrance-occupying equipment makes that sort of thing especially problematic.On the positive side... um... It's kind of hard to say what's to like? I clearly *did* enjoy it because I played it for 27 hours. The generated puzzle-ish nature of the dungeons is pretty good. The combat is meh, but the mechanisms for *avoiding* combat are decent. The music and graphics are pleasant enough (though sometimes the stylized graphics make it hard to distinguish stairs from cliffs, or stairs from flat surfaces). Would not recommend at full price, but would recommend on a good sale.
