_childDocuments_.review: This game is difficult.Its mechanics to some part concealed, goals only hinted and the way how to achieve them foggy, stony, long.If you do not want to give up early, heed my advice:Make this game on your first try as easy as can be. Don't only choose easy difficutly, but use all extra user defined modifiers to make it more forgiving. The extra easy difficulty setting is your true tutorial. This game is brutal and designed to give you a challenge in repeating runs. It is not good at explaining how things work, at times it seems unfair and the prologe tutorial is a joke. The tutorial is not bad per se, but the world and its mechanics are too diverse to be packed into 15 minutes playtime.But now, 15 hours in, I start to understand what is going on and Unexplored 2 has rolled out a red carpet in front of me.This is MY adventure. The game engine has created a unique world and it works! Farms, mountains, woods and rivers. Dark caves and shiny temples. Riddles, monsters, bandits, greedy traders and the helping peasants hand.I unlocked my first fast travel option, gathered knowledge (additional skills) for coming generations (runs). I know where to store my equipment. I understand where I want to travel and what gear should be equipped. I can form beneficial relations with neighbouring clans.And still, I feel like I have only scratched the surface.This is just my first run and this was money well spent! I highly doubted that in the beginning.6 days after release only 2.8 % of players unlocked a fast travel route (achievement), which is not a good sign. I fear many of the early buyers did not make it over the first obstacles and might be giving up too early. If you think you can invest 15 hours to learn this game, go ahead, draw your sword and bash the door in. Adventure awaits! But if this time investment sounds boring or too high, move on traveller, there are other worlds to explore.And one more thing. The world generation is patchwork. There are many tiny instances crudely stitched together. First I found that off-putting, but got used to it. Just don't expect hand crafted levels, merging seamless into an open world.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Now that I have finished the game, I have to say that there is a lot more going on that I initially saw in this game, but this is also because recent updates have made it significantly better experience. When I was playing near the release game progression was way off balance (the quests unlocked too fast, there were too many gift items, too many sigils and abundant amounts of loot), so majority of the game’s features did not feel as interesting as these could have. But after the passing moons update, the progression is much slower, so the player has enough time to explore the game more gradually. Making friends and alliances feels more meaningful when you must consider what clans to support. Combining sigils to make magic items that fits your playthrough is some of the many great mechanics in the game, and now that the game is much more balanced, thinking what kinds of magic items you need is much more meaningful. There are still some bugs that can be game breaking. In my last game where I cramped the difficulty almost as high as I could (no healing brews, less health, more hardships, tougher enemies, and encounters) the game generated in one of the Raaf temples a cliff that I could not pass, because the way through was too small for my character. What felt especially irritating was the cold winds in snowy areas. I think this is a bug, but because I could not see some of the wind hazards that took my health and gave a cold status, I could not progress by taking calculated risks. In easier difficulties these kinds of bugs do not really matter, because hazards are not life threatening most of the time, but in higher difficulties these bugs can ruin the playthrough. I am going to wait more updates and give another go after a month or two.In my opinion, what this game needs (aside of bug fixing and some balance changes) are more items, different encounters, enemy and hazard variety, and more custom difficulty options. Wolves and spiders get repetitive fast, and because of this, encounters and hazards are often pretty dull to pass through. Although the game can still generate really interesting scenarios, majority of them are just running or sneaking past them in almost linear corridors. If there are more variety in what you could face in the world, encounters and hazards would feel more interesting and exciting. It would also be nice to have an option to make more caves and temples completely dark and maybe even to toggle a circular line of sight system, where I cannot see beyond the walls. In terms of atmosphere, this game really shined in those areas where I did not have clear picture of what was ahead of me, and this was largely because the areas were completely dark, requiring torches or other light sources. Solving puzzles and navigating in these areas felt exiting, because the layout of the area and secret rooms were not that obvious. There still surely are some things that I forget to mention, but I wanted to update my review to reflect my recent experiences. I cannot emphasize enough how much I like this game and how much I anticipate future updates. Unexplored 2 gave me the feeling of playing something that resembles the depth, complexity and decision making that are mostly only found in p&p rpg’s (a feeling that not even most of the recent crpg’s cannot give). Developers have made something unique, and I really hope that they succeed with this game. Really good work! 😊

_childDocuments_.review: A Reward For The PatientUnexplored 2 is a visually appealing journey that rewards patience and experimentation. With a beautiful art style and score, and boasting good depth to its procedural generation, this is a game for when you're in the mood to relax and immerse yourself. Patience, reading flavor text, and experimentation is essential to enjoying the game.If you're looking for action-adventure, Unexplored 2 does not have the most thrilling of combat, and the pace can be slow. Pick this up if you're looking for the wonder of travel and exploration.Pros:⚪Beautiful Visuals⚪Sweeping, adaptive, well orchestrated score⚪Interesting skill check system ⚪Good depth to resource management⚪Highly customizable difficulty settingsCons:🔴Large amount of reading bogs down the beginning of the game🔴Some gameplay and visual bugs e.g. torches on wall sconces not emitting light🔴Contradictory instructions vs gameplay e.g. "combat is not required!"+ "cannot leave area, hostiles nearby!"🔴Overly simplistic combat given the depth of other aspects of the game🔴Insufficient difference in zoom levels makes details sometimes hard to make out.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're reading all of these reviews and chewing it over and you haven't already bought the game, this game is probably not for you. No, this game is instead for people who are willing to explore, take risks, fail, and learn. This game is for people who like games that break convention and that aren't afraid to do things 'wrong' to create an experience that feels powerfully new. This game is for people who like slow, ponderous games and for people who like making their own stories.What's the point of the game? To destroy the  Staff of Yendor. That item is both boon and bane; a necessary and useful tool that is also the source of much of your strife. And, like the game's clear fantasy corollary, this world and story is about the journey not the destination.There are so many magical mechanics at work here: the barter system, the travel system, the encumbrance system, the simple but brutal combat system. The audio is usually exquisite, the visuals are noteworthy, and the lore is pleasingly diegetic. It all reinforces that feeling of exploration and journey. We're still discovering the depths and corners of this world, and it sounds like there's much more to come.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very special but it is not for everyone. Because of the nature of procedural generation it has it's flaws but the qualities make this a underground gem. Gameplay-wise it is a adventure simulator. You are going on a journey so you have to manage fatique by sleeping, you have to bring food with you to regain HP and bring a coat against the cold weather of snowy mountrains or water if you are going in the desert.The world is open but it is not an open world. The map is like a board game with points of interest that you travel between.  The points of interest are small levels like Caves, fortresses, dungeons filled with traps and treasure, Trading outposts or even other civilisations. But on your way there can happen a lot. And here comes the shiny part of procedural generation in play. This game throws random generated things at you at your jouney. Hostile encounters, friendly encounters or maybe some sort of nature wants to kill you so you have to doge living trees or you just get wet because it rains.  And the things the random generator can create are mindblowing. Every world that is generated feels different. The layout of the map can vary heavily and what you find and where you find it also. That comes with different problems you have to overcome each map. Because the exploration of the world  is the center of the gameplay that makes a very intriguing gameplay-loop because you never know what to encounter. If you are searching for a random generated skyrim where you  fight hordes of enemies you are looking at the wrong game. You have to pick your fights wisely and sneak or run past most enemies because you're healing capabilities are limited and you don't know when you can find or buy new supply (or you get wounded for example what will come with disadvantages). So this game is a lot heavier on the survival side than on the action side gameplay wise. But since your charackter can die fast all the time and loose every gear besides some legacy items a journey in this game feels like one. This game simulates the tension of an adventure like no other game. But the game doesn't end there. There are an incdredible amount of features for example a very unique magic system, a crafting system, you can empower weapons and armor with sigils that you find on your adventures and a lot more. And everything is wrapped up in lovely RPG mechanics that define your charackter. Are you charismatic and can talk yourself out of situations? Or are you strong and can climb easier for example. At every start you make your charackter and what attributes you choose make a difference that gives you bonuses in a minigame that display obstacles the player has to overcome like lockpicking, talking, climbing, decipher inscriptions and so on. But the RPG doesn't end there. You can become friends with other civilsations and build a bond of allies with your hometown called haven. Or you steal from another village and they turn hostile against you. Pretty awesome if you ask me.The combat may feel clunky especially because of the movement of the player that feels like car with a lof of weight. But the movement makes dodging, parading, positioning and attacking at the right time  very rewarding. If you have gained some experience with it your skill as player plays a huge role in the outcome of your encounters. Also very cool is the procedural generation of dungeons. Dungeons are the place to be. There you'll find the treasures that will make the journey pay. But they are full of traps, puzzles and enemies. As with a lot of things in this game, the procedural generation keeps the dungeon crawling exciting because they seem very different and you never know what is behind the next corner. But with time you recognize the layouts. And that is where the dark side of the procedural generation comes in. First this game won't tell you intriguing story or lore. Second everything you explore is not a handcrafted dungeon with a special story and clever designed puzzle or another village won't give you an exciting clue about an ancient sword hidden in deep their catacombs. So the world feels a bit bland by nature because it is build by a programme. But if you can oversee these shortcomings the procedural generation makes the exploration and survival mechanics so immersive.If a procedural generated survival-exploration-RPG game sounds interesting to you try it out. It has a lot of charm, the procedural generation technology behind the game is incredible for a little indie game, there are a lot of things to explore and discover, very cool mechanics to play with and as I said this game will give you an adventure-feeling like no other game. It is hard, it doesn't hold your hand, it is frustrating sometimes, but it is also rewarding figuring your stuff out. And to everyone who is scared by the difficulty-level that a lot of people are describing here, when you start a map you can adjust the difficulty to your likings. Very cool feature. There clearly went a lot of love and passion into this game. It is so unique that you can't compare it to anything else. I can't thank the developers enough for trying something so niche and new. The game isn't even my type because I don't like survival mechanics but it is so special and cool in it's own way that even I pushed through the hard learning curve this game has. This game has a special place in my heart for being the most unique gaming experience I ever came across.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm coming back to the game a few months after release and revising my review since the game breaking bug that prevented me from continuing a number of my characters after a certain amount of progression has been resolved.Overall, I really enjoy this game.  The game takes a different approach to many rogue-like RPGs in that the preparation and travel for your adventures is just as important, if not more so, than the more action heavy parts. You'll need to make sure you have the correct equipment, such as boots, warm clothing, and food, to survive the obstacles you'll encounter on your journeys.One thing the game could do better is more thoroughly explain the permadeath progression systems. In order to ensure that your next run is easier than the last, it is important to obtain "legacy" items (which can be procured by finding a smith that can upgrade one of your current "well-made" items, trading for them, or less often, finding them in the world), which are passed down to every subsequent character. It's also important to store useful items in the vault, which are also passed to your next character. Without these, it can be difficult to make progress in the game, and the importance of doing so could be explained better.Also, although the game breaking bugs seem to be fixed, there still seem to be a number of non-edge case bugs that will force you to exit out of your game and re-load it to resolve them. These annoying bugs I have encountered are:-  If you reassign a two handed weapon to a new preset, you will not be able to add a different weapon to the old preset.- If you set up a camp in an area, you will not be able to set up another camp in the same area.- Enemies will sometimes get stuck below the ground, preventing you from camping near where they are, due to their being hostile.I always enjoyed the camping and travel aspects of RPGs, such as in the original Baulder's gate games, and if you also enjoy those aspects, you may enjoy this game as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game for the art style, knowing absolutely nothing about it - and while I will update this review once I actually finish the game, I already have enough thoughts on it to write a full review after about 5 hrs of playing (despite what steam says about my playtime). Unexplored 2 has some of the most beautiful visuals and environments I have ever seen in a game, especially in an indie game. This game knows exactly what it does when it comes to color schemes and asset design, with every time of the day looking unique and beautiful. And really, if you just want to look at a beautiful world, play the game in easy mode, and you already have your money's worth.Unexplored 2 is a game that takes a lot of inspiration from pen and paper games like DnD and Pathfinder, but is incredibly rule-light and elegant in how it's implemented. This is not a hack-and-slash adventure, but one where your life bar depleting literally means you die and lose everything - combat is only encouraged when you see an actual gain out of it, and you can never beforehand know if an encounter may not actually cost you your life.Aside from the main quest, the story is fully procedurally generated, and so is the world and each encounter in it. This makes the game replayable and creates a world and a story probably only you ever played. At times, I really was amazed by how dynamic the generated levels felt, with ledges to climb and traps and enemies and dangerous environmental hazards. I still have to say that procedural generation always has its errors - there are encounters I already had 3 times, while I feel like there are tons of content I haven't yet witnessed, some areas feel like they don't 100% make sense, and you sometimes just don't know if a key that you need to open a door is really somewhere nearby or in an unforeseeable corner of the map, because you just can't put your trust into a level designer who would have put it somewhere you would find it.There are tons of plants and environmental aspects across the world that don't explain itself to you - you usually walk into a plant and realize it hurts you, and then you are smart enough to never do that again. Everything in this world teaches you a life-lesson in a very Dark Souls-esque way, that I really enjoyed - the way I found out aggressive bats can live in tree stumps which I was looking for loot in, was being jumped by 5 of them and running away in panic. Unexplored 2 has tons of stuff like that - rocks that explode, ledges that give in, any new thing you find that looks strange to you will teach you how it works by you trying to interact with it and I found that to be really refreshing, because no one needs a pop-up before every dangerous new item saying "by the way, these plants hurt you", because learning it yourself is a lot more fun and way more immersive.The game is really smart about giving you quests and ideas of where to go, because rarely someone will actually tell you that they want you to do something - most of the time people just say stuff like "I heard there is a hidden library somewhere on the map". With that you never feel forced to go to a specific spot but rather can go explore with some goals what to bring back home in mind. So many small parts of the game are so fun and smart - there is no money in the game and everything is very trading-based, though I wish they would have gone a bit further and wouldn't have added items that are meant literally only to be traded away. Trading in some of your good food for a health potion would have been (to me) way more interesting than finding a valuable little figurine I can give someone that has no other purpose for me. Trading in general has some cool hidden "features" that I found so interesting to use: Instead of a trader having separate menus for "repair a weapon" etc. all of these services are incorporated into the trading menu, making you barter some of your items for a repaired blade or giving up a weapon you don't use for passage to a city somewhere else on the map. It's such a small thing, but it really immerses you into the world.The way weapons work is really simple and still incredibly strategic, because everything is slow and has cooldowns and fighting more than two enemies at once is incredibly dangerous and will probably lead to your death. The combat isn't hard to understand or to master, but it is risky enough that you never just barge into a fight without first trying to sneak past or look for a trap to lead your enemy into, etc. The game really encourages creative solutions to problems. The skill checks in the game are a GREAT addition to the gameplay and are a lot more than just rolling a die and seeing if you can make it or not - every skill check forces you to strategically think whether to invest into success or whether this isn't that important to you. This kind of check would be really convoluted in an analog pen and paper system, but in a video game it works perfectly. The music and the visuals are absolutely beautiful, and that the game is an indie game is actually insane to me. You can really see how much thought went into the design of the world and the systems within it, and how much effort they put into making this feel like a fun experience. This game is ambitious from a visual standpoint, as well as from a system design standpoint, as well as from a level design and programming standpoint, and I am amazed that the devs actually pulled all that off.Some negative aspects: I found the game to be a bit more aimless than I had hoped until now - I know, that you have an actual objective in the game, but no one told me where it really was, so I just did other stuff and tried to explore the world a bit, which also wasn't very helpful, and nothing really told me how to figure out where the place I should go to actually is. Exploring the world rarely gives you really cool stuff, which isn't bad, but I felt like exploring a place was often more punishing than just moving on, which I am sure wasn't the intention of the game devs. From a game design standpoint I think there were some items I found unhelpful and really just clutter - there is a mechanic that makes travelling more of a challenge, so you can be faced with heat, wilderness, cold and at least 4 or so other status effects - each of these can be cancelled out by having the correct item equipped. These items clutter your whole inventory and take up half of the inventory space, and I think having them in a game that has an incredibly small inventory isn't a good choice, given that they aren't actually fun to use, and the mechanic does nothing other than discourage you to travel. I wouldn't actually be all that annoyed if it were more of a "be prepared for the region you are going into"-mechanic, but they aren't reliably bought anywhere, so you can't really say I could have prepared for the cold weather, if no one is actually reliably selling me warm clothing. Also, I still don't really understand the magic staff you get and haven't found a single place to use it in yet. I also still experienced some minor bugs, e.g. a scene wasn't loading and when I restarted the game, everyone in the scene had a clone of themselves standing next to them. There are also some things where I am not sure if it is a bug or if I just didn't understand what I was doing wrong - one time everyone in my home village suddenly became hostile and attacked me etc.Really, if this game sounds like you will have fun with it, go buy it! It's beautiful to look at and fun to play. I don't think a procedural exploration rogue-like adventure is for everyone, and if you don't know if you'll like it, maybe watch some gameplay first.

_childDocuments_.review: I have quite a few more hours on Epic during this game's Early Access period. Yes, I purchased it twice to support the developers. I adored Unexplored 1, and Unexplored 2 is on a whole new level.Let's go over some highlights: - A multi-generational quest to destroy a magical object. - The whole world feels magical and alive. - One of the few games I actually read the extended lore for. - Extremely smart procedural generation. Lock + Key puzzles that require exploration to solve. - Much of the game can be bypassed without combat.  - This game's version of a "skill check" is used for getting information out of people or ancient text. - Preparedness is rewarded. Don't forget to rest, repair your gear, and bring the tools you think you'll need. - Limited equipment inventory makes you really ponder if heavy loot is worth bringing. - Barter system in place of "currency" with various NPCs which want different item types. - Combat is very tactical. You can't just charge in and expect to leave unscathed. - Beautiful art and music. - Etc etc...I have a couple gripes. - The procedurally-generated maps sometimes fail to produce a level you can complete. That or I'm an idiot who missed something. It's hard to tell. There are so many elements that go into each area. - Traps feel extremely hard to bypass without getting hurt. Again, this might be a "me" problem.Want a solid adventure that expands as you play? Get the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Unexplored 2 captures the feeling of being on an adventure as few games do. Would compare it to Wildermyth in that regard (by the way, how about adding the history of previous fallen wayfarers to the journal as Wildermyth does?). The procedural generation does wonders, lore is intriguing. Special mentions to art style and soundtrack: just amazing. Trading and skill check mechanics are very interesting and fresh.Some cons I can name is that it is a bit buggy (hopefully that will become less true with every patch) and the combat feels kind of meaningless as many reviewers have stated. The developers already expanded on their point of view regarding combat, and I can see their point of not incentivising players to fight every creature they encounter, but I think some small thing would go a long way as for instance a bestiary with some lore that is unlocked by beating a monster X times, as well as keeping stats on how many times you killed/got killed by particular enemy (I haven't played enough to tell if it is already not there, but the nemesis system would fit the game perfectly). Maybe I just played to much of tunic/death's door/elden ring lately, but i feel severe lack of dodge/roll button while in combat. Also would love to see the equipment I have on my character, for instance seeing the cape if I have it equipped ecc.All in all, great and very unique game, the developers clearly have a vision for it, and I can't wait to see what's next for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very tentative recommendation for now. Would pick it up on sale, or if you really want something kinda weird and fascinating, if a bit rough around the edges atm. The gameplay concept is weird and interesting and feels like what people thought No Man's Sky was going to be. The bones are there, the game is fun, I find myself obsessed for multiple hours at a time.But there are a lot of issues. Loading times feel absolutely brutal at the moment. There are very occasional world generation bugs, some of which are very significant. In a more traditional roguelike I wouldn't mind playing around this, but the very long  multi-session run times makes this brutal when you get 9 hours into a world only to find out that one of the mid-game major quests might be bugged? The game also has some extremely challenging to solve procgen puzzles, which can make it difficult to figure out when something is bugged or just confusing. There are also some weird combat bugs (throwing weapons in particular tend to just not work on certain types of enemies).Despite all of these issues, I've still put about 20 hours into the game, and I'll probably put more in. In its current state, I find the game hard to recommend. Based on the dev's previous work on unexplored 1 and the cadence of updates, I feel confident that this game will solve a lot of these issues in the long term, and is still very engaging in the short term.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I love this game, and If you like exploration and being led on by 'whats over that hill', you may like this too. You ever sit down and play a game, only to find yourself 1000 hours later wondering how something so perfect for you came into being? For a lot of people it's something like Rimworld, or Kenshi, or any other number of weird, niche games that fulfill something inside you that nothing else does. This game is that for me. It's the essence of exploration. Its an OSR Tabletop game in video game form. Its something I can sit back and play with a controller (Dwarf Fortress please) while being one character - my character - and not controlling a group of outlaws like a game of starcraft (looking at you kenshi). It fosters my curiosity and desire to explore and it can continue doing that with the procedural generation. This isn't your Early-Access-Roguelite generation that a lot of games are coming out with though - it has purpose. Each node you visit on the map with something interesting in it feels designed, and like it tells a story, if you listen for it. I came across and abandoned mountaintop ruin, which had no bridge leading to it from the stairs up. With as old as it is, the bridge must have collapsed, so I started looking around and found a cave - Turns out the spider infested cave was an escape route for the old tower, so I fought my way through and made it to the ruins at the peak. When I arrived however, it was locked down. Of course, like any good adventurer, I brought my trusty lockpicks along, but failure after failure led to my final ones breaking. On my way back down, I spotted an extra path I hadn't seen before. I followed it along until I reached an open cavern with a Big Mama spider who was not happy to see me. After sustaining mild injuries, I killed it and found a key it had been guarding. I took it back to the top of the tower, and opened the previously locked door to claim my loot. Another ruin I entered had some statues with pedestals in it, obviously meant to be a puzzle to open the nearby locked door. After exploring for a bit, I found a slate of ancient text which detailed how 'The Moon would Set me Free'. One short cooking montage later, I returned to the keys at night, only to see the moonlight shining down on the key I knew would open the door. I picked it up, and was immediately barraged with the gunfire of guardian turrets. Confused, I ran to hide and lick my wounds, only to find another slate telling me to 'leave the key in its place and take the others'. I went back, dropped the key back in place, and took the other 4 statues from their pedestals to be rewarded with an opening door. Some may find this 'deterministic' generation boring, in the sense that they know answers will exist for the questions they find in the place they find it, but I love it. Each Profile you make creates a world (Dwarf Fortress Style), and every character you make each death lives in that persistent world. The world created really is an amazing feat. It feels so interconnected due to the rumors you hear, lore you decipher in ancient runes, or random encounters with local folk who put you onto interesting things in the area. There are even things you can stumble across (that probably exist in every world due to overarching lore) that you can impact to make permanent changes in the world. Things like ancient magic devices that protect a region can be shut off to steal the power source inside. That of course, has consequences though. There's also not a lot of the world explained directly, which some may not love. Instead, you can find lore books and scrolls in areas of interest, and return them to the 'Loremaster' in town who can give you rumors/info based on some of them. Im curious how much 'crossover' there is in things happening in worlds though. Ive read epic poems in one world detailing the life of a brave warrior, then followed the path to where he died, and looted his corpse, but I wonder if that same 'hook' shows up in every world, or just occasional ones.The best part though is that it has different 'factions' that get a 'faction turn' between deaths. Factions expand, attack, or get attacked, and you can influence all of these things. I cleared a cave of kobolds terrorizing a nearby town, and found a copper ore vein inside that cave. When I returned to let them know of my success, I handed over the info about the copper vein, and they expanded a mine into it.There are no levels, but instead you gain skill by doing 'feats'. Some areas will have a task for you to do, like defeat bandits, explore a portal in the area, or discover a hidden treasure, and when you do one of those tasks, you're granted a feat next time you rest. Noncombat encounters - like social encounters or climbing a cliff face - use a weird 'gumball machine' style mechanic to visualize your chances of beating something. Your equipment, skills, feats, and relations can add or subtract things from 'the gumballs' that drop out of the pool with each interaction you push. Theres a 'reroll currency' you can earn/find that acts like a meta-currency to pull a new draw from the pool if you don't like your outcome. Learning what is worth pushing for a success on vs what is okay to fail is a really fun skill. Maybe you want to push your luck on convincing a local in a hurry to give you a rumor, but that means you may not have the option to do it later when you're attacked by bandits who are hearing you out first.It handles the issue of you dying by letting you find 'Legacy Items' - Items that return to town for your next character when you die. Its a really nice system for the game, because as you risk diving into barrows rumored to hold the remains and treasure of a great adventurer, you come out with a permanent upgrade. If you die though, you don't lose *everything* and have to start from 0.While I do love it, there are some qualms I have with how it presents information. In the tutorial, it tells you that combat is deadly, and its best to often avoid it, but more often than not you're forced into encounters with monsters along the road. There is a stealth system, but you usually end up fighting anyways. When you camp, you draw attention to yourself as well, causing encounters to happen, but those, more often than not, can't be talked out of. I understand its about managing your risk of camping, but sometimes it still feels odd. What about encounters like the game 'Outwards' deaths? While you sleep, some people take you away to another node, or spirits around you whisk you away and you find yourself in a spirit prison needing to escape?The devs explained their reasoning for the way combat works in a forum post here, and after playing more I think I like their vision of it more than traditional RPGs. Ive come to like not being overburdend with loot, but I also feel like the options for avoiding combat are really slim when they make up so many encounters. Id like to see more encounters on the road that don't involve un-initiated combat. If you're going to throw wolves at me on the road, show me a wolf den I may find something in. I hate the random enemy encounters with no reason to want to engage.Ive also had more than one crash (probably 4) as Ive played, usually happening between scene transitions or looting a bookshelf/chest. Its not super annoying, since you start back at the latest node, but still.One last Major issue I had was that one of my worlds was deleted. Im especially annoyed about this one, since I had some rare dungeon loot that I'd retrieved from a named dungeon, and lost it. I did die  but I don't think it was meant to completely wipe my world from existence.

_childDocuments_.review: The game makes a good attempt, but not really recommendable at the moment. Firstly it lacks polish like creatures getting stuck or small things being off. Then, everything feels wobbly: the camera moves strangely and jumps around, the characters control feels unresponsive and overly smoothed, creatures are straving sidewards like they are on ice skates. The gui lacks refinement with big ugly buttons and small chunky icons. The graphics style is based on only few colors and has too much contrast. Shadows are way too strong and sometimes feel random. For example with those random directional lights in caves. This sometimes makes it hard to parse the scene and is tiresome on the eyes. I don't expect high-production voice acting, but the squeaky character / NPC sounds are not really adding anything. Then it calls itself an "RPG", but character development is not even close to any typical RPGs. There are no attributes, no exp, no specialization and a major skill is "+1 to attack", or "+1 to social checks". Combat is kind of left-click-to-attack + run-around-cluelessly. Difficulty scales with just adding more monster which do more damage. No depth whatsoever. Lastly there are really frequent and long loading times. It takes about five+ seconds to load a map and as maps are tiny with just a couple of areas you will see plenty of loading screens.

_childDocuments_.review: I started up a new game as a Human Disciple, a skilled pathfinder with natural charm. His name was Arneld. He wandered around the hub town, and from reading books in the archive and speaking to patrons of the inn and passing traders, he picked up some rumors about several nearby locations. one was a cave with Kobolds nearby, considered a nuisance, but not a threat. Excellent. A great start for a young adventurer to hone his skill and earn respect for mighty deeds.I made my way to the cave, but on the road got waylaid by bandits, who knew turning me over to the Imperials would make them a pretty penny. I managed to sweet talk my way out of it, and they let me pass, but wouldn't let me camp with them. Avoiding the fight was lucky but I was dead on my feet and the night was closing in.I needed to camp as I was losing light, so I stopped at the next location, a lakeside. After disturbing some bats who took a fancy to my neck, I made my way to the waterside and set up a camp. I caught a fish and ate it, and then rested until the morning.At daybreak I managed to reach the cave. The signs of Kobold activity were obvious. I tried to sneak in, but stumbled onto two kobols on patrol, and luckily again my silver tongue saved me, and they let me pass. "This our home" they said in gutteral common tongue; "make visit but not trouble."Heading inside and down a precarious path beside a seemingly bottomless chasm, I stumbled into what looked like a ruined shrine, and also into some chittering horrors in the dark. I pulled my lamp and trusty blade to ward them off and dispatch them; the biggest cowering from the light while I drove my blade home.Venturing futher into the shrine, I came across the leader of the kobolds and his second in charge, examining a locked container. We exchanged greetings; word had obviously been sent down about my arrival. The room contained some kind of coloured pressure plates, and by tinkering with them, I managed to open a nearby door, but was immediately set upon by garguantuan spiders, the largest spitting balls of goo from which swarms of smaller terrors burst forth. I loosed arrow after arrow at the broodmother while dodging her younglings vicious maws, and eventually dispatched her. Deposited in the corner under many webs was a statuette; a roly-poly bug. I had seen a plinth with similar carvings earlier, so I tested my luck and placed it upon the plinth, which rolled (and polled) back a sectionof wall to reveal a downward stairs. Praise be to the rolypoly gods.Taking rest with the kobold leader, I ate bread to recover myself, and then set off for the unknown stairs. Id lost track of how long Id been underground- I had no idea of the time, but I was low on supplies and was eager to see the back of the place. However, in the depths I hear the faint crackle of electrical static, and was soon face to face with a horde of some kind of lightning bugs, led by brutes that punched through my blocks and electrocuted me. I dispatched two and several of the smaller ones, but rounding a corner I cam face to face with another brute, who headbutted me, and ultimately, ended my life.This was my first run in this world. Now, years will pass, tribes will shift their territories, and the Imperial menace will encroach on the lands more. The next wayfarer in this world will inherit the memories of his ancestor and hopefully learn the lesson: take more arrows and don't go toe to toe with lightning bugs

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very unique and amazing game. I like games with a really good sense of exploration and mystery, which can be hard to find these days with most overly Ubisofted to handhold and highlight at every turn, but this game does it wonderfully. Really great world and level generation. Unique and beautiful art and environments. Interesting bartering system without any money. Just lots of interesting and fairly unique mechanics and systems. I'd say it is great role playing from the adventure aspect, though shallow currently in the story and relationships aspect, relying mostly on lore.Bugs and rough edges have been an issue, but the devs improve it constantly and if Unexplored 1 is any indication, this won't stop for a very very long time. Although they improved it some, I do hope they will make the carrying capacity less restrictive in the future. I understand the need to impose limits to enforce hard choices, but right now I feel it is quite severely limiting my options instead. I also hope in the future the character interactions and quests can be made deeper and more interactive so towns feel more alive and interesting. Right now it is more at an early 90s console RPG level of repetitive NPC one liners. If they could turn those generation algorithms in the direction of Witcher 3 quests and story lines, this game would rocket off into the stratosphere. Maybe they'll do that for the next one.

_childDocuments_.review: If I didn't know coming into this just how different Unexplored 2 was from Unexplored, I might have ended up down-voting this game. However, forewarned as I was, I downloaded the demo and realized I had to keep playing. The feel of the game is so emergent yet engaging, and I really enjoy how the world changes based on my actions (and between my runs). For me the only real downsides are minor: there are some typos that could use addressing, and every character is either ungendered or is so androgynous that nobody is comfortable hazarding a 'he' or 'she' (everybody is 'they'). The constant use of 'they' as though nobody knows anybody does get a little confusing at times; I don't know if this is an off-putting political consideration or if it has something to do with simplifying the dialogue due to the practical considerations of procedural generation, but either way it is constantly odd and sometimes genuinely confusing.  Overall, the game is a wonderful fantasy escape, and I very much recommend it (just know you aren't getting a souped-up version of Unexplored 1; this game is it's own thing).

_childDocuments_.review: Warning: This game behaves as spyware and collects "telemetry" and personally identifying information.  While there is an option to disable this, there's no guarantee that will work.  Worse, the developers turned this on by default to try to spy on as many gamers as possible.  The developers will make the unverifiable claim that this data isn't personally identifying, of course that's BS as they're collecting IPs and all kinds of other information about gamers, when combined with other profiling data this can 100% identify an individual.  They say it's for "QA" purposes but there's no guarantee they're not profiling you or selling your data to third parties as they spy on you.  Should you trust them?  Of course not... if they had any concerns about user safety and privacy, .  There's simply no reason to trust them and gamers should avoid this game because of this unacceptable privacy invasion.Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy is yet another of literally hundreds of console ported (3D rendered) 2D retro top-down brawlers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.This is an unusual entry, however, instead of being a wave survival game or some such, they opted for a lightweight RPG "exploration" experience (but you'll spend a lot of time playing, and hating the badly done combat in the game anyway), then decided not to add any content to the game and decided robotic, samey AI algorithms would be a perfect substitute for doing the job of a game developer.   You're supposed to explore these endless, samey maps all day long and pretend it's fun.The second gamekiller is that, even if this did have any human generated content, it would be unpleasant to play because it's less about exploration and more about really clunky, badly done top down brawling... it's unpolished and unpleasant to play, but there's a recurring theme of the developers here doing everything possible to make a game without doing the basic, standard things.  Although they didn't find time to polish and test the game properly, they did have plenty of time to infest it with spyware.  Game development sure is a mystery. The game features low-polygon "retro" assets with a cel-shading type shader effects instead of doing their job properly and texturing the game assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capabilty to create highly detailed, high poly models and instead use shader effects to disguise that shortcoming under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It's far below the state of the art visuals gamers expect as a result of their decisions.Another defect in the game caused by the console-peasant-centric design is the intolerably bad camera, you're just looking at the whole game from a top down perspective, and this isn't great.  There's no effective mouselook, and control of the viewing angles is deliberately outside of reasonable control from the user.This defect springs from the limitations of inferior console peasant children's toy gamepads, but on PC we don't have this limitation due to KB+M controls... however, the developer deliberately chose to arrogantly foist this handicap onto PC gamers.  Out of spite, or laziness, it's unclear, regardless, once more console peasants and console devs have made gaming worse for everyone.Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.As mentioned, the game features no proper level design or game/story flow/plot, as they opted to try to use samey repetitive procgen algorithms as a substitute for adding such content to the game, to avoid doing the important job of level/map design.  As a result, the game doesn't actually have any content worth mentioning, just endless, boring, repetitive, soulless algorithmically generated sameyness.  Developers must learn that procedural generation is not an acceptable substitute for content.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.The game never really caught on with the millions of gamers on Steam, with a very low peak player count close to launch, and then just a handful of players launching this game every couple of days.  This is undoubtedly caused by factors such as those raised in this review.  It's always helpful with buying decisions to consider how popular and successful the product is, and unfortunately while this did accumulate a few participation trophy reviews, overall, people just aren't using it.Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy has the completely unrealistic cash grab price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  For comparison, the $20 asking price for this game could get you games like "The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt", "Stellaris" or "Deep Rock Galactic". _childDocuments_.review: Very cool game that right now is a diamond in the rough.  Visual design and soundtrack are excellent, and its mainly general bugginess and lack of content depth that hold it back.  However, given that the dev(s) are pushing out weekly updates--- not just hotfixes but actual content patches and gameplay changes as well--- I do recommend this game, with the caveat that you realize you are getting the game at an incomplete state.  TBH, I'm surprised it's not early access.  If you're seriously on the fence about the game, read through the latest announcements (and check the dates!) to see how swiftly it's changing.  I put 10 hours into it months ago, and then decided to wait a while before playing more, and from the announcements I can see that it will be a much more polished experience when I do come back!Secondary note, but this is one of those games where the developers had a very clear vision that they are executing on, and since it's different from what the general gaming audience expects then it will not have universal appeal.  All the design decisions point to the fact that this is a game where exploration is first, and everything else (combat, etc.) is a secondary concern.  The game reminds me more of Outward (another game with a strong and divisive vision) in that you'll either "get it" and this will swiftly become one of your favorites, or you'll play a few hours and be like "not for me".  The game has a demo, which I love to see and I wish were more standardized, so go play that and see if it's your jam.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really fun game. I'm not usually into roguelikes and play a lot of easier rpgs so combat can be difficult for me, but the game allows you to really tailor your play difficulty in a non-judgemental way. You definitely have to learn how to play defensively but each time you die you pick up on the mechanics a bit better. I really like the barter system. In other rpgs like Skyrim it's easy to amass wealth because you can trade your valuable things that weigh a lot for coins which weigh nothing. In this game you have to think about what you carry around because there is no currency, just direct trade.The most frustrating part of the experience so far is movement. Your camera is locked in one angle and wsad moves you north, south, west, and east (relative to the camera). The character will turn in the direction you're walking. The problem is the character will *also* try to turn in the direction of your mouse. It's a fairly smooth system for exploration, but in combat when you're moving a lot it can kinda reduce your accuracy, since your character is fighting which direction to look. There are settings for lock-on but I wish it was just one or the other.This game is definitely worth buying, but if you're unsure, go for the demo. It lets you have a sizable chunk of the game and you can get a feel for it before spending any money.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like Unexplored 2, but it never really gripped me. The constant loading screens hugely hamper the experience and this may be a fatal flaw. I did give it a very fair shake (5+ hours), but this was mostly out of desperate deference to Unexplored 1 (plus maybe hope?). With a game this punishing, the game play simply cannot afford constant interruption. It's like watching a pirated movie that's constantly buffering.It's a crying shame, because Unexplored 1 is one of my favourite games of all time. The original walked a tight-rope between being completely obtuse and unfair, yet also just fast-paced and zany enough that it always kept you coming back for more. This title feels slow and plodding. Each death, I audibly groaned, and after about four attempts I just wasn't sure that I felt much urge to try again. YMMV. I think if you're looking for an exploration game this will scratch the right itch, if you're more looking for a roguelike sort of experience it's probably not the best fit. _childDocuments_.review: Recommended with reservations. This is a good game but it's flawed in potentiallySetting:- Interesting and unique setting with various cultural factions and non-standard fantasy races. I wish more was done to differentiate the factions.- Story is kind of cool, revolves around unraveling traditions and myths, but it's dense and not written in a very compelling way. (It's unclear if anything you read matters or is just fluff or is meant to be important but is effectively fluff.)- Plot is good, combines LOTR-like motivations with temple-raiding investigationsGameplay:- Combat is fun, but it's difficult. I'm still in early game, but I am not sure there's enough depth to entertain for dozens of hours.- Feels like a solo adventure in a well-crafted, lightweight D&D game. You need to carefully choose your weapons and supplies, trade for upgrades to cover your weaknesses, and take calculated risks in overcoming challenge events. You can specialize in certain kinds of challenges, but the downside is that they all use the exact same system and I wish there was some mechanical difference between scaling a cliff and convincing a hostile king to become your friend.- Traveling across the map is great. It's a simple system that offers you meaningful choices at every turn and gives you real incentives to balance travel time against safety by showing you (almost) exactly what hazards you'll encounter with each leg of a journey.- Exploring maps is a mixed bag. The maps are generally small so it doesn't take too long, but you will do a lot of exploring dead-ends, a ton of backtracking, and too much searching for small keys/clues/etc that *may not be there at all*. Because it's possible for an unsolvable puzzle to be generated, every time you get frustrated, you will ask yourself, "Do I do another pass to see if I missed anything, do I risk using the in-game cheat to bypass this possibly broken puzzle, or do I just leave?". The cheat I mentioned is a really good system actually, but I would much much much rather just have confidence that the puzzle in in fact solvable.Bugs:- AI is really buggy in regards to NPC hostility. If you run into bandits and talk them down, be careful not to talk to them again because you will have to complete the same challenge again or they'll attack. Except sometimes they just become normal NPCs, so don't miss out on talking with them. If you successfully intimidate wolves to make them run away, watch out, because instead they might just run in a circle and then attack you.- There are some game-breaking bugs. I lost an entire world because one of my characters died what felt like a bs death (see above), so I alt-f4'd in frustration. Unfortunately the death was already saved, so now that save file is stuck in limbo and when I try to load the world it just freezes. There was also a bug where if you start with a bow you can never unequip it - this might be fixed, but I haven't checked.- Fortunately, this game is still being actively updated and bugs are being fixed right now.

_childDocuments_.review: 56 hours into this game and I still don't know all the mechanics! The game presents a beautiful, interesting world and lets you experiment, yielding the magic of discovery at every turn. Can't seem to finish a dungeon or puzzle? Come back later, armed with knowledge and understanding of not just the Lore, but many new and interesting mechanics and interactions available in the world. The rogue-'long' formula means each death really stings, but each new start is, importantly, in the same world, so it's not a clean slate. Between Wayfarers, time passes. Areas you've previously explored might change. Factions take new claims on the map, based on how well you helped them, or hindered, as the case may be. Unchecked hazardous fauna and bandits also get some love between lives. Couldn't kill the big spider in that cave? Now it's offspring are attacking local farms! I love how much I feel like I have an impact on the world, with favored clans having the weapons and knowledge (thanks to me!) to push out and take new territory, and I often go out of my way to exterminate local vermin. Regrettably, the world is a big place, and you can't be everywhere, so you have to pick your battles wisely.Another call-out feature is the Token system they use to represent skill checks; the sort of thing typically covered by dice rolls. It's possible, even likely, to fail a check and _permanently_ lock a Wayfarer out of a dialogue option, puzzle element, or whole town! Fortunately, the next Wayfarer will have a chance to make amends, as well as getting a head start by capitalizing on all the sweet loot their predecessor was able to stash for them! In addition to the Stash, you'll also be able to find and modify weapons, armor, etc... with the 'Legacy' mod, which returns them to another box near your stash should your Wayfarer die, preserving powerful items for multiple runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start off with the best things about this game. Unexplored 2 is a gorgeous looking game, unique in its style and designs. Beautiful areas with bold color choices. Tons of diversity in environment design. The game is full of cute, lovable, quirky characters. And the game is beautifully scored with great music.This game is hard to get into for new players (and even the ones who played the first one), but that does add to the feeling of accomplishment when you do figure things out. Not much is explained. I recommend using the very intuitive game difficulty settings at the start of a new world. It gives you more freedom to discover this beautiful game and its rules.Unexplored 2 is very different from Unexplored 1, like a big brother. Players of the first game will encounter recognisable monsters, items and other hints to the first game though.As much as I want to love this game, it's not as fun as Unexplored 1 (yet). For me, anyways. I see what Ludomotion was trying to do, but it feels like the game is not quite there yet. The devs created a huge procedurally generated world, but feels like 20% of the world's content is still missing, which makes it a bit empty (BUT! The devs are constantly patching the game, fixing bugs and adding quality of life updates, which makes me excited). I miss those crazy moments from the first game, when you open a door, not knowing what you'll find and you fall off the couch yelling 'Nooooo, trooollll!', cause there's a random troll there and chaos ensues. I miss the surprises. Part 2 seems more predictable, you know what encounters you're going to have when starting your adventure. You spend more time running away from monsters than fighting them.All in all I would still recommend the game, even though it has its shortcomings, it's unique and the creators were willing to make some ambitious choices which almost all worked out.

_childDocuments_.review: The follow up to one of my favorite games of all time DOES NOT play it safe. Where the original used the classic dungeon crawl to showcase a revolutionary procedural generation system, this game uses procedural generation to emulate the sprawling, exploratory gaming of the hex crawl sandbox.  You need to take the Staff Of Yendor to the First Valley and destroy it before Sauron, er, I mean the Empire, take the Staff from you and seal their control over the world, but other than that, you are free to explore the world as you wish in order to discover how to destroy the staff and find the tools you need to survive on your journey. Multiple characters will live and die trying to complete this quest, and your actions, and the Empires growth, will slowly change the world that future wayfarers will need to navigate.  All this happens in a world that  world is completely randomly generated, with reoccurring predesignated set pieces. The world you save is unique, different from any other player. And the world you explore is truly beautiful like if Moebus and MIyazaki were hired to work on an adaptation of Lord of the Rings, but decided to adapt Wizard of Earthsea instead and hoped nobody noticed.  It's one of the most ambitious games I've ever played.  It's also very hard (although there are a lot of tools to generate easier worlds) and doesn't do a lot of hand holding.  It takes about 2 hours of play to really get into it's groove. The combat feels chaotic and dangerous (like real combat) which means it's best avoided when possible and doesn't really contribute to the power fantasy,  The permadeath system - where you loose all of your equipment that isn't specifically charmed to return for the next character when you die,  and the Empire continues it's advance while the next wayfarer is recruited, is brutal befitting a rouge-like.  And because the game is so ambitious in it's use of procedural generation it is, at the time of writing, a bit buggy, although it's clear the developers are taking a very active role in correcting them.  The original game also had hundreds of potential  pre-designed set pieces to interact with in the procedural generated dungeon and you could play every day for weeks without seeing repeated content.  At this time a lot of the quest-lines you interact with show up again and again.  I personally hate dealing with the same road hazards over and over again (damn you roots! Curse you, falling rocks!). Nevertheless, I've never played a game that promises so much game play, and delivers so well on the exhilarating feeling of exploration and discovery. The game is extremely well named, as this is one of the greatest games for creating the thrill of exploration, one of the feelings Video Games are uniquely equipped  deliver as an art form.  Overall, I highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that is monumentally difficult to put down.  I was mostly drawn in by the gorgeous, stark aesthetics and the dungeon-delving gameplay loop, but there's so much intricacy to love.  There's really organic world-building and a lot of gameplay systems that work together in interesting ways, and the way the world is set up, there's always one more point of interest to visit.  Looting is a core aspect of the game, but you have to loot intelligently and plan long, hard trips around obtaining and then depositing loot.  It makes small tasks, like taking a book to a library, feel rewarding, and puts the scale of the world into focus more than any other game I've played.  You may die, but the changes to the world remain.  Even now I struggle to come up with the perfect words for a game that's fundementally unique.This experience is not going to be for everyone.  It's obtuse by design and often hostile to the player.  You will be required to fail many times before even understanding what to do next.  But if you want a game that's granular and emergent--and especially if you like procedural story-driven games like Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress, or Caves of Qud-- please do yourself a favor and check this game out.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game if you are into -procedural generated adventures-being a thoughtful planner-satisfying growth of your charaters-semi high stakes game play (ablative health, "perma" death *its not very unforgiving like other games)-a legacy system where important items can be passed down to later characters, like weapons or relics. Avoid if-if you're looking for an action rpg/challenge combat sim. This game is more of light D&D simulator.-expect to be hand held. This game kind of just drops you into it, with not much prompting on exactly what to do, but not so little as you won't have any idea. You have to be observant and pensive. People trying to blitz through areas or challenges will often get ended, there are many hidden traps and hazards. A lot of time avoiding an encounter is far better than going in swinging. Death isn't the end of the journey but it sure does put a hamper on things.I really like this game, I play a lot of indie games, and a D&D and similar games have been a love since I was a child. This game really hits a lot of the good feelings you get when playing a game like this. Truly wish it was co-op, as that would really seal the deal as an RPG tabletop sim experience. The one thing, the ONLY thing I have to gripe about is the optimization of the game itself. My PC is a pretty decent rig - 3070, all the ramz, good processor and all that jazz. But for some reason this game heats up my GPU FAST! Like really fast. It doesn't get OVERWHELMINGLY HOT (between 50-70 Celsius) but it's like as soon as the game starts it is ramping up the GPU for no particular reason - the requirements are not absurdly taxing on a system, so why the massive heat spike when running the game compared to other (frankly more graphically intensive) games. I especially noticed this while in the menus. Being in a menu would spike my GPU heat a good deal. leaving it paused to get up and get a drink, come back and the GPU was ramping up for no real reason that I could discern. Anti aliasing seems to be disproportionately taxing on the GPU for some reason. I routinely find myself taking a break from the game that I would rather not take because I live in a decently hot place already, and it's summer - I don't want to risk any stealth damage to my PC. Hopefully the game gets optimized a bit more for the future because it really is a charming game that I want to play more of. 8/10 would buy again. probably only going to improve with time as it get's updated.

Most bugs can be resolved by quitting out and reloading. I've had some a bit more severe and save-breaking, but the developers are responsive to bug reports and the process to do so is straightforward.Despite the bugs, I keep playing it. It's just a delight. Even if I'm more familiar with some of the larger structure and system of the game now, it still finds ways to surprise, and keeps pulling me forward.
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Only look at recent reviews because devs have changed this game drastically since release! My play time reflects the joy of a game that no longer exists. I can no longer recommend this game. The most recent update changed the game to force players to play the way the devs intended for it to be played. It used to be that you could make a character and try to accomplish as many quests and as much as possible before you died and had to make a new character to continue your progress. Now, you ask? Now your character is automatically retired after one quest and forced to make anew one meaning onwards players must make dozens of characters to finish the game.I felt the previous iteration was challenging but gave players a lot of freedom to explore, learn the lore, make a checklist of quests, and try to do as much before (inevitably) dying and making a new character to continue the legacy, It was harsh, but players had autonomy to do things their way. Now, there continues to be so many changes that have radically overhauled the game. I disagree with the direction the devs are going and am a little resentful/disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played a lot yet on the full release  yet (I did the demo though), but this is what I was looking for.This game is a real adventure. You will encounter foes and friends, find amazing artifacts, climb high mountains , explore dark and dangerous caves, discover mysterious ruins and so much more.Wanna negociate with that big root thing? Why not. Wanna steal this guy's turnips? Face the consequences (I felt so guilty afterward...). Its your adventure, your choices. And it feels great.Combat is only an option, as are negociating or sneaking, and it is all about exploration and dealing with situations.The world building, general ambiance and procedural generation are also top notch.If you are not expecting a classic combat only roguelite, but instead a thoughtful journey and an amazing world to explore, you'll enjoy it a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: So, my experience with the game so far:I played the tutorialThen I played the prologue with the questline to visit the first villageI explored the village, bought some goodies, chatted with NPCs, brought A LOT OF questsI gloriously started my journey saying good bye to the good folks in the village, looking forward to my great and lengthy adventureThen, literally as I exit the village, I encountered 3 bandits on the road. I dispatched 2 of them. But the last one killed me. And that's it, end of the story :D======The bottom line is: I love this game, its randomness and its freshness everytime you start a new journey. This might be the true gem among the roguelikes :)
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: It's still buggy as hell, but oh my do I love it. It's intended as a resource-management obsessive-compulsive discovery simulator with neat Unexplored1-like puzzles. Some say mechanics doesn't work for them (they kinda don't, but it's not the design fault: bugs are not fair), but hey: now it's not about combat or story (yep.), currently it's a story generator.Last run I had my bird sold all of their possessings in favor of gaining health potions and a neat sword, and raided the Garden of Yendor for the sake of further generations. It survived. It's just, the game bugged and deleted the Raaf Disc (quest stuff) from the world save completely, and now my Wayfarers have to figure out how to pass the main quest without it, stealing stuff from unexpecting travellers with bad AI (I'd call 'em "unobnservant")), travelling w/o boots and writing bug reports.Bugs are magic. Explore 'em, 'till they Unexplore 'emselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy

_childDocuments_.review:
Unexplored 2: The Wayfarer's Legacy is a roguelite action-RPG and prodigious sequel to the critically acclaimed indie gem, Unexplored. Leave the Dungeon of Doom behind and venture into a vast, wondrous world as you embark on a heroic quest to destroy the mysterious Staff of Yendor.

Explore beautiful landscapes and discover hidden marvels. Encounter magical creatures and dangerous foes. Make brave choices and put your faith in good fortune. name: Helheim Hassle
detailed_description: Helheim Hassle is a narrative adventure game that is as much about friendship as it is about body parts. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ From the same universe (and set on the same Tuesday in fact) as previous hit Manual Samuel, comes this macabre adventure where you play as Bjørn, a pacifist Viking who hates the idea of dying and going to Valhalla… who then ends up dying and getting taken to Valhalla. When Bjørn is resurrected to assist with a task for the mysterious Pesto, he sees a way to negotiate his way out. Using Bjørn’s undying corpse with its ability to detach and combine limbs at will, players must solve challenging puzzles and navigate tricky levels in order to retrieve a certain magical item... In return, Pesto will try to grant Bjørn a permanent residence in Helheim - what a hassle! ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ 14 levels 90+ puzzles 80+ interactable characters 3,700 lines of spoken dialogue performed by 24 professional actors ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ What people are saying: 'Helheim Hassle is a colourful puzzle-platformer that consistently tickles ribs while you’re tossing around its protagonist’s limbs.' - IGN 'Helheim Hassle is a phenomenal adventure game and a creative puzzle platformer.' - The Escapist Magazine '...Helheim Hassle is a consistently fun, creative blend of narrative adventure and puzzle-platformer with an amusing spin on Norse mythology.' - Adventure Gamers '«Helheim Hassle» is the funniest norwegian game ever. And additionally it's a very good adventure game.' - NRK 'Simply put, Helheim Hassle is one of the best puzzle adventures I’ve ever played.' - Total Gaming Addicts

short_description: Helheim Hassle is a narrative adventure game with puzzle platforming elements. Play as Bjørn, a pacifist Viking that can detach and combine limbs at will to solve challenging puzzles and get out of uncomfortable situations involving desperate Norse Gods, Goblins, Dragons, and angry skeletons.

_childDocuments_.review: The creators of Manuel Samuel is back with another game! And just with how Manuel Samuel was a unique adventure will humor surrounding Samuel’s unfortunate situation, so is Helheim Hassle. And fun fact, Helheim Hassle and Manuel Samuel takes place in the same universe and even on the same day.Helheim Hassle brings us to a young teenage Viking named Bjorn Hammerparty who isn’t like his Viking brethren. Unlike everyone else, he is a pacifist. He doesn’t want to go out fighting so he makes sure he doesn’t get into a situation where he has to and he sure doesn’t want to go to Valhalla. However, during a battle that is sure to wipe out his whole village, Bjorn gets into a fatal accident while he was running to his hideout. The sketchy bridge he was crossing may have made him fall straight onto a bear. Once Bjorn comes to, he’s a ghost and his body is limbless. Before moving on, Bjorn attaches his limbs back on his body and talks to Modgunn to be granted passage into Helheim. However, his cowardly fall to his death was counted as him heroically killing a bear without a weapon and is brought into Valhalla by the Allfather.And that’s where Bjorn stayed for centuries. That is until Pesto comes across his body and resurrects him since Pesto can’t read Old Norse to get through the door to Helheim. It doesn’t take that long for them to find out that Bjorn’s limbs can detach from his body, make a deal with Pesto so Bjorn can enter and hopefully stay in Helheim, and find out that Helheim is getting a bit of a renovation. That renovation being a bunch of puzzles being installed along the road to Helheim that is strangely perfect for Bjorn’s situation. Though, Bjorn’s absence in Valhalla doesn’t go unnoticed. Mostly because the Allfather is very into shooters and Bjorn is his team’s healer. Well, this sure will be a hassle! A Helheim Hassle (haha, okay I’ll see myself out).So to get all the way to Helheim and ask Hel if Bjorn can stay, you’ll need to use Bjorn’s new ability to use. At first, you’re only able to detach one or two limbs, along with the puzzles starting out easy, to get used to how each limb controls and so you’re already prepped to think about how you’ll get your limbs up there rather than your whole body. As you progress, more are unlocked until you can detach and move every limb. Each limb have their own way of moving, how it’ll affect the main body, and how it’ll affect the movement of a group of joined limbs. Your arms are great for climbing, legs are great for running and jumping, and a head, well, is just a heavy blob that weighs your body down. When you’re combining limbs, or detaching them, you’ll need to think about these aspects. If you need to jump high and climb, for example, you’ll need to combine a leg and an arm.The puzzles here mainly revolve around this unique mechanic as you need to maneuver your body parts to the needed pressure points to open doors so you can take your whole body through. There are also situations where you need your head or your arm as you need to read or grab something as part of the puzzle. Finding those gaps that your limbs can squeeze through, or figuring out what limbs you need to send, so the pressure points can be pressed. Throwing your limbs around in cases where it’s just too high for you to jump to. Or even figuring out the sequence you need to send out your limbs to so you can open up an opportunity so you can get the other limbs there or to release them in cases where they’re trapped. Later on, you’ll be tasked with bringing specific limbs to pressure points, making it harder as a result. There are also a couple puzzles that emphasis speed, but they are few and far between.I also can’t write a review and not mention the immense amount of extra content. If you’re just going straight from beginning to end, just doing the puzzles and quests you need to do to continue, you’re pretty much missing most of the game. Even if you are doing some extra things along the way, you’re still missing a lot. There are a lot of optional puzzles that you can find, optional notes scattered around, berry bushes hidden in places you can either easily reach or barely reach, side quests galore, races, and a whole convention where you can fund and play game parodies. Though, it’s important to not get hold up if you’re stuck on a particular side quest. Doing the optional puzzles will often lead you to chests with gold or soul coins that you can spend and berries can be made into smoothies so you can gain abilities to help you. Luckily, the map does let you see if you got everything in an area. There are also one time things that you can only do once so you’ll need to at least play twice if you’re planning to get every achievement.Also for anyone that’s going to pick this up, you do get notified of a point of no return, but it’s only until you finish ending sequence. You’re brought back so you can get anything you missed once you complete the game, so no need to worry.The humor will, of course, be hit or miss. Even more so than the humor in Manual Samuel. Here, the humor is more around the Allfather being an announcer tryhard dude, Pesto mispronouncing everything (and I swear it’s on purpose) and cringing at everything, breaking the fourth wall to make fun of the game itself, and putting humor with Bjorn’s situation. Most of the humor did hit for me, with some even growing on me as I progressed through, but Pesto never grew on me.Helheim Hassle may have went with a different style of humor that is kind of annoying, but the game itself is solid. When I went into the game, I just expected a straightforward game akin to Manuel Samuel, but instead we get a game filled with a bunch of stuff to do and explore. The puzzles are well designed, this unique mechanic works pretty well with how it was implemented, I adored most of the characters (not you Pesto) and the art style is great as always. It may also help to know that you don’t necessarily need to play Manuel Samuel before this one as there are only a few references to loosely connect the two games. If you loved Manual Samuel and/or love puzzle platformers, Helheim Hassle is definitely worth it. I really hope Perfectly Paranormal will come back with another title.
