_childDocuments_.review: I love time loop stories. Nearly every time loop movie I've ever seen has been hugely entertaining. This game seems like it exists just to prove that time loop stories in fact, can be terrible. This game has nothing going for it. It's a bad story, bad game play, bad voice acting (even though they hired very talented film actors-- the bad acting clearly is not their fault), and one of the worse, nonsensical plot twists ever conceived.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: What initially swayed me to buy this game was the creative top-down 3d art style and the name Twelve Minutes excellently capturing the idea of the gameplay and what the game's plot entails. The story is good but confusing having many obvious plot holes, the voice acting feels natural, and the animations and art are solid. Without a guide, I definitely would not have figured out the entire story let alone get every achievement and ending by myself, but it was fun to play through the game and discover many of the endings on my own. Resetting each time the loop ends can be annoying, but at the same time, that's kinda what the game is meant to be and feel like. The ending of the game is super ambiguous to the point where there really is no correct way to view the story of the game. Maybe too confusing for its own good. I've read so many different theories trying to piece together the ending and close all the plot holes. I'd like to believe that there is a theory that encompasses everything and makes sense and that the writers didn't just take the time-loop and make it a gimmick with a forced twist. Regardless, I will admit it has been fun reading through forums and posts of other peoples theories.

_childDocuments_.review: Starts good but a lot of stuff makes no sense, and it is not obvious when the looping ends / what is the final objective. I would suppose the "best scenario" would be to somehow get rid of antagonist without being the obvious murderer -- but that appears impossible. Gets pretty frustrating and one can get easily blocked by having no idea how to progress. I haven't finished and I don't think I want to. I suppose that replicates the main character's change in state of mind over the repetitions. So I suppose it is a faithful experience in that sense (you get the same frustration as the main char would get) -- but that is not a very good experience.Regarding the plot holes. I won't go into detail (no spoilers), but main antagonist is behaving inconsistently -- there appear to be some safeguards in the game to "make him catch you", even if it were extremely illogical for him to search for you there (e.g. he has searched for you in the same place before, even though he doesn't even know that someone hidden is in the room). Or that sometimes he needs light to see and sometimes he does not. Or other kinds of plot armor

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of a time loop adventure game is brilliant. Unfortunately, it misses the mark in execution. The game feels short and long at the same time. Moving animations are incredibly slow, conversations cannot be skipped as a whole, and some scripted animations cannot be skipped at all. This gets frustrating very, very quickly. If I subtract the amount I had to wait impatiently for the previously mentioned actions, not much gameplay time is left. That's why the game also feels short. I finished few endings in 5 hours. The story is good, but too much over the top that I had a hard time believe it - not counting the loop itself, of course. Overall I did enjoy the game, but I have to take into account the price. It is way overpriced for 21€. I suspect that a lot of money was spent on voice actors. They're great, no arguing there, but the gameplay should be the top priority. That's why I cannot currently recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Elsinore  2-7 hrs depending on how much you experiment and how many endings and achievements you are willing to pursue. You have twelve minutes to get things right... or you have to do it all over again, and do it all over again you will, the game is at it´s best when it encourages you to experiment with different approaches and gives you new information and clues based on what you did, and it´s as it´s worst when you have it ALL figured out but forgot to grab a picture in the fridge, that is this game is VERY arbitrary in what the correct solutions are, and finding them on your own feels great, but sometimes you HAVE figured it out, you DO have all the pieces but you cannot advance because the game requires something very specific of you. The story is cool, I enjoyed it, but don´t expect a satisfying ending. + Time looping that requires constant experimentation + Cool story with an all-out star cast as voice actors+ Cool presentation (not mind blowing but if you like the screenshots you will like it):- VERY limited controls and interaction (This is just a point & click adventure game at the end of the day)- Some solutions are very specific or require a very specific item or have triggered a specific conversation before starting the event, something that you didn´t had any clue about needing to do at the time and have no way of solving without starting another loop- Game resets your progress after some endings, granted, once you know the answers you can get back to the last parts of the game extremely quickly, but that repetition is completely unnecessary and only artificially extends the already lackluster game duration, and makes a game that by definition is all about repetition, even more repetitive- VERY short game, this feels kind of like an interactive movie, only this is REALLY interactive and let´s you do a lot of random stuff, even if the path forward story-wise is only one

_childDocuments_.review: The writing for the story of this game is the worst I have ever endured. I am not even kidding - this is literally the concept. it is stupid. Literally stupid. And, as a capper, the gameplay is dead boring, repetitive, and arbitrary. You will not solve this ridiculous story without using a guide to cheat to the ending. Zero reason, zero intelligence, zero fun. I have played worse games, but only in the 80's, and from a bargain bin. Run, don't walk, from this impossibly dumb piece of deeply awful writing. You play an amnesiac accidental father murderer who accidentally married his own sister after accidentally making her think she is the murderer and the only way not to die is to be accidentally hypnotised by your (still alive) mutual father in a time previous to the story so you forget loving her. Seriously. That is the story. You have been warned. I am trying to get a refund right now.

_childDocuments_.review: When Green Goblin come after your wife who is Rey Skywalker inhabiting what appears to be a "Pixar Mom" in-game model, you know you have to get to the bottom of this as a young Professor X. This clearly has Disney written all over it.TL;DR (Serious) - Pretty fun game and definitely worth playing, but price is real steep so "wait for sale" for sure. Actual detailed explanation below:-  For a short game I think the writing is alright. I do, however, feel like the story could have been longer or expand on various things to give more gameplay for players while enriching the story even more. I will elaborate more but it may contain super minor spoiler, so I will put a "block" around it and you can just skip that part**********Potential Spoiler Warning for this section**********It may break the "12 minutes" mark which is the title, but disappointingly they never explain why this "Groundhog day" happened or why it is "12 minutes" to be exact writing wise. So I am going to assume it is strictly for gameplay reason. **********Potential Spoiler Warning end (You can continue below safely)**********-  The game offer small degree of replay value as it has multiple endings. So once you beat the game once and get the 1 ending, you can replay again to try to shoot for another ending. There is no manual save, so you cant save scrum and try to just get all endings by loading at the loop that will lead to the finale. Once you get the ending, you basically have to just start over. Similarly, if you messed up something you best bet is to just trigger the loop reset. Aside from the looping mechanic, the way to handle information can be a pro or a con, depending on who you are - the game offer no way to write down information you come across.. so anything trial and error or potential intel you best write it on a notepad or something outside of the game. -  It exists.-  It seems weird I put the 2 together in one category, but please bear with me. This is honestly the biggest "con" for this game. The scale/scope of this game is nowhere NEAR the price it is trying to charge you for. I feel like you are paying for these famous actors/actress's voice.. and honestly they arent even that impressive... I would rather spent this same amount for better or amazing voice acting from a proper voice actors and actress instead, and with the dev help promote these talents. If any game can make the most out of voice acting, is these narrative driven games where a lot of "feels" comes from the conversations beside in-game discoveries.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes is a top-down point-and-click game that plays like an interactive movie. As advertised, the main premise of the story is that you're a man who's being forced to live through a sickening but sometimes endearing purgatorial-esque time loop wherein a cop comes to the door of the apartment that you and your wife live in and accuses her of murdering somebody; that somebody being her biological father. As you go along with the narrative, you begin to learn more about your wife's past, the "cop"'s background, and yourself. It initially escalates from a murder mystery thriller to something much darker than you would be able to predict or imagine. There are themes of an affair, hypnotization, incest, family, & plenty of symbolism indicating these things all around you, which are manifested in the paintings and objects around your living space. All of this reminds me a lot of both simulation theory and the Sims, and sometimes it feels like the husband knows he's in a video game.Even though the playstyle would seem as if it would be repetitive, it rarely feels that way. There are always new things to learn about your situation by exploring your environment, along with the items and decorations placed in and around it. Throughout my playthrough, I only encountered 2 to 3 glitches where I'd both clip through my wife and the blood on the ground, my wife had repeated herself like a broken robot, and I had gotten scene locked, but it wasn't detrimental to my view of the game in any way, and I quickly forgot about these things. No matter how biased we are in our opinions towards things, nothing is ever absolutely perfect; and imperfections show sincerity. Only one of these bugs was somewhat game-breaking.In other news, I think the sound design of the game is masterfully done. The scores can induce anxiety, appreciation, and many other emotions. I really recommend turning on spatial sound to hear how realistically the thunder, rain, and lightning reverberate against the panes of your windows. The graphics are practically perfect except for the fluidity behavior of the liquid substances in-game, such as blood and water, and clearly, you don't just clip through people in real life. I think it appears a lot like whatever engine the Sims 6 would be advertised with. The game does get confusing in its attempts to guide you through the story without holding your hand, along with other aspects like the father and the cop sharing the same voice actor. It can be fairly frustrating to figure out what your objective is without looking up a walkthrough, which I had to do at some points, especially with attaining multiple endings. Some actions you're able to carry out make you believe that you'd get a trophy for it, but overall the achievements are quite convoluted and you'd likely need outside help to 100% Twelve Minutes. Regardless, I still feel like the first half of the story is very captivating until the second twist, and then it becomes anticlimactic. (Spoilers ahead.)(Spoiler ending, continue here!)Anyways, even though I had a few small qualms with the game, I wholeheartedly recommend it. I had waited for this game to come out for a long time, and I'm not unimpressed at all with my experience. The game can siphon you in for about a few hours or more if you want to get every achievement, but I loved playing it the entire time. I don't really understand or agree with the bad reviews at all, and I believe this game is worthy of anybody's playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: Infuriatingly repetitive. Fun for the first 2 hours or so when you're still experimenting with all the things you can do, quickly becomes mind numbingly dull when you realize that the only way to progress is to do the same highly specific sequence of events over and over and over with the most minor of variations until you gleam a tiny bit of new information for you to do the whole thing over again with.Especially maddening towards the end when it feels like you've figured everything out and the game should be over now, but it still makes you do the loop countless times until you find the right order of conversation options to choose that doesn't result in the game arbitrarily deciding you messed up in some unknowable way.Also your wife's a ♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: Intriguing - would be a good way to describe this game.It has it's flaws, and I wouldn't say it's a masterpiece, but I can say for a fact that I was pretty excited to continue playing it once I started, even though I had to repeat loops over, and over, and over, and over...Not now....and over... and over...and over again. I think it fails a liiittle bit at trying to be self aware and getting more complex than it is, but honestly that might be my fault for not understanding it completely yet, plus once you get a little far in talking to some insect person, the role of this person and how things unroll from there are pretty hard to believe.I do however know a game that does the same premise beautifully, and was also published by Annapurna: Outer Wilds. In conclusion, I would recommend this game if you are up to try something new and enjoy cracking your head a bit to figure out your way through a story.

_childDocuments_.review: Man I sure do love time loop games where I have to wait ten minutes to slightly progress the story only to learn a tiny bit of information so that the main character can ask about it in the next loop... like five times in a row...Game has great visuals and good voice acting, but there are barely any interesting red herrings that you'd expect from a time loop game and instead you just flounder around knowing how to complete the game yet not knowing what specific minor actions you have to do to finish it (dude just show him the damn photograph why do you just stand there as your wife gets beat up).
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed the game.Let me get the bad out of the way first:-Sometimes conversations are strung together in a way that doesn't make sense. I noticed some flaws in the logic of conversations where I was able to say something to Her that I hadn't actually previously learned or known.-Controls can be a little wonky.-It's too short to justify the price tag. I know we get to experience these huge behemoths of the cinematic world as voice actors, but the length simply doesn't justify the price.Now the good:-The story is quite gruesome and interesting. I felt genuinely interested in the characters and the development of new information. Despite the aforementioned gripe about strung conversations, I feel that generally speaking, they are quite well put together and are generally believable interactions. I mean c'mon, it's a time loop. He could figure out how to make his own wife believe him on something given several iterations.-The voice acting is obviously phenomenal. In some ways it was a sort of buzzword cast of huge actors, but at the same time, it was well executed enough to the extent that it doesn't feel like a cash grab.-The mechanics are sometimes hilariously interesting. The interactions I was able to perform with certain items was, at times, shocking. You will know what I mean.Overall I give it a solid 8/10.

_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Game started off as a fun mystery, but eventually became too repetitive. _childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: In Twelve Minutes you work throught a repeating night to discover a dark secret. The game features multiple endings, with most of them being quite vague, leaving the player in thought about not only what the ending meant, but what the story as a whole and certain details about it and the apartment you're stuck in mean as well. Overall, Twelve Minutes is a good mystery for anyone interested to figure out.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: So overall, the game is fun, for the first hour. The whole idea is repetition, doing the same thing over and over but in order to achieve a different result. It is in its own right, a puzzle game. The exception here is that this puzzle becomes so tedious that the game loses its flair not long after starting. Restarting and not knowing how to progress is part of the premise of the game but it is what makes the game more frustrating than fun. To add on, the twists in the game are not rewarding enough to justify the time played to reach the end result. To add on to the pile of negativity, the entire game only has one scenario. That, to me, makes it absolutely not worth $25. $25 for a few hours of game play and absolutely ZERO replay ability SHOULD keep you from buying this game. Do not waste your time or money on this game as I painstakingly did.

_childDocuments_.review: This will contain SOME story elements, but nothing you haven't seen in the trailers.Have you ever watched "The Edge of Tomorrow"? It's a movie adaptation of a story in which the main character, after an encounter with an alien threat, becomes pretty much immortal. Every time he dies, he returns to some point in time before it all went down and, with the acquired knowledge of the last attempt, tries to move forward bit by bit.The movie (which is really good btw, worth a watch) does an amazing job in portraying just how many loops the protagonist has been through as the story progresses. You don't actually sit there and watch hours and hours of loops, each one being slightly different. You see the most important bits, but everything else is portrayed in how this endless cycle of life and brutal death almost breaks him. It's almost as if he goes through the stages of grief, and in the end he's a different person. All of the dying, the killing, over and over again, it changes him.This game is very similar, but instead of a death loop, it's simply a time loop. Whether you die or not, 12 minutes is all you get (or 10, depending on how the story goes). The issue, however, is that this totally shouldn't be a game. Having to sit through literally hours and hours of the same thing over and over again only to make some tiny bit of progress by pure chance which then prompts you to go through it all yet again is just not fun.Not only that, but the protagonist literally sees his wife getting murdered multiple times. She gets kicked, punched, shot in the head while screaming. He gets killed himself multiple times. His behavior barely changes, he remains the same person and reacts the same way through the entire game until a really odd revelation breaks things.I'm usually good at brainstorming SOME workaround to issues I find in games, specially when they are related to gameplay or mechanics. I just can't do that with this one. This is just not something you can fix in a game unless you want to take away the controller from the player and do a bunch of cutscenes.You also end up having to write so much for the game to feel reactive to your choices, and often these studios just don't have the budget for thousands upon thousands of voice lines, specially when they hire the likes of Daisy Ridley or Willem Dafoe. I don't know, I guess I don't recommend this if you despise back tracking in games, going over the same place or event over and over again without much progress being made.What a shame.

That is, until I broke the loop by saying I love her and she said "lol 1252 loops have passed and now you come with this" then left me and moved half across the planet. Then I thought to myself, damn, maybe I should have tried saying "I love you" before we reached the 1252nd loop. Maybe her response would've been different and I would have gotten the good ending.Then I realized real life doesn't have a reload last save button. Anyone knows when that's getting patched in?

_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first review I've ever actually written for a steam game, and so that should mean something when I say that this game is not great.Don't get me wrong. The voice acting is brilliant. The sound design and soundtrack are beautiful. But the game is clunky, characters clip all over the place, and you really don't have as much freedom as you'd think you do. Whilst I did enjoy the story, somewhat, I don't think this game has been worth the wait at all. It's repetitive, which granted, is pretty much the premise of the game, but each cycle there is nothing new. Not once you've completed a specific cycle once already and then have to complete it another 30+ times to get where you need to be. It's a shame, because I had such high hopes for this game. I was so excited for it. The premise, the voice actors, the style of it. Everything seemed like this game was going to be incredible. Unfortunately, it was too good to be true.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy a good story and good storytelling... Well, this game is not for you, then. There are major plot holes, very implausible character arcs and the more details of the story you discover, the less sense it makes. Seriously, I don't buy it. And not in a "lol, time loops aren't a thing in real life, I don't buy it" kind of way, but in a "I can't believe the story could even get more stupid, nothing of this fits together" kind of way. Seriously, my mind felt insulted after playing it through.So no, I personally don't recommend it. I am in fact a little angry I spend money on that. And yes, I played past the credits, hoping for something to make sense, but my point still stands.What I liked about the game was the unique perspective, the good voice acting and the limited items to interact with. This way the puzzles don't get too complex. The complexity of the game comes with all the different possibilities to do the wrong thing at the wrong time so the time loop gets messed up and you don't get the desired outcome. Can be a little frustrating, depending on your patience. I think it can be a nice game for people who are here for the puzzles and not for the story, who are patient and don't play a game more than once.

_childDocuments_.review: A superbly interesting concept and neat story, ruined by a mind-bogglingly awful (as in, stupid, not believable, and badly-written) twist. There's a solid foundation here, and unlocking new dialogue options is very rewarding as you make progress, but you often get caught on really trivial details only for the rest to be locked behind something pointless.To be clear, this isn't a *bad* game, it's just a very mediocre one. But at $25, I can't even come close to recommending it. It's worth maybe... 5? 10, tops. Wait for it to go on sale and then maybe try it. Keep your expectations low though- the plot becomes trite at best.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I'm usually willing to ignore problems a game has if the game is ambitious. Twelve Minutes is certainly ambitious with its Groundhog Day conceit, but the problems make it impossible for me to recommend this game. There's been a lot made of the lack of content warnings on the game. Content warnings are fine as long as they are voluntary. (I find they can sometimes spoil key moments and prefer not to look at them.) However, I also see some criticism of particular characters being bad people and I've never understood the need to have nothing but kind relatable characters in my media consumption. I think the bad things some characters do make sense given the characters.What I do have a problem with is bad animations, awkward voice acting (especially when you have three competent actors), and bad writing. I blame the third for the game seeming to want to have the ending be a crescendo of surprise and revelation but the ending somehow straddles being both disappointingly absurd and boringly unsurprising. I don't mind a short game, but at this price, with all the aforementioned problems, I think, if you really want to play it, wait for it to be at a deep discount.

_childDocuments_.review: As my night with  draws to a close, I wonder only how I managed to so royally waste money and time on this game, conned by its initial intrigue but let down minute after minute with its tedious gameplay and superfluous ending. I simply can't believe, how bad this game is. I sit here in disbelief that anyone at the studio actually played the game they were making, and thought it made even an ounce of sense. Part of why it lacks so much cohesion is that, in a genre of puzzle mystery game based upon logical precedence and skills of deduction, it has a story so overly convoluted that it angers me to think about. The game presents with a story of man and wife, and their happy evening destroyed by the most disagreeable armed robber in all of New York City. So what do you immediately think? How do I stop this man killing me over and over and over and over again? A scene that played out a painstaking amount of times because of the inability to skip it, mind you. You think.... well, I should arm myself with a knife! Nope. Well... I should hide! Nope. Well... I should call the authorities! Good luck with that. But wait... what about... mixing sleeping pills, drugging my wife, waiting for her to sleep, turning the light switch off and on, then hiding while we wait for the intruder to turn the light back on? Resounding ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ success! He's now unconscious on the floor so I can finally call his daughter and chat about movies!It makes so little sense that it actually made me laugh at points, the experience I can compare it to most closely is that of throwing darts while blindfolded. One string of events somehow leads to another, and what makes it worse, is that when you get this preposterous combination of actions even slightly wrong, you have to restart all over again. At the end of this game, I had given up, having already figured out the terrible shock ending that awaited me about an hour beforehand. Literal primary school grade writing. From one thing to another, you cannot figure out what to do. It lacks direction and purpose in almost every way. The story doesn't even end when you beat the intruder, and it gives almost no pointers as to how this story could even be resolved. You just bash your head against the wall until a spoon becomes a vicious weapon or a babies's apron has the answers. Not to mention the jankiness, multiple loops retried because dialogue wouldn't activate until my pretty little character stood in the pixel perfect spot to announce his discontent. For nearly four hours, I was confused, angered and upset that I had to start my year with such a bad game. It's ambitious for sure, in that it disappointed me more than I ever thought possible.I have an aim this year to play as many Annapurna titles as possible, because multiple titles from their catalogue were groundbreaking and touching in ways I haven't seen in this medium before. But I'm sorry to say this isn't one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: This game starts of with an air of intrigue and cinematic flair. When I first booted it up, it felt like David Lynch, Wes Anderson, Michael Giacchino and Alfred Hitchcock booked one of those hidden rooms behind the bookshelf in a mansion in the middle of nowhere, sat around a table smoking their cigars and drinking well aged whiskey when they came up with the concept and presentation of this game. I can positively say that, the charm doesn't last for very long. Within the first twelve minutes you will experience two maybe 3 time loops and begin to see the frustrating flaws that lie at the core of this game. With having to repeat every action almost mechanically and without many options to get from point A to point B, you'll be stuck spending the same repetitive evening putting together the most tedious trial and error puzzle in the same order. This, more often than not will only lead to failure and have you start over just to follow the same steps until you hope you've done something right. Now, to those who feel like the breadcrumbs you get at the end of every loop help the game stay coherent in it's element, I say, good for you because you definitely got more enjoyment out of something that i didn't.Voice Actors aside, the voice acting itself just feels like robotic and mechanical. The sheer hilarity that ensued when I'd click on the "COP" when I was tied down went a little something like. And I paraphrase."Listen... uh, sir""Shut your mouth.""Uh... oh, uh heh heh nevermind heh"It's like Vaas Montenegro once said, "Instanity is doing the same f***ing thing, over and over and over again, expecting ♥♥♥♥ to change. That. Is. Crazy." And this game, even with competent presentation and somewhat satisfying mystery and intrigue, felt frustrating and honestly, after 3 hours, quite boring. There's a really niche set of people who will enjoy this game and I feel like they should really celebrate what makes it great. Unfortunately, that's not how I felt.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes was definitely a good experience for me. I loved the atmosphere and the gameplay throughout the game. The 9 hours I spent with it felt like an intensive, immersive movie.Some stuff I didn't like. The second half wasn't as engaging as the first half, and while in the beginning the choices felt endless, the ending felt somewhat forced: the items got boring, the gameplay was a bit repetitive, and the actions needed to get in the end were very specific. I had to Google instructions to get past one of the loops, which sucked.But yeah all-in-all, one of the better interactive movie-type games I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn. I was not expecting to enjoy this game as much as I did... Bought with a main seller of Willem Dafoe, stayed for the story. While nothing crazy unique or new, the performances really sell it, that's what happens when you get incredible actors playing these roles. I particularly liked James McAvoy's performance so props to him, reminds me a little of his performance in split.Enough on that though, what really got me hooked was how insanely invested I became in the main characters relationship. I got really hooked. Maybe I saw this guy trying to make everything work whilst experiencing the day over and over again and damn did I want to help him. I wanted everything to work out. And the more invested I got, the more twists came my way the further into the game I got. And those twists really had an impact on me since I was so invested at this point.I would really recommend playing this game, not just for the acting, but it's got a unique visual style with a really investing story, and imo worth a pick up at sale price.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting games that sours after the first half. Don't buy it unless you like the premise and it's on sale. I'm not going to bother going spoiler free so don't read beyond this if you want to play the game.* ******Spoilers about to start.** * * Ok. First half of the game is interesting. Going in with no idea what the game was about was very rewarding at first - You slowly find out the rules of the timeloop and that you can change/short circuit conversations with your wife to get more info. There a bunch of Interesting mechanics when interacting different objects, sometimes together(IE- watering the plant) - it would have been nice to have a short tutorial on things, like watering the plant to help demonstrate that something is up in the time loop. Another nice touch would have been the husband commenting that something has changed in each loop - the posters, the plant or whatever. But nope - no such luck. As the second or thirdt timeloop concludes, the game holds promise as a potential "who dunnit" but with a payoff that is coming closer and closer. You find out your wife is a killer! And she did it! She even admits it in a few different ways in a loop! Then, you push against the hitman/cop and find out wait! She didn't! And that's the high water mark of the game right there. If Annapurna rolled credits right there, it's be a short but sweet game. Yeah - the audio being a bit weird in spots, I give it a bit of a pass as the production of this game took place during 2020/2021 COVID - the teams did the best to get the talent to produce given the circumstances. The interactions were frustrating at times. For example, in the first loop I knocked the cop out, I went to check him but, right after I clicked on him, he woke up and killed me. Plenty of these little frustrating moment litter each step of the plot but ultimately didn't ruin anything. But, they can't help themselves. No - this can't be a weird but fun little game. It's got to be another "let's give you a psychology study in trauma and memory repression - is your narrator reliable? is this real?" schtick worthy of an Abrams plot. The game, being straightforward in it's mechanics up until now, decides to screw it up and make you do a nearly impossible to find interaction with the cop and the onesie. Keep in mind any other time you tried to do something with him, you get killed or ignored. The game even seemingly has a bug when you try to show the cop the photo of your wife that he ignores you despite telling his daughter he would listen.So of COURSE you confront him with the onesie in that 2-3 seconds after a specific setup in a timeloop. So it drags on with unnecessary twists and turns, undoing all of the build up and trying to do some weird riff on "The Shining" or David Lynchesque plot. But with none of the investment from the beginning to underpin the psychology thriller aspects - no where during a timeloop does your narrator start to question if anything is real or show introspection in a way that might lead us to question what is happening from the sandbox point of view. The result, sadly, makes me bin the game at only a few accomplishments, not really caring to find out what else the game holds.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this while it was on sale. While I do recommend this game, I recommend it only when it is on sale.The good: The general idea of time looping and solving a mystery is very appealing and mostly executed well. The interactions with props in the world was well implemented (minus one important aspect explained later). The voice acting is incredible. The graphics are aesthetic and feel very well put together as the style is cohesive and moody. Dialog overall doesn't have any glaring bugs or issues that I noticed. For specific sections I was completely engrossed by the results of my actions. There are multiple "endings" some of which don't end to credits completely but keep the loop going which was really neat. What is also awesome is that you and a friend can play with totally different loops and decisions and eventually end up at the same conclusion over time in a way that feels natural.The bad: I felt like I was grinding the same dialog over and over and over again with one change to hope it was the correct change for me to progress only to find out 30 mins later that I had actually done the correct order of actions. However I needed one super tiny / hidden event to occur before it would do what I expected. Some items and interactions with people didn't do anything at all when it should have warranted some kind of response. Getting the supporting characters to draw dialog connections from items was not just a struggle at times, but also tedious and frustrating. When I did find an answer (never searched online for any tips), it was fairly disappointing in the result only to realize I need to redo the full 10 min loop over and over and over and over and over. It feels like something interesting unveils itself only once every 30 mins on average out of sheer trial and error. Even then, the major twist at the end was somewhat disappointing to me. I feel a bit conflicted about the ending because it wasn't the worst ending ever, but I do think they could have gone with a much more interesting twist.Overall, you can tell a lot of quality work was put into this game. The actors are marvelous, even the script was well written despite the disappointing ending twist. It's a pretty well made game but feels very drawn out and unnecessarily repetitive and frustrating at times. Some of the mechanics feel a lot like trial and error instead of natural problem solving. Every once and awhile the game actually makes you feel smart (I wish they had more of this). I wouldn't pay full price $24.99 for this game, but I think it was worth the experience on discount $10.00.

_childDocuments_.review: Very Interesting Story. A Mysterious Killer, your wife has a dark secret and in the middle, you nwho has to discover the truth and a way to escape the loop. It is really enjoyable and discover more and more about the past and your wifes secret, by failing over and over again in the loops. But the end of the story is pretty dumb. Its a good twist at the end, but if you think about it, it doesnt make any sense. Despite the weird conclusion of the story, this game is very enjoyable and surprisingly long. It took me 6 hours to get to the end of the story, which is just perfect in my opinion, not to long not to short. So i recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve minutes is a time-looped story about a man arriving home from work where his wife greets him. During the sequence of events, he will eventually return to the beginning of the time he will repeat the time loop.First of all, this game is well written, it comes with twists that I didn't expect, but it makes sense. The dialogue is written well and is voiced by an A-List team of celebrities (Willem Dafoe, James McAvoy, and Daisy Ridley).There are, however, a few bugs with character collision and story dialogue overlaps, however, this does not take away from the immersion that much.Nevertheless, this is a game worth playing; it is a captivating and story-rich game that immerses you in psychological horror.I grade this game a B+
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: 12 Minutes is a game hard to review, since its premise, story and game mechanics are very interwoven. The most basics: You play a nameless husband coming home one evening to find your wife in an excellent mood having prepared desert because of a special occasion. The romantic get together is interrupted by a surprise visitor and … well things escalate quickly from there. But not to worry: After your visitor most likely used the Heimlich Maneuver wrong, you will get a chance for a new start … and then again and again… Like Bill Murray you are stuck in a time loop and now have to gather clues and piece together the story.The idea is interesting, the game in its simplicity well designed. There are a lot of nice ideas and turns, and also well lets say gimmicks. Personal however I found the overall story arc not that great. It is an interesting concept BUT for me it was predictable and stale. Also in my eyes there is no proper resolution.  Not everything has to be spelled out always, but some more information, hints or so would have been great. Also the repetition gets tiresome at some point and some of the achievements are ridiculous and or stupid. There would have been better options for those.  Should you play it? Yes, if you are in artsy little games and human relationships as well as nice little puzzles. But most likely you should buy it at a good discount.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to play a game that uses timeloops to tell a story, you should probably buy sexy brutale instead. It's the same price as twelve minutes and tells a better story that "clicks" better, and uses its mechanics with more consistency.My issues with the game:- Twelve minutes tells a confusing story that gets more confusing as you start to understand the plot.- The game teaches you that some game mechanics lead to death & dead-ends only to change its mind once a few conditions are met... For no understandable reasons.- The game has ONE "good" ending, and is only "good" by some guy's morality code. Morality is a "grey" thing, and depends on the culture and era you live in. Having the devs force feed us their morality is kinda hard to swallow. (Note: I kinda agree with the dev's "moral choice" but it should NOT be "THE" end.)- Some things are not possible to do, but I should be able to do them (such as getting the policeman's phone number, among other things)- Once you want to achievement hunt, the options to skip dialog & time (or replay a known loop) are very limited- moon logicThings I liked:- timeloop- decent "closed room mystery" (but once again, once you understand the meat of the plot, the games becomes too moralizing)
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game suffers from one major issue and that is the loop mechanic. There is nothing wrong with a game that is meant to be played again and again to find new information to progress further. But there is something wrong with making the player sit through the same scenes over and over again. You cannot skip stuff you have already done and therefore waste a HUGE amount of time before actually finding a small hint that you have to use when you restart the loop and sit through EVERYTHING again. It's like a visual novel with multiple endings not having a Skip button and a Save/Load function, you would not want to be pressing A for 15 minutes, only to choose the dialogue that led to the wrong route and have to restart from the beginning. Underneath that major flaw though, it is a decent mystery/thriller story that for most, has shock value. But it loses its spark while you sit through the same dialogue, scene and actions again and again... again. Overall, that major oversight of the gameplay mechanic ruined the experience for me and in the end made me lose interest real quick afterwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I like the concept, the time loop. Every new choice you make could help you unravel more parts of the story, thus unlocking more options / interactions. This is a big plus for me and possibly a reason why I like the concept. The execution however, is not entirely smooth. *Gameplay:*While there are many paths you can go with, the issue I have is that the paths feel very restricted. Basically, you need not only follow the path, but that path seems to be hidden and you can only see it if the circumstances are set up in a specific steps. This feels correct while typing this, but in reality while playing the game it felt very limiting and when I exhausted all options I had in mind that I was allowed to do, I, myself, was also stuck in a loop trying to brute force for a new path, trying to learn something new, which was rather frustrating at times, especially when doing the paths I have visited 10 times already - hearing all the dialogues again and again (you can skip them to ease the pain).While some things on the gameplay could be improved, I would say I generally liked it. With every new step and new dialogue options towards the end, it always unlocked a new part of the story and I began theorizing about it all over again. Major plus for multiple possibilities (that may not lead anywhere) but were still part of the game. *Dialogues / voices:*Dialogues were great, they help a lot to dive in to the story and the situation. The acting felt real and played a huge part in the game. There were a few moments where I told myself that "I could use a [dialogue option] for this specific case because I think it makes sense and would help me", but I understand it'd be very difficult to have the game prepared for everything that a player can think of.*Graphics:*I had no issues with graphics - no need for super-real graphics in this type of game anyway.*Story:*The story was very intersting from the beginning. At the very start, you know nothing and you need to play multiple iterations (loops) to understand more, until you understand the story as a whole. This in itself felt very nice throghout the game and has a major role in the game. However, I did not like one of the revelations in the story, Overall, I did enjoy the game, and I would recommend you to at least try it if you feel interested in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this if you like story-driven games or groundhog day-like stories. It's a bit short and simple, I beat it in one sitting without ever really getting stuck, but I really enjoyed my time with it. It was slow but satisfying to watch the story unfold little by little, adding more complex twists throughout. It reminded me a lot of The Sexy Brutale, but I think I enoyed TSB a little bit more because of its length and harder difficulty. Overall a fun experience and an interesting story!
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I completed this game, which is something I won't do for a game I hate, so this is a pretty soft "Not Recommended," but this game just had too many issues for me to recommend it. The plot and uncovering the twists is very enjoyable and you will not see them coming. But unearthing the clues needed to progress the plot is arduous. The setting is so limited, you will be seeing the same area and hearing the same dialog over and over as you try things to get different responses. It is not a very fun experience. When you do unearth something new it feels great! But it's just too tedious.Compare this game to a game like Outer Wilds. Outer Wilds is just in another league compared to 12 Minutes. Outer Wilds has the same idea of an emergent story through repetition, yet it rarely lags and presents a vast world for you to explore. Somehow the tiny world of 12 Minutes is also much slower to explore than the huge world of Outer Wilds. That's not great.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest, I didn't finish this game. I couldn't - I didn't have the will to continue.Maybe it's just me being a dumbass, but I seriously ran out of ideas to try after interacting with all the things I could find, combining everything that made any kind of sense and flushing everything I could carry down the toilet. Feel like maybe I could have possibly got it eventually, but the game is so boring sitting through the same events over and over and over again, It gives you no feedback about any good decisions you make, it just expects you to make very specific actions at just the right time. I ended up just getting frustrated.So I looked up a walkthrough. I read that the [blank] can be found in the [blank] under the [blank]. I went and looked, and the [blank] under the [blank] is completely hidden from view because the screen is blacked out at the top and bottom. I would have had to just stumble upon it by moving my mouse over it. That's dumb. Maybe at some point you can find out where it is through dialogue or something. I don't know because again, the game is so tedious I couldn't be bothered.So anyway, I grab the [blank] from the [blank] and give it to the guy when he comes - That's the thing he's asking for, right? So I give him what he wants - the thing that he's after - and he kills me anyway, starting another loop.♥♥♥♥ this stupid game.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game is advertised as being interactive, but you have to spend hours and hours clicking every possible combination until you find the right one, as there is only one "correct" option for you to progress forwards. The combinations that you need to get are so ultra-specific that there's little chance of guessing them and I ended up just following a guide, because there really is only one way to progress and I wanted to see what the ending was. It ended up being very underwhelming and it wasn't really explained how they managed to do the things they did - it felt out of place with the rest of the game. Furthermore, if you got a single step wrong, you had to repeat the sequence all over again until you got it right, including the minutes of dialogue which you have to skip one line at a time. The twists got more and more ridiculous as the game progressed until I was rolling my eyes at everything the characters were telling me.Some of the dialogue didn't make sense in context (I guess because it is difficult to create dialogue that works in any situation regardless of action). The game definitely has promise, but it isn't where it needs to be at the moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I like the idea, the presentation, and the overall plot, but sadly I found the implementation to be lacking.* It ended up being very repetitive. I often repeated the same steps over and over again, just to do a small variation of it to see if anything is different.* Sometimes I do the right thing, but my timing is just slightly off, so it doesn't count (and I don't know whether it was the timing or the thing I'm trying just doesn't work)* Many times the thing that makes the most sense to me just isn't an option. That is especially horrible with dialog options. I often find myself wanting to tell one of the other characters something I learned in a previous loop, but there just isn't a dialog option for it.I was very intrigued at first, but it ended up just being tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: As many others have said, frustrating as hell. Still, the story is cool, disturbing but cool. And that is the only reason I kept playing (the fact that I had to use a guide/Spoiler free tips), and the great performances of the actors. The gameplay/mechanics the game is based on need a lot of work, since the game won't let you try new things or paths, you must follow specific actions to go forward, otherwise you're gonna be stuck for an hour at least until you have exhausted all the different things and found the actual working actions.The ending might be disappointing for some, but it was a nice conclusion/wrap up of the whole mess the story is (which will keep you interested). _childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a janky game, but I'm pretty much always up for a time loop. I do like the lack of hand-holding going on in the game. It's all about discovery - of story as well as of systems and interactions. The story is nothing special but it served its purpose. This game will not end up on any top list of mine but I would still recommend it so anyone who likes to try new things and can accept them as they are.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly I can't recommend this game. There's a lot of cool and interesting things this game is going for, and there was clearly a lot of talent put into orchestrating it, but the ending is sufficiently bad and the puzzles sufficiently frustrating that it brings the whole experience down.Some puzzles involve a disconnect between intent and action, which means you're never really sure if your idea is bad or you just got unlucky. Sometimes you cannot perform an action until you receive other information, but because you failed to do that action earlier you assume it can never be done. Sometimes you fail to do something simply because of a bug, and continue onwards assuming this mandatory step towards completing the game is impossible. Sometimes you need to do something not because of the obvious consequences that it'll have, but just to see what will happen, which makes it feel less deliberate and more brute force-y. There's also a lot of spam-clicking through cutscenes and other tedium which ruins the lategame's pacing - resulting in especially frustrating moments where you have to restart because you forgot to do something five minutes ago.It's a shame a game with a lot going for it got bogged down by all of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game was wonderful, well made, and strange, and the frustrating thing about it is that it requires patience. I mean, it will lose a lot of people because it doesn't really flow the way you might want it to. It's more like a nut you have to try to crack. I personally didn't find it to be particularly frustrating but I also simply love the concept itself. Like, the core mechanic for me is like this toy that I can play with, and so the rough edges and stuff that might have been done better just didn't really matter to me. And it isn't so difficult that you can't solve it. Like I said, it takes some patience and sometimes we just don't have that patience, for better or worse. It's very cliche but this one is "stay with it, it'll grow on you"

_childDocuments_.review: F-R-U-S-T-R-A-T-I-N-GI would recommend, but strap yourself in for annoyance at this game. We need to be able to skip more dialogue/actions in an easier way please! That is where all the play time comes in...oh whoops, I forgot one minute detail?!? Or oh what does this do? Time to replay the whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing again. I know time loops are supposed to be annoying... but I feel in game play we need a bit of leeway. Sometimes I would just . There is no clear objective for this game other than getting out of the time loop, there is no guidance...you just have to guess. _childDocuments_.review: OK, so this game is pissing me right off! It's a great game and I am enjoying it immensely but as soon as I make progress, BAM, the loop resets. _childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying that its not that i dont recommend the game entirely, its just that i dont recommend it at this price point. Simply because there are better options out there. To elaborate in just a few words before i go into more details the game has a cool concept but fails in gameplay and story aspects, even tho some parts are good.So this game is trying to tell the story of the main character that is trapped in a time loop, the cast consists of 3 characters and the world is basicly 3-4 rooms. Now thats a small cast and a small space for a story to take place, but since its a time loop game it can work. Well it doesnt, the start of the game is the only good thing about it imo, and thats because your actions are basicly actions anyone would take. For example call the police, try to explain that you are in a timeloop, etc. Well you do those tings for an hour or so and then you hit a wall, thats were the problems start. Here there is a puzzle (spoiler about the lightswitch) that you just have to get lucky and find it to progress. There is no hint about it and because you can use all the items in the house you are stuck trying them out while they are just decor and do nothing. After that part you basicly stuck in repeating 2 scenarios until the end so you can get information about the backstory of the characters. I think thats handled in a bad way, with characters believing you way to easy, ignoring obvious answers that explain the situation in a more logical way. And thats the game, a good start and everything else falls apart. It starts as a game about getting unstuck from the timeloop and ends as a game about finding your story, basicly rendering useless the timeloop mechanic.Well ok, the gameplay might suck but the story might be good right? Well actually no, the story for me is the worse part, i never was inclined or had the urge to find out what was going on, i really didnt care the dialog didnt make me care, to be honest i dont thing it really needed a story, it just need a concept. Oh i am stuck in a time loop because of this this and this. Anyway i wont go into more details because of spoilers but i will give you a small spoiler for anyone that gets it, here it is. The story is basicly poor man's oldboy but also simplified.Lastly i would go into a few technical details. The game runs like ♥♥♥♥, its unable to keep 60fps, the framerate is all over the place, you get 60 then 40, then you click on a painting it goes to 30, you click on another painting it goes to 60 again. Just a mess, thankfully it doesnt affect the gameplay. Personally i think for a game that consists of 3 rooms a few animations and doesnt look that incredible it should reach at least 60 easily. I would also like to mention the cast, 3 known actors that did a good job with what they had. This was a major selling point and marketing so i would like to say that actors in games that consist of basicly 1 page of dialog for each character doesnt really matter, it would have the same feeling with unknown actors to be honest. They are just there to say "oh that dafoe".Thats it, if you are interested in the game get it on a sale. If you are interested in the concept of the game just get Outer wilds or life is strange, much better games.

_childDocuments_.review: Really interesting concept, but the illusion of this story being a game that reacts to a player falls a bit rapidly. After trying several things that you'd think would do something, you end up realizing that the game has only one path it wants, and will actively reject any other option you come up with.Combination that should work will not, AI behavior will change to make you fail, it will do things that it does not in other contexts (because if it didn't, the script would fail).And to try something new in the next loop, you will have to do everything all over again, and spend minutes (times the number of tries) just to explore something you think would work but does not.So, all of these things, coupled with the fact that the game does not tell you what you are supposed to do to break the loop (which increases the number of tries) makes for a quite frustrating experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Minor spoilers for the mechanics of the came, but no content.The game is a classic time loop game, where you have to figure out what triggers the loop and how to get out.And it is very fun for the first 2 hours, but the fun quickly fades away as you get stuck and have absolutely no clue what to do.The game gets super tedious and boring, having to sit through the same dialogue again and again, trying little variations to see if that will unlock something new.The changes between every loop are so small that you barely notice them or think of them as changes at all.The game has infinite loops but only so and so many endings, with only one being the correct one, making the game reset without explantion or a conclusion to the story.I find myself very good at puzzle and detective games, but when I reached 6 hours being stuck in this game, I gave up and looked up a guide, which revealed that I would never ever in a million years have come up with the solutions for the various endings and loop resets.The things you have to do is so random, and you have to do them in a very specific order for them to trigger. There it's not logic and it just makes the game frustrating to play.The game does not tell you when or what you did right to make something new happen, so you have to go through every scenario and dialogue option again and again to see if something new has opened up, often making you wait the full 10 minutes before revealing that nothing you did this time changed anything, which is really frustrating and boring if you ask me.Lastly, the game has some minor bugs that led me to believe I was stuck several times, when it was just the game bugging and it took a restart of the game to realize it was a bug and not a game design feature.And the game is called 12 minutes, but every time loop only last 10 minutes, so that also frustrated me a bit."But whyyy?"I know that if you add some specific moments in the game, it adds to 12 minutes, but that is only 1% of the game, the rest of the loops are 10 minutes max before resetting automatically for no reason at all.The idea for the game is very good, but the execution is very poor.The game is way to hard, tedious and frustrating, when you are stuck and have abselutely no clue what to do, and when watching a guide you just go "Okay, well I will just do that then for some reason"The game is not hard because stuff is hard to figure out, it is hard because the game does not give you any hints what so ever after a while and the things you have to do are so random, and has do be done in a very specific order and in a very specific place on the timeline to trigger.The game can be completed in about two hours if you know what to do, but I reached 6 hours being stuck before watching a guide, and even with a guide I hit 9 hours before completing the game almost 100%The game frustrated me more that is was fun, which is why I don't recommend it.Is has nothing to do with price, but purely the clue design of the game, the frustration of getting stuck with no clue what to do, and the missing conclusion to the ending.Buy it if you like puzzle/time loop games, but be prepared to get stuck and be very frustrated.Because as most other reviews here say, is that the games puzzles rely mostly on trial and error, not being able to "figure it ot" whick is why it gets boring and tedious quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: There used to be talk of how deep a simulation game could go. People would converse about the idea of a simulated neighbourhood, a small block of houses where anything is possible, sure the game wouldn't be as vast as an ocean but it would be as deep as one. In my opinion, while this is a very small piece of that cake, it embodies the idea rather well. Twelve minutes is a game where you play as a protagonist trapped in a time loop who must figure out how to escape. While the median of choices does appear somewhat limited at first, its the order in which you play and the way you use them that dictates the length and flow of the game.Yes, it is somewhat short and yes there is some level of limitation, but overall I think as an experimental game that really wants to create an open ended version of a choose your own adventure, I think this game gets it astonishingly well. I'd reccomend it even more if you got it for around 15 bucks or less as the 20 dollar tag can be steep for some. The game is a little clunky for interaction and movement but fortunately its a rather small play space and dialouge can sometimes get skipped - albiet only a few words in my own experiences. Certainly worth checking out if this game intrigues you to any extent

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. This game took a very interesting concept and absolutely ruined it by trivializing some very dark issues. I'm so glad I figured out how screwed up this game's plot was at the 105 minute mark because if I hadn't done so, I'd have ended up outside the refund period -- and this is a game whose treatment of heavy issues is not at all deserving of financial rewards.I'll start with the positives, not because they outweigh the negatives, but because they are easier to articulate without ruining the game. I very much liked the idea of recurrence and the way recurring memories are handled so you don't have to redo the same click sequence each time -- contextual actions make it clear that not only you as the player but also your character remember each loop. The contained space also makes it very easy to get where you need to go when you need to get there so that the game's sometimes-clunky navigation interface (point and click even when using a controller? Weird!) doesn't get in the way too much. And the plot even starts out interestingly and mysteriously... but then!Spoilers follow.

_childDocuments_.review: 3rd and final edit review: TLDR: 4 hours of brilliant gameplay and voice acting ruined by a last 1% of that feels tacked on by a team which, unlike masterpieces like "Detroit : Become Human" (75 different ending), couldn't handle a *single major twist* alongside 12 minor achievements. Not to mention, a 'oh-hum' ethics in the final chapter that might see many upset by the lack of options at our disposal.. And '12 minutes', for the most part, is really good... for its first 36 or so loops, which lasts about 4 hours.Sadly, as mentioned in my intro, the last 12 loops (3 minute long at most each , as you'll be whizzing through endless series of dialog at this point to get it 'done and over with') that mark 12 different achievements feel like they have been 'tacked on' by a different writer and even different programming team. I get it - it's meant to be the twist behind the twist thing. But with Dafoe voicing 2 characters instead of one, it ends up being a confusing mess. Imagine 'memento' meets David Lynch but only for the last 10 minutes of the movie. You'd walk out disapointed. I did here, too.There's even a series of bugs raised and acknowledged by the developers that 'some elements of gameplay inconsitent with the overall playthrough' may confuse a lot of players. These players are like me, downvoting the game because they got stuck at 99% of the game and couldn't finish it without going through some impossibly complex dialog branching, Now regarding the cost. You know the movie '12 angry men'? According to IMDB, it's one of the best movies ever made according to both critics and the public alike. Yet, the movie takes place in a single room and has only 12 actors that never move. The hordes of people complaining they paid 19.99 for a game that takes place in a single room is akin to complaining that the ticket price of movies should be proportional to their production costs. Let's imagine now the opposite proposition: one where you pay more if you REALLY enjoy a title or movie. You are enjoying Final Fantasy? That will be 5,000 dollar please? Or what if games charged per hour of content available? I spent 2,500 hours on morrowind - that game would have bankrupt me. Do these model sound fair to you? No? Then the opposite shouldn't either.In conclusion, it's okay to criticize games, but do so for the quality of their content, not their setting/budget. Whether '12 minute' had a cost 600 or 6 dollars, it wouldn't remove or add from its terrible ending mechanism, and total lack of replayability.Thumbs down from me despite really enjoying the first 4 hours of the game out of a total playtime of 4h30 (5h if you count attempting to get all the achievements).

_childDocuments_.review: A fundamentally flawed game. The concept is really cool but it is badly executed. I like the puzzle element of being stuck in a time loop and learning about future events so you can plan your actions and prepare accordingly, but that only lasts for the first 30-60 minutes. After that it is basically brute force to try and find the "correct" set of actions in order to unlock a piece of dialogue for the next loop so the story can progress. There is a lot of work and very little payoff. The story is weird and moronic. The writers are way too far up their own ass. I think this could have been a short and sweet puzzle game if they just focused on the freedom of choice and allowed the player to get their own endings. The game already kinda does this; first thing I did when the game started is pick up a knife and stab my wife. Amazing. But if you want to progress you are pretty much forced to play it the way the devs intended.It's a good game but it's a shame that the devs take away the players' autonomy and spit in their face when they play it their own way. It's also impossible without a guide. The hour of freedom and exploring the different possibilities are worth it imo.

_childDocuments_.review: ** There are no spoilers in this review.This isn't a game I either wholeheartedly disregard or recommend: there is much about it that is really quite impactful and well-crafted, such that it leaves a mark and is a game that is likely to be one you remember.  On the other hand, there are significant holes in both plot and mechanics that ask a lot of the player to look past in the desire to have that emotional resonance.Functionally, the time loop works well.  It breaks when you expect it to and you end up agonised at repeating a lot of the same thing over and over, much like you might expect if you were trapped in such a thing.  The way the story unravels and you discover different parts based on what you learn in previous loops works well and for the most part makes sense, there's not a lot you are guessing and the things you try in desperation convey that sense well.  The acting is, as you'd expect for the pedigree, on point and makes the story much more credible, although the decision to hire two famous British actors for voice only and then have them affect American accents is a strange one.The story, for you to get the most out of it, relies on the player being willing to suspend their belief on constructs more than you really ought to for a game set in a contemporary real-world setting mainly rooted in feasible than incredible.  This results in a third act which stretches to breaking what it asks the player to accept, and resultantly is where it falls down.  There are one or two too many tropes and twists thrown onto an already heavy wagon, and that it is delivered with the same earnestly po-faced auteur devices as the more conceivable, more engaging earlier acts mean that it comes off as insulting the player's intelligence rather than continuing to allow them to be part of the journey.Some of the impact it is capable of delivering, despite these problems, in that third act *is* heavily impacting and the game definitely has stories and messages worth listening to and experiencing the telling of a story with multiple interpretations and different shades of grey in every aspect.  In that regard, it has a resonance and it delivers.If you go into this with eyes open and willing to move past what are pretty hefty asks of you, then there is a good chance you will enjoy this work and experience.

_childDocuments_.review: What to say about Twelve Minutes. I think you should buy this game. Not at $25. But if you can pick it up for $9.99 or $14.99 it's worth a go I think. I think in many ways the plot is brilliant, but I have SO many problems with this game.1) The voice acting.When you read the opening credits, wow, Willem Dafoe, James McAvoy, Daisy Ridley, holy crap, what a cast.Willem Dafoe is clearly in this game. James McAvoy, maybe? I think, the main character sort of sounds like him?Daisy Ridley, absolutely not. I just played 9 hours of this game over 2 days listening to my "wife" say the same lines of dialogue about 1000 times and either that's not Daisy Ridley or she tried (and succeeded) so hard to sound NOTHING like Daisy Ridley it may as well be anybody. They could have paid me $50 to play "wife" and I would have sounded much more like Daisy Ridley. Get ready for some great Willem Dafoe and not much else.2) The characters. (minor spoilers)Pretty much everyone in this game sucks, including yourself. Sometimes you like one of the characters but they all inevitably turn out to be horrible. Your wife will lie to the point of you getting killed for it. When you call her out eventually to the point of "Hey babe,  you need to tell the truth or I'm going to get killed in the next few minutes", she still denies the truth until you are literally getting your head beaten in and THEN she's like, "Ok, you got me, lolllll". Too late, you're dead.3) The game ends 50 times. (minor spoilers)I'm not kidding. You will have no idea when, if, or how the game ends. Early on, there's an ending where somebody dies and it's kind of fitting ending. However, the game doesn't end. it's a game "achievement", but not an ending. However you will have NO idea what to do with this newfound knowledge. You will desperately want to say to Willem or Daisy, "Hey I know who the murderer is!" But will have to bang your head in a car door for many hours before you figure out how to convey this to anyone. Best of luck with this bit, you can piece it together, but it's not intuitive. All this said, I did ultimately enjoy it. But I can't give it a positive because the developers need to learn how to end a game in a way that the one playing the game can say without question, "I just finished this game!". Not "I just finished this game?" for the 12th time.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes gets a lot of undue hate for being essentially a short game with only a literal handful of characters (3 of which are only voices), but it's an interesting spin on the "Groundhog Day" trope: the day starts, something happens, it starts over. Choices lead to results.And really, that's what the game is about: you are presented information, and then you are given choices of how to react to that information. You face the same scenario again and have the opportunity to make a different choice, with your previous choice not being an influence (at least not directly) on your previous choice in the same scenario."If I had it to do over again..." is what this game answers.Now, those choices may be considered limiting and unrealistic by some, but I like to think there's a specific, story-related reason for that, and I'd like to believe that you actually learn the reason for it at some point in the game.I found it entertaining, and well-made, for what it does. It doesn't have what it doesn't need, IMO, such as a desirable soundtrack and skins and mods and all that, because it's not that type of game. It's not a perfect 10, by any means, but it's well above a 5 in my opinion.Those who like fast action and loud music and shouting at other people in multiplayer will not find anything here, thankfully. Those who like mysteries and watching a story unfold (or unravel) might like it.A lot of to-do has been made about the talent providing the voices, but don't get your hopes up; you're not really going to get the experience of Rey Palpatine and Professor Xavier having a chat with the Green Goblin. They do a fine job, obviously, but I didn't find anything in the dialogue or its delivery that was award-winning, or that made me think about who was delivering the lines (although Willem DaFoe's voice is rather distinct and suits the character). Any reputable voice actors could have done as good a job, but there's not really much to work with here. Overall I'd give it an 8 out of 10. It sets out to do a certain thing, and it does that thing it set out to do. I haven't completely completed the game, as far as I can tell (there are supposed to be Achievements, which I haven't achieved, yet I've seen the ending credits twice), so I can't really say if some of my questions will eventually be answered, and it can be a little frustrating the further along you go, but it's a solid experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen a lot of reviews about this game that were pretty critical, but let me give another perspective: It's a role-playing game. You're a guy trapped in a time loop. You don't understand why, or how to end it. Some things that you might not normally consider as that character are required to finish the critical path. This is not poor story design, and I think a lot of reviewers are missing that. It's a pretty good game for what it is. It's a philosophy piece. Just buy in. Play the role. Suffer, try, fail, die, and get creative. Do things you'd never consider doing unless you have been in the same time loop a hundred times with no apparent way out. Give up and try nothing. Try letting terrible things happen and watch from the closet. Betray your wife's trust. Drug her. If you catch the guy who wants to kill you, and he won't answer your questions, torture him until he does. Be so desperate to get out that you'll try anything, and do the unthinkable. That said, I did get at least one game ending without ever personally murdering my wife.Oh, and listen to the dialogue. Sometimes they say random stuff that's actually the developers trying to give you a hint of how to approach a problem differently. A guy tells you he isn't willing to listen because he only listens to x kind of person, maybe think about how to make that happen.

_childDocuments_.review: I like adventure games. I like puzzle games. I like narrative games. The puzzles in this game are actually very clear, not the "moon-logic" I've seen some describe them as. I want to make that very clear going into this. If you listen to the dialogue given, you can get through almost every puzzle posed to you in the game without too much of a sweat. However it is all given a framing device that makes the experience feel tortuous. Your willpower will be driven down to loathe doing anything in this game, to the point you will resent its insistence on not ending sooner. As you repeat the same actions again and again and again, without an option to skip the whole section so you have to click a dozen or so times through all the dialogue (each run!) in order to get back to where you were making progress. The narrative, the story, the entire reason for playing this game however, is absolutely shamefully bad. This game has the gall to rip off movies better than it and pose as its own piece of work. A premise was thought up for this game first, one that was seen in its trailer back in E3 2019, and everything else feels ripped from other films and slapped onto this work. It is a pretentious Frankenstein's Monster of other ideas done better. The entire *ending sequence* is ripped from *MASSIVE SPOILERS AHEAD*  WHOLESALE, with none of the narrative pay-off that the film it rips-off contains. It is a hollow and vacuous twist that hours after beating it, I am still wondering why things played out the way they did?MORE ENDING SPOILERS| Credit where credit is due: The acting talent, as expected, is superb. Which makes sense as it feels the game is riding the coattails of its talent into legitimacy. But even great talent can read horrible drivel, and as the faux-Hitchcock poster for the game and The Shining Carpet shows, these are people who want to pretend they're among the finest craftspeople of the arts, but instead play dress up in thin costume to fool people into thinking that they actually are that good.Also the game was buggy when I played. There's no fancy way of talking about that. A character who had died suddenly came back to life to tell me a clue before somehow dying again immediately after. My wife began telling me deep secrets as Willem Dafoe broke down my door, but then he stopped, as the door lay open to the apartment, to let my wife finish, as if no-one had heard one another. In a moment of madness (CW: Suicide, Self Harm) I don't recommend Twelve Minutes. It goes to show that over-hyped marketing campaigns and stunt casting count more than artistic merit. Even if David Cage disappears, there will be more people on the creative talent of him that will get inexplicable amounts of money.
