_childDocuments_.review: = Long Review (No Spoilers)= This review is about 12 minutes (“12M”) – a point and click adventure. What is this game about? The game begins when you (as the player) return home to your apartment and your loving girlfriend. It looks like just like another nice and comfy evening at home as some events unfold that dramatically change your lives. Without spoiling any of the further content, I must mention that the story of the game is centered around a “time loop” that the protagonist lives through. You relieve the evening again and again, trying to change the chain of events that is about to unfold. In order to do so, you can walk around your apartment (3 rooms), interact with some items (pickup or use) and you can interact with and talk to people. As time progresses and you “live” through loop after loop, more and more of the story is revealed and you gain knowledge about what is happening and how you can change the outcome bit by bit.The story sounds mysterious and interesting – you do not have the slightest clue about what is going on in the first few minutes or even the first hour of gameplay. Should make up for an interesting puzzle game, you might say.Yeah - so far goes the theory. Unfortunately, 12M fails to deliver a good gameplay. That has multiple reasons I would like to point out (now switching to my subjective views):1)	Time-Loop scenarios in movies or literature can work quite well. Movies like (e.g.) “Boss Level”, “Butterfly Effect” or even the Star Trek Episode “Deja Vu” from TNG are examples that I really enjoyed. Of course, due to the nature of the “loop”, the audience experiences the same events over and over again. This is bound to get boring, so one major element to prevent this is that each “loop” must be engineered to be different enough that the attention and curiosity are peeked and that new aspects that come to the mind actually feel like progress. For the first hour or so, 12M delivers a similar experience. After that, however, the changes in the loop dramatically decrease to being absurdly superficial – you really feel like you are stuck in an infinite loop (in the negative sense) and this almost destroyed any joy I had in playing the game.2)	The actions you take in the game and the events that unfold are playing out in “semi real-time”, meaning that it is relevant which action you take at which precise moment in time. Unlike classic point and click adventures, where the “world” you act in is static (apart from changes you actively induce), time-based puzzles are a crucial element in 12M. While this may not be a bad thing as such, the required precision with which you must time some of your actions in order to progress is sometimes very high – make just one tiny mistake, and you can “re-loop”. 3)	This leads me straight to the next point: The game requires a very, *very* particular set of actions with a very particular timing in order to progress, but there are little to no clues which steps are required in the mid-game and especially the end-game. This “railroading” effect is taken to the extreme and effectively reduced any fun I still had playing after 2 hours.4)	As if that were not enough, the solutions to the so-called “puzzles” which the game expects of you are often so flat-out illogical and far-fetched that I would call it absurd: Things that would make perfect sense are just not “designed” to be possible – with no explanation at all. Additionally, some items are hidden in a way that it may be pure accident whether you find them or not – even *although* you already know (from a previous conversation) where an item should be.5)	Then there are the dialogs: You can talk to your wife and several other people in the game. Unfortunately, I must say that I do not find most of the dialogs and especially the choices in the game very well-written. There is hardly any depth to the dialog options and even the conversations themselves are stale, stereotyped and boring / uninteresting. What is far worse, though, are the characters themselves: The way they act is simply ridiculously illogical. I cannot go into detail here without spoiling, but let’s just say that the actions of the “visitor” in the apartment cannot be brought in line with the motivations of the character – it makes even less sense in the end. 6)	As mentioned above, repetition is an essential part of time-loop scenarios, but since a game (and especially an adventure) lives from how it lets the player interact with the environment, how it encourages and rewards exploration, and last – but not – least – how the player perceives progress. In order to progress, you will have to relive the *exact* scene of events many times. Imagine that – the exact same conversation, no changes, the ever-same introduction, the ever-same midgame. Just to change a few sentences in a dialog after > 5 minutes after which you need to do it all over again. And you cannot even skip the dialog! You can just “fast-forward” it by having to click and hold after each sentence – this is pure punishment!In a movie scenario (e.g. in “Boss Level”), the writers cleverly circumvented such a situation in skipping events or drastically changing them in the beginning of a new loop to explore new, undiscovered territory. In game, this is similar, yet not as easy to achieve: The parts you as a player are bound to (re-)play most often must have the most diversity to prevent boring you to death. This is where 12M fails miserably.7)	Finally, there is the story and the narration itself: I honestly do not think it makes any sense at all, “plot twists” especially included. Yes, there are multiple possible endings, but none of them left me “fulfilled” or “enlightened” in any way. It all feels utterly pointless, artificially constructed and completely far-fetched.Take all those things above and add to that the very limited, enclosed space you can explore and the small amount of true puzzles you need to resolve, I end up with a game that could entertain me for 1,  maybe 2 hours. Then, I quickly lost any fun in playing and it was my sheer will and curiosity whether it all “makes sense in the end” that kept me going nonetheless. Needless to say, I was disappointed and the “replay” value of the game is non-existent.  And yes – W. Dafoe participates in the game as voice actor (“WOW! How cool is that!?”), but that does not help matters if the dialog is just badly written and the atmosphere is lacking. That the publisher self-advertises the game as 12M “blends the dream-like tension of THE SHINING with the claustrophobia of REAR WINDOW and the fragmented structure of MEMENTO.” is a very bad joke – all those three titles are very cleverly done in their own department. 12M falls behind them all in each and every single aspect – a very bad comparison, indeed.Sorry, but I cannot recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A husband, James McAvoy, comes home to his loving, occasional baker and jedi wife, played by Daisy Ridley. Everything appears to be the stuff of fairy tales one minute but the next all hits the crapper… That is when a cop, Willem “The Foe” comes pounding at their door rooting out secrets, lies and won’t think twice resorting to violence. But James has a secret of his own; he’s stuck in a 12 min loop! Now go crazy persuading, intervening and learning the truths~  Quite a few games have incorporated time loops;  but none have been as minimalist and drilled in your head as TVM’s! And no, the Sims-like controls don’t make it any easier or happier as time plays an integral role. The first few attempts will be overpowering but soon through experimenting with deaths, crank calls, thorough apartment inspection, you can begin to regain some control and access shortcuts.Some design choices are delightfully clever; the pause menu is a real-time clock and there you can observe, take note of which events start on the schedule. Employ these to your advantage to prove points, contradict or confront characters, bad cop style. Soon the shenanigans pile up, stink eyes are given before bitter realities set in… TVM will occupy you for hours on end with its various endings and getting to exhaust every possible reaction there is from the single setting and ensemble cast is a deliverance in itself~1) Messed up somehow? Walk out the door.2) Combine objects even without picking them up!  Has one of the most burning, multifaceted plot I’ve ever lived through in a video game, which is a marvel because you’d expect this sheer level of detail to analyze more from a book or film. A story caked in suspense, deceit and obsession. Think of it as an onion, just as you think you’re done with its many layers, you’re not and look you’re tearing up. The pivotal theme is time- and the loops become even torturous and your sense of it, transient… With each one, new facts can surface, meaning gets developed but also lost, feeling more illusory the further you’re adrift in the temporal maze. You make connections of your own, read into every line of dialogue or quote seemingly to no end. Like the husband, you just want it to stop and enjoy the evening with your wife no matter how short-lived. Luckily, there’s a point to all this madness and though it may be a contested take as it’s heavily “cliched”, it’s executed with tact and poise, I excuse it~ The top-down perspective got me startlingly anxious. For one thing, it prevents the audience from fully gleaning emotion. Not that they all have faces, as you’ll soon find out from a few first-person viewings. Instead, you have to trust the weight in their words and mannerisms. It’s unpleasant and there’s a jarring detachment between characters and yourself… The apartment is essentially a gritty stage or set piece, one that is exposed to flashes of lightning, smeared with blood but for all intent, framed perfectly still. But you rarely get tired of it, if ever. Thanks to the rich, ample motion-capture animations and simple but shocking changes in mood lighting. Passage of time flows when examining an item and a reflection of what’s behind you get cast, wherever you’re positioned. It’s like an interpretation of a painting, where your conclusion changes depending on your state of mind at a given moment~The star-studded casts’ voices were barely recognizable, except for Willem Dafoe who is as iconic as ever. Both James McAvoy and Daisy Ridley portray, deliver believable and emotionally-laden American accents… I was really taken by them, their transition from a field that relies on facial expressions, body language to game voice-overs was a major success I’d say, though not without issues. More on that later~Sound design is magnificent, with all those ordinary household and street noises to give a sense of normalcy but that plunges to shi* and hell thanks to the score. Which arranges from casual, romantic to “make it go away” tenseness. Then advances to more tragedy has struck, deepened nihilism and tears you can’t jerk out anymore. It’s a roller-coaster of emotions, all in such a short duration~Some dialogue paths and choices are insultingly linear, for even though you “safely” bypassed that stubbornness or ignorance- speaking out of turn, or trying to show an item in your possession even when the situation has been defused, could get you choked, shot or walloped to rib-tickling effect.Characters’ bipolar emotional swings and their change of hearts so instantaneous are also distracting. While I appreciated how more summarized versions of explanations are made available for use, certain options are locked out and require that exact phrasing, prodding to progress~The voices are great but sometimes there’s a hint of their accents breaking and you can tell a lot of work went into fabricating the voice that it doesn’t come off naturally. That’s also what I meant earlier with “barely recognizable”. Also, some lines just sound amateur, in terms of the script. I’m not wholly convinced of the married couple’s relationship, let alone eight years of history. Again, it could be because of the “12 minutes” selling gimmick~TVM’s $25 isn’t exactly worth it at this period. Sure, there are many endings, subtle line changes, intonation for the most part- but everything will get tiresomely linear fast and its flaws become apparent over time. Which I guess is the point, seeing as it’s a game about a 12-minute loop after all~ x Wife's head faces the foot of the bed.x Cop's trajectory gets stuck by characters' feet or objects. I had to try to escape to let him kill me.x Voice lines being lined up wrong / awkwardly continue.x Woke up stuck inside wall unable to interact or see anything besides blackx Husband’s tie cuts his spine.x Everyone phases through objects and each other!~ That one "...babe!?" line is unflattering. On the level of Heavy Rain's "JASON"!~ Making open phone calls and revealing incriminating information in the presence of other characters have no effect (save for one response).~ Actions feel sluggish even during heated moments; a delay between thinking and doing!~ The way the “skip dialogue” works will give your finger a workout.TVM will drive you curious, annoyed, mad and on your knees as it subjects you to an eternal hell. Its biggest achievement is having stood the test of time but ironically also its ultimate downfall~If you like a modern game gushing out classic thriller nuances from its exhibition to its mind-bending plot where you can write a detailed analysis essay afterwards. If you’re someone pressed for time, rest assured for you can squeeze TVM’s brief sessions at least once or thrice daily then continue on weekends. If you’re a fan of the three prominent celebs and want to see them in different, yet similar content to their filmography- this is as good as it gets~

_childDocuments_.review: This review took longer than expected, not because I didn’t finish the game (in fact I finished it the very same release week) but because my own opinion about the title has been changing since I finished it. Not going to lie, every Annapurna published title excites me a lot as it’s a publisher that offers a very specific type of experience that I enjoy a lot, 12 Minutes wasn’t the exception, since the reveal trailer in June 2019 the game has been under my radar due to the core mechanic of time looping (Annapurna wasn’t an stranger for this as they already published Outer Wilds by that time) and here we are 2 years later, before I start with the review I must say this, even at this point I’m still undecided about how to feel about this particular game, here’s why.Game’s premise is quite simple but gets deeper with each time loop, we start this story by coming back to our apartment after a long day, wife is waiting to enjoy dinner with us and perhaps surprise us somehow, the moment gets interrupted by a mysterious detective that muzzle both of you while asking again and again about her father and a watch we don’t know nothing about, after this the time loop will start rolling over and over again until we discover what’s going on with this detective, our wife and that watch.I must say that the story at first sounds interesting and the more you learn about it, the more interesting it gets, each time loop is an opportunity to learn more details about your wife’s past, knowing more about that detective and of course unveil dialogs that will open new paths to new situations, you could say that both the characters and your own apartment are both part of a giant puzzle that you will be completing piece by piece and everything goes well until we reach a certain point on the story.Without spoiling anything about the story, there’s a twist in this story that should have been the “Woah” moment of this game but it just doesn’t work, why? Because it’s an unlikely situation based on the chances, not only that, it feels completely disconnected from the main plot line and yeah, it explains the why, the who, the when and the where but I still don’t think it works at all, I’m going to say that it’s sad that a promising starting point gets smashed by a disappointing ending but I don’t think it ruins what the game does right.Characters are really interesting and the more you learn about them, the deeper their arcs go, the way you unveil every piece of data and how you use what you learned to open new dialogs and trigger new situations is fantastic and in general I think that the story had a lot of potential even though it didn’t deliver at the end of the adventure, but overall I think the intention for an intriguing story is there and most of the adventure it is like that.I think it’s a good moment to jump into the technical aspects of the game like visuals, sound and gameplay loop.Overall I think it’s a beautiful game, it doesn’t really stand out on anything in particular but everything it does, it does well. We have a zenith point of view most of the time which makes us feel like observers out of the scene, as we have a complete view from an upper perspective the map feels like a doll-house in which we can do multiple actions, some of those actions will switch our point of view to a first person perspective in order to see what’s going on with a very specific situation or to solve a puzzle.When it comes to visual style, the game pursues a very realistic style so nothing to comment here, however animations are quite good, sometimes they feel robotic or doesn’t interact correctly, however, most of the time you will see a very interesting animation job between character interactions or character with environment interactions, in that sense I can say that the game is well done.Same goes to sound in general, the game takes place in a completely normal house so most of the stuff is mundane but voices are really well done, not surprising considering that the staff they have in place is quite good which reminds me about the second problem I have with this game, I feel like having such big names was a bit of a waste of resources as I think it was a wasted opportunity to make them shine, I don’t think it was something that necessary to have all this hollywood stars but what had to happen, happened, they don’t do a bad job at all, it’s just that I feel like more could have been done having this staff.But let’s talk about what’s really important, the time loop mechanic and gameplay.A lot of people consider this game quite repetitive (heh) and they are not wrong, even though it’s a time loop game there are different ways of approaching this mechanic, we have multiple games that have experimented with this mechanic, a few examples would be Outer Wilds, The Sexy Brutale or Deathloop, in all cases the approach is different, this is the same case as 12 Minutes.12 Minutes plays similarly to a point and click adventure, the inputs needed to make progress in this story are minimal, you click a place and the character triggers an action over and over until the time loop repeats, what’s the problem with 12 Minutes then? Where does the action take place, we are not talking about a Mansion, an Island or a micro solar system, it’s an standard apartment with one room, one hall and one bathroom, as it’s a small place it is more likely you feel like it’s repetitive or not quite dynamic and you are not wrong, this game’s approach is slow and you must understand this as soon as possible, my playtime was around 4-5 hours to get some of the endings and the interaction was minimal and the loop was repetitive, however, it was not something that impacted in a negative way my experience.And that’s about it, overall I liked the game and I recommend it because I didn’t have a bad experience, I was just disappointed about the ending and a few smaller things but overall I can’t say I had a bad time, on the contrary, I enjoyed it quite a lot as it was something smaller and that was what I was looking at the time.It’s not a bad game, can’t say it’s one of my favorites but I think I can say that you should probably play it and see if it “clicks” on you, I feel like it’s a mix bag of good ideas, bad executions and probably too crazy and incoherent plot lines, however I don’t regret playing it and it was in general an interesting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore any review that complains about "the ending". There are many. This game is one of the most unique and interesting point and clicks I have ever played. With clear inspirations from Groundhog Day and the Shining, the game takes elements from both and combines them to create an "almost horror adventure". The game contrasts the modern era of "we went larger" found in most "AAA" games. With the polar opposite to giant maps with nothing in them. This game opts, instead, for a tiny map absolutely filled with lore for those who are willing to go digging.The story is definitely dark, although it is ambiguous enough that you can make you own mind up on what is actually happening.The gameplay is simple, it's a point and click, but it integrates the time loop aspect well. While most point and clicks want you to figure out the solution to each puzzle, this game rewards you for getting creative, almost anything is worth trying, in fact, almost everything is required to try to unlock the story.This does, inevitably, lead to a LOT of backtracking, a LOT of "failed" attempts and a LOT of replaying once you have finished the game once. You *need* to finish the game multiple times to get the full story, although I bet many players stop after one ending.TL;DR If you like point and clicks, you are the kind of person who loves searching for clues in games like Little Nightmares or Fran Bow and you don't mind replaying a game many times to figure out something new, this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend anyone buy 12 minutes? Yes. Why?I whishlisted this after E3 2019 and somewhat forgot about it. I knew it was published by annapurna and their last time loop game was Outer Wildes (not worlds), which I consider to be one of if not the best game ever made. But different developer made me go in with ZERO expectations. For this review I assume you watched the trailer.So what did they do wrong? Mouse controls are fine, and the game sometimes struggles a bit performance wise, but nothing major or game breaking.No major bugs were encountered. The character animation are stiff and since the game used motion capture this felt odd. The animations also tended to be stiff. With characters walking through one another. Again, not in a game breaking sense, hell I'd be willing to bet it was a choice to ease player frustration. But these things do add up. With quality dropping slightly with each.Voice acting was... not great. Not in that it lacked emotion, but some of the lines were full of happy energy or excitement and others sad and slow. But they were spoken right after each other. And not appropriately. Like the same lines were used at different times for different purposes. They could have recorded the 20 or so repeating lines twice if need be. But they didn't. And It felt like less of a story and more like a, well 'game'.Sound effects were nice and music was great. I will give them that.Art was nice, nothing special and playing on Low vs High didn't make much a difference. Lighting was lovely and weather or not the lights were on or off the rooms looked well perceivable.All in all sounds and arts good. Animations and Voice acting were ehhh. And no bugs, which is most impressive. No reason not to buy the game.And trying and figuring things out for the first hour or two is great if you love the "what if I try..." question.However the story is as simple as it gets. The puzzles are childish and mostly rely on setting everything up correctly and seeing what happens.Whenever you figure something out, at the start of the next loop the character will give you a quick tip to point you in the right direction. And new conversation paths may have opened up to that clue, or a nod to an item to use. Simple useful tips. But for a story puzzle game, it had poor simple time sensitive puzzles, that gave you tips on the first try. The felt less of a "ohhh I see" and more of "yea no ♥♥♥♥ Sherlock, let me do it" or "I heard that too, the clue is just useless repetition". And to give the devs the benefit of the doubt, I don't see solutions to these problems, not simple ones anyway and twice in the game it did tell me what to do. But once it was "wait I forgot about that" and the other was "wait THAT was the clue?" and in both I continued to solve the puzzle within the next few cycles.But even if you did get what to do, both doing and figuring out how to apply your understanding in game, felt, what others have described as "trial and error". And while I would not apply that title, the game doesn't stem far from it.For the story? There is little to none. No big reveal. A poor twist and lackluster writing. Again a puzzle story game without a story isn't much to hear. And without puzzles there isn't even gameplay to look forward too. I don't know what to say without spoiling the already short and lacking experience. This may not have been a problem if the game did one of the two well and another poorly, Or if it was rushed, but after a possible 3 years of development, I have to ask. Why so little game? Why so little polish? Why such elementary elements?Old point and click games had more content than this. And possibly, a higher quality of story telling.Based on the credits and the announcement being 2 years ago, I can't money for staff or publisher deadlines to be the killing factor. But I have ♥♥♥♥ on it a good bit now. Why do I still recommend it? Because the game is a play in one 3-4 hour sitting experience. And the first 3 are great if you have any interest in puzzle point and clicks. I enjoyed it and I don't even like point and clicks. The game is a good even somewhat unique experience. The devs tried something and it works, not perfectly but it does work well.So I say wait for a sale, the game price falls into 10-15 range. Maybe take an offer or 16/17 if you have cash or like the theme the game provides. But don't hold back on this interesting and fascinating experience.

The story has some nice twists here and there and there are 6 endings to get. It's pretty interesting to learn bits and pieces going through the same little time loop over and over again.+ The freedom in learning the pieces of the story in any order. There's no right order of finding clues so it feels pretty nice that your own little experience is a bit different from everybody else's.+ The voice acting is very nice. I enjoy it quite a lot even tho eventually you start skipping through the same dialogues.+ The simplicity of the game is very appealing. I think that 12 minutes is long enough to be able to alter the events quite a lot but at the same time short enough that it doesn't get repetitive.- It gets a bit annoying when you have to get through the same dialogues or actions to progress and one little mistake or impatient click makes you go through all of it yet again.- The game is rather expensive for what it is, I would recommend to get it on a discount.- There is only one solution and only one way to get to the ending. And tho your experience is still unique, eventually the game forces you into making a very particular series of actions which is rather upsetting.- Still has some little bugs here and there, people going through each other and through objects sometimes.Overall:I'd rate this little indie adventure 7 time loops / 10. _childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes is one of the most thrilling and immersive games I have played in a while.Recently I have struggled to focus on a game for longer than an hour, but Twelve Minutes sucked me in for 4 hours non stop after purchase.It's a mystery point and click adventure that takes place in just one location - your apartment and the corridor leading up to it.You get back home from work to your wife, who wants to spend a romantic evening with fancy desserts, surprise presents and dancing. As you dance, a shifty-looking man who claims to be a police officer kicks his way through the door, cuffs both of you and eventually murders you as well.The protagonist then wakes up at the entrance to the apartment once again, clueless about what just happened.He quickly learns that these 12 minutes will loop endlessly until he discovers the cause behind this curse. I will not go into too much detail on what the mystery is or what kind of actions you will have to take to solve the puzzle.Spoiling anything would literally ruin this game as the story and the suspense holds things together.However, you will start point and clicking on everything in the apartment to pick up items and try them out on other points of interest.Eventually, you will start discovering new clues during conversations that will unlock other clues.This will throw you into a rhythm where you can plan out your actions for the next loop, and step by step, you will beat the game.Point and click adventures have a bad reputation or a stigma even of having illogical puzzles.However, to my great pleasure, I have not seen anything ridiculous like this in Twelve Minutes.Sure, I did get stuck on a couple of puzzles here and there, but by the time the solution clicked, I didn't hate the game for making it awkward.The solutions always seemed perfectly logical. There was only one instance where somebody asked me for an item that I did not have in my inventory, which led to that loop ending there.I don't know why the game just didn't let me pick an option to quickly go and grab it.Graphically, objects like furniture have quite nice but simple textures, just good enough to give an impression of realism. The character models and their textures are also hanging on the balance between realistic and clay. Still, the art style is consistent throughout, so nothing really sticks out as bad or exceptional.The only bone to pick is the absence of presentation of the facial features of the characters.The main protagonist probably works in some office as he wears a tie and a white shirt, but not quite a full suit to assume that he is doing really well.The police officer is a bald, scarred old man with a beard who looks more like a hitman. Thus we can assume that he is not an officer.The wife - well, we don't really know much about the wife.Still, although we can tell a lot from the costumes, we don't really know the characters as we can't see their faces. The soundtrack mostly consists of atmospheric string instruments and piano, quietly humming along to the story in the background.It isn't something that comes through a lot, but it can add more gravity to certain moments. Notably, the voice acting is where Twelve Minutes has put a lot of resources.The studio managed to get James McAvoy, Daisy Ridley, and Willem Dafoe of big-screen fame to act the main characters. This investment has really paid off well, as the trio has delivered the dialogues perfectly.I managed to complete Twelve Minutes in 3 and half hours, adding another 30 minutes after the credits trying to see a few things I might have missed at first. However, by looking at reviews on Steam, it took some people around 10 hours to complete the game. Considering that it can be completed in one session, is this game worth £20 or 25$?No, you can get more for your buck somewhere else.However, when Twelve Minutes goes on sale with 50% off, I strongly recommend giving this a go.Alternatively, you can also access this time through the Xbox Game Pass, but the game would not launch on my computer, so this is worth keeping in mind. The story and acting are thrilling enough to keep you on the edge of your seat as you play through the 12 minutes loops. The mystery and the puzzles are not too challenging but logical enough to make you feel smart when you crack them.But, this is a tough recommendation to make at the £20 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, meanwhile, Twelve Minutes is very simplistic, and eight hours is a long time to be looking at the same top-down view of your apartment. The frequent clipping issues and very rudimentary Sims-like animations don’t help, but it’s the kind of nitpick I learned to live with as I became engrossed in the central mystery.It’s difficult to convey my enthusiasm for Twelve Minutes’ time-loop mystery without discussing what happens at the end, but like Inside, I’d be doing you a grave disservice by giving anything away. What I can say is that the payoff is worth it, and the clever way in which writer-director Luis Antonio flips the traditional point-and-click adventure on its head makes for a compelling bit of unconventional storytelling that could only have worked as a game. Throw in great performances from three respected actors and the result is a memorable crime worth solving.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: If you're very on the fence about the polarizing nature of the game, get it on XBox Game pass! I'm going to do that to give it another try because I love a good plot twist, but I'll get a refund here because it really did feel like a waste of $30 on Steam.This game is super vague, and gets on your nerves if you don't get the solutions quickly. I've been playing for an hour and I already feel agitated and annoyed; that's how you know it isn't designed well. The puzzles are cool, and the story is great, but when I have to redo EVERYTHING every time, what seems like a groundhog day puzzle becomes a slog of repetition where you have to redo everything you just did if you mess up or miss the timer. The puzzles are also so vague and complex, while also needing to be done in such a specific order that I felt more annoyed than rewarded when I solved one. Everything can be brute forced to completion if you waste enough time, which made all of it feel unearned and lazy. But when you mess up and have to replay the same ~10 minutes again, it gets on your nerves more than anything. I found myself scrambling and skipping voice lines because in my hour of playing, I had already heard the same 12 minutes of voice lines over and over and over again. Many of the lines are super weird as well; they just play lines that seem to have little logical connection to what is going on. I don't mind the poor animation quality, but that, the poor voice line timing and disconnected writing pulled me out of the immersion way too often. I got the first real puzzle the first time, but the solution felt cheap in some ways, and after looking up a guide, I know the game is much longer and I have no desire to see how it ends. Just the thought of repeating and redoing everything over again with brute force trial-and-error seems like no fun. Maybe I'll pick the game up again on sale, but for now I'm going to refund.TL;DR Repetition and filler, slog down what could have been an incredible indie game. Combine that with the very small dev team and I think this game just got expectations too high. Overall, still highly disappointing and not fun to play. Your mileage will vary though depending on whether you happen to really get sucked into the story and like the puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: I love time loopy movies, like Groundhog Day and Edge of Tomorrow(I've re-watched them so many times), so I thought this would be right up my alley. Twelve Minutes has lots of potential but it falls pretty flat in its execution and delivery. The potential does shine with its interesting mysteries and twists. Subtle hints will give you clues to any interesting plot that you find out after each loop, and there are some moments when the game gives you the impression you can do so much more, but you really can't. In both Groundhog Day and The Edge of Tomorrow, the main characters are fairly blank ass-hat characters. They develop and grow as they live through their loops, but oh no, not so for Twelve Minutes. The main protagonists bloody regresses.  As you learn more, you find out that you actually have very little control over what goes on, unlike what this genre usually portrays. Now that I think about it, not all time loop stories are good. This is basically a shorter version of Re:Zero. Please, don't watch that.The power to relive history is meant to be almost godlike. A person can make so many changes and grow but not in Twelve Minutes. In Twelve minutes, there are too many unsolved mysteries for a psychological horror and too little control for a time loopy story. The game just leaves the player unsatisfied.In other words, this game is like a fruit that's rotten inside but clear on the outside. With a few careful bites you'll be having something delicious but eat too much of it and you'll realise it's yucky and rotten.

_childDocuments_.review: *SPOILER FREE*Twelve Minutes is a novel idea and works decently well as a mystery story. As a game though, it's significantly tougher to recommend. At first, the idea of repeating the same 10 minutes (you read that right, 10 minutes.) and getting to try new things to progress the story sounds fun. The problem is that the game is extremely specific about what you have to do and the order you have to do it in to make any progress. This winds up making the minute to minute gameplay (no pun intended) more frustrating than cerebral as you struggle to think of what other possibilities you even have open to you.The game presents you with an illusion of freedom from the start. It feels like there are so many interactive items crammed into this small, three room apartment and the possibilities will be endless but in fact, it only took me a few loops before I started feeling overly restricted. For example, there are windows in every room but these cannot be opened. By the time the credits rolled for me, I had never been allowed to interact with the windows in any meaningful way. Several other items and even whole areas around the apartment left me feeling the same way by the end. If there was any use for them, I never found it.There are several technical problems as well. Animation glitches are frequent, even when the characters follow their standard, scripted path. Even on my gaming desktop, my frame rate dropped significantly at specific times for reasons that are not clear to me. By no means was it ever unplayable but it was noticeable and occurred often enough to be annoying. The dialogue feels stilted more often than not, forcing your character to say specific things in specific ways, even if you the player have a better plan in mind. I also can't help but be disappointed by the voice acting. Don't get me wrong, I'm a fan of all the actors involved, but this was far from peak performance for any one of them. Daisy Ridley and James McAvoy in particular were bland and having these famously UK actors fake American accents seems pointless. For a game that marketed the voice actors so heavily, the end result was wildly underwhelming and based on the pedigree of the actors, I'd guess this has more to do with the directing and script than anything else. That or maybe it's just an example of why it's better to hire voice actors to do voice acting roles.This doesn't mean there isn't fun to be had in Twelve Minutes. It's an impressive idea and many of the small details are neat. Having an entire game in such a small space was an accomplishment and the first few loops offer some real entertainment. The story isn't perfect but it does have some unpredictable twists and will likely please any noir or psychological horror fans. I doubt that it will blow any minds though and there are some leaps in logic that will be difficult to stomach for some.Twelve Minutes is an impressive experiment but for the typical gamer, I can't really recommend it. The conceit is underutilized and the puzzles are more about discovering the path the developers want you to take rather than creatively solving problems yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: There is something to the tone of the story. A certain dark tone that I like. And I think the looping works well. The early events work great as you slowly unravel the story. _childDocuments_.review: This a fantastic piece of media everyone should enjoy. This type of scenario or predicament in the game's story (the time-loop) is commonly found in film and movies, and I always wondered how someone would go about creating a video game with this same idea. If you have ever played Stanley Parable, you would love this game. I was too young to play the game when it came out (didn't have a pc) so all I did was watch YouTube videos on my ipod touch of walkthroughs and all the endings, ultimately spoiling the fresh experience of going into the game blind on my own. Searching for where I could find another similar game that could offer me the feeling and experience I knew others got from Stanley Parable, I found 12 Minutes, almost 10 years later, and it offered me just that. I am not comparing the two game at all, other than the fact that they both are specific forms of media with an extremely unique method of storytelling that in all form and glory are "videogames" and can almost only be depicted and consumed in no other way possible. You can make a book into a movie, vice versa, or movie/book into a videogame. But you can't make all videogames into a movie or book. If you ever played P.T, try to envision that as a book or movie, just wouldn't be the same, wouldn't even come close. This is one of those games. What I'm trying to say, is there nothing like this. Reminds me of the old age of film making. Where we didn't have crazy special effects, and high tech cameras, so directors, writers, producers, etc explored and came up with new and unorthodox methods to get the viewer into the story, creating an atmosphere. I began with watching a stream of this game, and clicked off immediately because of how cool I thought this games concept was, bought it right away and began playing. I am very content with my decision. If you have not yet seen gameplay of this or seen very little, do yourself a favor and play this. 12 Minutes and its developers are another testament to how less is more. Commonly recognized, but it's insane how a point n' click indie game can be more compelling, immerse the player far more, and have miles of depth (not referring to content) compared to most new age triple A titles. The price for gameplay hours is a off in my grading scale, HOWEVER the experience that the game delivers is so new and refreshing, where multiple times I audibly exclaimed "THIS IS SO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ COOL", makes it is worth every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ penny. I have never played something like this, and I wish I could re experience it already. 10/10 this is a rare treat

_childDocuments_.review: The game doesn't allow for nearly as many choices as it should when dealing with the problem -- mainly dealing with the main antagonist. There are options like leaving what you might think it's the goal for him on a table that he should be able to see, or trying to give him a very important piece of evidence that should change his mind, but for the game doesn't acknowlodge it, often causing you to die and having to spend 5 minutes or more setting everything up again just to try something else. You'll be spending so much time setting up everything and trying to find out just what you have to do next that by the end of it you might have more fun stabbing your wife and yourself to death than actually advancing the story. Again, some of the choices you'll have to do are super contrived and you might even miss them because you didn't know it was an option in the first place.The controls are clunky at best. The animations while looking nice can break easily and by your fourth loop you'll be wishing you could skip them altogether. The top-down view, while a creative choice artistically, only makes it harder for you to actually select what you wanna and move around.I have 4 hours played in this game. At least two and a half of those are me repeating the same thing over and over to see what I could do different -- by the end I gave up and looked up a guide. Not only two of the endings I tried are super contrived and rely on meta-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but I couldn't even access them, no idea why not. For those who might wanna know, my clock didn't go backwards not matter what I did.For what I saw the ending to the story is also pretty contrived so I don't think I might've enjoyed it either way.

_childDocuments_.review: It is said that the definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again, expecting a different result. Indeed, one would have to be insane to enjoy this game. Twelve Minutes is a top-down click-and-drag puzzle game that holds an interesting concept and story and executes it very poorly.My opening first impressions were initially good. I felt the game looked and sounded alright for an indie title, the concept introduced was interesting, and the controls were fine. I initially thought this would be a puzzle game to remember, how ever, I quickly found myself in a frustrating loop that felt like I was just wasting my time. Unclear puzzle solutions and having to re-watch the same situation play out repeatedly is not what makes a game in my opinion. I quickly lost my interest, and it is a shame because the concept was something I was genuinely interested in.Perhaps it might be a game you would deeply enjoy. I, how ever, cannot see how anyone could willingly succumb to the insanity that is playing this title.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished playing twelve minutes a couple days ago and I marinated on it and I have to say the story and the idea was good in theory but in execution not so much. I felt like the premise of the game was super intriguing and it hooked me in and drew me to find out the whole story. However when I found out the key factor of the story I was needless to say repulsed. There were also a few things in the story that didn't make sense or just seemed irrelevant to the story. like what is the point of the daughter with cancer other than being a facet in an interaction to trigger a conversation? Why did the "cop" and the "father" both have the same voice actor and look? What really annoyed me was the fact there was no way to streamline the experimentation with the time loop and the interactions without having to start from the very beginning. it became extremely tedious after the first few hours of having to rush through dialogue you read multiple times over, just to glean the smallest amount of new information. Also one huge gripe I have with it is to get the true true ending you had to play from the start of the game with no memory of the previous loops and make the correct decisions to get the correct interactions in the right loop. Which when you think about it after playing quite a few hours already made me shudder. I got maybe two different endings but I did not have the strength to play through the game multiple times again to achieve all the endings. it just didn't have the same draw to it each time I played it again.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a puzzle / logic game, but things play out in such a strict order that it breaks logic.For example, you can get your wife to the point she believes you're in a time loop, but you can't plan to ambush the cop.  Once she knows, the cop always goes right for you and knocks you out.  There are many other examples, but I don't want to spoil anything.  Basically the game won't let you play out logical ideas that you have.  You have to figure out the logic that the game wants, which becomes repetitive and boring.Another problem is characters will have random mood swings because the narrative wants to connect two branches.  You can jump from sobbing on the floor to making wise cracks about time loops in a second.  It's very odd.It seems like this would have worked better as an episode of the Twilight Zone.  Everything is scripted to the point that there's no reason this needs to be a game.  As a show, the story would at least have better pacing.I should also point out the final big twist was very surprising.  However, that's only because it's completely insane that anyone could believe all the coincidences required for such an outcome to occur.

_childDocuments_.review: Please be civil in the comment section.If you find this review hard to read or comprehend, I apologize for my poor writing skill as this is my first long review in English. I would greatly appreciate any feedback on how to improve or general applause for my little courage and passion. You are stuck in a 10 minutes loop when you (The protagonist) enter your apartment. In these 10 minutes, you have to gather information about your wife’s past, a self-claimed cop who will interrogate your life about her father’s watch, and your past as well. In , you can grab an object, investigate it, or interact with it at a particular location/character in your apartment. You can also move around in your apartment and have a conversation with your wife and the cop (When he is willing to listen to you for whatever circumstances). This level of interaction is acceptable for a 90-degree third-person puzzle-solving game. It is not very fun, but enough for you to focus on the puzzles. Still,  has one characteristic that can make this pretty unbearable at a certain point: The infinite loops. The process of getting more information out of the cop and your wife can be extremely tedious and repetitive. The excitement I feel at the first couple of hours would wholly dissipate at the third hour as the story progresses in an unsatisfactory way. It doesn’t give you much hints to tell you what you might need to do next to get out more information. You might need to move your cursor thousands of times to drug your wife, interrogate the cop, only to receive the same outcomes over and over before you have an “Oh, I could’ve done that?” moment.  Hints could've been done better with just some dialogues! However, if you are a quick puzzle solver, these would be less of an issue. The environment of the game is excellent. A small, moody apartment and the pressure from the very scary time make a good combination. There are also paintings in the room to look at every different loop to unlock the achievements.  The driven force of the game is, unfortunately, the weakest part of the whole package. The story’s pacing heavily depends on how quickly you can solve the puzzles. It gets tedious if you aren’t fast enough to move on to a different scenario after several loops. The dialogues are OK alone, nothing too cliche, the actors are executing them with weight and passion, but the whole story is just wack. You married your sister who has a different mother. What kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ setting is this? Disgusting. You would think the game would put something in the story to make this having an appeal, but it doesn’t do that at all. You’ll just have to eat it up and keep playing. Father doesn't want you to lie to her about this relationship, but you panicked and shot him. So eight years later, you are stuck in this ten minutes loop, and it forces you to remember everything you want to forget. Great, more BS. I'm not even going to talk about how anti-climactic the six endings are. I sincerely don’t find any character in the game relatable or charming. You (The protagonist) is an  is anywhere interesting. Her (your wife) is a bland character as well. Her past is f**led up as much as yours is. We don’t get much beyond that. The Copis somewhat relatable and fascinating as a character, but this kind of impression shouldn’t only exist in the antagonist. Music sounds good when I listen to them for the first time, but then it gets stale over time, just like the story. There is not much to be said about QoL other than some bugs I’ve experienced. They are minor and don’t harm the overall experience very much. There is no issue with optimization whatsoever in case you are wondering. Visuals…Uh what can I say it’s a 90-degree view third person game, definitely not looking at the right game for some super fancy graphics. Let’s just say it is good enough for you to solve the puzzle just like the gameplay. Even with stars like Daisy Ridley and James Mcavoy in, that would still be a hard pass. ' concept is quite creative, but gameplay and story are just dragging it back... If you are not a quick puzzle solver, don't consider buying this game because you are unlikely to find doing investigations and looping fun. Furthermore, staying in the same apartment and dealing with the same characters for the nth time can gradually kill your appetite for playing it. If you are, this is a decent adventure. Though you still probably don’t want to pay at the full price due to the short length story (4-6 hours, 8 hours for completion).

_childDocuments_.review: Good voiceacting and atmosphere, but it suffers from the "what do I do now" problem that most point-and-clicks have. The true ending of the game is only accessible through a series of counter-intuitive actions, and leaves you scratching your head as to what the moral of it all was. There's a "midpoint" in the story where you save your wife, redeem the villain, and create a happy ending for everyone. The game really should've stopped there, but instead it resets and makes it abundantly clear that there's more story to uncover. None of it is happy, and there is no satisfying epilogue.At least the game is short... but I still feel like I wasted about half the time and money I invested into playing this.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game with some interesting puzzle mechanics. There was just two major problems. And that was the story and pacing. The story would explode with information I wanted, then grind to a halt until the next solution. It really took the wind out of its sails. I'm not even sure how they would be able to fix that with this narrative.Games like Firewatch and Edith Finch and a lot of those story games end up with me watery eyed. This made me kinda go ugh 3/4 of the way through at a pivotal moment. 6/10. I think it's important to experience it once, and see some of the possibilities. Beyond that it hasn't left any lasting impact on me.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This bored me to sleep. Literally.The concept is great, they have huge names behind it and the trailer is extremely eye catching. So where did it go wrong?First,  there's maybe 30 minutes of original lines and possibilities. After that it's all repetition. But you need to get trough it to get to the good parts and endings. Over and over again. At least 4-5 turns just to get all the pieces into place. And then the progress resets so you need to do it again. If the game had save points, chapter select, better skip buttons, ANYTHING to cut down on hearing the same line over and over again.Then there's , they're clunky and not very responsive, making every step literal hell when timing and precision matters. And for certain endings it matters a lot.You tried to convince your wife to explain why there's a murderous Willem Dafoe with a massive strangling fetish after you two? Click. Click. Oh for fudge's sake you clicked on the knife instead of the dessert and accidentally murdered her. RESET. Again from, the start, go talk to her and oh now shes throwing a tantrum cause you clicked the wrong menu and you're both getting killed. Thanks honey. There's also a particularly annoying scene where On that note the artstyle is pretty ugh. Characters move and look like bad tech demos. The credits claim mocap was involved but its not very noticeable. The movements are clunky and rough, not to mention there's like 4 different rooms in the entire game and there's reused assets with the same texture, not even a color change...its ridiculously bad.Damn you Daisy Ridley. The entire ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ neighbourhood knows about your secret by now so just tell the [s]Green Go[/s] cop so he doesn't strangle me for the 5th time this evening.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: A modern way of telling a story featuring traditional point-and-click adventure features. Quite a few different, small ways to explore while still maintaining a mostly linear shape. If you like point-and-click genre games, I would definitely recommend this one. Word of caution: If exploring similar decisions, expect similar results. When trying to make forward progress, small steps can lead to a stale and repetitive experience. Don't overthink it - let the story play out.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes is a game developed by Luis Antonio and published by Annapurna InteractiveI was genuinely excited for this game when it was first announced, interesting concept, nice graphics, star-studded cast and overall, an Annapurna game but unfortunately, I was sorely disappointed by how the game turned out in it's final releaseThe game offers some nice graphics and overall a great aesthetic, although some ugly glitches here and there, it is pleasant all the same. However some of the animations are really bad and make me feel like I'm playing The Sims and not an adventure gameTwelve Minutes is boring. Just plain boring and incredibly repetitive. Some games, especially with some basic to mid-tier mechanics can be repetitive and boring if played for a long time, but, what separates those to Twelve Minutes is an interesting and gripping story, recent games such as Road 96 and The Forgotten City, which, although are repetitive in their own right, their stories are interesting and captivatingBut with Twelve Minutes, it overall has an interesting premise, but it's just boring and the endings - which by the by, I had to force myself to finish the only four hour campaign, unless you want to push yourself even more to find the hidden extras, which, guess what, I don't, are just underwhelmingThe game heralded at trying to be "like a movie", with a gripping story and a Groundhog Day-esque premise and, again, a star-studded cast but it just falls flat on everything except for the casting which was okay but nothing to write home aboutTwelve Minutes overall, however, is an okay game to play but a massive disappointment, and it does get boring really quickly, but I guess is an okay-ish to meh time travelling adventure game, but don't expect much else
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Playing a game that has James McAvoy,  Daisy Ridley, and...Willem Dafoe??Sitting through the opening credits, I get the same vibe I'd have watching some Awards-season arty-fartsy movie. I hope the experience matches the vibe..But I  gotta say, gaming sure has come into its own as medium over the years...Looking at the game mechanically, the whole "Groundhog Day" aesthetic wears itself out pretty quick. The story does play out slowly as you piece together train wreck of events. Despite "many angles" you can approach this game, I did feel ultimately  shoehorned to making very specific decisions.  I will say it's worth a spin. And that the Bad Ending (I did two of six endings) was probably one of the best bad endings I've seen in a game. I mean, I. FELT. GROSS/AWFUL.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Wild ride of a game, pretty good. Though its a bit too short to justify the pricetag. (but they do have some big name actors in it, so that probably has something to do with the price) Its fairly challenging to figure out. And it definitely wont give you any hints as to what to do. (outside of dialog and situations you find out yourself). Its a fun ride, but i would definitely wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: A-MAZING! I was really excited about this game since the first time I saw it one year before it's release. It was waaay better than I expected. Annapurna Interactive deserves an Oscar or something for how amazing they story telling skill is. _childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes is a complex, story-lead solo puzzle game with multiple endings and countless interactions to be had to uncover the interesting story.I played through the game initially but returned to try to complete all the endings and achievements which was a challenge to say the least...Twelve Minutes uses a birds eye view camera to try and distance yourself from the characters but with the unravelling story you cant help but feel yourself get dragged in...There's not too much more to say about this game, but if you've got the patience and motivation to uncover the story, it is well worth playing
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: The first hour or so of Twelve Minutes is when the game is at its best. The concept is still fresh and interesting, you haven't played the game enough for the long, unskippable dialogue to be annoying yet, you hear the phenomenal voice cast deliver new lines bit by bit and the story is still being puzzled out. For the first 2 hours I was really enjoying myself.Then the game gradually got more and more boring over time, the time-loop became grating and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot twist at the end really soured my experience. The game is okay, but if you're considering getting it, wait for a sale- it isn't worth full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Simply: It's not worth $25. At all.  ($4.99 mobile game, honestly)The first 2 hours is AMAZING!!!!!! And finding new "streams" and loops is very rewarding. As you start to figure out more and more, about half way through, it feels like a total slog fest. The payoffs are no longer rewarding and the actual "plot" makes less and less sense. By the end, the game endings felt more and more nonsensical and cheap. Because progression needs to be perfectly executed, it's easy to miss ONE little detail or timing and bring progression to a hault. There were two things that delayed progress for me until I found it on a guide (while expertly avoiding getting further points spoiled).
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very special game for a specific kind of gamer. I love time loops and point and click adventure games so this was right up my alley.There's a huge attention to detail. There are so many subtle ways the dialogue can go depending on your behaviour and the context. The puzzles were devious, the mystery was intriguing, the voice acting was great, and for an indie game the attention to detail is top notch.My only criticisms are:1. As the story unfolds, some specific chunks of dialogue become very annoying to repeat (please let us fast forward through multiple lines of dialogue instead of just one at a time)2. The ending doesn't meet the standards set by the rest of the game.But overall it's a positive experience and I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Is it possible to dislike a game after  enjoying 9/10ths of it and the puzzle construction of the time loop before hitting the ending where the whole thing falls apart? Well, yeah, demonstrably so. The unfortunate reality with endings that swerve out of nowhere like this, and stumbles with it like a Spirograph plot, is that the more you roll them around in your head, the worse they get and leave you with a bad taste in your mouth.The thing is, I can't think of a single reason why  had to be the big twist of the story (you'll know it when you see it) other than being for the sake of shock factor. By that, I mean I can think of several, and none of them are good.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: The first hour or two of the game are great, as you constantly feel like you're uncovering new secrets and slowly progressing the plot while figuring out puzzles.However, the second half of the game really drops the ball, as it drags on far longer than it needs to and starts to lose momentum. The writing in the first half is semi believable and pulls you in, but goes into completely absurd territory in the second half as it unleashes one 'twist' after another until the whole thing becomes ridiculous. Each 'loop' through the game events feels like it takes even longer than the previous ones as you have more and more steps to remember and perfect, causing the game's later stages to drag on forever.Finishing this game also requires completing exact specific steps in a specific order, with little to no variance on how those steps can be completed. If you miss one item or even so much as miss-time your click, even with the correct items, you get forced to restart. This leads to some serious frustration at the end of the game once you've gathered every clue and have a complete understanding of the story, since even with all the information, you'll still have to resort to pure trial and error (repeatedly) to finally get through to the end credits. Each time you experiment to find the solution and get it wrong, you have to sit through the entire sequence again.I really enjoyed the beginning of the game, but man, the last couple hours are pure pain and it really sours the experience.Consider looking at Sexy Brutale instead if you'd like a good time looping mystery game.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes provides an interesting, engaging way to tell a story, it just doesn't have an interesting story to tell. Big name voice actors are completely wasted on what I felt were poorly written lines and dialogue. It must have been extremely complex and I respect them for writing and plotting everything out. It feels like a very, very well polished proof of concept that managed to get full funding and big stars attached. If you really want to experience an interesting way to play a game and explore a narrative through time loops, just play Outer Wilds. Twelve Minutes locks you into tedious dialogue that you've seen at least a dozen or so times. It gets a little frustrating when you think you know what's going on but can't articulate it through the dialogue options. There's a very obvious tell right before a major plot point that you're not allowed to come to on your own, you have to awkwardly clunk through the controls to get there.It's a great concept. The art is interesting, the concept is intriguing, the story is just boring and uninteresting.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: A cool concept that just ends out being poorly executed and incredibly tedious. The route to the final parts of the game requires several stretches of the imagination and sitting through the exact same dialogue multiple times. The story has potential but is also deeply uncomfortable and should absolutely come with a content warning on the box as it deals with multiple incredibly sensitive subjects like  Most of the games budget has gone into getting big name voice actors who do excellent performances in a game that would be otherwise immensely forgettable without their presence.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: It starts out with an interesting premise, but it doesn't go far enough with it. Instead, it opts for an M. Night Shyamalan–esque twist that made me want to stop playing. Regrettably, I continued playing, to see the "ending", if you can call it that.Along the way, there are a lot of things that feel like they "should" work, but don't for reasons that feel very arbitrary. You can do things that seem to affect Willem Dafoe's behavior, and he says something different at first, but then justs go back into the same routine, and you have to do the whole loop again to try something else. In one case, a character searches rooms in a different order than usual just to prevent you from doing a seemingly cool and useful thing. In another, Daisy Ridley is upset, and says something like "Will you just say something?" but if you try to talk to her, there are no useful options, and then she gets upset that you aren't talking to her, even though you tried to, and runs out the door, ruining the loop. If you try to do certain things to throw off the timing, Willem Dafoe just shows up early and ruins it.There is a little bit of fun experimentation at first, but for the most part, it is a designer saying, "You didn't do it the specific way I decided, so you fail. Try again."Also, I spent an entire loop on hold with an insurance company, and it didn't even do the joke that I got connected right as the loop ended. Come on!
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: While it was a decently good experience. Looking back on my playthrough there were several elements I didnt like and make me say pass on this. Its a fun promising and unique game. But there are only so many elements to choose to do or not do and really the biggest change is the order in which you do things and which combination of things you choose to do. Often times you dont progress the story and you end up needing to repeat and only one path progresses things making this more linear than it comes off as. Realistically theres only one right answer. In the end it felt like a very slow paced game that takes probably under 4 hours to beat. I applaud the devs for trying something new. Good idea, just poorly executed
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game's worth a play-through. The acting's good, the writing's decent, the twists are intriguing, the concept's interesting. If you allow it, Twelve Minutes will make you feel for the characters and their dilemmas. It stands up well if you're looking at it as a choose-your-own-short-mystery-story rather than looking at it strictly as a story-driven game. Execution's maybe a 3.5/5. Overall, I'd give it a 4/5 for the concept, sound design, and the tricky landing. Go in mostly blind and you should have a good time--or twelve. How much you'd want to replay it for the various endings is probably hit-or-miss depending on how generous and patient you might be for a story like this.That being said, there are some problems that could turn someone off from liking the game. Soft-spoiler: Ten minute loops get really cramped after the 3rd or 4th loop when you've already been through the investigation part of the mystery. Don't ask me about who made dessert. Point is that if you don't have patience for doing the same tasks with interchangeable steps 20 times or you aren't genuinely interested in the mystery-story aspects and so you aren't willing to forgive some rough edges, this game will probably not be for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Congratulations to Willem Dafoe! Netflix's Death Note is no longer the low point of your career. Fire your agent, Billy.It's difficult to nail down exactly what the worst part of this game is. The models clipping through every surface is up there, Daisy Ridley dropping her American accent in literally the first line of dialogue, the puzzles are bad, the game doesn't let you try anything interesting. _childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: The storytelling carries the game. Exploration, changing things and living the same scenarios again and again is at the core of the game. The game relies on you figuring things out through trial and error, and by tampering with things.For such a small and short game, the aesthetics and animations could/should be better in my opinion. For me, picking plates and mugs out of your pocket in GTA style is a little immersion breaking, especially when the objects glitch in the characters hands. This could have used a little more effort and attention from the developers. Also, You might get a little frustrated at times when you can't skip the dialogue faster.The issues I had with small glitches, animation and graphics are not something that ruin the game, but if done properly, they would make the game more immersive.In the end, the game is fun to play and it will force you to think about the consequences of your actions and what to try next. Trying different combinations and seeing how things turn out is fun to follow!ProsStorytellingAtmosphereGameplayVoice actingConsSmall glitchesAnimation qualityPoor graphics, considering the game came out in 20218/10
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: On a scale from one to ten, I would only give this a generous 7. Game's a little bit glitchy though I wouldn't mind it on the second day of launch. Everything was great, but it felt more like a film rather than a game. Actors, soundtracks, the story line, everything is amazing, but I must say the gameplay is just unpolished. I did manage to finish the game, but only with the help of walkthrough at the later stage of the game because the experience is just unbearable.The reason why I say the game is unpolished is because every single stage of the game is so "scripted". The stages are designed in a way that you must complete those actions in a very specific order in order to progress, otherwise you have to go through everything again and again even with just one single misstep. In addition to that, the dialogues that are supposed to make up 90% of the game sometimes just don't make sense because it's so damn scripted! Not to spoil the story, but when you make your wife mad, she would refuse to talk to you anymore, but as you click on her again, she just acts like nothing happened. Or when she tells you she needs some time to think and you leave her alone, then all of the sudden she "calmly" asks you "cAn YoU sAY SomETHing??" like wtf?Overall the game is pretty great, but if you can bear through the experience that I mentioned above, then this game is definitely worth your time, though I might have set the standard a little too high considering it's an indie game.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Quite an interesting concept, reliving the same period of time over and over with elements changing as you gain more knowledge of the past with every loop. Definitely a great experience for anyone that likes a good mystery, well that and having your brain hurt. Having a blast! One of these days I'm gonna show that cop whose boss, probably, well maybe, if I get get him to stop punching me in the face first. Ouch!Finally shown the cop who's in charge, lets just say I had a bit of a light bulb moment and I'll leave it at that.Every time I thought the game couldn't get any stranger I was proven wrong, just wait until all is revealed and prepare to cringe like you've never cringed before.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible time loop/detective game with simple enough gameplay and an immersive storyline. It had both it's highs and lows, but as with any information based game, taking a break and thinking about it will help you tremendously and the moments when you figure something out makes it definitely worth it!I especially loved the sound design and atmosphere of the game, and with great voice acting you never feel like you don't want to listen to them.If you like Outer Wilds, you'll probably like this one! That goes the other way as well, If you like this game and haven't played Outer Wilds, you will most definitely like it so go play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: 12 Minutes is an excellent addition to the trifecta of psychological thriller/horror games that I have! The two others bein' the Five Nights At Freddy's series, and the Outlast series. The graphics is ok (at best), the overall story is very interesting, and the voice acting is fantastic!If you're a fan of Groundhog Day, then this game is for you! If you are into psychological thriller/horror games, then this game is for you!If I were to rate this game, I would give it a solid 4.5/5 stars!
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: A game with a very good idea and concept, but becomes increasingly frustrating (as maybe a time loop should feel?). The story unfolds quite fast, you learn everything in just under 2 hours, and then it becomes just trying to use the right dialogue line to get the credits. I have finished the game with 2 different endings and still am not sure what was everything about. The twists are very predictable at some point, the story takes an extremely dark turn and in the end nothing is explained to a player. There are many questions that are just left hanging in the air. Also it is quite expensive for a 3-4 hour experience. I feel that the design and ending should have been much better for a game of this calibre.Voice acting and idea is terrific though. If this gets adapted into a movie, it will probably be much better.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended but with a caveat - this game does outstay its welcome rather quickly. Its a great premise, excellent mystery, and i really enjoyed figuring out different things about the mystery each loop. I thought the style was good, the voice acting was excellent (especially Willem Dafoe), and in terms of technical performance i never experienced a bug or crash, just some performance dips and frame stuttering.But when progression through the later loops requires very specific sequences of events, where mistakes cannot be undone with a simple rewind function so you have to restart the loop and play through the specific sequence again, things start to transition from mysterious to tedious. And the ending, there wasn't a huge pay off and in my opinion it was way more edgy than it needed to be given how the story had progressed up to that point.Simply put did i get my moneys worth? Yes, but only just. Pick this up at a steam sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game! Very well written, interesting mystery to uncover.It actualyl feels like an interactive movie, with the characters reacting to all minor changes you make. I have never seen this in a game before.I do however think it does not have a satisfying clear ending. You can go to YouTube ect. to see what people theorize about the endings.If you are looking for more info:-) Point and Click/Dialogue driven game-) Playtime: 7-8 at least for the "true" ending, more if you try to get all achievments (= mostly all "endings").Negative points:-) Slightly grindy: You repeat a lot of stuff over and over. You get a lot of options to shorten certain parts or skip time, but it some parts are unskippable/have to be manually repeated.-) There are some bugs in the game, causing you to "lose" the current loop (i.e. you have to use the built-in time loop reset). It occured 2-3 times to me and costs you the loop each time, so around 5 minutes wasted for each attempt. These bugs can be avoided by letting the characters act the way they want to (instead of talking to them at weird points or standing in their pathing).
