_childDocuments_.review: Wow!!! I just cant believe what have I experienced. I was so hyped for this game since Microsoft e3 I guess, I thought the bald dude is a hitman like the actual hitman 47 but I was in the wrong :)) I really like time loop plots, and this game smashed it. I thought this game would be short but damn it's 8.5 hours and I just finished the first out of six endings! for people who have a sensitive spirit I recommend you don't play it cause " *****spoilers***** it made you stab your wife or hide and watch your wife gets murdered, I personally lost my sh*t after witnessing those things over and over ****spoilers**** " at some point, I just started crying because I couldn't get out of the loop. the plot twist is huge you cant never see it coming trust me xDDD.Graphics are acceptable but characters in first-person look like ps1 one games, since this game is the first of its kind I hope in the future they put more effort into this subject. The soundtracks are great Neil bones didn't disappoint hats off to him and the voice acting was on point!This game is the second masterpiece after "life is strange" which messed my mind and emotions. bravo10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game a lot and I think the psychological aspect was a lot of fun. I also really enjoyed the twist and finding all the little ways you get the game to move forward. All the voice acting is great, the top-down view is odd at first but I think really adds to the experience. The devs were extremely creative while making this game and I love the progression and finding out all the little hidden things.That being said, i do have to say that a lot of the endings, in fact all of the ones that actually complete the game, are incredibly difficult to get to. I enjoy games like this but it gets incredibly tedious in the ladder half of the game. I wouldn't recommend not buying this game because of this, but if you get easily frustrated with tedium then I would say you should reconsider.

_childDocuments_.review: Was waiting for this game since it was announced- I am sure the story is great but within the first 10 minutes I had character clipping into objects, characters talking over each other etc. It feels unpolished, animations feel janky and unfinished. Overall feels like an early access title unfortunately. Would pick up in sale for maybe under £10.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: After four hours of random clicking I got the "blissful ignorance" ending. I will admit that I got stuck twice, but with random clicking (actually NOT CLICKING AT ALL) I moved forward.Now I guess the true fun starts. Looking for different endings, paths and choices. No... this is not a game for everyone, this game could be boring, stupid, repeating itself, fun, multi-layered, ethical, philosophical and the plot twist can be seen from far away if the player has seen at least one time-loop movie. (I have realized the plot twist pretty much in my first loop, because it had to be set up that way. It actually reminded me of one great movie from an Australian production, also about a time loop.)But! James McAvoy and Daisy Ridley both provide an amazing performance. If I didn't know better, I would assume Daisy is American.Willem Defoe's performance is top notch too as one would expect from him. Overall I would say that in this (sub)genre of point-and-click games Twelve Minutes have enough to offer, but I can see why the game can be not as appreciated as it needs to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

Sorry but I really can't recommend it.(Although, besides the stupid story, the game mechanics are great. Using objects is performed well in the game)

_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything I thought it would be and I adore it. Having to try and figure out what to do and pay attention to all the little details is just fabulous. Add to that James MacAvoy (I adore him anyway, to get to listen to his voice and picture him saying the words is just auditory candy) and the extremely talented Willem Defoe (also a fan of his) and this is the perfect game.If you're all about running and gunning or can't think past your tanks and guns, this is not the game for you. But if you're a thinker and like games with a heavy dose of reality mixed in with your fantasy. You can't go wrong with this one.  I don't recommend for kids though.  Some of this is rather graphic. I'm not a squeamish type woman by any means but even I found myself turning my head...or maybe it's just the really good story telling that made me turn my head....or I may or may not have a photo of MacAvoy from Split on my other screen. Who knows...

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately Twelve Minutes is a letdown. Some negative reviews have said that the presentation is bland, and I think that's partially true, but there is something interesting about what they were going for. However, all of that potential is squandered by the uninteresting and cliche story. Anyone that's paying attention will see the final twist coming probably four or so loops before it's revealed because it's just the only thing that could happen next, and it's not even that interesting -- just shocking to be shocking. The gameplay is what you're expecting of a point-and-click adventure, but the puzzles require trial and error and one misstep can waste your entire loop (which was likely spent doing the same thing you've already done and watching the same reactions for 5+ minutes). And for what should be pretty simple dialog to script together (considering you do the same thing all the time), there are lots of awkward cuts and jump-ins and unfinished lines that draw you right out of any immersion you might have had. I understand that the forced waiting is meant to mirror the experience of the protagonist, but this forced waiting has absolutely nothing to do with the larger themes of the story.So much of the game is just screaming, "We made a time loop game and that means the writing and gameplay is smart and innovative by default." It isn't. Don't bother with this one -- if you want a good time-travel story game, give the re-release of Ghost Trick a try instead. It's much better written, has much more content, has incredible presentation and gameplay, and is only $5 USD more expensive (as of the time of writing).

Perhaps this kind of game-play can be considered to make you an active participant in the time-loop process, the feeling of frustration as once again you relive the same moments only to change one thing, fail and do it all over again.  Speaking of endings, I wasn't aware I had finished the game for the first time till after I looked at guides. In this sense, depending on where you end up, there may be a lack of closure. Further, it's reading guides which will largely strip the mystery of the game. It's like peeking behind the curtain of a magicians act. Looking back at how one played you will see at any given time you were likely performing the actions of several loops in a trial and error process to find the way forward. In actuality the way forward is pretty simple on a loop-by-loop basis. There's more to say, but I think many of the other reviews (both positive and negative) hit the nail on the head.

_childDocuments_.review: I set my expectations correctly given that this is an Annapurna game and to be fair, the concept is a great one, but for all its attempts at being compelling and layered, the end result is mostly just frustratingly bleh.  As well you know,  is a narrative game in which you find yourself trapped in a short time loop that you must relive repeatedly until you figure out how to escape it.  The story it tells is passable for the medium and it's a noble attempt at doing something different than its peers.  Obviously, the game relies on you trying different things as you repeat its short loop.  However, its heavily-scripted nature means that you're not really experimenting and more just hunting for the triggers to find another route and it often feels - at least to me - like the director (Luis Antonio) doesn't like to step aside and let the game be a game.  This is more like an arthouse film masquerading as a game and there are fewer considerations on how to make the game play well than on how to tell a convoluted tale.  And given the publisher, that's kind of on-brand and not necessarily a bad thing.Where the game feels weak, though, is in how it approaches the repetition.  Given the nature of the central mechanic, of course the game is going to be repetitive, but you'll be doing the same things over and over again only to change one minor thing here or there to divert the narrative flow, so to speak.  In other games of a similar nature, the loops allow for tons of variation where grander gestures or completely different routes can be explored by making choices early; in contrast, a lot of 's choices are made at the mid or late points so unless you give up and look at a guide, chances are you'll be repeating the same opening half of the run a tremendous amount of times before you figure out how to avoid it only to then find yourself in a different, repeating opening half.  In film form, we'd only see one or two complete loops before jumping 'in media res' so we can see what actually changes each go.  Ever seen ? Imagine if every cut had the entire running sequence in full, or maybe a  where we see each and every day completely - that's kind of how this game plays out and it's annoying.  This is what I mean about not allowing the game to be a game.  On top of that, you can sort of semi-skip dialogue, but it's more like a fast-forward than a full skip so you only save seconds.  Then you have camera work and artsy dissolves and slow zooms, etc.  It makes it a lot less fun to explore than if there were some sort of tree to navigate like in .  This results in the game becoming rote and mundane instead of fascinating and compelling because you're so bored by the time something new happens and well, the payoff isn't ever that mind-blowing except perhaps once.On a technical level, it's well put together.  There's no weirdness I encountered and the graphics and lighting all serve their purpose.  The A-list actors don't really bring much to the table, though.  Anybody could have lent their voices, probably at a lower cost, and nothing would change.  The core of the game is centered more on presentation than anything else and as far as that goes, I think it succeeds.And it kind of make sense - Antonio's credits are all art-based (on fantastic games, mind you) so  has an artist's eye rather than a game designer's one.  I don't mean that as an insult, either; as an art piece,  is a fantastic piece of work.  It just could have played a lot better.

_childDocuments_.review: I was intrigued at first, but gets old and repetitive real quick. I know its meant to be frustrating as with any protagonist that's stuck in a time loop, (and I think that's quite a genius ludonarrative consistency) but Imagine watching groundhog day but you have to watch the loops in its ENTIRETY EVERY TIME, no cuts, no montages. That's how the game is like, only with 12 minute loops.PROS:High production value, clear and easy to understand UX. I appreciate the few 'shortcuts' that the devs implemented into the conversations, though I hope there were more of them. dialogue and voice acting has a lot of variety, and reacts appropriately to context in a surprisingly flexible way.Mysterious and intriguing story that hooks player to find out more.CONS:The puzzles are convoluted and contrived, only to trigger in a very specific and sometimes illogical condition.The game functions sort of like a real time point-and-click adventure, but instead of making you feel smart that you solved a logical puzzle, in Twelve minutes the puzzles are largely conversation/dialogue based, which some times feels stiff and unnatural, and less rewarding. There are many situations where I know what I want to say or ask the other character, but because I haven't said or went down a specific dialogue path, I don't have that option and its frustrating to replay the whole loop again just to find that one obscure thing to unlock the dialogue. It feels very 'gamey' at those points in the game, where you KNOW the answer to the puzzle but the game decides not to let you progress. This breaks immersion as the game tries very hard to be serious and dramatic, but fails as there are many instances where the most rational or logical way to deal with the situation wasn't an option simply due to the way the puzzles are designed/structured.OVERALL:I feel like the game's scope is a little too small and simple, the characters are not fleshed out, has questionable motives, and the conclusion doesn't make much sense and is disappointingly contrived.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game blind not knowing anything about it until yesterday when I booted it up. It's good. The acting is great, the optimization is great, the art is great, the music is great. You can play through it without really needing a walkthrough--which helped my immersion a lot. It's got all the components you need for a point-and-click puzzle. The writing may be hit-or-miss with some folks, but I personally liked it. As-of the time of this review: the game *does* get repetitive towards the later parts of the game while you're going through the steps required to reach each new 'branch' of the twelve minutes you're afforded. A lot of the paths overlap and the game  to alleviate some of the tedium by making the protagonist skip dialogue that's already been done--but the game really could use a rudimentary "undo" or "rewind" function even despite this. If you've got the patience for that kind of thing, then you're golden. If they ever add a rewind feature: even better.There's only one part of the game I feel is truly sinful in its poor implementation. The game up to a certain point teaches you to leave certain items in-place where they are (), until all of a sudden the game punishes you for not having picked something up (). But even this "sin" is relatively tame and just makes you roll your eyes for one loop. The game is worth playing for sure. I hope they can churn out similar games in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this is a pretty okay game. If you're super into the timeloop theme and or point and click puzzle games then you will most likely get some enjoyment out of it. On top of that one or two of the puzzles are way to specific in the sense that you have to do a specific thing after doing all these other things in a very specific order, without any good hints on what that exact thing is. For the most part, everything you do makes sense, however the way you get there can be a little obscure or hard to find out at times. This can get pretty frustrating considering the game gives you little to no help with puzzles, and failing can force you to sit through a minute of dialogue that you have seen countless times before. The story also is pretty decent up until the twist, which is very laughable and hard to take serious at all (when i reached it i was in awe at how stupid it was and just sat there for a whole timeloop dumbfounded). Either way, even through its flaws, this was still an enjoyable experience for me. I'd give it like a 6.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: The non-spoiler part: Wow this game is awful. I went in entirely blind to play on stream. I knew the basic concept and found it really interesting, but progressing through the game got more and more absurdly bad, to the point where I could barely make it through the ending because I was laughing too hard. The writing is comically terrible, with pretty extreme emotional non sequiturs. It plays like a university film student's "edgy" senior project. If the egregious story problems weren't bad enough, there are also plenty of little annoying things that just make the game unpleasant to play, like the inconsistency of when and how much you can fast forward, some inconsistency in when conversation options are grayed out or not, some timing issues that can ruin a whole loop just because you attempted an action a fraction of a second early, etc. I cannot recommend enough that you do not waste $25 on this. The whole thing is bizarre to the point of absurdity, and while I enjoyed sharing my disbelief while playing with chat, had I come to it just wanting to play an interesting game I would have been very disappointed.On the upside, you can make your character sit and noisily eat the lovely dessert your wife made you while she sobs on the couch or gets handcuffed and thrown to the ground, so plus one star for that. The spoiler part: There are a lot of pretty distasteful choices and statements that you're forced to make over and over again to progress the game. You're forced to drug your wife, to tell her that you'll support her and then immediately not do it, and to watch her get beaten and murdered. A major storyline point is all about calling a child born to unwed parents a "bastard" and "monster" because...??? I guess just because he was born of an affair??? And then suddenly there's an incest angle that feels built exclusively to be edgy while 1) not making any sense at all and 2) not even being really explored in any implications? It's bad. Watch it somewhere if you're curious, but don't bother playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Mediocre story, production values, and the voice acting is surprisingly bad from two and a half talented actors. Falls into the usual adventure game trap of trying to guess the developer's logic, which is pathetic for a game that has three characters and maybe fifteen-ish interactable items, and another half dozen things to use them on. You'll be asking why interacting with a thing or person with an object gives you only one possible interaction.The game is easily limited enough that, had they just gotten cheaper voice actors, every potential interaction could have been explored. Why can't I throw water at my wife? Also, that's her name... wife. Is a name to help me get attached to the character too much to ask? I don't believe anyone who says this game is longer than 8 hours. You might get 10 out of it if you go for the alternate endings, but the ending you're most likely to get the first time feels like the canon ending, so why bother going for the rest. Especially when you have to repeat even more of the same boring loop that you will be sick of by that point. And, as for the endings... Well, if you want to feel like you wasted a few hours of your life, play the game, because terming the big reveals in this story unsatisfying would be an understatement. They're utterly contrived and pointless. Since you have no investment in any of these characters because they're all cardboard cutouts, the reveals don't even matter, leading you to think "Huh... That's stupid. Did M. Night write this?" rather than anything about the plot. I'm a sucker for time loops. Groundhog Day, Majora's Mask, a dozen other things that it'd be a spoiler to reveal they were time loops. But this is the Endless Eight of video games. You want time loops done right? Go play Outer Wilds.

_childDocuments_.review: There is A LOT to be desired here, and A LOT MORE missed opportunities over a 7 year development period. I'm questioning why a game so hollow had so much time invested into it, only to give us what we have. That being an illusion of a much bigger title that doesn't exist.+ It's a Time Loop mechanic. That is fun+ Plenty of things to grab and use and talk about and explore to slowly uncover the story+ Great voice acting and performances+ Solid music and visuals+ Clever ways to introduce story elements- Story is bad :(. - Endings are pointless, as they're all the same. So it should be "ending".- Time looping because you choose a single incorrect dialogue option gets very tiresome, and there isn't a way to really reconcile. Other time loop related games give you opportunities to reconcile by allowing you to do other things to forward the progress/understanding of what is happening before re-looping. This game has no such thing. You screw up, you may as well start over. It gets very exhausting very quickly.- Big missed opportunities that feel like the developers wanted to implement but did not (such as items or objects carrying over from one loop to the next). Whether it was because they needed to get this game out or couldn't figure out how to code it well is beyond me. - As stated, unused items or pieces in the environments are basically just filler. _childDocuments_.review: I was really excited when I first saw Twelve Minutes at E3 2019. Timeloops have always been a facinating concept to me and I am always happy when developers utilize games to tell a unique story. Luis Antonio have created a great story with Twelve Minutes, which definitely has grabbed my attention.I don't want to spoil anything from the game itself, as most of the fun comes from discovering how to unfold the plot. However I would have liked more objects and ways to get different or similar scenarios, as the way to achieve the endings can be quite repetative. I understand it is a timeloop, but even more ways to achieve the same outcome would be a great addition to an already great game.The voice acting is done beautifully with great voice acting from James McAvoy, Daisy Ridey and Willem Dafoe. Some parts of me would have loved to have even more intense confrontations between the voice actors as some interractions seem a bit hollow at times, however with the pandemic and the structure of the game I can see how this would be difficult to attain.All in all I think the game is a bit short and would have loved to play and interact more with the game, however the story itself creates a great mystery ontop of an already interesting concept. I love how the game turned out and watch with interest in the next stories Luis Antonio and his team have for us!If you don't want to pay for the already low price I would highly recommend it on any sale!

_childDocuments_.review: Christ on a cracker I had issues with this game. For a game that's selling itself as "blending the dream-like tension of THE SHINING with the claustrophobia of REAR WINDOW and the fragmented structure of MEMENTO" you'd think think it would actually hit any of those beats. Game play wise: it's a point and click, but it's a specifically timed point and click. If you fast forward at the wrong moment, you brush off your wife and potentially derail your loop. Or you fail to get to the closet before she sees you. It's a precise level of timing that could be interesting, if you had any clue in terms of escalation. The only way you can tell by sight is the paintings. You will most likely hit a dead end of cycling through bland loving dialogue and brutal murder, which gets grating since your time loop is literally twelve minutes at the longest. Oh, and if you reached an ending you have to completely wipe your progress to see alternate scenes/endings, in addition to collecting achievements (unless you magically know to check paintings every loop progress and water the plant every loop). So a fresh start every time, which means you sink another 2-3hrs of figuring out what to do with the two other vents in the apartments. Graphics: Once you cross the intro screen and get into your apartment, you spends almost the entire rest of your time in a one bedroom. You're faceless, your wife is faceless, and the cop has a beard. That's what you get. You get nothing more, nothing less. Story wise: what the hell is the writing? It's a deluge of edgy writer cliches stacked onto each other and wrapped in a time loop trench coat. It's needlessly brutal to the female character and shallow as hell towards the male characters, to the point that only my burning desire to finish what I start. It's taking the concept of a tragedy to 90's era extremes to the point that it was funny to get to the point where the main character wakes up again, after being exposed to the dark heart of the game, and has to continue with his time loop because I forgot to use the spoon last loop. Sorry mate. TL;DR - game is tolerable, but unsatisfying. Don't trust games that use the Shining carpet.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't mind the bad graphics, I expected that, since this is an indie game.I don't mind the glitches and bugs, I expected those, since this is an indie game.But to have such a simple and generic story, with no depth at all, that I did not expect, and cannot excuse.And the design, while somewhat unique, is just so flat. While the story is just boring, finding the gameplay in this state feels even worse, there is just so much unused potential. Your choices are very limited, and the interesting implications of the time loop are basically not explored at all.You might say that this game has a great voice cast, and that is true. But the sound design just ruins it! How can the voices of these famous actors flow when the lines feel so crudely put together, not to mention the wholly uninspired dialogue?The only well-crafted aspect of this game is the advertising, and it certainly fooled me. There have been a number of great indie games that are so unique in their composition that even explaining them would be a spoiler. Stanley Parable, Outer Wilds, Undertale, these are games where you have to say to your friends: "Don't read any reviews, just play it, trust me!" It's clear that the trailers for this game are meant to evoke this feeling.This game costs 20 dollars, and it's just 5 hours of... nothing. There's really nothing there. If it cost 5 dollars maybe I could play it and put it down without thinking about it again, without feeling so cheated. I never review games negatively, but Twelve Minutes just convinced me. 5 hours is enough time so that a refund is impossible. I didn't want to stop playing the game because I seriously thought something interesting was still coming. But then the game just ended without anything memorable happening.In conclusion: Do not buy this game, it's a waste of money. Play Outer Wilds instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Good start, terrible ending. Very repetitive.*The Good*The beginning uses the time loop very well, the mystery is fresh and there's a few things to unravel. The atmosphere is great, and throughout the start I was intrigued to what would happen next.The voice acting is very good. There is a caveat to this. The voice lines themselves are great. The direction and utilisation of them could have been much better.There are a lot of minor details the game does right. The main character adjusts their reaction to the wife initially as the time loop continues. They get more used to things happening to them, like getting hurt. They are quicker to rudely brush off the wife initially to figure out whats going on. *The Bad*The game as it progresses after a certain point becomes nonsensical. The story felt like it was trying to throw you for a loop for the sake of it, rather than trying to create an interesting story. And the way they try to "shock" you is extremely dumb and makes no sense. A much simpler story would have been more interesting. Honestly, the game's story is like a roller-coaster except the track breaks two thirds of the way into the ride.There are not a lot of interactions in this game. There are limited items and limited environment pieces to use them with. The game felt like there were two distinct paths and they were the only paths that mattered because you just had to talk to people, that was it. There was very little experimentation on what you could do in a time loop game which felt very disappointing, and it felt like a repetitive chore half way through the game.The voices themselves are great, but the direction is off. You could go from an emotionally sounding voice line, to one that is happy when that clearly makes no sense. Generally this is hard to do in games and would require multiple different versions of the same voice lines to convey the tone and feelings of the character based on prior moments, but for a game built entirely on these kinds of interactions and how you manipulate time for desired effects, this is something that is sorely lacking in this game.*Conclusion*If you care about story, you will either not mind the last third of the game, or dislike it immensely. If you care about gameplay, it is a very good start, but it gets repetitive quickly with its lack of items and object interactions.If you love the idea of time loops like myself, I would buy it on sale. The game is very short. Get Outer Wilds instead if you don't mind a sci-fi setting, it is a much longer game with a mystery that is brilliant throughout the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks shiny, but rotten at the core.Twelve Minutes has all the trappings of an indie gem.  It's got a high-concept premise, a unique visual style, and prestigious talent attached.  But it ends up being one of the most profoundly unpleasant things I've played in quite a while.The premise is simple enough: you play a nameless man (voiced by James McAvoy) coming home to his wife (Daisy Ridley) who has something happy to tell him - but the evening is interrupted by the arrival of a cop (Willem DaFoe) who proceeds to "arrest" and murder both of you...... and then you wake up, and it happens again.  The loop resets if you die, or if you leave your apartment, or if the titular twelve minutes runs out, and the only thing you keep between resets is any knowledge you've acquired.The entire game is presented from a top-down perspective (pictured) and gameplay is point-and-click adventure-game style shenanigans.It looks good, and initially it hooked me.  But by the time the credits rolled, my viewpoint had changed.  (And it's not a terribly long game, although it often feels like it is.)There are three key problems with Twelve Minutes.The first is that it's tedious.  Solving the mystery requires watching the same scenes play out, again and again, as you experiment with minor changes and hope that this time you'll unlock something new.  Often you don't, meaning you've wasted your time and will have to do it again.  To add insult to injury, sometimes the game is finicky about recognising when you *have* unlocked something.  I had to repeat some loops to re-hear a piece of dialogue that I swear I'd already heard.  There are some concessions to avoiding tedium.  You can fast-forward dialogue that you've heard before - but not if you could theoretically interrupt it but are choosing not to.  There are also times when you can skip straight to the cop arriving - but even then, there's still a lot of waiting around.  I ended up using a walkthrough for some of the later bits because I couldn't bear the idea of another 12-minute loop with nothing to show for it.The second problem is that it's ugly.  This game needs content warnings - and so MANY content warnings.  Violence (and particularly violence against women), pregnancy (and violence against pregnant women), suicide, domestic abuse, sick kids, police violence, torture, murder, home invasion.... the list goes on (including a couple whose inclusion would spoil the ending of the game).  And it's not just that these things happen, but that in many cases the player is actively inciting them, or choosing to stand by passively while they happen, for the purpose of advancing the plot.  And it's not cartoonish or heightened - they're presented with the intimacy and emotional weight of a real home invasion.  And you watch them *again* and *again* and *again* as you try and work out what to do next.The third - and most overwhelming - problem with the game is that there's nothing at its core.  When it's all over, you realise that all the gimmicks of the game exist only to hide the reality that both its central mystery and its resolution are exceedingly juvenile, deeply contrived, and chosen exclusively for their shock value.Nothing that happens makes sense when you think about it even a little.  It's a Rube Goldberg machine of plot, self-justifying and wildly implausible, but unlike the tradition of twist-ending short fiction it's drawing from, it doesn't ultimately *mean* anything.  There's no lesson here, no philosophical question.  It's a "gotcha" moment, stretched excruciatingly into a tired, hacky game.  I've given it a grade of "C", and it really only rates that high because it's (unfortunately) memorable, and because it's undeniably made with imagination, enthusiasm and innovation.  It's not the kind of complete train-wreck I give Ds or Fs to - it's just deeply misguided.Not recommended.  Feel free to spoil yourself on the ending by Googling.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a preliminary review with which I'm basically recommending to wait with a purchase for now. The game isn't terrible, but it's definitely not the intricately designed, well-polished time-loop experience that many of us have hoped for. In fact, I find it thoroughly mediocre so far. While there are some interesting ideas, they are outweighed by lots of issues and signs of shoddy design:- Conversations often make no sense, characters often say things that don't reflect what they already have been told. Having renowned actors to voice the characters isn't worth much if the game fails to build believable conversations out of the voiced lines. This happens throughout many conversations, and it is even more problematic since the dialogue makes up half of the gameplay.- The game often doesn't give me the option to say things that, in my opinion, would be helpful and make sense. This is frustrating because it feels like the game has artificial difficulty; it ignores actions that would make sense and instead forces you to find solutions that actually make less sense.- Interactions with objects often follow arbitrary rules that aren't clear. This can lead to situations where you tried something already, but it didn't work, and you came to the conclusion that it's just one of the many things that the game doesn't let you do - when it in fact just wants you to do it in a slightly different way or at a different time.- There aren't enough different things to do to make the start of the loop interesting after the first 10 times or so, and there's no way to save a state within the loop, so the game gets repetitive and a bit boring rather fast.- The game seems very eager to kill me or otherwise set me up for failure, which means that I have to repeat everything from the start of the loop again. It feels like the game doesn't actually have much content and uses this mechanic to stretch out the somewhat thin experience, but I can't say that for sure yet.I'll probably continue playing it, but unless the game has something splendid in stock for me that I don't see yet, I really don't think it's worth the asking price and wouldn't feel comfortable recommending it - as sad as that is, for a game that sounded so interesting in concept. It's still worth a shot if you like puzzle thrillers with a time-loop mechanic and can look past the issues, but I'd wait for a 40% off sale at least.I haven't completed the game yet and my opinion might change depending on how things go, but the problems that I listed above are definitely present. If someone's interested, I could give a list of concrete examples, but it would spoil parts of the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Say what you will, but I thought that this was a really neat game. (Mind you, I absolutely adore the "Groundhog Day" genre, so any attempt to capture it in a video game will get a lot of grace from me.)Now, you've likely heard some complaints about the controversial storyline that unfolds, but so long as you're not squeamish, it's pretty impressively shocking. (If you are squeamish, then... yeah, you might as well just head on over to a safer game.)The game is still pretty short and simple, however, so keep the smaller price tag in mind and -- as always -- try to buy while it's on sale.That said, for those obscure decisions that you might make and for which the developers DID account (of which there are a decent number), you'll find some entertaining ways to mess around with the game world. If you pay close enough attention, you'll also notice some fun details in relation to how your character becomes more accustomed to the repeated horrors over time.The only other thing that I'll say is that I could only picture Chris Pratt as the voice actor, not James McAvoy; James clearly did his best Star Lord impression during recording.

_childDocuments_.review: I could just be like others and tell you how great the graphis, animations and the voice actors are. I could tell you how aMaZiNg these narrative twists are, and that this game is perfect for people, that love to solve mystery. But then I would just describe you how literally all narrative games are based on.So let's get real:After some hours of playing, you'll get sick of it. In the first few, you'll listen to every detail of the conversations, afterwards you just start skipping and already know what you want to answer to this and already know where you have to move and what to grab. You are constantly prepared. This argument is mainly used as a reason for why this game is not as good as everyone says. But isn't this "mechanical, always prepared and bored or uninterested attitude the exact representation of how the protagonist feels after hours of repeating the same minutes of his life over and over again? You hate specific people at the same time he hates them, but start forgiving as soon as he does. This influence Twelve Minutes has on you, is exactly the reason why this Game is so playworthy!I also like the way how the psychological, dark atmosphere maintainly grows in each loop you discover new informations. I'm not only talking about the music. THE WHOLE STORY tests your morals and forces you to think about it. In this game you've got many opportunities. You can take it seriously or just fool around and stab everyone! It doesn't matter anyway since the day repeats itself over and over again, at least until you found out the truth. Even when you finished an ending and replay it, you'll realize a lot of easter eggs in this game the more you repeat it. The "mission" to solve the mystery though, becomes exhaustingly boring.This game isn't for people that cannot see any violent actions, but the game is PEGI 18 rated.However, I really enjoyed playing this game and I'm waiting for more!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very good and I love it,     however it takes forever to progress in the game, and if you're just learning the game like I was, it takes forever to try and find the next step in the lore. There are way too many options to choose from and a lot of the times the right one never seems to be the on that's your first pick.     However i DO love the story line, beautifully made and is very easy to see how much work went in to this. The animation could be smoother, but it's still good for a free-moving game.    I totally recommend this game, but I would only suggest it if you have a lot of time and patience. There are subtle hints in the game here and there, but not enough to really get it unless you keep replaying the scene over and over again, and at that point the hint it worthless. That's really my only suggestion for this game. Definitely will continue to play every now and then for the different endings, but I know it'll be boring. I do think each day should have a little more variety, instead of having the the dialogue each time you replay the scene. But it's fine to me.In conclusions, boring game play after a while, but the lore makes up for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Captivating, Addicting, Entertaining and many more that I can't put out in words. For such a simple game, and the old fashioned concept of a time loop, Luis Antonio makes a game truly like no other. With help from the wonderful voices of James McAvoy, Daisy Ridley and Willem Dafoe, this truly fascinating thriller is a must play.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: A well-paced time loop mystery, with a great score and a good cast.It does need to be said this game doesn't give you much in the way of 'next steps suggestion' as is often seen in most modern games (arrows, blips on maps, characters blurting out the answer) so you may find yourself a bit lost at times.But that's when you can just loop again and try something new (try anything new). There'll always be something to pick up on.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I have a love-hate relationship with this one. this review will contain spoilers.--the game starts off extremely strong. the topdown aspect keeps it impersonal enough to view it extrospectively, but you still become completely immersed in the narrative.but then you get stuck in the loops.... at first, you simply appear to be experiencing the frustration of being stuck in the loop. as it goes on, it becomes apparent that you are just experiencing oversights in design. not being able to skip dialogue you have heard exactly the same multiple times around in any meaningful way is super frustrating from a UX perspective. I question why they were able to recruit a star studded cast like this but weren't able to record them speaking the same lines a couple of times so you wouldnt have to hear the exact same cadence time after time. I found myself getting irritated at Her humming the tune at the start of the loops, even though it has a role as a timer, because of its repetition. narratively, I was extremely capitvated at the early and mid parts of the game. The research system they have implemented is really intuitive! but as you go through the story, becoming more detached from the story due to UX oversights, the drive to discover more slowly gets squashed.  I have 6 hours at time of review and 3 achievements, but discovered more endings before having all the requirements to unlock the achievements. there is more things I wish i knew about the narrative, like I recommend it for its creative use of video game as story telling device, but ultimately i think this one was a little undercooked and would have benefit a lot from an extra year in development. 5.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game thinks that it's way better than it is. Cool concept but the only reason anyone would really like it is because it makes them feel smart for doing the same thing over and over again, in a slightly different way each time. Repetitive and convoluted, whilst also just plain not fun. The main redeeming quality is that the story is quite good but even that becomes predictable, and once you already know what is going to happen you still have to do the same thing over and over again unless you do all the exact right things in a short number of loops.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the name, the game is, in fact, longer than 12 Minutes...Jokes aside, this game is an interesting experience. It can be described as a "point and click" heavily narrative driven game. Upon reaching their apartment, the protagonist goes about his night with his wife, some events take place but after about 12 minutes, time will loop and he will restart at the beginning. Likewise, the loop will trigger if he tries to leave the apartment, or if he somehow gets hurt or injured. To uncover the lingering mysteries behind the surprise appearance of a police officer that wants to arrest the couple, using the time loop you should strive to uncover more and more information each time, pursuing more avenues and different tactics to reach a different outcome within the limited options you have at your disposal. There is a deep story hidden within to uncover.The concept is interesting and enjoyable, though I will say sometimes it becomes a drag to have to wait for some events to happen, there are certain actions you can do to fast forward time on the loops, but sometimes some necessary sequences will take up more time that cannot be sped up in any way, this gets kind of annoying when you're trying to re-do some set of actions to try something else at the end, only to have to wait for some characters to finish a dialogue. If you absolutely know what to do it is possible to minimize the amount of repetition, but for a first, blind playthrough, most players will probably use several loops to learn some necessary information to proceed with the deeper plot.That may just be nitpicking though, the game on its own is very enjoyable. Depending on how much you'd like to experiment on different outcomes of doing certain things or choosing certain conversation options, the main game should take at the very least 6 hours. For me it was worth the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not worth your time or money. I don't know what was the point of hiring all those big name actors just to voice a plot they found on a used napkin. The ending is garbage. it's not 'artistic' its not even giving some kind of moral message, it's just dumb.The puzzle solving is mediocre at best and dodgy at worst. in a time loop game, consistency in the way characters act is the only thing we have going for us, so why do the characters sometimes act in inconsistent and illogical ways?It took me 10 hours to reach story end, and for $35 that's one hell of a scam. If you really want to know what happens, watch a play through on youtube. You will get all the frustration of the terrible ending without the insult of being charged for this crap.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: There seems to be a lot of blind hate on this game due to the looping nature of it, but... That's kind of the point of a game that has a timeloop as a mechanic, is it not? I'll try to give a slightly different perspective on this game.Twelve minutes is a relatively short but very intriguing adventure puzzle game where you have to figure out the root cause of said time looping, allowing you to make different choices every time to see what new information you can extract. From the start I was intrigued, since I always find time paradoxes to be conceptually very interesting, though I reserved my judgement since getting time paradox stories right is difficult.I have to say that after playing the game and getting every ending - I am very happy with the experience.The game is not perfect, it has some logical flaws and I understand why some people can get frustrated by the looping nature, especially if you get stuck. However I implore you to persevere and give this game a chance.There's nothing else quite like it, the story is intriguing and interesting, the gameplay loop whilst not groundbreaking is perfectly fit for this type of game and the level of detail on the branching story is really well done.Given how cheap it is and how you can finish this game in 5-10 hours (depending on how in depth you want to explore and how many endings you want to reach) I think this is a solid game and worth a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: This one... is a difficult one for me. I am really torn.This game does a lot of things really well, and a lot of things not so well. It's got a great concept, but falls flat on the execution.I'll go with a thumbs down for this, because of the really steep price for so little game, but it might be nice on a strong sale.Very light spoilers ahead.The game is basically a puzzle game, that works with time-loops, and expects you to basically solve a sort of puzzle per loop that you do.Now when you think of good puzzles, you think of how all you need is all the pieces, and that you, as the player, have to figure out the solution. That part the game does really well.However, one thing you rarely think about, since it is usually obvious, is that you also need to have an idea for what the puzzle will look like once it is solved. And that is what this game really struggles with. It expects you to do something, but you don't really have a way to tell if you solved anything, or if you did anything right.Imagine you were solving a jigsaw puzzle, but every time you put a piece in the wrong spot, you get reset to the beginning. But then, you have that one go at it where you do everything perfectly, and all the pieces align and you think you are done... but then it resets anyway.That's what this game felt like around the middle point. It felt like I solved everything I had to and I just had to finish it off. But then that... didn't finish it off, and I didn't know what the game expected me to do anymore.The beginning of the game starts fairly open, where you can fool around and figure some things out. As mentioned, it all comes together in the middle point, where it feels like you finally solved everything, when in reality you didn't.The end part of the game is... very repetitive, dragged out and unforgiving. The game expects you do a number of things in a specific order. I am willing to bet there's people out there that took things a step too far, because it made sense, and ran into a wall, because they were supposed to do that a bit later.And, honest to god, I would have never figured out how to finish off the game if I hadn't resorted to a guide. The ending is... really disappointing, to be honest. All that good buildup, only to slow down and end so poorly.The game is fairly fleshed out, though not to a degree a game like this needed. Again, it does a lot of things really in some parts, and falls flat in others.As for voiceacting, it is just as mixed. Some voicelines are done super well and convincingly, while others don't make a ton of sense in the way they were emphasized. It feels like the direction wasn't really there, and the actors had to voice each line separately, sometimes without enough context.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Looping is fun. But only 12 minutes til the loop reset (which actually like only 5min of free roaming then the rest is just follow the script)? That's hardy allow players to do anything *meaningful*. It's so frustrated being in the middle of a conversation and then BAM!!, try talking faster again next loop. Besides, the more we progress, the more the game need us to "set up" those steps. Combining with the clunky control, and don't know what to do next, it's so annoying to redo another loop. Which ruin the fun of this game as "a game". Despite the acting and story is somewhat great, it doesn't save the game from this thumb down.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story but repetition gets old fast. I tend to agree with what appears to be about half the reviewers of this game that the repetition and cost of mistakes really saps the fun out of this game. And I typically enjoy a good thoughtful puzzle with interesting story lines. I was hooked for the first hour or so and then, well, see below.There were three puzzle items in this game that were very difficult to figure out and I don't feel the game gave enough hints in character dialog as to their importance, I doubt I would have figured them out without looking up hints. However, my frustration also could have been due to finding out several pieces of information out of order. Game appeared to be confused about who I had talked to about what and what dialog I had chosen to skip, leading me to get dialogue about a particular subject before I initiated the first dialog about it in the intended way, which ruined the immersion (this was before I looked up any hints and what started me down the path of confusion/frustration).tl;dr Game gets repetitive, is short game for the price point (ignoring the time it takes you to fix your mistakes), wants you to do things in a specific order that is not always apparent.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: The game is alright, beginning to middle, but the ending, specifically the twist, ruined most of the experience for me.Spoilers beyond, obviously.Emotionally manipulating the player with a "you were the bad guy the whole time!", with no way to act on it or figure it out beforehand.Just watch someone else play it, and save yourself the money.(FYI my internet was out while I played, so it didn't save most of my play-time. I have indeed beaten the game myself, and thoroughly enjoyed those 8 hours until the end.)

_childDocuments_.review: very good but short and with a really weird twist ending. Best to play this game immersed like you are in a movie. also some of the puzzles are frustratingly hard because you have to keep repeating the same loop with random ideas in your head on what to do next until you finally figure out the next step. _childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty fun and intriguing game! _childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of writing, visuals and concepts -absolute trash. The game has a top down view for some reason that just makes the game look awkward. It doesn't do anything visually interesting. In terms of music, it's equally trash. The devs spent all budget on big-name actors. Should've spent more on writing. I get why this game only has a 74 OpenCritic score.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I really like puzzle room games, but this misses the mark for me.In most puzzle games you find out a big step, and then each loop you progress a little further. This one feels far more minor increments, and often you're stuck with the same ending because something doesn't work quite the way you want to.The stellar voice cast was pointless. You can not tell it was James McAvoy, or Daisy Ridley and as good actors as they are -- their stardom is lost. Dafoe you can tell it's him, but it doesn't have the same power I've come to expect of him.Also, there are bugs. Which is surprising considering it's a finessed small gameplay loop. At least once the cop dragging me got me stuck on my wife's body.I feel sad giving this a thumbs down, as I love the idea. It's just not it.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Light spoilers within: I really wanted to love this game - I love groundhog day tropes! But then I played it for a couple of hours and got SO annoyed and bored that I looked up spoilers, because no matter what I did, I couldn't finish the loop. And then it turns out the only things I did wrong for each of my approaches were little small details that don't totally make sense structurally (like, they don't seem like they would be critical to the completion of the loop). And some of my approaches IMO should have worked because I survived them. Add that frustration to the general slowness of redoing the same. dang. thing. over and over again (yeah you can skip forward dialogue and fast-pass time but once you realize you've messed up with the cop, for example, you have to sit through the whole dang thing until you can try again). This game wears out its welcome really quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes has a bunch of good ideas that end up going nowhere. The gameplay is interesting, but incredibly repetitive. For example, if you make progress but forgot to pick up a specific item, then you have to do all that progress from the start. It may not sound bad, but having to go through the same dialogue multiple times because of a small slip up gets tiring very fast. The ending itself is unsatisfying and to be honest, ruins the entire game. If you are really curious, watch a walkthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: So this is an interesting little game all about reliving the same 12 minutes and trying to solve a mystery in it. The premise is good, gameplay wise its a point and click puzzle game with realtime elements. Super intruiging as well!  So I got it after not paying to close attention to reviews and avoiding most spoilers for the game. aaand...  TL;DR its disappointing.The game itself is incredibly short with just about 2 hours of gameplay, usually Im not upset by the short game time, in this case however I am.The time would be a lot shorter than that because most of your time is spend being frustrated and feels artificially padded.  The real time element keeps a tenseness up, however if you retry loops over and over again without being able fast forward it quickly becomes annoying. If you mess up you also cant rewind time by a minute, you can only try and restart your loop completely. Actions you have done must be repeated multiple times as there is some trial and error involved... yet you cant fast forward animations or walking speed. A little pet peeve is also the movement itself, the whole game is played via point and click. This leads to situations where you wanna go out of a room and suddenly close a door instead... All of that combined is..... not great. So far Ive only complained about mechanical aspects and not delved into the puzzle solving and story though.The puzzles start out great. It feels intuitive, it feels like you have a grip of things and can find out information by logical deducation. The mystery in the first few loops of the game is well done and feels rewarding to do. The early to mid point being the strongest part of the game... however it drops quickly once you hit the first barrierOnce you hit your first big wall the puzzles feel counter intuitive and convoluted (sometimes extemplified by the mechanical shortcomings) For example, at one point you need to (spoilers from here on out about some puzzles, setting, part of the plot)In conclusion. This game had high potential, the premise was interesting, the mystery was super intruiging at first. Genuinely during the first handful of loops and getting a grip of things I was super immersed, I was very much into it, was scared about what if that is one potential solution, etc.  It plays with a lot of good ideas and as a proof of concept it has extremely high merit. The mechanical limitations are however frustrating, the story is stifled by its restrictions, the puzzles get frustrating and counter intuitive midway through and the game at the same time overstays it welcome and doesnt last long enough.I dont want to hate this game but if I had one sentence to describe it its: "Mediocore game with unecessary (and self imposed) restrictions with frustrating mechanics that pad an already short game"If you like mystery games and time travel mechanics... probably wait for a sale.I cannot unfortunately recommend it with good consience for 25$
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is good, and I'm sure it took a great deal of work to create, but considering Outer Wilds is being sold for the same (or cheaper) price tag, I don't think this game is worth full price.It has a decent amount of jank in the voice lines and in the animation, and is by all measures too short. I think my 4 hour blind run was about average; there were a few puzzles that I stumbled on but for the most part I think most people can beat it fairly quickly.The story is fine, the voice acting is good, but I'm frankly a bit disappointed. If you were as hyped up by the trailers for this as I was, then I think you'll enjoy your experience with the game, but I think you'll also be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. Too short.  Feels like this game should have been a chapter in a much larger game.  Nineteen hours to complete and mess around a bit after for achievements. Great and interesting story. Wish they had a fourth actor rather than reusing one... and I've been up and down the story... but it still doesn't make sense to me the way it was told.

_childDocuments_.review: So the story was interesting but the gameplay was so tedious, annoying, and frustrating. The fun thing (for me at least) with timeloop games is experimenting and seeing what happens, but it feels like you are punished for that in this game. You spend 4 minutes getting to same part over and over again and it makes it so painful and frustrating and not fun to try something out cause you dont want to accidently reset the loop and spend the next few mins doing the same thing, if I wasnt streaming it i probolly would have quit the game early on by the amount of frustration it was causing.  On top of that you cant really play at your own speed, you need to so stuff in certain orders even if you figured it out and have all the pieces needed to trigger the next part. And the ending is so so so unsatisfying, to achieve the "best" ending involves just timing things in certain orders and if you click a second too early or too late you have to restart the loop again. Imo the story would have been so so much more satisfying after you find out the big twist and reveal it. That would have been satisfying, insted it gets dragged out and made more confusing for no other reason than I can assume to pad out the play time. TLDR id just watch a letsplay/story breakdown. It'd be more fun for you

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: I received this game for free as a tester, I did not give a negative pre release review, because I understand being a developer is not easy and a negative review can kill hype, even if I didn't enjoy the game I still respect and love game developers.So first off, the premise of the game is super exciting. I was hyped for the idea that there were multiple choices, multiple endings and fully voiced characters! However the negatives were not something I was prepared for. Below I'll start with the positives then dig into the negatives.Positives:-Character voicing was awesome with lots of variety-Graphics were decent, animations were mostly good with a few hiccups. (characters clipping etc).-Sound effects and OST were extremely beautiful, I even cried at one point.-Initially all the options and choices make the game seem exciting (INITIALLY)Now for the dreaded negatives and reason I DON'T recommend the game.-I played the game for over 10 hours, and NEVER left the single level. That's, right, TEN hours in a single room. I don't know If I am just really really stupid or what, but even when I made a ton of progress and understood most of the story, progression was in fact impossible. Unless I am given a cheat code sheet of phrases to use in a specific order "figuring" out the game is a daunting unrewarded task. I also found that even though the game gives you 100's of options to choose from in dialogue, most of it is either only for lore and meaningless after the first time you hear it, or it actually just resets your run to the beginning. The choices are as wide as an ocean but as deep as a puddle in most instances. -There are no checkpoints as far as I know, I would spend 20 minutes listening to dialogue just to try another option that led to a reset AGAIN. I don't know about you but constantly repeating the same level over 80 times, over TEN HOURS is aggravating as all heck. I mean I like puzzles, but when you are given 100 plus options and none of them lead to an ending and they all reset each time the game makes you think you are making progress, it makes me want to turn the game off and read a book or something.-Inconsistencies in the story. Throughout my playthrough I found many inconsistencies that meant things that should have worked did in fact not work.  It was aggravating to say the least when the wife asks you to prove you are in a time loop, you say a storms coming and she says she already knows, but if you dont tell her a storms coming when thunder sounds she stupidly says "OH I WaSnT ExPeCtInG a StOrM" LIKE REALLY, REALLY!-Character choices don't always make sense. For example at one point you can hide in a closet while the main antagonist has his back to you. You can practically touch him through the opening in the closet, but if you select the knife and click him the character OPENS THE CLOSET DOOR AND PROCEEDS TO GET HIS ASS KICKED. A common theme in this game is that no matter how clever you think you are only a few methods work and even fewer progress the story. I eventually figured out the story and how to deal with the antagonist and without spoilers it just resets you again even when things are about to progress. it was so frustrating I actually haven't played the game since it happened.In Short: Without spoilers I liked the story, but who wants to spend 10 hours in a single room listening to the same thing over and over with no progress? I don't recommend it unless you wanna piss someone off as a joke. I swear if I have to hear the wife do an impression of Mario Kart Toads OWOWOWOWOW one more time or "help me, can you come help me, HUSBAND WHOS TRYING TO HIDE TO SAVE YOUR LIFE, I might just break my keyboard!I really wanted to like this game, I tried day after day in total 7 days of playtime to like this (I was a tester), but I could not change my opinion. I almost did when I progressed pretty far through the story, but when I was reset again I immediately lost all interest. In the future if changes were made to make the game player friendly I would consider coming back to it. However I shouldn't be given 100 options if only 1 leads to progression. The game makes the player feel stupid, and doesn't reward you anytime you do happen to make a little sliver of progress. By the end of my playthrough the wife was annoying as hell to listen to and hearing the main character say "Well that didnt work, or I HaVe To FiNd AnOtHeR WaY" was absolutely excruciating.In conclusion I at this point have to wonder if the developer was in fact doing some sort of psychological experiment to see how long people can play a game before getting pissed off at the fact that nothing they do in any order makes any permanent progress.EDIT: Comments are now disabled do to toxic unproductive comments practically cursing me and my ancestors. This review IS an opinion based on one persons experiences. You don't have to AGREE with me, but everyones opinions should be respected.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I love time loop stories, and have been excited for this ever since it was shown at E3 2018, but this was just way below my expectations. I went in open-minded, understanding that this would probably be a "short" game, that the game would take place within the same 3 rooms, and that it'd probably be repetitive each loop.But even then, I just look sit back and look at everything in the game and think "that's it?" Don't get me wrong, I did get one or two good moments of various emotions, but I don't think it did anything "unique" when it comes to the time loop genre, or anything with the story that kept me invested enough to finish it.I really wanted to like this game, and was so excited to play it the moment it released, but I'm just left with disappointment, and the desire for something more out of it.It also doesn't help that I just came from the great time loop experience of The Forgotten City, as well as playing and loving Outer Wilds earlier this year, that just make this game feel so much more barren in comparison.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Escape room aspect and mystery seems interesting but the writing and "twist" ending is awful and gross. The writer definitely thought it was "clever" and trying to pull people in with shock-value. I've never had a game leave such a bad taste and make me feel like I was trapped in a weird train wreck of trauma-porn.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the engaging premise for the first hour or so as well as what seems like a game loop with the potential for tons of depth and opportunity, I found this game to be frustrating, excessively repetitive, and disappointing. From the disjointed voice acting due to the different dialogue options to the immersion breaking animations at times, I soon was unable to feel as immersed as I thought I would be. Without spoiling anything I also found the story to be more convoluted than it needed to be. There are plenty of twists, but some of the final turns are baffling in my opinion and take away from what could have been an interesting climax. Overall I will give this a 5/10. A unique concept that lacks some of the depth I thought would be there and frustrating loop mechanics takes from what could have been a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: The novelty of a puzzle game involving time loops is fun at first, but the pay-off of this particular game is lacking. The endings just aren't satisfying, and it's frustrating that once you do reach "an ending" you have to start aaall over again to get a different ending. And at that point, the game is just so unsatisfying you really don't want to play again. I get you're supposed to feel the anguish of the protagonist as they experience the same loop over and over again, but like watching a film, after a couple of hours of this, you kind of get sick of it. Interesting concept, but falls flat.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely such a waste of time. The initial intrigue devolves into a convoluted, unimaginably dour mess made worse by the abysmal voice acting (except for Willem Dafoe, as expected). Twelve minutes is the amount of time you should spend with this game before returning it or deriding your friend for gifting it to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most compelling mediums to tell a story in meets a fantastic look at the game mechanics of every other game. The "loop" of this game plays on the respawn element of other games, but twists the outcome to fantastic results. I recommend playing organically, going through a guide would not have the same effect. I personally haven't seen every ending yet, but I am working through the puzzles looking for alternate options. 25 dollars may seem steep to some, but I have enjoyed every minute and will continue working for other endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely great game with so many twists and turns in the plot. Extremely good story along with very clever puzzles. Some things get a tad convoluted and redundant at times as well as some puzzles being seemingly impossible without a guide but it definitely does not distract from how good the game's narrative is and how good and intriguing the gameplay is. Definitely a must have for players who want an extremely good story along with entertaining puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: I did not mind this game, but it just didn't do it for me. YMMV. I was initially not feeling great about the premise once I had gotten through a couple loops. I think the pressure to get the story moving forward just really hampered my experience, and no amount of fast forward mechanics would make that any better. The time pressure to do things correctly took over the feelings of progression and just increased frustration.I felt that some of the interactions felt a bit off or a bit stiff at times. Overall I liked how it moved forward and how things slowly got uncovered, but I couldn't help but feel annoyed with hearing the same voicelines and gradually disconnecting from the characters and the story itself. It became less about the story and more about how I could speedrun my next loop, just to eventually screw up one detail and have to start over. Some argue that's meant to help you empathize with the main character, I just found it to draw me out of immersion. I did enjoy the endings, but it did not feel like the well-earned payoff I was looking for.Overall I really didn't think this was worth the $25 for the amount of time or satisfaction it provided. I was hoping for some more classic point and click fun, but I feel that the game's ever-changing, time-sensitive magic formulas of progression made it hard for me to enjoy in one or two sittings.

_childDocuments_.review: When considering movies and games such as , , and  - all of which involve replaying moments in time - they limit how much of the repetition to showcase before switching gears and focusing on how the loops change instead. These changes are often significant, which imbues these stories with more textured and entertaining content. takes the opposite approach. The entire game unfolds in a tiny apartment where there isn't much to do, and the changes between most loops are minor. Meanwhile, you have to bear the full brunt of the time loop's repetitive forces, as you relive the same conversations and events over and over again. The dialogue-skip option offers little comfort, as its reach only extends to the ends of currently-spoken sentences. To make matters worse, the game description inaccurately frames the time loop as 12 minutes long. It's actually hard-capped at 10 minutes, and in practice you'll often die as a result of the event that takes place at the 5-minute mark. So you typically have way less time than the game's title and synopsis suggest.Things really suffer whenever you get stuck, as the game will come to a screeching halt. It's very frustrating, especially since you still have to deal with the monotony that comes with restarting a loop either way. Without any kind of clear goal, your only option is to experiment - and most of it will be in vain. There are several things you wish you could do but can't, and some things that  work but don't. Even when you think you're moving in the right direction, most forms of progression lead to dead ends anyway. Our protagonist, at one point, sums up the experience perfectly: "What am I supposed to do?! I did everything right!" The correct pathway feels no less arbitrary than the other pathways that happened to not pan out.Admittedly, I thought the story was interesting at first. There are a couple of neat twists along the way, and I was enjoying the mystery up to a point. But the ending veers sharply off the rails in poor taste, tries too hard to be clever, and becomes muddled in its implementation. And I know this is just a video game, but it was a little messed up to see such a wide array of awful fates that can befall your pregnant in-game wife. This game is a lot more violent and graphic than I was expecting. As you make your way to the endgame, you will have watched your wife get violently restrained, kicked in the stomach, shot in the head while awake and bound, shot in the head after you've drugged her unconscious, electrocuted, slit across the throat, stabbed in the gut, and forced to watch while the protagonist gets strangled to death. A lot of the necessary information you need in order to progress comes from either torturing the antagonist or watching your wife get tortured. Especially after what happens in the ending, I couldn't help but feel like this game was built solely as a vehicle for some developer's psychosexual snuff/trauma porn fantasy. Maybe I've just gotten softer in my gaming sensibilities as I've aged, but if I had known how much of this game would involve watching a pregnant woman get brutalized, I would have passed on it. I suppose I have only myself to blame -- I had asked a few friends what they thought of this game, and the feedback was negative from all of them. Against my better judgment, I bought the game anyway because I am a sucker for time travel stories. But, eesh, I really should have listened here.This game's only real saving grace is the voice acting. Dafoe, McAvoy, and Ridley are big draws, and they do a good job. But other than that, this is a mediocre 6-8 hour-long game with a poor ending. It's certainly not worth $25.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though this may be a rather short experience, it's definitely something worth playing through if you enjoy story puzzles, don't mind click-based mechanics and if you have a little patience. I rather appreciated unpacking the story incrementally as I did. It made the simpler choices feel a little more weighted and impactful as I progressed. I also didn't experience any noticeable bugs as some others had mentioned. I'd gladly play another title like this. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game ... to me, "Twelve Minutes" sounded like a whodunnit in a time loop, more and more knowledge uncovered and new dialogue options offered over time, with twists and turns along the way.And the game does indeed start quite well; the story feels interesting, interactions and logical combinations make sense, and all the possibilities of interactions / situations are covered surprisingly well in behaviour and dialogue / voice acting. And with that, even with the repetitivness that comes with such a type of game, a sense of meaningful progress is there - up until about two thirds in. Then comes the big twist, and it's a huge disappointment. It feels misplaced, and doesn't really make sense at all? At this point it becomes clear that the actual story pretty much has ended, without all the suspense, the twists and turns, the shocking revalations I was hoping for. The last third feels like a chore, progress slows down immensly, time loops become frustratingly slow and boring, and consequences of actions and dialogue options are suddenly unpredictable. You hope for the game to finally end, but it takes loop for loop until it finally does. What happened here?Overall, an interesting experiment that sadly wasn't able to convince me in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: — The acting is as good as the medium would allow it. I say aye. The motion capture here deserves a highlight, this is nothing like what I'd expect from a top-down view and outside of live action. If video-game violence we inflict on each other had this much realism — instead of ragdoll models  — we'd all be in therapy for PTSD; I'm reminded of the intro level of Fahrenheit here. — Considering the sheer complexity of cramming so much detail into a small flat and a 10-minute span, however many painful bugs you'll come across are not enough. The game is polished, there are a couple bugs, they will hurt the unfortunate, but the game is polished, . Just restart the loop a couple of times.— One caveat is that there is a bottleneck or two where the requirement for perception or intuition is unevenly — perhaps, unreasonably — high and you might find yourself stuck and angry. I had to peek into a walk-through on IGN once or twice and would advise the same if you find yourself running in circles for a couple of hours.
