_childDocuments_.review: An overall enjoyable game, yet hard to recommend. There are many disconnects between the player and the character, as the player will be a step or two ahead of what the character knows, forcing the player to go around clicking stuff and cycling through repeated voice lines to try and find out what to do to progress the game. It's quite immersion breaking and frustrating at times, especially as a few puzzles are rather contrived. The story is alright. There's not much to say without heading into spoiler territory. A couple of twists are just plain absurd, and not in a good way.The design of the level, a lot of the puzzles as well as the quality of acting and attention to detail are really quite nice though. Sounds are good and graphics are quite nice. The value proposition though is borderline. For AU$36 it's a little steep. In actuality my playtime is closer to 4-5 hours rather than the 7-8 on my profile. Coupled with the polish this game really needed but didn't receive I can understand why some people were left a little disappointed. However, on sale, this is totally worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of the game is interesting, albeit unoriginal. But where the game fails is in execution and story. The voice actors are great, of course, but it's irrelevant if the dialogue is clunky and unnatural. I understand it's hard to write dialogues that'd work regardless of player choice (I wrote a timeloop game myself) but it's no excuse for characters saying things that make no sense with the info they have (protagonist speaking about knowing about wife's father's murder even though it was only alluded to), react in ridiculous ways (husband proclaiming how good the dessert he's eating is right after wife reveals she's a killer), or just forbid you from talking (characters are talking about a polaroid picture, so I show it to them and they're like "Don't interrupt us!" and I then get killed for interrupting...).Also it's a buggy mess. The cop model loaded during the father flashback, two endings played out at once having voicelines and subtitles not matching, and now if I start the game up I only see the UI and the rest is a black void. If I click on objects it just plays the door unlock sound in loop for hours of exciting gameplay. I don't think I'd be able to play the game again as it seems irreparabily broken, but luckily I have no desire to do so.And even if I'd be able to ignore all this, the story is actually quite dumb. It's basically every soap opera cliché smushed together complete with illegitimate children and amnesia. Discovering the full story is NOT a satisfactory reward for suffering through the bad dialogue and gameplay. Also half of the achievements are "look at the painting 4 times". Riveting.

_childDocuments_.review: My score: 9/10Overall review:The story is interesting and for an indie title there is just a ton of branching paths and outcomes. There's plenty to uncover and I really was shocked when I came to the conclusion (there's more than one conclusion) of this game. I love the story and the way it's told feels pretty unique. The story felt pretty engaging and very intriguing.My one critique:My only major critique of this game is that you can't skip conversations you have to sit through all the long winded dial even when your trying find all the possible paths going through the same conversation multiple times after the loop resets again becomes quite exhausting.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this game just loves itself far too much. All of this is based on contrivances and expecting the player to make leaps in logic. The game is a looping narrative, which is great, this has worked really well in other games such as Outer Wilds or even Road 96, both of which encourage repeat play-throughs to get the most out of your experience... 'Didn't like your ending? no problem hop back in where you left off and find a better one'. In Twelve Minutes, the devs decided to ignore this trope and make the entire game loop after you hit your first ending, revoking all learned knowledge for your game, including the 'tutorial' section which I must have played no less than 10 times now. As the game is you have to repeat looooong sections over and over with no changes each time. It feels like watching an episode of a serial TV show over and over and over, every time you watch it is exactly the same as the last bar the final 30 seconds. This decision makes going for 100% a nightmare. On that topic, achievement hunting in this is just ludicrous, all the achievements are hidden so how the player is supposed to even know where to start on these without a guide is beyond me, but sometimes you can work out clues such as "hmm that painting is changing, if I see all its different forms then maybe ill get an achievement". Congrats, you'd be correct with that assessment however knowing when the painting triggers a change is cryptic beyond cryptic. It will only change after certain plot points play out, plot points mind you that can be skipped on a run. So you can get two of the three variations on a painting before you get to an ending and then as I said earlier, your progress is revoked and you're sent back to the tutorial. "Better luck next time Bub!" the devs of the game say behind their massive ego...So disappointing, the story that is offered is almost really cool, as it stands is nothing more than competent. It requires far too much guessing and random clicking, hoping for the best to get to an ending that actually makes sense. But it won't ever make sense because they couldn't afford a fourth voice actor to separate two very similar but important to distinguish - in order to understand what the heck is going on - characters. This of course being after they blew their load on Daisy Ridley, James McCavoy and Willem Dafoe. All of whom are doing a decent job, Willem being the stand out. I still have no idea why they cast a Scotsman and an English woman to voice two generic sounding american people. Their voice talent is clear because their accents are flawless but they could have just cast people born with those accents, these roles aren't exactly requiring Hollywood talent. And again, why the voice of the Dad and the voice of the cop are both Willem I will never know, it just makes it so confusing to know who is actually with you in your ending...I do not recommend this game if you are wanting to see everything it has to offer. The pain it puts you through plus the lacklustre destination just make for a miserable experience. If you are desperate to see the story because you just love Willem Dafoe or something then honestly just watch an LP, it will save you time and frustration. The only way I can see this being enjoyable to play is if you play it once through to an ending and then never pick it up again, maybe that's how it was intended but it just seems like you miss so much like that - like 90% of the game...

I wont complain about repetitiveness and how hard to find the right sequence, because that the frickin point of the game. But some sequence do make a result that for me doesn't make sense, and probably will frustate me and others. But once you got the sequence right and have a new information, it felt damn satisfying.My experience with this game is like doing the programming, where you got error and unable to find it at stack overflow, you stuck, try solution, stuck again until you finally run the program and got another error, back to square one, and repeat.I have mixed feeling about the story. The mystery-thriller story was excellent and very well excecuted, i always got hooked up and drive me to find a new information. The climax twist was really good and pretty shocking one......... until you got the ending, dusted up all the good story above. It confusing and when you finally understand you still felt dissapointed, too bad indeedStill recommend to for you that like puzzle-mystery game, but keep your expectation low after you finally found the answer of the big mystery, because there is not really a story after that

Story wise it took me around 5-6 hours to reach a real ending in this time loop game.That would be no problem, if the game mechanics and/or the story would be above average. For example you have a usalbe toilet where you can flush down nearly all objects.But this seems to have no effect at all on the actual loop. So there are nearly no "nonsense" loops possible, which is a shame in a "time loop" game.And then the story. This murder mystery took a very weird turn. Maybe this was done to get a "Woah", but at least for me it is more like a "Meh".Thats not so much because of the general idea behind it, but more because of the problems it causes in the plausibility of the game (if that can be used for a time loop game).

_childDocuments_.review: I was immediately intrigued with this game when it was first announced at E3 back in 2019, not only because of the time loop storytelling device but also the unique prospect of playing a game with only three characters in a three-room studio apartment.  Just how much gameplay can you milk from such limited resources?  Roughly 8-12 hours based on my personal game time and research of others’ experiences, and that is likely to get you only one or two of the multiple endings, which may not be the “true” ending, but by then your brain is mush and “truth” is merely a concept.Without giving away any spoilers you play as the husband (James McAvoy) who comes home to his sparsely furnished studio apartment where his wife (Daisy Ridley) has big news and a tasty desert waiting for him.  Only a few minutes into their celebration a police officer (Willem Dafoe) starts banging on the door saying he has a warrant for your wife for murder.  Of course things aren’t as they seem (the understatement of the century) and your life keeps resetting after twelve minutes (or sooner if you die, get knocked out, go to sleep, or leave the apartment).  It’s up to you to solve the mystery of the pocket watch, a dead father, and a diabolical family legacy that will have you on the edge of your seat until the jaw dropping twist.  Can you repair time and escape the loop?If Steam is your only option I might recommend waiting for a sale or perhaps doing a free Game Pass trial and playing that version.  As much as I love what Luis Antonio was trying to do here, Twelve Minutes is not a $25 experience…in my opinion; especially when the game will most likely leave you feeling icky and unsatisfied with the intended ending.Read the full review at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -

_childDocuments_.review: An ingeniously minimalist time loop game that is at once very satisfying and very frustrating.It's a masterpiece in terms of the breadth of narrative expressed with such a limited and narrow set of tools. The puzzle of its plot is exquisite. When all is put together and the credits roll you will clap your hands, tip your hat, and yell "bravo".But you might not have the best time getting there. It's a very short game if you just measure the amount of content, but unless you figure things out effectively you will repeating a lot of it, a lot. Experimentation is the only way to get ahead in this game, but it will punish you with repetition as often as it rewards you with something new. And though the repeating segments have an upper limit of 12 minutes, which seems like not a lot, even a few repeated minutes can feel tiresome when you do them five times in a row.On this, two things to say. First, the game is just short enough that the frustration doesn't overstay its welcome  much. I got annoyed, yes. But not enough that I didn't want to keep trying. There are online walkthroughs, too, and don't be afraid to use them if the alternative is to rage-quit.Second, the game suggests more than it can deliver. It's so great in anticipating the various combinations of actions that you might assume it's smarter than it is. A few times I came up with some great ideas on how to solve a problem but the game could only offer a select few options. You can only do what it lets you do, and that's intentionally minimal. You need to play it at its own terms, as a puzzle rather than a sandbox.Recommended for time loop puzzle fans!Note that the use of famous actors is 100% a gimmick and would have no effect on your experience. These expensive actors are not any better than other video game actors. If anything, the voice acting is just mediocre.

_childDocuments_.review: Well... this is pretty much everything I was expecting. No less, but also no more.Twelve Minutes is as much a videogame as Los Cronocrímenes is a movie. And they got the same price too.I watched both, believe it or not. I dont mind cheesy low budget movies and I dont mind small indie videogames either. There have been a grand total of 3 times where I have been stuck for a couple minutes trying to figure out what to do, but to be honest its nothing major, the flow of the game as well as the story is so linear and overall well crafted that a regular amount of thinking will get you where you want to be. I thought I had to decrypt mysterious paintings at first but no nothing of the sort, there's not even a math puzzle involved, praise be the heavens for that.It is a very linear, very simple, straightforward time loop videogame that plays like a 75 minutes low budget movie. _childDocuments_.review: Just finished "12 Minutes"... definitely one of the most disappointing games I've ever played. Majora's Mask is one of my all-time favorite games, so the Groundhog Day premise had me excited and the first few time loops were amazing and exciting but the direction it went wound up being one of the most tedious and obtuse puzzle games imaginable with such a lame and frankly gross story. Absolutely do not recommend it, especially not for $25. It's like a 5 hour game but that's with 3 of the hours being frustration. It gets to a point where you'd think it would open up (when you convince the wife you have powers) but instead it closes off completely and the "solutions" become insanely ridiculous. Like one would think "Ok, now I have a partner so we can setup a situation that will work well"... but you can't. All she does is sits there and you can't even explain to her what actions to take in any capacity, and the game devolves into doing the same long segment of moves multiple times and hoping something accidentally is different.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: i HAVE PLAYED THROUGH 3 TIMES NOW. Amazing story, crazy twists and fun achievements! If you don't like solving mysteries and want a game to point everything out for you, don't play this please. I also saw other reviewers complaining about wasting time but yes, the point of the game is if you're stuck in a time loop you wouldn't quicksave and go back. It takes 12 minutes to redo a loop, stop trying to take the easy way out! This game is a 9/10 from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Faux deep BS that feels like it's entirely trying to ride on the shock of the one real twist.Other reviews talk about the repetitive gameplay and the way highly specific combinations are required to progress, and I could forgive all of that if one thing were true--the thing which every stylistic aspect of the game and every trailer--all indicate that the developers  was true. If the game had something to say, if the story was in any way deep or compelling or even just memorable and distinct-then I could forgive the gameplay. Alternately, I could forgive the writing if the gameplay was interesting. When I saw that I could put one of the fake candles in the vents, I thought-- oh here's something. Maybe if I knock the wife out, hide, and leave the candle in the vent with the pocket watch the "cop" might do something different. Hell, even if this hadn't progressed the overall story in any way, it would have been . It would have felt engaging and interesting to see even the same outcome if the path to it was slightly changed by your actions. Why even make it possible to pick up and stash the candles there?In short, the makers of this game were too busy thinking they were VERY CLEVER to actually write a good story or create engaging gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Be warned: TRIAL & ERROR!I finished the game in about 6 hours. It was a lot of fun. There are no controls as such, just a point & click puzzle game but with a good story and great acting!Due to this being a Groundhog Day-esq type game (you re-live the same 12 minutes over and over) repeating some of the dialog can be tiresome and if something doesn't go the way you intended, you have to start over. This is really a trial & error game. There's nothing to really get stuck on, you just keep trying things in different ways. You can look for a walkthrough but you probably wont get much satisfaction out the game if you do because the game is about discovering things through trial and error. Overall, good fun, unique style. Not something I would play again, maybe in a few years when I have forgotten the story.

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is interesting and it's fun to experiment to come up with different solutions and finding new clues.There are small details within the apartment that changes. Though, why or how I don't know.It is exciting to gather the pieces of the story throughout the game. However, the story goes down hill towards the end with a big plot hole. A character doesn't know what he did but at the same time he did know, and there was no explanation to why as far as I know. _childDocuments_.review: Does a nice job with the time loop mechanic, giving the player lots of options to learn its rhythm and manipulate it. _childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: My first loop I used the knife on myself out of curiosity, but unfortunately the game doesn't really know what to do with a player whose choices deviate a lot from the intended solutions.  The subsequent loops presented me with dialogue that alluded to events that never happened in my first loop because of my actions trying to play around with the tools in the game.  My advice to anyone playing this game would be to not approach it like a puzzle game.  This is not a game that wants the player to experiment because experimenting frequently causes hilarious malfunctions in animation, voice acting, and continuity.  The solutions are more often than not just to keep choosing dialogue options and the apartment is rife with things that could have been great puzzles but are not.  It feels like it should just be a linear game without scripting that shatters when brushed against but then I guess the lackluster writing would be harder to forgive.I recommend eating dessert during any and all emotional climaxes because you almost always can and the protagonist will moan "milky!" and "i love you" while the other characters discover dark truths out loud.  That's the best experience I had playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Super Mindblowing story.....There are certainly frustrating moments; trying to coax characters into particular conversations or specific positions in order to enact your plans can take longer than necessary, even though you’re able to fast-forward through familiar conversations.What I can say is that the payoff is worth it, and the clever way in which writer-director Luis Antonio flips the traditional point-and-click adventure on its head makes for a compelling bit of unconventional storytelling that could only have worked as a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but at the same time, I wish I had a maybe option for this one. The game is good, very interesting and challenging, but after a while becomes very tedious, repetitive and unsatisfying to play, especially as you slowly start to solve the mystery.The first couple of hours were the best as I felt that each time I hit a roadblock I would come across some new detail or information that helped me to progress a bit further. This was fine, until closer to solving the mystery where I had to replay certain scenarios over and over again, just to progress a bit further than the last time. I get the point of it, but it doesn't change the fact that it's repetitive.I won't spoil anything, but the ending was a major letdown for me. There are actually multiple endings. The core mystery being solved is quite the unexpected turn of events, but I none the less felt empty afterwards, not really satisfied with all the effort I put into solving this mystery. The endings are influenced according to what you choose to do with this information.I'd say the game is worth giving a shot. It's easy to play and will definitely keep you busy for hours. You might find yourself wanting to look at a guide from time to time, but I'd recommend trying to figure it out yourself, there are multiple things you can do to gain a bit of information and it's really worth tickling your brain.There's no replayability though, and you can attempt to get all of the achievements, but honestly, I don't see the point in putting in all that effort, unless you're like me whose a bit of a completionist.If you decide to get the game, have fun, you're in for a rough ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes is a time-travel mystery point and click game. Your wife and you have a pleasant dinner in your house when a cop arrives searching something of value and arrest your wife. You have 10 minutes to solve the mystery, after that time you will go 10 minutes back in time. A VEREDICT: Not recommendedI have a high tolerance to the try and errors and I don't mind if a game is very short, so this game seemed to be made for me. Sadly, the game has been a disappointment and I don't recommend it. If you're very interested in the premise that the game proposes, please, wait for a big discount.PROS:+Great premise. The first loops are something special.+Great actors. Even if the dialogue isn't outstanding, the actors delivers most of the time.+A lot of your actions have a unique response...CONS:-... And even so, the game doesn't take advantage of it. The game is extremenly linear, each puzzles only has one possible solution, and the game only let you solve it at a certain time. This isn't a new problem in the genre, but in a game with so little interactable characters and objects, it's easy to think find a valid solution for a puzzle, and the game doesn't let you solve because is not the one moment the developers made it solvable.-The writing is bad. Is appreciated that the game answer all the mysteries it proposes to you, but all of them are very weak or laughtable. Poor character development, and some unrealistic reactions thanks to the extreme linearity of the game.-Glitchy. I suffered some t-poses and unreponsive mouse clicks. Some animations are wonky.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes has a great concept and, for a while, it feels like a cool mystery that you're piecing together. But the game doesn't work like you might think it does. It's not solvable in a single loop; there's this whole investigation arc you need to undertake by learning things in previous loops and bringing them forward. I wanted the time mechanic to work more like Outer Wilds, and a little bit less like Groundhog Day.The worst part for me is that, past a certain point, the things you're solving in each loop have a lot less to do with out-of-the-box puzzle thinking, and more to do with finding the right spot to click in the world. I ended up completely stuck on one step of a loop, and it turns out I actually did most of the right thing... just clicked in the wrong spot. Since I missed the click, I ended up doing a solid number of loops trying to figure out what to do before I resigned myself to looking up a hint and realized that I just needed to click an inch lower.Couple that with the part where you're going to be re-doing some progressively more unfun dialogue/scenario set-up in each loop in order to get to where you think you need to be to try and figure out the next part, and you have a headache. I wish Twelve Minutes wasn't so "on-rails" with the puzzle. It feels like such a cool idea, and there's so much potential to have fun, whether it would be through setting up weird situations through previous knowledge or by having interesting failure states, but unfortunately it feels like an oddly linear puzzle where you have to repeat the first ten steps multiple times until you either give up and look at a guide, or just give up and uninstall. There isn't enough of a sandbox here for me and no reason to get excited about what Twelve Minutes does. I just couldn't help but get the feeling that this game fell far short of what it could have been.I honestly feel like you'll get most of the same experience watching a youtube walkthrough of this game. It's legitimately that unengaging. If you think, "What if you did this and this?" chances are, it doesn't do anything. You have to ride the rails to the end, or you just end up in an unenthusiastic fail state where you either wait for the loop, or force the loop.I can't recommend or vouch for  this game, and I genuinely feel like I wasted a bit of money on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I misjudged this game earlier. It's definitely not bad. But it's a concept that's far better narrated passively in a movie rather than a game, because the translation of such high end concepts in difficult. Time loops look fun passively in a movie or a show, but when it comes to active engagements, any momentary branching that doesn't sit well with the player might kick them out of the experience and never want them to try it again, given how the game is insanely sandbox by nature and doesn't give any prominent lead for players to proceed to do something. There is dialogue but it's very easy to either miss at times or just pass off as a repeat in script.But as an experience it's definitely something unique which urges you to peer deeper into it. Maybe try it on a sale if you don't want to risk it on full price.

And the short time loop (less than 10 minutes) allows for lots of experimentation without feeling too tedious.Full review is available on my personal blog:

_childDocuments_.review: A character placed in a time travel narrative is tasked with slowly puzzling through the circumstances they are experiencing; being placed in a sudo isolation until the "problem" is solved. This can have severe consequences on a characters mental state and can lead to a character unwillingly taking actions against their normal judgment. The actions we are allowed to take in this game completely break the idea of our character being a normal person placed inside of a time loop. You can do some awful things that are not made suddenly okay because we are in a time loop. Obviously to a player these things are funny, what else would you use a knife for? But the main character is just a puppet for us even though he is supposed to be an integral part of this story. According to his actions he was a terrible person before entering the loop, no normal person would immediately go to these solutions when trying to escape a time loop. There are many other issues with the game but at a surface level it is trying to tell a story based in a time loop and completely fails to ground it and make anyone take it seriously. If you want a story puzzle game like this go play Outer Wilds instead.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very disappointing review to write, because by all means this game should be amazing! It just falls flat on SO MANY levels that I cannot recommend it. I recommend experiencing it, but it's definitely the type of game that is much better to experience in the back-seat.My play through of the game was relatively well for the most part, to avoid spoilers I won't explain too much about what happened in it, but I will point out some of the more specific issues I faced. Starting with some minor ones, the animations in this game leave a LOT to be desired. It really seems like someone tried way too hard to make something complex, but had no idea what they were doing and over-looked some very key aspects of them, though this may also be the fault of whatever system they used for the AI's tasks, as there is a lot of jarring moments where the player has no control over the game, and others where the player has control, but is unable to move due to another AI's task, or the game glitching out and endlessly looping a task. Another minor issue would be the gameplay loop itself. As someone who is addicted to time-loop and point-and-click games, I was drawn to this instantly, but what is initially a fun mechanic to mess around with quickly becomes extremely tedious as some of the dialogue options seem to exist for the sole purpose of ruining a run with no gained information. Which from a player perspective feels soul crushing. You finally unlock new dialogue options, and it takes 3 loops just to find out they're all useless? What amazing game design...One major issue I faced would be the game's delivery of the events. It sports a cast of terrific, professional voice actors, and it feels like the developers just took the lines and smashed them together wherever they thought they would work. Some of the dialogue is repeated multiple times in a single loop, and even though the game seems to provide slightly different dialogue after exiting and reopening it on certain story segments, if it's all done in a single play through these things don't seem to be taken into account. Part of me wonders if I may have had a more interesting experience having closed the game down after literally every loop, which should not be necessary. There are moments when talking to secondary character where the given dialogue flips between emotional states, some of them are not even mixed the same, and it just sounds absolutely horrendous. Just goes to show that when it comes to games, a voice actor is only as good as the developer implementing the voice clips. What a waste.I would like to say the story feels well designed, but it really doesn't. I definitely did have a moment of feels after doing something naughty and finding a phone with messages from a loved one, but it was very short lived as I happened upon it much too early in the game for me to have an attachment to that character. Which is kind of the problem with games like this. Not to mention the entire premise of the game is flawed from the start. It seems like the type of game where, if you know exactly what to do you could get a "successful" ending in one loop, but that is just not the case. The time loop mechanic seems to specifically be a time wasting mechanic, keeping you from realising there is very little effort put into every aspect of this game.I feel bad for the amazing voice actors who took part in this. This game is not worth $30. Just watch someone else play it so you can enjoy the moments where the developers purposely screw with the player for no reason other than to waste their time.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: - Very well written story and great voice acting.- Nice looking environment with great use of time based lighting.Cons:- Voice acting isn't stitched well together; oftentimes certain lines would interrupt other ones, two dialogues would play at the same time leading to awkward situations, or complete tonal shifts would happen without warning.- Too many collision bugs and jerky character animations that really messed up the immersive experience. Most of the time these didn't affect gameplay except once during my playthrough where two characters got stuck on each other and I had to restart the game to continue playing.- Not enough player agency. There is pretty much only one correct way to advance the timeline, and certain actions that seem sensible are impossible in the game. For example (HEAVY SPOILER): - Too many red herrings that acted as timesinks. - Too short. I completed the entire game (including the true ending) in 6 hours. I feel like a proper price for this length of game would be around $15-$19 CAD instead of $30 CAD.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: YOU'RE IN FOR SOME HEAVY SH*T!That's the warning you should see before playing this game. Before writing this, I took a while considering if this game goes too far. I still don't know for sure.Yes, the story written by the portuguese Luis Antonio and beautifully portrayed by a stellar Hollywood cast has several different triggers for SUIClDE, R4PE, ABUSE, among others that would be a spoiler to enumerate. They can and will be quite disturbing. But that's the idea of the game: pushing the protagonist to do horrible things in order for the story to progress.It all makes sense in the so called "true ending", which unfortunately is a little difficult to reach. The good thing is: the game is enticing enough to captivate your attention until you ultimately find that one way out of the spiral of chaos and get to watch the credits go by your screen.In conclusion, you will find a very controversial narrative and some design bugs (clunky character movements, people going through objects, etc). If you don't mind those, dive in and you might as well have a thrilling ride onboard this very disruptive title by Annapurna.

_childDocuments_.review: Best thing about this game is that it really makes you feel the emotions of being stuck in a time loop: frustration, boredom, insanity, only to later be absolutely delighted at a new hope when you find out about a new interaction, before being let down again when you thought you've done it all correctly but are sent back to the start of the loop. A very thrilling rollercoaster for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say, the game was a very profound experience regarding trial and error and what would one do if they could turn back the clock. Brilliantly voice acted by its A list Hollywood cast. The top down perspective is implemented in one of the best ways I've seen in a video game, while maintaining a very cinematic sense of direction. It's very stylized in the sense it feels like a game made by David Lynch, Twin Peaks fans are gonna have a field day with this one. Not only is it Lynchian in style, but also in terms of story telling, bizarre, dreamlike, and proceedingly twisted... The time loop scenario/mechanic fares perfectly within this aspect as well.The only two cons in the game in my opinion are:1. That there's quite many house items and vents and interactables in the house that aren't fully utilized, don't get me wrong, most of it is very creative, but there's some missed opportunities/potential in this specific aspect of the game2. You have no idea where the plot is headed, it starts to unravel itself so subtly, and that's awesome! But there comes a point where it starts to get a bit predictable. It redeems itself a bit later by going back to it's twisted unravelling nature. But I feel that I have to mention that when it's managed to do it so well for the majority of the gameI hate number scores but if I were to rate it that way, maybe a 8/10 or 8.5/10.If you love indies, love arthouse films, love Lynchian work, and Willem Dafoe,and at this price point, I 100% recommend this game.This game gave me a lot of laughs and wow moments, its wild, go play it.EDIT: Last note, this is the first game to make me lose my track of time(no pun intended), I always game for long hours, but I can always feel it, this game made my senses go bonkers in that regard.
_childDocuments_.name: Twelve Minutes

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes starts off as a brilliant game that becomes difficult to recommend playing because of how hard it trips over itself in the final moments.The first half of the experience is filled with an awesome sense of discovery and mystery, the story elements are being laid out for the player and there is a real sense of open ended freedom. The story revolves around a man stuck in a time loop, his wife and a mysterious cop. The dynamics that play out between these characters and the room they are staged in is a real treat to see unfold at the start. So many things change depending on what the player chooses to do and this is where the real height of the game is. It feels open ended and figuring out how to advance the story comes with a truly rewarding feeling.After experiencing several loops however, the game very quickly starts to crumble. The player is simply punished for experimenting. There is no checkpoint system and you can only skip dialogue one line at a time. This doesn't sound too bad on paper, but in practice it leads to insanely boring sections of time spent setting up the scene and skipping a bunch of dialogue just to alternate between two different actions at the very end of a long sequence of identical events. *calls a character BEFORE the cop enters* or *calls a character AS the cop enters* I found myself making these tiny alterations trying to push the story forward, and having to sit through very similar events each time got so jarring. It isn't obviously expressed to the player when they have managed to make a breakthrough in the story. The game relies on the player hitting very specific sequences of dialogue in very specific moments that aren't always obviously or reasonably related to the current story unfolding and it results in the player setting up lots of the same scenarios just to see if anything has changed.Only after completing the game is it obvious just how few the number of events and loops needed to reach the finish actually are. This is because while playing the game its very hard to discern what the overall goal of the game actually is, Are we the player trying to break the loop, find justice, create chaos or seek some sort of moral victory? The lack of a clear direction in what actually results in breaking the loop makes striving for a goal kind of difficult. There are several endings but ultimately the game never feels like it properly ends. It's worth noting that the game builds a really nice tension and sets up a lot of questions that the player wants answered only to crush all of that with a really big plot breaking twist. The twist was crazy but makes any chance of a cohesive story end in a total joke.Overall though I do recommend this game because of its unique presentation, incredible voice acting and great and simple gameplay elements, I really enjoyed the game; the first half is especially excellent, just don't expect this game to somehow avoid the limitations that it has set upon itself.

_childDocuments_.review: While the voice acting, visual art style of the game are done fantastically well, the story isn't. The game will constantly punish you for doing the right thing, until you do the exact thing the game wanted you to do. I always have this issue with time travel movies, books, and games. A huge amount of them don't get it right and end up digging holes in their own worlds. Let me give you an example of why this game does it terribly wrong. Act A: You arrive from work, wife greets you with exciting news and dessert. Sometime during dessert a cop will arrive to arrest her and eventually kill you.Act B: You now know of the cops arrival so you prepare for it, grab a knife form the kitchen and play the day out as usual. You cut yourself free and try to attack the cop from behind only to miss. (you can repeat this 50 times and your character somehow fails to learn from his mistakes) Act C: You grab the knife from the kitchen, hide in the closet ready to ambush the cop only for your character to somehow manage to eff it up or the cop find you.Act D: You kill your wife, leave the door open making it seem like a killer showed up and left, cop will always find you like a bloodhound.Act E: You anger your wife to get her to leave 11 minutes before the cop is ever to arrive. Somehow cop arrives in the nick of time like a sitcom and game takes a giant turd on you once again. Nothing you do is ever right in this game despite knowing the loop and knowing exactly when things are suppose to happen. The game always makes up it's own rule for the cop to kill you unless you do it exactly the way it's meant to.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most disappointed I've been by a video game in quite a while. I remember seeing this at E3 when it was first announced and I was so excited for it, but the actual implementation is pretty garbage.The character development is mildly interesting at best.Hard to explain without spoiling, but some of the solutions to the puzzles are really dumb imo.I encountered multiple game breaking glitches and more immersion breaking bugs.The timeloop mechanic gets really tedious by the end, it takes 5+ minutes to get back to the moment you want when you start a new loop. There's no way to skip entire convos with people (only individual liens) or events that you aren't interacting with (ie convos between other people). NPCs often talk over each other making it hard to follow along with the actual convo you're having.At several points I found character interactions didn't make sense for the timeline I was in (ie someone punches me when they were not hostile to me in that timeline, or seems to forget something we had previously discussed in that timeline).And the ending is really dumb. Hard to explain without spoiling, but holy cow, I can't believe I powered through four hours of this game just to find _that_.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not even close to worth 25 bucks. I put 5 VERY REPETITIVE hours into this game, and saw all there is to see. I get the game is about looping, but it gets old FAST. Even with all the huge amount of padding, the game is over before it even really starts. Not to mention that the story is so far up it's own ass, that it can see teeth. Its SO nebulous and SO metaphorical that there is no concrete basis for any kind of story to stand upon. This game is the equivalent of listening to Data from Star Trek explain how the holodeck works for 5 hours. This game is all of the poetry ever written by an angsty teen, complete with a total lack of self awareness. _childDocuments_.review: Mechanics, acting, techs, idea, all great. Enjoyed it immensely. THE ENDING. I am very disappointed about the big so called twist, which frankly, should have a massive TRIGGER WARNING. It's disturbing, and should not be giving an option to 'carry on' when you get there to make the final choice, it should not be the end all to be all in the first place, and just made it feel like it was was thrown in to be 'extremely edgy'.Quite frankly, I suspect the people who will love this game's ending, will be a certain type of people. I am saddened that a game with so much potential went this direction, a game I was looking forward to.If you still wanna play this game, I recommend you wait for a sale, with at least 75% discount, for the price I paid, the disappointment wasn't worth it. Also, game designers? Put a warning on your game please. You have no excuse when games like Doki Doki Literature club did so. None at all, and this was hundred times worse than what they offered. Do better.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since the first trailer for this game came out I've been looking forward to playing this. I am always interested in stories that feature time travel or time loops so this seemed right up my alley. So after plaything this game for around 6 hours and getting a few different endings I can happily say this game didn't disappoint.There are some shortcomings that I didn't like in regards to how voice lines are being played or overlap each other. More often that not it comes off as somewhat janky. For example when lines are delivered one by one. Meaning someone says something and the other person is clearly meant to interrupt but there will be an awkward pause until the line that's supposed to interrupt will play.Other times voice lines overlap that aren't meant to.Sometimes interactions seem weird in your character has clearly more information because of the loop and will just blurt out stuff because of dialogue choices and whoever you are talking to will queue there answer to that line which a lot of the times comes across as unnatural.Animations can come off as weird but I feel this is more about that the game has to react wherever you are in the apartment and has to accommodate for it.I know the things I mentioned are more nitpicky because of how the game is structured there are so many variables and accounting for all of them at any given moment seems like a monumental task that is probably way outside the budget of this game.Nonetheless I loved every second of 12 Minutes. The story had me hooked from the start and while it didn't completely stick the landing for me it has so many cool moments along the way that I am not disappointed in the slightest.Though the worst part for me after finishing the game (getting to the credits) is that I need more of these type of games/stories.All in all this is an easy game to recommend to any fan of time travel/looping stories or people who are looking for a great narrative experience.

_childDocuments_.review: It so happened that I have been waiting for this game since the announcement, having become interested in it from the first trailer. Perhaps this is what played a cruel joke with me - maybe there would not have been high expectations and obvious interest, the game would have turned out to be treated somewhat more tolerantly than I did. Well, okay, what happened, happened.Well, there is not much to say here - in fact, there is none. Yes, yes, we have a classic Point & Click, with all that it entails - a small location, several points of activity (where you can take or break something, as well as shift it from place to place), and that's it. However, this was just as expected.There are actually no graphics either. No, it is somewhat better than in the first trailer, but this does not save the game in any way. However, since I knew in advance what to expect, therefore, there is also no particular point in finding fault, so we will also leave this aside for now (as well as the question of why such a modest game in terms of graphics consumes so many PC resources, not lightly loading not the most powerful , but still a discrete card). But there are some questions about the animation - not only is it extremely twitchy and torn, but also the norm is, for example, situations when characters simply walk through each other or through objects. Which is no longer good.And here you will have to answer to the fullest extent - since this is the only thing that in such a game should be at the highest level, but ... no. There is actually no plot here either. No, it kind of is, and in the first couple of loops it even causes some interest, but then it all comes down to a strange, completely unrelated game that makes you ask only one question at the end - what was it? Senseless and merciless, this plot destroys (in a bad way) all expectations, it looks so ridiculous and crookedly glued together in this game. Maybe if his pitch was a little more even, he would look a little better, but ... what is not, is not.Another important aspect in a game tied to time loops. And here the situation is basically similar to the plot - the first couple of loops are all cool, but then you realize that there is actually no replay value here either - each loop (except for those that can interrupt the cycle) ends with one of two not very impressive results, also actually which boil down to the same thing - restarting the loop. The only question is whether we restart the loop voluntarily or forcibly. The rest is a search using logic and the good old method of typing the only (actually not)) the right way that will finally allow you to finish this game. So-so perspective, isn't it? But this is one of the few aspects of the game, which turned out really not bad. Voices sound good, changing depending on how the characters react to certain events. Let's be honest, the use of well-known actors is more of a marketing ploy, since many lesser-known actors could voice this game just as well, but oh well. The soundtrack, by the way, is also quite good, which is also worth noting.Neutral (actually negative, but expected) aspects:1) Graphics2) Animation3) GameplayNegative (unexpected) aspects1) Plot embroidered with white threads2) Virtually no replay valuePositive aspects1) Voice characters2) Musical accompaniment in general3) If there is a Disappointment of the Year nomination at the Steam Awards 2021, I know for sure which game deserves it this year like no otherSeparately, I would like to note the general psychedelic nature of what is happening in the game, sometimes seeming simply meaningless. Who, why, why, why the hell did no one understand this before and why no one was interested in it for so many years. In other matters, a number of even more far-fetched fan theories than the main plot provide answers to these questions, but the main question remains unanswered - do we need to look for these same answers at all? Maybe it's better to close this game and forget it, as another fake, which turned out to be somewhat worse than our expectations? Well, I'll leave that choice to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve minutes is a game about a man (you the player) stuck in a time loop. You get home from work and walk into your apartment, from which you are greeted by your girlfriend. You have desert that she made, and chat, when all of a sudden you hear a knock at the door and a mysterious man yelling for you to open it. When you do so he zip ties you and your girlfriend. He begins interrogating both of you and asks for a pocket watch, you exclaim that you have no clue what he's talking about, he promptly strangles you and you die. But wait you wake up at your apartment door again, what just happened are you going crazy or are you in a time loop. That's the beauty of this indie game, you keep restarting the loop to slowly uncover pieces of the story. Also Daisy Ridley and Willem Dafoe are voice acting in this game. I will say at times it can be quite tedious and draining but if you go into this game with knowing that, it can be less painful. this game is quick (i beat it in 4hrs) but beautiful at the same time. If you like steam achievements this game can be completed in about 2-3 hours and get all achievements. But all in all its a decent indie game, i wouldn't say it's the best indie around but its definitely worth playing. The price tag is a bit steep for what it's worth so i would recommend only purchasing when there is a steam sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Twelve Minutes is a point and click adventure in a timeloop scenario about a mystery revolving around a long forgotten tragedy. While this premise might sound appealing, its execution is unfortunately lacking. For the first two hours, I was enjoying myself as I suspected to come closer to the truth. However, the quality of the mystery eventually deteriorated.The nature of a time loop requires the player to experience certain dialogue over and over again. The provided means to skip dialogue that you have already heard does not work towards the end and that makes the experience rather exhausting. The puzzles are not exciting and often rely on obvious hints by the protagonist. This should not be the case. Hints about puzzles should be planted in the environment and dialogue not in a monologue that feels out of place.Finally, I would like to express my utmost confusion about this game's overall positive reception on this platform. I cannot understand how one might recommend this game, especially at the steep price tag of about  €20. I do not recommend this game to anybody particularly not to those who are into puzzle or point and click adventure games. It is a disappointment.

name: The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance Tactics
detailed_description: UNITE THE CLANS In The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance Tactics , you will lead a fledgling resistance of Gelfling against their oppressive overlords, the Skeksis, across more than 50 unique turn-based tactics RPG battles. Along the way, you will recruit and customize new allies by assigning them jobs, modifying their abilities, and outfitting them with equipment to ensure victory. With 14 playable characters, including familiar faces from the classic film and the new Netflix original series, build your own teams and devise winning strategies to overthrow the rule of the Skeksis and restore light to the Gelfling homeworld of Thra! The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance Tactics is an upcoming turn-based strategy game for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation®4, Xbox One, PC and Mac (via Steam)! LEAD THE RESISTANCE A Twisted Fairy Tale Full of mystical creatures from faraway lands, experience an expansive fantasy story through the vibrant world of Thra, where innocent Gelfling lives are consumed for their essence by the nefarious Skeksis. Unite the Gelfling tribes and drive the rebellion to success, or defeat... Strategic Tactical Battles Decades of developer experience building strategy games brings multi-layered, tactical role-playing game combat. Units can be customized for specific fights with unique gear and varied abilities across an expansive job system. Use guile, planning, and cunning to overcome superior foes. The Clans of Thra Thra is full of a variety of Gelfling homesteads and unpredictable environments, from arid deserts to lush forests, each as dangerous as they are wondrous. Brave the wild lands of the Gelfling clans to unite them and obtain unique strategic benefits.

_childDocuments_.review: I am pretty far along, and my starting lineup is 20+THE LOOK AND FEEL:Considering Netflix has more money than god, this feels very low budget. From modeling, to avatars, to combat, it all feels like a decent IOS game vice a solid PC tactics game. The menu gives you next to no options. The UI has real issues. It looks dated and explains nothing. I was just playing some old C&C games recently and I am not being hyperbolic when I say the UI felt similar to those. Yeesh.I'd bet my bottom dollar they used the default font in whatever software they worked with. It's like reading a sign a coworker printed out for the work fridge. There's almost no voice acting, the soundtrack is nice but limited to two songs... and there's way less art work than I would have thought. Still, I keep playing it. It's the friggin' Dark Crystal universe. Wholly unique and wonderful and sincere. I love that about it. HOW IT PLAYS:The combat is totally passable. There are some synergies you can explore at later levels which gives you something to look forward to.Also, it's not pay to win.However, the in-game store (where you buy gear for your roster) doesn't allow items to be recycled or traded back in. The store reveals higher tier items seemingly at random. This makes it tough to know when to save and spend. Your only income are pearls (which you only get upon completing a mission). The prices of higher tier items aren't MMO grindy, but you'll never have top gear on several characters at once. My power level might read 178, but then I only hit for 68. Why? Armor? Not sure. It makes it impossible to really min/max your moves. The jobs and class system is not bad in theory. You can level two jobs and then create a new more powerful job. Sounds cool, but how do you earn XP for your secondary jobs? I don't know. The game doesn't tell you squat. My secondary jobs don't seem to be leveling at all after several battles' worth of XP. I am pretty sure they only way to level a job is to set it to 'primary'.But then... say you level your soldier to 10 (and get three skill slots to use from the soldier's 7-10 actual skills) if you switch solider to a secondary role, you now have only two skill slots and you have three slots in your new unleveled primary job/class. You now have a bunch of skills you unlocked you can't use. The game also switches your characters loadout based on the primary job you've chosen. Ex:The Stroyteller advanced job combines scout and mage classes, but once you switch your primary from mage to scout, you have to use and wear scout gear. You now have a character with a bunch of mage skills you unlocked (all require MP) with a now smaller mana pool... and a dagger. It's like a bad Skyrim build. Way I see it, you have to take two steps back in terms of power in order to take three forward. Sound fun?Also, there are 'encounters' on the map which are kinda like skirmishes. They help you earn XP and pearls and keep some characters at or above level. At first I thought, this is a great way to keep my roster up to snuff! I can try out different combos! Tavern brawls whenever I want! But the problem is that encounters level up at random. Your bench players quickly become underleveled. Half of my roster is unusable. They just fall behind and there's no easy way to get them caught up.Have a level 7 soldier you'd like to use?  The encounter is now level 14. Too bad little one. I tried bringing one low level character in a 5-man encounter. My team wiped and that encounter now says 'completed' Even though I was defeated. So...SHOULD YOU BUY THIS GAME:For 20 bucks? Maaaaybe. Ugh. I guess? Probably not. There are better tactics games for less. With more polish and some performance issues ironed out, I would say yes, buy it right then.But we're in now, now. When will then be now? Soon...(gulp) I hope. So unless you are a die hard Jim Henson fan (which I am), I would wait and see if the team begins to engage the community and drop news about updates before you buy. HOW TO MAKE THE GAME BETTER BECAUSE I DON'T JUST WHINGECC skills aren't reliable. The wording of the skill leads you to believe it will just work. My stun, stuns like 25% of the time. How is it being resisted? Who knows. Probably just RNG. So is there a way to increase stun chance? Nope. Is there even a way in game to test builds? Nope. Because of this, damage reigns supreme. No point in trying a stun a minion with 213 HP, only to end up doing 48 damage, when you could just do 128 damage with a normal attack and save your MP.You can't unequip items either. You can swap in an item, but you can't remove an item. This is a game about characters and items... and yet you cannot complete the most fundamental video game task. Nintendo games in 1986 let you unequip items. We are in 2020. At least one encounter on the map should allow you to choose it's level (the podling tavern would be great for this). Hell, make a custom encounter on the map that lets you choose the layout and enemy roster. Actual fun!Show all items in the store from the get go... for the love of Thra. Let us choose between default and currently equipped armor appearances. The skill circle needs it's size or transparency adjusted so you can actually see what's happening. Icon size needs tweaked and the icon's names actually fall out of the circles. It looks like powerpoint. We need a way to reset character skills, or adjust them or SOMETHING. As you progress through the game, your tactical options actually become more narrow and therefore more repetitive. Seriously, the font. You already have the Dark Crystal and Jim Henson fonts on file. They're great! Use them. We only see them on the main screen, then it's hours of reading 'Arial Black'. I will update this once I beat the game, if I can stomach the journey. Thanks for reading, and go watch the show. It's beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, at least for me, it has ACTUAL turn order, none of that "all your side goes, then all your enemies go" that just encourages dogpiling and prevents all kinds of time-based mechanics (haste, slow, stun, etc.) from being applicable.With that said, I'd really say this game is pretty solid - not mind blowing, but solid. It uses many of the Final Fantasy Tactics ideas - elevation, for example - while introducing a few of its own. Rather than missing you 'glance', doing reduced damage and no extra effects, thus protecting against an unlucky streak of misses against an enemy at a shred of health, while also allowing you to build evasion-focused characters.The aesthetic is lovely, the art in the cutscenes is delightful.. ultimately I feel pretty happy about this purchase. And, I mean, especially considering it's only $20, totally lower than I had expected. I will say that if you haven't watched the new Netflix series at all this could be a little spoily, but there's enough detail and such missing that it'd be plenty fun to watch afterwords anyway, I think.A surprisingly solid Tactics-style game from a recently revived IP that nobody asked for.. but I'm sure extremely happy to have.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all I am 35 and grew up playing Final Fantasy Tactics and original X-Com, and I've played a lot of the new X-com and X-Com 2, they're some of my favorite games and I know them in and out. This game is definitely a simpler version of those games. If you like tactics games and Dark Crystal, this would probably be a fun distraction. I beat it in a few days, I don't think it has a lot of replayability but I may play it one more time. Basically it is challenging enough to be engaging, I put it on hard and I often lost battles and had to try them again. Even the level up side battles are often tough to win. There is a decent variety in abilities and combinations you can use for different strategies. Some of the levels are creative and interesting, like levels where water rises and falls and you have to play around it. Or levels where you are trying to get from one point to another without having to kill all enemies. (hint, don't forget about flying) There is some problems though, mostly from the feeling that the game could've been a lot better if they put more into it. It ends a little quick, and some of the tier 3 jobs don't seem worth the time. The items could've been better, all of the special weapons and armor you get from beating bosses are outclassed by the top level stuff you can buy.  The Dark Crystal fantasy element is ok but not really that engaging, it mostly takes from the new tv show. I loved that show and it was fun to play as Hup and the Fizzgigs and Brea and Deet, but it didn't really add much to the story or characters. The cut scenes are simple without dialogue or fancy visuals. All in all, if you're looking for a fun strategy distraction during quarantine, you could do much worse than this. _childDocuments_.review: The only person (because  is being optimistic) I could recommend this game to is someone whose number one video game is Final Fantasy Tactics, and whose all-time favourite film is The Dark Crystal. Otherwise, I can't think of why anyone would want to play this over the myriad of turn and tile-based tactics games that have existed over these past few decades, and have long improved upon since. If there's a mistake the turn-based tactics genre has made in the past, be it a painful user interface, poor level balance, a necessity to grind that affects the flow of the story, or too many mechanics spread too thinly, The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance Tactics does it willingly, and does so even in New Game Plus.You could instead be playing Enchanted Arms.Despite the amount of hours I've put into the game, having all the achievements and buying the trading cards, this was not because I enjoyed the game, rather because I had to see everything to know that I would have no reason to return to it. The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance Tactics is mercifully shorter in its New Game+ mode thanks to insanely more powerful items with greater stat boosts and effects than before, and levels stop meaning just about anything despite enemies always managing to say they're more powerful. Not to mention it adds nothing new to the experience; it's only there to say if the game was too short, you can play it again.You could instead be playing Shadowrun: Dragonfall.The truth is the game isn't too short, rather the opposite, but it doesn't use the 20 hours I spent grinding levels to get to where I needed to be in my first playthrough at all well. The developers clearly knew enough about the Netflix show to pad out what can only be described as a "90s movie tie-in game except it's not as good as the Disney ones" (which should be a genre, only with a catchier name). Lazy is not a word I'd use to describe any game or developer, and Age of Resistance is no exception. Rather, it  to making a bad game. Whether this is for some compensation, tax scheme, a statement on the human condition or quite simply punishment for Gamer Rage in general, I'm not entirely sure. I'll take the last one though, I don't think I deserve games better than this with how I rant, but surely the late and great Jim Henson and the success of his properties post-mortem deserve better.You could instead be playing The Age of Decadence.Mechanically, it's very much like all other RPGs that have stats which are incalculable and you just have to hope that bigger is better. Which, thankfully, is true of The Dark Crystal. Damage, health and magic pools are easily read and mostly understandable, but knowing if a hit will be a glancing blow or a crit, you can't say for sure. Magic and physical defence are just as nebulous concepts, as if thrown in because "that's what video games do". They're not wrong on that I suppose. However, what stops Tactics from being like other turn-based JRPGs with verticality is how everything takes more time than it should. You can't simply right click on an enemy to perform an attack. You have to click on your current character, navigate the radial wheel, select the ability, select the enemy if you're in range. If not, move. If you're still out of range, undo the move and retry. It sounds like a silly thing to get worked up over, but it's the way one interfaces with the game and it's an immediate annoyance. The only way to overcome this is to play more aggressively with better equipment, so you can end fights faster. But to do that you need to grind for Pearls to buy said equipment, and to grind you have to get into combat.You could instead be playing Fallout.But as far as The Dark Crystal influences go, there's not that many. Tilesets are overused, with landmarks and other points of interest barely having any presence in the deadened woods, murky swamps and a sandy level. There's also painfully little to no voice acting, with some squarks from the Skeksis characters and not much else, not even for the few "cutscenes" which are comic book panels fading in and out, not even daring to bother footage from the show it's based on. There's appearances from the antagonists and plenty of named characters but beyond that, not a whole lot else that makes you feel like you're playing the show itself, and hardly a loose adaptation at that.You could instead be playing Divinity: Original Sin.Movie tie-in games have come too far for this to get my praise. In a world where we had the Battle for Middle-Earth games, Arkham Asylum, Mad Max, Alien: Isolation, The Godfather 1 & 2 and most recently Spiderman, this feels over 20 years out of place. If you want a tactical JRPG there's no shortage of them on Steam with far greater replayability, skill requirements and are memorable in every other way.You could instead be playing literally anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: is a tactical turn-based strategy game based on the Jim Henson movie and then the Netflix TV series.The story is simple, help the Geflings against the Skeksis. To fully understand the background lore, I would suggest that you go watch the TV series. I have not seen the TV series, but I did watch the movie in 1982 (yes, I know I am old).The game has three difficulty levels built in along with a tutorial. Everything is easy to understand.When you play, you will see a map with various nodes that take you to different battles. Most of these are story-related, some of them are not. If you need to be stronger for certain fights, you can use these individual nodes to grind for levels.The game goes from battle to battle, so understanding the lore is not really all that important. In these battles, you will select party members. It is advisable that you level up the lower level characters so that everyone keeps up.During the battle, each party member has a primary job. There are three different jobs and with leveling up, you can unlock a secondary job as well. Each job has its own abilities for variability.Each battle is different, and you will find out the objective as you play. You will have to kill all enemy units in some, while others involves you making a clean escape, etc.Winning a battle will earn you experience points, loot, and also money, all used for progression. If you fail, you can just go to redo these missions.They are absolutely beautiful, everything appears right out of the TV show.There is no spoken dialogue. The music is awesome.You can play the game completely using a Mouse, a Keyboard, or a Controller. I tried all three, and I prefer using the Mouse.In Europe the price is €16.79 which is absolutely fair. You get enough playtime and quality of game out of this money. It’s regional priced also (USA $19.99).As mentioned above, I never watched the TV series, and I had seen the movie a long time ago that I cannot remember much from the story. After spending some time with the game, I now want to go watch the series so I can understand the story better. One thing to note is that you really do not need to understand the story the enjoy the game. You go from battle to battle and so the story is a bonus, not a must. This style of progression may be boring for some people. However, the battles are tactical and not too long--the ideal combination.If you love tactical turn-based games, I would recommend this game. For people who are new to the genre, this is not a bad starting point either, as it's fairly easy even on Normal difficulty.Overall score: 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Solid casual tactics game, if you are into the genre I highly recommend to play in hard mode from the start, I played the first few missions on normal and I was getting really bored, hard makes you think about units placement and priorities a lot more and when I changed difficulty suddenly the mechanics got more interesting. I'd place it somewhere between Mario Rabbids and Mutant. The main loop consists in doing main missions that follow the show storyline while using side ones to acquire equipment and level up, there's no permadeath so you can always make a story mission easier by grinding side encounters first. Pawns that "die" during a battle get less experience (half?) so there's still an incentive of trying to keep everyone alive. Considering that it's a low budget game from a small studio the story is surprisingly well recreated. Don't expect cinematic cutscenes, it's just text most of the time, but the battles often recreate the show key moments, a shame that they've not integrated clips from the show

_childDocuments_.review: I am just so dissappointed in this game.  I had it on my wishlist forever, and bought it on Day 1.  Unfortunately it was a huge let down.  First let me say this game could have gone 3 ways.... fan service for those that love the series, fan service for those that love tactics combat, or the best option: fan service for those that love both.  Unfortunately, as someone that was looking for a good tactics based combat game... this falls VERY short.  Everything about this game screams "MOBILE GAME"... from the oversized chunky GUI and radial menus, to the hardly-there graphical options, to the tight FOV and simplistic graphics.  It feels cheap, and thrown together like a free to play mobile game.  There is no voice acting, no impressive FMVs, nothing original or breathtaking about the presentation AT ALL.  I watched a dozen or so hours of gameplay on stream before I loaded up my own game.  I was horrified at what I saw on stream, and it didn't get any better when I tried it.  I sat through the FORCED tutorial that teaches you the most retardedly simple movement and attack coontrols, that anyone who has ever even SEEN a video game would already know.  And did the first few battles.  After that I just couldn't take it anymore.  It was simple, unchallenging, and bland. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - 7/10 - Not a must play, and the storytelling is very weak, but it is a good tactical strategy game with plenty of character customization, abilities, and difficulty options to keep you busy for a while. Can be slow and boring if you're not into turn-based, slow-paced, tactical strategy. I thoroughly enjoyed it because I like that kind of thing. If you're into turn-based tactical strategy, pick it up. If not, maybe on sale.And now, the long, boring review.STORYTELLINGI originally picked this up hoping for expanded lore in "The Dark Crystal" universe or an alternate or parallel storyline to the Netflix show. What I got was a disjointed and confusing narrative that follows beat for beat pretty much all of the same events in the show, but doesn't explore them even a tenth as well as the show does. The characters, with the exception of the Podlings, and, oddly enough, the Fizzgigs, all seem pretty generic. "The Dark Crystal" has an incredibly rich and vibrant universe with diverse and interesting characters, locations, and lore. This game makes those characters seem more like lifeless puppets than the actual puppet show! The game completely and utterly fails on a narrative level. If the Skeksis didn't look like Skeksis, you could literally insert any random bad guy doing evil things and it would make no difference. Now some of that may be due to budget, but even taking into consideration that the story is conveyed through speech bubbles and comics, there are lots of generic elements that could have been so much better with a little creativity and embellishment. FOR EXAMPLE: The "Defeat" banner when you lose with genericevillaugh.exe... how much more satisfying would it have been to have a full screen comic book graphic pop up with one of the Skeksis hurling an in-character insult at you?GAMEPLAY AND CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATIONThis is where the game won me back. I absolutely love the gameplay, tactical strategy, and character customization in this. It is slow, turn-based, tactical strategy, but I really like those types of games. There are plenty of maps with good variety in environmental hazards, lots of character customization options (if you take the time to unlock them), and added difficulty options that should keep you busy and thinking for a while. I was engaged by the gameplay and thinking about how to do things (sometimes challenging myself by taking in my least qualified characters just to see if I could make it work). I really loved playing with all the different abilities and trying things out. It's the type of game where I should go to bed, but I just want to play one more map. In short, I had a lot of fun playing the game itself, and this overcame pretty much all of the problems I had with storytelling. It's clear this is where all of the effort went, and it absolutely shows. Of note... you can only level up secondary abilities if you set them as your primary abilities. Also, there are some abilities and specialized equipment that are absolutely essential for certain missions. Specifically, with The Chamberlain, The Scientist, and The Scientist's nurlock experiments. INTEGRITYMy first run was pretty much glitch free. The game did not crash, and I did not encounter any game breaking issues. On the "New Game +" mode, I had a bizarre glitch where some of my equipment would disappear, but it reappeared after quitting and relaunching the game. Overall the integrity of the game is pretty solid. It's always helpful when I don't have to fight the game at the same time I'm fighting the enemies in the game. And using another definition of integrity... I'm happy to say there are NO microtransactions and NO annoying pop-ups urging you to spend more money in the online store. They don't nickel and dime you for hero characters, special skins, PTW, or other BS. You get the complete game when you buy the game and that's always, ALWAYS appreciated.OVERALL: I liked it. I would have liked it more if it had better storytelling and more creativity and personality in the embellishment, but the gameplay alone made it worth it for me. I do feel like I got my money's worth. Your mileage will vary, especially if you're not into slow, turn-based strategy. As I said, not a must play, but if you like tactical strategy games, you'll probably like it.

_childDocuments_.review: A richly satisfying tactical game with a complex combined-tree skill path system and strategic squad assembly that gave me a real challenge on the hardest level. Nice (colonial uprising) story, graphics, interestingly-varied creatures and comic-book cut-scenes to drive plot. Almost every battle introduces a new skill or way to gain an edge. And it is a pretty forgiving system, encouraging experimentation with picking your team and varying their jobs. The equipment system provided a good balance as your opponents get harder to beat, with fewer weaknesses. The relatively simple square-grid 3D-battle-maps were less of a constraint than I first expected, since you have to work hard to get the best out of varying formations and changing threats/opportunities. The order-of-battle system was very clear, which is good because it is pretty essential to master the sequencing of your, foe's (and allies') turns.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't remember if I've ever seen the original Dark Crystal and I haven't seen the Netflix show. From what I know, the game's story is a retelling of the show. I am in no way compelled to continue on playing from where I stopped. The game plays like an older Tactics Ogre game but without the lovably cliche and stupid characters, interesting narrative, and great gameplay that I expect from Tactics Ogre. There's no hook for anyone who isn't familiar with the Dark Crystal property. I don't care about these characters because they haven't shown me any side of them. I don't care about Rian or Gurjin or the Skeksis. If the characters don't hook me into the game, then the story should and does the story do that? No. I wouldn't be writing this review now if it did. I honestly have idea what the hell I just witnessed and I certainly don't care about it at all. The gameplay should interest me seeing as there hasn't been a proper Tactics Ogre since the Seven Years' War but even then I don't enjoy playing this game. I was just bored. The game isn't caught up to modern SRPGs like Disgaea 5. I can't just click on any enemy to attack them or click on a square to move my character. You have to navigate menus and windows to do everything. This isn't 1992, we can use modern SRPG mechanics. The game is pretty ugly design wise. I know the original Dark Crystal had more "mature" and interesting puppet designs than what Henson and co. did previously but I wouldn't call these mature or interesting. These characters are just ugly. The comic-like art style doesn't do wonders here. The overall presentation is supposed to be like a comic book and while the game does that, it certainly doesn't do it in any meaningful way. Netflix is sitting on a mound of cash and the game doesn't even look like it got an ant hill of a budget. What a shame. R.i.p Jim Henson.
