_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a nostalgic love letter to the early Sierra adventure games, especially The Colonel's Bequest, but with a modern twist. What stands out most is how the game expands on the classic formula, staying true to its roots while introducing improvements that make it more engaging and accessible.The game gently nudges you in certain directions, but ultimately, it's up to you to piece together the mystery. This design strikes a perfect balance between being story-driven and player-driven. Unlike many modern adventure games, where you feel like you're simply along for the ride, The Crimson Diamond gives you a real sense of agency. The choices you make have tangible consequences, which makes the experience more immersive.Another clever touch is how the scoring is built into the story. It doesn't feel like a superficial points tally but rather an integrated part of the experience. For fans of classic EGA graphics, this game delivers in spades—the pixel art and colors hit hard on that nostalgia. While almost all of the puzzles are logical, I did encounter one that left me stuck for a bit. Getting the  could have been handled more gracefully, but overall, the puzzle design is solid.While it might not be a popular opinion, I loved the text parser. It gave me a lot more freedom in exploring the world and solving problems, and the decision to avoid using "use" as a catchall action command was brilliant. This forces you to think more deeply about your actions, which adds another layer of immersion.That said, there were some rough edges. While the pixel art is fantastic, the animations are a bit choppy. Text parsing could also use some refinement—some logical inputs weren’t recognized, leading to some trial and error. Additionally, I encountered several minor bugs that, while not game-breaking, were noticeable. Hopefully, these will be addressed in future updates.Despite these small issues, it's clear how much care went into making this game. The developers took the best parts of older adventure games and layered in modern standards, avoiding many of the pitfalls that made early Sierra titles frustrating by today’s standards. I sincerely hope the developer continues to create games in this style. The Crimson Diamond stands out as one of my favorite detective games, and I would love to see more titles inspired by this classic genre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A great throwback to the Sierra Online days. If you were a fan of Colonel's Bequest you will love it. Julia put a lot of love and effort into making this and it shows. The art could fit right into the SCI era Sierra games, and the music was created with a real MT-32.It uses a parser to interact with the game, but there are lots of shortcuts and quality of life enhancements. The puzzles aren't too bad and there are multiple things you can miss and find on different playthroughs. It can be a bit wordy at times but not overwhelming. The ending bits definitely take a page from the Laura Bow games, so you might want to take notes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game so far! Having a great time. The art is incredible and every scene is a joy to explore, incredible EGA pieces. The puzzles (I'm about 3/4 of the way through) are challenging yet very satisfying. And the music is very very catchy. A wonderful homage to classic text parsers! There are some really lovely QoL additions that make this a great way for newer players to get into this older style of game. Lastly, as someone from the same part of the world as the game is based, I'm enjoying the neat niche references that are fun while not being necessary to understand to play the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson diamond is a fantastic game! I have been following it's development and it has been awesome seeing it release and be so well received! I did not grow up with old adventure games and this was my first introduction to text parser and I ended up really liking it m(even played old school text parser games after trying TCD demo). The parser is very beginner friendly and easy to use, but also challenging when it needs to be. There were a few bits where finding the solution was harder, but it was a good challenge.The story is also intriguing and characters have very distinct personalities. It starts off slow as you get your bearings on the lodge and it's inhabitants/guests and then picks up quite rapidly. There is more than one thing happening at once and the game will reward you if you pay attention and inspect everything you can. I love eavesdropping in particular, it is so much fun. I cannot go more into the story, because of spoilers. Needles to say it's a good mystery.The retro graphics and EGA color palette are very nice and beautiful. The closeup shots are gorgeous and the limited colors have been well utlizied.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: What a gem! The atmosphere is on point, the graphics take me back, and entering commands through the prompt gives you that feeling of freedom of exploration and wonder that all good adventure games instill in you.And it's all the work of one developer! Wow.If you dig retro style adventure games true to their stylistic inspiration, this is one to get today.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a true "love letter" to The Colonel's Bequest. The game offers a nostalgic experience reminiscent of old-school text parser adventures. It blends the simplicity and charm of early adventure games with modern sensibilities, such as a more forgiving approach to player mistakes compared to its inspirations. The game requires you to explore environments, gather clues, and solve puzzles by typing commands, similar to how text parsers functioned in classic Sierra games. However, it doesn't punish the player as harshly for every misstep, making it more accessible while still maintaining the feel of the originals.The parser, while generally effective, occasionally led me to seek hints while solving a puzzle, only to realize that I was on the right track all along but needed to phrase the command slightly differently. However, this is exactly the kind of challenge that characterized those classic games, and in the end, I have to admit that this quirk might very well be part of the nostalgic experience for me.The adventure begins with two women deeply immersed in their passions, whether it's studying birds or mineralogy. This instantly evokes memories of books and films from a few decades ago, where adventures were driven by characters fueled by their great passions, be it archaeology (“Alessandretta, of course!”), science (“Great scott!”), or paleontology (“They’re moving in herds”). I particularly loved the game because the protagonist shares knowledge about mineralogy, genuinely teaching something valuable. And she does so in a way that makes the information memorable, as it is woven into the gameplay and essential for progressing in the game. The narrative is incredibly enjoyable.Guiding us through this adventure is a third woman, Julia Minamata, who is driven by her passion as well (developing video games ofc). She tells a story that is both classic and new, filled with intriguing ideas and emotions. I also found her special tribute to Roberta Williams at the end of the game to be very touching. In the final credits, the creator thanks the player with a heartfelt "thank you for playing," and I know for sure that she truly means it.In the end, I'm deeply grateful that there are still people driven by passion, who find joy in discovery and in sharing it with others. I sincerely hope that there will be more opportunities for Julia to explore and marvel alongside all of us.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. There are few games out there this committed to the style and even then they don't have the same quality of graphics and puzzles. But just in case you're scared of classic Sierra-style gotchas and walking dead scenarios you have nothing to worry about here. You can die but it's usually pretty well signposted. If you've got any nostalgia for the EGA graphic adventure era you've got to play this one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this game wishlisted forever, and I'm so happy it finally became available this year! It is beyond charming--a perfect retro throwback to text parser adventure games. With that kind of gameplay comes some inevitable hiccups (trying to get the phrasing just right, making typos and getting aggravated), but overall, it felt like the game was pretty intuitive about doing what I wanted it to do.The story is a mystery wrapped in a mystery wrapped in a mystery, and all of the layers were compelling. I don't usually say this, but one of the best things about this game was that it was possible to miss clues depending on how you approached certain tasks. Normally, I want to discover every last detail in a game, and in most mystery adventure games, you're pretty much on rails, and you can't proceed without finding all the clues. Here, you can proceed by attending key events without discovering something important, which will change the outcome of your game.Because of these miss-able clues, you feel like a real amateur detective, trying to piece together information from your limited observations. I didn't find it hard to get enough information to solve the mystery, but I imagine it WOULD be hard to figure out every last detail without a walkthrough. Still, with limited help, I was able to get a solid positive ending, and I don't have any major remaining questions.The graphics are great--even in the pixel art, it's usually pretty easy to see important details or when something has changed in a scene. There aren't TOO many areas that aren't important, and there's relatively minimal backtracking. I also feel there's very little moon logic, to the point where I found myself intuiting what to do with objects before their ultimate use became apparent. It's by no means an easy game, but it felt like a logical one, and I simply loved it.A small list of nitpicks: I did see one reviewer complaining that there isn't enough sound, and I agree with that. It would have been nice to have a bit of ambient noise, but honestly, I'd rather there be too LITTLE sound rather than an irritating repetitive soundtrack. I did sometimes get frustrated when I thought I had looked at something only to find that I had to "Examine" it. At one point I typed "pick up strip of paper" about 20 different ways before I realized I had to examine something first, find out what that strip of paper was, and then type that. I also found the tasks in the notebook a little hard to parse. I think this is a game where you'd benefit from taking your own notes so you can remember whom to talk to about what; I didn't ask people enough questions!If you love a classic adventure mystery, this IS your next game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful journey back to my childhood era of games. Sometimes I wish I could go back and play Sierra games again for the first time so I'm having fun enjoying every second, trying bizarre actions and getting to know the characters. Great quality of life settings compared to actual retro text parsers. I can't wait to see what speedrunners do with this game, there's an amazing community of Sierra and Sierra-like games speedrunners out there. This was a labour of love and I hope it does well. Congrats!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: What a treat! I won’t spoil anything, but The Crimson Diamond is packed with mystery. You get to be Nancy Maple, who finds herself stepping into the shoes of a detective. There’s a big map to explore, and a bunch of characters to interact with. You’ll be listening in, sneaking around, asking questions, finding clues, grabbing items, and solving puzzles - just like you’d expect in a game like this.The artwork is stunning and so detailed, full of dramatic close-ups. You’d never guess it’s just a 16-color palette! Plus, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing!I’m having so much fun with it. I can’t recommend it enough!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm an adventure gamer from way back. I've been playing my whole life, and I've played many of the modern entries into the genre.It's been a long time since I've played a game that took me back to the good ol' days as effectively as this one did. The text parser is a nostalgic favorite of mine. This one is a lot more forgiving than the adventure games of yore, inviting you to try typing anything and everything you can think of. The puzzles were challenging, but not so challenging I ever wanted to rage-quit and stop playing. I'd get stuck for a day or two, but I'd be thinking about the solution and then it would hit me and I'd open up the game and try things out. It's one of those games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've played all year! The Crimson Diamond is a wonderfully written, dazzlingly faithful homage to DOS-era text-parser adventure games that avoids the most common pitfalls of the genre with its wonderfully intuitive puzzle design.The only reason my playtime is so low is that I needed to play this game with a CRT filter, so I ran it through RetroArch instead of Steam. I'd love for an official CRT filter option to be included in the base game, but I intend to revisit the game in the future to see the alternative endings and get those achievements.If this became a series, I would play every entry. Here's hoping for more adventures with Nancy, the cunning young mineralogist/detective!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A really excellent mystery adventure. I almost avoided it because i didn't grow up playing any of the text-interaction adventure games growing up, they were slightly before my time. However it was actually just a really fun and dynamic way to interact, i learned alot playing it. I assumed I wouldn't enjoy such a finicky system and I'll admit it wasn't 100% perfect but overall being able to directly input written commands felt really free and dynamic. It was very immersive and the mystery itself is surprisingly complex, 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I think I've never played a Text parser before, so I was kind of hesitant to get into this game – despite it's great reviews on trustworthy sites. But I decided to give it a try and loved every second of it. The texting actually gives you a strangely liberating feel as if you're able to do almost anything. It's really impressive how many different (wrong) interactions Julia considered and wrote an answer for. You always feel like the game knows what you mean which is definitely not a given for a game like that. So the puzzling always seemed fair and logical.Additionally the story was really nice. As much as I enjoy Point and click adventures I am really thrown off by their humor quite often. Obviously a video game doesn't have to be super-serious or anything, but it's just nice to meet a game that takes itself serious enough once in a while. Doesn't mean Crimson Diamond is super bleak and without any fun, but really it seems more focused on telling it's story than entertaining you with countless dad jokes.A few additional things I want to point out that I really enjoyed:- the hint system (which is basically a website) is awesome. There are numerous clues for each potential issue so it doesn't give away the answer immediately but tries to lead you in the right direction step by step.- the graphics are really beautifully done- there are several different endings one can explore and the ending really gives you the opportunity to show how much of the story you actually understood/uncovered- one character in the game () basically has my dad's name. <3Overall really recommend this one. Give it a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm currently in chapter 3 and so far The Crimson Diamond is probably the best 'modern' adventure game I've played in the last 10 years. TCD absolutely nails that classic Sierra style without feeling like a copycat. Exploration actually feels rewarding and the puzzles have all been logical so far. Compared to The Colonel's Bequest, TCD communicates clearly which tasks in your notebook advance the world state and you can explore as much as you want without missing any optional events.The music is also very good and I wish there was more of it. Even if it came at the cost of authenticity.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played and enjoyed those old Sierra adventure games where you have to type in everything you do then this might be for you. The Crimson Diamond is a well made and fun game, with a text parser and has none of those click and point interface options that came later. The game autosaves though, but I can live with that.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a fine Canadian Whiskey. Aged for many years by a mindful developer in the old EGA graphical style. I detect a homage to the old point and click adventures, then hints of the developers own unique witty writing and flavours of modern quality of life design. The nostalgic taste lingers while still being its own unique game.But I am certainly no expert!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a modern retro indie masterpiece and an absolute breath of fresh (Northern Canadian) air to those of us who love those old 80's and early 90's graphic adventure games. The amount of care and detail that went into crafting the game's exquisite art, meticulous writing, complicated story mechanics, and mood-setting music is obvious throughout the entire experience. I've been fortunate to know Julia for several years on Twitch and been able to follow along with some of the design/development process--and I was still blown away by the final results. If you love Laura Bow: The Colonel's Bequest, then The Crimson Diamond will transport you back to that era just like stepping in a time machine, although it is arguably a cozier and more relaxed experience overall. The game is also more accessible to modern audiences who may not have played text parsers before, offering tutorials and a helpful goals/objectives list that get checked off as they're accomplished, along with a list of events that Nancy Maple has witnessed or participated in.In a world where so much media feels increasingly soulless because it is obviously marketing- and "bottom line"-driven, The Crimson Diamond sparkles as a true piece of art and a labor of love. While I am being transparent that the game was gifted to me, I believe that the price point is extremely reasonable given its quality, and countless people in the retro gaming circles I travel in ended up purchasing it and loving it. You really can't go wrong buying The Crimson Diamond, and I believe that it's important that we support endeavors from creators whose work embodies genuine care and artistry so that we can hopefully enjoy similar-caliber titles in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic.  I was worried that the game would be unfair and require the use of walkthroughs to complete (PTSD from my Sierra days), but it was wonderfully satisfying to play through "blind" and I did not have to have any hints to finish the game.  My second concern was that the game might be overly simplistic and rely mostly on nostalgia and the (admittedly lovely) art style, but it did not disappoint on this front, either!  There are layers to the story and even potential for more than one playthrough (with a clever and optional hint system at the end, for those who want to dig deeper but might be pressed for time).  Of course there are a few bugs (I mainly noticed some displaced/ out of time dialogue), but they'll probably be cleaned up going forward, and do not affect the gameplay.  Julia Minamata has done a fantastic job and I'll be eagerly looking forward to anything else she comes up with in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is an adventure game by Julia Minamata, the game is based off of classic Sierra adventure games, specifically taking the most inspiration The Colonel's Bequest. This was one of my most anticipated releases this year and Crimson Diamond definitely didn't disappoint. The game seemed quite straightforwards compared to it's inspiration to me initially, but my jaw was agape when the game tallied my score up at the end, showing that I actually missed quite a few possible encounters and wasn't quite able to tie up quite a few loose ends; and it made me ravenous to give it another playthrough as a result! (I'll definitely give some further thoughts in regards to that in the future but I shall continue.)Julia Minamata did a fantastic job creating EGA graphics that genuinely feel like they were ripped straight out of the era, plenty of stunning backgrounds and closeup shots rendered in that wonderful limited color palette that a lot of us retro enthusiasts have come to adore deeply. (Always loved that deep red that they used for Caucasian skin tones!) It's very clear that they have tons of love for not just Sierra adventure games, but the genre as a whole. It's really hard for me to find anything particularly negative about the game to say, maybe I felt a *bit* confused about how the game wanted me to type in certain actions but that's just how it is with text parser games sometimes, really hard to knock it for that. I also found the music, when it comes on to be excellent and suited all of the scenes perfectly; definitely going to have to get that soundtrack eventually...The story is paced well enough, at least I was triggering the right events at the right time (mostly) so I felt that I was moving along nicely. There's a nice build-up of tension as you proceed further into the game and witness all of the plot threads start to intertwine together for the latter half of the game. I felt really smart for finding the right commands to be able to eavesdrop on certain events, though as I found out; I missed quite a few! And once it all starts to boil over at the end, there is truly a sense of urgency in the game that feels incredibly strong and had me on the edge of my seat. With so many different ways that story can seem to end, it really just makes me want to replay just to see what kinds of thing I can do. (Including the many possible ways to get a game over, I only found a few!)I do actually think that this game could be a really good jumping on point for newcomers to the genre, as the puzzles aren't so crazy that it devolves into the utter wackiness a lot of the classic adventure game puzzles fall into. Everything makes sense and collecting items, evidence, and samples is a complete breeze once you understand what you're looking for exactly. My one tip to newbies is to make good use of not only the Look command, but also Examine, and Look In; and of course, examine everything you pick up closer as it could be the one thing that helps you get even closer to solving the countless mysteries occurring in Crimson, Ontario.All in all, if you like Sierra adventure games, adventure games in general, or even a passing interest in them, it's hard to say no to such a low price point for a game that exudes so much charisma and charm while telling quite an engaging story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely solid, throwback adventure game! Even with its old-school Sierra trappings, it goes out of its way to make you comfortable with its combination text parser/menu-based controls. Even more impressive is the level of granularity to your investigation: even if you miss an important scene or two, there are other ways to find the information you need and solve the case. And despite a few death scenarios for the sake of it, they never feel unfair or set you back too far (thank you, auto-saves). A game well worth your time, regardless of your experience with older adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Have been awaiting this for a while (Julia's dev logs have been great!) and have not been disappointed so far - the quality and attention to detail make it feel like an instant classic, beautiful art, catchy tunes and a gripping plot. Have been playing on a steam deck and works great - Will update once I've completed...
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game obviously filled with so much passion. As much as it initially appealed to me in a nostalgic sense, that soon faded away and I found myself appreciating it not through a lens of how much it reminded me of games from the past, but how much of an achievement it is in its own right.The art was the initial appeal but the story was really captivating and I felt like the writing maintained a high standard throughout, after finishing I felt compelled to immediately load some saves to try some other things out, but decided I'll just be ending up doing further playthroughs anyway. The characters all feel distinct and interesting, I really want to discover what's going on with each of them and I feel like I just scratched the surface. I also really liked the music, I sometimes found myself wishing there had been more of it sometimes but what's there is great. I found myself stopping to listen to the main menu music for a bit every time I booted it up, I love that track in particular.Ultimately it's a game set in 1914, drawing heavy inspiration from a game released in 1989, and yet for all relevant metrics (for me) it manages to feel timeless. I have no doubt this is going to be considered a classic in the genre and I hope the sales reflect that, and we eventually see some more of Nancy Maple.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Something about the text parser makes games like this so immersive. I think just the way you have to think about what you're doing more really  brings you into the world. If you haven't tried a text parser game this is the perfect one to dip your toes into. Persist and you'll be rewarded!  Crimson Diamond itself is a work of art, beautifully pixel arted in luscious 16 colours! I love this, partly for the nostalgia reasons, but also the contrast of light and shadow, and brilliant colour that it brings.  I wanted to leave an early review to support this kind of game getting made, and can't wait to dig into the mysteries more!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes when an independent, solo developer creates a game, it's easy for them to run out of creative juice. Making a project like this, over multiple years can be extremely difficult. But Ms. Minamata made it work. You can tell right away how much passion and energy went into this. The game is so wonderfully rich and dense. The art is gorgeous, even scenes you may only see once! I was a bit worried, because the game is quite obviously inspired in part by The Colonel's Bequest, a legendarily hard Sierra game. And this game does have easily missable scenes and character deaths but they're not random or unfair and the game has an autosave feature. It was clearly made with love and passion. The creator deserves a long break but I will be guaranteed to buy her next game, should she decide to make one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a love letter to retro adventure games with modern player-friendly considerations added to it. An attention to detail and respect for the player is at the forefront of this game, and the way it allows you to approach the experience is top of its class.Some of my most fond memories of old adventure games is struggling to progress but being engrossed in the story being told, and pushing on no matter what. After getting older I still enjoy that feeling, but this game launches with a player-friendly hint book (like the old ones!) that opens in your browser. It's even formatted like the old scratch-to-reveal-hintbooks with gradually escalating hints which was a really nice touch. Partaking with it is left at your own discretion (as it should be!).The artwork is true to the EGA roots and faithfully retains the palette many of us grew up with. Animations, character portraits and backgrounds are sublime and well-designed. Seeing the palette shift between night and day outside the lodge is an absolute delight! It helps that the writing is snappy and dished out in perfect rhythm. It never overstays its welcome or bogs you down in extraneous dialogue. If you like geology, there is a ton to learn here with some nice crash-courses provided in the form of puzzles and insights by the protagonist. If you don't like rocks or gems, these things might be annoying, but as someone who is an ardent amateur geologist it's hard for me to judge if this is annoying for other people. The music is sparsely used - giving it a nice punch when it's called for. As an aside, all the tunes sound like I remember the old Adlib music sounding like back in the day. There is some dissonance in the sound effects which are a lot higher fidelity.Overall, as life-long Laura Bow fans playing this game together with my sister was a delight. Playing blindly (with just a few hints, I swear!) earned me an ending that felt deserved and earnest, and the game asked me if I wanted hints on what I missed. It gave me a really good idea of things that, in hindsight, I should have realised I missed! Knowing what was left unrealised in the game, I feel the vigor to replay it that I feel with the old Sierra classics.Cannot recommend this game enough for people that enjoy mysteries and wonderful art and characters. The game is a comfortable romp at about five to six hours, comparable (or a bit longer) to the classics.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's been following the development of The Crimson Diamond for a few years, my expectations were high. I already knew the art would be a wonderful throwback to the Sierra games of the late 1980s, but I wasn't sure about the story, puzzles, characters, and overall gameplay elements. Likewise, I've never been much into text parsers even when they were a popular interface.And I'm happy to say that The Crimson Diamond lives up to expectations-- particularly with the parsing! For one, the creator has taken great pains to make the user experience as streamlined as possible, with many, many shortcuts for typing common commands. These are easy to find in the manual and fairly intuitive even if you want to jump right in. Additionally, there's many different ways to type the same command, so you won't often get frustrated trying to guess precisely what sequence of words the game wants. Similarly, you're never expected to write out a novel -- most of the commands needed are comprised of around three to seven words or so.Most importantly, the choice of making the game a parser really adds to the feel. There's dense backstories waiting to be discovered in every part of the game and in every character, and a parser game captures that feel of mystery and depth by encouraging the player to test and explore different things, as opposed to having all the options laid out for you as you would in a verb-based interface. This is an easy world to get swept in, and it rewards you with many mysteries to solve.Along those lines, there is a lot of investigating to do! The Colonel's BeQuest has been mentioned as a precursor to this in several reviews, but with that game many of the events occur whether you investigate or not. Other mystery games in general swap out detective elements with more generic, tangentially related puzzles. Not here -- there's a lot of detection -- establishing who was where and when, often why; what certain conversations really meant; what belongs to whom, and more! In fact,almost every puzzle takes the form of some kind of investigation, and the game rarely strays from that, while still keeping the puzzles from being repetitive. If this is your first parser, it's an excellent introduction that doesn't cheat the player with sudden deaths or unwinnable situations, and if you're a fan of the genre, this is a wonderful entry! Also, special kudos to the music, which similarly captures the look and feel of both the game's period and the classic Sierra games. I still have the opening theme in my head.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: so far I've only played through the demo (the game's first of 7 chapters), but I've been following the game's development for nearly a year, and seeing the amount of passion she's poured into it has been very exciting and inspiring.  Julia started this project with no experience in game development or programming knowledge, she was simply an artist who wanted to experiment with the limited color palette and resolution of her favorite retro games, but her enthusiasm grew until she decided she needed to see her creations as a full game.  and her passion doesn't just extend to the artwork and gameplay, almost every facet of the plot and characters is a reflection of something she's knowledgeable about or means something to her, from the main character's interest in mineralogy, her friend Kimi's interest in bird watching, the local history of the setting... it's all very authentic and you can feel the love poured into it.  on top of all that, she's put as much as thought as she could into making sure the game is approachable to people who've never played a game with these kinds of retro mechanics, because naturally you dont just want your game to only appeal to niche retro enthusiasts, you want everyone to enjoy it as much as you do!if literally any part of this game seems interesting into you, give it a try; I highly doubt you'll be disappointed!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The platonic ideal of a cozy adventure game. Incredibly charming visually and very well-paced in a way few other modern (or classic) point and click adventures manage. I do think that there could have been more opportunities for unique dialogue based on parser input and I think the conclusion is a little rushed, but I loved this game and will support all future Canadian geological adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent new point and click adventure game in the vein of the Laura Bow murder mystery games from Sierra. I thoroughly enjoyed it. I was fully immersed in the writing and loved how each character I felt were unique and actually properly characterized. Julia did an EXCELLENT job of recreating the feel of the old SCI0 engine Sierra adventure games and I am very impressed that she managed to do this in Adventure Game Studio (it helps that I love both those engines for adventure games) and at times I couldn't tell the difference. I appreciate the quality of life additions to the game over CB such as Nancy going through all the evidence and objectives in speech and thought bubbles and how that dynamically changes depending on how many of the objectives you have completed. I greatly appreciated that the notebook clearly defined what were the objectives at any one time during a chapter and kept logs of every single thing that was discovered, and the lightbulb pop up and associated dings whenever you found something; this is something SORELY lacking from the Colonel's Bequest, especially in regards of getting the Super Sleuth ranking.It is a little rough in some spots, but for a one woman job that has never made a game or done programming in anything else it is quite impressive. I know Julia is very receptive to the glitches people are finding so they will be ironed out over time. One small critique I can give is that it is almost *too* much like the Colonel's Bequest and Dagger of Amon Ra in characters, setting, etc, but that isn't a bad thing as those games did the murder mystery genre for adventure games very well, and TCD just expanded upon that. I did feel like I had to try and reload my games quite a bit as I realized later on in a chapter that I had missed something in the notebook, and I know that I *shouldn't* do that as whatever ending I get is just a result of my sleuthing, but I couldn't resist; just an example of how immersed I was in the game that I was pining for the best ending possible.If you are a fan of murder mystery and enjoy the old style point and click parser hybrid Sierra titles, then don't even think about and it and buy The Crimson Diamond.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A pitch-perfect tribute to 80s Sierra adventure games. Very forgiving compared to those games, too, with no "moon logic" puzzles or way to really get stuck, and there's a notebook to make sure you don't forget what you have to do at any given moment. That's not to say that the game holds your hand the whole way through, though. The game is very focused on detective work, and you'll need to be sure to explore and examine things carefully if you want to achieve the best ending (you'll be quizzed at the end to determine how well you understood the events of the game). This is never dull, because the lodge is portrayed in such a charming EGA style, and full of interesting characters. There is still some leeway to get the best ending, though. I missed a few things and was still able to achieve it. I'd definitely like to go back and achieve a perfect score. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed classic point and click Sierra games such as Colonel's Bequest, Crimson Diamond is a must have! its creator Julia Minamata has done a lot of hard work to bring this game to fruition. For those of us that love the feel of old school graphics and mysteries, this game is a trip down memory lane and more. Julia is also a fan of these older games and when I saw their influence- tapestries and items on shelves that refer back to beloved old titles-- I know that we are in good hands for a wonderful game that deserves to take a place of honor beside the classics that inspired it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first venture into text parser adventures and it serves as a good stepping stone for people looking to explore the genre. Crimson Diamond is a fantastic game that brings the classic genre into the modern age without compromising on what makes those games special. The story is a fun mystery to solve, the characters are lively and the atmosphere immaculate. Certain puzzles do have that moon-logic element to it that leaves you scratching your head quite a few times. The game has a lot of fail-safes in place which prevent you from hindering your own progress. Had a great time with it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I occasionally was able to catch Julia Minamata's streams on Twitch when she was developing this game in real time. She was always pleasant, knowledgeable, and an exceptional pixel artist. It is nice seeing everything come together into such a great retro inspired game. I am a little rusty with text parser adventure games, but their are plenty of text shortcuts and quality of life improvements baked into this game for returning hard-core fans and first-time players to appreciate. I can't wait to see what is next from this talented developer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is an evolution of the adventure game genre and a real triumph!So many other games done in the spirit of adventure games of old faithfully copy everything, flaws and all. The Crimson Diamond, however, brilliantly sets itself apart by keeping the unique flavor of those past games (the beautifully detailed EGA graphics, the affecting Roland MT-32 music, and the limitless feeling of text parser gameplay), while tossing out the dated and frustrating design elements that make them so difficult to engage with in the modern age (copious unfair deaths, soft-locks, nonsensical puzzles, and finicky, narrow text parser command parameters). Developer Julia Minamata clearly put a lot of thought into building something that celebrates what was so endearing about those old games, while also making the game accessible to new players (as well as us seasoned players who have gotten sick of obtuse puzzle design).The Crimson Diamond fashions itself after the look and feel of The Colonel's Bequest, combining it with modern design niceties (auto-saving, a notebook of objectives a la Thimbleweed Park, a robust dictionary for the text parser, and multiple ways to solve some puzzles). It marries old and new in such a unique, thoughtful way that there's really no game on the market that altogether looks, sounds, and plays quite like it! I'd put this game up there in the same category as Return to Monkey Island, as they are both games that have a foot in the past, yet are designed with respect for modern players' expectations. But Return to Monkey Island was made by developers who have been doing this since the nineties, while The Crimson Diamond is, amazingly, Julia Minamata's very first game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully crafted adventure clearly inspired by a certain era of Sierra games, which for the most part eschews the moon logic of its forefathers for grounded, logical puzzles that wouldn't feel out of place in a police procedural.The story is well paced and intriguing and its protagonist, Nancy, very endearing.It all culminates in a beautiful finale that you can influence in a multitude of ways, be it positive or negative. The best ending ties everything together very nicely, and I recommend going out of your way to experience it.  (keep some saves to previous chapters!)There are some flaws, like a few interactions that are clearly bugged (I would go into details, but that would be spoilerish) and some actions you have to repeat a bit too often to the point they become a bit annoying.All in all, I highly recommend this game, hoping for it to be only the first of many for its author.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I am a life-long Sierra & Lucas Arts (no surprise there) adventure game fan, so when I saw screenshots of The Crimson Diamond years ago, I added it with the anticipation of reliving what I loved so much from the EGA Sierra text parser games (Steam wishlist said that I added the game in March of 2019, if that gives you an idea of how long I've been waiting for this game!). Those years of waiting have allowed the author, Julia Minamata, to write a love letter to the EGA artwork & experience of The Colonel's Bequest, as well The Dagger of Amon Ra. Fortunately for us, we get the chance to read that letter.I have played other modern adventure games, and thoroughly enjoyed them, but The Crimson Diamond manages to allow me to reexperience the joy of exploring an adventure game that I haven't had since the release of those original Sierra text parser games, all while having the modern quality of life touches that some of the early adventure games hadn't developed yet. The EGA artwork is spectacular, and manages to live up to the peaks of The Colonel's Bequest, which is some of the best EGA artwork I've ever seen in a game. I also took note (pun intended) of the Roland MT-32 soundtrack - a hallmark of the SCI Sierra games , where Sierra was pushing the envelope of what games were capable of  in terms of sound & music. There is a lot of silence, but the music kicks in when it needs to, and when it does, it's incredible. The dialogue is witty & cheeky, with some of the subtle touches & style that make you feel like you're reading a novel. The characters are fully fleshed with their own personalities (much like the Laura Bow games), and I was consistently intrigued to learn more about them. Having finished the game, I can say that I was extremely satisfied with how well written all of the layers of the characters & plot that the game had to offer. Much like the Laura Bow games, your ability to deduct what happened, as well as your ability to understand it, will alter the end results. Fortunately, I found that the mechanisms that the game uses to apply what you've done was a much more effective method than the Laura Bow games. I look forward to going back & playing it again to find all the little things that I missed!I cannot recommend this game enough, and I think it's one that will appeal to old school adventure game players, as well as those who have never played a text parser before (the game does a good job of giving you a tutorial to acclimate the player to the style, and the parser itself is easy to work with). I hope that this game inspires people who are new to the style to go back & try some of those Sierra & Lucas Arts (and other developers) adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Outside of the nostalgia of its presentation and gameplay, this is also a lovely detective story, with a small cast of allies/suspects, and some detailed geologist lore from our sleuth protagonist. Although some may find elements frustrating (even in the end game I was still trying to 'use' objects, and helpfully being reminded that verb is not allowed), this is definitely a strong homage to old adventure games and sits well alongside other old school games such as Perfect Tides. (If you get very stuck, there is also a link ingame to a hints page set up by the creator.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game should become an instant classic. It is amazing. The story and characters are engaging. The puzzles and mysteries are deep and satisfying and always logical. The text interface combines the best of retro and modern. It forces you to know exactly what you want to do (you can't just click your hand icon on a spot hoping something interesting will happen), but it's rich enough and forgiving enough to almost never stand in your way. The graphics are top-notch and very detailed. There are plenty of interesting descriptions of scenery and objects even when you can't interact with them. I like that you can miss things, but not in a way that causes you to be stuck and be unable to finish the game. There are some spots where you can die (I found one), but since the game auto saves often it's probably not going to be a huge backtrack if you do.Basicallly this is what Laura Bow was trying to be. All the richness and complexity without the clunkiness and headaches.The developer has hinted at a sequel, and I can't wait to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The oldest of us shall remember the gold era of Sierra-on-line games. Amongst them, was a gem, a true gaming experience that remains unmatched to me today : The Colonel's Bequest. A mystery game in an eerie, woodunit style. Now, playing the Crimson diamond, i have the feeling i'm playing the C.B's sequel ! It's a great odd to old Sierra graphic games with mystery, a murderer on the loose, great character and story-telling. I DO Recommend !
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a welcome throwback to the golden age of adventure games. I'm only a little way into the game and it's already clear to see the love that has gone into this game. The game has a beautiful intro sequence with many 'close-up' cutscene animations that sets the stage for a grand and intriguing narrative. I've been enjoying exploring the manor, searching everything I can get away with and learning about the guests. The text parser is very well implemented with lots of handy shortcuts and the writing throughout is great. Highly recommended if you're a point and click fan!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic walk-and-talk (the text-box parser version of a point-and-click). I've been waiting for this game for the better part of a decade, and I'm extremely pleased with it now that it's been released. Easily worth the price. Great little minigames and puzzles with only one that I found genuinely irritating at the time (melting the wax). There's a preponderance Epilogue, and there's basically no major character that you don't learn a ton of stuff about.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game. The visuals are a beautifully hand crafted homage to the EGA era, you can fell every pixel is placed with love. I really like revisiting the text parser interface. It feels fresh again. Investigating feels natural and curious through it. It's all quite chill and has a lovely atmosphere. I can't wait to dig deeper into this adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond takes me back to Roberta Williams King's Quest series, albeit with much more quality of life features :)The characters and dialog are very interesting and the story has some unexpected twists and is told beautifully.I love the visuals and how much work has gone into them.This is an easy recommend for anyone who loves adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Was fun, story and characters were decent, I felt like the puzzles were fair and I did not need to look up help... mostly.  I am pretty sure I did some things out of order due to searching and trying things.  People really did not seem to care if you rummaged through their things right in front of them.  I missed opportunities to ease-drop since I didn't realize I could at first.  I did skip the tutorial so that is definitely on me.I had one particular moment when I tried a thing.. rub thing on thing (trying to not give spoilers).. and the game was like "oh no, I just couldn't risk doing that".. and then later I was checking a guide for help and it was like "btw you can do that exact thing if you want".. I tried.. and it gave different dialog this time and worked!  I felt like I was robbed of the satisfaction of it working when I tried it earlier and the game not allowing it in that chapter.  It seemed like the smart thing to do at the time but the game was like "nah".I wish there was more ambient music or sounds throughout the scenes, the game just seemed too quiet.  Fire could be crackling, something?I feel like some tools are just way way way overused  (dust that thing x1000).  I would have preferred if at the end of a chapter we tripped and lost the dust, brush, and all!Overall it was a positive experience, I like that there was multiple stories being told and many things to discover and collect for completeness.  Not certain I am the type to go for that perfect score but thanks for the journey
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game overall, it's a good text-adventure/point & click entry. I was a little disappointed in how straight-forward the story was, there aren't any twists & turns. The story, setting, plot and characters are all overtly simple.The game is not hard to finish, but if you want to 100% it there are a few easy things to miss. You could walk into the dining room and forcibly advance the 'plot', now having missed any sort of necessary cut-scenes in other rooms, which is actually a pretty annoying game mechanic. I wish the game didn't advance in such a way without prompt.I recommend playing using the shortcuts listed in 'help' menu to alleviate quite a few tedious actions. Anyway, there are a large number of dialogue options you can have with each character, it's actually a bit surprising how you can ask them about so many different topics and they often will have a response. Though, sometimes they say things that don't make sense in the current context.There are a few moments where the prompt gets really irritating to work with. E.g. throwing a work into a doorway took a lot of rewording attempts to work. Doing any one-time action was a bit tedious. Some others just would ask "be more specific" to the point that I couldn't even be more specific. . Just expect it going in.Took me quite a few hours to beat it with 100% completion, with a lot of replays and loading since it was so easy to miss one-time opportunities. Got both endings where you choose to keep the 'secret' or expose the 'secret.' I think I prefer the 'bad' ending honestly. Ah well, the good ending at least adds some bonus content.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend for anyone who likes investigative detective games and is nostalgic for retro adventure games.Note that this isn't a standard point-and-click (though you can click to move around and examine inventory items), and everything from comparing evidence to talking with other characters is done through the in-game text parser -- I might suggest playing the demo if you've never tried this type of game. Outside of a few moments where I had to struggle to rephrase things, this system is implemented really well.Just buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is SO good! If you played the EGA Sierra games back in the day, The Crimson Diamond will feel very familiar. It's almost like playing a new Laura Bow mystery. The characters and plot are great; it's clear that Julia put a lot of love into this game.The text parser can be frustrating (just like back in the day), but it understands more than i expected. There aren't a lot of deaths, which is either a good thing or a bad thing, depending on your perspective. The game auto-saves at important stages, like at the beginning of a chapter and in at least one case, before you do something that might kill you.I love this game and highly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only a few chapters in but I'm hooked. Pitch perfect adventure game. Cosy and interesting setting. It's very engrossing and I've had a few good laughs too. You gotta be cool with typing "open door" a lot (or at least "o d") but if you're into that I highly recommend this game.Adding more: after just finishing the game for the first time, despite a satisfying conclusion it was very clear there were so many other things I could have tried and I'm already beginning a new playthrough...
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a great time playing The Crimson Diamond so far! I'm just enjoying exploring because it is so beautiful. I will update this once I've played more.UPDATEI've finished my first play through (although I did load a saved game to get an alternative ending). I would play again to try and work out what I missed, and because I really enjoy exploring the lodge. I would recommend this to fans of Cluedo / ClueI appreciated the notepad, map and the ability to 'review' progress.I also loved music.The text parser is comprehensive but there were a couple of occasions where I had worked out the solution to a puzzle but didn't input the answer into the parser in the way it wanted.Overall, I think this game is great value for the money and worth playing.My adventure game of the year!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing trip down memory lane - as well as providing a feeling of playing a new game, with some neat quality of life implementations that we could have needed back in the day. The graphics are awesome, the 16 colour EGA palette really shines throughout the game, and the story and puzzles are both challenging and fun, without being to "moon logic-y". If you liked playing text parser adventure games in the 80s and 90s, this is 100 percent going to do it for you, of course. But this is also sure to hit home of any fan of story driven murder mystery adventure games. All in all, an amazing indie dev effort, and obviously a labour of love.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid I never had a computer so I missed out on many PC games and when I was a teen I tried playing a text parser game (Leisure Suit Larry 1) and was not a fan of it since it just seemed to enjoy killing the player more than telling an interesting story, guess this is what they call Sierra syndrome.After playing this game I can say I was a little too harsh fobbing off text parser games since this game weaved an interesting story and rewarded the player for actually paying attention to the plot and trying to figure out whodunit.I have never experienced a game that actually played out like this before and a game that actually wanted you to pay attention and then tell the game what you think happened and then judge you on a point based system for what you got right inspiring the player to go through the game again to get even more of the story. I'd love to see more games like this so thank you Julia Minamata for expanding this reviewer's horizons on video games. I have also picked up the Colonel's Bequest since this game is highly inspired by it because I enjoyed this game so much.So if you are looking for a game that actually is a real mystery, wants you to pay attention, wants you to figure out whodunit and then wants to hear your theories about the mystery then pick this game up because this is one of the few times I actually felt rewarded for paying attention and trying to figure out a mystery instead of having the whole thing just spelled out for me time after time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm an old man. Some of my earliest and fondest memories are playing Sierra adventures way back when. Among all the fantastic series done by that amazing company (Leisure Suit Larry, King's Quest, Quest for Glory, Space Quest, etc...) was a rather short lived two game series involving the titular character Laura Bow.Growing up as a kid who watched a lot of TV and read a lot of books whenever he wasn't gaming my favorite genre was mysteries. Agatha Christie in particular so it shouldn't be a surprise that my favorite Sierra games were the Laura Bow games. The Crimson Diamond is a rather loyal homage to The Colonel's Bequest.The story has you playing as Nancy Maple who is an amateur geologist sent to a small Canadian town to investigate the discovery of a new gemstone. When she gets there she meets a number of eccentric characters each with their own reasons for being there as well as the owner of the estate. Given that this a mystery it's not long before some shenanigans happen and Nancy decides to investigate.The game plays just like an old school Sierra text parser and all. I did not run into too many instances of the game not knowing a word I had typed out and was able to complete the game after about nine hours (although I will admit I did not get the best ending or all the achievements. I'll have to replay it again soon).The game has great old school Sierra styled graphics and sound and plays just like a classic. If you're a fan of those then you should absolutely pick this one up. Julia Minamata has done a wonderful job her first time out and I hope to see more games from her in the future. I do highly recommend this one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely adventure! ✨ It manages to stay original to the EGA text parser style while breaking free of the not-so good qualities of the era.The writing is excellent and the mystery and the characters are very well presented. Kept us eager to unravel and engage with each chapter of the story! (playtime not accurate as we played on a different family member's account)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally a fan of CGA/EGA graphics as they're before my time... but this game is awesome! The writing is excellent and while some of the stuff is telegraphed a little too transparently it feels like the game equivalent of a page-turner. Definitely sat down to play it and finished it by the time the sun came up. Oops!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredible throwback! I felt like I was a little kid getting another Laura Bow type game and the mystery did not disappoint! I really enjoyed the incredible detail put in the items, art, and story of this game and learned quite a few things I didn't know about Canada in that time period! 10/10 will be recommending this game to all my friends! I already can't wait for a sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Thumb-up to, but please notice that the game could be sometimes frustrating if you are not used to this type of adventure game.Crimson Diamond is a retro-adventure in the style of Sierra On-Line: in particular, the game is an obvious tribute to Laura Bow's series (some locations and Nancy herself are basically lifted from The Colonel's Bequest).In this kind of game, instead of using your mouse pointer to do interactions, everything is managed through a text parser (i.e. "get the pen", "ask Jack about lodge"). You can use your mouse to walk around or navigate the inventory, but it is possible to accomplish everything through the keyboard.The story is a classic Christie-like plot: a bunch of characters confined in a mansion, with some mysterious things going on. Each NPC is very well portrayed: everyone is interesting and shady in his own way... I couldn't wait to progress to discover the truth!The gameplay consists mainly of eavesdropping, collecting evidence, and analyzing the environment and items. There are a lot of things to uncover and you will likely miss something on your first run, so the game has replayable value too. There are some clever puzzles, too.The main problem comes with the text parser: if you are used to IF/text adventures, you already know that one of the most annoying things is the "guess the verb" situation, when it is obvious what you are supposed to do, you *know* what you have to do, but you can't accomplish it because you are not using the supposed verb. This happens quite often in the game and particular verbs are required to solve crucial puzzles (fortunately, the game comes with a hint book that will help you in these situations).Another aspect that could be worth improving is Nancy's notebook, which I found messy and confusing to consult.Anyway, the game is recommended if you like old-school mystery adventures, especially if you are nostalgic for Sierra's Laura Bow games!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: With love and care apparent in every pixel, The Crimson Diamond evokes the magic of older titles, but with much less frustration.  It is a mystery adventure in which the player steps into the role Nancy Maple, an avid and intrepid young geologist, sent on a mission to the Middle of Nowhere, Canada, to investigate the possibility of diamonds in the region.  She winds up at an old-fashioned lodge with a somewhat curmudgeonly owner and a hodgepodge of guests who all have secrets and grudges and hidden agendas, and the tensions all start boiling over almost right away.  Nancy comes off as a total goody-two-shoes, but she’s got a mischievous streak – as the player, you can poke your nose where it doesn’t belong, snoop around in people’s belongings, and eavesdrop all over the place to get to the bottom of events as they unfold.It’s a massive achievement for first-time solo developer Julia Minamata, who wrote, programmed, animated, and did all of the art for the whole game.  There was a deliberate aim to make this game feel as though it could have been made 40 years ago.  This game is developed using a strict palette of only 16 colors, which was pretty much the limit of what a computer could do in the 1980s.  The developer is an incredibly skilled artist, though, so each screen looks like a painting, and just wandering around the lodge is almost as fun as the game itself.  Additionally. the music and sound effects in this game were composed on a genuine Roland MT-32, which is the pinnacle of computer audio engineering… in 1989.  The game’s soundtrack, composed by the very talented Dan Policar, is robust and authentic-feeling.  The music is only intended to punctuate key story moments, though, and you will have long stretches of silence as you explore.Furthermore, the Crimson Diamond is a full-on text-parser adventure.  Text-parsers are what all the cool kids used before they invented the computer mouse.  This is one of the most under-utilized game interaction mechanics these days, and it’s just so, SO fun.  Part of the reason they may have fallen out of favor is because many games that used to implement parsers also tended to have wacky puzzles, dead ends, player deaths that came out of nowhere, etc.  That can be fun, too, but maybe that stuff isn’t so mainstream these days.  Anyway, there’s none of that nonsense in the Crimson Diamond, and if you’ve never played a parser game before, this is the perfect place to start.Here’s why parsers are so great: it’s like you are having a conversation with the game.  It rewards paying attention, and stopping to smell the roses.  It’s a bit like hunting for buried treasure.  Sure, you can fly from objective to objective, but good parsers grant freedom to think laterally, to find all sorts of fun lore and dialogue buried below the surface, and it’s very rewarding to type some unusual, out-of-the-box command to Nancy and then to be pleasantly surprised when she actually does the thing.  And the Crimson Diamond parser is softer, more forgiving.  First, there’s a full-on tutorial available from the main menu.  Second, the game recognizes many, many synonyms and it’s not too picky about syntax either, so it feels more natural than some older parser games.  Third, there’s a handy autosave that kicks in at key moments.  Fourth, the game has an in-built notebook feature which automatically tracks objectives and key pieces of information.  Finally, there’s an absolutely genius shorthand system where the most commonly-typed commands, objects, and names can be abbreviated with a letter or two.  You don’t have to use it, it’s totally optional, but I  being able to shorten “open cupboard” to “o cu”, or “Ask Evan about Margot” to “a ee ab mm”.At any rate, I totally love this game.  I want to share it with all my friends.  I even have a T-shirt with the logo on it, so you know I’m a true fan.  But on a more personal level, I also logged in to Twitch every Tuesday night for several years straight, especially during the pandemic, to keep Julia, Dan, and about 50 other regulars in the “cTuesday” crowd company as she poured passion into each and every screen in the game, even the ones that the player sees for about 6 seconds in the intro and then never again.  I just want to say thank you.  Thank you for the informative geology show-and-tells, thank you for the very convincing sermons why you really only need 16 colors max to accomplish anything, thank you for all of the cat watercolor postcards, and really, truly, thank you for making this game.  I have many, many games in my collection, but there’s really something special about this one in particular, and it will always be one of my absolute favorites.

_childDocuments_.review: Superb game. The retro pixel art style is beautiful and nostalgic. It's cozy. Game play is reminiscent of Colonel's Bequest but its fresh and modern. A lot to discover and explore. The story is quite interesting, lots of things unfold, you think you've got everything and there's another turn. Very enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a masterpiece, for several reasons:I don't like very much detective games because they seem cynical - but this one is very different. It made me care for its characters, and it hit me hard emotionally when bad things happened to some of them.  It's difficult to say why it's so good at this - is it the abundance of closeups and talking portraits, the fleshed out motivation and personality everyone has, or the gradual progression of things getting worse for them but in any case, it's very well written. The Crimson Diamond isn't trying to just tell you a story like most story-driven adventures. It is an actual game.1) There are a lot of  that you may fail to find. This makes the exploration and the conclusions that you make really meaningful. At the end the game points you in the direction of the things you missed, so this also makes it . But you may get a satisfying end of the story even if you weren't perfect.2) There are layers of problems, small scale (personal) and big scale (political). There are  at the end, again, a small scale and a big scale one, and they both made me reflect and clarify decisions in my own life.The elegant storytelling and design can be seen even in the movation of the protagonist (she's a mineralogist that has to turn into a detective). This is great, because initially I cared about my own goal (scientific exploration of minerals, finding diamonds) until I found some injustice that I cannot easily ignore. It means the player can identify with any motivation he or she likes: 1) fame and riches, 2) advancing science or 3) setting things that are very wrong right - and then  this motivation. I've played a lot of LucasArt style adventures from the 90s and there was something distorted, fake, lifeless and wrong about them that I could never explain. The Crimson Diamond demo (released several years ago) acquainted me with Sierra's style of adventure games. I was 42 at the time and because of this game, I played through half of Sierra's catalogue without any nostalgia. But they were made just for the type of person that I am and I felt excited as a child again to discover something so fresh and so wonderful.Even though in TCD everything is scripted and relatively static:1) there's  that feels "systemic", eavesdropping that can fail and situations you can miss. NPCs move around and do things. Let me repeat, this is  compared to even more advanced adventures such as Elsinore, but it is super important that it's there and unlike the rotten 90s trend.2) Dangerous situations may result in , just like in real life. It's nothing unfair, just an invitation to use common sense, which raises the stakes and makes things more immersive.3) At the same time, the game feels . It has very nice onboarding, an optional tutorial, it has a lot of quality of life improvements and won't be as frustrating as some people find the 80's games that inspired it. Very elegant design that manages to both lean into the design pillars of the 80's games and at the same time translate them for a modern audience.The game is:It's amazing, and it's done by someone who just loved something a lot and wanted to share this love with us.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I've only been playing for half an hour and I'm already in tears because this game is so amazing. The graphics are stunning, and the atmosphere is incredible. Even simple tasks like picking up items are fun and engaging thanks to the great interface. I'll update this review once I've played more and have a better idea of the puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game was surprisingly easy to approach, considering the genre of text parser games being often very specific in how you need to approach them. Rather than restricted, this game is enhanced by its genre. There are some deaths, but not around every corner, the main risk in this game is losing an opportunity to uncover a clue or two. The puzzles occasionally stumped me, but were mostly well signposted with the protagonist giving gentle hints on what she needs to do (still ended up using the hintbook on four occasions).
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic. It's the perfect take on the old formula. This game presents a challenging mystery and plenty of threads to investigate. While it doesn't hold your hand, it does offer you some hints (should you choose to take them) that can help you untangle all loose threads the second time around, giving it some nice replayability if you missed anything. Can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is an amazing and charming love letter to old mystery games. Both game play wise and visually the game is stunning and with a larger variety of events and intrigues it is well worth several playthroughs. The attention to detail is really amazing and I can do little more than recommend this game from the bottom of my heart!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: bought on a whim, was pleasantly surprised. it has nostalgic ega graphics and text parser control scheme combined with modern game design features like variable endings and alternative solutions. it has none of the frustrations of older games like getting stuck on some silly, illogical puzzles. generally it feels like playing a mystery novel.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this is not even my usual type of game but I still had a blast going around and doing detective work, asking questions, finding clues and solving puzzles (apparently I was even worse at it than I initially anticipated). The only small complaint I have is that as a non native speaker it has been challenging at times to tell the parser what I wanted to do as it only accepted very specific words, so I would definitely add some sort of glossary to help, but overall it didn't hinder the experience.Maybe the real diamond was this game all along :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Julia Minamata understands why these games sold for $30 back in 1988, and it's not just because nothing else was around to play. Unlike most of its predecessors, the game is thorough and complex enough to justify multiple playthroughs, and I only encountered maybe two puzzles that were a bit too frustrating.Some of the art could be improved a bit, especially the character sprites when they move vertically (they appear to hover north and south). There are also a few bugs but nothing game-breaking.I hope the next game doesn't take so long to complete
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty good.  The only beef I have is that even though it plays like an old skool "Hugo" game, it does not give you nearly the amount of options for executing a written command.  Which I find kind of sloppy, considering how much technology has progressed.  Or as Hugo would say " I find that befuddling".It is fun to bring back the old idea of these games.  Just work on the amount of verbs and object names that can be used to execute a action to make the playability smoother, instead of being so specific.7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first gameplay. It's a fun retro detective game and awesome that they consulted someone with indigenous knowledge in the staff, however, the stereotype towards the Asian female character, Kimi, is disappointing from Chapter 1. Kimi approached me on the train and said hi to me first, yet she was described as a shy and petite woman over and over again. It doesn't make sense - seems like you're describing Kimi based on your stereotypes, not the behaviours you actually assigned to the characters.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond, the game you want to give a thumbs up but just can't.So, this was a project made by one person and is clearly a love letter to the Laura Bow series, except unlike the Laura Bow series, which has obnoxious timers, countless deaths, and text parser blues, TCD is a game with more of a classic adventure game formula which makes a few things better but has a weaker story which is still hampered by archaic game systems.Let's start with the good:1. It's the perfect length and difficulty. It gets rid of Sierra-style nonstop deaths and nonsensical logic problems. Only once or twice did I feel like I needed to look up a solution or what to do next, and often, that was due to fighting with the parser.2. The graphics, sounds, and general aesthetics are a perfect time travel machine for Colonel's Bequest, which brings back good memories of childhood. It's charming and does feel like an old DOS game.3. Bug-free for the most part. I tried breaking the game a few times and found a few minor errors, but nothing game-breaking.Now the bad...1. The story - Laura Bow, I mean Nancy Maple, who is pretty much a clone of Laura Bow, is a geologist in Canada! So, the most boring profession in the most boring area in the entire world. In her tedious quest to study rocks, she meets equally boring characters when a murder occurs. The murderer, who you will determine who is in the first two minutes of the game, does a terrible job of hooking you for the whole mystery portion. The characters fit the Canadian love of blandness by making them easy to read with motivations and methods, so the mystery, if you can call it that, is solved within two seconds, eventually sadly ending with a lack of luster. "Let's review your knowledge and actions and give you a detective score!" similar abysmal finale to that which occurred at the end of Laura Bow 2. 2. The Parser - The game tries to hook you with the parser. It really wants you think this is good - It's not. In fact, it's pointless. The conversations, branch dialog, and actions are so limited in number that they can all be done with a basic choice of action. Thrill as you have to type "scratchplate with a sample" instead of just clicking and hovering one item over another. People say, "But it has that Nostalgic vibes!" and to that, I say, even Sierra would say that system is annoying and obnoxious, especially in the year of the lord in 2024.3. The Fun—Nancy Maple is a slow game but also a boring game. There is no fun to be had with the parser, and there are no countless violent deaths for Nancy Maple. The only time I got a chuckle was a clear Easter egg to The Colonel's Bequest regarding a death while taking a shower, which doesn't work with the story at all, but it is still interesting. It just seems so bland. The world is so dull. The characters are uninteresting. The big morality choice at the end for your ending type is so eye-rolling long, simplistic, and dull.So, would I recommend the Crimson Diamond? No. Don't get me wrong; the creator did an amazing job on a one-man project, but the game itself is a love letter to a gaming relic that didn't need anything dedicated to it. Adventure games, in general, should stay dead and remain buried in the ground. Let the dead rest in peace.
