I hope Juila Minamata makes her future games but does something original and unique to her interests instead of copying the same flawed game I played 30 years ago yet somehow making it worse in the story and in some mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Blame Steam for the thumbs down, I'd give it a sideways thumb if I could. My feelings are mixed as are my feelings today on the Sierra graphical text adventures I loved as a kid. I liked and still like the introduction of Colonel's Bequest, which I first saw on a demmo machine at Computer Village, Palmerston North at Xmas 1990. When I finally got to play it I was disappointed in many ways, but even if not very fun to play, the game had a strong atmosphere through to the end hence when the game appeared at GOG in early 2017 I was keen to buy it and play through it again. And looking back, I'm glad Roberta took a break from King's Quest to make something a bit more mature. Then I discovered Julia's demmo, at first glance thinking it was some sort of remake of or sequel to Colonel's Bequest. I played the demmo and at the end of it had mixed feelings even at that stage. Of all the guests/residents, three stood out as "bad" while the others were, at most, rough around the edges. So I was concerned that the game was making it way too clear who was going to do the dirty deed(s). I couldn't be sure though and I messaged Julia to tell her I was interested in seeing how the game progresses after the collapse of the bridge ending Chp. 1. It was nice to follow Julia's gradual game-building via blogs and vlogs and she often responded to little comments I made (I also talked to her about my own text adventure hobby projects in AGI Studio and SCI Companion). When Julia FINALLY linked us the finished game on Steam last Friday (New Zealand time) I was keen to give it my best shot and played it good over the next few days until I'd got all the achievements plus looking through Julia's online hint book to see what I'd missed.You could say I like a lot of little things about the game, but there's some big things I don't like. So I think the Crimson Lodge residents are good for having a lot of depth, there's so much you can ask them about and get a good response to, fleshing them out, also the close-up, face views are very detailed and expressive, giving everyone more charracter. I started to feel close to them especially Jack, Nathan and Kimi. Colonel's Bequest is obviously the main blueprint for Crimson Diamond, but its wealth of history and science got me thinking of another late '80s Sierra adventure, Gold Rush! by Ken and Doug McNeill one of the last text adventures made for the earlier AGI interpreter, Gold Rush! turned out to be one of the most fun ways to learn about American history and geography, Crimson Diamond doesn't have the travelling of Gold Rush!, but you learn North American history and geography in a fun way, including the Klondike Gold Rush, NW Canada, 1896-1899. Learning about and practicing mineralogy was fun too, I'm sure I've played other games where you have to learn a little scientific fieldwork to solve problems and puzzles. I think some people have talked about the puzzles being a little too easy to solve, it's true that back in the day, Sierra adventures would take me months or even an entire year to solve and I finished Crimson Diamond and gained most of the achievements without the hint book or the forum in just a few days, but for me a game can still be great even if the average gamer finishes it in about a week, some games have enough going for them that you enjoy playing them through again and again like watching a good movie. Crimson Diamond is certainly replayable what with multiple endings, achievements, missed evidence and cut scenes etc. The fingerprint dusting, footprint studying and other detective work of course recalls another Sierra adventure, Police Quest 2.So my big dislike was the whodunnit, murder mystery part of the game.So yeah, I liked a lot of little things, disliked a couple of big things, I don't want to give it a thumbs down, but Steam is like Siskel and Ebert movie reviews, you either like it or you don't, besides there are so many positive reviews that it a red thumb might make the review page a little more interesting. On a five star rating I guess I'd give it two or two and a half.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've been legitimately sad to have finished in a long time. A perfect text-parser EGA graphics throwback, but with all the quality-of-life updates and thoughtful points that you'd expect from a modern game. The art, the music, the sound effects, the writing, all come together perfectly for an incredibly satisfying game that I can't wait for more of.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you like old Sierra games, like Colonels Bequest, then BUY THIS GAME!!! If you don't like them, probably avoid. If you are unsure, there are some quality of life increases in this game that make it stand out some, but it is not that different from many older games. Must buy for fans, worth considering if you are unsure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, this is going on my list of favorite detective games of all time for sure. The Crimson Diamond is a cleverly written whodunnit with layers upon layers of detail, and it gives you an absolute buttload of ways to approach solving the (multiple!) mysteries. You will be rewarded for being thorough and looking for every clue you can, and I guarantee you won't find everything there is to find on your first playthrough - especially because sequencing is critical. Beware of accidental story progression! While that might sound frustrating, it makes every clue you find or every deduction you make is all the more satisfying. I had to really engage my brain with some of these deductions too, and I really enjoy that the game makes you do a lot of the work with its parser command system. The notebook can help guide you and there's a handy dandy Hints page to refer to if you REALLY need it, but otherwise the game's puzzles are logical enough to work out almost all the time. Loved the artwork, loved the writing, loved the setting, loved the gameplay, loved the narrative, I just loved it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Kings Quest IV was the first video game I played, and I still remember it with extreme fondness. This game took me right back there, though with some nice new features to make it (slightly) less punishing than those old classics used to be. Just a fantastic and beautiful game! (Only comment is that I felt a bit battered by all the detective questions at the very end. But this didn't at all detract from the joy of playing the game.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Dear Julia, for a certain type of players you created the most stunning game ever. Buying it was out of the question of course, but had I known what awaits, I would gladly have paid double the prize.First of all the setting. Early 20th century in the deepest woods of Canada, the perfect scenario for burglars and murderers. With the charming style of those pixel graphics the game already pulls you in. And in a positive manner I already felt like Nancy - no way to escape! As for story and the proceedings I don't want to spoiler anyone. Every action is a surprise, every riddle solveable. Of course it gets harder as the chapters pass on, but that's just fair and well done too.All in all you made a childhood chapter of every 40+ player come back to life. The Colonel's Bequest is revived in the best of all manners. And for everyone younger than 40... just drop in and enjoy a great story told without the need for fancy rendered graphics. Just like a grand novel read with a cup of tea by your side on a foggy Sunday afternoon. Absolute 5 Star game!! Thank you Julia and pleeeease make another one!!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Play:-If you like your game with a hand-drawn atmospheric look that is clear, focused and beautiful.-If you like your game with a bit more grounded mysteries.-If you like your game to make you feel that you accomplished something with your wit instead of your hyper-active hands.-If you like your game to have an easy-going and non-stressful feel. Chill out, man! Breathe deep once in a while!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Being a fan of the adventure games from Sierra I found this game very enjoyable. It has a look and feel like the text parser adventure games Sierra put out in the late 80s, but the gameplay is friendlier, with no possibility of getting stuck in a state where you cannot finish the game but don't know that you cannot. In that way it is a good introduction to players unfamiliar with the genre. Also there is none of the, for me, dreaded arcade sequences that appeared in some of the old adventure games.The game markets itself as a "cozy mystery game" and I think that is a very fitting description. You play as Nancy Maple who at the start of the game arrives at what used to be an inn, the Crimson Lodge, and soon gets involved in the dealings of the other people staying there. There is a lot to explore and ask the different characters about.  The pacing is good and you are given hints about what you need to do to advance the gameplay all through the game. The story is divided into chapters, and the final chapter gives you clues as to what you may have missed in the earlier chapters, adding to the replay value of the game.In sum it is a very good game, all the more impressive that it is made by a solo developer, and I definitely recommend buying it even if you are unfamiliar with this kind of game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Not quite through yet, because I'm trying to get everything perfect the first time, but I'll probably get there soon :D My impressions so far:The Crimson Diamond does a phenomenal job of capturing the spirit of a classic whodunit murder mystery in game form, maybe moreso than any other game I know (and I've played lots). It gets plot, characters, atmosphere and gameplay perfectly right at the same time.It was really fun using a text parser again after many years and having to come up with my own ideas of what to ask people about and what to examine more closely. I am also glad that the game always remains fair to the player and is far more forgiving than classic Sierra games in the 80s. Deaths are present, but are either hinted at or directly after an auto-save.Many thanks to the talented indie developer Julia Minamata who has obviously put her heart in this work. I would buy a sequel without even blinking an eye and recommend this game to anyone who likes classic mystery stories and/or classic adventure games. Just give it a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The atmosphere and overall vibe of this throwback game is a total treat. It really feels like an authentic 80s Sierra title but with far fewer of the frustrations that would date it poorly. Sometimes the music/sound feels a bit too sparse, but what’s there is totally lovely. I can’t wait to see how the mystery resolves!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game for all the same reasons more eloquent people have stated; I am simply adding another well deserved positive review.  Though I will say one thing -- there was one instance where I wept, not from sorrow, but from the true beauty of a particular statement made by one of the characters, so I give extra high praise for that.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I always loved the idea of some of the old mystery games Crimson Diamond draws inspiration from, but their often arbitrary consequences and softlocks marred the experience in practice. Julia Minamata has crafted a charming puzzler with an even more charming amateur detective at its heart. The Crimson Diamond takes inspiration from its predecessors without being beholden to them, eschewing the ethnic stereotypes that could plague old Sierra games in favour of more well-realised characters, and providing more modern quality of life features like an in-game notebook and autosave feature which avoid aimless plodding and losing all progress to a sudden death.My first playthrough did not result in the best ending, so I will be returning to Crimson soon. If I eavesdrop at the right doors, find the right clues, perhaps it will be different. Even if not, I will enjoy wandering through its EGA woods and searching for precious stones. It was a pleasure to be budding geologist Nancy Maple, and I hope this is just the start of her adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: There are many classic adventure titles I’ve not played. Some I probably never will. Some do intrigue me still. For example – I heard very interesting things about The Colonel’s Bequest, an investigation focused title where you could completely fail solving anything and still finish the game. Hopefully I will eventually play it, but the reason I’m bringing it up is because The Crimson Diamond seems to have been influenced not just by any Sierra adventure titles, but this one in particular. And it’s not just the EGA-styled visuals that call back to the long past era of adventure titles. Far more interesting is the fact that this is a text parser based adventure. You don’t see these often anymore.As you might’ve guessed by now, The Crimson Diamond is a modern adventure game, designed around concepts and mechanics that hasn’t been in use for quite some time. Just like most classic Sierra titles, this game is controlled with arrows and typing short phrases into a command line. You do get a visual inventory screen and mouse can be used to examine inventory objects or move the character on screen, but for the most part you better get used to quickly typing combinations of “verb + something” if you want something done. And seemingly to avoid ambiguity and motivate informed actions, the game does not accept “use” as a verb, requiring you to think about how exactly the object must be handled. As was always the case, this approach feels a lot more investigative and gives the player more chances to feel smart. But also has a downside of making many actions slower and more repetitive.But it all works when the story is interesting and the mystery is gripping… Which is not something that happens in The Crimson Diamond. Don’t get me wrong – there are curious mysteries and the more you play, the more drama happens. It’s just that… I suppose, what I expected was a 2024 game using 1989 technology and what this game is feels more like a game you’d get in the middle of the 90s. What I mean by that is – stories and character motivations has gotten quite a lot more complex and engaging over the years. Characters in “serious” adventure games feel more like real people rather than weird adventurers who put junk into their pockets and ransack random people’s rooms for no reason. Heck, you can die in this game very early on for seemingly no reason and it doesn’t feel like cool foreshadowing, it feels silly and out of place.Though the biggest “old game” feeling comes from just how underutilized the text parser truly is. The potential of a text parser is in the idea that you can talk to characters about basically everything and expect to get a reaction. You could experiment with item usage and get results. But this game immediately kills that promise by showing just how limited and context specific most of these interactions are. Writing “ask X about Y” very often gets no meaningful result even when it clearly should. Why is the bird watching lady who is watching birds right this very moment “doesn’t know anything” on the topic of birds? Things like this, along with the repetition of tasks you often must perform to be a good investigator (whom you are not, by the way, the character just decides to act like one), really made me wish the game would drop the pretense and work like a LucasArts game with a mouse control and a contextual “use” command. Because in reality that’s how most of the things in the game are, just made less conveniently. Maybe I just expect more from a modern investigative game, with examples like Lamplight City, but investigating in this game felt like I was constantly going against what game wants me to do and it rarely felt right or exciting.Which is not to say that The Crimson Diamond is bad. It very much isn’t. There are cool moments, yes including those that do work better (or exclusively) with text parser. And I did like playing it overall. It simply feels like a disappointment when taking the setup into consideration. Text parser, limited location, few characters – setup for a truly fantastic tightly made investigation game where characters feel alive and selection of verbs comes naturally. Instead, it’s just a good Sierra-like adventure game that feels like something from the 1990s, with a few modern quality of life features. And that’s alright too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond has been a wonderful way to experience a mystery, and a mastering of its retro inspirations. The writing has been wholly enjoyable, the puzzles delightful and creative, the background art fantastic: with everything making have to know what happens next, and whether my detective skills will be up to snuff. Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent homage to the old Sierra text parser games! Fantastic expertly detailed EGA-palette artwork, contrasted with simpler sprite animations. The writing is excellent. Each character speaks in their own "voice". Julia Minamata has actually researched mineralogy to make it convincing. The game evokes an Agatha Christie style mystery, while avoiding veering into ridiculousness (a la the Laura Bow series).Although it uses the Adventure Game Studio engine, it's customised enough to avoid feeling like "just another AGS game".The music is quite good, using a deliberately synthetic MIDI-soundfont style.There are a few quibbles I have: the animations are sometimes a bit slow, and the game is silent at times. The text parser is fairly generous, I only got stymied by it a few times. There are lots of things you can miss while playing, often without hints that they're happening or available topics of conversation, so I ended up following the hintbook.Get this if you like detective games with a retro aesthetic, or you have nostalgia for the classics!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: As an adventure enthusiast, I can say that everything about this game is excellent. The wonderful 16-color EGA style graphics are a work of art. The story and characters are very well written and interesting to engage with, The gameplay is a lot of fun, and in contrast to the classic Sierra adventures that the game takes it's inspiration from, it is entirely fair. That means, there are no dead ends, no silly deaths at every corner, like in the classic Quest games. I was able to finish the game without a solution, something which I was never able to do with the old Sierra games.The puzzles are logical and fair, and while you can miss some things, you can still finish the entire game. And maybe discover additional stuff in a 2nd playthrough – the game has different endings, and there may be some questions left open at the end if you missed certain clues. There are a few possible deaths, but they always come with a explicit warning (and an autosave).The UI is of course pretty old school, with a "text parser". That's how the text input was called back in the day, a word a friend of mine did not understand when I used it recently to describe the game. So basically you move the player character with the cursor keys, and enter orders like "open door", "take cup" etc. when standing next to the object. For the typing lazy, the game also accepts shortcuts, an innovation that was missing from the classic games. Example "o d" for "open door".You can really notice at every aspect of the game how much love for details, how much research for the setting and characters, the game's solo developer Julia Minamata has invested into it over the many years it was in development. It still blows my mind that it is not only done by a solo developer (with only additional help for the sound track), but that it's also Julia Minamata's first game. An amazing debut and instant classic for adventure fans.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the limited colors, sounds, and animation, this is a fully developed mystery made for fans of detective adventure- painted lovingly with a brush of VGA graphics and scored with nostalgia-inducing chiptunes.You'll need to be clever if you want to get to the bottom of the mystery, but whichever way you tread the paths of Crimson you will be rewarded with satisfying text parser gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is SO GOOD!As a kid/teen, I played a lot of the Sierra games (Kings Quest/Space Quest) and this gets the feel of those perfectly, from the graphics to the game mocking you for ways you can die (hilariously, too!). The game also is full of puzzles and makes you think quite a bit! There also seems to be multiple endings, based on how you play the game. That's a surprise to be sure, but a welcome one!!!I highly recommend this game to those that like mystery/investigative games, text parsers, and/or retro games. The Crimson Diamond delivers a solid experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: wow, i've played for only a couple of hours but I'm super impressed with the game so far. I love old school adventure games especially EGA text parser games and of course I love the Colonel's Bequest which has a strong influence on this game. First off the introduction is fantastic, the animations and artwork are reminiscent of the good old days while also being even more impressive technically than some of the games that influenced them. There is a large amount of detail in the artwork early on and the parser has a wide range of text that you can input. I also appreciate the help page in game that lists all the verbs and shortcuts for navigating the game easier! I played Colone's Bequest with my family and we started playing Crimson Diamond together and so far we love it, its great going through the story and mystery as part of a small group, the more heads the better!So far so good, hopefully I'll remember to come back and edit my review when I'm further along.BTW the fact that the developer Julia did most of this on their own is a testament to how passion can drive a project and I hope this game is a great success for Julia and I wish Julia to contiune on developing games because they proved they are an asset to the field of game development. A+
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of nostalgic adventure games, check out Crimson Diamond. It leans very heavily on Laura Bow (one of my favourite adventure games from the time) for inspiration.A murder mystery presented faithfully as a graphic adventure with text parser in gloriously garish EGA colours. A touch tedious at times but has an interesting story & characters, well-written.Want to know more? Check out  my bite-size review here:For more niche curation, follow me at:
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely delightful game.  Great main character, interesting NPCs, a good story, and an interesting mystery to solve.  Great parser: this is definitely the best part of the game compared with the old text parser games.  I very rarely had to sit and try command after command, trying to figure out what the game would "understand."  The game had a very high amount of synonyms it understood, so I was very rarely stuck trying to figure out what to call something.  It happened now and then, sure, but even then I was usually able to get my second attempt to work.  Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I was so pleasantly surprised by this game. As a fan of Laura Bow I was pretty sure this was a game I would like, but I didn't expect to like it so much! Great storytelling, really clever ways to feel like you are doing an investigation, and the whole epilogue is so cool and interesting. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Feels just like similar adventures of olden time and it is mostly well done and interesting. Story and characters are pretty good. Didn't like that there's barely any music or sounds and also that the game moves on without any warning preventing you from solving a lot of the mysteries just because you solved a specific problem too early. Puzzles are a mixed bag. There are some good ones but also, a lot of time is spent walking around trying to collect footprints/fingerprints which just isn't that interesting. Then there's a ton of drawers, cabinets etc. to open and look inside and the vast majority of them are completely empty, which would already feel wasteful in a point & click adventure, but here you have to type in the commands each time in addition to walking to each spot first.Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game and there seems to be high replay value with all the things you didn't find out the first time. Would also like to point out a lot of effort was put into creating a satisfying ending as the story doesn't just go "the end". You'll see.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fitting love letter to the old Sierra games, most specifically The Colonel's Bequest, but it definitely also has its own identity.It plays to a point like Colonel's Bequest, but with a more modern approach: there are less random player deaths, the text parser works better, so does the pathfinding (no more "you need to get closer" when you want to interact with something), and the graphics are wonderful while still retaining that old school EGA vibe. The pixel art is truly amazing and I can't imagine how long it took to get it done, especially knowing it was the work of a single developer!As a horror/thriller fan, I did miss the bloodbath of Colonel's Bequest, with dead bodies showing up left and right, as this is a more peaceful and comforting game... but this is clearly a deliberate choice, and one I can respect. There *is* still death around the corner though, so the murder mystery element is still present.I had a lot of fun playing this, and am hoping for a future sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful adventure game that hearkens back to a bygone era in gaming history. I thought that l would hold off reviewing until I got all the achievements, which has helped me develop a clearer picture of the game as a whole. Some of the achievements might be a little buggy or unclear as to what is actually required (even with outside help). Aside from that, the game can be a little frustrating at times. But I don't hold any of that against this game. There's more depth and luster to this rough little gem of game than I would have expected. It was quite nice to see a game take place in a Canadian (ultra) small town. I keep imagining a movie version in my head.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly cozy game. Sometimes the text parser is a bit frustrating but that's the nature of text parser games. If you enjoyed The Colonel's Bequest it's a no-brainer to play The Crimson Diamond. Even if you haven't heard of the former, I'd recommend the latter IF you like the art style and the idea of the text parser.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A charming adventure game that looks and feels exactly like the classic Laura Bow: the Colonel's Bequest by Sierra. The gameplay is fun and it features a simplified version of an old text parser adventure. The puzzles are difficult but fair. The story is rich and the characters are interesting, specially the main one. Highly recommended for fans of old style adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The beginning of the game is a bit slow: a long cutscene followed by a multitude of empty drawers to open and information getting often repeated through dialogue. But it gets better with every chapter, with more threads to follow, more freedom, and the strong sensation the game won’t end abruptly if you let a few details slide.What impressed me the most is the amount of customization the game opens up to the player - you may use more awkward, “retro” commands instead of the more convenient UI. You don’t have to use the in-game notes to track your quests. You may accept the game over screens and start from the beginning, but you may also save at any time.And the game's conclusion is especially good at allowing the player to decide how much they want to learn about their mistakes. You may try to answer some questions blindly, you may ask the game for some pointers, or you can avoid any tips at all, to replay the game some time in the future. Which, to me, sounds like a pretty alluring option.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I suspected it would be better than Colonel's Bequest, and it was; It lays down a more coherent mystery for you to solve. I suspected it would have a lot of beautiful art, and it does. But what I didn't expect was a sensitivity towards the characters that you rarely find in a mystery. I felt BAD for what happened to certain characters. I glimpsed the life that was robbed from them.  It's written with a strong emotional intelligence.I wish it had more puzzles, though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is an incredible game, full stop. I've played several Sierra text parser games in the past year or two, and have loved all of them. This one stands among the best.The story is well written. What begins as a simple rock hunt balloons into various plots and subplots by a fairly large cast of characters, all of whom seem suspicious at one point or another. Everyone seems to have secrets in this small neck of Ontario, and it's honestly amazing just how much you can learn (and miss) as you play.The graphics are a massive highlight, with absolutely beautiful pixel art complimenting the EGA style late 80s graphical look. It draws clear inspiration from the likes of King's Quest IV, Space Quest III, and The Colonel's Bequest. More importantly it absolutely exudes that classic Sierra atmosphere. There are even times where the atmosphere and art direction even stands firmly above the best of Sierra's art at the time.It's no surprise to see a glowing endorsement from Roberta Williams in the game's description here. I'd even argue that if creator Julia Minamata were crafting The Crimson Diamond at the time of Sierra's heyday, Ken would've likely hired her on the spot, no hesitation.I've gotten only one ending, and while it was satisfying (and likely the second best ending), I felt like I was missing several answers.I don't often play a video game more than once after finishing it. I will be playing this again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a most welcome sight for those of us who grew up with adventure games like The Colonel's Bequest. It nails the vibe of that and other games that inspired it, but stands on its own solid two legs as a modern adventure with a compelling mystery to solve, beautiful art and a pleasing soundtrack. I will play through it again in an attempt to unlock all its secret plots and find more incriminating evidence, and I recommend it to fans of the genre and newcomers alike.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Very well done. It was everything that was good about the old Sierra Kings Quest, Space Quest and Police Quest games before they tried to update their look and lost their appeal (ill throw Lesuire Suit Larry in there, too) but cleaner. The connections made sense and were mostly intuitive, tho there were some complex actions to achieve some results.. tho, they didn't bring the story to a grinding halt. It was possible to miss some things and I really appreciated how it gave a breakdown of how well it was done at the end (though, It gave me a 0 out of 9 for Margots death... a ZERO?!) . I found myself looking to see if this studio, pardon me, this DEV, this solo DEV! had any other, similar games besides this. I am really looking forward to see what she comes up with in the future and hope that, if she does branch out into other genres and more complex game designs, that she also does a few more like this, pixel style, old school games..   I'm sure there is copyright issues involved, but her version of kings quest or space quest would be awesome. Even if it was an homage and not a true reboot in name...        The absolute ONLY thing I would add is the humour of those games..  where, in certain places, if you type in what would normally not be a command that was recognized, a witty response instead of the standard 'does not work' message .. or even a quick animation for pure humour that doesnt affect the story or game.. just recognizes what someone might type as input in odd places...        But, overall, WELL DONE!  thank you!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game was so much fun! It really brought me back to my childhood when I played Colonel's Bequest. It was challenging, but not too difficult that I wanted to give up. I can't wait to play it again, get all the deaths, see what else I can find, and get the different endings. This game made me feel like a kid again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game! I've never played a text parser game myself before, so I was thrilled to see this game pop up. I greatly appreciated how the game did a good job of (optional) hints/tutorials so that even someone unused to the genre could figure it out. I liked that the mystery/puzzles were challenging but still felt fair. I've never felt more accomplished finishing a game before! I spent about 13 hours on my initial play of the game, but someone more experienced with the genre/style of game might do it quicker. The scenes are beautifully done and I find the whole game extremely cozy and enjoyable the whole way through. Even if you've never played this style of game before, you should give this one a try!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you're nostalgic for the days of Sierra's EGA-era adventures, The Crimson Diamond is a must-play. This game nails the aesthetic—from the pixel art to the catchy, retro soundtrack—perfectly capturing that old-school vibe, even if you experienced those classics on a Hercules graphics card with a monochrome monitor like I did. It modernizes the experience just enough to be more forgiving, making it casually enjoyable without sacrificing the charm. I managed to complete about 95% of it without resorting to external hints, though I did get tripped up on phrasing a couple of times. Give it a shot; it’s worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a classic game in the stye of sierra on-line. Like those games, the story and characters are excellent, but the puzzles can be obtuse. Fortunanetly, there is a built-in help guide. No longer will you have to call a 900 number for hints, or go to the Sierra BBS. What a wonderful age we live in. Seriously though, if you want a loving recreation of text parsing games from the 80s, this is fantastic. (Don't feel bad about looking at the hint guide either.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I was born after the text-based era of these games. But I did grow up with point-and-click adventure games so this was a new experience for me in many ways. Overall, I think this is a very well designed game for what it is. If you get stuck it will give you hints and there are different routes and many different things to find. The more I look into it the more things I find. Some commands and words are a bit annoying because you have to be very, very specific to get it through sometimes. Some words I did not even knew existed, but that might have to do that I am not a native English speaker.However, the game dev is super helpful and willing to listen to feedback and has added content and commands based on players critisism and feedback and is very willing to improve their game based on that. I think over time the Crimson Diamond will only improve and get even more accessible. The love and passion for creating these type of games really comes through. I enjoyed the characters and stories. It's a lot more slow-paced to what I am used to but it was a different experience which I appriciated. I would recommend it overall to people who can appriciate a more slow-paced adventure and fans of detective like games or just retro titles in general. Overall, I really liked this experience. I am certainly going to replay it in the future and see what I missed in the game. Kudos to the creator for both creating this and being very kind and helpful to feedback and fellow developers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow I completely missed the news about this game before it released on steam. I don't think I've ever bought a steam game upon first glance, THIS game was insta-buy. I still remember walking into a radioshack about 30 years ago and buying a copy of The Colonel's Bequest. Thinking back, I suppose that game was insta-buy as well. I knew nothing of the game at the time, thought it looked really interesting, and took it home. I was enthralled by the mystery, as well as the detective-work. So unique, I'd been wishing for someone to pick up the mantle of that style of game (of course I played the sequel).The Crimson Diamond did not disappoint. I dusted off the mental cobwebs, and the 'ol parser ones as well, and got to business. The work that went into the game was fantastic. Totally took me back to that great time I had after coming home from radioshack that day.If you played the Sierra adventures back in the day, I highly recommend this game. If you didn't, but you think the game looks interesting, I highly recommend this game. Just be warned, while you can finish the game without TOO much difficulty, actually solving the mysteries that come up and being able find all the necessary clues is where the true challenge lies. It's immensely rewarding to be able to put all the clues together at the end, and there's still some I missed out on! I'm looking forward to going back in and finding those last clues though.Thank you to the people that worked on this game, especially to the developer. I truly hope that a sequel is made. Until then, I'll continue to enjoy my vacation in Crimson.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Right from the start you’ll be hooked in with the charming graphical style and the spunky music with an interesting premise, a diamond was found in a fish and you’ve been sent to the lodge to investigate as Nancy, an amateur geologist at the Royal Canadian Museum, diamonds could be a big discovery and help immensely in your career. Things quickly go awry and your mineralogical study turns into a thrilling adventure. A small cast of characters awaits at the lodge each with their personality and motives leaving you unsure who to trust.The level of mystery and intrigue stays high from start to finish revealing bits when seeming necessary (and through your detective work) without overwhelming the player, everything ties together and is told extremely well, it’s up to you to ensure there are no loose threads at the conclusion. This is all helped by some very likable characters who feel both alive and complex, much thought went into each aspect.Gameplay is a text parser that allows shortcuts, and the game is mostly able to figure out what you mean. Doing this well makes the experience more enjoyable, for the most part, the puzzles don’t require specific wording and it’s broad with what it allows alleviating some of the frustration that could emerge. While simpler words like ‘use’ aren’t allowed, this means you’ll have to think about what exactly you want to do with something, making for a more immersive experience. How you can find or reveal information can change from playthrough as you can miss some things or go down a different path, I missed several things in my first playthrough but despite that, I never felt I was missing out on anything too important. The only aspect I struggled with was that sometimes the character would get stuck on doors and not go in, an easy fix with some repositioning but it was a bit frustrating.    There is enough to be able to figure out the mystery, especially by the end, I was able to mostly piece it together just missing a few things and only totally wrong on one aspect, there won’t be any completely unpredictable twists here.Some themes present involve Indigenous treatment and especially the theft and improper use of their land, it does a good job be respectful of these things even if it is only a minor aspect of the whole thing, it does help to add some more weight to decisions you may have to make and about how you want to shape what happens at the lodge. Tying into this are also ideas of disruption to wildlife, especially birds. Despite the rather serious nature of aspects of the plot it still finds time to be lighthearted and comical in some parts and overall an enjoyable experience that will keep you wanting to see it through to its conclusion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely recommend to players that played text prompt and/or point n' click puzzle in the past. If you are new to the style it is not too hard to get into because the game guides you well.The game is not too hard because it's not abstract, it unfolds in a logical way and in a pleasant pace. I don't want to say any spoilers but there are more things to discover in the game than you may believe at first.The story and character development is really intriguing and will sometime leave you to laugh sometime it will leave you wonder.Thank you for this amazing game and I'm really looking towards buying Julia Minamata games in the futures whether it is with Miss Maple or in another theme/genre. The pixel art is exquisite and interactions with the game is witty. I would definitely would like to see a new game with a fantastic/sci-fi/horror/less-realistic game.Thank you Julia Minamata and all people involved for this fine piece of art and entertainment :) .Buy now and enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and lovely adventure game where you actually have to type everything you want to do. Makes me nostalgic for some Space Quest game that I often played in my childhood but never finished due to every floppy disk used for saving corrupting after a while. None of that frustration here! Just a cute little story and some fun investigative work. Looking forward to the rest of the story and unfolding the mysteries of The Crimson Diamond.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is a well made mystery adventure game that about the discovery of Diamonds in rural Canada, and the subsequent intrigue around the event. I really enjoyed it for the most part, though some of the puzzles felt extremely obtuse or illogical at times. Still, the game comes with a guide to help minimize frustration and there are still a lot of smaller smart bits of design to help prevent annoyances. Overall quality of it makes it easy to recommend for fans of the genre or for people who have an appreciation for authentically old school sensibilities in video games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A truly wonderful game that took me back to my childhood playing Colonel's BeQuest which it clearly plays homage too but in many ways surpasses with novel puzzles to solve and sleuthing skills to develop. It is so nice to have a new ega text parser game to play. It's like wearing a favourite piece of clothing.  Definitely reccomend to all the sierra lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved The Crimson Diamond. The text parser allows for so much freedom, creative thinking, and humor (try swearing at it, or seducing people). The art is gorgeous, with so many screens making me exclaim "that's so pretty!" - it's seriously impressive what is achieved while adhering to a specific style of art direction. It’s an amazing homage to the Laura Bow series while carving out a space of its own; it's nowhere near as unforgiving in terms of either deaths or precise timing. I highly recommend playing with a friend so you can bounce ideas off of each other - had a wonderful time streaming it together with my dear friend!Kudos to Julia Minamata, who clearly put an incredible amount of love into The Crimson Diamond.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite games this year. The puzzles are well thought out, I love the characters, honestly I cannot say enough good things about this game.I do wish that there was more music in the game, there are some times where you feel it's absence and sometimes the puzzles can feel a little arbitrary. This means we are looking at a solid 8.5 out of 10 for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely retro text parser detective game. The text parser gives it a lot of depth, there are many things you can miss or different ways to get to the same conclusion which is really great and engaging.There are a few moments though where it's a bit too rigid on what it expects you to type.Interesting story and characters who you want to overwhelm with questions from the get go to learn all about them.Funny deaths included.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Sierra's "The Colonel's Bequest" with Laura Bow (a personal favorite of mine), or detective/mystery games in general, I recommend this game.  It was a lot of fun!  There was a lot to see and discover, too - I appreciated the attention to detail - and there is more to discover on the next playthrough.  A few things I needed help with, but this game's text parser was more user-friendly than some games from back in the day.  Addition of an auto-save function, in-game notebook to keep track of main objectives, and keyboard shortcuts were welcome additions.  The keyboard got a workout with all the typing, hence the helpful keyboard shortcuts, but some of that is dependent on how thorough your playthrough style is and if you look at everything there is to see.  I will let other reviewers go into the nitty-gritty, but wanted to leave feedback since this game was very enjoyable for me, and hopefully others will agree.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so I have a lot to say about this game and ALL of it is POSITIVE.First up - yep absolutely nostalgia fulfilling, it feels a lot like Laura Bow (except not ridiculously punishing) but with plenty of original flourish. Even though Crimson Diamond is inspired by the classics, it still has a lot of its own feel which is incredibly nice to play.Second up (but my no means lesser) the pixel art of this game is SO GOOD. Its really funny there is this one scene with a balcony where you can look at the view and it will give you a written description of the view and I was just like SHOW ME MORE, you do get to go all the places described - but at that moment I was like I want to see from all the perspective thanks!!Finally the game was a really good vibe and level - its not brutal, but not completely cosy, there are death scenes, but unlike a Sierra game its not like if you cross the road wrong you'll cark it twice. I'm not 100% sure but I don't think there are walking dead situations but as a mystery story there are discoveries that might require a few playthroughts.To concluse THIS is the point and click nostalgia but also new game that we've all been hungry for for a while, I love everything about it and hope its successful beyond Minmata's dreams (because a sequal or another game would be awesome) :D
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Great game inspired by the classic Sierra games. It reminds me a lot to the first Laura Bow game. It's incredible that it's made by just one person! The story is well written and the puzzles are fair.If you don't like games where you have to type, or either your English is not very good, this is not the game for you. But if miss the era of old parser games or you are just curious and don't mind typing this might be the game for you. Give it a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute sleuthing delight.I am never replaying Laura Bow again, but I can guarantee I'm coming back for all the secrets I apparently didn't unearth in my first playthrough.Of course it speaks to the heart of an old Sierra player, but I won't say this is just nostalgia, the game is incredibly fun, challenging and atmospheric in its own right, and I cannot wait from more by this developer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game that pretty nicely captures older sierra parser adventure games feel.But is also same way annoying.This game in question mostly reminds of first Laura Bow sierra game.You type words on the parser/text input and character does what is suitable for them.However, parser in this game is in my opinion pretty dumb at times and you really need to figure out the correct way to input something for the game to understand.VERY frustrating when you know what you're supposed to do, but game only understands certain words or phrases.Game doesn't give any hints and some things it really could give a hand, example my struggle to fail the damn  game. No idea what i was supposed to do because i had no words what to input.At one point i had to ask something from someone, but i couldn't progress because my phrasing was off.I literally lost my mind when i googled for right phrasing.Some things are well thought after, for example closing and opening like a door can be shorthened to just C D or  O D and you O D a lot in this game LULMovement is simple. You can use your mouse to move around game area, or use keyboard arrow keys to move around. You can use old sierra style to one click and character keeps moving, or holding and moving. Game doesn't backseat and you can and propably will miss a lot at first playthrough.Good thing is that you really don't get stuck and if you progress you don't miss anything that prevents you from progressing.Also i am annoyed how game uses too much animations for like searching or opening like drawers. Character opens or closes double doors separatelly and player character opens each drawer separatelly.And you have to do this a lot. With different cabinets and whatnots that are right next to each others.Player character can evesdrop on lot of conversations and can find different ways to progress and questions you can ask from other characters.In the end you are given sort of score of what you may have missed and player keeps track on notebook what you have found.Easily accesible even.Game would really need more work to do with phrases and words it understands but as is it was still enjoyable journey and gladly will give this another go to try and get more secrets revealed.Hope we'll have a sequel someday. Maybe even with voice actors.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I loved every moment I spent in the Crimson Lodge, and I am looking forward to replaying the game to get all possible endings. I grew up with adventure games and all their idiosyncrasies. Not only was this game true to the experience, it ironed out all the things about Sierra games that drove me nuts (dead ends, nonsensical puzzles, etc.).  This game is truly one of a kind and I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Hooray, no in-game clock! I can't tell you how relieved I was to just be able to take my time in this game. "The Crimson Diamond" is a fantastic experience that stands on its own while being an excellent tribute to "The Colonel's Bequest." The art and music are gorgeous, and the story is compelling and specific, not just a rehash. Like a lot of great murder mysteries, it pairs a clear plot with deeper themes, specifically global politics, colonialism, and environmentalism. I even learned things about geology! The text parser is subtly brilliant: while you will inevitably get "I don't understand" messages, it has an impressive vocabulary and is mostly pretty lenient. This game kind of reminded me of "Undertale" in that it was extremely detailed and created almost entirely by one person, heavily inspired from a single game while adding some new ideas. True, "Crimson Diamond" is nowhere near as boundary-pushing or subversive as "Undertale" (the twists in this story are far more modest) but there's a similar blend of passion and creativity. And both have excellent soundtracks.You can talk to the characters in "Crimson Diamond" about a lot of different topics and the game will take your position on the screen into account when typing in actions. Most actions will have multiple possible ways to trigger them. There is an important difference between "looking" and "examining," as well as "talking" and "asking," but the game helps you learn this early on.I loved the tutorial and ESPECIALLY the "review" command! Even as an expert old-school Sierra gamer these were great ways to get oriented and keep track of your objectives without giving too much away. Sierra (or whoever owns the rights) should seriously hire Julia to add these to the GOG versions of their older games. Also, the hint page you link to was a good, fair way to help players along slowly.I have a few minor criticisms. First, I wish the notebook had tabs for easier navigation, which would have definitely helped in the later chapters. I wish there were more options to "tell" characters about things. And without spoiling anything, let me just say that the resolution of the story probably won't blow your mind or even surprise you very much, especially if you have any experience with murder mysteries. But that's not entirely a bad thing: the focus is less on finding out "whodunnit" than gathering enough evidence to prove it. In most cases, the game will warn you when you're missing something, so if you don't get an 100% ending, it feels less like you screwed up and more like you decided not to pursue certain things and press on. I'm sure I'm not alone in hoping we see Nancy Maple return. Despite their issues I always wished there were more Laura Bow games, so maybe the success of Crimson Diamond will lead to further adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: It's wonderful to see a Sierra-like text parser adventure game in 2024. I'm a huge fan of Sierra adventure games, although by the time I started playing them in the early-mid 90s, they all used point&click interface. In a few attempts I made to play older, text parser-based titles I failed miserably, what due to the objectively higher difficulty level of those earlier titles, what due to not being a native speaker and not having that large vocabulary at that age. And thus "The Crimson Diamond" became the first text parser adventure game I actually completed without a walkthrough. While the game is not very difficult, I wouldn't call it too easy (I would give it a thumbs down if it was, as I do like to have actual puzzles in my adventure games, even if it means getting stuck). Additionally, the "novelty" of the text parser interface makes it interesting to solve even the easier puzzles since you really need to know what you want to do and can't just randomly combine objects. I also like how the "use" verb is banned.However, the game isn't without its flaws: - It pulls a trick on you where you can't progress (or at least can't progress to the best ending) if you failed to pick up an item in one of the previous chapters. The game also has optional objectives in some of the chapters but won't always tell you if you missed those. I realize this makes it more authentic for the time period it gets its inspiration from, but personally, when it comes to the elements of the older adventure games, I'd prefer to have more difficult puzzles (bring on the moon logic!), but not letting me get irreparably stuck. - Some of the puzzles are hinted too strongly (fortunately, not all of them), where Nancy or other characters tell you exactly *how* to do something instead of just what you need to accomplish in general. Additionally, the "Review" command that is meant to give you progress towards the end of the chapter will actually give you pretty strong hints. I hoped to use it to find out if I completed all of the high-level chapter goals, but after using it once, I considered it cheating and avoided using it again. - Although the story is meant to be a mystery, it becomes clear "whodunnit" pretty early on and there are no big revelations, at least not around the main plot. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed the game and the characters, I just prefer more "mystery" in my mystery stories.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm Nancy Maple, a mineralogist student sent to the town of Crimson to investigate the discovery of a large diamond in the belly of a fish. When I arrive by train, my luggage has been stolen and it turns out the inn I was supposed to stay at isn't an inn anymore. Its owner, one Evan Richards, is so kind to allow me to stay the night, but he will send me back on the first train in the morning.It's a text parser game, which means you have to type in what you want Nancy to do instead of clicking on hotspots. It's heavily influenced by the first Laura Bow game, The Colonel's Bequest. You also find yourself in a huge mansion with lots of people whom you can eavesdrop on. But next to being text parser, it also uses the old EGA graphics style with a limited, 16-color palette. You can move Nancy with the directional keys but it's also possible to click with the mouse where you want her to walk.It's very handy that a message pops up about muffled voiced whenever you near a door with people behind it having something interesting to say. I remember in The Colonel's Bequest you were pretty much left on your own to figure out where to go, and there everything you saw, heard or found could progress time, and then the NPC's would move positions, so you might miss some things during the earlier time. I'm not really sure if The Crimson Diamond uses a similar technique or not. There's no in-game clock, but there definitely is story progression after doing certain tasks, usually indicated by an auto-save message. So I try to make sure to know every NPC's whereabouts before doing something I think leads to such a progression, but I'm sure I'm still missing lots of stuff. I finished The Crimson Diamond in a little over 7 hours! But I'm not too happy with the result! There are three "report cards" so to speak. The first two weren't too shabby, but still okay. But I got zero on the third one! What?! Where did I go wrong?!Also, I redid the final showdown a couple of times to get a better ending. There are several steps you need to be perfect at, otherwise you'll trigger quite a long cutscene followed by the Q&A sessions that result in those report cards. So, I had to reload a couple of times, but then for the last step it turned out I didn't have the necessary inventory item with me.But just like I had to play The Colonel's Bequest a second time before I got anywhere near a decent result, The Crimson Diamond is a joy to play. In itself it isn't such a difficult game, you just need to be aware of some strategies you can employ in how you can find the necessary clues and evidence. The game is addictive; I had a hard time letting go of it, and I would have preferred to play it in one sitting. It's a great location, an interesting set of characters, a cool Agatha Christie style and gathering clues type of story. I had great fun with it and I hope Julia Minamata will make many more games like this!Oh yeah, I found a couple of death scenes as well, but there’s no rewind function here like in Beyond the Edge of Owlsgard, so remember to save!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely game! I've been following the development of this game for several years now, and I was so pleased that it was finally released! It didn't disappoint, but instead it was even better than I thought. Upon first glance, the game might seem like a pastiche of Colonel's Bequest and Laura Bow, but fortunately it is much more original than that. I really loved the mineralogy aspect of the game. I really recommend this game and hope that the developer decides to make a sequel at some point :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: An innovative twist on classic graphical interactive fiction and point-and-click adventures, with an engaging story, an intrepid protagonist, and a host of memorable characters whose backgrounds and agendas added color to the story.  The puzzles fit the storyline and were rarely frustrating, and the notebook helped avoid aimelss moments.  After finishing it, I immediately wanted to replay the game to see what I missed the first time through.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A modern adventure game with beautiful EGA graphics and a text parser. A true work of love and a sincere homage to the classics.The game is good, but not perfect. There is a lot of exposition through dialogues, several parts of the world feel rather empty, and the game is a bit light in puzzles. Also, the characters have very little depth and the story barely has any twist.Finally, the achievements are currently broken on Mac, but I’m sure this’ll get patched soon.The non-playable intro and epilogue have some absolutely gorgeous environments. I’d have loved a bit of gameplay there so I could enjoy them for a little longer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A truly wonderful game, with a setting that's a joy to spend time in, interesting characters, beautiful writing, and gorgeous art and music.The parser is used brilliantly, giving the player a level of freedom that just can't be found in other games. I'll give just one small example (without spoilers)…At one point in the game, I knew I needed to somehow manipulate an item in my inventory (I won’t describe how or what, to avoid spoilers). In most games, I’d have needed to use an extra inventory item on it. But in reality, it’s something I could do with my hands. Well, in this game, I just typed in the action that made sense to me – and it worked! It felt electric, and incredibly immersive. There are many, many moments like this.Also, there is no need to have played a text parser game before this one. There's a simple standalone tutorial for those who need it, and the game itself does a great job of easing you in slowly, and giving you plenty of time and opportunity to learn and experiment. Also, an in-game notebook keeps track of your goals, so you never feel too overwhelmed.All in all, I can't recommend this enough, as it's perfect for text parser adventure newbies and aficionados alike!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game, the creator has brought back a beloved style of awesomeness from the late 80s/early 90s that I cherish, and has done so much hard work on The Crimson Diamond. Looks like some serious heart and soul was poured into this little masterpiece. Makes me happy knowing someone exists that took the time to make a great game like this!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I love you Nancy... please tell me more about rocks...This game is a wonderful little tribute to old Sierra games, specifically the first Laura Bow game (in case the protagonist looking a lot like her didn't tip you off). Aside from there being only seven ways you can die (I got five during normal gameplay), The Crimson Diamond is very accurate and wouldn't be that out of place next to the classic Sierra titles. Some of the puzzles do have that good old Sierra "how the hell was I supposed to know THAT?" feel, but there is guide that you can pull up ingame if needed. You play as Nancy Maple, an aspiring geologist who is staying in Crimson Ontario to see if diamonds can really be found there as reported. There are also a lot of different characters you'll get to know throughout the game, some being clear references to Laura Bow characters. That said, this game definitely has its own charm and appeal separate from its inspiration. It's clear that a lot of love and care was put into The Crimson Diamond. You can gather fingerprints, investigate the environment for clues, look at rocks, rummage in drawers, and a lot of other things. I found myself invested in the story and characters, and it was a bittersweet feeling when I finished the game. I got what I see as a 'bad' ending and what seems like a 'good' ending after I reloaded my save and tried again. I was pretty damn thorough in my investigation, but I still missed a few things and didn't get a perfect score. There's a decent amount of replay value here, clearly. Overall, I would 100 percent recommend this to any fan of Sierra adventures. If you're not familiar, I would watch a video or something first before buying.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A very pleasant and nostalgic game. I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing the game. The game emulates the gameplay of The Colonel's Bequest and fixes most of the problems that game had. It was basically impossible to finish The Colonel's Bequest in a first try and understand what actually was going on. The Crimson Diamond has an ingame tutorial, it has a notebook and at all times you can ask Nancy what the next step should be. And to make things even better, you always know what will trigger a step forwards in time. I never felt I had to rush or missed out on anything.The story is interesting and easy to follow. It's a classic murder mystery story without any sense of parody (which is a good thing). You can basically search anything, even if there is nothing to find. Character answer most relevant questions you have. And from what I've seen some puzzles have multiple solutions. The thing I also liked was how Nancy, the protagonist, has an actual job to do. She isn't just there accidentally. And throughout the game she is actually doing the things she is supposed to be doing. Now my nitpicks. The mysteries are too easy. I did play the game with pen and paper, making notes. Maybe the game is harder if you don't do that. Quite early in the game i guessed most things that were going on. And those things turned out to be true. This game isn't so much about finding out who did it and what is happening, but more about how you can proof it to the authorities. It's more CSI than Poirot or Marple. I did enjoy finding fingerprints and shoe prints and matching them to the suspects though. But it also made figuring out what happened a little to easy.Another minor thing is that there isn't a lot of music. A lot of the time the game is eerily quiet. Especially when you're walking around the main house. That said, the music that you do hear is very good. You can only have 50 savegames. Near the end of the game I had to delete savegames to make room for new ones.All in all I can recommend this game. If you're in the mood for a classic murder mystery, this is what you want. Especially if you want to play a game like The Colonel's Bequest, if you're nostalgic for old Sierra games or you just want to try out a very different way of playing a detective game than you're used to.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: An instant classic! If you enjoy cosy mysteries this is a fantastic game and I highly recommend grabbing your notebook, putting your detective hat on and checking it out!You play Nancy Maple, a plucky mineralogist student sent to the far North of Canada to look for diamonds, but mystery and misadventure awaits! The story and cast of characters are intriguing, and after arriving at our accomodation - The Lodge, a beautiful and expansive wooden mansion - we are very soon pulled into the mystery as things go awry.There is so much detail here, both in the incredible graphics, with lavish rooms to explore and constant beautiful detailed close-ups of objects you can examine, but also in the research for the Canadian ghost-town setting and the mineralogical aspects. I know Julia did a lot of research for this game and it really shows - you feel both immersed in searching for diamonds but also immersed in the remote Canadian wilderness - and it’s a perfect setting for a cosy mystery as you explore the warm rooms of the Lodge where you are staying and venture out into its surrounds, nestled amongst cosy pine trees.The text parser adds so much richness and interactivity. There are many actions your character can perform, including many little fun things you can get your character to do. It’s a joy to think of some funny thing and then when you type it and try it the character actually does it, or you get a funny refusal from the parser. Try getting in a cupboard, for example, or using the Lodge’s lavish bathroom facilities. But the parser interactivity goes beyond funny jokes - there are many investigative actions you can perform.I strongly recommend doing the tutorial and also checking out the Help screen to learn the parser shortcuts - things like ‘L’ for Look and ‘X’ for Examine, ‘O D’ for Open Door - as these will help out a lot as there is quite a bit of typing, especially if you want to be thorough. In this game Look and Examine are two separate actions, don’t forget to Examine things! Nancy will examine things with her mineralogist loupe - which is really a genius idea as she can both perform geological investigations with her loupe but also examine clues!The game finishes with an interview testing your knowledge and investigative skills - I was quite surprised here, the test of knowledge is a lot more extensive and tricky than I was expecting, which is great! You can go through the game just completing the tasks your notebook tells you to do, but there are a lot of extra things to miss here! The investigative aspects are quite rich and complex. I recommend taking your own physical notes too as this will enrich the experience and the in-game notebook gets a bit cluttered by the end of the game with all the things going on.Buy the game! And bring on The Crimson Diamond 2!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up playing Sierra games and The Colonel's Bequest was my absolute favorite. If you enjoyed that game, you'll love this one too. It felt like I had just stumbled on an old Sierra game that I had never played because the local Sears computer section didn't sell it back in 1989. The graphics are amazing, the text parser was surprisingly friendly to use, and the story was multi-layered with many threads to chase. When I completed the game I found I had missed out on quite a few things, so I am definitely going to go back and replay. There are multiple endings depending on what actions you take and how much you have uncovered of the mysteries. You'll be asked to provide answers at the end of the game, like Dagger of Amon Ra.Like the good old Sierra games, you CAN die. However, there aren't that many and most are pretty obviously avoidable. If you turn on autosave it usually saves fairly soon before a death, but like with any Sierra game, I'd still recommend saving often. I really loved the game and Nancy Maple's character, so fingers crossed that there will be more detective adventures in Nancy's future!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: LOVED Sierra games - especially the Laura Bow mysteries! This game was very reminiscent of those earlier titles (though I perhaps encountered nothing as creepy as when Laura finds Lillian in the playhouse). I enjoyed the exploration and how many puzzles/mysteries there were to solve. Definitely planning a second play-through to catch the things I missed. Well done!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Playing The Crimson Diamond feels like curling up in a big cozy chair with a cup of tea and a good mystery novel.Taking on the role of plucky geologist-turned-sleuth Nancy Maple, you'll embark on a journey to a rustic, isolated lodge in the northern Ontario town of Crimson. While the lodge is normally sleepy and peaceful, recent events have shaken things up: scheming relatives, mysterious new visitors, and the discovery of a diamond in Crimson (Nancy's reason to visit) have filled the lodge with tension and upset. It's up to Nancy to meet the residents, untangle the secrets hidden throughout the lodge, and uncover a greater danger lurking under the surface - all while completing her collection of rock samples!Text-heavy adventures like this live or die by their writing (which is not to detract from the top-notch retro graphics on display) and there are a lot of ways to get it wrong. But The Crimson Diamond is warm, funny, detailed, clever, and feels very comfortable speaking to modern audiences while staying true to its 1910s setting. I laughed a lot, and even gasped at a couple of reveals. And though the game is not a long affair, it's well paced, and it pretty handily earned a solidly cathartic and emotional ending for its memorable cast.One other thing I quite liked was the way that so much of the mystery was optional to progressing in the game. I really felt like a detective picking up clues from eavesdropping on conversations, finding useful objects, and making connections all under my own direction. I felt really accomplished at the end when I had a chance to show off my knowledge (though I wish I'd been less shy about stuffing my pockets - I didn't realize how much I'd be expected to provide physical evidence of my assertions). The central mystery is solid, there are side elements and plot points to flesh it out, and overall it just feels worth your time to investigate. You really get a deeper sense of the cast in a meaningful way, and being able to talk to everyone about these discoveries just feels really organic in a way I don't always associate with adventure games.All of this would be remarkable on its own, but as a solo dev effort it's a real feat. If you're looking for a strong story well-told, this one is well worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I was following the GameDev Vlog of this game for a while, and indeed the game did not disappoint. The reconstruction of the graphic design and the EGA of back then color pallete is above and beyond any expectation, and looks absolutely gorgeous even on today's hi Res 27" screens. Regarding the game play, it really keeps up the tension of similar games in the genre, like Laura Bow 1 and 2. Excellent game play. Interesting and drifting plot. The beginning of the game is a bit tedious needing to visit each and every room in the lodge, but once the Dinner begins the game gets much more interesting. 5 out of 5 for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Having an absolute ball playing 'The Crimson Diamond,' a retro-modern text parser adventure.  It looked like a long-lost DOS adventure, but it's a recent release!  The designer deserves praise for the faithfulness of its presentation and the authenticity of its atmosphere. I appreciate the smart, subtle QoL features, none of which betray the nostalgic charm of its text parser. I've been having a lot of fun with the story and old-school gameplay. I'm a touch typer, so the interface has been a delight.  I can't wait for more story to unfold (and to take more things from random drawers). Please, please pick this brilliant, well-designed game, and support amazing creatives like Julia.  The Crimson Diamond stands on its own strengths and creativity, and I hope Julia continues to develop more wonderful adventures for years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is a completely delightful game, a true love letter to Colonel's Bequest from Sierra On-line. If you like OG text parser games or really, any retro adventure games, this one is a delight. It combines mystery, puzzle-solving, intrigue and then there's the amazing music, sound effects, and lovingly made EGA art. I can't wait to finish it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: For starters, I'm not a big adventure game enthusiast (the only ones I've ever completed were the old Infocom text adventures, The Dig, Full Throttle, and the Legend Entertainment adventures based on novels). So this was a fresh experience into the older kind of adventure games I hadn't played. I was coming into this expecting to be polite and gracious for receiving an early copy, playing a couple of hours, and then moving on.This game has literally haunted my dreams (in good ways!) ever since I started it! I've only been able to get a couple of chapters in, but I plan on completing it as soon as my very limited free time allows!The graphics hit that retro-styled pixely itch that I very much enjoy. The cutscenes and animations are very detailed, and watching Julia's art streams were quite engrossing to see how they were drawn up! I also really liked the music, which feels era appropriate not just in the retro stylings that the game was based on, but also for the time period of 1914 that the game is set in. The characters all have life breathed into them through dialogue that draws you into the game even more, and want to find out more about each of the characters' past, and how to help (some of) them with their current endeavors! The puzzles have been a little challenging for a non-adventure gamer, but there are a couple of very handy QOL features that present a light guide for what to do (your notebook and the 'Review' command). I never felt truly lost, and the only thing keeping me from completing the game is just time!I highly encourage everyone who is a fan of adventure games, retro-styled games, or a well told story, to purchase this game and support Julia and Dan in this, and hopefully future games down the line!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond
