_childDocuments_.review: As players of virtually all the old Sierra titles, my wife and I were really looking forward to this game - and we were not disappointed! The art is wonderful. Nancy's portraits are endearing, the scenery is highly detailed and showcases a lot of variety. The music is wonderful (though I did feel its absence at times when wandering the lodge). The story has a lot of depth, with the ability to ask characters about a wide range of topics to glean their backstories and motives. We enjoyed roaming every corner of the lodge searching out clues and conversations, and despite cataloging a trove of data, still missed some key points of evidence. Having just finished the game we plan on immediately starting another run tomorrow night - determined to cement Nancy Maple as a master sleuth and mineralogist!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Not since The Colonel's Bequest has my soul been this happy! I feel like I'm nine again. As mentioned by another reviewer, this game does a marvelous job of honoring the spirit of Laura Bow, while improving on what didn't work (i.e., the fingerprints actually amount to worthwhile evidence in this one, and the characterization is much more nuanced). While the puzzles are nowhere near Sierra-preposterous, it is exceedingly difficult to always be in the right place at the right time (I'd actually say this one is worse than the Colonel on that front). No matter--having played it twice, and getting drastically different endings each time, I look forward to my third round (which will hopefully achieve the optimal ending). Also, the hint book is great--an indispensable resource! Thank you, Julia Minamata, for bringing this nostalgic delight into the world!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Quite enjoyed this. Excellent EGA art, scratches a specific nostalgia but is a lot less stressful that those Sierra games. Hampered by a pretty limited text parser and some hand-holding with the notebook feature. (Biggest peeve: no "use" allowed. It's not an adventure game if you can't sit and "USE item on item" for 5 hours.)Not the most novel plot but it's charming and dorky and pretty well written. Wish the parser allowed more freedom but it's a singe dev game I get it. Definitely going to replay (I did bad at detectiving, despite what I thought was too much hand-holding haha.)Very Canadian, FYI.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Great game! Fun mystery, great personality, nostalgia inducing. You can take your time playing this and finding all the secrets is highly satisfying.  I grew up playing Sierra text parser games (the Colonel’s Bequest and Quest for Glory 1 and 2 being favourites). The Crimson Diamond easily recalls the nostalgia of those games while smoothing over barriers that text parser games can be known for., this game wonderfully captures the EGA look but renders environments beautifully with great composition and use of pointillism/dithering. Any significant details are animated to help them stand out. Honestly, there are close-ups and cutscenes that added a lot of charm and thrill (particularly eavesdropping on conversations). Characters are animated well and convey personality (my only critique is that the walking animations are a little stiff, but it helps with the walk speed so I don’t mind). , text parser games are all about using keywords. This game easily lets you do what you need to do without much difficulty. There are some moments when I had my own idea or solution but the game wants me to do specific actions or keywords. Thankfully, the writing of the game is easy to follow and there are plenty of opportunities to figure things out by looking and examining things more closely. The game does well to train you to use these actions frequently and the writing often reveals breadcrumbs of where to go next. To let you know you're on the right path, the game is very satisfying giving you get ‘good job’ notes when you’ve done particular tasks. It’s not a score, but it is helpful. The notebook is also incredibly helpful at keeping things organized! I just wish it was maybe a bit bigger and easier to navigate (it gets long by the end of the game).  : This game is really well written! The cast of characters have interesting motivations and quirky personalities. It’s clear that there was plenty of research into all of the aspects of the story, location and mystery. Crimson is fictitious but it could easily fit in as an old Canadian mining town. I’m also glad there was an Indigenous consultant to ensure that the portrayal of the time was accurate.Another reason why the writing is so great is that, with an inquisitive mindset, many clues are revealed from asking questions, examining items and being the best Miss Marple (that’s a great wink and a nod) you can be. Fingerprints are copious and fun. The game does a fantastic job of explaining minerology procedures needed and, as long as you’re consistent, I think most will be pretty satisfied with figuring things out. There are multiple endings to explore which all depend on how clueless or how astute and thorough you are. The end of the game quizzes you on evidence gathered and it could be a little cumbersome to know the exact keywords to explain everything, but I managed to be within one or two points from perfect during my run. Overall, this game is a , imperfections and all, and I’m thrilled to hear that the developer has plans for a sequel! There’s so much great potential for text parser games and I’m glad she’s pursuing them!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved The Crimson Diamond. It's the first full-length adventure game I felt compelled to complete in one sitting after starting it.Although the EGA-style graphics and text parser UI could be considered throwbacks, after just a few minutes of playing, I completely forgot about the UI and the graphics and was 100% drawn into the intricate and beautifully woven story and characters.Seriously recommended, loved every minute of it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Holy bajeezus I'm at 5.7 hours already? As with most great text parser games, they really immerse you in the story to the point where you completely lose any sense of time in the real world. You'd think entering a new chapter would be a good excuse to take a break, but it's hard to put down because you want to see what's coming next.The art really helps immerse you even more because it feels like I'm back in the 1990s playing games like Hugo's House of Horrors or Leisure suit larry. With better graphics of course, but it still strictly conforms to the EGA palette.It comes with some conveniences like typing shortcuts. For example, you can use ctrl+t for talk to, or ctrl+l for look, type in "o d" for open door (which you'll be doing quite a lot). The notepad is a nice touch, too. It's like a journal that keeps track of your progress. Even it tells you to do something, you should probably keep exploring, because there's side bits you can miss.There's also a hints page for when you get really stuck, but I'd recommend trying to play without it as much as you can. There's not much point if you're just looking everything up.If you're a fan of text parsers, which you probably are if you're here, then this is a must buy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm absolutely delighted by this game - the visuals, the storytelling, and especially all the surprises and discoveries found along the way. Growing up with the Nancy Drew games, this scratches that same mystery-solving itch but it brings its own special flavor and an extra level of difficulty + creativity that comes from typing text prompts. Now I have to go start over and find all the clues I missed the first time ;)
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game rocks, so to speak. Gorgeous graphics, an exciting set of mysteries, interesting characters, and many locations to explore. On top of all that, the game has a replayability factor that a lot of other mystery games tend to not have because you can progress without seeing everything, and I'm planning to revisit the lodge to round out the mystery! The game feels very Agatha Christie and Clue-like, with a suspicious cast of characters stuck in an expansive lodge together, each hiding their own set of secrets. This was my first ever foray into a text parser based game and I thoroughly enjoyed the experience which feels more immersive than a typical point-and-click adventure game. There is a bit of a learning curve, but the tutorial is helpful for newbies like me. I found the puzzles to be an ideal level of challenging that kept things satisfying but not frustrating as long as you were thorough in your investigation. Highly recommended to fellow mystery lovers!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I just have to gush.This game is gorgeous. I've been waiting for it for years and it was so worth it! Such care was taken to not spoil anything past the 1st chapter and I could not have been prepared for what has been released. This is the EGA text-parser that I always wanted growing up.  Julia Minamata took everything from the adventure games of my childhood and gave us something that was MORE. The pure joy in doing REAL detective work (though cumbersome at times, the victory was all the sweeter!), the helpful nudges in the right direction, the delight when the game auto-saves before you do something stupid and the hilarity when it doesn't (collateral damage, am I right?), I have not been so thrilled at every twist and turn in a game since I was a little!I highly recommend this game to any and everyone who enjoyed these type of games as a child, and those who did not, this is not something that anyone should miss out on!Side note: play ALL the ways, super sleuth, brain dead, the writing is brilliant with whatever route you chose!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gorgeous, very polished adventure game. A Lot of care has been put into the graphics which are sumptuous. Characters are well scripted and seem to respond to several topics, which is something I appreciate a lot. There are many locations, all with beautiful designs, it's a pleasure to walk through them. The writing is excellent and the story looks great even though I am just at the beginning. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is the parallel-universe third installment of the Laura Bow series this world deserves. So very happy to see this released and be amazing. A must-play for any old-school Sierra adventure fans.Very minor nitpicks: In a few instances the text parser was not as forgiving as I'd like. Had to try a few variations and think a bit. Expected this for the genre, but some might be frustrated by this. Aside: I applaud the effort to ban "USE" and feel it's the correct choice here. There could be more music and/or ambient sfx (e.g. character theme music when on screen?). Some of the animations are simple (e.g. carriage)But forget about all that! This is FANTASTIC. If you're at all any bit a fan of these games: Buy it, play it, love it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid text parser adventure game with really nice pixel art. Choices matter in the sense that there are different ways to approach problems, and depending on your approach certain characters may live or die. There's a surprising amount of depth.The only major con I have is that the story is quite straightforward - I had figured out who the killer was and what their motive was far, far before the reveal. This led to the last couple of chapters feeling very anti-climactic. That being said, the gameplay is interesting and modern enough that it's still quite fun and definitely worth a try if you're interested in old school adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Great example of the genre.A couple of the prompts it wants are a bit super specific.For example, some of the prompts around dealing with the icebox were a little unnecessarily annoying.For the most part, it works just fine.The first couple chapters, I took my time, opening all the drawers and such.After that, it really picked up the pace.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: First, I love the graphical look.  This review isn't 100% positive but I'd still recommend it if you're craving a classic adventure game. I maybe played a couple EGA games in this style, like maybe PQ2, QFG2 and such, but of these games that was my favorite visual style.  So thumbs up for the look. Second, the gameplay is pretty good, albeit maybe an automatic icon to open a door would have been alright.  My only gripe and this isn't just this game, but all the "classic" games is that they're sometimes too classic in this kind of way where they lack a certain QoL.  It's a nitpick but there's a lot of doors.Third, the story is pretty good, the characters are interesting enough, and the dialog is well written.  In the game you can really be creative and try out any combination of phrases to reveal hints or just information about the world around your character.  It's very much a classic Sierra-style, parser-driven adventure game.  Mostly finally, the music is okay.  It's nothing too interesting, but it fits the setting.  There are some times when a particular tune with a particular wind instrument keeps playing over and over that gets kind of annoying (to me!) but other than that, there's some good little tunes! Finally, the game is not very challenging, so if you're looking for a real head scratcher-mystery, I don't think that's here.  It's relaxing though, it's fun to learn about the characters and it's a good time.  Personally, I did not love the animation.  This is just my taste.  The animation feels more choppy than even the classic games, unless my memory is fading, which is totally possible.  Alright go get it! Have an adventure!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond is definitely worth a try. First of all, the game is beautiful. Even if the retro palette isn't normally your thing, Julia wields it masterfully to create a world that feels vibrant and real. Subtle use of dithering adds depth and richness to the environments. It feels like you're really there, staying at a cosy lodge in Northern Ontario, surrounded by wilderness and wildlife, and solving real mysteries. The music is also expertly crafted by Dan Policar and fits perfectly with the atmospheric setting.The story is clever, and rewards the player for getting to know the complex and multidimensional characters. Everyone at the lodge feels like they belong there and each comes with an interesting backstory that gives the world an authentic "lived-in" feeling. The puzzles are intuitive and engaging, and although there were times that I felt stuck, persistence often revealed that the answer was staring me in the face. There's also a helpful online hint book in case you get into a real jam.Like any good mystery, there's a lot that can be missed on a first playthrough so if you try to barrel through the story like you're going for the glitched any% speedrun, you will certainly miss out. I encourage players to take their time and stop to smell the flowers. The game offers a surprising amount of replayability, and having just finished my first playthrough, I already feel compelled to return to Crimson to get the complete picture.A beautiful experience, and a work of amazing Canadian art.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully crafted and sharply executed, this mystery-adventure game is absolutely worth your time.  I truly enjoyed the compelling mystery and the quick-witted protagonist; the game play and story is well-paced by the author.Look forward to revisiting previous titles and upcoming entries; support indie developers whenever you can!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Every aspect of Julia Minamata’s The Crimson Diamond is filled with a deep reverence for the classic Laura Bow series by Sierra On-line. It takes the majority of its inspiration from The Colonel's Bequest, the first entry in that beloved series. Julia did a wonderful job of emulating her inspirations while putting her own unique spin on the game. Every component of The Crimson Diamond; the text-parser interface, the EGA graphics and Dan Policar’s MT-32 composed music, is a loving tribute to the glory days of Sierra. Julia used the components to draw players into a compelling original, and challenging mystery. She packed this game with plenty of shortcuts and modern conveniences so that  players never get stuck in the story. Many players will enjoy The Crimson Diamond Thanks to Julia’s passion, hard work, and attention to detail, but for a Sierra fan like myself, playing The Crimson Diamond  was like reconnecting with a beloved, and sorely missed part of childhood.  The Crimson Diamond has every right to sit on the same shelf with  The Sierra Classics  following in the grand tradition of its predecessors, The Crimson Diamond will enthrall gamers of every generation.The foundation of The Sierra Classic was always the story. The Crimson Diamond follows that golden rule. When a fisherman discovers a diamond in the belly of fish while camping near the town of Crimson Ontario, things develop quickly for aspiring mineralogist Nancy Maple, who is tasked by her boss Professor Plummer to see if the story is true, and if more diamonds can be found near Crimson. Nancy gets mire than she bargained for when a geology trip becomes a mystery filled with robbery and murder. Nancy needs the player to help her get to the bottom of things, and to survive.Continuing  the Sierra tradition, the player helps Nancy through typing commands into a parser interface. If the player wants a description of a scene, they type  “Look Around” and hit enter or return. If they want to open a door, they type open door. If they want to talk to someone they type talk to person, or the can use the characters name or several other words. A helpful tutorial ensures that even rookie players will use the parser like a pro.The interface lets the player help Nancy with many tasks from being a detective and a mineralogist. Nancy will need to eavesdrop many times. Players type Eavesdrop and she will overhear the conversation.  I enjoyed the mineralogy puzzles. Nancy must identify many rucks by rubbing them on a plate an analyzing their residue. You do this by typing Rub [name of Rock] on plate Nancy will reveal the results of the test.  I found “Review” to be  the most helpful command. Typing this compel Nancy to recap her achievements and ponder what she has yet to accomplish. She also takes copious notes notes in a helpful notebooks. There’s even a hint book for players who need help.Julia’s world of nostalgic mystery is realized through lovingly constructed EGA graphics and wonderful music composed on the MT-32 by Dan Policar Visually, my favorite scene of the game occurs at the end of the story when Nancy returns home after a long day. The presence of Nancy’s landlord made me smile when I discovered her identity I also enjoyed the sturdy house and blue sky Dan Policar outdid himself when  composing this music. I especially enjoyed the suspense-filled track during the introduction when driving to the lodge at night.Thanks to Julia Minamata’s attention to detail, and attentiveness to feedback, The Crimson Diamond  is a wonderful piece of interactive art that will appeal to generations of gamers.   I m glad I played it. I urge gamers of any skill level to solve its mystery.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a little lovely gem for all those who loved the Sierra text parser games of old and who also likes a detective story. It is very clear that the game is a love letter to the old Colonel's Bequest by Roberta Williams, but in my mind it beats that game when it comes to the story elements and the general plot. As a Swede I also must give a game which makes a reference to "Hallongrotta" a thumbs up. I'm definitely going to re-play this game at a latter date to see if I can get a perfect score (and find all ways to die).The parser can at times be a bit clumsy, but that's the only negative critique I can give this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: While reminiscent of the classic Sierra games in its artwork and text parser interface,  this game is its own masterpiece.  The amount of work and attention to detail presented in the plot, the characters and the setting are extremely impressive.  The artwork is exquisite.  While there are a few bugs, they seem to be minor.  Not only entertaining, the Crimson Diamond has tremendous educational value, both in the field of mineralogy,  which is essential to the plot, and in teaching deductive reasoning.   The game's creator, Julia Minamata, has done an amazing job.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I had my eye on this since watching One Short Eye's video about Colonel's Bequest and hearing Minamata discuss how they made the graphics look so real despite only having 16 colors to work with. After playing the demo and getting a callback to one of the deaths from CB, I realized that this game was going to be special.This is a game that's best done at a leisurely pace, when the characters are new and the mysteries are yet to be solved. Having a notebook keep track of things to do and an autosave system really elevates this from the Sierra game of old, and I look forward to spending more time with this game like I would reading Agatha Christie novels when I was growing up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game was amazing. I admit I was never a big fan of Sierra adventure games and their approach to puzzles, so I'm glad The Crimson Diamond took the best bits of those classics and made a clever homage with gorgeous pixel art and music, approachable puzzles, and a very helpful notebook. I was absolutely immersed since minute one and loved the use of parser controls that made me feel like a real detective. It was a joy to play.I hope Julia keeps developing brilliant games like this one for a long time!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game, definitely catches that Laura Bow vibe. Very atmospheric and the music is great. Unlike most retro-like adventure games,e.g. built in AGS, this one scales fine on a 4K monitor.The art is very well made, I actually think the developers should have used the game-style art for the thumbnail instead of a regular 2d drawing to better showcase the vibe.Definitely make sure you use the shortcuts like 'o' for open etc. because typing the same words gets old a bit fast for me. With the shortcuts it's actually great.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Like others have said, very Colonel's Bequesty. Which is a good thing, for me. Less ways to die, maybe, and easier to get to the end having done (most) all the things. It felt like the complexity of Dagger of Amun Ra, with the interface of Colonel's Bequest. But also with Christopher Plummer.There is a built-in hint document (website) that is accessed via the game menu, and I did have to go to it for one thing that was not intuitive to me, personally, but generally I felt everything made sense. That might be because I'm one of those people who goes to all the wrong rooms first (on purpose) before I get to the room that will advance the plot.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: I'd been looking forward to this game and it well exceeded my expectations!The art is absolutely stunning. Every scene looks like it was made with such care.I hadn't played many text parser adventure games before this but I'm happy to say I had very little trouble with it, aside from my own spelling errors.The story is like a love-letter to the mystery genre. I found it gripping the whole way through and I had oodles of fun snooping about and being as nosey as possible.I highly recommend this. I think it's one of the best adventure games I've played and I'm looking forward to playing through it again sometime to see if I can catch what I missed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This was a lot of fun. I've played through once and know I've missed at least a few clues, but the game is very forgiving - no ticking clock like The Colonel's Bequest. The art style is absolutely beautiful and I enjoyed the slow reveal of the story while being able to look back and piece things together.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: The Crimson Diamond keeps all the best parts of 80s parser adventure games and reinvents the annoying bits. Autosaves. A competent parser that accepts shortcuts. Beautiful dithered EGA. A main character who knows her stuff and uses that knowledge. An in-game notebook that keeps track of your progress. Wonderful attention to detail. I could go on and on, but really, you should just hit the buy button and download. Julia Minamata has truly made something special with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Crimson Diamond is a labour of love and extremely charming. The time period, literature, and art of 1900's Canada is well researched and loved. Scenarios are interesting and puzzles are built around very practical tools and resources. The characters are fun and unique with a good range of emotions and motives to make you remember them. The setting is lush with a great sense of place around the lodge. The handful of Sierra booby traps are entirely of your own volition. They're funny little Easter eggs with an auto-save to let you go nuts and get back to the story. If you do ever feel lost, the notebook gives you both great progress feedback and threads to pull on. It's en engaging romp through a mystery novel you should definitely play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: A solid classic-inspired adventure game with intuitive text parser actions which do  fall victim to the old age of blindly using every x on y to solve obtuse puzzles. There is enough context to have a good idea of what you need to do at any point, the notebook and review keeps you on track without holding your hand, and there is even a level of redundancy in a number of spots so you need not check every nook and cranny to get what you need. There is a need for thoroughness in some aspects, namely in the multiple means of inspecting, collecting and  items to get all the info you can out of them.While the player may intuit a few things right away from the earliest clues, the characters' knowledge being too limited to point fingers so soon is reasonable, the need for more solid evidence is rational, and there was enough misdirection (and a lot of drawers) in the secondary plot threads to maintain a level of intrigue. The game was an enjoyable, smooth, completion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: If you like retro style adventure (specifically Laura Bow) games, then pick up this love letter to the genre. Julia crafts both a good and fun mystery, with some Canadian historical flair, and I already look forward to the next title in this series.There is a little bit of "syntax quest" but the text shortcuts included are a great feature. If I had any complaint it would be that I wish some of the clue gathering and notebook keeping were maybe a little more streamlined, but overall it's a solid game,  impressively done by a single dev.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful game! If you love old adventure games and/or classic murder-mysteries a'la Agatha Christie and the like, you will absolutely adore The Crimson Diamond. One of the most original storytelling, mystery adventures I've played in years and cannot recommend it enough! Give it a go, and discover the mystery of the Crimson Diamond!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This is an outstanding improvement on the design of The Colonel's Bequest, an homage without being a pastiche. It retains the investigative elements of Bequest while making you a more active participant in the plot instead of a passive observer, and rewards being thorough in ways that will give quite a bit of replay value to pick up what you missed.The parser system is more versatile than old AGI and SCI games, although there are some thesaurus issues: you need to be aware that "look," "examine," and "search" do very different things, while "use" gets avoided in place of more specific verbs.Overall an excellent modern approach to parser-based adventure games and very accessible for anybody interested in trying out the genre. It might spoil you on older, clunkier games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game is clearly a work of love, to Colonel's Bequest and the EGA era of Sierra adventure games in general.The polish and the attention to detail is impressive, considering it is mostly a one-person effort;  I haven't found a single glitch in my playthrough and the parser interface has plenty of quality of life improvements, which makes it more accessible to modern gamers (although the main audience is clearly those nostalgic for that era). It is also a surprisingly meaty game, it took me about 10 hours to get through it, trying to solve as much as possible (like the original CB, a lot of stuff is optional and you can finish the game without figuring out most of the plot, if you rush through it). The puzzles are varied and rewarding, and in general much fairer than you would expect from a game of this kind; but the art is where the game really shines, with a style completely faithful to the EGA palette with many lengthy animated cutscenes,Some minor criticism I can throw at the game would be about the characters. While the protagonist is really likable, I found the supporting cast kind of bland; possibly there was a deliberate effort to make the characters more realistic than than in old Sierra games, but they end up being less interesting and memorable. In a similar way, the writing is well done and interesting, but it lacks some the wit and irony of the old classics. Finally, the game lacks the sense of tension and peril that Laura Bow games had, especially in the mid-late game.Overall, if you enjoyed the games The Crimson Diamond takes its inspiration from, and old adventure games in general, this is an easy recommendation to make. At this price is also a steal and I'm happy to support indie games with a nostalgic bent... buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes me feel like a kid again. Though it's inspired by classic point-and-click adventure games such as The Colonel's Bequest, The Crimson Diamond really is a beautiful gem that stands on its own. The artwork gives me heavy nostalgia vibes. Everything is beautifully rendered and animated with the classic EGA-style palette. The parser interface is expertly crafted, and there's a response for just about anything you can think of doing in the game. Trust me, I tried everything I can think of, and I do not lack imagination.I'm about two hours into the game and I'm enjoying the story / writing so far. I anticipate that I will not be disappointed as the plot unfolds! The love and attention to detail throughout the game is very apparent to any adventure game fan, but you don't have to be a Sierra or Lucasarts fan to enjoy this experience. The Crimson Diamond features many quality-of-life improvements that the older generation of adventure games lacked severely. I can't wait to make it all the way through, but I'm also taking my time and enjoying the journey in this new classic. Thanks, Julia and team, for making such a wonderful new world for seasoned adventure game fans and newcomers to explore!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Who knew I missed text-parser adventure games so much? What an absolute joy it’s been playing The Crimson Diamond. Captivating characters, compelling mystery, and fun puzzles, who could ask for more?TCD sure brings back fond memories of playing quest games in my youth, but I think the game transcends nostalgia. Whether you’re a seasoned adventurer or a budding explorer, I bet you’d enjoy the hell out of this game.And it was essentially made by one game developer!? How? Phenomenal achievement.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: One of the things I love the most about The Crimson Diamond is its pacing: how each of its chapters prepares you for the one that comes next.Without ever feeling heavy in any way, it's a game rich in detail, atmosphere and polish, with beautiful EGA art and animation, and spot-on MT-32 soundtrack! Growing up I mostly played point-and-click adventures, so I didn't play many of the early parser adventure games, that's why I'm thankful for how many shortcuts and synonyms are available in this game! They make navigating it a very pleasant, immersive and rewarding experience, even just considering how many unique responses and animations are available. There is a lot to explore and investigate and both the notebook and a clever hint system makes it very engaging to play.It's very hard for me not to recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of fun and hits you right in the nostalgia.Pretty great game that has been in development for years that I have been tracking off and on.  Really excited to finally see this come out.It's like if Laura Bow: The Colonel's Bequest and Laura Bow 2: The Dagger of Amon Raw had a Canadian cousin living in northern Ontario.  Yeah.  Just like that.There are a couple of small bugs I've noticed so far, including descriptions in some places not updating after items have been removed/used, some glitching through items to disappear, and some weird verbiage limits that I think could and probably should be added in a future patch.  Ultimately, I have to say buy this game if you liked games where you have to type your instructions.  It definitely helped my typing speed growing up!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: You can tell how much love went into this game. There are so many nods to the past with some appreciated Quality of Life updates (auto-saving at important places, a little bit of guidance to prevent the 'what else am I supposed to do?' blocks, the classic hint book that isn't behind a pay wall, etc.). If you enjoyed Colonel's Bequest and replayed it dozens of times, The Crimson Diamond will bring you joy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Just made it to chapter 2. This game is a blast. If you're into old-style adventure games, you're certainly going to be into this. But unlike those old games, this one is very helpful in trying to make the experience as smooth for the player as possible.Love the graphics, the music, the writing. Very good stuff, can't wait to see where the story goes!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: As you might gather from the screenshots, The Crimson Diamond is a something of a retro throwback to the classic Sierra adventure titles. It especially bows greatly towards one of my favorite titles, Colonel's Bequest. This it does fantastically. It's a game made with love and care, down to the SCI engine style graphics and text parser you use to interact with the game.The Crimson Diamond is one the best retro throwbacks I've ever played. It oozes charm and the mystery is fun as well.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: Loving the game so far.  Definitely a love letter to the old school Sierra games, and I appreciate the choice to keep the text parser interface while implementing other modern 'quality of life' enhancements.  Never quite agreed when the industry considered the move from text parser to entirely point 'n click as it's own QoL improvement for all adventure gamesI learned to type on the old Sierra games and my kids and I have been trading off chapters and save games as they learn to actually type and explore with TCD.  They're having a blast as much as I am.Great game, congrats to Julia!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review: This game provides a good exercise to enhance your typing skills, so you'll type faster!But it isn't your typical classic adventure. It's more of a mystery/murder type. Otherwise, why (spoiler alert) would someone murder me, while I'm taking a shower just a few minutes into the game? I haven't done anything wrong! What's wrong with this game? This doesn't make any sense.Anyhow, solving mystery murders isn't my cup of tea. But! I do like the EGA graphics! Those are excellent!
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

_childDocuments_.review:
The Crimson Diamond is an EGA text parser mystery adventure game where you play as amateur geologist and reluctant detective Nancy Maple. Nancy is born and raised in Toronto, Canada, where she works as a clerk for the Royal Canadian Museum. She dreams of attending university to study geology and mineralogy, and she's prepared to venture into the unknown to achieve her goals!

Follow Nancy as she travels north to the ghost town of Crimson, Ontario to investigate the discovery of a massive diamond in the area. Eavesdrop on conversations to learn more about the eccentric cast of characters who find themselves gathered at Crimson Lodge. Explore the lodge and its environs to evaluate the diamond claim, and maybe solve a mystery or two along the way! The Crimson Diamond is a cozy mystery that encourages reading and engaging in the story over devious arcade challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: The Crimson Diamond

name: A Total War Saga: TROY
detailed_description: In this legendary age, heroes walk the earth. In an act that shocks the world, audacious Paris, prince of Troy, elopes with the beautiful queen of Sparta. As they sail away, King Menelaus curses her name. He vows to bring his wife home – whatever the cost.  Fight to save or conquer the kingdom of Troy as one of eight iconic heroes, including the infamous warrior Achilles, noble protector Hector, wayward prince Paris and vengeful king Menelaus.  Lead an army across the fabled lands of the Aegean, recruit special units inspired by creatures of Greek myth, and charge into battle against ferocious foes.  Build your empire through strategy, statecraft, diplomacy and all-out war, as you conquer this vast and striking recreation of the Bronze Age Mediterranean.
about_the_game: In this legendary age, heroes walk the earth. In an act that shocks the world, audacious Paris, prince of Troy, elopes with the beautiful queen of Sparta. short_description: Inspired by The Iliad and brought to life through the award-winning strategy game series, A Total War Saga: TROY brings a blend of grand, turn-based empire management and spectacular real-time battles to the heart of the Trojan War.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing since it launched on Epic. I was actually able to get it free on there and felt compelled to buy it on steam as well. I've played every TW game and while some of the games do have their faults, I'm having a hard time finding any with this one.The art style is great for the UI and the different research/diplomacy/cult tabs look amazing and are comparable in style to TW Three Kingdoms. The hero/general component is closest to Three Kingdoms vs. the extensive skill usage of TW:WH but the units they added in Mythos and the abilities you gain through cults add a bit of the magic flair back in.The agents are actually effective and necessary cults. The mythic agents have great bonuses (can't go wrong with a blacksmith who equips your entire army).The added components in Mythos are pretty great too. (I've got Odysseus with a Cerberus and an army of the damned)Also a big fan of Ajax but I could probably do with the Amazons.If you're complaining about the "pay wall" you're not talking about the game.I've seen complaints about the AI armies but most of them are from people who fail to recognize effective campaign tactics. "Why does the AI keep sneaking past my army and attacking my cities?!" You obviously realize how effective this is if it's stopping you from crossing the Aegean to wage a real war instead of trying to mop the smaller factions you're supposed to engage in diplomacy with.People complaining about historical accuracy don't seem to know that this isn't history... it's mythology/fairy tales that ancient Greeks incorporated into their history like every ancient civilization did.Go watch it on Twitch if you're debating it, but if you're a fan of the other TW games I doubt you'll be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: Huge TW fan, own literally every game and every DLC piece, but this is just pathetic. -No sound on loadup or ingame. Nice bug to start. -Can't change sound settings, they just reset themselves.It's been 5 minutes and it's already to the point of demanding a refund.Edit;I've decided to give it another try. The problem is simply that the game doesn't justify the price. They're charging with the Mythos DLC, as much as a full Total War game like Warhammer 3, but it seriously lacks enough to justify its price.
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: There is not too much to say about this game, it is the same as any modern Total War with the addition Mythos in the sense you have a campaign ripe with features and unique mechanics. The only real wish I have is that they did more with the special units other than make them ridiculously overpowered early game. The recruitment system with city specific unit unlocks was really well tuned, though if there was a global recruitment in Mythos such as WH2 I feel the mythos experience would be even better and lessen the waiting game when moving all your armies from the Greek Peninsula to Turkey or visa versa. The graphics engine is where this game really shines on my mid tier level tower this game runs smoother than melted butter and it such an amazing thing seeing that happening with new titles coming soon. I will say the game also plays pretty well, I'm not too sure what the issue with the A.I is that everyone seems to be going on about, all of my play-throughs that I've had since even epic launch have been fine, nothing about treacherous A.I and such other than the clearly designated traits.Overall I'd give this game a solid 8.5 I'm a sucker for ancient myths and this scratches that itch with usual high quality game play from TW.
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: After putting in a million hours into Warhammer 2, I have to say that this game really highlights flaws in the Warhammer series.  Troy's battle maps are far superior, with really fun geography which you can use strategically.  Where WH2 has largely open, flat maps with the occasional choakpoint, Troy's maps have lakes, cliffs, mountains, impassable areas.  All of these really make battles more exciting.  Night battles are back.  Let's not forget sieges.  WH2 siege maps are terrible, so it's nice to go back to more interesting Rome2 style siege maps.The mythic units are generally fun, without being over powered.  I'm certainly enjoying myself.
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, Probably my least favorite so far and I have played every total war series. There is too much going.. too many cities next to you..when you take territory and look at the map in other games you feel accomplished and have some since of strategy but this is just a mindless ok lets take that territory... now this one cuz they declared war on me for no reason ect... They did all the other total war games perfect but this just seems to lack something. Feels more like mind numbing no point strategy game now. Graphics are great tho!
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: I skipped Warhammer II and Three Kingdoms, so I been away from Total War for a while.After a few years away, I found the historic verse the mythical game play having the best of both worlds.  I didn't think I would be interested in the mythical version, but I guess this old Armchair General needed something new and different.  And, there have been a lot of new features added since Attila too. So yeah, Troy is leaps & bounds over Attila.
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, Troy. You're not a bad game, in fact, absolutely polished!  (For a CA Game that's Wow!) Alas, just, too narrow in scope.  Having come from Rome 1, Med II, Rome 2, Attila: I expected THE WORLD to be on the map.I was really jazzed about Troy (Oh boy, a BRONZE AGE Total War!!!)Who would I play? A Trojan faction, or, some other world power, ready to pounce upon the Greeks as they are busy in the Trojan war.  Would it be like Age of Empire I - Hittite chariot rush! GG!  (Also, chariots, wow!)But, upon loading the game, the first shock hit.- No other nations.  Just Greeks.Wat!  Where is Egypt? The Hittites? Scythia? Minoa? I didn't expect them to be playable, but I expected them to be THERE. So I thought:Oh well, maybe they'll be in expansions? I mean, WOW the Mythological richness of Egypt would be AMAZING!Can you imagine Egyptian Gods on the battlefield? Horus? What about Sumer - Gilgamesh? War wagons? Nubian archers!They can add this later, right?  What about an expansion for Jewish peoples, WRATH OF GOD! The religion mechanics of Troy + Ark of the Covenant would be incredible. A campaign to leave Egypt, take over the Levant and fight Philistines would be incredible.  They can add this, right? Other cultures will be next, right?Second Shock: - The map - just Anatolia, and Greece. Oh the lamentation!  It was then I knew - this game was a one-trick pony. Greece, Greece, Greece.A brief glimmer of hope came with the release of the Amazons!Oh boy, as a female player how I WANTED TO BE ZENA! And scream the battle cry "Ei- li - li - li - li -  li - li li - li li - li li - li li - li!"  Alas, this DLC was another disappointment.Why?Because it wasn't part of something bigger.Everything rotates around the Trojan War - so you just never feel like you're in an open-world sandbox with open-world possibilities.The Amazons, far from being their own distinct people, feels like you're playing a side-show.  Taking control of mercenaries.The Mechanics:Actual conquering - is quite difficult and un-fun.- Rome 1/2/Attila: Felt like I was in an immersive, dynamic world where I was managing real people, real armies.  My goals/targets were strategic.   Sometimes, holding a mountain pass for 10 turns was more important than moving your armies.- Troy: You stop your army, you die.- A frantic GO GO GO, race-race-race is the result.  (Until I finally find it tedious/exhausting, and don't load my saves.)- Troy felt like the most important thing I could be doing - was chase "bonuses."- That's right: You don't take a town because of it's strategic location, or resources - no  just, cause taking it gives some magic +3 to spear unit damage, and my units are spear units, so I'll chase it.- Wow - talk about taking the strategy out of a strategy game.- Buff-chasing - reminds  me of the gameplay of that WWII arcade game 1941. You fly your bomber directly INTO power-ups.- And, the power-up bonuses of Troy - are too damn powerful.- The game is too difficult/frustrating without power-ups.- Too boring/easy once you gain them.- This makes your rise to power a flatline-struggle, suddenly, with a power-up, you're at the pinnacle. High above anyone else. It's all downhill from here, for them. The rest of the gameplay is a boring "cleaning up the map" from helpless enemies.I still recommend the game to fans of the Trojan War / Total War games.But - you must know what you're getting.It's not worth $60.00.  I don't think it ever was.Honestly it's probably more interesting to people who like Warhammer and want an entirely new take on things.The Good:- Time Period - quite interesting/novel.- Polished!!- Doesn't crash.- Looks great.- Good optimization. (No need for super-computer.)Gameplay:- 3 modes of playing, each with good challenges. - UI has incredible art. It's stunning.- UI / tooltips / instructions make it finally CLEAR - what you can build, units you can make, etc, so you can plan long-term.(Other Total Wars are as clear as MUD, like the horror show that is Attila "help" menu, which is just a browser window that bizarrely opens in a pop-up screen on top of the game - and, crashes instead of showing units you can create.)- Religion mechanic is pretty neat.  (As a base mechanic, although one can argue it's too powerful.)- Sound is pretty good. (Your troops blow horns and shout in unison as they march.) It's neat.The Bad:- Music - unlike Rome I / Med II / Attila - nothing memorable about Troy.- Very disappointing after the masterpieces Jeff Van Dych made in others.- There's lots of "unit diversity."  However, I still can't tell the difference between them.  Subtle manipulation of attack/defense numbers and re-skins - don't matter a bit. The (non-myth) units all react similarly.  One mid-tier spear unit feels exactly the same across all factions.  So there's 8, or 10, or 20 spear units to choose from - who cares?- Means there's a heck of a lot less re-playability than other total war games.- Since all factions (barring amazons) feel the same - choosing a "new campaign" is just choosing a new starting location.- And who your nation is default-pissed-off-with.- Follows history a little bit too inflexibly.  I can't take my faction in a new direction, i'm pretty much stuck being anti or pro-Troy.- Map is too small.  Feel fenced-in.- Completely lacks the "epic" scale/feel of the other Total War games. - Conflict feels like a bunch of scorpions thrown in a bucket.- Heroes are supposed to duel each other, and the camera is supposed to zoom-in on their exciting battles.- However, no matter the settings, I could never get the camera to EVEN ONCE show me a close-up of a duel. - I just heard generic talk of my hero being victorious/defeated. Snore.The Ugly:- Armies march HUGE distances in a single turn. Resulting in "I just left Greece for Anatolia. Soon as I got to Anatolia, I saw the enemy get on a boat, and sail all the way to my capital. They'll take it on next turn if they "assault." I have no time to get back and defend!"  This happens a lot.  Zig-zags across the pond.  Battles where cities are entirely defenseless, cause their army can't return in time to defend.  Soon as you take a town, and walk 3 steps away, BOOM they take it back.- Collision Mechanics:   Knockback is still bad.-Still too much like Rome II - the game where unit collision was (disastrously) removed, resulting in the new "ant swarm" effect when armies clashed.   It's too hard to disengage enemies.  They get stuck like magnets in combat.- Was hoping for the amazing physics seen in Rome I... You know, the unit collision system that allowed elephants to toss people like rag dolls, and cavalry/chariot charges to cut a swathe of downed/dying men in a unit, without getting stuck and insta-dying? Sadly, missing here.  (There's some knock back, but not what you'd expect. Mostly from giant myth units.)(How many years must go by before you realize that's what's MISSING from your Total War games CA?)- This also makes chariot units worthless. (Like elephants of Rome II, they needed to knock down / toss people away from them to survive. So - they don't. - Tunnel-vision on Greece in a time period of flourishing cultural diversity.- Mythological beats were a SWEET touch.  However, with only Greek mythology, it feels like the game is just - empty. - We'll never see Greek beasts fight Egyptian myth units, or any other culture.- Lack of sea-based beasts. (Could you imagine Leviathan of Caananite mythos vs The Kraken?)- Sea myth units would have been great to protect my homeland, once I left for overseas war.- Heroes - are a neat addition. But their abilities are so over-powered, I'd actual perfer them to stay off the field.- Would have been better to implement a duel-to-the-death 1v1 BEFORE battles commenced, just like in the Illiad.  - Hero battles for ancient peoples were about taking a chance to demoralize your enemy. Overall, ok

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving the game a negative review right now because I feel it has been released too soon. It's still a total war game, so it is still an above average title, but right now it is battling with Medieval for the honor of worst total war game.The AI is probably the worst I have seen in a total war game and the computer has no clue how to siege a city. I got two heroic victories defending cities not due to any brilliant tactics on my part. The first army to siege the city brought 6 battering rams and sent one to my main gate as the battle began while a few units tried to assault the walls with ladders. After my ranged units and the city towers caused the first battering ram unit to route they sent in a couple more battering rams, only those rams could never get to the gate because the first battering ram was in the way so they stayed outside the gate getting pummeled until eventually all 6 rams were done for and the entire army ended up routing. After that battle a second army from a different nation immediately besieged the same city. They did better in that they brought four rams and attacked both of my gates and actually bashed through the gates only to immediately turn around and slowly walk back to their spawn point and then the entire army routed a few minutes later.The economy has been completely changed from any previous total war game and now revolves around about a half dozen or so resources. This is a good concept but it also causes the AI to constantly beg you to give them resources for free. I even had a nation I was at war with suddenly request I send them food and wood, and they didn't even request peace. They just straight up wanted me to give them my stuff.And probably the worst faux pas of all was the game caused my Windows 10 desktop to blue screen. I've played tons of games for hundreds of hours on this computer and this was the first one that was ever able to do that.I'm hoping CA will patch out some of these issues and if they do I may change my review, but in it's current state I can't recommend this title.

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be one of the most highly underrated Total War games out there. There is a split in the community for TW between people who enjoy fantasy aspects in the games like Warhammer and the hardline historical people. TW Troy is the perfect balance. _childDocuments_.review: I've got about 3.6 hours in this now, and I feel fairly experienced enough to give an honest, if not complete, review.To make this quick...Goooooood stuffz:- Beautiful. Simply gorgeous.- A fair amount of units without extensive complexity.- Leader duels are fun to watch, and rather cinematic. It's like watching Troy all over again.- Units look nice, later troops have fairly pretty armour styles.- Something about it makes it feel like Total War: Lite, and that isn't actually bad.- UI is easy to understand- Resource management is easy to learn that is nicely challenging without head-smackingly difficulty.- Dialogue is pretty fun. Hearing what I believe is Hector shout, "How could you do this, brother!?!" when he's actually the one invading Paris' city will never get old, unless I discover it's Paris justifiably bawling. The funny would be gone then, but regardless the situational dialogue is always great to hear.- The option to play with either historical accuracy, historical with romanticised leaders, or full blown mythological battles (DLC) For those who complain about historical Total War games taking the fantastical route (even though the story of Troy is a fiction but...whateeeeeeevs) this enables you to literally alter the gameplay with a single click to your preferred gameplay style. Personally, I cannot wait to go full-blown mythical.Baaaaaaad stuffz:- A feeling of Total War: Lite may be unacceptable for some.- Without Blood and Glory, the battles both look and feel...well...crap. Sometimes great charges end, not with epic crashes, but a sudden stop with an almost stereotypical British sense of fair-play. "Are we all ready? Fabulous. Alright lads...and...stab!"- There doesn't appear to be a feature where, on the very slim chance an arrow hits Achilles in the heel, he is insta-killed. Shame.- Sound design...is...AWFUL! I mean, truly...what are they doing? I've always felt the Total War games outside of the Warhammer series had rather dull sound effects, but this seems to be on a whole other level of unimpressive.Let me paint a picture for you...Menelaus charges with righteous fury towards Paris of Troy, the memory of his wife's betrayal fresh in his mind. With four bounding steps, he leaps into the air, sword raised high above his head, the deadly point aiming to pierce the boy's throat. Paris' eyes widen as the larger man descends upon him. His mind flurries with panic, but he has enough sense left to remember some semblance of his training, and raises his shield just as the blade tip comes crashing down with a violent...dink.Didn't that abrupt, anti-climactic word just take you out of that scene? Now picture that in the visual art space. Where I should have been able to say, "a violent splintering of wood and crashing of metal" I can only say..."dink". I have no issue with the vocal effects as soldiers battle one another, but the effects of wood and metal, flesh torn and armour rent are utter...I don't want to be mean, but...it sort of half rhymes with yardage.Overall:Love it as an RTS, recommend it highly, just be prepared for a sound design that seems to have been directed by a person who's never heard a large piece of metal strike another large piece of metal.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a promising Age of Mythology Total War to-be but wow is it ugly and repetitive. It can be daunting for a new player to open up the brown UI and see oceans of nearly identical-looking brown-armored, brown-background units with little stat variation, moving the units around brown maps with brown skies, brown fog, brown shaders, and brown pop-ups. It's the bronze age but damn, chill with the brown! I didn't buy Total War: Sepia! I appreciate what they were going for and indeed it does work sometimes, but right now it's difficult to play without workshop overhauls that can file its rough edges. If they hadn't incorporated the Mythos DLC, I would have never been interested because classical age Rome 1 mods exist. Right now, it just can't compete with the Rome Remaster in historical or TWW2 in its fantastical creatures and magic. In contrast, those two games are bright and vivid in art direction and highly diverse in what they offer. Troy's in a hard place and almost every aspect of it is under-par. The only aspect I enjoy is the resources and the trading of them, it adds some depth and feels a bit like Catan. I'm expecting to return to this game in a couple years to see if it's playable then, if it survives. Overall, it's not a bad game by industry standards but it's just ugly, repetitive, and can't compete in what other titles in the series have to offer. I hope they can change that.

_childDocuments_.review: The whole "sagas" thing made me hold off on this game for a long time, but after just a few minutes I've realized I was missing out on something good. The visuals are nice which is always a plus, but the faction variation is what does it for me--I haven't played much yet, but compared to other total war titles this one seems to have more promising replay value. Both historical and fantasy fans will have a good time, the mythos dlc shouldve been included in the base game but it's nice to have 3 levels of realism to choose from. This is my favorite total war setting by far, either I'm really autistic about classical antiquity or the setting just really lends itself well to diverse and unique factions. I used to find the Iliad boring but this makes me want to pick it up again, the underlying thematic content of a "Total War" game pairs extremely well with Troy. The mythological tone makes it feel like witnessing the birth of true warfare itself. Maybe I'm overhyping a game I haven't played enough of yet, but I haven't felt this happy looking at a main menu or campaign selection screen since Rome II released. I'll update my review if the game betrays my expectations.update: now that I've played more, I still have a lot of appreciation for this game but there are definitely some negatives worth pointing out. The biggest issues are with balancing and AI. The behavior of individual soldiers feels like a step back from titles that used matched combat animations like shogun 2. Troy attempts to do something similar, but it often comes off looking extremely janky, especially in mythos mode--sometimes i find 3 or 4 soldiers far away from their unit just frozen in an idle pose, non-hero units surround heroes in a circle but then fight them one at a time like they're in a bad martial arts film, and when a hero is routed they become practically invincible. Generals simply have too much hp, good luck running one down before they get away--a serious amount of my time in battles was spent chasing down fleeing heroes and only sometimes killing them. Fights that are literally 1000v1 should not be ending inconclusively like this, it's infuriating watching an army of fresh units jogging or even walking behind an exhausted routed general like he's the CEO at the company marathon and their job security depends on him making 1st. You can blacken out the sky with arrows and it still won't be enough. They are just too powerful, most battles I saw around half of all enemies killed by my general alone. Historical mode solves this problem by upping their mortality considerably, but it just feels kinda bland without the other mythos content. My other biggest complaint is some of the design choices made to support variability in faction mechanics. Mainly, it seems that unique faction abilities are just mechanics that were standard to multiple factions in previous total war titles but have been removed from Troy. For example, Agamemnon is the only one who can have vassals or demand tributes. So rather than praising the "unique," maybe we should just say that factions play quite different from each other.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying this game far more than I thought I would, but only after using the Mythos DLC. However the graphic engine is extremely powerful and provides lots of options to tweak and get the graphics how you like them. Here is one example of mine.The performance of the game is amazing, I had to lower some of the WHTW settings, but here I am at 60+ fps all the time with everything maxed.All factions have unique rosters with weaknesses that make you switch up your gameplay, if you play for example odysseus or achilles. They're both achean culture, but they play vastly differently.I also have to mention that CA Sofia is unusually quick with doing bugfixes, compared to past TW games that were lefts on weeks or months unpatched, so kudos to the bulgarian devs for their dedicated support.The historical mode is disappointing in my opinion, so if you plan to get this game, I would recommend to get it with the mythos dlc to get a much better experience.The game isn't  perfect, but it is damn good at what it does. _childDocuments_.review: I do NOT recommend this Total War entry. It's overpriced, including when on sale, and it's very shallow. Graphically it is great, but you need more than that. I purchased the Complete Edition with the Mythos and all other dlc's, but have not touched the Mythos campaign. As of this writing, I am attempting a refund though I have been denied once already as it's over 2 hours. That's a fine policy, but any strategy game player knows it takes more than that to delve into one, especially a Total War game.Unit wise, this is a joke. It's a mobbing mentality and if you use ranged, you win. Ranged is utterly broken with no real counters as they are extremely quick and will outrun your troops with enough of a gap to return fire multiple times before continuing their retreat. The morale is almost instant break and the lack of formations is pathetic.The gameplay  side of things with your currency being food, wood, etc. is a nice addition, but it's annoying as you must take settlements with those, especially food. If you are not near those, you will be steamrolled quickly as the other mechanic of the Trojan War will see 2 sides basically fighting it out. You will be spammed with multiple full stacks while you are doing good to have 1 stack. The full stack spamming has plagued TW games off and on for years, but this entry is particularly bad in that regard.With the Mythos dlc you have 3 different modes to choose, Hero, Normal (can't remember exact name), and Mythic. Hero has the characters play as actual heroes, like Warhammer or Three Kingdoms, while Normal gives your heroes an actual unit like in standard TW games. There are other differences as well, but imo that's the biggest. Mythos is supposed to add alot of mythical units and quests, but I have not played that mode as I was trying to keep my play time down while figuring out if I would enjoy this game or not...obviously it's the latter.If you can get the complete version for 75%+ off, then maybe try it, but overall, there are many better choices for a TW entry.EDIT: Denied refund again, which I assumed would happen. Learn from my mistake and don't get this or wait for a STEEP sale! Current sale at $57 for Ultimate Edition is awful and I regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Troy is plagued with more than a few issues that have existed for a long time in the Total War series:- Dumb, rabid AI that will target your undefended settlements with no concept of self preservation. You could be sieging the gates of Troy and on the verge of stealing back Helen but Paris' AI will be far more interested in playing whack-a-mole with one of your armies over some of your undefended settlements in the middle of bum ♥♥♥♥ nowhere. This issue is particularly highlighted during the late campaign, with the AI abusing the Aegean with the full speed stance looking to wriggle past your armies for those oh so tasty undefended settlements.- Siege battles are still broken with extremely over-powered settlement defence towers and piss poor unit pathing. This issue is exacerbated by the condensed nature of the world map with many settlements being one turn away from each other.- The resource system means the AI spams diplomacy even more. AI can be overly aggressive and abuse diplomacy to get at the player - such as some of the major players forming military alliances with a 3rd world one settlement faction in the corner of the map which then declares war on the player for absolutely no conceivable reason, bringing in half the map to fight you alone.- Units wipe each other out so quickly that battles are reduced to how fast you can click spam fest- You're essentially penalised for trying to build decent settlement garrisons against aforementioned dumb, rabid AI. In the case of this Total War game, garrisons should have been tied to the main settlement building with a basic garrison with the chance to expand it at a discounted rate towards your administration tier and treasury imo . How it works in Troy is that you really need every settlement slot for resources, special mythical buildings etc and the garrison debuff of minus public order is also daft. - Great power penalty is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dumb - at the very least this should have been tied to the administration tiers and not be implemented so harshly.- The administration tiers in general are under utilised and could have been made so much more interesting with the aforementioned points, instead of CA trying to make the game more difficult for the sake of it.- The difficulty levels tying together AI stat buffs and supposed increased AI intelligence - an asinine decision to say the leastNow for some of the positives:- I absolutely love the Mythos world map with so many interesting features and places to look at. The sea is beautiful and the day/night cycle with all the settlements lit up at night is the cherry on top. I also like the background imagery and how the fog of war 'burns away' when you discover new areas.- I think the mythical creatures are fantastic and have been implemented and balanced really well. They fit into the world and look amazing, the fact they are tied to different settlements around the map via special buildings is great, encouraging the player to explore and expand.- The administration tier system works really well here, it encourages the player to explore different unit compositions and recruit units that they might not usually go for. On a side note, in other TW games such as Total War Warhammer they should do away with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ supply lines system altogether and let the player go nuts.- I think the special recruitment pool is a very cool idea, allowing the player to get hold of special units that they wouldn't get otherwise. Unfortunately, the events and other ways to fill this pool are extremely sparse when it should function a bit more frequently and consistently like with the events tied with the Lizard men's blessed units in WH2.- The Expeditions are a fun and interesting feature that allows the player to put together a team and guide them through a mini text adventure game in order to gain a special gargantuan monster unit as well as new units and mechanics which I think are great.Overall I really like the concept of this game, with two major uber factions in the form of the Danaan Pillar and Trojan Pillar clashing across the Aegean. It's just a shame that as you progress through the campaign things like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥, dumb, overly-aggressive AI can ruin this by creating bizarre, annoying and frustrating situations that pull you right out of the experience amongst other neglected areas of the game which gradually start to wear you down. I very much enjoyed the beginning of the campaign in this game, but as I reach the later game it starts to get more and more tedious. CA seems to have this obsession with making it's games more difficult for the sake of it as apposed to making it's games interesting. Although it has got admittedly better over the years there are still issues with some of the difficult for difficulties sake mentality and game design choices. As much as I would like to recommend this game for all the good points, I can't.EDIT:I'm trying to stick it out to at least complete a campaign, but the more I play Troy, the more annoying anti-player mechanics I keep finding:- The chronic issue of random neutral/friendly factions declaring war on the player seems to be tied to player progress. If the game decides that the player is 'doing too well' it will quite literally keep dog piling you with factions to fight from every direction until you start going backwards. Which is ironic because it feels like the AI itself has gone backwards. I have done a bit of testing through saving and reloading and it seems some factions will be absolutely hard set on declaring war on you no matter what agreements you make with them. The close proximity of a lot of the settlements on the world map means that if this particular anti-player mechanic kicks in, chances are there will be more than a few occasions in which an enemy stack will instantly take a settlement without warning or without you being able to defend yourself. Nice.- Now that agents can't be used in battle or attached to armies more meaningfully like in Warhammer, the problem of AI agent spam has come back in full force. Have fun watching a dozen or so enemy agents pinball between your settlements and armies every turn.-  There are some nuggets of fun to be had - Diomedes (all Danaan and Trojan factions at the very least should have been free with the base game) has a couple of very fun mechanics, essentially allowing the player to build their own custom regiment of renown pool and also build up 'domination, to get more favourable diplomacy. It's just a shame diplomacy is already pretty broken for a variety of reasons.A couple of things I forgot to mention previously:- Another positive is that the vassalage system actually works now, without your vassal breaking away and declaring war on you anywhere between 1-5 turns after being vassalised. With a faction like Agamemnon's (he has a specific vassal mechanic) it can however work a bit backwards at times because it is easier to keep vassalising one settlement AI factions that are liable to double doomstack for you, as apposed to directly taking said settlement for yourself as yet another very vulnerable settlement you have to protect. You can eventually have the AI, in essence, playing the game for you to a large degree lol.- Having the ability to region trade is great. Your AI 'allies' are opportunistic little ♥♥♥♥♥ that will retake settlements that were once yours and this mitigates the issue a bit. It is also a good way to trade your AI allies all of your vulnerable regions for more well protected ones at the back of the map.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much enjoying the game. (With the expansions) There are 3 different modes to play it. "Historical", "Semi-Mythical" and "Mythical". You can play as one many Greek or Trojan factions or Amazons - the later can be played as a normal faction or a horde faction (as in Attila). So there is plenty of variation. There are also quests of various levels with rewards. Mythical allows you to quest for mythical monster units. Semi-Mythical represents your heroes as single "Hero" units. Although you can easily build a pair of "killer" stacks, it is a challenge to ward off multiple attacks (up to 10 or more stacks) invading your base areas and also manage the economy to supply your armies and gain bonuses from worshipping the various gods. There are various levels of victory conditions allowing you to avoid having to conquer the whole map. But sometimes you just want to conquer it all and the game allows you to continue after you gain victory. I recommend it, but expect to spend a lot of time on the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this after Total war warhammer and 3 kingdoms and it definitely is not on par with those. World looks nice but enemy AI seems lacking, the armies the build have have very little variety and usually just spam the same few units to fill a stack, and even with alliance colors on I have a hard time telling my units from enemies in combat. Tactics like ambush are of little to no use since you cant use it in sight of other armies or move after going into it, and allies are completely useless so far in my experience. Playing as Menalaeus I allied with my brother Agamemnon and built a full stack of 20 to help him fight his neighbor he was at war with. Marched way up there after he agreed to the war target to which he sent 2 armies, one with 16 units and one with 10 leaving his other two forces at home. Enemy has 13 units in his army stack and a garrison of 14 so a total of 27 units that we could easily crush if AI actually helped, but it doesnt. It just runs every time I siege them or if I start raiding his land myself so ai can siege instead.  So in the end its just my stack of 20 vs his 27 units behind walls while my brother runs home to let me fight his battle for him for no logical reason despite having 4 different armies to use to help. Had better allies in Total War Warhammer, that were literally my enemies who simply fought alongside me because it was strategically in their best interest. I know catapults werent really used in the era but neither were cyclops and minotaurs and would be nice to have some siege artillery options which I have yet to see. Its not a horrible game and has some enjoyable parts, but for the same price you will pay for Warhammer or three kingdoms, you would get more miles out of either of those.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, Total War:Troy is a fun and refreshing experience. The addition of the mythos dlc adds some fun changes and just enough fantasy roster to keep it exciting while not going full fantasy genre.Where this game lacks is in the depth of the building chains, the "historical" scripting, and the strategic battles. So, essentially all the main reasons to play a total war game (you had one job CA).It seems like CA were going for a Total war game that played more like a freemium mobile game than a detailed Strategy game.Around turn 65 as Hector of Troy the historical accuracy script kicks in; at this point, whether you have meticulously fostered relationships with greek states or not, they will all go into the negative and declare war on you. Makes sense for historically accurate accounting, IF  NOT FOR THE HYDRA IN MY ARMY AND THE GIANTS SIEGING CITIES. Seriously CA, these scripts, like the one in Shogun 2 that kick in halfway through a campaign need an off switch, especially for multiplayer campaigns. Siegies are useless. Garrisons have been trained by meal team six and could not defend against an attacking wind. If you do decide to defend a siege on the map, don't defend it like a city with walls. That is a mistake, the ai will charge your walls at full sprint, and ladders will appear from a portal. This was my biggest gripe with the game, it just seemed like the biggest broken game mechanic in a game named after an impenetrable walled city. This is further worsened by the changes to the battle strategy. Units get lots of buffs against flanking, and battle speed plays out as if it is 2x speed default. The terrain strategy is nice, but seems a bit empty when all the intricate details for battle strategy like formations and flanking are removed.TLDR; This game plays more like a mobile strategy game, not the total war of old. If you want a superficial RTS this game is great. If you want a detailed grand campaign RTS to test your tactics against opponents, welp this is not it.
