_childDocuments_.review: I have never felt the need to review a game, but this one deserves far less criticism than it got, so I want to leave a review.CA, this is the quintessential Total War game. I own about 10 of them I think and this one in a short span of time has become by far my favorite. The Mythos DLC is scummy, but it hardly matters when weighed against all of the positives here. Excellent map design, campaign map is vibrant and runs well. Music is absolutely off the charts stellar, attention to details is crazy, and the game runs perfectly even on older graphics cards. If I could add stuff from this TW game to every one after it, I would in a heartbeat. It's not boring, the UI is excellent, if a little crammed onscreen due to how many features there are, and every play session leaves me feeling excellent and satisfied, excited for the next one. There are only two legitimate downsides I can give this game, so I will list them here for anyone wondering.1. Not nearly as strategy based or formation centric as older historical Total War games, this game goes for a healthy balance between that and the Warhammer series. What it delivers is a game that is much less focused on battle preparation, and a lot more on micromanaging the battlefield. This can feel amazing when you make an excellent flank, but not as good when you get outmaneuvered. Unit difference is definitely noticeable when unfavorable matchups happen, and often times even when I'm winning battles in reality, individual units caught up with allied units can find themselves losing battles based on stats. This is balanced out by hero characters as well as how much more responsive units are in this game.2. This one is not the game's fault frankly, but I'll have to list it because it's true. Because this game unfortunately didn't catch on as much, the modding scene is very shallow and unfortunately lacking. This is a special tragedy because this game is probably the best Total War in the series to actually mod on. It has a great mix of creature. hero, and line units to use for major mods, yet very few if any exist sadly. I hope this will change in the future, as any large mods on this game would no doubt be amazing.In conclusion, this is a must have for any Total War fan, historical or fantasy. While not an era everyone may be a fan of(myself waiting for Medieval 3), it is a total blast and a breath of fresh air that was much needed to revamp the feel of a Total War game. While a future game of this style may be less colorful or epic, I'm hoping CA takes notes from this game for any future endeavors.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the game's setting , aesthetics and music, its really enjoyable but even then i recommend getting this only on sale. There's some major flaws that result in a tiring and grindy mid - end game campaignThe concept and structure is there, with each faction playing completely differently due to mechanics unique to them and rosters specific to them. A campaign as Odysseus will play completely differently than Menelaus due to campaign story/choices and faction mechanics.Resources are a new thing for this entry too, restricting you somewhat but at least giving you something more to manage besides growth, pop and money, lacking bronze and gold for example means you'll be fielding few if not no armored/mythic units. Influence is also another mechanic, allowing you to reap more resources in high influence zones.Gods are a nice touch, allowing specialization or generalization, they generally help a specific unit type and provide either a unique unit at the end or an epic agent at the highest tier of favor, combine this with specific buildings and with enough time you can really make a nice doom stack of melee specialists or ranged units with drastically more ammunition.The AI is a mixed bag, the battle ai does try to overwhelm you, but there's nothing special most of the time. The campaign AI is, horrendous with the current patch overall, it becomes a nasty tug of war with no concern for attrition over the seas, most of the time you'll be bogged down by any faction that isn't a pillar making it a home conquest first - its safer to make a damned land route to Troy or just outright conquering through Crete and making your way from the south.Combat is to put it mildly, lackluster and by far the weakest in this total war, charges sometime lack impact, no formations for infantry units and most of the time it boils down to a grind fest at one to two points in a siege where the AI usually just tries to overpower you.

_childDocuments_.review: Played through one Truth Behind the Myth Achilles campaign on normal. Sparta pretty much solo'd Troy and the entire eastern side of the map. I had a lot of fun playing it. You absolutely need to get all the DLC to make this game worth buying. I bought the game and all the DLC during the Winter Sale for a total of around $60. I don't think I overpayed, as I was able to get about 60 hours of gameplay out of it from 1 campaign. Before this game, I mostly played Shogun 2 and this was a huge improvement. I'm on a high end PC (specs mentioned in the Pros) and it runs perfect.Pros:+ The different resources really makes things interesting early on. You have to leverage what you have an abundance of to trade for what you don't have. It really makes diplomacy essential at the start. If you don't focus on having a good income of all the different resources, you will put yourself behind later in the game. It's best to start gathering early, which adds a layer of complexity.+ Battle map variety keeps the game interesting. Rather than battling on a flat plain, there are a lot of hills, forests, mud pits, rock formations, and high grass that make the battles depend a lot more on the terrain. Some battles I would've lost had it not been for the map giving me a very strategic position to use to my advantage. This makes the battles a lot more engaging for me, as the standard plain open field gets rather dull.+ Variation in the starting regions. Each faction has a very different start and there are a lot of options on how to play each faction. + Graphics. This game is absolutely gorgeous. I'll be disappointed if WH3 isn't as good graphically. I'm on a Ryzen 9 5900 and a 3080Ti 12GB and this game runs smooth. I only get the frame rate slowdown notification when the AI is taking their turn, which is not at all a problem.  Cons:- You really need the DLC for this game to have a full Total War experience of today's standard. With WH2 being the most popular TW game atm, and WH3 about to release, not having the Mythos campaign included in the base game is disappointing. That being said, if you can get the base game and all DLC on sale, definitely go for it. - Diplomacy seems a bit off. Maybe other factions don't like trading with Achilles, but the diplomacy function is definitely an area that could be improved. Confederating another faction required giving a lot of gifts and regions to the other faction. It seemed odd that on one turn I could give another faction a bunch of regions, then on the next turn they're all happy to confederate, so I get the regions I gave up back and more. Also asking another faction for a region seems next to impossible. Sometimes I wasn't able to trade resources for another region. The game would just not give me the option. The only option I had was give me the region or war. I also wish there was an option to spend resources on a confederation and then not get access to the confederated factions armies. Like suppose I give one faction 2000 gold to confederate. They accept and they're heroes go off and retire somewhere. I think this would make confederation more viable, but sometimes it's just easier to go and conquer that lone wolf faction that doesn't want to confederate. You may get a diplomatic penalty, but you can easily overcome this after some time. - Unit variety. I know this is the bronze age, but I just wish there was more unit variety. I wish that I could get axemen as the Greeks once I capture a Thracian region. Making cavalry units difficult to access turns archer/slinger/javelin spam into a problem. All you need are like 3 or 4 spear units and a deathball of ranged units and you're pretty much unstoppable. In a siege, just wait it out until the enemy attacks. They will be helpless as their blobs of infantry run into a deathball of archers.- AI does some dumb stuff on normal and hard, especially during sieges. They shouldn't every try to run through a choke point and attack you when all they have to do is sit back and defend. Yet if you push forward with archers enough, they will slowly move one unit just into your range and do nothing while you kill them off. Eventually they will decide to full charge you while they are on defense and end up losing half their army before they engage your infantry. Why are they doing this on defense? The normal AI shouldn't be dumb. It makes it too easy to cheese on accident.- Auto resolve could be tweaked. There were a lot of battles the autoresolve said would be a close defeat for me, but when I fought it, I lost like 20 guys. Again, normal AI should not be dumb AI.That's all that mostly stood out after 60 hours of gameplay on normal. I'm going through a hard mythos campaign now with Thrace and it seems a bit more challenging. Thrace just has a different play style which makes it fun. Overall, if you love the time period, want to play a beautiful game, and enjoy Total War, I would pick up the base game and all DLC next time it's on sale. Yet with WH3 about to come out (less than a month from this review), maybe just wait. I wouldn't pass this game up because of some negative reviews. It might not be the most loved Total War game, but it's absolutely a fun game for the casual Total War fan.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my impressions of the aesthetics, and new gameplay options (historical vs myth). Firstly, I LOVE the new option in 'TW: TROY' to choose between the more historically accurate units/ battles; legendary human units with divine blessings (i.e. single heroes like Achilles); or mythical units (gods/ monsters on the battlefield). It adds replayability and caters for different player tastes. I also LOVE the more colourful and mythological art style (it is vibrant and engaging).I really hope Creative Assembly take a similar approach for future Total War games. In particular, I would LOVE a Norse/ viking themed version of this!! 'Thrones of Britannia' felt very uninspired to me in terms of muted colours, and importantly serious lack of distinct faction appearance, and fun heroic warrior unit types. I appreciate it was more historically accurate to have all the factions look very similar with very similar units, but imo it was to its own detriment as a game - and I personally found it too boring. The more fantasy style units could be added separately as FLC or DLC (or simply an option in the game - like 'TW: TROY' where you can choose as a player what level of accuracy you want with the unit types that appear. Win win!).  I personally would like to see Viking units with tattoos, war paint, furs, as well as different wild berserker units! I really think a new TW version of that era with Celts (woad warriors and head hunters), Saxons, and Vikings - leaning into this colourful art design, myths, heroes, and Norse/ Celtic gods could be a massive hit for CA! (particularly given the popularity of 'God of War' right now).As an aside, I hope CA approve a PC remaster of Medieval 2 (like the recent original ROME remaster)! Bringing it back to 'TW: TROY', I think this new approach (of allowing the players to choose the level of fantasy and historical accuracy depending on their own personal preferences), and the vibrant art style breathes new life back into the franchise! I'm excited to get back into TW!

_childDocuments_.review: I've have played every Total War game outside the War Hammer series since Shogun 1. And played Troy at release when it was just on Epic games for over 200 hours before the Steam release. With the Mythos DLC there are now 3 campaign modes. Historic, Mythical, and the in between. Creative Assembly have done a good job with the Saga games in my opinion. There is a lot of controversy around all the DLCs for these games: if they are over priced, should be free, should be part of the original game itself, etc. But taking them as a the sum of their parts these Saga games each do a great job of making you feel immersed in the epic periods they are set in, and this game is no exception. To play as the mighty Achilles, the huge Ajax, the cunning Odysseus, or the respected Hector is thrilling. I like how you can build your character with different upgrades, equipment, and skills gained from battles. I think Three Kingdoms character upgrades was better, but Troy's element of skills like sapper from doing more and more sieges with that character was an improvement. I like what they did in some story building through character missions, but seems a bit shallow overall. Good first steps, but would like to see more story driven elements especially during time pieces that feature epic heroes like with Troy and Three Kingdoms. Maybe even introduce cut scenes unique to the decisions made in campaign rather than standard ones like in Three Kingdoms.    While I personally find more enjoyment in strategic campaign management over tactical battles it does feel great to win against insurmountable odds. The ability to micro manage your forces to do things like draw in your enemy, split their forces, utilize your forces specialties in either speed, defense, or higher quality troops to flank or outmatch your opponent feels great. To go up against multiple armies with your one and use actual tactics like defeat in detail, hammer and anvil, and force concentration is something no other game has. And the real life tactics aren't lost even when introducing non-historical elements like heroes and mythical creatures.     However, the place this game is lacking most is in the strategic campaign elements. In an effort to streamline empire management good things were introduced like less buildings, automatic garrisons, and regions with capitals and smaller cities/villages each with their own type of resource or specialty like unique unit recruitment. But in reducing some campaign management complexity to reduce the learning curve for new players, or those who mainly just want to focus on fighting battles, the game loses its competitiveness. Mid and late game are boring because you're just steam rolling everyone. What fun do tactical battles present when you OP army can easily stomp 3 armies of standard troops. To me those battles become mostly chasing trash mobs down that I'd rather just auto resolve as it detracts from the goal of conquering. There needs to be a way for smaller nations to grow tall rather than expand out as the only means of gaining strength. But that requires more in depth campaign elements.    The greatest thrill of winning a battle you shouldn't is what that means for yous overall game on the campaign. You're in a war, and your forces are there toed down. You are unexpectedly declared war on by a different neighbor, and now have a 2 front war. You win a defensive siege battle that you shouldn't have, or take a higher toll on the enemy than expected giving you time to raise another army or conclude the first war and move your forces. The battles should mean more than just winning a battle. The game loses that element in the Mid and Late game.   Overall, this is an enjoyable game, and I like to see how Creative Assembly is progressing their games by adding in new elements rather than copy pasting into a new set time piece.

_childDocuments_.review: Not as bad as some reviews say the game is. The diplomacy and resource management is better than most of their previous games, it really forces you to manage resources carefully especially in the early game. I also enjoyed the Amazon unit progression where the only way to upgrade your units is to rank them up in combat, wish they applied this in more of their games. However, I can see this being a problem for the AI late game who regularly wipe out their armies, this would enable the player to snowball before mid game.The combat itself forces you to flank instead of just sitting there launching arrows or sitting in a phalanx. The graphics are better than most of their other games, if you are playing the game above medium graphics (some people are complaining it looks cartoony, but that's more if you play on lower graphics.). My main complaint is the AI, in my game I have a bunch of Greeks sailing across the sea to wage war against me alone at times. They are at war with other factions, but in my game it seems like I get the full brunt of it. Also, like many of the historical total war games, the main factions in the conflict seem to get confederated or destroyed by lesser factions. This seems to be more prominent in the Trojan side than the Greek side. The main Trojans (Hector and Paris) got confederated by the Dardani, while the Greeks main players(Sparta, Phthia, Mycenna, etc) are still top dogs as they should be. They really need to make it so Hector and Paris are the spear heads in the Trojan campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel the campaign's economy, unit upkeep, and AI are absolutely garbage. I started off as Hector everything was fine at first. I was completing quests and conquering territory. Primarily at the behest of Troy. Eventually I had more territory than all of my allies. My buildings, especially in production zones, are up to date however I feel it really has no real benefit. I am always short on resources while having multiple territories of each. I have upgraded heroes and researched upgrades yet it feels my economy is too small for more than two large armies. Then there is Paris who has way too little territory to have multiple large sized armies wandering about. Same goes for enemies who at times have dozens on dozens of mid tier units while maintaining one or two territories. Whats worse is when we go into negotiations they seem to all have massive stockpiles of this or that material, sometimes all of them. Yet I'm constantly begging for scraps?So instead of having properly defended territory, Im constantly dragged into wars by allies and when my few troops are far off on some front, I lose an important city. Then the enemy AI always seems to walk away leaving the door wide open to that lil shyster Paris. Sure cyclops' and centaurs are cool but how about a decent, balanced economy and AI that actually does something besides piss off everyone then take your territory when you are off fighting for him.

The wars felt a lot more personal to me for some reason, and finally getting to the point where I could bring the fight to my enemies and destroy them was immensely satisfying. _childDocuments_.review: This game is boring.I haven't played a Total War game after Rome 2 and Attila.  I am kind of an originalist, thinking RTW and and M2TW were the best in terms of campaign and UI, even after hundreds of hours in Rome 2.  Despite that, I wasn't bothered by Troy Saga War basically retaining the same UI style as Rome 2.The problem is there's a whole bunch of new features offered, but strip away the veneer of "newness" and they're exactly the same as Rome 2.  The decrees, the province-wide edicts, the building trees, the agents system, the "only generals can recruit soldiers", all of it is exactly the same.This would be great if it was great to begin with.  There's a lot of flaws with the Rome 2 UI system, and absolutely nothing has been done to fix them.The distinct resources, expanding from just gold for so long and now including Food, Wood, Stone, Bronze, and Gold, is pointless.  Nothing is done with this as well, all it does is add a pointless metagame where you have to balance resources, since some soldiers require just food for upkeep while some require food and bronze, or food and wood.  Certain buildings require stone to build instead of wood.None of this matters.  Philosophically, it's a downgrade, going from a currency system to a barter system.  Gameplay-wise, it doesn't add anything new.Speaking of not adding anything new, this is set in the distant and murky Bronze Age, with barely any sources on military hardware and specifics, the core of this game's focus.  It's wide open for interpretation, which they very clearly did when it came to the armor and weapons used by the Homeric Heroes.Why didn't they bother doing this with the other combat units?  There's barely any variety among them; most units are barely armored, if at all, wearing plain clothes, plain brown armor, plain spears and clubs, plain helmets.  The number of units available is similar to that of previous Total War games, but so many of them look alike and function alike that they may as well be the same unit.As for the campaign....This is a short period being covered, 10-20 years of the Trojan War.  Short timescales usually work out well for most Total War games (like Total War Napoleon or Fall of the Samurai), but, once again, NOTHING IS DONE WITH THIS.Playing with the Agammemnon tutorial campaign, the game carefully guides me around all the "new" features and guides me for about 3-4 turns or so, occasionally popping up with new information as I advance missions and upgrade buildings.Now I'm 71 turns into the campaign, and nothing has happened.Where is the war?  Where is the call to arms?  Where is Menelaus raging over Helen's abduction, which was depicted at the start of the campaign?  Where is everybody?There's been no call to war, no mission telling me to gather everyone up for an invasion.  Troy itself isn't even visible on the campaign map, and hasn't been mentioned at all except for an earthquake brought about by Poseidon around turn 50 or so.  Since then, nothing.Literally no one is moving except me and the Amazons.  Diomedes has a small army on the border with me.  It came up around turn 3.  Turn 70 it's still there, unmoving.  An agent keeps merging with it, then leaving it, then merging again.  That's the only campaign map action I see unless I go and declare war on someone.What is happening?  Where is this so-called Trojan War?  Why is the AI completely dead, deader than Rome 2's AI on release day?This sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely good for those who like the historical aesthetic Total War has catered to for most of its history, but also want some mythical units to spice things up as well (when bought with the Mythos DLC). This game is beautiful, the colors really pop and the UI is smooth. I love the unique unit rosters too. They carried over the improved diplomacy system from Total War 3K, which is necessary at this point. I also love the map. I don't mind a larger, more in-depth map.This game is fun enough to play obsessively for dozens of hours. But the more I play, the more the imperfections become apparent. There are a few bugs. Sometimes units seem to ignore orders when there is seemingly no reason not to. Trading materials in diplomacy is sometimes bugged too. I've given another power fewer resources for them to accept a deal, but when I give them more they refuse.Sometimes the reliability and disposition systems can be a bit vague, and it is not always transparent that some diplomatic actions you take will have a significantly negative impact on your reputation with other powers.Most of these issues are fairly mild. But personally, my biggest complaint with Total War games recently are the naval battles, or lack thereof.I understand the reasoning that CA has for not including naval battles in recent games. They have been heavily criticized in games like Rome II (even though I still like the naval battles even if they are hard to control). However, just because CA hasn't always had the best designs for naval battles doesn't mean it's a positive thing that they aren't including them. Any time there is water in the form of oceans, rivers, lakes, etc. in games like these, excluding the possibility for battles on ships is completely immersion-breaking. Naval warfare has been instrumental in influencing the outcome in most conflicts that involved troop movement via ships. To me there is no excuse to force 2 armies to land on the closest island when their fleets meet in the middle of the Aegean sea. No navy would realistically do that. The absence of naval battles in these games is a consistent missed opportunity by CA to really explore the nuances of different forms of warfare, and the diverse strategic outcomes and gameplay elements that can fulfill the depth that a game like A Total War Saga: TROY really deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: Frustrating new problemsI certainly do not recommend trying to play this game, even on 'Easy' level without going and subscribing to a whole range of mods first. There are many of the usual Total War problems that they never seem to correct, such as opponents able to produce huge armies when they have meagre resources and them knowing from hundreds of miles away when you have moved and losing a single town seems to wreck your food supply situation.Additional problems come with the geography of the region featured. Almost every town is on the coast or on an island, so enemies can fall on you almost wherever they choose. You might think to garrison your frontline towns but a new feature of Troy is that heroes - your generals - who stay garrisoned quickly gain negative traits. The alternative is to follow enemy armies on land or at sea, though as others have commented, no matter what skills you develop among your heroes and agents and even with special boats or chariots, you will find almost all enemy armies can escape you, they are always just out of reach, often ploughing through your towns with you unable to bring them to battle.As with previous Total War games, the navies appear to have technology many centuries in advance of the time the game is set. Even Admiral Nelson would have welcomed the ability to find out a fleet hundreds of miles away had left port so as to line up two fleets to capture it precisely with no chance of escape. Reinforcements keep on being sent to the bottom of the sea, no matter what route you send them. In contrast typically, no matter how close your fleets may be to each other - as often happens with armies too - for some reason they seem unable to support each other, let alone together pursue an enemy trying to  contrast to slinger units in the Total War: Rome games, in this they are useless. If one of your slinger units, even the advanced ones, can kill a single enemy soldier then it is cause for celebration.There are a couple more difficulties which are particular to Troy. One is that some of the heroes cannot be killed. You can defeat Rhesus of Thrace, ten, twenty, one hundred times and he pops up again in a couple of turns with another huge army. You end up with the majority of battles not being between the main forces but between small town garrisons faced with some unkillable general with overwhelming numbers. It is not particularly fun to play.If you do have the Thracian DLC then given how powerful Thrace is - Aethiopia which comes with it is less difficulty - it is quite likely that your game will change from being the Trojan Wars to the Thracian Wars and you will devote a great deal of time to chasing after Rhesus reappearing once more with huge armies to lay waste to whichever part of your kingdom he picks this time. As others have noticed, no matter what items and buffs you may have, it seems that the enemy can always move that bit faster than your armies leading to a frustrating chase up and down the map.The other new problem is the bureaucracy. As your empire grows and in this game restricted to a chunk of the Mediterranean it is never big, it becomes less and less efficient, meaning you have to seek out more resources simply to stand still and very vulnerable to that one raid meaning you have run out of food. I do not know what games testing they do, but it is clear that they do not test it on ordinary gamers or ones like myself who has been tried out the Total War games in hope, since 1999.Aside from the challenges with getting resources, the barter economy around food, wood, stone, bronze and gold, is interesting. These things do not simply work as money but are needed for building structures, equipping armies and for effectively researching some new abilities or upgrades too. The prime flaw is holding on to a decent amount to run even a handful of armies, let alone anything equivalent to your opponents and that very soon it seems that even the smallest of factions have ample quantities of everything and have little interest in trading with you.There are some nice elements. The music is great; the numerous quotes from 'The Iliad' are interesting; the portrayal of the landscapes and the graphics, e.g. on load screens all work well too. I like the choice to make it historic, the truth behind the myths or mythological. In the latter you get interesting units such as giants, centaurs and harpies. Other mythological creatures are hard to get but interesting. The quest facility to gain others is wasted. Given you will be scrabbling around trying to hold on to the territory you have, there is no real chance to go on a quest or as the Greeks, really even to get to grips with Troy. The mythological special units are tough but not so overwhelmingly as in the Warhammer Total War games, where it seems flying dwarfs can nuke almost an entire army. The paragon units, specially trained elite units are a decent feature too. However, as always the AI side seems to have far easier access to special units than the player ever will which combined with unkillable heroes means you are likely to be fighting a lot of battles in which you stand no chance as another garrison army is overwhelmed in a couple of minutes.Even heavily modded, this can be a frustrating game. On top of the things complained about Total War games down the years, there are some new ones, which I do not really know why they bothered to include.

And that would be incredible!The majority of negative reviews all seem to converge on price. It seems that if CA ever put a price tag on their games/Sagas/DLC that the negative reviews come flooding in. Games are a business. Commercial success is essential if we want more content. And, clearly, we want more content.  Warhammer got the DLC:FLC ratio roughly right so there's a commercial model to copy. _childDocuments_.review: Troy A Total War Saga embarks on one of the most ambitious updates ever done for a Total War Game to date. When Troy was initially released, there was mixed reception over the Truth Behind The Myth Approach, as it did not fully embrace the mythological nature of the game. Now with the Mythos Update bringing massive changes to the game, with three new campaign modes (Historical, The Truth Behind the Myth, and the Mythological Campaign) and three new legendary beasts to hunt down and recruit in your armies in the Mythological Campaign. They have reworked the three new campaigns in ways that make sure that each campaign mode is distinct. In this review, we’ll cover the three campaign modes in-depth. Note: I am a content creator for CA and I received early access. All thoughts are my opinions only. I really enjoyed this game tbh, and I didn't find much to criticise about. I honestly enjoyed it. I've tried to be as critical as I can, but at the end of the day, my review is my opinion only.  How you will find Troy, is up to you. I think it's def worth trying out at the end of the day. I do think the pricing for Mythos could be more heavily discounted imo, and when I mention it's a potential AOM, I mean in the sense, that this Mythological DLC opens up a possibility of adding other potential Mythological realms such as Egypt - it doesn't mean it's getting added but there has to be a hint at it. They need to EXPAND this game to EGYPT, ASSYRIA, AND BABYLON imho. Historical Mode initially strips away all mythology, instead introducing a grey muted colour for their battles, including battles being more infantry based combat and less reliance on missile infantry even they can still turn the tide of battle. Your heroes do not fight like absolute machines on the battlefield and they retreat like normal generals. The diplomacy feels that it could do with some improvements and the diplomacy could act more historical in some ways. The diplomatic AI offers good deals for bronze and wood, and food. But it often does it to be unhistorical. Essentially, Troy Total War is a sandbox game. So what may have happened in the Iliad is rarely needed to happen in this game.Battles are where I’ll certainly give credit to CA for taking community feedback and improving upon it. In one of my battles, I fought as Agamemnon and besieged a city. An epic battle ensured where rain poured down upon this miserable day as the city walls looked intimidating to my troops. The enemy had brought forward slingers. Slingers! A majority of their army comprised that only. With that in mind, I sent forward my shielded warriors, and we fought a tough battle. Not one side gave up their ground. The enemy’s missiles kept on peppering my troops with their deadly rocks. It was a tug of war, for the enemy had been wiped out. Only their slingers remained while mine kept retreating. Exhausted, my troops retreated. They erected a historical landmark at the city gates on the campaign map. Troy can create these epic stories from your battles. That said, I disliked the grey-coloured outlook of battles and in the campaign mode. An option to have a colourful mode and a non-colourful mode would have been much better to do between switching colours in the campaign mode. In the battle mode, if you go to the menu, you can select Photo Mode, which means you can switch and adjust the lighting of battles that persists in the campaign map. Some criticism that I would add is that slingers felt too powerful in battles and sometimes entire battles can be decided on that outcome. Garrisons are sometimes too strong even if you have an army that’s got elite units for historical mode. An improvement that was welcome to see was that during this battle, when the enemy slingers attacked my heavy shield infantry, the shield infantry didn’t break. That said, I prefer this. There was a time where slingers can wipe out entire units in the previous version of Troy before the Mythos Update. It is a definite improvement and one which I welcome. Chariots needed more of a presence on the battlefield and need to have a more devastating impact on the battlefield. They are powerful but can be easily defeated too quickly. Since Chariots were the battle tanks of the Bronze Age, some changes to their stats would be welcome. From an overall view, the technology tree didn’t change throughout the three campaign modes, and I feel they could have improved upon this aspect. Making each technology tree distinct from each other would have added more replayability. Historical Mode definitely achieves a gritty grounded feeling and is a recommended campaign experience to try first. Before you start the Mythological Mode, getting acquainted with the Historical Mode allows you to understand how to fight battles, and how you will play in the Mythological Mode. The Truth Behind the Myth approach has been revamped, giving the campaign map a more colourful mode to play with. In terms of preference, from the start, I had always wanted Troy to expand out of the Bronze Age and add different factions. I can say with no doubt that it has been improved. Mythical units have been revamped and re-skinned to make them appear Mythical as much as possible. The Gods give passive abilities within battles, and heroes are your typical one entity that charges into battle. The best comparison would be to compare this to Three Kingdoms, which period is renowned for Generals charging into armies alone many times. Mythological units are mostly humans wearing animal skins, but that’s a wonderful concept. The way the three campaigns works is this: Once you’ve had your share of the Historical Bronze Age, it may tempt you to try out the units that were mythical in legend but having a more human approach. After that, it might tempt you out to try out the Mythological Mode in its full glory. In this mode, you are witnessing the truth of what was really behind the Mythological steroid filled fest of the Iliad. It’s a campaign that improves upon certain mechanics in Historical and introduces other elements that you might not have been aware of previously. Overall, it’s worth trying out.Troy has definitely embraced the realm of Greek Mythology for its Mythological Campaign mode and battle wise. This was my most favorite campaign out of all the three modes, and it is a definitive moment for CA to expand this mythology mode and add in other unique factions of the Bronze Age such as Egypt, the Hittites and Assyria. It could become the next Age of Mythology Contender and I will keep on championing this cause until the day I see CA does a full scale Bronze Age Total War, or hopefully decide to make this Saga Title and expand it further. It is where Troy excels at. This mode adds three new legendary mythological creatures most famously known in the Ancient Greek World: Cerebus, the dog of Hades and Persephone that guards the Gates of the Underworld, the Mythical Hydra that guards the entrance to the Underworld, and the Griffin of Greek Mythology.For an overall conclusion, this game is totally worth it in my opinion and I give it a 9/10. It's fun, solid and it really excels with the Mythos update.You can find the rest of the review here: Link to the review since I'm new to Steam Formatting: You can find my youtube review here:

_childDocuments_.review: It's actually better than I thought it would be. People complaining about it "not historical" also don't state there are actually three ways to play the game, much like 3K. Personally I enjoy the mid tier, but am welcome to all the game modes. Honestly I think the historically "accurate" game mode is probably the most dull - yes we all know that Hector and Achilles probably didn't fight and kill hundreds of people in a single battle, but were good fighters in their own rights. The actually AI can be a little bit annoying doing random acts, but it isn't much different than the newer TW games as of late. I can't tell you how many times in TW:WH 1-2 an army would force march just to either avoid my armies or spearhead further into my territory - this isn't something new to Troy. I am glad that the factions actually have different unit varieties for different styles of game play.Having different resources can actually make it interesting in trying to develop settlements and armies, but the development and army building actually seems rather slow going as food is a huge factor into army maintenance, but it is difficult at times to acquire enough food to support your empire on your own (personally I don't like bartering for food per turn due to unforeseen events to ruin your army capacity). I don't mind having to struggle to get things like stone, gold, ect - but food settlements are a huge key to victory and they can be rather sparse - some regions not even having one to speak of. Lastly one of my biggest gripes is playing as the Trojans getting your fathers favor he often issues missions that are counter intuitive to what you should be doing - such as going to war with a faction you just made peace with. Or capturing a city/settlement that is under an allies territory. I know they aren't required to advance your favor, but it still seems rather TOO random and should adapt to your campaign rather than just willy nilly. Overall - it's fun, its a TW game much like 3K, but I find it much better executed and personally I find the era far more interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic themed total war. Not sure why it gets so much hate.The campaign is distinctively purposeful with missions and mechanics that pitch you and your allies against half the map. On veteran difficulty, I had to restart each campaign multiple times.- playing as Paris was epic and I had to make crucial strategic decisions every. single. turn. After many hours of defending and bartering every turn for the resources that you likely won't have for most of your campaign, I was finally able to turn the tide of the war. V epic.- playing as Achilles, I was constantly pushed to attack and grow my armies to the point of exhaustion. His units are great, but the emphasis on light swordsmen forced me to be aggressive. Again, I was only able to really make a move against Troy after many hours....Battles are also epic. The rareness of cavalry forced me to really think about the differences between each type of infantry units and how you can compose your armies. An army of light or medium infantry or even archers can be much much more effective than a heavy infantry stack once you start looking deeply at stats and abilities. Anyways the food shortages upkeep will really make you think twice about having any armies at all for most of the game.Also the bartering system REALLY gives new purpose to conquering.Only downside is that the siege battles on minor settlements really really depend on the layout of the buildings. Some have very poor chokepoints. I often gave away settlements whose layout didn't favor the defenders.Fantastic game, 100% worth it on a sale. Really wished the modding community focused on this because the engine is much better than Attila or any other... plus the mythological units are already there and work very well.

_childDocuments_.review: 9.5/10 with mythos 6-7/10 in historical Don't even attempt Truth behind the mythTotal War collided with paradox games would be my dream game. A fantasy or historical mashup of real time tactical battles, character management and storylines and political/economic manuvering. I feel like this game is the closest total war game to reach that fantasy. For the short verdict, go to the very bottom.On the battle field, I have a solid line of elite club infantry, shining in heavy bronze armour, crash into a trojan spear wall. Hector and Achilles replaying their iconic duel. Meanwhile on the flanks, my centaur lancers devastate lightly armoured skirmishers while my own archers are picked apart by sirens and harpies. In the midst of all of this, Cerberus reinforces from the East with shades of the underworld while the hydra lobs acid spit all over my reserves. Lightning strikes and tidal waves roar over the land. This is the average endgame battle for this game. By the endgame, on higher dificulties, you can get battles of like 3 stacks vs 3 stacks with mythic monsters and divine boons. These are cinematic and very entertaining. The normally dry infantry vs infantry combat of the bronze age is spiced up and you are really able to cut loose with tactics that blend a tradtional Rome 2 vibe with Warhammers fantasy additions and three kingdoms style single entity duels. Battles can be epic in this game.The political side of this game is just as epic, there are 2 major alliances that fight through the game and the diplomacy system really works. This is the best total war diplomacy system ever as it seems very real. Alliances work and if you put in the effort, you can really feel like the man leading 1,000 ships to Troy. Particularly with Agamemnon, political manipulation and conquering Troy together is really fun. You feel like you are part of something greater than a simple total war campaign, you feel like a player in the world's first major western conflict. The resource system also works extrordinarily well and province development and the way you p[lan your conquests really is just so different from only addressing gold income from other total war titles. The buildings are also unique and each faction has different ways to progress to make money and make new troops.The Map really lends itself to the game as that really facilitates a sense of the clash between 2 major alliances. This theme is very central to the gameplay loop and I think that Trojan war is so well encapsulated by this. A homeric victory is enough to have a great timer and complete a story driven campaign but you can always go for a total war campaign which asks for global dominance that requires some commitment but is quite fun the first time you do it. The characters and epic missions are quite well fleshed out and provide a fair representation of the true war. There were no real good guys and bad guys. Only two brothers with a ton of allies reclaim a wife and in the mean time confronting the largest empire at the time.Achievements are a fun way to add a storyline to your campaign as neglecting Aphrodite as Paris of Troy and devoting oneself to Athena gives roleplaying qualities to your campaign and also gives a fun alternate history aspect to the campaign. ach faction has an achivement for completing a homeric victory and two more that either center on their campaign mechanics or narrative arc. By the end of each campaign, you should have 3 more achivements and will have played through a fun and immersive story.The modding support is also amazing. There are some good combat overhaul mods that tweak numbers to make everything better and there are more combat animations added. There are also two major overhaul mods but in my opinion, the best mod is the expanded factions mod that add a multitude of new factions everywhere. These have unique units, buildings and victory conditions along with missions. This gives an almost unlimited replayability andthis lets you play anything from Hercules descendants to sea raiders who are so fun. Supporting 5 armies from 5 settlements by raiding, sacking and razing literarly anything you can get your hands on is ridiculos. The unique buildings provide unique opportunites to have cool play styles. For example, the sea raiders, you can get massive upkeep reductions, to the point where you pay 5% wages for armies and get over 50% bonus to sacking and razing income.To finish this all up, I want to share an experience that I had that made this game all the much better. I had recently wrangled the varius greek kings(no small feat with the complex diplomacy) together to go to Troy and started island hopping towards Asia Minor when I reached a road block. There were 5 trojan stacks sitting on a two city island in the middle of an archipelago. What followed was massive showdown of me (Mycenae) with 2 armies, and with Sparta, Salamis and Argos each having one, confronting the defending Trojans off the coast of Greece. The Ithacans with Odysseus were comping but it would take time and the Pythians with Achilles were combating Hector of Troy on the shores of Greece. What followed was a ten turn death match for the main island which was the lynchpin for the whole archipelago. my Spartan Allies took an early victory in taking a staging ground island and after a swift siege, I took one of the main islands cities. Then I engaged in a open field battle to fight 3 trojan armies with my two and I was forced to use evry tactical bone in my body to properly use my centaur cavalry to keep the enemy armies separated while my infantry tried its best to rout the enemies by pulling off daring flanks. I won the battle but then, with my allies help, had to siege the final city of the island. It eventually fell but not without causalties. The whole experience felt like truly fighting a large scale war on the macro and micro lever. I was directing Agmemnon to duel Aeneas on the battle filed but on the strategic map was atchjing Spartans fight Priam while I kept the Dardanians away. I had many moments like his later, major flashpoints in the war that made a massive difference, like on the shores of Troy.All in all, I love this game. This game is a political contest of herding your alliance together in your homeland and then going to confront your enemy after an extensive island hopping campaign. All the while using mythical units and divine boons to send enemies to Hades. 9.5/10 definitly would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Another "Epic bot" here who spent more time with the game on another platform. I am addressing the game mostly from perspective of Truth behind the Myth approach as historical mode is a very sad and unnecessary afterthought and Mythos is a full-on warhemmerisation of a game that wasn't conceived to be another warhammer. Troy is currently being  review bombed due to CA's practices, but for what this game is and offers it is completely unwarranted. Currently, patch 1.6 broke something and there is an omnipresent chromatic aberration and blur effect that's likely to be fixed soon enough. You may consider waiting with a purchase until it gets addressed. If it won't be addressed or acknowledged within a reasonable time frame, I will change the review to negative because this has a fair potential to cause discomfort during play, completely eliminating all the upsides. Done by "team b" from Bulgaria, Troy offers something really special and amazing. A visual feast not only in quality of its assets but also representation of a historical period that is most authentic to date, with obvious artistic freedoms taken. Most people aren't that familiar with the period and history so it will be difficult for them to appreciate the work, research and clear passion Sofia team put into this project. This has to be one of the more SOULFUL games released in recent years. All of the visuals are accompanied by wonderful ambient music and memorable themes and chants performed by  a Bulgarian ethnic choire. This is the best soundtrack since Jef van Dyck's work. This is also the best optimized Total War to have come out. I saw people complaining about UI but I find it serviceable and fitting the theme without causing distractions or confusion like rome demaster have. Graphics aren't everything. Troy offers experimental and new campaign mechanics based around multiple resources, expanded diplomacy (as always, AI can get wacky...), ritual hecatombs and prayers where we spend resources for faction and army buffs from the gods. Each faction and hero has their own, small unique flavour mechanic similar to what we know from Warhammer games. We also have agents fulfilling all the roles (and more!) we've come to be familiar with from other titles. Otherwise, it's pretty much what we're used to but those small changes add a lot to turn-based campaigns campaigns we're all familiar with.  Battles are the most visually stunning in the series, although sync kill animations do not exist contrary to the trailers (booooo). Being a time period where cavalry just did not exist, designers really put a huge emphasis on creating a varied infantry roster to fulfill a variety of different roles, resulting on a diversity and options that make other games of the series look pale. Beautiful battle maps are really well designed to account for terrain formations and even new terrain effects that affect infantry performance. This creates many options and approaches to play with and keeps battles very fast and dynamic which works for a video game. Each faction is very varied with different playstyle variations being catered to between them; for example Diomedes has virtually no access to ranged infantry whereas Odysseus excels and utilising ambushers and shock troops. Balance is just fine to keep the game interesting and fair for the most part but single entity units are just too powerful and take away from the suspension of disbelief. I highly recommend against purchasing Mythos. Base game and faction dlc is where it is at. Mythos, despite being visually stunning, is an attempt at appeasing a warhammer fanbase. A sign that Troy is undergoing and identity crisis and loss of direction. Not only it diverted from the brilliant, original vision that received unnecessary mockery but Mythos itself feels more like just one big reskin that adds Warhammer creatures to the game that even utilise same animation kits. Certainly not worth the price tag. Mythos also feels completely out of place for this setting and given the original vision for the game. I also do not recommend historical mode. Originally something I was looking forward to, but in the end it was just a quick, content bloat-oriented afterthought which strips the vanilla campaign of all its flavor and completely diminishes roles of heroes rather than looking at balancing it out for a good, really grounded experience. Troy is in a good spot. Its vanilla content got patched up and expanded upon to the point of becoming one of the best Total War games and its limited scope does it a huge favor. Mythical expansion is completely unnecessary and uncalled for. Truth Behind the Myth mode is what everyone should give a chance to. I have read too much about our history and was raised on mythology. This game is as much a historical title as Three Kingdoms and Rome 2 with its diversity updates. No one can tell me otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being released over a year ago, this game remains fundamentally broken. The resource requirements are stupid. It makes it near impossible to maintain more than one decent army before you fall into the red. The defending garrisons are terrible and may as well not be there.Somehow, AI factions have no issue with generating tens of thousands of resources or stacked armies to plague you with. They'll still spam you with nonsensical diplomacy though... EVERY. SINGLE. TURN.The difficulty settings are pretty pointless too. For example, Playing as Achilles in my first run-through, Hector of Troy and his merry band of Trojan allies declared war on me, totally out of the blue in turn 3, before proceeding to dominate most of Greece within 30 turns. This made the very idea of an invasion on Troy utterly impossible, simply because I had no way to raise the armies required to fight back and was stuck with defending my one or two settlements for dozens of turns. Playing as Hector, it was vice versa but in turn 11 (except that Achilles wasn't involved - he decided he would rather spam me with resource requests instead, whilst the Greeks dominated Troy and her allies). I could go on and write a huge list of the many issues but you'll find that in the other reviews, which is a shame because it had serious potential. It's almost as if the developers thought it would be a great idea to build a game with all of the annoyances of previous Total War games, leave out most of the good stuff, then sell bits of it to you behind the many paywalls after you've already brought the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I played through once, and probably will never return to it. That said, there are still things it does that would be great to see in future TW games.Overall, the main issue is just that key mechanics are poorly implemented. Diplomacy, something the series has never done well, is at its all-time worst in Troy. There's seemingly no logic to when I get DoWed and when I don't. Neutral sides will go hostile when they are wildly out-gunned by my forces. In sharp contrast, when I am weak I feel like I am less likely to be preyed upon, even by my enemies. There's just no obvious reason why things happen in diplo, and previous games that had realm divides (Shogun 2) at least let me know clearly who was on what side. Part of what breaks diplo in Troy is that it is surprisingly difficult to know which factions are in which groups; it should be *far* easier than it currently is to know who is aligned with whom.Trade is also an enormous mess. I like the idea that resource management is more than just gold and food, and would like to see this type of resource management aspect continue in other TW games. But the trade system in Troy is not up to the task of supporting this type of mechanic yet. Unless I missed it, there's no way to auto-block trade deals by resource... as in, stop asking me for gold and offering food that I don't need. If resources are to become a bigger part of the game (itself a good thing IMO), then the trade mechanics also need some tweaks. Worse, there's usually 2-3 trade deals every turn during CPU turn-taking, which slows the game down a good deal. And worst of all, the UI for trade is hard to see and not as informative in some ways as I would like (it should be easier to see if I am gaining or losing something per turn).But the biggest problem is combat... the pace is ridiculously quick. It feels like eSports SC2 levels of micro are needed when units are under attack and need to be moved. Heroes, even on Mythological, take damage fairly quickly at times, and holding/fodder type units don't stand up long enough in melee to allow for much flanking. The battles end up being repetitive, with a focus on getting into melee as fast as possible and committing everyone at once. While there's some thought that has to go into positioning during deployment, after getting underway battles depend more on reflexes and hotkeys/control-groups than on any real tactics much of the time, and even in my large battle to take Troy, it mostly devolved into pulling blobs apart and monitoring which units had for some reason stopped running towards the capture point.Finally, the difficulty of Troy is its own problem. Nothing against a game being hard, but it's incredibly hard and then suddenly fairly easy, and then back again. The see-saw diplo of neutrals means that out of nowhere, a faction not far off of your flank will send a stack at you. They will take a settlement, force you to raise an army and spend resources doing so, then 10 turns later make peace and give you a bunch of resources back in the peace deal. You never know when this all will happen, or for exactly how many turns they will menace you, so in the early game it can be a huge issue. But in the late game, they settle for peace more quickly and will toss you 10,000 food in the process. All of that being said, the resource management, art style, and events are pretty well done here.P.S.: CA, figure out naval battles please. This isn't Warhammer, so you don't need a license to have naval battles in Troy. It's beyond bizarre that the campaign map centers on a body of water that takes up a sizable portion of the game-space, yet you didn't add naval battles. It's time to address and figure out navies again, because it's alarming that a game with so much water in the middle doesn't even have ships.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War games, at this point, has very few new things to offer except how the campaign flows. Troy's combat, for the most part, feels like Three Kingdoms, which is perfectly fine. The combat animation is a bit lackluster, but it's quite forgivable. What is really frustrating is how the campaign map flows. In the end, the campaign map turns into East vs West  scenario: Greeks in the west, Trojans in the East. Much of your time is spent consolidating your flanks so that your allies are flush against the boundaries of the map. Although your main enemies in Greece or Troy is just 3 to four turns across the sea, the campaign AI (at least in the higher difficulty) prevents you from placing a foothold in your enemy's homeland due to the fact that your coastal regions will be constantly under attack. Because coastal towns lack a lot of natural barriers where you can bottleneck enemy movements, you are forced to move back and forth picking off enemy armies gliding across the Achaean sea. What you end up doing is keeping 1 stack to defend your shores and send 1 to 2 stacks inland, capturing minor factions to buff up your flanks. Since so much of your time is devoted to conquering minor factions, you don't really get the "feel" of the great Trojan war.By the time you make a landfall on the other side and fighting on main enemy faction's enemy soil, your armies are stupidly strong as it would be quite late in the game. All you end up doing is auto-resolving until you achieve your victory objectives. Consequently, the campaign gets boring. Quick. TW: Troy was a novel idea on CA's part. But, if you're going to sink in 100+ turns into a campaign, I suggest you skip on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Troy - despite the mixed reception it got from the community - is one of my favourite Total War titles of all time. There's an almost perfect balancing of so many positive qualities; the lighting, the campaign map, the art style, the multi-resource economy, and that's without even talking about the battles. While a lot of the factions do seem a bit samey, there's enough personality and difference in the Hero unique mechanics that makes the factions distinct.What I love about this game too is the battles. Not only have they reworked the unit roster to use different classes of infantry as the backbone of your armies, which really does make a difference, but the battle maps themselves are so well done. Both from a visual perspective and the actual terrain features. So many choke points to pin enemies down and send fast light troops around to flank them, so many high cliffs to position your missile troops on, and the different types of terrain (mud, grass, trees etc) really make a difference on how the battles play.With the addition of the Mythos campaign too, I think there's a bit of something for everyone. It's definitely worth checking out, and it's super fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War Troy depicts what is one of my two most favourite historical periods, classic/pre-classic Hellas/Ellada (the other being Feudal Japan). And as such, TW Troy is a clear 10 out of 10. Its a really cool version of the ancient fabled land(s) of Hellas, especially with mythos active. Its almost like re-living the epos of the Illiad. But that, the setting is the main stage of all that is good. Then comes the game itself.As a Total War game, or more generally as a modern game, TW Troy does not impress. Some things are good, as the barter system where you can see how the other part values stuff. The music and sfx is ok. The absence of "time/date" is also a welcome stance (in my opinion). I also like this five asset system where different settlements produce one specific asset and you have the need for all five assets (for different reasons - Food for armies, Wood for construction, Stone for advanced construction, Bronze for advanced troops and Coinage for advanced tech, troops and construction). This incentivize expansion and conquering partly to attain those resources you lack.But, the AI is just terrible, has it devolved from earlier titles? I don´t remember Shogun II being this retarded when it comes to the AI. Allies never lift a hand to help, even if they have armies nearby and you are being slowly conquered. AI armies can be found just aimlessly walking around in circles. The Skirmish stance for archers and javelinthrowers are abysmal, I don´t think I´ve used it a singel time without my units just running straight into the enemy lines - instead of just the opposit direction (which should be the whole point of it). When I ask my charioteers to go north to avoid the approaching enemies - they seem to think it´s a swell time to run around in circles until the enemy locks them in combat and kills them.  Even minor stuff can be a needle in the eye, details that has been there before but now has been streamlined. Like remember how in previous titles, how settlements literally "grew" when you expanded them? you could SEE them actually grow, thats not here anymore. No mercenaries to recruit on enemy soil. No animations for agents actions. No taxation levels. No family tree or similar system. No formations per troop (tight - loose etc) etc etc.

_childDocuments_.review: TW Veteran here. I like the game a lot but it has its downsides for me. Specifically, it's way too hard even on Normal. It's not that I'm afraid of a challenge. But it's too hard in an annoying type of way. For example in TW:Attila, it's so dramatically difficult and the AI is so shrewd on the campaign map and in battle that when I get my ass handed to me, the defeat is so thorough and complete that I can only tip my hat and respect the AI for the humbling beat down and abrupt end to my campaign that I would otherwise win in 250 turns in say Rome2. It's very shocking. TROY has too much whack a mole and this is because of the lack of navies.. Without navies patrolling your coastal territories, the player is forced to travail back and forth the Aegean with your land armies to defend which is not fun. I'm one of the rare few who enjoys the naval battles from Rome2 and Attila and I think it was a bad decision not to include naval battles in a game set in Bronze Age Greece of all places. TROY and TW PHAROAH should be combined maps into one game just like zoomer fantasy title Warhammer. Troy is very well-optimized but I suspect that is because of the smaller map, less factions and near complete removal of the lovely matched combat animations from Rome2 and Attila that sadly is not present in TROY. Thus, when opposing units are engaged, the units from the middle to the back just stand around and do nothing while only the front lines are  fighting.My career advice to CA is not to give up on their Grand Campaign multi-continent sized historical titles. Attila, Rome2, Medieval2, Shogun2 were the best games they ever released. Make Rome 3 with all the features from Attila like siege escalation, fire, dynamic campaign map, vicious AI, family tree, governors, matched combat animations in battle, non-combatant civilians walking around in cities and towns, etc. It's been 10 years of lessons learned since the release of Rome2. A Rome 3 w/ Attila features would be an instant classic instead of a belated classic like Rome2 and I would gladly pay 60 euro for it ;)JUPITER GIVES US STRENGTH!

_childDocuments_.review: TW has a fundamental problem: The AI hasn't really evolved. That was fine 20 years ago when I played my first TW game, Medieval. In 2022 it's pathetic and, in fact, TW: Troy is less of a strategy war game than 20 years ago. Creative Assembly's solution for this is to make the game harder (and less realistic) but not more challenging. Huh? Challenging to me would be a game of TW RTS chess. To make it harder TW just piles on enemy factions, cheats against players, NPC buffs, etc. The game starts off promising. The factions are well thought out and differentiated. On paper they have well defined strategic differences and play styles. Ditto factional units (more on that later). Regardless of mode, classic, semi-mythical, or mythical, it starts of with well designed, if largely recycled, cuts scenes laying out your faction's situation and starting strategy. Once in game you have 2 victory conditions: Homer or TW. Additionally you have epic missions (usually 13 needed for a Homer victory) and regular missions that offer rewards, often too meager for the trouble, that early on act as a tutorial to get you started. Later regular missions make little strategic sense to me and are just inviting endless wars in distant regions to gobble up historic areas. Each region has a settlement with a fort and typically 2 settlements with resources. Resource settlements can't be walled. It's all downhill from there. Fairly early on you'll be given a mission to control 4 regions (nomad factions are a bit different). About the time you complete it all strategy ends and TW: Troy becomes a game of whack-a-mole. Inevitably you'll be tagged a threat, assigned an antagonist faction you can't negotiate with that will compel countless factions to brainlessly declare war and swarm you. I've played 100s of hours and at this point in every game strategy, goals, objectives, plans all cease for pretty much the entire game as I'm in reactionary mode responding to endless invasions outnumbered anywhere from 3:1 to 8:1. Yes, it's a war game but this gets extremely tedious very quickly because no progress is being made except exhausting NPCs.It's not too long into the game I just want to auto-resolve many battles because most aren't very interesting. But you can't because, as expected, auto-resolve is so heavily nerfed TW forces you to manually fight all but trivial conflicts. Manual combat isn't even as good as old TW: Medieval, IMHO. The first problem is the unit selection isn't very diverse. Calvary is very limited and most of that is skirmish. The 2 mythical game modes are a little better offering cavalry like centaurs and even some flying units like griffins. But there still isn't enough variety. Resources are tight plus there are limits on many elite units so mostly it's about fielding as many mediocre armies as you can. I find it hard to get past 2-3 full (20 units) armies until the mid to later stages - about the time I'm bored and about to stop. I should add here most factions have an administrative burden nerf so the more armies you add the more they cost to buy and maintain. Ditto adding/upgrading settlements. Siege equipment is pitiful. Ladders and battering rams. That's it unless you go through a very long buff cycle to develop a "Trojan horse". I was so eager to develop one only to find it isn't what I hoped for. It's just a recycled siege tower from TW: Rome, et al. The walled city layouts aren't very interesting and battles are just slow hack and slash. If you ladder up a wall you're stuck on the wall until you pretty much control the gate and by then the battle is almost over anyway. Battering rams often get slaughtered before they do their work. Unwalled resource settlements are contrived geographic locations with typically 3 canyon choke points. Again, hack and slash. Few tactics.Open field battle (sea battles are resolved in open field too) doesn't offer many tactical opportunities either. The big thing pushed in TW: Troy is flanking but it's harder than you'd expect to maneuver units. Units are stupid and often non-compliant to your orders. They require constant monitoring. The game always assigns the player a disadvantageous starting position like lower ground. Terrain doesn't simulate reality (I've been to Greece) and is contrived with obstacles and lots of trees and hills because TW likes hidden units. The problem with hidden units is their visibility comes and goes so units can't lock onto the enemy and will just stand around awaiting further orders - that constant monitoring problem. Missile units in brush or trees won't fire and often won't easily leave cover with enemies near. Also, all units slow to a crawl in brush or trees and they aren't quick to start with. Beyond these issues the AI doesn't follow orders very well. Units tend to get hung up on their way even on clear terrain frustrating any flanking or rear action plans (like harassing NPC missile units). I'm not a big fan of the superhero army leader idea either in the 2 mythical modes but it's the price you pay for an expanded unit roster. Classic offers traditional leader units.One quick thing. TW: Troy discourages army garrisoning. Settlements can be reasonably garrisoned through settlement upgrades to a degree but if you add an army due to a larger threat it won't be long before your hero is penalized for laziness and procrastination. I'll add the hero buffs and penalties in this game are numerous to the point of confusion.Diplomacy is mostly a joke. It is most helpful in barter trading. The AI will always brainlessly make a trade if they're not at war with you. Otherwise, it is pretty resistant - and awful. NPCs will arbitrarily declare war on you and if you look up the reason it's because they're at war with you. Silly. Often in a turn or two you can make peace with them and they will pay you for it! Huh? Only for this silly cycle to repeat itself with the same NPC a few turns later. Mostly you can't negotiate with anyone beyond non-aggression except when your faction is part of a larger shared culture like the Danaans. Then you can form defensive or military alliances with cultural peers but they are only useful to the extent they won't attack you while they're in them and might pose a target for your enemies. They won't help you fight and will betray you without penalty. You break an alliance and it's a huge diplomatic penalty leading to almost every faction in the game wanting to fight you plus barter earns a huge cost penalty. Vassals and confederations are an option in rare instances but I find it best to avoid them. Wrapping up game play there are agents: priestess, spy and diplomat. They're not as useful as I hoped and just as NPCs swarm me with armies they swarm me with agents who typically kill/wound my agents over and over and over. In the mythical mode there are also mythical agents that infrequently auto-generate but they only last 8 turns. The turn limit renders them mostly useless in my experience. The bottom line is I find the early game play fun and can typically last 80-100 turns until I'm sick of the whack-a-mole. Playing 100 more turns to get into an end game isn't worth it so I rarely try and only forced myself to gut out a win once in a little under 300 moves just to say I did. By then I had overwhelming power and finally could strategically choose to declare war. Unfortunately it was on leftover minor NPCs until I reached an unrewarding TW victory. A Homer one would have even taken longer in that particular game.

_childDocuments_.review: First off I waited a year to purchase and play this game because f*** Epic Games....I've been playing Total War since Medieval Total War 1 and have enjoyed just about every product that has been put out since then. I, personally, L-O-V-E this game! To me I grew up on Greek Mythology and the stories of Orion, Jason, Perseus, and the Homeric Poems of the Iliad and the Odyssey (HBO please do an awesome series of both of these!!) . This game captures all of the elements I love from both the games and the stories..for me. I know A LOT of people will disagree with me on this, but I like this more than the Warhammer series....now before I am pelted to death with stones hear me for my reasons why. For me, I connect with all the characters, creatures and monsters presented in this game. I've read about them, watched all the movies out there (Jason and the Argonauts, Clash of the Titans, Troy, The Odyssey etc..) and to see it come to life in a release like this is just AMAZING!!...for me...I imagine this is how fans of the Warhammer Universe feel when they play Total War Warhammer 1 & 2. and eventually 3. Don't get me wrong Total War Warhammer is awesome and I've played a decent amount of that too but I personally prefer Total War Troy over the latter. I like that I have the option to play a full historical campaign more akin to Medieval, Shogun and Rome series if I choose and on the flip side can ratchet up the Mythology with a Mythos campaign. This game is INCREDIBLE and I love it! I highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Guys, this game is good. Is it perfect? No, but it is a lot of fun. The campaign map is gorgeous and strategically interesting, the way you can customize your heroes and armies is great, the mythic units add a lot of fun flavor and diversity to battles, the battle map terrain is brilliant (love the implementation of things like mud patches that slow down heavy units and make you think about how you're moving your units around), and I'm surprised at how much I really enjoy all of the incentives to ally up with your "team" and explore rather than simply gobble your neighbors and blob out - really captures the hodgepodge-alliance feel of the era as described in the source material and other era-appropriate literature I've seen.My only real gripe is that some of the mounted javelin units I've encountered (specifically in the Griffin Mythic Quest) have such obnoxious "scurry away" programming that the end-battle turns into an endless cat and mouse game where you can never get quite close enough to hit them for long enough to get them routed, so you end up just chasing them around the map in frustration for like an hour - but that feels like something that could be easily patched out by putting a stricter limit on how many javelins they can throw, and is rare enough that it doesn't significantly detract from the enjoyment I've had with the overwhelming majority of this game.If you're on the fence at all, I say go for it with this one. It's a lot of fun if you know what you're getting and are excited for (or at least willing to indulge) a fresh take that's a bit different from standard historical TW fare.

_childDocuments_.review: So far this Total War is very enjoyable.  Being able to Siege the entire city and not just one wall is great.  Combat feels good, units have a weight and density.  Collisions are good.  Upgrading units and RPG elements are also nice. I'm not a fan of the Province system,  I like any town being able to grow into a major city, but it was done well enough here it doesnt bother me.  Some of the building bonuses are great and figuring out each provinces maximum output design and structure was a minigame in itself. Heroes and storyline plus the triple campaign based on how you want to play was very cool.  I really liked going back to having a hero lead a unit like a normal human warrior would, but also the option for single entity.  The best release of a Total War game in a while!  Great Job 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: So, a year after it was given away for free on the Epic Game Store Troy comes to Steam. And it's honestly all the better for the extra year of dev time. I never minded the behind the Mythos mode in the basegame, but the Mythos mode makes it feel like a whole new game, one that seems to step out of the screen in the same way the old Hollywood films of the 50s and 60s did, full of bizarre creatures and imposing sights that add a huge amount of weird wonder that is both intimately familiar and alien. Mechanically it's also interesting, especially on the strategic map, in that it dabbles with true diversity in resources beyond single province buildings giving bonus stats to units recruited there. Food is important, stone is important, gold and bronze are vitally important. Trade isn't just a "click button make number go higher", but having to actively seek out AI trading partners to buy bronze from in order to keep your armies going, or stone to build a new temple or upgrade your capital province. Wars now aren't simply a matter of unceasing expansion wherever the AI is weakest, but have a measure of strategic impetus as you seek out provinces with additional Bronze, stone, or gold to keep your armies growing. It's a system I'd love to see brought forward to newer Total War games as it adds a lot to the tbs side of the game, one that would go perfectly with a return to population systems seen in the original Rome. The AI is the AI. It's not been any dumber than Warhammer or Rome 2 from what I can see. I know that's not a ringing endorsement, but if you have fun playing those games you'll likely not notice here, I certainly haven't. More importantly though I think the thing the game has most made me want is a true Total War Mythology series, expanding the map out to include the entire Fertile Crescent, with Egyptian, Hittite, Sumerian and proto-phonecian civilisations and their many and varied mythic heroes and monsters. Who knows, if enough people buy Troy they might even do it.
