_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, Total War "fans" are braindead. I also find it funny that some people whine about historicity in a game based on The Iliad.Anyway, this is a very nice addition to the Total War series.First of all, the game is absolutely gorgeous - similar to 3K but a little bit more "stylized", which makes it look even better IMO. The UI is also very nice to look at. Performance is great too, much better than WH2 - battles are smooth and there are no random frame drops on the campaign map.There are several additions to the gameplay which I like, such as the administration system - makes it a little bit more interesting to manage your empire as it grows and you build more armies. 4 resources are also better than just one currency to use on everything, and it made trading more useful. Diplomacy is not on the level of 3K but definitely much better than most other titles.The design of battle maps is probably the best in the series, there is more terrain variety and you can't just use the same formation every time. Campaign map is also decently sized, obviously not on the level of mainline games but a little bit bigger than I expected.Overall I think the game is definitely worth getting if you're interested in this period and appreciate the Age of Mythology vibes.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War: Three Kingdoms was my first Total War game, and I fell in love. I tried to play TW: Rome, but refunded it because I felt that the quality of life and management systems were poor compared to TW: 3 Kingdoms. It seems like TW: Troy implemented a lot of Rome's systems, and totally threw away a lot of good features that were found in TW: 3 Kingdoms.PROS-Upgraded the Talent Trees for characters-Monsters are cool-Playing as Hector or Achilles is fun if playing for narrative purposesCONS-They took out administration positions, so now if you purchase an NPC the only thing they can do is be an agent (special spy unit) or a general-They also took out the ability to tax your realm on a sliding scale, now its either tax that region or dont tax them, there is no in between.-They rendered all of the NPC portraits in 3-D and it looks clunky and bland. I liked the 2-D artwork that 3 kingdoms had-In 3 kingdoms, the seasons would change when you progressed in turns. I get that this is in the Mediterranean, but losing the seasons changing really kills some of the immersion.-BUGS:  long load times between turns, completely absurd barter requests coming in from random NPCs (I really dont get how this game determines wealth. I read the tutorials, thought I understand, and then I have some guy refuse 50 gold coins for a little bit of food... when they have tons of food, no coin, and we are in good standing with each other. Very weird system), Combat is finicky... you need an entirely full army just to take down a minor settlement just because the garrison troops are stupid strong.- You can only have one general in an army.. Also the generals are all bland, most of them have a similar name that starts with Poly. I missed the special characters in Three Kingdoms that you would sometimes get and would be other worldly on the battlefield. I also miss teaming up commanders in an army to satisfy all the needs. Commanders/ Generals are no longer color coded by type, they are just the Warmonger, Fighter, and Defender, and it really doesnt seem to matter which one you choose other than some minor personality traits. Those are some of my basic complaints. Honestly, if I could refund this game, I would. However, before the thought even crossed my mind, I was already 2 hours deep into it, so the game still does that classic time vanish technique that symbolizes Total War games. Its not bad, but its not what I was wanting. TBH, I would have rather just played TW: 3 kingdoms again.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the worst TW game released in the last decade in my opinion. The game crashes more often then it should, and the game's balance is pretty poor. A few examples of issues I ran into with gameplay:>Getting soft-locked because capturing another settlement puts me over an administration cap that tanks my income to the negative, and being unable to capture any territory near me or develop my own fast enough to be able to not get killed.>Getting war declared on me by neighbors I have good relations with for no reason.>Allies may agree to join me in a war when I'm attacked but then before my next turn will make peace with the factions that attacked me, making the alliance virtually meaningless.>The AI can confederate way faster than you. If you confederate with another faction you have a 10 turn (or 12?) cooldown where you have a bunch of debuffs and you also can't confederate during that time. Meanwhile the AI can confederate 4 factions before your cooldown is even up. >There are SO MANY negative events that you get hit with, seemingly for no reason. Very commonly you'll have one of the major gods just wreck one of your cities for no reason. Having a higher level of worship for the gods I believe does decrease it, but I've still had gods that were tier 2/3 (respected) by my faction just decide to devastate one of my cities for no reason. Doesn't matter how many altars or temples of that god my faction has they'll just crap on you for no reason sometimes. Furthermore, i don't think I recall a single random event having a purely positive effect like in other TW games. You either get one with a little good and a little bad or just all bad.Were it not for the setting of this game I most likely would've quit after only a few hours. I've played almost every Total War game and have over 1,000 hours in the series last I checked. Every game has it's own BS to deal with but it's usually nothing too crazy, but this game is far more poorly balanced than any of the other game's I've played. If you want a similar experience just play the Greek campaign for Rome 2, it's much better.

It sort of looks like all of the soldiers have heat stroke, and some are hallucinating while others are feinting. :)I have watched this franchise slowly take a turn downhill, and I think it's finally gotten to a point where the games are not fun. There's probably a lot of tech debt that this franchise has accrued over what must be a decade of using the same tech. _childDocuments_.review: Edit UPDATE 10.9.21: A small petty, irrelevant kingdom with 3 settlements declared war on me at the very late game, where I can finally start taking Troy on their own territory and sack their city, a requirement for victory. This little useless achaean kingdom was also allied with my allies (Mycenae & Sparta), who are "Achaean Pillars" which means they are supposed to NEVER BETRAY YOU (i'm playing as Odysseus, a historical ally of all Achaeans). Both Mycenae & Sparta rejected my alliance to join this small tiny kingdom against me, their longtime ally, in the middle of war with Troy. This effectively ends my campaign and ability to sack troy for at least another 100 turns, only after i literally have to destroy every other empire first. BROKEN DIPLOMACY. I double down on my recommendation that this game is worth it for the first 50 turns alone, after that, this game severely suffers a lack of direction, balance and composition to bring its vision to completion without extreme frustration, annoyance, and more labor than fun. If you are an ancient history buff and liked Three Kingdoms, this game is worth it for the first 50 turns to experience the ancient Agaean warfare, even if its only for 20 hours of gameplay before it gets incredibly stale and repetitive. The voice acting, design, and maps are beautiful, as is leveling up a Homeric Hero and sending them into battle with impressive bronze age armies.           Mythos expansion is worth it to experience the "expedition" narrative where you make choices to shepherd a chosen expedition army to a final epic live-action tactical battle against a legendary monster that you will recuit after and control in battle against your enemies.            Aside from these highlights, the game suffers from an overall lack of depth, diplomacy, and a overly-simplistic economy & bartering system that is too repetitive and basic to not become annoying over a long campaing. Definitely get the bundle with Mythos as that's worth it if you want to enjoy some of the really cool mythical monsters and "expedition" feature to capture a monster and control it in battles. Overall pros/cons per my 150+ turns played experience across agaean side & trojan side (about 30 hours gameplay): Pros:- historical map and beautiful environment- UI design and character design in general- solid fighting as usual for total war- armies move across the campaign fairly quickly and the map is dense with resources and settlements to capture without much down time- voice acting is spot on- the "epic missions" feature is cool- Narrative of sacking troy or defending does feel very very cool. Combined with great voice acting, beautiful map, and other historical tidbits included. Neutrals:- endgame is always west vs east / east vs west- basically must ally with the same factions per the narrative for every play thru, depending if you're on the trojan side or achaean side, so there is limited replay-ability outside of playing once for achaean and once for troy. - Narrative appears in "epic missions" that are unique to each faction. These feel great and provide much-needed direction and story in an otherwise chaotic and often unfocused campaign. But there needs to be more development of this and it needs to be more pronounced than it is, which is currently very sparse. Cons:- no cavalry (except for Mythos expansion), so the tactical fighting gets stale and slow after many, many battles. There are chariots which are fun, but they are not easy to get quickly as you need special military building to access them.- garrisons are very strong, and you need two armies to effectively conquer even small factions. Waging war on two fronts is very difficult and more annoying than it is fun, and having more than 3 armies is not easy to manage with an annoying resource system and "anti-steamrolling" penalty applied to growing empires- administration penalty is there to increase food upkeep and recruiting costs to prevent players from "steamrolling" and making the game too easy. there is nothing fun about administration upkeep and it's clearly a last minute bandaid for a larger balancing / pacing issue- have to basically dominate your side (east or west) before embarking on major expeditions into enemy territory, or small powers you left alone will just declare war on you and cause a massive headache while your armies are away. This creates a less-flexible playthru as you are forced to sweep your side of the board first which could take 70+ turns or more before you really start the "grand adventure" to sack troy or, as the trojans, bring the war in earnest against the achaeans. - diplomacy is very basic and almost non-existant. I still don't know how to create a vassal, there is no button or options for it, but other AI factions create vassals.- the constant bartering and trading of resources is the only way to survive, but it gets very annoying and repetitive and takes away from the immersion as you are constantly rejecting stupid AI barter offers and you have to keep renewing necessary agreements every 5 to 10 turns. This becomes a chore and there is no redeeming narrative quality or immersive benefit from having to do this.Bottom line: fun game, great setting, incredible map and environment. The game desperately needs a deeper narrative focus and more engaging empire management just for the sake of immersion and enjoying your conquests.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review of Troy with Mythos. It's the only proper way to play this game.Yes, Mythos should have been a free DLC update, but I couldn't resist getting it being a massive fan of Greek myth and classic Harryhausen films. This game scratches that old itch better than any of the recent Clash of the Titans movies. As a Total War fan, I'm only slightly (read slightly) disappointed. The campaign- objectives, map, diplomacy, etc. is great. Everything is beautifully rendered with a damn-near perfect UI. There were some genuine surprises from the AI that kept me on my toes. Heroes determine objectives and play-style like they did in Warhammer and Three Kingdoms, but the system is further refined, making the whole thing more replayable.The battles- are where this game does not shine. A competent handle on combined arms will devastate the AI all the time. There is nothing in the way of cool formation options (shield wall should be in this game, maybe a nascent version of the phalanx, Aeneas could use testudo as a nod to Virgil, etc). Terrain is there, but its influence on the actual fighting is negligible compared to earlier entries. They're still fun! I can't think of a Total War battle that isn't fun except back when Rome II launched, but CA needs to replay Napoleon and Shogun 2 to remind themselves how battles can be story-worthy without adding more stuff like monsters and heroes to them. I partially bought this game for the gods and monsters, but they should enhance the battle experience, not be relied upon to fix it. All that said, this is my favorite Total War entry in years. As a Greek Myth man, I finally know what it was like for the Warhammer and Three Kingdoms fans out there. It's downright awesome to build a labyrinth, recruit the children of the Hydra's teeth (zombie edition), and see gods in the sky. This will do until they finally come out with an Immortals sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been one of the better Total War games that Creative Assembly have made in recent years (though there is room for improvement with how aggressive the AI can be (even on Easy difficulty)).  If you are a fan of Greek history, and/or Bronze Age warfare, there is no better game out there.  This is the story of Homer's Iliad with 3 different game modes to experience it: Historical (no mythical units; heroes have bodyguards), Truth Behind the Myth (mythical units are in-game, but presented in a way that is grounded in reality; heroes have superhuman strength and ability), and Mythos (mythical units are in-game, as they are described in the legends; heroes have superhuman strength and ability, and the gods play an active role on the battlefield).There are plenty of ways to experience this story in TW Troy.

_childDocuments_.review: WHY TOTAL WAR? _childDocuments_.review: A Gem in the Total War FranchiseHonestly, I think the team that worked on this one deserves a raise. It managed to take the best aspects of Three Kingdoms (heroes, diplomacy) with the brighter, more colorful, more immersive campaign maps of Warhammer. Cult Bonuses are a nice touch and something I hope will carry over into future (historical) titles. The mechanics are simple, the learning curve is fast if you're familiar with the Total War basics, and each character faction has truly unique goals and play-styles that make for a lot of (sometimes game-breaking) fun.Not to say its perfect. The early game has a lot of useless factions on the Greek side that should already be vassals of Agamemnon at the start, but they're not, so the Greeks are gonna spend 25 - 50 turns getting their act together before taking on Troy. The Trojans, on the other hand, don't have this problem, instead of the games mechanics directing the action towards the plain of Illium, the Greeks more often than not have to fend off the Trojan invasion. Also the map includes all of Northern Greece and Makedon which I don't think were really settled nor are really relevant to the poem, and that added front, again, takes the action away from Troy.But if you like any of the Total War series, whether historical, fantasy, or romance: Troy will suck you in. Most of the DLC is pretty good too and has something for everbody. If you like Warhammer, get Mythos. If you like 3K, get Diomedes. If you like Atilla, get Amazon or Memnon.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this one as things aren't as gonzo as you'll find in some other Total War titles.  It doesn't mean that it is boring, it just means that you'll be hitting the END TURN button a bit more, often without doing too much that is meaningful.  There is a considerable amount of pacing that might bore some, but I find it an interesting take on conquest.  For example, a province typically have 3 or 4 towns in them.  If you are very quick about conquering all them, the citizenry will be almost ready to revolt immediately which makes it mandatory to leave a sizable garrison force while they calm down (and you build a few things to make them happier).You should know that sieges are especially effective in this game.  They both take a shorter overall period of time than some other Total War titles and the effects once starvation set in are almost immediately crippling.  Generally speaking, you are good to attack a besieged force after 4 or 5 turns.  If you combine single-stack sieges with the pacing that I spoke about earlier, you can get a little bit of extra conquest done while a partner stack is tied down keeping a rebellion from happening in a newly conquered province.Battles are more than a bit about money.  It costs a lot more to field an armored unit and wealth allows you to have a higher percentage of heavily armored, difficult to beat units.  I usually have my primary stack which is expensive and then a supporting stack of 14-20 units that helps eat some of the attrition.  The goal is to be big enough so that I don't experience many losses and to be large enough to besiege heavily fortified towns without losing much of my fighting force.The reason that I am concerned about losing units is less about cost and more about diplomacy.  You want to get into the top 5 list of military strength ASAP and stay there.  Factions are less likely to declare war on you if you can fight back.  I picked up the entire package for ~$40 and so far I've been in a historical-based campaign.  Even so, it has some favor of the gods elements that are based on the beliefs of your citizen solders or your heroes.  I feel like they've done a good job of capturing some of events and beliefs of the time period while not drifting too far from being a simulation. That's my take after 10 hours....  If you don't see my time advance beyond 50 hours, maybe it wasn't that good after all :)

I also come with a background interest in the Odyssey and all the Greek myths so the mythos expansion with cyclops, cerberus and hydra is awesome! Adds good variety to the gameplay where spears and slings can get a bit repetitive. Gameplay - for a first TW game, it's easier enough to pick up, game dynamics and controls make good sense. The wider strategy and map play (outside of battles) does feel slightly overwhelming to begin with, and there are a lot of options which I still don't fully understand, but it does mean it has a good empire building feel to it. Visuals - BEAUTIFUL. Particularly when you play with the myths version. Really colourful and bright, with lots of lovely references to the ancient greek world. Battles look great and the colourful soldiers really nice. lots of bronze!!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a first look review on Total War Saga: Troy. I will be basing most of this off the Mythology DLC that I play with.Graphics: 8/10Graphics are pretty good and are some of the best we've seen in total war. Similar to the graphics of Total War: Three Kingdoms which had very good graphics compared to some of the other releases.Gameplay: 9/10In my opinion at first look I really enjoy the gameplay of the game. I play full mythology mode so it may not be the same as historical mode but I am really enjoying the mythological aspects brought in. The new resources add a whole new level to gameplay. In other total war games you would use the currency as the recource for everything but now currency/gold is very rare and valuable and are only used for special buildings. The other ones; Wood, Food, Bronze, and Stone (I might be missing one) are used for anything from building fortresses to recruiting units and upkeeping them with food. Depending on where you are some recources will be rare and some recources will be in surplus making bartering with other factions very important.Units: 8/10There is good variety per individual person in a unit and units overall can range anywhere from spartan soldiers in bronze armor to giants with massive clubs (that are very op). If you are planning to buy just the historical mode then you can get militia men with nothing more than pants and a wooden sword to soldiers from Troy whom are adorned in gold.Campaign Map 5/10: The map covers Greece/Hellen - Western Turkey making variety very hard to come by but the game is able to do that with small changes that don't do too much to give variety.Battle Map 7/10: The Battle maps also don't have much variety for different sides of the map but the detail is very nice and the massive skeletons and armor of beasts in the background make your battles all that much more epic.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favourite Total War games to release in quite some time. I am admittedly quite biased by my love for the setting, but I also feel like this game presents some of the most interesting and innovative concepts in the series history, with one of the best campaign gameplay experiences ever (annoying barter diplomacy AI aside). The battles are as you would expect for the Bronze Age setting. Seen a lot of people complain about a lack of variety...but what exactly would you expect? What is great is that CA have done such a good job bringing variety and dynamic gameplay to quite an infantry focused time period. The Mythos DLC just adds to the fun, though I do wish they had gone more crazy with the 'god powers'. That being said, I am sure that this is something modders can expand upon! And this is not even to mention just how gorgeous and stable the game is with one of the best soundtracks in the series. Simply put, this game may not be for everyone, but if you like the setting and a more unconventional and challenging campaign experience then this is a must buy. _childDocuments_.review: As much as I have played this game to DEATH ever since it came out, that has mostly to do with Total War games being very good at hitting my addiction brain. When it comes to being a good game, though, TROY is a mixed bag...While I did not like Three Kingdoms butchering the combat in exchange for a spy mechanic that frankly did not work, playing a more traditional entry like TROY also highlights and exacerbates the problems with more old-fashioned agents, being incredibly unbalanced. Priests and spies especially feel broken, and a single successful action by one of them can put an entire army out of commission for multiple turns.Combat, on the other hand, has its own problems. While a lot of complexity was added, with new terrain types and spearmen being able to switch between a two-handed grip and one-handed with shields, it feels wrong. That doesn't sound very professional, but its the only way I can describe it. I'm one of the few people who like TW: Attila, because its combat had weight behind it; it felt impactful. When fighting in TROY, however, models float around without a care in the world, and their animations are very simplistic. On top of that, battles have gotten even shorter than they were, with no time of room for strategy. How can I move my chariots or light units around to perform a pincer attack when battles often last less than five minutes? For me, the Shogun II, Rome II, and Attila eras were just right, allowing plenty of room for strategy in a battle that wasn't overly-long, unlike in Medieval II, where a unit of trained knights somehow would need five whole minutes to rout a bunch of peasants. The world has regained a bit of colour, and the maps are interesting, but all that potential was lost when you zoom in, and it all goes wrong.Lastly is the optimisation, or lack thereof. Ending turns takes forever, even when your speed up movement in the options menu. This gets especially tedious in the late-game, where the AI has so many armies that even the campaign map started to somehow lag. Just keep churning out the DLC, guys! That'll fix all of your problems!In conclusion, while TROY was a step in the right direction, a pretty campaign map and soundtrack doesn't solve boring battles and lag!FINAL SCORE: 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A Total War Saga: Troy has been a controversial TW game: it is a smaller scope Saga game, it was released exclusively on Epic Games Store, and the Truth Behind the Myth mode was neither a historical nor a mythological game mode. The Historical and Mythos modes solved the latter issue, but you can sometimes notice that the game wasn't initially developed with these modes in mind, so they are a bit lacking.Nonetheless, Total War Troy has become one of my favourite TW games. Actually, it is my most played TW game with over 400 hours recorded! If you love Greek mythology like myself, you will have a blast reliving the adventures of the characters of the Epic Cycle. While it is true that vanilla factions have limited replayability due to vanilla factions playing similarly, DLC factions and the custom Homeric victory questlines made me play all factions in the game and complete all achievements! Moreover, the multiple-resource economy is one of the best mechanics of the TW franchise. Finally, unlike any other TW game, alliances work surprisingly well in the game: your allies won't betray you if you remain loyal to them, and you can coordinate them to help you destroy the enemy alliance!In conclusion, I believe that Total War Troy and its DLCs are all worth their value (except for the blood DLC, which is a scam). I recommend playing on Mythos mode with mods, Heroes of Troy and Gods of Olympus are awesome if you want to have all the characters and gods from the Epic Cycle in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This phrase from Homer I dared to butcher perfectly summarizes my time with , which makes me sad, as this instalment, set in the Bronze Age, had the potential to bring a bit of fresh air into this franchise.Alas, that did not happen.While one of the main selling points, the “Truth Behind the Myth” campaign mode, has an interesting premise of interpreting both historical and mythological aspects in a semi-realistic way, it does not fully commit to them, resulting in a weird, bland mishmash. Instead of taking advantage of its setting, it delivers half-baked mechanics and simplifies, even omits at times, well-functioning aspects from its predecessors, presenting a mediocre turn-based strategy experience at best.Let us start from the beginning, though. I decided to start my campaign in the said mode as the kingdom of Ithaca, ruled by a cunning Odysseus. We know that he is cunning because he repeats it every single time you click on him instead of, you know, having some unique tactics or mechanics that would do justice to his character and change the classic  formula a bit. Nevertheless, I started slowly expanding and conquered a few neighbouring factions, who were apparently surprised by my cunning strategy of attacking their settlements by sending armies via the main road.With enough cities, you can decide whether they will focus on industry, agriculture or military by constructing various buildings that either provide resources and bonuses for its region or allow you to recruit units and generals for your armies. There are also special agents who can, for example, poison the supplies of your foes or boost your production. However, my faction has an illogical disadvantage, as it cannot build anything in territories that do not have access to the sea. Barracks or farms on an archipelago? Sure! In a vast, inland region? Even our cunning Odysseus cannot figure out how to do so.For all of that, you will need enough resources: food, stone, wood, bronze and gold. While I adore this change, as it is more interesting than having a singular currency for everything, it becomes unbalanced after a few hours, as you will have tons of them anyway. I thought I would have to carefully decide whether to use bronze for an armoured unit or some buildings, but I could do both and much more. Having five different resources also means that other factions will keep sending you several trade requests per turn, which is pretty annoying. Moreover, it seems that opposing factions do not play by these rules, as they always recruited a lot of elite soldiers despite lacking the materials, making this mechanic purposeless.I am also disappointed by the outdated diplomacy system, in which factions ignore most of the options, following only the simplistic loop of sending you trade requests, declaring war and pleading for peace over and over again. While this might be serviceable in the  franchise, as that compensates the lack of diplomatic options with different aspects,  does not do so. Moreover, artificial intelligence is truly on the verge of intellectual disability at times. I have witnessed Menealus leaving Sparta, ignoring Helen and the counter-offensive of Trojan forces, and sailing across the sea to conquer a neutral settlement on Crete, resulting in him returning and trying to take back his regions. If only he was as cunning as my Odysseus...The last crucial campaign element is communing with the deities of Olympus by using food and gold in exchange for powerful passive bonuses that influence both the main map and battles. However, as it is effortless to have a lot of resources, this system becomes easily exploitable. Thus, I had the support of the gods for most of my playthrough. That becomes problematic, especially during the said battles; benefits like having a +20% range for missile units when worshipping Apollo is powerful, and the artificial intelligence is not competent to deal with you in such situations. This system is also not thought out well, as some deities punished me for no reason despite being fond of my faction. For example, Poseidon kept unleashing earthquakes on one of my islands, which even had a temple dedicated for him. I guess that gods work in mysterious ways… Even the multiplayer works in such a way, as it is in “beta” despite being released a year ago, so good luck finding a match there.Anyway, let us mote to the real-time battles, where your goal is to obliterate enemy forces or capture/defend points of interest. Even though  respects its Bronze Age setting by not having many cavalry units nor proper siege weapons, it does not bring anything to compensate for it. Sure, it is nice that it tries to be historically accurate, but I would expect that it would give more depth to each unit or provide more tactical possibilities, but that does not happen. Due to that, the battles feel more limiting and the same throughout the whole game, as you only upgrade to better versions of soldiers.One could argue that the special units, like Minotaurs or Cyclops, add to the variety, but they are not enough to fill that vast, empty hole. They might be useful in the first hours, but once enemies get access to elite troops, their effectivity decreases even when supported by an additional unit or two. Moreover, due to that semi-realistic approach in the “Truth Behind the Myth” mode, it is a bit weird to watch a half-naked guy with a club pretending to be cyclops while bonking everyone in the head as in the “Go to horny jail” meme.On the other hand, heroes like Achilles or my cunning Odysseus are far more enjoyable to use in the battle, and they do justice to the pompous tales, as their abilities can both increase their effectiveness or even provide bonuses for other soldiers. However, I feel that ranged heroes are a bit overpowered, as they manage to heavily damage or even wipe out enemy generals or elite units before they get close to my position.If there is something that  excels in, it would be its audiovisual presentation, as Greece and a part of Anatolia looks stunning, and the day and night cycle works beautifully, adding to the immersion. Additionally, it portrays Ancient Greek art at times, which is always a welcome addition. As for sounds, I already mentioned those annoying, reoccurring remarks, but the soundtrack does a fine job, underlying the overall qualities of the audiovisual.That is not merely enough, though.While I criticized  a lot, it does not mean that I did not have fun at times. However, that was because of the solid foundations that the  series already have—not because of  additions. For me, the base game is a simplistic version of its predecessors, and I do not see a single reason why would I recommend this one over those.

_childDocuments_.review: I can not recommend this game due to technical difficulties. I'm running the game on an i9-11900KF with 32GB RAM and a Geforce RTX 3080, and after just a few turns it always causes the blue screen "Clock Watchdog Timeout".Therefor I've checked my system for hardware faults, clean installed Windows 11, made manually sure every component has the latest driver and the issue still persists.I've run multiple diagnostics, stresstests and benchmarks to make sure the issue is not with my system. My computer passed every one of them with flying colours. The BSOD can not be reproduced with anything but Total War games. Funnily enough Total War: Warhammer 1 and 2 can reproduce the BSOD as well, it just takes more turns.I've checked for faulty hardware, none was found. I tried the game after a clean installation of Windows 11 without updating Windows and with it's default drivers, then with an up to date Windows 11 and the latest drivers, while nothing but Total War was running on the system. The BSOD still occured quickly.The BSOD can not be reproduced with benchmarks, actual stress tests or other games beside Total War games, so I assume that there might be a conflict between some of my systems components and/or Windows 11, with the Total War engine. Way more demanding games also run without any issues on this system. If a BSOD can only reproduced with a very specific software, then it's likely that the software is the cause for said BSOD. Therefor I can not recommend the game to anyone, especially not to people with newer systems and/or Windows 11. So far it was impossible for me to find out what exactly causes the BSOD's. The system ressources and it's power consumption are in the green when it happens.I assume it's some sort of compability issue. SEGA's support was not helpful at all by the way, which is another reason for why I can not recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Im a big fan of traditional total war games, the bronze age period, and the Homeric poems.Not sure why people complain it's not "historical", the stone age period is pre-historic; the references that are left of it come from pots, poems and insurance disputed etched in clay. TROY has clearly been developed by a team with a passion for the Classics, and it shows. The chants, battle roars and call-outs fit. You will stumble into the most obscure characters only peripherally mentioned by Homer and Hesiod. Each hero has a mechanic specifically tailored to their character (IMHO they especially nailed Achilles, Odysseus, Hector and Ajax) and their roster of available units ties you into a play-style that actually fits the character (Odysseus has only a single front-line unit available, hidden away behind a tier 3 building upgrade, whereas Hector has almost nothing but sturdy front-line units)The prayer/hecatomb mechanic is really fun and dynamic, you have to plan ahead early on in order to have the right boons active at the opportune moment.It's not like traditional TW games, no siege weapons/artillery and barely any cav to speak of (even for the amazons it won't make up the bulk of your army for at least until the early endgame).However I like that. TW was getting a bit stale: siege, drive you arty in, bombard pull the enemy close in, panini iron them with you line inf, and bob's your uncle. That ♥♥♥♥ just don't work here.In addition, the terrain is FANTASTIC. The most dynamic use of terrain in a strategy game I have seen thus far. The diplo AI might need work but its set up really well. Differentiating the resource pool is a welcome change. Also, with Mythos, you get to chase down routing troops with a griffin.

_childDocuments_.review: Objective note about troy : (after a hundred hours on epic and several more in Mythos on steam)Pros : - New period, always nice for TW to cover more- Great sounds/music/looks in general- Multi ressources system - Awesome battle maps - unique scenario when assaulting troy- all factions feel different- you actually have to play in team- 3 campaign modes Cons : - Battles can be repetitive, but this is the case for all TW titles- too much bargains asked by bots during end of turn sequence- siege maps are great, but the AI isn't, just like ToB there's lots of space to defend and retreat to, but by the time they choose to do it, the battle is over due to the morale loss- never had a siege battle where i was the defender Overall note :  17/20-1 : little things there and there that could be changed (bargains thing for example)-2 : for being a TW game, again with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AIBackground around Troy that might explain why the harsh reviews : The whole "problem" with troy, is that what interest historical fans is pike&shot / medieval 3 etc. And for those few who would care for a bronze age TW, Troy total war don't cover that much (trojan war scale is by definition much smaller). In the end, what works the best is mythological stuff, because it gives AoM vibes to the gaming community. But in the end, it just makes troy another fantasy game. But fantasy fans are waiting for warhammer 3. Even if the game is good, the actual TW trend does not lead to this game.Reddit TW is now swarming with warhammer posts, because warhammer has a VERY huge success. The only way to get some more love for a pure historical title, would be to release a solid title that follows the community desires.So in the end, just like ToB and 3k, the game is just being stoned to death because they want something else? There's no objectivity here. Instead of not buying the title because they aren't interesting, people will just buy it, try it anyway and indeed see that they aren't interested and then complain. Love you guys, don't change. Oh, and about the price. Fanatical offer + code, i had the whole thing for 40 euros. Try calculating Warhammer 2 plus several DLCs now. Always a pleasure to see that studios should still release their games for 20 euros less, why should we pay people for working after all.(And here I am, a bronze age avid reader, enjoying troy, knowing I won't ever have more love for this period in TW)

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up on sale recently thinking it wont be that good. The campaign detail is beautiful and the detail to the heroes of the time are great. Each faction has its own playstyle and goals with its own unique units. Some factions are harder than others and thats great. I really enjoy the economy system (im a old school gold per turn kinda game guy). The new(ish) system really makes you think and care about your settlements and upgrades and what path to go down. diplomacy is good too, being able to barter goods easily and make allies. The most impressive part was the Mythic campaign not just because of how beautiful the maps were but weaker or harder factions get access to powerful mythic units and it makes life so much more fun and easier.After my Ajax and amazon campaign victories were done i did notice how the AI behaves and how poor it can be at times. The game is a repeat of left side of map vs right. The princes of Troy will randomly attack small islands out of nowhere while Agammenon is razing their lands, Only for him to leave and lose it all few turns later to some random trojans vice versa. i played Ajax on very hard and didnt have to take much land - just play out the story - wait for troy to send a bunch of armies and counter attack. It all seemed a bit disappointing towards the end. I did however manage to turn the Amazonians against them by taking random regions and gifting it to them for a military alliance so in some aspects its possible to make allies on the other side of the map. All in all the AI is just repetitive and boring, By turn 100 Paris was still pumping out armies with rubbish tier 1/2 units - simply to sail the whole way and die. Its a shame that there isnt a random generate feature that scrambles all factions to spice things up.Apart from that, the lore, economy, units, heroes, and detail make this game a very fun play. I picked all DLC up and the game on sale and suggest you do the same - its a steal for that price. Im only 38 hours in and will be playing much more - next up Odysseus VH!

_childDocuments_.review: This is no historical title, and the Mythos DLC's "Historical Mode" is a marketing joke. BUT this game is a solid Bronze Age Total War game, given that the era is steeped in mystery and lack of records (outside of epics and poems). Because of that, this seems fitting.Graphically this game is excellent. The UI is mostly good but could use some tweaks/mods with displaying faction flags a little bigger (instead of city type icons). The campaign feels mostly balanced, though the AI all seem to struggle/excel with the same types of resources, meaning little supply/demand diversity.  Battles are what you'd expect, although units still move through each other too quickly (it's harder now to exploit, but the AI will still sometimes break from combat and charge straight through you to chase a retreating unit of yours, ignoring all your fighters and running as if unimpeded).  I wager we'll get some great mods on the Steam Workshop, and I'm glad I got to wait that year to buy this, because I avoided giving EGS my money and I now have a more patched, optimized game than when this launched.Don't buy this game expecting a full-blown historical title (or fantasy title). This is a "Saga". It's a weird blend, but it works. I don't see any glaring flaws and the *feeling* of the period is there. I don't know many TW fans who won't enjoy this other than the folks who are on a mission to dislike it. At the same time, this game isn't likely to blow you away, so if you feel you should wait until a sale--you probably should.  I rank it lower than 3 Kingdoms or Rome 2, but higher than Thrones of Britannia and Warhammer 1.I just hope that the "Historical mode" in this game & the "records mode" in 3K aren't signs of what's to come from TW's historical department, because so far we've had nothing even remotely respectable or innovative from a historical mechanic/gameplay loop standpoint since Attila.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. If you like Total War, Greek mythology and Total War Warhammer 2, then this is a sure bet for you.Campaigns: There are three campaigns: Historical, Truth Behind the Myth, and Mythos. Historical should be easily understood. In Truth Behind the Myth, your hero is a true demi-god (just like in Iliad), and they add quasi-mythological units to the game that are actually just humans. For instance, giants aren't really giants. They are just a group of bigger than normal human warriors that entered mythology as giants. Minotaur? Just a very strong man with a bull helmet. It's all kind of cool. In the final one, Mythos, all of these mythological creatures are truly the creatures of myth. You can have flying harpies, centaurs and even a monster like a hydra. Mythos has a similar feel to the Warhammer games.Difficulty: I'll talk about the good AI in a minute, but one big difference between this, even in the Mythos campaign, is that the game's balance has been very fine tuned. There are limits, for instance, on mythological units, so you can't just build doom stacks and win every battle. It's a bit more challenging in that way, and that's a good thing. You have to use better strategy instead of just buying up 20 star dragons.Gameplay: This is very similar to Total War: Warhammer 2. If you've played that game, you already have the basics down. The major change (there are other changes, but not as big) is the inclusion of various resources that run the economy. Every minor settlement produces one of the following resources: food, wood, stone, bronze, or gold.Food and bronze pay your units. Wood and stone are for building. Gold is used for very high tier buildings or troops.  Each settlement has various buildings that pay out a certain amount of the resource they are tagged with. It's quite fun to look around the map and find the resources you need and then either bartering with that faction or going to war with it.Bartering is another great addition. Need stone? You can try to set up either a one turn or a multi-turn agreement with someone. This is a part of diplomacy, which is a bit more robust than in recent games.AI: The AI has been significantly improved, and Troy boasts the best AI of any Total War campaign, both on the strategic map and in the RTS battles. If you are defending in battles, you can expect to be surprised about how the enemy is approaching and have to move your troops around. If there's any way at all the enemy can flank you, it will. The AI also does a good job of defending against being flanked.Just a last note. I hate to talk about other people's reviews, but when they are wrong, you need to let people know. One of the popular reviews talks about 6 AI factions declaring war on you on turn 10 and sending a 12 armies to you by turn 15. From my experience, this reviewer is playing as Achilles and exaggerating quite a bit. Achilles is the hardest hero to manage by a long shot. He's sort of bipolar, and you frequently have to make tough decisions due to his mood. It is very possible to have a few factions declare war on him in the same turn if you make a dumb decision (you can choose options that the game flat out tells you is going to cause serious problems with your relations with other factions). It is extremely unlikely that his happened in turn 10, and I'm just going to go ahead and say that the 12 armies by turn 15 statement is inaccurate. It probably felt like 12 armies, but there is no way that happened on turn 15 on Easy.

_childDocuments_.review: Troy is one of the most underrated and underappreciated games in the TW franchise. This is mostly because they originally released it exclusive on the Epic platform (for free) which is where I originally got it, so a lot of people just refused to even consider it. It's such a shame though because Troy has a huge amount of character and charm as a bronze-age semi-mythical strategy game, and has far more depth than a lot of people in these reviews are letting on. Character-wise it's similar to Three Kingdoms, with the major players in the Trojan War each having unique traits on the campaign map and in battle. You have characters like Achilles being nigh-unstoppable beatsticks with a focus on elite heavy infantry, then more subtle characters like Odysseus more focused on colonising coastal cities and exploring the map, and other unique playstyles I haven't even delved into yet. The game gives you three different realism modes depending on your tastes, with the suggested mode being 'Truth behind the myth' - the semi-mythical mode that sees characters be powerful heroes as depicted in the Iliad, and mythical units being imagined as special human tribes that superstitious Greeks interpreted as favoured by the gods. This interpretation of how these myths might have come into being is one of my favourite aspects of the game flavour-wise, but the game does allow you to switch all that off and play on realistic mode if desired.Sadly the true mythology mode is locked behind the overpriced MYTHOS DLC, but in my view that DLC is totally optional. Troy by itself provides a fantastic Bronze Age total war experience with tons of mythical character sprinkled in, and the base game is well worth your time now that it's on the winter sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played (and enjoyed) all TW Games since Medieval 2 and can say that Troy is a mixed bag but has a lot of positive and unique things going for it. Firstly I think it may be somewhat misunderstood to be a 'historical' total war game - it isn't. It's heavily influenced by Warhammer/Warhammer 2 both in battle and campaign and it feels closer to those games in how it plays than a historical title like 3 Kingdoms, Attila, Rome 2, ToB etc. This has a couple of effects on battle and campaign:Battle: The upside of using Warhammer as a starting point are that the heroes and mythical / pseudo-mythical units 'work', they look good and feel unique in battle, more familiar to those who've played TW Warhammer (monstrous infantry, single entities, flying units etc.). The downside is that for conventional units matched combat is reduced, formations are limited/non-existent and infantry vs infantry combat feels less visceral/physical than in Rome 2 or 3 Kingdoms and more gamey. I can understand why some people aren't a fan, I found that turning off always-on unit selection indicators (little yellow triangles on the ground under each entity) which appear to be on by default in Troy and no other TW game helped make it feel less gamey for me. Campaign: On paper the campaign experience of Troy is great; each faction has a very unique feel and much more significant faction mechanics than typical historical total war factions and the agents, cults (gods) and multi-resource economy add a lot of depth. The issue with the campaign for me ultimately comes down to difficulty (as somebody who plays TW on hard+ typically) and in particular the aggressiveness of the campaign Ai early on, even on normal difficulty. They have a tendency to declare war on you quite lightly and then attack your undefended settlements which isn't that unique to Troy but part of the issue is the multi-resource economy which makes your minor settlements way more important than in other games, especially early on (you might have 7-8 settlements but only 1-2 of a particular resource and losing it can massively hinder you) with your choices seemingly either to sit in an endless cycle of defending or strike out but inevitably lose important parts of your economy both of which get frustrating and tedious. My tip would be to mirror the Ai's behaviour: recruit multiple small forces for defense (garrisons in Troy even in minor settlements are quite sizeable and often just a few extra units and a hero can protect from most attacks). With the changes to the 'supply lines' system this is now much more feasible. Once getting over the initial hump, I've found that Troy more so than any other TW game I've ever played manages to keep the campaign interesting and challenging into the mid-late game without using emergent 'end game' factions, with 'snowballing' having been an issue in almost every other TW game, this is the first where even with 60+ settlements and 5 armies under my control it still feels like the Ai is putting up a good fight and could turn it round. I wouldn't recommend Troy to a TW newcomer over Warhammer 2, 3 Kingdoms or Rome 2 but if you've played a lot of Total War and are looking for a different experience, I'd recommend giving it a go (or another go if like me you've come back to this game after initially not being sure about it).

_childDocuments_.review: I still enjoy the Total War series of games, even after 20 years. They certainly scratch my tactical battle itch. Could they be different, could they be better, have less bugs, for sure. But as Creative has proved over the years, they do address most issues, fixing their games over time, and they allow for others to mod to their hearts content.  Troy is a further iteration of the Rome series but on a much smaller map. A little different from Alexander, as it holds to the more traditional style of play where you conquer and build up your regions and create higher tiered armies to conquer still more regions. But there is a bit more of a time constraint to get your objectives done and win the game. As it is the map could be increased with additional DLC, even adding new goals or an earlier time period like Shogun's Rise of the Samurai. The Mythos DLC might be a nod to that direction. An expansive map like the XGM mod for Rome might be too much, but as Rome Remastered shows, anything is possible. If they could merge the politics and strategy of Paradox's Europa Universalis with the strategic battles of Total War, the game would be perfection. But then there are not enough hours in the day to hold a day job and play that game. Are they hiring for strategic game playing?    If you are thinking of getting the game because you have not played these sorts of strategy games before, do it. Any buyers remorse will fade as you approach Troy's walls, or have your carefully built up army wiped out.

_childDocuments_.review: (This review is based on me buying the Heroic Edition of the game at launch on September 2nd and will consequently reflect that)Wow. This game genuinely took my breath away.I'm a Classicist in training at University, whose focus is on ancient Graeco-Roman religion and mythology; however, I know a bit about ancient warfare. And though there are errors here and there, the general attention to detail in portraying Greece during the Bronze Age had me screaming. For example, though some errors and creative liberties are taken, a lot of the armour is reimagined genuinely based on material and artistic evidence from the Mycenaean period. The style of warfare is also awe-inspiring. For example, calvary is sparse during this period. Instead, early on, you'll be using light infantry to try to flank enemies before eventually unlocking units trained in calvary. However, when you begin to unlock them, you can truly see the impact on the battlefield. Chariots are also fierce weapons of destruction and can be used to support armies with devastating effects. In the broad strokes, A Total War Saga: Troy's art direction and gameplay are spot on (even if the latter does require a decent amount of fine-tuning).But most impressive to me would be the Mythos mode, sold as a separate DLC. I am someone who loves to play Total War: Warhammer I and II, but has zero care for the Warhammer setting, which doesn't appeal to me. But as someone passionate about the ancient Graeco-Roman world and ancient mythology, A Tota War Saga: Troy is now the default game I will turn to if I want to play a fantasy Total War game. Yes, I have some criticism of such a mode being sold separately and not being part of the base game. However, playing with Mythos mode, I don't think I could play A Total War Saga: Troy in any other manner, nor do I have a reason to go back to Total War Warhammer. Mythos mode makes the game truly feel like a Homeric epic, and in my opinion, it's how the game should have launched to begin with a year ago. For starters, the maps in default Troy were already gorgeous. But with Mythos, they become stunning. I find myself actually pausing battles just to observe where I am. In battle maps, you can see things such as the skeleton of the giant ketos (sea-dragon) that Herakles slayed when it assailed Troy, and the Gods above overlooking the battles. With the overworld map, the sky becomes filled with beautiful scenes styled after Greek pottery that depict scenes of myth relevant to the direction. The geography of the overworld map itself becomes decorated with sites and objects that reference ancient myths, and in short, it is a candy to the eyes for anyone as big into ancient mythology as myself. Another thing is that with Mythos mode, the pre-existing "Truth Behind the Myth" units also get a facelift actually to be the creatures of ancient myth that they're meant to depict. And something about the design needs to be particularly applauded. Rather than being dull and going with the boring designs of 1963's Jason and the Argonauts or 1981's Clash of the Titans that permeate popular culture (yes, those designs annoy me and are disloyal to the ancient world), CA Sofia once again showed loyalty to the ancient cultures that they depict by portraying monsters as they were thought by the ancients to appear, drawing from ancient art to recreate beasts of legend. The Harpies and Sirens went from looking really out of place on a battlefield to a genuinely scary reimagining that captures the spirit of what they were in ancient myths. A cyclops and minotaur went from human-sized bandits in stupid-looking skull masks to actual massive cyclopes wielding clubs and actual massive minotaurs who are part bull, part man. Rather than just being regular dudes on horses, the centaurs are real centaurs, half-man and half-horse. Giants-- they look great, even having serpent legs, something media has rarely ever depicts them with. And so on. The reimagining of every pre-existing "mythic" units to actual mythic units is a genuine joy, and it's not merely about cosmetics. Most of the units are given entirely new powers, giving them excellent battlefield utility (e.g., Harpies/Sirens fly, Giants can regenerate health by touching their mother Gaia/Earth, etc.). And that's not even to mention the fact that there are also new Mythic Expeditions that allow you to recruit truly legendary monsters of Hellenic legends, such as Cerberus, the Hydra, and the Gryphon, who come with their own unique mythic unit roster.And what did this all remind me of? The first PC video game I ever played, and still do actively play, Age of Mythology. Mythos mode turns the game into a genuine spiritual successor to Ensemble Studio's classic RTS title-- except on a much grander scale, within a sandbox world where you can redirect the course of the Trojan War however you want, with decently accurate armour and playstyles that also do a good job at representing Bronze Age warfare. As a Classicist, this is my wet dream.Though I am enamoured with the game, I have some criticisms that I feel people should be wary of before they consider a purchase: -There aren't quite as many mythic units as I'd like (why can't I bring my gorgons or satyrs into battle!?)-Some places where I can recruit mythic units are a bit awkward. For example, I find it odd that Hector can immediately begin to recruit giants, rather than go to Thrace to do that, which would make more sense.-Battles feel like they can happen a bit too quickly before I have any time to set up a complex plan. I hope future patches will allow matches to take longer.-UI can feel a little awkward at times.-Historical mode feels like it could be more fleshed out. I also strongly dislike Truth Behind the Myths mode, and that makes Mythos more or less necessary to purchase to truly enjoy the game. Again, Mythos should have been part of the main game as a free update.-General bugs and glitches here and there.In short, do I recommend this game? With the Mythos DLC, that is a resounding yes. Although it has issues, I feel this game is a massive joy to play. I think the game particularly appeals to people like me, people who are in love with the ancient Graeco-Roman world and enjoy fantasy RTS games. This appeals to me far more than anything Warhammer related.I hope this game receives the proper post-launch support it deserves. I particularly want post-launch content that brings in Thracian heroes like Rhesus or the East African warrior-king Memnon (the latter of which could act as an opportunity to bring in Upper Egyptian and Nubian mythical units). More Akhaian heroes like Idomeneus or Nestor would also be great, as well as heroes who led nations but weren't directly involved in the Trojan War, like Cleodaeus, King of the Dorians.

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly good Total War game!Having played most of the rest of the games in the TW series, I came into Troy cautiously optimistic, but not much more. The Mythic game mode sounded interesting. However, having completed my first campaign (as Diomedes of Argos), I can honestly say this is a really fun game and a lot better than I was expecting. So far I have only played on the 'Mythological' mode, and haven't tried 'Historical' or 'Truth Behind the Myth'. I've seen other reviews complaining a lot about the 'Administration' system. This causes unit upkeep to increase as your nation gets bigger. Although this takes some getting used to, I ended up finding it wasn't too bad. It also makes sense that a city state in Bronze Age Greece or Anatolia can't just casually build a massive empire without serious admin problems!Good Points:+ Beautiful visuals: fantastic looking campaign and battle maps, love the black-figure pottery art style. + The Heroes: each hero feels distinctly different, with unique mechanics, such as talking to the dead or training elite fighters.+ Siege maps: massive improvement on, say, Warhammer 1 & 2. Cities and towns look great and are fun to both attack and defend. + Diplomacy: maybe the most surprising thing this game does well is how strong the diplomacy is. The AI still makes weird decisions (it's still TW!), but you can see exactly how close to agreeing to a deal the AI is and why. A great tactic is to sack settlements and then sell them off to another nation.OK Points:~ Battles: nothing unbelievable, but enjoyable.~ Myth units: having cyclopes, giants and the hydra is great fun, but it would have been nice to see more variety. Some units feel a little lazy, especially compared to Warhammer. Age of Mythology did it better!~ Unit variety: Better than I had expected, but not amazing. Limited by the time and place.Bad points:- Gods and god powers: Trying to keep the gods happy often feels like a chore. Building temples gives you big spike in favour, but this drains away overtime. You need to constantly use priestesses and prayers to keep them happy. Not a terrible system, but not very fun. The powers the gods can give you in battle are underwhelming, especially compared to magic in Warhammer. Most are just coloured lights. Even thunder bolts from Zeus don't look that impressive. Again, acceptable, but not great.- Confederation: Because factions can confederate (annex) each other, it can often be a very long job to wipe out an enemy completely. In my Diomedes  campaign, I destroyed Troy itself and took out all the key settlements of the Trojan heroes. However, Hector just kept confederating other minor powers. It took me until past turn 200 just to finally hunt him down!- Very aggressive AI: Often I had minor powers that obviously didn't stand a chance against me, declare war and then, a turn later, ask for peace. Overall, a fun TW game. Especially recommended to anyone with an interest of either Greek myths and epics, or the Bronze Age.

_childDocuments_.review: Got Total War Troy for free on EPIC where I have 100+ hours, but bought again on Steam as the Mythic Bundle was actually cheaper than buying all the DLCs separately on EPIC. TLDR; Total War Troy accomplishes exactly what CA intended their Saga titles to accomplish. It experiments with new features (like multiple resources, bartering and terrain effects) and narrows the geographical and temporal scope of the game to bring a more focused experience. It does this while somehow being both the best looking and best running Total War game to date.The Good:+Best graphics in the series at present while also boasting higher framerates than Warhammer 2 or 3 Kingdoms due to great optimization.+ Has region trading, although a faction can only receive a region if they are adjacent to the region. +The trade barter system is fun and adds more flexibility to your play style than you might think. For example, I am currently playing my Ajax campaign as a "realtor" where I will go and conquer some far off territory and then trade it to someone in the area for a 10 turn barter agreement for bronze or gold or whatever it is I need. This nets me both a big diplomatic bonus with the recipient and more than enough resources to fuel my next "acquisition". +A well defined campaign goal (take or defend Troy). This isn't for everyone and is a reason many dislike saga titles, but I feel the smaller scope let's you focus in on details that would otherwise be lost and also lets the game tell a somewhat more character driven story.+ The monster units add an interesting strategic element since you have to control the corresponding "monster spawn" on the map to recruit them. Since these units are fairly limited, they actually feel special and impactful on the battlefield due to their relative rarity and unique abilities. + Monster units are strong because they fill a strategic gap, not because they have OP stats. For example, with the unit roster primarily consisting of foot soldiers, adding some centaur cavalry makes you stronger not because they are great cav units, but because your opponent most likely will not have cavalry at all (unless you're fighting the amazons). Note that this does not apply to the 3 big Mythos monsters (i.e. Griffin, Hyrdra or Cerebus) who are strong due to great stats. + Sense of Exploration and Journey. With unique resources and monsters spawns, exploring the map actually is a bit of a mini-game in and of itself. It felt pretty cool leaving Ithaca with just a bunch of chump infantry and arriving in Troy with harpies, cyclops and a gold income from the goldmine I found along the way. Not to mention the usual mechanics of finding equipment and gaining character traits.+Terrain effects (mud, water, etc slowing movement of heavier units) are also pretty cool and a first for the series+Bronze age is an interesting time period that doesn't get covered all that often in video games anymore+Great presentation. Lots of nice small touches like the sky being a having a bronze age pottery motif, mini cut scene after every battle of your general dueling the other, and excerpts from the Iliad peppered into quest text and loading screens.\+Relatively bug free. I played this game Day 1 release on Epic and it was probably the smoothest launch Total War has ever had. 1 year later I haven't encountered any bugs that compromised my experience. The Bad:A lot of the negatives I am seeing in the reviews here apply to Total War game as whole. Diplomacy spam is very present in Warhammer, 3 Kingdoms, etc., and AI has been pretty dumb for as long as Total Was has existed. If you're new to Total War entirely, these may be things to consider. If you've played TW before, however, then this is pretty par for the course and Troy has not fixed these long standing problems (and I doubt WH3 will either, tbh). As for negatives that are unique to Troy, however, these are my thoughts:- Unit collision is more "fluid" than in a number of other titles. You would, for example, with enough clicking, be able to move your regiment of light spearmen through the enemy's regiment of light spearmen - although this becomes much more difficult to do with heavy infantry. Personally this didn't bother me, but I do see a lot of people complain about this and it is a valid concern if this sounds annoying to you. - Fatigue is too arcadey. This isn't so much a Troy problem as it is a "modern" Total War problem. Units can run across the whole map and only go from Fresh to tired. This makes positioning less important and makes Total War play more like a traditional RTS than it does a Total War game. This can be fixed pretty easily with mods though, and I recommend the longer battles mod if you prefer more of a Rome or Atilla type fatigue system.- Price. During the current sale, you can get the base game with all DLCs for 50 bucks. I think this is a pretty fair price for the game. Full sticker, non-sale price would be more like 85 dollars though and that's really pushing it. I get that CA is in an awkward position in that the revenue model for this game was to give away the base game for free on Epic (even if they did get paid by Epic for this) and then charge for the subsequent DLCs, but that means little to those users picking this up on Steam for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: It comes as no surprise to find a game that was given away for free only a year ago is not particularly good. As someone with several thousand hours across every Total War to date, this game was a clunky, confusing mess that cannot decide what it is and where it belongs. The time period is interesting, the Bronze Age features some interesting stuff but by placing itself within a mythologized version of events this TW comes off as cartoonish. It does not know if its a "History" TW or a "Fantasy" TW and therefore ends up as neither, with none of the strengths of either type. Warhammer was successful for Creative Assembly so I guess this is them trying to bring that crowd to their historical titles and subsequently not being satisfactory to either of the two groups.The UI just "feels" odd, unclear and clunky, much like the rest of the game, with a cluttered UI of Unit Cards and missile trails dominating battlefields, making them look like an overly colourful mess. Attempts at bringing Three Kingdom's excellent Quick Deal and politics system to Troy failed by creating an intrusive and cumbersome diplomacy screen where its difficult to find who you want to talk to and then to distinguish anything about them from anyone else. Speaking of which, although it makes sense for the period, removing money and adding tradeable resources to the game only results in every single AI faction pestering you about them every turn without any reason whatsoever, with each deal being more unreasonable than the last. It also removes some depth from the game as money used to be another way of tracking how well you were doing, but now with it stretched across several resources that becomes difficult and as different deals with different factions end its hard to know what your wealth will be from one turn to another.Buy it on deal for less than £10 in a few years, maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing Total War games for approximately five weeks; I am a former U.S. Navy UDT-SEAL/combat medic/propulsion engineer living on a disabled veteran pension. Purchased six total war SEGA Creative Assembly games and gaming desktop PC-- after watching many hours of Total War campaigns and battle videos. Troy has a huge learning curve for individuals new to Total War games!  I have watched at least 20 hours of how to YouTube videos for Troy and have played over 100 hours and still have not learned how to caste spells and have not built a confederation. There is absolutely NO attention to detail on envoys, priestesses, special abilities.. A manual needs to be at least 10x the size with examples to save time searching the internet, Reddit etc... for answers to mechanics, strategy and battlefield tactics. It was not made clear: that an ally can randomly attack you; when your forces are vulnerable. If you have not saved your campaign at an opportune juncture, in the campaign, tens of hours of game play in a campaigned are ruined, which can be very very frustrating.    The game is gorgeous with a lovely soundtrack. The battles are truly stunning and can be replayed and reviewed. You can pause, fast forward or slow motion the action in battle or in replays. The commerce and diplomacy gets repetitive and annoying. The movement in the campaign is very difficult to estimate: when you need to change from raid, march to encamp or ambush? Traveling across the map takes very much attention and planning, because you can be attacked at any moment or ambushed- including by an ally.   The take away, while I have had many frustrating moments with Troy and many more heart pounding thrills as well as hours of boring waiting for the program to move all the factions about the map. The adviser gets annoying as well speaking the same phrases over and over and over. Unfortunately, I need the adviser on. The game is a complicated and complex dynamic gaming program with a gigantic learning curve for a newbie desktop gamer. It is a good fit for a disabled veteran on Covid-19 isolation, but I would not recommend the game to a newbie used to console games, such as first person shooters. I understand the negative reviews, but for me I am "over all" having fun and enjoying Troy very much. Cheers and HooYah Hay

_childDocuments_.review: One of my only negative reviews, but to be fair, its negative because I read a lot of Greek Mythology, so just a warning to anyone who is the same, and a note to people who don't already read that stuff, if you liked this game, have a flick through some greek myths. I should have loved this game, I read and delve deep into greek mythology, but I kind of knew I would be disappointed when there is a game called Troy, but a myth DLC. Troy is a fantasy story (epic poem), by a chap called homer, titled the Iliad. the Sequel being the more famous Odyssey. But probably my own hype built up my disappointment here to be fair.So fantasy should have been the focus, but it went more hollywood Troy, which is boring to say the least compared to the actual story, because it is a fantasy story.Helen of Troy is a demi god, daughter of zeus, with a habbit of being kidnapped, there is a point in the iliad to make you question the whole premise, did she run away, or was she kidnapped? Why was she looking for her brothers (castor and pollux) at the walls of troy. Homer gave two versions of Helen, and what happened after, essentially one of being kidnapped, the other of running away, but her sister is the wife of her husbands brother.... which is why there is another version by the original author clarified in later works.Now as it is a game, and should explore beyond the source material, there is so much opportunity to do something really good with paris, basically, a choice, in the main story he picks Aphrodite, she gets the apple, and empowers paris destiny. But what would happen if he chose Athena or Hera, making Hera work is easy into the same game, but very different faction and bonuses etc. no helen at all.Anyway, enough ranting, that is why I didn't like it, it is 100% not about the game and completely because I have read a lot of this stuff and my imagination ran wild with possibilities but the basic concept delivered was very disappointing to me, but can compeltely see how if you have not dived into this stuff, seen the troy film, that it delves into a lot more stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: I changed the review to a positive review as I love the Greek mythology concepts and heroes more than archers, cavalry and artillery...I love Greece, Greek mythology, etc.I have myself Greek ancestry as a US American.The Total War series I usually play on my PC. It is an excellent series.Total War: Troy has beautiful graphics, runs even on older systems beautifully, it has a wonderful focus on gods, heroes, etc.However, the negative issues hurt... There are very limited archer units available. Not every faction has normal archers.There are also zero cavalry units present. Except for mythological units that can only be build in 3 parts of all of Greece.And... no artillery.This is unacceptable. I expect from a game with a historical theme and military composition a bit accuracy. At least as much that basic units styles in form of cavalry, artillery and archers are available, especially from a time where archery, artillery and cavalry defined warfare.Even the flags of the factions show horses.All other Total War games have cavalry units from the start, except this game with a Greek theme. I bet that Turkish Germans have been involved in the production of the game with hate for Greece.There are furthermore no trade agreements, no faction VIP's management, etc., no research, and other major issues that take any form of fun away from this game.You are overwhelmed with countless types of infantry units, but no archers and no cavalry units... and also no artillery units... *handpalm against head*Which are essential basics for a military strategic game in a setting based on this type of warfare. And yes, these essential basics that are missing ruin all the good stuff of a Greek theme, wonderful graphics, excellent gameplay mechanisms, etc.I strongly suggest to get books about Greek mythology or Homer's Iliad and Odyssey on used book shops for 2,50 GBP each and read them. This will create a proper atmosphere while you play a very nice and beautiful looking with a lot of Greek cultural elements...At the end might I definitely buy all the other DLC's in order to complete this game...I can live without artillery, but not without cavalry... That is really the main disappointment in an otherwise very atmospheric, Greek cultural and outstanding strategy game...If you love Greece, the Greek culture and can live without a basic cavalry unit... then buy it... It's worth then even at full price...

Most of the monsters you read about in Greek mythology are there, and a few not-so historical mythology units make it into the game. Want to see the Cyclops from The Odyssey fight the Minotaur? Or the Hydra fight Cerberus? This game  can do it. What's great about this game compared to TW:WH is that the monstrous units are extremely rare to come across in campaign, so when one finally appears, it's awe inspiring. If you're Total War fan, you can tell that the development team is different, based on how actions are mapped compared to the primary title. Not a huge deal, but some quality of life aspects of the UI in other Total War games are missing in this game, like using the side scroll key in the recruit agent menu. The battles are also really quick compared to other entries in the franchise, so I find myself going into slow-mo more often during battles. TLDR: Recommended if you're a fan of Total War, Greek Mythology, or Homer's stories.
