_childDocuments_.review: I've got a weird relationship with this game. I can't decide whether it's good enough a game to recommend, or a game bad enough to slam. Having played this on release for free on Epic Games, putting it down after 30 or so hours, and then forgetting about it for a few months, I hoped that with the coming of the Mythos DLC (and release on Steam) that Troy would finally become my new go-to Total War game. Alas, my hopes were dashed. . . but the game has improved a lot. :Pros: . Hands down one of the prettiest campaign settings out of any Total War series. The arid scrub lands of Attica, the forested hinterlands of Macedonia and Thrace, the mountainous regions of Anatolia, and the azure waters of the Aegean Sea are simply breath-taking. All of this is given a little bit of extra flavour in the Mythos setting, where the player can see the remnants of old Colossi, the ruins of ancient Olympian shrines, and several cool mythical creatures just chilling in the environments.. Although it's not a leaps and bounds improvement from previous titles, Troy's UI is functional and surprisingly artful. Click on a Divine Will tab, and you get a window to the Greek pantheon that looks just like those famous Greek vase painting. End turn icon is depicted a bronze shield, very thematically consistent! Building and unit icons are also on-point and pretty intuitive for the most part. These things might not seem like a big deal, but since you'll potentially be staring at these for hours it's crucial that the devs get it right, which in my opinion they did.Cons: as far as gameplay difficulty is concerned. I'll not nitpick the location of resources or special buildings, some of which are absolutely busted, but I will complain about the starting situations of some of the factions. Troy's got this current issue (has been since August 2020) where the AI aggressiveness has been dialled up to 11. Now couple this with the fact that a faction like Achilles (Pythia) is right on the doorstep of three Trojan main factions, as well as several angry barbarian minors, and you've got a recipe for frustration. Often mid-late game experience involves long periods of "whack-a-mole" where you'll constantly be chasing down the AI's half capacity trash-stacks, who for some weird reason are coded to make a beeline for your weakest settlements, rather than protecting their own or going for your closest army. For some reason also the devs included a mechanic where some buildings have a negative modifier that INCREASE the likelihood of rando factions raiding or attacking that building's home region. Who thought that would be a fun addition? Seriously.. Yes it's easier to navigate, and the biggest exploit on launch has been nerfed, but as far as balance goes it's still as aggressively nonsensical as America's foreign policy. AI will straight up ignore non-aggressive pacts and truce break if they're allied to one of your enemies. RIP Sarpedon! Agamemnon STILL has an exploit where he can vassalize the world with scummy turn-based trade deals which he can then cancel after with no reliability cost. Some AI factions will just horde resources, making them literal piggy-banks for the player. Zeus gives a massive diplomacy bonus that makes all deals a cake walk, i.e. who needs careful planning? Not that any of this matters because by turn 20-40 everything devolves into a confusing mess as the Danaans and Trojans declare war on each-other. How has this issue still persisted? Couldn't they just extend the peace until a later time then pop the cluster-cluck around turn 100 or so a-la Chaos Invasion in Warhammer?I'm spending way too much energy spewing on about this so I'll keep this section simple. Troy added a few interesting gimmicks, and a big emphasis has been added on infantry and weight classes, nonetheless the strongest units continue to be ranged and chariots for these simple reasons: 1) missile units are busted because they deal damage without taking any 2) Chariots are bent because they have zero collision and roll over units like your kid cousin rolls over his army men with his toy monster-trucks. Morale also seems to be a issue, even at higher difficulties. It's easy to inflict enough enemy losses with a few well placed units and then see the enemy army break within a few minutes.If you're a Total War fan, wait for a sale that includes all the DLCs. If you're new to the Total War franchise then you should probably do the same. You won't regret the purchase, but there are much better options on the table than A Total War Saga: Troy.

The soundtrack is subtle and I find myself enthralled by some of the hypnotic themes that play in the background while idle. _childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of Rome total war 2 and previous entries from total war... but this one... The setting, depth and detail is nice but it´s the gameplay that just falls short.Never a fan of single hero units that are stronger than entire regiments, but it´s a nice touch that you are given the choice to play "historical" in which the heroes are just part of a unit of bodyguards like generals always have been.Now the issue: The maps you fight on are incredible small and just ooze "arenaesk" out of every inch. They feel like artificially created for the sole purpose of pvp combat and are so small you constantly bounce of the borders with the camera when trying to place your troops...And balancing never seem to have been a thing that they have been bothered with at all.. the "bonuses on top of bonuses" idea might sound great but when you have an army with 5 heavy archers each with 210+ range and 150 damage each! and 60 ammo... than any fight becomes just a "machinegun the enemy down".Moral is broken to quickly and generally does it seem that any engagement is supposed to not last longer then 3 minutes... which is bad for a game like this.And large city sieges... oh boy... there are no catapults or such, and you can only climb walls with ladders... but the pathfinding is at times horrendous, when a troop is in process of climbing the ladders don´t give them any orders or half of them might take the now the gate engaging just another enemy.Also anyone interested in this title might look for a mod to nerf the turrets, they gun down your troops like machine gun emplacements. Which makes them way more dangerous as the defending army + reinforcements. Would i recommend the game? No. Probably for a new audience for those that are to impatient for the genre and want short 3 minute bashes on small maps where everyone just runs his troops into a big ball till one side wins as the other runs out of moral. For anyone who likes medieval 2, rome total war 2, attila etc... this isn´t a game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: As a major fan of Greek Mythology and having recently read the Iliad and the Odyssey as well as a previous major fan of the older total wars (RTW, M2TW and ETW) I was very much looking forward to this addition. After playing 2 hours I found the cut scenes not very captivating and cartoony in retelling the Homeric Epic.The battles are a little lack luster as in you feel its a 50/50 whether your units will win a 1 on 1 fight even if you outmatch the enemy unit, and there's no body in the units just a bit of a mosh pit in the battle compared to the long battles you know whats going on in RTW and M2TW and you know where to look to identify the major breaking point (perhaps I just prefer the old engine). It was far easier to identify what was happening in these older iterations (even if you turn all flags off). The campaign seems a bit overloaded in new things (6 different resources instead of just money - or perhaps they could have used bronze as currency) and a whole host of agents including mythological ones. It feels like the attitude from the developers "more is better" in terms of features and options has made myself feeling no single choice makes much of a difference, so end up playing 1 campaign hours reading everything, deciding and deliberating everything barely making progress and then the next campaign spamming through options and not really thinking about the consequences.Another minor criticism is that the units do not seem very diverse or believable in their appearance (lack of armour), that being said it can be incredibly difficult to create authentic looks on 1200 BC bronze age units with the lack of sources.The mythological units are pretty cool and different to me as I never got into the Warhammer games. I feel like they have missed quite a few iconic ones however such as the Chimera and Talos just to name two which already has me thinking that there will be even more DLC for more units.I do quite like the concept of the divinity table in where you can prioritise certain gods over the others for buffs and I found it fun to role play certain characters in the Iliad in their preferences for certain Gods.But when I think about M2TW the Lord of the rings mod this is a level below this personally speaking, which is a tremendous shame as I am an avid Greek Mythology fan and old (maybe ex) total war fan. With much regret, unfortunately I cannot stomach the price for this game (which I consider you need to buy the Mythos DLC to really consider buying this game - otherwise you could just as easily play one of the more historical games) in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm in two minds about this game, but after about 40 hours playing time won't recommend it. My first impressions were great, the interface is probably as polished as it's ever been and generally it's well laid out. The management side of the game is the best and the intricacies of the pantheon and the effect of religious buildings is a nice feature. I've enjoyed the battles too, there's a lot of potential and long-time fun to be had there and units generally seem more responsive than in Warhammer. Unit variety seems pretty good and all the best TW games have been fought with swords, shields, spears, bows and other pointy things. I think the setting is great, too. Troy is a great piece of mythology and the game graphics shine. Diplomacy seems fine, I haven't really played the game long enough to know if allies are really good for anything other than barriers against enemies and bartering resources. It seems to be fairly quick to load too, compared to Warhammer II at least...The problem is that the campaign seems broken, the AI factions seem to have one setting and that is to build armies and attack, or build armies and then stand aimlessly next to your settlement, not even raiding, just messing up the public order and forcing you to declare war, usually while you're tied up elsewhere. Resources appears to be another issue, while I quite liked the use of food, wood, stone, bronze and gold, it's very hard to maintain large enough armies to stay competitive with the AI, who don't appear to have any such issue. Factions of only a few settlements somehow amass 30k-40k of everything except gold, with no apparent way of building up such numbers. So for the first two games I've played at least, it's felt as if I'm basically running my armies between the four to five provinces I've managed to conquer, defending against AI throwing darts at the board.I thought Attila was one of the harder TW installments, but this feels like it's difficult for the wrong reasons. Furthermore, the game suffers from the same problem Warhammer (and some others do), which is down to a basic part of the game design; the time between turns takes extraordinarily long if you don't fast forward it, even if all factions' movement is set to Fastest. But fine that's not something you can really do much about when so many factions are included and I guess the answer is to exterminate them, it is Total War after all.tl;dr it's alright and I might still grow to love this game like many of the others, but while there's a lot of potential I'm not really enjoying it yet.**update after 95hrs played, changed to "recommended"**If you're a long-time Total War fan then I recommend buying this game on sale, get the "full edition" rather than the bare-bones version that CA loves releasing. I've only played this game with the DLC and on sale it's a good deal. If you're new to the TW series, a better entry point might be Attila or Shogun 2, unless you're in for the mythology then give this a shot. Troy is unique in the TW series (as far as I've played) in that you can get both historical and fantasy gameplay such as what Warhammer offers. Why did I change my mind? Well I persisted with the campaign I was busy with, settled into the grind that comes with TW games and changed to a more offensive stance. A big difference was settling on a cyclops island that gives a big food bonus with the appropriate building when the city reaches level five. Active bartering with allies helps to balance out the resource load and if playing as Mycenae, vassalising states further adds to resources gained per turn and eventually I got to a stage where I could command three or four medium to large armies in the 2nd quarter of the game. One of the biggest annoyances though is gold. Regions where gold is present start the game with a limited deposit, which makes sense in a way, but the problem is that the AI goes for the building that depletes it the fastest so by turn 30-40 most deposits on the map are depleted and then you only get 10% of the total gold supposedly produced per turn. Gold is obviously a rare and precious metal, but elite units and some third-tier buildings need large amounts to recruit and build, so if you didn't start with a gold producing region or capture one early on, you're in for a tough time.The game probably shines most in the battles, even though there are only two formations to choose from (melee front/missile behind and vice-versa) it wasn't much of a bother, fighting is more mobile than in some other games so commanding smaller groups around the battlefield makes up for it. The use of ambushes, skirmishes and creating cauldrons made the battles fun and kept it interesting over the different terrains. (The terrains are generally similar, but at least the maps don't repeat or didn't repeat enough for me to notice. Unlike my first experience of Warhammer II, when I stopped playing because I got bored with the same two or three maps. Luckily that was eventually sorted out.)Heroes' skill trees are also done well in this game and the usual items and retinues they can collect makes building characters more interesting. The Homeric story line is nice too, even though it's a fairly superficial layer on the campaign so don't expect too much from it. The voyages across the Aegean sea and saying prayers to Poseidon to prevent attrition is a nice touch though, so are the bonuses and mythological units that the other deities provide.  So overall this is a good Total War game. It seems fairly well optimised from a PC perspective and the UI and gameplay is fairly slick. Some TW games tend to hide information although here it seems to be where you need it. I have no doubt I'll play this game some more, but I'm not sure if it could stand next to Rome, Medieval II, Attila and Shogun 2 in the pantheon of TW greats.

_childDocuments_.review: The campaign of Troy certainly can't be played as conservatively or practically as other Total War Games. Like Achilles you have to choose Glory over a long life. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This is my new favorite Total War!After finishing 4 campaigns and playing half-way through a multiplayer campaign I can definitively say that this game is a hidden gem when it comes to the Total War series.Set during the Bronze Age and based on the Iliad & Odyssey it brings the rich story from Homer's epics and puts you in charge of one of its Heroes. Carve out a kingdom, pick your side in the Trojan War and appease the meddling Greek gods, or ignore them at your own peril.For a more traditional TW player, the game offers a Historical mode allowing you to play as you would normally. Whereas the Truth Behind the Myth mode is a nice blend of historical and mythological ideas; and the Mythological mode is, perhaps surpisingly, a lot of fun, adding more mechanics and replacing some of the units with their mythological counterparts.The strongest points of the game:- Every Hero faction plays uniquely, due to having different game mechanics. This makes every new playthrough be a refreshing endeavor.- Performance-wise the game is very stable and well optimized.- The game has an amazing art style that immerses you into the age of mystery that was the Bronze Age of the Iliad.- Resource mechanics. Having separate resources (food, wood, stone, bronze, gold) makes for more interesting decisions during gameplay.- Attention to detail. One can see that developers poured a lot of effort into the lore. I love seeing the map burning away as you explore the Aegean, the old Greek alphabet and much much more.The game is not without its issues, however.- Bugs! Unsurprisingly this game still has many bugs. I haven't encountered any blockers, however, no crashes or the like, but quite a few minor UI issues and achievement bugs.- I'd like to have a wider variety of battle maps, especially when it comes to the city maps (after a while all sieges start to look very similar).Final verdict: If you are a Total War series fan, this is a MUST BUY!PS. Do yourself a favor and watch the movie Troy before booting the game up for the first time ;).. or, even better, read the books first.

_childDocuments_.review: (TLDR): Incredibly frustrating without the right mods (see below). I wish Steam had a "neutral" recommendation because there's a lot I enjoy about this game.Each of the heroes feels suitably distinct, with interesting mechanics that had me wanting to try out different ones. Unfortunately, with a few exceptions, the legendary quests/heroic mechanics don't really change up the experience. The campaign map is beautiful, the legendary monsters are fun to hunt down and recruit, and the battles are...fine. I didn't expect overmuch from a Total War Saga game, and Troy basically checked all my boxes.Except one, where it woefully and egregiously failed.The point is to recreate the Trojan War--Greeks hurling themselves at the walls of Troy for literal decades. Fine. I get that. In practice, what you get is a malicious AI that will SPRINT across the Aegean to brutalize undefended player settlements. Does it matter that it's at war with ten other Greek factions? No. It will double-time around their cities just to raze one of yours. Building a garrison in every town mitigates this a bit, but with the auto-calc heavily favoring the AI I REALLY hope you like siege battles, because you're going to be fighting DOZENS of town defenses in a single game. (Side note: I'm not sure why every minor town is built in a crevasse--seems like that'd be bad for drainage.)Sure, you can raise a army to deal with the AI ravagers, but since settlements are so close together, that only means the AI will switch to another, less defended target. You could be literally besieging Troy and Paris/Hector will charge across the sea to raze some worthless settlements in southern Greece. The only real solution is to cheese the AI by  leaving an army in ambush stance near your most succulent settlements, which is...not fun. It got to the point where even looking at real-world maps of the Aegean made me nervous.Thankfully, there are a couple mods that help with this issue:-Double Garrison (Maximus): Does exactly what it says. Saves you from having to put garrisons buildings in every settlement and forces the AI to actually marshal a credible invasion force to threaten your lands. That, or besiege your settlements, which gives you a turn or two to respond. Of course, this makes it harder to take AI settlements as well--but, I mean, the Iliad is LITERALLY about an extended siege, so that tracks.-Cataph's Unforced March: Tweaks the double-time mechanic so it adds only 20% to movement--which means you can actually see the invasion forces coming (mostly) and move your armies in response. It helps a bit, but doesn't really mitigate the AI dodging along the Grecian coast to try and outmaneuver your defenses.These two mods changed a fundamentally frustrating experience into a genuinely fun game. I was able to send my armies abroad without having to worry about wave after wave AFTER WAVE of AI stacks ignoring my allies to seek out the weak points in my defense.There's a lot to commend about Troy. Overall, I would recommend the game--if you're a TW fan and can get it on sale. Once I'd dealt with the glaring AI problem, it kept me pretty engaged.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, Ive been a huge fan of the Total War series for over 6 years now and played multiple titles like Shogun II, Rome II, Attila, Thrones Of Britannia and now Troy. After a complete playthrough of the HISTORICAL CAMPAIGN, I think that Troy is the worst of all Total War titles and I am quite unhappy with the purchase. But what exactly is it that makes Troy so unworthy of a Total War title? I'll start with the good innovations and move over to the bad ones:1. Graphics are crisp and clear and really look amazing if you can afford to play at a high resolution with everything on Ultra or even Extreme. 2. I like the introduction of ressources. I think that it helps deepening immersion.3. I really like the historical theme with all the heroes, the mythical references and legends around.4. Diplomacy was quite to my liking with the ability to single barter ressources and to trade regions and stuff. As sad as it is, this is all I like about the game.What Troy makes a bad game in my opinion:1. The most terrible factor is definitely the lack of battle complexity. Battles always have been a key element of the Total War titles and this is definitelöy the worst title concerning this fact.You cant have formations to line up your soldiers, everything looks really untidy, you cant form shieldwalls to protect your soldiers from missiles, you cant improve your charge with abilities, nor anything other complexity enhancing elements are available. Only your hero has abilites which he can use from time to time, e.g. if his battle rage has built up enough to use some of them, Since heroes end up going down quite easy when caught in the fray, you dont get that much out of their abilities, since their either too far away from the soldiers or to close and he'll get slaughtered before being effective. 2. Cavalry is completely gone. The only way to have some mounts is by using chariots, which are a total desaster, since theyre being successfully chased by mere footsoldiers and then slaughtered. This was actually one of the most depressing factors for me about this game.3. Many buildings in your provincial capital almost make no sense and/ or have very little effects.4. The most absurd element though is the artificially boosted strength of the Trojan forces, when you reach their homeland. Not only are most garrisons as strong as a full stack of your own 20 unity army, the elite stack of Hectors army beats the ♥♥♥♥ out of every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ army you can build up. The worst of their units are the Trojan Princes, who slaughter every highly armored stack of yours from miles away, with no cavalry being able to shut them down, you'll simply bet butchered by them. I only managed to defeat them, cause I was able to starve their army after taking all of their food producing towns.All in all, I wouldnt recommend this game, if you'd have to buy it. For free it might give you a worthwile pasttime activity of about 40 hours playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: A Total War Saga: TROY is a really interesting testing ground for Creative Assembly's ideas for the future of the series and has tons of engaging content. However, it's definitely got issues.Cons:1. The AI. Non-playable faction AI is essentially brain dead on lower difficulties while on higher difficulties, EVERYBODY is extremely aggressive. They will cross seas, mountains, forests and rivers just to raze your tier 1 settlement on turn 10. They will sometimes declare war on you out of nowhere, immediately sue for peace or ask for ridiculous concessions over something trivial.2. Resource balancing. I really love the idea of having different types of resources and that they're weighted differently. But in the course of an average game, the same situation always crops up: everyone gets an extreme surplus of food, you're starved for wood in the early game and stone in the mid game, gold is always at a premium and very difficult to find and bronze severely caps how many elite units you can field. Food is essentially worthless while every other resource, depending on the stage of the game, is both difficult to maintain and desirable to obtain. You can counter this with smart choices in your tech research and expansion but there's just something missing here.3. Unit balancing. It's nowhere near as bad when I played Troy back on the Epic Games Store when it first came out but there are certain army combos that are essentially unbeatable against 90% of what the AI will field against you. Also, while I love the idea of singe entity hero units, having these guys capable of tanking 2-3 enemy regiments (hundreds of soldiers) is both hilarious and dumb.4. Epic Missions, basically quests, can have some extremely inconvenient tasks to accomplish whether they be conquering a settlement on the other side of the world or making friends with an enemy who you've been fighting for 30 turns now.5. Historical mode is a joke. It has basically no content and is undoubtedly the worst way to experience this game.6. The game doesn't have a huge amount of replayability because there aren't that many factions and certain ones, like Sparta, just aren't that fun to play IMO.Pros:1. Bronze Age! The setting is extremely underrepresented in games and media and is a treasure trove of awesomeness. I hope we'll be seeing further expansions to the setting like the Sea Peoples or at least mercenary Hittite units.2. UI, graphics, art design and music is incredible. The stylized Greek ceramic drawings, the genuinely memorable tracks and the world and battle maps in Mythological mode especially is stellar!3. Epic Missions, while still having issues as stated in the Cons section, is a great way to learn of the history and drama of the Trojan War. I personally found it very immersive and interesting.4. I really like how the emphasis on infantry doesn't detract from a diverse battle experience. Tall grass, forests and bodies of water all have important tactical aspects and your units can have some real nuance. Too bad that in the late game, I was always fielding just one or two types of min-maxed armies.5. Mythological mode is great! The original Truth behind the Myth mode just pales in comparison and I'm kinda upset that it took them an entire year to realize that going full mythological was always the right way to go.6. Diplomacy is streamlined and very easy to use. While it doesn't reach the complexity of Three Kingdoms, it puts the Warhammer titles to shame.Conclusion:All in all, I'm a fan of this game and I think it gets a lot of undeserved hate both for being an Epic exclusive for a while and for being a Saga title. And while it's not perfect, it certainly has a lot of fun and interesting elements to it that anyone interested in the Bronze Age, the Trojan War, the RTS genre and the recent Total War games would enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a giant problem: Player agency. This game doesn't want to be played by you and it makes that perfectly clear. You buy it - and then you rarely get the chance to play it. Not because of bugs. Not because of difficulty. But because, and I am pretty sure about this, the AI is programmed to not let you play this game. The AI will do everything to get you as player out of the game as soon as possible, no matter if it makes sense.The anti-player bias of Warhammer III is bad. But it's nothing compared to this game.You can play this game like any other Total War game. Until the "Antagonist" feature kicks in. After the game reveals your antagonist, all factions that are against you get stronger and they don't care for anything else but you anymore. 50 to 60 armies when you cna field two is not rare in my games.And to make matters worse: All factions of the cultures you chose, seem to be purposefully programmed to lose all kind of AI programming. Not sure about that, but it seems so.Example: I played as Ajax and had a good few provinces built up as the greeks decided to go to war with Troy. I accepted aaaand - the Greeks suddenly stop all their armies. No matter what they did, they come back and sit in their cities while not three roudns later, a giant invasion force of everything that had the smallest connection to Troy came and wiped the floor with me. They left everyone else (who were, as said, blissfully unaware of their own existnce) alone. It didn't take long till that game was over.I tried Agamemnon. Same thing happened.I tried Odysseus. Sad that you can't built buildings. Nice units, though. And after same time, the same thing happened.I tried Achilles. The same.Only good thing where Memnon and Rhesos. And they were a DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to give this one a proper review as I think it's pretty maligned and - for a long-time Total War fan (played 'em all since Rome 1) who put off playing it - I don't think its low review score is helpful for players in 2024.Short Review: This game is great fun, the most fun I've had with a TW since Warhammer 1, if not Fall of the Samurai. That doesn't necessarily mean it's the best (the games are so complex that singe playthroughs can vary a lot in fun factor for all sorts of reasons) but it's definitely a game I would enthusiastically recommend.Long review:I played as Diomedes, with the Mythos DLC. Reviewing this game kind of comes down to two questions: is it good (yes), and should I play this over other TW games (maybe). If, like me, you're happy to play ALL the TW games then no need to answer the second one. If you're coming in fresh and want to prioritise, you could do a lot worse than Troy.Pros:It's Total War - still the first, last and only real name in full-size strategic and realistic tactical historical(ish) wargames. There hasn't been a Total War I haven't enjoyed and every one of them (including this one) is a recommend from me. It's a worthy addition with lots of unique mechanics and I'd recommend it to anyone interested in expanding the number they've played.Greek Mythology is great, although you'll need Mythos to really enjoy it.I like the rarity of cavalry, it makes the battles more tactically interesting and, in the early game at least, makes every remotely fast unit very valuable.The battle AI is, based on my experience, relatively strong - certainly better than Warhammer 2.I like the new resource system (food/wood/stone/bronze/gold rather than just money), it makes trade meaningful for once, distinguishes between settlements (aka targets) in a single and simple way, and reduces (although doesn't eliminate) the usual choice between building armies and developing economy.Diplomacy is pretty good (for a TW game at least).Cons:I have nitpicks but they don't affect my overall recommendation and are mostly about the religion system and agents.FMMV:I can see why some people might not like the new resource system as it removes the choice between army and economy - basically the same reason I like it.I'm not really sure what the criteria of a 'Saga' game is - this was still a ~90hr experience to complete the campaign.The Minotaur in the room:A lot of the criticism this game gets is about making a game about Greek Mythology without any Myths in it. It was a pretty baffling decision and then charging extra for the Mythos DLC to have those elements that should've been in the game from the start is pretty rubbish. But, in 2024 with the game price hugely reduced, does that make it a bad game that should get a thumbs down on Steam? Of course not. If you like TW, you'll like this - it's a further refinement of the gameplay and it's a lot of fun.Conclusion:If you're fresh to the series looking for  way in, as a whole package it's probably not as good as Warhammer (1, ME or IE) or 3 Kingdoms (although I felt 3K would be very intimidating for new players). That still puts it in the top three for the series for me to play in 2024.

_childDocuments_.review: To be perfectly honest, I held out on purchasing this game for a while in anticipation of it's mediocrity and I'm sorry to say, that my preconceived prejudice was confirmed. Whilst not a terrible entry to the total war series, this game unfortunately is just mediocre and frankly forgettable. Whilst the artistic design is impressive, this game suffers from a queue of poorly thought out mechanical features which goes out the door and around the corner, both on the battle field and the campaign map.  Due to the absence of cavalry and artillery units, the battles are merely drawn out melee slogs, with grand strategic maneuvers being almost pointless, thus rendering the battles laborious and frankly boring. The campaign also suffers from a terrible economic system which can be very easily exploited and cheesed to death, with an absence of political systems and a diplomacy system which is also highly exploitable,  owing to the game's economics. There is also a distinct lack of playable factions, with those that are playable being virtual carbon copies of each other, in terms of their units and settlement management. The feature of mythology and mythological units in this game may bring a degree of elevation for some players (primarily those who play war hammer TW), but it is an acquired taste and for the total war enthusiast invested in historical themes, this unique feature won't do much for you. I'm also saddened to say that upon recent first glimpses of the up and coming Pharaoh entry, it would appear to be little more than a copy of Troy, both in design and overall game mechanics. I'm not holding my breathe...

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Troy is a great Total War game that focuses on infantry and the titular war. Each faction is pretty unique and plays differently than the others. Definitely a buy.  8/10Has some great moments during the game; voice acting is also on top. 8/10As the years go by, Total War just keeps getting better, and with Troy you can see siege battles and settlements in all their glory; among other things.  8.5/10Combat is pretty solid, seriously improved with terrain and unit class playing a bigger role than previous games; even more so because of most of it focusing on infantry. Settlement management works the same. Each faction has its own units, that is a big plus and each faction has interesting and different gameplay styles.Regarding the three campaigns, I have no issue between a fully historical, in-between or mythical campaign; in fact, I enjoy that since it gives the campaign a fresh take when you play them.The biggest downside for me is that the research tree is the same for all factions. I’d love some variety there or at least some differences in some technologies.  8/10While the general story is the same for all factions, their epic mission or what leads to the Homeric victory is usually very interesting and tells the story of the faction or character. They are really enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended with reservations.Enjoying the game so far, added Ajax DLC whilst on offer to give more characters to the game. I do enjoy the Ancient periods and generally play the sagas on historical mode. If I want monsters and unbeatable generals I will play Warhammer. Fed up with heroes destroying my army single handed in Three Kingdoms..Upsides? nice graphics and soundtrack which doesn't grate on you after a few minutes. Tech trees quite clear and understandable to use. No problems with battles as the variety of units available without using expensive specialist units makes for a effective army (whopped AI every out of settlement battle so far and ambushed AI in two settlement battles)  Six to eight shield units will give you an unbeatable army in attack or defence (as long as you don't screw up, keep 'em together)Downsides?Map doesn't expand to an overview or I can't find the icon. Very cluttered when trying to find other factions or pathways, No wonder Odysseus took ten years to get home! I haven't managed to even contemplate attacking Troy as I am busy trying to expand my faction to gather resources to support three armies. Hector seems to roam the islands at will attacking different factions, I thought he would be busy defending Troy??You have to attack a faction to gain a needed resource held by one of its settlements, trade doesn't seem to work nor does non-aggression pacts with the AI. Distant factions declare war for no apparent reason then will make peace two turns later - unsure why this was built into the game as it is about as useful as a chocolate tea-pot. Agree that the AI can support armies without any settlements remaining is uneven and annoying, best bet is to totally destroy the faction!In all with the lowered price not a bad buy, maybe Pharaoh when it is on offer. Please can we have a Genghis Khan game, with a bit of thought it would actually make a great saga game.2nd review - well playing as Agamemnon is a non-starter..His brother has mopped up all the surrounding settlements and resources. Any attempt at conquering an isolated settlement/faction results in five or six factions declaring war instantly and the remaining five turns (I gave up after five) were spent in repulsing enemy armies...so much for the "historical" alliance setting sail for Troy. Trying Achilles but although enlarging my territory am now under attack from four enemy factions, armies invading all over my territory (how the h*** can the Amazons pop up in the middle of my territory??) No-one even near willing to sign an non-agression, defensive or military treaty...an there's me thinking Achilles was vital for the assault on Troy!Ajax DLC was on offer and adding this gives about the most satisfaction although treaties are still nigh on impossible. My copy of Homer must be completely different to that of the developers...

_childDocuments_.review: Total War Troy is a perfect example of why Steam needs neutral review option. For every plus this game has it has an equal negative quality. I'll hit a few of each, but try to keep this brief.First the positives, region trading, no unit caps, no needless timers, and best of all, 5 resource types make for a much more interesting and fun play through of the world map that most other total war games. I also found the Mythos DLC pretty fun, but that's extra cost to play, so keep that in mind.And the negatives, The big one is a complete failure to recreate the Trojan war. CA, in a bid to make the game more open ended, doesn't have a lot of alliances or pacts at the start of the game, and thus, in all my play time, I have never once seen Troy, Paris and Hector, at war with all of the factions they are supposed to be at war with. How irritating is that? And worst of all, the AI will almost never join a war against one of the main factions, so you can't even work around it. And because of the "Join War" BS, the AI will constantly join the war against just you, avoiding any allies you have. Basically the entire diplomacy system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up beyond repair. Also, the usual anti-player bias is back. AI will focus on you to the exclusion of rational choices most of the time. AI behind your line, hitting a settlement, then forced marching away from all your armies is back (never left without modders, I never understand how CA keeps messing this one up).To sum up, I hope they take the good from this and more forward, but the diplomacy system is so broken it's hard to find the fun in the campaign even though individual battles are pretty fun. Too bad CA put out half a game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is weird, in a very bad way.It has some really nice features like trading for specific resources and locations that produce those resources, unit maintenance is also split across 4 different resource types, so securing a supply and using it wisely is key.A big improvement for me is the averaged melee damage, similar to how ranged damage is averaged over 10 seconds in Warhammer.That's something desperately needed because without easily accessible information on attack speed it's impossible to accurately access its true damage output.But it inherits all the fault that Warhammer has, the unit responsiveness issues have never felt worse, and the DELAY for any action is absolutely massive, ESPECIALLY ranged units that will casually stroll into their neat little formation in the middle of a desperate fight because their IQ will not allow them to fire even 1 pixel away from their designated grid formation.The game also shares many faults of Thrones of Britania, the engine is simply unable to provide good historical gameplay, no formation, no execution of running enemies with the backs turned, a very limited firing arc for ranged units, and weird and unrealistic hiding mechanics.It lacks the redeeming factor of Warhammer; the massive, MASSIVE unit variety and diverse faction play styles, even Britania managed to have some unit variety between its factions.At the very least we're back to uncapped unit recruitment and no arbitrary timers...I don't want this review to drag on too much but this game is just... a bad version of one faction in Warhammer, painted onto a single map and forced to fight itself for pretty much the entire game, with almost no truly unique gameplay to units exist in the different factions and when they do, they are either completely pointless or overpowered, rarely in between.Get Warhammer, or even better, get Warhammer 2 with its QoL upgrades and faction reworks.This game is nothing but a bone poked at people like me who are desperate for a good historical game, desperate, but not enough to be grateful for this mess of a game. IT'S NOT WORTH YOUR MONEY.and it defiantly wasn't worth mine even at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried really hard to like this game but the lack of walls on minor settlements plus administration costs of having multiple armies, plus other anti-snowball mechanics just really turns the campaigns into a slow grindy slog. Diplomacy is possibly the worst I have seen in the series with war declarations coming out of nowhere. The focus on different resources does not add anything to the game except being starved for different resources at different times and being spammed by the various AI for trade requests every time you click the end turn button.The AI also seems to really struggle with settlement and fortifications, sadly the campaign cheating seems to be at its most apparent yet. With the AI managing to spam multiple resource intensive armies while they only have a single province while the player often ends up struggling with gigantic administration costs.The administration costs themselves feel like unnecessary padding put into the game only to inhibit the player at the expense of the player and affecting only the player, leading to campaigns to feel much more bloated and drawn out. I would strongly suggest to the developers to reduce the administration costs or make them a toggleable option.  There are some good things here the mythos setting is great and the art direction fantastic, but too much of the game is bogged down in tedium and padding.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad it's finally on Steam, where I can get all the DLCs and enjoy the game fully. By the end of it, there was no corner of the map unconquered and Achilles has transcented as a literal immortal god (being max level and with the best items) defeating entire armies on his own.The Steam release brings quite a lot QoL improvements and most importantly the Mythos DLC, where CA decides to go full mythological and bring fresh life and replyability into the game. I've started a new campaign as Paris and can't wait to see all differences in abilities and units in Mythos from my original playthrough!Also lets not forget the game just looks beautiful, has nailed that 'bronze age feeling' with an amazing art style. _childDocuments_.review: Pleasantly surprised by this game. I never expect much from a Total War SAGA game, they always have issues (I don't consider Fall of the Samurai a SAGA game). They're usually a buggy mess, have bad gameplay mechanics or are boring. But Troy feels different and fun.-It's a beautiful game with a great soundtrack-Despite the setting, the factions feel very unique, each with their own mechanics and special units. We've come a long way from the basic spearmannii vs spearmannii battles.-The Homeric storyline missions give each faction their own direction and role to play in the Trojan war. You have proper victory conditions that are more than just painting the map.-Probably the best battlemaps I've seen in a long time.-The new administration system that replaces the old supply mechanics of Warhammer. Now you actually have a viable choice between multiple low tier armies or 1 doomstack, without gimping yourself with massively increased unit upkeep.-The use of multiple resources like food, wood, bronze,... means you no longer have to choose between building your settlement or building your army. You can also focus on building a lot of 1 resources and trading it with the AI for whatever else you need.-The EGS exclusivity put me off from buying it initially. I hope this is not a trend that will continue.-You will fight A LOT of battles. The entire game is basically Realm Divide from Shogun 2. Your massive alliance vs the entire enemy alliance. Lots of enemies means lots of enemy armies that are focused on taking out the player. You have to play slow and smart or you're going to be playing a lot of whack-a-mole deep inside your own territory.-Auto-resolve is absolute garbage and heavily skewed against the player. Even with top tier armies facing off against militia half-stacks, the auto-resolve will completely kill off several units. This means you have to fight a lot of very trivial and boring fights. I remember a battle that would supposedly completely kill 8 of my top tier infantry units in auto-resolve. So I just put them all with their backs to the enemy and went afk. I won the battle with less than 50 casualties out of 2000. It's a solid game, with some issues and annoyances. Def worth a buy, especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent Total War game. I had some fun with it, I like the era, and adding the proper mythology stuff certainly helped. But the battles feel terrible. It's buggy. Ranged units don't shoot because they get stuck in a movement command even though none of them are moving, pathfinding is worse than usual, it just feels like you barely have any control over your army. Also CA asked us, paying customers to check our privileges. Since I think it's my RIGHT and not a PRIVILEGE to criticize a product I purchased with my own money, here is my review: the company is in the gutters, you shouldn't support them. It just sours the gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: Great campaign- good alliance and resource systems. The same for their last 3 historical titles : boring, blob battles with little unit variety. It is honestly puzzling that CA lacks the basic analytic abilities to understand why their games get mixed reviews since Attila. The battles are just not fun despite really interesting maps. There is very little need for tactics or strategy, just mash everyone together. :( There are also broken systems that have not been fixed- like enemy unit breaking through your units just to turn around and back charge your units (like wtf is that ♥♥♥♥?). It is clear they are desperately trying to bridge the gap between Warhammer and their historical fans, ruining the game. The game is not warhammer enough for those fans, but ruined for historical fans...hence the heroes, blob battles, "magic".
_childDocuments_.name: A Total War Saga: TROY

_childDocuments_.review: This total war game is very atmospherical and nicely designed. the battle maps are awsome. The new trade system is quite interesting. Heroes and units have been well designed too. As bronze age units show  an inherent lack of variety, Ca did a pretty good job at diversifying the infantry. Unfortunatly,  the campaign is flawed beyond repair. Because the greek world more or less divides into two super coalitions, you ll be forced to pick a side whatever the faction you play. As a result, every campaign just play the same. At turn 30+, dozen of stacks wil converge to the player faction and you will have to fight endless battles while advancing toward your objectives.The replayability is thus very poor...

detailed_description: TEST YOURSELF AGAINST CAPITALISM JOIN US ON DISCORD About the Game Jack Move is a fresh take on turn based Japanese style RPG’s. Promising a unique blend of gritty cyberpunk storytelling, turn-based battles, and beautiful modern pixel art. Take on the role of Noa Solares: An up-and-coming vigilante hacker from Bright Town. When the overreaching mega-corporation Monomind, kidnaps Abner, her estranged father, Noa has no choice but to get him back, before it's too late. Why is Abner researching digitised consciousness? And what does Monomind want to do with it? Noa won't be alone on her journey. She'll be helped out by her best friend and tactical planner, Ryder, as well as her Martini drinking uncle and ex-corporate spy, Guin Blakely. Battle Noa’s foes in the unique single-party-member turn-based battle system, featuring beautiful animation and tactical gameplay. Customise the software of your Cyber Deck to switch roles mid-battle, balancing offense, defense, and buffs. Choosing which software you load during battle is the key to victory! Hardware upgrades can help boost your stats, increase the amount of software you can install or give Noa extra abilities. Gorgeous “Hi-Bit” pixel art inspired by retro RPGs and enhanced with modern techniques. Battle your foes in cyberspace. Take them down using a multitude of sweet hacking software. Explore the dangerous world of Monocity One and takedown Monomind, the evil mega-corporation that controls it. Play as Noa Solares, a sassy hacker out to save her father and the world. Fight your way through dungeons filled with all sorts of cyberpunk villany. Street punks, gangsters, corporate militia and horrific cyber-experiments-gone-wrong will all be vying to take you down! Bite size 7-10 hour campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: 8.1h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. No. No. is a turn-based RPG game with a hacking theme. You won't do any hacking at all, although there are some computer-related terminologies like installing programs and making sure you can fit your programs with the amount of RAM that you have.- Unique, simple-to-learn gameplay- Customize the encounter rate as you like- You need to talk to everyone to get and finish sidequestsIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 looks good with its pixelated visuals. The game tries to portray its hacking theme well into the environment, making the internet UI look a bit blurred while the real world looks clearer. I also liked how the buildings were designed. Each building was given enough care to make them look distinct from each other, in a style that blends well into the theme that was set up for each area.I found the story to be weak. The dialogue might be clever, trying to use hacking-related words as swear words, but the main plot is lackluster. Moreover, the same can be said for the ending, making the journey to be disappointing They seem to talk about a big, evil plan, making it seem as if there is a threat that might destroy the whole world, although it then being scaled down and toned down into a simple case. I know the developer tries to tell that people have motives to do things, but I don't think it's presented well enough to make it captivating. is a turn-based game. You can explore a dungeon, where you can set the encounter rate yourself. Fighting an enemy can be done just like other turn-based games, except that you can accumulate a Jack Move meter whenever you are hitting or getting hit by an enemy. Having a full bar means that you can do a Jack Move, a move that can hit all enemies with bigger damage. It's such a convenient move, especially in the early game since you don't have to use any MP for it.You are being forced to use skills. The skills that you can use depend on the programs that you can install, which are limited by the number of RAM that you have. Better programs will have a higher RAM, although they also have some level requirements to install. That's mostly not an issue, though. The issue mostly lies in the limited number of RAM that you have, even after you upgraded it to the max. That and the fact that you have to use MP whenever you use a skill or have to deal with a very weak normal attack.Skills are mostly just a way to implement the rock-paper-scissors mechanic on the enemy. Most enemies are weak to one element and strong to one element, forcing you to use the right skill to kill them. Using a skill several times will increase its experience, which will lead to higher damage whenever it is being leveled up. I enjoyed the skill level-up mechanic here - it encourages me to keep on using different skills.That being said, it's easy to get over-leveled. I turned the random encounter rate to the highest one because I wanted to level up my skill, and I didn't notice that I was several levels higher than the recommended level by the time I reached the final dungeon. I ended up deciding to skip the entire dungeon completely with no encounter rate, and just as I expected, I managed to kill the boss at that level. However, I found that it's hard to level up your skills to the max; even with all of those levels, I still haven't managed to level up all of my end-game skills to the max.One thing that intrigued me when I played this game is the way the NPC talks. They always have a new dialogue after almost every major event, especially at the beginning of the game. Sometimes, I even find it to be annoying whenever I want to continue the story, especially since people might give you a side quest. It's impossible to distinguish between the two, although luckily, the game gives an indicator whenever you already read the dialogue with that person. Still, it can take a long time to explore the whole area to check if there's a new quest, though, especially when you unlock the biggest town in the game that has so many people in it.I finished the game in 8.1h. The game is easy; you can just grind if you are having trouble with it. Moreover, there is an overpowered item that can make sweeping random enemies easier if you are having trouble with the numbers.However, I don't like the fact that you can't recover MP freely in battle. Leveling up might recover it and I was grateful for it, but there are times, especially in the early game, where I had to go back and forth between areas just to recover my MP to be able to continue exploring the area. is an okay turn-based game. The story is weak, but I enjoyed the gameplay. It was fun to level up your skills, and although it takes a long time to do that, it still manages to hook me up. That being said, those who don't like grinding might find the game flat, especially since there isn't much that the game can offer gameplay-wise. It's a straightforward game that can be finished quickly with unique, leveling-up gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Context: Completed game after about ~9 hours. Game looks good and soundtrack is decent, but that's really all there is to compliment. Story is cliche story beat after cliche story beat, battle system is shallow and full of mechanics/abilities that serve to do nothing but bloat the number of "abilities you could use but never will". There was not a single fight in the game that could not be resolved by "spam the ability target is weak to and heal after you get hit a bunch". The side content is middling and I found myself skipping side quests after consistently being rewarded with a handful of easily purchasable restoration items. The default encounter rate is VERY high, but the game allows you to adjust or completely turn off encounters.This feels very much like a (admittedly with incredible potential!) proof-of-concept release rather than a game I feel good about spending $20 on. At risk of being contrarian, I was very surprised to see the large number of reviews praising the story and gameplay. Some reviews highlight "build customization" and "unique battle system" but I just can't see it. You are in an area with enemies weak to wetware -> you equip your strongest wetware attack and a healing spell, and completely roll through the area. There's no point to debuffs or buffs as enemies generally die in ~2 attacks. It is worth mentioning the spell animations are VERY cool.Despite my generally negative take on the game, I would love to see what comes next from this developer if it's given a little more time in the oven.

_childDocuments_.review: 1 week before release i played the demo, it was a 20 minutes demo that was very underwhelming, but i still thought i should give the game a chance to see if it gets better later on.It doesn't.So the first thing i read about this game in the embed of the steam link was "a fresh take on the jrpg genre", and its probably the biggest problem of the game. It is really the most basic, mediocre turn base combat you can find.Turn base combat, rock paper scissor elemental types plus physical, materia base skills with few spots (i had only 4 skills activated),  no gear, no party. Does that sound like a fresh take to you?So if the gameplay is so barebones it means is at least hard right? Well no, it is basic and easy. The start is easy, in the mid part they blow up the HP of enemies so you understand you should buy new skills, and once you do it the game is easy again. Mob enemies are generally harder than bosses because you are 1vs3 most of the time, while in bosses you can just debuff it and make it slow, while you have 2 turns to spam healings and hitting. There also some questionable decisions on the minor mechanics of the combat system but i don't think they matter (see some paragraphs below)Now here is what is really the "fresh take": the setting being cyberpunk. Everything is written with tech terminology. The mana is called data, block and delay turn is called cache, melee combat is called hack? some of the terms don't even make sense of what they actually do. Also because we obviously live in a technological society we have people called "V-sync" or "Nullpointer", expresions like "Digits!" or "Oh my grind!", you know, normal behaviour if you ask me.The story is pretty standard for a futuristic setting, it wasn't bad but also it wasn't good, pretty normal.The artstyle is cool, the music is generally cool, which i think its why most people would don't mind the boring gameplay and will just play for the story, which is also present in the game itself because you have options to either skip every random encounter (yeah we have those here) or to insta win every battle when you want it.So if you want to try this game because of the "fresh take in the jrpg genre" you will be disappointed, if you have played jrpgs before there is nothing new in this game, you have already played it before.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: To start with, I cannot, in good conscience, call this a  game.Still, it leaves me underwhelmed, and not even because it's short. It's just not living up to the promise on the cover. It is billed as a JRPG, but mostly borrows traits from them without actually making sure they work well together. The cyberpunk plot is not really  but is nothing new nor original, nor really brilliantly executed. More importantly, the combat system doesn't really go well with it, it just feels silly. Boss battles are a long, drawn out,  slog, especially the final boss, which rehashes every other boss battle... multiple times... yes, seriously.The artwork is cute, the NPCs floating around always have something fresh to say and their own storylines, the side quests are all tied together, but in the end , this just doesn't make a good enough game for me to enjoy it.Which is honestly a crying shame, I was hoping to like this a lot more than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a fan of JRPGs and Cyberpunk, I want to love this game, but I can't.From a gameplay perspective, this is basically just an extremely simplistic "fantasy" combat system, with a superficial cyberpunk coat of paint. You spend you "data" to "execute" "software" to heal your character, and the "data" only comes back when you rest or use specific items. That this is obviously just magic thrown into a world without magic kind of makes it throw you out of the experience. Beyond that, the combat is extremely simplistic. You only have 1 party member, and all but maybe 2 boss fights boil down to "hit the enemy until you need to heal, then heal". There are a few buff/debuff/status spells, but they don't seem worth bothering with except in those maybe 2 fights.From a story perspective, the game can't decide if it's a goofy comedy or a somber reflection of the pain of seeing your loved ones die. The story is at its best when it's the latter, but those more somber story moments feel so rushed and so infrequent that they are more disorienting than impactful when they pop up. Much more of the the dialog is devoted to really terrible technology puns like "chip-squeak." It feels like the developers didn't have the confidence to tell the story they really wanted, so it ends up drowned out in the not-so-good humor. There are actually some interesting ideas in the story, and a few good twists in the later plot, but they come at you so fast and so briefly that they feel surreal.All that said, there is a lot going for this game, the visuals and music are mostly pretty good, and it feels like there is a real story buried in this. I'm hoping the developers can learn from this to fix the gameplay in whatever they do next, and have the confidence to really tell a story.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine hours... Seriously? This game is only nine hours long? This might've been the dealbreaker for me if I didn't actually enjoy the game. When I checked out the Shop for the first few hours I thought, oh, maybe when we get to MonoHQ the world is REALLY going to open up, and I'll get to buy new Decks, new Software, and new Hardware! Checking the achievements, I've only unlocked like 4 out of 13 of them. I'm sure there are more content and more levels down the line! Turns out I was wrong. Some Pokemon fangames probably have longer total content on their third/0.3 update. Words could not describe my disappointment when I blazed through the rest of the achievements in the last 4 hours. And it only took 9 hours because the final boss bugged like hell on me and I spent almost an hour trying to beat it. Like wow.The maps aren't particularly varied, but I feel like there could definitely have been so much more sidequests and more visiting old maps. There are SO. MANY. interesting characters in the story and the large majority of them don't even get a sidequest. Right now, it really feels like the game is the FIRST arc of a long series or the first 3 chapters of an 12-chapter long game.Gameplay was great, mind you. If it wasn't I absolutely would've put up a not recommended. Music was really great, pixel art looks fantastic (though the constant "mini screenshake" when moving around is a tad disorienting), and combat was really stylish. But all these positives just barely edges out the big negative that is IT'S JUST TOO SHORT MAN! There's not even an ominous after-credits epilogue or something like come on!

_childDocuments_.review: Steam Deck Performance - 10/10PC Performance - 10/10 Gameplay - 7/10 Graphics - 9.5/10Style & Sound - 9/10Story - 7/10A absolutely stylish romp through a neon arcade Cyberpunk world with a turn-based JRPG style twist.This game simply oozes with style from every point, graphics and animations for its 2D style are absolutely top notch for this type of game.  Gameplay wise its a JRPG style game through and through, with turn based combat and a rock-paper-scissors style of weakness vs defence that you'd be right at home with if you've played things like Pokemon or Final Fantasy, except all the moves and customisation come from your Cyber Deck and your hacking programs. Very unique take.  Music is very good here and stands out as a high point, unfortunately though there are only a handful of musical tracks so it does get a bit repetitive, luckily the tracks there are excellent so it never feels annoying. Story wise the game is pretty easy to follow and pretty good. I think the story gets a bit -too- silly sometimes, I  realise this is an intentional choice by the developer but there are certainly a few moments where I found myself rolling my eyes a bit at some of the story takes and silly dialogue.  Overall though it is a decently well written and easy to follow story that seems to make sense and come together well early on without feeling like it drags or feels grindy. Definitely a recommend for fans of 2D JRPG's and Cyberpunk.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Jack Move as soon as it came out, and only just got the chance to play it. To a degree more than less, I like it, but as of about 10 minutes ago, I decided not to finish it.Overall I found the game with pluses and negatives. The early game is quite nice with good enemies and bosses, while the late game I feel it notches it up too high, with some common enemies literally becoming their own bosses. The ram function makes your playthrough unique, but the slot limitation makes it difficult to use around half of the software, and hardware accessories feels limited and underwhelming. Combat isn't unenjoyable, it's just a little tedious and limitingThe story itself is pretty basic, with some nice touches like the billboard questline. Graphically, the game is nice with a lot of neon light personality, although i'd gripe that game banner Noa, Animation Noa, and game Noa are 3 completely different character designs, and personally I just feel that game Noa's design falls the flattest with the bob hair, while the banner Noa, jacket, flowing hair in the wild and all, has so much personality in design that just doesn't exist anywhere in the game. Although crude to say, I admit I loaded the game for the first time, looked at Noa, and my first reaction was "uhh..that's it?"I persevered and got quite far I believe, but admittedly I stopped. Had the game flowed fine, i'd probably be at the credits now and considering fan art, but I resigned to never finishing it after, during one of the longer bosses within the game, I got stuck within a menu changing my software, and for about 10 minutes, mid-boss, I couldn't exit the menu until I ctrl+alt+del'd the game, and this was not the first time either. The menus just either are a nightmare to navigate on occasion, or they bug out and remove the option to exit them, when i've changed stuff in the menu multiple times over throughout the game no problem, but a magical moment decides "no, you're locked in here now". Might get it in your playthrough, might not, but you'll definitely see the npc's that spawn in completely different locations, that start walking and clip through entire walls of the map just to get back to their original spot. Why they do this I have NO idea.I want to like Jack Move, I really do, the initial presentation is great, and I don't mind that it's short. Even though the enemy balancing falls hard at the end, the combat has great visuals and overall it's a good idea with a lot of potential. It just has a number of issues that make me scream. Metaphorically, It's a balloon of your favourite food. Looks great initially, deflates once you pop your fork into it, but there's enough real chocolate sauce over it to see you through to the end, if you want to. I just don't want to redo an entire boss due to a "twice in 5 hours" supposed menu glitch.

_childDocuments_.review: First thing you should do is not to think this would be a JRPG genre game or any of the movies / characters design you see on the store page would be present inside the game.Saying that, the game is pretty okay adventure with nice atmosphere, good music and some funny jokes here in there.Has no replay value, not challenging but makes a nice title for kids.Narrative is nice yet plot is pretty much naive.In general I would recommend this if you prefer some slow passed cute adventure games.

_childDocuments_.review: Fans of the turn-based RPG genre tend to get excited over new games to experience the story or combat system. However this genre also these tend to get dragged out way too long, till the novelty of the combat system and even the story starts to feel like it's not worth the time investment.Jack Move is a refreshing change of pace, it's a bite-sized game that just takes an idea and a story, and just presents it to you in one streamlined package. It's a really great weekend title, though the price might be a turn off considering how short it is. So I say it's definitely a must-get for fans of the genre when it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a strong recommend. It's very linear, and expects the player to do a little grinding. I think the game really expects you to buy ALL the software, and near endgame, lean on the swap mechanic to load them.I was, by the end, quite glad to have the option to turn off random combat.Final boss was somewhat interesting, but... the combat was nothing much.It's pretty, it's fun, there's some minor plot holes towards the end... honestly, most of the plot just didn't need to happen. _childDocuments_.review: Ah Jack Move. It's a game that makes it very hard to dislike and I believe that explains the somewhat overinflated review average. It's not terrible and there is clearly a ton of love in it, but there is also a lot of wasted potential. Let me try to explain.The story is a straight forward nice little SciFi story. It could have been an episode of Star Trek really. Someone invents a new tech that is sure to change society forever. An evil megacorporation wants to control it for their own gains. Our protagonist is stuck in the middle. It serves as a motivation for our PC to do things, not much more, nothing less.The animations are really gorgeous and the art has really vibrant colors. It's quite charming though I personally feel the backgrounds do it a disservice. They are super busy sometimes and it can be hard to discern what parts are traversable and what aren't. It's pixels but relatively high resolution. Personally not a fan of this art choice. I prefer proper high res 2D or something that could have been from the 16 bit era, not a hybrid somewhere in the middle. But you might see this point very differently. Now to the meat of the game - the game mechanics. Here is where the game loses me and where I'm struggling to find the motivation to finish it even though it's reportedly not that long to begin with. You only have one character you control and that severely limits how battles can play out. Basically you get 2 or 3 attacks in before you need to heal and that's all there is to it. Enemies have elemental affinities (which are impossible to guess, so you'll want to equip the auto scan accessoire) so it's just a game of Simon Says. Equip one skill of each element and use the one that's needed two times, heal and repeat. That is every battle. Another weird thing is that you don't unlock or find new skills gradually over the course of the game, instead you just go to a shop where you can buy basically everything from booting up the game on. Some things are level locked but they still show up in the shop. Despite the systems being so simple it's actually quite overwhelming at first to go to a shop and having to parse and chose from a list of 50 things. Especially since you don't know yet how simple it is in practice.There is also a really high and annoying encounter rate in dungeons. It can be turned off at any time but the game warns you that you'll be underpowered for scripted fights if you do and I have no doubt it's correct. There were enemies that I struggled with that I could easily one shoot after two levels. So you need to take all the battle you can get to be at the strength the game wants you to be.Overall there is unfortunately not enough there to keep me interested in the game. Because of the high encounter rate coupled with how pointlessly simple the battle are dungeons are more annoying than fun. And the story and characters aren't interesting enough to compensate for this by a long shot. I feel bad but I can't recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: 1. Go to the Slums area immediately outside Cash City.2. Wander around until you find a random encounter with a Lackey - dude wearing blue clothes with a gold chain.3. Kill every enemy except the Lackey. The Lackey will summon reinforcements.4. Repeat step 3 for as long as you have the patience and resources to do it. Each reinforcement you kill counts towards your rewards for the fight.By this method, I got to level 15 very early in the game, had enough money to buy all the chips I wanted, and from that point on I just coasted on my high stats and arsenal.When you get to Level 20, get the Beast and Linkman hardware upgrades. These two together let you destroy enemy groups with minimal effort. The defense debuff that comes with the Beast can be cured with Patches or Software for boss fights, allowing you to enjoy all of the perks with no disadvantages.

_childDocuments_.review: Ratings:---------------------Story - 3/5Its pretty average as far as fantasy storylines go. Protagonist and her best bud against the big bad evil corporation. All in a stylistic retro style turn based rpg. I will say I really enjoyed the friendship with Noa and Ryder.---------------------Difficulty - 1/5There's no difficulty options for this game and well there's really no challenge in the combats either so that's pretty much that. There are a lot of different options for skills, like standard buffs and debuffs, however they're completely useless as you're pretty much one shotting normal encounters very quickly.---------------------Graphics & Art - 4/5I like the retro artstyle and the combat animations were great. Some of them were recycled especially the early attacks. But I dig the whole vibe of Bright Town.---------------------Combat System - 3/5Turn based combat with Rock Paper Scissors element weaknesses. You have a bar that you charge up and do an ultimate attack. ---------------------Final thoughts:Total game time is about 10~ hours. If you gun down the story and ignore sidequests probably even shorter. If you expected a lengthier rpg or something more, don't get this game or wait for it to go on a sale. Its a really short game. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's your classic JRPG gameplay with a different coat of paint. The story is fine but linear, and the combat is boring and repetitive. Thankfully i got it dirt cheap in a game bundle.The story is kind of interesting but it's not a big part of your time playing. It's also completely linear so you're kind of just along for the ride and grinding level-ups in between story events. By far the bulk of the time spent is in combat and it's just your typical classic JRPG turn-based combat you find in something like RPG Maker (this game was made in Unity btw).The combat looks cool at first, especially the Jack Moves, but then it's just your usual boring grind that wastes your time as you try to get to the next story event. This has all the mechanisms you'd expect like guard, attack, skills, items, etc..., they're just here under different labels: cache, hack, execute, patch... The biggest issue with the combat is that there's tons of skills and items that you'll never use and Port Scan makes fights really easy. As long as you don't disable or lower encounter rates, you'll have no trouble winning fights in just a few turns as you reach mid-game. I don't think i used a single buff/debuff in the whole game. They're just not necessary. Items would be far more useful if they didn't count as your turn in combat. But trying to buff/debuff is just wasting your turn. There's also no reason to have a short QTE for Jack Moves--it's completely unnecessary.I was really disappointed in the end of the game. The hints were too direct if you're not lazy, and the final boss fight was super easy with the right skill that i happened to try. The story could have ended with a lot more impact too as i found it pretty weak.
