_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is a fantastic game. I particularly love the beautiful pixel art, it really helped convey the aesthetic well. The story is also well written, has some grit to it but ended waay too soon! Overall, I enjoyed my time with Jack Move and will be eagerly anticipating the sequel! My only complaint is that this is basically a no grinding game. I've been playing jrpgs since the original Final Fantasy in the late 80's, and grinding has been a quintessential part of that experience, and one that I truly enjoy. I did a bit of grinding near the beginning of Jack Move and consequently breezed through the entire game. The only challenge came in the form of the final boss, which I won't spoil here, but that was a much more enjoyable fight. I would definitely like to see the ability to scale the difficulty in the following games, or make the inherent difficulty higher. Also some power re-balancing would be great, such as lowering the damage on the Jack Move abilities, for starters. I'm considering a second playthough with the intentional limitation of no Jack Moves in order to increase the difficulty. With a little more effort put into the general game balance, Jack Move could really shine past it's current 10 hours of playtime and provide a much richer and more rewarding experience. I definitely recommend it to fans of cyberpunk storytelling and gorgeous pixel art, as well as those looking for a lighter jrpg experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: A short indie RPG with turn-based combat in a cyberpunk setting.The story: Rescue your father and his research on mind-upload from the big evil corporation. A pretty standard cyberpunk story with a focus on loss and grief-handling.The gameplay: The gameplay is a love letter to the old JRPGs on the Super Nintendo. You explore the world with a top-down view and when you randomly encounter an enemy it moves to an over the shoulder view. Combat is turn-based with a simple rock-paper-scissors system. Attacks and actions are technical named.  For example delay your turn until later is called Cache and using an item is Patch. You also build a power meter for devastating special attacks which can be boosted with the correct button prompts. A nice touch is that the frequency of the random encounters can be modified.The graphic: Like most indie games Jack Move uses a pixelart graphic style. Not to fancy but with some nice details like flying drones.The problems: My main complaint is that the game is a bit short and quite easy. Even the last boss is no real challenge and only has just a ridiculous amount of health. At least this means you don’t need to grind experience or money to finish the game.So if you are looking for a JRPG which does not take dozens of hours to complete Jack Move is a good choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game knowing nothing about it 'cept that it had been a surprise indie hit last year and that it was a jRPG. Bought it on a whim to treat myself and I couldn't be happier with that decision!I think something that jRPG developers need to learn is that more is not better, and less can definitely be more. Final Fantasy VI and Chrono Trigger were short experiences compared to later games in the genre, and those are yet to be beaten in terms of quality. Shorter allows for a tighter pace, a more focused focus (pardon the alliteration) and less pointless side-content. Jack Move definitely knows the story it wants to tell, the characters it wants to focus on and who they are and their role in the story and it does its best to excel at that. Some things are basic yes, and you can see where it is going but, it's about the quality of the storytelling over the direction of the ride. Eight hours is perfectly fine and I think I only missed one sidequest (and these exist only to flesh out the world a bit), A++ on that alone.Pixel art is some of the best I've seen and I can only image how good it would look on a CRT. Absolutely gorgeous and made me fall in love with the whole aesthetic of the game.Combat reminded me a bit of Shin Megami Tensei I and II, dunno why. But that's a positive in my book. I really enjoyed it and it was simple enough to be quickly understood, while throwing a couple systems that allows you to shape your play-style to what you prefer to do. Stat growth on the character is fixed, but that's a staple of jRPGs by now.Music was excellent but not that memorable I'd say. It's perfect for its setting and while playing I did find myself humming the tunes as it went along. That's a good thing.As another reviewer said below, it's excellent at its base price, a steal on a sale. Loved my time with it.Edit: Played it on the Steam Deck running Windows 10 at 3W and it worked perfectly.

_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is first and foremost a lot of love. The pixel art and animations are neat, it's J-RPG but at the same time it stands out for a different artistic choice, and it works. The music fits perfectly with the cyberpunk vibe. The story is captivating, the characters endearing. The player is invited to think about love, the meaning of life, what makes a human.Thank you So Romantic, I really enjoyed myself with Jack Move. I sincerely hope there will be a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: What a joyous game!JRPG-wise it's pretty streamlined - no party system, a rock-paper-scissors-punch damage type system, some buffs and debuffs. Doesn't overstay it's welcome in terms of game length and I feel like the end challenges put the combat system to good use. Side quests were kind of sparse but the NPC's always had more to say after every checkpoint so you really got a feel for casual friendships the protagonist Noa has, she really lives in this place. Main quest isn't anything special but it's a good driven story.My favourite part of this game is the genuine adoption of 90's hacker talk type dialogue and turning it into something endearing. I also really like the animations and music, they're in a word 'hype', although this effect wore off over time.If you're looking for an approachable, charming and medium-sized game, I recommend this even if JRPG's aren't quite your jam.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to love with a game like this one; however, playing the game is a different story. For all intensive purposes, I think this is a good game. Unfortunately, it's not a great one when it could have easily been so. Gameplay-wise, the turn based combat and Hardware/Software system is a great addition. It's too bad that you only really utilize it at the final boss. Speaking of combat difficulty curve in the game is jarring with enemies and bosses throughout most of it being really easy. But at some random encounters you can easily lose in one hit, and being ill-equipped and not using specific moves against the final boss I can imagine leaves you easily softlocked, which is never fun. Story wise, even as someone who can really turn a blind eye to aspects like it, I could not stray away from how mediocre the plot and writing can be and in my opinion not even take itself seriously. Don't take that comment to be all-encompassing of the dialog in the game as some lines and interactions really do shine. It's just something I took notice of. Even accounting for its short length, Jack Move should have been a game I loved but didn't. I wouldn't stray away from it cause it has its charm and its good moments, but it really stumbles at every opportunity. As a remedy, I feel like this game could use some type of sequel or another chance to really show what it wanted to be about, that implements and fixes a lot of what it has, because I do believe in its theme and concepts in addition to its battle system that the game simply does not deliver on. As a last note, I found a review taking note of how our protagonist is wildly different than what you expect, which is a great point and a shame because if you expected what seemed like a stylish, rebellious, and maybe cocky girl, from the trailer or the cover, you're simply not getting that in the actual game. Game Noa, although not perfect is cool though. There's a handful of issues, and no replayability, but I would give it a try if you have some time to kill. Just don't go in expecting something you'll reminisce about.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I generally don't go for cyberpunk, but this was an amazing JRPG, one of the best I've played lately. Amazingly well-paced with a good story and well-written characters and a fun combat system that centres around exploiting weaknesses to 4 different types of damage. I never had to go grind for anything and was appropriately levelled and I LOVED the system where you can set enemy encounter rate, even turn it off, which I did during some puzzles and backtracking. The final boss fight was genuinely one of the best I've played in ages, I truly had to pay attention during the fight. I also did not experience any particular imbalances that are easy to fall into one 1-character JRPGs. Genuinely a fantastic game.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Short, breezy, cyperpunk with a soft edge, Jack Move is a stylish throwback to 16-bit era turn-based RPGs, without drawn-out grinding and empty spaces. Players can adjust the encounter rate whenever they want---I made steady progress on the base setting, which made for an enjoyable balance between exploration and random encounters. RPG aficionados, please note: This game might fill a day or two at most, so I recommend looking elsewhere if you crave losing yourself for days in an intricate epic and detailed world. Also, although the story brushes on serious themes, this is definitely not Cyberpunk 2077---the most grit we get in Jack Move is some goofy toilet humor and a silly take on the mob. Don't let me set the wrong impression: It's not all goofs and slapstick, but the plot and dramatic beats are certainly never that heavy. If you are on the fence because of the short length and simple combat, I recommend buying it on sale. For me, the plucky lead character, distinct aesthetic, and terrible puns are worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Solid battle mechanics, great atmosphere and art style. Story is good, and the world definitely feels alive with the ever-changing NPC dialogue. Definitely a bit on the shorter side, but well worth the price.Only nitpick is that the final boss ended up being a bit of a HP sponge, but that may just be a personal experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. The humour is amusing, there's the odd charming techy pun. There's enough depth to squeeze out of the combat systems for its length. Even the system for choosing moves using RAM, or your "Defend" command being Cache which stores a command so you use two commands next turn. There's glorious quality of life things, like.... knowing if an NPC has something new to say or not. And the NPCs do have a lot of dialog that changes over time. It's completely reasonable to recheck every area just to see who's got something new to say, and then realize it's practically everyone. This game was loved when it was made, and the quality of it shows. Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't remember whether I heard about Jack Move through a gaming journalists article or an ad on YouTube, but it seemed like an interesting RPG with very stylish presentation. Roughly 10 hours later, was the game style over substance?Sort of. First, the game play:--------------------------------------------------------------------------For the most part, Jack Move is a very basic RPG. It has a very unique flavor to its presentation, but underneath the hood, everything anyone who has played a classic JRPG would expect to find is present and exactly the same. You have stats for Attack, Defense, Software Attack, Software Defense and a few others. These increase as you get EXP from winning fights, or can be modified by equipping Hardware mods (you start with one Hardware slot, and unlock 2 more). I should mention that while the game explains most of its mechanics very well, I inferred what most of these stats and their effect were as I played through the game; it's not like that was hard to do, but if the game gives an explanation for them, it was quick, I missed it, and there was no way to access that information later. Anyway, moving on:You have 4 types of attacks: "Physical" (red moves, listed in quotes because in-game descriptions state that all battles are virtual hacking sessions), Cyberware (green moves), Electroware (blue moves), and Wetware (Magenta moves). These are essentially equivalent to the elemental attacks you would find in a conventional fantasy RPG, and come in 3 levels of power that you can purchase from Deck Lord shops. There are also moves you can purchase that represent Healing, Attack Up/Defense Down, Slow and Haste, Poison and Sleep, Reflect...you get the idea. There's also a Scan move, but enemies are color-coded; if you know how the game handles its not-Rock-Paper-Scissors arrangement, you don't need to scan anything to know how to kill it efficiently unless buffs and/or debuffs are heavily involved (as in boss battles). Then there are the "Jack Moves" that the game is named for. These are a cross between Sabin's Blitz moves from FF6 and Limit Breaks from FF7. You have a Jack Move energy meter that fills up as you take or deal damage, and when it's full you input a 3-button DDR-style combo to execute a super move. There's one move for all 4 types of attacks, and the game gives them to you one by one at different points in the story. Enough said about that.What this game tries to do differently is wrapped up in a system that limits the number of moves the player can access at one time, together with the way the player and enemies take turns, and a pair of moves the player can use called Cache and Install. Basically, the player is given a certain number of "RAM" slots, and each move you can use takes up a certain number of those slots (from 2 to 5). You can upgrade the number of RAM slots you have, but the game starts you off with only a few. When you go into a battle, you can see a timeline of icons representing the player character (Noa) and the enemies (which are numbered, so you know exactly which enemy is going to attack you). If you decide that the moves you've equipped are the wrong moves for whatever strategy you want to use, you can use the "Cache" move to temporarily increase your defense and forfeit your current turn in exchange for two turns after all the enemies have run through their next attacks, which lets you use the "Install" move to (if desired) change any or all of the moves you currently have equipped to something else. Now, back to the style over substance thing. Everything I just described about what was unique about this game's core game play loop was a completely unnecessary, tiresome pain-in-the-butt extra step for me. With the exception of some of the boss fights (and when I decided to go into the area to the right of the game's main hub area (Bright Town) *way* too early), there is never a reason to bother with the Cache-Install mechanic. Cache by itself is helpful as a limited defense buff + a setup for move combos/buying time to heal, but otherwise, I was able to just equip the most powerful elemental attacks for Cyber-Electro-Wetware + a healing move and blast through everything. To mix analogies, I played this game the way I tend to play Pokemon: by brute-forcing everything with my starters. I don't play with my food, I eat it. Extra steps just draw things out for no reason. I don't start developing more complicated strategies unless the game *makes* me. It not that I don't enjoy strategizing, I just don't see the point when the simplest solution is right there. This game only really forced me to do that for the last two bosses.--------------------------------------------------------------------------Now, about the story:--------------------------------------------------------------------------Without spoiling anything...it's passable. I've experienced worse. It kept me kind of invested. The characters are well-realized, to the extent that you spend time with them. The world-building could use some work. The things that I was most interested in had to do with the world outside Bright Town, and Slums, and MonoMind. In other words, literally everything other than what you see. The game eludes to the fate of the rest of the world, but you never see any of that, and the game doesn't talk about it much either. That leaves what we got, which is a tiny chunk of the world which revolves around programming with the same immersion-breaking zeal with which the world of Pokemon revolves around...Pokemon. Ideologically...the writers have their heads on backwards. This game is yet another example of people reinventing a setting with corporation-based governments and an oligarchy represented as capitalism so that the writers can have another anti-capitalist straw man to burn down. It's the same tired, idiotic scenario all the leftists are spewing anywhere they can today. This isn't even the first game I played through that uses this premise this *week*. This in spite of the millions of deaths from Communist regimes that prospective writers are a few keystrokes away from learning about at any given time. Seriously, just STOP. The other major concept is the question of whether an AI-based simulation of a consciousness is the same as the original person. The game itself debunks this notion fairly early on in the narrative (which was a pleasant surprise), then keeps going with it as though the matter wasn't settled with about 10 seconds of dialogue after the question was first posed.--------------------------------------------------------------------------With all that said, do I recommend this game? Well if you can get past the story and the setting, enjoy the polished presentation, and appreciate the game play for what it is, then yes. Small side consideration: the only reason this game took as long as it did for me to beat is because the game implements some small but super-awesome refinements to its dialogue system. There are icons that appear over NPC's heads that tell you whether or not they have new dialogue, and nearly all dialogue can be skipped unless it's only one line anyway. This arrangement triggered my OCD, so I was running around talking to almost all the NPCs after every major event in the story. Most of them add little or nothing of value (except a few side quests that don't give you anything for rewards that you can't just buy), but I talked to them all anyway. That jack-moved out my completion time. I imagine the game would actually be very short for anyone skipping all that.

_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is a tight little RPG. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, if I could've given this game a sideways-thumb, I would've. There's certainly a lot to like here - the art's beautiful, the animation's marvelous, the characters are likable and the Cyberpunk Classic setting is well-executed. The core mechanics - the turn-based combat and progression-system - aren't particularly EXCITING, but they're functional and don't get in the way, though some parts of it feel rather overblown for such a short game. Not that the shortness is a bad thing - it's about right for a narrative-focused indie-game like this. Bigger isn't always better!So what's the problem? Well, basically, while the first couple of hours are a great time, the game just starts to steadily decline after that. Dungeons become cliché (how many times have I changed the water-level in a sewer in order to progress by now?), the bosses become dull damage-sponges, the random battles follow suit in the final level... and that's just the start of it. The story falls apart altogether, and I don't (just) mean in the narrative sense. Sure, there's a fair bit of "Wait, that makes no sense!" style fridge-logic moments, and some shaky characterization, but I could've overlooked that. What is HARDER to overlook are a ton of COMPLETELY GARBLED DIALOGUE-SCREENS! We're talking outright empty text-boxes, repeated lines, nonsensical conversations where lines seem to have been randomly swapped around, the works! There's probably a pretty good story underneath it all - at least, there BETTER be, since in a game like this the story's very much center stage - but it's like watching a grade-school theater troupe perform it, with much stammering and many forgotten lines.How does something like that make it past basic QA? I don't want to take shot at a developer who obviously has some very talented people working there, but I genuinely can't think of any explanation that doesn't involve somebody somewhere in the process going "Eh, don't bother with the rest, if they play that far they won't be able to refund it." And I just DO NOT want to support that kind of thinking - hence why I ultimately decided that no, I WOULDN'T recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet, this game evokes the random battles of games like ffvii, but a protagonist takes on the whole show. I like the focus on the struggle of the individual while also trying to maintain our consistent relationships. There are tons of lines of dialogue in small interactions, they're quirky and fun. _childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the game, nice graphics and art style. The history is not boring, actually i got into it and i enjoy the campain. The boss figths are not big deal, or at least interesting enough, the bosses are pretty much as a normal enemy, but they have a unique mecanic that take us more turns to kill.I don't like something about the combat though, the combat is boring, most of the times you'll face the same enemies and most of them are the same, the only strategy you need is hit them with the counter "element". _childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Short game.  Great game. Touching story and light-hearted laugh-to-survive comedy woven into the gritty reality of the cyberpunk genre. The combat is a turn-order sort of affair with ways to buff/debuff, manipulate turn order, and other features all neatly rolled into a system that rewards paying attention but doesn't punish casual play. There is even a handful of difficulty modifiers to further tailor the game if it proves too challenging. The game circumvents the common random encounter struggle by putting the dial directly in the player's hands.  All in all, one of the best sub 10-hour game experiences I've had in years. I hope for a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I tried out the demo for Jack Move one a whim when it came out and found it to be a super charming game. When the full game finally came out, I jumped on it! This game is just lovely. The atmosphere is really nice, and feels quite realistic. As a love of cute cyberpunk girls, I really enjoy Noa and can sort of see some of myself in her. The music is likewise great and I utterly adore the post-combat jingle! Cannot recommend Jack Move strongly enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is a stylish cyberpunk JRPG. Graphics look great and the characters are fun. Enjoyed the dialogue and specifically the inventive lingo for the futuristic time. Soundtrack is a lot of fun to listen to while playing as well. I could not stop bopping my head to it. Gameplay is fun once you figure out how to open up more abilities and RAM. Loved skulking around in Noa's dad's huge lab and fighting enemies. Love love love it! Gameplay video below

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Great pixel artExpressive animationAbove average characterizationTight map, no fillerAccessibility options are helpfulVaried perks and buffsEasy to grasp combat systemShort lengthCons:Gameplay loop is repetitiveEnemies pose no real threat by endgameMap becomes unclear and confusing after the "Point of No Return"Short lengthSangamon's Review:This game has so much heart. It is clear that the devs poured their talents into this game. I love the pixel art! The animation is expressive and the world is interesting to explore. The game is short which is a pro or con depending on how you value money vs. time. For me it's a pro! I'm old and my time (and attention) is limited, which brings me to the cons ...Unfortunately, the gameplay loop doesn't evolve after the first hour or so. The map is easy to explore, to a point, then it gets confusing after the "Point of No Return". I beat a giant robot, then got lost and wandered around for about 30 minutes. I decided that I got my money's worth, and stopped playing. I did not beat this game because I got lost, and the gameplay wasn't compelling enough to continue. Once you unlock buffs your character becomes OP and the combat becomes repetitive. The accessibility options help a bit, but not enough for me to complete the game.I do still recommend this game despite my criticism! It's worth a playthrough and you may not hit the same snags I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game, the mechanics make you feel a bit like a hacker, especially with the code input of the Jack Move. _childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it a tepid thumbs up. It's got an immense amount of style and charm with the visuals and sound, but the actual meat of the gameplay is pretty weak. Bare bones RPG combat, with the same enemies seemingly being repeated throughout. I found an area early on where the enemies were hitting three times as hard, but were still identical in terms of models and attacks. What was irritating is that I actually managed to cheese a couple and kill them with a combination of Jack Move and heal tanking with Counter-Hack, and they didn't even reward me any extra EXP or money than a battle against weaker enemies. Maybe EXP is calculated based on what level YOU are, rather than the level of the foes you fight, or these foes' EXP gains were intentionally reduced. Or something. That was pretty disappointing, since exploiting systems to gain massive power boosts is basically the nature of JRPGs, and it was sad to see Jack Move making that a possibility, but not letting the player actually realize it.Anyway, decent game, though maybe get it on sale, since apparently it's short.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game dripping with style, including fantastic art, music, and characters. The 'type effectiveness' combat is pretty simple, the story's length leaves you wanting more, and the game's final boss is way more challenging than the rest of the game's enemies would lead you to believe. Despite this, I still enjoyed myself and had a lot of fun. So this gets a thumbs-up from me!Edit: This game feels right at home when played on Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is another one of those small, but fun Indie titles.The story's interesting (if relatively short), with a bunch of side quests spread around the map and quite a few character dialogue lines partially commenting on the game's events, if you're willing to listen to them every now and then. Some of the jokes and expressions are a little on the nose, but they do fit the classic cyberpunk setting.The combat is relatively easy without needing to grind levels or use consumables unless you make major blunders - some kind of difficulty setting or more sophisticated enemy reactions couldn't have hurt here - but the variety of combat options you get along with boss fights being somewhat tactical is enough to not make it boring.Definitely a recommendation from me, though you might want to wait for a sale. (Or not, supporting Indie studios is a great way to get more charming games like this one.)
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: A really lovely RPG with some clear retro inspirations from all forms of media. The story is simple and has a clear draw from the get go. Dialogue, artwork and the music work in tandem to draw us into this cyberpunk/dystopian world. Everything in the game works so well together. It's easy enough to plug in and play the game just to enjoy it as it is but if you want to dig a little deeper into the world the player's time is still rewarded and respected. The mechanics are fairly straightforward as far as JRPG combat is concerned. X beats Y beats Z beats X. The animations are crisp and inspiring. The music is fun beeps, boops, and bops I found myself bobbing along to on accident at times. The story is memorable and succinct with enough seriousness to enjoy but it doesn't take itself too seriously. The dialogue was so refreshing throughout the story. Absolutely pick up this game when you feel like relaxing into a great cyberpunk adventure for a couple hours. It's a little on the short side as far as RPG's go, but after playing it through I find it refreshing to be playing a game that respects my time and knows when to progress and when to end.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, my biggest gripe with this game is its length. I completed everything, all side quests, max level, etc. in around nine and a half hours. I wanted more of this story, more of these characters, more of this world! Other than that, this game deserves at least a 9/10. The characters are actually rather complex, with a world that feels like it has developed around them and having a history outside of them. The environments are well-realized, and motivations make sense. Finally, in my limited experience with Cyberpunk style games, there's one constant: incredible music, and Jack Move does not disappoint. Overall, the experience was well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Very beautiful pixel art in modern 16-bit style!- Turn-based RPG in the traditional way, which is a plus for fans of this style.- The music fits the style of the game really well.- The gameplay feels like it's well polished, and despite the flaws of the game it feels good.- Nice RAM-system where you choose which abilities matter to you.- The story and characters are about average, but it's definitely not bad enough to be a "con".- The game has random encounters, but you can adjust the rate, and even disable it.Cons: - The game is way too easy. No bosses really requires any clever strategy, even though there are a lot of available abilities (called "software" in this game). If you like a challenge, this is not the game for you.- Despite a good combat system, it's not utilized enough to keep the game interesting in the end.- At the very last dungeon the random encounter combats really just felt tedious, not challenging, and not rewarding enough to endure, so I ended up doing something I would never expect I'd do for this type of game: Disable the random encounters entirely.- There is no party. All you have is the one main character, which I think is one of the reasons why the combats gets boring after a while.Overall a game worth playing for JRPG fans that does not care too much about the challenge. The good outshines the bad all in all, but I think I would give this game a neutral score if that was possible in Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Upfront, the best thing about this game is the pixel art. everything else is honestly underwhelming. However I do think there is a lot of groundwork for improvement in a potential sequel with the gameplay mechanics set up.The enemies need more battle variety: 90% of the games enemies do something too simple like do damage or raise allies attack. when you finally do encounter any of said variety it's right before the end of the game which ends in an underwhelming slogfest of a bossfight. If enemies were able to inflict more creative status elements it'd make for much more interesting battles. Why can't an enemy scramble my ability to read my moves or take damage for its ally?There are some serious oversights in terms of progression:For instance you can level up to having max ram and hardware (active move pool size and number of equipment slots) before you even reach the second boss and within maybe 30 to 45 minutes of the first. (please balance the lackey enemy)There is also an oversight in equipment progression, the ram expansion equipment should either not exist or allow for an amount of ram that is balanced but allow for an amount past the standard static upgrades. essentially unless a piece of hardware is the lesser version of another, no piece of equipment should be rendered completely useless like this. finally the penalty for death shouldn't be experience but credits. credits are much more valuable when it comes to expanding the player's capabilities and ultimately still gate the player despite the additional hurdle of having to be a certain level in order to buy end-game gear from the shop.The early to mid game ends up being quite boring because despite the somewhat interesting rock paper scissors elements system they've set up for you it can be completely ignored in part because of the above exploits. I honestly think the elements should stay but the predictable rock-paper-scissors nature of them should be removed. What I would be interested in is a change in the relationship enemies have with the elements. Punish me for spamming a particular element across the board by having it heal the enemy instead or reflect the damage, not just do a little less, and uncouple the type of damage dealt  from the weakness of the enemy or I'm just going to either run odds on what element spam I'm going to do for an area based on who deals the most damage or the rate of encountering a particular weakness,The story beats vacillate between being pretty decent and cringe. Guin is easily the most interesting character, if a sequel were made I'd definitely like his past to be the main conflict of the story. The Ryder-Ming sub plot had some of the better and worst story moments of the game. You had me that Ryder was angry and I felt that but then he literally lights up an almost person-sized portrait of Ming to emphasize the point and I lost my immersion. Ryder is a genius cyber hacker in a cyberpunk setting, why does his character have a portrait of anyone rather than some other kind of medium? If you wanted to do that for anyone it should have been Guin and his sister. otherwise the npc dialogue varies between neat to understandably boring for the more myopic characters like random corpos. I wish there were more than three sidequest lines, its especially frustrating that it can appear that you've started three separate questlines near the start of the game only to have them to be the same one but you've forgotten to deliver a single item that linearly progresses to the next leg of the quest. Best feature of the dialogue is that the devs thought to let you know you've expended someone's dialogue I just wish some npcs were replaced with journals since a couple literally drop exposition the character already knows aboutI really hope the developers continue this game as a series, the pixel art is super solid and will definitely bring people in if they just continue to improve and tweak the game to make it more engaging gameplay-wise
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: The one word to describe this game is FUN. This game was A LOT of fun! If you like games like Final Fantasy VII, you'll like this game. It's a very charming game. I made the mistake of assuming this game would be too easy. I paid for that mistake late game. I will say don't underestimate the game late game. Make sure that you're prepared before you go into the sewers. Be sure to buy Hyperderm, which is a major healing upgrade. Also, buy lots of Super Health Packets and Super Data Packets for late game. If you get stuck somewhere like on a boss, my advice to anyone is you can ALWAYS level up near one of the soda machines without using any items. When you level up, it will make your health bar number greater. You might have to do that if you get stuck on a boss. You can turn on and turn off your encounters by hitting Escape and changing it there, which I did when I didn't want to use items and instead leveled up around the soda machines. I only did this late game, when I got stuck on a boss and didn't want to use the limited items I had. For some reason I assumed that after I beat the game that I could go back and finish side quests. Apparently, you can't do that, so if you have any side quests you want to do, do them BEFORE you go into the sewers. I would have liked to have been able to go back and done the side quests after I beat the final boss. I was a little disappointed that the trailer animation for this game was not used in the game itself. There weren't any cut scenes with that smooth animation. Even with a few things I might have changed, I still love this game. The environment, music, and characters draw you into the game's world. I found that to be very enjoyable. This game might not be as long as other JRPGs, but I found it the perfect length for this game. The story moved along at a good pace and didn't drag on. The late game is way tougher than early to mid game. Just be prepared. Otherwise, you might get a real workout like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard review to write.. At the end I've chosen positive, What game there was is fun, the music is good. the animations in fights were good. Though the game has serious problems. A: It is very very short.. like flash game off newgrounds short. Few hours max.. B: Even with it being short. it quickly runs out of equipment and character upgrades before it's already short clock runs out. C: Alot of the non attack abilities and non healing items just don't have a point. Fights are never long enough for the defensive items and skills to matter. It's always better to attack or recover.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed playing this game quite a bit. TL:DR. Buy this game if you're looking for a nice solo play game that scratches that RPG itch without sucking the life out of you.It was addictive, quirky, interactive, and fun! I liked the following features: 1) When you're done talking to a NPC, it'll let you know. I think this allows for an immersive environment. I was able to know if someone was going to say something different from my last encounter with them, or I can just pass by them. Each "chapter" allowed an opportunity for the world to expand a little more. The future is 5 minute pizza delivery!2) The encounter rate system. I plan on testing this a bit more, but, the game allows you to just explore without encounters, until you're ready. You can have that traditional JRPG feel of wandering in a dungeon, get random encounters, crank it up to 11 and have every hacker at your every footstep, or cruise down the streets without a care in the world about encounters. I plan on running through this again with a mix of the different encounter rates.3) The battle system. Rock, Paper, Scissor....Bazooka? I like that each enemy had their own weakness/strength, and it would be exploited. It was fun to test out different abilities to see what was weak to what while also leveling up my skills.4) Leveling up your skill. Use them, level them up, MOAR POWUH! 5) The environment. It was fun to stroll around the slums and talk to people. There are side-quests to be had, and the provide decent reward. It was colorful, imaginative, and felt like it could be a real place.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, yet short, experience (100%, including secondary objectives, and saw the credits in 7 hours). Enjoyed most of my time playing, but is easy to get some upgrades and become near impossible to defeat except for the odd boss fight. Some bosses are noticeable difficulty spikes as well, but can be overcome surprisingly easily with the right gear.Was always interesting things to do, none of the characters were annoying to interact with and the music was stellar (will be listening to the OST on and off in my own time).My only real complaints are the game's length and lack of replayability. It is very short as mentioned previously, and paying full price for the length is questionable at best. I'd wait for sales or bundles before purchasing. If the game was longer, I'd more recommend the full price.Still, for what it is, Jack Move is simply fun and that's what matters to me
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cute game, with some decent dialogue going for it and not too complicated technique involved. _childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: First off: Great game, but not without flaws.Ascetics: very nice visually, honestly was not enjoying the background music.Game play: fairly standard for a turn based RPG.Game length: 4 hours in, and I think I am close to the end.Difficulty: sadly, too easy. The problem with this is the game wants you to push the difficulty to HYPE. All that did was increase the spawns. Don't have a grievance with that, but it does not modify the mob spawns in the slightest. With how much damage you can deal opposed to how much damage you take, scaling is almost required to keep things interesting. Honestly, I have been breezing through with hack, counter-hack,  the jack moves, and the high level heal software.Last boss: it needed to be long and drawn out, and did not disappoint. Getting nailed by Jack Moves every couple of rounds actually brought a smile to my face. Would of liked if the attacks I took had more of a SLAM verses a WHAP, but can't win them all.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: I was surprised at how good this was. I loved the traditional turn-based fantasy RPG game mechanic re-themed in this 90's hackers-like-cyberpunk theme. In the beginning the language used to describe some of the buff/debuff software and hardware equips did get a confusing to understand. Luckily as you play it starts to come together. The visuals and animations are what originally drew in, and they are gorgeous. The game definitely scratched that traditional JRPG itch. The magic/software system has an easy to follow elemental wheel which will be the bulk of your combat skills. And the RAM slots to which you use to the manage which software to equip was clever as well. Some of these concepts might be common among cyberpunk table-tops, idk i've never played one but they are well done here.My only complaint is that game was too short and that's not as bad as it sounds. I'm completed the game at the Max lvl, most side-quest completed and most software skills maxed at about 10.5 hours. I would think if one were trying to breeze through, they could do it in about 5.5-7 hours. The story was enjoyable and complete. The game just release last week on PC and I'm already wanting a squeal or dlc story updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing really wrong with the game, but also nothing that was innovative or memorable. The best part about this game was the art. Story felt like a copy-paste from tons of other games. Nice time waster to play for an hour and then move on to something else. All the achievements are story based so it's an easy completion. Wait for a sale. Overall a generous 7/10, more would have been better. Probably the most average/generic RPG I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: * Story - If you have a thing for Sci-fi/Cyberpunk-esque stories, you'll like this.* Music - It slaps, all of it.* Combat - While it's good, I do have some qualms against it* Game Length - May differ from person to person. It took me just under 10hrs to complete, others were give or take a few hrs. If you want a game to complete over the weekend, or binge through in a night, or an hour here and there over the week, this would be great.* Difficulty - This game was pretty easy. I had some issues in combat, but I realized it was a bug or maybe misplaced design which I'll bring up after.If you, like I did, decided to use the Linkman hardware that allows your offensive software (spells) to target all the enemies, for whatever reason if 1 enemy dodges, i miss, or however the accuracy system works (which isn't explained anywhere), all of the enemies will dodge. If 1 of the targets triggers a counter (which also isn't scanned) the whole ability just doesn't happen. It feels SO good when that happens.

_childDocuments_.review: So i just came from finishing the prologue and absolutely loved it so now i've purchased the main game straight away . Honestly this thing is superb on the steam deck. _childDocuments_.review: Really liked it! anyone who's looking for a turn-based, fun, funny, interesting, and nerdy/geeky cyberpunk feel of a single player game, this one's for you! _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game with the Crosscode bundle for 15 dollars since I already owned Crosscode and I more or less got my money's worth. Like other people said, this is a fairly short game. I beat it in 8 hours but I messed around quite a bit so it's certainly possible to do so faster. Definitely the strongest part about this game is the presentation. The sprites are extremely well animated and very lively, which really does a lot for the experience. As well, the music is fantastic, there are some real great tracks and some are damn catchy.The battle system is interesting but underutilized. I initially farmed credits just to get some customization going, but unfortunately most fights in the game do not require it. For the most part, going for the three elements + healing or physical will do just fine. I like the idea of on-the-fly customization, but it needs more depth than just "slot in the purple spell for the green enemy"That being said, I appreciate this RPG being one where status effects work on bosses and I always like RPGs which let you use the turn order for planning.People bag on the writing, but I honestly enjoyed the silly slang. It reminded me of Shadowrun or other similar sci-fi TRPGs so I was alright with it. I never felt like it got overbearing but YMMV. The writing gets into some real issues in the final act, it feels like it's trying to juggle too much and ends up feeling very rushed. Others said this game ends up feeling like a prologue and I have to agree.I recommend this game if you're looking for a bite-sized RPG. I can't say it's revolutionary, but it's very enjoyable as it is and I hope the ideas introduced here will be expanded on.
_childDocuments_.name: Jack Move

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of the JRPG genre, with some caveats. As others have noted, the game is short. I took my time and talked to everyone, hit the level cap just before the final boss, and took about 10 hrs. The gameplay and combat are reminiscent of old SNES RPGs like Final Fantasy, though the pixel art animation reminds me more of old PC adventure games like Beneath a Steel Sky (although Jack Move is a far more upbeat future dystopia, if that makes sense). The music is great and the game overall has a nice sense of polish -- it played well with a controller and I didn't encounter a single bug. But as you'll see in other reviews, the combat system is a bit simplistic. You have a physical attack (Hack) that honestly became useless for me after the early stages, since it can't be effectively upgraded (there are no equipable weapons) and is quickly outpaced by your "software" attacks (basically spells). As with classic JRPGs, you don't distribute ability points when you level up -- that's all automatic -- and the character stats listed on the inventory screen still remain a complete mystery to me (with names like "toughness," "grok," and "sass"). The software attacks (i.e. spells) and the corresponding "jack move" super moves fall into 4 different classes: cyberware, electroware, wetware, and physical. Each one is strong against one class and weak against another. What this means is that you basically spend most of the game deploying the appropriate software attacks depending on the enemy's class (helpfully indicated by their color). Without much enemy variety and with no equipment or party members, the combat gets pretty repetitive and predictable. The challenge comes in determining which 4 software abilities to equip at any given time, depending on how many RAM slots you've freed up (more advanced tiers of software requiring more RAM space). You can hot-swap your software choices during battle, which costs you a turn. It's a nice feature but I only ever had to do it in the final boss fight. What's more, pretty much all of the major software in the game is available from the start in the main shop in town. There are a couple other stores in different parts of the map but their inventory -- with a few exceptions -- is exactly the same. By mid-game, with a little grinding, I bought the highest tier software attacks available and had all the RAM slots unlocked; I basically didn't need to change my strategy at all from that point. I completely ignored the host of buffs and status attacks, since the combat was so straightforward.The draw here is the story and the cyberpunk setting. The main narrative is interesting and the characters relatable, with grief and loss being prominent themes. There are a few side quests but they're very minor and don't contribute much other than a little extra color. If you're interested I'd recommend checking out the demo: it'll give you a good sense for how you'll be spending the 8-12 hours it takes to finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to finish the game before I left a review so I could fully grasp the entirety of the game and what it had to offer.TLDR at the bottom.So Jack Move for the most part is a very well put together game. However I have some reservation about it that  rub me the wrong way.Gameplay: The game play is fun, smooth and not buggy or broken, granted it is a pixel game, so this type of thing is less likely to be a problem, the game did work for me flawlessly. Navigating the map is easy however that is because there are only about 5 areas of exploration. Battles are fun and really easy. A bit too easy but this is most likely a design choice so that players regardless of skill can flow through the story unimpeded. You can turn combat off which is welcome because you do abit of backtracking through previous combat areas. Boss battles are fun and some even have puzzles to figure out but are still really easy. This because of a skill you have called Jack Move which obliterates most bosses for at the very least half their health is not most of it, (The next to last boss I killed in two turns.) There are shops in the game that allow you to buy restorative items, new moves and equipment. Most of this is fine however there are alot of items that for me are just not necessary. You can a set number of hacker skills which can be increased through purchasing upgrades and you can also equip "hardware" or accessories that add a smidge of variation to combat. Can they be utilized in someway to make the game interesting? YES. Did I just buy and equip Silicon Beast and the Combo Link mod and process to split the game in half? ALSO YES. So all in all the game is fun but its not very complex. But this is also because the enemy varieties are sorely lacking, Most enemies you fight have a color coded weakness which there are 4 of and you can basically see what color they use and guess, often correctly, what their weakness is. At times I would be experimenting with different skills thinking "IT CANT BE THIS EASY." but alas, it really is essentially rock, paper, color red. This is actually compounded by your party composition...or lack there of. When I first saw this game I got a strong JRPG vibe and I believe it was marketed as such but a staple of JRPGS for me has always been a quirky yet often effective band of party members that even you out. The main character in this game can equip everything you can buy and has not weakness other than she is by herself. You meet people in the game that I swear could be party members but end up being support characters. NOW this could be a prequel of sorts introducing characters for a later installment where they are in fact party members. (I was praying for Guin as a party member.) So Ill leave this aspect of the game alone for now but I was disappointed. Gameplay flow is good but uneventful. Its smooth and it never feels bogged down by any distractions other than a minimal side quest fetch quest. I really felt like this was going to be a normal thing throughout the game until I realized that the map was super tiny. This is good for time but not good for content. Talking to people is fun and some of them have interesting things to say. There is an indicator that will appear above their head to let you know you have already spoken to them and they have nothing new to say. Story: The story is well written and fun to experience but it doesn't do anything risky or new. It is satisfactory. Like a ham and cheese sandwich you will eat it because you are hungry but you'll wish it was something abit more unique.  The writer was very careful not to really do anything that would make the person experiencing the story really think. There is nothing philosophical or morally grey about anything you are doing or the main antagonist. WHY THEY BAD. THEY BIG CORP. WHY WE GOOD. WE STOP BIG CORP. WHY. BECAUSE BIG BAD CORP DO BAD THINGS. There is a point towards the end of the game where I thought the antagonist was going to have something similar to something that could be considered layered but then the writing just goes BECAUSE BOSS LADY BAD! and at that point I lost all hope for thoughtful writing. I have to honest its written in a way that really appeals to people that see things very black and white. I get that the game is in some ways possibly a proof of concept of a prequel of sorts but most indie games tend to have their writing on point and challenge new ideas and concepts while introducing nuance and complexity that makes the player go "well if you put it like that then I dont know" or "Yeah if that were me I would have done the same."I may be being to harsh for such a small title but there is alot of good dialogue in the game and I kept waiting for something pull me in and challenge my beliefs or pre-consious biases but it never happened. Music and Sounds: Its really good. Im not a fan of the kind of sounds that usually accompany cyber punk style music but it fits the game and gameplay and it never felt out of place. Sound effects are amazing, and I recommend using headphones when using Jack Moves. There is alot going on technically that speakers dont do justice.Art and style: I believe this is why most people including myself were so excited for the game in the first place. It has FANTASTIC art and animation that really shine in combat. It is very smooth and the main character as well as enemies and especially the bosses all look phenomenal. I really cant say enough about the artwork in this game. It is the reason to get this game however;Price Point: Is the game as a package worth 20 dollars? Now I received the game as a gift but I was prepared to buy it so I believe I can say this and still be honest with you and myself.It is not worth 20 dollars. The game doesnt really do anything wrong because it plays it very safe. It plays it safe with the combat, it plays it safe with the gameplay flow, it plays it safe with the writing. (Like baby wrapped in blankets in a playpen wrapped in more blankets safe. Its really a shame. The writing. I get that the meat and potatoes of the game is the combat and art but writing is so unoffensive that it almost seems like its patronizing me. "We dont know who you are dear player but our goal is to not offend you because that would be bad and the only thing bad in this game is BOSS LADY BECAUSE BIG CORPS BAD!"Sorry. Price point should be close to $10.00 USD or dare I say even $5.00. Im sure the dev team worked hard on it but its at best a 7 hour game. Level cap is 30. 2 side quests. No party members, and a story that is very forgettable. But hey. They didnt hurt my feelings which hurt my feelings. FINAL SCORE: 6/10 because the gameplay is fun but short. The music and sound effects are great. You will stay for the artwork and animation. You will leave wishing the story took more risks and was not so mediocre.

_childDocuments_.review: The presentation is spot on. Excellent visuals (with impressive lighting) and quality music make this an indie attraction. The final battle is a bit of a slog and somewhat anti-climatic. Also, the game is very short, clocking in about 12 hours. That includes the (few) sidequests. Your mileage may vary on if this is a good thing or bad thing. The characters are more than one-dimensional. It's amazing how much you learn about the main characters without there being a long arc or over-dramatic cutscenes and the NPC's are also amusing. Jack Move actually encourages you to talk to NPCs not just for questing but for funny banter. Noa is a very good lead, balancing sassyness with enough vulnerabilities to make her enduring.Despite the issues, I would say this is worth a playthrough. There is no new game+ nor any difficulty options so replayability is low. But there is potential for a sequel and the developers clearly have talent.

_childDocuments_.review: While not the longest game (I have already completed it at the time of the review), Jack Move shows that you don't need overly complicated game play systems or hyper-realistic graphics to create a good game.A Turn-base battle system based on coding and hacking terms as attacks, it incorporates a straightforward rock-paper-scissors battle system that is easy to understand and pick up. Graphics fits really well with the theme of the game, effectively conveying the ambience of each level and area to the player. The story line is simple enough with so much potential to grow should the developer decide to create a sequel.My only critique is that I kind of hoped for more of the JACK MOVE system, one of the game's highlighted feature where you keyed in directional commands to execute a finisher-like move.All-in-all, Jack Move feels like a fun demo of what it can be should it decide to expand as a sequel, it knows what it can do and it does it right. I'm excited to see more of Jack Move should the developer decide to start on it's sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is a game about a cyberpunk dystopian future where corporations control the world. The player character is a young woman named Noa who soon finds out her father has been involved in some research that has made him the target of the main corporation of the game, Monomind. The story is about Noa's journey to rescue her father (and maybe even take down an evil corporation on the way).The story was... fine, I guess, but suffered from pacing that was far too fast. Events escalated far too quickly and then at the end of the game it seems like... everyone is fine for some reason? Even though much of the game was about them not being fine. I can sort of suspend my disbelief a little bit but it felt like the story would have been served better by a longer game (my 5.4 hours represents a full play through and basically a 100% of the game, including side quests).The gameplay is fun and interesting with a single character party that allows you to swap moves in and out during battle. However, this really only becomes relevant during the final fight (which is kind of a slog, though satisfying to be able to build up so many buffs), otherwise it's not really necessary. I also found the combat to be made trivially easy after getting the piece of equipment that lets you deal more damage while taking more damage, because you can simply remove the damage taken increase buffs with a single skill at the beginning of battle.Speaking of combat though, the quality of life features in this game are amazing. You can freely adjust the encounter rate and the game lets you know when you've talked to NPCs already. You can easily check main and side objectives from your menu as well. The only thing I didn't like is there seemed to be no encyclopedia of various status effects, and you mainly have to rely on context clues to figure out what they do (and some things I never figured out what they did, e.g., some kind of fire looking buff that is on the aforementioned piece of equipment).Normally I recommend games based on my enjoyment at their base price point, and it's a little hard for me to do so here... Still though, I can't say it wasn't enjoyable, just short. It had some flaws, but nothing unforgivable. I would say to pick this up at maybe $10-15. $20 is a bit much considering the length. However, I certainly hope the developer creates more games along this vein, I think they are onto something solid here and a second attempt could allow them to fix all of the issues I mentioned. Keep it up!

_childDocuments_.review: Jack Move is a RPG/adventure that proves you don’t need epic set pieces or countless locations to make a fun game. Everything is packed into a few locations that don’t feel boring or overused. It’s also very accessible. If you’re not interested in battles and only want to enjoy the story, you can enable auto win and even remove random encounters altogether. Which would be a shame because of a fun battle system. Your main weapons are software and hardware. Software are your classic attack and support “spells”, and hardware act as special perks that improve your combat. The couple I couldn’t go without are auto counterattack when you get attacked and linked attack that gives spells the ability to target all enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: fantastic little gema) the game's structure is like an oldschool jrpg (the good ones)it's turnbased, combat mixed with realtime explorationyou kill enemies, get exp and cash. levelups increase all your main statistics, whereas cash allows you to buy new active and passive abilities and items.b) everything is centered around the Cyberpunk setting (the genre, not the IP). which means your abilities, stats, everything pretty much revolves around hacking, cyberspace and co. ; imagine Shadowrun's deckrunning.c) the game realy doesn't take itself to serious, but serious enough not to be annoyin. it's less constant slapstick and more tongue and cheek with a more upbeat vibe. d) the OST is perfect. there's little else to say. it's high quality, offers what you would expect from a Cyberpunk-game, but with an 80s twist in some tracks (even spottet a track having oldschool Ridgeracer-influence).the same goes for the soundeffects, they are meaty, they are well mixed and fit always the happening onscreenfor the pricetag there's actualy a lot hereprogression mechanics are layered. basicaly your active skill-slots revolve around RAM, which you can perma upgrade along the way. each active ability uses a certain amount of RAM (imagine spells in other games, but to slot em you neet a limited ressource, which you can change and mix'n match at your leisure) to be slotted, using your limited "mana" to cast inbattle. active abilities range from direct damage spells and attacks, to buffs and debuffs for specific damage-types, to haste-like overclock spells and utility and healing-spells. then there's the permanent hardware you can carry. which means auto-active/passive abilities you can slot. like getting certain buffs precast when combat starts, or staring combat while having the first turn always, increased crit chance, etc. spells you use in combat level up to increase their damage.then you get a special-move bar (the titular Jack Move), which fills with every action taken in combat and can be spend on high damage aoe attacks (including a very basic minigame).the rest is you running around, doing small sidetasks, or searching for hidden chests in the enviroment. textboxes and writing are pretty good; yes, there's no voice acting, but conversations aren't drawn out, so reading the textboxes doesn't get annoin.the 2D backrounds during normal exploration are pretty good, the screenshots definitly do em justice. but the combat realy stands out. it's hard to describe, but the art-design mixed with the banging OST and soundeffects is just a joy to behold.the sudo 3rd person approach to combat inclusive perspective change and dynamic backround was a great idea, so was the way grinding and random encounters are handeled. basicly with 1 button press you can access your "deck" and change the intensity of random-encounters. want to grind? just up the frequency. want to just progess? turn it off. it's neatly integrated into the game's vibe. there are some minor glitches/bugs i encountered, nothing you cannot work around. the save everywhere feature mixed with the auto-save also saves you alot of headache. looking at the trailers and me beeing a pretty big Cyberpunk fan (genre, not the IP...well probably both) i already expected a pretty good game, but tbh. it's even better. very fun, very enjoyable. hope to see a sequel. 0

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this game was great. I really loved the extra nerd that was in this game. It made the programmer in me very happy. I only wish there was more game left to play. Would recommend if you like turn-based JRPGs.Here are more details if you care to read.I bought this game the day it was released, and I was very surprised at how few bugs there were as I was playing (granted, I didn't go looking for them). There were a couple glitches here and there, but overall it didn't get in the way of enjoying the game. The overall experience was very clean for me.The beginning felt like an information overload, especially with the game using different names for some of the traditional RPG mechanics. (Data = Mana, Software = Spells, Hardware = Equipment, etc.). However, I did like how that's pretty much all the tutorial in the game, and then you are left to figure out your own strategies. Along with that, I felt like the enemies were well designed to incentivize you to actually think about the moves you use in battle rather than just using your most powerful moves like I've seen in a lot of turn-based RPGs.I also really loved the implementation of some of the battle mechanics. Cache (blocking) felt like an actually useful action. In most turn-based RPGs I've played, blocking always felt like a waste of a turn except for very specific occasions. On top of that, the ability to change your software (spells) mid-fight as a turn action was a really cool way to add another dimension of strategy to the battles.Last couple of thoughts. The art was really good, kudos to the designers. The story felt rushed to me, but I still enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: So far so awesome!I am really loving the turn based attacks, they give me time to think and react without feeling the stress of time pressure.The art is undeniably beautiful and the depth of personalities in all the NPC's makes the world extremely immersive. I particularly like the level of detail to the curated language terms to represent a new sociolect in this modern world! I also appreciated the very British terms I came across on occasion.So far I highly recommend this game. Although not the style game I usually go for, the clever story building from the start has me hooked, and I will certainly be clocking a few more hours in soon.A few suggestions might include:-Lower xp reduction upon death for the first few deaths. (I thought I had to go up to the river, and was shocked to lose 25% so easily)-Health counter for enemies? Or make it clearer, I was not able to locate it when fighting. The boss at the end of the tutorial especially had me confused, I thought I was doing something wrong after they didn't die to a Jack Move-Player guidance might be a little better. I really like the open world feeling, but I think a minimap or guidance markers might be beneficial? This could help with primary and secondary quests too.

_childDocuments_.review:
Jack Move is a unique blend of gritty cyberpunk story telling, turn based battles and beautiful modern pixel art. Take on the role of Noa, a vigilante hacker determined to rescue her kidnapped father and take down the overreaching Monomind corporation.

They whisper her name on the streets: Solares. A mysterious veteran of the Data Wars, Noa Solares keeps the fight against the Corporations alive as a vigilante hacker-for-hire, empowering the downtrodden and undermining those with power. When she receives an emergency message from her estranged father - the eccentric Dr. Abner Solares, whose wife's death spurred him to become the leading researcher of 'digital reanimation' - Noa is thrust into a world of murder, kidnapping, dark research, and the corporation that would steal it for their own ends: Monomind.

What starts as fight to save your father will become a fight for the future of mankind itself...

The past has been altered! Team up with up to four players as you level up, claim legendary loot, and take on the armies of enemies that await you! _childDocuments_.review: [Revision 7/7/2023]With the announcement that this game will be dropped in favor of a new project, aside from some very minor QoL/Kickstarter promises, this will most likely be my final revision to this game review.  I guess the best place to start would be the initial "sell" of this game: the penultimate reimagined Dungeon Defenders experience that was meant to be the definitive game in the series.  Another way to phrase this would be a remaster of DD1 taking all the lessons they've learned with a more modernized game design.  Did this game accomplish that?  No.  No it did not.I don't hold it against this game that it doesn't have all of the maps that DD1 has, it was clear that this would gradually be updated until it reached that point.  Many people didn't give this game a chance because of that, which I think was wrong, you obviously can't release a new game with the same amount of content as a game that had been developed for 11 years.  What I DO hold against it, however, is that the development was always focused on shoveling out "new" content, rather than polishing the existing content, largely because the developers really only cared to listen to a small, loud group of players.DDA's biggest problem wasn't bad ideas, but bad implementation.  Or rather, releasing unfinished work.  There are a lot of good ideas worth praising conceptually, but criticizing in their unfinished state.  Runes are a great example of this.  Runes offer the potential to customize towers and really play with the strategy of the game, but there's only one rune per tower (meaning it's just outright upgrades) or some either don't work or literally make the tower worse (like the reflect beam rune.)  The idea is a great concept and very much belongs, but the developers haven't fleshed it out fully, and now they never will.DDA struggled because it was always in a rush to win back diehard DD1 players who were never going to give it a chance (because it wasn't DD1) so it never courted a playerbase that was either new to the franchise, or people like me who loved DD1 but can't play it anymore due to the lack of QoL and aged content.I'm disappointed that this game isn't going to be developed more, because literally it just needed more thought and polish into its systems.  I will not be supporting whatever their new project is, so I can only offer some meager advice:  Whatever your new game will be.  You need to release the content when it is ready, and you need to make sure to polish it enough so that the game is foundationally fun to play.  New content is good, yes, but if the core gameplay is suffering, more content is just going to be a temporary bandaid.  And that's exactly what happened with DDA.  Shoveling out new maps and heroes brings temporary activity to the game, but if the core problems aren't addressed, it's not going to survive.This game was horribly mismanaged, when it could have been an absolute banger.  No matter how flashy their next project looks, I'm not interested.  DDA deserved better.  This community deserved better.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not ready for a publicly available early access. There are two other games in the Dungeon Defenders series available on Steam, and you would have a better time playing either of those. I would recommend waiting on Dungeon Defenders Awakened. The game has less content than the previous two games in the series, and has significant technical problems at the time of this review. I want to see this game improve, but it will take time. I played the beta for this game, and the lack of improvements from the beta to the current early access version are disappointing.Edit:Dungeon Defenders Awakened has officially left early access, but the game still feels like it is in beta. Do you like items with useful tooltips such as <MISSING STRING TABLE ENTRY>? Then this is the game for you. Are you a big fan of randomly disappearing ui elements? Check this game out then. Technical issues aside the game has improved since it left beta. The ui is more streamlined and easier to use. There are more maps and game modes too. _childDocuments_.review: TLDWR: The game doesn't appear to be finished. Wait until when and if content and patches roll out. So, I played the first Dungeon Defenders a fair bit and quite enjoyed the whole game play loop. I even tried to play Dungeon Defenders 2, but I did not enjoy the route that they took for a multitude of reasons.I figured that a reboot or 'rework' of the first game would be pretty interesting. The same old Dungeon Defenders, but a bit better and on a newer engine. I didn't really expect that as a backer I would be paying at least ten dollars more than someone who purchased the game on release...I also did not expect to see such an incomplete game considering that it was just more or less making the previous game 'newer'. Weapons with Stats that literally have <missing string table entry> on them... Add in things like cryptic and misleading dialogue that is later revealed to mean that the shop (For buying weapons and the like with the gold you've been getting) just isn't implemented. The important mechanic of upgrading your gear is hidden behind a right click menu (not speaking with the blacksmith of nothing doing) with no button prompts to point it out. The game loves showing you all the buttons you can push for various actions and things that you can to, just not that. At least game play is a bit nicer and less clunky. The 'helpful' auto adjusting shots don't seem to be a thing which is nice. Double jump is a helpful thing for getting around, and there are other improvements to 'useless' abilities from the previous incarnation. Currently there seem to be missing aspects in animations with the enemies however. Notably Ogres. I haven't seen all of the enemies just yet, but a typical 'end wave' or semi-boss creature that you see somewhat frequently throughout the game seems to have very little done in their animations. You'd imagine a big lumbering creature to create shock waves and particle effects when it swings it's weapon (Once a spiked club that is now a ham... because... sure.) just like the previous game but no. There is little indication of it doing anything which makes it look unpolished or lazy. Most of what I'm seeing are missing things that would make a fairly decent if not good start of a re-release of the original game. I say start because the first dungeon defenders had oodles of content to it including alternate heroes, items, and other promotional content that this does not and may not ever have.It would be easy and beneficial for the devs to add that back in with packs similar to the first game. Just update the models and maybe adjust a few mechanics and it would be easy money.Then again I'm getting the impression that there wasn't as much interest as the Devs may have wanted so the game will not be receiving as much (If any) additional work beyond patching the most broken aspects of the game. That may not be the case, but I'm a bit salty about the ten dollar price drop on release which I also think is a bad sign.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not generally one to review games but reading some of the negative reviews i felt the need to counter them and not just as positive reviews but to address the complaints. I am thoroughly enjoying the game, though i am admittedly biased as i have enjoyed all of the dungeon defenders games, and i absolutely recommend it even in it's current state and price but only if you fully understand this is EARLY ACCESS and the content has a timetable of release that will expand the value of this purchase over time... i repeat the value is not there right now... it will be later and the point of early access is for those excited to play early to get that opportunity while also supporting the developers in continued development and content delivery.The game is a reskin of the original dungeon defenders with better graphics better environment effects and some slight tweaks to gameplay.... as advertised so that really shouldn't be considered negative as it is openly acknowledged and it is a successful return that brings back all of what made the original great in my opinion and eliminates a lot of the bad that was holding dungeon defenders 2 from being equally as fun.There is not a lot of content, it has the main campaign (minus bosses) and survival mode for leveling and gear grinding and that is about it...also as advertised, again there is a timetable release from the developers that shows planned release times on more content, also those reviewing negative about that seem to forget that the original dungeon defenders had very little content in its 15 dollar original release( it had the campaign with some bosses and survival mode) the extra content they are remembering was all free add ons later like insane mode(which is already in this one) and nightmare mode(coming soon) or paid 10-15 dollar mini dlc's generally in the form of new classes.If you take early access for what it is and understand more value is coming your way over time and like tower defense games and don't mind a little grinding for gear and levels then this is absolutely a fantastic game and buy =)
