The mechanics are familiar (besides the 'Morsel' mechanic, which is one I haven't seen before, but is a lot of fun) and the game's ability to summarize the outcome of a turn (sometimes a turn that lasts upwards of 100 attacks) at a single glance mean that all the strategy is still there, but people new to this sort of game and veterans alike will be able to determine the outcome of a played card to a much more effective degree. It's tough to explain in a Steam review, but it's honestly amazing from a design standpoint given the amount of information that is being calculated from various abilities across a ton of different units. The designers and programmers deserve a serious high five for this.I was drawn to this by Northernlion's series on it. It's a ton of fun to watch and it's a blast to play. I'm 6 hours into it, but from my experience with it and my love of the genre, this may just be an early GOTY contender for me.Highly recommended, 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster train is a cardgame/tower defense roguelike that has you defending a pyre atop 3 levels of a moving hellbound locomotive trying to re-ignite a literal frozen-over Hell. You play monsters and spells in synergistic ways do defeat waves of enemies, with the ability to upgrade you spells and units as the run progresses, picking up relics which give various unique effects.The closest similarity is Slay the Spire, but the game has various differences that make it stand out, I won't go into details about specifics as that requires familiarity with the game but just broad strokes: The runs in this game are quite short compared to most others in the genre, averaging between 20-45 mins, what this means is your deck and options scale fast, meaningful decisions happen early and often.This encourages multiple playthroughs and definitely has that "just one more" quality. In addition the game informs you of all the main bosses, the end boss and gives a complete map ahead of time, so pausing runs for later is never a problem, just take a look at the map and you can easily figure out what you were building towards The game uses various levels on the train, with enemies starting at the bottom, in addition you always draw your champion who is powerful and consistent at the start of each battle along with any banner(class) units every turn, this leads to runs where variance occurs but you never feel outright screwed because you didn't draw your block in time. The game actually starts out pretty easy, the card variety is far more limited, you can't play the hard factions before unlocking them and there is a lot of discovery and experimentation, which is really fun! It's so easy in the beginning you get to check out the cool bosses and experience a lot with little pressure and it makes unlocking and beating the harder difficulties more rewarding in comparison. The game has an amazing soundtrack, interesting lore and an abundance of easter eggs and little quirks like any good roguelike, it also has a speed up option and various set speeds, with a logbook that shows your progress in terms of unlocks, wins, cards etc, which is really handy and motivates you to play more. The presentation is excellent which is a welcome surprise because a lot of these mechanics first games have pretty meh aesthetics.  The game has 5 different factions to mix and match with two champions each, when playing you chose a main faction which supplies your champion and a supporting one. This leads to a ton of variety thematically and gameplay wise, covering all the archetypes you would expect such as graveyard synergy, big bois, spellslinger, consuming to grow etc. It also draws out many players to various favorites, which is always a good sign. Playing demons, hellspawn, imps and eldritch horrors is just more fun and interesting than being the good guy like in the majority of games.At the current price its a steal, tonnes of content, great music, replayability, challenge and with it's excellently paced difficulty curve you can be a complete newbie to this genre or hardened min/maxing theorycrafting veteran and have just as much fun. Edit: So I've put more time into the game, and after reaching Cov25 the game just doesn't really feel balanced at all, doing a random-random run feels like banging your head into a brick wall, there are so many synergies that flat out don't work and the path to victory often involves ignoring half your deck and just focusing on what synergies jump out while removing as many cards as possible. I feel like if it wasn't for the upcoming DLC I would honestly give up on the game at this point, although it did give me a good amount of hours it doesn't really live up to games like Slay the Spire etc, the attention to detail regarding balance just isn't there, some classes struggle too much to clear backline and the vast difficulty jump between most Seraphs and The Patient is sort of glaring when you look at it, you can have a perfectly valid strategy but the Patient can kinda just shut it down.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game a bit and progressing through the game a bit, I can say that it doesn't have the depth of other turn based strategy games in this category. While you can certainly influence the game by placing your units in different ways on the levels decks and the decisions you make about which cards to keep and play in your run are very important, if you don't get the right drops of items, units or special effects throughout the run, it will be very difficult for you. I know this feature is present in many other games, but in this game it feels heavily present and effectual. Each run just feels like a lottery, hoping for the right items or drops. If you don't get them, it will very hard for you and  perhaps no fun for you (or less). If you do get them, you will steam roll to victory and the margin for error will be so high. It can be a bit boring that way. You know if you get the right items, it will be easy. Or that if you don't it will be hard and a grind. There is no mystery to the run. I don't feel like I can pull myself up by my bootstraps and make a bad run good. I just feel like if it is bad, it is bad, if it is good, it is good. There isn't a lot of complexity there to the gameWhile I get that that art of this game is good and they have put effort into the class system, ultimately it feels a bit 2 dimensional, especially compared to some in the genre. Once you understand how each champion works, whether you will win the run just depends on what items you get in the run. You can't turn a good run bad, or a bad run good. Or at least, it is very difficult to do so. You will either be having a party on round 2 cause you are steamrolling your enemies without any effort on your behalf, or you will be sweating away round by round, hoping not too much damage gets done to your pyre in that one..

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: - Unique spin on Slay the Spire formula, with floors, minions and very impactful artifacts.  - 5 clans, 1 main and 1 supportive, which makes for many unique combinations (even same two clans make the run very different depending on which is main one and which is supp) - Kind of mobile game-y but still solid animation and art style which grows on you - Interesting hidden events and decent storyCons: - Could use more events\artifacts\cards - Gets repetitive if you don't switch clans for a while )

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad I bought this game. It's heavily inspired by Slay the Spire, and I'm enjoying it at least as much as I did STS. The card mechanics are well designed, and there's more diversity between runs compared to STS because of the ability to choose a primary and allied clan. The innovation of the multi-floor tower-defense-like mechanic is clever, and it keeps the battles interesting. So far my biggest complaint is a lack of variance with the boss fights. The bosses switch up their minor mechanics, but you fight the same bosses every single run, and their main mechanics are always the same.  Overall it's an awesome game if you enjoy card battlers, and you can easily find it on sale for <$18 if you check a price tracker like IsThereAnyDeal.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly fun deck builder. While superficially similar, it's very different from 'Slay the Spire' in that you manage a roster of heroes and spells, levelling them up and deploying them on three levels to fight the increasingly difficult waves. Although you start out with only two factions, there are five factions in the game which you unlock by summoning heroes. from these, you choose your main faction which gives you a champion unit witrh special abilities and a support faction which gives you spells and unique heroes.The very early stages are a cake walk which can lure you into a false sense of security because the difficulty ramps up after three of four encounters. Then you see the need for devising a consistent upgrade strategy. Levels are quite short and can be played through quite quickly and then you get to choose your upgrade path, allowing you to upgrade your spells on one path and your heroes on another. And you can discard some of your cards or heal your pyre.There are a tremendous number of synergies to explore here. How you upgrade your champion, which heroes to pair it with, there are so many possibilties here.  I've yet to unlock the last two factions but I'm already spoiled for choice as to what to do each run. There are even a selction of really powerful spells which can only be cast on the floor below your pyre so there's a lot of fun to be had here.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent evolution of the deck-building genre.Clearly inspired by Slay the Spire, this may be the first game to challenge the mantle for best in the genre, and is truly a unique game in itself and re-think of this game loop, rather than a cheap knockoff with a few twists sprinkled in, like most of its recent competitors.An extremely polished and unique game with great replayability, highly recommended for any fan of this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game through the Humble Monthly Subscription.It feels awfully similar to slay the spire, turns out it's from the same studio and follows the same gameplay principles, for the most part. For those that played Slay the Spire and loved it, this is a lighter, more fast paced take on the same idea. You move through 8 different stages, pick some semi random drops and bonuses as you go along, eventually trying to defeat the final boss and earn yourself the chance to do it all over again, only harder!It doesn't have the deepness or seemingly endless combinations you'd find in StS, and games tend to finish fairly quickly. That's not necessarily a bad thing, it's nice to get into it for 30-60 minutes of fun, wrap it up and go on with your life.Does tend to become addicting despite its apparent simplicity.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: It's Slay the Spire in many regards, except instead of a mission to try and defeat an evil Spire, you are delivering a burning Pyre to reignite the flames of Hell. I do feel like Slay the Spire is the more elegant, timeless game of the two, but Monster Train has a lot going for it in terms of build diversity with the varied clans and their synergies. It takes many notes from it's predecessor, and while in some regards it does things worse, in many ways it offers some interesting new ideas, like upgrading cards and the multi-floor strategic layer. Monster Train may be a bit more cluttered in it's design, but it is definitely scratching the same itch as Slay the Spire. RNG is still king here, but in many ways I feel it's a bit more manageable. Runs are not super long in general, and the graphics and sound design are top notch. It warms by cynical heart that the goal of the game is to save Hell from oblivion, and that the 'Winged' (aka Angels) who have frozen Hell over are depicted in such a dark manner. The lore tidbits attached to cards make for an interesting read, something I feel StS lacks. I do hope future games in the genre take notes from some of the design choices made here. There have been quite a lot of these roguelite card games of late, but this is the one of the few that I feel moves the genre forward somewhat. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good that it got me to write a review for the first time. Incredibly fun, addictive and skill-driven. Sound track is awesome, gameplay is diverse and cool. Love the art and the silliness of the whole thing (which does nothing to detract from the seriousness of the strategy). 10/10 awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I prefer it a lot over Slay the Spire. Extremely well polished. It's at the level of dead cells for me where I was blown away by how well made, and cleverly crafted, the game is. It's gotten rid of most of the monotony and time-wasting that comes with the genre. You're straight into the action and kept there until you finish the ride.Synergies are well thought out and directly rewarding for your forethought and investment in them. Most importantly synergies no longer rely completely chance and can be planned accordingly. While synergies in Slay the Spire were fun, even if you planned for one you often had to rely on RNG for whether your acquire it. This game does them much better.It's incredibly fun to start with the champion or an item and think 'oh cool I could do this'. My last run I had a starting artifact that majorly buffed my initial (extremely) weak creatures and my immediate thought was 'how can I capitalise the ♥♥♥♥ out of this and make them OP' and I was able to do just that because I could plan for the forge (spend money to buff a creature) and duplicate which copies a card. I nearly won with my silly build but lost at the end stretch of the last boss.The devs should feel proud, and maybe a bit smug, for what they've made.  Much rarer these days then it should be, Monster Train is a game about having fun and I'll certainly be continuing to take it up on that offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you're like me, you've seen many games try (and fail) to capture the magic of Slay the Spire. I've played many of them myself, and this is the first one that has not only come close, but has potentially more depth replayability. And I say that having poured a frankly irresponsible amount of time into Slay the Spire. This game is clearly a labor of love, absolutely worth full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you like magic the gathering, or slay the spire or both, this game is for you. It has hours of content, with two free updates that brought even more. There are 5 factions with 2 champion and unique cards per champion to chose from and you chose 2 different factions per run, giving a huge amount of combinations to play. Not only that, you can add a little bit of madness to the game with the wild mutations content, there are daily challenges, hell rush where you face off against other players to be the first to the end, and the ability to send challenge links to friends. The game is one of the best deckbuilders I've ever played, and I 1000% recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid deckbuilder. Lots of variety for highly-varied runs. Nice gradual progression of difficulty allowed for a satisfying victory at the hardest challenge rating. I found this game more approachable than Slay the Spire on the whole, due to its slightly shorter runs and slightly less punishing RNG.My main complaints are a lack of variety in enemies and too large a power variance among artifacts and caverns. Overall a good entry-level deckbuilder that is approachable for casual players.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Slay the Spire you'll love Monster Train.I was put off at first by the weird name and cartoony, hearthstone-clone, F2P-look the game's store page has, and only bought it because it was heavily discounted. I needn't have worried - underneath the slightly strange branding there's an absolutely stellar game.The mechanics are perfect - it's easy to understand but hard to master. Card games can be difficult to get right - it's often fairly straight forward to play 'optimally', and then you're basically at the mercy of the RNG and just along for the ride. That's certainly how I felt with Hearthstone. But Monster Train gets it right: there's still a lot of RNG - it's a rouge-like after all - but there's a lot of strategy as well in terms of what you play where; which battles you choose to fight and which you leave to a different floor. There's also a good amount of 'right, how can I make this deck work?' too; there's not  many opportunities to draft units, so while you can have an ideal build in mind, you have to be willing to change direction.I've spent many happy hours playing Slay the Spire, but this has replaced it as my 'I've got an hour to kill, what can I do?' game. It's easy to drop into and easy to save and come back to if you can't afford the full hour a run typically takes. There are still cursed runs, just like in any roguelike, but it's still enjoyable even when you're never drawing right. And when you get a bit of luck and a build that really synergizes: it's a blast.My only critique is that I wish it were easier to 'come back'. Usually when a run starts going bad it's really difficult to recover. I think slightly more choice on some of the rewards would serve that purpose - it would let you tailor your build better and fill in that one card your build needs but the RNG isn't giving you. But that's fairly minor - and I find exactly the same thing in StS (in fact in StS it's worse - while your demise is still assured, it's much more drawn out).
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10, the gameplay somehow has more depth than , the only point of comparison I have.The minions are both your main character and expendables, this makes for tough choices, or at least meaningful choices, nearly all the time. Spells also have a lot more variety since they need to be relevant for more types of situations.There's also a very good amount of replayability, and 5 different factions, each accompanied by one of the 4 others.As long as you have some affinity with the genre, or are curious to try it out, this is definitely something you should buy. Maybe wait for a discount, but I think that fullprice it's nearly worth it, so if you're itching to try it out, you should be satisfied even with a small discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Like Slay the Spire but worse. Runs are extremely dependent on luck. The covenant mode gives you random extra cards to your starting deck, which range from busted OP to useless garbage. This encourages you to restart until you get an appealing deck, as restart abusing gives no penalty. Many clan combos have absolutely zero synergy together and allied clans just end up cluttering your deck.

_childDocuments_.review: good roguelite.   Handful of different factions to choose from for your run, as you unlock them.  You pick 1 main faction and 1 secondary faction.  Playing around with different faction combinations has  kept the game feeling fresh.  Additionally each factions has 2-3 ways you can play it, making each run different than the last while still giving you a fair shot at a good run.   I have sunk about 20 hours in and could easily see sinking at least double that.  Well worth the price of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is good at two things:- Making you frustrated when you lose a run.- Making you overly happy when you win one.And the happiness largely trumps the anger. When you win, you go "Wow! That was awesome!" with a big smile on your face. It's a good "Take that, bad guys" kind of joy.Also, Monster Train is very good at:- The music.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I personally don't like how you only get one turn to destroy enemies on a level; otherwise they move up. Since this mechanic is core to the game - I cannot recommend it.I love card games. I've tried, and tried, and TRIED to also get into Monster Train but.....I just can't. Don't get me wrong, I love literally every other aspect to this game. The classes are unique, the cards are interesting, and there's enough randomness to make each run different. However each time I start up a new run I tell myself "Okay  time will be different and I'll finally get into it", but it always ends up with the same routine:- I'd change it so that enemies stay on their level until they have cleared all of my creatures on that levelIf you can get past this mechanic, then it's a fantastic game and would recommend it. Before buying I would recommend watching very closely how the game is played, and make sure it is right for you.

_childDocuments_.review: All the comparisons to slay the spire are apt, but there is a little more depth to this game. The multi tiered fighting areas make for some tough decisions on where to put units, and the all of the different races you can choose to play as add a lot of variety to this game. I can see myself sinking a lot more hours into this jawn. Hop off that fence and buy it, it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster train is hands down, one of the best video game card games I've ever played. It's a perfect blend of risk, reward, luck mitigation and replayability all neatly packaged together in a solid core gameplay loop.Firstly, the game offers a lot of different combinations. You pick your main deck which has a powerful, free and scaling champion unit you get at the start of every combat. You then pick a secondary faction which opens up a roster of card and game play mechanics exclusive to them such as unit upgrades, card upgrades and artifacts to augment your abilities. Your goal is to find syngeries and abuse the hell out of them. In the base game, there's 5 factions (an extra sixth is included in the dlc), and all the factions have an alternate side which replace the starting card and champion. Furthermore, the champion units themselves have 3 different paths to upgrade as you progress. Admittedly, some of these are more niche, less viable and ultimately less reliable than others which becomes more apparent as you scale difficulty. Although, this only mildly undermines just how much the game gives you to play with in terms of content.The general gameplay loop is you pick one of two paths before each combat, get stronger and then fight. What makes this so crucial is that the game gives you near complete information of what rewards you'll get in the future. At any time you can scroll further down the map to see what your options are, including the kind of flavour the end boss is and what his mechanics are. There are some fixed reward types and general flow to each run and unlike slay the spire, there is absolutely no negative events to worry about. You feel completely in control of your decisions and most of your failures will be your own rather than at the mercy of the game. Certain rewards can also be skipped and will give you some gold to use as compensation such as cards and artifacts. Even better is that the game generously gives multiple draw pick 1 reward types so you always get strong choices to make.Before each combat you get the choice to add an additional modifier to your fight to get extra goodies. The DLC also adds shards which you can take to get more rewards at the cost of fighting randomly buffed enemies depending on many shards you've willingly taken on. Most of my failed runs are out of making bad calls without consulting what information the game was giving me OR by biting off way more than I could chew. This is what makes the game so immensely fun.Combat is fairly simple. You control 3 levels and a core level. You plonk down dudes to defend and play cards to buff or kill foes. Enemies pop in the bottom floor and will ascend a level after each round of fighting until they die or reach the core. Once you take too much core damage, you lose. After you end your turn, your enemies attack FIRST then you. You'll need to make clever use of your units and cards to either mitigate the attrition or plan around it. After some rounds of combat you'll fight a boss who will make his way to the core and the cycle repeats. The game will tell you who dies and damage before you end the turn so you know how badly you're losing or well you're winning so you can better make decisions.Finally, after a successful run you'll unlock a new covenant level up to the max of 25. These add additional handicaps to keep the game challenging as you push through to new heights. The first covenant in particular adds random cards to your deck from your factions as a way to incentivise you trying them out or making a strategy with those draws in mind.Monster train is hands down the most cleverly designed card games. It's addictive, challenging and all the while makes it so most losses will boil down to you rather than bad RNG. You can't ask for much better than this. Even if the main game gets tiresome, there's the daily challenge and mutators to make runs more wacky. An absolute gem packed full of content.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic roguelike deck building card game. The tiered minion-placement system is great. The deck building aspects were different from what I'd seen previously but once I got accustomed to it I loved it. The difficulty is easy enough and scales smoothly. I hope to spend much more time in this awesome game.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Would rate 8/10Pros:- It's good.- It's fun.- There is little like it. (it's not quite like Slay the Spire)Con:- Limited replayability.- There is no enemy or map variations. You fight the same 9 "rooms" in each run, with identical waves of enemies in the same order. - This gets really tiresome after 10 runs. Would rather play something different.Multiplayer is early access:- All players are doing individual solo runs. It's not really multiplayer. The player going further with the better score "wins".- You can't inspect other player decks.- You can't spectate other players.- There is a horrible timer forcing exactly 5 minutes per room, before proceeding to the next room. Except a room takes only 2-3 minutes to play and you're bored to death waiting another 2-3 minutes to continue playing.The game is good but doesn't deserve more than 8/10 due to the lack of diversity and replayability. Don't expect to get more than 10-20 hours out of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Once you get into it, by it I mean: get used to the gameplay, mechanics, memorize the Races, the overall deck builds, spells, combinations, shop items, artifacts; then you will be overwhelmed by the insane amount of the replayability. Not only the fact that most run can be totally different, starting from the Champion Card upgrade path right to the overall cards drawn after the mission, but also due to the fact, that there is Covenant system, which changes the game every time you beat it.Basically, if you want "truly" beat the game, you need to do it with a Covenant system active 25 times, and each time pick the higher Covenant for the run.Verdict - If you like rogue card games, deck building, replayability, challenges, randomized runs, unpredictable outcomes and fast pace (the average run will take you around 30-40 minutes or less), then it is a definitely a game that you need to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is an unique deck builder game that I have really enjoyed. I have played many deckbuilding games and Monster Train is the game that extended my perspective on this genre. The main mechanism of the game is what creates the "Train" part of the game. Your chosen units, with potenital upgrade attachments, is placed one of the three floors, and fight with "Monsters". Floor switch mechanics, floor related upgrades, minion buffers and debuffers, the choice of cards in the overall game is perfectly fit into the mechanism of the game. I strongly recommend this game, especially if you enjoy deckbuilding games! If not, there is no shame to try it :) Might change your mind!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite roguelite deckbuilder. The amount of variety possible in each deck is incredible. The engine building is also very satisfying. If you find a powerful strategy, the game rewards you greatly and you can snowball very hard. But it does take some trail and error and a bit of thinking to find a strong strategy like that, but it is so worth it.The game is also easy to beat on this first run, it only took me 2-3 tries. I personally like this because I don't like getting stuck on my first run for many hours. However, later runs can be modified to be much more difficult, which I think its a interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a ridiculously addictive rogue-like deck builder. The premise is that you're racing to Hell with the last spark of demonic fire to reignite the bowels of your home. Heaven is trying to stop you. The demonic fire is called your pyre and sits atop the fourth story of your train. The bottom three stories is where you defend against the waves of attacking Heavenly mercenaries. Gameplay is excitingly quick and punchy. Power-ups galore. Oozing with upgrades. Full of rare cards.This game has an unusual idea packed into a fun as Hell package. Love it!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I love the theme of the game, and how each faction feels. The gameplay is simple enough to grasp but deep enough to have you want to play one more run late at night. Managing the deck is just as important as playing your cards while fighting the angels off the Boneshaker. All of this has me excited to spend more time playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Having high expectations (I'mcoming from Slay the Spire, which is an excellent card battle game), I'm really surprised by the fun I'm having with Monster Train. The gameplay is neat, the animations great, and fighting aboard a train really gives a special energy to the battles.Being able to accelerate several times the fight, or stay with normal speed, is interesting, depending on what level of understanding of the effects of the spells or attacks you need.Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Great card game in the same vein as Slay the Spire and just as addictive! Instead of controlling one character like in Slay the Spire, you play several monsters which you use to defend a central nexus at the top of your train. The game has a bunch of different factions all with different unlockable card sets and has many different difficulty and modifier options to spice things up. It plays slightly faster than Slay the Spire but needs just as much careful planning and management of your deck to maximise your power!The only really bad point I'd say was that there isn't really much of a tutorial, the game throws you into the deep end very quickly and you're just expected to get the hang of it. However all card abilities and types are explained clearly and I found after only a couple of runs that I completely understood it. Regardless, I'd probably recommend playing Slay the Spire first. Once you're tired of that and looking for something else, come try this!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an innovative gameplay that i like very much. Moving from battle to battle with its different bosses with decisions to be made on the road in form of events, upgrading your units, spells, self defending train core and that you have to protect. In battle you have multiple stages of the train that you defend in terms of preventing enemies to move up a stage which march towards your core to  destroy it. Distribute your units wisely. You can choose from multiple factions, each of has it's own heroes and abilities. Battles can be made faster through settings. One whole round takes about 20-30 minutes, i am guessing here. No regrets on buying this.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: As someone new to gaming, at the tender age of 33, I have really enjoyed this game so far. I found it a little overwhelming learning what to do and what it meant (I need instructions but I have learned this is not how gaming works haha). I really am not a simple person, just a slow learner, now I know what I'm doing it's great! It really is a fun one and not fast paced, you can really take your time in deciding what to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: When making a deck builder roguelite, one is instantly posed with the question: why not just play Slay the Spire? Monster Train I feel answers that question so well that I find myself asking why even play Slay the Spire? It may sound blasphemous but the multilayered gameplay of Monster Train coupled with the general speed of its runs makes it an experience I have found deeply rewarding and even more fun than the game it shares so much DNA with.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Esports superstar and 30 year old boomer Ryan 'Northmillion Lionshares' Letourneau brought me to this game and I was initially sceptical about the 'train cart' gimmick but I quickly fell in love with the diverse and interesting card design. All 5 different hell races are unique and interesting, the ability to pick 2 per run adds much needed depth to deck building and an incredible amount of replayability. There is even multiplayer where you can race against your friends and compete for high scores in the same seeded run, a feature often neglected in roguelikes.The game isn't without flaws, certain events feel extremely situational and are often just passable, a number of bosses hard counter certain builds and there's very little you can do outside of a handful of tech cards that you may not have unlocked, and lastly the stygian guard feel a bit below the curve in terms of power. But overall the game is a great card builder/roguelike and definitely worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the Spire is nothing short of a damn good game. I've played it a lot and I highly recommend it. From its Roguelike elements to its random events to the cards themselves and the very lore of the spire itself that your character is trapped within...The game is just phenomenal. Many games since have tried to emulate and mimic Slay the Spire as it seemingly has set the bar to a new level within the Deck-building Rogue-Like genre that is so sensationally high that I never thought it would be possible to raise it further.Until now.Monster Train has many elements from Slay the Spire which is why you see so many comparisons and correlations to it. However Monster Train's unique take on the genre from its own very rich lore and incredible visuals to the cards and bosses you run into is just a blast to play. From the "professionals" (masochists?) that play the game on an incredibly high level at the highest difficulty to someone who has never before experienced the genre, Monster Train is truly an amazing game to play right from the beginning. The amount of possibilities that lie within its system of "take one clan as your primary clan and another as an ally" and all the various abilities and combinations that follow allow for a truly deep level of complexity yet introduces the player slowly and subtly enough that it never really feels overwhelming to learn.The upgrade system seems better overall though a bit more RNG heavy than Slay the Spire. The difficulty can scale to truly masochistic levels so if you're someone who enjoys a challenge this game has that too.Its biggest faults are that sometimes you just aren't offered what you need to win the run. And while that feels bad, it isn't so disappointing that it angers me. I usually just say something to myself along the lines of "Guess I'll see where the next deck takes me."And that's the greatest thing about this game. Seeing what heights you can take your deck to soar at... or plummet below the gates of Hell itself.Welcome to Monster Train! - the game where Hell itself has already been frozen over and your job is to reignite what's left of the Pyre at the center of the nine layers of Hell. Don't let the Angelic forces stop you though - they're here to snuff out what little hope remains. Will you succeed in reigniting the very Pyre of Hell? Or will Hell remain a frozen wasteland for all eternity? Only you can decide.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Finally reached covenant 25 and won the game this day. So many failures and rage was had until that feat. This is like a tactical Dark Souls. Sometime the game purley hates you and the randomness never seems to work in your favour. But in the end I found out that the Melting Remnant (the kid) / Stygian (frostbite) combo was the only way to do it for me. For some reason I stayed with this game and I am glad I did.Do not touch this if you can´t stamina a game that´s doing it´s hellmost to make you fail and also don´t give any rewards at all for a succesfull run.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great but it is plagued by unbalance gameplay. Doesnt matter if you've got a perfect strategy and build really good decks from there because there will always be that one boss  a particular enemy placement that completely counters your entire strategy towards the later stage of the game in the form of artificial difficulty. Also, there is only 1 way to beat some bosses or enemy placements and if your deck does not have that one way, you are guaranteed to lose.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Um so I dont have a ton of time played into this game, but I have quite a bit of experience with deck builders and games in general. So this is my opening statement, its a decent game, I dont think its worth its price tag though. I actually beat this game on my 2nd run through. It just wasnt all that challenging or complicated. Some of the cards dont seem very balanced (looking at you cards that buff when healed). I had 4 cards in my decks almost immediately and thought to myself, yea i could probably win with these, and sure enough i did. Theres not alot of  strategy. You end up playing the same monsters in the same spots every level and essentially do the same series of moves no matter who you face. Run 3 with a different deck and I again was able to beat the game. I think its ok if you're new to deck building, But i would say Slay the Spire tops this game. Id say this is a $10-$15 game. Its fun enough but just not as in depth as i hoped
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I hopped on a bit late on the Monster train , but the ride so far has been very enjoyable ( pun intended ). I enjoy the fact that even though some combinations and archetypes seem to be incomparable to other combos on the power curve cards seem to find their way into winning decks and still not feel like complete dead weight.Also infinite damage/gold/heal etc. are really hard to build and require a lot of rng even with good deck building and a lot of experience. If/when you manage to pull off one of those that run feels memorable and extremely enjoyable since it's really rare and hard to replicate again. It's a game that similar to Slay the Spire made me feel like I should be recording my runs to share with people later, yet I never do.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually play card games, but I found this one enjoyable. Monster Train is one of those that falls under don't judge a book by its cover. I like how it has different approaches to whether or not you should thin your deck, stay away from buffs or debuffs depending on the various forms the last boss takes, Seraph. For example, Seraph the Diligent will cause each card played at the beginning of a turn to have the consume trait, and Seraph the Chaste will half all buffs and debuffs that do not benefit him. Taking this into consideration is necessary to have a successful run, and each run has its unique concerns. I recently played Roguebook, and the latter seemingly had more limited options; for example, their answer to disincentivize deck thining was to have cards that add damage based on how many cards are in the draw or discard pile. Overall, Monster train is the best deck-building game of the few that I have played.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: But I can't recommend it because the visual style is just too damn lousy. Generic, full of meaningless detail that leads to no coherent picture, lacking in personality but offering a profusion of fantasy tropes that go nowhere. You've seen this in a hundred games and other media, and not once did it make sense, look good, or help readability.Getting an artist to come up with something that's unique, aesthetically pleasant and readable is difficult. I won't expect it. So could I just have all the visuals replaced with geometric shapes and text, please? That would turn this around.Also, we're on the wrong side here! You're supposed to kill the demons, not help them!  hasn't DOOM taught you anything?-------------------------Edit: After some more time spent on it - no. I'd rather play more Slay the Spire, which has far tighter gameplay while offering far more interesting setting and presentation.

_childDocuments_.review: Heavily-inspired by Slay the Spire, but lacking much of the nuance that made StS so great. Still, the game is very fun. There's much more focus on broken combos in this game, but the tiered levels add a nice twist that can give fresh entertainment in the genre even to someone who has logged almost a thousand hours on StS and its associated mods. Higher end graphics and animations are well done. 35 hours in and still looking forward to more. Excellent value, thanks devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a Deck Building Rogue Lite, bearing some similarities to Slay the Spire and other Deck Builders. Aesthetically it is very pleasing with pretty visuals and impactful audio. The general plot is that you are a denizen of hell, taking the last remaining pyre to the frozen heart to reignite it. This pyre serves as the health points for your run (situated on the top floor of your 3 floor train), and should it be reduced to zero your run is over. Your run will last for 8 battles with overworld sequences separating these. You start the game by choosing a guild and a sub guild; these have their own cards and strategies which in most cases will compliment each other. To begin with you have access to two, eventually accumulating 5 with a handy option to randomise your choices for some extra challenge. Your primary guild also decides your champion, a 0 cost unit that can be upgraded to become a powerhouse. The game is broken into the overworld, where you choose your route between battles, and the battles themselves. The route splits offer run-duration upgrades for units and spells, regeneration for your pyre, artifacts, troop recruitment points and other more interesting points such as card duplication and removal. Some of these are immediately more useful than others, such as removing two vanilla troops or spells from your deck at a single stop. You make your initial choices of starting artifact and champion upgrade at the start of a run and then you're on to your first battle. You're treated to a splash screen which displays the enemies you will face, and importantly their Keywords. Keywords include such traits as incant (gains buffs when spells are cast on the same floor) and sweep (unit will apply its damage to all of your units on the floor when it attacks rather than just the frontal unit). The game will also offer you the chance to increase the challenge of the battle at this point, and offer rewards for doing so. These are on a per battle basis thankfully, as your composition may not always be suited for the challenge, for instance an attack heavy deck may not be well suited to take on an enemy force where each unit has damage reflecting thorns. The battles as previously mentioned take place across 3 floors, with a fourth floor being your pyre. Each room has a population capacity, with creatures having a size stat. Your job is to prevent enemies from ascending the train to the pyre by placing monsters strategically so that they combo with one another on the same floor. Typical card game mechanics apply here, such as draw amount and the energy reserves you use to cast each card, with cards having an energy cost typically ranging from 1-4 with some exceptions. With the knowledge that the enemy troops will generally attack yours first you must weigh up the outcome of the battle, and then intervene by dropping stronger creatures, killing enemies with harmful spells or healing and bolstering your own units' attributes. after each scuffle, surviving enemies will ascend a floor. Certain rules allow enemies to ascend faster, but if they make it to your pyre they will begin to damage it. Thankfully your pyre takes none of their nonsense and has a sweeping and very damaging attack it will use once they have finished their assault, but this is a last resort and to be avoided if possible. After several waves, the boss will spawn. Bosses will attack the same floor relentlessly rather than ascending after a single round of attack. This means that Your floors need to be strong enough to take a sustained assault while also dealing enough damage and debuffs to hinder the boss. Certain bosses will be present before they begin their climb, laying traps and augmenting their units before making their final approach which leads to some great and flavoursome battles. Should the boss kill all of your minions on a floor, they will seal the floor in ice and render it unusable for the remainder of the battle. Killing the boss will take you to the rewards screen, with points deducted for pyre damage taken and every floor the boss successfully ascended. You are then offered a selection of cards from each of your guilds which you can opt to take or, importantly, leave. The joy in the game comes from finding silly combos, finding that way to perpetually feed sacrificial creatures to your tank, increasing its power every turn or stacking hundreds of stacks of life draining frostbite onto an enemy. The guilds are varied and each is genuinely a joy to play as. Finding the synergy between each is a lot of fun, especially considering the vast amount of card and artifact unlocks that factor into this endeavour. Optional "Covenant" levels add self appointed penalties which make runs more challenging, ensuring a challenge no matter your level. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who wants a game that is accessible but has a learning curve that is not afraid to punish poor synergistic choices. As an example, I had a unit that would bring a unit back from the dead every turn. I ended up with a perpetual cycle of him bringing a morsel, (a small sacrificial creature typically destined to be eaten at the end of the turn) back to life instead of a worthwhile creature simply by playing the cards in that order without thinking. Well worth the retail price point for the depth, and the love that has clearly gone into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics is decent, difficulties are just right. You don't lose a run and lose everything. You still gain stuff. The runs are short - about 15-30 mins. As a man in his late 30s, I would recommend this game if you are looking for something cute, slower paced yet action-packed and intellectually challenging. My thanks to the developers of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Monster Train on and off for a while now, but it's a really fun game to come back to. There are tons of fun ways to build your deck and even though the bosses are the same through each playthrough they often change their tactics which makes you need to adjust your strategy for beating them. The art for the game is imaginative and vibrant and I love how colorful the game is. The game has lots of replayability with multiple class combinations, card unlocks, and special challenges.Slay the Spire is still the premier deck building roguelike in my opinion, but Monster Train differentiates itself from it enough that it's well worth giving a spin.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a good, fun time. Start with a deck of crappy cards, fight angels, and slowly turn that deck into an unstoppable force of destruction. It's well paced with a lot of variety to keep things interesting. The big weakness is that as you rise to higher difficulty levels success feels more dependent on getting lucky with a killer combo rather than a well balanced strategy. Still, it's satisfying to pull those combos off.It's not as good as the finely tuned machine that is Slay the Spire, but it's still quite a delight.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Compared with Slay the Spire, here a casual old guy like me can actually win a game or two after work. The game has only minimal buildup time, the upgrade system between the fights is more about good choices than about missing out and the artwork with its Magic the Gathering meets Hearthstone just pleases the eye. I love Monster Train for being chill and turning into unexpected wtf synergies in a single game session.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Very Slay the Spire-ish game with interesting mechanics. I think the branching paths are better executed with more meaningful choices - do I upgrade my spells, my minions? do I get an artifact or rather remove cards? - rather than just how many elites and how many campfires I'm going to get.The game is more snowbally in nature, and you often end up with some broken combo by the end of the run. This is reflected in the enemies' HP which progresses much more exponentially than in Slay the Spire. This also means the balance is more sensitive and randomness can have a meaningful influence.Nevertheless, Monster Train is really addictive and rewarding when you get things right. It feels less clean and polished than Slay the Spire, but it dares try more ideas mechanically speaking.A very refreshing game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: At this rate I have become a sucker for Roguelike Deckbuilding games and don't let the cash-grab-mobile-game-like art style fool you! this game is really good!- It has the usual elements like in StS but it adds some kind of tower defense mechanic to it- The synergy relies on combination of clans - It has a mastery system for each clans / clan synergy- TrainsFrostbite is ridiculously op
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is decent but is far from the best game in the genre. The Good:- easy to learn- combat feels unique compared to other games in the genreThe Bad- card art is meh- the sound effects are VERY annoying- poorly balanced which results in either an easy run, or a hopeless runIf you're a fan of the genre, its worth trying. If you're new to the genre, buy Slay the Spire instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: It's deceptively easy to spend hours on this game. A run takes me about an hour and that time is filled with constant progression and leveling up. Satisfying. That's how the game feels. Yes, it's frustrating to lose a couple of runs in a row on level 6-7 but it doesn't feel like a huge deal to just try again. I'm a big fan of deck building board games and this scratches the same itch and gives something extra that would not really work in physical format. I like that the combat resolution is completely deterministic. So first there's the puzzle on how to optimize your deck and then there's smaller puzzles in each battle.I think this will be one of those few games that I will complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Looks like a simple deckbuilder but it is actually super complex on your first run u may be like i got this in the bag but as you climb the ladders with each run it gets harder and something u thought was good early ends up being bad constantly have to refine a new combo to master the game a must buy for any fan of slay the spire style games
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: first few hours i really enjoyed this game, the artstyle the mechanics and choices interested me and the game has a lot of potential but sadly things get boring really quickly unless you enjoy replaying the same bosses over and over with just slightly more damage and health then i'd wait for a big sale before spending £20. What annoys me most about the game is the fact it took me 2 hours to complete the standard run, there was no difficulty and expected more than 8 battles to complete the game. Hopefully they add in way more content for me to change my review because the game has got a good foundation

_childDocuments_.review: Great deckbuilder that took inspiration from Slay the Spire but still put forth a lot of new systems and mechanics to add its own spin to the genre. The result is a high quality game that is up there with Slay the Spire. The artstyle itself is also really good and the soundtrack is superb. Definitely would recommend, and for the price the game is, you're getting a lot more back than you are paying for.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I only recently discovered the joys of Slay the Spire. And then the Monster Train rolled through and took me with it. What a ride! >30 hours in and there is still so much to do, so many combinations to master. Every run is its own thing. The choice to combine two of five very different clans to set up your deck is genius. Finding the synergies, weaknesses and strenghths of the decks you can build out of these (depending of what you get in your current run of course), together with upgrades and artifacts, is a lot of fun. There is a surprising amount of depth here. Yes, some combinations are more potent than others, but it is still fun to go for a more unlikely combination and lead it to victory. The covenant ranks keep things interesting, even as you progress. I'm honestly not sure if I will ever reach rank 25, but that's not gonna stop me from playing!Highly, very highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a card game wherein cards are divided into clans and each clan has its own specialty. You choose a primary and secondary clan at the start allowing you to mix match different clans and see how they synchronize with each other. Each clan also has 2 different champion cards that you can choose between at the start which have their own skill set. These features allows players a variety of gameplay every run.The game also has a covenant system which is similar to Slay the Spire's ascension levels wherein players can choose to play the game in a harder difficulty after they finished the difficulty level before it for a challenge.Similar to Slay the Spire, Monster Train also has daily challenges that gives players different additional conditions in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Very varied, plenty of mechanics. You have ample ways to prepare, yet your choices matter from each phase of battle to the macro strategy of planning your deck and pathing. Charming setting, EXTREMELY addictive gameplay. If you like Slay the Spire, I feel like this is an even more complex and fun game of this genre. Plus, the devs added several major content updates and a new one will be coming soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike Slay the spire which the first completely run through took me forever, Monster Train started out a lot easy, but then as the covenant goes up after you beat it every time, it becomes increasingly harder and addicting. There is just so many combos you can play with on each run and it is extremely satisfying when everything works out in your favour and you start steam rolling enemies. I highly recommend this game, it is just a ton of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you love Slay the Spire then this is the next game you should check out. Love the combined deck building and tower defense aspects which make such a unique play style. I could take or leave the expansion. I like being able to merge units and have more ways to increase difficulty for big rewards but I'm not a fan of the new clan. It's just not really my thing. But I absolutely love this game and am glad it finally came out on mobile!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Fun until its not because Cov 25 runs don't start until you get past your 2nd to 3rd floor. RNG non-option challenges you have to take because of the way the game exponentially snowballs your victories means that you are basically on auto pilot and waiting 2-3 runs before you get an actual run going. Devs seem focused on nerfing what is consistent as well to push you to picking other cards, despite the fact that a lot of the low pick rate cards are niche because of the draft mechanic and relic mechanic. Rare minion are most likely to appear floors 1-4 and relics start appearing around floor 3. This makes it very risk to take a rare minion that is essentially dead if you don't hit the right relics, but if you do find the right relics you have a very low chance of getting the minions that go with it. All of this means its just brain dead clicking the buttons until you get combos that get past the first 2-3 floors. I prefer my input to actually mean something from the start of the game and not just go through the motions. Other deck builders like Slay the Spire are much better if you prefer that. Also the mutators aren't why I played the game in the first place and only serve to further splinter the playerbase and keep hellrush a dead game mode unless a popular streamer is playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and highly addictive deck-building game.There are five clans in this game. Each of them plays very differently and very unique. And since in every single run you can bring two clans (one main clan and one ally clan), there are 20 clan combinations to play with.Each run can last from 15-30 minutes, so this game is good for a quickie if you don't have much time to play. The game is casual friendly but also pretty challenging, especially if you have the highest Covenant unlocked.I'd give this game a 9.9/10. The missing 0.1 is room for improvement. Would love to see more clans to be added to the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is the best deckbuilding roguelike I've played, after Slay the Spire. The gameplay is a fusion of "summoning followers" style card games (MtG, Hearthstone), deckbuilding roguelikes (StS), and tower defense Games.   Despite its flaws, Monster Train is still an amazing game, and I believe it would keep improving. At of time of this review, I have been playing at the difficulty of Covenant 1/2, so my opinions are based on that.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I love -- love --  Slay the Spire. Played it for a few hundred hours on the Switch. But eventually everything gets old.This scratches that itch. It has enough similarities that you feel like you "know how to play" right at the start. But at the same time, it's different enough that it feels fresh and completely new. 25 hours in at time of writing and I feel like I'm still just starting to explore all my options. We'll see if it really goes the distance but it's already worth the money and then some.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you like card games you'll probably get some fun out of this. I don't typically like card games but this still caught my eye and the way it was described to me I figured I'd give it a shot. I got roughly an hour and a half into the game when I quickly realized that this game may not be for me. So before I went over the two hour mark I decided to pass.My main issue with the game wasn't the fact that it was a card game/tower defense mixed together. I actually liked that idea a lot. My issue was the power spikes. I played three runs. The first run I got absolutely destroyed, it lasted all of maybe ten minutes. My second run I got really far in comparison. What happened was I got a really good card, duplicated it with some good modifications, and between it and my hero card I had a single slot left per floor for a powerful imp card I found. This power spike literally carried me through the entire run. I made small modifications to a few others but they were on cleanup duty taking out whatever was left of the mangled enemy that crawled it's way up the stairs on the next turn. Point is, it wasn't even a contest. But on the third run (after you "beat" a run it goes into another run but NG+) the enemy got it's power spike and rendered everything moot. I didn't make it two more than two stops on my train ride. And therein lies my issue. This game is wildly inconsistent and all over the place. This isn't a bad thing, I can easily see people liking this. It's how rogue-like games thrive, in chaos. But it's not for me and I imagine not for others as well the lack of predictability leaves me feeling like I have no control over the outcome. You can perfectly play a level and still get roasted. Overall, the game is well built and the developers should be proud of the work they did. But it definitely won't appeal to everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a deck builder / tower defense that invites comparison to Slay the Spire. This game is less elegant (the numbers are much bigger) but far more mechanically dense (summoned units and limited capacity thereof, multiple floors on which fights play out, activated effects that you'll need to chain together in order to succeed, finer control over your starting conditions). This is disorienting if you try to play like in StS (or Dominion or any other deck builder), but not overwhelming, and new mechanics are parceled out at a good pace. With 20 hours, I have most of the major unlocks but plenty of minor ones are still out there, and I'm still encountering new events, artifacts, and cards. Most importantly, when the game copy uses gift as a verb, it does so correctly, describing a gift given to a stranger in a hospitality-exchange: It means so much to me, devs. Thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I tend to disregard games similar to games I've played before. This looked a lot like Slay the Spire, and I was about to just let it pass without giving it too much thought, mostly because I hadn't heard of it. Very glad I got introduced to it on launch day. It's fun to play, and takes most of what makes sts great and does it a tad better. The only thing I find I'm lacking now after around 24h playtime, is a bit more content. More artifacts and more bosses mostly.Great fun, give it a go. Also perfect for couch co-op
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Slay The Spire, Inscyryption, etc., this game is a no-brainer. There's enjoyable "game-breakers" occasionally and uniquely there are clans that you can level up, which give you different decks and strong "champion" cards that lead your gameplay style. It's quite addicting and I keep finding myself coming back, so far. There's also daily challenges that you can progress along-side seeing other players' progress at the same time, it's kind of a neat feature. Overall, if any part of you wants something both different and more than Slay The Spire, but similar in the good ways, this is a must-buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Slay the Spire, you might enjoy this.Unlike Slay the Spire, you do not play as "your character". Instead, think of all the characters as minions, and yourself as the "Boss". If your minions do not stop the enemies ascend through 3 floors, the enemies then attack you directly and damage you. Every faction offers different minions, spells, and mechanics. Some focus on healing and buffing, others on giving your minions temporary health (Armour) and damage, others focus on using LOTS of throw-away minions that they can remake again and again, and those minions grow stronger with every remake. The spells are a nice advance from Slay the Spire. You have the standard fare of damage dealing, healing, buffing, and debuffing cards, you have cards that have strong effects but require you discard cards, you have cards that affect your minions and the enemy minions, there's an evne that lets you build your own card from a selection, and there's cards that grow permanently (as in during that run, not between runs), as well as cards you can only play in specific floors, albeit there's only 1 or 2 of those. Overall, a very good selecton of effects, and quite a few that allow you to really strategize your turn.Without the DLC, the base game has, basically, NG+25, as every successful run unlocks a new difficulty, with different effects. Up to Level 25. the DLC adds a new, tough endboss, a new mechanic, and new cards, as well as a whole new faction to play as.I whole-heartedly recommend it. The game is very stable (for me, I have not had a single crash or freeze in all my hours). I did have two instances of the game not reacting for a few seconds, but I cannot reproduce those.The difficulty curve is smooth, the factions you play as are all very interesting, the learning curve is not too steep, but you will repeatedly find yourself thinking "Hmm, I wonder if this combination works" and it will work more often than not. Cards are well-explained and tooltips are precise. All mechanics work well togetherThe translation seems good, but I cannot say much about it, as I usually play my games in english.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This has lots of varied cards and they are all combo pieces. This game has really high difficulty and the cards are purposefully not balanced at all. In slay the spire sometimes you find a game breaking combo and its a lot of fun for one run, well in this game that's what you're supposed to do every run.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent Deckbuilder that I honestly liked more than slay the spire. There’s a lot of strategizing in terms of unit placement - do I place a unit in front to sacrifice it as a meat shield to protect the unit behind it, or do I play it safe on a different floor? Runs also feel a lot faster and more dynamic, and I like the ability to choose which set of rewards you get after each run. Highly recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a deckbuilder game designed around a custom mechanic: we put monsters on the floors of a train. Train has 3 floors, and after each turn our monsters fight against enemies on the same floor. Then, enemies ascend, trying to reach a Pyre, which is mounted on the top of our wagon.The base game contains five fractions, and in each run, we choose two of them - a main one and a support one. These fractions vary a lot - each one of them is based on another mechanic (even two mechanics, in fact), and these mechanics are really fun and original, different from what can be seen in other games. Thus, each run may be a totally new experience, when the player has to discover a way to win from the ground.And this is a point that requires emphasizing: Monster Train is designed to discover. Not only it has many fractions, but it also rewards the player for discovering - the game contains a logbook that marks each fraction combination we have won with, and even each single card we have won with. And I had much from filling this logbook, the game strongly encourages players to do so, so they are not bored by playing the same optimal tactic again and again.And here comes main disadvantage of Monster Train: although fractions and cards vary a lot, enemies are not that different. Yeah, some of them have some special traits, but most of them are not very surprising or don't make that big difference.  That's why choosing the best fractions and cards every time may become boring very quickly. Even though the game has 25 ascension levels, each of them making the run slightly harder. In other words, if you are 100% focused on playing the best tactic every time and you don't have fun from experimenting or taking suboptimal choices to fill the logbook, Monster Train may be not for you.A small, but appreciated accent is that the game likes to give the player many statistics. After each run, it shows us some records we broke (and there are so many records that you will almost surely break some), and compares us to friends.Summarizing, I had lots of fun from playing Monster Train and I really recommend this game. It brings some fresh ideas to deckbuilding genre, and it executes them very well. It's a great choice for anyone who likes deckbuilders and wants to try something new.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game better than Slay the Spire. I haven't felt like a run was hopeless, and the path to making overpowered decks is a lot more intuitive.If you're on the fence, but you know you like Slay the Spire or any other deckbuilder, just get this game. This is the gold standard for deckbuilding moving forward.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really like most deck building rogue like games. They tend to get boring and tedious, sometimes even just too random with none or little actual strategy leaving you relying on luck only. Monster Train does a better job with the strategy aspect of the game. You still have to rely on luck but generally not as much. The design of the three train track levels makes it much more interesting to think over your next move.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterclass in balance. To an insane degree too. Probably the most balanced game I've ever played. Example. I thought I had the most unbeatable run. Had a card that had multistrike and gained attack after every strike. He had something like 200x7 attack by the end of one fight. I had prepared backup of other cards with high health. I was unstoppable. Thought I broke the game. But he had one weakness. Low health. I hit a boss that had a sweep attack. Lost the run. That's the kind of variability you'll experience here. You even have access to modding in case the game is too hard. Like having cheat codes. There is nothing I can complain about really. Maybe that it would be nice to have more clans. But that might break that perfect balance. Every clan and clan combination (you get a 2nd backup clan to combine two in a run) is worth a try and plays competently. Adds a new flavor to every run keeping every play different. Seems endless. I hope they do a sequel.  Great job devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic deck-building game with some of the most interesting gameplay mechanics that I've seen in a long time. Despite the complexity, the game somehow makes everything feel extremely accessible right from the start, and only deepens from there. If you're at all interested in deckbuilders or rogue-likes, you won't be disappointed in this.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Fun gameplay, each of the different factions provide 2-3 different playstyles that you can mix up with the secondary faction. The artifacts are weighted pretty heavily into either useful or useless, but that also makes the game interesting. The Last Divinity expansion definitely skewed the game balance towards certain builds, but you can switch it off for the original playstyle.All in all, I would give it a 7/10. I like it, I'd buy it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like real life. It gives you ♥♥♥♥ ton of choices to handle a situation, sometimes you make the perfect choices with poor execution, sometimes it's bad choices but you just play em right and turn the situation in your favor and sometimes it's just the whole world throwing poop at you so you gotta step back and start over. Got a lot of high and lows.So it's pretty pog if you into deck building games or want to get into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game should have a warning because it's sooooo good it's addictive. One of the most fun games I've ever played. 10 out of 5 stars. Only thing I can even think of is missing is maybe the possibility to play this game with a game pad instead of a mouse, though this might still be added and I'd much rather prefer they add it later but refined (slay the spire has this implemented really well in my opinion). **Edit: what do you know, they've added gamepad controls ;)It's so cool that they're still adding new (endgame) content. I have to say, after unlocking everything and getting all achievements I do not play the game a ton anymore, but it still took me almost 140h to do so, so that's absolutely fine for me and in any case absolutely worth the money. I do still watch videos on the daily challenges because I love the crazy combos used there (costumization to more directly try some of that would be a cool addition I think - maybe like a "training room" where you can freely set up enemies and define your deck). Also, I will definitely come back to it once the new content is available (wouldn't even mind paying for it to support the game) and again, better add some solid endgame content later than just anything boring. _childDocuments_.review: 10/10 one of my favorite card battlers and probably the best card battler out there in my opinion. Other games like Slay the Spire of Ring of Pain rely too much on luck and random chance to be successful. Monster Train allows you to make strategic decisions on the fly to turn the tide and achieve the win. There are five unique champions (six if you get the DLC) and for every run you choose a primary champion and a secondary champion whose deck gets incorporated into your starting deck. The game challenges you to win the run using every combination of champion deck. Not only that but there are 25 different "covenant" challenges that change up the rules or increase the difficulty. If you get the DLC there is yet ANOTHER challenge to try to beat, once again with the challenge to beat it with every combination of champion deck. It's so satisfying to win a run with a new combo and get that little check mark in your logbook.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like slay the spire and other card game rogue like hybrids, this is another very good game to spend your money on.  Plenty of content, excellent graphics, lots to do and definately scratches the slay the spire and magic the gathering itch without having to spend hundreds of dollars on card packs to get good cards (looking at you mtg).Definately worth your dollars if you need a card game battler to waste time.  Loads up easy, gets a game going easy, and easy to get right back out of.Great relaxing time waster.   'Nuff said.

_childDocuments_.review: Just three standard runs.. But low playtime couldn't hold me back from writing. I liked relatively shorter challenges compared to similar games. As you invest less time and effort per run, the pressure on decision making is less. Resuming a run is less needed. It leads to less "where were we?" moments. Persistent progress/unlocks and endless challenges are there for great replayability, long playtime and more challenging runs. Do I recommend? Definitely yes for the lovers of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Doing a review way earlier than I usually do, but this game is super fun! I'd put myself in the more casual camp of Slay the Spire (StS) players, so I was really surprised that I beat the final boss on just my 2nd run. I don't think I had one of those "broken" builds, but maybe I accidentally stumbled into one without realizing it. Monster Train feels more "streamlined" compared to StS. I'm sure the game gets more difficult as you go, and there are optional ways to increase the difficulty, but if you found yourself getting frustrated with StS but want something like it, pick this one up. And while it's 75% through November 29, it's a no-brainer - get this game!My primary gripe at this very early point: The enemy noises on attack/hit are a little harsh and don't have a lot of variety, so it's kind of an unpleasant cacophony if there's lots of enemies you're tearing through, or fighting a boss that you slowly whittle down. It's just *SKWAK*SKREE*SKWAK*SKREE*SKWAK*SKREE*SKWAK*SKREE* until the boss is dead.Replayability is a key part of any roguelike/roguelite, and I don't anticipate that being an issue - it seems you're incentivized to try and beat a run with all the possible combos of clans. The music is rad, art is great, and I appreciate that you can speed up the animations once you end your turn. I'm looking forward to seeing more of the cards, too - I can tell there's going to be tons of fun combos to discover.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Roguelike (or light) deckbuilders has become a crowded genre, but this is one of the few real stand outs that does more to define the genre than participate in it.I would argue the real draw here is in how overwhelmingly well balanced the individual cards and enemies are. The power growth curve is steep and the synergies are many, complex, and deep. Getting the core of a genre just right is always hard, and here they've done it better than any but the best of the best.If you're new to the genre, this is a great intro. If you're a fan of the genre this is competing for the best of the best. Either way, go for it!
