_childDocuments_.review: If you have ever played Xenoshyft (an irl deckbuilder lol) this is pretty much a digital version of that.  I really enjoy that game so all the possibilities that come from being digital make this a no-brainer for me.  I love Slay The Spire, but this takes from that, adds Xenoshyft, and runs.Another thing I love about this is the difficulty.  Instead of starting off impossible and slowly getting more possible (like 99.9% of roguelikes/lites), this one started easy and seems to get more difficult as you go on a win streak.  Three runs in and I haven't lost yet, but I can sense it coming.  A lot of people would count this as a strike against the game, but I really don't understand why more games aren't diverting from the norm and taking this route.  I do love roguelite elements (Hades, For the King, etc.), but it is refreshing to be able to start off easier and progressively ramp up the difficulty until you lose and break your win-streak.  I hope more games take this route.One extremely minor gripe (not even so much against this game specifically) is that I am sick of this look/style.  I know there are limited budgets regarding how these games look, but it'd be cool to see it done "better".  I don't know how else to say it.  At the end of the day though I completely play these games for the mechanics, as does nearly everyone else, I'm sure.  So again - just a very minor downside IMO.  Nothing that would turn me away from the game.  I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes deckbuilders.  You do not need to be a fan of roguelite mechanics to enjoy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is perfect for killing time doing something solo. _childDocuments_.review: This is a deck-building game with rogue-like elements that borrows a lot from Slay the Spire, and at least for me is actually better than Slay the Spire. A lot of that has to do with the way the game is laid out. I did not go into this game expecting anything and found myself playing it over and over again.The actual gameplay is standard deck-based battling similar to Slay the Spire, although with a bit of a tower defense twist because over the course of a battle you play minions to different rooms and enemy units arrive in waves and move towards your core. In between battles you can choose between different types of upgrades (artifacts that grant permanent passive buffs, upgrading cards, getting rid of cards, random events, etc.) and in my opinion those choices feel good and less random. In many rouge-likes there can be a feeling that success and failure is highly dependent on getting lucky drops and battles as opposed to unfair ones, but the difficulty and amount of good upgrades always seems consistent.Outside of the runs themselves, the systems around progression feel great. Instead of a simple win/lose system like most rogue-likes, the game has an ascending difficulty system so that your first runs while you are learning and struggling to find good synergies can still be wins. The game also keeps track of how what difficulty level you have beaten different combinations of classes with, and which cards you have used in successful runs, which lets you decide on your own challenges to pursue. Part of why I stopped play Slay the Spire is that once I was able to beat it with each class there was not a lot to do.In terms of negatives, the theme of the game is both bland and a weird attempt at being edgy. The game balance could be improved which is always difficult in rogue-likes, where some strategies that the game clearly pushes the player to choose seem completely non-viable. Also, one of the major parts of the game is that you are given a special hero character at the beginning depending on your class. This hero is always under-powered compared to the best normal minions in the game that can be bought or drafted as the game progresses. I guess that is a good way to encourage the player to find and build around a new set of minions each run, but it feels bad to find success in just completely ignoring your hero character every run in favor of upgrading and buffing regular minions until they are much more powerful.

Draft cards and upgrade cards throughout an 8-boss run, including spell cards, unit cards, random powerful artifacts that provide constant effects, with a variety of card types each with drastically different playstyles. by earning experience in game,  more cards become available for players to draft / use in runs, as well as artifacts and spells. _childDocuments_.review: Short looping games with escalating difficulty only work when they are about player skill, whereas watching an avatar grow stronger is only satisfying when it's a single long journey/story. Monster Train, though, like many such games, quickly ends and restarts with escalated difficulty but immediately undermines this by strengthening my deck too. Instead of me or at least a character experiencing progress, the one "getting better" at the game is the game itself--a faceless deck locked in a short loop. So,  is going  in this game's design philosophy. It's a quagmire. Monster Train is faulty on the foundational level.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly no, at least not yet. Monster Train runs through an uncanny valley of likeness to games like Slay the Spire, but with a sort of tower defense twist. It's a novel idea, but suffers from a kind of balance malaise that's hard to pin down in specific. And yet, you'll go through runs seeing card after card that doesn't appear to fit into any strategy anywhere. Predominately, runs often blend together with each faction feeling there's only one (maybe two) good builds per faction with a matter of luck to see if you end up with the support to make it happen.Maybe check in with Monster Train on sale if you're really hurting for another deck builder, you certainly won't start to see the seams until 30+ hours in, and/or after a MT has had another year to develop.I wish I could recommend Monster Train, I wanted to love it, but it just feels worse and worse as time goes on.(Edit after playing the Friends & Foes update): Balance issues and UI readability issues remain. The new champions add some new options for specific faction combos, but the underlying problems remain.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the Spire-esque deck drafting with a unique take on strategy. I would say this can be a bit tamer compared to Spire, at least until the later Covenant levels. There is tons of variety, but once you start building your deck the upgrades and decisions usually seem pretty obvious. Although I think Slay the Spire is a more polished, enticing game, I have put more hours in Monster Train and it hasn't been a regrettable experience. Working up the covenant ranks will take a while and it adds just enough extra difficulty to make things interesting. Also while I don't play it much myself, the online mode offers some enticing modes if you get bored with standard runs (not to mention mutations to change your game up)With the free updates, the devs seem dedicated and if you are at all into this type of deck building/strategy game, you will love this game too.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game rocks. If you like Slay the Spire, check this out. You won't regret it. Got it on sale, but knowing what I know now, I would have easily paid full price for this. _childDocuments_.review: This game is everything I love about Slay the Spire (RPG style deck building), and everything I LOVE about Legend of Keepers (order of attack, and different sections to disperse your troops), all rolled into one game AND THEN SOME. I love the art style, and it seems like each card is made with a bit of love. Being able to play the evil side is a great way to win me over, for sure, so the game started off on the right foot.

_childDocuments_.review: 87min: Great game, really fun to deckbuild in, though it does often feel kind of surprisy whether they're gonna be enough to kill the final boss or not (which comes down to me not being able to easily do that kind of math in my head), fortunately it was.8.4h: It is starting to dawn on me how genius this is designed, the way that there are so many different combinations, each of them playing out differently. In many tower defense games, if you let enemies through, they will instantly kill you. Because the Pyre is itself quite strong, but doesnt strike first, you get a health system where health decays if you dont play well rather than getting obliterated in one go.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Now even though I selected not recommend, I want to say this comes with a lot of caveats.I would still recommend this game to those who wish to sate their thirst for a decent deck building, rogue run game, but currently this game still lacks polish, even when in comparison to Griftlands, a game still in early access.  Therefore I won't recommend it to anyone new to this sub-genre, I would rather point them to Slay the Spire instead.For one, other games in this sub-genre like Slay the Spire and Griftlands, all recognize that it is frustrating that a half an hour to one hour run can be easily ruined by a bad draw in the first one or two turns, so they mitigate it with setting certain cards to be drawn on the first turn; this is a feature that Monster Train sorely lacks and has resulted in many of my runs ruined.Certainly RNG is an essential element of this sub-genre, yet when other games do it better, it is hard to see Monster Train as anything but lacking.  I have some other minor gripes but they don't come as close as to the one I just mentioned.  I know it is unfair to compare this to Slay the Spire, an older game that had more time to fix itself, but when an early access game can do it better, then I see no reason why Monster Train can't improve on the same thing, especially when there are other examples to borrow from.So yeah, here is a bit of my rant.  Hopefully it doesn't come as too condemning.  I still like this game and don't regret buying it, but it still needs a lot of works.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Its a neat game,But it seems you quickly get pigeon holed into a certain build if you are going to play the Covenant rank 1.Stygian Frost Bite stacking, or spell weakness stacking is mandatory or you cant kill bosses with huge life pools (2600!) Then it seems you need Umbra for any reasonable defense.Maybe awoken and hellhorned have useful units / builds as they level up?, just not seeing the balance there by comparison.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Having watched some pre-release videos of the game before it came out, I was very much looking forward to playing the game.However, once I got to play the released version, it did not take me long to realise that the game is absolutely imbalanced and even outside of incredible luck with the RNG (which yes, it's a deck-builder game, it's expected to a certain degree, but in this case it's absolutely ridiculous), there are only a couple viable "builds" or "strategies" that are capable of winning a run.Either you are able to create a beat stack in one room, which is capable of outlasting the incredibly exponentially-scaling enemies and especially bosses (while there only a couple options which "exponentially" increase the player's capability to keep up with the nonsense), or you manage to get a rare cheese combo of effects that allow the absolutely pathetic damage spells to nuke the boss.Not to mention that you are forced to start with a "dual-land" deck, in a game, where synergies between the 5 available card factions are very lacking.Overall I truly hope the "balance" gets addressed in one way or another (nerfing the enemies/bosses, buffing most of the cards and faction mechanics or slowing down the pace and adding more "rings" to Hell, in order to smooth out the scaling curve, etc.)TL;DR: At the moment, the game is a hilariously imbalanced RNG-fest, even for it's sub-genre, and I do not recommend you buy the game now, unless you're okay with such.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game enough.  I enjoyed slay the spire but this one is a step above that imo.  The variety you get by mix and matching the factions together adds a ton of replay value without even including the "ascension" level style of difficulty progression. _childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game with lots of variety. 5 clans (+1 with DLC), each with 2 champions that require different strategies to play, combined with the fact that you choose a primary and secondary clan each run gives you plenty of room to experiment.The most fun part of this game is coming up with broken builds and doing so is not only encouraged but also required when playing in higher difficulties.The speed setting is also a nice touch to cut down on wait time.All in all great entertainment, but terrible for my sleep schedule.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This review will be a bit biased. This game very much reminds me of Slay the Spire, and I loved Slay the Spire! It's a very similar game, except the fact that you have a few levels here with the pyre on top, and you can go up and down based on your cards. I look forward to the challenges everyday, sometimes I wish there were more. There are player made challenges now too, which are fun to try. Pros:It's a rogue-like card game with a lot of replayabilityFairly easy to get intoEasy to create builds as you goA lot of fun, with a lot of optionsCommunity Challenges adds more replayabilitycons: Some of the mutations are much harder to counter than others. Some mutations don't seem to fit, for example sometimes you get hollowed as a mutation (Friendly units get Heartless which means they can't be healed) and then get very unlucky and get a bunch of healing cards. Another crazy one is Permadeath, in a game where the point is to build a deck, if your units are going to be purged completely from the deck, then the game won't last long.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Fun as hell (no pun intended) and well worth the asking price.That's the long and short of it but I'll try to elaborate a bit more.If you like deckbuilding roguelites like Slay the Spire then this is an absolute must.It borrows some of it's ideas like the ascension mechanic and artifacs but also introduces new ideas like the 3 stage arena and clan combinations ( essentially allowing you to mix and match 2 deck archetypes). Speaking of Clans ,there are 5 of them (2 unlocked from the beginning ,the other 3 trough gameplay), and all have very interesting and diverse gameplay.While the Stygian Guard is all about frostbite ,sap and spells , the Umbra are about the comsume mechanic and buffing units .Seeing how you can combine any 2 clans ,you have the potential to get some pretty juicy decks that are extremely satisying to play .Besides the wonderful single player experience where you can climb covenants ala AScension in Slay the Spire; this game also offers daily challenges ,competing in multiplayer with other players in a "rush" style game mode and you can even create custom Challenges that you can post online so that other players can compete in them.All of these are great activities that offer Monster Train a lot of replayability.Like I said : Great game ,great fun.It will be interesting to see where the devs thake the game next .Personally I would love to see more Leaders cards and floors and maybe even some sort of coop game mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves card games, and especially the deck-building kind, I can wholeheartedly recommend this.Pros:- 5 very distinct clans, each with a handful of different playstyles. your deck combines 2 clans, which might uncover some really cool synergies.- Nice art style with nice attention to detail, such as units adjusting their size based on how many slots they take up.- You can enable combat preview, which is very handy (I'd even go as far as calling it a must-have) as it helps you track very complex interactions.- You can pull off some insanely powerful and fun combos, and it's incredibly satisfying when you do so.- Great replay value, as you can always go for different builds and/or increase your difficulty. Cons:- This is not a train game. The train is there just to add some flavor to the game and its lore, but nothing more beyond that.- It could use more content of some kind, such as more cards, artifacts or more scenarios to play through. But there is some more content coming, so this is really just a temporary issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write many reviews so forgive me if I get of track a bit. Monster train feels like the strange offspring of Slay the Spire, Binding of Issac, and MTG (Magic the Gathering) after a wild night and no one really knows who's kid it is. The game revolves are using 5 base decks that all have their own specific themes as well as champions that also have different play styles to them within that base deck. You play two decks at a time between any of the 5 base decks with one being the main one that your champion is from and the other being a deck you just pull cards from.  For instance the hellhounds, one of the first decks you play is pretty similar to something of a goblin deck from MTG at times. Where the monsters synergize together to be far greater than the sum of their parts, with a heavy emphasis on aggression and relatively well stated early game monsters. And the second deck you have access to at the start  is a lot like a usual green deck from MTG with large monsters and an emphasis on large health pools and ramping damage, ect. Even though I say that, that doesn't necessarily mean that you will be locked into those kinds of play styles. How you play that deck and champion will be based on what kind of drops you get, the stats of your champion,  and what ways you can best make use of artifact synergies and events that happen in a run. Now take the MTG systems and add in vertical layers along with the usual roguelike elements, random artifacts that could drastically change any given run, random events, shops to beef up spells or monsters with different semi random effects or stats. The amount of wildly different and viable deck styles I have won with already is absurd to be frank. With me only being 13 hours in, the single player alone seems to have a couple hundred hours worth of content before you have seen all the different possible combinations. This doesn't even include the multiplayer which has weekly challenges,  mutations akin to hearthstones brawl's, as well as races with other players to see who can finish a run the fastest. With this much content at this price point if you are even remotely interested in Slay the Spire then I think you will be hard pressed to not find something to love about this game. I am very much looking forward to what comes next for this game and its developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a REALLY well done roguelike deck builder game. Similar to Slay the Spire. You build your deck as you go along, trying to create a deck engine that can overcome challenges and make it through the final boss.There are so many well thought out game principles in this game. Everything is "plannable". You know ahead of time how each turn will play out with live preview numbers as you consider different cards to play. You know what the final boss' "gotcha" mechanic will be, so as you go through you're run, you're constantly working on weaving your deck in a way that is going to be powerful against that particular boss.It's a super great game for people who enjoy puzzling, planning, and figuring creatively.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Great deck builder roguelike, the modifiers on the bosses and the prestige mechanic make every run unique, would just with for some more different bosses altogether. The train level mechanic differentiates the game from other deckbuilders like Slay the Spire and gives it a lot more tactical depth in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster train is a complex and wonderfully addictive combination of a roguelike deckbuilder (such as slay the spire) and a tower defense game. Interactions between factions are complex and interesting, strategies change a lot from game to game, and the progression is at a satisfying clip. Really strong recommendation for this one, as few games seem to illicit the sort of addictive glee this one has. 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This is not only a well made, fun game, but it seems to have solved (or at least vastly improved) the "lane" mechanic attempted by other games such as Artifact, Elder Scrolls: Legends, and Gwent.  The aforementioned games approached lanes in their various ways, but the approach in Monster Train feels not only the most intuitive, but genuinely adds to the game's strategy and fun, while feeling streamlined instead of cumbersome.  Even without the lane mechanic, Monster Train would be an interesting and enjoyable card fighter, brandishing a personality that sets it apart from the saturated genre.  It's smooth, fast, interesting, fun, has professional quality and depth, and just downright feels good to play.  Definitely compels the "just one more run!" user experience that signals the hallmarks of a good game.  Highly recommended!Edit: Updated for 2020 Steam Awards; nominated for "Sit Back and Relax Award".

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, a tad on the easier/forgiving side. If you've played Slay the Spire, you'll have a MUCH easier time at this game. Spire can be downright brutal even at the early levels, but Monster Train is just more forgiving. The graphics are gorgeous, and I didn't see any inconsistencies with language or keywords - which is paramount for a card game that relies on such nuances.  For the negatives here, balance of factions comes quickly to mind. Some are just obscenely easy to finish consistently with, and others rely on outright tons of RNG (both in what cards you take, what artifacts you gain, and your literal draw in a match). Overall though, the curve is much smoother even with the most RNG-based faction than Spire. The other big negative is the "roguelike" aspect where finishing and leveling up factions can actually hamper you - when you first unlock a faction, it's SUPER consistent because your card pool is so limited. You know what you are going to get in virtually every run. Once you level up and unlock more cards, well... that dilutes your card pool from the initial starting stock. Some of the additional cards can be great, others not so much. In the end, you play with what you are dealt, but it's an aspect of the game that feels out of place. Instead of earning more, it can feel like a punishment.

_childDocuments_.review: Update 11/27/2020 - After sinking about 80 hours into the game, I have to say this is my choice for game of the year.  The mechanics are a combination of Slay the Spire and Darkest Dungeon with the visuals of Hearthstone.  When starting out, it is best to experiment with each clan with the following recommendations:*  When selecting units or spells  it is best to take the paths towards your primary clan.*  When you only have spells or units from your support clan look for ones that offer the best utility.*  You want to have a Tank, DPS, and some type of buff unity.*  You will typically want to place your hero on the top or middle floor so you have time to setup floors.*  Look to add units or spells that offer incant or buffs.*  You typically want to take additional draws or add draw cards to your hand so that you can buff your primary damage units.* For unit bufffs. you should prioritize add health to your tanks, and multistrike & damage to your damage heroes.* For spells you should look to reduce the cost for your bigger spells, add endless to your best buffs or sweeping spells.* Make sure to also remove the Train Stewards and starting spells.  I typically will add a damage / consume to spells and prioritize removing stewards first.The skill ceiling gets progressively harder as you complete covenants with each level adding changes to the the play environment.  You will had to adjust your approach in order to put out the needed DPS and debuffs.  That is why having additional card draw is important.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics aren't anything amazing, UI is polished but presumably pretty standard for a single-player deckbuilder, there's limited enemies you play against, so far for my four wins bosses are all the same. Yawn city, right?But it's a playground made for one reason: for you to do what you can to turn whatever cards you get into an unbelievably explosive strategy. "Take more spikes!" you cackle madly, as your unit gets spikes on its spikes as you heal it so that it lasts longer for enemies to smash themselves against the spikes. "Take more magic!" you cackle madly, as your unit sweeps all the enemies (including the boss, hovering around like a concerned fart) on that floor and giving them increased levels of weakness to spells. And you have a spell card with +10 magic power and holdover that you can use to cause huge damage that will be multiplied hugely."Take more frost!" you cackle madly, as on each level you have a 1 pip imp unit that adds more and an artefact that stops the frost from reducing, meaning when the minions are gone the boss is already labouring under intense amount of damage every time.It's FUN. And these are just the first three demon clans -- there are more, and I've heard they have new strats and synergies.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I was perusing the message boards on random games, trying to get a pulse on a few of them, when someone recommended this specific game, said something to the effect is was ostensibly better than "Slay the Spire"...I looked it up, kind of smirked to myself, then saw that it was on sale via a flash deal for $4.99 USD and I thought, "Why not?".  Installed it and well...almost five hours later I was still playing it.  I do not know whether the hook is as good as Slay the Spire, it is a bit different in that instead of a lone warrior you have clans, but the deck building and the overall presentation are superior in some ways.  Further, you are not at the behest of the RNG and pre-destined deck outputs, which is what Slay the Spire is...what this means is, at least in the base game, you are given more leeway if you happen to make a mistake.  Always good for a roguelite deck builder, and for beginners, and for anyone who lacks patiences for these sorts of nuances that come with new deck building systems.  In other words, it's intuitive, it is fun, and most of all, accessible.  If you like Slay the Spire, of deck builders generally speaking, then this should be an instant purchase, especially at $4.99.  I did not purchase the expansion yet as I wanted to enjoy the base game first.   I highly recommend this title.  It is an intuitive, addicting, roguelite deck builder with some truly sublime music to accompany it.  Look forward to more from this developer. Rating: 90/100 -LoA-

You have to place unit to defend the floors, each floor has a max. capacity of unit placed, enemies will move up a floor each turn, final boss can freely travel between floor.3. You have limited mana to play cards.4. You have spells to damage/heal enemies(you can damage your units as well), heals, draw etc. like StS5. You cannot replace a unit until its dead.6. _childDocuments_.review: My vote for the best game of it's kind!The emergent "Deck Crawler" genre is most popularized by Slay the Spire, though personally I consider that sort of near the middle of the couple dozens games out right now (production values in StS are fantastic, don't get me wrong, but the card game is good rather than great, really). It's a real "Shut up and take my money" niche for games in my book, and there's steep competition near the top of the pile for my affections, with games like Nowhere Prophet, Chrono Ark, and Gordian Quest making competitive cases for my stop spot...At least they did, because I feel like Monster Train just blew every other game in the genre out of the water for me.Oh man, this game is so good, I don't even... I'm gonna have to bullet point this so I don't gush past the review character limit- The game involves a mechanic to modify individual cards in your deck. You can really strategically run wild with novel combinations of traits in this sort of system, but to date, other games I've seen try is largely faceplanted because it was too difficult to balance these mechanics... Monster Train is the first game I've seen not only make it work, but nail it in a deeply satisfying way.- Balance and difficulty is always an issue in these games, and Monster Train takes the approach of "It everything is overpower, than nothing is unfair". You can make so many busted combinations in your own deck it's headspinning, just "it feels like I'm cheating" with how severely you can break mechanics... thing is, you NEED to do that, because the later bosses are JUST as relentlessly unfair and over-powered... you WILL NOT beat Fel or Seraph without some form of exploit, so "Break the game" is built into the game due to a difficulty curve that would be unrelentingly savage if you don't... Even then, you'll be surprised how often a deck that feels unstoppable can suddenly lose due to a complex misplay... with 25 difficulty levels (apparently, I'm not very far into them), if you ever feel like things are too easy, the upscaling of challenge is quite high... it's an excellent balance of rewarding high strategy, being approachable for more casual players, but offering a huge difficulty cieling to hardcores. - The game involves doing runs with a modular 2-faction deck, similar to card games like Smash Up... but whereas the biggest difficulty I find with those cardgames IRL is seperating the decks after every game, it works excellent in this digital format. The faction choice influences the two halves of your starting deck, what cards will be available to gain in play, what traits will crop up to add to those cards, what passive-granting relics will crop up, and your "main" faction will even grant you a powerful "Champion" unit that costs 0 mana to play and starts in your opening hand each fight, which will eventually "Evolve" down a tree to 1 of 10 final forms, which will likely be utterly crucial to your strategy in most runs.- The 5 factions all have a few themes connected to them... Umbra are ramp, sacrifice for buildup, and X-Cost; Horned Devils offer aggressive attack units, direct damage, and on-kill effects; Awakened have ample healing, defense as the best offense tactics, and units that have lot of potential for enhancement; Stygians synergize incredibly well with spellcasting and can dish out savage damage via debuffs; and the Remnants offer rapid minion spawning, deck thinning, and sacrifice effects. Any of these factions can chose to focus on just one or two of their mechanics, and of course you have two faction sets to choose from... this makes replay value almost staggering, as Remnant/Awakened, Stygian/Remnant, and Awakened/Stygian are likely to look UTTERLY different from one another in terms of strategy for a run. - The game prides itself on a mechanic of having multiple floors you need to defend, forcing you to make calculated decisions about where to place units so as to best use your resources and minimize weak spots in your defenses. This is probably the LEAST interesting of the innovations to me, but it is novel and works well... The implication of it I like more is that it creates a game of 9 long battles rather than dozens of short ones... which sounds unpleasant at first blush, but actually works well... rather than choose paths of "Fight/Treasure/Camp/Shop", every match WILL be 9 battles, and you get an "Intermission" of the other things in between each, making your choice "Do I want to enchance spells, cull cards, and heal; or would a random relic, an event, and unit enhancement be better for me right now?" and so on. It makes an interesting "preparation phase" between each combat... the "One more turn" effect is so REAL here, after every fight, you want to do the prep phase to check your spoils, after every test phase, you want to do another fight to test out your new tricks.- Production qualities are solid... the graphics are charming, but more relevantly, the soundtrack was downright impressive... there's a lot more tracks than you tend to see in these games, and I REALLY liked the majority of them... I usually put on a podcast while doing dozens of hours in these games, I tend to just listen to the OST with this one.On some level, it's hard for me to even know what to say reguarding why you should buy this game... it feels like a no-brainer. If you're into strategy, board/card games, roguelites, and DEFINITELY if you're into deck crawlers, you really MUST try it, it's the best game of it's kind to date.

The different types of gameplay really help keep it fresh, especially as they interact with each other and either make up for or exacerbate each other's weaknesses. This game certainly isn't for everyone, but the people who it is for are going to know that on sight and have a great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This is basically Slay the Spire in another skin, and that's a good thing!Okay, okay, to be fair, the combat in this game is a bit unique, as you have 3 layers of combat field and a heart to defend, so it's more like Slay the Spire + Artifact. Still, you build a deck, decide what goodies to pick up, you create synergies or at least you hope you do, etc. etc. - a roguelike deck builder.There's a fair amount of replay value and I really like the combat to deck building ratio. In Slay the Spire, you often just get stuck in a string of 3-4 fights back-to-back when you just want to get to the next ? room. In Monster Train, you get to do these miscellaneous stuff after each and every fight, guaranteed and with how long the fights are, I feel like this is paced perfectly. Quantity wise, I think there's more cards to mix and experiment with than StS, but slightly less miscellaneous stuff like mystery rooms and artifacts (which are this game's equivalent of StS' relics).The production values are particularly noteworthy, everything is crisply animated and well drawn. The music ranges between many meh tracks to some really memorable ones you can listen to even outside of playing. The vocalizations of units are kind of phoned in, however and one particular winged angel boss will make your household think you're blasting porn on your PC with maxed volume.All in all, if you liked Binding of Isaac and Slay the Spire, this is a must play for you. Though it doesn't reinvent the wheel or blow your mind, it doesn't have to, because it's good.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I am in love with rogue-like deckbuilders since I played Slay the Spire. This is the best one I've played since then. It's a blast to play, and isn't too hard (unless you explicitly ramp up the difficulty).Most things are extremely well balanced, though I feel like the Stygian race is noticeably weaker than the rest. Though I might just not be seeing the power plays they can make as easily as the other races. The only way to I can do well with them is if I use the first hero with a focus on frostbite. But I've not found other winning strategies for them.The art is good, the music and SFX are excellent. It all feels like a AAA game masquerading as an indie game. It's an easy 10/10, which I don't give often. I'd probably give the Slay the Spire a 9.5/10 due to its difficulty curve.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool Rougelike Deck Building game! Very interesting main mechanic with enemies moving floors as to punish you for putting all your strong units on the first floor, if they do reach the top then they damage your "pyre" health total and once that drops to zero your run is finished. Replayability is a 8/10 as you unlock more cards which then opens different ways to build your deck however Bosses are repeated.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a gem! It is the best of all the card games combined together with a good story and in-depth lore. Every bit of the game feels premium like it has been given a lot of time in the making. I have played many card games before like Slay The Spire and The Darkest Dungeon, this feels like a combination of both with all the unique cards and abilities and game changing artifacts. _childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Slay the Spire, this is better. This is a deckbuilding game that is also pseudo-tower defense (in that  you place your units on various levels of a train and they fight units as they go up) with auto-battle elements added in. The game is great for two major reasons:1) Customization. As you progress you get spells and units, then you can augment these units at the various shops, by default you can enhance cards twice, but it can be increased. You also get to pick two factions to only get cards from those two factions, so you could for example go Melting Remnants with Awoken, Melting Remnants focuses on reviving dead units and Awoken is very durable allowing you to have a strong tank while throwing units at enemies and reviving them even stronger.2) Controlled RNG. There are so many elements in your control that losing a run is really on you 95% of the time - I say this losing plenty because I dink around with cards and make enemies stronger at the same time - But it's enjoyable to do so sometimes just to watch a unit hit 8 times and return to the top of your deck when it dies. This is the best deck-building game I have played and will recommend it to anyone that likes the genre. Also - Melting Remnant's Exile Champion is fun as all hell, that is all.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I got this as a gift and this is by far the most time I have spent on a gifted game. Turn Based Roguelite Card game... it can mean only one thing: lots of math. Don't worry, you can suck at it and still have fun (I lead this by example, although I shouldn't be sucking at math). But, wait, while we are at it, let's see the numbers.Each run of the game is set when you pick one of races for your main deck and one for support, after which you can pick your champion (tempted to use the word hero, but from story point, you are a "baddie"). So, there are 5 races, and each "deck" can be split into usage categories like... Long-term offensive, Healing, Passive defensive, passive offensive and explosive (short-term offensive). 5 choices for main deck, thus 4 for support (since you cannot pick two of the same decks for one run). 5*4=20. Not bad.Then there are champions. 2 champions to choose per main deck, thus: 5*2*4=40. Neat.Each of the champions has 3 of different upgrade paths; so... 5*2*3*4=120. WHAT?120 of different STARTING combinations! This is also disregarding the fact that there is DLC that brings another race/deck!And possibilities just keep pilling up as you go, since each champion's upgrade path has 2 upgrades, and you can even intertwine upgrade paths. After each battle, you are given randomized possibilites, out of which some consists of upgrades, acquiring more cards (some that are unrelated to any of starting decks too!); all in all polishing your deck.Each run is crazy and we are introduced to very progressive and fair unlocking system - that way, you may feel slightly overwhelmed only at very beginning, but once you get used to how mechanics work, game will guide you as you go. More you play, more stuff you will unlock. It took me about 30h to unlock all cards and I am not done playing. Did I also mention you have other modes, other than standard run? Yes sir/madam, there are even more stuff! I haven't even tried all the cards yet, to be honest!If you have played Slay the Spire, i.e., I could say that Monster Train is like upgraded version of the game. I feel I devote more of thinking to tactics in here, there are way more things to juggle with and certainly, way more fun for me. Like in StS, you have here difficulty rise as you succeed in each run and from what I can see, the last "difficulty" is 25th.  All in all, this game will challenge you more than one I previously mentioned, but possibly bring you more fun too. OST is pumping, sound effects are quite decent, artwork is very imaginative - each of the deck is a theme that relates to its "power". It is blinding with how much love this is all built. Kudos to devs. Long ago, one steam user once said - if it can bring you 1h of fun for each 1$ you spend on it, game is then worth the price. So... yeah.... very worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: The king is dead, long live the king.We should salute Slay the Spire for being the first of its genre and defining the standards, but Monster Train outshines it by far in terms of gameplay, pacing, aesthetics and... fun. In fact, I'm uninstalling StS right now, because I for one welcome our new master. Exit the sadistic RNG, the stupid boss artifacts you have to refuse because they will f**k your run up and the murky fights spent waiting for an unfair death. Monster Train is smart and fair. Get it.It works perfectly on Linux (thanks to Proton).

_childDocuments_.review: OK. I have perhaps 20 reviews of Steam games. More than half are good reviews, and a sprinkling of games that didn't meet up to my expectations.I won't review a game until I have played it enough to learn it. It doesn't do YOU any good if I am making half-assed comments about the game, and I don't understand the mechanics.OK...let's start with the graphics and polish. Similar to Hearthstone, with bright colors and sharp detail. Sounds are excellent, and the presentation is very good.But...I don't care about graphics. I still play Master of Magic, and the original X-Com. I am all about the gameplay.I keep discovering new things about the game. As I blasted past the two hour refund point, I never hesitated. I knew that this game had legs, and was a keeper, and will be a favorite of mine for a very long time.I don't have anything to fault here. If you win, it is very, VERY satisfying. I have had 25 "runs", and have one just once. It's a roguelike, and the stars have to align for this to happen.I think that what I enjoy most is the sense of progression. Even if you lose, you gain experience in your main army, and the secondary army you choose. Play enough games, and you unlock levels, and unlocking levels unlocks more cards, better cards, and a better chance to progress deeper in your next game.There are five armies in the game, with two unlocked at the start. After 15 hours of gameplay, I just unlocked the fifth one..so everything is unlocked.After my one and only victory, the challenge level increased. I didn't realize it, but I was getting smoked pretty good. In complete honesty, I am not great at strategy games....but I am doing OK here, trying to figure out the synergies and relationships between the cards.There are MANY variables on each run through. I haven't begun to believe that I have remotely seen the content. Under 10% at this point. This game can be played for hundreds of hours, and still have unique combinations and synergies uncovered.Each run starts with a base set of cards, and some standard, non-army specific cards using generic units. There are units and spells, and each has their own purchase price. You can increase the cost or their efficacy, or make them stronger at the risk of consuming them - one shot. If you don't use all the cards in your hand, they go into your discard pile, to be recycled. This really is a terrific gaming system. My grandson was looking over my shoulder as I played earlier today..he's ten, but smart, really smart, like his mom. I think the Bank of Grandpa is going to kick in here....
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Only 7 hours of gameplay but I can tell this is going to be a game I'll be spending tons of hours and will find myself coming back to. It's just so GOOD! I'm a big fan of roguelites like Slay the Spire and I can say Monster Train is at least as good as StS. And I can't compare the two further cause they are just so different, even though both are deckbuilder combat roguelite games with a path that offers multiple possibilities and there are many common elements in both games like relics, all the comparisons stop there. Monster train has you protecting a Pire with multiple dimensions to combat, both horizontal and vertical, it has deployable cards that are gone on that particular combat, it has upgradable cards, lot less rigorous calculus but keeping the same (or more) complexity and density where you're just optiziming to the max.... Well, I could go on forever, this game is really good. TL;DRIf you're a roguelite or deckbuilder or card combat fan then you must get this game. If you're not then you must get this game, it'll turn you into one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the only really great roguelike deckbuilder thing. There's a ton of variation both within each faction's cards/units and in the combinations of such, even more variation in the (well-balanced) events and artifacts which are thrown up along your run, and the card upgrades you're offered - and even more variation in the combat system, which is inherently much deeper than the typical slay the spire setup a lot of these games have. I'm highlighting opportunities for variation, because that's what will make it worth coming back for run after run after run. You have many chances to try different strategies, and you WILL get the chance to try them because you have much greater control over how the gameplan of each run develops. You're almost always presented with multiple choices whenever you get new cards/artifacts/upgrades, and unlike many other games your runs will essentially never depend on specific high-rarity enabler cards to come together. The design of most factions and their mechanics is cunning enough to have them be viable in different strategies for completely different reasons, which makes it feel more like you're actually discovering archetypes and putting them together yourself versus following one of a few preset lanes. Unlocking more cards and seeing more of the rare events and archetypes over time keeps things fresh, as do the various challenge modes. Even having gone out of my way to try all the options the game has to offer, I find myself still as engaged at the end as I was at the start, as I'm able to enable challenge run modifiers which make things harder in interesting, beatable ways.All the small bits of polish here help as well - the lore and aesthetics of the game, while not front and centre, are actually quite compelling. The UI is very readable, and the thoroughness and completeness of tooltips means I never feel lied to about what's happening in combat. Even complex interactions resolve along logical and consistent lines, and the designers have been quite open minded in how cards and upgrades can be used, so you never feel like your cool ideas have been shut down. The logbook makes it easy to keep your progress through the game tracked for when you get to the completionist phase of play. I can't speak to the quality of the expansion, but the base game is a 10/10 for me and my only complaint is that other deckbuilders look worse by comparison. Please make more games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like Slay the Spire but you do all the combat at once, then you do a lot of deck management / shopping. Repeat.It feels like less of a slog because everything is so condensed. Both games are great but you'll probably like one of them more than the other. For me I think this one is better.The only complaint I have is that the RNG seems to swing way more on this game. It's pretty easy to get artifacts or shopping options you don't want. But when you do get things the way you want, you can do some pretty fun strategies.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love slay the spire, you will love this game. I believe at the time of this review I have just shy of 100 hours logged into STS. I FINALLY beat the final boss in STS and now am basically just grinding all my champs to 100%. I was beginning to get a bid bored of that and a friend had recommended me this game so I picked it up.It is similar to STS in a LOT of ways but it is NOT the same game. With this game you have a train in which there are 3 floors and 1 room with essentially your nexus / heart. If the enemies climb from the bottom floor to the hear they will attack it and it can fight back but once it dies its game over. So you basically have to play 3 different floors of strategy at the same time and have to worry about your heart. It can be a little bit chaotic but once you get the hang of it, it is extremely fun!!! I have about 10 hours logged into it now and there are probably 30 something different combinations in which you can pick your "Heros" and each one has its own deck, similar to STS with Ironclad, Silent, Defect and Watcher. So you get to fine incredibly good combos with the deck building and sometimes it will be a good deck up till the last boss fight, sometimes you die on the second boss.Overall it has a LOT of replay-ability and a LOT of potential. I am very excited to see some new updates in the future but in the meantime I will continue to play and try to get 100% on this game as well!

Those mechanics and the rest of the expected mechanics from this genre are very well executed.If you like roguelite deckbuilding game, this is a great game to have!

_childDocuments_.review: Balancing issues aside (I mean when are there not going to be balancing issues) this game delivers on all fronts. With fights that play out with substantially more control than Slay the Spire, Monster Train has me a lot less frustrated than that game.My only concern is card bloat, and I'm too new to the game to see if there's a plan to deal with it. If every run starts you fresh, how are you expected to craft a themed deck when the pool of available cards continues to grow larger and larger upon unlocking them? With a total card pool so large, the odds of you acquiring the ones you want grows smaller and smaller with each new card unlock.But aside from that it's amazing. The sound design delivers on the hits each monster exchange, and some of the noises they make are properly weird and unearthly. The run length feels good. The art direction is fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't bad, but it is poorly balanced.  Once it gets some fine tuning, if it's acceptable, I will change my review.  As of right now, you will often run into a few very annoying issues.  Your starting deck, for nearly every clan is stuffed with too many of certain cards.  You will find that you are constantly pulling an entire hand full of nothing but Regen spells, Morsels, or other spells that don't let you develop your "train" to face the upcoming waves.  And there are ZERO opportunities to tweak these until you clear the first train... even then, the next tile has to have spawned a node that allows you to remove cards.Just to clarify... there are 10 regen/spell cards in the starting deck, and only 4 monsters to place down other than your champion.  So of the 15 cards in your starting deck, 66% of them are useless for developing your train layout.  Doing the math you will see why it's so common to get screwed with a hand full of garbage, instead of monsters that you need to place in your train.  I am all for having a bit of RNG and luck involved... this is a Roguelite afterall.  But these percentages are a bit extreme if you aren't going to allow us to remove cards from our deck before clearing the first train.   My suggestion, is limit the Regens/Torches/ or other spells to 4 each in the starting deck, and give Train Stewards or weak clan monsters to 6.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster train is a rogue-lite deckbuilder with a surprising amount of emergent depth of play. The good: Like other games in its class (such as Slay the spire), the focus of MT is on building and enhancing a deck that can scale to exponentially increasing levels of difficulty. This is easier said than done, as the playing field has a fairly large number of variables to consider and balance such as draw count per turn, space for units on each level of the train, ember (action points) to spend per turn, unit defensive and offensive power, etc. To balance this out, MT provides a generally higher degree of player agency than other games in its class. Rather than being entirely beholden to the RNG, players are subject to making impactful trade-offs at regular steps along the way. A winning game session requires about 1 hour and 20 minutes at a relaxed pace. A primary/secondary faction system provides ~13 deck combinations for good replayability in conjunction with a system of gradually progressing handicaps.The bad: MT is a mixed bag in terms of permanent player progression. Wins and losses unlock more factions to play, more cards per faction, some purely aesthetice enhancements, and an increasing difficulty scale in the form of player handicaps. The card unlocks, in particular, seem a bit contrived, as though players need to "earn" the right to access the complete game. The faction unlocks serve as a good way to gradually introduce players to the complexity of the game, but progression is very uneven. For example, I had to play close to 10 rounds to unlock the 4th deck, but the last two decks unlocked in two rounds each.Finally, I would be remiss if I didn't note the overall *cringe-ness* of the overall game theme. I wince whenever the game forces me to click a button labelled "Hell Yeah!".
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: hehe monster train go wooooFavorably compared to Slay the Spire for being a similarly well-constructed deck building roguelike, but blended with a sort of Darkest Dungeon Lite flavor to the combat. Ramping difficulty is cool. Choosing a main and support race is really cool. Having a champion for each one is cool but I wish there were more than one for each race, though the choices in building them is arguably enough. Maybe one more choice of upgrade for each one? I've only seen 3 different ones at max.Could use more enemy variety (mostly bosses, two runs and you've seen them all). Again, the variety is a little padded with modifiers, but another couple bosses would round it out nicely. Slightly longer runs would be nice too. But then, it may be that they just seem short because I'm enjoying it so much, as the runs tend to be around an hour long each. Still, it can feel like you're just getting the ball rolling on a build by the time you reach the final boss, or you may have duped 5 strong, multi-attacking, sweeping monsters with front-liners to tank for them within the first few lucky rounds. Such is the fickle will of the cards.In any case, this is a great initial release, and scratches an itch I forgot I had.Edit: I said nothing of the online features, of which this game packs 3: a daily run, a race run, and customized, submittable runs with mutators and predetermined race choices, which makes this pretty robust overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This is currently my favorite game of 2020 so far.  Hell has frozen over and it's your job as "bad guys" to protect your pyre long enough to reignite the frozen heart at the end of the rails.  With only your units, spells, and a train you must fend off the various creatures and angels attempting to make sure your pyre never reaches the end.  Friends will join you, your train will upgrade, imps will die.  This is he nature of Monster Train.  With a full length soundtrack to play behind each three-leveled fight this game provides an enjoyable experience that really makes you consider if "bigger" minions necessarily means "better" minions.  The Friends and Foes update adds a wide range of play styles and card builds that help to add an extra dimension to this game that on release, I thought it was missing.  Now I have found this game to be one I love dearly and find myself playing at least a run a day.  Sometimes it's difficult and frustrating knowing you're just one turn away from being able to save your pyre, but it's the growth and overcoming the odds that makes this game worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game but I really, really don't. You need to scale so much that it rarely feels like my decisions matter in the fights. Fighting all of the enemies feels exactly the same because the answer is always "scale as quickly as possible or get overwhelmed". The only decisions I make that really feel like they matter are deckbuilding decisions, and while it's cool to assemble a strong deck, it got old for me really quickly. I have 100 hours in Slay the Spire and 8 hours in this one, and I have no plans to play it more.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game but one bug the devs refuse to patch is annoying the hell out of me. For some reason it's called 'Monster Train' instead of 'Crazy Train'. So I don't know why they won't patch this or if they ever will, but I can tell you that every time I go off the rails of a Monster Train I weep for the potential this game could have had.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Like card battlers?  Like randomized procedural runs?  Like planning several moves ahead?  Monster Train was made for you.  I was hesitant as it might seem like a clone of popular deckbuilders at the time, but Monster Train stood out and on its own two legs nonetheless.  The music is great as well.  There are also random daily challenges with a leaderboard to mix it up once in a while which I found to be very fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: A solid roguelike deck builder in the vein of Slay The Spire, but with some key differences it to make it a unique experience that stands above the hordes of StS clones. The multi-tiered unit-based combat is fun and strategic, with plenty of decisions to make per turn. The card upgrade system is fantastic, adding to the already impressive deck building scope built on a foundation of a plethora of interesting units, spells, class synergies and artefact effects.Monster Train is another great addition to the roguelike genre, and one of the best deckbuilders I've had the pleasure of playing. Definitely worth picking up at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Having played over 40 hours and still enjoying it i would recommend it to anyone who likes deck builders. Its a fun game with amazing combos you can build into.  the deck building is compelling and you can stop a run and resume it again when you want. My only gripe is lack of variability in enemy types that i think will be fixed with more content releases.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train brings something new to the roguelite card battlers. Everything has a purpose and everything feels like it was designed to be effective. There are very few cards that you look at and go "maybe if I get this one trinket/card/upgrade this will be good" and that is how a card battler should be. The only concern I have is how pigeon-held you are into certain strategies but there is enough variety that it doesn't get too wrote.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Excuse me hi wow this game is addicting.  I love that Slay the Spire came out and popularized deck building roguelites because between that, One Step from Eden and this, there is a vast amount of potential in this style.Monster Train has a lot in common with Slay the Spire; card drafting, slow methodical gameplay, predictable interactions, fun synergies, artifacts, and bosses that make you want to tear your hair out.  In spite of the similarities, the game plays so much differently that you could tell me that the developers never played StS and I'd believe you.The thing I was most excited about once I finished my first run and realize that multiple clans existed was the breadth of different play styles that you can create just by mixing and matching each clan.  Each clan has a completely different focus in how it plays: red is direct nukes and high damage creatures, green is tank and heals, blue is spells and... wait is this just Magic: The Gathering?  Anyway, that by itself isn't so special... what makes it special is that you pick two of these clans for each run, which directly effects your play style for that run.  Also, your primary clan comes with a champion creature that costs 0 to play and is always in your opening hand and can be upgraded with some CRAZY synergy powers, so there is DEFINITELY a huge difference between a Green/Red playthrough and a Red/Green playthrough because of this!If you had even a passing interest in StS, you owe it to yourself to take a good look at Monster Train.  I'm very excited to see how this game grows!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game. It's basically a mix between Slay the Spire and a Tower Defense game. The card mechanics are very STS as well as the rogue-lite card collection and ascension systems. The battles play out using a tower defense system where you are trying to kill enemies before they get through the levels of your "maze" and start beating on your core.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is an incredible deck-building game that offers a fresh take on the genre. With its unique blend of tower defense and roguelike elements, it's a game that's easy to pick up but hard to put down.The game's card mechanics are deep and strategic, allowing players to build their decks to fit their playstyle. The five different factions each have their own unique strengths and weaknesses, creating endless opportunities for experimentation. The game's difficulty is also adjustable, ensuring players of all skill levels can enjoy the game.The presentation of Monster Train is exceptional, with gorgeous visuals, a fantastic soundtrack, and a dark and twisted art style that perfectly matches the game's tone. The game's story is also surprisingly engaging, with a variety of interesting characters and a well-crafted world that will keep you hooked from start to finish.Overall, Monster Train is an absolute gem of a game that deserves to be played by anyone who loves deck-building or tower-defense games. It's a game that's easy to get into but hard to put down, with endless replayability and an exceptional presentation. If you're looking for a game that will keep you hooked for hours on end, Monster Train is the perfect choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: More addictive than crack.Amazing game play variation - after hundreds of hours I'm still coming up with new decks and strategies. There's a perfect balance of RNG, every run is unique but I always feel that I'm steering the boat and not just "in for the ride"... Buy it (and the DLC - it's damn worth it)
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I do like the game but the Overwhelmingly Positive is not accurate. Its a fun game but if you already own slay the spire there is nothing to see here. What i dislike the most about this game is the only two path route you can take throughout the run, you always meet the same type of enemies and bosses. It's fun for a couple of hours untill you complete a run and have to do the same run again just with stronger enemies
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who got to beta test this... This game is very solid for those who appreciate the Slay The Spire / Fate Hunters type of game. Sure, you have an "army" of unit cards instead of a single hero, but it keeps the deckbuilding spirit. Between each battle, there are opportunities to improve your situation, and each battle you must choose whether to take on a special penalty for extra loot. The "quality of life" details in this game are pretty outstanding (numbers in battle advise you of how much damage will be dealt and who will die with current arrangements, you can pay extra to refill most of the shops with new options, etc) ... I definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: It may look like a cheap Slay The SPire knock off, and while a lot of its mechanics are heavily "borrowed" from it, this game has surprising dept to it.Smooth gameplay, has pretty polished mechanics as well as a nice soundtrack. Only remark would be that the balance feels a bit off sometimes. Some cards feel game breaking, some absolutely useless. But these things will get ironed out over time no doubt. Definitely worth its price and your time!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun card game, a little bit like Hearthstone or Gwent as you summon monsters from your deck and utilize spells. I find this more fun than those, though, as the singleplayer (or competetive challenge run) nature of the game allows the balance to be in the players favour and to create ridiculous combos, which is certainly positive. The runs are quite long for a cardgame, but you can leave whenever not in a battle and return to it later. And battles are fairly short. It has quite a lot of replayability, not only because you choose which cards to draft into your deck during the run and how to upgrade them, but also because there are 20 possible combinations of different decks to start the run with! There are also about 20 difficulty levels, so even people who want a real challenge get their fun out of this.The only thing I would say is a negative is enemy variety, I hope they will add more enemy decks in other updates or DLC.If you enjoy Gwent or Hearthstone, you will enjoy Monster Train. If you did not enjoy those two (I did not lie Heartstone much), you might still enjoy this one, as it feel much more casual and fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: the best of the best.I tried numerous card games and this game deserves more hype.Slay the Spire comes nowhere close to Monster Train, I bought multiple copies of the game for friends and can highly recommend it. Contentwise you are looking at 80hr+, I wish the game would have gotten more updates because this is a one of a kind game, pure addiction.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal game! If you like Slay The Spire then you'll love this, and I truly think it makes StS seem basic in comparison.What I love the most about what Shiny Shoe have done with the formula is really worked on combating the early-game staleness that other card-battler roguelites tend to get: Selecting a primary and secondary deck that combine together feels fresher than just a single character with a single deck, you get given a random selection of cards from those decks along with a choice of an artefact right at the start of the run which stops the first fight being the same every time and the card upgrading system offers many more choices.The events system is far more positive than StS too; the only negative effects you'll receive will be alongside positive ones, and the game always allows you to choose none of the given options.I highly recommend :)
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Its fun and all but its highly repetitive almost to the point its annoying. There is no incentive for actually leveling up. The mob cards get stronger but yours don't . Still wish there was a neutral rating on steam. It not that bad for a thumbs down considering the price. In a nutshell you don't get the rng right then your screwed.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good it makes Darkest Dungeon, Slay the Spire and Teamfight Tactics (each the titan of their genre) entirely obsolete in comparison. It's not every day a game is so innovative and so perfectly executed that it dethrones entire, brand-new genres of gaming all by itself - and every fan of the aforementioned games or card games in general owe it to themselves to give Monster Train a try!The game looks, sounds, controls and has a soundtrack that is exactly what you'd expect from it and it runs like a charm even on integrated graphics cards (tested on an Intel HD 4000-equivalent). I wish there were more keyboard controls but I can't complain about the current control scheme either.EDIT: no longer working on Linux through Steam Play (Proton).Other than needing to skip the non-playing introduction video (black screen) with a mouse click, it works flawlessly on Linux through Steam Play. Being an Unity game, it's confounding why there isn't a native download of the game at all!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like STS - you might like this better actually. this game satisfies every possible itch i have with anything roguelike cardgame the class diversity - and mixing them, opens up so much fun gameplay. Me talking about the depth of the games mechanics would not do it justice, but i can safely say i wont get bored with this for a looong time, and even if i do ever - i will absolutely come back to it.

You never really run out of spell cards. So experiment with purging cards and not accepting a reward too often to make all the cards you draw relevant to whatever strategy your's trying.

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the Spire, but better in some ways. The mechanics have a nuance to them that isn't immediately apparent. You really understand the depth when you play it. Tons of replayability mastering the various clans and experimenting with clan combinations, discovering new and interesting card synergies, basically everything you would want in both a card game and a roguelike.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I'm not liking the game. I quite liked Slay the Spire, and I have been playing many roguelites recently. Many reviewers here will praise it for being fast paced and allow a lot of variety. I think it is too fast, and doesn't allow you to really do much deck building. Once you are getting close to a fun build, you are done. And a part of the difficulty scaling in the game is adding bad cards to your starting deck, that you have to spend the short game removing again. Very bad mechanic, in my opinion. I would also say, that there might be a decent amount of variety yes - but a lot of cards are deadweight if not in the correct build, meaning less flexibility. Overall I feel like there is more boring or wrong choices in this game, and many of the choices I get to make during a game is either: boring or meaningless.I've been playing it a bit more to try to give it a fair chance - and maybe after 15 hours or more my thoughts will change. We'll see.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best deckbuilder I've ever played. Game starts out easy and lets you get the hang of the various race combos and mechanics before ramping up the difficulty through the standard ascension mechanics found in these games (each playthrough is harder after a victory, completely optional though!).More dynamic than Slay The Spire with a stronger ability to save runs through player skill or a lucky card/artifact which leads to less restarts and more exciting moments. Add in the ability to configure a bunch of fun "mutations" that will make your run easier or harder and the fact that once you beat the highest ascension there are some pre-built mutation sets called elite challenges to keep you playing it is a must play if these kinds of games are your jam.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: (Played this for about 20 hrs at review time)TLDR: If you're considering buying this or Slay the Spire, buy this.I got into Monster Train on a recommendation and loved it, then got Slay the Spire because hey, it has amazing reviews and it started the deckbuilder/roguelike genre! About half an hour in my jaw had almost hit the floor - I was shocked by how poorly StS compared to this game. It's improved on nearly every basic feature: more exciting items! More character choices! Better turn flow! I credit the StS devs with inventing a new genre, but hey...I'd rather buy the new and improved version than the first stab at the concept.Monster Train is perfect for strategy gamers and trading card players (I'm a longtime Magic fan). It might be hard to beat the bosses if you don't have much experience with card games specifically, I'm not sure - Slay the Spire might be the better game for new players. But MT has it beat on depth of mechanics and overall quality of life. The one major drawback is the lack of boss variety - you ultimately "beat" the game by beating the final boss 25 times, which is a 30+ hour time commitment and starts to feel repetitive (although they add modifiers to the gameplay as you go). I'd really like some sort of built-in Endless Mode or just more boss variety to make for a longer, crazier experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic addition to the ever-growing rougelike deckbuilding genre. After falling in love with Slay the Spire I was gifted this game by a friend, and I don't know if I can ever go back. The wildly different factions you can play as and the multiple floors add so much strategy and potential for fun decks.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: It's as least as good as slay the spire, better if you like a bit more forward planning with the multiple floor setup and combinations from two different clans worth of cards.  If you like deckbuilding strategy games then you should try this.  Each combination of clans (there are 5, you pick 2 to start) plays quite differently from each other, some synergize well, some don't but you can usually eke out some unusual strategy if you try hard enough.  On top of that there's a goodly collection of artifacts, clanless cards and other bits and pieces to give a massive amount of combinatorial variety.  Everything is pretty well balanced, with space to find things that seem (but aren't) completely brokenly powerful, which is always fun.  Then, often, you run into the one thing that counters that, which has never been a problem before but now is what's stopping you from just rolling over the whole game, and you see if you can adjust your strategy to cope with it.  Overall it's a game full of small but meaningful decisions adding up to an overall effect on how successful you are, and everything looks nice, sounds fine, and plays smoothly.  You can also stop and save at almost any time (I believe you only lose anything already done on the turn you exit), which is nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train stands apart from other deckbuilders by making every decision exciting and bombastic. Where Slay the Spire decisions often give the player small and incremental benefits, Monster Train encourages you to break the game with absurd multipliers and combinations that feel fantastic to pull off. Monster Train focuses on minion combat rather than a main protagonist, which means that you build little connections with each card and you'll find yourself getting excited to find an Overgorger or a specific power-up (StS has this as well, but I think it shines through a bit brighter in Monster Train). The custom soundtrack has gone way under the radar and should really be appreciated more -- I think it's pretty neat.In my opinion, this game can be enjoyed by two types of gamers:For someone who is new to deck games or didn't like Slay the Spire:If you aren't familiar with deckbuilders, this game has enough beginner elements that it's a good jumping-off point into the genre, and it isn't reliant on a ton of experience to get a few wins. If you didn't like Slay the Spire, Monster Train is a bit less math-y at the lower difficulties and the minion elements and sound effects give the game a lot more character. I recommend the base game to anyone who wants to try someone new, but I would save the DLC until you're beating the higher difficulties consistently. You can buy the DLC, switch it off within the main menu, and then save it for when you've gotten the hang of the game.For the hardcore deck builder:This game belongs in contention with StS for the best deckbuilder created as of 2021. The control that MT gives the player over your deck in each run, combined with the build-diversity and variety of random events make it infinitely replayable ang every run is winnable. The difficulty curve within a run and as you move up the difficulty tiers feels great, with enough random events and rotating bosses to break up "meta" builds from carrying each run. The Last Divinity DLC is another level of complex, for better or worse, but overall it accomplishes the goal of keeping MT fresh and adds an absolutely massive amount of new content and mechanics. There are daily challenges (using positive and negative modifiers) and the ability to create and share your own if that's your thing.

The unlocks and stats are great and give the game a lot of depths. As a little downside the enemies/boss are always the same which makes it less varied but also more consistant. _childDocuments_.review: Okay - so I almost didn't download the demo because of the name; "Monster Train"?  Sounds kind of lame.  Well, I couldn't have been more wrong!  This game rocks.  Within about 15 minutes of playing the demo I knew this would be a day-one purchase for me.  I love it so much I called my brother and told him to download the demo.  He too wasn't sure about a game called "Monster Train" but decided to give it a chance.  He ALSO was a day one buy!  This game scratches all of the right itches for me.  It's a deck builder (which I love) but also feels sort of like a tower defense game?  It's very unique.  When I played the demo, there were only 2 races you could play as; now there are more that you can unlock.  Given how many different cards you can unlock for each race, this game seems to have endless replayability.  I can't stop playing it!  If you like it even half as much as I do then you'll be in good shape!

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Slay the Spire, and this is basically everything you love in that game plus. It's an amazing deck builder. You have different races to choose from each with 2 champions. You can choose a main race and a sub race for each run. There are a ton of things to unlock, so lots of replayability. _childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I can't think of a single negative thing to say about Monster Train. The art, the creativity, the design, the music, the replayability, the difficulty; I wouldn't know how to make any element work better than it does.
