_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game! Beating later bosses requires some clever floor setups to maximize damage and survive. Like a mix between a tower defense and Slay the Spire. Setting up your floors with so many constraints even feels like a puzzle sometimes. You pick 2 clans each run, which change how you approach your deck and defense building significantly. Haven't even unlocked the last deck/clan!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: The strategy and complexity of this game is hidden under a "cute" exterior. Quality of graphics is great, smooth game play and great characters keep me coming back to play. The deep complexity of game means there is plenty of re-play-ability. The challenges are fun and put a great twist on the baseline game. You won't be unhappy with a purchase of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Some games are so good they inspire an entire generation of games. The most notable example of this is obviously Dark Souls, but I would argue on a smaller scale Slay the Spire spawned an era of turn based deckbuilder videogames. In the same way the best "Soulslike" games are not mere cheap ripoffs, but rather build on and advance the ideas pioneered by their namesake, Monster Train stands head and shoulders above other "Spirelikes" as in my opinion one of if not THE best deckbuilders out there. Without going into detail on the specific mechanical distinctions between the two, the part of Monster Train that most improves on the Slay the Spire formula is the mix and match mechanic where instead of getting locked into a single class you are given five different "decks", from which you select a primary and a secondary, This combined with a few other smaller design choices ultimately results in an absurdly high amount of build diversity. I'm 80 hours in and still discovering new combinations and strategies I'd never considered. Sometimes the game does feel like it has strategies that are a bit broken, but I think that's less of a criticism and more of a design philosophy, it feels like the emphasis is always erring more on the side of letting the player have fun breaking the game than creating a strict competitive balance, and frankly, I think it's more fun that way.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a massive Slay the Spire fan, and got this game after seeing it compared to StS so often, and Jorbs playing it on his YouTube channel.Monster Train is decent. Not nearly as good as Slay the Spire, but decent. If you have a ton of hours in Slay the Spire and are interested in playing something new, give Monster Train a shot. If you haven't played Slay the Spire though, I'd say go buy that game instead. It's a masterpiece of a game that's honestly just better than Monster Train in almost every way.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Linux! Okay, now that I have your attention: first off, I really, really wanted to buy this but then saw the Windows only logo. So I put it off for months. I finally got my gaming rig fixed from Microsoft's latest incompetency and made the leap. You can read comments way more articulate than mine about how awesome and balanced this game is. I'm hardly a veteran of deck builders but this one has devoured at least 2 hours of my life, maybe even 176 at last count.While killing time waiting for the week or so it takes QT to recompile on a system update, I popped into Steam and saw a little green Play button for Monster Train. , I thought to myself,  as my ultra portable Arch Linux laptop was trying its hardest at heating the neighborhood. But the cats huddled close to it so somebody was enjoying the electrons.Back to Linux.Flawless. Absolutely and completely flawless. Vulkan with Proton 5.1. System utilization never got above 2% on my 4 core i7-8550U, the RAM utilization didn't even show up on my top 10 offenders Top chart. And the Intel UHD 620 was able to rock at 1920x1080 at 60FPS. Admittedly my Windows box rocks a whole lot harder, but the GPUs in that monstrosity dim the neighborhood when I'm training a neural network.There were a few hiccups on the larger, zoomed out screens; but that went away as soon as my QT compilation was complete so I'm going to chalk it up to either disk IO or forcing gcc to work threaded.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: GREAT deckbuilding Game that's kind of an evolution of Slay the Spire. Instead of copying the concept the devs smartly expanded it and gave it a very cool twist that completely changes gameplay experience!This time you are the monsters and you need to stop these pesky heroes & Angels from snuffing out the last embe rof the fires of the underworld!The gameplay is diverse, the concept is familiar to those that love deck building game yet brings a LOT of New concepts and ideas, It leaves you with this itch to instantly try this new strategy you just thought of when you finish (or fail) a run. The game is also pretty challenging which again is good as it spurs you to try new strategies.The most amazing part though is the potential. I can already see 40 different avenues how this game can expand with DLC / more features very easily. More Heroes is no 1 I am thinking of. But also new artifacts, new bodies for the heroes or branching paths for the train. Maybe an overarching story as you climb the covenants!Great great game and worth every penny. If you love deckbuilding games a must buy <3
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It's fun to have a rogue-like that expects you to scale like mad in a span of 45 minutes. Every run comes with a feeling of satisfaction and there's always a risk that you'll die if you aren't paying attention. This is probably the best card-based rogue-like on the market right now - especially if you don't like the slow place and poor scaling in Slay the Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Waited after I tried Slay the Spire to write the review for this game. After all, this is a more casual roguelike deck building game compared to Slay the Spire.The pros: the art design and animation of this game is probably one of the best for this genre. With the double clan combined game design, it does have a decent more variety of potential combos. Core gameplay very simple, easy to learn and easy to control.The cons: The combination of clans doesn't always work, this directly resulted in a big reduction of the actual combo of clans that's viable in the game. There will still be more variety, just nowhere close to what there seem to be. The overall deck building is not as tight as StS, it's fun for casual play, but the depth of the game as a deck  building is a bit lacking imo.Overall, Monster Train is still a fun game, if you've get bored with StS, this is a great game to try. However, don't expect the same level of serious deck building experience like StS. For some people, this could be a better game. If you are not a hardcore deck builder, I'm sure you will enjoy this game for many hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely well made and endlessly replayable.Monster Train is a rogue-like deck builder with a bit of a tower defence twist to it. Instead of building a deck around your attacks you collect units and spells. Units are placed in one of three lanes and attack at the end of every turn and spells are used to support them. A big part of the game revolves around finding strategies that allow you to adequately defend all three lanes until you get your wombo combo going.With five different factions, each featuring numerous unique mechanics, and numerous game modifiers you can sink a lot of time into Monster Train. If you enjoy deck builders it is definitely worth a look.Additional reading material that goes over how I enjoy finding new synergies every time I play:

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the game the first few times I felt it was 'only' a decent game. I guess I kept comparing it to Slay the Spire. But the game just pulled me in, and now I cannot get enough of it. There are so many combinations of heroes and cards and all encourage different play styles and kindless need combos to discover.I thought the character art was a bit off-putting honestly, but otherwise this game looks nice, sounds nice (great music and sound!) and feels nice (smooth and clear UI!)There is so much to come back for and the idea with the floors is so clever, definitely a recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Had this game for less than a week and already put 18 hours into it and have not even scratched the surface of all the builds, cards, synergies, etc.. that this game has to offer. If you like games such as slay the spire you'll love this! I personally have found this to be even more enjoyable than StS but that's just my personal opinion. If you are on the fence about buying this game ill help you out with your decision. BUY NOW! i think it's still like 10 or 15% off at the time of writing this review for the Steam Summer Sale but even at full price it is worth every penny!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Slay the Spire, except better. Let's be clear here, I love Slay the Spire, it is one of my favorite games of the past decade and basically invented an entire genre. Monster Train takes that formula, and improves on it in every way. Choosing 2 clans essentially lets you mix colors, meaning that there are 20 different clan combinations to master. I loved this, as my biggest frustration with Slay the Spire was that there was a very limited amount of characters to choose from. The game starts out easy, but don't let that fool you! Once you start climbing the ladder, the games difficulty ramps up significantly. Some days I will go 4-5 runs without a win! That is okay though, that is the life of a rogue and I wouldn't have this game any easier.Buy it now!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly fun card game, plain and simple.5 Races with 2 unique champions/starter cards per race. You pick a main and a secondary race. Some have better synergy than others, but winning setups can be made with all the possibilities. Starter cards, upgrades, boss fights etc. are all randomly generated with several choices. _childDocuments_.review: Scroll down for full GameplayAnother entry in the roguelike card game genre and what a hell of an entry it is!With the addition of customizable card upgrades, introduction of unit summons and the ability to create sick combos, Monster Train stands proudly among other titans of the subgenre. Things really start to heat up once you unlock more clans, cards and difficulty levels. Plenty hours of fun, card diversity and fun cardplay, earns it a very warm recommendation (promise, no more puns). + Excellent card play. The core card mechanics and the way cards combine offer plenty of great deckbulding opportunities.+ Card customization. The ability to upgrade both units and spells, is by far the most fun aspect of the game for me as it opens the player to experiment with pretty crazy combos.+ Diversity. Anywhere from picking different starting champion units, over different starting clans to just picking and upgrading different cards, the game offers near endless diversity in how you make your deck work.+ Fairly quick runs. Defeat doesn't feel as bad, as a single run can be done within an hour.+ Aesthetics. Personally I enjoyed the art style and on top of that the cards are slightly animated which is nice touch.* Empowering players. The players are given a ton of tools to create their own perfect deck, with plenty of options to remove cards or duplicate the strong ones. This can make runs less difficult, but most runs will not be as easy as it may sound. * Math problems. Although the game does the hard calculations for you, sometimes it's very difficult to foresee the output until you actually play the card, especially for units. This could be resolved by showing results before you play a unit card, but the game currently does not support that.* Slower unlock rate. The last clan together with some end cards take a bit more time to unlock than I would have liked personally. Thankfully, the game is fun enough so it doesn't feel like a chore.* Some items seem a bit overtuned. This can make some runs a lot easier, but at the same time broken combos can be super fun to pull off. Some players may be bothered by it, but I found it more enjoyable than not. - The single biggest downside of the game is the very notable lack of boss diversity. Each major boss has some slightly different mechanics, but ultimately you will be seeing the same faces over and over again.  As typical with games in the genre, you will fight a series of fights, earning cards and items along the way, only to face the last boss. After each run you will be unlocking new cards and difficulty levels.Aside from the tutorial, you start off by picking one main and one allied clan. The game introduces 5 clans (some locked), each with their own unique cards and mechanics. Some clans rely on summoning morsels which are eaten by your other units, other clans rely on summoning powerful minions that have a burnout mechanic,  making them expire after a few turns.Each clan also starts with unique a champion, that can be upgraded into 3 different paths or you can even mix them up to align with your playstyle. Each fight you will summon units on one of three floors of your train and try to prevent waves of enemies reaching your Pyre, not unlike a tower defense game. Where and when you place your units is extremely important and positioning matters with the front units taking damage first and once they die, they can't be summoned back for that fight (with the exception of some clan spells). On each level, after the last wave the boss joins the fray, usually possessing an additional gimmick. Unlike tower defense games, the boss can't slip by, so if you have the damage/health to deal with the boss, you will. In between fights you can choose one of two sides of the railroad track, each giving access to different set of locations: shops where you upgrade cards or buy items, healing sites, sites to duplicate/remove cards or special events.One thing that sets this game apart from similar games is the card upgrade system. Every card can be upgraded (spells and units) in a number of ways (e.g. stat improvements, adding special keywords etc). This small mechanic can greatly supplement your strategy. One example is adding the keyword Holdover to a card, which puts it on the top of your deck when played. If your strategy relies on playing some key cards, playing it every turn without having to clutter your deck with copies, can be immensely powerful and satisfying.The game tries its best to give the player all the tools he/she needs to succeed with plenty of ways to remove cards from your deck, get new ones or duplicate/upgrade existing ones, all in the effort to create a super deck. Lots of fun, lots of diversity, excellent card play and deckbuilding.Royally recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is a very fun roguelite cardbuilding game! This game is similar to other games in the genre (e.g. Slay the Spire) in many ways like designing combat around defense/shields, damage, DoTs, and other common abilities/mechanics. Monster Train is also unique in ways that make it interesting and distinct from other games. Instead of a single hero you deploy several monsters over multiple floors, so who and where you deploy is important. Choosing a primary and secondary for each run from the four factions with unique abilities keeps the game engaging. You choose between two simplified paths between each battle with a few rewards. Overall a great game that's definitely worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR; A great take on the Sly the Spire genre, Monster Train provides more accessible tower defense gameplay (i.e. easier to get into). While less technically complex, Monster Train's skill ceiling isn't low so there's plenty of longevity.  The different clans (like Magic the Gathering's different mana colours) also provides plenty of variation to keep gameplay fresh.----Not going into too much detail in this review. Unlike say Griftlands (another game inspired by StS), I found that I could get into the gameplay for Monster Train almost immediately. It's that easy to grasp (at least for me), and it works well. A few points:1. The main gameplay is tower defence-like. Kill enemies with static units on each floor (as in they don't chase the enemy) and spells, before they reach your pyre you are trying to protect,2. The units & spells you use remind me of Magic the Gathering's summoned creatures and spells. There's limited place on each floor though, so choose and position your units carefully.3. Also like M:tG, you can mix two clans (colours) to try different sterategies.4. Each run is significantly shorter than StS, maybe a 1/3rd.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of rogue lites and deckbuilders (e.g., Slay the Spire or Dominion) this game will most likely be fun for you. It nicely combines the deckbuilding aspect with strategic elements of unit positioning and synergies (similar to Darkest Dungeon, but on three levels). Your overall goal is to avoid that enemy units move to the top floor, where your pyre rests. Once its destroyed, you're dead.The replayability is huge, since there are different clans (i.e., card decks). The clans play very differently due to different card mechanics. Furthermore, you not only select one clan but two for each run. This increases the combinations further. And there are ascencions, steadily increasing the difficulty after each successful run. The difficulty is pretty challenging once you reach a certain ascencion level. Similar to other deckbuilders, it's very satisfying to find a powerful deck, but it can be a bit tiresome to get there. But there is no heavy grinding, most card unlocks happen pretty quickly.Overall, the game is worth the money if you are up for a rogue lite challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm revising this because it doesn't seem fair to play a game so much and give it a negative review. My complaints are the same, but it's still an enjoyable experience despite the annoying parts.This game has a ton of promise, but the amount of luck of the draw and variance in usefulness of artifacts and if you get the right cards is absurd. It's not difficult to play this game well. There's a lot of strategy and synergy. Instead, the problem arises from being unable to do the super cool combos you want to pull off because you just didn't get the right cards.For example, I got an artifact that gave me plus 3 to all x cost cards. Cool. This gives me a clear strategy of pursuing and upgrading certain x cost cards. And then I didn't get offered a SINGLE + x card. Another issue is that artifacts are absolutely not balanced. Some are miles better than others. That's fine for a game on launch. What's worse is that some artifacts are clearly good, but offer literally no interesting decisions, like giving your pyre 40 health. These artifacts do not affect your play style literally at all. Also, some of the statuses are an issue. For example, thorns. It's an issue because some unit leaders only have a couple of hit points, and it's not like you can stop them from attacking. Thus, you can play your leader and hope that he just never engages an enemy with thorns, because if he does he will die and there's nothing you can do about it, or not play your leader? I guess. Stealth is equally stupid. There's genuinely nothing fun about the stealth mechanic. It's just a boss taking 8 free shots on your units so you better hope you went with a beefy boy strategy, because if you went for a glass cannon big damage strategy you're definitely going to lose.The foundation and variability is great. This is a fully fledged and well thought through game. But it needs a lot of work to get it out of the frustrating stage of just getting totally boned by bad luck.Even offering 3 cards instead of 2 after each fight would go a long way, or have  a card shop, or any number of other things.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: After logging over 1200 hours on Slay The Spire I was looking for another good Rogue-lite Deck Builder and Monster Train has nailed it! It is a blast to play. Where it shines brightest is in the tactical game; Set up your monsters across the 3 floors of your train to protect your Pyre. Attackers will board your train and combat your defenders before advancing to the next floor. Defeat them before they get to your Pyre.Once the Boss arrives, it will relentlessly attack all creatures on that floor until either your defenders die, or the boss is dead.Move your train through 8 fights to secure victory.Oh and it's got freakin multiplayer too! 10/10 game of 2020.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is my favorite game of 2020!Like Slay the Spire, this game is a mashup of  the roguelike and card battler genres, but it also has some tower defense elements as well. While the card pool doesn't offer the same strategic depth as Slay the Spire, the difficulty is also not as brutal. Monster Train manages to keep things fresh enough with the different clan and champion combinations that I've been able to enjoy over 300 hours of gameplay so far!I recommend Monster Train to anyone who enjoys games like Slay the Spire, but prefers a more chill and player-friendly experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game that builds upon Slay the Spire's legacy. I was sceptical when I read it had elements of deck building and tower defense (though I do love both genres), but I was very impressed at how they combine the two. The biggest gripe would be balance and variety. At least one of the classes feels much more limited than the others (hellbourne), and often times there seems to be fairly limited routes to true success for each class. As well, the enemies scale a bit too fast vs your monsters for my liking.That said, there is a lot of depth here and what's already here is worth the price -- especially if there's a good sale. For those that like Slay the Spire, this is kind of a no brainer. Definitely a step forward for that style of game, though not quite the masterpiece that Slay the Spire is. Graphics - GreatSound Design - No comment as I usually listen to podcasts, but from the little I heard it seems to suit the game very well.Gameplay - Good to great. Engaging gameplay loop, fun upgrades, but sometimes finding the optimal strategy can feel constraining. Quality of Life - Great. Everything you'd want in terms of a low spec graphics mode, speed options, easy to navigate menus, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: A ridiculously clever and well-designed deck building game with remarkably deep but easy to understand mechanics. Draft a squad of monsters from several varied clans with their own gameplay styles, mix and match clans to see how their playstyles complement each other, then do your best to survive challenges that always seem fair but never seem boring. Time and again a strategy you never thought would work will reveal itself, or the moment you feel that you're unstoppable something will happen to snap you back to the edge of your seat again. Beautiful presentation that never feels grating and fantastic character design on the factions. I feel guilty having slept on it for so long.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Same genre as Slay the Spire, felt familiar with the mechanics rightaway.  While it's incredibly easy to get into everything and understand the mechanics, Monster Train surpasses STS  in terms of variety and tactics. It's challenging. I'm not an experienced card/rogue like player but the way it motivates me after each run is just great! Even if you lose, you literally feel the progression of getting stronger. Imo more than in STS. The new/fresh feature that it brings to the table is that there's multiple floors to manage at the same time. This opens up many new ways to fight if compared to one single encounter. I really enjoy the artwork, the progression, the tactical variety and the content(lots of different decks with 2 heroes each). A no-brainer for everyone if on discount. A no-brainer for fans of STS for the full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: It wears its Slay the Spire influence on its sleeve, this is a great evolution of roguelite deckbuilders. If you are fan of StS, you will love this. If you are fan of turn based games in general, you will love this. I feel like you are given a lot of agency to build your run the way you want. After every stage you are given lots of strategic choices to make, and it feels like all of them matter. The tactical game is not on rails either, you have to make choices all the time, which is what makes a turn based game. The difficulty is pitched well - its not so difficult it becomes frustrating, and when you fail you feel its your own fault rather than being at the whim of the RNG, given the agency you have to mitigate bad luck. Pacing is good, with a run weighing in at about an hour - short enough that a failed attempt doesn't feel like a waste of time, but long enough to feel meaty. Really the only negative I can think of is the name, which could not be less inspiring if it tried. Thanks to Northernlion for featuring this game on his channel, else I would probably have missed it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Basically Slay the Spire made sweet love to a train, and Monster Train was born. From the 'artefacts' to the ascending (or descending in Monster Trains case) gameplay mechanics, and the obvious deck-building aspect, it screams STS, but to me fairer in difficulty, and very well balanced in the card game they have created here. I can easily see myself putting tens of hours into this game, and even more with continued updates, its that addicting and fun. Highly recommended for anyone who likes deck-builders and the many mechanics in STS, with or without a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train Review:First of all, just have to give a quick shout out to Conan The Librarian for recommending this game to me.TL;DRAwesome deck builder, lots of options, challenging, and has a ton replay-ability. Highly recommend.The Good:The way the two clans are set up, and the variety of units, artifacts, and spells, make so many fun combinations, and it's not even the full game yet. It's challenging, but not completely unforgiving. I still haven't completed a run on covenant difficulty. ( I am not great at these games, I just enjoy them). The play-throughs are all so different that while I have a strategy, the randomness can upset the best of plans and I have to adapt.The clans: At this stage, and to oversimplify it, one is more offensive based, and the other is defensive. Each has a few units to balance their weakness, but they feel different enough for me. Good news, whichever clan you don't select is your ally at this point (I'm sure the possibilities will open up even more when they release the rest of the clans).Update: There's a whole lot more clan goodness and combinations. Outstanding, but I won't spoil anything. Just sayin' 5 clans each with unique play strengths, lots of vairation and replayability.Building Your Deck:After selecting your clan, you start with one artifact (enhances your race as while in a variety of ways, multi-strikes, cost decreasing, additional armor etc,). After each battle, you have two different route to choose. One usually has an artifact, health, and shop, the other a unit, or duplicator, and a different shop (right now three merchant, some sell artifacts, some sell spell enhances, the other unit enhancers). Utilizing the different cards you pull there are shops that enhance spells and units in a variety of ways (utilizing gold earned in battles). All this to say, even in the beta, it was variety done right.Update: As time has gone on, the variety increases, making it more interesting, without becoming overwhelming or unbalanced.The BadI don't have much bad to say. In part because I haven't played a lot of deck-builder games, but I have done rogue, rogue-lite. This game brings in a lot of different elements, and for a newbie, the learning curve was little much, but not a turn ( I accept that a. I'm new to these games and b. I'm not that great at them). I would like to be able to for my own broken ego, have run that let's me choose any of my unlocked items to create and OP deck and go to town on some of the bosses that have really given me the most trouble. Just a recommendation, and one I'm sure many would find unnecessary. My only other complaint would be, I just want to play the rest of the game (I'm a little impatient too).Conclusion:If you're new to deck-builder, rogue-lite, mash-up that this falls into (I know that's probably not the most accurate description, but that's not more forte either)  then get this game. I've heard references to Darkest Dungeon and Slay the Spire, but once again, I'll leave that to other better at those descriptions. It's a great game, with an active development team and a growing discord community. If the rest of the game is as good at the beta(UPDATE: It's even better!), I would recommend goin in on the full price, it'll be worth it.Update: I used other games to reference what Monster Train was like, tbh, it really is a gem in own right. While it has some elements of the games I mentioned, in all reality ,it has so much individuality that separates it from other games in this genre that make something other games aspire to achieve. The devs have been amazingly responsive and I have so much I love about this game. (That said, a lot of people are streaming it right now, so go check it out.)Final Score:10/10 would and get pwned for poor strategy again (...and again, and again...)

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure what I was buying/getting with this game, a blind purchase; but I enjoyed it enough to put in over 100 hours. The gameplay involves you choosing an alliance between two factions and getting a hero unit in which you will use to defend the bases core in a 3 tier tower defense style play.The fun comes from all the support units and spells you get that are represented as cards in a deck. You draft from a selection in the overworld and then play them out in turn based combat.The challenge comes from punishing Rogue-like mechanics which reset you back to start should you lose.The variety is that everytime you restart a new shuffled game awaits.What stinks, but sometimes doesn't smell is that the difficulty mostly scales by forcing you to begin with a worse deck.Good game, plenty of frequent updates for now, I bought it at 30% off and was happy.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is like Magic: The Gathering and Slay The Spire, but also better in some ways. The devs are really friendly, and the Discord chat is super active. Definitely worth buying if you liked Slay The Spire, especially as they give a 10% discount if you already own STS. Extremely worth the 20 dollars I paid on launch week, still worth the 25 you might have to pay.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of deck building games, I personally find this one to be one of the better ones available. Unlike many of the games of this genre which I've played (mostly on ios), a run in this is a lot shorter which means over time the deck feels more and more tailored/controlled as opposed to the RNG-ness of others. I'd like to call out the length in this game specifically because it's very well paced. A lot of these type of games last too long and allow you to go overboard with the deck/items which isn't a bad thing, but in my opinion makes the genre less strategic and more random, so this is one thing this game excels at.Aside from gameplay, the art direction and music is also very good. Overall I'd say this is a very polished game that will keep you entertained for a while especially in bite sized runs/playthroughs. I haven't tried multiplayer yet but it seems like they're just competitive modes... I'd like to see a co-op mode in the future if that's a possibility, but other than that I'd give this game a 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I've put quite a few hours into Slay The Spire and if you enjoyed that game you'll feel right at home with Monster Train. The biggest difference between the two is that while Slay The Spire is a deckbuilder rogue-lite mixed with RPG style exploration  and combat, Monster Train is a deckbuilder rogue-lite mixed with a tower defense. Because of this while Monster Train is still enjoyableI found it to be lacking a lot of the depth that Slay The Spire had that made me want to do 'just one more run'.Despite that Monster Train is still very much worth playing if you enjoy these types of games. Good visuals, easy to pick up and play, and plenty of ways to experiment with combining different factions.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Even as a regular Spire player, the tower defense aspects of this make it very interesting and unique. Characters like the wonderfully nightmare fuel-ish Umbra champion (personal favorite), and the Melted Remnants as a whole, show that a good amount of thought went into the characters. The difficulty is generally well balanced, some game breaking setups exist, but most of them can be countered by the AI, so while you may spend some time feeling invincible, it'll be well spaced between plenty of times getting stomped. Comparing Seraph to The Heart, in my personal experience, Seraph will kill you faster, but the heart is harder to set up an "I definitely win" against, so that's a decent tie.I can resist the urge no longer, so this is a hell of a lot of fun, especially if you like the genre itself. Get the soundtrack too, there are some really solid tracks there.

_childDocuments_.review: Positive - a refreshing take on rouge-like deck builders, offers a streamlined satisfying game play and the replayability is shockingly high. they have already gave the game a few major updates, no doubt more to come.Negative - from the outside looks like a bad mobile game, can very occasionally a run can end out of your control near the start because of RNG. also I stopped playing Slay The Spire because of this game

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like playing deck building games? Do you like Slay the Spire? Do you like trains? If the answer is yes to any of those, then you owe it to yourself to buy this game. Well maybe not the train part... There are a total of 5 characters and you pick two to build your deck. Two unlocked at the beginning and as you play you unlock the other 3, each one plays differently and each have a different way to build your deck. Excellent deck mechanic in the game keeps each new game interesting and different. Music is also great, which is important because you will listening to the same tunes multiple times as you play.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a fun deck building rogue-like with tons of replay value, this is the game for you. This game has 5 different colors of cards to choose from (6 if you include the DLC), and you can mix and match 2 different colors to create decks with specific strategies you build up during a run. If you like card based Rogue-Likes this is a must buy, especially if it ever goes on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: Bought at  discount.Very gorgeous graphics. Most animations are top notch.The music fits the ambience, it's a lot of action and voice sound effects, so it fits the genre of fighting. There is enough variation to not get the player bored of listening.It's great for passing up time. You will have a game where difficulty between learning how to play the combination of cards/factions and how to master them rise up nicely and can brake if you feel it's going too fast for you. The challenge modes spice things up and you can unlock golden border of cards, which is nice because it's a purely cosmetic reward which doesn't impact on anything if you don't care.Each run feels different if you try to experiment with different cards and heroes. Even if you go for the exact same strategy, it STILL can feel different due to a lot of random rewards / choices you have to do along the way. The mini bosses are varied too and the final boss behaves differently each time you run against him, so the same strategy might not work all the time.It have a unique layer of customization/strategy which is the floor you put your units or cast your spells. It's better if you spend your last 'mana' kill that soon to be attacking minion which barely escaped your monsters or it's better to buff your units on the front?There is also plenty of achievements and challenges to complete if one is interested on it. And even a few secrets.Story is encouraging. You are responsible for maintaining alive the last piece of hell and to rekindle it. It also explains why you run a lot of monsters in your train and why they all team together despite being different races. There is a lot of lore to chug if you take your time to read the story of each card while not in combat.My notebook is an Acer VX 15.  It ran smoothly to me, no stuttering, nothing. I didn't notice any bugs.9.0 / 10A great rogue like which successfully maintains the variation and the action pumping, not getting you bored if you are willing to try different things.Some cards DO feel underpowered compared to others. Like for example, card that just move your allies on the floors and heal for the cost of [2].OBS: I didn't feel the need to buy the DLC as I believe it didn't really go well and is unnecessary.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's a great take on the roguelike deckbuilding game that does a great job distinguishing itself with its layout. Each of the clans has a unique feel to them, and finding new combos makes the game feel fresh and new with each playthrough. I'm hoping for even more clans in the future, so there are even more things to experiment with
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: A finely polished deck-building game.   It's a pleasure to play, but it's also  in desperate need of more content.    + This is a huge: After three runs, you'll see all the enemy content this game has to offer.   There are no different levels, the boss rotation is anemic, the enemies are the same except for a random stat modifier.    Please, devs, mix it up!      + Visuals, audio, and UX are very polished for an indie title.  It's very enjoyable to interact with the game.  Your minions make satisfying crunchy sounds.  The graphics are engaging and informative.  The fallen/angelic soundtrack fits your ride into hell perfectly.+ Card design.   Lots of interesting combos await your discovery.+ Strategy.  Your train consists of three floors, and each one is a place where battle can be waged.   There's a bit of tower-defense strategy here, as you try to anticipate when enemies will hop floors and optimize your resources accordingly.The inevitable comparison to :  Monster Train is superior in every way, imho.   Game mechanic-wise, it's a v2 of Slay the Spire, with more gameplay variances and a better multimedia experience.(edit 1 min after posting: grammar.  sigh.)
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: It's like if Slay the Spire decided to make half the bosses depend entirely upon rng instead of game knowledge and personal skill. This game was better on launch back when it was only the stealth boss that made you instantly lose for no reason half the time, but unfortunately the devs thought that was a good way to go with things and made the alternate bosses in line with that one overtuned ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.It's still a good game, but if you intend to play in Covenant (it's StS Ascension mode but in this game and goes up to 25) just keep in mind it's a hell of a lot more tedious than STS's Ascension mode. You'll end up needing to restart a lot of runs right at the start just because you got bad cards or two trash artifact choices. Even when you get a good start you'll still fail half your runs just because the game decided to give you bosses you were never going to beat in the first place. If you can deal with that then the runs where the game doesn't cuck the ♥♥♥♥ out of you are actually quite fun, and the mutators are a good way to spice things up and add replay value.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review for the game as it is after the Last Divinity DLC.So, there's not a lot of deckbuilding Roguelike games out there but with this latest update this is basically the best one. Also, if you are a fan of more turn based games where you can mull over your decisions, this is the best one of those with a roguelike bent (not even sure if that's a thing). The amount of new decisions added in this latest expansion increase what was already a deep game to upper tiers of deep thought you don't always see in solo card games.With 6 factions and now a second final (optional) boss and new ways to upgrade your run, even the same starting point will be drastically different from the last end point you reached last time with that same configuration.Simply put, this is a great game that the reviews aren't BS'ing you on. It may look less exciting when you watch streamers play it but only in the same way that watching someone read a book isn't anywhere near as interesting as reading it yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: As a avid Slay the spire player I have been tiptoeing around this title for a while. Decided to get it during the summer sale and it was a great choice.If you like Slay the spire and other deck builders this is the game for you a purchase well worth it. Not into the nuances yet (takes a while just like spire) but already have tons of fun and can't wait to get into the meta.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Slay the Spire, and I liked this even more.Chance plays a part in every run, but you still have a decent amount of agency over the outcome. When I lose, I usually can look back and see a better strategy I could have taken advantage of. There's enough control over deck composition that you can alter your strategy as you progress. No hoping for a single run-defining card or artifact to make the different.The possible card pools are smaller than Slay the Spire's, but I enjoy that. It cuts down on the possible pool of cards you'll see, so you can actually plan ahead towards some possible synergies. Some artifacts are very powerful while others are so-so, which makes getting a good one make a run feel unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Watched many YouTubers play it (Northernlion, Rhapsody and MichaelALFox mostly) while playing or even in free time. It's an extremely entertaining and fun game, with excellent replayability from a quick run every day or just to slam failed run after failed run trying to make the cards you're given work. The difficulty ranges well as it is easy to pick up but incredibly hard to master and perfect each run. With devs working super hard and pumping out consistently great updates the game is positively going to improve even further.Highly recommend the game for those that enjoy roguelikes, deckbuilders or those that love a good time sink; reviewers hours speak for themselves in many cases but here the case is especially true. 10/10 A true gem from this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Train

_childDocuments_.review: You carry with you the last flame of hell on a train. You need to protect it while the good guys want to take it from you and kill you and your monsters. It's a strategy deck building game with random elements and card drops so each run is different. A run typically takes about 30 minutes so it's easy to play and if you need to leave the game automatically saves your progress so you can continue where you were without much issues.It's colourful, the level design is great and the music is cool. It's super addictive as there is so much to unlock and then new mechanics are introduced after you progress making the game a little bit more complex but still rewarding. There are different races and you can combine them to make your ultimate deck. If that is not enough there are daily challenges and you can compete with others or try a custom challenge. You can also make your own challenges by adding mutators to runs.I also enjoyed that there are multiple events that usually give you a nice reward. There are even some secrets to be found.It's super addictive :-) you will end up spending hours on perfecting your run. Then you discover multiplayer and daily competitions and you can't stop playing :-)As you progress in the game it feels the solution to a run, narrows down to a few units or combinations. If you have an unlucky hand, you will lose and have to restart; at times this can be a little frustrating. On the other hand, you will learn strategies as to remove cards you don’t need and not to pick all the cards that are being offered. This ensures your more desirable cards show up more often.It's a great rogue-lite deck building game. You become more efficient as you discover what combinations work well. The music is great and adds a lot to the game. Graphics are OK. The game is optimized for small 30 minutes runs. Highly recommend if you want to play in short runs (although admittingly I played for hours just to find the right solution 😊).

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, like many of you, I'm here from the STS route. And I've downloaded and played this for a handful of runs three separate times now, thinking I'll get into it more (mostly because I find my way back to the reviews and they're so stellar, and I appreciate that other people like the game), but I just can't recommend it.I appreciate the work the devs have put in here, it's clearly noticed, but it just feels like every element of what makes something like STS successful is turned up to 11 with no thought for balance or cohesion. The design is overly colorful and cartoonishly garish, but not with any real sense of storytelling. The world doesn't really make sense, like why are we on a train?? The music is nice! And I like that it displays what tracks are playing as you go, in case you want to look up the music later, that's a nice touch because I can never figure out the titles of tracks in games otherwise. And the gameplay...I've seen this listed a bunch already, but it feels like if you haven't locked into an overpowered setup by the third battle...it's not going to end well. And if you have, you're essentially just waiting to win. I'm sorry to compare it to STS so often, but because the market is so oversaturated with these games, it's hard not to. I don't have any of that joy of overcoming something that I really thought I might not like I get from STS. There's no sense of danger, only futility if your run is bad.

_childDocuments_.review: I lost my Roguelike virginity to this game!This game wasn't a simple, seen it and bought it... I went on a flippin' journey for this one!Welcome to my essay on why Monster Train can have my babbies:Let's set the stage: I got 3 free months of XBox Game Pass from Discord more than a year ago.Not wanting to waste those 3 months, I held onto the code right before it expired, then activated it and started to explore all the possibilities. I didn't wanna waste time trying to download Halo or something, so I just downloaded a bunch of games that were small in file size. However, even after downloading these games, I struggled to play them... The thing is, I like to consider myself a Gamer, but I find myself lacking in what the kids call "Gamer Energy," and because of this, more often than not, I stick to a small handful of games I enjoy, barely straying from said games.Modded Minecraft, Terraria, Stardew Valley, Sudoku, Picross, A whole lotta Nintendo Gams!I enjoyed playing games that had a story, gave a bunch of tasks to do, or just let you solve some ♥♥♥♥♥.RPG, Action, Adventure, Survival, Platformer, Puzzle, Strategy, Rhythm, Shooter, Beat-em up, Fighting!I liked many genres, and my indecisiveness helped me not stick with a single genre for long.Though, with all these great genres, there was one genre that I really despised...  No, but seriously... I didn't like Roguelike games for the longest time.Since I lacked that "Gamer Energy," playing a game where starting over again was the main idea had me looking at these games as if they were just throwing your hard work away to start a fresh game... Since I was having a tough time playing the games I downloaded from Game Pass, I felt that I needed to force myself to play ANYTHING before I lost my membership. - Said the naive Roguelike Virgin.I played a round and lost. I played another round and won. I played ANOTHER round, and then I realised that the round I was playing was actually my 10th, and it was almost 5 in the morning.After that night, I felt like I needed to show this new wonder I found to someone.So I got my lil sister to sit down and build a deck with me; after that round, she asked me if we could do another one. Then, the next day, she asked if we could play it again.This game surprised me... I played Slay the Spire before this game, and yet, for some reason, Slay the Spire didn't click with me. Though, after playing this game, I went back to play Slay the Spire and found that I was able to enjoy it a bit more the second time... I also started to try out other Roguelikes, and now I have many new Roguelikes occupying my wishlist. Monster Train changed me.When the 3 months were up, I went straight to Steam and bought this game without a second thought. I haven't done something so impulsive in years, and usually now-a-days when I buy something that isn't groceries, I get a bit of buyer's remorse... Yet, this triggered no such thing.I did it for the core game, and the moment they released DLC, I did it for that. LATER, when it was released on the Switch, I bought that motherducker without ANY restraint!They're still working on the Google Play version of the game as I write this, and I'll tell you this now: I'm buying it. I love this game and only hope that it can grow in popularity.Ever since they released the workshop, I've checked on the mods all the time to see whats new, and for some time now, there hasn't been anything...It has its fans (*points at self*), but there just isn't a lot of noise going on for it compared to other Roguelike games doing similar things. Though I still cross my fingers every night when I drift off to Sleepytime Junction for this game to blow up and get all the attention.Sorry for this long-winded review... I just really love this game, dude!Please, for the love of all that's lovely in this world, It's a great Roguelike card game where you are trying to save Hell from freezing over.So, jump on that train and fight off those pesky Seraph for all of us, okay?

_childDocuments_.review: If you like deckbuilder roguelikes like Slay the Spire you'll PROBABLY like this game. The positives - the game has a lot of personality, the different clans that serve as the base of your decks are unique with their own fun mechanics, there's a good amount of depth, there's lots of ways to "break" the game, and each run doesn't demand too much time so this game works really well if you only have a short time to play. The negatives - the game can be really chaotic and it's often easy to totally lose track of what's even going on, the game falls into the common pitfall of "some cards are must picks and many cards just straight up suck", and other than a couple bosses most enemies feel pretty samey. Though to be honest those negatives aren't huge. The game is a lot of fun. I think the most important thing to call out here is that this game is NOT Slay the Spire. They're very different games with their own take on the deck builder genre. A lot of strategies that Slay the Spire rewards will backfire on you here. This isn't a bad thing. The reason I'm mentioning this is because I immediately got a lot better at this game and had way more fun once I stopped trying to play it like StS. For example, StS encourages you to ramp up energy per turn and your strength scales largely through passive powers. In Monster Train you're encouraged to double down on strengthening a couple cards and playing them as frequently as you can. Card Draw as a result is waaay more important in Monster Train than in StS. Slay the Spire is the better game between the two, but Monster Train deserves a spot in your library if you like deckbuilding roguelikes. Pick it up, it's a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train is as the developers have touchingly put it, "A strategic roguelike deck building game with a twist." Monster Train is in essence heavily inspired by the title Slay the Spire, yet commands many differences. For the sake of selling Monster Train on its own merits, I will avoid comparing the two from this point forward.I would hope that I'm versed enough in the workings of Monster Train by now to sell you on it. Over the course of roughly four months, I have sunk just past 260 hours on the game, a feat that very few titles have captured me enough to do.When I first began my journey four months ago, I was seeking out a new rogue-like that had chaotically fast pacing. Stumbling upon the title right as it released onto Steam, I saw that it was quickly blowing up. Choosing to fish out my wallet and give it a go, I was soon enraptured in an intensively dynamic experience that promised one of two paths per run:  While slowly adjusting to the game's style of multi-unit/spell combat amidst a juggling act of three separate 'floors' for the placement of Monsters, I was able to sink several hours into understanding the mechanics as I worked my way to my first successful run. If I was to judge how I as a newcomer to Monster Train felt in my first five hours, I'd have to say I was an addict to a punishing experience.What I find is one of the most enthralling elements of Monster Train is how tightly it doubles-down on a refined experience of building your team's strategy that can somehow still end up in the deepest pits of  Each run generates a total of   'stops' that you must travel through on your journey to the hellish depths of  Throughout each of these stops will be  separate paths that you are able to choose from, each containing a slew of potential elements for pickup. Be it health, coins for purchases, unique artifacts to empower your journey, shops to upgrade your Monsters and Spells, new Monsters of a specific clan, or lastly randomly generated event caverns that provide choice upgrades that can assist your run in different ways.Through a mashing of these varying elements, Monster Train empowers the player by providing a constantly rolling wheel of dynamic game-play. Every single choice you make can dictate a drastic shift in how your 'build' (deck) will continually play out. This can allow for careless decisions in which players whom do not pay attention could alter their strategies in harmful ways that prevent further progression and prematurely ending a run in defeat. On the flip-side, it also thrillingly provides a unique element of strategy for players that maintains an addictive hold on them with the mentality of 'Just One More Run.'From the onset, Monster Train seeks to expand player choice through build variety. This is done by use of the Clan System. Upon starting a run, you are given the ability to pick two clans out of a (current as of this time) pool of five choices (though for first time players - the 3rd, 4th, and 5th clans need to be unlocked first).You are given both a Primary Clan and a Secondary Clan, which allows for the development of a synergy through the two. Each Clan plays wildly different from one-another, and can serve in either role effectively. What properly differentiates your two Clan Slots is that your Primary Clan dictates the Champion that you may use, with each clan giving you two choices for Champion (as of this time). Your Champion is an empowered Monster that is upgraded three times throughout the course of each run, spawning two generated choices per upgrade to pick from. Because of Champions and their upgrades, each Clan has a plethora of build options for how they play depending on whether or not they are the Primary Clan or the Secondary Clan. In my humble opinion, I find the Clan System a tightly refined mechanic that allows for explosively dynamic play-throughs and is a victory for player choice through build variety.Designed as an empowering feature for unique fight strategy, Monster Train's 'battles' are fought across primarily three lanes, with a 'mini' fourth lane, which houses your Pyre - the fuel source that powers your train and something to be protected at all costs.Across these three lanes, portrayed as scaling floors aboard the Monster Train, you have the ability to play your Monster and Spell cards drawn from your hand. Each floor has a Player Unit Limit of  at one time, most likely for both performance and balancing reasons. Outside of unique modifiers and conditions that alter spawns or unit advancements, enemies will generally spawn on the first floor at the bottom of the Monster Train, working their way up once per Turn. On each turn, you are empowered with  to spend on both Monsters and Spells, and may place your Monsters strategically in an order that adheres to a left to right mentality, where the rightmost Monster both attacks and is attacked first.The ultimate goal of Monster Train is to survive and defeat all enemies on each stop while defending and protecting your Pyre's health. This multi-lane combat is thrillingly engaging, as every single move you make could single-handedly derail an entire battle in the flick of a wrist. I heavily recommend thinking before you place, as choices have consequences.In an effort to offer long-term engagement and unique additions to dedicated players, Monster Train offers an 'end-game' mode in the way of the Covenant Ranks. Spanning a total of  ranks altogether, each Covenant rank that you advance through adds another modifier to your run, either positive or negative. You must complete the prior numbered Covenant before you are allowed to advance to the next, and this provides a clear line of progression for players while also steadily ramping up the difficulty over time.I feel that the concise development of the Covenant Rank System allows for a constantly provided sense of fulfillment and achievement for players of Monster Train, and I am excited for a potential future expansion that could further empower the System.In Conclusion, I would like to thank you for reading this review.I believe that Monster Train is far more than the sum of its parts. It is a delicately refined yet explosive package wrapped in a cohesive concoction of addiction. It has certainly consumed me for many hours and I imagine many more.  I can not recommend this title enough, and I would suggest that you buy your ticket to come aboard the Monster Train.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing card battle game with a unique twist: you play your cards on a train with 4 floors. Monsters always appear on the lowest floor, and ascend a floor when they survive your attacks. On the top floor there's a crystal that should be protected at all costs, so it's necessary that you beat all monsters before they reach that floor. This is done by playing cards, which spawn a creature on the floor of choice, or cast spells that can heal, apply buffs and debuffs etc. These mechanics work incredibly well, making Monster Train one of the most enjoying card battle games I've ever played.The game contains 5 different decks, and you can combine two decks for each playthroughs. Each deck has a completely different playstyle, and also has two heroes to choose, who can be upgraded in several ways. To increase the replayability even more, you can switch to a higher covenant after beating the game, which adds extra challenges to your run. I have beaten the game with each faction for the first five covenants, but I'm sure I will do many more runs in the next few months. Oh and the game works great on the Steam Deck; just press a button when you see a black screen and change the video player in the settings screen. Next time you boot the game everything will work fine. Very, very recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to play Monster Train and not compare it to Slay the Spire. It certainly scratches the same itch as Slay the Spire for me and whilst I don't think it's quite as good as Slay the Spire, it's certainly a very good game in its own right. I think Slay the Spire really has perfected it's own formula and Monster Train adds a fun twist on a lot of familiar elements. Things you may dislike are being a card game it's very RNG based and you can have runs that fall apart through no fault of your own. _childDocuments_.review: I generally don't write reviews because most games don't scratch many itches I have as a consumer. But monster train hits a lot of these points to create a truly great game which I'm afraid many will miss. So if you're finding something niche, I hope you give this game a shot.Also, my review assumes you played slay the spire.Monster train is what a proper spin-off, homage and spiritual successor should be.Every aspect of Slay the Spire, MT has integrated their own spin to the formula while leaving what makes StS fun intact.MT has a dual faction system that offers a lot more replay value and mastery with being able to mix and match regions, creating deck-building variety like in Magic: The Gathering. Each faction has cards similar to how a character in StS has cards, different archetypes and they are surprisingly synergistic across regions.Runs are also generally shorter (personally), one run is condensed to 7-8 boss battles as opposed to dozens in StS. These fights are still fairly long so runs can still take awhile if you want to methodically think about things but there is less of the annoying health min-maxing in StS ascensions and more focus on the decision making.There is also a real-time multiplayer gamemode, each player is still plays as if it were singleplayer but they compete with speed and efficiency to gain score to see who scores the highest in end while you are on a clock. It's very intense and a good change of pace to the singleplayer mode and I highly recommend it, it has an adrenaline rush very unlike anything out there in the multiplayer market.My only minor gripes about this game is that some UI elements are not clear, information is crucial, same with StS. There isn't a clear breakdown of overhealing/damage, at high values you will have to resort to a lot of manual calculation. There is also no way to see what each unit is doing to who, especially important when fights span between multiple attacks amongst multiple units. Lastly, the unit's speech can block the room size which is crucial in speedrun type playstyles.Finally, I hope you don't judge a book by its cover. The visuals are a bit "crappy mobile game" but there is a lot of world-building delivered similar to StS, neat character designs and that subtle mysterious lore. Also the name is very mobile gamey and I hope that doesn't detract you from buying it because I know many will.And if you do buy it, let me know about your experience and hook me up for a Hell Run! >:D

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like a much denser experience than Slay the Spire. If you're like me, you may miss the more intricate combos, and free-er expression and exploration that Slay the Spire offered.What you get in place is chunky combat, with a number of important decisions and a number of trivial decisions. Often it's not difficult to end up setting up a powerful engine and watching the game play itself past the first few rounds of combat.Non-combat decision making is similarly dense. Between each fight, you'll choose one path or another to explore, picking up some upgrades and losing out on others.It's a fine experience, and a good distraction.

Because of this, I'd say Slay The Spire is the better designed and more challenging game, while this one is more fun to mess around with and tinker new ways to torture holy beasts.Little Fade best girl.

name: The Room VR: A Dark Matter
detailed_description: Fireproof Games continue their award winning game series, The Room , with The Room VR: A Dark Matter . The British Institute of Archaeology, London, 1908: The disappearance of an esteemed Egyptologist prompts a Police investigation into the unknown. Explore cryptic locations, examine fantastic gadgets and uncover an otherworldly discovery which blurs the line between reality and illusion. Designed from the ground up for the unique capabilities of virtual reality, players can inhabit the spine-tingling world of The Room and interact with its strange contraptions in this compelling new chapter. Fireproof Games are a small independent team working in Guildford in the UK. We self-published our first game The Room on iPad in September 2012 and were stunned with both the critical success and our new-found fan-base, not to mention multiple international awards. The Room games have since changed our lives and we hope you enjoy our Virtual Reality take on the series.

_childDocuments_.review: (Played on a Valve Index with Vive controllers, Windows 7 Pro 64 bit)Wow.I've played every room game, and I've seen Fireproof's gradual improvement with each game. This game is no different; the improvements between this and Old Sins, the fourth and prior game, is very good. From storytelling, to puzzle complexity, to attention to detail, this is a step up from every previous room game. That's not to discount them, they're all wonderful games, and I would recommend buying and playing them. I'd highly recommend getting them on mobile, since (to my knowledge), the previous games are made for mobile rather than desktop.The visuals of the game, especially for VR, are very good. There's a *lot* of detail put into all of the objects, but sadly most of the detail is lost due to then screen-door effect and the lower resolution. I didn't actually realize that the player's gloves have a pattern to them until looking back at the store screenshots while writing this.The controls are pretty good in terms of VR games. Many games offer alternative movement modes, be it joystick, teleport, an armswinger-like one a-la H3VR, or something else. This game only offers teleport, but I think that works in its favor rather than to its determent. This allows for the developers to define areas that they want the player to focus on, and eliminate ones that would do nothing but act as clutter or red herrings. One problem that I do have is that the teleport button is forward, while inventory is back. Players coming from a game like HL:A are used to teleport being the back button, and that tripped me up a bit when I played. I got used to it by the second scene, but I think it's still worth mentioning.The story in this installment is well made, but is instantly spoiled by anyone who's . If this is your first Room game, then you'll have no problems, but for people who've played all other installments, . The puzzles in this game are mostly pretty good. However, their quality can vary wildly. Some puzzles are what I call "nothing puzzles," where solving it is basically just moving something from point A to point B on a slotted track. There are some others that require minor memorization, and others that are more related to spacial awareness and looking through the environment, which are probably the best out of all of them. The cynical part of me thinks that the "nothing puzzles" are there to pad out playtime, but in reality, I've played all of these games, and I'm probably mislabeling some puzzles because I've solved similar ones in previous installments.My main issues with this game are not really problems with the game itself, but more with the price versus time. Your mileage may vary, but I was able to finish the game in just over 2 hours. I bought the game on sale for $20, so that's about $10/hr. I understand that developing a game like this is no easy feat, nevermind for VR, but the sum of the other games' prices is $6 on the App Store, and at minimum offer around 10 hours of content. This isn't Fireproof's first foray into VR, so besides porting parts of the pre-existing mechanics to VR, I don't see why this would be much more expensive than the others. I believe that at release, Old Sins was around 5 bucks (at least that's what I remember picking it up for), so I guess my question for Fireproof is, is marking up the price this much worth it? This'd be the perfect opportunity to pull in a demographic that may not have heard of your games,  but the price of entry for VR players is super steep. I love this series, but I still waited for it to go on sale because I couldn't justify buying a shorter game for $25. I still don't think that $20 is justified for the amount of time it took me to complete it, but I didn't want to wait for a larger discount before playing. If anyone looking to buy this game takes away anything from this review, let it be this: This is a really good game, but wait until it goes on sale. If you're brand new to the series, it'll probably take you around 3-4 hours to finish the game, so buy accordingly.All in all, this game's a solid 7/10. If the price were dropped to $10-$15, I'd up it to an 8/10, but the buy-in price is just too high for me.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like puzzle games then you will almost certainly enjoy this one! I've been a fan of "The Room" series since the first one came out on mobile platforms many moons ago. Playing the same styled puzzle game in VR was just a plain joy. Being able to manipulate all of the various contraptions just has a great feel that you can't get outside of VR. The only major negative I can think of that might concern someone about to take the plunge is that the game is short. Please take into account I play many puzzle games and am very familiar with this series. I finished the entire thing in about 4 hours, but I could see it going up to 6 if your new to puzzle games. Final Thoughts:- Rock solid puzzle game! No weird VR jank, puzzles are fun, locations are wonderfully crafted and have a spooky, but not terrifying atmosphere.- The puzzles are tricky, but not enough to light your brain on fire. If you're used to games like the Witness, The Myst series, etc, don't expect the same level of challenge. It is still a great experience, but you won't be pondering most of the puzzles while you eat lunch at work. - The game is rather short, but every minute was worth it to me. If you've got the cash I can't see how you won't enjoy your time spent. - If you have trouble with VR locomotion and smooth turning you shouldn't worry. The game only lets you jump from a few points in each room to figure out the puzzle via teleportation and snap turning. It works great and I don't feel you lose much by not having free movement. - They let you sit down! Right off the bat they ask if you are standing and sitting. This is huge for someone like me who is usually on their feet all day at work. When I get home, I usually just want to sit for a bit. Having a fun, VR puzzle game that allows me to chill out and sit down was such a nice feature. - Sounds and music are well done and atmospheric. It puts you in a creepy and foreboding place, but no jump scares or any demons reaching for you face. Think the overall vibe of H.P. Lovecraft. - If you're on the fence I recommend purchasing one of this devs cheaper mobile games within the same series. They are some of the best mobile games I've played and they will give you a great idea of what to expect with this game, except in VR. I Hope they release another title in VR because this was a rad experience!

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid fan of all of the "The Room" games, I was blown away by the immersive experience of playing it VR. I guess it must primarily compared with the first edition of the game on the iPad in terms of duration of the game, but for their first foray into the subject matter they did a stellar job. The animations are awesome, the riddles not too tricky to bore you and with some of the puzzles it really screams "we have wanted to do THAT for ages". I consider it a great entrance into the world of VR both for new users and Fireproof and just with the first installment I am waiting for many sequels.A small aside: I very much enjoyed the several tips of the hat to other games in the series.Perhaps next time they should focus a bit more on telling a coherent story (either there was none here or it just went by me) and switch the dramatic arc a little - the final "world" of the game felt a little rushed and out of place with the rest. Having said all that: Here you have a great puzzle game that not only uses VR as an immersive setting for the brainteasers but at times as an element of them, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Buy on sale.The Room is a rather nice VR game, but the length just doesn't justify the 30€ (or 20€) price.The puzzles are somewhat simple, but unique and I genuinely enjoyed solving them.Other than length I really hated the movement. Just like in other The Room games there are certain spots you go to and stand there. Sure you can move around yourself, but you're not supposed to. Turning around with the thumb stick resets your location in game meaning that it's harder to "feel" where you're standing in real life. In other games even with snap turning I had an idea of where I was, but with this game it somehow messes up with your senses when the location resets in game.The game is actually shorter if you don't miss anything.

_childDocuments_.review: As an rabid fan of Fireproof and The Room series.  I have been waiting for ages to finally purchase this game.  I have an OG HTV Vive and it works phenomenal for me.This game has to be like the greatest culmination of a story line I've encountered.  After playing through 1, 2, 3, and Old Sins.  I have been curious if they were going to continue the series.  When the VR game was announced I was happy there was another entry, but I wasn't sure if it was going to be a sequel, a mid-quel or something else.This was a capstone to the series.  They sorta left it open for maybe another installment, but my goodness what an ending.  If you spend any time getting wrapped up in the story of 1 through 3 and get through Old Sins, this episode is the last one.  Don't skip, don't miss anything.  There's some subtle callbacks to a few of the previous episodes.The only thing I can hope is Fireproof ports the rest of the series to VR.  I would love it so much.Unbelievably great game.  Thank you, Fireproof, thank you for a wonderful story.

_childDocuments_.review: I've completed the Room 1-4 and must say that VR is great for this type of game. The movement is good and has been designed to be comfortable either standing or sitting (I did both in my playthrough). VR really helps with the immersion and enables puzzles and interactions that are not possible in the 2D games. Would definitely recommend if you enjoy puzzles and/or The Room series and have access to a VR headset.A few minor criticisms:- The game is quite short and only took me about 3 hours to complete. There are only three full size chapters, with a quick tutorial chapter at the start and two short end sequences that are fairly straightforward. It would have been nice if the last two sequences were fleshed out a bit more.-Sometimes it can be unclear that something can be interacted with. This issue is common in the other Room games where determining what to touch can often be more difficult than the puzzles themselves.-There isn't as much interaction with items in your inventory compared with the Room 3&4, but I imagine it is a limitation with how VR works, i.e. using two hands to interact with the same item.
