_childDocuments_.review: Best enjoyed whilst blind drunk.A legendary dragon recommended this game series for me, so i bought it, even when it really isn't my usual cup of tea. This was my fifth Yakuza game so far.STORY:The story is about people planing schemes upon schemes. Some smarter, some dumber. Those in low in the power ladder with everything to gain and those high up with everything to lose. There is betrayal of trust, the breaking of old brotherly bonds and the founding of new ones. But to be honest, the story can be quite wack. It start really strong with new amazing characters with interesting personalities and motivations. Sadly the story starts to slowly deteriorate longer it goes on. One characters motives break down and is replaced with another one entirely, one is simply simping for a woman, one wants simple revenge and the last one just gets dragged along for the sake of the story. The side characters and bosses are amazing and the substories are great.GAMEPLAY:And a another great thing about Yakuza 4 is the improved gameplay and quality of life improvements compared to Yakuza 3. There aren't many, but they are noticeable, with the very slightly improved graphics, animations and combat.Speaking of combat, Yakuza 4 has 4 different characters with their own unique fighting styles. Akiyama destroys anything on lower difficulties, but suffers on legendary. One valid tactic is just running around and doing charging attacks.Saejima destroys everything on any difficulty as he is simply a massive beast. When you get the upgrade where enemy attacks no longer stun you if you have heat, you can bulldose everything in your way.Tanimura has a very technical fighting style and does ok on any difficulty. Though on legendary he has to rely on his signature parrying skill. Either parry bosses into walls or normal enemies and instantly doing a heat action. Also Tanimuras last boss fight really sucks. You WILL NEED the sacred wooden armor set you get from doing all of the training from the masters.Kiryu is Kiryu, i ain't going to sugarcoat it. Kiryu is the strongest beast in the game as always.OTHER:All of the main characters have their own main things to do. Akiyama has his hostess maker, which sucks, Saejima with his fighter maker, which is the easiest and best, Tanimura with his radio thingy and Kiryu with gang fighting thingy.Amon fight is great, with each main character fighting their own Amon. Though Kiryu goes last and has to essentially fight everyone back to back with Jo Amon switching his fighting styles on the fly. The only sad thing about the fight is that you only get one pair of Amon sunglasses from the fight.But there is one thing i absolutely hate about Yakuza 4. It is the random jazz music. It comes around when there is a important mission coming about.CONCLUSION:Great game to enjoy casually if you don't mind the aged gameplay and graphics compared to the newer games. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: While the early Yakuza games kind of have a rocky start, I think in chronological release, 4 was when the franchise really hit it's stride. The focus being placed on the city of Kamurocho instead of solely relying on Kiryu was an excellent decision that added a breath of fresh air to the series, and still makes this entry stand out today. Yakuza 4 is a great display of the series in it's early days, as well as just a damn solid entry.The most unique aspect of 4 was the introduction of multiple playable characters, an amazing change that really freshens up the gameplay. Each of the three new characters has a very unique identity that helps them stand out from one another, emphasised further by how they interact with different parts of the city in with unique perspectives. I enjoyed experiencing their separate connections to the story but the most exciting part was their distinct approaches to substories, covering a much wider range of fun or comedic bluntness. Their combat spices things up a ton as well, with a character built around speed, strength & defence respectively, each character brings their own style to the table, all of which are compelling. I love Kiryu's combat, but I'm glad we didn't have another full game slowly progressing through his moves, instead by the time you get to him, he's a complete monster with most of his abilities from 3 already intact. That's another thing, the upgrade system is far more flexible and fun, this time you're given "Soul Orbs" to spend on any abilities in favour of linear progression, and it's a lot better being able to buy the abilities you want immediately. An emphasis on training and activities to unlock moves returning from previous entries also further enhances the individuality of each combat style. It's a shame that with so much depth present within combat, that it feels incredibly easy, even on the highest difficulties. They've swung in the complete opposite direction of 3 here, a huge improvement but still a problem. Enemy AI is so non-aggressive and willing to take punches that most encounters can just be mashed through without much substance, even bosses aren't that tough anymore. It's a shame cause you ultimately have so many mechanics to play with, I just wish you got a couple more opportunities t hat squeezed out that potential. Nevertheless, the combat is still dynamic and interesting, staying fresh through the multiple character you get to experience.With multiple protagonists to manage, Kamurocho becomes the star of Yakuza 4, with the smaller scope allowing the city to truly shine in it's full beauty for the first time. All of the familiar sites are back, but terrain has been fleshed out with rooftops, underground paths and compressed alleyway areas that give the city a lot more identity and variety than it's earlier counterparts. A new perspective is added to the city through each character and new areas, but it's still the same lovable open world ripe with hilarious content. The introduction of more interactive businesses and concepts helps break up the standard gameplay formula, and it's nice having minigames that you can dedicate tons of time to, Fight Maker was my favourite. I think this is also the first game where substories started to get really good There's way less than the first 3 games, but they all carry more weight, with memorable characters, story arcs and just sometimes pure hilarity. It's the first entry where I really wanted to seek out every substory. However, despite all this new content, Kamurocho can get a little stale to roam around in the later game, especially with how slow your characters can feel. The new areas are great for each character's story too, but they could've been a bit more interesting, only the rooftops truly stood out (a huge shame these never returned). You'll likely be very familiar with Kamuorcho at this point in the series, but 4's interpretation is mostly a joy to explore.The big dud in Yakuza 4 is it's story, a fun but ultimately messy experience. The initial hook of the Ueno Saiwa is interesting, but the plot line that follows takes a while to go anywhere. Relevance to the plot varies with each playable character, so the plot can start and stop at very unnatural speeds, creating a very off pacing, as well as continuously adding more and more plot threads to an already dense story. Saejima's the perfect example of the story at it's worst, as he really doesn't achieve much in his chapter despite his significance to the overall plot, leading to a series of long combat sequences and just straight up walking down paths for far too long. On top of that, removing a decent chunk of open world content while playing as him and restricting your exploration of the city just results in a complete lack of desire to play as him. I think what they were intending here could've been handled much better, but as it is, Saejima's sequence is mainly just a noticeable pain in the overall campaign. Yakuza 4 revels in complexity, but it doesn't get more out of it other than having a ridiculous plot that takes far more dramatic turns than necessary. There's also a reliance on some really bizarre plot threads that just don't really make sense  but you can still have fun with the story. I really enjoyed the constantly shaken up plot for its pure insanity, but I did have trouble being invested due to the poor pacing and some really stupid character decisions.Favourite Moment: I have a lot of respect for Yakuza 4 with it's various experimental ideas, as well as nostalgia for being my first Yakuza entry past the PS2 titles. It does a lot right with it's expansive world and characters, but misses the mark in areas such as story and difficulty. I'd recommend Yakuza 4 to anyone interesting in continuing the story, as well as anybody wanting to see the franchises roots and one of the key growing points for the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is an enjoyable change of pace after the atrocity that was Yakuza 3. The big deal of this game is a multi narrative story with 4 playable characters, and while most of you all have played Yakuza 0 by this point, Yakuza 4 was actually their first try at adding multiple protagonists, but was it a good try?Let's discuss the gameplay first, cause that was Yakuza 3's weakest part. Yakuza 4 vastly improves the gameplay in every way, heat actions feel strong, a fun to complete skill tree, and an enemy AI that is worth fighting. Every punch you throw lets you feel the impact, and the stronger you get, the stronger you feel. Yakuza 3's revelations make a return, and I must say, they still are fun and goofy, I'm happy that they didn't scrap everything from the previous title. What was scrapped is Yakuza 3's enemy AI, constantly blocking each attack, getting almost no hits in, and in this game the enemies are much smarter, they actually throw punches, and aren't camping during the entire fist fight. They sometimes chain grab you though, which ends up in you getting beat up while mashing a button to get released, however the more you level up the better your options get to combat that.Chase sequences from Yakuza 3 return too, and they're fine. They aren't necessarily worse, or better, but they're mostly used for side quests.While we're at it, the side quests had somewhat of an improvement, they often call back to past games with past characters you already helped, or tried to help. Some even have short cutscenes, which make them feel less like your average quest, and more part of the overall package.The gameplay is fine, so how about the story?The story of Yakuza 4 introduces us to 4 protagonists, each getting 4 chapters to shine. Akiyama, a loan shark with a bizarre way he runs his business, Saejima the escaped death row convict, Tanimura a crooked, but ironically very justice-driven cop, and Kiryu, the man himself, the Dragon of Dojima. Each character has their own style, and each character is interesting in their own way.The plot makes you invested in all of them, questioning their morals, their plans, and even their backstory. For the first around 10 chapters, I was surprised at how connected the story is. It ties up loose ends from Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 1, but mostly relies on the new characters, which is a breath of fresh air.While the first half of the game makes each plot twist exciting, unfortunately, the latter half struggles to connect the dots and turns the story unreasonably complicated to the point that I couldn't sympathize with most side characters. Yakuza 4's plot turned from a straight path with occasional left and right turns, the plot twists, to an entire spiderweb. The closer you get to the resolution, the more plot twists you get. Some of these feel nonsensical and don't change a lot when it comes to the bigger picture. Some of them simply feel so unneeded that it barely even affects the story. During the last few hours unexpected plot twists became expected, cause many of the characters became inconsistent. Kiryu also has little to no reason to fight the final boss, he's just like "Yeah, you kinda suck" and they start fighting.Another issue I had is the typical trope of disarming an enemy, and then acting like the gun vanished to the shadow realm, until the enemy picks it up again to try to get one final shot in. How were the protagonists able to understand the plot, but keep doing the same mistake over and over again? It happened twice, with the same villain, in the same cutscene. They disarm him, the gun is a few meters to the left, and no one decides to pick it up and get rid of it. It's such an odd way to create tension.Last, let me tell you about the protagonists, and how much I enjoyed them.Akiyama - He's a fun character who's at the same time mysterious for how his business stays afloat. He is no Yakuza, so it's neat to see the story unfold in the eyes of an outsider. He has a Rush style move set, meaning fast kicks, but little damage, good to introduction to the game.Saejima - He probably has the most heart-wrenching story in Yakuza 4. He hits like a truck, and has a Beast style with chargeable finishing blows, frustratingly his last 2 chapters aren't really enjoyable, it is just badly implemented stealth.Tanimura - story-wise he was alright, but gameplay wise I loved him. He's more of a brawler, but also has a parry that is fun to use, especially when you're next to a wall, since the environment plays a role too.Kiryu - The embodiment of pure testosterone, the legend himself, tries to fix what others couldn't. As the last playable character of the pack, he's also immediately decked out with most moves, a joy to play.Yakuza 4 is a big improvement over Yakuza 3 in every way, it is a good first take on a multi narrative story, but the overreliance on plot twists gave it a bad aftertaste. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played such an intriguing game since Yakuza 0 last year. Yakuza 4 is the 5th entry, chronologically, in the Yakuza series. Featuring four playable characters, this is the most varied game until now, and (in release order), the first ever Yakuza game to feature multiple playable characters. Playing as these new protagonists was really a breath of fresh air after three consecutive games with Kiryu only. The gameplay in this game is much more balanced than its predecessor, enemies don't block as much anymore and the progression system is much more fun to use. Four characters also mean four distinct fighting styles. The visuals are pretty much the same as 3's. The soundtrack is, once again, pretty good, maybe my favorite after 0's. The story is complex yet amazing, you have all these different plots full of twists and emotional moments that in the end converge into one epic finale. It might have some flaws here and there, but overall it's very enjoyable and possibly one of the best stories in the franchise. This game is close to be a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 puts a twist on the franchise and not only takes the multiple protagonist route like 0 would later do but it even doubles it!This game finally feels like a true continuation to the franchise and not spending most of your time in Okinawa.I'd say the multiple protags is definitely a double edged sword, on one hand that allows the game to experiment with 4 decently different styles of combat and keep the constant upgrades feeling fresh and rewarding. On the other hand though it constantly feels like I just started the game and that I haven't really built up any of the characters.Another thing about it that's kinda disappointing is that if you don't really vibe with one of the character's play styles it feels like a quarter of the game is gimped, This game still retains some of the clunk from 3 but definitely improves upon it at the same time. For instance there were multiple times where I'd get absolutely mobbed by a ton of people and there'd be one enemy with a gun just taking cheap shots while I'm stuck in animations from either getting my butt clapped by enemies or stuck in grab animations. These instances were some of the most infuriating.A place the multiple protagonist feature is really utilized well though is in the now vastly expanded open-world. Each character has specific parts of the city they hang out in during the story and it kinda changes the way you interact with the city. The now expanded rooftops and underground portions are also very interesting. (This also answers the question I was having over the past 4 games and 150hrs of playing of "Where the ♥♥♥♥ do all these people park cars?")I definitely plan to revisit this game eventually since I apparently only finished with a 5.4% completion rating. At the end of playing through the story though I'd rate the game a solid 8/10, the story is great for sure, but it still doesn't really shake some of the clunkyness.

Minigames are alright, and there's enough of them to keep you busy if that's your kind of thing but I'd recommend newer games in the series where the minigames are done better. _childDocuments_.review: Yes, I recommend this game, as opposed to Y3 which I advised against playing (you can check out my profile for that review.) Built on an evolutionary iteration of Yakuza 3's engine, the game will feel familiar to those who did bother with playing Y3, but it feels tighter and more well-conceived overall, with numerous positive additions and enhancements to the combat and general game flow. The "bounding" system introduced in Y3, which allows you (and your enemies) to bounce opponents off walls if hit close enough to them for extra damage and potentially annihilatory combos, is great fun to experience, unlike 3 where it seemed to hardly ever function right. Y4 introduces an improved leveling system, as well as three other playable characters in addition to Kiryu. No longer are you beholden to vague descriptions and a completely linear skill unlocking system -- you can now earn 3 skill points per level which you can then allocate to a wide range of skills at your leisure, so you can prioritize abilities and buffs that suit your playstyle. The three new playable characters all feel unique with their movesets and their personal stories are well written and executed as well. It is absolutely worth completing their substories which helps to flesh out the characters since many of them are less random and more personal. As you would expect, all four player characters will have their stories intersect and eventually converge for an epic final showdown at the game's climax, and it's pretty dope. I can't sing too many praises about the main overarching plot, however. Even for Yakuza standards, which eschews sensibility and rational decision making in lieu of characters doing braindead things which leads to very  results to say the least, tips the scale in such a way that you'll be audibly groaning and laughing at the sheer absurdity of many of the twists and turns that occur. Some of these plot points are monumentally dumb, and not even Yakuza's inherent charm can save it sometimes. Thankfully, the characters themselves manage to do a decent job of salvaging much of the nonsense, which is why ultimately I will still recommend this game, especially if you plan on going to Yakuza 5 and beyond afterwards, as the newcomer player characters return in 5 where they are once again playable.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is the fourth installment of the Yakuza franchise, like Yakuza 3 being a remaster of the original PS3 game. Still being a beat em up, this is one hell of a different game, this time it's not only Kiryu who is playable and it's not only 2 playable. But a total of four playable characters, that's right 4 playable characters. As there are 4 playable characters, I've decided to not give a short summary of each character, but I'll give some of my thoughts about the story and some insight of the characters. I want you guys to experience these characters yourself, that also includes for Yakuza 5. Chapter wise it's different as well, this time all characters having a total of 4 chapters as it switches of character after the end of one character's story also having a big final chapter in the end.-Shun Akiyama. A loan-shark that gets twisted with some inconvenient things-Taiga Saejima. Big buffed guy that tries to learn the truth about the past with a lot of regrets in his life.-Masayoshi Tanimura. A detective who tries to search for answers as to why his dad got shot and what it has  to do with the 1988 shooting,-Kazuma Kiryu. Mainly a support guy who learns more about the truth that happened past games.The story to me is good, it feels somewhat like Y2/Kiwami 2's story, feeling more standalone and giving other characters more of the focus instead of Kiryu alone. With altho some hit or miss moments in the story.The location is mostly set in Kamurocho, what's also a lot less in the game is the mention of the children at morning glory or not even one mention of Mikiyo and Nakahara, even Saki is no more at Morning Glory either it did bother me a bit, but this game is also mostly about Saejima and Tanimura. Akiyama plays a role bigger than Kiryu but not as much as the other two, and Kiryu he's just there, just wait for Yakuza 5 tho ;)This is the game that reinvented combat for the Yakuza games as you have 4 play styles to fight with, with 2 being an influence to Kiryu's styles in Yakuza 0 and Kiwami, those being Akiyama and Saejima.Akiyama has mostly kicks as his attacks and is fast as well, combos are the best bet with him from wall combos to some like juggles, he also has a tiger drop like counter where he kicks the enemies when timed he is very fun and my favorite playable character in the game.Saejima is more of a power house, let's say more of a wrestler/grappler type, his attacks are also a lot slower but pack a lot of punch, when you charge his attacks he continues his grappler moves instead of mashing light attack. As fun this might look, I still didn't really enjoy playing as Saejima as I thought, his move list is just so less compared to the others, and he could be a drag sometimes when fighting a huge amount of groups. Tanimura is quite unique, his fight style is more of, and I'm the parry guy as you can manually parry enemy attacks into walls or to defend yourself, as you attack them from the back, you got quite some martial arts moves with him from strangling enemies to breaking bones and holding them down or to simply cuff them lolI enjoyed Tanimura a lot in this game, next to Akiyama my favorite to play as well.Kiryu. We all know how Kiryu fights, not really needed to talk about, however there are some things I do want to mention that I find less about him in this game.From every play through I had playing as Kiryu I could not find any moment where I could wall combo enemies and some moves are gone from him as well and given to others like the ground sweep when you get downed to the ground, Akiyama and Tanimura got those moves now.Kiryu is still fun to play (definitely over Saejima) but just not the same as Yakuza 3 Kiryu. Oh, and most of the problems that Yakuza 3 Remastered has, has been fixed in this game so like no more overly long blocking enemies and frame attack are fixed as well, altho some jank is still in the game but yeah it's only a remaster...Some new things as I mentioned before, the upgrade system is with XP points as you got upgrades where you need 1, 2, 3 and 4 XP points to upgrade your character's stats as your characters have a level limit of rank 20. Revelations return as well, everyone has them this time.The next addition is the debut of Rooftop exploration, before in the series they were used as combat locations, but you may actually traverse using them by accessing specific locations.All the beloved substories return from the OG PS3 Yakuza 4 in Yakuza 4 Remastered.Something to note here, each character has a total of like 15 to 16 substories in total.As always you can come across them randomly when completing a chapter or when going to certain places, each character also has a personal focused substory so that's a nice touch as well.My favorite of Akiyama was his version of ''Fake Kiryu'', someone imitates as Akiyama and is like a scammer instead of a helper to people,For Saejima it's the one personal one the is my favorite as it gives more character and lore to what happened to his clan, for Tanimura it's also his personal focused substory where he tries to find more answers about his father as he meets another detective named Nadine.For Kiryu however, all his substories are great too me, a lot are callbacks to stuff from the past games which I really like.All the minigames return as well, this time Pachinko is actually kept instead of removed like Yakuza 3 Remastered, it also has a new addition that beingTable Tennis. As for Side Content, every Character has their own side stuff next to Substories, you'll have to see for yourselfYakuza 4 like I said is mostly involved within Kamurocho, as always you can come across enemies. There is some enemy variety for each character with a unique kind of design, but still most enemies look like basic residents. Also, a lot of groups you fight like Yakuza 3 have some of an original theme, altho quite a lot do you have moments where you hear the same battle theme when fighting groups of enemies. The bosses in this game are quite good, it has epic moments in it as to who you are fighting against, and yes a lot of bosses also have dynamic intro's and a great boss theme.The special one to me tho are the boss themes used in the Final chapter, ♥♥♥♥ the last boss tho, that ♥♥♥♥ is like the one in Y1/Kiwami but on steroids.The Yakuza 4 OST like 3 is louder, hardcore, rocked, metal, techno, beat, mixed into one. And this time a new thing to it is the amount of Jazz and Moodiness it hasyou can't even begin to count how many times you'll hear a saxophone, and you'll notice some funk in it as well. But man it's so good, and it fits perfectly with the setting this game is in.Each character also has their own battle theme, which is very nice and great to fight with as well.Of course the game has some great long battle themes, my favorite being Solitude that plays near the end of the game, trust me it's worth the wait!But to me the best theme of the game has got to be the main theme For Faith, it's so good to listen to it, yes it has broken English but the theme itself is such a big part of this game and has such a meaning!Yakuza 4's soundtrack is really great in every way, and like I said, it's something that RGG Studios does for every Yakuza game of theirs.Having an absolute banger of a soundtrack.That concludes my review of Yakuza 4 Remastered.The game feels better to play then Yakuza 3, altho to me, it had some slight hiccups in the story element and of the less use of Kiryu, but we got that more in 3, so I don't mind it actuallyI very much enjoyed a lot of the combat, especially Akiyama's him being my favorite to play as in the game.Overall great time of a game to enjoy!(9.3)

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 does a much better job of sticking to its core narrative than Yakuza 3. Where its predecessor was weighed down by sub-plots and side-plots, Yakuza 4 focuses on its four intersecting stories which culminate to the grand finale. But, unlike previous instalments, Yakuza 4 is Kiryu-lite. Although Kiryu is still a playable character and is important to the plot, Kiryu's playtime is shared equal to the three other protagonists. Each of the four protagonists has four chapters of gameplay. While an interesting tweaking of the formula in the series to date,  each character feels spread thin compared to previous Yakuza titles. The skill tree, as an example, never feels fully fleshed out or explored and is generally fully populated with experience points by the end of each character's tenure. Unlike previous Yakuza games, you don't fully feel the "journey" or skill development given that each character is playable for only a finite and linear series of chapters. But, each character furthers the story and is a welcome deviation from a Kiryu-focused title. Meanwhile, the difficulty offers some brutal and unexpected spikes (which could be attributed to the above limited time to develop a character's skill tree). In previous Yakuza titles, the more difficult moments of a Yakuza title is mostly in the first third of the game with the combat becoming more manageable as the title progresses. Yakuza 4, alternatively, will unleash boss fights that unexpectedly test your fighting skill. So, more than ever, knowing the moves are essential and button mashing is less likely to get a player through the fight. It is, however ,a very welcome change to the formula. Visually, the remaster may not look as glossy or as polished as the 'Kiwami' remakes, but it still presents well enough and the cinematics still have their signature polished look. Overall, Yakuza 4 is an improvement over the disappointing predecessor, but still not quite the definitive Yakuza experience as compared to the likes of Yakuza Zero through to Yakuza 2. 4 out of 5

The story is interesting, but it begins to build up so many twists and surprises that it starts to feel a bit ridiculous. Series protagonist Kazuma Kiryu also feels a bit out of place, like a special guest star in his own series. It makes me wonder if the devs were considering tying up his story even back in 2010. _childDocuments_.review: Overall: 7.25/10Story:Yakuza 4 Remastered is an action adventure beat 'em up game with a narrative that embraces the usual the high-stakes, over-the-top drama tones, but ultimately stumbles under its own weight a LOT. The premise is genuinely intriguing, especially for those who can set aside realism and simply enjoy the dramatic, soap opera-esque twists the series is known for. However, the story gets increasingly convoluted, especially by the end, where the sheer number of intersecting plotlines and twists feels more contrived than convincing. As much fun as it is to watch everything spiral out of control, the suspension of disbelief reaches its breaking point.One standout feature is the multi-character structure, which adds layers and variety to the plot and new faces to the world of Kamurocho. This is an exciting change, adding fresh perspectives and backstories, but this structure proves overwhelming pretty early on, as the need to reinvest in each character’s story arc with every switch detracts from the coherence of the overall plot. Just when you’ve settled into the rhythm of one character’s tale, you’re forced into another’s, making for a jarring, somewhat exhausting experience as you scramble to keep up with each story’s exposition.The character arcs themselves are pretty solid. None of the playable characters feel uninteresting by any means, but some certainly feel more fleshed out than others. For example, I felt Tanimura’s arc had plenty of potential, but the story doesn't fully explore it, leaving him feeling somewhat underdeveloped by the end of the game. In relation to this, while I didn’t mind Kiryu’s presence in the game by any means, his place in the story almost feels like fan service that overshadows the other characters, which detracts from the deeper novelty and life that any of them could have seen. Yes, he is what connects the other three character's narratives together, but I feel like his inclusion takes valuable screen time away from those who needed more character development.Yasuko, on the other hand, falls flat as a character all around. Her role as  is limited to serving as a plot device for other characters’ development, with little personality or agency of her own. It’s a wasted opportunity, especially in a story that thrives on larger-than-life characters.Then there’s the infamous  twist—a jaw-dropping revelation in all the wrong ways. This plot device doesn’t just strain credulity; it practically snaps it in half. The game clearly shows us blood during  only to later insist  This absurd twist is compounded by the scene where  It’s insulting to the player’s intelligence, doubling down on a flimsy excuse that even the game’s visuals contradict. Additionally, in the finale, no one  which leads to another frustrating scene where logic is sacrificed for the sake of drama.If you’re willing to just go with the flow, Y4 has an enjoyable, if absurd, crime drama at its core. But even with lowered expectations, the pacing issues caused by the abrupt character swaps might make for a bumpy ride.Gameplay:The gameplay of Y4 builds on the foundation of Y3, refining the combat system in several ways that make it feel much more engaging. Each of the four main characters comes with a unique combat style and set of heat actions, which gives the game a fresh feel with each new chapter. These varied movesets add diversity and depth, though some elements come with a few rough edges. For instance, while Kiryu, Akiyama, and Tanimura have distinct and enjoyable fighting styles, I found Saejima’s combat far too slow and stiff, even with upgrades. His heavy, sluggish style just didn't match the fluidity of the others, leaving it feeling like a chore rather than a highlight.Speaking of the combat, one of Y4's strengths is how each character’s combat feels tailored to their personality, but the switching between characters comes with drawbacks. Just as with the story transitions, investing time in a character’s upgrades and moveset only to reset with a new character can feel jarring. Unlike previous games where you gradually refine only Kiryu's skills, here, you’re forced to start from scratch each time. Fortunately, Kiryu’s chapter stands out as it begins with many of his upgrades unlocked, making the shift to his familiar playstyle feel like a reward after all the character switches. In general though, combat improvements are noticeable across the board, especially with heat actions that are far more aggressive and impactful than those in Y3. Additonally, the return of the “Revelations” mechanic is a nice touch, adding fun flavor to each character’s journey. However, seeing multiple characters share the same Revelations hurts the immersion a bit. Despite this minor drawback, one advantage of juggling four protagonists is how Y4 spaces out side content. It’s balanced well, providing breaks in the action without ever feeling like too much at once. I personally enjoyed side activities like Saejima’s Fight Maker, although the minigames overall aren’t the strongest in the series mainly due to their age.Y4 also alters enemy behavior; while Y3 was known for foes that relentlessly block, this game introduces enemies who are equally aggressive with grabs. Thankfully though, these grapplers are easy to spot due to their arm positioning, which makes it easier to target them first, making group encounters more manageable.World:In Y4, Kamurocho returns almost identical to its layout in Y3, but with a few big improvements. The map now includes more taxi fast travel points, addressing a key issue from Y3 and making navigation more convenient. The biggest new addition, however, is the expansion into both rooftop and underground areas, which I found to be a cool and refreshing way to explore. These new layers add verticality and variety, offering new shortcuts and hidden areas to discover. While still familiar, these changes make Kamurocho feel more dynamic, enhancing the city’s immersive urban atmosphere.Visuals:The graphics also stay mostly consistent with Y3, maintaining the same PS3-era foundation. While this limits visual fidelity, minor improvements are subtly woven throughout, adding a touch of polish. Lighting is marginally enhanced, creating slightly richer contrasts in nighttime scenes, while character models and textures feel a bit smoother, especially on the main cast. These refinements aren’t drastic, but they make environments a bit more immersive and enjoyable to explore. Despite these tweaks though, the reality is that Y4 remains visually tied to its era.Music/Sound Design:The music and sound design in Y4 quickly cemented its place among my favorite OSTs from the mainline series. This soundtrack strikes a perfect balance between emotion, funk, and crunch, keeping you immersed in the story and gameplay with high-energy tracks and impactful, emotive pieces that set the tone for each intense encounter. The sound design, however, provides a solid, serviceable experience without introducing major innovations. Overall, the soundtrack elevates the experience, but the sound design feels more like a steady continuation than a step forward, which I can respect.TL;DR:Yakuza 4 Remastered is an action adventure beat 'em up game with a very over the top narrative that, despite having lots of emotion and flavor, sometime struggles with pacing and a general spaghetti plot. Despite this, I still think Y4 is a great entry to the series, and if you can accept the narrative for what it is, the general energy it brings, along with the side content, combat, and even soundtrack make this game well worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: One thing is certain. Yakuza 4 is way better in general than Yakuza 3, that's a relief.It is about Yakuza, not about politics, there is enough drama which is not overdone (looking at you Morning Glory).My main technical issue - audio synchronization is broken, some cutscenes have a several second difference by the end of said cutscene.Chase/Escape sequences are better than in Y3, but honestly, I wish they were stupid QTE for plot reasons. Some of these sequences are unnecessary long.The game is divided in 4 character arcs that you play one after the other uncovering the main plot of the game. Each character has different combat style and to anyone who have played Yakuza 0/Kiwami/2 it can be described exactly as each character using one of the styles (Beast, Rush etc). Of course those styles are less polished and not that over the top since this is not a remake. Still combat system is more fluid and less clunky, so kudos for it.It should be noted that Saejima (beast) has a prototype version of this style, so he has no cool moves like auto picking up items laying around and smashing faces with it and in general is the weakest of the bunch who requires (not kidding) some decent planning on how to level up his abilities, otherwise you will suffer and boy does he suffer. Eventually you are able to overcome these issues and he gets tolerable, but it's a horrible ride. He has a  huge health pool, I guess to cover his weakness.Other characters are fun to use, have some cool move sets (Kiryu has his usual style of course which is "complete now") and useful Heat abilities going beyond the usual - Grab/Knockdown/Counter Heat. Besides Saejima of course.In terms of characters and Plot.Arc 1 - I'd say it's fresh, the perspective, the character himself and the majority of what you do.You unlock Hostess maker here (should've been earlier though) which is identical to one from Yakuza 3, but with different makeup/outfit combos, and with no ability to have the "Ultimate" combo. You will have to use 2-3 sets (never used Cute for some reason) to win the mode. As In Y3 it's slow to wind up, equally slow to unlock new items and in general I got bored doing this AGAIN.Arc 2 - There are upsides and downsides. In general the overall idea here, the motivation and the logic didn't appeal to me, so sometimes I felt frustrated and annoyed. Here you unlock "sewers", use roofs extensively for plot reasons and boy it's one hell of annoying experience to deal with. Mostly it's connected to the new activity you unlock here - Fighter Maker, which I fully completed and was surprised there is no achievement for it, only for getting 1 fighter to the top.Mini game itself is pretty cool not going to lie. Many options and variations are available for you to work around. 5 different fighters to train with different move sets and their individual differences.The only issue - save scum. There is no way around it. Combat is AI vs AI and it's randomized, so there are fighters that suck no matter what you do with them and it's a tedious process.Arc 3 - This is another fresh perspective and character himself has some sick moves. This arc is mostly plot driven and it somehow felt rather short.Arc 4 - It's also a short one, but it fits well and doesn't have to be long for reasons. As usual there is some cinematic stupidity in Y4, that happens generally throughout the series, where some moments happen because Drama, but don't feel organic, but hey if you have survived Y3, not much can surprise you anymore. There is also an issue of pacing, where it gets into gears pretty slow, but eventually they simply throw a bunch of answers/events at you where at some point it gets confusing as to who what where when. Pace could definitely be better. They delivered with the ending though, didn't mess it up and it felt satisfying after going through this game.Age of the game shows as I don't really have any wish to 100% it or play it again, but that's what made remakes 0/Kiwami/2 this much better than the originals.TLDR Yakuza 4 got the series back on track, with better combat system, less annoying boss fights, better pacing in general, with some questionable ideas/features but it gets praise for actually been about Yakuza for a change. It took some mental strength to end Yakuza 3, which was not a problem here. Also, playtime is wrong, I had the game minimized for unknown hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 was a big step up from the previous entry. It was more fun, engaging and the new minigames were fun as well for the most part. That's not to say the game had no issues because it had quite a few which at times made the game a little too repetitive and tedious.In this game you get to play as 4 distinct characters, all with their own unique fighting style, upgrades, story, sub stories and certain mini-games. I think it was very smart from a design choice to make you play the 3 new characters first before getting to play as Kiryu. It helped establish a personal connection with the new characters as well as help you learn about their backstory, purpose and morale. Plus when you finally get to play as Kiryu, it feels as if you are rewarded with what I can argue is the best character since we all have familiarity with him and this series is more or less about him and his struggle of being a former Yakuza member. All the Sub stories in the game were very well made as each Sub story was written to match whatever character you were playing, it was less about wacky random missions from strangers and felt more as a catered experienced towards the current selected member of the story. That is not to say that there is no funny wacky missions, you still get some for each character but they were more in the context of who you were playing. Akiyama dealt with Money lending missions as he is a Money lender, Saejima dealt with getting accustomed to the world after spending 25 years in prison, Tanimura dealt with cop related issues as he is a cop himself and Kiryu dealt with certain returning characters and some Yakuza related things. The mini-games were done in a similar fashion as each playable character had their own mini-game that matched with their personality as well. Overall I had a lot of fun playing this game as the introduction of a new character every so often changed the play style throughout the story which made things feel fresh throughout the play session. The music is also probably my favorite so far from the series as each playable character had a different track that would play when you would get into a fight that would more or less match their tone. Every Character was very well personalized, they all felt unique with their own quirk and views from one another and I commend them for doing so as not a lot of games would go the extra mile to make sure of that.so the issues I have with this game are more centered towards the combat. The combat for the most part is a huge improvement from the previous entry and it is very fun since each character has their own fighting style but sometimes this could be an issue. A lot of the times, if you made enemies fall, they would take AGES to get back up. Even after hitting them on the ground, sometimes you would knock them to the ground consecutively which made them spend more time in the ground and just made fights take longer since you cant just aim at the floor. A lot of the bosses and mini bosses constantly blocked, which got very annoying after a while since it would take long to complete these fights. There were also certain mini bosses that would wield weapons and you were not able to knock down or stagger these opponents so they would just hit you and knock you down, which in turn you also took too long to get back up after getting knocked down (there is an ability to minimize this but even with that sometimes your character would take a while to get back up). Not only that but the bosses seem to repeat the same attacks multiple times in a row and not do much else besides block immediately and do the same attacks again. Because of this, you had a potential of getting stun locked when they would do the same long chained attack multiple times in a row. Saejima was probably my least favorite to play as because of how slow he is as a fighter, he is the strongest hitter but the game would put incredibly fast opponents against him which made his fights a bit tedious.  I also think the story is not as strong as the previous entry, its still narratively good as the other games, with your twist and turns, drama and action, but I just felt like it was not as strong as the others, not to dismiss it though the story was still very good since it would keep me invested during my playthrough but towards the end it felt like it lost its structure and started to get messy which in turn did not give me much of an impact as the others did.I think anyone that wants to play the Yakuza Franchise or is a fan of the series should play this entry. This game did something different from the previous games and did a lot of things rights. It was fun to go through the story and fun to play all the different styles and sub stories as well as the mini-games. Give it a playthrough as I think its well worth your time but do not play this game if you haven't played any of the previous games as you will be missing context clues and references from the other titles such as characters and events.

_childDocuments_.review: had some rough gameplay, clunky controls, and an upgrade system that did not feel rewarding, but it did provide a solid experience overall.  improves on everything that the previous entry lacked, with some new features added in as well. This time you will be playing as four characters, each divided into their own segments in the story.The story for  takes place in four main segments and a final act, with four of them having their own separate characters to play as. There is , a successful entrepreneur who runs  and will lend money to anyone who needs it. , who is on death row for murdering 18 members of the . , who is a corrupt cop who is trying to avenge the death of his father, and  runs  orphanage and is trying to live in peace with the children he takes care of.What do all four of these characters have in common you may ask? Well, I can’t exactly say much as they are in their own perspectives, so you will have to find out yourself while playing the game. It’s really good, just like any  game, the story is what will keep you invested and have you wanting more.The gameplay is a huge improvement over the previous entry. When you get a certain amount of EXP, you will level up, increasing your health and heat to do more special moves. The new moves you can learn in the game are moves you want to use and they feel very satisfying to pull off, it’s a big improvement. There are objects for you to pick up and utilize that offer more variety in your attacks as well, pulling off a heat action with them sometimes. However, there are four characters for you to play as and they have their very own unique play styles. has an easier difficulty overall. I rarely felt challenged throughout my playthrough, and the few times that I did feel challenged I could just sweep the fight on the next life that I got. I did not experience any bugs outside of a few occurrences during the quick-time events where the game did not recognize my inputs causing me to fail the event.  This didn't happen often, but it was very annoying when it did. are much better than they were in the previous title as they feel smoother and you don’t have to deal with much this time around. Your objective is to chase someone and take out their health bar, if you do that you will successfully catch them. Sometimes you may have to run away from someone chasing you. However, you should be careful because if you go down you will have to redo the mission all over again.The graphics have also been improved and look much nicer.  I liked the way  looks and it feels more alive than ever. I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM. The game runs at 60 FPS no problem and I did not experience any issues during my playthrough.I love the soundtrack! There are so many songs worth mentioning that I could make a long list on them. makes you feel like you are in a fight and also making sure you are ready to beat down some enemies.  is one of the best boss themes in the game as it really captures the feel for the boss and tells you who you are dealing with. However, my favorite would have to be , as it’s just so damn catchy and it feels as though I'm in a nightclub. is a great entry in the series as it improves on everything that  suffered from. If you are a fan of the  series then this is a must-play no doubt about it. There is so much I love about this game that I just want more of it.  The improved gameplay and soundtrack really helped to bring me into the experience. It may be on the easier side, but being easy doesn't prevent this latest entry from being a blast.Welcome to Sky Finance, we made a partnership with  they make some good quality reviews, feel free to follow them

_childDocuments_.review: The story is a convoluted mess, there is an insane amount of twist that it got to a point where just trying to piece everything together and trying to remember everything just gave me a headache. The villains are very mediocre when it comes down to their writing and their reasons for being evil, which makes them very forgettable and the supporting characters in the main story are also pretty forgettable At least, the new playable characters had a solid introduction and the characters themselves are pretty interesting (even though it kinda felt like a waste of time getting to know Tanimura since he never appears in the rest of the other Yakuza games (because the VA did cocaine or something).Playing as Kiryu and Akiyama was pretty fun (Especially since Kiryu is pretty much the same as how he was in Yakuza 3 and Akiyama is very fast and plays smoothly, at the cost of being too fast making him overpowered), but Saejima is too slow, his attacks have little range and his skills near the beginning of the game encourages you to hold guard to build up heat and to spam dash since his dash is one of his only good moves near the beginning, once you are near the end of the game, Saejima's playstyle switches to centralizing around spamming finishing moves which is kinda fun at first but it becomes repetitive fast. Tanimura is pretty gimmicky since his playstyle centralizes around parrying (especially near walls) or spamming grab, since his attacks are also pretty slow but at least not as slow as Saejima. The way you grind exp in this game is either by doing allot of substories or destroying every bicycle you see which is a pretty slow process. The enemies don't hold down block the entire time like in Yakuza 3, but they dodge your attacks almost perfectly leaving you almost no room to punish them, since they're the ones usually punishing you and enemies tend to stun lock you with attacks like its Dark Souls. The prison section where you play as Saejima, was horrible, first is that in your first fights you have a pretty tight time limit where enemies tend to grab you to stall for time (especially since they just hold grab until you finally escape while staring deep into your soul), to progress your escape you basically go around the tiny prison, picking up items and talking to people while they each send you off to do one fetch quest after another. Second is that once you are in the middle of your escape you end up fighting hordes of guards with police baton in which the fights drag on for way too long with the player being provided very little healing items and a character that sucks with melee weapons (since he's too slow at swinging them), forcing you to ignore the melee weapons that the guards drop, after you get through the first few guards you have to run on top of the prison roof where you have a sniper that shoots you every three second forcing you to slowly chip away the hp of the objects that block your path (which there are multiple), while also having to deal with heavy enemies that have infinite flashbangs that stun you for five seconds. Third is that after you finish the horrible sniper section you have to fight yet another bigger horde of guards and a boss at the same time, but thats not even the final and worst part since after you finally escape from prison you fight another final boss (with no additional healing items provided) that perfectly counters your attack with one counter move that takes almost half of your hp and another counter that cancels your combos completely. The plot twist for Tanimura's arc felt like a stereotypical mystery cop drama with predictable outcomes, also i wanted to point out the brief case section sucked, all you do is just spam the weak attack button for like an hour, and it basically ends with a weak chase minigame and a heavy enemy with the health bar of a boss. The final boss was a worse version of Jingu, since you have to fight twenty minibosses and the actual boss that runs away from the player if they get too close and the final boss also constantly shoots you if you are too far away. The game has some very good tracks, but the rest of the ost is just decent.Overall the game is an improvement from Yakuza 3, since they improved the combat by making it faster, the story doesn't have as many fillers and it is faster (at the cost of making less sense) and the minigames are better, but despite all of this I still think this is the second weakest Yakuza game because the issues outweigh the improvements.Finally, I recommend you skip this game and just watch the cutscenes on Youtube, but if you want to play this game I highly recommend you play in normal mode since you still can't change the difficulty throughout the game like in Yakuza 3 and because the game itself is not too difficult (excluding the prison section and the final boss), the problem is that it gives you little freedom as to how you face enemies and bosses like in Yakuza 3.

_childDocuments_.review: The game that pulls no punches! You play as 4 characters Shun Akiyama, Taiga Saejima, Masayoshi Tanimura and Kazuma Kiryu in the relentless streets of Kamurocho. There's a huge city to explore with secrets and collectibles to find both above and below the city, be that on the rooftops or in the sewers. There's a slew of wacky zany Minigames and Substories to play which can serve as a nice distraction from the brutal street fighting action that these games showcase and the story in this game is one of my favourites in the series. The climax is incredible and seeing 4 characters with vastly different personalities and experiences coming together to stop the crime that is ruining their beloved city is...awesome!  The game doesn't take itself too seriously and has a kind of honesty that you don't always feel from a game, the characters are very likeable especially Akiyama he's lackadaisical but competent and full of charisma he's the star of the show in this game. I want to see more of him in later Yakuza Titles, I can just never get bored of his swagger. This was the first ever Yakuza game that I had played back on the PS3 and it got me into the series for the first time and because of this, I'm now a huge fan. For what it's worth the game is old, but the gameplay absolutely holds up and the story and characters are still as entertaining to watch, as back when the game came out. There's some serious quality here that only improves as the franchise moves forward. 8/10 I really really like this game. In these games there's always more content to play once you finish the main story and experimenting with the combat system to make it reach it's limits really keeps this game fresh for me.

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone who started with Yakuza 0 and has been playing the games in order, this one is really a step into something different - mostly because you don't have Kiryu as a playable protagonist until like 70% of the way through the game. Before that, there are THREE other characters whose stories all come together in the end. Two of these guys have nothing to do with the yakuza world we've come to know so far. For me, this was a nice departure, because there is space for more stories to be told in Kamurocho than just the ones that directly touch Kiryu.My two main complaints about this game are: After you've played 0, Kiwami, and Kiwami 2, 4 (much like 3 before it) has a really rough feeling to it, even with its remaster. The character textures are not as smooth. What you might generously call technical eccentricities pop up at random times. The two that were present for much of my playthrough of this game were: Cutscene audio being ahead of cutscene video by 1-2 seconds, and when pulled into a street battle or dialogue scene immediately as a location's name popped up on the screen, that name (e.g. Nakamichi Alley) floated frantically in its little box.Second complaint: Normal difficulty is comically easy. I experienced difficulty in exactly two fights. That was not the case from 0-3, and it's not because I've gotten that much better at playing these games (although I probably have, a bit). You could get by with XXXY even more than the previous game. In no portion of the game was this more apparent than Tanimura's part, since his fighting style allowed him to activate heat by default at the end of any 3-4 move combo.That said, the drama and the silliness that anyone could have come to expect from playing this series up to this point is definitely present. They understood the assignment and they delivered.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, where do I begin. The 4th title in the series gives a lot of mixed feelings for me especially since the plot has the most twists I've ever seen. It's like one minute you're friends with xxx and the next thing you know xxx is actually working against you. This happens multiple times in the story and has made my head spin faster than a merry-go-round. Whether the ending mitigates that for you is variable, but it is one of the hardest endings in video game history (I visibly pumped my fist in the air when it happened). Horrible final boss though. Regardless that seems to be the only major flaw in this game. Combat's improved drastically since Yakuza 3. Akiyama's a fun lad to play as. Saejima's a bit rough around the edges but he does boast a lot of strength and the ability to grab every enemy without them breaking free,   included (his part's a bit tricky to pass though, especially in Legend). Tanimura's another one that takes getting used to but once you do you'll find out just how fun parrying can be. And Kiryu's just a powerhouse of abilities (this is one of the few times where you don't need a training master to teach you how to do the Tiger Drop, again). Characters are a bit of a hit or miss in terms of how well written they are in this title . Visuals are pretty much the same from 3 but with a few QoL updates, like turning animations. This is also the first title in the series where they started using direct face capture for their models so if you're well versed in Japanese media you might recognize a couple of faces here and there. There's only one map for all 4 protagonists but Kamurocho's been expanded with a few more areas for you to explore. Soundtracks an absolute banger and I guarantee For Faith's melody will be stuck in your head for a couple of weeks. All in all, Yakuza 4's a solid Yakuza game to play alongside 3 and 5. P.S. Both Tanimura's are fine in their performances. Narimiya's (1st) is more down to earth and realistic while Masuda's (2nd) fits more inside the Yakuza universe. Whether you want to mod in Narimiya or not will not affect your playthrough much.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 does a great job at shaking things up for the franchise, literally having quadruple the amount of playable characters as compared to the previous games in the franchise (in release order of course). This game does a great job at making all 3 of the new protagonists really likeable and fun to play as. However, the main issue I have with this game is definitely the length. You play as 4 characters, but the game length is still the same as usual, meaning that you're cramping 4 main character arcs + their storylines into only 4 chapters each, which really isn't much. Now the storylines for each character I don't actually have an issue with, but how they intertwine gets confusing near the end. For example, the first character Akiyama (best character btw) has his arc end roughly a week in game date before the rest of the gang. So when the protagonists start to group up, there's an entire week of storytime that's left completely untold. And it really feels like 4 chapters is nowhere near enough time to make a dent on what stuff you can complete with each character. The most substories I was able to get done was like, 4 or 5?Back onto the story itself, the individual character arcs I definitely still enjoyed a lot. In particular, I probably liked Tanimura's the most, I was honestly surprised at how invested I got into it and he ended up having my favorite fighting style. On that topic it was cool to see how the 3 fighting styles Kiryu has in 0 and 1 were basically inspired by these 3 new protagonists (Tanimura with rush, Saejima with beast, and I guess that leaves Akiyama as brawler). Yes the story was solid as per usual, but of course there were issues with it besides what was mentioned before. There were a lot of plot twists just as other reviewers have mentioned, but I think that they were not as annoying as in some of the previous games (cough cough 2 cough cough). That was probably because they were a bit more spread out over the last few chapters, instead of having 3 plot twists back to back to back dumped on you right in the final 30 minutes of the game. But although this game doesn't win the "most plot twists in final chapter" award, it does win the "most cancerous final boss fight" award! My god the final boss of this game is something right out of video game hell. It's not even in the difficult way, it's in the "we combined every annoying enemy feature into a single fight" way. Besides that, most of the Yakuza formula is still present in this game. The substories are still good, revelations are still some of the most enjoyable parts of this game (although I had an audio sync issue for some of them), and the minigames remain pretty unchanged from my experience. Karaoke good and hostess management bad. To sum it up, Yakuza 4 is a breath of fresh air for the franchise in the big steps it takes storywise. It does a great job making and developing memorable characters in such a short amount of screentime. It's brought back by some confusing timelines and overall short length, but hey it's still just as good as what you can expect from the franchise. This game has Shun Akiyama, of course you should play it (after going through the previous games of course).

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 Remastered is the fourth entry in the series and builds off of the groundwork laid by 3. The gameplay is largely the same but feels fresh with 4 playable characters and a story that links all together for one final showdown as allies. I had a lot of fun overall, but some issues definitely made me annoyed at times. The story follows our 4 protagonists: The game has 5 parts (1 for each character and a final battle with all of them present) in the order above. As a result, the overall story feels rather disjointed at times as it is split between the 4. Once you reach the end of someone’s part, you are suddenly thrust into the role of the next and have to pick up the story from another new perspective. The end result is feeling like you have to start the story completely over and recontextualize everything that has happened thus far with new information. It makes sense that they all learn different things, but having to start a new character after a drama bomb feels weird. The overall story is good. It is mostly about dealing with the past in the present and all the complications that a 25-year gap creates. One issue I had is that there are a LOT of twists and it got a bit hard to keep up with all the revelations, especially with the story splits. As a result, the true Big Bad reveal made me more confused than surprised. Likewise, there were multiple times I guessed a death or wound and was right. The story leans a bit too heavily into crime drama tropes this time around, but is definitely an entertaining journey. The beginning with Akiyama is a bit plodding since he is the establishing character for the mystery and introduces the uniting force for the 4, a mysterious woman, but things pick up with Saejima. She also could’ve been fleshed out more as a character instead of being a plot device to create more emotional weight.      There are more save points available but all of them are only available in part 5. There are more taxi fast-travel locations now so navigation is a bit easier. However, the lack of a sprint button is much more annoying in 4 than 3 for a few reasons: The largest change to the formula is having 4 playable characters. Each has their own moveset and niche which makes them feel distinct. They also have their own inventories which makes gear management a bit annoying.   The upgrade system has changed from Y1-3. Instead of investing in 1 of 4 categories to level them up and gain the attached rewards, you now passively gain max health and heat by leveling up and gain 3 Soul Orbs per level. You are able to freely choose how to upgrade your character from a list using your Orbs. Staples like re-guard and taunt heat are present but unique moves and abilities spice things up. Revelations return with some really useful moves for everyone. Unfortunately, most are for naught as the overall game is rather easy. The perma-block enemies of 3 are gone which is a big factor. It looks like most fights were rebalanced with all characters in mind- the end result being a fairly breezy trapeze through the main story. The only real difficulty I had was against certain (mini) bosses who can counter/ super armor through combos and using Tanimura, who I just couldn’t get the hang of (his final boss is just miserable as well). The game is unfortunately confined to Kamurocho although Saejima has an exclusive level. Kiryu has a scene in Okinawa but you cannot return there. Tanimura opens up Kamurocho a bit via access to Little Asia. Likewise, the aforementioned underground and rooftop areas also make it seem more open. Chase scenes return with some tweaks to make them more engaging and are used much less frequently. Graphically, the game looks the same as 3 Remastered- a nice facelift but some textures look bad/off. Kamurocho looks the same as it ever has but the new areas are nice and realistic. The new character models are good and animations are good across the board as well, especially for the 3 new player characters. Pre-rendered cutscenes definitely show age but are well directed.     The soundtrack is still great overall. I honestly paid more attention to the action, but stopping to take in the music was really nice. There is a smattering of jazzy tracks for common themes and it was nice hearing them with more traditional rock fight themes. The commonality and differences in the final boss themes were also beautiful. Each playable character also has their own battle themes to further cement their individuality. Sound effects are mostly carried over from 3 so good overall. Overall, I had no major issues while playing the game. However, the 60 FPS bug is still present (objects freak out/ vibrate in world/ cutscene). However, it wasn’t as bad this time around and I didn’t notice any z-fighting either. 4 received very few changes from my research. The biggest one is the recasting of Tanimura. The original version was made after his actor’s likeness. After drug use allegations, the actor announced his retirement and disappeared from the public. Tanimura’s character model and lines were all redone. Aside from that, it appears that there were some translation/ localization changes, but nothing else major.  4 overall feels better than 3 but the overall lack of challenge was a bit disappointing. The improvements in gameplay and 3 new playable characters feel a bit wasted as a result, but they all presented new and interesting ways to approach combat which made the journey fun. The overall story was good but weakened due to the split narrative device of 4 protagonists. Graphics are on-par with 3 but the new characters and animations were nice. Music was great and the game ran well. A bit light on changes to be a “Remaster” but better textures and framerate are always welcome.Overall, a very fun journey with a solid main cast but some flaws hold it back.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is disappointing because the first half was genuinely the best the series has been since 0, assuming you're playing in chronological order. However, at about the halfway point it's like both the original writer and director died and they just had to pick a replacement off the streetI'm not exaggerating when I say this is the worst written video game I have ever played. The story is a convoluted, complicated mess. Seriously. This game would make Hideo Kojima look a Nobel laureate of literature. The plot is so complicated and bloated. There are too many horrible twists, such as the famous  twist that completely ruins one of our main characters arcs as well as the most emotional scene in the game. Or characters with no motives or reasoning being revealed to be villains all along, with no foreshadowing. Or characters who get shot a dozen times turning up alive and well. Or the main villain being a nobody who only shows up at the last chapter of the game. There is a character that changes allegiances at least 4 times throughout the course of the game.It's such a damn shame because the writing of the series has been very good so far, and the first half was amazing. I don't know wtf happened here but it's like the writers collectively had a stroke after finishing the first half of the script.There's also the combat. You play as 4 different characters during the game, but the third character (Tanimura) is genuinely useless. If you thought Yakuza 3's combat was bad, wait until you play as this guy. His main gimmick is cool, but he has low health, and does no damage unless you spam staminans and heat actions. He can chain heat actions off his combo which is super powerful, but his combo is so damn slow that you'll never be able to do it against a boss. _childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 Remastered : By Triple F“Yakuza 4 Remastered” brings a fresh twist to the beloved Yakuza series by introducing multiple protagonists, each with unique backstories and combat styles. Originally released in 2010 for the PlayStation 3, the game was revolutionary for the series, expanding the story’s complexity and giving players a broader perspective on the criminal underworld of Kamurocho. This remastered version offers improved visuals and smoother gameplay, making it the definitive way to experience one of Yakuza’s most ambitious entries. While the core gameplay and structure remain true to the series, the multi-character approach adds a new depth to the storytelling and diversifies the overall experience.The story in “Yakuza 4 Remastered” is divided into four distinct arcs, each following a different protagonist before converging in an explosive finale. In addition to Kazuma Kiryu, players control three new characters: Shun Akiyama, a charismatic moneylender with a complex past; Taiga Saejima, a stoic convict on a quest for redemption; and Masayoshi Tanimura, a morally ambiguous cop with a personal vendetta. Each character brings unique motivations and perspectives, creating a layered narrative that explores loyalty, revenge, and survival in Kamurocho’s criminal world. This multi-character structure not only enriches the story but also provides insight into how different lives intersect within the gritty cityscape of Kamurocho.One of the game’s highlights is its diverse approach to combat, as each protagonist comes with a distinct fighting style that changes the dynamics of gameplay. Akiyama, known for his speed, uses flashy kicks and acrobatic moves, allowing for agile, crowd-control techniques. Saejima, in contrast, is a powerhouse, wielding slow but devastating moves that make him feel like a wrecking ball in close-quarters combat. Tanimura specializes in counterattacks, bringing a strategic, defensive style to the game, while Kiryu’s balanced brawling remains as satisfying as ever. This variety keeps the action fresh, as each combat style requires players to adapt their tactics, offering a sense of progression as they master each character’s moveset.Kamurocho, the series’ iconic urban setting, is as lively as ever, brought to life with improved textures and lighting in the remaster. Though the city’s layout remains the same, each character’s unique circumstances reveal different parts of Kamurocho, both literally and figuratively. New locations like the rooftops and underground passages add verticality and depth to the environment, encouraging exploration and giving Kamurocho a fresh sense of mystery. This layered design emphasizes how each character operates within different layers of society like Akiyama’s high-rise office, Saejima’s prison background, and Tanimura’s police work expose different sides of the same city. The remastered version’s graphical polish enhances these spaces, making the city feel gritty and immersive.Side activities and mini-games are as abundant as ever, offering players a break from the main story and adding layers of immersion to the Kamurocho experience. From engaging in hostess clubs and trying out karaoke to playing mahjong or managing a cabaret club, the mini-games bring a lighthearted touch that contrasts the intensity of the main narrative. Each protagonist has unique side quests and storylines tied to their backgrounds like Akiyama has business ventures to manage, Saejima has underground fighting clubs to conquer, and Tanimura can investigate local crime cases. These activities not only enhance the world-building but also allow players to feel like they’re living out each character’s life in Kamurocho, giving them a connection to each protagonist’s story.The remaster includes additional content that was previously omitted in Western releases, such as certain mini-games and substories, giving international players a more complete experience. These additions enhance the authenticity of Kamurocho’s vibrant, gritty life and offer fans more reasons to engage with the game’s numerous side stories and hidden details. Additionally, the remaster has improved the frame rate and resolution, providing a smoother experience than the original, and while it doesn’t reach the visual standards of the Kiwami remakes, it looks sharp and runs well, allowing players to enjoy the game’s details without noticeable performance issues.In terms of sound and voice acting, “Yakuza 4 Remastered” maintains the high-quality performances that Yakuza fans have come to expect. The Japanese voice cast brings emotional depth to each character, particularly during intense moments in the story. Each protagonist’s dialogue reflects their unique personalities—Akiyama’s laid-back humor, Saejima’s brooding intensity, Tanimura’s street-smart charisma, and Kiryu’s stoic resolve are all delivered with authenticity. The soundtrack complements the tone of the game, ranging from fast-paced battle themes to reflective, somber tracks that highlight the emotional weight of the story. The music and voice acting work together to heighten the impact of every scene, making the story’s twists and turns resonate with players.To summarize, “Yakuza 4 Remastered” stands out within the series as a bold, innovative entry that deepens the world of Kamurocho by broadening its perspective through multiple protagonists. The diverse combat styles, interconnected storylines, and expanded city exploration keep the gameplay fresh while immersing players in a complex, morally ambiguous narrative. While the game retains some of the series’ classic design quirks, the remaster’s improved visuals and restored content make this version the best way to experience this chapter. For long-time fans and newcomers alike, “Yakuza 4 Remastered” offers an engaging, multi-faceted journey into a world of crime, loyalty, and redemption, solidifying it as an essential installment in the Yakuza franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 has taken me by surprise with its introduction of a new character in the first cutscene, Shun Akiyama, enough charismatic sequence to rival the likes of Goro Majima in his Yakuza 0 debut. You're thrown in dismay in the beginning however slowly you'll get to pick up what happened since the ending of the previous chapter of the series, a lot of excitement with many new characters and their ambitions. The combat experience is also vastly improved and diversified thanks to 4 different styles you get to master and dedicate yourself to by finding what's their best most destructive, ruthless & flashy combos. This means you're offered on the plate 4 different playable characters as shown on the cover which left me confused when starting, although it made sense answering all my questions later. Every new main playable or unplayable character brings their own burden on display, some more villainous and idealistic to their cause while others have a scarce sense of true justice that won't let them sleep until all matters are solved just. On a technical standpoint it's not a huge improvement since it's using the same engine with minor improvements but it does contain quality of life upgrades for those playing the series in chronological order from the previous. As always there is abundance of substories, minigames and encounters to explore with its newly introduced rooftop and underground locations that have shortcuts and offer sections yet to be seen behind the glamour of Kamurocho. - story & character quality- OST & sound design- top notch voice acting- fighter minigame- machine gun kiss- minigame variety mostly same as Yakuza 3- some slight pacing issues
