_childDocuments_.review: Out of the 3 "Remastered" games (3, 4, 5) I would say that this one is hands down my overall favorite. The combat is great thanks to each character having a unique play style, there is a variety of fun side content, and the story is one of the better ones (if not the best) thanks to its' pacing and buildup to a great payoff. (Also the game introduces Akiyama to the series so it's automatically a 10/10)This was the series' first attempt at having multiple protagonists and it does a great job at it! Each character fights in their own unique way with exclusive moves and heat actions. Although a bit broken, I do enjoy the level up system in this game as it allows for players to pick and choose what abilities they feel are more important to go for first. I also like the "mastering" system where some heat moves if used enough will allow them to unlock a follow-up attack to add on some more damage. Lastly in regards to combat, the boss fight QTEs and their "Essence of counter attacks" are a great step up from Yakuza 3. In Yakuza 3, most QTEs were simply Kiryu dodging attack and nothing more. However in Yakuza 4 characters will dodge attacks while also laying on some of their own. This will lead to the "FEEL THE HEAT!" section where your character will preform a powerful counter attack in a stylish way. I like this system a lot since it doesn't feel as one sided.All four characters have their own importance to the story and it was fun to see how they interacted with one another as the story progressed. I think the story is one of the best in the series thanks to how well it builds up the mystery and interest as you progress with each character. Each time I finished one character's section of the story I would always be more invested in the story and excited to see where it goes next. This interest and excitement is also thanks to how the story's combat sections are designed. The first character's long fight is nothing too special with there just being some small time goons in grungy hallways. However every proceeding character's long battle gets larger with more set pieces that make it feel like ♥♥♥♥ is getting real. The final long battle in this game is probably one of my all time favorites in the series due to its' various settings you punch your way through with each one displaying unique ideas all while some amazing music plays in the background to really set the mood. When comparing the first long battle to the last you can see how everything progressively ramps up. On a final note in regards to story, people tend to complain about a certain plot point and act like it ruins the story but I beg to differ. All I'll say is that if you pay close enough attention to the cutscenes you can see when something suspicious is up.Lastly is the side content which I will admit is not the strongest in the series. From my experience most of the side minigames are basically just enhanced versions of what was found in Yakuza 3. Boxcellios got a sequel which was fun, but other than that it felt like most things were upgrades and tweaks. Each character has their own unique side activity to do, but most of them are pretty meh. I'm not too big of a fan of Akiyama and Saejima's activities due to them being slow management minigames which I find pretty boring. Tanimura and Kiryu's activities are alright but are basically just street fights with some story. (I can't hate Tanimura's activity though as it was how I first discovered Yakuza without even knowing what it was thanks to ). To conclude this section and the review I have to mention that the Karaoke in this game is at its peak due to it having all songs from Yakuza 3 plus many new ones including my all time favorite MACHINE GUN KISS!

_childDocuments_.review: The Yakuza series has some of the best narrative design in all of video games. This entry is no different. The play is a little clunky, definitively a few steps up from Yakuza 3 but not yet what it would be in Yakuza 0. If you like this series, especially because of the story, characters, and setting, you owe it to yourself to play this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Classic Yakuza game. The story isn't very good, as with other early entries, but it's at least better than, say, 2 or 3 (but not by much). The combat, however, feels completely refreshing after the terrible combat of Yakuza 3. The minigames are still normal Yakuza minigames - I particularly enjoyed Saejima's dojo minigame, and I spent 4 hours on it to finish it, but things like Akiyama's hostess minigame were just really boring. _childDocuments_.review: Worst Yakuza Game so far. The story is all random plot twists and forced drama that couldn't be more conspicuous and we're not talking about 2-3x what you would even expect from a yakuza game, but constantly. It also constantly breaks with its own continuity (Feels like an 80s morning soap opera)The fighting is terrible, the characters are all slow and you often hit nothing. You constantly lose control of your character through knockouts, knowdowns, etc. Dodging or special move timings are super low or bugged I don't know, polish is simply missing here. They should have focused on 2 characters as usual and not 4. The fighting just isn't fun. Being able to walk underground or across rooftops doesn't add anything to the game, it just makes it the orientation more difficult. It probably only exists because it was needed for the story....what a waste!It's the first Yakuza game I turned off and uninstalled immediately after the story. Normally I had all the others installed for a few days to complete missing substories, play a few minigames or just look for locker keys, Cards etc. I even thought about playing some of them again. That's not the case here, I don't care at all as this game just isn't fun, everything feels forced and irrelevant and just unfinished. I even lost the desire to start with the next part soon -.-I'd still say it's kind of a close 6/10 but it's such a massive step backwards that it just deserves a thumbs down.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 feels like the more balanced game of the three present in this remastered collectionFirstly, compared to Yakuza 3, the game opens up a lot more when it comes to exploration and we get to play in a very nice expanded Kamurocho, with rooftops, underground areas and even sewers. It feels great to revisit our favorite city but expanded.Then the game introduces new playable characters, each one with their own part and chapters in the story. At first it feels weird but that feeling goes away pretty fast because the new characters have incredible personalities and backgrounds. It feels like we’re being given a huge lot more of story with each of these characters, to discover, compared to just playing as Kiryu in previous games, and it also feels quite refreshing.Similarly to Yakuza 3, on my Ryzen 5 3600 and RTX 3060 Ti I’ve played this game at 4K DSR Downsampling and 125% extra Resolution Scale on top of that, and still enough GPU headroom to keep the 60 FPS cap. Keep in mind this games, all of them, have an issue with variable frame-rate, and if you cannot keep either the 30 or 60 FPS cap, the game will slow down; to avoid this, either use the “Auto” FPS cap (but that makes the camera motion stutter a bit, for me at least) or make sure your settings and resolution are good enough to keep either of those FPS caps, at all times.Once again, the PC specific settings like keybinds and remapping are great in this port, mouse input doesn’t feel perfect though, and you may prefer to use a gamepad, but definitely it’s not impossible to play with mouse and keyboard, especially because we can remap actions for all the side activities as well, something we don’t see in many PC games lately, some actual effort put into the keybinds, so good job there, QLOC.The game has an adequate length, considering we play four characters, and the story is quite enjoyable in my opinion. By the time each character’s story reaches their “end point”, things get very intense and epic and, of course, the final boss battles are fun and flashy, as usual.For being a game originally released on PS3, the animations and facial expressions on the characters’ faces is great, it’s a staple on the Yakuza series, I reckon, and they only keep better and more detailed in newer entries in the series.I had one other small glitch in the game, related to entering cabaret clubs like Jewel or Shine in Kamurocho, at times the game could get stuck in an infinite loading screen, but found out that doing a combat encounter before entering again “fixed” it, and also going to a phone and save the game. Still, an annoying issue if you want to do the cabaret mini game, need to take this bug into consideration and save often. Hopefully they can patch this at some point, so far they have not.In any case, it is an excellent game, needs a patch to fix at least that infinite loading issue, but it only happens in cabarets AFAIK, so if you’re careful and do what I said, it can be avoided.Overall, a solid and fun experience and one of my favorite games in the franchise so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is so much better than in 3 they actually do more than just block!Story-wise though i felt the villains weren't as good as 3. _childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I've been disappointed with the story in Yakuza, it's very shallow and predictable, but it's not a big deal. There are only two reasons why I hate this game, which convinced me to give it a negative review (although my review doesn't matter since I bought this game via retail).1. Combat MechanicsI finished this game on hard difficulty (which I then changed to normal using a hex editor to get the achievement) and managed to beat it relatively easily, so I wasn't too burdened by the enemies, but they were very annoying, dealing with most of them is not fun at all.- Blockuza is still a thing! Enemies don't block as often as in Yakuza 3, but their blocks are absolute and cannot be broken. This makes Saejima completely useless because his attacks are very slow and entirely dependent on charge attacks—which can be easily blocked by enemies.- Grapple, this is the most irritating thing about this game, the frequency of grapplers spawn is very high, and they can grapple consecutively without any break, it's truly broken! When you press your x button repeatedly to escape from one grappler, another grappler will immediately catch you. The best way to get away from the grapplers is to let yourself beaten till down so you get thrown far enough to keep your distance from them. Fortunately, this issue has been fixed in Yakuza 5.- Stunner, this is also quite annoying, almost all the minions in this game can make you stunned. Why did they think it was a good idea for the player to constantly lose control of their character?- Fighting style, only Kiryu is really enjoyable to play with. Akiyama is okay, but his attacks are very easy to block, Tanimura is very boring because of his automatic heat action that makes fighting just a button-smashing, Saejima actually has great potential but is hindered by Blockuza in this game, making his charge attacks useless.2. MinigameJust like another RGG game, the minigames are quite fun, but there's one minigame that really made me hate this game, which is hostess maker. Basically, it's a mix of a loading simulator and a walking simulator spiced up with RNG elements packed into a minigame.- There's no clear indicator on how to increase the hostess's stats, you have to go through trial and error like pocket racing (or look at a guide, of course). Not to mention, you could only try once in every shift. - The transitions between segments are very slow and cannot be skipped, especially the "before-after" part.- The only way to reach the first rank is to get maximum service in 3 shifts, there's no accumulation of scores, so no matter how many times you play, you will never beat this minigame if you don't achieve maximum results for 3 shifts, which is entirely dependent on RNG.- When I give the hostess free time, their stress actually goes up, causing their performance to drop. That's happen almost every time. This is why I call this minigame full of RNG, even the catfight in Yakuza 0 is much more enjoyable than this minigame.- Finally, and most importantly, the player doesn't get anything from this minigame, unlike the cabaret czar in Yakuza 0 that generates a lot of money. Moreover, this minigame can no longer be played once the three hostesses have reached the first rank, as if the developers realized that this minigame wouldn't be liked by the players.Doesn't generate moneyDoesn't provide enjoymentDoesn't mean anything to the storylineThe purpose of this minigame is purely to torture the player

_childDocuments_.review: Yuck.  Remember all those crazy side quests in 0, 1, and 2?  They're gone - or at least there was no sign of any in the first 3 chapters.  In Yakuza 3, they were replaced by teaching life lessons to cute kids.  In this one, you're just kinda doing stuff - sometimes good, sometimes not.Worst of all, though, is that the game is far too easy.  On normal difficulty, there's really no challenge at all.  And by that I mean you can put the controller down for a minute and still have plenty of health in a typical street battle.  With no challenge, there's no need to buy any health boosts or buy food.  At level 11, I had 18 skill points unspent!  Why bother to get new skills when you can defeat everything the game throws at you with simple kicks and throws??  A ton of the gameplay becomes pointless when a game is this easy!If you decide to play the game anyway, for pity's sake, set it on Hard, because you can't set the difficulty higher once you start to play.  (Though I hear the game will lower the difficulty if you get beaten on Hard too many times.)

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is an improvement on Yakuza 3 in some ways, and a bit of a let down in others. In general though, it's a pretty good game, but it's not flawless, and feels like it doesn't have nearly the impact that it should.Yakuza 4 introduces the player to 3 new playable protagonists beyond Kiryu himself, those characters being Akiyama, the new introductory phase character, Saejima, who probably has the best narrative tied to him, and Tanimura, the sort of crooked but not so crooked cop (an interesting take on a character, playing someone who is actually on the total opposite of the Yakuza).To keep things short and simple, all 3 of these new characters are fitting members to the Yakuza cast, and they more or less play well, with fitting movesets for each of their respective characterizations. Akiyama is all about taunts, combos, and mobility, while Saejima is all about slow, but devestating strikes and grabs. Tanimura is probably the most interesting of the bunch in terms of mechanics, coming out of left field with a built in parry button for his block and his very unique and somehow powerful grab mechanics.Revelations are back, and are unique across all 4 characters, all of them having different things to say about the wacky events that happen in front of them and different ways of obtaining their "revelations." In the case of Saejima, there's actually a reason to fail these because you get new sculptures when you fail. Some revelations do get repeated across the playable characters, so it kinda sucks you have to sit through doing the same button prompts again to improve the heat actions, but not all of them repeat, and some of these revelations could be played on repeat due to how great they are. The first one is probably the best.The Sonic 06 Mach Speed sections I gave Yakuza 3 crap for are back, but surprisingly, this mechanic has 1.) gotten more polished, 2.) is used all the time as a secondary gameplay mechanic to the combat, and 3.) isn't nearly as annoying and is genuinely more fun. I must commend the developers for improving one of the aspects that I found VERY lacking and bewildering as to why it was even in Yakuza 3. Kudos.Yakuza 4's combat is better than 3's in the sense that enemies aren't block happy. However, it seems that the developers may have over corrected, because to compensate for the fact that enemies don't block everything anymore, grabs are nerfed unless you're Saejima or Tanimura (Akiyama's grab is ass and Kiryu's is about as good as it was in 3, you just have to deal with stronger enemies), enemies are more aggressive, and some of them are VERY GRAB HAPPY, leading to incredibly frustrating gameplay sections. I swear the Komaki Parry and Tiger Drop don't activate when I wanted them to, and there was no way to apply pressure onto enemies to get them to attack me. In Yakuza 3, even on hard, you could condition the AI to attack, so you could MAKE your opportunities to strike. This doesn't happen in this game. They just block the combo, and then you either dodge and get your combo, or don't, because enemies STILL BLOCK YOUR ATTACKS MID COMBO WHY IS THIS A THING I SWEAR TO GOD I HIT YOU I LITERALLY GOT THE HIT SPARKS WHY ARE YOU BLOCKING!The most glaring section of the game that I found to be abysmal was Saejima's prison section. Absolutely god awful. You have nearly no abilities, enemies are horrendously grab happy, so you end up getting stun locked, and because Saejima has no mobility, you break out of a grab only to get punched, fall into hitstun, and get grabbed again by the same freakin' dude. Oh, and you have like no healing items. Horrible section and I don't want to play it again. I don't think I want to play any of Saejima again at all, actually. Unlike the other characters, Saejima can't roam the streets of Kamurocho freely, and instead, either gets constantly chased or you have to use the sewers in a round about way to get to where you need to go. It was kind of annoying. In terms of narrative, Saejima had one of the best parts, but gameplay wise, sheesh.Tanimura's story isn't all that great either. It's just...kinda there...and the reasons why certain things happen are a little nonsensical/predictable. I can't give Akiyama much flack because he's the introductory character, so his story is more so to draw you in rather than keep you captivated; the rest of the cast is for that.Kiryu is shoe horned in at the very last second so the fans can play Kiryu. That's basically it. He's got like no reason to be part of any of this at all, other than some seriously convenient plot fiddling. To be fair, I like seeing the redemption arc of a character who really didn't get as much screen time as he should have in Yakuza 3.Tanimura's final boss (yes each character has their own respective final boss) completely sucks. It's Yakuza Kiwami all over again. I suppose it's not AS bad because there's no grenades involved but still. Bleh.All 3 of the newer playable characters pale in comparison to Kiryu. Maybe not so much in terms of narrative. Obviously, Kiryu doesn't have much going for him there other than, well, he's the legendary Dragon, and you obviously can't NOT put him in the game that he's been the main protagonist of right? Problem is, he is literally the best character in the game. Canonically, and literally, the best character. None of them even compare to Kiryu's kit, flexibility, and naturally fun gameplay mechanics. Akiyama has combos but Kiryu has more and better, and he can actually grab enemies without getting trampled on. Saejima is slow and even though he has super armor he's prone to taking damage because of it, requiring the player to have to heal a lot. Kiryu has similar levels of power, and unlike Saejima, he has the speed/mobility to avoid getting hit. Tanimura's gameplay is by far the weakest, being unable to use extended combos much, his heat actions lack punch, and though arresting enemies leads to instant take-downs, it doesn't help that he has the smallest health bar of all the characters. His only saving grace is his on demand parry, but the problem here is that YOU DON'T GET TO COMBO AFTERWARD. It's only to protect you. Meanwhile Kiryu over here can destroy a health bar with his tiger drop and get free combos with the komaki parry.Perhaps you could say it's intentional that Kiryu is so unbelievably good. To really drive home how he truly is the most powerful of the cast. And to be honest, I don't have a problem with that. The problem that I have is that Kiryu's kit is basically perfect, and the other 3 characters are just parts of Kiryu split apart to give them "weaknesses." Akiyama has the combos and mobility, but lacks the power and crowd control. Saejima has the power and grabs, but lacks mobility and combos (practically all of Saejima's good combos come from charge attacks, which aren't true and can be blocked). Tanimura is somewhere between Akiyama and Saejima, so he has combos but they aren't as flexible or fast as Akiyama, nor as damaging, he has grab power like Saejima but he's got a gimmick around the whole akido crap.The point that I'm trying to deliver here is that once you get to Kiryu, there's basically no reason to ever play the other characters beyond liking their battle theme, or wanting to go for completion points. If you want to play them for their gameplay, well, just play Kiryu, because Kiryu can do everything they can do better. I want unique gameplay to them, not a nudered Kiryu moveset.If you're coming from Yakuza 3, and hated the combat, you'll like this title a little more. However, as for story, this game is kinda weak. Yakuza 4 isn't a bad game by any stretch, but it didn't quite meet my expectations both narratively and gameplay wise.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 Remastered is the remastered version of Yakuza 4 (2010 in Japan and 2011 for North America), originally released to the Playstation 3. The PC version was released in January 2021 as part of the Yakuza 3-5 Remastered Trilogy pack. The story takes place in 2010 and for the first time in the series, the player gets to play multiple protagonists. This ranges from the fan-favorite Shun Akiyama, Taiga Saejima, Masayoshi Tanimura, and of course, Kiryu Kazuma. The plot follows of a young woman and all the characters mentioned in the previous sentence has some connection or association with her. In some ways, Yakuza 4 feels more of an anthology to expand the Yakuza/Like a Dragon’s lore. Is Yakuza 4 worth playing?Yakuza 4 and the remastered version feels more of an improved and refined version of Yakuza 3. It’s a good thing since the game engine’s improvement changed the “janky” combat to a tolerable state. Since the player gets to play multiple protagonists, there are different combat skills and fighting styles that are enjoyable. For example, Shun Akiyama primarily uses kicks whereas Taiga Saejima uses brute force and Masayoshi Tanimura utilizes Taiho-Jutsu – Japanese martial art for law enforcement. Gameplay is great yet also similar. I won’t go further details as I already mention on my previous reviews for earlier entries of the series. The environment and audio immersion are impressive, particularly when rain appears in Kamurocho and jazz soundtrack rings out on my headphones with Dolby Atmos. It feels like a neo-noir film in some situations. Hidenori Shoji and the RGG audio team have done an outstanding job. As much as I like some features in Yakuza 4, there were some significant flaws to the plot and felt like major hinderances. I can’t explicitly say what the plot holes/flaws are, but I found it very disappointing. RGG studios usually does the main plot well for the most part in the series, but Yakuza 4’s plot was insulting as I played through. In some ways, Yakuza 4 feels like a filler and lost track on where the series would go from there. Few can interpret Yakuza 4 was at a “low point” for the series’ writers on what to write about (luckily, the recent entries improved significantly – including the Judgment spin-off series). I agreed. In addition, the boss fights in the game aren’t too great, specifically Saito and another character I won’t spoil because of plot. Yakuza 4 is an “middle entry” to the overall series, depending on what the person can interpret as based on the game’s chronological timeline or the game’s release date. Yakuza 4’s gameplay is an improvement and a better refinement than Yakuza 3. The new protagonists and their motivations are intriguing and interesting. I really like Tanimura’s character and his combat style, but it’s unfortunate for the character as a one-time encounter. Unfortunately, the main plot did place a sour note on my mouth. The overall score, in my perspective, leans towards a “mixed” reception. Steam’s review policy does not feature a “mixed” review for individual reviews. When factoring the pros and cons, I marked the score as a positive because of new characters, new gameplay combat styles, and outstanding voice cast. I factor a game’s story a lot in all my single-player game reviews based on how good it is. The overall story is all filler and little substance. I still recommend the game for fans of the series, but be aware on the plot and its flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: Typical Yakuza game with a deep twisty turny crime drama and lots of minigames and substories (I completed The Main story + all The Sidequests (Yep including amon)). The highlight of the substories are the Akiyama Hana-Chan loan sharking stories and the Saijima karate dojo training. There are about 62+1 substories total with about 15 for each character. The story can get a little convoluted and too much nonsensical video game logic infested but it's going to be highly entertaining for sure. The only Problem: You can see at chapter 4 (with the fourth Character) that the story kinda falls apart. It's introducing too many new characters and clans under the tojo clan and all the Plottwists kinda lost it charme later on. Too. Many. Plottwists.A good and refreshing entry in the franchise. Definitely an improvement over the prequel. It has the innovation that you do not play as Kazuma Kiryu alone. Instead you have 4 playable characters.All these characters are drawn into ramifications from things that happened 25 years ago that play into the events of the current year. I actually truly enjoy the characters. Each of them has an own story line that lead to the climax as those are connected to each other. While the story itself is really good the separate episodes weaken the performance a bit. Everything makes sense at the end and the motives are believable but you are a bit puzzled until you get the connections and reveals. I should point out that it is a remaster not total overhaul like Yakuza 1 and 2 (Kiwami) but aged better than the prequel. Gameplay wise I love how different the characters play. Akiyama has lightning fast kicks and moves fast (Kinda like rush from yakuza 0), Saejima is durable and hits like a tank but is slower and you have to adapt to this. Tanimura is a master of grapples and throws with auto finishers you can unlock. Lastly Kiryu has the same style as before. You can unlock a lot of abilities for each characters and the revelations return. A true strength that made me praise the game. On minor misstep is that you get Saejima after Akiyama which is hard to adapt in the first chapter as he is nearly the opposite. Of cause there are some new and familiar faces. Everyone woks really well. A character from the last game I cant name because of spoilers surprised me and won my deepest respect. The strengths of the Yakuza games are the activities. You have tons of side quest and mini games. Be it a battle coliseum, poker, black jack, shogi, bowling, darts majong, koi koi, cee lo, darts and more. You can easily sink in more times in these as in the main story. I like the side-quests and craziness involved. For the mini games I especially like the improved hostess maker, the excellent fighter maker and the police scanner which I must say can become annoying if I played longer. Also they gave Kamurocho more depth as they added an underground and rooftop instead of "new cities" which I highly welcome. Early in the game it feels a bit empty at the rooftops. Like I said the enjoyable crazy side quests and stories are a plus for me. Graphically and soundtrack wise I say it is a good remaster. Nothing is ugly while I will say graphic fetishist will complain. I also absolutely adore the revelations (I did every single one of them) and It made me laugh so bad especially two of them - it literally made me cry because it made me laugh so much.Overall this is a truly good entry in the franchise (Please play Yakuza 0, Kiwami 1, Kiwami 2 and 3 first before going into this) and a strong 8/10 for me. Would recommend this on any day but the many new faces, names and confusing plot is something that can really downgrade the experience since its ... Plottwist upon Plottwist... It lost it charme later on sadly.

However, the plot is ridiculous...but in a good way. For starters, it is definitely better than Yakuza 3's, but tends to get really convoluted because of the many (and sometimes not so brilliant) different elements thrown in there in such a small time window. It is perfectly fine, though. Yakuza is a series that puts the words "fun" and "interesting characters" in first position, so I am honestly ok with having a messy plot, as long as it means leading the story to interesting and fun scenarios (which is something that Yakuza 4 does really well). In fact, I loved playing this game, because the dynamic storytelling and fast paced rotation of the 4 playable characters never gave me the time to get bored. Not only once.In conclusion, Yakuza 4 passes with flying colors the "Is it fun?" test, but unfortunately fails the "Well written plot" one.Thanks for reading ♡

_childDocuments_.review: Coming off the heels of Yakuza 3, Yakuza 4 is just... mwah. It's better in every way than its predecessor and, other than Yakuza 0, it's my favorite game in the series to date (though I'm excited for 5-7!)Largely, I think my sunny disposition is because a lot of the annoyances from the first game are gone. There's still a small intro to battles but it's a few seconds shorter in length. The archaic leveling system from 3 was improved in a way that makes late-game leveling decisions surprisingly relevant. And most of all, you can craft using items from the Item Box, yay!The story is one of the more memorable ones of the series, though it has more than a handful of contrivances and plot conveniences. Guns are apparently of zero consequence in Yakuza 4 and loyalty means nothing as everyone backstabs each other multiple times. But the story winds the threads of a likable, interesting cast of characters into something cohesive and enjoyable. Even if the big showdown involves a pile of money... again.But at the end of the day, if you're considering Yakuza 4 you're already knee deep in the series like me. You don't need convincing. So instead, let me offer some assurance that the slog of 3 is worth it for the joy of 4.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, without a doubt, my favorite Yakuza game, after 0 and 3. I say this as someone who has played all of the RGG games available on PC. Why?The tone game initially sets in Akiyama's part will make you think it's just a fragment of what's to come from the other protagonists at the start. This then reinforced by  cutscene at beginning of Saejima's part, possibly one of the best in the franchise. From that point on, the expectations set couldn't be any higher.So you would think, unfortunately,from that point onward, which marks the beginning of the Saejima section, things begin to fall apart. The early game with non-upgraded Saejima and Tanimura is abysmal, and the second half of the game feels rushed, lacking both sense and depth due to its ridiculous plot twists and turns. Even the main character Kiryu somehow feels shoehorned in his own game.Everything comes crashing down in the infamous chapter aptly named, perhaps summarizing the entirety of the game,  This insane chapter completely shatters whatever faith and expectations you had held, abandoning all of it's sense to a point you can't take it seriously anymore.So, as if the developers too are beign aware of this, fully embrace the absurdity, delivering an utterly nonsensical, balls-out, epic finale chapter. It's so over-the-top that it feels like a finale from a B-tier superhero movie.My favorite part was; during final confrontation the cunning evil mastermind turns towards our group of heroes and asks, "Who are you?", and in perfect unison, the gang responds: As For Faith with all of its glorious engrish kicks in following this line, i was completely won over at that moment and found myself forgiving all of the previous blunders.Just with that finale Yakuza 4 has solidified its place as one of my favorite Yakuza games, if not one of my favorite games overall.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from Yakuza 3 you may be discouraged to see the same engine, graphics, minigames etc., but this game is actually much better than the previous installment. Most importantly, writing is undoubtedly the best among 1-4, leaving the orphanage and twins' shenanigans behind and returning to where Yakuza's best: inter-family politics. This time, you experience the story from four different character's points of view, which gave writers lots of opportunities for mystery and plot twists. Each protagonist takes a while to develop, but eventually I found them all very likable and charming. As they all fight using different styles, brawling gameplay is much more varied, and AI keeps all fights interesting - combos stick easily. There are some minor unique minigames later in the game too. No exotic locations this time, but Kamurocho has twice the content as usual, because you get to visit lots of new, previously inaccessible areas. Certainly a high point of the series, although it does suffer from too much reused side-content compared to other Yakuzas. So if you're coming fresh from 3, many side quests, interactions, club management, minigames and even the UI will feel very stale.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about Yakuza 4?It’s a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ masterpiece.In my  I had spoken about how it was a welcome breath of fresh air and a satisfying departure from the dismal experience of , whose broad variety consisted entirely of fighting, fighting, and more fighting with breaks between the fighting consisting only of—you guessed it—more fighting.To me Yakuza 3 seemed like a really good game, but something about it seemed off, filler-y. It wasn’t until I played Yakuza 4 that I realized why I felt this way. Compared to Yakuza 4, Yakuza 3 feels like a tech demo showcasing what the studio could do on the PS3, and Yakuza 4 feels like the studio hitting their stride as they discover that bad ♥♥♥♥♥ can do more. There’s a total of four protagonists, and honestly that had me concerned at first, but it shouldn’t concern you. The game is set up to be a true sequel, the story right where we left off, and with a protagonist explaining as he goes through his own story just how Kamuro-Cho has changed since the departure of the Dragon of Digimon. You start off playing as Abracadabra, a magician who uses his feet to shine the faces of those who ask for his lunch money on the wrong day, which is every day. Akihabra makes his money by giving money away, and taking money from the sidewalk he just kicked his foes through. No one seems to know how he stays in business, and that’s likely because he doesn’t know what the words “business plan” means when combined. Once you’re done playing as Adidas you take on the role of Kitty, a man from the past who we all should recognize from our time together in Yakuza 0. Ol Wildcat has been in jail for the past 25 years for a crime he may or may not have actually theoretically in practice simulated. Despite being a powerhouse of strength, he has the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ start considering his fighting style seems to be taking 8 years to wind up a punch, and doesn’t seem to like counting past 3. After spending four hours of being everyone’s punching bag, I decided to do anything else other than fighting, and fell in love with the game as I discovered ol Housecat has his own set of diversions, including training the underground bum fighting championship. He also has his own set of navigational paths, and ultimately he is a great departure from traditional gameplay. The more I played as him, the better his fighting style became, and soon I was maxing out his extracurricular activities so he could become the fist-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fighter of legend everyone makes him out to be. Every character plays like Kiryu or Majima from prior installments, except Whiskers, from fighting to exploration he stands out, even his speech is different as he sports a nifty Osakan accent.After Garfield you get to play as Shifty, a man who sidesteps and counters more than he beats women in abandoned buildings. That entire sentence is lore-accurate, anyone who says otherwise hasn’t played the game.Lastly, after seemingly getting all pieces of the puzzle, enter our champion wrestledad, ol’ Kiwami or Salami himself, Pikachu.If you’re a veteran or fan to the series, I don’t know why you’re reading this review. It comes part of the legacy collection which goes on sale for $20 while this game alone is also $20. I don’t know what sociopath is buying the games separately and reading these reviews, starting with mine, but you should reach out to me so we can hang out and discuss your supervillain origin story. I’m here for you.So for new players, why should you start at 4? I don’t think that’s a good idea, however I do think it wouldn’t be a bad idea if you played Yakuza 0, Kiwami, then skipped 2/Kiwami 2 and 3 before taking this one on. Why do I say that? The story for 2 seems largely ignored outside the joke in 0, and the first like…ten minutes of 3. Similarly, the story for 3 could be understood in a single cutscene since there wasn’t a lot of depth or complexity, and in hindsight I don’t think I want to replay it again.With character-specific side quests, excursions, mini-games, and entertainment each journey through the main quest feels like a treat, and I’m reminded how much these games redefined my standards for what a single player game should enjoy.Yakuza 5/4

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is yet another solid entry in the franchise. It has you play as a variety of characters in its 4 acts with flashbacks to different time periods; namely, Shun Akiyama, Taiga Saejima, Masayoshi Tanimura, and last but not least, Kazuma Kiryu. Although being able to experience the story via 4 distinct perspectives is awesome, it was hard to shake the feeling that it's too similar to Yakuza 3. Not only is the combat mostly unchanged, the graphics haven't aged well either. Some NPCs are downright ugly with visible polygonal features so if you were expecting Yakuza 3 and 4 Remastered to look as good as Yakuza Kiwami then you'll be disappointed.Graphics aside, Yakuza 4 remains one of the most varied campaigns in the franchise due to its amount of extra content as well as the ability to play as 4 stand-out protagonists who each have their own fighting styles even though they don't feel all that different. Some notable additions include pachinko, hanafuda, table tennis, and there's now some hostess-style stuff that takes place in a hot springs area. Of course, there are tons of substories to complete, restaurants to eat at, and shops to visit as well which help flesh out the marginally expanded city of Kamurocho. Overall, it's a solid game and feels like an expanded natural evolution of Yakuza 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is my favorite in the series. Going back to it on PC has only confirmed that. I get that a lot of people will come into the remastered games having touched 0 first so there may be disappointment with the gameplay, for some. Yakuza has always felt like an evolution of the classic beat 'em up design and that's how I personally like it instead of the faster, style switching design. Instead, this game offered each character a single, distinct style that represents their uniqueness without completely changing the gameplay philosophy.       Some say 4 has a weak story because of how ridiculous and nonsensical the twists are but I think that's part of it's charm. It presents things in a serious tone that are ridiculous as opposed to the substories which can be ridiculous and are acknowledged as being such. You'll either like it or hate it. I like it, but I also liked 3. I recommend getting the mod that replaces the "new" Tanimura with the original. Just preference here but I don't like recasts and the original actor was done extremely dirty by the industry with drug allegations that were proven to be false.     Port is totally fine. Didn't crash, ran as expected. Looks fine for being a remaster of a game from the PS3 era. I fully recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: So you've finished Kiwami 2 recently, and then took the deep plunge into Yakuza 3, downgrades and all. You finished Yakuza 3 and you're ready to play 4 next. Well there is some really good news for you. Spoiler free.+ Yakuza 4 is overall a very big upgrade from Yakuza 3. Graphically, gameplay, and side content+ An extremely satisfying and new look on both the regular game and the endgame segments (playing as different characters at different points in time, but done correctly)+ Story is overall good, with a couple questionable twists+ Visually, if you max the game out, it passes the bar for today's age, but also shows signs of retiring. This is in comparison with Yakuza 3 Remastered where it's already retired and we brought it back out of the nursing home+ New characters introduced are top notch, especially Akiyama+ As said, all the minigames are there, and a few more+ An overall more satisfying way to level up and get abilities vs how Yakuza 3 did it+ A MUCH BETTER completion list. No longer staring at just numbers, but now we have this nice clean UI to look through that is nicely organized+/- Story twists take some hits. It's a "don't-care" or "hate" situation. Hell, maybe you'll love it. Everyone is different. I didn't care.- Still can't Sprint- Some side content is extremely grindy (Hostess Maker) while other side content is actually fun to watch the actual stakes and progression (Fighter Maker). I just wish it was all great.- Fishing. I may get flamed for this but man do I hate fishing minigames. I 100%'d this game and this was the only minigame I actually dreaded. It turned out to be kind of fun, but also kind of not when you fish for a Steel Barrel thinking it was a massive big rare fish you've been spending an hour trying to catch.So get excited. It IS an upgrade from Yakuza 3. You may still not like it as much as 0, K1, or K2, or even 3 (story wise), but take the dive so you can fully experience the series (as I slowly am). Let this review encourage you that there will never be a leap in this series again when it comes to going from Kiwami 2 to Yakuza 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 doesn't fix much of what made Yakuza 3 a chore to complete, but it's a vast improvement in one area - variety. While I loved Kiryu's mundane adventures in running Morning Glory Orphanage in Okinawa back in the previous game, the minigames and side content were nowhere near polished enough to engage me, and the story's collapse in the back half made even focusing in on the main plot a bit of a drag. Yakuza 4 doesn't make the combat any better on a base level, nor does it make stuff like the old cabaret club management game any less of a massive bore. What it does do is give you far more variety to make chasing the main quest and substories that much more interesting. I'm a sucker for multiple protagonists with stories that intersect in interesting ways, and Y4 has that in spades. Even during a rare weak chapter or two, you're much more quickly pulled into something new and interesting. The four protagonists also have the 70-ish substories split between them, so they're much more likely to tie into their backstory, with way less filler as a result. Combat still isn't great, but there's a lot of variety between Akiyama's slick, speedy basics, Saejima's heavy brawling and Tanimura's counter-focused guards. I do wish each style had slightly more depth, as none of them are as complex as Kiryu's returning Dragon style, but you can see the beginnings of the multiple styles in Yakuza 0 here. Similarly, Kamurocho now has 4 levels of its own - in addition to the city streets, you can explore the underground garage and mall, along with some even deeper sewers, and the rooftops of the city. The latter is an annoying pain to navigate and has basically nothing to do, but the lower levels of the city have some cool atmosphere and are interesting to explore. I've seen a lot of people complain about the story here, and while there are some eyebrow-raising twists, none of them truly feel like they betray what we've come to learn about the characters. While there's not much here that reaches the heights of Y0, we don't have some of the inscrutable choices in the latter half of Y3, or the really poor PS2-era writing of Kiwami 1. Every Yakuza game is a bit dumb in a pulpy way, as long as the twists don't hurt the characters I'm fine with them. Anyway, I'm pretty glad to be done with the games on the super-old engine. This one is worth playing for the story, but you aren't missing much if you skip everything but the main missions and substories.

_childDocuments_.review: After 3, I was a bit hesitant to get into 4 but it has been more than a pleasant surprise. If 3 put you off due to the block spamming in combat or the Morning Glory Orphanage segments, there's a lack of that this time around.The story wasn't anything special in my opinion but playing through as new protagonists and learning each of their unique fight styles was what made the game for me, not to mention Akiyama being one of my new favourite characters. Saejima was also a fun character to meet and I'm looking forward to seeing more of him. Tanimura didn't really grow on me but I liked his fighting style. The usual mini-games and side diversions return alongside some new ones like the fighter maker, table tennis and pachinko machines as well as the revelations which spoiler alert, keep delivering the most bizarre moments I've seen in the series. Only gripes I had were that Kiryu's involvement felt a bit forced or convenient and the antagonists weren't very memorable and very few of the end boss fights had any real reason to occur in the first place. There was also a lack of sub-story markers which made it easier to follow their progress in other games but it's only a minor issue. You're probably looking at this game because you've played the first few, it's worth the dive.

_childDocuments_.review: Still amazes me how each title brings different gameplay mechanics and scenery to spice up the formula of the Yakuza franchise. I honestly thought that the 4 playable protagonists would make the story have terrible pacing or the issue of quantity over quality with how the characters operate. But im happy to say that that is not the case here.Akiyama - I adored the lore and whole idea of a loanshark with an absolute ♥♥♥♥ ton of money but rather than making more money he uses it to change people with his tests. His part in the story was the weakest out of the others but that does not mean it was bad, in fact I felt attached to his character by the final chapter. His gameplay evolves around his huge rush combos and agility, which was interesting to play through but just wasnt as fun compared to the other characters.Saejima - Saejima's section was definitely hands down my favorite section in the game, his story was compelling, his character was compelling, and his insane burst in charged attacks or bounding heat animations was not only satisfying to pull off, but satisfying to play through. Tanimura - Taking a look at Tanimura for the first time I felt like he was going to be a snooze fest to play through but I ended up being surprised again and enjoying myself. A corrupt detective on the force looking for his father's killer by any means necessary totally blew away my expectations and I was hooked from the start of his chapter, and his gameplay MMM. His whole kit evolves around his invincible parry which I had a lot of fun throwing enemies into the wall or each other. Kiryu - I am happy to see that upon returning to the main protagonist of the previous games, your abilities and heat actions learned from Yakuza 3 are unlocked or unlockable. I thought the game would pull a restart on Kiryu and make him forget the abilities all together but im glad to see that did not happen, and well its Kiryu. Of course he was fun to play, you got your bounding combos, tiger drop, and other utilities you know and love.Map - The whole game takes place in Kamurocho and Kamurocho alone rather than the standard 2 locations you would travel to in the previous games. You would think trailblazing through Kamurocho the whole game with 4 protagonists would get old and boring quite quickly but along with the new decoration and establishments you can now visit, they gave Kamurocho some insane verticality. You can now jump through the rooftops to admire the view and skys of kamurocho, visit the underground mall for some pool, or even go through the sewers to get to point B quicker. It was very intimidating at first but once you get the hang of it, you come to appreciate the detail.Minigames - The minigames have a lot of improvements from 3, either refining presentation like the hud in karoke, or just making challenges a much more better player experience like with the very hard mode in batting cages and not removing the crosshair like in yakuza 3's very hard mode. I really like the mini games in the Yakuza franchise, in fact its where most of my hours are and is my favorite franchise for these side activities. So when I found out that Pachinko/Slots were removed from the remaster, it got me puzzled to why? I read that some people said it had something to do with gambling laws, but that makes no sense seeing how the American gambling games like poker, blackjack, baccarat, and roulette, along with the Japanese gambling games koi koi, oichu-kabu, cee-lo, chohan, and mahjong are still here. I have no idea to why it was removed, another mini game was removed called Answer X Answer, but since the game was out of date Japanese trivia I could understand and live with myself with that being removed. But Pachinko, bummed me out. Another thing that bummed out is that they havnt fixed how ♥♥♥♥ the controls are in pool, I finally caved in and remapped my joystick to only move horizontally, and guess what. I started having fun and it played like an actual minigame. Another complaint is the hostess mini games, by now I have started to get the cabaret club fatigue and these hostess clubs have started to bore me. I reached fatigue already in Yakuza 3 on the 5th out of 9 hostess, so by now I was already checked out. The variety sounds good on paper but for completionists like me, its very tedious.Those were some big complaints but I actually still enjoyed the mini games despite those hiccups. I really like the oldschool fishing rather than the Yakuza 0 fishing, gives it more action, and is exhilarating. Boxcelios and its sequel is still a vibe to play. It was interesting using the hostess maker to create hostesses and have them seduced later in the game by the other protagonists, and the fighter maker was unbelievably fun, that one shocked me tbh.This game surprised me, I have heard nor seen nothing in media surrounding this game so I came into this game blind and I came out of it very satisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: Almost makes me wish Yakuza 3 was the last game in the franchise.I've played Yakuza K1, K2, and 3 back to back and loved every moment in them. I remember being upset about Yakuza 4 having four protagonists back when I first heard it because I loved playing as Kiryu, but kept my hopes up since Yakuza 4 was being praised and sometimes getting called the best in the franchise. Now, after finishing it 8 months later because I kept taking breaks either out of boredom or annoyance, I'm at the point of considering skipping 5 to get straight to 6.It has the worst story by far, with AoT levels of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ twists on top of other equally moronic twists. It does nothing interesting, has very shallow climaxes, hollow emotional scenes with no punch, and no big 'oh ♥♥♥♥' moments from the other games. The ending of the game has the worst parts of K1 and K2's endings combined in one package, both in its story and gameplay. A story needs build-ups. This game has some, don't get me wrong, but they all get shattered and ♥♥♥♥ on by the writers trying to conclude them with sudden and moronic twists for a quick gotcha. It was tedious, that's all it is. Shibata, Sasai, Hisai, Sugiuchi, Mishima, Katsuragi, they all get moronic conclusions and feel pointless as characters. They obviously didn't know what to do with Kido and Arai, it kept jumping from place to place with them and each twist was worse than the one before. I hope they won't appear in the future games and get erased from existence. The only side character who was fine was Hamazaki, but even he had his moments of idiocy.Akiyama was the only interesting character out of all the newly introduced characters, including all the side ones. His personality and combat style made the beginning of the game hopeful at least. Instead of being a punch heavy guy like Kiryu, he's using his legs instead during combat. His charm, backstory, mannerisms, and relationships made Act 1 a breeze. And right after things start to get complicated, the torch gets passed down.Saejima's act's beginning was fine but after getting to Kamurocho it becomes a snoozefest. His personality is comparable to a pile of bricks, just like his combat style, and wasn't used that well. His relationship with his sister and Majima was interesting but we don't see enough interactions with them. His shootout scene was cool but the twist that involved it later on was so majorly idiotic that I had to turn the game off for a while.Tanimura was actually tedious all way through, both him as a character and his act. He didn't belong in a game like this, and his entire existence was to introduce the police side to the story a bit more, which was executed poorly in itself. At times I even forgot that he existed. His 'cool guy' personality got lame real fast. Saejima's combat style was basically the beast style from 0 and K1, so I expected Tanimura's to be the rush style but his abilities felt very shallow compared to the rest of the cast, and his automatic heat move ability made it really boring in fights. Apparently he gets erased from the franchise after this game so that's good at least.Kiryu's act was great, of course. It would be a hard task to mess it up and I'd congratulate the game for managing it. You start off really strong since he has most of his essential kit, and tiger drop is only a couple steps up. His interactions with the characters were the highlights of the game. The only bad thing about his act was how short it was. Don't need to say more about it, really.The game has the worst levelling system by far, even worse than 0's money based system. It feels really arcade and way too easy. It's kinda understandable since grinding for abilities on each 4 characters would be annoying, but getting all the necessary abilities after like an hour with each character made the whole system pointless. I didn't care to get new abilities after a while since I had everything I needed after spending a little time with each character and got op already. The only map in the game is Kamurocho but they expanded on it with new underground and rooftop areas. Too bad they're all empty with nothing to do in them, and only a few quests take place there. They only made the game even more unbearable, to say the least.The substories, which are one of the biggest reasons a large part of the community likes these games, were mostly lame. If you don't do them all when they appear and if you think about doing the slightest thing in the main story, say goodbye to them until the after-story premium adventure section because you're not getting them back.In my eyes, the substories were complimentary to the main story of the games. They were there to get you immersed in the world after getting through the story after a while and when you wanted to take a break. Now, majorly with the result of the game's structure of multiple protagonists, you get rushed to do them all. And as I said, getting op in this game is easy so they're not needed for their xp either. It's a horrible entry considering the previous titles but it was an OK game. Had a fe— a couple cool scenes at least. I genuinely wish Yakuza 5 will be better but I'll need some time off after this... 5 protagonists, man..

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is yet another masterpiece from the Yakuza series, right up there with Yakuza 0 and 2. This time, however, you follow three new protagonists in addition to Kiryu.Shun Akiyama is the loan shark with a heart of gold (don't call him that to his face, though). He's an incredibly likable character from the outset, other than one line of dialogue where  that is way out of character for how he's written for the rest of the game. His fighting style is very kick heavy and is very fun to play. Taiga Saejima is a hardened ex-Yakuza with a soft spot spending time in the joint (wait, deja vu...). He is a character you really grow to appreciate through his side stories, so it's somewhat of a shame that  Unfortunately however, similarly to Akiyama, he has a moment that feels incredibly out of place with his character that leaves a very bad taste in the mouth. His fighting style is very defensive and the fighting early on is a bit rough. I  recommend  spending points on  as soon as possible, followed by  and  to make the early fights in his part easier. The beginning gameplay of his part was easily the worst part of the game for me, but it's worth sticking through.Masayoshi Tanimura is a police detective with his own brand of justice. He frequents Little Asia and is something of a polyglot. Interestingly, he's almost a prototype for the future Judgment games. There are even police scanner events that pop up throughout Kamurocho from time to time. His fighting style is based on the real life Taiho-Jutsu and has an absolutely busted parry mechanic. By and large, the gameplay is pretty similar to Yakuza 3, but one interesting feature new to Yakuza 4 (and hasn't returned since to the same degree) is the addition of explorable rooftops and underground in Kamurocho. The series has many great substories and Yakuza 4 is no exception, having some of my favorite ones in the series thus far. All in all, Yakuza 4 is a fantastic entry in the series and I came to love all 3 of the new protagonists, with Akiyama being my favorite by far.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're considering if this game is even worth playing after playing Yakuza 3, I can tell you it is, but you may be disappointed for entirely different reasons.First things first, the gameplay in this game is much much better than Blockuza 3. Enemies are not nearly as passive, so you can do things other than just spam grabs which is very welcome. On top of that, this game boasts 4 playable characters, each one with an actually unique moveset, playstyle, and upgrade tree, so it keeps combat feeling fresh in a way that previous games excluding zero haven't been able to compete with. This game plays just fine, and only has a couple annoying bosses, compared to blockuza 3 where every single boss was annoying. ♥♥♥♥ Blockuza 3. All my homies hate Blockuza 3.The only thing is that the final boss in this game is a joke. The following is a rant about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it is, so don't read it if you care about spoilers. Just know that however bad you're thinking it could be, its much much worse lmao. Still, one fight out of the whole game being bad, as opposed to the whole game being bad, is quite an improvement.TL;DR The gameplay is great. If you were worried that the gameplay sucked after playing Yakuza 3, don't be. Its not at all like Yakuza 3.The story I am not as positive about. It starts out strong, really strong, but somewhere in the second half of the game it just stops being interesting. This game is also filled to the brim with plot contrivances and offscreen bullets, and much of it never ends up making sense. By the end, I was able to accurately predict when someone gets shot through the chest with absolutely no warning or buildup for stupid dramatic reasons. You really can see the director's hand just manipulating things because they needed the game to be longer, or they felt like there needed to be an arbitrarily shocking moment, or they really needed an excuse to use a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boat chase minigame. The first half of the game is super interesting and fun, and then half way through it becomes like a cheap knock-off parody of what a Yakuza story is like, made by someone who hates Yakuza.The ending two chapters are particularly egregious. The characters become mind numbingly dumb and senseless for no reason  presumably because the plot would resolve itself if they didn't behave like idiots. The build-up to the finale is incredibly flaccid and weak, and this ending lacks any of passion that I've come to associate with these games. Its really disappointing because the gameplay is pretty good and the beginning was amazing, this game really just fell flat on it's face in the delivery.If you just enjoy these games for the plot, I am fairly certain at least one of the new playable characters in this game is a frequent returning character, so I would still play through this game so you're not missing context. Just don't expect to be thrilled with the story like you might've been with previous games. Again, the first half of this game's story is genuinely really good, it just falls apart later on. Temper your expectations, and enjoy it for what it is, and you'll be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a step up from Yakuza 3, but that's a really low bar to clear.  The idea of having 4 different playable characters is completely different.  However, the implementation of it leaves a lot to be desired.  There is no sharing of items across characters, so things you may have gotten the first time around, not realizing you didn't need them are sitting uselessly in your first storage and when you could use them with the second character, you have no access to it.  You have to learn 4 different fight styles, starting right back at the bottom with each new character.  The fighting system is old and outdated.  If you are going to sell it as remastered, at the very least improve the fighting, especially in a fighting game.  The damage system is flawed.  If your character can rip a manhole off the ground without special tools, or pick up the heaviest object or enemy, but when you hit someone with a crowbar , you do minimal damage shows that the game developers were not even paying attention to the game. Still working on the second chapter, and its tedious.  The whole dynamic of avoid the cops or else you go back to a previous save, without having save options easily accessible is pathetic and frustrating.  Not to mention, if you put a cop in the middle of the street looking one direction, to have the game force you to turn around because they can see you BEHIND THEM on the sidewalk is unnecessary  and tedious.  The mini games for each character is nothing more then random number generator results that make no sense.  The same crap of hostess trainer, dojo training, and so on.  The results are nothing more then the computer doing a rng.  You don't even control the students you are supposed to be training when they fight in a battle,  You just sit there and build their heat up to maybe use a finishing move, which does little to no damage, and if you don't QTE right, you take the encounter ending damage instead. Save your money for Yakuza 0, Kiwami 1 and 2 and Yakuza 6.  They are much better games that are fun to play and won't leave you ready to smash a controller into the monitor.  They are worth the money to own.  Go to You Tube and watch the video cutscenes for this game, it will save you hours of your life you won't get back.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a blast.The second of three titles collectively known as The Yakuza Remastered Collection changes things up in dramatic fashion after the laborious Yakuza 3, it’s a much more enjoyable game for the average player in both gameplay and story.Four heroes! We have not one, but four protagonists to run around Kamurocho with, all with a unique fun approach to combat, their own sidecontent and a unique outlook on not just the story, but the world around them. Kamurocho itself becomes a fresh face again, new areas to explore and character-specific routes give a lot to hand a newfound appreciation to the district. Entertainment wise, this will gripped you as much as the other titles did.About the story and narrative, you know what to expect and I can assure you it won't disappoint. The story is again as usual very good and intriguing with plot-twists, melodramatic moments and of course, action, lots of violence. It starts with a very good pace and the longer you play the more complicated it becomes and it lasts until the very end. Honour, love, betrayal, death, friendship – you'll witness all of these. The franchise signature.I would say the downside is having to introduce a new character multiple times throughout the game, altough the experience feels fresh, it might feel a bit down since you have to start from the bottom and learn how to play each time. The use of multiple protagonists also interrupts the flow of the overall plot. While it starts out very strong in the individual chapters, it goes completely off the rails by the end of the game, with way too many tangents.Gameplay-wise controls are more responsive and the game isn't as janky as Yakuza 3, Yakuza 4 feels more fluid and welcoming to players, overall i'ts a slight improvement over Yakuza 3. Some of the new features in the series is introduced here, you now can climb on roofs and explore the underground of Kamurocho. Like always you're bombarded by substories, some good, some really fun, some weird. If you've played it's previous titles you already know what to expect.As a remastered title, graphically it looks slightly better than Yakuza 3 as well. In general they're very similar when it comes to looks. The city looks improved and character models are slightly better, pretty decent considering it was a PS3 release game. Sound as usual is very good, a large variety of music, voice acting sounds great, believable and dramatic. Part of the fun of playing a compilation of remasters is that you get a chance to see how the series evolved overtime. Overall a very good game despite some downsides, it does not show its age as poorly as Yakuza 3 does. Good character design and story outweigh the negatives by a large margin. If you play through this series blind, as always you'll gain an unforgettable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 features the same gameplay structure that fans of the series will be familiar with from the previous games, as you explore the open world city of Kamurocho while playing the main story, substories and minigames. The biggest change is that in addition to Kiryu, the player will control three other characters in different story chapters.-	The new characters include Akiyawa, a loan shark who runs his business more like a charity,  Tanimura, a cop searching for answers about his dad’s murder, and Saejima, a yakuza who was sent to prison for murdering several members of a rival family.-	I really liked Akiyawa and Tanimura, both are very interesting, but Saejima has zero personality compared to the other characters, so playing through his chapter was the least enjoyable part of the franchise so far in my opinion.-	Saejima does get the best minigame though, which is basically a Kobra Kai simulator where he trains students to try to win a martial arts tournament.-	Story is excellent because of the way each of the four playable characters’ personal stories slowly link together, while also featuring lots of NPCs from various yakuza families and the police force, all of whom have their own agendas. Expect lots of deals and betrayals, twists and turns, all played out in highly entertaining and dramatic cinematic cutscenes.-	Combat feels much better, smoother and more responsive than Yakuza 3, which felt a little clunky. Bosses no longer block 90% of your attacks, so those fights feel like the epic showdowns that they’re supposed to be.-	Again, Saejima was the least enjoyable to play as. His combat style is really slow and his attacks have a very short range, which makes some early boss fights extremely tough. Saejima’s strength allows him to pick up and throw the largest enemies, but of course the bosses that gave me most problems were immune to being grabbed. One boss fight against a very important character whose name I won’t spoil almost made me drop the difficulty down to easy out of frustration, after at least 10 failures I was in “one last try” territory when I finally got it done.-	Combat with Akiyawa and Tanimura is much more enjoyable, being fairly similar in style to Kiryu. With all of Kiryu’s moves unlocked in the final chapter, I really felt like the Dragon of Dojima, just absolutely destroying everybody.-	It took me 42 hours to complete the main story and over 40 substories, so value for money is great.-	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.-	Controls worked great on my xbox 360 gamepad. This also includes chase sequences, which didn’t work properly for me in the previous game, but now have improved control mechanics (your character now autoruns, so you only have to control the direction).Yakuza 4 is a return to the high quality that I’ve come to expect from this franchise. The gameplay of 3 really felt like an old game, but 4’s gameplay and story are both comparable in quality to Zero and Kiwami 1 & 2.

_childDocuments_.review: With almost 76 and a half hours put into this game, this marks my fifth game that I've managed to fully complete on Steam. Will this game be a better pick for me than Yakuza 3? Or will this game fall flatter than the flat earthers that we have in the world? Let's find out.The game begins a year after the events of Yakuza 3, however not with our beloved protagonist Kazuma Kiryu this time. Instead we're forced into the shoes of Shun Akiyama, a moneylender who runs Sky Finance, a rather unorthodox moneylender as well. The Tojo Clan has taken blow after blow, and it seems the structure within the Clan is shaking. Behind the scene however it seems that a dark secret had been brewing for over 25 years now. As you go through the game you play different perspectives, of four different characters as they uncover the secret and do their best to stop those leading that dark, grim secret.One of Yakuza 4's biggest pros is that the combat has been changed and revamped, and the addition of three additional playable characters, other than our beloved Kazuma Kiryu. We have Shun Akiyama, who plays similiar to Kiryu's Rush Style in Yakuza 0/Kiwami. Very fast paced, additional quickstepping. Those who enjoyed Rush will enjoy him. Next we have Taiga Saejima, who plays more like Kiryu's Beast Style. Very heavy hits, but very slow. However his hits have a tedency to give super armor to muscle through. Lastly we have Masayoshi Tanimura, a more technical based character that's unlike anything in the game thus far. With a focus more on using grapples and submission move based heat actions. Another pro I'd consider for this game as well, is the fact that this game doesn't have an Exposed Dragon achievement. It still has a Mahjong based one, but not a tedious one. Additionally a feature I enjoyed was the Police Scanner, which is an activity for Tanimura. Quite fun in my opinion to do. Trying to stop crime in between substories and minigames.While Yakuza 4 has improved combat, for me it's still one of its largest cons. It's clunky and outdated. Simple as that. You don't feel it as much, but it is. What Yakuza 3 had too much of, in enemies blocking, and heat actions not doing enough damage, Yakuza 4 comes with new issues. A lot of the bosses have these aggravating 'super armor' moves that simply go through your combo while you're performing a Rush combo on them. Good examples are Saito and especially the last four boss fights in the game. Maybe it's the fact I play on a higher frame rate, but not even being able to get in a full combo, only to get punished with a super fast, unavoidable, super armor attack that deals a chunk of my HP on Legend? That's simply unfair. Even the Super Boss of the game felt more fair to fight than the last four boss fights. Additionally I feel like Yakuza 4 added a bit too much to the game. Every character has their own minigame. Akiyama has Hostess Maker (it returned), Saejima had Fighter Maker (Hostess maker meets Spectator mode), Tanimura had Police Scanner and Kiryu had the return of hunting gangs. Overall I felt like there was a bit too much to do in the game, and it dragged it out too. And the story, well, it isn't as strong in my opinion as Yakuza 3. Multiple characters, with shifting perspectives sometimes don't mix well. Yakuza 0 did it perfectly, but I felt like Yakuza 4 did it poorly.In comparison to the previous Yakuza games that I've written a review on, I feel like Yakuza 4 was my least favorite and the weakest game in the series in both combat, its minigames, and its story. I'd rate this game a 6'5/10. It's not a bad game by any means, but it's not on the same enjoyment scale as say the other games. I had heard how people praised Yakuza 4 for being 'much better' than Yakuza 3. Yet I feel the opposite is more true. I feel that Yakuza 3, despite its flaws, was a superior game in terms of its story. Not to mention its story didn't drag out the same way that Yakuza 4's story did. And the shifting perspectives, again, to me was confusing at times. Seeing you don't always know /what/ had happened for the other characters. And timeline wise it wasn't shown very well either. And while the blocking in Yakuza 3 was tedious, and the heat actions not doing a lot of damage was too, I'd rather take that, than unavoidable, super armor hits during my Rush Combo any day.
