_childDocuments_.review: The Yakuza 4 Remaster is the second stop in my ongoing Yakuzathon. Set one year after the previous game and originally released only a year after Yakuza 3, you would be excused to assume the two games would be quite similar. Indeed many of the core elements are the same, this game in fact expands on several mechanics from the previous game. Of course, not always successfully. Yet, what is arguably the biggest change is that this time around long-time protagonist Kiryu Kazuma takes somewhat of a backseat. The game stars, besides him, an additional three more characters. All of them new to the series.The game starts with Akiyama Shun, an eccentric Kamurocho moneylender who asks for no interest or collateral, instead he lends to people that pass his seemingly arbitrary tests. It continues with Saejima Taiga, a death row inmate and legendary yakuza, who has spent the last 25 years of his life behind bars. Then the game proceeds to Tanimura Masayoshi, a maverick cop who follows his own Robin-Hood-esque brand of justice, taking from the rich and giving to the poor Asian immigrants whose community he has adopted as his own. Before finally returning to Kiryu as he gets inadveredly dragged in yet another yakuza power struggle. This time a reprise of a conflict that started 25 years ago and originally sent Saejima to prison.To call the plot twisty would be quite the understatement. The game seems hellbent on pulling the wool over the player's eyes whatever the cost. Even if that means the main story will attempt to weave together several past events and give them a different spin, by introducing a powerful new actor that apparently was pulling everyone's strings all along. Even if it means the plot will serve you straight one of the most ridiculous plot twists in modern gaming. I won't spoil, trust me you will know it when you see it. Now, this is a Yakuza game, the ridiculous is to be expected. Often, it serves to enhance the game's cool factor. This variety of ridiculous though disestablishes the background of one of its primary characters, severely damaging the narrative. All in all, the plot may have its moments, but generally fails to impress when it doesn't outright exasperate.Of the new characters, Akiyama is arguably the most fun to play. Not only is he an interesting character, his devil-may-care attitute belying his powerful sense of altruism, but he also handles quite well and has the coolest side-character, his chubby secretary Hana-chan. His fighting style is quick and involves primarily kicks. He is not Kiryu but going through his section is a breeze. As a contrast, Tanimura is probably the game's flattest character. His primary motivation is simply to discover who killed his stepdad. He fights in a, fairly weak and repetitive, parry focused style. More so, he doesn't really seem to fit the game's tone. I mean he is a police officer, yet he rarely even bothers showing his badge to the various gangbangers and hoodlums he encounters. So what's the point?Then we have Saejima, perhaps the game's most compelling character storywise, since much of the main plot revolves around events he played a part in. That said, unfortunately, his game segment is a slog. Saejima's fighting style is slow and rather cheesy, starting in prison with no healing items, the prison break involves many difficult battles and tons of frustration. By the end of it, you will really hate Saito, the warden, with a passion. Even after reaching Kamurocho, you'll be constantly hunted by the police and forced to stick to the sewers. Yes, that annoying chase mini-game from Yakuza 3, it returns here with a vengeance. Let's just say, by the time you are back to playing Kiryu you will be really quite grateful. Just like in the previous game, Kiryu is a beast.By now it should be obvious that the game is quite uneven. Some segments play great, others not so much. Some of this can be attributed to the new playable characters. It must not be easy to create fighting styles as interesting and fun as Kiryu's, imagine three of them. Still, I believe, that much of it was due to completely avoidable bad design choices. Why have such a difficult entry boss for Saejima? Why so many lame chase scenes? Why make the awful hostess management minigame from 3 a part of the main story now? Why have the player finish with each character before playing the next? Sending them after hours of progress back to level 1. So no, I don't think the new characters were the main problem. Besides, Tanimura-excluded, I did find them quite appealing, I believe they have potential. When it comes to content, yet again it's a mixed bag. On one hand, the main story is significantly longer than that of the previous game. On the other hand, with four main characters, it's nowhere near long enough. By the time you start getting the hang of one these characters, oops his segment is over. The same goes for substories. There are several great one here, but there are also some quite vague ones. They are also few in number. Only about 15 or so per character. Compare with the previous game that had over 100. Even map-wise, Yakuza 4 only has one open-ended area to explore. Good ol'Kamurocho. Only Yakuza 1 I believe was so narrow in scope. I mean sure, Kamurocho now has rooftop areas, sewers and underground malls and parkings. But those are a bit of a maze and take a lot of getting used to, without offering quite enough in return for the investment.This game was a surprisingly underwhelming experience. Coming in hot from Yakuza 3 I expected more of the same. A somewhat imperfect but still highly entertaining Yakuza game. What I got instead was a game with lots of unrealized potential and flaws too glaring to ignore. I certainly don't regret the time I spent on it. In fact, I would say that for Yakuza fans, uneven as it may be it remains a must play, as long as you are prepared and can tolerate some frustration. Overall though, much as I would like, I can't really give this a thumbs up.Finally, I would be really quite remiss if I did not exclaim, for the sake of posterity, a loud and clear: F*CK Saito!

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is in many ways the bridge between the modern era where Yakuza fully coalesces into the phenomenon it has become and the somewhat jankier history of the series. It's a great game that is at times held back by its older contrivances and cases of the devs getting to grips with a game of this size and scope. This is my second time around playing it (as I played it when it originally came out on PS3), and I've completed a basic run of the main story line with sub substories from this release.Firstly, in some ways, it is an absolute miracle that in 2024 we have the absolute slew of mainline Yakuza/Like A Dragon releases available on Steam and multiple platforms. At the time of Yakuza 4's original release in the West in 2011, nothing of this scale had been localised into English. While JRPG releases were regular occurrences, games like this never usually made it beyond Japan and were dismissed as at risk of under performing and being costly ventures with little to no return. The games had their fan base, but for the longest time, this was looking like the LAST English-language release in the series (until the 5 year wait for a digital only release for 5).While Yakuza 3 was a bit of a diversion, 4 returns to Kamurocho in full, but with a major distinction: for the first time in the series' history, the game had multiple protagonists in an interlinked crime drama that explored experiences of civilians, police and the yakuza groups. The game starts with Akiyama, a money-lender and kick-centric style user, who becomes embroiled in clashes between the Tojo Clan and a competing group in the opening act. This is followed by Saejima, a brawler and grappler yakuza who is on death row, Tanimura, who is a semi-rogue cop with a grappling/counter-focused style, and finally a return of the man himself Kazuma Kiryu. Much like the later release Yakuza 0, this game has an interlinked plot that brings all of the protagonists together. It has its ups and downs, but it all builds to a very strong finale and many of its sequences became the template for what we love about the series. High drama, flying fists and excellent crime twists are all a highlight. Likewise, the performances of all key characters are on point.While the above is very much one of the major steps towards the modern state of the franchise, there are elements of Yakuza 4 that are held back by its past. Admittedly, it wasn't until Yakuza 0 in 2015/2017 that the franchise perfected its combat. While all of the four characters are perfectly serviceable and fun, there are jankier elements that do feel a bit rougher. While there is a defined improvement over some of the cheapness of Yakuza 3, some encounters may still frustrate players. It does feel like some encounters have been tweaked since the original release, but enemies with large weapons, firearms or rapid dodging can still feel awkward and a bit cheap. The new trio's styles are all good, but your mileage may vary in terms of how well they work for any given player, given their individual quirks. In many ways, these styles feel like the prototype for the multiple styles featured in Yakuza 0.While I didn't spend too much time with the expansive side content, Yakuza 4 has a wide range of options that are very much in line with what's expected of the series. There's a good range of side stories, revelations for each character, and even character-specific ongoing side-quests. However, unlike some later releases in the franchise, the side-stories may be set to the side as the main plot progresses. It's actually quite possible to finish the main game while barely touching this content. As said above, given that this is my 2nd time around, I mainly stuck to the main story, with some diversions. There's still plenty to do, but it doesn't feel quite as essential as some entries in the series.The Remastered package presents a fully functional port that smoothly runs at 60FPS, which is massive upgrade from the original PS3 port, which fluctuated in its frame rate. While the age of the game is still apparent (particularly when compared with Yakuza 0 and later entries), it still looks fairly good for its time. The little details like crowd density and lighting are a nice touch as well. There is one major issue with this Remaster which may impact some older fans' perspectives towards this release - the previous actor of Tanimura was arrested in Japan due to drug-related charges and because of this, Sega scrubbed him from the release and replaced him with a new actor. In all due honestly, I wasn't really that fond of the original choice for Tanimura and I do really like his replacement. Beyond that, there's a series of quality of life improvements that collectively make this a far better version than the original release.If you're a fan of the series, this game is essential. Much like Yakuza 3, there are parts that show their age, but this is very much the beginning of all the pieces coming together to make the franchise that we all now adore. If you're dabbling in it, it's best to check out Yakuza 0 and take it from there. Onto Yakuza 5!

_childDocuments_.review: Of the Yakuza games I've played at time of writing this review (Zero to 4 + LAD), this is easily the worst one in terms of combat.Yakuza 4 uses the same combat mechanics as Yakuza 3 - so you've got somewhat janky controls compared to newer titles, wall-bounding and so forth, though the developers made an active effort to reduce how much even regular enemies block your attacks, which is a welcome change.That's where the positives end, however: As instead of blocking, enemies seem to have a fetish for grabbing the player, and their ability to do so is even worse than Marth's grab range in Super Smash Bros Melee! Case in point: Not to mention that enemies seem to have a habit of course-correcting around to hit you in the back - despite starting in front of you - means that you can and you WILL be stunlocked to oblivion. There's been countless of random street fights where I've been completely unable to do anything because a knife-wielding enemy charged at me, spun around and hit my back before the recovery animation of whatever attack was finished (or in some cases, even as I was getting back up from being stabbed in the same way just 3 seconds prior).Akiyma gets an ability that lets him quickly recover from knock-downs and a get-up attack, but is a sitting duck when grabbed.Saejima is screwed once he flinches and gets combo'd or knocked down, but has a move that lets him escape from grapples easier... Which never seemed to work in my experiences, and NEVER works against bosses on hard mode.Tanimura is in a similar situation as Akiyama, but at least has the ability to parry any melee attack if he blocks just before getting hit, which at least gives him a CHANCE to escape from being surrounded. He's still the weakest of the four in terms of pure stats and moveset (tho I found him at least fairly enjoyable despite that).And Kiryu's got it all: Get-ups, knock-down recovery, and anti-grabs (this one HAS worked a couple of times for me on hard, but still useless against bosses), making him clearly the only character worth using. Shame he's the last one you get to play.Overall, if you have to skip a game in the series for whatever reasons (being on a budget, already knowing the plot, etc.), this is definitely one you ought to avoid just from how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the combat is.

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike Yakuza 3 where most of its problems lie in how the Remastered port functions (or, fails to), Yakuza 4 was a pretty alright time. The game is essentially one giant expansion to Y3 minus the part where you're stuck in only Kamurocho the whole game, and being just a few months off of finishing Y3, I sorely miss Okinawa (or at least having a second city). My initial playthrough was on hard, 100% completion. The combat functions well enough, the minigames are mostly fine, and the multiple characters helps keep the experience from becoming too stale. I can't really say the same about the story, as when it's time for all the pieces to start fitting into place, they start forcefully pushing corner pieces into the center stage. Motives start to become blurred and characters feel like they're constantly changing allegiances, which just makes things a bit tiring to keep track of. This game is essentially Tanimura and Saejima's story, with Akiyama as a nice side dish and Kiryu for.. what? He's just kinda there because of some Y1 ties, but he's still very much appreciated. The finale fights are cheesy as hell, yet despite this, they still feel necessary. They feel good. They put a smile to my face.My only real minigame complaints are with darts, fishing, and table tennis. Darts and billiards insane difficulty seemed to have swapped between 3 and 4, resulting in a far harsher darts experience this time around. Table Tennis, with or without using the "heat generation" function, takes a long time to complete an actual match. As for fishing, man. I like the system that exists here, but pulling trash every other pull (especially at distances of like 100m+) starts to get really annoying quickly. Every guide on what fish to find where is wrong - I'll often find them never within the day or distance provided and the bait you choose actually matters (I don't mind this, I just hate being lied to). A lot can be said about each character's unique side content (Hostess(es)/Fighter/Dispatch/Gangs) taking a long time to do, but since I was 100%ing it anyways, I just took them for what they were.Outside of those few sore spots, I don't really have much to say. Game is solid. They are definitely the Yakuza Four(some).

And these guys here, these guys are nasty bad bad people. You're looking at four of the most brutal and committed individuals ever to grace Tokyo's infamous underworld, the Yakuza. Cross any one of these badass big shots and expect to be stripped of your pride dignity and limbs. One by one. Nice. These monsters have shot stabbed punched strangled kicked and scrapped their way to the top of the pile and they're not likely to be stopping anytime soon. And just to add a little more fuel to their angry angry fires the big bad boss with a checkbook has been sliced and diced and payed the ultimate price. So now understandably all kinds of ♥♥♥♥ is going down here in which anything could happen, and I mean anything. Sushi showdowns? Sure. A motorcycle to the skull, hell why not. These guys are so tough they don't even use umbrellas, and that's saying something. And you wanna know the craziest part about all this is? The ladies love it. _childDocuments_.review: The middle child of PS3 Yakuza.You probably wonder why it's the cheapest key you can buy. I think there are reasons for that but bear with me a bit.Yakuza 4.You'll start with a new protagonist, Shun Akiyama, known as "The lifeline of Kamurocho". He's an owner of Sky Finance, a money lender company without interest or limit. The only thing they have to do is pass his test, varies by how much they're going to ask for.One day he got a visit from a mysterious woman, asking for 100 million yen. And that's how the story start.You'll play 4 characters, probably already spoiled by the game cover, and 4 chapters per character with chapter 17 serves as the finale.The gameplay.+ Vastly better than Yakuza 3. There's no blockuza BS. However, you'll still need to use your head to fight against bosses.+ Not so much grinding in the game. I mean you still have to fight in the streets a bit but you don't need to grind like it was in Y3.+ Money isn't that needed in Y4. Unless you're playing at Hard or Legend difficulty then you probably will have a grindfest and that's quite hard to do so.- Minigame is boring af, probably worse than Y3. I don't even think there's any minigame I want to spend my time on.- You'll encounter many side stories within a span of like 100m walks and the worst thing is that there's no menu for it so you have to remember where you need to go or you'll probably forget there's a side story at this place. And there's no marker in the map for that like what's in the newer games.The storyIt makes sense if you can keep up what's going on. I mean the whole thing, apart from past event, happens within span of a few days which somehow doesn't make much sense compared to how big the event is.It doesn't feel rush, don't get me wrong, but it's probably the weakest story in the series.It's still fun to play and stuff but the reasons behind everything is so damn too convenient for the story to conclude like that.I think if you want to rush the game, you'll probably finish it under 10 or 15hrs.Graphics.Well, they probably think Y3 is a bit stiff with face animation or something like that so they went all in with Y4 by making it the funniest, goofiest face animation in the series.But visual-wise, just crank it to 200% rendering scale. I think it hold up pretty fine.So why it's the cheapest?Well. Mid gameplay and mid story. Pretty mid like a middle child.Y3 nailed the story much, much better. I mean it makes sense and not making me feel "Well, ain't that too damn simple?".Y5 nailed everything that's not the story. From minigame, side stories, gameplay and everything. I think I can play Y5 just the side stories and minigames alone for 10-20 hrs and not bored out of it.Y4 doesn't. Very boring minigames, forgot where to go next for the side stories like most of the time. The story doesn't have much weight and just throwing a plot convenience to make it "make sense" when actually there's plenty of way to solve the problem.Overall.It's probably the weakest of Yakuza game when you consider both the gameplay and the story.While Y3 just need a Kiwami treatment, there's probably no way to save Y4.By trying to tell 4 characters' stories, we don't have time to develop the character (figuratively, not literally) and by the end of the game, some character is just there like a cameo (which is actually true as one of the protagonist is just a star guest which appeared only once) that's nothing more to just a piece to make the plot moving on.Still recommend?Yes. _childDocuments_.review: Welp, seeing as I've left reviews for every Yakuza game thus far, looks like it's time to review Yakuza 4!(For a TL;DR: 0 > Kiwami 2 > Kiwami > 4 > 3)Yakuza 4 is a little bit of a divergence from what you've had time to get used to with this series, though it isn't a bad thing! In fact, it does this new structure fairly well, although a prototype of the mechanics we will later come to know and love. What is this new structure? Well, it's actually the implementation of a multi-protagonist system! Unfortunately, though, since this is the first Yakuza game to have this kind of mechanic, it does have its fair share of flaws.One of the main flaws of this game is how it begins to fall apart in the plot department around halfway to three-quarters through. I honestly didn't have a good idea what the hell was going on past the halfway point. This game suffers from way too many betrayals and backstabs, some of which I seriously don't understand the motive of even now Also, Kiryu feels like an afterthought compared to the other protagonists. Out of the four, he is the least important one, and I really wasn't too sure how I felt about that. Unsatisfied, is probably what I have to settle on.However, despite some plot failings in the ending half, the first half of the game has amazing plot and story progression! The second part was probably my favorite, and . There is some much-appreciated backstory on Majima as well, , so I enjoyed that a lot. The combat is good, better than Yakuza 3 by leaps and bounds, and it's varied due to each of the four protagonists having unique fighting styles. Akiyama's is particularly fun. There's something for everybody in the combat department this time!The minigames still haven't been refined, but some primitive business style substories do appear here. Most of them feel extremely grindy rather than fun, though. Completion for the minigames is a little bit too much of a chore for pool and darts in this game, in my opinion, but much of the other minigames are doable, if rather difficult.These are all nitpicks, though. In the end, this is a solid entry into the Yakuza series, and you can definitely see it beginning to refine itself into something more like some truly great entries, like Yakuza 0, and setting up for the next game to build upon these building blocks. Not too much else to say but to play this game!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR This is a great game in a great franchise, one of the best of the series imo (mind you I've only played up to this point as of this review, I'm on to Yakuza 5 fairly soon after I do more of the side content here). However, the story here ties in very heavily with all the previous games, so I'd recommend playing those first if you are new to the series.Coming off of Yakuza 3, this game feels quite more bold and polished. unlike the previous two games, which felt a bit "episodic" in their stories at times, this one does a great job at pulling everything together from the past games, and showing the results of everything that has happened over the course of the series thus far. The four different main characters each with their own section of the story was quite interesting, and really changed up the way that storytelling is approached in this game, seeing the plot unravel from multiple different points of view, until it all comes together for a big finale, which I quite liked, and I feel like it worked very well as a whole. All the protagonists were likable, and different in their own ways. It is a little weird having to use different move sets and restart upgrade trees every time the game switches main character, however. There wasn't a character that stuck out like a sore thumb in terms of combat, they are all similar enough, but after playing all previous games in the series you generally stick with the same move sets all game, with the only exception being 0, in which you do have a bit more control, and there are only two characters to swap between instead of four. All in all though, I felt combat was much improved over 3, while by no means the best in the series imo, but overall solid and it didn't ever have me crying at general jankiness and stupidity. The upgrade system, which RGG Studio seems to love changing every title, is pretty good here too. It's a bit watered down compared to previous titles, but I still quite like it because it's not an eyesore or unnecessarily complicated.The side content here is just as good as ever, however I do think that being constantly swapped between different characters kind of discouraged me from doing it in a weird way. I pretty much waited until the game finally swapped me to Kiryu before doing much of any of it besides some karaoke as Akiyama. Which, karaoke in this game is quite weird, since each character has their own libraries to choose from, with Akiyama and Kiryu being the only two with anything notable. Tanimura has two mediocre interjection songs, and I didn't even try it as Saejima. Kiryu does have quite the selection, however, and there is also machine gun kiss in this one, which is easily one of the best karaoke songs in the series.The map is also quite different in this one from previous games, since you have access to not only the rooftops of Kamurocho, but also the underground. These sections of the game are interesting additions, but I feel like they don't really add a whole lot other than serving as locations for a few campaign sequences, and a couple of substories. They are also a tad annoying to navigate, but maybe that's just because I have the streets of Kamurocho engraved in my head at this point.As a whole, a very good entry in the series, those of you like me who slightly struggled with Yakuza 3, hopefully you will find this one a whole lot more fun. Not that I think 3 is bad, the gameplay, specifically the combat, left a bit to be desired imo. Either way, great game, if you like the series, buy it now.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is my new favorite from this series and I think that playing through this game has led me to finally understand why I loved Yakuza 0 more than the other titles so far. Imo Yakuza as an entity is at its best not because of Kiryu in a vaccuum but because of all of the interesting characters around him. Kiryu is a great character, dont get me wrong, but kinda like batman you know he's going to punch people and that will fix everything. Without compelling villains/side characters you'd get tired of it eventually because they feel static and unchanging, they have their moral codes and stick to them. Yakuza 4 having 4 playable protagonists allows for so much more intrigue, as introducing 3 new characters with their own angles at work in the scheme of things leads to so many new and exciting situations where you can't just assume that it's going to work out how it always does. That's why I loved Yakuza 0 so much with playing as Majima and that's why Yakuza 4 works even better.The writing and plot of this game is the best it's ever been, hands down, and piecing together the timeline of that fateful incident 25 years ago never leaves a dull moment. You'll play 4 chapters as one character and as you reach a big reveal, you get switched to someone entirely new. Every time it kept me wanting more from the previous character but within minutes the new protagonist grabs your attention and holds it just as well as the previous. Then once the squad is assembled it's time to finally finish things in possibly the biggest climax yet.Combat and leveling is real nice, and each character has meaningful differences in fighting styles. Akiyama moves quickly with long combos, Saejima is slow with short combos but they hit hard and can be charged, and Tanimura gets a cool new parry mechanic and has flexible branching combo options. Then Kiryu, being the last character you unlock, is generally good at everything but gets a much larger pool of heat moves and can activate them in so many different circumstances, making it super satisfying and raising the intensity to match the high stakes.For side quests they largely seem to be fewer but longer, but the ones I did do were still fun as per usual. Revelations are still absurd and are always a treat.Minigames are mostly the same as in Yakuza 3 plus some character specific minigames like running a hostess club as Akiyama, running a dojo with Saejima, or handling disturbances around kamurocho as Tanimura. The karaoke scenes are relatively tame but still fun (very disappointed that Saejima is too serious to go sing though, would have loved to be able to see a song with him)Overall, 9.5/10, new series favorite, would have been a 10 but you can't make any of your characters equip the purchasable cat ears or a maid dress. Cowards.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has 100% Yakuza 4: Remastered, here's what I think about the game:This game breaks away from the usual formula of having one grand story following Kiryu Kazuma, instead we have (in my opinion) pretty bite-sized stories following the odd loan shark Shun Akiyama, the fabled Taiga Saejima, the rebellious officer Masayoshi Tanimura, and of course, the legendary Kiryu Kazuma. Every single story was nice to follow along and I think for just 4 chapters each, they did a pretty good job with creating depth and life to these characters, however I believe Kiryu's side of the game was just surprisingly short to a fault. My only real complaint for the story itself is that it's pretty easy to get lost early on in the first section of the game if you're not drawing connections yourself without the game having to really explain it much, so I found myself having to really look things over again to really be on track with things and understanding who is associated with who, names and clans, etc.For the gameplay itself, the combat handles itself VERY nicely. For those playing the games in order like myself, starting with Y0, you'd know that Yakuza 3's emphasis on wall bounding was pretty stressed and if you eventually learned how to utilize it as much as possible, coming into Yakuza 4 and seeing how much easier it is will feel very welcoming. You are also rewarded handsomely for going out of your way to do side activities instead of breezing through the main game with things such as gear, abilities, and even stat boosts.For any fellow achievement hunters and completionists: This game will definitely take a moment. There are MANY things to do in this game. Side quests, weapon modding, hostesses, minigames, etc., and it definitely gives this game HUGE amounts of play time with the wide range of activities to do. If you're looking to earn all achievements, though, prepare yourself and buckle up for a whole three playthroughs of this game because there are two achievements that are tied to difficulty settings. One is on the "Legend" mode as common throughout the other games, and one is for Normal difficulty. I initially played this game on Hard and learned the hard way that difficulty settings don't stack, meaning that my first completion of the game didn't net me any achievements aside from the one for completing the game.To say the least, this game is a time and a half. It's enjoyable and has nice combat to go along with it. I have high hopes for Yakuza 5 and I look forward to writing another review there!

_childDocuments_.review: That was a pretty grand recovery. Everything that was wrong with Yakuza 3 was either fixed or improved upon, and THIS is the entry that is good enough to be compared to Yakuza 0 and the Kiwami games. The combat is still kinda clunky, but the rate at which you gain new abilities feels so much better. There is only one map to explore this time, but Kamurocho's new rooftop and underground areas are big enough to count as an extra location anyway. By the way, you play as 4 different characters that each have their own individual progression. You may or may not like all of their fighting styles, but I thought they were all at least reasonably fun to play as. In terms of their personalities, they're all welcome additions to the Yakuza cast. The story does a fantastic job of fleshing them all out, and they each have the potential to be your new favorite character. The middle of the story is somewhat weak, but the final act is probably one of my favorite endings to any game ever. I would overall consider this game better than the first Kiwami, but still behind Zero and Kiwami 2. Not by much, though.

_childDocuments_.review: 🗾The first impressions I got from Yakuza 4 were insanely positive; in fact, . What I saw in the beginning (and what really took my breath away) were immaculately crafted, riveting cutscenes that I could just keep watching for days on end. Most cinematics in videogames are focused primarily on raw action and rarely deal with pure character portrayal, presumably out of fear to bore the player silly. Yakuza 4 subverts all expectations and first shows you some dude you don't even know chilling on the sofa and reading a magazine, then napping and doing his best to ignore a persistent phone call. Full of tiny little details and seemingly insignificant actions, this cutscene achieves so much in the character development department where an hour of boilerplate dialogue wouldn't even scratch the surface, and it does so in this mesmerising, ocean-breeze fresh way that wins you over instantaneously. I couldn't help but keep shifting in my chair and looking at my backseating partner every 15 seconds in complete awe, unasked question written in bold all over my dazzled face:  If only they kept this going, Yakuza 4 would be a strong contender for the best interactive media experience available.Unfortunately... they didn't. For whatever reason, things fell apart in a hurry. Like discovering that the pasta carbonara you ordered at a roadside diner contains a secret ingredient – a long strand of black, greasy hair covered in lice eggs – playing Yakuza 4 can be one nasty surprise. Actually, not even one, but several. Let's examine the strand of hair more closely and count the white-yellowish nits: one...two...three. Oh, four. Four big ones! 🐜 To be fair, each Yakuza game has its stupid moments and its gaping plotholes, but it feels like  decided to use every dumbest trick in the gоddamn book and quickly mutates from a charming 'femme fatale' into a ludicrous, negative-IQ Bollywood monster who incessantly spews one tired cliché after another seemingly at random, screeching and wailing and covering itself in a spray of its own noxious bile. Witnessing this was strange, almost surreal, like watching how a dear friend of yours (who you know is a good guy) drinks way too much, gets into a fight with a Christmas tree and then wets himself in front of everyone, but it was also mildly amusing and at times infuriating.  🐜 In any Yakuza game, there are substories that exist to help you get distracted from the main storyline and enjoy some zany adventures on the side, usually with a bizarre premise and an unexpected twist. Since basically nothing could remedy the stinking mess that the main storyline is in this game, the devs decided to not even bother and nipped any fresh and interesting ideas in the bud. Almost every substory with very few exceptions is a dragging snoozefest that simply involves running to different places. 3 was also guilty of this, but not to such an awful extent. For the first time in the series,  I can't even believe I'm writing this. 🐜 I still have songs from 0, 1, 2 and 3 that I listen to on a regular basis. 4, on the other hand, sounds bland overall, and sometimes straight up weird and unpleasant. I don't know how this could have happened to a franchise that has constantly delivered one musical masterpiece after another, but looking at the first two glaring issues, lacklustre audio design somewhat pales in comparison. 🐜 Not all of them are bad, of course – but this time we have  people (!), and it's not just your best boys Kiryu and Majima anymore. Now there are guys whom I would call arsеholes any day of the week without as much as a hint of regret or uncertainty. Awful, awful folks. One of them is particularly bad – this dude's story doesn't inspire me, his struggles make me roll my eyes, and this stale  talk he loves regurgitating so much got way too old long before I was born. For some reason though, this very person is kinda the most important guy all of a sudden, but it's like chewing on a plastic bag. There is no substance. No emotional investment. Every previous Yakuza game hit me in the feels, some made me cry. This one made me yawn so hard I almost dislocated my bloody jaw🙄  😌 Yes. Yes, there is, as always – nothing in the world is absolutely good or absolutely bad, and Yakuza 4 shines sometimes and makes you laugh and is fascinating and inventive in its own ways. But I can't really think of any saving grace truly worth mentioning here besides the fact that since you're so deep into this fictional universe already, you might as well pick up the fork and dig into the lice carbonara before it gets any colder. Be a good boy and clean your plate to get a dessert – Yakuza 5🤫🥇 From a completionist's point of view, this game is (thank you, Lord, oh, thank you, thank you) the shortest of them all and the easiest one to 100% – as if the devs felt bad about making you stick around any longer. Taking all aforementioned things into account... this was clearly a good decision.

_childDocuments_.review: FORGIVING THE WORSTI've wrote a review here but somehow it didn't save. Having a break and recollecting my thoughts, I face this game again with a new perspective.Let's get with the negatives first. This is the weakest story in the Yakuza franchise. Kiryu Kazuma, the main protagonist from the first three games is shoehorned and got nothing to do with the plot. The reason for Kiryu to step in is also kinda dumb. Although I took a long break and have soome of my thoughts and opinions changed, I still haven't change my mind on the main story. Enjoyable in a 'so bad its kinda good' way.I do commend the writers on creating multiple characters and tie em up into this one whole plot. Other than Kiryu, the other three are lovable and a joy to play. Each of them have their own stories, backgrounds, personalities that creates a dynamic that bounces off well on each other. This feat is then shown again  but better in its sequel; Yakuza 5.Onto gameplay, combat first. Just like the characters having a diverse of personalities, they also have very different fighting styles. The old and brute Saejima hits people like a tank, while the wormy corrupted cop Tanimura have a more counterattack style and use a more non lethal approach. Each of them have their own movestyle that never gets bored when switching characters.Typical Yakuza style, the side content are fun and is half of the experience. Lots of minigames, quirky substories, and also a sideactivity for each character. Saejima has his own sideactivity in training a young apprentice while Akiyama runs a hostess club. Dismissing this aspect of the game is a huge sin any player can commit.One thing that I noticed that I haven't mentioned before is how atmospheric the open world of Yakuza is. The dev team manage to create a living, breathing city. Walking through the streets of Kamurocho you can see many pedestrians doing their activitie. Lots of diverse animations that is borderline realistic. Sound design is amazing since you can hear the city ambience and pedestrians' footsteps or shouting. How alive is the city in such a compact size when compared to other open world games. Really shows that quantity is not the best quality.Many praise this game for the soundtracks and song. For me it is ok.Overall, a decent Yakuza game. Probably not the weakest gameplaywise since that belongs to Yakuza 3, but it is the weakest storywise. A must-play if you're binging since future games will bring elements from here and make up for it.3/5

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR, the same issues with Q-LOC's other Yakuza Remastered ports are still here but Yakuza 4 is a solid entry with some fun characters, a fun plot (although That Scene with Saejima is still weird as ♥♥♥♥), and enough switchups in playstyle to keep things interesting.Yakuza 4 is the first time the franchise got to experiment with multiple playable protagonists, and it manages to pull it off surprisingly well.Shun Akiyama, owner of Sky Finance and widely regarded as 'Kamurocho's Lifeline', primarily focuses on speedy kicks and evasion.Taiga Saejima, Goro Majima's sworn brother and former inmate, primarily focuses on hard-hitting attacks and decent crowd control.Masayoshi Tanimura, corrupt cop with a heart of gold, primarily focuses on speed, chicanery and single-target attacks.And... Kazuma Kiryu. He's Kazuma Kiryu.Each character has a personal story that ends up tying together with everyone else for a (IMO) satisfying conclusion, albeit one that may end up confusing a more casual player. I wouldn't say everything ties together flawlessly, but it works well enough frequently enough that it works. It probably won't surprise you if you've seen my other reviews, but I wholeheartedly recommend Yakuza 4. It's not my favorite, but it's still rock solid.

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime fan of the Yakuza series, Yakuza 4 left me feeling somewhat puzzled and disheartened. It deviated from the engaging side quests that had previously made the games so immersive, offering activities that felt disjointed and shallow. The surprising part? The lack of challenge, even on the standard difficulty setting. Fights seemed unusually effortless, making upgrades and skill improvements almost irrelevant. It was disappointing to witness the game lose its usual flair without a genuine challenge to keep me engaged.Initially, the storyline seemed promising, sticking to the typical Yakuza storytelling that I've grown to appreciate. However, midway through, things took a turn. The plot became a tangled mess of forced drama and unexpected twists, lacking the depth that usually keeps me invested. Instead of staying captivated, it felt like a shaky balance between compelling storytelling and predictability. And the combat? Well, having been through previous Yakuza games, playing as Tanimura was quite underwhelming, especially during those pivotal boss battles that felt more like a grind than a strategic thrill.The boss fights lacked the stimulating challenge I've come to anticipate, and the mechanics felt a bit off. Even the usually captivating substories felt lackluster this time around, leaving me yearning for more depth and coherence.True, Yakuza 4 did introduce some new characters and expand the game world, offering glimpses of the classic Yakuza storytelling that usually keeps me hooked.But, overall, as someone deeply immersed in the series, Yakuza 4 fell short. The lack of engaging side quests, the absence of a challenge, the inconsistent storytelling, the lackluster combat, and the forced drama just didn't resonate with me. For those seeking an immersive and fulfilling Yakuza experience, this installment might not quite measure up to the series' usual standards.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is a big step up from Yakuza 3 in any possible way:Greater scale, a plot with a lot more depth and it introduces new characters to the cast which since then have become fan favorites. Yakuza 4 is an icon of what every sequel should strive for. After Yakuza 3 RGG was like: We have to rush out another game. Yakuza 4 was released one year after Yakuza 3. Which is way too short for such a game, if you could ignore the asset reuse.Yakuza 4 completely reuses the whole area of Kamarucho which is the only city in Yakuza 4 but adds new areas to it which are somewhat relevant, but give the city a lot more depth and character. Always keep in mind that in Yakuza games the cities are as much characters as actual people. In Japan every Yakuza game has a subtitle, in the case of Yakuza 4 it was:“Successor of Legend” as they had the idea to replace Kiryu as the protagonist. This got handily thrown out of the window, because one character could not be reused as the voice actor got accused of drug use. Additionally, RGG was afraid that not using Kiryu would alienate their audience which was probably the right call. Yakuza 4 builds upon the foundation of Yakuza 3, but it impresses with quality and quantity. Featuring four characters with wildly different move sets, protects from fighting fatigue as fights actually feel different and provide variation in approach. And RGG fixed the blocking problem:Yakuza 3 suffered from enemies that block throughout the whole fight and forced you to use throws which dealt little damage. Yakuza 4 had to do one thing, and they did it:Enemies block less and the characters are fast enough to circle effectively. Although this does not mean that all characters are equal. Funnily enough, they are about as strong as in the story, but everyone still feels better to use than Kiryu in Yakuza 3.The only real flaw is the amount of grabbing going on. It is still way less atrocious than blocking, but it becomes annoying real fast. While not every character has a way to escape or counter grabs.Combat aside: Yakuza 4 does add some new mini-games, but not enough to actually warrant a new game.Everything got refined so that the controls are actually working quite well, but it is mostly still the same stuff as in Yakuza 3. Most of the side content is forgettable, at least the scale of Yakuza 4’s story makes it bearable.This was probably the high point of the Yakuza series in terms of storytelling, and it really shows. The story was written with a lot of fidelity and strong characterization for the newcomers while also integrating them well into the plot.And then it committed the crime of the dumbest plot twist in the Yakuza series which to this day is infamous by fans and gets repeatedly brought up, when discussing the most questionable decisions in the series. In spite of that, if you can ignore this one mistake and some weak side characters, what is left, is downright epic and fun. RGG is in on the tropes, but instead of subverting them, they play it straight and add their own twists to it. Although it is not groundbreaking, it has been refined to such a degree that no one ever will doubt that Yakuza 4 had not an ambitious story.Yakuza 4 does not have the chill vibes from Yakuza 3 and Okinawa, it is more grim and less bright. A perfect fit for the general theme of the game. If Yakuza 3 was about the bonds between people, Yakuza 4 is about responsibility. Every character carries burdens that they have to shoulder one way or another. It is haunting to see people who had such hard lives needing to step up for others, at one point you may ask if this is fair, yet this question is irrelevant. At some point what needs to be done, has to be done. And this is when Yakuza 4 peaks, it uses the set pieces for mature discussions about life and how one ends up in their respective situations. An effective way to showcase of how the road to hell is paved with good intentions. Then the music picks up, and the player connects with the game, feels the flow, this is when Yakuza 4 becomes untouchable. I have to stress that the music is fantastic, it contains some tracks which are the best of the franchise.Apart from these mature discussions, a good amount of substories is still very funny and well-written. If compared to the almighty Yakuza 0, they are still worse (on average with some outliers) though.Yakuza 4 is the point the series became great without any doubts or questions. While there are some hiccups, it is a captivating thriller that perfectly sets the precedent of how to utilize an ensemble cast.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 brings to the saga some fresh air needed after the formula for the three first games started to become a little rusty, and even if it performs really well in the early and medium stages of the game, it fails to give us a fulfilling finale. The main difference between the game and the previous ones is you can play with four different characters, including of course Kiryu, but letting the player feel other characters with the same quality as protagonist of the game. The story developing presents a solid construction and a slow-cooked style along with tons of cliffhangers and plot twists, nothing strange in the Yakuza saga. Corruption, betrayal and murder will be again the routine along the 17 chapters in the game. However, I think the plot is more interesting than the previous games, as I love stories where different characters have separate paths until they converge towards the end. And that's probably the only flaw the game has, the end. When I was completing the chapters of the game, I had the feeling a massive and outstanding finale was on the way. Without spoilers, the final chapter felt a little bit underwhelming from me, having in mind the potential for an instant-classic was there. Still, it's not bad, just on the same line as other Yakuza games. This time we only have one city to explore: the everlasting Kamurocho, but thanks to the addition of the rooftops and the underground system on the city, it gives a new way to explore it compared with previous times we've been here. With plenty of substories, minigames and secrets, you'll never get bored and can take a break from following the main storyline. Overall, the B-side of the game is like the rest of the saga, but I missed a little bit more complexity on the hostess management minigame that was features in earlier games. About the difficulty, I always play in normal mode, and while other Yakuza games felt more difficult combat-wise than it should be, Yakuza 4 was way too easy, so have that in mind if you want to face a challenge.  If you're following the story of Kazuma Kiryu the game will work wonders, as it's the same formula with more memorable characters and situations, but I think Yakuza 4 could be a little bit more than it is. Enjoyable game, nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 has a hilariously bad story that has you sit back and wonder what the hell they were thinking, but it's VERY entertaining. It's so ridiculous that you really want to know what else the writers are gonna pull out of their rear-ends, and occasionally, they show up with some hype moments and well-written (or at least likable) characters. What really makes Yakuza 4 a solid entry in the series though is the gameplay and side content. The combat and upgrade systems here are some of the best in the series (barring a few REALLY annoying boss fights). The substories were also quite memorable for the most part. There aren't as many substories in 4 compared to other games, but they're a good example of quality over quantity. There are some issues with this port of the game, though. All of the complaints I'll mention here are not exclusive to 4, but the entirety of the Yakuza Remastered Collection on Steam (aka, Yakuza 3 through 5.)1. Some of the cutscenes are in even worse quality than the original PS3 version due to compression.2. The analog stick is extremely sensitive. The pool and darts minigames are atrocious for some, but the biggest issue for me is that traversing the city in a straight line is difficult. Even the slightest tilt of the stick will have the character jerk to the left or right. 3. The quickstep distance is halved from the PS3 version, seemingly because of the upgrade to 60fps from 30.4. Certain licensed music from the Japanese release is absent.5. The game isn't as optimized as it could be, and depending on your hardware you might have some high CPU Usage.However, almost all of these complaints are relatively minor and have mods to fix them, with the only exception being what is for me the biggest issue, the stick sensitivity. There may or may not be guides to adjusting the deadzones for the analog stick in Steam controller settings, feel free to poke around on the Steam forums and look if it bothers you. As for me, I have played through this game entirely on vanilla and despite these complaints, I still had a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: A mysterious woman arrives in Kamurocho just as conflict is brewing within the Dojo Clan. Her sudden appearance also triggers a series of events that leads to four seemingly unconnected men to become tangled in her affairs and with each other. These four men – Shun Akiyama, Taiga Saejima, Masayoshi Tanimura, and Kazuma Kiryu – serve as the playable protagonists of .Akiyama is a moneylender with an unorthodox method of determining one’s borrowing worthiness; Saejima, an escaped death row inmate; Tanimura, a police officer with a strong sense of justice and a gambling problem; and Kiryu, a former yakuza who needs no introduction for fans of this franchise. Each protagonist has a four-chapter part that tells his side of the story in the broad narrative. The game culminates with all four storylines converging for a grand finale.It’s very refreshing to have  start off with Akiyama’s story. It signals  being a different game than its predecessors in terms of narrative and gameplay. Akiyama is suave and laid-back, but can deal serious punishment with his fast kick attacks if needed. There’s an air of mystery about him that reminded me of Goro Majima when I was first introduced to him in . I’d have been very satisfied if Akiyama was the game’s only playable protagonist.As Akiyama learns more about the mysterious woman, the game’s narrative transitions to the story of Saejima. Unlike Akiyama, Saejima is no charmer, but has a bleeding heart; he’s a tank, with powerful, slow charge attacks. He may not be as instantly likeable as Akiyama, but serves as the linchpin to the game’s story. From there, we’re introduced to Tanimura, who provides the law-and-order perspective of Kamurocho. His parry counterattack offers something new to the combat in the  series, and is effective when managing large groups of enemies.And then we have Kiryu, whose story frankly feels tacked on. By this time in the  main series timeline – whether you begin with  or the original  for the PlayStation 2 – there’s really not much more to tell of Kiryu’s story at his stage in life. I felt the story of  could have been told well without Kiryu, but I guess it was too much of a gamble for the developers to leave him out of a  game at the time.The noir narrative of  is comparatively more grounded and sombre than . (It's still absurd to a degree, especially with one truly ridiculous plot point, since this IS a  game after all.) The parallel storylines, with some scenes suggesting that our heroes could or might have crossed paths at some point, showed improved sophistication and maturity in writing. Akiyama repeatedly referring the mysterious woman as a femme fatale, however, is still indicative of the game series’ trademark lack of subtlety.Gameplay-wise, each protagonist’s part lacks substance to expand into a full game. But together, they form a whole that offers variety in adventuring and combat. Akiyama’s part is most similar to previous  games, including an improved, but still tedious, Hostess Maker mini-game. Yet, your participation in it affects Tanimura and Kiryu’s hostess club visits, thus offering incentive to work through the grind.Saejima, as an escaped convict, needs to be mindful of police patrolling the streets of Kamurocho. This is where the newly introduced (but underused) Kamurcho rooftop and underground levels come in handy. He also has a Fighter Maker mini-game, in which he trains Coliseum fighters, that is too confusing for its own good. Tanimura has Police Scanner missions, in which he responds to calls for help, apprehends criminals, and earns additional money. He’s also the only one who has access to high stakes gambling games.Then there’s Kiryu’s part. Aside from Gang Encounters side missions in which he fends off gang members hunting him for prestige/bounty, his part plays similarly as Akiyama and Tanimura’s. In the end, Kiryu’s bit in  makes the game overstay its welcome. Even his segment in the finale feels boring compared to the other three characters’ boss fights. Overall,  is a very good game that redeems the  series after the narrative, gameplay and technical mess that was . The story is restrained yet interesting; gameplay is varied but feels harmonious as whole. Technical flaws in the previous game (especially with framerates and enemies over blocking) have been addressed; even many (not all) upscaled pre-rendered cutscenes look more in line with the in-game cinematic sequences. One missing element that could have elevated the game to the next level is giving each character’s part its own colour filter/theme to give it a unique personality.More importantly,  shows that there are stories that could be told in the  – now  – universe in which Kiryu is not the focus. It paved way for  and , since Tanimura’s part showed that playing good guy in Kamurocho can be fun. The protagonists’ unique different fighting styles ultimately led to implementation of multiple fighting stances/styles in  and . Is  a home run? No. It has its share of bloat and missteps (including a final boss battle that is challenging to the point of annoying). However, it’s a solid, entertaining game that stands on its own and manages to steer the  game franchise back in the right direction.

_childDocuments_.review: As always, it's a delightfully goofy yet serious game, and I absolutely love it. It took me several months to beat this one. The constant change of characters always disrupted the flow for me, and as a result, I found myself frequently pausing for extended periods of time. In the end, I pushed through the long introductions, and it was an incredible experience. The combat is amazing; it's weighty and makes you feel like an absolute badass. It can also be very challenging at times, and some enemies can be infuriating to deal with. The lesson is: never attempt to play this game on hard without properly leveling up your character! I always end up making the same dumb mistake.The story can be very, very convoluted. The sense of mystery is always present, but some revelations can be incredibly goofy. The standout feature of these games has always been the characters, and this game doesn't disappoint! The plot can be dificult to follow at times but the characters carry the game with their incredible presence and charisma. Side note: For some reason, villains always resort to pulling out a gun after being defeated, and it's always incredibly silly.In the end, It was clunky, at times frustrating, and hilarious, but it's a Yakuza game after all. I definitely recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: A late and edited review, because Yakuza 4 was a mixed bag, and then I replayed it and loved it?Despite 3 being hated by people for it's gameplay, and 4 being praised because of it, I had the complete opposite idea going into this game for the first time.A few things in 4 made it feel more of a slog compared to the previous game at first. In 4, there is only one city, Kamurocho, which shouldn't be a problem since Kamurocho is an absolutely fantastic location that shines every single game, especially since Kiwami. In 4 however, additions were made to Kamurocho. You were now able to get to rooftops to traverse the city, or go underground. However, these areas are absolutely pointless, except for a handful of substories, a few useless shops and admittedly some nice locations, the traversal aspect of these locations does not work at all. These aren't shortcuts, instead they just make traversing the city more tedious, especially when you are forced to with a certain character in the story. Sitting through multiple rooms of loading screens does not help this game, and the map doesn't do a good job of explaining where the hell things are either. However, after playing the game again much later? I had no issues with any of these locations, and traversal didn't feel slow down compared to 3 anymore for some reason.Combined with walking around the city just feeling... slower for some reason in the first place, it was not fun to roam Kamurocho like usual, and for the first time after finishing this game I didn't feel like doing any of the substories or side-content, I did all of those in 3 after finishing it, just before jumping into this one, although admittedly, maybe there was a bit of burn-out? Coming back later I absolutely loved doing the side-content though, and each of the characters when finally leveled up are fun as hell to play with. Substories are an upgrade too.The story isn't all that great either. I think it's also because the bets moments were spoiled to me, so they lacked punch, because I can definitely see a lot of worthwile things in the story. On the other hand though, there are certain scenes in this game which hit really hard, but there are also scenes which are better on their own than when they're connected to the story. And admittedly, the characters are still as good as ever. While the story itself isn't too good, the locations and battles 4 takes you too are an improvement over 3 in some way, and the combat is more fun too.Akiyama's part was... less good than I expected. I thought there was more to his character from what I heard, but admittedly, he's still a great one anyway. If you're new and you know nothing you'll probably love him. He's the first character and it's nice to have a different look at the city through another character's eyes. His combat style is focused around legwork, and it's quick, basic and satisfying. Coming back to replay 4 later though, and loving Akiyama thanks to 5, there seems to be nothing wrong with his character. He's amazing, he's handsome, and he's the best boy. Same for Saejima and the others.At first I thought Saejima was also less good, but I have quite literally seen almost everything that happens to him beforehand. I'm sure that, as a new player, he could end up as your favourite. His combat style feels heavy, and he has some extremely brutal attacks. Tanimura is the third character, and he has an experimental combat style that doesn't quite work at times focused on parrying. His story was all over the place, but it had some really nice heartfelt moments. He's more of a niche character.Kiryu is the Dragon of Dojima everyone knows and loves, and despite his short and simple part in the story, some of the most interesting and heavy-hitting takes with his character are in this game. And for all of you who only played 0, his Dragon of Dojima style he gets since 3 is as fun and powerful as always.I finished the story and dipped, so unfortunately I can't say much about substories and the like. I have to say that 3 looked a little uncanny at times, and 4 looks way sharper in terms of graphics and all that. However, the gameplay and story are a notch down surprisingly. But it does make for a bigger, more experimental, funnr game, and I feel like some stuff pays off in 5 at least.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is one of the greater games in the series, you start out with Shun Akiyama, a loan shark who is a bit different from all the other ones. He keeps the story going nice and fast with his speedy kicks and laid-back attitude. Akiyama is one of the best characters in the series that just keeps growing. Akiyama's part is a bit too fast and you don't get to enjoy him for long if you just play through the story. Next is Saejima's part, an ex-yakuza with a past (I ain't telling you about what happened), his story starts when he transfers to a new prison. Long story short, he has to escape, so he does so with a returning character from Yakuza 3. His part is the 2nd slowest of the 4, but it is fun with his huge attacks and over the top heat actions. At the end of his part, we are shown the same cutscene from Yakuza 0.Next is Tanimura's part, which is by far the slowest, but it has by far one of the best character introductions. His combat mixes up the whole game, as he has a defensive style in a game series with offensive styles. I think there is too much story in his part, I wish we could learn about Tanimura more, but at least he has one last kick-ass boss before the last part. The last part is Kiryu's, he has the shortest part, but it is sweet, as his substories make this seem like the last game in the series, with returning characters from older games. He has the most developed moveset in the game, but he is a side character. He even fights two of the other characters from the other parts. The Reqium Chapter, is the ending part of the game, the first three boss fights are good, but the last one is a pain in the ass, his damn ARMY just keeps on you for so long. After his painful fight, the story ends and it turned out to be a great game.For just casually playing the game, it is amazing, but when completing it, hoo boy!!  It is a lot of grind and it becomes very tedious, but at least you get the satisfaction from completing everything. Casual Gaming, 7.8/10 Pretty GoodCompletionist Gaming, 5.5/10 Tedious and Grindy

_childDocuments_.review: This game is better than Yakuza 3. The story is just as good as previous games in the series and draws on elements that took place back in Yakuza 0 and 1 for some really neat moments. You might be a little put aback by the fact that you start playing as a new character, Akiyama, at the start, and you work your way through various protags until you get to play as Kiryu again; but don't worry, the characters are great and each person's story culminates in the finale really well.I did all the substories and beat the game on normal on my first run through, and don't have plans to replay on a higher difficulty, but it's definitely a fun game and worth the money to go and enjoy 40 or so hours of gameplay that stays interesting pretty much the entire time. The Amon fights after you finish the substories are pretty awful if you're unprepared, and Saejima's round is the most frustrating fight I've ever had in a Yakuza game, but one sour point isn't enough to dampen this review's thumbs up!

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a mixed bag with this one. Slightly near them? Grabbed. They're behind multiple enemies? Teleport towards you and grabs you. Just got up not even for a second? Grabbed.When you do the prison break part it can be a form of torture. Little to no healing items. All enemies have melee weapons, always a grabber and the main warden is some sort of legendary dark assassin being able to dodge attacks in an instant and doing never ending barrages of attacks. Which is funny since when you break out of prison and fight Kiryu I beat him in my first try when he's the main protagonist who's taken down all different types of enemies including legendary fighters and trained CIA agents.Later on through the game when you start playing as Kiryu the game starts to actually get fun with his move set being more fun compared to the other three and I didn't notice any grabbers anymore.The final boss fights are great as well until you get to the final boss where they thought it would be FUN to give you a crowd of enemies who love to dodge every second they can while carrying knives and giving the main boss a gun who shoots you every second he can and if you get near him he starts to run away and run around like a baby monkey.I'd say only play this if you want to play all Yakuza games but if you just someone who wants to play a game to pass the time I'd pass on this.

_childDocuments_.review: Great continuation of the saga. Much, much better than Yakuza 3 remastered! Great story, where we finally get to know exactly what happened in 1985, with the whole hit that lead Saejima to prison and Goro to lose his eye and then to be "encarcerated" in Osaka. Great characters too! Including the secondary ones (shout out to Hana-chan!)Loved the fact that we could witness the story from the perspective of 4 completely different characters, who have very distinctive fight styles. I realized that is one of the reasons why I loved Y0 and YK2 so much. It adds to the experience and fun - because always playing with the same character and executing the same moves over and over becomes monotonous after a while. Saejima and Kiryu can be fun at times, because they are stupidly strong, but I much prefer faster characters like Akiyama and Tanimura (and Goro) when it comes to fighting, so I had a lot more fun with this game than I did with Y3.Most of the issues present on Y3 are gone (namely the annoyingly stupid enemies that defend all the time). The minigames are good - the karaoke songs are pretty cool! (as opposed to Y3, where I didn't like any of them). I think Machine Gun Kiss and Pure love in Kamurocho are going to be playing in my head for a while xDThe revelations are back! And I love how ridiculous they are! Oh and please do complete all of the massage courses, to get to the extra special one! You're in for one of those funny wtf moments :PSo, highly recommend! Especially if, like me, you're in the journey of going through the whole Yakuza Series.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this for 34 hours, I asked myself, "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, why is this game STILL picking up the pace?????". It took me 50 hours to complete the game, and do a few things on the side I liked, and then the game tells me that I only completed 20% of everything. Talk about a lot.Now, before I go on to explain why you should definetly buy this game somewhere in your life, allow me to explain the state of quality of Yakuza 0,1,2,3,4. Yakuza 0 is a prequel, it was made after Yakuza 1,2,3,4, to add to the story in the past. Yakuza 1 and 2 were remade entirely as Yakuza Kiwami 1 and 2, those are the ones you can find on steam. Yakuza 3 and 4 were simply "upgraded" into modern times, and are available as Yakuza 3 remastered and Yakuza 4 remastered.The result is that Yakuza 2 Kiwami uses an incredible new engine and tons of fun stuff, and then you get to Yakuza 3 and it's all gone again. To me, this made Yakuza 3 feel a bit weak (for a Yakuza game), but I still recommend it to high heavens, it just...took me off-guard to see such a step back.But Yakuza 4 remastered makes it all better. When I played Yakuza 0,1,2, I kept thinking about Yakuza gaming every day, while I went shopping, while I was working on my career, while on the toilet. I kept talking to everyone I know about Yakuza gaming and I kept wanting to do more. With Yakuza 3, it was like seeing this same feeling through milky glass, felt like the game series that once washed me away is now an old grandma. Still as lovely, still as much Yakuza as the previous titles, but not the same as playing these games for the first time. Yakuza 4 relives that wonderful feeling for me, in all its glory, and more. I live in this game.But how did I get into this situation, you may ask? Well, I was just an ordinary guy. I play a lot of videogames, a whole lot. I'm not some quirky game critic or something and I don't really like most mainstream games simply because I see them in an ad. I'm more the type to play videogames only if they're truly, honestly fun for me, and not something tedious or repetitive. Then, I bought Yakuza 0 on an impulse, because I saw a few Yakuza memes. I knew absolutely nothing about the game, I read no reviews. I just bought Yakuza 0 on sale for 5 bucks, booted it up, and started playing. After 137 hours of playtime I finished it. I craved more. And more. And more. Every game delivers, somehow.So, I'll give you two recommendations, depending on your situation:You're like I was back then, you have never really seen or heard much of the Yakuza series? Hey, do you like strong men with good hearts duking it out for justice? Then stop reading reviews right now. Trust me on this one, even if I sound like a paid advertisement. Start the Yakuza series from Yakuza 0 here on steam, and just play. As blind as possible, look no further, just do it. It was one of the best decisions I've made in my life overall, and it might be the same for you. I'm really begging you to give this one a shot, soon you might look back and think "how did I miss this huge powerhouse of a video game my entire life?", and friend, I have no idea how we both missed out on this.Or are you like me now, did you think "hm, I played Yakuza 3, and I'm not sure if Yakuza 4 won't get monotonous..."? If so, rest assured. I've been playing Yakuza nonstop for hundreds of hours at this point. I haven't played anything with a story in between actually! So yes, I can clearly spot a few weaknesses Yakuza 4 has, but after I finished this game, I can only think "Man, that was so good again. If quality is already this high, then I can't wait to see how awesome Yakuza 5 remastered is".I finished this game today, less than 30 minutes ago. And I'm gonna install Yakuza 5 and play it tomorrow. Yakuza 4 remastered completely satisfied that itch, you don't have to worry. If you liked the previous Kiwami and Remastered and 0s, then you'll really really love this one. It doesn't get monotonous, it's awesome actually. Awe-inducing it is, too, really.Thanks for reading a bit of my mind. It's become really personal to me to try to convey how much genuine fun and happiness this game has brought me, without telling you anything about the content in the game. I think, if you play through this series blind, you'll gain an unforgettable experience. Of course, that is if you have any interest at all in seing buff men with wonderful hearts in their chiseled chests, fighting for what they believe in.
