_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 3 was a good game, but Yakuza 4 is a significant step forward. Even though it is almost the same game in roughly the same engine and only released a year later in 2010, it feels different enough. It's still noticeably an older game, but it doesn't impact the experience that much. Where Y3 I felt didn't have as compelling of a story, Y4 is far more interesting with its intertwining narrative of Akiyama, Saejima, Tanimura, and, of course, our boy Kiryu.There is one patch you should really get. As far as I know, there isn't the same kind of frame rate issues as 3 Remastered, but it does lack the higher resolution PS3 cutscenes, some licensed music, and more importantly, there was a significant change with Tanimura, the 3rd playable character in the game. For the Western release they completely changed his appearance and voice lines due to drug use allegations and there's a mod that restores his original likeness (guide on the community hub called "Yakuza 4 Hiroki Narimiya Restoration Patch"). It also includes the aforementioned cutscenes and licensed music, so it's a perfect all-in-one patch.Not to continually crap on Y3, but Y4 is much more compelling, a little convoluted, and harder to quickly summarize. These won't be spoilers, but I'll set up the premise more than the store page's super vague and useless paragraph. You start as Akiyama who runs Sky Finance, a loan shark business without the shark part that gives massive, interest free loans to people provided they can pass a series of his tests meant to gauge their character. A low level yakuza friend of his gets involved in a murder and disappears, sparking a conflict between the Tojo clan and the Ueno family. Daigo is still chairman and the usually insignificant Ueno group has this murder as a bargaining chip. Akiyama also meets a girl around this time who came in for a massive loan who's clearly running from something. Things happen in search of his friend and for answers about this woman. Then you'll switch over to Saejima. His chapters initially feel like they go in a different direction from the main plot (for most of the time I was left wondering what Akiyama was up to) but eventually work their way back in. I had a similar feeling with the Tanimura (except I was wondering what's Akiyama AND Saejima up to now), but this is to be expected for any story with multiple perspectives.I was hooked from the beginning in a way that 3 didn't until its middle/end. I think by now if you're a fan of at least a couple of these games (especially the older remastered ones), the handful of trope-y and goofy plot stuff can be given a pass. But I do have to say that one twist choice in the story annoyed me. It'd be a spoiler to say what it is so read this hint of the twist your own peril: , but that's a nitpick. Some other nitpicks would how some aspects of the ending felt a little too similar to Y1, actual spoiler: , and lastly the bosses and main villains. I think 0 and Kiwami 2 spoil first time players with awesome antagonists and if you're playing chronologically, the ones in 3R and 4R are a little lamer in comparison.Anyways, multiple main characters was definitely the right choice for the series at this point. As much as I love him, 7 games of non-stop Kiryu would run the risk of making his character boring and stale. All these other playable characters breathe new life into the series, lending it more narrative depth and the freedom to explore different themes they otherwise couldn't with Kiryu's personality. Each character has their own 'angle' with a different fighting style, personality, and activities to get up to. I was somewhat worried upon starting that the multiple characters were a 'sequel gimmick' introduced because they were running out of ideas, but fortunately they all play differently enough and have enough going on in their own respective chapters to feel truly inspired narratively and not a bunch of reskinned Kiryus.Substories aren't that different from Y3, but they feel a touch more inspired, probably because you're experiencing them as different characters. By now, Kiryu's character is pretty well developed, so the way he reacts to his stories is much more predictable and borderline formulaic. Now you've got these three other guys, and while they do share some characteristics and have similar motivations as Kiryu, they're different just enough.Where Y3 got slightly tedious due to its single fighting style, every fourth chapter in Y4 you get to switch to a new character who has a different one, keeping the whole game fresh for its extended 30+ hour playtime. Some people complain about how Saejima and Tanimura's styles are hard and stink, but that's kind of overblown; I like that they all play a little different. Yes, the first part of Saejima's story is definitely much more difficult than what you might be used to, especially on hard, but it's not unfairly so (though still frustrating and takes a bit of getting used to). Also enemy AI does seem improved and not as stupid as 3, though it is still a little dumb.What does feel like a sequel gimmick are the rooftops and subway/parking garage/sewers. Sure, new areas are always nice, but they seemed to exist only to give you new places to go, with very little consideration of what they actually add to the game. They're annoying to traverse and are ultimately forgettable as they weren't included in later games (I think?).Even though it's roughly the same game, in the same city, with similar characters, and a story similar to and as trope-y as the ones you've played before, it's different just enough to be noticeably better. If you're a near-completionist like myself who wants to do almost everything that isn't extremely painful to do (♥♥♥♥ shogi and ♥♥♥♥ mahjong), you'll get 40-70 or so hours out of this. If you just want the story and like ignoring substories, then it's more like 20-30 hours. You don't necessarily miss much that's important if you're speeding through it, but there's a good deal of fun in (most) of the side content.

_childDocuments_.review: My Best Soundtrack Award nomination for the Steam Awards 2021. I actually like Yakuza 5 Remastered's soundtrack more, but I had already nominated that game for the Game of the Year Award (sorry Halo Infinite, but imo there's basically zero chance that campaign is gonna be good enough to make up for the so far meh multiplayer compared to The Master Chief Collection's and top the masterpiece that is Yakuza 5).Anyways, Yakuza 4 still has one of my most beloved soundtracks in the series (I'd place it in 2nd behind Y5 actually and very narrowly ahead of Y0), and the series as a whole  has come to have my most cherished soundtracks in gaming beating out Halo. While Y4 is my least preferred out of Y0-5 (not sure yet where to rank LaD/7 as I'm still playing through it), it's still a brilliant game much more fun and full of soul than most releases these days. If anything, I just hope both it and 5 one day get free DLC similar to LaD to restore the Slot & Pachinko minigames cut from the PC releases. I highly recommend giving the Yakuza series a try, starting with 0 and going in numerical order from there.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 introduces a lot, maybe more than you can chew, which naturally leads to a game that is a lot of fun in the moment and retrospect, but it’s easy to be frustrated inbetween.The biggest change are the four playable characters, all with a unique fun approach to combat, their own sidecontent and a unique outlook on not just the story, but the world around them. Kamurocho itself becomes a fresh face again- the new locales, areas to explore and character-specific routes give a lot to hand a newfound appreciation to the district. As for the characters themselves, Akiyama steals the show from the start, and Saejima shares with Tanimura the role of giving us a new perspective of not just the Tojo but the world that sorrounds it. The newcomers are the highlights of the experience and carry the whole game to it’s conclusion as Kazuma shows up in the final act to break any skulls left untouched.Aside of this, if you come from 1-2 in PS2 and 3, the quality of life improvements are seen from the get go, with a better upgrade system and a nicer approach to encounters, sidecontent and clearer explanation of most elements at play. It’s a much, much more enjoyable game for the average player in both gameplay and story.There is however a point of mayor divide- the story itself, or should I say the conspiracy in it. While retroactively most of the points of contention can be reasonably be found as properly hinted, forshadowed and it’s possible to connect the dots yourself, the pacing of the scenes and the absolute drag of the cutscenes at times cause the revelations to feel like something pulled out of a hat.The pacing issues have most of the blame, but the amount of conviniences and writer tune does get in the way a lot. It’s not the worst story per say, but it has a lot of problems telling it, causing the frustrations to multiply.Yakuza 4 is still for the most part a net positive, with a lot to like, but I feel ironing out the flow a tiny bit would have made the game a almost unanimous positive. Also the soundtrack is fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another entry on the long running Yakuza series, 4 picks up the ball after it was dropped by 3.The story beings a bit after the post credits scene from 3 and has a far better pace.It tries to tie all the loose ends from the previous games and there are an insane number of twists and betrays.The only problem that I have with this game is how dumb the characters get when something related to guns is happening. Stuff like "leaving the loaded gun at the enemy arm's reach" (surely the defeated boss won't try using the gun and we won't have unnecessary deaths happen) and "rubber bullets" (just HOW you didn't notice the guy you just shot at point blank didn't had his brains fly all over the room??).The gameplay is still similar to 3, but has a better pacing. Enemies still have the same problem of always blocking and being almost immune to throws, but the game was rather easy on normal.I only had problems on two bosses, the prison guard that has super armor, blocks all your attacks and has several lenghty combos that can stun you and the secret boss Amon, that just cheats.Adding new playable characters brings new life into the series, its nice to see the world through a different point of view.You can see that the new characters were the base for the stances added in 0 and Kiwami.Akiyama has long and quick combos and better dodges, being the base of the Rush stance.Saejima has slow, but powerful charge attacks, with some super armor so he doesn't gets stunned while charging, being the base for the Beast stance.Tanimura probably has the worst moveset, his combos are weak, but he has a rather overpowered parry move that gives him invincibility for like 3 seconds when fully upgraded. You can easily lock enemies into a loop with a few moves. Other than that, he has a different grab move (that is useless on most bosses and bigger enemies) and can trigger a heat action on the end of every combo.Okinawa didn't return for this game, but Kamurocho is still full of substories and side activities. All gambling minigames are present (although pachinko was removed for some reason), baseball, bowling and billards are also here.All characters also get a side story:- Akiyama gets the bad hostess club side story that is so boring that I couldn't bother finishing it.- Saejima has a fighter maker side story that is also super boring, but you also need luck to finish it since the AI is too stupid to actually use good moves and will mostly quickstep around and get hit.- Tanimura has a very basic side story were you just have to walk around and sometimes a crime will happen in a street nearby, then you will get a fight or a chase sequence.- Kiryu has a gang side story that takes quite a while to finish, since most of the times you are looking for one of the gang members to fight and they barely spawn when you need them to.The graphics look pretty good for a Remaster of a PS3 game and I didn't had any problems with errors or crashes, aside the depth of field effect looking really bad, plus the fact all characters have this "aura" around them that makes the post-processing effects get a bit crazy and look terrible.In short, great game, picks up after the letdown that was 3.

_childDocuments_.review: For the first time in the series, we get 4 protagonists! (Gosh Akiyama is so cool)An action-packed beat'em up RPG game from 2009, remastered with better texture and frame rate. With the 4 protagonists system they introduced, Kamurocho suddenly feels much smaller, so they introduce the rooftop and the underground part of the city for exploration as well. I consider it good for its era: the story doesn't quite match my preference, substories shine in this game, the combat system is much improved compared to Yakuza 3 and leveling system is my favorite too. Compared to other games in the franchise, this game is where it gets real close to our "Yakuza standard", it has all the over-the-top hilariousness we seek and offer great experience, but still holds some drawbacks like graphics quality, CPU consumption, scarce save points etc., but don't be discouraged to try it.be warned: second part of the story has a difficult long fight and a legendary boss fight so do some research online for levelling tips, also the final final boss can go to hell.I give it a 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you need to know the story, play the game up until the final boss fight. After that, alt-F4 and watch the ending on YouTube. Trust me, it's not worth it.EDIT: It's been a day since I've "finished" this game and I can now properly articulate why I hate the final boss. Spoilers from here on out.Every final boss in Yakuza is meant to be a test of your strength and a way to put what you've learned to the test. Munakata does not do this, and instead opts to be an unfair situation that Tanimura has never been put in before. Kiryu and Saejima both have great crowd control, and almost every fight with Kiryu even in this game has you fighting multiple enemies at once. Tanimura always either fights one singular enemy or a group of enemies that are fairly spread out.The final boss requires incredible crowd control, something Tanimura has never needed before. I've seen many people tell me to just suck it up and go get sacred tree armor, and I would be fine with it, if not for the fact that Munakata is the final boss after a rush of three other bosses. I'm sorry, but I don't want to reload a save file and then grind a bunch only to go through those three bosses again and only have a CHANCE of the final fight even being fair. THAT'S why it's not worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 was strange... to say the least. I still enjoyed it because its more dumb Yakuza fun and this franchise has solidified itself as one of my favorites. However I did have some personal gripes with it, for starters the story and plot was great right off the bat to where I didn't mind that I wasn't playing a Kiryu but after a while it started to lose me to a point where I would forget scenes and events from my last play session. Akiyama and Saejima were so cool and Tanimura was not my favorite but I still enjoyed some of his scenes. The story would eventually pull me back in with a plethora of great Yakuza series styled twists. Finally while I didn't much enjoy Yakuza 3 all that much when I first played it, I've come to appreciate it a bit more after beating 4, and I bet I'll feel similar once I get through Yakuza 5. I also would like to add that the soundtrack in this game was really good as I found most of the songs super enjoyable to listen to, and it was not just the karaoke tracks that got stuck in my head.These technically are the oldest Yakuza games I've played since they are the remasters of the ones from the PS3, you can definitely feel their age as the controls aren't as modernized and some enemies and certain boss fights are just brutal to get through. The final portion of the game where its essentially a boss rush between our four main heroes was so brutal to get though on normal mode, I barely managed to scrape by it seemed. However I can't really fault the game too much for being a bit outdated in certain spots. While just like Yakuza 3 this game wasn't my favorite I still have to recommend it to anyone who loves this franchise as much as I do.(This was also the Yakuza game that I got the least amount of achievements in... so far at least.)

_childDocuments_.review: Before Playing Yakuza 4, I played Yakuza 0, Kiwami, Kiwami 2, 3 and 6. I enjoyed all of these games despite their flaws (yes even Yakuza 3). I previously just completed Yakuza 3 and while the combat and pacing of the story wasn't the best, I still thoroughly enjoyed the game thanks to it's great story and good soundtrack. So coming into Yakuza 4 I excepted a good story and soundtrack at least, surely it would improve a bit on it's predecessor right?   it's poorly written, predictable and generic so much so that the point that it becomes boring and hard to enjoy. It's full of plot holes and poorly written plot twists. The new characters are not given enough time to develop. While I did have a bit of fun in the chapters where you play as Akiyama and Tanimura, The chapters where you play as Kiryu and Saejima and Kiryu were overall bad.  So from what I heard the gameplay in Yakuza 4 was meant to be better than Yakuza 3 and while it is true that now enemies don't block a lot, I still find the combat worse because you will frequently find yourself getting  by enemies with batons only to then get instantly  by another enemy as soon as you get back up and then subsequently get  by another enemy. This is particularly infuriating when you play as Saejima who's an absolute unit and yet still gets smacked around like a punk by the enemy AI. Also speaking of gameplay, the ratio of gameplay to cutscenes is the lowest in any Yakuza game I've played, so you will spend most your time watching a crappy soap drama of a story instead of actually playing.  This game easily has the most generic and worst soundtrack out of all the other Yakuza games I played. I don't remember a single song standing out as particularly good. This game also easily has the worst bossfights. (with the exception of 1-2 actual good bosses) Also remember combat training to unlock new abilities in other Yakuza games?  They had the stupid idea of making training into mundane and annoying tasks like avoiding bullets, withstanding gunshots, digging a tunnel, and punching falling rocks. How they managed to mess up something as simple as training and making it into annoying gimmicks I don't know.Don't buy this game unless you're an absolute diehard Yakuza fan who wants play each and every single Yakuza game. Upon completing this game I feel burnt out and will be taking a very long break before I start Yakuza 5. Overall I rate this game 4  bullets out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is through and through a rollercoaster and I mean that in every way possible. To start with you do not play as Kiryu to begin with, he is instead the last character you play, if you inform yourself on games before you play them unlike me you may be aware of this. The next rollercoaster part is that there are 4 playable characters and two of them have awful combat but through endearing personalities and fun substories we tolerate them. This is alright as exploring is fun as always with new characters making you really feel different interests and stuff. A good example of this is 3 characters can go to the cabaret clubs, all three will be able to request different girls that they hit it off with upon second visits, just a nice bit of characterization for all of them.The next thing I feel a great need to talk about is the absolutely insane soundtrack this thing goes way harder than it has any right to, recieve and bite you is probably one of the best battle themes ever and every battle theme in this js mad.Enough talking about ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this games story is unhinged. I cannot stress enough how enjoyable this is though. Nearly every major showdown involves like three twists and betrayals. I won't spoil anything but I can say that I had a big goofy grin on my face with the last two big cutscenes and how wild they are, all of this isn't even to say the story itself is bad it is still great. And lastly mostly for anyone who played yakuza 3 on pc, the ai is much better, no more stuck fighting a guy who blocks for ever, the ai is also a fan of grouping up on you now so the bigger the mob the worse the fight is kind of, especially since most characters unless equipped with a pole or anything that does a lot of  aoe. I'll also say that grouping isn't the worst until the final boss then yeah it can kindly ♥♥♥♥ right off, I spent an age just widling them down. So all the stains of y3 are really gone in this one and treat you a lot better hereAll of this said, yakuza 4 is a great time and you should really play it if you've played the others.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is truly a game.As always let's start with the story, it's rough. The story really isn't even that bad but the antagonists make you feel nothing, none of the have any compelling motivations. Katsuragi wants to take over the Tojo, Munakata just wants control over everything, I don't even know what Arai wants, he switches sides so much in this game and his motivations are never being made clear and Kido just wants to make it big in the yakuza world. Such compelling characters. Sugiuchi could have actually been a decent antagonist for Tanimura with him killing his dad and all but the problem is the game expects us to care about Tanimura's dad because he's... well, his dad, the absolute minimum they could've done is showing a flashback of Tanimura and his dad having a sweet moment or something like that but we never get a proper connection between Tanimura and his dad leading to the reveal lame. Now as many people have pointed out the rubber bullets plot twist is not good. Not only is it really stupid in general but it overstays it's welcome, by a lot. Story aside this game is actually really fun. The different fighting styles between the four protagonists are a lot of fun to use and have a ton of variety. If you properly learn the techniques for each character, taking down enemies is really satisfying. Finally, while I said all the antagonists were ♥♥♥♥, the protagonists, thankfully, are not. Akiyama is one of the greatest characters in the franchise, Saejima is actually a compelling character in this game (unlike his other appearances), Tanimura is just the greatest character ever made, and Kiryu is kinda there, you can tell they had no actual plan for his character. It really shows how good the other characters are when Kiryu is the worst protagonist.Y4 is nowhere near the best game in the franchise. But no matter how much I criticize a Yakuza game, each of them hold a very special place in my heart which is why I can't bring myself to hate any of them

_childDocuments_.review: I would legitimately rather play 3 over 4.The story has this really cool feature where the writing takes a turn from bad to good and vice-versa every 30 or so minutes - to the point where I started predicting when characters would die from off-screen gunshots, only to later come back from the grave due to an completely horrible plot device.The final boss battle is the absolute worst in the entire series, from 0 to 4. I'm writing this as I play it. It's absolutely horrid.There are so many bosses and mini-bosses that have a combination of guard-breakers, constant super armor, or attacks that have less startup frames than yours. Sometimes all three, and to be honest, it's really annoying, especially when every other character is weaker than Kiryu and it feels like an uphill battle to do anything. You cannot mash out of some of these bosses unless you absolutely strain your elbow, and without upgrades, sometimes you cannot do this at all.Substories are sometimes convoluted to find, or are not described very clearly. If you miss out on these substories, you cannot play 1-2 more locked behind their completion. Not only that, but a lot of the substories in this game feel incredibly weak and also very boring at times. It's wholly and entirely disappointing, to say the least.The only redeeming parts of this game are the new characters, expanded kamurocho, and a slim portion of the plotlines. That being said, I don't  think this game is entirely unplayable and should not be played. It has a lot of moments where it has a lot of the Yakuza charm. If you want to complete the series, then go for it. However, if you're going to skip any game, I'd say to let it be this one; read a catch-up summary of the game or watch a video if that's the case.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is one of my personal top 3 Yakuza games as far as the story category. It was really refreshing to have a Yakuza game that allowed the player to experience the story from the viewpoint of four different protagonists, which all had compelling and interesting personal stories that each tied nicely to the overall story of Yakuza 4, as well as some great connections that were made to the previous games. It was nice to continue Kazuma Kiryu's own story while being able to branch out to the lives of other living legends in Kamurocho. I thought it was really cool that each character you play as had their own unique playstyle, which made leveling each of them up from scratch less repetitive, while also nicely changing up the gameplay throughout the game. One thing that I haven't talked about much in my other Yakuza reviews is Yakuza's soundtrack. From Yakuza 0 to Yakuza 4, I have loved the soundtrack of each game, especially 0 and Kiwami 2's soundtrack, and Yakuza 4 has continued to impress me as far as the soundtrack category goes.TLDR: Yakuza 4 was successful in making me look forward to playing Yakuza 5 because of it's pretty great elements of storytelling and keeping me emotionally invested in its characters and themes.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: gameplay, technical stuff like performance, graphics are good. story is very good, though knowing Y3's plot is a prerequisite.PREFACE:there are a couple of things i did that diverge from how the game is played "normally" that may have affected my experience.1. real yakuza use a gamepad. sadly, i am not a real yakuza. i used a mouse and keyboard to play this game.2. whenever i play a game, i spend a large portion of my time achievement hunting. yakuza 4 is no exception.3. i did not even attempt to fill the completion list aside from substories. i only played four minigames more than once: pool, karaoke, bowling and darts.TECHNICAL STUFF:the game runs well. i had one severe drop in framerate that i had to close the game to fix, but no gamebreaking glitch occurred in 88 hours of gameplay.there is one minor gripe i have that i think is a bug: some quicktime events don't register the first time you input the correct key. you will have to hit the key twice for the event to succeed, for some reason.GRAPHICS: i had no issues with the graphics of this game, aside from the fact that some cutscenes are higher resolution than others. the inconsistency bothered me more than the low res, to be honest. there's also some inconsistency with animation in cutscenes, with some being well animated, and others being clearly made with stiffer gameplay animations. again, this was not all that bothersome to me, but you shouldn't play this game expecting kiwami 2 level graphics.GAMEPLAY:i'll split this up into 3 subsections for each of the gameplay aspects.when it comes to the map, not much has changed from previous games. unlike the two preceding games, yakuza 4 takes place almost entirely within kamurocho, and you cannot go to any other cities. however, the game has added rooftops and some underground sections you can explore. while this is cool and all, i don't feel like either of these add too much to the exploration or gameplay. enemies spawn in one underground area and not at all on rooftops, and there's honestly not much going on in either aside from maybe one or two shops and a few collectables.while the AI has improved since Y3, with enemies no longer constantly blocking or dodging for no reason, enemies in this game grab you a lot, which is rather irritating (especially since enemy grabs drain your heat) and odd, considering Y3 didn't have this problem.another issue is that the "lock on" doesn't track enemies. instead whenever you lock on you permanently face the direction the enemy was when you started the lock-on even if the enemy moves, which is one of the strangest and most self-defeating ways to implement a lock-on system i've seen.yakuza 4 has multiple playable characters. this allows for two really good styles of fighting to be included as opposed to the third game, which only had kiryu's. if you've played kiwami or 0, you can think of each character's way of fighting as an ancestor to the "styles" in those games.the problem is that there are four playable characters, and you cannot switch between them until the final chapter of the game. i'll start with the good.the first playable character is very good, being built around speed and dodging around strikes to land massive numbers of small blows. think of him as a "rush style". weak damage per hit and health, but overall  high DPS.kiryu is kiryu. he's somewhat fast AND hits hard. no real complaints there, it's a strong balance. think of him as a "dragon style".as for the other two, there are some considerable flaws.the 2nd playable character is meant to be the tank/strength character. he's slow, but can absorb damage and does a lot of damage per hit. while you may understand this as a "beast style", it's important to emphasize that the characters are not direct analogues to the fighting styles, but more inferior ancestors. in this case, the sluggishness of the 2nd character is very hard to deal with, since enemies and especially bosses are quite agile in this game, which will often mean getting combo'd with no means of dodging or escape. ironically, the first few hours of this guy teach you that all your strength doesn't mean much of anything without agility, as you have to dodge sniper fire and fight an extremely agile boss.the 3rd character is kind of odd, and is where the "style" analogy breaks down completely. his style is built on two things: parrying, and heat. he's both slow (though not even half as bad as the 2nd guy) and weak, but his heat actions can all but one-shot most enemies even at the beginning, and he is the only character who can parry attacks, which forces the attacker a few feet away from you and stuns them. the big problem is that due to the aforementioned slowness and weakness, his fighting style pretty much devolves into cheesing enemies by parrying them into walls and kicking them a bunch. that's the only way to fight bosses or large groups without getting walloped, aside from heat actions, which are actually quite scarce, given how often enemies grab you. it's really uninteresting and disappointing given the wealth of moves that would have been worth using had they been attached to a stronger or more agile character.as said before, i didn't play a lot of minigames. i will give two thoughts on two minigames, one positive and one negative.positive: the darts in this game are much easier to control with a keyboard than in yakuza 0 and kiwami. you can actually control the speed at which the dart is pulled back and when to release it (which is essential to aiming) whereas in kiwami and 0 merely clicking the mouse pulls the dart all the way back at max speed.negative: this is the most nitpicky gripe possible, but they really needed to color code the inputs for karaoke. seeing a line of black squares makes my eyes glaze over very quickly, and distinguishing what's a left key from a right key becomes a bit of a hassle. thankfully they added color coding in yakuza 0 (but got rid of it in 6???).STORY:i don't intend to spoil anything, but the story is fairly par for the course for a yakuza game, which is not surprising, since yakuza has always set high expectations for plot. there is one plot twist that is kinda dumb and commonly memed, but it's not anything that would completely ruin the experience.you shouldn't get this game as an introduction to yakuza, which should be fairly obvious since it's the 4th game, but i should also clarify that there are plot moments that may not make particular sense or lack context absent playing the third game, which happens to be the "black sheep" of the franchise. if you skipped the third game, at least watch the cutscenes on youtube.

_childDocuments_.review: Continuing the epic saga of games that is Yakuza, the 4th entry was pretty good aside from a few hiccups. I will say the story in this one was really good as it tied a lot of loose ends from the earlier games, but I found a few things lacking.Yakuza 4 has you playing as 4 different protagonists. A loan shark, a death row inmate, a cop, and Kiryu. All of them seem disjointed at first, but as the story progresses, we see that they are all connected to events from the past few games. Mainly, the 1985 hit where Majima didn't join his brother Saejima, the missing money that the Tojo clan could not find, and the explosion at the Millennium Tower. With all these old problems being dredged up again, will the Tojo clan survive?Gameplay-wise, Yakuza 4 is like previous entries except now you play as 4 different characters. Each one has their own unique fighting style that you can level up and strengthen as you do substories and beat the crap out of enemies and bosses. While I did like how this worked storywise, gameplay wise it grew a lil annoying to level up a protagonist and then have to go back to level one with another when the story switched them. Luckily, in the final chapter, you can freely switch between them to finish substories and level them up before the final battle.Music and graphically, the game is mostly the same like previous games which is good if you played them so you can dive right in. I found the substories lacking in this one minus a few that were really nice. The main story was definitely really good in this one. It was so amazing seeing the answers to questions I had since playing Yakuza Zero finally being answered. My gripes in this one was how annoying it was to have to start over 4 different characters, sorta threw off the pacing gameplay-wise, but I understand it. Some bosses were still annoying to fight, but not enough to cause me to want to quit. A lot of the substories were really hard to follow and I wound up having to use a guide just to figure out where to finish them. Final verdict? If you've played previous Yakuza entries, this one is a no-brainer. I know Yakuza 3's story was pretty lame, but 4 really came through and knocked it out of the park. It is a decent length, and the gameplay between the characters was unique enough for them all to stand out on their own. Here's hoping that 5 is just as great! Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing the story I just can't bring myself to play Yakuza 5. Funnily enough I thought that I would just get on with Yakuza 4 as soon as possible so I can finish playing the entire series.Gameplay is simply amazing. You get to play four characters - that's a given. Their playstyles are completely distinct and unique from one another, but mastering them are so satisfying thanks to the new 'Soul Orbs' leveling. You have more flexibility in choosing the skills you acquire which makes for a more fulfilling gameplay progression. Without spoiling too much: one character makes you torment enemies with relentless attacks while another makes you take on a more disciplined style and be rewarded with punishing finishers.Story-wise, all I can say is that it's executed really well. At first, the story is seemingly very slow and monotonous - that is because you haven't got the bigger pictures in the story yet. As you progress through every character's chapters, the story picks up and becomes clearer. You'd even notice subtle symbolism and hints throughout even the earliest parts of the story that makes you go "Ah, so that's why it's so and so". There's a lot of play around dialogues that I noticed too and I'm not too sure if it's just the story team's ingeniousness or the translation team's. Either way, I can't not love the story in this game.This pc port still has some issues hardware-wise but there's a lot of help that you can find in the guides and the forums. 9.5/10 I guess? If I'd be a little more critical, probably 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the "worst" of the Yakuza games I've played so far (0, Kiwami, Kiwami 2, & 3 Remastered) which still makes it a really, really, really good game.  Shifting to a new protagonist after Kiryu was a gamble obviously, and they hedged their bets by makes THREE new protagonists AND keeping Kiryu in the mix.  The result is 4 characters who are interesting in their own rights, but slightly diluted by the necessity of each getting less screen-time to fit all four in.  This also means there are some odd patches in the story that never really get patched up, with things (sometimes MAJOR plot-related things) having apparently happened off-screen.The main plot is fun if over-convoluted (not unusual for Yakuza games), with a game full of betrayals, twists, double and triple crosses and secret allies and secret enemies and bizarrely pointless retcons of things introduced only a few hours earlier in the game.  But the characters are fun, and of course all the usual substories, mini-games and collect-a-thons are there in full force as always. Seeing how each of the very different protagonists deal with the madness of Kamurocho's assorted weirdos, oddly wholesome horndogs, slightly mad/obsessed hostesses, wannabe tough guys, mad scientists, stray animals, d-list celebrities, useless rookie fighters that need training, underground passages and a cucumber loving kappa... well, it's as fun as any other Yakuza game.  All Yakuza games are worth playing, and so is this one!

_childDocuments_.review: After not enjoying the kiwami remakes and suffering through yakuza 3, This opus was a breath of fresh air.The plot started off incredibly well, with the introduction of Akiyama(smoothest mf on earth) and his fighting style/arc. Writing is fantastic, and i truly missed seeing Kamurocho and its criminal underworld through the eyes of someone that wasn't Kiryu(even if he does come back for the last part of the story).Admittedly, the story becomes disjointed, with asspulls and twists that are as idiotic as they are fitting for this series. Gameplay is MUCH better than 3, however this one has the worst designed bosses so far: Right as you get to play as him, Saejima has to fight a boss that is fast, powerful and agressive with the starting moveset while Tanimura, the young detective that is built around parries, fights a boss that is immune to said parry. WTF...Add to that the technical issues of the PC port like not being able to break grabs due to the higher clock speed. The list of frustration goes on and on...However these new characters make this game worth playing. Akiyama is the sleek, suave city prowler every dude would love to be. Tanimura, the cop in search of the truth with a super fun fighting style using aikido and judo. Saejima stands out especially, with powerful scenes filled with emotion, this guy's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ badass with big muscles and even bigger sense of honor. I found myself enjoying the series again, it has everything i loved from the previous games while smoothing out (most) of their issues. A ♥♥♥♥ ton of memeable moments, a ♥♥♥♥ ton of goons to fight and a ♥♥♥♥ ton of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the original, there aren't many significant changes here.Some small features like exclusive food & magazine items were removed despite the game mentioning you can still do them.They removed the pachinko minigame supposedly due to potential gambling laws some countries have, but that'd be a really stupid reason if that were true when the entire series has been full of gambling games. You can still enter the one pachinko parlor in the game, but you won't be able to do anything in there except listen to NPC's.This game takes place a year after the third game, and actually has little to do with it outside of this one other character and when Kiryu finally gets involved. The game has four stories going on, each one for its four characters. You start off the first three stories with the new characters until you finally get to playing as Kiryu once more.The characters are generally interesting in this series, and this especially goes for the new ones introduced here; one's a money lender, another's a prison convict, and the other's a cop.Each of the characters' stories get really intriguing. Its main plot, however, takes a huge downfall in the later half when some big reveals & twists start happening. Never mind the really dumb things this series does like characters turning their back on enemies who have or are near a gun, but in this game, they go really overboard on the "they're not actually dead" plot element, which practically ruined the story for me; this is where that "rubber bullets" meme you've probably heard about came from, which is real and it's stupid. In addition to that, the amount of constant betrayals is pretty overwhelming. The series is known for characters betraying a lot, but in this game's plot, it can make trying to understand each character's motivation extremely confusing.Unlike the last two games, you'll only be in Kamurocho this time around instead of being able to go to another town. You can finally walk in the underground areas and some rooftops in the city, but they're mostly empty and are just used as convoluted shortcuts.Just like with the previous "remaster" they did some "re-translating" for this game as well, as in really "localized" it as opposed to direct translations for loads of places, so it's still kind of hard to tell when characters are at times being obnoxious or if the translators are just having too much fun seemingly rewriting the script.The combat here doesn't feel like much of an improvement over the previous game, as it still feels like I'm playing the previous game's combat, but with different characters.Hard mode and later, however, is vastly improved, as enemies no longer block all the time. The only really annoying enemies in the game now are the enemies who can constantly grab you from weird distances.Each of the new characters are interesting to play as at least, with none feeling like they're no better or worse than Kiryu, so it's more up to personal taste if you'd really rather just have a character that Tiger Drops or something. It makes for a really good change of pace when you've been playing as Kiryu for a lot of games in a row.Compared to the previous game, this port is a little more optimized somehow. I'm not sure if that's because of the fan-patch, though in the previous game, the fan-patch only mostly mitigated the issues. It still skips frames at times, but they weren't as prevalent as in the previous game.The substories are mostly short like the previous game, and aren't really much better if at all.If you didn't mind the previous game, you most likely wouldn't mind this one.Its only real problem is that later part of the main story.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 was unexpectedly different. I was aware that there would be new characters but given the central portrayal of Kiryu it felt more of a cameo when he does show up and then like a guest appearance when it's his turn in the story. Its not a complicated story but it does well making it feel as if the characters are interwoven in backstory. The annoying part of the story is the frequent use of Yakuza of death as a fake out. It sometimes feels like the story was written one way then changed midway after cutscenes were already made so they did a work around. Gameplay wise combat is fairly diverse. Different styles that were in Yakuza 0 are present but spread to different characters to make each feel more distinct. The finale showdown is more of a fan service though as storywise it was unnecessary. Cutting out the fights would have resulted in the same end. All in all it feels more satisfying than Yakuza 3 and ran well on steam deck despite the unsupported rating.

_childDocuments_.review: I have not much to say other than this is not a game I will be revisiting. It baffles me that people find this to be one of the better games in the series. It takes the game engine and combat AI of the previous game and puts it into the ground. The story is disjointed and quite boring, with many 'twists' just being there for the sake of 'twists', while it is interesting to have 4 stories come together at the end, there isn't nearly enough of a connection to warrant such a story telling method, this could have just been a spin-off staring Tanimura.Many say that the side-content is some of the best in the series, but the game drags and the characters don't matter to me, by the time I get to do any of the side content I'm sick of the protagonist and I want to move on. And even when attempting to do any of the side-content, the sub-stories are not straight-forward enough to do them in any reasonable time, I struggled to do even the most basic subs without looking up a walkthrough. Taiga's section just sucked, evading the police became infuriating cause they would spot you with no explanation, the game would block off the world so it was hard to figure out when I could go back to exploring, and his story was pretty lacking.As mention in the first paragraph, the combat it busted, main enemies will just steam roll you over and over, but grunts will just get washed by your protagonist even with no ability upgrades. The final boss with Tanimura was just impossible, I actually started raging even when I put it on easy. I ended up having to look up endless combos, which would help me beat the boss, but it took forever and it was not satisfying at all. I didn't feel I earned anything in the game due to the outrageous difficulty. I can't believe they made a 20 hour Yakuza game with 3 hours of Kiryu. Should have been a spin-off...4/10 Just skip the game, it's not even contextually important in the greater Yakuza story imo

_childDocuments_.review: Now, as this is  we’re talking about, this is obviously not a good starting point for the franchise. That’d be  or  - depending on who you ask. As such, moving on, I’m going to assume that you’re familiar with the franchise and maybe even already finished the previous entries.So, what does  bring to the franchise? For the most part, exactly what one can expect from a -game. We’re once again back to Kamurocho and as usual, the story starts small before growing in scale. There are the usual minigames to explore, locker keys to find and substories to engage in. As with , this game did not receive a makeover similar to that of  – but the game still looks serviceable and runs without any problems or crashes.However, even though much remains the same, there have been some changes. Kamurocho features more verticality now, for example, with explorable sewers, an underground mall or rooftops. However, combined with the extremely basic map, I felt like these extra zones did more bad than good. I stopped completing substories halfway through the game because moving around and finding the right spots got extremely tedious. As Kamurocho is the only proper visitable location in this game, I appreciate that the devs were trying to spice it up – but ultimately, I felt like the added verticality only added some tedium to the game.The biggest change, however, would be the four playable main characters. While the previous entries (not counting  as it released later) focused on Kiryu alone,  adds three new characters to the mix. This might not be exciting news for those who play the  games mainly because of Kiryu – and I wasn’t too keen on playing as someone else in the beginning as well.Even so, I was pleasantly surprised with the three new faces. Of course, as we’ve accompanied Kiryu through a few games now, they couldn’t possibly live up to him. But nonetheless, they all mange to bring something new to the table, be it their personality or unique fighting style. As such, over the course of the game, they actually feel like proper main characters and not just one-time sidekicks. Still, as their stories are destined to intervene with each other, they’re not as detached from Kiryu & Kamurocho as could be. In retrospective, I would’ve liked some even more unique viewpoints. But what’s important is that they manage to hold their own and that they do.In terms of the story itself, expect the usual twists and turns. In terms of the overall quality, the general opinion is a bit mixed as you might’ve already realized by reading other reviews. Personally, I’d say that while the story has some good moments, it has a lot of flaws as well. It’s still as easy to feel lost with all the different characters and Yakuza families as ever. Some plot developments feel extremely forced and others are just too predictable. There is one scene involving the orphanage that made me extremely uncomfortable and feels really out of place. Also, you might not see some characters as much as you might hope.Still, what the story does achieve is to create the typical -atmosphere – including some surprising ties to previous entries in the franchise. Also, as you’ve accompanied some of the characters involved for a few games now, you probably want to see how their journey continues anyway. Overall, the story of  certainly isn’t the best the franchise has to offer but it’s still a -story that’s not going to stop anyone from playing through the rest of the games.That’s basically what could be said about the gameplay as well. The usual mix of minigames is here but unfortunately the club management minigame heavily disappoints this time by dragging on way too much. The new fighting styles are fine additions but there are extremely annoying (boss) fights in the game that are devoid of any fun. There are too many street shakedowns as well. However, in the end, beating someone up with a bicycle after throwing their friend into a wall just never gets old.Concluding,  is just another entry in the -series. I wouldn’t say it’s the best game the franchise has to offer – by far – but it’s still enjoyable for the most part. You get what you expect and while there are some changes, they’re not really changing the core experience. And hey, you wouldn’t consider playing the fourth/fifth game in this franchise unless you enjoyed the previous entries, no?

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4's story is the narrative equivalent of the old adage, "If you don't like the weather in New England, just wait a few minutes." If a story beat is confusing, you needn't fret; by the next cutscene another character will be dead (shot from offscreen, as most Yakuza characters meet their ends) and another will reveal their true loyalty lies elsewhere in an unexpected (actually fully expected at this point) twist, completely changing everything. At one point  and it was here that I realized the writers must surely be having a laugh. At the very least I was, and I'm glad I saw this game through after initially thinking I might skip it to expedite my Yakuza journey (it wouldn't be complete then, would it?)Akiyama rules.

_childDocuments_.review: While Yakuza 4 has some weaknesses, it is one of my favourites of this series. It introduces some great new characters, has an interesting plot and all of the familiar gameplay features you'd expect by now.Interestingly enough, the biggest weakness of Yakuza 4 is how easy it is. The fights in Yakuza 3 weren't hard, but got dragged out a lot by enemies dodging and blocking constantly. Yakuza 4 is the opposite - enemies almost never block and hits barely hurt you, making most of the game very easy. The game's side modes are also not very interesting and mostly feature modes from previous games or are very repetitive.Still, Yakuza 4 is fun and sets up the stage for future games. As usual, the story is great and the characters convincing. And I mean, if you got this far in the series - why wouldn't you play this one too?

_childDocuments_.review: I know a lot of people have speculations about this game because for the first time since Yakuza 0, Kiryu isn't the only protagonist- and even then, in this game, he's not one of two protagonists, he's one of FOUR. I myself was also very skeptical about whether or not I would like this game, I don't adapt well to change and meeting new main characters is just not something I usually enjoy.However, all it took was the first cut-scene of the game and I was honestly hooked entirely. Akiyama and the others have SO MUCH personality and it brings so much more perspective into the stories, I actually ended up hoping there'd be more and more time between me and having to play Kiryu's part. Saejima, Tanimura, and Akiyama are such deep and rich characters that overall made the game play a LOT better and brought a whole new level of depth and entertainment to the story. Now all I can say is I'm more than excited to see the new protagonist added in Yakuza 5.No matter how much you think you're gonna hate the next Yakuza game, it ends up being your favorite out of them all.

_childDocuments_.review: There is something about the Yakuza franchise that just hooks you in.. In this review I will trying to explain what that something is while talking about Yakuza 4 without giving away spoilers.Yakuza is my all time favorite franchise and I don't think I've ever felt attached to a gaming series like I have with it. The beauty of all the Yakuza games (I'm currently on 5) is that it is all an overarching story-line centered around Kiryu and the people he meets along the way. It is really more so of a character journey that goes from being a young, innocent, but smart kid in Yakuza 0 to experiencing the full world of what it means to be Yakuza.. a world so cruel yet adventurous. There is nothing like in gaming. You can go from experiencing the most heartbreaking cut scene that leaves you in tears to doing the most ridiculous side stories involving grown men wearing diapers. It is the definition of a gaming franchise that caters to the player in terms of how the user would like to experience the story. You could spend 100+ hours easily having nonsensical fun doing all kinds of mini-games to side stories in a vast world that offers so much.. or simply enjoy the main story itself at your own pace. Yakuza 4 has all that in abundance.. Awesome mini games to crazy amount of side quests but the difference here though, there is a little twist compared to the previous games. You actually get to play as several main characters. Going into this I was prepared to not enjoy it as much since there is less of Kiryu but I was very, very, wrong. You meet Akayama who is a hopeless but careful romantic set on helping people, Saejima a man burdened with a terrible backstory with a surprising connection to one of the all-time great Yakuza characters (I wont mention who), and finally.. Tanimura who is hell bent on finding out the truth at all costs..You have three diverse characters with very different personalities but their story-lines are incredibly compelling that it makes you want more. It is also refreshing to experience a new take on the already established Yakuza world. All three of them compliment Kiryu perfectly, and the fact you still get to play as him makes it all the more fun. It doesnt just end there, you also an amazing ensemble of characters that make the story even more rich.. Returning legends in the franchise to new scary looking villains that make up this twisted world.It also amazes me how everything connects at the end.. You're experiencing a giant story through the eyes of four different characters that flows together so perfectly. Each chapter will leave you with more questions than answers, a perfect deep rooted crime thriller befitting of the name Yakuza.In a nutshell if you're a fan of the franchise period, you dont want to miss on Yakuza 4 but the uniqueness of having a new cast complimenting the returning ones makes it standout for me as a refreshing chapter in Kiryu's Saga.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good entry into the Yakuza series; however, this is easily the weakest of all I've played so far (0, Kiwami, Kiwami 2, 3). The game starts of strong with Shun Akiyama, who is a charismatic banker who lends money to people with no interest or collateral (seems no matter the amount either), given that they pass a test of his. Akiyama's story is fun and interesting, and his substories are quite humorous. Saejima's tanky style in the 2nd part offers quite a departure from the kicking-style of Akiyama, but it is a very welcome change. Taiga Saejima is a convincing character with a big heart who wishes to find answers for crimes he committed decades ago. Masayoshi Tanimura is a police detective who is trying to find out the truth behind his father's mysterious disappearance that coincides with Saejima's crimes decades ago. Tanimura's fighting style is satisfying, but missing something. Being parry-heavy, Tanimura had a chance to be the most fun out of all the characters, however, his potential was waaaay under-utilized. I had fun with Tanimura's substories the most. Tanimura's story is where the game starts to fall apart at the seems. The infamous 'rubber bullet' moment didn't bother me nearly as much as other ridiculous plot twists that occurred later on. I can say with 100% confidence it only gets worse from there in regards to the story. Finally, we have Kazuma Kiryu. What else can be said about the Dragon of Dojima that hasn't already been said? It was nice to see Kiryu back in action and an old rival of his team up to fight corruption at the Tokyo police department. Kiryu's section of the game also suffers from the plot-twisting mania, but at least Kiryu's fighting style is A++ great. Despite all the positive things I mentioned, one thing needs to be stated: this game drags on and on and on. I remember playing this game a while back, and I thought it was much better. Replaying it however after finished 0, Kiwami, Kiwami 2, and 3 made realize the amount of flaws this game has. Many substories are just copy-and-paste from 3. Nothing new is really offered to the game, and some of the Side-stores (different from substories) are painfully boring and completely uninteresting. While I had fun with the hostess game in 3, Yakuza 4 literally does a copy-and-paste with many hostess situations that occurred in 3. Boy, what a waste!Overall, a 6.5/10 for me. Above average, but easily the weak link in the great Kiryu saga. Re-playability level for this entry is very low. 100% worth it though if you're a Yakuza fanatic like me.

_childDocuments_.review: It may be one of the larger entries of the series with a larger main city, 4 playable characters and the same but different selection of mini-games and challenges, but it’s not necessarily any better.  The new areas are mostly empty of meaningful content and having to swap between characters, who each have their own play styles, makes the story and experience rather bitty.  Combat is far too easy and unchallenging, making much of the side content unnecessary, and having to learn a new playstyle every few hours isn’t great.  The story isn’t very engaging or memorable, partially due to introducing too many new characters who the player has no connection to and making them play the same plot period over a long period of time.  That being said, the writing is good and each character will become your favourite at some point.If you’re a fan of the series you know exactly what you’re going to get, which will either make this stale or comfortable entertainment-wise, but it doesn’t really bring anything new or remarkable to the series.  It has the same great graphics, music, drama, wacky comedy and massive volume of content (including end game grind to get 100% completion), but it lacks that special something of the previous titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 is the point where some of the elements that began to shape some of the best received titles of the franchise began to be experimented with. This game features four different playable characters, each has their own combat moveset, as well as story, background and motivations. The main plot of this game revolves around a series of events that will eventually bridge the paths of all four protagonists joined with a common goal. The presence of multiple fighting styles and characters was born here and further used in some future titles along the line. Comparing it with Yakuza 3, it's predecessor, the title which it shares the most similarities to, they improved on the combat side where enemies guarded too much, here it is much more balanced and enjoyable. The experience system once again works differently which can be amusing. Experiencing the city of Kamurocho from the eyes of four different people helps create a similar, yet different atmosphere, as each character will have different side activities and meet different characters only available to them.Not to say it doesn't have side effects or issues. Inventories are character locked while playing the main story and if you picked up something that another character may have benefited more from, they cannot really use it until the inventories merge near the end. Also, having a reset on your money every 4 chapters didn't allow for certain side activities or minigames to be enjoyed right away, since I lacked the funds necessary to pay for stuff like gambling minigames or hostesses. Overall in this game I did the least amount of side activities before beating the main story due to this side effect.On the Completionist side of things, I was relieved to see that most objectives as compared from Y3 were severely reduced in difficulty, without downgrading the amount of stuff. This was a good thing in my opinion given how extreme certain requirements were in the previous game, requiring hours and hours of practice to perfect a specific minigame. There are new additions as well so it's not the same thing again, certain minigames also were modified in an unique game on this entry, which I found amusing too.In my opinion the story isn't as emotional as most of the previous entries, there's a few moments but they're tamer compared to earlier title's. But overall I really enjoyed the converging stories and the many sides of Kamurocho the four legends were able to see through.

I loved this one a lot more than 3. It does some interesting stuff with 4 different protagonists. At first I didn’t like that idea, but all of them grew on me fast and they were all awesome in their own way. The best part about this game was no grinding mini game! Hostess maker was there again and the dating thing was there again, but they both didn’t count for any sub stories so you could just ignore them fully. And because the game is split up into 4 parts with different characters, there aren’t that many subs to grind out either, that alone really helps this game stand out as being one of the better ones. Akiyama is such a fun character. Saejima was actually seen in 0 but I forgot, and he’s a badass, specially 1 scene is awesome. Tanimura was cool but the least out of the new characters. The subs were pretty fun again, great comedy and just fun storylines throughout the subs and main game. Could have used a bit more Haruka though! Hype for 5.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely, an upgrade compared to Yakuza 3 in terms of gameplay, which is much appreciated.Yakuza 4 tried something new, which is to divide the game in 4 different parts (plus a grand finale) with one character involved in each of these parts. This was great a challenge to the team, I suppose, but it works very well as you keep shifting from one angle to the other in the story of Yakuza 4, the stroytelling is supreme on this one. Sometimes, this is challenged by the pace of the one game, as some chapters feel really empty gameplay-wise compared to others, but it is still a fulfilling approach. Not to mention that each character has his own motivations in this entry but also many individual perks when it comes to gameplay: Akiyama is the speed-oriented character, Saejima is the burte force, Tanimura is more technical and pary-focused, and Kiryu is a master of all trade, the god-tier powerhouse he is supposed to be.Putting that aside, same old yakuza - beating people up in the streets or in massive battles (there were a lot of these last one in these entries, and I appreciate it,  I like them better than street brawls and boss fights), completing substories and minigames, etc. I might be tempted to say that after playing the first five games, I'm starting to fell a bit "Yakuza-fatigued", so trying to keep things fresh with the individual chapters and the multi-angle story was much appreciated, character development was on point for all four protagonists and the game felt way "fresher" than in Yakuza 3. My only concern is that the story kind of fell a part towards the end, and while I loved the last chapter, it left me bittersweet, specially the "villain" was lacking compared to the previous entries.Having said that, while Yakuza 4 doesn't reach the god-tier of 0 and the Kiwami's, it is way better than 3. Here's hoping 5 steers towards the same direction.Overall, I'm giving it an 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 game. Each of the 4 protagonists were likable and good characters. Kiryu and Akiyama had great fighting styles, Saeijima's was decent, and Tanimura's was mediocre. The very enjoyable main story took me 20 hours to complete on normal difficulty. The pacing was much better than Yakuza 3's and overall just better. The only problems I had in the game were combat related and the severe lacking of Majima. The issues I had with the combat are few but annoying. There are way too many enemies that grab you. Grabbing enemies deplete your heat and make fights take an annoying amount of time. When there are multiple grabbing enemies in one fight it can get downright infuriating. The other issue is that in certain fights, one of the boss enemies will be given a gun while you have to fight 5-12 other guys. You cannot beat the gunman quickly due to the large amount of health and the fact that the other enemies will swarm you. Gun wielding enemies ruined some fights as they would double shot you and leave you to get violated by their allies. But overall I must say this was a great Yakuza game.

_childDocuments_.review: Considering a lot of people are going to end up playing Yakuza 0 and Kiwami 1 & 2 before they get to this, the whole "multiple characters and multiple fighting styles" thing might seem like nothing new (0 and the Kiwami remakes modified the fighting systems), but I remember that when this came out I was really impressed with the idea. Playing as Kiryu is fun, but it was time for something fresh.My biggest gripe is probably that the multiple character system creates a disconnect that never really solves itself until the very end (and Premium Adventure mode) when they combine the inventories and cash of all the characters. Before that, every character is very independent of each other. It definitely feels like you have to take your time with each character on your first play through and try to discover everything you can do before it's time to switch characters. Maybe not a big deal for some, but it does change the way you think about side missions and all the other fun stuff you can do besides the story line.It's a bit of a convoluted story line, but it definitely improves on all the things that Yakuza 3 didn't quite have right and ends up being a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Yakuza games, and this gets a recommend simply because it's part of the series. It's one of my least favorites though due to the idea of having four main characters. Due to this, I was never motivated to actually explore or improve any of them, or feel like I'm the main character that's part of the story. It was the first Yakuza game I kind of just rushed through to get to the ending due to this lack of investment in any of the characters. Technically it's a large improvement over Yakuza 3 and you can see how the series was progressing. The main plot was kept interesting from start to finish too, and I can see how they though having multiple characters will allow the writers to come up with some interesting new ideas and side-quests. Sadly, this approach does not translate to a good experience for the gamer, making you feel like you're watching a couple of dudes from the sidelines rather than feeling immersed as the main character throughout the story. Yakuza Like a Dragon nailed it perfectly with having multiple companion characters with interesting stories and side-quests, while still retaining you as the main protagonist. I hope they stick to this formula. I'm already dreading playing 5 with multiple protagonists again until I can get to the apparently excellent Yakuza 6 to play the entire game properly with Kiryu.

_childDocuments_.review: A step up from 3 by a long shot in the story department. The new characters that are introduced as protagonists are all interesting. No story time is wasted on random filler like basically all of 3. The upturn in the series after 3 is evident.Still the game is not without its problems. Some characters feel better than others and the encounter design is still sometimes horrendously bad. Of the 4 final bosses 3 are fine (in that they are 'balanced' yakuza bosses but that doesn't make them very fun in my book) one of them is horrid for no particular reason. The fighting game is still not fun in my opinion. Yakuza has always been a game about getting hit and it leaves most things very unsatisfying when you can do nothing about the boss throwing his own parry at your attacks and then railing you a couple times. I played on hard but honestly you could just do easy there is nothing to gain here from compelling combat. Always keep your restoratives stocked, you will need them at the weirdest of times.

_childDocuments_.review: If you couldn't finish Yakuza 3 Remastered like me because of the combat: Don't worry, this game is heaven in comparison. _childDocuments_.review: Some may call me crazy, but this game was low key peak fiction at a variety of points, it surpasses not only the somewhat average Yakuza 3 in every regard, but also Yakuza kiwami 1 and 2. The game was the freshest Yakuza has ever felt and I wanted to absorb that ♥♥♥♥ right into my veins, it was so good my muscles started quakin. The cast was superb (- Hana because she sucked and I was glad she wasn't in it for too long), the main characters of Saejima, Akiyama, Kiryu and Tanimura were all a joy to play and were a large part as to why I enjoyed this game so much, each of them not feeling like a re-skin of one another. The supporting cast was equally superb with the repurposed Hamazaki being the highlight and the best thing to come out of Yakuza 3 (with him and Saejima's story being where the game peaked for me) and characters like Sugiuchi and Kido both being extremely well-done. The villains felt a little undercooked for me personally and I struggled to really feel anything towards them aside from Katsuragi and Daigo (although Daigo definitely needed some more screen time and development of his motives this game since we hardly saw him). Arai, Kido and the deputy police guy were kind of frustrating I guess but lacked much impact in any department (the latter especially), but I guess that's always going to be a problem when splitting the game across so many perspectives and introducing the latter so late in the game, Kiwami 2 at least had Goda which is still something that makes 2 especially great.The combat system this time around was superior in just about every regard in comparison to 3 and I don't think I need to say much more other than I would like to be able to change direction mid-combo but that isn't particularly important all things considered.The karaoke was caught lacking again sadly, aside from MachineGunKiss which is a classic no cap, the duet with Hana was a bit of a laugh though (best use of her character).If I were to rank each part I'd place them from worst to best: Kiryu (shocker I know), Tanimura, Akiyama and Saejima. Saejima's was GOAT'd and cant be topped, only if it lasted longer, nothing more to add it was just that good and his fighting style was the most fun with the best premise, gameplay and supporting cast by far. Akiyama's was a great start to the game, hooked me and gave me a great idea of how good this game was going to be. Tanimura's was slow at the beginning but once the police conspiracy kicks in and we meet Yasuko it gets so much better and I liked it a lot by the end with Sugiuchi acting as the best part of his story (not to mention Tanimura's fighting style with the satisfying parry system). Then we have Kiryu's which was just a weak climax to the whole thing and just felt like sloppy seconds with none of the same greatness the prior three parts possessed, it was forgettable for the most part and can be summed up as anti-climatic. Not to mention the disservice Kiryu is done throughout (I can't help but feel his character lacked about 90% of the legendary status he deserves by this point and is told/ it's implied that he's done a ♥♥♥♥ job or not good enough the whole game like he owes anyone ♥♥♥♥, I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I just want my legendary bad ass to be cool and not feel like a middle aged altruistic loser.Aside from that last incredibly biased and petty criticism of Kiryu in this game, I loved it and cannot wait for Yakuza 5, the only thing that this game needed was a second location on par with Kamurocho (more like Sotenbori in Yakuza 2/0 and less like whatever that place in Okinawa was in Yakuza 3). I am also ashamed to say I did not engage in the game world and did very few side activities, as has been a recurring theme across all my play through's (minus Karaoke), however, I will likely return to the premium adventure in due time as I can accept the very few side stories I completed/started were somewhat entertaining and engaging (at least more so than Yakuza 3).Overall the game was superb and an easy 8.75/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much enjoyed this one!First of all because the combat is fixed from Yakuza 3...!All 4 protagonists all have unique fighting styles, which is pretty satisfying. This is also what I think was the start of the multiple fighting stances in Yakuza 0, Kiwami, 6, Ichin, and so on. It's very refreshing to be able to switch to different combat mechanics.Of course having that many characters could make the story confusing, but it actually flows quite well from one to the next. The only complain I have is that there are WAY TOO MANY PLOT TWISTS. So much so, that it makes it exhausting and confusing at times... but I guess that when I'll replay this game I'll notice a lot of foreshadowing, making it interesting.The map of Kamurocho is pretty much the best it ever was. The street floor, the rooftops, the undergrounds, the sewers, everything is interconnected, which is pretty beautiful.Now, having done the completion list. Yakuza 5! :)

name: Yakuza 5 Remastered
detailed_description: Experience the fifth chapter of the Kazuma Kiryu saga in 1080p and 60fps. In December 2012, Kazuma Kiryu left his past as a ''legendary yakuza'' and his place of peace in Okinawa. He now spends his days as a cab driver in a corner of Fukuoka's red-light district, hiding his true identity. All for the sake of fulfilling the ''dream'' of an important person. However, a disturbing atmosphere begins to drift through the supposedly well-balanced society of the Kanto and Kansai yakuza, emerging as a plot to drag all of the yakuza organizations in Japan to war. In order to protect the ''dreams'' of his loved one, Kiryu is drawn into the vortex of battle once again. This is the story of four men and a girl chasing their ''dreams'' in five major cities in Japan, presented on the largest scale of the series yet. Complete The Dragon of Dojima’s journey.
