_childDocuments_.review: KIRYUThe main story was really good overall. Kiryu’s part of the game is almost the strongest part of the game. Instead of being an OK caricature of the wise cool dude we know him as, like he was in Y4, he’s the most lonely and humble he has ever been in the series (well at least he starts out that way). Kiryu’s substories are overall the best since they force him to think about the course he’s currently taking in his life. Later in his story, what entails is one of the best power trips in the series where Kiryu crushes dozens of goons like ants and where that rage mode is in its element. Though the best part is an iconic cutscene where Kiryu dodges two rockets nonchalantly as a massive explosion erupts behind him. The man is BACK!SAEJIMAAfter hearing the news of Majima’s assassination, we’re shown a scene of Majima and Saejima 2 years prior. Majima isn’t acting like a lunatic anymore. He’s mostly being straight up, which is surprisingly refreshing to see. The rest of Saejima’s section is just passable, his substories may actually be the best part since they’re wholesome and Christmas-themed. His combat is just a smoother version of Y4. At the end of his part, he finds out Baba, his prison buddy, betrayed him this whole time and has an obsession with suicide.HARUKANow for what might be the most controversial part of the game. While a lot of people have voiced their discontent with Haruka’s part, I actually think it’s better than Saejima’s part and it’s the emotionally powerful part that Y5 needed to land its tear-jerking ending. I might as well talk about her gameplay now. While simple, she has decent rhythm games, one for idol concerts that are really simple but with great vocal music and visuals, and the other for dance battles that can actually get quite challenging on harder difficulties. As time goes on, Haruka ends up seeing Park, her trainer, as a surrogate mother, but only when it’s too late. In a long car ride that should really be about 30 seconds long, Park opens up to Haruka and gives Haruka the pen she uses to open her safe and she leaves Haruka with some encouraging words. The next morning Haruka finds out Park “committed suicide” on top of her own building. I really wish I could have seen more of Park. She was hot.AKIYAMAIn a wave of irony, Akiyama is back but he basically has no character development throughout this game and he somehow is one of the best leads in the Yakuza series. Going off of Y4, he already has the perfect mindset for Y5. It’s his self-assigned job to help people achieve their dreams. So all the story asks of him is to do exactly what’s in character: help people he cares for and kick ass while having the sexiest face and voice in the series. This is a good time to talk about his combat. Akiyama has some of the most interesting combat in the series, only using kicks and juggles people in the air as if he were in an anime. There’s more I want to say about his time with Haruka, but it’s best for me to move on. This segment of the game made me wish other games in the series combined two characters into one chapter so seamlessly. It’s a great way to stir up some chemistry but I doubt that will ever happen.SHINADAShinada’s chapter starts out with him hitting a very unlikely home run, but he later wakes up in a dingy apartment. Clearly, he’s not a baseball hotshot anymore and he isn’t doing well financially since both his best friend and a loan shark come to his doorstep within the same minute, demanding he pays up. This was a great introduction to Shinada’s loan shark, Koichi. He’s portrayed as a charismatic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who pretty much has Shinada on a leash, taking any bit of cash he earns right out of Shinada’s hands, to the point that Shinada would go hungry at nights if there weren’t other people who were so nice to him in town, which is actually a great strength of Shinada’s story. Later, he leaves for Tokyo after Daigo. Back in Shinada’s apartment, Koichi enters uninvited but only finds the 20 million yen and the baseball Shinada left as a token of their bond. I actually think this is one of the best scenes of the game, Koichi just sits there bottling his depression. I personally think that Shinada’s story is the best part of this game. The one thing I despise about the English port is that Shinada's vocal theme Wild Romance, is nonexistent. It is the best and most thematically relevant song in the game and it makes Shinada's arc that much better.FINALEThe Amon challenge is, funnily enough, the easiest in the series so far. Though Shinada’s boss, while still easy, was incredibly annoying. The Kiryu v Amon fight was legitimately hard though, and it felt cool as hell to have them both fighting each other in rage mode. Besides that, the only other stuff mentionable is karaoke. The highlights being Baka Mitai, So Much More, and Machine Gun Kiss. My favorite is So Much More sung by Haruka and backed up by Kiryu. It is incredibly wholesome and it can only be played after finishing the story since that’s when Kiyryu and Haruka reunite. It was an excellent way for me to close the game. The song is about Haruka having to hide her true self from the rest of the world since having Yakuza connections would foil her chances at fame. She is “so much more” than she’s letting on. I liked Kiryu and Saegima’s showdown with each other, Watase, and Naoke.  I also really like Saejima’s heavy conversation right before they’re about to kill each other for Haruka’s safety. I actually really like seeing Majima act all serious. I thought I’d miss old kooky Majima but he works almost as well as his Y0 self. After flooring Baba at Haruka’s concert, Shinada watches Haruka in the distance and sees how small she is from the stands. He then questions if that’s how everyone saw him when he hit that infamous home run. He has an empty look as a tear drops from his face. That is probably my favorite frame in the game, and one of the best in the series. A nobody contemplating what the dreams he was gripping onto for almost two decades really meant. It could easily be the game’s thesis. Shinada thinks about how he doesn’t have a home like Baba has. That’s when Koichi calls him and tells him he and the whole town misses him. This makes Shinada break down. What a great way to end his arc. Back with Saejima, Kurosawa watches in horror as Shinada props up the camera Baba had and makes a hilarious face with a peace sign. Shinada just owns all of the best frames in this game. I like Akiyama’s humble ending. It doesn’t give him an emotional exit, but it’s still a fitting conclusion for him since he doesn’t care about fame, just helping others. This leads to Kiryu’s part where he faces Aizawa at the Tojo Headquarters. Before that starts, we cut back to Haruka preparing to sing her debut song, “Dream”. It’s a song directly meant for Kiryu about how she’s decided to come back to him. Despite his profusely bleeding bullet wound, Kiryu charges into battle, shirts off. Kiryu, weak from blood loss, still wins and before Haruka sings another song, she gives a speech to the entire world. She confesses her origins to everyone and says she loves him deeply while fighting tears. As she says this, we watch Kiryu struggle his way back to her. This is the only part of the game to make me cry. While this game’s story might be the most unorganized in the series, its strongest parts like Kiryu, Haruka, and Shinada’s arcs make it an incredibly powerful experience that is worth playing. After the credits roll, Kiryu succumbs to his injuries and passes out. He’s woken up by Haruka screaming for him and as he sees her, he asks if this is a dream, alluding to what he wants the most. She says no and tells him she’s really there for him. Finally, Kiryu and Haruka achieve their dreams, and the game ends. Despite this game’s flaws, its long runtime really accentuated how powerful its ending is. It’s a great game overall and it’s very worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this franchise in numerical order, Yakuza 5 is the first game to truly rival Yakuza 0. The pacing of the main story, edgy anime battles, goofy side content, a wide array of likable and interesting characters. This was just ticking all the boxes for me. Yakuza 5 took the concept of having multiple playable characters and really took it to another level, embracing Japanese culture from so many more angles and offering incredibly diverse gameplay experiences that kept everything feeling fresh the entire way through. There was also such an emphasis placed on the values of these characters, and delivering not just a grand action experience, but something heartfelt that will leave you glad you invested the time into the franchise.Now, do I recommend Yakuza 5. That is a bit harder to answer. This game does a very poor job at introducing returning characters to the point where I would say playing Yakuza 4 first is a must. And to play Yakuza 4 you probably want to at least play Yakuza 0. Point being in order to enjoy this game you need to be sold on the franchise to begin with. So if you enjoy these games, Yakuza 5 is fantastic. If you maybe tried one of these before and are on the fence, Yakuza 5 will probably be more of the same and confusing from a narrative perspective. But as a whole, I loved Yakuza 5 and strongly recommend playing through this franchise to get here.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this is THE 2nd best Yakuza game in the main series in my opinion. Doubt me all you want but this is peak brawler Yakuza experience (excluding Judgements since they are not neccessarily Yakuza games). -Sure the story is a bit overwhelming and progression is boring at times (Saejima's prison escape ugh) but it's not bad by any stretch of the imagination. The plot expanding all across Japan is what keeps me interested. What happens over there that contributes in any way shape or form to the previous place's events? How do the characters get to the classic Yakuza stomping grounds once again? These two characters are nothing alike how can they work for the same goal? These questions keep me playing the game and finding out these things give me great joy. The story also has some big time cliffhangers. They ramp up everything until a certain point, then gives a second of climax and moves on to a completely different scenario, which is honestly pretty brutal but a minor setback in my eyes. -The side content. OH THE SIDE CONTENT. Almost every character has a side story in addition to substories (rip akiyama) that explores the characters main activity. Kiryu has his taxi driving work as his side story, Saejima picks up hunting and we get to see it on a deeper level, Haruka does her idol work and Shinada picks up his bat and ties any loose ends he had from his career. These are interesting, provide tons of xp and good rewards. Substories are once again enjoyable and interesting. Minigames are a bit of a let down in some places (arcade, bowling, cochin) but most of them are good. Almost every character has a minigame thats unique to them (they did akiyama dirty) and they are decent. Not the best but definitely not bad. -Combat feels like the best out of all of the games that do not run on Dragon Engine. Its smooth, the controls really punish you from button spamming if you want specific combos or abilities, and every character has a moveset fledget out for every situation imaginable. Sure unarmed Shinada is kinda weak and lacks a real counter but he manages without weapons and the sturdy weapons, while weak offer really open and high skill cap combat with him. Enemies recycle moves from previous games which is stupid but thats an issue in almost every Yakuza game not just this one. Also the heat actions are brutal and theres a TON of them to do, I'm especially happy about the return of Hells Gauntler from Yakuza 3. (In case you're wondering, its Essence of Armbarring for Shinada) -City exploration is also huge. Each character has their own cities and they all share Kamurocho. Everyone in their own cities have a form of collectables to look out for, tourist spots to photograph and eateries to recommend to a famous chef.  Its a great change of pace from the basic eat if you want and collect coin lockers that almost every other game offers. -In the end, the 2nd biggest Yakuza game also happens to be the 2nd best. The story, while being what it is in terms of progression had me hooked from the start. I'm a big fan of the combat and the side content is so interesting I want to experience it all. The game has its flaws, but that goes for every game on this planet. Definitely play this one and every other Yakuza game preceding this one if you haven't done it. Honestly amazing.

The characters all end up coalescing in Kamurocho, Tokyo, naturally. Each character also has their own fighting styles. Kiryu is balanced and aggressive, Saejima is strong, Akiyama is fast, and Shinada  uses weapons.Haruka doesn't get in combat, but she does dance battles and singing competitions to become an idol.The story is fairly convoluted and feels kind of messy to me. _childDocuments_.review: Man, Yakuza 5 is a mess. It's a good mess, like a sloppy joe or a massive breakfast at a local diner that you put too much cheese on, but still a mess -- full of empty calories and extra fat, and certain to give you a premature heart attack if you try to go for all of it at once.The series' weird decision to amp up the number of playable protagonists throughout the PS3 era is on full display here, and it suffers greatly for it. I'm not sure Shinada even needed to be included in this story, but I guess Japanese baseball is serious enough business that they had to  to tie it all into the greater plot of the series. Go figure. In Yakuza 4, they used the new characters to try to tell a different perspective on life in Kamurocho, since by that point Kiryu and Haruka had long since left for Okinawa. Not the case this time.In Yakuza 5, it's clear the creators were trying for something bigger, a game spanning all of Japan, sending our heroes to corners of the country we'd never seen in the series before and wouldn't see in the series since. Without a doubt, this is the BIGGEST Yakuza game, full stop. It is an absolute heavyweight of content, with minigames, side stories, substories, hostess dating, gambling, arcade games, and the most expansive combat mechanics the Y3 engine would see. And, unfortunately, a lot of it just isn't worth the time. Sure, the substories are amusing and the side stories are dramatic, but so many of the minigames and other optional content just aren't worth the effort -- especially since the only thing required for the Amon fights this time around is completing all of the substories, as usual. The Side Stories are just a nice way to watch your character get wrapped up in something different from the norm.That said, once you separate the wheat from the chaff (and can sit through 30 plays of KONNAN! as your ears bleed the whole time), Y5's an excellent... Story? It's hard to call it that, because it's really a quartet of vignettes that come together into a greater overarching conspiracy. Each of the four chapters is loosely tied together at first, though around Part 4 if you're paying attention you start to notice that everything you've observed thus far has been incredibly meaningful. Really, that's the big weakness of the story -- even moreso than most Yakuza games, the story drops all of these hints about who's who, who's important, who you should be paying attention to, and it all just goes over your head until the big twist comes three chapters later and you're like "wait, who was that again?" because it's been *forty fluffing hours* since you've last seen that character.Also, the resounding success of Yakuza 0 and Yakuza 7 in the US guarantees that most people who play this game, on this platform, will know right off the bat that . It's not the same as playing it for the first time on the PS3 eight years ago, but RGG boomers like me have long since learned to sit and watch the kids recommend Y0 as the best game to get into the series. It's fine, I can deal with it.Anyway, if you have the patience for its incredibly long and meandering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (and you must, because you sat through this review), this game's a definite recommend. Just, strap in. It's quite big.

_childDocuments_.review: What would you do for a dream?  What would you give up for a dream?  If you had to give up your dream, what would be the circumstances?  Is this a dream?All of these questions and more are answered in this game.I've been playing the series in release order.  That means I've been playing the criminally(no pun intended) underrated Yakuza 1 and Yakuza 2 PS2 games.  I've played Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 4 on PS3 already.  I own Yakuza 5 on PS3, PS4, AND on PC now.  This is the first time I've found myself completing this game.This is definitely one of the longest games in the series.  There's tons of side content and there are a whopping 5 characters to play as.  They're all fun and unique.  Yes, even Haruka.  My biggest gripe with the gameplay is a a nitpick and it's series wide.  The QTEs are a bit excessive.  Not only that, this might be the easiest game in the series next to 4.  One last nitpick, but Shinada's story starts off fantastic.  However, the after a while Shinada's story becomes boring and he ends up becoming so baffling and irrelevant that even the other characters are looking at him like he's drunk or stupid or both.One of my TWO continues was because I was nodding off during his final cutscene and it turned out to be a QTE...oops.Also, the final boss of this game might be the best final boss in the series.  The other best final boss is from Yakuza 2.  It's just so special and hype and perfect thematically.  The music is bombastic.  The choreography and the visceral brutality of it too.  It's perfect.I highly recommend this game and the other games in the series.  If someone were to ask me how to get into Yakuza, I would still say release order is the best to appreciate the gradual growth of the series and the changes of the engine and writing style and characters growth.  Otherwise, just go with Yakuza 0 like everyone else I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: Being able to play this collection of games on the PC has been an amazing experience.After Yakuza 3 and 4, it is clear from the very first moment that Yakuza 5 is a huge game. Once again, we can play as different characters during various parts in the story, like we did in 4, but this time we get to play in several areas/towns.Some of those new cities I didn’t like that much, like Tsukimino, due to the layout, but then it was great to play in Sotenbori again (since I already did that in Yakuza 0/Kiwami 2) and by the time I got to Kamurocho again…wow, it looks amazing in this game.Surely…I was really impressed by how much bigger Kamurocho got from 3 to 4, in Yakuza 4 we get to explore the rooftops, underground and even sewers, so I kind of missed some of that freedom in Yakuza 5 here, yet the city feels really detailed this time around, more than ever, at least to me (up to this game that is, excluding their remakes).The characters are quite likeable, not only the main ones, or the new ones we can play, almost every character involved in the story here feels well written and developed. As usual in these games, the facial animations and expressions look really great for a game initially released on the PS3, despite being a remaster.Like the previous two games, 5 runs great on my Ryzen 5 3600 and RTX 3060 Ti card, I played this one at Ultra Settings, 4K DSR downsampling and an extra 120% Resolution Scale as super sampling, on top of that, and still enough headroom to keep a steady 60 FPS at all times.The controls are great, I used my Dualshock 4, but keyboard and mouse have lots of remapping options available, although there’s some mouse acceleration that I believe cannot be disabled, it’s not terrible but I do prefer gamepad for these games, as recommended by the developers.I found the game a bit easier than the previous one, and I beat it on Hard difficulty but well, it is what it is, wasn’t a walk in the park either, but I expected a tiny bit more challenge on some boss fights which, in any case, most of them were pretty awesome.All in all…wow, what a journey this has been, this collection of games, to me are something special. Yakuza 3 felt like the weakest of the bunch, but still I enjoyed that one quite a bit, especially after some time since I played a game in the series.Yakuza 4 packs a very serious punch, new characters to play and a great expansion to Kamurocho’s layout…it’s great. And Yakuza 5 feels like it had a really important budget, it’s a long game in comparison to the others, I think the story was great and, as always, it teaches us some important messages about life and family especially. Lots of feels and stuff packed in this one, just like in the other games, and it is really good.If anything, I felt that Yakuza 5 was a bit too long for my tastes, but considering all the content in the game, it’s understandable. Yakuza 4 felt quite balanced when it comes to length and pacing, in that regard, but I can’t say 5 was a worse game due to this, it’s great too.With this one, I’ve played all the games available on PC with the exception of Like a Dragon, which I’m waiting until I get to play Yakuza 6…in a month. It feels weird being able to say that…Yakuza 6 is also coming so soon, but yeah, I cannot wait to continue. When Yakuza 0 came out for the PC, thinking of having so many more games in the series on PC was only but a dream…today is a reality, at last.The PC is the first platform where I’ve ever played these games, so I thank SEGA and the studios porting these games (QLOC in this collection) for the chance they give us to enjoy these titles. These are my kind of games, for many reasons, and the fact that they can now be played on PC is great. They may not be 100% perfect in all aspects, but well for what they are, they’ve been pretty enjoyable to me.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 Masterpiece!This game is fantastic. It's a better version of Yakuza 4. This time we play five characters (Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama and Shinada; Tanimura is no longer playable). I think the story is really great. In my opinion, it has the same level of hype and emotion as Yakuza 0. The graphics and soundtracks are also fantastic. It's also cool that we can play in five different locations in this game, whereas in the previous games there are only one or two locations available to explore.But my highlight is the gameplay. The combat system is almost the same as Yakuza 0 and I got along well (much better than Yakuza 3 and 4). You can also automatically assign the points you earn when you level up. But that's not all. I think it's cool that the characters have different jobs: Kiryu as a cab driver (almost had a GTA vesion to Yakuza/Like a Dragon T_T), Saejima (then as the game progresses) as a hunter, Haruka as an idol pop star, Akiyama as a laid back loanshark (like in Yakuza 4), and Shinada as a journalist who used to be a baseball player.  Overall:Anyway, I'm grateful that you guys released the series on PC, Sega.It might almost be my favorite Yakuza/Like a Dragon game. The lovable, pseudo-psychopathic Majima is in the game, but is getting less screen-time to the point that he's becoming nearly forgettable. Missed cash money opportunity by RGG.Fear not though, because one of the new playable characters, Tatsuo Shinada, is just as loveable in a wholesome way. He's charming, very honest, athletic, loves baseball, was a pro-baseball player, borderline homeless, gets beat up a lot, is in crippling debt, eats leftovers and expired foods from the local konbini, and is an underpaid porn journalist. Gone are the days where getting shot in the head or getting pushed off a tall building doesn't guarantee that they are dead (at least for this game 😬). Nothing else much to say here; most people play Yakuza games for their legendary side content and minigames, and it's there in Yakuza 5.Combat is re-adjusted for characters coming from Yakuza 4, but core gameplay is still maintained except for one massive inconvenience that for some reason was added to the game. , unlike most other RGG games. This means you will encounter a time where you will complete a battle you stumble into, walk 2 footsteps and then somehow get into another battle. _childDocuments_.review: After the previous game, I can see how the RGG team decided to expand on the concept first experimented with in Y4. Yakuza 5 is a complete evolution of the gameplay and game structure first explored in the last entry. They went from four protagonists playing their stories in the same city, to having five different protagonists with an entire city for each of them (almost) to explore. This game is MASSIVE in all aspects that you can consider, which really surprised me when I first started playing it. Like the previous game, the story is split up into parts where each character takes front stage, with each restart putting you into a new city to explore, often filled with new activities to perform on as part of the many side contents you'll find around. On top of the main story which is connected to a bigger plot in between each of the character's segments, each protagonist also gets a side activity that gets briefly introduced as part of the main progression, that you can follow to take a break from the main gameplay loop and arguably play a completely different game on each. I do personally enjoyed these side modes a lot as I enjoy the great variety that this series offers on their side content.As part of the main combat, it's pretty similar to the previous game's styles, besides the one character who is swapped for a new protagonist. One addition is a character specific way of spending their heat, which can be fun or annoying, depending on who you're using, Saejima's isn't that great and is more annoying than not when it triggers.Completion wise, as expected from having five different cities, there is A LOT to do, as evident by my high play time logged, it is certainly a challenge for Completionists. Most of the actual objectives aren't all that difficult, there simply is an insane amount of things to do. One tip however: Play on Normal difficulty, Akiyama's Coliseum matches are NOT balanced for him and it is a pain to do them in Hard or higher. There's also the fact that for some god forsaken reason, they do not allow you to create Clear Save Files from Premium Adventure, and they explicitly tell you this. This means that if you plan to do future replays, you are only able to carry whatever progress you had at the Finale. I have no Idea why they chose to do this and I understand it's the only time they did, so... there's that.Performance and engine wise, there is a massive improvement from Y4 Remastered, having played Y0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2, this game feels like a middle point between 0/K1 and K2, it is still the older engine but I really felt a big improvement that it almost feels like it's the Dragon Engine at times, transitions into battles are smooth and instant almost always, the other times they play a small cutscene to begin the fight, but that's mainly an aesthetic choice, though it can get annoying after repeated occurrences.As a final comment, I often see people disliking this game a lot, and I feel like it mainly comes from it's massive length, I get it for a bit, but the game being built in five different stories and cities are what enable it to be this way. Another point may be that Haruka's sections are so different and pretty much it becomes a rhythm game altogether, as a fan of that genre myself I adored this part, but I could understand someone who may not be as ecstatic to be more annoyed by it than not, I do enjoy the big variety offered so I enjoyed this alternate play style when it came, it isn't as hard as I wish it could be at times, but mastering the harder opponents was a fun challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through the entire Yakuza franchise, and 5 is a new low. I can appreciate the ambition and scope of the game, but it very clearly collapsed under its own weight. Narrative-wise, it is easily the messiest game in the series, somehow surpassing 4's laughably awful story with its exposition, conveniences, and surprise reveals. The Kiryu section was entertaining enough that I was hopeful that it would be a better experience overall than 4. Kiryu is still very fun to play and has by far the most options during combat. The story for his chapter was also decently intriguing and was set up pretty well. Saejima's section is where it all goes to ♥♥♥♥. His gameplay is fun enough, when those charge attack hits land they are incredibly satisfying, but his section is an absolute snoozefest to get through, and I genuinely can't believe people thought it was a good idea to add in a hunting section in the game. Starting from the prison section which goes on far too long, to being forced to play through an imaginary Sapporo, to the mentioned hunting village, it legitimately made me drop the game for a month before I finished it again because it was so exhausting and mindnumbingly boring. Akiyama and Haruka's section is incredibly mixed. I actually found myself enjoying Haruka's section and gameplay. The story is no Perfect Blue but it still does a pretty good job making me feel repulsed towards Japan's idol industry. I can definitely see why people would hate it though, I'm sure it's jarring to go from a beat em up game to a rhythm game for the next 5 or so hours. Akiyama's story I don't remember at all, and his gameplay is atrocious. He does pitiful damage, has almost no defensive options, and in general feels incredibly scuffed compared to 4. His final fight where Kanai gangs up on you is just miserable to play through, almost as bad as Tanimura's fight against Munakata in 4. I get that I'm playing Hard mode but I don't see how being knocked around like a pinball by Kanai and his goons are supposed to help me get better at the game. Shinada has an interesting story but the way its connected to everyone else is nonsensical and felt like the developers pulled it out of their ass. His gameplay is also incredibly unfun, and using weapons doesn't make it any better. The final chapter is just exposition, exposition, exposition. At that point, I genuinely couldn't care less about what was going on, because it was just convenience and contrivances one after another with exposition, exposition, and exposition. Has it sunk in yet? This game in general has the most egregious usage of unskippable cutscenes and dialogue in any of the Yakuza games to date. My E key is probably broken from skipping all the worthless padding and filler for so long. I feel like the story would've been nonsensical even if I didn't start skipping everything, the plans that the characters come up with are so incredibly dumb, like that mastermind reveal ploy where they all fight each other. Maybe it's recency bias, but this game is easily the worst in the series, because while 4's story was awful and ruined Saejima's character as a whole with rubber bullets, at least it wasn't this long or this much of a slog (although it was because 4's continuous backstabs from characters reached comedic levels). The only new character I remember from this game is Shigeki Baba, who is admittedly handled well because I found him compelling with his split loyalty. Every other new character I've forgotten already. As a whole, I'm just done with the multiple protagonist route with Yakuza and can't wait to just play Kiryu the entire game in 6.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 - The most ambitious game that RGG studio had ever done.Story- 5 Arcs. Each arc for each characters, except Haruka shared her arc with Akiyama, and the Final arc.- You'll start with Kiryu then Saejima, Haruka and Akiyama then Shinada.- Kiryu arc is pretty much straightforward. He tried to put his past behind, living as a taxi driver in Fukuoka when suddenly problems came to him. Again.- Saejima arc tells the story when he's back to prison a year after event of Yakuza 4. Then things happened and he's now in Sapporo (the northern land of Japan, close to Russia).- Haruka arc tells the story about her path to become an Jpop idol and somehow cross path with Akiyama in Sotenbori.- Shinada arc tells the story about his struggle as a penniless writer who try to put his past about that faithful day 15 years ago, living as a freeloader in Nagoya when he discovered the dark truth.Gameplay- Probably the best fighting mechanic of the PS3 era Yakuza.- A bit grindy. I finished this game in Normal and it's pretty sweaty to fight against bosses.- Vast selection of minigames and side quest. Kiryu's Taxi driver, Saejima , Haruka's activities as a J-idol and some insight into the Japanese entertainment with various cameo from irl and Shinada's battle against his former teammates.- I'm not sure if Akiyama has one apart from dancing battle (overlapped with Haruka).Sounds pretty much a good combination between the story and gameplay so what's the catch?- Well. It's pretty much can be sum up by one sentence, "R1+A" simulator.- I don't have exact number but I think this game could even surpass GTA V in terms of word count in the script.- I mean - point at my hrs count - that's what I got even with holding R1+A to skip the dialog and skip cutscenes. I already finished this game once in another platform so I didn't miss anything.- I'm pretty sure that if I play the game without skipping the dialog or cutscenes, the hrs count when finished the game would be double.So just dialog simulator is the problem?- No. The gameplay also dragging and the story writing is pretty much... not as bad as Y4 but dragging.- They tried to do the same formula by telling the story of each character, build the background then sums that up in Tokyo, Kamurocho.- The problem is by the time I finished Shinada arc, I don't recall what happened in Kiryu arc, and barely Saejima's, and had to rely on YT for summary. That's how dragging and the amount of sidestories/gameplay in later arc are.So.. dialog simulator and dragging story?- Another thing is that this game is grindy.- For example, if you're playing on Hard or Legend difficulty I think you probably have to grind for a Tiger drop for both Kiryu and Saejima in the underground colossium.- I didn't do that and I spent nearly 20 mins to fight against the boss with Kiryu, which could be just 5 mins or 10mins tops if I have tiger drop.- Saejima also need to grind for his 3rd heavy attack to play this game a lot easier.- While Haruka doesn't need that much of grinding, it would be nearly impossible to continue her main story without doing the side stories/tasks.- Shinada is pretty much tragic. If you don't have any interest in baseball or his past (like me), his fight in the final arc is pretty much a nightmare. I finished his fight with health bar flashing.... Akiyama?- The problem with Akiyama is simple. "Why did Akiyama have to be in this game?".- His story is ridiculously short, like 2-3 chapters and it shared with Haruka.- And the writing is so damn bad like they just offed one significant character just for him to be there.- I mean it'll be soooo much better if they didn't off that one character. Nobody cares about the characters that sprout from his arc.- He had to be there just to get that final ending scene. But I don't buy it. They put him there just to make sure he's not the one off character like Tanimura in Y4.Overall.It's a good game but it's one of those game that "you finished once and never want to play again".It's not  because of how bad the combat was like Yakuza 3.It's not because of how empty the NG+ was like Yakuza 4.It's just ... nobody wants to play another 30-40 hrs of dialogue simulator, grinding festival and a mediocre story.And that's so unfortunate. Because this game is probably the most ambitious game RGG has ever done since. They dare to put 5 cities from Fukuoka, Sapporo, Osaka, Nagoya and Tokyo in one game. 5 biggest city in Japan. And we probably won't get anything like this again. Ever.

_childDocuments_.review: First, the bad: Yakuza 5 suffered from the same pacing issues as Yakuza 4, where you're given very little in terms of coherence for most of the game. Everything falls into place during the final 5 chapters, so it was still an amazing, intricate story, probably the best of the pre-0 games. Next, the good: literally everything else. Everything is an upgrade from Yakuza 4, except for graphical fidelity, though the environments still manage to look better. The Side Stories (not substories, though those were awesome too) were amazing. The soundtrack slaps harder than Nishiki. It was incredible how the game just kept getting better, generally speaking; part 3 felt a little weaker than part 2, but part 4 more than made up for it. Also, I want to thank RGG studio for teaching me that "yume" means "dream" about fifty thousand times. Now I will never forget it for the rest of my life.

_childDocuments_.review: As For The Game:This game tries a lot of new things, and not always do they pan out well. Despite that, I'd say it is as good as Yakuza 0. This game tries to do a similar thing to Yakuza 4, with playing as different people that eventually meet up to fight off the big bad. While I believe Yakuza 4 still did that better, 5 does did it with a whole lot more ambition, and it damn well payed off. This game is the longest so far, at around 45 hours for me, and it feels like it. It feels like I just went on a huge journey, even more so that some giant JRPGs that were longer just based off hours alone. I don't want to spoil absolutely anything about the game, but it is HUGE.As For The Port:Actually pretty solid this time around. Didn't crash at all for me, with only a few minor hiccups that were barely noticeable. It did pin my CPU to full, but I have since upgraded and it runs fine. A couple of disappointing things, the textures in the game seemed to be weirdly low in resolution, maybe even lower than 3 and 4. The draw distance of NPCs and the resolution of the FMVs are also pretty low, though that is an issue in the whole remastered collection even on PS4. Hopefully modders will fix this eventually, if they already haven't.

_childDocuments_.review: Worst Yakuza game?! There is no "worst" Yakuza game, only least favorites here and Yakuza 5 is my least favorite. The story and the main villain's plan are convoluted and filled with excess. The four individual acts and finale mirror Yakuza 4's plot except longer and somehow even more things to do. Each character gets their own little side story with a bunch of side quests and it's a lot to go through if you want to beat everything, which is saying a lot for this series. The new mini-games are so-so, Kiryu's and Shinada's are actually fun and then you get to Saejima's and Haruka's games and it just sucks all that fun away when you have to play them. It's not that they are bad, it's that they are boring and waste time, just let me beat up on dudes! This game has a lot of pacing issues, especially around Acts 2 and 3 when it's a bunch of "go talk to this dude, to talk to this dude, to talk to this dude" type of game design. One part in Saejima's story almost made me want to quit playing where he had to go on a wild goose chase just to get one password; I know these games have those padding moments but this is so purposely long and mind-numbing for no reason. However, this is not a bad game, at all! It's still good and worth at least one playthrough, there is a lot of stuff to do, so many substories and mini-games to play. This also may be the longest Yakuza game yet in the series (maybe besides Like A Dragon and Infinite Wealth) so completionists are going to have a blast playing those. Most of the story elements are not too bad and the combat is still really fun. Just wish it was a lot better. That finale is insanely good though, I do not care what anyone says!

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a bit of an interesting case for me. The game is stupid fun and easily my favorite game gameplay wise but the story is probably the worst Yakuza story, which sucks because I really like parts of the story. Kiryu's part is really good story wise, but Haruka/Akiyama's part falls flat story wise because of a character who just isn't fleshed out or written well, and the final boss fight narratively doesn't make sense (although it is one of my favorite bosses in the series, I have to stress, in GAMEPLAY.) Seriously, get to the end of the game and you'll be scratching your head why he's sitting there. However, the gameplay is stupid fun, and I believe I like it more than 0's style switching. I think having a style fit for a character adds more personality. I think that Akiyama's swift kicks and Saejima's slow, strong charge attacks are cooler than Rush and Beast, as I think that there's more personality in these styles. The three main characters from 4 return: Kiryu, Akiyama, and Saejima (sorry, Tanimura!) and Haruka is playable for the first time! Sadly, no beating down thugs though. Dancing happens instead. It's a controversial gameplay change, and while I think it would be miles more entertaining to see the Dragon's daughter tiger drop a hopeless thug, I'm not too peeved about this. It's a fun holdover for a bit and breaks up the monotony. Plus, Akiyama's there! For chapter 3 and 4 at least, so the required dancing's only for a bit. Who knows though, my opinion may change going into Legend. We also get a new character who gets shafted in the next game like Tanimura, Tatsuo Shinada, disgraced baseball player turned nightlife journalist. I think his chapters are definitely hard to talk about: his fight style doesn't achieve maximum potential until you play a good amount of his baseball minigame. His story is a little bit out of place, but I like it. Only gripe with Shinada is in the finale, but eh. Whatever. Every street encounter is also beefed up to the max, and contains a lot of enemies for you to beat down. I love this for the game, as not only does it allow me to listen to the music more, but also use every character's kit to the max. Every character also gets a heat-consuming super move that is unique to every character. Kiryu receives the Dragon Spirit mode, an unwieldy but massively satisfying mode that allows him to dash between enemies and destroy them with speed, making for a kit that destroys large groups of enemies. Saejima gets Tiger Puppetry, where he gets more fleshed out throws and a big ol' swing. Akiyama gets Launch Strike and air combos, allowing him to defy all laws of physics and start levitating to destroy some poor sap caught off guard by his knee. Akiyama also gets heat moves pertaining to Launch Strike, with big single target damage using his Alpha/Beta/Gamma Drive moves and his revelation that allows him to knock two enemies into the air for crowd control. Bit easier to pull off then his triple kick which forces him to start running in a crowd. Shinada gets My Meteor Tackle, a move that he is only allowed to do without weapons, where he, well, tackles the enemy for crowd control, heat moves, big damage, and grabs to set up for Shinada's other big attacks without heat moves. Weaving in and out of his weapons and unarmed stances is very hard to do, but incredibly fun, making him the hardest character to master. Definitely worth picking up his infinite use weapons from baseball minigame, which we'll get to. Overall, I adore Kiryu's Dragon Spirit and Akiyama's air combos, and the other two character's moves are also very fun to use. Haruka doesn't get one of these moves due to her fighting style being a little bit on the different side than the other four.Right, side stories. Every character gets one. They're tiny, but detailed minigames. Kiryu gets taxi racing and taxi driving, aka the only racing game that forces you to follow the law. Mad amount of fun for whatever reason. I really liked it. Saejima gets hunting. I do not like this one as much, probably just because of how much time the story takes for it. It is one of the longer chapters in Saejima's part, and it is all for hunting. No main story progress as all, so I see why people are mad about it. Haruka gets idol work, which is her entire main story section so I won't touch on it. Akiyama gets no side story because of Haruka and his part being mashed into one. Shinada gets baseball, which I warmed up to after a while. Good fun but I stopped playing after I got all the infinite use weapons. There is a stupid amount of content in this game, definitely the most jam-packed Yakuza. You get a lot of bang for buck. This is also the first game I fought Amon in, and his fight definitely took me for a spin. I'm not the most advanced Yakuza player in the world, so your results may vary, but Jo Amon vs Kiryu definitely took some time to master. The substories (not to be confused with Side Stories, the additional minigames, yes this did take some time to get used to) are very good and are generally very solid parts of the series. I did really like Shinada's sub stories, as they focus on him being a broke bum and working to get some money, even working in a convenience store. Now I get the other side of buying 12 Staminans.I don't normally like talking about the soundtrack in these games at length, as music is subjective, but this game has the BEST ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ soundtrack in any Yakuza game, as well as one of the best soundtracks in a game I've played. Every song fits every occasion. From the street fights to the idol battles to the final boss of the game, every song fits every occasion. The final boss music is the BEST final boss song in any Yakuza game. It represents everything I like about Yakuza, from an incredibly hype guitar part to a slow moment to take some time and realize how far every playable character has gone back to banging drums and guitar solos. It's seemless and frankly amazing. I do not think I dislike even a single second of the soundtrack. Maybe the generic boss theme, just because of how much it plays for a song that's a bit one note, but damn is it still good.Overall, this is my favorite Yakuza game, but not because of the story. I had the most fun playing this game compared to the others, and while the story falls flat, the other games generally have pretty good plots, so I'm not too torn up on it. At least it's fun to make fun of. Highly recommend it, especially if you intend on going on with the series with Y6 and YLAD. Things will make more sense.

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game this was. The story is on par with 0 for me, like the whole sequence was so emotional and played like a fever dream. The gameplay and graphics is pretty much the same as 0 if not better and you get to play as Haruka for the first time. Also Shinada is such a hearty fellow, his scenes made me cry at the end. Even though the story has a bit pacing issue, and goes on for a very long time, the entire game is a really nice experience. So many good characters in here and the ending was stellar nonetheless. In terms of gameplay it is similar to 0 and kiwami but the upgrades system and a few other thing plays out more like 3 and 4. The influence for 0's amazing story is visible as well. The best gameplay system for me in here was the idol dance battles, a refresher from all the fighting and a surprise as well. There are also tons of minigames to play, actually it has the most number of minigames out of all Yakuza games so that's a big plus in my list. I'm a bit sad that Pachinko Parlor minigame is removed without any notice from 4 and 5 but it's fine. Also the side stories were pretty good as well. Especially the Taxi Driver side story, IT'S AMAZING. Fishing is improved in this game from previous 2 titles. Kiryu in this game is like, balls strong. The strongest so far out of all games I've ever played and that alone makes this game worth it. Obviously there are a few flaws here and there like enemies are too fast and you can't avoid having a battle unless you run like an idiot and the PC port being mediocre at best crashing randomly making you save every 15 mins out of fear of losing progress. But the latter can be fixed through patches unless QLOC doesn't abandon this game. Overall the pros outweigh the cons and makes up for a really great game.Well that's all I have to say about it, hope you guys give it a try as well even if this game is old, it's just the same experience as 0 in my opinion and it's definitely in my top 10 games now.  I give it a 9.5/10.Edit: Can't really stress on how great this game's story is. You should really give it a try if you are a Yakuza fan.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of effort went into this game. The combat was improved once again, and there are now 5 different cities for 5 playable characters to explore, which is a big step up in terms of location variety. One of those playable characters changes the genre into a rhythm game, which is a bold idea, even though it wasn't my cup of tea. So, the thing is...There is a MASSIVE underlying problem with Yakuza 5 - the story. Not only is it the most boring story of the series with the least interesting supporting cast, it's also the longest. This is a KILLER combination - and by that I mean I was KILLED by boredom throughout ~80% of the story. Kiryu's first part is fine and that's about it. I seriously have no idea what happened here. The story has a ton of filler, and even in the final chapters, most cutscenes are just endless dialogue with barely any interesting plot developments. For what it's worth, a large majority of the story's cutscenes are fully voice-acted this time around, so at least there's that. I'll just end on this: if you're a fan of Yakuza games for the quantity of their content, you'll have little reason to dislike this game. This entry in particular is GREAT for side activities! But I play this series primarily for the main story, and that is Yakuza 5's biggest weakness.

_childDocuments_.review: "Let's do what we did in Yakuza 4 but make it much longer & the story much more convoluted... and have 5 main characters 'cus... 5 is in the title." - Yakuza 5 DevelopersFun and big. It all comes together with a huge finale that seems like it was meant to end the series, but then they did one more to finish Kiryu's story. _childDocuments_.review: NO SPOILERS HERE.(I am still in the chapter before the finale, so I haven't beaten the game yet. However, I am at around 70% of the main story, and I am confident in that the game will continue with the same quality, that it expressed until now.)I have played Zero, Kiwami 1 & 2, Y3 and Y4. And from all those games, I would rank Y5 the lowest, or at least in the lower ranks.What is the reason?However, it is not the good type of lengthy videogame (being filled with entertaining content), but rather the wrong type (being filled with unnecessary sequences, elongated dialogues and lackluster fighting styles).This is interesting and multilayered, but the design falls through when you realize, that you can only control one character at a time, meaning you only have access to one combat style at a time. Much worse than in (some of) the previous games.There are some funny jokes and cool sequences here and there, however, a lot of content could have been cut down into a neater package, I feel.From what I could gather online, Y5 marked an anniversary, which is why the developers wanted to deliver something big: instead of only Osaka and Tokyo, they also included Fukuoka, Nagoya and (again) Sapporo. With each place comes (generally) one character.The idea of it is well meant; the possible greatness of such an undertaking could be remarkable.However, this is where the heaviest flaw shows its head: because the scale of this videogame was so big, the quality is stretched thin. Whereas the two cities in Zero were polished to almost 18 karat, the cities in Y5 are far from it. The same goes for other areas of the game (fighting system, side stories etc.).This game is approximately 36 hours long - double that of almost all the other games, except Zero, which sits at 31.5 hours. And it has been a slug to get through it.As a side note: I originally picked this game up in March 2021.I only pushed myself to finish it now, because the new Yakuza games seem fun and I wanted to finish every main title and not just skip some of them.(Also: I can't spend more money on games I don't finish. I'M STARING AT YOU, SAINTS ROW 4!)------------------------------------------------------Can I recommend Y5?No.Would I recommend Y5?Only to a hardcore fan, who wants to follow the whole story of Yakuza.TLDR; if you do not want to spend 36 hours with, in comparison to previous titles mediocre content, then I'd recommend you to watch a summary on YouTube and go on to the next title.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gonna take you a long time to finish, mainly because of how big the world is and how interesting all the characters are. Hell, it took my 70 hours to finish the story and I only hit 22% completion. Then again, if you're playing Yakuza 5, you've already spent a long time with the previous installments. Shinada replaces Tanimura from 4 as the "new guy", and he fills in that role well, dare I say better. His move set, character, and dynamic with others tops Tanimura, but he really stays as the side character, which is fine.The side stories in this game were amazing breaks from the typical beat 'em up that Yakuza is known for, but I understand that it isn't everyone's cup of tea. This is also the first time Haruka is playable, and in my opinion they hit it out of the park. She's the character I spent the most time with. Saejima's hunting side story was also a lot of fun, and the final boss is even more fun, Yama-oroshi.The finale does run on a lot longer than the previous games, but now there's the ability to select characters for fights, and to complete substories you've missed before. The final fight with Aizawa was a lot more fun than Munakata in 4, mainly because Kiryu is my favorite for tackling boss fights. It isn't the hardest fight in the game though, that would be explaining to your family who walked in on you playing the Princess League Finals that you're playing a super serious game about the Yakuza. All in all, I loved the game. While not my favorite story, it definitely has the best charm out of all the others.

_childDocuments_.review: 169 hours and 4 minutes to finish this game as a completionist-type gamer, with 90.26% done in the stats.Unfortunately, Yakuza 5's length feels like it's biggest drawback. Only played 0-4 and none of the spin-offs so far, though.After playing 0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2, I can see how the developers really evolved and refined this series. Yakuza 3 was interesting but felt rather disconnected from everything else that came after. And in 4 and 5, I was mainly there for the story after all is said and done.For comparison, I put...140 hrs - Yakuza 0 (enjoyed nearly every minutes)60 hrs - Yakuza Kiwami (felt like an expansion to 0)130 hrs - Yakuza Kiwami 2 (enjoyed much of it almost as much as 0)100 hrs - Yakuza 3 (?!? and somehow liked the combat more than 4 and 5)95 hrs - Yakuza 4This game was still enjoyable, make no mistake. It's Yakuza. Being able to play as Haruka was pleasantly surprising and a breath of fresh air. I might be biased because I love the karaoke so the rhythm-based way that she plays was a breeze and pretty fun. Her story is a very nice interlude that made me appreciate her as a character that much more.Any Yakuza fan should buy this game. On a side note, I wouldn't want anyone to play Yakuza without first starting with 0, now that I know the quality of the games as they've progressed.Love Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and Sega for keeping this franchise alive!

I thought the pacing in Yakuza 4 was awful but this game takes the cake in that regard. Many boring parts and the Story is dragged out way too much. Of course this is still a Yakuza-Game, it has the humour and some really good parts. In regard of the Story-pacing and Mini-Games, Kiryus Chapter is the best in the entire Game. The Taxi-Sidemissions is the the best Mini-Game in the entire franchise, even better then cabaret club. Kiryus fight against the Tojo-Clan is one of the best in the entire Series (Kiryu doging a Missile is freaking awesome). I never was a fan of multiple characters in the Yakuza Games in the first Place. It dragges out the tension of the Story. This is the case especially after Kiryus part, where the game lets you run errands in the prison for 3 hours without any Mission-Markers. In Yakuza 4, the Prison was the worse part and now you can do the same ♥♥♥♥ again in Yakuza 5.The reason I gave this game a thumps down is that they failed the balance between the serious stuff (Story) and the unserious parts (Side Missions, Mini-Games, etc.). I mostly enjoyed the Mini-Games, but if the other 50% of the game is poorly made, it is not fun anymore, especially if you played Yakuza not only for the Mini-Games, but also for the Story.I know that Yakuza 6 will only have Kiryu as a Main-Character, on top of that, it is way more Story-focused then this Game, I will probably enjoy that Game more then Yakuza 5.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Next stop in my ongoing Yakuzathon, after the relative disappointment of Yakuza 4, is Yakuza 5. This time we are dealing with a much more modernised game, using what appears to be an engine similar to that of Yakuza 0. Just like Yakuza 4, it has multiple playable characters, 5 this time around, one more. So immediately I was concerned that it would repeat the failings of its predecessor. A convoluted overplot, repeated starts from scratch mid-game as you switch characters and so on. Indeed it does repeat many of these failings, but still something is different, something shines through. Yakuza 5 seems to work.The game begins with a very somber tone. Kiryu Kazuma, the legendary dragon of Dojima, is no more. He vanished a long time ago, left his orphanage and adopted family behind for places unknown. Enter Suzuki Taichi, a humble taxi driver living in Kyushu, Japan's southern island. He conducts his business with care and honour, has the respect of his boss, a woman that cares for him and a painful past he is trying to leave behind. He is of course none other than Kiryu and on the first segment of the game we get to follow him as he tries to live a simple civilian life. There is something very grounding about the whole experience and an opportunity for introspection. Naturally being Kiryu, it doesn't take long before he gets involved into yet another underworld plot and whatever life he managed to build comes crumbling down.The stories of the other protagonists are also intriguing. Yes, Saejima is back in prison, for another prison break, because every game has to have one it seems, but even if it sounds unnecessary the execution this time around is great. Haruka's idolmaster in Osaka segment is truly odd, as the gameplay revolves around dance battles and the game for a while transforms into a rhythm game. Her story did feel a bit like a mexican telenovela at times, but that doesn't mean it wasn't interesting. Once Akiyama, who is trying to expand his business into Osaka, joins the fray it gears up further. Even newcomer Shinada's baseball corruption story is interesting during his segment. Plus, unlike Yakuza 4, here each segment is fairly long. There is a satisfying amount of content. Unfortunately, the main plot, into which the stories of all these segments are woven in, is once again rather underwhelming. There is a fair amount of hijinks the main plot pulls to justify things. At least, as the player focuses on the individual segments, the main plot simply retreats somewhere in the periphery and doesn't offend. On the other hand, the substories are largely on the good to great side. It's no wonder I happily finished them all. Finally, each segment includes a lengthy side-game and all of them have at least a few points in their favour. Kiryu can drive his taxi, Saejima hunts in the mountains, Haruka is trying to become an idol and Shinada plays baseball. Adding all this up and considering the game takes place in 5 different open world areas this easily becomes the lengthiest Yakuza game yet.Combat feels snappier and more impactful. Kiryu as usual shines, but even the other returning protagonists have been greatly improved. Saejima in particular. Yes, he remains painfully slow and his reach is shorter than the Black Knight post amputation. Still, this time around the guy does feel and play like a tank, he actually has viable strategies. Newcomer Shinada is probably the least impressive, but when considering he is replacing Tanimura it's hardly a loss. Combat is also less filled with annoying grab-spams that force you to repeatedly press the same button to break free. With the notable exception of some extra-challenging fights. Then things are bad. That Amon fight probably ruined my gamepad. Nevertheless, overall combat plays out a lot better than in the previous game.Gameplay wise there is generally a lot that has been improved. That includes the new game modes, like those found in the side-games. Yes, they may feel a bit janky sometimes. Yet, they are quite fun nonetheless. Yes, driving around or hunting is definitely less polished than combat is. Yet, I kept doing it for hours and hours. Naturally, there are a few pet peeves here and there. The frequency of random encounters is something I have criticised before in this series. This time, it seems to be on steroids. Sometimes, you can't even take 3 steps without getting involved into some street fight with some hopelessly outmatched loser. Another issue when roaming around is just how packed the streets are. There are civilians blocking your path the whole time, as if the Covid anxiety this caused wasn't bad enough, it's actually really hard to push through them too.Overall, this game was exactly what I needed after Yakuza 4. It fully restored my somewhat damaged faith in the series and is arguably the best Yakuza game since 0. Sure, the main story is nothing to write home about, but it hardly matters. There is so much to see and do here, the individual segments are by themselves more than enough. The game does experiment quite some. The rhythm game half-way through for instance. This may surprise returning players and it would be good to be prepared and willing to try something different. But it's worth it. This game, as a package, is a great Yakuza experience. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 Remastered saw the franchise get back on track after Yakuza 3 Remastered was a slight misstep. Yakuza 5 Remastered continues that trend, being a quality offering that will leave Ryu Ga Gotoko fans satisfied once they’ve had their fill of Kazama Kiryu and co. First off, Yakuza 5 Remastered looks pretty fantastic. It’s clearly a step up from Yakuza 4 Remastered and Sega were doing all they could to crank out a quality looking game. Graphics are sharp and more vibrant.  There is still pop-up issues that said and while it’s quaint to see some restaurants you enter use pre-rendered backgrounds, it does take away a little from the overall presentation. But overall this is still an impressive game to look at. The cities, Kamarucho, Tsukimino, Sotenbori, Kinecho and Kamurocho, have their distinct look and feel, especially Tsukimino because its taking place during Christmas. The UI interface has once again been tightened up. They’ve decreased the sizes of text and boxes but it’s still very readable and just as importantly allows you to see and view more. Plus it looks really slick and impressive.. There is still has that weird design choices such as only being able to select one item at a time mechanic e.g. when getting reward items from a store) and now you can’t advanced conversations with the B/Circle button meaning you can easily select an option you don’t want, making it somewhat easier to fail sub-stories/sub-missions. This is all topped off by the fantastic music with a lot of emotional scores, as well as diverse ranges you expect from the series (playing as Haruka will expose you to some catchy bangers). Another audio triumph us that we now have speech for the majority of the important in-game scenes. It makes the story seem that much more important. Once again we are now playing as not just Kiryu, but as three other characters; charismatic money Lender Shun Akiyama, gruff but kind-hearted Taiga Saejima, the naive but determined adopted daughter of Kiryu, Haruka Sawamura, with dreams of being a Japanese Idol and newcomer, disgraced former baseball player, the somewhat sleazy but lovable Tatsuo Shinada. Once again we have different fighting styles with Kiryu being the all-rounded powerhouse, Akiyama being speedy and technical, Saejima with strong man moves and great crowd control and Shinada with weird grappler style backed up by being a weapon master of sorts. This sees the side-stories back but they are much more involved. Kiryu drives a Taxi (it makes sense in context) in not just getting fares but also providing customer service via conversations and engaging in speed racing (again, it makes sense in context,) Saejima gets to go hunting! Haruka goes through the trials and tribulations of being a Pop Idol and new character Tatsuo Shinada rediscovers his baseball groove (and makes the baseball mini-game fun!) Only Akiyama lacks one. At least he gets a dance battle against an old lady as a sub-story. In terms of story, Shinada may seem like an odd duck, but he ends up fitting in regardless and it's another interesting well-executed story with the usual Yakuza story beats; you kind of know what to expect but you still feel rewarded for going through it. The main story cutscenes are longer than usual but they don’t feel dragged out. Gameplay has been refined once again. We’re now using a hybrid of Yakuza 3 Remastered and Yakuza 4 Remastered experience system; With now having to choose from Soul, Tech, Body and Heat to increase (Yakuza 3 Remastered) but instead of spending experience points, you now spend soul orbs you gain from levelling up (Yakuza 4 Remastered). While it’s somewhat restrictive compared to Yakuza 4 Remastered, it’s nowhere as bad as it was for Yakuza 3 Remastered, thanks to experience points gain being less stingy. That said, you can’t max out your level until the late game (and only if you complete a sidequest) so it can be frustrating to see your growth stall. Speaking of levels, you now have “weapon skills” that gain levels depending on how much you use them. Not only do you do more damage the higher the level, but it’s required to use many weapons with have a level requirement. This actually encourages you to NOT avoid fights, as many places will have a weapon of some kind to build up those vital experience and unlock cooler and much more useful weapons, but to also use weapons you own constantly, even the least effective ones and not just chuck em away once you’ve done their heat actions. A nice improvement is that each character can now use all weapons.This ties into the modding which is less of a hassle. Now you can repair and reload more than one item at a time. Now Kamiyama does everything, rather than having to run around different vendors trying to find bits and pieces. You have to unlock his wares through investment but this brings a happy medium of working towards unlocking powerful and effective equipment while not sandbagging you and making it feel restrictive as it did in Yakuza 3 remastered (and to a lesser extent, Yakuza 4 Remastered.) That said, you still have to wait till near end-game to fully take advantage of it. At least now you can fix weapons without having to go to the modding shop!The main meat of the game, combat, is much faster. Enemies encounter happen either almost instantly or at the very least a lot more quickly (no more weird dialogue from enemies to fight you), it feels faster and the heat Actions are revamped for the better. They look more visceral and violent and there’s more of them, with weapons sometimes having more than just one Heat Action belonging to it. There’s also some new mechanics which is nice, with the Dragon Spirit making Kiryu go all Super Saiyan for a limited time, as well as activating (for him and the other playable characters) a Super Extreme move that does good damage but its costly all the same. There is some additional quality of life improvements with combat; It’s easier to avoid being thrown by enemies, they can now be targeted by weapons on the ground and you can pocketHowever, we have something different. Enter Haruka Sawamura, the adopted daughter of Kiryu. For the first time, we control her in her own exciting journey and story. Does she take on guys twice her size and beat them down like fools? Well no. Instead Haruka’s scenario focuses on her rise to being a Japanese Idol in the music industry. Cue Dance battles, concert singing, handshake events and even miscellaneous side gigs like interviews, quizzes and being in a show panel. While its nice beating the crap out of thugs and smug villains, its relaxing and refreshing to see this side of the story. Of course, it being a Yakuza game, its not smooth sailing and has the usual tense, whiplash and bittersweet moments alongside the positive upbeat moments. The substories for each characters feel a lot more involving, not just gameplay wise but story wise too. As stated in past reviews, they feel like the soul of the Ryu Ga Gotoko games and each instalment seems to improve on them and Yakuza 5 Remastered is no different. A nice handy addition is there is now markers for where they are (as well as where to go next). It may take the exploration fun out of finding them but for others, it can feel like making doing them less frustration. Really the biggest drawbacks with Yakuza 5 Remastered are the usual pains with any Yakuza game before this one; weird design choices, some mini-games being just pure pain, save points being far apart making doing so a hassle. But Yakuza 5 Remastered has shown that Sega can put love and care into an established franchise such as the Ryu Ga Gotoko games, trying new things, learning from past mistakes and still making sure it carries that insane charm, energy and great execution, it’s still a joy to play.

_childDocuments_.review: series’ writer, Masayoshi Yokoyama, once commented to  that 2012’s  would be like  in terms of scope – it would be a huge game with expanded core concepts.  – and by extension 2019’s  – notably ended up featuring 5 explorable locales, 5 playable characters, and 4 side stories on top of the already plentiful side content that games in the series are known for. It, in retrospect, was more ambitious than 2013’s  in some ways. not only whisks us back to Kamurocho and Sotenbori, but also introduces us to Nagasugai (based on Nakasu, Fukuoka), Tsukimino (Susukino, Sapporo), and Kineicho (Sakae, Nagoya). It brings Kazuma Kiryu, Taiga Saejima and Shun Akiyama back as playable characters, with pop-idol-in-training Haruka Sawamura, and disgraced former baseball player Tatsuo Shinada being the surprising and welcomed additions to the roster.If you’ve played the mainline remastered  games so far, you’ll find ’s gameplay to be very familiar. There are ample substories to complete, minigames and gambling games to play, food and drinks to consume, hostesses to meet, fighting abilities to unlock, and trinkets to find. Not only do these side activities make locales more alive, they’re necessary for levelling up the protagonists for boss battles.Yet, there is plenty that makes  different from its predecessors. The five playable protagonists each has at least one master to train with; extra training with Sotaro Komaki can raise the level cap from 20 to 25; health and abilities can be enhanced by dining in restaurants; Revelations are expanded to include some weapons; character- and region-specific minigames are added; and of course the 4 side stories.All this new content is certainly impressive on paper, but sadly, bigger and more don’t translate to better. Although gameplay is diverse and abundant, the game is so bloated with content that the main story gets overshadowed and sidelined. Perhaps that was intentional because the main story was poorly thought out and is unnecessarily convoluted. More poignant themes and emotions were ignored in favour of forced storytelling and poor character developments, which Yokoyama tried to present as shocking narrative twists.Just how bad is the main story? Prior to the final boss fight, Kiryu asked the antagonist, “What are you doing here?” (The actual reason for this is so ludicrous that I couldn’t blame Kiryu for asking.) Just when you thought the enemy’s motive is tied to the running theme of realizing one’s dream, and help other people fulfill theirs, he answered, “To be honest…I’m not really sure myself.” That was it – absolutely lazy writing to tie up a major loose end.With 5 playable characters, pacing of the game dragged. Although Kiryu’s part kickstarted the story well, it stopped at a cliffhanger so that the game could shift to Saejima’s. However, Kiryu’s actions had no impact on Saejima’s adventures; Saejima’s exploits had no effect on Haruka and Akiyama’s experience; and Haruka and Akiyama’s deeds had no influence on Shinada’s circumstance. Each of the 4 parts exists in a vacuum, thus bringing the main story’s momentum vexingly to a halt 4 times, with no payoff for each until a huge exposition dump in the finale.It was as though Yokoyama got tired of writing gangster stories, and was more interested in exploring other subject matter and telling smaller, more intimate stories in the  universe. Thus, we got a slew of side activities and 4 side stories to distract us from the poor quality of the main narrative.Although the 4 side stories have little impact on Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka and Shinada (Akiyama doesn’t have one) in the main story (except for earning XPs), they’re memorable and touching. Kiryu getting caught in the world of street racing; Saejima confronting the harshness of nature in winter; Haruka balancing fame and friendship; and Shinada resolving old feuds with his rivals – they all have their moments that made me want to go the extra mile to finish tasks or missions. I actually cared about the characters involved.Haruka and Shinada’s side stories and main story parts are particular standouts. Haruka’s section is full of positivity and hope, and allows for hassle-free exploration of Sotenbori. Shinada’s is full of pathos (and a laughable disguise from a masked individual), making you want to root for his comeback. Plus, Shinada is unrefined and rough around the edges in a funny way, but also feels real. I was really glad he was added as a playable character, even though his story is actually superfluous to the main narrative.As bloated as  is, the gameplay is still fun overall. The most important part – the combat – is slick and tactical. While plenty of Heat Actions were at my disposal, I needed to learn to use them strategically for filling the Climax Heat gauge, which would allow me to use Climax Heat techniques during boss battles. With that, boss fights never felt very challenging at Normal difficulty level.There was one detail that the developers included that I particularly loved. Because Shinada respects the game of baseball, he will not use a baseball as a weapon. If you try to pick up a dropped bat when controlling him during combat, you’ll see a unique animation of Shinada picking it up, inspecting it, then putting it down. It’s a small detail, but has great impact on characterization!Yokoyama also once said to  about , “Outside of whenever it’d be useful to preserve the tempo of the story scenes, we want to avoid cutting things off as much as we can.” Perhaps he and his fellow developers should have rethought that approach. Since more emphasis was put on the side content than the main story, valuing quantity over quality,  ended up being an uneven game. But, it’s still fun depending on the part you’re playing. is a product of the studio’s overambition, but it’s also proof of their collective creativity. After , the studio went on to make , which is arguably one of the best games (if not THE best game) in the series to date.  – a game that also features multiple playable characters, concurrent storylines, and multitude of side content – feels more cohesive as a whole; it’s what  could have been if the developers’ creativity was expressed with restraint.As much as I’ve bagged on this game’s story, Yokoyama is not without talent. The game’s side stories were interesting; he also wrote a powerful scene in which Kiryu asked himself after seeing someone he holds dear got hurt, “Why does this happen whenever I get involved? Why does someone else always have to pay the price?” If only he went with this theme instead of spinning yarn about fulfilling dreams., in spite of its flaws, is still worth playing because there are plenty of good bits in the potpourri of content. If you plan on experiencing all that the / series has to offer, the good news is that  is far from being the worst game. Somewhere in this game, you’ll likely find some elements that will be of interest to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a fantastically weird game that offers a serious and amazing story that juxtaposes the ridiculous but good gameplay. The game has decent graphics and good characters that make you care about their struggles and motivations. However, it also disappoints in some aspects compared to Yakuza 4.One of the main drawbacks is that Shinada, while a great character with a compelling backstory, is not as interesting as Tanimura from the previous game. His gameplay is much better though. Another issue is the hunting section that ruins Saejima’s part. It is tedious, boring and frustrating to deal with the wild animals and the harsh weather. It feels like a chore rather than a fun activity.The game also introduces Haruka as a playable character for the first time, but her dancing section is unnecessary and out of place. Even though it is fun to play as a pop idol and perform on stage, it does not fit well with the tone and theme of the game. It also takes away from the main plot and the other characters’ stories.The game also suffers from awful PC optimization, as it has frequent bugs and performance issues. It is not well ported from the PS3 or PS4 version and it shows. The game could have used more polish and testing before being released on PC.Despite these flaws, I still bought the game twice, once on PS4 and once on PC, because I love the Yakuza series and I wanted to support the developers. The game is still worth playing for its engaging story, its quirky side quests, its diverse mini-games and its charming characters. The game also has Akiyama, who is the best character in the series and should have been the protagonist of every chapter. He is smart, funny, generous and badass. He steals every scene he is in and makes the game more enjoyable.Overall, I would give Yakuza 5 a positive rating of 8/10. It is not perfect, but it is still a great game that deserves your attention if you are a fan of the Yakuza series or if you are looking for a unique and immersive experience.`
