_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 takes what Yakuza 4 accomplished and amplifies everything in it to create a brand new experience that is bigger and better than before. It is the most jam-packed Yakuza title yet, the longest-running in the Kiryu saga, and contains the most playable characters. But it also is a case where it becomes too much of a good thing that finally reaches the series’ breaking point, and causes some issues for the franchise. Yakuza 5 has returning characters from the previous game with Kiryu, Saejima, and Akiyama, but adds in two new playable characters, an ex-baseball player, Tatsuo Shinada, and for the first time in the series, Haruka Sawamura, Kiryu’s adopted daughter. Each of these characters gets their own section of the story, with Haruka and Akiyama sharing their portion, giving players four distinct parts of the game, with a rather large finale at the end.Due to those sections, Yakuza 5’s story is massive. Kiryu’s section starts with the series’ main protagonist hiding in Nagasugai under an assumed name. Daigo Dojima, the leader of the Tojo Clan finds him and explains what’s going on.  He details a brewing war between The Tojo Clan and their long-time rivals, The Omi Alliance. This is the major backdrop for much of Yakuza 5’s story, however, each character has a personal story that will weave into a full narrative in the final sections. Like always, Kiryu ends up getting involved in the Tojo Clan’s affairs. This time the cause is that Daigo goes missing after their discussion. This part of the game feels the most at home for the series and shines, it’s the strongest of Yakuza 5’s storylines, though this means Yakuza 5’s peak is the first section of the game. After Kiryu’s story is mostly resolved, Yakuza 5 then hard cuts to Saejima. Saejima’s story begins with him returning to prison to atone for an undescribed “assault”. Where Kiryu’s story is strong, Saejima brings the entire experience to a firm stop, focusing on prison life for an entirely too long time, and then a large side game that takes a decent amount of time. Each character’s section starts with a hard stop and feels like the game is starting over, which means there are three dead stops throughout the game. Besides, each character has different pacing, where both Shinada and Kiryu are what fans will expect from the series in its storytelling, Saejima focuses on long and pointless dream sequences that add very little to his story.Then there’s Haruka, who finally has the series focus on her, but her story is about being an idol for a tv program. It’s such a strange and unique departure for the series. But it’s also Yakuza at its most pure.  It feels appropriate for the series, even as the story completely departs from the series’ comfortable niche. Though the addition of Haruka causes some issues with the gameplay, we’ll discuss that below.Finally, Tatsuo Shinada is a new face to the series, but his story is a redemption arc for a disgraced baseball player who was called out for stealing signs.  He was banned from baseball, and now years later, plans to find out the truth of what occurred many years before. It’s a story that should resonate with players and is an enjoyable story.The experience of each story is good, but besides the pacing where the game has to restart the story three times with entirely new characters and no firm connection between them, Yakuza 5 also has a bigger issue. Yakuza 5 is a very long game. If played at a reasonable pace and ignoring all side missions, players are likely going to spend at least thirty hours, however with the ease of getting distracted, it’s more likely that players will spend at least fifty hours or more. I spent eighty-four personally. That’s a long time, but with the story having four distinct sections with no overlap, stuff that happened in the original section is forgettable when there are over twenty hours or more hours of gameplay before returning to those characters. In the finale, characters showed up and I had forgotten who they were or what their relevance was in Yakuza 5. This is even true for the final boss which feels like a character who comes out of nowhere.As for the gameplay, Yakuza 5 is filled to the brim with different modes. The typical Yakuza battle system is back, and similar to Yakuza 4, each character feels different. There’s more variety with each fighting style this time. Where Akiyama played similarly to Kiryu in Yakuza 4, a firm effort has been made to make each character unique, and it has paid off, giving four distinct brawlers, which becomes more noticeable once players use these characters back to back in the finale. Each of the four sections of the game also has a unique “Side mission” which is a major mini-game that is exclusive to that character. Kiryu has Taxi missions, Saejima goes hunting, Shinada has a fresh baseball minigame that is extremely enjoyable, and Haruka performs in musical numbers, as well as being tasked with typical Idol duties such as shaking people’s hands, or going on game shows. At the same time, the main story relies on many of these. Saejima spends a decent amount of time progressing through his hunting before he’s allowed to continue with the main story and Haruka has to do many idol performances, as that’s her main gameplay mechanics, rather than having her fighting system.  Saejima’s entire section feels like it goes on too long and while I enjoyed it, it felt like the side mission became more of the main story than optional gameplay. Haruka’s idol story though can be painful as the section focuses on her performing in a tv idol competition but to become good enough for that players will have to practice quite a bit. By the time you finally perform the musical number for the show, the player will likely become sick of the song. It’s an interesting experience that made me realize all performers must practice far more than Haruka does to become proficient at the music that has made them famous, and it made me wonder how many of them must grow to hate their most popular music.Still the side missions here are enjoyable, but then with the massive number of minigames added in, fans may be in danger of drowning in the side activities. The problem is that the story doesn’t treat them as side activities as they are often required such as making the player play a game of pool here, or a game of baseball there to progress. I’ve always been a big fan of the mini-games in the franchise and I do enjoy the majority of them in Yakuza 5, however with the massive sum of time already in the story, and the fact that the story feels like it's needlessly adding them to pad the run time, I question if it is really necessary. Putting a mini-game on the player's path makes it less special than if players accidentally stumble upon a mini-game on their question of vengeance. Yakuza 5’s additions to the series aren’t isolated to the minigames, the Yakuza world has expanded massively.  While Kamurocho and Sotenbori are familiar locations to fans of the series.  Yakuza 5 has five distinct cities, with three of which are new to the series and players barely spend any time in Kamurocho this time around. Each section of the game is set in a new city and it means players will explore their city as their story plays out. The newer cities are smaller than previous locations but they are fresh additions to the game and one that helps Yakuza 5 feel brand new even with the game using a similar progression to the previous four games.See the end of the review with the score at: If you enjoyed this and want to see more from me, you can check out my youtube channel at

_childDocuments_.review: Overall satisfaction: Recommended, the quality of this game is comparable to Yakuza 0.Storyline: Good. We play as 5 protagonists with their own stories in 4 different cities. We can now control how many street fights to participate in (as opposed to Yakuza 3 and 4). The game has a lot of new side contents. There are 4 sets of side missions (side mission is like Real Estate and Cabaret in Yakuza 0): Taxi, Hunting, Idol, Baseball. There are also a lot of new minigames such as snowball fight (yes, you read that correctly), making ramen, etc.At the start of part 1 and 2, we will be given a city tour, which is an awesome way to learn new cities. Moreover, the game also includes the minigames (karaoke, dart/pool, Cabaret Hostess) in the story progression, so we have some basic knowledge of the minigame.Character depth: This is one aspect that Yakuza 5 excelled in. Side characters are explored with more depth, including their character and their relationship with other characters.Substories: I think Yakuza 5 has the best substories set out of Yakuza 0 - Yakuza 5. Yakuza 0 branded itself as having 100 substories, but most of them are very short. Meanwhile in Yakuza 5, the substories are much more meaningful. _childDocuments_.review: Five character to play as, five cities to explore & all the gameplay that fans of the franchise expect:  doesn’t want to innovate,  wants to expand. As such, there's more of everything - even if that everything is mostly what we've seen in previous  games already. Just reaching the end of 's story, ignoring all side content, is going to take even experienced (!) players between 30 and 35 hours. If you fancy taking a look at some of the side content as well, you can easily put a few dozen hours on top of that:  is simply bursting with activities to participate in.Unfortunately, more doesn't always mean better. That is, unless you're only mostly interested in side-activities to begin with - if you just want to participate in karaoke with different playable characters, well, there you go.No, the main victim of 's content expansion is the main story. Just like , it's spread across different playable characters, each with their own parts & chapters - culminating in a finale where everything's supposed to come together. While its predecessor featured four playable characters,  ramped that number up to five. How does that work out?Unfortunately, for everyone expecting an interwoven storyline with frequent crossovers between the (playable) characters, I'm going to have some disappointing news:  has chosen a different approach, a sequential one. To put it simply, you're playing through the story of the first protagonist, get a cliffhanger to set up that finale and then start from zero with another protagonist in an entire different city/setting. Rinse and repeat until the finale has been reached.Considering you're not allowed to transfer anything - be it items or money - between characters up until that finale,  feels more like a package deal for a bunch of separate games rather than one big title with a steadily progressing story. It's more of an episodic title with a big crossover at the end, if you will.There are three problems with the approach  is taking: the need for good pacing, delivering satisfying end points for each individual story part and lastly, offering a finale that manages to tie all loose threads together. And as you guessed it,  has problems with all of these.Let’s start with the pacing issues. What’s the most important part about a story which is supposed to come together at the big finale? Getting the players to stay interested until the awaited conclusion arrives with a bang. In an episodic title, this means giving the players a constant stream of plot development or clues throughout all episodes, without running out of steam in-between. That is unfortunately nothing  can provide.In a game as filled with potential side activities, it’s easy for the player to stray too far from the story, creating their own pacing problems by spending too much time perfecting those karaoke numbers for example. But  manages to create its own pacing problems even when ignoring side activities. The pacing of the game changes constantly. Sometimes it’s pressing on rapidly, queuing long cutscenes and dialogues without breaks. Sometimes it stalls you, forces you to run through a city multiple times before the story really continues.This isn’t a new issue for the franchise - but it gets worse thanks to the game’s length, constant progress resetting by switching to new characters and the unsatisfying end points of the story arcs, which brings us to problem number 2: None of the character parts have a satisfying end. Instead, the endings all point directly to the finale, leaving you with just a feeling that the “princess is in another castle”. Nothing really gets resolved during each part,  just dumps a lot of loose threads on you with the promise to tie them up in the end. Completing an episode, which – again – takes a few hours, doesn’t give you the feeling of completing an interim goal – it feels like someone just pulled that dangling carrot in front of you a little further away.And then, lastly, we get to the promised, solve-it-all part: the finale of the game. Of course, due to spoilers, I won’t go into details here, just let me say this much: First, you’re going to see a lot of dialogues painstakingly trying to tie everything together. Second, you’ll realize that thanks to the length and uneven pacing of this game, you’ve already forgotten some of the earlier plot details. Third, even with all the time to build things up,  still decides to throw some last-minute surprise developments into the mix. Lastly, while some of the character moments still work due to the attachment we’ve gotten to them over the last few games, others are just bafflingly stupid.That’s not something that just happens during the finale, by the way. Of course, being a  game, a bit of stupidity is expected – like the inconsistent use and power of guns in these games. However,  takes things up a notch at times, which made me really wonder if some of the characters are just plain idiots. And this is a franchise where you fight a tiger with your plain fists as a boss battle.Overall, the story of  made me tired, scratch my head and even consider dropping the game a few times. Still, I do have to give the game some credit where it’s due: the voice acting remains fantastic, and I can’t help but love some of the characters. Returning to Kamurocho, with Kiryu standing under that big neon arc, is always a pleasure. Punching gangsters with a bike feels great (even though this game has way too many random encounters in narrow streets & blocking enemies). I enjoyed the gameplay change introduced with the third playable character, even if they overdid it. And well, there’s always baka mitai.Still,  is probably my least favorite Yakuza game I played so far. It didn’t stop me from trying to get all the way to  but it sure did test my patience a few times. If you’re like me, you’re probably going to play this game regardless, just to continue Kiryu’s journey. But if it wasn’t for this and the attachment I developed for the franchise, I doubt I could’ve seen this game to its end. Replaying it is certainly out of the question.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like this game. It's hard to tell whether RGG Studio was running out of ideas or had too many. Things I don't like about it:- The story is split between five characters and the narrative suffers for it in the same way 4 did, i.e. it has a stop-and-start cadence where every time the plot picks up and gets interesting their part suddenly ends and you start from zero with a different character. I thought this would be less of a problem in 5 since most of the characters had already been established in the series, but their circumstances here are completely new so each character ends up with hours of individual exposition at minimum, and most chapters after Kiryu's don't really fold into the main plot until near the end.- A lot of the central narrative is just flat out tangential or barely relevant, e.g. a troubled hunting village, idol competitions, baseball drama, etc. It's like half the staff didn't actually want to make another Yakuza game.- Part 2 is miserably linear and three of the four chapters take place outside of any city, in scenarios where you walk around and talk to people to advance the plot, with a few scripted fights. Someone actually looked at the prison chapter in 4, said "yes, we need more of this", and put two chapters of barely interactive cutscenes and dialog here in 5 as well. The third chapter of Part 2 is basically plot setup for a minigame and has no relation to the plot or even the basic themes of the series. By the time you end up in a city and are free to move around on your own, it's underdeveloped like the other two new ones, with invisible walls everywhere. Somehow Saejima can shoot up a noodle shop, head his own organized crime family, and beat crowds of people half to death every 15 feet when he goes outside but jaywalking is beyond the pale.- I don't like Shinada. His nasal voice is annoying, his fighting style sucks, and his whole dumb baseball story (minus the scant parts that relate to the yakuza) is really boring.- The new cities are underwhelming. Play spots and other points of interest are sparse compared to Sotenbori and Kamurocho. In contrast to 4 where they fleshed out Kamurocho with multiple levels and collectables the cities in 5 all seem barren and undeveloped with nothing to explore. Just move from cutscene to cutscene and run through the substory checklist. Subjectively, I also just think they're dull to look at.- The new minigames seem like obviously bad ideas, mainly in the sense that they all seem to revolve around established genres that usually get their own games with more thorough treatment (racing, hunting, rhythm). The racing and hunting minigames are on the level of mid-90s shareware and unsurprisingly not very great. I don't fault the devs for this outside of how they could have chosen something more appropriate. The rhythm parts in Haruka's section were sort of enjoyable and it's nice running around the city and dancing with people but the difficulty even on Hard is pitiful. I'm guessing since the rhythm sections are unavoidable, RGG Studio decided to tone down the challenge for everyone who isn't into this kind of thing and who expected a beat-em-up game like usual. That's understandable but if they couldn't go all the way with it, it probably wasn't a great idea to start with.- The usual minigames are barely accessible for most of the game due to them being absent from cities or plot-restricted, sometimes for reasons that make sense (Haruka doesn't gamble), sometimes for reasons that don't (Kiryu can play exactly 2 (two) games of shogi in Kyuushuu before his opponent randomly packs up and leaves). Making things even worse is that the game has a random luck mechanic where you'll get cellphone messages periodically announcing whether you feel lucky/unlucky; this is basically the game announcing to you that the PRNG is now tilted for or against you in games of chance. As an example, I suck at mahjongg, yet on the first hand of my second game I scored suukantsu, the most improbable yakuman (outside of tenhou and chihou). After I picked my jaw up off the floor I realized the game had probably cheated for me and playing an honest game of mahjongg isn't an option in this installment (putting aside the fact that mahjongg isn't available for 2/3rds of the game anyhow).- They went overboard with the heat attacks. I have no idea how many times I rolled my eyes after mistakenly pressing Y with a full heat gauge during a fight with random thugs and got stuck watching a 15 second movie of Akiyama kneeing some guy in the face. It gets old fast.- Even though this has one of the best final chapters in the series, the plot twists and overall writing get pretty stupid toward the end.

_childDocuments_.review: As both a PC port and the game itself, some words of warning.By this point, it's almost guaranteed that you are already familiar with this IP and either are buying the full collection in a go, or are waiting for a sale. Regardless, two things must me mentioned.First, this port is the only one I had any real issues with, three freezes to be precise. I didn't have any other technical issues, but other people did. There has been some patches so it's at least better now, pick up the fan-made Silent Patcher if you want as well..The second one, is that subjectively, this game is like a wasabi-filled sushi, a tasty affair that is a pain to swallow.You get five different characters with their own city, content and stories, intertwining in the full plot, but the game will first introduce them in a long as hell start, build up their role in the big picture, and then finally open up the fun.I personally ended up enjoying all of them and the variety they had in every regard, but let me be sincere, this will either be a game you discover you love, or you will bitterly endure it for the qualities that brought you to this series.I have to respect the commitment to have so much variety, content and unique ideas for everyone, but at the same time, it makes the padding and pacing issues of 4 look thin. Story wise, the pieces do fit nicer in place, even if by this point they clearly were trying to amp up the ridiculous excuses to get a really cool boss fight or a devilish villain twist.In the end, it's more of this damned Yakuza franchise , which let's be honest, if you are even reading this on the store page, you already know what's up by this point.When the game finally ramps up, it's a complete party of joy, and the pay-offs create what might be some of the best peaks of the series, but the lows are considerably steep in contrast and are certain to test your patience.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 takes on an ambitious scope, introducing four new cities and featuring five active main characters, each entwined in their own compelling subplot, all of which are individually impressive. However, the game grapples with the challenge of uniting these diverse elements, resulting in difficulty tying everything together. The main story, marked by a few notable highs, often falls short. A pivotal moment occurs when a main protagonist questions the purpose of their journey, encapsulating the sentiment that permeates Yakuza 5's main narrative. While the character subplots are exceptional in their own right, the cumulative effect feels a bit overwhelming.Despite these challenges, Yakuza 5 boasts the most extensive collection of mini-games in the entire series. The combat system, unfortunately, remains largely unchanged from Yakuza 4. However, within Yakuza 5, one can discern the early DNA of Yakuza 0, with this game laying the foundation for the exceptional aspects later refined in Yakuza 0. Despite its shortcomings, Yakuza 5 retains the quintessential Yakuza charm, offering hilarious subplots, intense action, and a unique style synonymous with the series. On these merits alone, I recommend Yakuza 5 to devoted series fans looking to complete the entire saga. However, for others, it may be prudent to consider skipping this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a game with such a diverse range of content you will fully enjoy at least one quarter of it, but on the same hand you might also completely hate a totally unrelated section.In this game, the central plot itself takes a backseat to the central theme. The theme of dreams. Each character is chasing or trying to fulfill a dream, be it there's or someone else's. This theme is not only present in the main plot but also pervades deep into the majority of substories. While everyone dreams do ultimately get them to come together and fight one antagonistic force, its the personal journeys that matter.The level system actually abandons the free leveling system of Yakuza 4 to return to the shingitai (body, tech, soul) system of prior entries. I don't like this decision as I feel Yakuza 4 nailed it, but its functional, and because you swap characters so often, you gain levels quick enough to mostly get what you need when you need it. Kiryu, Akiyama, and Saejima play for the most part as they did previously. However the series decided Tanimura doesn't get to exist anymore so this time around we have Shinada. He's clearly the basis for what would later become Yakuza 0's slugger style, but a little bit less fun. His unarmed style relies a lot on grabs, which I found most bosses quickly got fed up with and decided to just not allow. He gains access to unbreakable weapons which is great in concept and opens up a lot of options for him. Unfortunately these weapons are so pathetically weak you'll only be able to kill with them from one (sometimes two) heat actions.I would be remiss not to give Haruka her own section. Haruka is technically a protagonist. However, she does not get to fight. Instead she solves her issues through the power of song and dance in rhythm game battles. I personally do find these really fun. However, because they couldn't manage to write an entire dramatic chapter where problems are solved non-violently, Akiyama sweeps in during the latter half. My biggest problem with this is that its completely unnecessary. If the devs had just let Haruka, the child of the dragon of dojima, have even the most basic of combat abilities, she would have been able to solve her own problems instead of the plot needing to write Akiyama in and fight her battles for her while she's busy getting kidnapped and passing out. I can't help but be dissatisfied with the idea to create a female protagonist we've known for so many entries and still deny her any real agency. Haruka's "main character" status makes it impossible to ignore just how bad this series treats women, and once you've seen it you can't really unsee it.Moving on, the side content in this game is incredibly numerous. Each character not only has substories, but side stories. Side stories are incredibly fleshed out and unique minigames that have their own story about the main character who participates and their allies overcoming challenges together. They are worth doing if only because they could really be their own games. Side stories this time around were also very fun and interesting, if not a little unfair at times. Unlike substories in Yakuza 3 that tried really hard to highlight Okinawa's peaceful; slow pace, or Yakuza 4 which served to give you insights on what the new characters valued, Yakuza 5 uses the loose and open theme of dreams/desire to explore some truly wacky situations. Things like having to dodge a ton of random people slipping on icy roads or applying to company where everyone has to walk around naked are just some of the things to look forward to on the quest to unlock the Amon battle. Overall, Yakuza 5 is an amazing game, and I can see why some people call it their favorite Yakuza. For me though, I still think I liked 4 just a little bit better. Like I said at the beginning, with such diverse content, I certainly think Yakuza 5 has the highest high points, but also some pretty low lows depending on what interests you.

It starts out well, with each character having incredibly well told story-arcs, the gameplay and combat system have been incredibly refined compared to previous entries made prior to the Dragon Engine games (1-4) to the point where everything felt incredibly smooth.However, all this is slowly fading away as Haruka's story-arc begins and all the previously mentioned things fade away into nothingness, as her story is simply too boring, too drawn out and her "fighting" a.k.a. Dance Battles get boring real quick, especially with how weird and inappropriate some of the outfits during the shows are (Shes still Kiryus teenage daugher! Whats with all the weird f*in outfits??) only to then have it all end in a really boring, seemingly rushed end that brings all and everyone together in one final chapter. Now, why do I still recommend this game though? Simply because this game has so much more to offer. It is literally jam-packed with content (after finishing my first play-through doing various side missions for each of the playable characters I still ended up with only _20%_ completion!) and it really shows that they pulled everything out of this "old" engine they possibly could. Multiple playable characters, lots of incredibly gorgeous places and cities to visit and so much more. The fightings stil great, the divesities in each of the fighters movesets are (compared to the usual Yakuza lineup) very well thought out and its just fun to beat people up. While this game is definately the weakest installment in the series, its still worth checking out, especially if youre a fan of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I've finished the game now and my opinions have not changed.I haven't finished the game yet as of the initial posting of this review, but I feel like I've already got my money's worth. I feel like I've played 3 yakuza games and I still suspect that  I have about a little more than a third left to experience. The story so far has been stellar and thankfully less predictable than the last two games were. The amount and quality of game I've been playing so far is easily worth more than the entry fee. If you have 20USD to spend, this game is a fantastic choice. The value of my currently incomplete play-through is equal to the 40USD price of the remastered collection.I'll come back and edit this review when I've finished to give my final verdict.Final Verdict: This is a damn good game with some of the best combat in the series. The story is amazing but gets a bit convoluted during the finale. Everything that I said before still applies.PC PORT RANT:This is a ♥♥♥♥ port by the way. There is no 120fps+ support, and the game runs worse than it should. Yakuza 0, a more graphically intensive game that runs on the same engine, with 4x super-sampling, ran at around 110fps. Yakuza 3, 4, and 5 on the other hand run between 43-57 when I so much as sneeze on the super-sampling option. Also, the Ambient Occlusion implementation used for these PC ports is absolute garbage. It reeks of the type of quality that you associate with shoddy implementations of Nvidia Control Panel's HBAO+. The Ambient Occlusion does not respect any kind of visibly clipped(overly-exposed) surface and decides to make the white highlights a disgusting and unappealing grey. The effect covers way too much as well. As you move your camera you can see blobs of darkness disappearing and reappearing at the edges of your display. Its hideous. I'm aware that all of these problems could be solved quite easily. Just disable AO in the settings, but why make it an official option when it makes the game look worse?

_childDocuments_.review: My review for Yakuza 4 Remastered was pretty harsh, lots of hate for the multi-story setup, frustrating sections in each character, disconnection of difficulty between bosses and grunts, and NOT ENOUGH KIRYU.Yakuza 5 Remastered has gone and changed and improved many of the things that annoyed me in Yakuza 4, much of the story feels more engaging and more varied. I still feel there isn't enough connection between the stories themselves, but I do see an improvement on this aspect. Combat feels much better, each character that fights has had some minor changes in how they control, their move set, and how much of a beating they can take. The main bosses feel much more reasonable, a needed improvement from Y3 AND Y4, I don't feel a need to drop the difficulty down after dying 50 times to a single boss. I've focused on not blazing through this game like Y4, I managed to do plenty of side-content, including quests, mini games, general achievement hunting which all managed to be engaging and silly like a classic Yakuza experience. Still playing this game to do some additional content, but so far while this is not a must play, it is a decent and recommendable Yakuza game from my perspective. I'd give it a STRONG 7/10 .

_childDocuments_.review: The quality of the game was unexpectedly good. It was unexpected for me because I bought the bundle, and I thought that 3-5 would have the same quality but I was proven wrong with new gameplay mechanics, Better graphics than 0, and better story elements in general. There is a lot of things I would comment because this entry is drastically different from the other games in the same bundle.For the general things, I would like to put away first my nitpicks with the movement, there is STILL no sprint which can be annoying at times, and the run animations for when you first moves were a bit uncomfortable to get used to at first but you slowly get used to it. There is several new things to do, like driving wow! And of course one the new playable characters.. Haruka! Although sadly she doesn't fight, we can play her and play a rhythm game. Honestly at first I was skeptical of it, but I eventually grew to love her part because she actually has an engaging story and a cast of decent characters. The focus on the vibe and theme of the moments were amazing, unlike 3-4 were I barely felt anything, Yakuza 5 Remastered did a great job of setting the mood for certain scenes, although not perfect (Like suddenly switching to a light hearted segment after a really really heavy one. Other than those shortcomings I'm glad they set a focus on the mood of these scenes, massive improvement from 3-4 with story telling. Now for the actual story itself.. uh..They added a new combat mechanic which I think is called rage, basically it differs for the 5 characters on the purpose (of course Haruka still doesn't fight lol) But they surprisingly have different mechanics and not just a rage button where you are basically invincible. It's quite balanced for a game mechanic. But I do have to comment about my first loss it was from the new character Shinada Tatsuo. Man where do I begin, his fighting style is incredibly slow and they aren't stunning to look at. I get that he is supposed to be the weapon master and that is where I like him. But he is flat broke and he can't buy weapons unless you do side content. I literally had to borrow the weapons from the other characters and give it all to him. He is not fit to fight multiple enemies at once unless you stack him with a full inventory of weapons, other wise, it's gonna be extremely long dragged and unflashy fight. I honestly don't know about the linear leveling system it's easier to make a choice, but it felt like I barely knew the moves because looking at the info was a pain, just like the past 2. Haruka's part was actually pretty fun as a rhythm game segment. Although I can understand why people would be skeptical/bored with her, It actually grew on me and I started to like her gameplay. It just felt weird that one of the important parts were non violent.The story was okay at least, it got tiring because of the constant plot twists towards the end, but it had an amazing start with the mood, setting, and the characters, and thank God it started with Kiryu, I can see why people would be starved for him after 4 lol. Haruka's story was actually really good and it gave me the right mood to feel in the right moment, just really good story telling and she had a good cast around her and a very good individual story prior to her relevance to the first 2 characters. I have a complaint about Shinada's Placement in the story and his existence in general. His placement in the story was SOO bad, it was all starting to come together with the 4 main character's story but suddenly there is a reset and you need to get to know another character? He was irrelevant until the end of chapter 2. Of course, I grew to love him and his quirks, but I almost took my first ever Yakuza break because of him and his uninteresting hand to hand play style where you have to use weapons, but as my complaint earlier said he is FLAT broke you can't afford the weapons. And for his existence and relevancy, it felt more like he was a guest character compared to Tanimura (Rip Tanimura sent off to America). But for my conclusion to my Shinada opinion, he was actually a really good character it was hard to notice because we were just wondering when he gets relevant. Shinada actually has a very interesting individual story prior to his relevancy to the rest of the protagonists, and he has a good cast of characters around him, but as I said, he felt like a guest character.It surpassed my expectations and delivered well. The combat was comparable to 0 which is a big compliment, but what made 0 so good was it's dynamic feel of the 3 styles in 1 character. But this isn't about that. Definitely the best compared to 3 and 4 overall although this one was a bit lacking in the story itself, but it had amazing story TELLING. 9/10 Not my favorite, but it was honestly a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: all things considered, its a pretty decent port of a PS4 remaster of a PS3 game that was only released digitally here in the west. _childDocuments_.review: In this episode of Top Gear:KIRYU DRIFTS A TAXI IN THE HIGHWAY AT 300 KM/H!SAEJIMA GETS LOST IN THE MOUNTAINS AND KILLS TWO BEARS WITH HIS BARE HANDS!HARUKA TIGER DROPS KOMAKI AND AMON INTO THEIR GRAVES!AKIYAMA LOSES MILLIONS AGAIN!A BASEBALL BATTER TURNED BUM DESTROYS TWO MAFIA CLANS WITH ONE HOMERUN!Yet another Yakuza sequel and it still keeps delivering the good stuff.The story once again gets quite convoluted, fulls of twists and a few plot holes, but its still really good. The final boss gave me a good "wat" moment.Gameplay wise, its better than 4. All characters get new moves and a special heat mode gimmick to make fights more fluid.- Kiryu is still the basic moveset, but now he can activate a super mode that makes him invincible (for a few seconds) and lets him do some new combos, although the combo isn't that good.- Saejima can now grab people and slam them around, which is fun, but you always end up using your heat meter when you just wanted to do a normal grab.- Akiyama now can use a launcher move and start an air combo. Aside being strong and letting you stunlock most enemies, even Amon, the big problem is that it shares the same button as the Heat Moves and the Super Heat Moves, so you often end up using your heat bars trying to defeat a normal mook with the launcher combo.- Tanimura didn't return for this one, having his story pretty much tied by the end of 4, so here we have Shinada, whose moveset is very simple, but he had more moves using weapons and a grapple move at the end of his combos. Hes fun, but lacks good moves like a counter or a good quickstep.You also get to play as Haruka and this is by far the worst part of the game.The dancing gimmick gets old rather fast and there are not a lot of songs to keep things interesting. Hakura's chapters are entirely made of minigames (aside one that actually lets her fight, kinda).I feel that most of her chapter didn't add much to the story and most could be summed up in a few cutscenes.If anything, playing as Haruka can hinder your game, since unless you know about it to avoid it, you can't trade Haruka's items until the post-game, so opening lockers with her will cause several items she can't use be stuck with her pratically forever.Also, her chapters add the worst character in the game, Park.I actually have to complain about her. She shows up out of nowhere, blackmails Kiryu into entirely leaving his kids lives and cutting all ties, acts like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥ and scams the one character she shouldn't had, the game pulls the "oh she had a troubled past" (where all that happened was her fault for only thinking about her carrer), she freaking DIES off-screen and in the end her dream is stomped down like a barely lit cigarette and everything she worked for is thrown away for nothing.There are still dozens of minigames, with some new additions related to the characters side stories. Pretty much every minigame makes a return, except Table Tennis, that was replaed by Air Hockey.Every character but Akiyama gets a side story. They are basically really long substories.Kiryu can drive a taxi and do races in the highway, complete with eurobeat playing.Saejima can go hunting, killing animals for food and money, while trying to help a village with a massive bear problem.Haruka gets more of the same minigames she does on her chapters, but she can also do handshake events (which is entirely holding one button until you fill a bar) and lots and lots of quizzes.Shinada has a special version of the batting cages, complete with special equipment (that is entirely useless because his stats increase super fast) and some fun moments.The game is rather easy, I managed to go through it without any continues and the only times I got in trouble were the Komaki fights with Akiyama and Shinada (due their lack of counters and how relentless the duo is during the fight) and the final Amon fight (because not only he constantly gets invincible, he barrages you with explosives and is always dodging or countering).Visually, its ok. Still PS3 level, with some crusty textures when seen up close. The depth of field effect is still pretty ugly and I wish you could disable it, since it looks very bad on in-engine cutscenes. You can see the effect cutout around the characters and it gets pretty obvious around their hair.Didn't get any glitches other than some visual ones and only one softlock when I exited a minigame.Overall, yet another good sequel. The last using the old engine, as far as I know.Also the last one to feature that many minigames, since 6 removes most of them.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, but note that I have A LOT of issues with it. For me, the good was enough to outweigh the bad, but it was a lot closer than I wanted it to be. First and foremost: game runs flawlessly, and as with 3 and 4, is capped at 60fps. My main problem with this game centers around the playable protagonists/story choices, so that's how I'll structure the review. I'll keep this as spoiler free as possible, but will give some details to give context and to better explain myself. As for the typical Yakuza stuff, it's all here and largely great: minigames, substories, etc. Combat feels like an extension of Yakuza 4, and I thought 4's combat was good (not as good as later entries, but still solid). It uses the same level-up system, so once again our protagonist's skill trees feel a bit small, because they have to have 4 different skill trees - but they each have different fighting styles and feel appropriately different. The music is also particularly good in this game - I actually added quite a few tracks to my Spotify playlist. Now, for my explanations via protagonist. As with Yakuza 4, this game features multiple playable protagonists: 3 return from Yakuza 4, along with 2 new ones. Each protagonist gets 4 chapters (although one set of 4 chapters is shared between 2 protagonists), and then there are 4 chapters in the finale. Each protagonist also gets a new playable area, with everyone coming together in Kamurocho for the finale. These areas are all smaller than Kamurocho, but still expansive enough to have some depth.Kiryu: Kiryu's section is largely fine. Without getting into too many details, he's living on his own in a new area and has started working as a taxi driver. He has an entire taxi driver side questline that frankly didn't interest me at all (these missions require actually driving the taxi, and I did not enjoy this minigame), but he also has some of the standard Yakuza substories. Once the main portion of the story starts to kick in, Kiryu's portion gets more interesting but the first chapter or two are pretty dull. Saejima: Saejima returns from Yakuza 4, and his section is one of my least favorites. His 4 chapters are a huge slog, and one of his chapters has this entire hunting side questline that once again - did not interest me at all. The game takes so much time to introduce this (quite sizable, in all fairness) hunting "mini game", but it has absolutely nothing to do with the overall narrative. And the game spends so much time on it! I really liked Saejima's portion in Yakuza 4, but his part in 5 is so bad and it drags on forever. I could not get through it fast enough. Haruka/Akiyama: These are the two that split a section, with each getting two chapters. And strangely enough, this is the section that I enjoyed the most. Haruka is working on becoming a pop idol, so rather than combat, her sections have singing and dance battles and I enjoyed these way more than I should have. They're fairly simplistic rhythm-style games, but the music was incredibly catchy and overall I enjoyed them a lot. I would legitimately play a spinoff dance/singing game with Haruka. Akiyama's sections are also good, but that's mainly because I thoroughly enjoy his character. He and Haruka have a bit of a "team up" section, so it was fun to see them interact. Shinada: Shinada is the new protagonist introduced in Yakuza 5, and I didn't click with his story at all, but there could be an easy explanation for this. He's a burnout baseball player, so his side questline (and his combat) are all based on baseball, which I hate. I don't enjoy baseball in any format, I hate baseball minigames in any video game, and you're forced to play a baseball minigame a few times for the main story which annoyed me. If you like baseball (or even just baseball minigames), then you might enjoy his storyline more. Like Saejima, I couldn't get through his part quick enough. Although one thing I absolutely loved was his combat music - his combat music is fantastic. Finale: (no spoilers) Where the game redeems itself is during the finale. Frankly, this game has one of the best endings of the entire series. As much as I hated Saejima and Shinada's sections in the main game, their portions in the finale and their character's resolutions are amazing - Shinada's being one of my favorites. Sadly, Akiyama is just kind of "there" during the finale, but Kiryu has a good ending as well. I do have one or two issues with how some things are handled (which would require spoilers to explain), but for the most part the finale is fantastic and honestly almost makes up for the rest of the game. TL;DR: I don't think I will ever play this game again, as it has too much baggage. But I do think it's worth playing at least once, because the entire finale is utterly stupendous and incredibly emotional. The game is much more playable than Yakuza 3 is, and you might enjoy some of the gameplay sections that I didn't - you'll just need to be aware beforehand that the game is pretty bloated and has some issues.

_childDocuments_.review: "Yakuza 5 Remastered: Dreams Unleashed"  It took me about 80 hours to finish this game story. It was pure enjoyment all of the time because for me it's a masterpiece. Especially on the taxi minigame but that's a different story. In this review I want to focus on the story and the moral it gives to us. So, I recommend sitting back and relaxing because it might get a little long.   Yakuza 5 Remastered continues the tradition of delivering a rich and multifaceted narrative that immerses players into the intricate world of the Japanese underworld. The story is divided among five playable characters: Kazuma Kiryu, Shun Akiyama, Taiga Saejima, Haruka Sawamura, and Tatsuo Shinada. As their paths intertwine, players witness a gripping saga that explores themes of loyalty, redemption, and the consequences of one's past actions. The narrative kicks off with Kiryu, the series iconic protagonist, attempting to leave his yakuza past behind and lead a peaceful life. However, as is often the case in the Yakuza series, circumstances pull him back into the criminal underworld. The story seamlessly transitions between the different characters, providing a diverse range of perspectives on the overarching plot. One of the central themes in Yakuza 5 is the concept of loyalty, particularly the unwavering bonds that characters share within the yakuza brotherhood. The narrative delves into the complexities of these relationships, exploring how personal connections can be both a source of strength and a potential downfall. Loyalty becomes a driving force for many characters, pushing them to confront their pasts and make difficult choices for the sake of those they care about. Redemption is another crucial theme woven into the narrative. Each character grapples with their own history and strives to overcome their past mistakes. Whether it's Kiryu seeking a path of righteousness, Akiyama trying to help others as penance for his wealth, or Saejima attempting to reconcile with his troubled past, the story presents a nuanced exploration of redemption and the possibility of finding forgiveness. But what moral does Yakuza 5 give us?  It imparts several moral lessons throughout its narrative. It emphasizes the significance of personal growth, forgiveness, and the enduring power of loyalty. The characters' journeys serve as a reminder that redemption is attainable, even in the face of a tumultuous and often unforgiving world. The game encourages players to reflect on the consequences of their actions and the importance of standing by those they hold dear. Conclusion:  Yakuza 5 Remastered not only offers an engaging and intricate story but also delivers meaningful moral lessons that resonate with players long after the credits roll. It's a tale of honor, loyalty, and the enduring pursuit of redemption in a world where the line between right and wrong is often blurred.  To sum things up I just wanted to say it's the best Yakuza I played ever. It got itself a really special place in my heart with its beautiful story and overall gameplay. But if I had to focus on all the things in this game think it would take several hours for me to write it. So, to end this review I just want to say it's quite a literal masterpiece and I recommend everyone to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Shinada is the BEST character to play asTopic. While I want to like his sections and he is a nice character, he is just the BEST fighter in every aspect compared to anyone else on the roster.His combo game is GOOD, only going for 3 light attacks and not even getting double finisher like every other character. Even if you get the reinforced versions.As Kiryu, you can adapt to any situation with your extremely wide arsenal of moves. As Akiyama, you can use the speed of your combos to find the smallest openings and taunt in any situation for more heat. _childDocuments_.review: The story has Kiryu take the role of a taxi driver but of course, that doesn't last long as he's pulled back into the world of rivalling clans. As you progress through the story, you'll play as 5 characters within their own distinct locales: Kazuma Kiryu in Nagasugai, Taiga Saejima in Tsukimino and Kamurocho, Haruka Sawamura and Shun Akiyama in Sotenbori, and Tatsuo Shinada in Kineicho. Unlike Yakuza 4, the various acts actually feel distinct and memorable complete with changes of scenery, radically different gameplay, and fully fleshed out characters. Gameplay-wise, Yakuza 5's combat is fine-tuned and much more satisfying although it still isn't the greatest of the series. One of the most stand-out gameplay aspects is driving the taxi as Kiryu. Just like with driving in real-life, you'll have to pay attention to traffic lights, signs, and people walking and you also get rewarded by smoothly braking and accelerating. It may not sound fun but I found it surprisingly rewarding; perhaps because you can simply drive however you want in most games. Anyway, you can also take pictures around the cities, play air hockey, and enjoy arcade games like Taiko no Tatsujin and Virtua Fighter 2. Hands down, it's my favourite of the 3 games.

This game also features one of the most frustratingly awful written female characters I've ever seen in a story.Sadly, if the devs were more married to the idea of just creating a Yakuza 4 2.0, this game probably would have been better. The only saving grace is playing as Kiryu and Akiyama again (but realistically, if you wanted to play as them, just play as them in Yakuza 4, where their movesets are borderline copy/pasted from)A very big step down from previous entries. At least Yakuza 3's story was amusing to poke fun at. Admittedly, there's a ton of really (un)intentionally funny scenes to make you laugh in this game, but you have to deal with tons of filler, and mandatory optional content that you really wouldn't want to go through if the devs didn't force you to.God bless those pieces of ♥♥♥♥ at SEGA

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is an enormous game. Out of the 3 remastered games, it's probably my favourite. I'm not sure where to begin.After the little slog that was Yakuza 4, 5 feels completely different. The story picks up pretty darn well from the get-go, but it has it's ups and downs throughout. In terms of side-content, music, gameplay and so on, 5 is an absolute blast and peaks above even the current entries of the series, and it is certainly the longest out of all of them. But it also makes you feel like putting that time into it with the way it sets things up.Each character has a part in the story, and each character spends their story in a different city too, with different activities, sights, substories and so on. As the name implies, there are 5 characters, meaning that there are 5 cities. 2 of those you might recognize are Kamurocho, as always, and Sotenbori from Yakuza 0 and 2.I was spoiled on this game aswell, but except for the finale, the spoilers never really ruined anything for me. With 5 being such a big game I guess there were quite a lot of things I didn't know too. First, let's start with the graphics.The graphics might seem weird at first, this is running on the same engine as the beautiful Yakuza 0, and was released just 3 years before that, but the graphics are still a little bit of a ways from it. This game was still developed for the ps3 after all. I'll just give a fair warning that they might look horrendous or broken at first, but they're not. You start the game as Kiryu, beautiful cutscenes and everything. But the first time you can move around you'll be in an interior, because of the way some interiors are optimized, the inside looks a lil' bit pixelated in some of them, and this is one of them, so fair warning, the game is beautiful, just go outside. Make any sense?Anyway, Kiryu's part is an absolute blast to begin with with some really interesting story bits and takes on his character. As it progresses it dampens a little, but it ends on quite possibly one of the best fights if not the best fight in the entire series. Kiryu still has the Dragon of Dojima style as his combat style, albeit a little different. It's basically the same style you get in 0/Kiwami mixed with the 3/4 one, with some absolutely unique and brutal heat actions to boot.Same goes for the rest of the game. Although it's not on the level of heat action insanity 0 had yet, the many more things in the environment can be interacted with, and you'll see some familiar moves around.Kiryu spends his time in the district of Nagasugai. That might not mean anything to you, but this district quickly grew out to be one of my favourite areas in the series. I can't quite put my finger on it, but it's big, nice, and different from what we've seen before. Unlike the small or big alleyways of Kamurocho and Sotenbori, this district rungs along streets of cars, bigger restaurants, and bigger arcades and such, while still being nice and cozy. A nice waterway runs alongside it, too. Always nice to throw enemies in. Because of the disconnected feeling the game gives you, with a character in a faraway town, it made me feel like doing all the side activities possible in the town. Hell, I even enjoyed spending time with hostesses. Somehow. It feels more rewarding doing them at this point in the game too, since a lot connect to the themes in the story. Each character has a special sidejob too. Kiryu has multiple kinds of taxi errands he can run, on one hand you can... literally follow traffic rules as you drive people to destinations. Sound boring? It isn't, somehow. You'll see. On the other hand he can take the taxi for a spin to go street racing against an evil group, with Taxi heat actions and everything as he teaches people a lesson in his work outfit.Saejima has quite the hated part, no spoilers but you're stuck in a certain loop for a while, and only in the later part of his story are you able to do his side-activity, forced to sit through a very long back and forth tutorial. It has problems with pacing, but actually doing this activity was really enjoyable, and doing Saejima's side-content fixed the pacing issue aswell. For people just going through the story, this might probably be really annoying though.Haruka's part fixes that completely though. It is surprising, it is nice, it is awesome, if you've seen it you still have no idea what's in store for you, but it's fun and different and it's a breather. As the first female protagonist of the series, and none other than the daughter of Dragon of Dojima himself, and already one of my favourite characters, I loved that Haruka could really shine on her own. Her side-job is also absolutely amazing, and probably the best one in the game. Akiyama kind of got screwed over this game, his story is shorter than the others', and he has no side-activity specific to him either. However, he was MUCH better in this game than in 4, same with Saejima. The growth these characters had in this game, and the moments and such they had made Akiyama and Saejima both really great characters to me. I feel like not liking them as much in 4 somehow helped with that, so I'm glad I played that one anyway. Despite his shorter story, Akiyama is a good boy and he absolutely shines anyway. I just know that some Akiyama fans would've loved more of him, he shows plenty in the other parts of the game though, and I didn't notice a thing about his lesser presence.When things switched over to Akiyama, I took a break for a while from playing the game. Playing 3 Yakuza games in a row does that to ya, but as I said, coming back to Akiyama's story was great, and he was a lovely character throughout.Shinada, the last character, a former professional baseballer turned porn journalist, has an absolutely amazing story too. It might be the best one out of all of them. With a tidbit of dumbness in Kiryu's part, pacing issues in Saejima's, shorter parts for Haruka and Akiyama, Shinada's part was perfection. It stood on it's own, it gave us a wonderful and very different character, but it was amazing. Shinada has an amazing side-activity aswell, but it's quite simple, almost too simple even. I can't emphasize enough how much I love Shinada.Whatever the finale might be, I'll let you find out for yourself, it consists of multiple chapters and I really like how all the stories intertwine, but unfortunately the very last part of the finale was spoiled to me, and admittedly took a little Steam out of it probably. I'm still glad I experienced it for my own.Now for some extra notes. During the story I did almost everything I could, everyone's hostess, substories, maxing them out, eating everywhere, everything everything everything. Or well, sorta? My completion list says otherwise, but at least the big side-activities, the substories and such I all did. It felt really rewarding, it felt right, and it felt nice to do it chapter by chapter, and no game did that to me before. It felt like living a journey and really helped with enjoying the characters. But it made for a long journey, only after 90 hours did I close the book on the main story, and I even beat the ultimate boss in the game, Amon, before beating the final one. Maybe that's why the finale also lost some steam, but I'm glad I did it anyway.There's so much I could still talk about, like the music and everything, but the last of my braincells are dying. At 20 bucks a game of this magnitude is a steal, but don't let my words woo you too hard because it's not quite the magnitude you might imagine. Find out for yourself what I mean.Yakuza 5's narrative and such made me really enjoy living in it, and I'm glad I could. There's much I can say about this game, and although, as usual, it didn't turn out the way I expected, it also surprised me again and again and gave me something better. But I will be glad to go back to one, single, unbeatable character next game, and for the final time, in Yakuza 6.

_childDocuments_.review: If you play Yakuza games for the story and not much else, this game is pretty lacking.  It's basically like Yakuza 4's story but even more unnecessarily convoluted which a bunch of new names of characters you're not gonna remember.  Not to mention the main villain is very unmemorable.But if you're okay with the story being meh then this could be one of your favorite games in the franchise.Combat: 9/10.This game runs on the same engine as Yakuza 0 and Kiwami so the feel to its combat mechanics are overall the same, but with more freedom with what moves Kiryu and the gang can do, as well as another 3 whole characters' different movesets.  The only thing thing keeping it from a 10/10 is that you get stopped on the streets by punks practically all the time, to the point where it's a whole ordeal just to get to your location.Music: 8.5/10It's no Yakuza 0 or 7, but this game has plenty of amazing tracks.  Just the fact that both "Bakamitai" and "Machine Gun Kiss" came from this game is enough to raise its score.Characters: 8.5/10Sure, most of this game's antagonists are fairly unmemorable with the exception of Watase, but the main cast more than makes up for it.  Like, this game literally has Akiyama in it.  Buy the game.  Now.Graphics: 8/10This one's just my opinion, but I really love the more gritty, more shaded look of this game than most of the other games.  I also think that Kiryu's visual design is at its very best in this game.  Objectively, the game's graphics are nothing to write home about, but its style is very charming.Side Content: 10/10This is the real reason to play this game.  Five different characters to play as.  Five different locations to explore.  Every character has about 15-20 substories to laugh at.  And most of the characters have a side story to go through, kind of like Kiryu's real estate and Majima's cabaret club minigames in 0.  This game also has one of the best selections of karaoke song in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: ProsA jaw-dropping amount of content, excellent combat, improved graphics.ConsAn unfocused story, underdeveloped gameplay mechanics, glitchiness.VeridictBetween the minigames, side quests, substories, idol simulator, and main story, Yakuza 5 offers a truly stunning value for your money.General Tips:You can go back to any of the first 4 chapter's cities in the final chapter by hitching a taxi with the corresponding character.The only thing missable thing before the end of the main game can be Haruka's sidestory missions because her cut off point is a bit earlier than the rest of the characters, but you can always finish those off in the post game.In chapter 3, do not open any key lockers as Haruka, as she cant use the contents and her inventory is separate from the rest of the characters until post game. You can still pick them up however, as any she collects are shared with the other character in the chapter and he can use them to open the lockers.When you unlock the final IF8 station, you can invest in it which at the max will give you skill points(up to 8) for redoing any of the available battles you have completed with every character(except Haruka I think.) You need these to max out your characters.Don't worry too much about grinding/farming, the sidestories/quests give out more than enough exp and yen.When you reach the final chapter you can go to the dojo to raise your level cap from 20 to 25.

_childDocuments_.review: How to sum up Yakuza 5 Remastered,Welcome to Yakuza 5: Cabellas MLB Crazy Taxi Idol SimulatorAre you a fan of playing Crazy Taxi and Need for Speed? Do you like hunting wild animals like Cabella? Do you fancy playing a baseball game to pass the time? Or have you ever wanted to be a J-pop idol?Well Yakuza 5 remastered has everything for you! From fighting a gigantic bear with your fists to doing handshake events in your J-pop idol life, Yakuza 5 Remastered has it all!But in all honesty, this is a step-up from Yakuza 3's horrible combat and improves on Yakuza 4's combat and graphics.The story is good as any Yakuza game should be and the characters were fun to use (except for Shinada when you're starting out but this gets better as you level him up).As stated in my opening statement, Yakuza 5 has a lot of side missions that will keep you entertained for hours and substories that have always been fun and a staple of the franchise.It has all the crime drama in the main story and all the laughs on the side that the series is known for. (Sadly you wont get much Majima in this game but we did get Akiyama so thats still a win)This is the Yakuza game that I had the most hours invested in and to be honest is up there with Yakuza 0. Buy it at full price, don't wait for a sale, the Yakuza games are a gem of a series in this day and age.Now we all have to wait for Kiryu's last game as a protagonist this March in Yakuza 6: The Song of Life when it releases on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Completely disagree with other opinions regarding this as a masterpiece, or even one of the strongest entries in the Yakuza series.  This is one of the most  in the Yakuza series, which doesn't necessarily translate to good.  The problem is, the game is trying to do too much, and be too much at the same time.  This contributes to a lack of focus, poor storytelling, and pacing. There are multiple characters to play as this time, and each character has a story, alongside their 'regular activity' simulator.  Kiryu has his story in the first chapter, and along with it, you also drive a taxi.  A lot.  Saejima goes hunting.  But the worst... the worst is Haruka.  There's an entire seemingly interminable chapter dedicated to her.  It's a cliched, trope-filled 'story' as she chases a dream to become an idol because reasons. Instead of fighting, there are dancing minigames in which we have to match button presses as they appear on screen, while she performs passionless robotic movements with dull lifeless eyes gazing out in innocent wonder at the world.   I lost all interest in the game at this point and only continued as I had heard that Yakuza 6 was a direct continuation of this story.Speaking of which, the stories of each character is supposed to be interwoven, but they decided to go with a cliffhanger at the end of each character's chapter, which results in a rushed, dissonant final chapter.  It doesn't help either that the plot is very convoluted with a lot of references to other people and their machinations, and I am not convinced the writers themselves know what is going on. Several times, they had to rely on expositions and even then it took a long time to get through it.  The fighting itself, which is the main attraction of these games, is decent in its combos and heat moves.  Each character has their own best moves and combos, but due to the massive gaps in playing between them, I found I was forgetting a lot of what made them strong.  Despite that, I found that the boss fights weren't very action packed or satisfactory, they were just OK and most were quite simple, and over very quickly.An interesting mechanic that's unlocked this time is the second health bar, filled only by food but not restorable through medicine.  It makes for a nice advantage before you're about to head into a big fight.  The towns are, as usual, nice to explore; there's a decent amount of detail and places to shop and eat.  But, due to the multiple locations, eventually the exploration became a wearisome task.  I do hope Yakuza 6 isn't more of this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly quite mixed for me. If it wasn't for the fact that its a Yakuza game which generally have a good standard of quality I probably wouldn't have reccomended it. This is definitely one of those moments when I wish steam had an in-between option.The game starts out pretty strong, with you playing as Kiryu undercover as a taxi driver. There's a great minigame about said occupation and the town is lively with lots of substories. Its pretty awesome how you can just play Taiko no Tatsujin in the arcade, even if it only has like three tracks. The story is fairly intriguing, with a few interesting characters like Watase who seems like he's going to be a great boss to fight at the end of the game.But once Kiryu's section ends, the game starts going downhill a bit. Next you play as Saejima, who spends the vast majority of his section in very closed environments like the prison and the village with basically nothing outside the main story to do (apart from the hunting minigame which seemed quite fleshed out from what I played of it). Even once you do get out into the city of Hokkaido, there's not really a whole lot to do which isn't in every other Yakuza game. The only(?) exception to this is an atrocious snowball fps minigame which wasted about 20 minutes of my time that I very much want to get back. The story isn't anything to ride home about either.Next we have part 3 which is split between Haruka and Akiyama. Haruka's side-story is an, uh, interesting change of pace but I'm not sure if I want to sit through 5 hours of the life of a Japanese idol to get to the part of a Yakuza game which is about, well... Yakuza? The dance battle minigame was kinda fun but really gave me "porn is easier to explain" vibes. And then Akiyama just kinda shows up halfway through after a plot-twist happens.And then we have the final section before the finale. I'm writing this review about a month after I played the game and I can't even remember what this guy's name is without looking it up. That should probably tell you what my general opinion on this section is. The whole theme around this is baseball and unfortunately I don't think I've ever watched a game of baseball in my life so it was a bit of a drag having to sit through hours of Baseball jargon. This whole section seemed like it was shoehorned in to be honest, as it barely seems to really link into the wider plot.And there's the finale, which I won't spoil but it contains the Yakuza series tradition of having a shirtless fight on a rooftop which was honestly one of the best parts of the game.I think the main problem with this game is that it was waaay too ambitious. Each section has its own city to explore, and while that sounds awesome on paper this is definitely a case of quantity over quality. Visually they all look very nice but they all pretty much have the same activities between them. Maybe its because I was a bit burnt out from playing 3 4 and 5 back-to-back so take this comment about minigames with a grain of salt. The story was also very all-over-the-place and many characters are introduced and then completely forgotten about. I'm very dissapointed that Watase didn't get the spotlight he deserved in the finale and just becomes a side-character. This may be a bit of a spoiler but the final boss was a completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out-of-left-field villain which had absolutely no buildup. I haven't even mentioned the fact that this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ long too - its 50 hours and really just drags on for far too long.Overall: Really drags on and too overambitious but just barely makes it into a reccomendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Though it doesn't quite reach the heights of , this is still one of the strongest entries of the -series that I've played (0, Kiwami 1, Kiwami 2, 3 Remastered, 4 Remastered, 5 Remastered). In my eyes, it exceeds  in every aspect besides the story, which I found to be a bit too convoluted, even for the standards of the series.  While  continues its predecessor's theme of having multiple playable characters, it expands on the scale of the game in multiple ways: A whopping 5 completely explorable locations are spread across Japan, plus some smaller side areas and story-locations along the way. Though the new areas are all very welcome and fun to explore, I found a few of them to be less interesting than even Kamurocho, which fans can probably navigate with closed eyes by now. Still, the new areas were sorely needed and they do the job.Combat feels very similar to , though maybe with slightly more variety in the moves and fighting styles of the characters. The annoying weapon system is gone, being replaced by a much more clear and engaging system that simplifies crafting and introduces weapon classes, an overall win in my book. One thing that is still a slight annoyance to me are the couple of overly long heat moves that break up the flow of combat. Some of them can take upwards of 10 seconds to complete, at which point they are more annoying than useful, especially if they are very easily activated. I am also very happy to see the changes to the hostesses that the playable characters can meet. There are both fewer hostesses and chatting with them at the clubs is a bit more interesting and less frustrating than before, mainly because you don't have to do it as much to complete their little story lines. I still find them somewhat unnecessary, but this is a step in the right direction.The same variety of side activities and substories from  can again be found here, with some slight changes and small additions. Overall, there is an absolute wealth of these little "timewasters", many of which are actually quite enjoyable, and the ones that aren't can just be skipped. The new character-specific side stories are all unique experiences in terms of story and gameplay, and - though they are not all equally engaging in my opinion - are worth a playthrough. This is another aspect in which  successfully expands on its predecessor.The one weakness in my eyes is the overall main story of the game. In series tradition the story is very convoluted, involving dozens of characters, multiple locations, unclear or shifting alliances, betrayals, and so on and so forth. This time, however, I felt like the writers overplayed their hand by combining this complicated story with the aforementioned character-specific side story arcs. The result is a plot that is hard to follow if you don't play through it relatively straightforwardly, with little to no breaks and distractions in between. And unfortunately, a plot that's hard to follow is hard to care about. Other factors compound this problem, such as the relatively uninspired cast of characters as well as the cuscenes and dialogue sequences that seem to drag on forever. This trend continues to the very moment the word "FIN" lights up on your screen; The finale brings a decent and somewhat coherent end to the main plot, but it does so in a very drawn out way, leaving me a bit underwhelmed. Still, I was satisfied and had made peace with the plot problems by that point.
