_childDocuments_.review: This game is so big that my initial review draft couldn't fit into a steam review. Like I heard this game was big, but I didn't think it was BIG BIG. So lemme condense what I liked/disliked down for you.GAMEPLAY:You switch around to 5 different protagonists all with their respective play style and capital city. Kiryu Kazuma or "Suzuki" since he is under a new alias trying to escape from his life as a former Yakuza chairman, is quite busted gameplay wise being his most powerful iteration yet with his standard one shotting tiger drop, bounding throws off heat cooldown, and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ extreme heat that makes him immune, increase attack damage, and teleport to the closes enemy all in a short time. What. The city of Nagasugai, Fukuoka was quite a chore to navigate through due to its limited amount of streets/taxis, and with the limited streets, random encounters happen way more often. The city overall just felt big and hallow, didn't feel like it had personality but maybe that's just me. Seajima Taiga's whole chapter is quite linear with him going to prison again for 2 chapters, diddling around in the forest for the next, then finally getting to his main city Tsukimino, Sapporo. His city unfortunately is the worst out of the 5 unique cities in this game, and is where the previously mentioned increased random encounters are more prominent and annoying with sometimes finishing one encounter just to step to the left once immediately going into another. Despite my issues with these cities im still glad they experimented and gave us these locations as each location gave you something fresh environment wise.Haruka Sawamura's whole chapter was very different from anything I have played in the entire franchise, distancing itself from the brawling combat we all come to understand in this franchise and focusing on its replacement "dance battles". Despite what a lot of people think about Haruka's chapter, I quite enjoyed it. It acted as a sort of breather from the mayhem, being the variety of plot threads, characters, locations, combat, and side activities. Sotenbori, Osaka returns as her and Akiyama's main city in my most favorite version of it yet. Combining Yakuza 0's south east areas being Ashibe park, and the market area along with Kiwami 2's beautiful canal docks.Shun Akiyama was very mixed for me gameplay wise. His single target damage is still insane with being able to loop combos and his new "launch strike" ability able to unload a full combo in the air immune to damage, but he really struggles at group fights, and that's a big problem because that is all of random encounters. Enemies block and grab a lot more making it easy for them to catch you mid combo and ♥♥♥♥ your ♥♥♥♥. I did like the weird ♥♥♥♥ like his different taunts being able to teabag the enemy or to quickly gain your bearing knocked down with a taunt. I love weird ♥♥♥♥ like that, and speaking of weird that brings us to the final protagonist.Shinada Tatsuo was a very unique character. His brawling was very slow but steady damage, but he excels at weapons. He is a weapon master being given whole new weapon abilities, heat animations, and increased durability along with infinite durability on some weapons. I'm usually more biased to characters whose whole tool kits involve weird abilities, its a reason why I liked Saejima in Yakuza 4, because his heats could only be executed off wall/floor bounding which was very weird but exciting to pull off. Shinada's main city is the streets of Kineicho, Nagoya and I actually really liked this city. In fact I would go to say this was my favorite city within the entire game. Very easy to navigate through the city with the amount of streets, and the landmarks gives this city a lot of personality the most. Like the ferris wheel off to the south, the park area featuring the big ass tower, or the baseball stadium on the very easy side. Loved it.Sidestories:Now the big thing I was really look for in this game was the variety in mini games, and the sidestory mini games were the focus of my attention. Kiryu got a taxi mini game, and the variety from just actually using the roads of Nagasugai to get your client to their destination while following the rules of the road was surprisingly addicting. Then all the sudden you can customize your taxi and take your car to the highway for the high octane road racing section and MMMPH. My only jib with Kiryu's sidestory is that there is not enough of it, I mean most of the missions are just multiple choice talk sequences and is just bloat. Feels and plays like bloat to pad out the run time of the mini game, and was done better in the other sections of the mini game where along following the rules of the road you had to quickly humor your client for max customer satisfaction. Saejima's sidestory was full blown hunting, and despite it being really grindy especially towards the end, it was different and very unique to anything that I have played in the series so far. Haruka's sidestory is being an idol and a combination of a bunch of sub-mini games. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like, handshake events, trivia talk shows, dance battles, and concerts. There was a lot of variety to be had in her section, and it got me really immersed during her section of the game. Finally Shinada's sidestory is just pro baseball in the batting cages. Despite how simple, and how we have had batting cages done before in the series, this was probably the most chill, and laid back sidestory of them all. Usually the batting cages mini game can be stressful at times, especially in Yakuza 0, but Nagoya's batting cages was just a vibe to play, and the over the top baseball animations were also fun to watch. Honestly I just enjoyed the hell out of the sidestories in this game, there wasn't a single one where I felt like I was wasting my time and should head back to the main story.Mini games:But does it stop there for the wacky mini games? No, they did not skip out with the variety in this game because there is more. You got air hockey which was way more fun then its predecessor table tennis in Yakuza 4, serving food at a ramen shop, an fps styled snowball fight, comedy club where you need the reaction time of a cheetah to read out your options which are Japanese in a short set given time, and cochin cup which is just ♥♥♥♥ racing. The sega arcade was also stacked with some bangers like Taiko (rhythm game), gunrhein (defensive boxcelios), virtual fighter 2, photobooth, AND probably the best claw machine in the entire series that isn't annoying and tedious to 100%. Now for the hostess clubs, I am usually mixed about the nightlife mini games of the series but I have to say, I am blown away at the hostess clubs. They revamped how hostess clubs worked where before you would respond to the hostess with the correct answers over and over again until times up, but now you can order a drink/food whenever you want between conversations instead of waiting for a set time for a refill, you can choose to ask her question and fill her in on some gossip you can get around town, the variety in different drink, and foods increase and can even get you special scenes if you play your cards right. The variety in locations from 5 different hostess locations all with their respective hostess kept things fresh, and the after hours dates are now very expanse and gives you a lot of freedom. Before you would go to set location like theater square or in front of the millennium tower and choose where your date was going to be from there but now if you wanna take your date somewhere, you can take her there. Without a doubt, my favorite hostess mini game in the entire series, they did not sleep on the mini games section of the game.Yep this was the my condensed version of my big review draft. It has some big flaws compared to the rest of the series but under it is a wild ride, and addictive adventure that will leave you crying and laughing.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're reading this review, then I assume you've played all or at least some of the games before this one. Otherwise, what are you doing starting with the 5th game in the series? At the time of this review, I've played and finished Yakuza 0, K1, K2, 3, 4, Like a Dragon (and this one) and I can definitely tell you this is one of the worst in the series and probably the worst. First things first. Is this a step up from 4? In most ways yes. Gameplay aka the fighting is great. I feel like the fighting has evolved a little bit from 4 with you having more tools at your disposal now. In terms of graphics the game is a slight step up but still good. If you're playing Yakuza games for the graphics then you're doing it all wrong. To add to this, there were some weird things I encountered at times. In the first couple of parts there's weird glitches with Kiryu and other people's faces. Also, for some reason, most characters' faces look like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ when you are inside a building. I played at 1440p and when you enter a building, it's like the resolution goes down to 720p. The minigames and sidestories are here just like any other Yakuza game and they're great. This game also probably has the best minigame in the series and what I would describe as the most Yakuza minigame also. And yes, I am talking about  These are amazing and should be played by any Yakuza fan. Sadly, the place where this game sucks the most is the story. Once again, just like in 4, you don't just play as Kiryu. You play as a number of other people each with their own stories and motivations. This time around, however, the story is so convoluted and so nonsensical that I was actually yelling at my computer at times. Yakuza stories have never exactly been Oscar winning stories but this one just goes above and beyond to be terrible. So many characters just do odd things, not at all in sync with what their character was in the series until now. Moreover, so many fights don't need to happen at all and it makes no sense for them to happen. This is the case with basically all the  fights. . The story is just so convoluted and confusing. The biggest slap in the face of any Yakuza fan, however, is that final plot twist and the final fight. Like wut bro? That stupid ass reveal just comes out of nowhere. Suffice it to say, I thought this story was the worst in the series by far (haven't played 6 yet).Overall, this game is still good. The fighting is still very solid and one of the best in the series. The minigames are all great and fun and the substories are the same they've always been, wacky, heartfelt and weird. I played 3 and 4 right before this one and I thought 3 was showing its age a lot and that it was probably the worst in the series. I thought 4 was great and one of the best, definitely up there with 0, K2 and Like a Dragon. After I've seen the story to its conclusion in this game though, I now think this is definitely worse than 3. If you're a Yakuza fan, I still recommend playing through this game just for the fighting, minigames and side stuff. Just know the story doesn't make any sense and it's downright insulting. Turn your brain off during cutscenes.

_childDocuments_.review: You know the one guy who isn't exactly the most sensible person, but is so passionate about things that you can't help but end up loving him for it anyways? That's kind of like Yakuza 5 Remastered. (I ran out of space the first time I typed this review so like 5 itself, it may seem muddled too)Yakuza 5 is a big game. Perhaps the biggest monument to the series as a whole in that it has the most characters, the most side content, and the biggest headache of a story to deal with if you're a guy like me who cares about that kind of thing. I don't even know how to begin this review if I'm going to be honest. Yume: The Video Game, everybody.So with that preamble out of the way, let's focus on series mainstay, Kazuma Kiryu. He currently resides in Nagasugai as a taxi driver, a stark contrast to how we've always seen him. Hiding his true identity and forced to live in a city unknown to him for six months, he is on the verge of breaking down from not being anywhere near Morning Glory and the kids he so affectionately loves. This is one of the reasons why as insufferable as 3 could be, is a necessary stepping stone to really understand the situation that Kiryu finds himself in. As is always the case though, Kiryu is brought back into the Tojo Clan's business yet again, being strung along by another conspiracy by another traitor within the Tojo Clan seemingly in a bid to start another war with the Omi Alliance. This section shines by showing Kiryu out of his element in another city trying to get by as he is forced to be here for the sake of Haruka's dream, crushing Kiryu's dream to be happy with his kids back in Okinawa. Kiryu's combat is as good as it's ever been, reaching 0 levels of modernity and having a general amount of versatility to his moves. The Komaki Parry now has the same timing as the Tiger Drop, so spamming the Tiger Drop during bosses is much more viable here (The window for it is not too hard either). His side story of being a taxi driver is rather amusing, following the rules of the road in some instances, making conversation with customers, in another, and then, finally letting it rip on the highway streets trying to take down a street racing group. As is no doubt what you've heard, this is probably the best side activity in the entire game. 5 tackles a lot of different gameplay genres, but they are very simplified, not to say they are bad by any means though. The racing sections in these are a blast to do (You can even blast Daytona during the race if you so incline). A very noteworthy part of his story is when he literally fights 100 men by himself to stop a war between two yakuza factions from instigating. A very good start, though it is sullied a bit by what's to come.Taiga Saejima starts with a mini section detailing his last day in Kamurocho once again, before being sent straight to jail...again. Yes, we start Saejima practically in jail again, just like last time, because the jail section was so fun in 4...you spend two chapters in jail, which is astonishingly quite dull and doesn't do a whole lot to make things interesting while you're there, even having bits of hallucinating you're visiting a city instead of actually, you know, hurrying things up to visit the city itself. Saejima also seems to have watched a bit too much of that video of that fisherman telling people to never give up, because he's basically discount Kiryu in terms of character and ideals, spouting flowery speeches to the most unnecessary things. It's a downgrade from his rough and blunt way of dealing with things in 4, and makes me sad seeing the character be done in this way. His combat is much better than in 4, and he's downright broken with Herculean Spirit, making him never flinch while in Heat mode, and with his extremely long health bar, this makes his sections a breeze. His side activity is a hunting simulator, so that could go either one of two ways for many people, where it either is okay, or is boring and dull. When you even get to snowy Tsukimino, you only have one chapter dedicated to it before you're gone to the next part of the story. A bit of a let down of a chapter.Well, this is the part where I have to commend RGG Studio for, making an audience that would usually come for brawler combat play a rhythm game. A very easy one, mind, because it kind of has to as I don't think the Yakuza crowd has a lot of Project Diva fans eloped in there. Enter Haruka Sawamura's section. She's trying to be an idol! Even though in 2 she literally didn't want to be one...but let's roll with it because it's her dream I guess? The circumstances of Haruka ending up in the seedy idol industry is what has Kiryu skulking away, and while it is super hype performing at least So Much More, I feel like this is more of trying to make me an idol fan, while at the same time showing how cutthroat and downright disgusting the idol business can be at times. It tries to make jabs at the idol industry but comes off feeling like how Persona 5 deals with its society theme, trying to say something, but really saying nothing worthwhile at all. Haruka's character itself also feels stifled by the idol section of this part, which sucks. Her side story is mostly doing busywork for her idol career and showing the life of placating the masses. Perhaps eye-opening, if anything to how some people treat idols. Midway through this part, we get a stab at everybody's favourite moneylender, Shun Akiyama, trying to set up a Sotenbori branch of Sky Finance. Circumstances lead to Akiyama and Haruka forming a dream team of sorts trying to uncover the murder of Haruka's boss. Her trying to fulfil her boss' dream, while Akiyama works to make it happen. While his combat theme is still the best one, he has most noticeably been nerfed in the health department and in the nature of his encounters. While Akiyama specialises in dealing with small groups, his longer combat scenarios sees him dealing with upwards of 5 or more people, not really playing to his strengths as a fighter. Another mixed bag when it comes to this part.And then, quite literally out of left field, Tatsuo Shinada. This washed up former baseball player in Kineicho that has people either loving or hating him. His story is that of a lost dream, stolen from him in his very first game. I ended up caring more for the lovable schmuck who writes smut for a living. His side story has a different baseball minigame altogether. The journey of him finding out what happened to his past may seem like it doesn't relate to the crime aspect, but it does to an extent, just not in the way one might think. Even then, some people may decry his combat as being too weird and unrefined to get much enjoyment out of it. I think that's the point, Shinada isn't a hardened warrior like Kiryu or Saejima, his combat is very scrappy and relies a lot on grabs to get the most mileage out of him unarmed. His weapon attacks are also all mostly unique to him, where even pulling out certain weapons is an attack and can chain into a Heat Action, so if you have the dough, it's worth having him be the one mostly using weapons.  Unlike Tanimura before him, he may seem like a gimmicky character, but he makes a much better and more lasting impression. Like him though, he is a one-off character which is a shame.The story is perhaps slightly less messy than 4 but makes about as much sense as that one at times. No joy for a satisfying logical story here, but the dream theme is so present in the best and the worst ways, that I can excuse it due to the amount of passion that's overflowing from this game. Logic aside, who could resist something like this? The minigames are abundant,  the substories are good and some things make their last debut (IF8, Revelations, The Florist). This does pave the way for the brilliant 0, learning from the mistakes 5 makes. Truly this marks the end of an era of sorts. Love it or hate it...there will never be something as big as Yakuza 5 again.

_childDocuments_.review: First of I feel the plot of this one is probably the most complex one giving the player a tenth of information through each character which makes it feel so overwhelming and lose interest the deeper in. This is also due to the fact that they've decided to go with even MORE protagonists then last time which imo made the game longer than it had to be. Haruka's part was fun for like ten minutes and then I realized I had to do the same songs 30 times over. It was a nice change from the constant beat'em up style of gameplay but in reality it's just a glorified karaoke minigame. Shinada felt like a rushed character trying to find someone to replace Tanimura so I didn't really get attached to him that much. Also with the Tojo Clan's only formidable enemy being the Omi Clan to spice it up I guess they had to make this overly complicated plot to make sure it wasn't just a re-run of 2's story.Plot aside though, this game has so MUCH content. From arcades with more games to two different types of fishing to each character's side story (taxi driver, hunter, idol, and baseball) there was so much even if you weren't going for a 100% run you definitely could see how much more content was put into this one compared to previous entries.The settings are also multiplied having a distinct city aside from Kamurocho which gives the player so much more to explore. I feel Fukuoka was the best of the new areas seeing how vibrant the city it really made it feel alive.Gameplay wise each character has their own niche which gives players a distinct fighting style. Some are definitely stronger (Kiryu and Saejima) which makes playing as the others feel like you just changed the difficulty especially in the Coliseum which was brutal on Akiyama and Shinada at certain fights. Each character also has an alternate mode only being usable in Heat Mode which was interesting and felt like the set up for Extreme Heat Mode but some had their cons. Akiyama's alt mode only worked if you could knock them up but you can't do it on bosses or enemies who block or if you accidentally do a heat mode. I feel for the sake of both story and gameplay they should've just stuck to two protagonists being Kiryu and Saejima similar to how it was in 0 so you could get invested in each of their stories more. QoL changes were added to like not having your Coliseum health being tied to your actual health so if you accidentally failed a Breakout stage you wouldn't be walking around at 1 mph. The yellow health bar was also a nice addition giving the player more room for eating food and giving you a buff along with the additional health.100% percent wise there wasn't anything too difficult imo just tedious tasks and careful planning and you have a long but clear way through. Amon was annoying for Shinada only because he would spam his parasol move, a move being difficult to fully dodge and also making his invincible. Kiryu's Amon was just a mashup of everything but after a couple of TD's hes nothing. Minigame completions aren't too bad with cheat items coming in once again to completely skip over roulette and mahjong entirely (the non-Western gambling games are still annoying though). Ultimate Matches in this game felt completely unnecessary as well the only ones that really were memorable were the annoying ones funnily enough only with Shinada involved having the battle where damage is only dealt with weapon drawing and his run away from the forklift, yup the forklift sequence where you can't even see where you're going hahaTD is still king and they gave it to Saejima :D (makes sense with whats on his back) and kinda Akiyama but his kind of sucks compared to the others.

It's bearable with kiryu's fighting style but once you get to saejima the game becomes unbearable. His style is so slow and his attacks cancel when you get it. _childDocuments_.review: This is my 2nd favorite yakuza game so far. By far the most optional content that I've seen in the series yet. Easily clocked over 100 hours. Multiple protagonists like in 4, cities, it's all here. Most of the cast has their own main optional content kin to business in Y0 (2 of them being insanely new feeling and phenomenal). A lot of love was put into this game. There's lots of small little things that really didn't need to be in the game but they decided to go thru and inject the game full of content.I have two major issues with this game. One of the protags just simply doesn't get a side story for some reason -- first issue down. Second issue being that there's a section in the game which KILLED my drive to play for a while. It absolutely shouldn't of been in the game IMO and just really derails the vibe and story. It stings a little knowing it could've been another new character or one of the many fan favorites made playable instead of what you get, but it's what they chose. Hypothetically I could've just rushed thru it a lot more than I did, but I decided to progress their side story which really made it drag out more than it should've for me -- whoopsie. This isn't a major issue for me since this kinda happens in every yakuza game to different degrees but the story is all over the place and really chaotic. Still enjoyed it though. Definitely a MASSIVE step for the series at its time. I recommend getting the HD text mod at the very minimum for this game. It was a bit blurry for me without it. And of course like 3 & 4 remastered it's 60FPS cap since they're PS3 games originally and probably hard to uncap.If you're playing this on steam deck -- cutscenes play the wrong audio sometimes and end 15-25 seconds early if you're unlucky. Thankfully there's a cutscene rewatcher as per usual, so you could just watch what you missed on PC.

_childDocuments_.review: I realize now that I played through the ENTIRE LaD franchise and forgot to review a lot of them, which is a massive shame in cases like 5 because it is by far one of my favourites. It's got the same amount of content as 0, but spread across multiple characters so there's even more variety! An entire characters story being based around a rhythm-type game that would normally be a side activity is so much fun, really loved Haruka's inclusion in the main chapters. My only complaint is the enemy encounter rates, and that's everyones biggest complain about it I'm sure, but other than that 5 is a highlight in the whole franchise. Adore it and can't recommend it more!

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a brilliant game. RGG studios really out did themselves with this one. This is chronologically the best game in the series since 0, and I think this is one of the best games in the whole franchise. i almost dare to say it's better than judgement, and that's a high bar to jump. For 20$ you get one helluva super sized 3 course meal to dig into. So many games have me ready to move on to something new 50 hours in, buy yakuza 5 had me fully engaged all the way through and begging for more after over 100 hours. Legendary story and characters as usual. But this story is so good, with some of the best charged moments, emotional highs and lows and one of the few time a branching 5 character story actually managed to be easy to follow, still hold surprises and manage to tie up well with a banger ending. Y5 has Some of the best fighting since 0, probably only bested by judgement. So many new cities to explore, if yakuza is considered a Japanese tourist simulator this game gives you a taste of everything north to south. So many unique and detailed environments filled with so many great things to do. Bowling is back and I couldn't be happier. Air hockey is great. Pool is still broken but fishing is fixed. The best thing about this game though, is 4 of the characters get their own 'jobs' which are basically sub games that turn yakuza 5 into a completely new experience. Putting down my real yakuza gamepad and hunting with saejima using mouse and keyboard is peak gaming. Drifting a anime taxi through the streets of japan is almost as exhilarating as carefully driving customers to their destination. The batting cages have never been this fun or robust and haruka miku deserves her own rhythm game. I have been taking my time playing the yakuza/like a dragon games. I don't want to burn through them and burn myself out. These games are like a fine glass of Yamazaki 12 years, meant to be savored and enjoyed at a leisurely pace. Enjoy the whole experience because there is so much to be experienced and yakuza 5 is the perfect example of this. I'll be sad when I run out of rgg games to play, but with 2 more announced they don't seem to be slowing down anytime soon. Tldr yakuza 5 is goat, and the perfect example of the framework of quality and greatness that every game that follows is known for. Not many series can be this consistently awesome but truly yakuza/ like a dragon games only get better the more you play them. I know my way around kamurocho better than I do my own home town and I love it. 1000/10

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely recommended (if for no other reason than Haruka's idol simulator chapter), but not the best entry in the franchise, though certainly the longest. Like in all Yakuzas the story and characters are engaging, it has an astonishing soundtrack and countless things to do, however more is not necessarily better and this game is a perfect example of that.

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, this is the worst mainline Yakuza game. Y4 had its problems, too, but I think this one is overall worse. Y5 has better fighting gameplay than Y4, sure, but:- the story is on par with the bad quality of Y4, which is an "amazing" "feat". - it has too many characters trying to share the spotlight; 4 was already crazy, and here we have 5- the characters are all just miserable in a way that just consistently brings the whole atmosphere down and is just exhausting to even watch- and maybe most importantly: some sections are just so, so boring. _childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, this is one of the best games in the series.  Just like in the previous installment, you have multiple protagonists, but this time, each has their own city to explore, and everything fits together pretty nicely.  Each character has their own side story (not to be confused with substories), and even though they largely center around minigames, I found myself enjoying them quite a lot!  These are almost exclusively things that shouldn't interest me at all, but they all found a way to hook me, and I played all the way through each of them.  The rest of the gameplay is largely similar to that of the rest of the series... until you get to Part 4.  Part 4 is just such an odd fit in almost every possible way, and I see what they were going for, but I wasn't a huge fan.The story is just what you'd expect from the series: same old over-the-top manly melodrama you've come to know and love, though this one comes with an ending that even got me all emotional.  Instead, I'd like to talk about the other toppings, mostly the visuals.  As I mentioned, each character has their own city, and these cities are GORGEOUS.  You'll see a few familiar places, but the new ones are absolutely breathtaking; I found myself wandering for hours, just because I didn't want to move on.  It's very rare that a game with a realistic visual style can grab me like this, but just about every place I went was exquisite.  On top of that, the soundtrack is among the best in the series, topped perhaps only by Zero (though I haven't played 6 or Like a Dragon yet).If you're a fan of the series, this entry is not to be missed!

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is the fifth installment of the Yakuza franchise, like Yakuza 4 being a remaster of the original PS3 game. Still being a beat em up, even this one is a bigger game compared to Yakuza 4, it's now 5 playable characters and a bloat of content in the game, like 4 I will not dig down on each character story but more of a short summary to what happens to them and what they're involved with and my thoughts of the story, however I will spoiler mark one particular character. With that said, the game is big, like literally big, the amount of things you can do in the game whether it's the story or side content, you'll have a lot of time spend in the game.-Kazuma Kiryu, this time he is a big character in the story and more involved in it as well,Kiryu is in such a broken state that it's quite depressing, his whole model even changed, and he's more Stoic and cold looking again, he separated himself from everyone, but even then he gets more involved again (give him a damn break already).-Taiga Saejima, personally, I didn't really like a lot of Saejima's chapters/moments in his part, his part drags insanely long like it goes very slow, but that doesn't mean everything is bad about his part no, the first bit before his chapter actually begins was a nice touch, and some bits of the prison moment. And his last chapter in Tsukimino, with a character named Baba, was also a great time as Saejima. But the rest? Hell nah, it's a waste imo.-play the game ;)-Shun Akiyama, Akiyama's part in the game is quite shorter compared to 4. He's still a support character but also adds a lot for the things that happen later on in the story, his chapter is split actually with that of the other character, primarily he is a support to that character you play like 2 chapters as that character and 2 as Akiyama. I do wish however that Akiyama could have had more playable moments in the story.-Tatsuo Shinada, the newcomer and honestly might be my favorite part of the gameI won't say much then that he is a very likeable character and a baseball player.It has changed quite a lot in the gameplay aspect, Kiryu has a whole revamped move list and new animations with it, a lot of new heat moves are added as well in the game. Kiryu is very broken in this game, like the most used moves are his extenders when you do an attack lets's say light, light, heavy and grab, he'll do like a back break or circle throws you, normally the heat in the other games get depleted when you do a move like that, however in 5 you earn more heat from it which is broken af haha, and also Kiryu in this game has got to be my favorite version of his DOD style. Saejima has also some new moves, like he has his own form of a tiger drop, and is still a powerhouse character and slow, but he is better than he was in Y4 because of the new feature . For Kiryu it makes him an angry beast, he is fast and invincible to no damage from enemies. For Saejima, it's the one thing that makes him better than Y4 Saejima, as you let's say when you let the enemy bounce you can grab the guy and drag him and spin him to the other enemies, and more. As for the heat mode, it works differently for each character.Akiyama, man Akiyama he is so stylish this time, you literally kick the enemies in the air like literally, you activate that with the heat that you have.Shinada is the newcomer, his play style is a mix of Kiryu and Tanimura for the way he plays, He has like Kiryu extenders and like Tanimura he has a slower move style, he pushes you far away to a wall, and you have the option to slam the enemy to the ground, his fight style is like a wrestler type, but the big thing is that he is more a weapons guy, as every weapon has a different animation and heat action, except for the baseball-bat, he refuses to use that as a weapon as each time he picks a baseball-bat he places it carefully on the ground. Sadly there is only like 1 revelation for each character, the upgrade system is with soul points as you got upgrades where you need 1, 2, 3 and 4 soul points to upgrade your character's stats as your characters have a level limit of rank 20. But when you do the training with Komaki you can go till 25. Speaking about Komaki, man are there a lot of masters, a new edition to the masters is Tatsuya, he is a chef, and he'll give you an upgrade that you can have a full second health from eating food, including stat bonuses for ,  and . Sadly, no more rooftop travel as they took that out of the game. There is so much more gameplay changes that you'll have to see for yourself.All the beloved substories return from the OG PS3 Yakuza 5 in Yakuza 5 RemasteredLike Yakuza 4 the substories are divided in like 13/16 each character in total. As always, you can come across them randomly when completing a chapter or when going to certain places. However, now comes one of the big things , For Kiryu we have taxi missions and races. For Saejima we have the hunting mini-game in the village, For Akiyama sadly nothing as a side story, the character that's with Akiyama tho yeah you're going to be thinking no way this is in a Yakuza game. For Shinada you have the batting center missions. It's a lot of freaking content, man, so you'll have plenty of enjoying the game and its content.There is even also lots of new mini-games, you have one where Kiryu is serving noodles, or Shinada doing chicken races, trust me there is so much more to do in this game.Man how many maps there are in Y5 is also insane, Nagasugai, Tsukimino, Sotenbori, Kineicho and Kamurocho. As always you can come across enemies also there is now a much better visible way to figure out who the enemies as they have a pink cloud above their head. But ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ are the enemies so annoying as to how rapid they appear and approach you, trust me you'll notice when you play the game. There is also something called the Victory Road Tournament, you'll have to qualify with each character that needs to do it in order to access the Colosseum in Kamurocho, yeah it's a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥ that you can't freely fight in the Colosseum anymore but oh well. What is really sad tho is the amount of dynamic intros compared to 4, It's just only 4, but man the dynamic intros are good tho ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.The bosses in this are very fun to fight as well, most of the main bosses also have their own fighting style. The final boss to me is like top tier boss fight, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great!The soundtrack of Yakuza 5 has again a different feel this time, a lot of acoustic and funk in it, and a lot of atmospheric vibes to it as well, especially when those dark and depressing moments hit. It's top 3 in my list for fav Yakuza OST, you'll also notice how many songs from different Sega ip's there are, especially sonic lol. Like always, each character also has their own battle theme, which is very nice and great to fight with as well. Long battle themes are also so great, two of my favorite being (36-Nocturne Strings), (Endless Fight). The best theme to me has got to be the theme of the final boss (The Battle for a Dream) as the word "Dream" has a huge meaning in the story as well! Yakuza 5's soundtrack is really great in every way, and like I said, it's something that RGG Studios does for every Yakuza game of theirs. Having an absolute banger of a soundtrack.(bless these composers man!)That concludes my review for Yakuza 5 Remastered.A big change from 3 and 4 because of the engine, and there is so much to do in the game.The story might not be everyone, but I really enjoyed it, of course do I agree that some bits and things could have been more fleshed out.Overall a great game with a lot of things to in it, you won't get bored!(9.6)

_childDocuments_.review: I remember being excited for this game hearing the different protagonists for this game, the amount of content in the game and the story. After playing through this game, I feel a little disappointed. I think this game is good and all, but I consider getting this on a big sale or when the collection is on a big discount (if you want to play Yakuza 3, 4, and 5).Here’s what I liked:- Soundtrack is a great soundtrack and the reason why I have a certain addicting song (sung by Haruka) constantly looping in my head.- Lots of different cities to explore- Akiyama dancing- Karaoke (it has Baka Mitai let’s go)- Saejima’s snowman heat action (the best heat action in the franchise imo)- Here are my main problems (spoiler free):- The leveling up system is the same as 4 which I wasn’t a fan of. It gives you options, but they don’t tell you what future upgrade will be. It’s not like in zero where you can see what skills to level up to obtain a desired skill.- The game throws a lot of stuff at you in the beginning which can be overwhelming considering there are 5 different characters with 5 different stories.- Haruka’s dance battles and overall dancing gets repetitive.- There are way too many villains in this game- Focusing on one character per part can be a weird way to formulate a story. By the time I got to Shinada’s part, I completely forgotten what happened in Kiryu’s part.- Frequent enemy encounters really frustrate me. In Yakuza 0, I didn’t mind since I had different battle styles and heat actions to make some fights unique. Here in Y5, you only have a certain move-set and that is the only move-set you use for combat.Complaints about the story:- - - - Conclusion: Should you go out of your way to play this game right away? No. This game is long and very painful to play through if you really don’t like the story or the characters. However, if you want a Yakuza game that you can spend lots of hours on completing and experiencing the loads of content in this game, then this game is alright (Yakuza 0 still does it better). Overall, this game is fine, but not something that had a big impact like Yakuza 0 or Yakuza Kiwami. This just felt like a longer version of Yakuza 4.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 walked so Yakuza 0 could run. After Dead Souls (and the fact that Yakuza sold like piss in the west) SEGA fully planned to just pull yakuza from english speaking territories all together. Petitions were signed and eventually someone from Sony stepped in and 3 years after the Japanese release we finally got 5 in 2015. 5 sold well enough (at least by standards of the series at that time) and because of that 0 scored an English release and its own dedicated localization team and the rest is history.Yakuza as a series almost single-handedly reignited my love for gaming, this is my third time buying the games in this trilogy and I don't regret it. A big thanks to Sega, the loc team (shoutouts to Scott Stricthart and his team, even though he wasn't involved in re-localizing the remasters), and Q-loc for making these games more known and widely available.(Localize Ishin and port Judgment please)Edit: According to some forum posts, the Pachislot minigame was removed from the PC version of 4 and 5, currently don't have time to confirm this but if that's a deal breaker for you watch out. The Qloc ports have been hit/miss but functional, but if they're cutting content that's present on the Xbox and PS versions of the game then that's just unacceptable

_childDocuments_.review: This is the beginning of the better Yakuza Games in terms of game quality if you're counting by release date.Karaoke, every minigame, things you'd expect from around this time (Yakuza 0's release date) is here, if not just still a little bit janky.Gameplay wise, its still as frustrating as Yakuza 4's combat, but less so just a tiny bit. Enemies block less but have unavoidable damaging moves you can do nothing but try and dodge against a invisible wall to get around. This game is one of the longer games out of the entire series next to 6 (third longest) and 0 (longest).I think the missions with Taiga were annoying, especially up in the mountains and into the snowy city, I just powered through that entire section without doing any side content because of how annoying that whole city was with combat, you had to stick strictly to the sidewalks, no way to avoid enemies in your path other than just fighting, most of them had weapons that always stunned you.Same with the 4th character that was playable, (not Haruka), his city was also annoying and his side content involved him getting better at baseball I guess. Didn't really know why he was even included besides having a Daigo subplot and boss fight.Haruka's section was probably the best because its the first time we're allowed to control her or do anything with a female protagonist in the entire series. It did only consist of things like Dance battles and idol things, but I still believe that side of the game was probably more of a highlight than Akiyama's own story.Weirdly Kiryu's side (while having the best combat) was lackluster, and consisted of a power scaling fight structure, where the devs would put him in a scenario where he would have to fight an escalating number of enemies each new game release. This time made it extremely ridiculous and hilarious, but also removes a lot of the tension because there's not much to lose for him until Yakuza 6 at this point.Overall I think this game is one of the beginning of the good Yakuza games, in terms of release date. Everything after and up to Yakuza: Like a Dragon is some of the best content gaming has seen in years.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5: THE LONG ONE.Hoo man. Yakuza 5. I'll be real with you, I don't like this game. Don't get me wrong, I do still like it and recommend it in the grand scheme of things, but Yakuza 5 is a game that really highlights how the series needed to change if it ever wanted to survive. This game has good core concepts combined with needless extras and a slog of a main story that, while good, feels like you are wading through plot pudding. The fact I've heard the exact same idol song around 42 times has not helped me or my developing psychosis on the matter.You follow the adventures of previous game's protagonists of Bazuma Biryu, Ahun Skiyama, Saiga Taijima alongside the new characters of Haruka and Baseball Dante as they try to deal with this week's wacky crime fight where Daigo has gone missing, there's a schism in the Tojo Clan and somehow it involves BOTH the largest idol competition in the entirety of Japan as well as a baseball game from the nineties. It's long. Very. VERY long. It's not bad, pretty standard for a Yakuza plot backed up by some very interesting characters like Aizawa, Watase and Park, but it's weighed down by the length. Yakuza 4's issue in my eyes was the fact you had four separate characters somehow stapled together into a big overarching plot. Yakuza 5 has a similar problem and it's only amplified to be longer with the addition of a fifth character. The extra mini-stories don't help, with each one easily adding another 5-6 hours if you want to be a completionist on the matter. It gives the game the feeling of a ship one step away from capsizing.A shame given this one plays INFINITELY BETTER than the others. We're in the fancy new Dragon engine we know and love from Yakuza 0 and Kiwami, which means nice new textures and models, and that glorious fighting engine that introduces the fun of the block break attacks. No longer will your attacks be stopped because one dude is holding down the block! You're still not safe from utterly tedious bosses though, those are STILL a problem!Lookin' at you Baba. As far as Yakuza games go, Yakuza 5 is good but incredibly long winded, and you can feel that this was supposed to be an endpoint that even RGG realized wasn't adequate. It doesn't really resolve much until the very end of the game, and what it does resolve feels weak. Had this been where Yakuza ended, I'd be more livid and go for a negative, but I know there's a better ending around the corner. An overall cluttered story is saved by critical characters, and your standard Yakuza fair shines as well as it normally does. Just tune out the mini-stories and you'll be good. You don't gain anything from winning the racing minigames, I assure you.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a fantastic climax to the Kiryu saga and while it's far from perfect, it deserves to be recognized along the best of whole series. This game is a celebration of the story, characters and lore that the other 4 games had built up until this point. The concept of "multiple protagonists, one storyline" is expanded and improved in 5, with 5 main characters, 5 cities and a single, long and epic story that might feel like the series ending, but as we know now, wasn't. The side stories for each character add a lot of worth and fun content separate from the main story. There's just a lot more to do and see than any of the previous games. My only complaints would be that Akiyama's inclusion in the story felt too rushed and unconsequential and that the finale was overdone with that last boss (and at least I felt this demerited the whole plot a lot).If you've played the rest of the games, you'll appreciate Yakuza 5 a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: I still think Yakuza 3 is worse, but for a different reason. Yakuza 5 has good moments and redeeming features and it's not completely BAD per se, but it has many issues that make it one of the worst in the series and one that I will never go back to.Basically you have 4 playable characters similar to Yakuza 4 and each has his own part with the main story and substories to deal with. But as it was in Y4 it strives further away from it been a story of Kiryu of it been someone else story whereas Kiryu is a kind of demigod bashing skulls and who, again is dragged into the story by "chance".Kiryu part itself is fine, it shows him trying to move on to a different path in his life semi successfully and it's ok and makes sense, while in the background there is a Yakuza plot with a bunch of new faces you don't really know or care about and none of them has any proper charisma like those in earlier installments. Which is an issue. The minigame of Taxi driving is fun, it's mostly a parody on Initial D arcades and it's clearly that. Kiryu is semi efficient as a fighter from the beginning and takes much less time to regain his full power, which is good. Obviously you need Tiger Drop as it's the most useful skill against all bosses. No surprise here.Saejima part is.. I didn't like it in Y4, but I could understand it plot wise, but here it's nonsensical, it does the same it did before it drags on forever, and it's a part where I have dropped the game for a couple of months. Saejima himself is as Meh as he always was. Slow, clunky, huge HP pool and all his style revolves around charged attacks which are not always useful. I dislike Saejima mostly for the way he himself is written as a character and everything that happens to him, I always want to skip it. His minigame of hunting is decent, but kinda slow paced as you have to move around the mountain hunting prey, and it's the one most profitable method in all of the game. There is an escape arcade sequence as well, that I should note is horribly made and honestly they should have simply made it a cutscene instead.Haruka is a weird one. It's more of a minigame like Karaoke, but with a story line. Haruka is okay in this part until she does stupid things as part of a story and piss me off again. Let's leave it at that. No fighting here and frankly I don't even know anymore what is the reason of all the "Idol" stuff you are trying to do. It doesn't matter at all, so unless you can complete Story missions you can just do that. I thought that what you do as part of Idol job has meaning and I was surprised. Especially considering this is all there is to it.Having Akiyama appear again is nice, as always he is a rather well written character who does the least amount of stupid stuff among all of them for whatever reason.Shinada is a new addition, his story is more of a sports drama and doesn't exactly fit into the series too well. It's quite well done, but the way it's tied to one other character of the series is a stretch. His combat style is a weird one, but he is semi decent once you unlock throws during combos. He does the least damage of all of the characters with his attacks, unless you use weapons which is a drag. The story isn't that long to even bother. His minigame is a chicken run game which looks like an afterthought by the way the menus are made and how uninspiring it is. The fact that only 9% of players have completed 1 race of second tier championship tells all.The Finale and the main plot once it starts accelerating towards the end becomes more and more nonsensical  and annoying. The writer/writers didn't care enough for many additional details that simply "happen" and explanations given are vague. Sometimes dialogues get to "we gotta do it" without proper discussions while at other times you will sit through ~10 minutes of dialogues trying to make sense of the story going in some excessive details about characters who you have barely seen before and usually it was somewhere in Part 1 of the game. The whole mastermind plot was cringe and showdowns happened for the sake of it. Haruka as always shines by making this story even more pointless than it already was. I somehow guess that it will affect Y6.Overall I was pissed by the end of it and while I'm used to Yakuza in general been clumsy in it's storytelling and quite often having some dumb things happen "because" or having "Teh Drama", they hit a new level here. Yakuza 3 had issues with the focus of the story on the orphanage and the main plot was boring, something out of Tom Clancy, but in terms of character building it was still good, and here they lose in every single aspect, which is sad.I heard polarizing opinions of Y6 so I guess I shouldn't expect any redemption from them.I was originally sad that I didn't play Yakuza 5 on PS3, but I guess I didn't miss that much.

_childDocuments_.review: FIGHTING, HUNTING, SINGING, RACING, ALL IN ONE GAMEYou play as Kiryu, an ex-gangster who is now a depressed man and is in a different place from before. In his shoes you will experience a tale of a man wanting to leave his criminal past behind but remnants from his history kept on coming back and haunt his life. This will make you have to fight numerous enemies, beat em up style, with brutal heat actions and animations that are a joy to watch and play. This goes the same way as the other three characters you can play as and experience their side of the story.You can also play as a female idol singer and fight with singing and winning competitions, win the hearts of the people, and also participating fan conventions so that your idol name and brand will rise up as the best in Japan. The rythm game they put in this game are very enjoyable and although the songs are lacking in numbers, I never get bored playing as her.You also play as a hunter in the cold region of Tsukimino, and try to hunt a wild bear that is terrorising a small rural village. And also you play as a baseball player (which I never got into it, yet). Oh, and Kiryu is also a taxi driver. You can play a taxi driver simulator, obeying traffic laws and try to send your passengers to their locations at the perfect time. And also you must participate in illegal street racing with your taxi to bring down an evil racing organisation.This game is bonkers even for Yakuza standards. There are 5 main games here and each of them you have to play in order to experience the whole main campaign. The first two paragraphs are pretty much what you'll get from pressing the Play button until the credits roll. After I finished the main story, I was suprised to see the percentage of the contents I have done which barely reaches 10% although at the time I had 40+ hour of gameplay. This game is a whole other beast when compared to most recent video games.This game refines many of the flaws of its previous installments (not counting the Kiwami / Remake ones) and created the most optimize experience of old-school Yakuza. The combat isn't as clunky as it was before, animations are over-the-top and fun to experience, substories, which are tales in the city, are brought up to another level, and also the main story is well crafted with likable characters, amazing set pieces, and also just giving a whole new vibe with good cinematography. You also get to free roam in five big cities which has their own substories and sidecontent. Yakuza is known for forming its own structure and identity of open-world games. Compact and small sizewise, but bloated and bonkers contentwise.Since this is a the fifth installment of the Yakuza franchise, I don't think I'll recommend it for newcomers. Well, duh, its the fifth game. Although with all the praises I gave this game, nothing is perfect. Which brings me to the flaws of the game which is the pacing. As much as I dislike to admit, but I had to take 3 three long breaks in order to finish the main campaign. This game plays in parts, and each parts is a different character and also different side activity to do, which is intergrated to the main campaign. This is the first time the dev team tryna do something different with the side activity you can do (Yakuza 4 was the first implementation), but right here they really went on a different level with it. But putting it midway through the story and forcing you to play through it in order to continue is kinda drags the pace. The sideactivities like hunting, idol singing, are fun if not forced.The second flaw that I encountered is that the encounter rate is freakin' high. It took me three battles, 30+ men defeated, to walk peacefully from Tenkaichi Street to Theatre Avenue. I don't know if there is an upgrade or equipment to lower the encounter rate but dayum, every ten steps is there's a battle waiting for you.Overall, best game ever made.5/5

_childDocuments_.review: I totally forgot to write a review for this! But I need to fix that!Holy crap is this the grand daddy of Yakuza games! The size, the scope, the sheer impossibly dense content! I really don't know where to start!Okay lets start somewhere! The gameplay. If I'm honest I have to consider this one of the better games in the series game play wise, baring Zero and Kiwami. Taking all the queues from Yakuza 4 and improving on them greatly the combat flows much the same way. Kiryu himself feeling entirely how he felt like in Y4 and only improves on the insane actions he can pull off. Although in my opinion, a lot of his heat actions feel... angrier this time around, which fits the story if I'm honest. Finding out that I get to play a literal taxi driver, moonlighting as a drag racer for his side story was absolutely amazing. Although the taxi portion was hit or miss. and the driving has a painful level of rubber banding. Overall I loved burning through the story and upgrading my ungodly hot wheel of a taxi was a treat.Also returning is Saejima, as the hulking powerhouse he always is. Now even more of an absolute monster with a plethora of pretty creative and humorous heat actions, fitting the areas he explores. His Side story, Hunter and Killer have to be the best side content in any Yakuza game to me. I genuinely adored going out on a mountain and hunting for game like a cautious game of monster hunter. upgrading my gear, buying traps and taking down a giant hulk of a bear with my bare fists -despite having a shotgun- is probably the craziest thing I've watched in a long ass time!As well with my boy Akiyama, coming in with the special ability to literally air combo a fool like he's in a DMC game. Akiyama's quick and darty game play will always be my class favorite.The two newcomers to the protagonist position are Haruka and Shinada. And come with quite different game play styles!Haruka's not a fighter, and that's alright, because at her core, Haruka is all about the mini-games and distractions that the series is particularly well known for. Her entire chapter to me feels like a long and necessary breather episode after the impregnable wall of content and drama that was Kiryu and Saejima's chapters. Dancing, and playing all kinds of fun little games while periodically swapping over to Akiyama was a delightful mesh. Although I feel because of this Akiyama's entire existence gets a little shafted. As despite doing everything I could for him I found him struggling to the finish line of his levels; largely due to not having any kind of side story to draw experience or techniques from. They kind of did my boy dirty here.Finally Shinada. Beautiful goofy Shinada. Coming in with two very great things: An actually useful weapon combat system and an actually enjoyable base ball mini game! I loved this guy, even with his attacks being shockingly weak, and his health pool painfully small (for real tho, why is his HP bar so freakin' tiny? This dude is in better shape than Akiyama!). His weapon combat felt like a strikingly fun departure from the last three games chunky and slow feeling. And his tackle gameplay was rather original in its own right; even though every mook with a subtitle could counter it. His side story being his baseball game play, shockingly simple, but oh so much an upgrade that I feel is a crime for them to just up and scrap in later games. Never have I loved Yakuza's batting cages as much as this game!Overall, between five protagonists, five towns, 4 side stories, and at least 30 sub stories for each of the protagonists. As well as every little ditty mini game. This game is the kingpin of content rich! And the Soul Orb leveling system has never felt more useful! Letting you chose your own skills and what you'd prefer to focus on!Whats more, the sheer variety of heat actions, and how crunchy, painful and insane they are has placed this game along side Like a Dragon 7 and Zero as the kings of painful heat actions! I love it!I won't go deep into the story, but this amazingly massive game, with a story about following ones dreams and the sacrifices and struggles that much come with following it are a powerful theme. And the depths that they went with it are incredible. It kept me going and completing as much as I could right up to the end! Amazing!9.5/10 Needed to give Akiyama a Money Loaner side story.

_childDocuments_.review: The problem with Yakuza 5 is the failure of it's penta-narrative. Y4 used a quad-narrative that worked, but only because each character was either directly impacted or entangled in the main narrative elements. Y5 fails because each character is basically doing their own thing unrelated to everyone else, until the last 15 or so minutes of their parts.	The biggest perpetrators of this are Haruka and Shinada's parts. Saejima is related to the larger plot, but spends a lot of time on irrelevant material. Kiryu's is the only strong chapter that directly builds up the main plotline. Let's delve into that first.	Kiryu is currently supporting his orphanage financially via taxi driving. Haruka was scouted by a talent agency, and without giving too much away let's just say that Kiryu leaves so that she can follow her ambitions untethered. Kiryu picks up a passenger early on: Dojima, the current chairman of the Tojo clan. We get the setup right away: the current Omi chairman is gravely ill and will pass soon, so the current alliance between them and the Tojo is under threat of dissolution. Dojima is therefore seeking alliances elsewhere. He goes missing soon after.	Kiryu, as was the case with the other games, doesn't want any part in underworld events. But he's slowly drawn into the fray, and with a resolution and drive that was missing in Y4 (which made his inclusion feel shoe-horned). Kiryu accepts his legendary status and reasons that it can be a force for good to protect those in his life. If the game stayed on Kiryu it would've had a stronger narrative.	But then we get the narrative switching. Seajima is the first up, and at first it isn't too bad. He's (willingly) serving a 2 year prison sentence, but abruptly denied parole for no apparent reason. Without spoiling a lot, let's just say that an urgent matter comes up with Majima, so we bust out of prison. Once out we patrol Tsukimino (the local city) in search of the local clan leader, who is  behind the transgressions.	The problem is that a large chunk of the chapter takes place in this tiny prison yard where you talk to the same 3 people to progress the story. And most of the story deals with Saejma's prison pals and the warden's ethics. It's not that interesting, or related to the larger narrative. When we finally get to a new city, the game rushes towards the end for the character switch.	Next up is Haruka, who is working at an idol agency and gearing up for a local competition. Where's Daigo? What's happening with Majima? Who cares; you have a handshake event today! I hope you enjoy playing Idolmaster for the following 30 hours! Haruka's part has a character switch to Akiyama halfway in, which ties it back to the main story via an Omi Alliance run talent agency. But this part also sucks because they NERFED THE HELL out of Akiyama's moveset. He's real weak.	Character switch to Shinada - an ex professional baseball player kicked out of the league for suspected match fixing. He lives life as an impoverished sleaze magazine writer. He begins uncovering the truth of his past as he seeks out the mysterious Nagoya family, whom are allegedly behind his downfall. His motivation being, at first, money from a 'mystery' benefactor (in a bad disguise). The mystery deepens as Shinada finds that the Nagoya family is seemingly nowhere (and everywhere) to be found.	I think by now the issue I talked about at the start is more clearly laid out now. Completely unrelated storylines that detract from the main narrative. There is a silver lining, which is that Haruka's part is at least conceptually interesting. You dance instead of fight. And Shinada's is a good mystery. But it's completely out of place in the game. Akin to filler material that barely moves the story. Remember, this is about Daigo and the Tojo alliance, so when we connect Haruka and Shinada to the main story it's both silly, confusing, and still inconsequential	By the ending, Kiryu is the only one with any real motivation for being there. Saejima is there as a Tojo soldier. Fine. Shinada is just helping out, I guess. Akiyama is there to take care of Haruka. And Haruka is dancing in the background at a concert. Which is under jeopardy for no discernible reason other than she is a main character and has to be in the finale. 	The writing is all over the place. It works for the most part. But you frequently have characters fighting for no reason. Like Shinada's fight in the finale. Shinada is attempting to stop a shooting, but the shooter decides to not go through with it before Shinada arrives. Shinada still fights him because we need a boss fight for Shinada.	Similarly, Saejima's part has him making up and shaking hands with an ally, only to fight him anyway because...I don't know, actually. There's no reason to fight someone after you've made up. We needed a boss fight to close up the chapter. Speaking of, after the fight Saejima is asked if he wants to know who the mastermind is behind everything and he passes because 'it won't change anything'. Just, really, the best writers behind this product! 	Oh, and let's not forget this 4-way boss battle towards the end between allies: “we have to draw out the mastermind by killing each other. Whoever survives can end this”. That's not an exaggeration by the way, allies helping each other bring up the possibility of murdering each other in the off chance that the mastermind might decide to show himself (and reveal his nonsensical plot of shooting a girl at a concert? Lol WHY?). Really, really, really smart and realistic writing here. Award winning brilliance. Don't think about the plot too much, because then it falls apart. The entire Majima story really went nowhere and was rather pointless. Sanada went to Tokyo because of his old coach, but we never meet him or resolve that matter. 	This game was hard to get through. Everywhere else it's typical Yakuza: boring hostess convos, the mini games, pool, darts, etc etc etc. You know what to expect. Each character has a unique side-game that is interesting, but nothing you can make a full game out of. Everything else is fine. But, this being a story heavy franchise, it fails tremendously at that. Certain plot elements (Majima's story, Shinada going to Tokyo to meet his old coach) either don't get resolved or go nowhere when you think about it. So give the writing as much introspection as the writers did: barely any. 	I'd suggest running through this quick and putting it behind you. Y4 may have been silly in it's plot elements, but Y5 is just trash.

_childDocuments_.review: As has been the case with nearly every Yakuza game, Yakuza 5 takes what the previous game did and improves on it in nearly every way. From having more variety in the side missions, refining the combat systems, or adding new cities, Yakuza 5 is a nice improvement to Yakuza 4. However, even though Yakuza 5 is a great game, it has two giant flaws: the story and how ambitious it is. When it comes to the story, Yakuza 5 is very inconsistent and often drags on. Moreover, with the many different plot points, you end up forgetting what the main premise is. Outside of the story, Yakuza 5 is just way too ambitious. While I appreciate the amount of content and new ideas that have made their way into Yakuza 5, it often just makes the game feel incredibly bloated. Moreover, considering the story alone takes around 40+ hours to complete, the extra content just adds to an already bloated game. If I had to summarize it best, Yakuza 5 is the San Andreas of the Yakuza series: a great game that improves on its predecessor in many ways but is too ambitious for its own good. Still, even though Yakuza 5 certainly has its flaws, it's still a fantastic game that was never not enjoyable. For fans of the previous games, as long as you're willing to deal with the amount of bloat, I'd highly suggest giving Yakuza 5 a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do you even start in Yakuza 5 there's so much thrown at you from the beginning you don't know where to pick it up from. It's a colossal experience once you've gone through early game you realize the amount of brilliance on a plate for you to explore and fully enjoy laid back like a true Ryū ga Gotoku experience. You get to continue the formula from the previous installment with a big step up in improvement, more stories independent of each other whilst dousing into deep routed minigames as the series has familiarized us with, on top there's also extra goods that are always well designed with shocking, entertaining or both moments. You will get to experience Kiryu's story through different lenses which you might have guessed from the logo and obviously more but I'll leave it to your imagination, all I'll mention is that there's so much diversity in side content to rival the likes of Yakuza 0. The graphics have been enhanced and decently boosted with PC port's upscaled textures to fit everyone's specs.OST (& sound design) is special and beyond splendid especially when you reach certain parts throughout the plot. The main characters are as always fitting the universe we've been accustomed to for so long, some may have petty reasons for doing peculiar deeds others less so and outright straight-faced. There's a lot more minigames this time around so if you're heavily into that sort of thing you'll obtain a huge time sink in its diversity. To my surprise we're introduced many new mechanics and refreshing new features for the combat which I might guess it'll be a thrill for everyone as we've had similar mechanics for the Remastered Trilogy. One of the most unique elements I'd say is the narrative which unveils very gently and methodically leaving you to manically try and guess whatever and whoever is behind the circumstances presented. Anyway, grab a seat and appreciate the thoroughly long journey you'll be toured.- characters & plot- improved & diversified combat- side content & minigame variety- baka mitai trilogy- voice acting quality- OST & sound design- a bit too many street battles

_childDocuments_.review: It is tough to evaluate the Yakuza 3-5 set of games. They are plainly a step back, graphically, mechanically, from the prequel Y0 and remade Kiwami 1/2. This feeling continues into Yakuza 5, which like Yakuza 4 before it is a narrative split with more playable characters than just Kiryu. Unlike 4, where Kiryu was kept in reserve until later, we start with Kiryu here and end up with a plot that involves five different characters in four different cities - including Haruka, Kiryu's (formally adopted? I forget) daughter, who is chasing her dreams of being an idol by getting into street dance battles. Yeah, really.There were big chunks of the game that actively repulsed me. Saejima's portion of the game, which is spent part in prison, part in a completely imagined version of a city, part in the snowy wilderness, and part in the actual version of that city, is particularly bad in this regard. I might have fought two tigers in Kiwami 2 but I'm not here to hunt bears in the snow, with traps and rifles and all that stuff. Haruka's part of the game, while narratively important, is also quite a jarring shift and while I didn't mind the departure, it's also a long interruption from the big yakuza plot that's been brewing now for two games. 4 was an interesting shakeup to the formula but this continuation of 4 was not a good follow-up to that shakeup. There were parts that I really enjoyed but overall... eh.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a bloated mess of a game, easily the worst story of the initial numbered entries. Haruka is a dreadful character, her inclusion is so transparent - big bad Yakuza man isn't all bad....FFS the writers could've handled this in a much better way but they didn't. Instead we have the Haruka segment (which should've been cut) - idol rhythm action and teenage histrionics are not what I play Yakuza for. Akiyama is wasted (after a promising start in 4), his appearance is fleeting at best and his fighting style completely breaks the combat engine. Saejima's segment could've been interesting but for the inclusion of Baba (second only to Haruka as worst character in the game) and a plot line that (like the other characters) goes nowhere. Shinada offers a fresh spin on the typical Yakuza protag but ,as with the rest of the cast, the Writers completely squander the opportunity this presents. Shinada and his "handler"  (played by the awesome Sho Aikiwa) are easily the stars of the show and it's shame the Writers didn't simply focus on their tale. The main antagonist's integration is laughable, far worse than any "rubber bullets". One horrifying aspect that permeates the final acts are extended Haruka monologues, these are thankfully skippable but I'd be remiss not to complain about their haphazard,unwelcome inclusion. The hodge-podge manner in which the protags are united is baffling though it does result in some cool character bonding moments. The momentum of the final battles waivers significantly though I must concede that Kiryu's final encounter is at least memorable. I'd recommend the game for series fans though Y5 only scrapes over the line thanks to the fun side activities (Taxi Driving/Racing and Hunting) and enjoyably broken combat. As for story, this is where Yakuza REALLY jumped the shark.
