_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 4 was funny, with all the twists being as ridiculous as they were. Even though it had some pacing problems and tedious minigames, it still felt more compelling and motivating to play through than 5. Yakuza 5 feels like they completely forgot the epiphanies they made characters declare in 4. the ending also makes no sense and makes everything feel completely pointless.There's no way to go through this other than every single chapter. I am going to spoil the entire game in this review.Beginning with Kiryu's chapter, did anyone else feel excited when Kiryu left off four saying, "I'm the one who forced the tojo clan on you. Left you on your own. But now.. Im done running. Its time I take responsibility for my mistakes." only for his chapter to start... And he is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ TAXI DRIVER., in another city, pretending not to know Daigo or the Tojo clan?It made me go wtf is he doing? and I was hoping they could explain this in a way that makes sense. But it doesn't because the game doesn't tie up loose ends from yakuza 4. I mean, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, we see Kiryu with the Tojo at the end of 4, swearing in the saejima family and all; he jumped ship that fast?This is all a part of Kiryu's internal conflict of not wanting to be involved with the yakuza because of his family. Yet, he involves himself in yakuza problems because he likes beating people up. I know everything Kiryu does in 5 is connected to how he can escape his fate as a yakuza, but Kiryu doesn't get close to solving this in this game.In fact, at the end of the game, Kiryu ends up in the same situation as y1, 2, and 3. fighting some guy that wants to take over the tojo clan or something.I started having a problem with Kiryu just because of this. He uses Daigo and everyone else in the tojo as cover for him until they can't cover for him anymore. He did that in the past games, but the nice part about 4 was him saying he'd stop doing that.Well, he didn't stop doing that, and now he will go superhero mode again to fix everything.Kiryu ACTS like he is some wise genius, but he doesn't think about his actions. He never takes responsibility. He only runs until he literally can't anymore. I wouldve been OK with this if they addressed how selfish Kiryu is and how he contradicted himself, but we get......nothingI would've liked the game 10x more if they developed Kiryu, but they make him go tojo superhero again. They also don't explain why Kiryu flipped the switch from his epiphany in yakuza 4. I get that it might've been because of Haruka pursuing being an idol, but I feel like it's different than that.It just sucks when they build Kiryu up to be something to admire. Yeah, his physical strength is crazy but everything else? He is a disaster.Very long Kiryu rant, but saejimas part is decent. It gets very dull in the last half, but his being in prison again is better than it was in 4. the nice part about his prison sequence is the people he meets; they are pretty interesting characters. Baba wasn't that bad either; they made a two-sided character that was good for once.It is funny that saejima wants to make everyone his sworn brother. His parts made me appreciate him more as a character; even the showdown between him and majima were good. How he consoles other characters honestly to God makes him better than Kiryu. He is a genuinely good guy who doesn't fake his wisdom like Kiryu.The fanbase of yakuza only cares about brawling mechanics, even though it steadily worsens from 3-5. Haruka's part of the story was a great breath of air. If I didn't have it, I would've suffered. They built up Haruka's character in this one, and it was great seeing her independent from Kiryu. It was also sweet seeing Haruka bond with the park. Park is one of the only exciting women characters in the series so far, as she is so ambitious. Seeing her try and be a mother figure for Haruka was great, and I liked that.It started great, so that they couldn't have ruined it. Surprisingly they did! Park ends up telling her sob story, but it's a pretty good one. It made me respect her a lot more, except she introduces the central theme of yakuza 5... which is following your dreams.She failed and couldn't follow her dream anymore, so she wants Haruka to pursue her dream. This wasn't a problem, but she got murdered for what we find out later, no reason. It's revealed that her ex-husband was majima, and majima wrote her a letter telling her he wanted to see her again??? So she was murdered for the letter, but they couldn't find it, and then they chased Haruka for it. They never get the letter, and it turns out that katsuya was best friends with park and didn't want her to die anyway.While her death was an accident because of ogita, the entire majima letter plotline was stupid.. as the Osaka enterprise family and Kurosawa family go from desperately trying to get the letter to literally never mentioning or caring about it ever again by the end of Haruka's story. Then we have yet to receive confirmation from majima that he even wrote the letter, or why he wrote that letter... or anything. We get speculation from Akiyama and no epilogue resolving this part of the story.I liked Akiyama's part in the story, but he served to get Haruka's part over with. What was ridiculous was how everyone gave everything to ensure Haruka finished the park's dream of the japan dome; even Haruka wanted to do it! She was super stubborn and didn't want NOT to do it. But as soon as she saw Kiryu fighting on tv after the first song they performed, she instantly gave all of that up. Like, are you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kidding me???????? This just proved Park's point that Kiryu doesn't seem to let his kids be independent; they all rely on him. they genuinely do. Park was never cruel. She was telling the truth. While it's messed up for park to have projected herself so much on Haruka, she indisputably gave her lots of care and opportunity. But anyway, she gives up after everyone fights to keep Haruka on stage. So much for the main message being "pass your dreams onto others."Then Haruka is running over the Kiryu as he's bleeding out... for the 3rd or 4th time in the series. That was incredibly disappointing to see. Especially when Haruka gave her speech, it was heartwarming until she said, "I can't keep singing!" like, are you for real? She had just left her role as the caretaker of the kiryus orphanage and the caretaker of Kiryu himself. Her character development seemed to be for nothing, all of everyone's sacrifices, for nothing. They could've had someone else rescue Kiryu instead of Haruka. If they had done that, it would've saved the entire ending. Overall the story had a lot of potential, but it didn't hit the mark. I would've been satisfied if they had made an epilogue that wrapped up some loose points.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 Remastered builds on the groundwork laid by 4, the end result being a very fun and varied trek. With 5 playable characters this time around there is a lot to see and do as you make your way through story beats.  Y5 has distinct character parts where you spend time as a certain character, get acclimated to their situation and find out how they are involved in the bigger plot. In this entry you play as the following:  The core plot is that the Tojo Clan and Omi Aliance are at each other’s throats. As the Omi’s Seventh Chairman is terminally ill, Dojima Daigo traveled around Japan and sent his men to broker alliances with smaller clans and families in an attempt to gain allies and dissuade any further Omi advances. Each characters’ personal stories get wrapped up in this drama as you uncover various conspiracies, deaths, betrayals and more. Overall, the story is still fun and interesting although the split narrative made me forget some finer details and the final boss was a weird choice. Saejima’s Ch. 3 takes a hard detour from the main plot as well.   The game makes it abundantly clear that the central theme is “dreams.” Specifically, the creation, nurturing, death, and passing/ inheritance of dreams and the hope they can bring. Although the final chapter went a bit too heavy with it, it was definitely a bit refreshing after all the crime and drama the series is known for. Can even a yakuza dream amidst all the hate and violence of the job? The game plays very similarly to 4 but the overall difficulty is much more challenging which is welcome and made certain situations/ fights more tense.  Additionally, there are certain set piece moments where you are surrounded by at least 10 enemies at once and have to fight all of them, sometimes with a boss in the middle. These were both fun and challenging. On the flip side, the overall enemy encounter rate is rather high this time around. Coupled with an additional change- pedestrians now having proper mass and can thus slow you down if ran into and box you in- means that you may be fighting more than you’d like throughout the game, at least until you get encounter-reducing items. The level-up system changed again. 5 goes back to the Soul/ Tech/ Body/ Heat categories. However, you still earn 3 Soul Orbs per level up and gain some max health upon leveling up. You unlock abilities by investing into a category to gain ONE upgrade per investment whereas you might get 2 in earlier entries. This definitely feels a bit weird but some powerful abilities can be learned such as double finisher in addition to staples like re-guard. A big change I dislike is that all characters have a level cap of 20. Although this can be increased to 25 in the last part, you might waste EXP by hitting the cap and not realize it. There is a new weapon level-up system. Kiryu and the other guys can gain proficiencies within weapon types by using them. Each level confers a useful bonus like more damage or more durability. Shinada is the weapons specialist and does more damage with them. Thus, I actively tried to use them this time around. You can now also keep certain weapons they find from enemies, allowing you to store them for later in your inventory but they take up a slot. Shinada uses punches, kicks, tackles and grabs when unarmed.There is now a food-buff system from completing a fairly short series of quests. You can get an additional temporary life bar and buffs to your unarmed damage and Heat retention/ damage. The bar slowly drains by itself in combat; losing the bar removes all food buffs. Thus, higher-skill play is rewarded more. Substories now have 2 states of completion- optimal (a silver star) and sub-optimal (a checkmark). You can still fight the series’ super boss with “resolved” quests however.  A new addition to the game are Side Stories, rather in-depth minigames with storylines pertaining to each character. These were really fun overall. Revelations return but each character only gets 1 through finding it in the map. The guys each get 3 weapon Revelations by using a specific weapon enough times. Chases also return. A 3 hit combo replaces the tackle and you can now dropkick. Neither is a game changer and Chases overall feel the same.  Overall, the game looks great. Textures are very similar to 4’s but there is a slight bump in quality. Animations were overall good although there is still clipping in certain in-engine scenes. Some facial animations (specifically smiling) were also pretty weird or bad to the point of being funny. The 3 new locations look fantastic and accurate to their real-life counterparts. Pre-rendered cutscenes definitely show age.  Music is still excellent overall. Each character has their own battle music again which is great, Haruka having many exclusive tracks for dance battles and performances. Overall, it’s very rock-oriented but getting into the mood to fight is no issue as a result. Haruka’s songs are pretty catchy. Sound effects are mainly the same as 4’s so good overall.    This was a mixed bag for me. Overall, no issues running, loading, etc. However, some bugs I found:The AI of the Mysterious Man in Saejima’s story chase broke. He ran 90 degrees left into a crosswalk wall; the quest broke since he was stuck and could not arrive at the scripted point. Akiyama spawned mid-air after a battle on Iwao bridge- it was a several second drop but everything loaded properly afterwards. The 60 FPS vibrating is less obvious but still present. Lighting and reflections were weird in some places. Shadows kept flickering on character models which was distracting. Apparently, little was changed aside from the improved graphics/ framerate and translations. Yakuza 5 is a game super-packed with stuff to do and people to see (and fight). The overall story was good although it kinda went too far with the “dream” theme at the end. I really like Shinada as the new guy and Haruka’s plot was nice. Each character plays differently, giving the game a lot of variety in terms of combat and Side Stories. Having 5 sandbox maps to play around in was a lot of fun and gave each character’s arc more identity. The graphics are overall great but some issues are present. Audio is excellent and gets you in the mood. Overall performance was good with some issues. A game jam-packed with fun times.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 iterates on its predecessor's introduction of multiple playable characters by giving them five different cities to explore, not just the usual Kamurocho. This goes a long way to making this entry feel much fresher than Yakuza 4, even if two of these cities are series mainstays. It also gets much more creative with differentiating its characters, with Kiryu, Akiyama, and Saejima being joined by newcomer Shinada, a former baseball player with weapon-centric gameplay, and Haruka, who has dance battles instead of normal combat. That's too say nothing of the taxi, hunting, and batting games that all bring a nice break from the normal Yakuza series action. And of course, the beat 'em up gameplay, substories, and crime drama narrative are firing on all cylinders as per usual.You probably know what you're getting into with Yakuza by now, so suffice it to say this is another strong entry in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not recommend this game except for die-hard fans of the series, and they shouldn't play the game without a walkthrough.  Most of the same problems with Yakuza 4 are in this game, so read that review for those things.  I played all the way through it on Normal difficulty.However, they introduced new problems with this game, mostly linked to switching characters.  First, DO NOT get any of the locker keys with Haruka.  During the playthrough, you can't move things from her item box to other character AT ALL.  For instance, the Chunk of Ash needed to make a specific weapon - if you get it with Haruka, kiss it goodbye, because you can't get it any other way.Second, the minigames cheat like hell this time, worse that Yakuza 4.  Sometimes your phone will tell you you have bad luck - believe it.  Sometimes it tells you you'll have good luck - DO NOT BELIEVE IT.  I like playing the Koi Koi card game, and on a "good luck" day, I got my ass handed to me and had to reload (and I play well enough to be able to score 9 platinum plates in a row, over 13000 points worth).  If you're going for 100% completion, you'll need over 20 million yen, because several of the weapons you need to craft are 800k - 1000k in price.  You'll need to gamble.  Save before gambling.Fishing is basically impossible without a FAQ.  Getting the Maguro and Squid (not bait) for the weapons required a Google search.  Trying to do it on your own is not guaranteed, because you can get several types of fish and junk items with the same bait in the same range depending on day or night - bait costs add up, and selling fish doesn't make enough to buy more bait unless you catch a huge fish like a marlin or coelacanth.The billiards and dart games get too hard at the advanced level, even with good dart parts.  It was better in Yakuza 0 where you got the best darts by buying them at the pawn shop, and when the game didn't mess with your aim in billiards - in short, it cheats a LOT.  And forget air hockey on the hard level - the only way to score is with heat shots, and the game loves to make you to chuck your puck in your own goal for no reason.No pachinko or slots for the Remastered version is unfair, considering the PlayStation version still has it, and they have other gambling games like poker, blackjack, roulette, etc.Winning at the gambling tables is more of a risk than the previous game, so keep those win items handy, and use them appropriately to win the most money.  The lack of save points make it a long run back to the casino, and you get in fights along the way, which is irritating considering the Kiwami 1 and 2 games allowed you to save anywhere.But the worst thing about this game, by far and away, is the Coliseum.  You have to get to around 200 rank points just to break the top 10, and you only get 3 points a match (3 fights per tournament, 1 point per win).  It takes forever, but worse than that, once you get there, you get beaten to a pulp.  I'm not a young gamer - I'm good at this game, but even I have endurance limits.  When you break the top 10, the #1 guy cheats ALL THE TIME.  How?  Mohammed Ali style - when you start beating on him and gaining heat, he grabs you, and half your heat disappears before your pounding the A button will make him let go.  He does this EVERY time you gain heat.  My only match with him went around 10 - 15 minutes on him alone, not even counting the first two hard fights.  I DAMAGED my wrist and arm because I was constantly pounding the A keep to stop him from throwing me.  That's never happened to me before, ever.  My arm was so hot I couldn't keep it up.  He finally destroyed me, and that's the last time I'll ever play the Coliseum in Yakuza 5 again - probably the last time I'll ever play the game, period.  I love the story and the general mechanics, but they made it far too hard on Normal difficulty.  It was impossible for me to win, with an inventory full of Stamiman Sparks (full heal, full heat).  That should never have happened, especially with Saejima.  Oh, and you can't get any of the missable items at the Coliseum (nor levels to get Spirit Orbs), so it's not really worth it except for 100% completion.But it did, and it happened again with the 2-on-1 fight in the Dojo with the baseball guy - they literally would not let me get a single hit in.  Without Kiryu's reversals and counterattacks, I just got beat to hell.  Saejima was the easiest to win with, and Kiryu was easy enough, but with the baseball guy it was impossible.  I gave up on Akiyama because of what happened with the baseball guy.The Amon fight was even worst than the Coliseum.  I got through the first three all right, but with Kiryu, I got wiped.  Not only did it grab me all the time, draining all my heat, but I couldn't grab him back, EVER.  That's cheating.  Worse, when I switched to my no-break katana, I could not hit him without heat actions.  I managed to get the guy down to green, and it uncorked everything it had, blocking everything I did, unable to grab, it hit me with unblockables to the legs, and finished doing two of the main character's super moves BACK TO BACK.  I didn't stand a chance at that point.  Remember, this is supposed to be NORMAL mode.No, you don't have to fight those battles.  I finished the game because I'd had enough of the AI cheating - the final story fight was easier by far, and I didn't even use any items to win it.  That's what made me angry.  The game shouldn't be this hard at Normal level, and it's not fun.  The inability to transfer items is not fun.  The game cheating at the minigames is not fun.  Yakuza 0, K1, K2 were fun, they didn't cheat so much.  Once you got all the skills, you were expected to maul everything in Normal mode.  Not in this game.One last thing:  If you have no rhythm, and you hate games like Dance Dance Revolution and Guitar Hero, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.  Haruka's story is all about getting into dance battles, and the interface sucks.  Not only are button presses needed to be done in time with the music, you have to use the D-pad to chose which line you need to press the buttons on (there's 4 of them).  It's actually far worse than the usual too-fast karaoke minigame.  I don't do well with DDR-type games, but I barely made it through.  There is an Amon dance battle near the end - I tried it, it was the hard version of Haruka's initial song (twice as many buttons to mash), and after three unsuccessful tries, I gave up.  It's too hard for me, just like the karaoke stuff.  I never get 100% because of this stuff, and I hate that it's so hard, especially since you MUST succeed at these to advance the storyline.  I only managed it because the story mission difficulty remains at medium throughout.  It's quite generous considering how many presses I missed.  Too bad the Amon fight couldn't have been like that.  Poor QA in not getting things level for Normal mode.So, don't play this unless you're a fan of the story and you're willing to skip 100% completion.  Play at your own risk.  It took two days for my arm to recover, and that was only playing games with my other hand (I'm lucky I use my mouse left-handed).  Stay away from the Coliseum, it's broken.  Save before doing the Coliseum, Amon or the Dojo fights, or you may burn all your items and still lose.  Same with the gambling.  If it's going to cheat, you might as well cheat by saving early and often.  If you have rhythm problems, take breaks between dance battles.  Save before every one.  Good luck, you'll need it if you play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the mainline game that released most close to Yakuza 0, and you can really feel it. There's lots of technical improvements that make combat feel smoother and more satisfying. Finally, you can hit people on the ground without using a heat action.Playing in 5 cities with 5 characters is a really fun experience, and we see the return of lots of cool characters, plus the best protagonist, Shinada. Everyone has side stories and minigames that could have been entire games on their own.It might be a little bit packed with content, but it's not too overbearing I don't think. There's a few issues with the story, but if you made it this far into the series, then you should be able to forgive that and just enjoy the ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 takes everything that Yakuza 4 stumbled with and tunes it up by a ton. The story now makes a lot more sense, while making some of the disconnection between characters a lot more intentional. With (almost) each character getting their own city to explore and set of quests, it really helps that each character is given their own larger substory which helps differentiate playstyles even further. I for one really got invested in the rustic and resolute hunting missions with Saejima. Some of the heat abilities can be pretty circumstancial, and Shinada isn't really given enough tools compared to Kiryu or Saejima to handle himself in the same style though. _childDocuments_.review: As far as Yakuza games go, this has both some of the  and the  points in the entire franchise.And it's It's easily the LONGEST Yakuza game, and the one with the most playable characters and places to visit , split into 5 characters across 5 towns. And the side content  that length.Every character has anywhere from 15 to 20 substories. There's more minigames than ever. There's THREE sets of "locker keys" to collect across dfiferent towns, plus even  extra collectibles outside of that.Every character has a SIDE STORY that's like a mega-substory centered around a unique minigame that only that character can do. Think the cabaret/real estate stuff from Zero, but .This philosophy of  kinda spreads throughout the entire game.The pacing is genuinely... . One second you're doing the hypest fight and setpiece of the last 3 games, and the next thing you know you're doing 4-5 hours of forced filler that barely advances the plot if at all.The whole thing just drops off a cliff after the first chapter and spends the entire rest of the game STRUGGLING to climb back up.Same thing goes for the gameplay.We've  moved past the Y3 engine, so gone are the super stiff, jerky and janky controls that barely work. This is the engine that powers Zero. The controls are good.But there's so much  piled on top of the gameplay.There's "extreme heat" mechanics that aren't that useful and half of the time just get in the way, and singlehandedly caused the addition of the "heat suppresion" button just to TRY to mitigate them.There's a "wall slamming" mechanic that's super janky and cheap-looking and ALSO constantly gets in the way.There's  that bars the use of certain weapons until you've grinded enough XP for that type of weapon with weaker variants of it.There is... so much. SO MUCH. So much EVERYTHING.The game constantly feels like it's crumbling under its own weight trying to add so much, and like 70% of it isn't that good, and the story and gameplay end up suffering for it....Not to mention how it harms . _childDocuments_.review: Let me start this review off by saying that yes, there will be lots of spoilers. I would attempt to stay away from spoilers but I think I can get my point across better if I don't have to tip-toe around things. Im not good at writing reviews or essay length ♥♥♥♥ like this so its going to be a bit disjointed, bear with me.Now I will continue this review by saying that Yakuza is my favorite series of all time, hell I have bought each game 2 times over. However Yakuza 5 is the absolute worst yet somehow best game in the series yet I've heard nothing but either blind praise or blind hate. I think the gameplay and characters are great, but the story spreads itself so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thin that characters get introduced and immediately thrown away or killed and many chapters reduce to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slog to get through. Let me start by talking about Kiryu, probably my 2nd or 3rd favorite chapter in the game, I mean its Kiryu who doesn't love this dude.Im gonna talk about some general design issues in this game, the biggest issue (that is present in 3/4 but sometimes worse in this game) is that street encounters are so absolutely ♥♥♥♥ that it sometimes just worsens the experience. Thugs either have a pink text box to indicate where they are or its suddenly not there, sometimes thugs are strewn into crowds and running through said crowds prompts a random attack, this isnt "cool and innovative" its annoying and lengthens the game by making you not be able to avoid encounters. Not to mention it seems the designers knew this as Kiryu can get an item through a substory that pretty much reduces the amount of enemies roaming to nothing. Apart from that each city apart from Sotenbori and Kamurocho is an absolute chore to run through, no shortcuts, bad taxi placements, and are usually just a boring grid. Apart from that the gameplay is probably some of the most fun in the seriesKiryu this time is in Nagasugai, a pretty damn beautiful city that's so absolutely poorly designed navigation wise it gives me an aneurysm. This map is 4 squares slightly slanted with an intersection running across them, not only is navigating it just holding forward but even worse is that taxi's tend to be either all the way across the city or 5 feet from each other (a common problem in this game). Kiryu's story this time however is one of my favorites, he has been separated from Morning Glory Orphanage following Haruka getting picked up by a big shot executive called Mirei Park. We follow Kiryu as he tries to balance his work as  a taxi driver while juggling the disappearance of Daigo Dojima and putting up with being spied on by the Tojo Clan. Overall, as I said this is my 2nd or 3rd favorite part of the game. Following this however is one of the most boring sections of the game.Saejima shows up again, and what do you know, he is in jail again! (yeah great choice, not like it was the worst part of Yakuza 4 or anything). Im going to go on a tangent just to say, WOW what a way to make an interesting morally grey character turn into a man with nearly the same ideals as Kiryu. This isn't to say I hate Saejima, but he really got the short end of the stick in Yakuza 4 and 5. Instead of Ryu Ga Gotoku Studios deciding that having a character that's attempting to atone for his crimes while still feeling the weight of the lives he took, they decide to pull a ♥♥♥♥♥ wucky and say he never killed because durr hurr rubber bullets. Now ill make this section quick-ish, Tsukimino sucks and has the same problems as Fukuoka, its a giant grid with like 4 taxis on each cardinal direction that forces you into random battles as theres generally no way to go but forward. The prison section is essentially running back and forth talking to people, playing detective, and having lucid dreams, I genuinely can't tell if I hate this or Yakuza 4's prison section worse. Other than that Saejima's section is boring and forgettable.Now we come to Haruka's section, probably one of my favorites in the game. You get to bop out to some amazing songs, relax from the usual "where the ♥♥♥♥ was that thug ♥♥♥♥ now im in a random battle", and play a rhythm game as one of the best characters in the series! Haruka's section is inter-spliced with Akiyama, another one of the best characters in the game, the story these 4 chapters are genuinely really good.... except for T-Set and Mirei Park. I swear this section has a hard on for introducing a character thats only mood is "im really mean for no reason" only to turn around a chapter or two later and say "whaaaaaat? they were mean???? no way look they are being super nice to Haruka now! Feel bad that you hated them and like them now!" Mirei's "redemption arc" I can forgive a bit more as theres some subtle hints that she starts to really see herself in Haruka and wants to be a bit of a mother figure for her. T-Set just randomly becomes nice just because. Akiyama is his usual self and I love him for it of course, his section is about figuring out the murder of Mirei Park and making sure Haruka is safe. The only downside with Akiyama is that his trainer Saigo is back, another horrible character.The last section is Shinada, god they did him dirty, a funny and somewhat interesting character shafted by a horrible moveset and little to no reason for being in the story IMO. I've played this game twice now and I have such a hard time just trying to rationalize him being there. I really just don't have much to say about this part or much about the game past this.The Finale is honestly where this game shines a lot, its brings back a lot of characters and has some amazing fights.... Except Aizawa, I swear this is the one point of the game people absolutely love yet the only reason I've read is that the setting of the Tojo HQ is cool (even though we have had multiple better sections in Yakuza 0, K1, and K2). To jog your memory since you probably forgot, Aizawa was Morinaga's friend helping to find Daigo until Morinaga "killed" him only for him to show up at the Coliseum and fight Saejima 12 chapters later and then disappear again until the final fight. For ♥♥♥♥♥ sake he says himself he doesn't know why he is there when Kiryu asks, how do you applaud a game with such a stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "final boss" as this. This is the one point I have the most contempt for, it was so jarring that they brought this character in after he had done literally nothing all game. You are to believe the big bad is the Omi Chairman Kurosawa who played as a Osaka Detective until suddenly Aizawa. This has gone long enough and I've rambled long enough. Yes, you should play this game. No, you should not expect a story as good and as well paced as literally any other entry in this series. If you liked the game and the ending more than me, I really don't understand but im glad you could take joy in something I had trouble enjoying.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, Yakuza 5 just doesn't cut it as a good Yakuza game. I tried it out because I had played 0 first, and this game inspired 0, so I expected much more from it, but this game feels so drag-on, tutorial-filled, and non-action-packed. By the time I got to Part 2 I just thought it was uninteresting, and returned to it after 2 years, and the story really didn't pick up until the Finale, apart from Haruka and Akiyama's part. I just thought this game was too packed with side stuff. This is usually where Yakuza games shine for most people but it can get repetitive and boring fast doing the same thing over and over again, and especially you'll have to do these things 5 times each because each character has something new for them to do. There also is no CP or unlockable abilities like earlier games so everything has to be done by constant trips and while walking, bottomless stomach, sprinting, or anything. This means that for each new character you play as there will be the same "Learn from Masters, Do Side Story, See all Revelations, Visit all Restaurants, Do Touring, Increase Weapon Skill, Play Minigames, Fight In Victory Road, Complete Hostess, repeat." for each character all while being hounded by the numerous fighting encounters that they can drag you into, as well as the countless backtracking and trips you'll have to do. The Level Ups also are so strange and disorganized. The fights also give out pretty cheap rewards, and also And the story? Ok but a bit underperforming in my opinion. Every time you get into the city there's always many things hounding you from progression, such as a substory or a revelation, or a certain enemy that sneaks up on you causing needless encounters, and there are far too many of these. And, even when it LOOKS like something interesting will happen, there are needless dialogue scenes between story events to make the game feel longer than it actually should be. The characters are also not bad, but a lot of them were a bit off to me, especially with the way they changed during the story, and some of the plot twists that occured for certain characters. There are returning ones like Yuya, Majima, Kamiyama, and Komaki, but everyone just feels so "meh". And I feel like the story just is poorly written, and replaying this to completion has showed me why I have stopped playing this, because it just is a long, gruelling journey with no satisfaction or reward. It's not a action-packed, immense story-telling game like the first 3 games (0,1,2) are. Instead, they were more content-hungry and less action and adventure here than ever. Maybe if you're a die-hard Yakuza fan you'll love this, but me, it wasn't as great just because it had the most content. I finished it but still my opinion hasn't changed. I don't know if i'd say I wish I never bought it, because I think this one is just ok, but it's nothing too special, although it's definitely better than Yakuza 3/4. After the Yakuza 0 Trilogy (0,K1,K2) it's the best of the remastered collection given it has 0 unnecessary changes from the original game unlike the other two games with an ok story and the biggest number of protagonists, but there are some other notable flaws that keep it from being as good.

_childDocuments_.review: When I completed what ended up being my first run of Yakuza 0 in September 2018, I didn’t think another game in the series would top it for me. I had given the franchise a try thanks to a content creator I used to watch a lot streaming 0’s first chapter one night earlier that month (hint: they’re most known for playing XCOM on Ironman Impossible), and man was I blown away. The captivating story; the well-written, memorable characters including my still favorite video game antagonist of all time ; the satisfying beat ‘em up combat supplemented by the rad Heat Actions; the amazing, diverse music which was the first to truly rival that of the Halo series for me; and the huge amount of fun, hilarious side content. Yakuza 0 handily won my GotY 2018, and slowly but surely my love for the franchise grew to the point where I ended up getting the Platinum (all achievements unlocked) in both 0 and Kiwami in the first half of 2020. Come September 2020, I grew impatient waiting for The Remastered Collection and 6 to come to PC so I decided to binge-watch game movies for 3 thru 6 before getting back to Kiwami 2’s Platinum. By the time I had finished watching Yakuza 5 Remastered, it had more or less stolen the crown from 0. By the time I had finished its Platinum 5 days before my 3-year anniversary getting into the series, Yakuza 5 Remastered cemented itself as my new favorite Yakuza game with 0 still being a relatively close second followed by Kiwami 2 (remake of the 2nd game), 3 Remastered, Kiwami (remake of the 1st game), and finally 4 Remastered, all of which are great games that I highly recommend playing. So how did the remaster of the mainline Yakuza game that’s right before 0 in development order manage to win me over?I’ll start with the story and characters. Yakuza 5 easily has my favorite story in the franchise. While Saejima’s part as well as the finale (before its final chapter) are a drag at times, the remaining protagonists’ parts are gems throughout and the finale’s final chapter is an epic, emotional treat which became my most dear in gaming . Each of the five playable characters are charming in their own ways and ooze genuineness, with Kazuma Kiryu, the legendary Dragon of Dojima, & Haruka Sawamura, his adopted daughter, being my favorite duo in any media only shared by Lilo & Stitch who were a huge part of my childhood. The remaining cast ranges from good (e.g., Aizawa, ) to amazing (e.g., Watase and Nakajima). However, if you’re looking to get into Yakuza, especially for story and characters, I would NOT start with Yakuza 5. Instead, start with 0 and go in chronological order. Trust me, you’ll be able to appreciate 5  if you take the time to experience the prior games.When it comes to the combat, Yakuza 5 Remastered is overall my chosen of at least the beat ‘em up entries in the series (I plan to buy Like a Dragon soon). Kiryu, Saejima, Akiyama, and Shinada each have a unique fighting style which feels very fluid on my Xbox 360 controller, and I overall prefer one style per character over multiple styles per character as was the case in 0 and Kiwami. Haruka, being a high school girl trying to maintain an idol image, understandably doesn’t fight like her adoptive father and the other guys. Her “fights” are dance and concert battles that are basically rhythm minigames. If anything, everyone’s fights are more often than not quite easy (though having Yakuza 0 thru 4 under my belt prior likely contributes a fair bit to that, not to mention the temporary double health bar upgrades each character can get & replenish). However, despite the lack of challenge most of the time, I still have tons of fun either directly, or indirectly in Haruka’s case, kicking peoples’ ***es.I’m a strong believer that every Yakuza game  has overall great music. With this game, I just have to hand over from Halo to Yakuza best music in a video game franchise. Yakuza 5 Remastered has THE best assortment of tracks in any game I’ve ever played. From Haruka’s delightful dance and concert songs (So Much More beats out the in-game version of Follow from Halo 2 for my favorite track in gaming) to the epic boss and long battle themes such as The Mutual Fists & Christmas Night Raid to the jams that play at the various establishments like La Seine & Kani Douraku across the five lively cities, I’d say there truly is something for everyone here. I recommend installing the Licensed Music Video and Uncensor Restoration Patch mod as it restores music cut from the Western release including what I find to be a better theme for the . Also, while on the topic of mods, I recommend the High res characters textures mod as the higher quality cutscene textures for characters get applied to their in-game models.In regards to side content, Yakuza 5 arguably has the most extensive lineup in the series to date. To start, each character except Kiryu has 15 enjoyable, varied substories (Kiryu has 18). While I still find 0 overall having the most memorable substories, this game certainly delivers here (especially  and ). Each character except Akiyama has their own Side Story on top of that. If you’ve played Kiryu’s real estate and Majima’s cabaret club minigames in 0, these are somewhat similar in terms of depth. Kiryu’s taxi driving/racing, Saejima’s snowy mountain hunting, Haruka’s idol simulator, and Shinada’s more advanced batting cages. All four of these were a blast to complete, with Haruka’s being my favorite (this game brings out your hidden yume [Japanese for dream and probably the most used word in the game btw] of becoming a J-pop idol haha). It’s a shame Akiyama didn’t get anything, but what’s here is good fun nonetheless. Besides those, there are 25+ minigames (including arcade and casino) which you can partake in. My top 3 are Air Hockey (which is exclusive to Yakuza 5), Mahjong, and Gunrhein (also exclusive to Yakuza 5), though all of them are wonderful entertainment (except Winter Combat battle royale on the harder levels where the “difficulty” comes from the 3 AI only targeting you like its classic Battlefront 2). The PC port unfortunately had the Slots and Pachinko minigames cut (probably to get around anti-gambling laws), and over seven months after release still doesn’t have a free DLC to add them back in as Like a Dragon’s PC version got. Also, I should note that in Yakuza 5 you cannot, for better or worse, carry over progress made in Premium Adventure (mode unlocked after completing the story where you can do all the side content with no story interference) to a new run of the story at all.All in all, Yakuza 5 Remastered is a spectacular experience that, without a doubt, earned its place as my new series favorite. It is a colossal, ambitious beast; a true diamond in the rough that steadfastly upholds Yakuza as my second favorite video game franchise of all time, only slightly beaten out by Halo who’s held that top spot for nearly 17 years now. Unless third time’s the charm for 343i and Halo Infinite’s launch knocks it out of the park harder than my man Shinada, Yakuza 5 Remastered is honestly a shoo-in for my GotY 2021. It was a solid entry to finish off my just under 3-year, 753-hour Great Journey across 0 thru 5, and I plan to keep it installed as my go-to chill-out game.  find Yakuza 5 becoming your favorite in the series too.

_childDocuments_.review: "Dreams, huh?" - AkiyamaThey really went all out with this one huh. This game brings 5 playable character to the table, with the inclusion of 2 new playable characters, those are Haruka and Shinada. This is probably the best Yakuza with the best story period, sitting right there next to Yakuza 0 or maybe even better. This game brings a plethora of contents for us players to enjoy, such as Taxi mini game for Kiryu, hunting mini game for Saejima, street dance for Haruka etc. The story is fantastic, each characters are fantasticly written, the amount of content is what really surprised me. They gave us so many contents I haven't even tried them all due to the compelling story that makes you just wanna continue on to know what's going to happen next. Unfortunately, this game suffers the same fate as Yakuza 4. Now, I've said earlier that the story is fantastic, but this game is so freakishly long and at times it's really hard to keep up to the story. There are so many swerves and it's just quite difficult to know what's going on really and it's just kind of a mess to follow. Putting that aside, this game really surpasses my expectation, I thought this game was going to be just a long messy writing all over again just like the previous title, but no, this game always finds ways to get me hooked up again and again. Kiryu's part is the perfect beginning for this game, Akiyama and Haruka's part are the most fun in my opinion and Shinada's part is also fantastic, in my opinion, this character is very neatly written because I thought he was just going to be a character that sort just there for the plot, he delivers everything perfectly and I think his part is my most favorite out of all. Saejima on the other hand... I don't know why they couldn't just make Saejima's part good but his part is just too darn long, and guess what? He's back in prison again! So you just have to sit there wandering the very limited space of the prison, going back and forth, talking to different people and it is so boring, I find it really really hard for me to enjoy his part. But I guess, it's worth mentioning that Saejima also get to go outside of prison and go to Sapporo but even that, his part is still so darn tedious, Sapporo is a big place and you have to sort of go back and forth to each corner of the end of the map and not to the mention unescapable street fight due to the limited area that you can actually explore. All that aside, this game takes place mostly outside Kamurocho, heck every character has its own place and that's is, in my opinion, a really nice change of scenery from the good ol' Kamurocho. For Kiryu, you'll be playing in Fukuoka, for Saejima you'll be playing in Sapporo, for Akiyama and Haruka you'll be playing in Sotenbori and for Shinada you'll be playing in Nagoya. Different places for each characters is what makes me love this game even more. The finale part... oh boy what a fantastic, fantastic ending. With this much characters, they managed to put all of them in the spotlight, giving them the opportunity for character development. All in all, I think this is a fantastic Yakuza title despite the length and a little messy but good story, it's is really up there right beside Yakuza 0. This game is a 9/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe Yakuza 5 in one word it would be ambitious. This game always stands out to me as having a ton of unique choices implemented in it, some good some bad, however the most ambitious thing in this game is by far the story, specifically the fact that this game is the only game to properly delve into a "theme" for it. While i wouldn't consider the start to be bad, there's a few things that slow the pace. Kiryu's chapter is fine however, Saejima and Haruka's part have some problems. First, the prison segment is boring. I get it's important to the story but idc, secondly the hunting part is completely unnecessary and drags on by a lot. Haruka, and by extension Akiyama's chapters aren't bad but on replays Haruka's segment is a boring and I wish we could've had more time to play as Akiyama. Now where this game really gets good is when Shinada's part starts, Shinada's segment is some of the best storytelling RGG has to offer. The finale also goes incredibly hard. As I mentioned in the beggining, Y5 is the first game to have a proper theme in the story. While the theme isn't something I would go nuts about I can appreciate it for what it is, especially how it's explored through the characters. Without the theme being what it is Kurosawa's plan and what he does with his power would probably not be as impactful. Speaking of Kurosawa, I think he's one of the most underrated character in the franchise, he might not be Ryuji or Mine levels of writing but he's still a good villain in my eyes. Staying on the topic of characters, Daigo truly shines in this game, we finally get to see him as someone worthy of leading the Tojo Clan through him trying to stop Kurosawa's plan.Now for the combat. Each fighting style in this game is fun and I appreciate the additions made to Kiryu, Saejima and Akiyama's fighting styles. Only bad thing about the changes is that Akiyama no longer has the juggles which removes a lot of the fun his fighting style had in 4, though I think the launch strike is almost enough to make up for no juggles. Finally, Shinada's fighting style, while lacking a bit, is still really fun.Finally, the final boss is perfect for this game. Like I mentioned, the theme of dreams is a huge point in this game, and the final boss is LITERALLY THE DREAM. Could he have been built up to better? Yes, but I still think he's a great final boss.Y5 can be slow at times, but overall, I really like this game. The story is unique and interesting, the characters are great, and the fighting styles are fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is considered to be one of the best entries in the franchise. To me, it’s the least enjoyable one so far.As before, Yakuza games are open world action adventure titles with beat ’em up combat and cinematic stories. And just as the previous wonderful entry in the franchise, Yakuza 5 is divided into several parts, with each represented by a separate character story. Except now every character gets their own city (well, a district in one) to explore, sometimes even more than that. There’s more of everything – more minigames, more mechanics, more things to do. Each character has their own mini-story, explored through unique mechanics, in addition to the overabundance of substories (the side quests of the franchise). And everything is (kinda) tied into one grand theme, that the game beats you over and over the head again – following your dreams and carrying the legacy of others.And I can understand why Yakuza 5 is so liked – it is the best implementation of the gameplay ideas first introduced in Yakuza 3. Arguably, even better than what was done in Yakuza 0 and Kiwami, apart from the combat mechanics. Everything is finally done well – chasing/escaping mechanic is fun, first person view isn’t annoying, revelations are just QTEs with no vague choice at the end, substories are streamlined in the best possible way, leveling up is simple, but engaging and much much more. There’s also so much stuff to do for those who like the optional activities in the franchise. Personally, I found the hunting story to be the most interesting one, but others might find more things to love. And it’s all so big and ambitious…But I like the series for the characters and the stories that they carry, and in that regard, I found Yakuza 5 to be mostly filler with some really stupid moments in-between. Kiryu doesn’t want to be in this story for most of the time, and I don’t either – his story has been done since 3, yet the story here is mostly centered around him and Haruka. Who basically has no character and never had, being a side-kick for Kiryu’s story. Yet, she’s the second arguably the most important character of this game. Saejima’s story says nothing at all, but at least you get to punch a bear a few times. Akiyama is, as always, the best, but he’s severely underutilized. Shinada is kinda okay, but incredibly one-note and doesn’t have much to do with the story, nor has the charisma of Tanimura from 4. And the plot is so full of itself, so incredibly stupid, while taking so agonizingly slow to develop…I dunno, sometimes I think that maybe the fact that Yakuza 0 was my first personal experience with the series and that game is still the high point of the franchise storytelling, is affecting my ability to like the rest of the games. But then, I really cannot see myself enjoying Yakuza 5 even without 0. In 4 I was so excited to follow every character in their stories that I didn’t care that the main plot was kinda silly. And in the first three games I was very interested to see how the series evolved and the character of Kiryu with it. Even if his solution to all problems is always “start punching people until the problems solve themselves”. Plus 3 had a genuinely engaging story, despite how painfully slow it was told. But here? I just couldn’t care. Until Akiyama showed up and gave me a much needed boost to be able to stomach the rest of the game.Your experience may be different – if you like “hanging out” in the world of Yakuza and just do activities, sing karaoke, run around and punch people, you might love this a lot. But to me that was always secondary. And this game is more or less all about that. And they did make the gameplay feel really great. But it didn’t click for me at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This is certainly, to me, the best of the 3 Remastered games, but it only really comes together and reaches the heights of 0, 1 and 2 in its final 20-odd hours (in all, start to finish took me 63 hours). It drags HARD in the middle, which sees you first playing as Saejima - a character I have always disliked due to his bullheadedness and proclivity for making really stupid decisions - and then as Haruka, wherein the game takes a hard left turn into the extremely uncomfortable world of J-pop showbusiness.I imagine some of this is just cultural differences - I read that Famitsu gave this an extremely rare 40/40 for this game when it originally released. My biggest gripe with the game is that in Parts 2 and 3, which collectively took me about 30 hours to get through even while giving up on the side content, it feels more like a Japan sim than a game, than a Yakuza game. Obviously, capturing the feeling of Japan has always been one of Yakuza's aims - in the behind the scenes book 'Destiny of the Dragon', Toshihiro Nagoshi talks about making essentially a nightlife sim for all those too shy to go to a cabaret club in real life, in Yakuza 1. But never before - or after, if the Kiwami remakes are anything to go by - has that felt more the focus than the story. Parts 2 and 3 in particular feel overridingly like whirlwind tours of parts of Japanese culture Ryu Ga Gotoku studio felt they'd missed in prior games. After a repeat of Saejima's prison episode, we're in the freezing forests of Hokkaido, to spend 5 hours with a hunting minigame; the plot stalls in Haruka's section to have you play pop star.The plot is also still weak in places. As I said, it only really coalesces in the final third or so, and even then, it struggles with some of the same issues as Yakuza 4's plot - the big one, namely, is being confusing. At this point, I think this just has to be chalked up to having such a massive cast - as in 4, every playable character, of which there are now 5, has their own antagonist who they split up to fight in the end. Add to that all the supporting characters and side story characters, and it just buckles. I wouldn't be surprised if this game was a big reason for the downsizing to just Kiryu and Majima in 0. 0, 1, and 2 all became quite clear in the end about what was really going on behind the scenes, but I'm still not entirely sure what was actually happening here.(Spoilers for 4)What really doesn't help is that, unlike in 4, the story is very disjointedly told. There isn't the sense of overarching narrative that that game had. In 4, every character was quite clearly forwarding the overall story - Akiyama's billions of yen kicked off Munakata's plot, Saejima's breakout triggered the coverup of the Ueno Seiwa hit, Tanimura was investigating the Ueno Seiwa hit to find his father's killer, and Jingu's 10 billion yen from 1 being a payment to Munakata got Kiryu involved. Here, it feels much more like each Part is its own self-contained story, until Part 5, Finale, where it all suddenly comes crashing together. It's like if you edited a season of Game of Thrones so that all the Westeros stuff happens in the first half, and then for the entire second half we're in Meereen following that entirely unrelated story. And as usual for these 3 games, this approach means a WHOLE LOT of exposition dumping in Part 5 to explain away all the mysteries they had not been effectively unravelling over the earlier Parts.That said, Parts 4 and 5, exposition dumps aside, hit it out of the park for me, especially the final chapter. This might just be my favourite finale of the series so far. That's a tough contest, to be sure, but this is very satisfyingly laid out, with gameplay, voice acting, cutscenes, editing, music, storytelling playing off each other perfectly. Part 4 follows a new character, Tatsuo Shinada, a former pro baseball player with a... painful past, shall we say. The baseball lingo - a whole lot of 'strike zone', 'bottom of the ninth', 'taking a walk', 'breaking ball' and so forth in this section - is a hurdle, but Tatsuo is so likeable and his story so good that you get over it. Hell, they managed to make an unscrupulous loan shark, who spends half his screen time threatening to shove Shinada's hand through a metal press for insurance money, one of the most endearing characters in the game. Shinada also gets a really addicting (Pringles, "pop and you can't stop" level) baseball minigame with really tangible progression.The finale also really makes good on themes that for me didn't work earlier in the game. A big theme of the game is dreams, and the lengths that people will go to to achieve them. They're actually really unsubtle about it - the word 'dream' has to occur at least 1,000 times in the script. But in Part 3, the first point I really noticed it, it just felt like a justification for really backwards thinking. Again, maybe cultural differences. In Haruka's Part, everyone is telling her "it's your manager's dream for you to become a celebrity, so become a celebrity, dammit!" Her manager is objectively awful, editing contracts to cheat employees out of severance pay, berating Haruka about the cruelty of the world, and blackmailing our dear, sweet Kiryu into abandoning her forever. No-one asks Haruka what she wants, they just tell her to do what her awful, awful manager wanted for herself.But in Shinada's section, it starts to take a more understandable shape. He had a dream, that machinations beyond his knowledge forced him to abandon for life, and his story is all about rediscovering it and choosing to start living again rather than just surviving. In the Finale, it actually starts to really work, as we see dreams giving strength to our heroes, and survivalist fear weakening our enemies. Haruka has an extremely touching finale, wherein she finally accepts that she can follow her own dreams, and fixes the biggest mistake she ever made. Kiryu gets what is easily one of my favourite boss battles in the series, with a really cathartic setting, lots of scenery changes, tonnes of awesome QTEs, and a really high-stakes feel.

_childDocuments_.review: - Story : Probably the longest Yakuza game in the series before Like a Dragon. This time with 5 main characters & arcs each with their own conflicts and underlying themes that is supposed to connect together but falls kinda flat in the finale for being too long & too ambitious that players might forget what happens in the early chapters. Sometimes it feels like the dev doesn't know what it wants to do with the characters from previous game since their character has been explored quite a lot already. The side quests this time is packed and has more story rather than being generic fetch quests. (8/10)- Combat : The combat in Yakuza 5 is similar with Yakuza 4 in that it's easy to advance skills using orbs and you can select which category of skill you want to upgrade. The fighting flow this time feels smoother considering the new engine that is used for the new Yakuza. Although i feel Shinada as a new character has somewhat clunky fighting style if you choose to play him without any weapons. (9/10)- Exploration : Probably the most fun exploration by far with a large 5 playable maps (4 new ones + Kamurocho). There's minigame, side quests, photography, food tourism, hunting, victory road tournament, and so much more. When i say this is the most ambitious RGG has ever been, this is what i meant. If you're like me and enjoy clearing substories & all the little stuffs, you might find this best one yet. (10/10)Overall : 9 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: Arguably the best in the series. 10/10 Combat: Yakuza 5 game has playable four characters five if you are including Haruka so naturally each character fighting style and boy none of them disaapoint (Yes including Shinada). Even if no one is as fun as good ol Kiryu its always fun and refreshing to have other playable characters and two if the playable characters were in Yakuza 4 so you don't need to relearn everything.10/10 Gameplay: This game has easily the most side activities the series has ever had (except for Ishin maybe). Everything we have seen from previous games is here in addition of many other fresh minigames we haven't seen before all of which spread across five characters and five cities with different substories and minigames.10/10 Story: One of the best stories in the series. Yakuza 5 probably has the biggest cast in series and yet they still managed to keep our beloved Kiryu's saga on a personal level and even got to see him in a vulnerable state we haven't seen him in before. We got to our favourite business man Akiyama which is always a good thing, Saejima our favourite guy who ends up in prison for no reason and Shinada who was such a a great character but sadly disappeared and never appeared in any other Yakuza game. The plot itself was good but I have seen better in the other Yakuza games and I could say the same thing about the villains. It was mainly the amount of amazing characters that hard carried the story but a 10 regardless.10/10 OST: Every character's fighting theme has absolute bangers and every single boss fight theme is amazing and memorable, especially the final boss. However this could apply to any Yakuza game since they never disappoint when it comes to OST.Overall: 10/10 Might be biased

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 takes the growth that Yakuza 4 had over 3 and sprinkles a bit more on top. Yet, it still fails to reach the highs of 0 and Kiwami.The game injects each character with some puddle-deep sidestories (Taxi, Hunting, Idol, Baseball) that keep items, exp, and money gated behind their respective (bland) gameplay loops.Only Kiryu and Saejima's stories were really worth their salt (but the Prison segment still sucked nuts, thank god they buffed him from 3 tho), Akiyama isn't dealt justice since half of his chapter is shared with Haruka on some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idol-arc tangent (love playing the same 3 songs for 5 hours), and Shinada is just a comic relief character shoehorned in so badly that they quite literally have a 20 second jikoshoukai-ass moment in the final chapter to try and squeeze him into the story - almost to the point where they'd both be better off as separate entities to not kill the main story's pacing (i will say that his story is strong - just doesn't add much to the main narrative in an organic way).But hey, at least side stories have a waypoint.While the combat has fundamentally improved a tad over 4, it's still blockuza (but not as bad as 3) and Akiyama feels worse to play as, and Shinada sucks donkey sack without good weapons and against enemies who can immune his tackle. Still a lot of cringe stun-locks, and shows that there's still a lot to grow in the gameplay department (which would reach its peak in 0 and Kiwami).- 60 fps cap- mediocre combat (still better than 3 and 4)- Akiyama and Shinada moveset was dookie- needs the cut-content and HD restoration + model texture patch (and HD font mod, but at least Silent Patch isn't needed)- character side stories were meh (taxi and races were repetitive, hunting was slow and repetitive, idol was easy, repetitive and trivial, and baseball was boring, repetitive, and hinged on training - starting to notice a pattern here)- the final boss/"main" reasoning behind what set the story in motion almost comes out of nowhere - like its pretty funny (light spoilers: imma die from canca so imma give my son, side character #8, the tojo and the omi like lol)- traveling around towns and doing side content still take 50 years - encounter rate way too high (you WILL be constantly stopped)- took away saejima's luscious mane- 夢5.5/10 its aight but HOLY was the story pretty dragged out and meh. The PS3 Yakuzas are NOT good dawg. Shoutout cheat engine speedhack for giving me the willpower to beat this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is by no means a bad Yakuza game - in fact, the content here is on par with just about anything else previously in the series and it's even more plentiful - however, I still haven't finished it. It's just too long. Each character has an estimated minimum of 10 hours of screen time and despite being interested in the story, the game just can't keep my attention for that long, especially seen as nothing really happens until the end of each chapter. Furthermore, the Yakuza gameplay loop has never been especially engaging but I've become comfortable enough now after 6 games to appreciate it. With this in mind, the sheer audacity of them to make no changes to the established formula in a game far longer than any other in the series is frankly absurd, especially when you consider that every other game so far becomes borderline tiresome by some point. Despite this, I do recommend it - I just don't have the patience to continue just yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is the worst game in the mainline yakuza franchise. You should still play it.To avoid writing an entire essay about why I feel the way I do about this game, in short the story is the worst story in any serious story based game that I had ever played, but the fighting might be the best in the entire franchise.The entire game is extremely ambitious and filled to the brim with stuff to do, with each of the 5 main characters having their own unique mini game, but it often times comes off as tedious rather than charming in comparison to the other games. It just throws everything at you all at once and it can feel overwhelming and exhausting at times.Also, like I said before the story isn't all that great either. While the Yakuza 4's story wasn't the best either and was extremely convoluted and all over the place with some real head scratching moments, I felt like the story struck an almost "so bad its good" note with how wacky and far-fetched some of the plot points were. Y5's story has some real confusing moments but they don't feel charming they just feel stupid. It just strikes a real ugly note where the story thinks its the most intellectual and meaningful story ever told, and it's all supposed to feel like this giant and grandiose epic, but in the end, it just feels so anticlimactic. 40+ hours of build up all for an ending you could see coming from a mile a way, and a final boss that doesn't even feel like a final boss. Y5's story summed up in one word is "unsatisfying" at best and "infuriating" at worst. It's not unbearable if you're like me and did a Yakuzathon and wanted to binge the whole story but GOD it feels like pulling teeth sometimes.But also like I said the fighting is some of the, if not the, best fighting in the entire franchise, even more so than Y0. I'm not a huge fan of the dragon engine combat and Y0 and Y1K can feel kind of sloppy at times, but in this game everything feels incredibly tight and precise, to the point where it's almost hard to go back to earlier games like Y4. Each of the characters you can fight as are incredibly fleshed out and add the right amount of variety to the main game as opposed to the other kind of "variety" the other endless amount of dull mini games provide (seriously I never understood that whole dress up thing with Aikiyama. They started it in Y3 and continued it through this game, and I don't know if someone working at RGG is a sadist because that is unironically some o the most boring ♥♥♥♥ I've ever played. It feels like it comes from a $20 shovelware game you'd get on the Wii).To wrap things up, this game is undoubtedly a low point in the Yakuza franchise, even more so than Y3 in my opinion, but I still think that it is fun enough to worth a purchase. Its almost worth it just for the story, even though it sucks because Y6's story might be one of best in the franchise. This the worst game to jump in on the series in, but if you want get the full Yakuza experience, give this one a shot.

Spoiler Free ReviewPros:- It has an awesome theme on it's story which is about "Dreams".- As always it has amazingly written side & main characters especially the new playable character, Shinada.- This game is probably the biggest Yakuza game up to date, you got 5 cities, 5 characters to play as, each character having it's own battle theme, and ♥♥♥♥ tons of mini games/substories per character.- It removed some cliche tropes you expected from the past Yakuza games (Yakuza 3 - 4 to be specific) so you will find this game a breath of fresh air.- Gameplay is similar to Yakuza 4 but just upgraded and enhanced. It's almost close to yakuza 0's combat, but the attacks still lack the punch (sfx specifically) like yakuza 0 has.- The OST is decent to best. Is this absolutely confusing and will never be brought up again? Yes. Does it make Park completely irredeemable in my eyes? Yes. Akiyama returns and continues to be lightning, idk why they skimped on giving us more of Hana but I can't make Sega change a 12 year old game to give me more of beautiful foodie lady who is weirdly their best written female character to this point if we're going by release order. _childDocuments_.review: The biggest Yakuza game of all with the most new content, but is so large it struggles to have any type of cohesion in its storytelling.  It’s more like 4 separate games added into one, but bigger doesn’t always mean better.Having the 5 distinct acts with separate playable characters, each with their own combat style, side quests and cities to explore makes this the most varied but also the longest game.  The pacing is extremely slow with lots of cut-scenes and conversations, often back to back, resulting in long times without any real game play.  It’s a long game even by Yakuza standards - each time you start as a new character, you basically start over again and each character has to complete their own set of same but different things to do.  There’s plenty of content, but getting into the meat of it takes a long time and completing it all is a lesson in persistence.The overarching story is slow and so drawn out that you’ll struggle to remember what the fuss was about.  It also doesn’t really feel like a game about an organised crime syndicate due to the extensive side-campaigns.  These offer a lot of content and have a surprising amount of depth, but thematically, can be quite distanced: * Taxi driving and street racing isn’t particularly good and gets boring after a while, especially after the taxi missions are changed to conversations and there’s only 1 race track.* Hunting in the snow creates flashbacks to Assassin’s Creed III, warts and all.  It’s not that bad, but lacks the polish and variety which the setting could have offered.* The song and dance routines are great fun and very different to what has gone before, but are very repetitive by their nature.  I guess this is what it is like being an idol is in real life.  The other fame missions showcase some variety, but leave one of the main characters especially short changed in content.* Baseball is a mini-game extended to breaking point but it’s not exactly engaging to play or varied in nature.  Thankfully, the character saves this with their charisma.Overall, it’s the same as every other game in the series and you can’t help but enjoy it, shortcomings and all.  The atmosphere, the style, the characters, the mini-games, the side content, the overly serious plot and the wacky side-quests all add up to an experience only the Yakuza games can deliver.  It’s got the same high quality production and formula, a mix of good and dated graphics which look fine for its age, albeit with more clipping, pop-in and other minor issues than before, and catchy music throughout.  The combat is solid and fun, the maps are different if a bit small (but with so many of them, you can understand why) and the set pieces up the ante and make you feel like a whirlwind of devastation.  The grind in endgame and other weaknesses are exacerbated when you have to do so much more of it, but if you pace yourself, enjoy the setting and embrace the culture, you’ll generally enjoy it.

To be clear, it’s not that his moves were bad in the slightest; it’s just the the first two were really done well this time and I had no choice but to place him here. And that brings us to . His fighting style has been my least favourite of any of the Yakuza games. His combos were short, and his main selling point, the ‘my meteor’ tackle just felt underwhelming. Skills: The skill menu is finally straight forward, with no room for confusion. You can choose to unlock abilities from the Heat, Body, Soul and Tech categories, in a linear fashion and as you unlock more and more abilities, the cost (soul orbs) goes up. Simple. Good. Map: The map is still similar to Y4 in the sense that you’re either zoomed all the way in or all the way out, and it’s still devoid of details at a glance. There is now, at least, a list of all places that can be entered and selecting one from this list focuses the map on that building. But if you’re just wanting to look around your immediate vicinity, you’re left to (hopefully) hover over the building long enough to read its name. Some buildings are very small on the map and are harder to get the cursor over than I would like. It’s a small gripe, I know. But in something as often used as the map, it’s just a layer of frustration that isn’t pleasant to deal with. Heat: The change to the heat system is good. You now have a red orb by your health and heat bar that fills up, and when it’s full you can press Y or Triangle to unleash a devastating attack. Minigames: The ramen shop minigame was quite fun as a one-off thing.  taxi racing was really fun, and you can even customise your car. The little stories you’d get into while driving customers around were enjoyable, but the real beauty of it all was the taxi company story. Tears achieved. It was the highlight of the first part of the game for me.  hunting minigame was a nice change of pace. The mechanics were a little stiff, and I would often have wildlife spawning on me once I’d entered an area, but aside from that, it was a good experience. The story of it was pretty good, too. In regards to , I never thought I’d be playing an idol simulator in Yakuza, but here we are. This type of gameplay is so far out of my normal purview that I would never have picked up a game that was purely based around this style. But the thing is, all the minigames are just so well done and so enjoyable that even though it’s not my usual cup of tea, I had a blast playing through them. But, as is the Yakuza way…it’s the story that makes this part shine.  Ahh, the tears, they come. minigame at the batting center was okay, but I didn’t really enjoy it all that much. It played well enough once you got used to it, but I just didn’t get much of a kick out of it.Side quests are as hilarious as ever.Miscellaneous: Not being able to cross big streets in the city was a pain in the ass. Street AI was the most annoying thing in this game. Get out of the damn way!  Not so much a bug, more of a coding issue, but sometimes funny things would happen during cutscenes like street AI walking right into a character and then disappearing. Once, a car actually drove through someone. It was hilarious, so I’m putting it down as a quirk rather than a bug. After Y4, I wasn’t certain of how Y5 would play out in regards to the characters that were introduced. I am pleased to say that I now see said characters in a good light (bar one, sorry Tanimura) and I have grown very fond of them. The combat is largely very enjoyable, and there weren’t any BS fights (excluding optional/hidden fights) that made me pull my hair out. The story was good, but again, I feel like they tried too hard, with so much going on that it felt a bit muddy by the end. The simpler story points like  hit the hardest for me. With some fun minigame additions and a little bit of polish, Y5 ended up sucking me in for a good spell. Yes. This is one of the better remastered Yakuza games, and a must-play for any fan of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 Remastered - 9.1/10Plot and Dialogue: 9.0/10, 9.0/10Setting and Art Design: 8.5/10Soundtrack: 8.0/10Graphics: 6.0/10Gameplay and Sound Design: 8.5/10, 9.5/10Plot and Dialogue:The plot in this game was a rollercoaster. Lots of ups and downs, plot twists, and an overconnecting narrative between all of them. This is definitely one of the best stories in the Yakuza franchise, only losing out to Kiwami 2 and 0 in my opinion. However, this game is super ambitious with 5 protagonists and so many supporting characters. I don't know how they managed to keep everything connected and cohesive, but it's super impressive they were able to do so. Setting and Art Design:We have 5 different locations, with each one having a unique feel to it. The art design in this game really does suit each of the locations and the cities don't feel as grey and monotone as it did in 3 and 4. Soundtrack:The soundtrack was very good in this game, as the songs really did help amplify each moment and they were very memorable. My personal favorite is Each of their dreams. Graphics: These graphics were definitely a step up in the facials department. The characters looked very realistic and it was clear a lot of time was spent on making them look good. In addition, the cities got the attention they deserved and were very well-fleshed out. Gameplay and Sound Design: The gameplay was extremely good in this game, with many different fighting styles across each of the protagonists and a simple yet nice leveling up system. Each punch and what not is very satisfying and really does make you feel like you are beating the life out of someone. Final Notes:In my opinion, this is the 3rd best Yakuza game behind 0 and Kiwami 2. I highly recommend this game, even at it's long playtime.
