_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a fantastic game. It's a huge leap in scale and quality over Yakuza 3 and 4, with neither of the mistakes that pull the previous two back from being better than they could be. What Yakuza 3 got wrong was its gameplay, and where Yakuza 4 falls on its face is the plot that I've got no qualms against calling some of the stupidest I've ever seen in any video game I've played. Yakuza 5 starts great and keeps going. There's some issues I have with it like some dated textures for a remaster, inconsistent quality on prerendered cutscenes, not being able to make a clear save in Premium Adventure, and the fact that you can't read the manga in the convenience store stalls like you could in the original version, but those are just nitpicks on a package that learned from the series' previous shortcomings while amplifying what those earlier games got right.A concern that I had heading into Yakuza 5 was if its expansion from four to five main characters was going to make this game's plot just as sloppy as Yakuza 4 ended up being later on. But that's far from the case. Like Yakuza 4, our main playable characters, from the three you'd already be familiar with, to our new baseball boy Shinada, and, in a refreshing twist in both plot and gameplay, up-and-coming pop idol Haruka, are all given ample time for the player to get used to their mechanics, from progressing their combat styles to all the new side activities (Kiryu's Initial D taxi races, Saejima's hunting, Haruka's idol jobs, and Shinada's baseball). But where it learns from Yakuza 4's mistakes is that the overarching plot that ties these five fully fleshed out characters is far better written and, I can't believe I'm saying this, believable... Well, more believable than I mentioned scale, and I wasn't kidding. Unlike previous entries where you're in one of at most two cities (one of which is always going to be Kamurocho), this game's got five. Kamurocho, Sotenbori, Tsukimino, Nagasugai, and Kineicho. And just as Kamurocho and Sotenbori have their real life analogues that the devs do a great job in recreating, so too do these three new areas. They're all wonderfully realized in this game, each with their own distinct local feel, even in how NPCs speak different dialects reflecting their region. The main characters are all tied to a city relevant to the plot, so it stands to reason that each character's substories will mostly be in their cities as well. It's also where each character's side story is present, so whether you do these side activities before or after finishing the main plot, you always have a ton of things to do that'll encourage you to take in each location, and it wouldn't take long to be familiar with each city in the same way you're already probably familiar with Kamurocho, Sotenbori, and maybe even Ryukyu from Yakuza 3. And of course, these new districts? They're ALL tourist destinations. Two of 'em are red light districts. Because OF COURSE they are. Hell, there's even a little side activity you can do with each character where you take pictures of multiple tourist spots in each city... I wonder what the Japan National Tourism Organization's cut on Yakuza 5's game sales is like...I have to talk about Haruka's mechanics. You'll be familiar with the game's combat. It's stayed pretty much the same throughout the series, with mechanical improvements, additions, and changes to progression that I'd rather you discover on your own. I will say that there's a ton more depth in this system than there was in Yakuza 4, which was already a massive improvement since Yakuza 3. But Haruka? She's the most drastic shift in gameplay that needs to be addressed, because you're either gonna absolutely love her section, or you'll see it as a jarring interruption. Not in the flow of the story, that's done really well, but in gameplay. Personally, I love it. She has no combat. No random spawning enemies that interrupt your peaceful jog around town. What she does have is dance battles in place of street combat, and the Princess League concert battles in place of boss fights. These are two different flavors of rhythm game, and I can sort of see in the dance battle mechanics the seed that would eventually grow and bloom into the wonderful bouquet that was Yakuza 0's disco minigame. Haruka levels up like any of the other hotboys to give it a sense of satisfying progression. And while, naturally, it's not going to have as much depth compared to the combat that's been refined for five games at this point, it does still have it. Haruka's got her stat increases, heat actions, her own trainer, and even a Revelation. At this point in the series, I really shouldn't be surprised that I'm thrown a curve ball like this, but I still am. Consistently. Besides, it's nice to have one character exploring a Japanese city without having to beat up several serious-faced goons every five steps. I can't wait for Yakuza 8 where Haruka becomes a vtuber or something.The big theme of this game is dreams. That even extends in the post-game where seeing all the characters together wearing goofy outfits felt like a terrible fever dream. But I digress. This game's plot is like a return to form. It's not perfect. I do feel like the final boss fight, while mechanically satisfying and the most hype since Zero, isn't really developed quite well. But the rest of the story that ties together our very well-written and fleshed out hotboys and gamer girl Haruka, is like going back to some of the earliest entries where characters fought over ideals than just having to stop a convoluted plot to take over Japan's underworld. The convoluted plot to take over Japan's underworld is still there. It wouldn't be Yakuza without it. But what I felt was a bit lacking from Yakuza 4 was this feel of fighting for a cause one believes in. There was a bit of a theme around trust, but it's overshadowed by the hilariously dumb overarching plot. It didn't really have a cheesy theme. Its levity was in how stupid its plot is rather than how endearing it is. In Zero, it was self-discovery. In the original Yakuza, it's love. In Yakuza 2, it's to settle who the REAL dragon is. In Yakuza 3, it's fatherhood and family. In 5, it's dreams. Fighting to make sure dreams come true, or so that people who are struggling are given the strength to make their own dreams come true. Or even passing on dreams you once held to someone new. YUME. DREAMS. It permeates this entire game from the main plot, to the side stories, and even some of the substories. See? Doesn't that sound cheesy? Of course. Because it is. But it is exactly the kind of anime af feel that makes these games so endearing. Yakuza 5 delivers on everything the series has done well before, and it now makes perfect sense why Zero is as good as it was, because THIS level of quality was that prequel's jumping off point.I find it hard to recommend any of the games in the Remastered Collection on their own, because for whatever flaws they might have, they're all still great games, and more importantly, they all build on one another and on the first two entries in the series. But if for some strange reason, you're only getting one of the three games in that collection, then get this. It's got a charming, well-written story centered around five characters across five beautiful cities without being difficult to follow. Its boss fights, while sometimes making very little logical sense, are still hype af to play. Its side stories are worth becoming their own individual games. And its substories are still hilariously goofy and endearing. It's a damn good time. Yakuza 5 is worth its asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone aptly put it, this game is big, huge, colossal, grandiose, towering, and pretty stonking large. It has moments that will make you like it, dislike it, love it, but never hate it. The game, like its overarching plot, is big and bloated but full of more heart than most of the prior games combined. It is one giant study on dreams – ones we make for ourselves and the ones we make for others, the ones we sacrifice for and the ones we make others sacrifice for, the ones that inspire us and the ones that corrupt us, and everything in between. Could have been a little more subtle in the dialogue. Get ready to hear “yume” (dream) a lot.Gameplay wise, it is the best of the remastered collection as it takes into account the successes and issues of prior games and iterates on that. With five different playable protagonists, each one has their own distinct style in fighting (of the ones that are able to fight). From Saejima who manhandles mobs of enemies to Akiyama with his Chun-Li kicks all the way to Shinada who can pull weapons out of his ass, each one feels equally as enjoyable as they are different.Personally, this is my favorite in the remastered series and high up in ranking across all of the Yakuza/Like a Dragon games. My only issues are that the bloat really needed to be edited down significantly and that the overarching plot is too convoluted to be gripping. The individual stories themselves are very well done, but they aren't connected as well as they should be. The beginning of the game is also a bit of a slog because of that bloat issue. But for every moment of bloat we got handfuls of crazy over the top action moments and emotional beats. Probably the best final chapter in any of the games so far. Definitely the best final fight of all of the mainline games so far.The game is pretty damn great. 8/10. Could have been a 9 if it was a little more succinct.

_childDocuments_.review: Man this one is absolutely jam-packed with content. Definitely don't skip this one, has so much to play here.You can really tell though that the multi-protagonist setup was starting to fall apart here, even Yakuza 4 started to show some cracks by the end. There's just too many perspectives in this game and its a bit awkward to play as one character for, depending on how much side content you do, maybe 10 or so hours, and then move on to the next character and just not see that character again for another 40 or so hours. It's unsurprising that the follow-up, Yakuza 0, dialed it back to just two protagonists and also had both characters alternate frequently throughout the game. Also, the longer you play this game the more frustrating it starts to get. The harder combat challenges for completion just become beyond tedious and require you to just use cheesey tactics to win. Running around town is annoying as well, as you can no longer push through pedestrians and end up getting stuck a lot.As for story, this one started strong but really fell apart by the finale. Twists just didn't make a lot of sense and some things honestly I felt were just left completely unexplained. Oddly enough, there was a very climactic showdown with Kiryu and Saejima, and then the game just didn't end and kept going a little longer, which just felt weird. Also, the actual final boss for each character was a repeat boss, ones that you fought a good 2 or 3 times prior in the game. Even the final boss of the whole game for Kiryu was a repeat, and the guy didn't even really seem to understand why he was the final boss! Really odd narrative choices in this one. At the very least, the final boss was still pretty cool despite being weird writing.Overall, a real treat to play. Each character has a dedicated side story with unique gameplay mechanics and plot, and there are so many minigames too. Haruka was also really fun to play as, having her own rhythm-based gameplay rather than the regular combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game between calls at work. Don't worry, it's not as long as my play time.This has probably been my favorite non-Kiwami entry in the Yakuza series so far. And each also has a side-story that you can play through, and overall I found it worthwhile and enjoyable to do all of them (Except hostess-raising, I've had enough of that by this point). You race taxis, go hunting, become a teen idol, and play baseball. Also speaking of characters, I found all five playable characters to be unique this time around. Kiryu is a badass as always, but I also found the others to possess much more diversity in their combat styles. One is fast with great combos, another is strong as hell and smashes enemies into the ground, and another is a weapon specialist who can unlock pretty potent techniques with each type of weapon. Oh, and one non-combat character, who although I enjoyed her portion of the story, she didn't contribute much overall to the rest of the game.In summary, if you're going to play one non-Kiwami game, I recommend this one.You Literally Punch a Bear/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing recommending it, however I've finished it having several issues regarding this game.Although Yakuza 5 never attempts to be a real simulation of life in Japan, the areas of selective realism within are one of its biggest draws. Yakuza 5 takes what Yakuza 4 accomplished and amplifies everything in it to create a very ambicious game with a brand new experience that is bigger and better than before. It is to this date the biggest Yakuza title and contains the most playable characters. Still, it doesn't surprass some of the best titles in the franchise, one of the reasons I could say is because it's a case where it becomes too much of everything that it starts to cause issues. Yakuza 5’s story is massive. The major backdrop for much of Yakuza 5’s story, however, each character has a personal story that will weave into a full narrative in the final sections. Just like Yakuza 4, this title has segments with each of the characters, as they get their own section of the story (including Haruka). The experience of each story i'd say is good, but besides the pacing where the game has to restart the story three times with entirely new characters and no firm connection between them, Yakuza 5 also has a bigger issue. Yakuza 5 is a very long game. If played at a reasonable pace and doing side missions, you are very likely going to spend at least fifty hours, with the ease of getting distracted, it’s more likely that you will spend more.In the beginning the game has a good pace, you are getting settled on a new enviroment never presented before, however as you go by the characters, each time the narrative escalate and you end up with a lack of pace and a rather large finale. At this point you pretty much forgot the thread of the story.Aside from the pace in the end of the game, another issue is that it has a lack of cohesion, Yakuza 5 tend to hard cut each time you are finishing a segment with a character. Each character’s section starts with a hard stop and feels like the game is starting over, Yakuza 4 had this issue, but you are going to feel it much more in Yakuza 5. There are some other issues, like focusing on sequences that add very little to the story, it all could be put as side quests.In the finale, characters show up and you might forget who they were or what their relevance was. This is even true for the final boss which feels like a character who comes out of nowhere.As for the gameplay, there’s more variety with each fighting style this time, a firm effort has been made to make each character unique, and it has paid off, giving four distinct brawlers, which becomes more noticeable once players use these characters back to back in the final segment where they are with their full abilities. One point noted, each corner of the map there's a fight, too many random battles, it's too much, even if you want to farm exp you will eventually get tired of it.As I wrote above, the game forces you on sequences that add very little to the story, I’ve always been a big fan of the mini-games in the franchise and I do enjoy the majority of them, however with the massive sum of time already in the story,  the fact that the story feels like it’s needlessly adding them to pad the run time, you start to question yourself if it is really necessary. Putting a mini-game on the player’s path makes it less special than if players accidentally stumble upon a mini-game. The newer cities are smaller than previous locations but they are fresh additions to the game and one that helps Yakuza 5 feel brand new even with the game using a similar progression to the previous games.Ultimately Yakuza 5 struggles more due to how much it tries to do, rather than any specific action it takes. It’s just too long of a game to be executed properly as it was planned, and with the depth and breadth of the gameplay offered, something had to give. Yakuza 5 though is an enjoyable experience for that I recommend it. The story is interesting once players can piece it all together over the long run time, the gameplay is engaging, you feel like some of it could have been better executed, It’s strange to both want more challenging content for each character, while calling out the length of the game, but that’s where we wind up with Yakuza 5.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 ReviewPart 1: The Gameplay Yakuza 5’s Gameplay was not enjoyable at launch, the game was very poorly optimized, and this has been recently fixed with a patch update, which made the Gameplay much more enjoyable.In my opinion, the game feels similar to Yakuza 0’s Gameplay as Yakuza 5 is built on an earlier version of Yakuza 0’s Engine.The Combat is nice and fluid, and easy to learn, but can be harder to master, the combat system is not as Stiff as Yakuza 3’s and Yakuza 4’s Combat System.There are also Five Playable Characters, and Four of them can enter combat situations.Kiryu: His iconic fighting style is still present, with the abilities to learn better moves such as the Tiger Drop or the Komaki Parry.Saejima: A More brute force Moveset. He can take heavy objects like Scooters and use them in combat, you can also charge up a damaging attack after a successful combo.Akiyama: His moveset is comprised of mostly Kick based attacks. He feels very satisfying to play as. But he does not have counters to being grabbed unlike Kiryu and SaejimaShinada: It’s interesting, but I’m not a fan of his moveset. Weak damage, but a lot of flexibility, he has access to an Iron Pipe that he keeps as a weapon that he can always use, he also refuses to use Baseball Bats in combat for Character Story reasons.Part 2: The MinigamesYakuza 5 has a lot of minigames, from hunting in the mountains as Saejima, driving a Taxi as Kiryu, all the way to being a Japanese Idol, Yakuza 5 features a lot of variety in its mini games.You got some of the classics like Karaoke and FishingBut you get a lot of new minigames, such as:Air HockeyCochins Cup ClassicComedy TeamDartsDriving RangePachinkoPoolShogiSlotsTatsuya NoodlesWinter CombatAnd much more.There are also arcade games available in the Club Sega’s on the Maps.My personal 2 favorites are the UFO Catchers and the Drum Master game.Part 3: CharactersYakuza 5 has some great characters.From Nakajima, a Taxi company president that hired Kiryu when he moved, Nakajima has also an interesting backstory, all the way to Kurosawa, an Osaka Police Detective which has some plans that I will not spoil here.There are also returning characters from other games:Diago Dojima: The Tojo Clan’s Sixth Chairman.Goro Majima: The Patriarch of the Majima Family and President of Majima Construction, but also a great Anti-Hero, Majima throughout all the Yakuza games is a greatly written character.And more characters.Part 4: The ProtagonistsYakuza 5 has Five Playable Characters:Kazuma Kiryu:Kazuma Kiryu is the most recurring protagonist of the Yakuza series. He is featured as the main protagonist and playable character in Yakuza/Yakuza Kiwami, Yakuza 2/Yakuza Kiwami 2, Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 6. He is featured as one of multiple main protagonists and playable characters in Yakuza 0, Yakuza 4 and Yakuza 5.His legendary accomplishments and ascent through the ranks of the Tojo Clan's Dojima Family, as well as the tattoo of a dragon on his back, have earned him the nickname "The Dragon of Dojima" He was the Fourth Chairman of the Tojo Clan, and previously managed the Morning Glory Orphanage, which was featured in Yakuza 3 and Briefly in Yakuza 4.Taiga Saejima:Taiga Saejima is a recurring protagonist and character in the series. He appears as one of multiple main protagonists and playable characters in both Yakuza 4 and Yakuza 5. He appears in flashbacks in Yakuza 0 and is a supporting character in Yakuza 6. He is a former member of the Sasai Family of the Tojo Clan, and later became the patriarch of the Saejima Family. He is the sworn brother of Goro Majima.Saejima became a legend amongst yakuza for carrying out the 1985 Ueno Seiwa massacre, in which eighteen key members of the organization were slain.Shun Akiyama: Shun Akiyama is one of the main playable protagonists of Yakuza 4, Yakuza: Dead Souls a PS3 Spinoff released in 2010, and Yakuza 5.He is a successful entrepreneur known as "The Lifeline of Kamurocho" due to his habit of lending money to people with nowhere left to turn. He runs Sky Finance, as well as Club Elise, a hostess club which he commonly uses in his tests to earn a loan.Tatsuo Shinada:Tatsuo Shinada is one of the five main protagonists in Yakuza 5. He is a former player for the Nagoya Wyverns and currently works as an adult entertainment writer.He takes the spot of Tanimura from Yakuza 4.Haruka Sawamura: Haruka Sawamura is a main character in the Yakuza series. She is the adoptive daughter of Kazuma Kiryu, whom she first meets and becomes close to during the events of Yakuza/Yakuza Kiwami when Kiryu helps her to locate her missing mother when she is 9. She would continue to feature subsequently in Yakuza 2/Yakuza Kiwami 2, Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 4. In Yakuza 5, she is now an idol, and appears as one of the five playable protagonists. She is a central character in Yakuza 6, wherein it is revealed that she has a young son named Haruto Sawamura.For most of the series during and after Yakuza 3, Haruka resides in Okinawa at the Morning Glory Orphanage along with eight other children Kiryu has taken in. As the oldest one living there besides Kiryu, she acts as the older sibling to the rest of the kids.Part 4: The StoryI Won’t say a lot here to spoil stuff.Yakuza 5 takes place Two years after Yakuza 4, The story spans the Five Protagonists, and is a very good one with some interesting plot twists and good emotional moments, if you like good stories, I think you’re going to like this one.Part 5: Should I start with this game if I never played a Yakuza game?Absolutely not.I Would Recommend to play at least Yakuza Kiwami to Yakuza 3.Yakuza 4 is also recommended but is not essential in my opinion. Yakuza 0 is recommended if you want to understand certain aspects of the Plot even better, Yakuza 0 is the First game in chronological order, Yakuza 0 takes place in 1988, Kiwami in 2005, Kiwami 2 in 2006, Yakuza 3 in 2009, Yakuza 4 in 2010, and Yakuza 5 in 2012If you want so start playing the Yakuza franchise, I heavily recommend to start with Yakuza 0 OR Yakuza Kiwami.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 was kind of a letdown for me.The storyline is quite messy for the first 16 chapters, but it gets more comprehensible towards the end of the game, in the last 5 chapters. The writing was...awful, to say the least. Characters get written out quite frequently, unnecessary and dumb plot twists, characters who do not have any building behind it and get to be a major part of the plot, slow pacing at times, "go to point A to point B" missions in the main quest, and the story constantly shoving down your throat about "dreams", that is the theme of the game, which leads to poor and inconsistent dialogue. And it also drags on for a lot of chapters, and it can get tiring to get to the end.But other than that,The game has great sidecontent, just the very best in the the yakuza series. It has fun and easy to do sidequests(by that i mean, it isn't locked between a minigame or anything you can just go and do it, which not many games in the yakuza series have), intresting side-stories for each character, with their own original minigames and storyline, many upgradable abilities for each character, which is really fun to do, to see how your character became a god to when you started the game is really satisfying, lots of fun minigames to pass your time, the combat is great in this game as well, it has a lot of fun and unique mechanics to it, which always makes it fun and refreshing for each and every character, which by the way, all of them are great to play as(even shinada's, don't let anyone tell you otherwise), great and phenomenal game OST, and the characters they get their writing right in the story, they get it right, and great cities to explore. And minus the obvious fact that, playing with 4(5 if you count haruka)characters, is really great. It really is the most ambitious title in the series ever.So, to sum it up:Pros:-A lot of great sidecontent;-Great combat system;-Fun minigames;-4 playable characters and 5 explorable cities;-Good OSTCons:-Terrible writing-Slow pacing-Bad storyline-Drags on for too longOverall, it could have been really great, the best game in the yakuza series. However, I could not get over how the ending disappointed me in terms of the story and writing. But it was still fun and a good time for the most part, if you're a fan of the series you should get the game after you played 4, but as a standalone title, you can pick up for the sidecontent I guess but don't expect much for the main story.I hope this review was somewhat helpful to you, cause really I just wanted to share my thoughts after playing this game, cause I've never felt so mixed after completing a game before lol. Have a nice day

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Big game is big! Big game is GOOD!Of all the Yakuza games I've played (0-5 at the time of this review), this is the... most!  It's HUGE! Absolutely jam-packed with everything you've come to expect from Yakuza: all the over-the-top dramatics, pointlessly convoluted schemes and double-crosses and ambushes and twist reveals and shock discoveries.  Plus of course all the bizarre and delightful sub-stories, the weirdly wholesomely horny middle-aged men, the ridiculous amount of extra content: arcade games, mahjong, gambling, underground fight rings etc with a whole bunch of new stuff thrown in: garbage collection! Baseball! Becoming a Taxi driver! Street Racing! Hunting! Dancing! Becoming part of the idol industry!The storyline doesn't make much of any sense but that's part of the wonderful charm of this series, and though I never warmed to Park in spite of efforts to explain her actions, she did make for a very interesting addition to the cast.  Speaking of which, Saejima and Akiyama return along with Kiryu, but newcomer Shinada is the star of the show and his storyline is both sweet, inspiring and also incredibly sad at times.  You can tell the developers really learned their lessons from Yakuza 4's multi-protagonist structure and improved on everything.It's Yakuza pre-Dragon Engine refined almost to perfection (perfection would be Yakuza 0), and it's just so gigantic and crammed with EVERYTHING that there is something for everyone.  You'll be hard-pressed not to find something to enjoy in this game, because it basically has everything there is to do in a game in it!A seriously great addition to the series, you could argue it's bloated but honestly, who doesn't want MORE Yakuza?

_childDocuments_.review: There is no denying that Yakuza 5 is immensely ambitious in scale and scope. Five playable characters, five cities, the longest story in the series (besides 7, probably), SO MANY moving parts...it's admirable just how much Yakuza there is in this game. And, for the most part, it works! That's maybe the most amazing thing about it all.Gameplay-wise, this is another clear evolution of the combat system in 3 and 4, feeling smoother and more cohesive. Kiryu, Saejima, and Akiyama return from 4, all of them playing basically the same as they did before, while new character Shinada feels a lot different from the others, and Haruka, of course, brings in a completely different style for her segment. I'm not sure if this is a new engine compared to 3/4 or not, but it does feel much closer to those two than it does to 0 and Kiwami after it. This similarity is good in some places and bad in others - Kiryu and Akiyama were very satisfying to play, while Saejima remained tedious and frustrating. The graphics feel like a clean midpoint between the two pairs - Kiryu in particular is very close to his "modern" look by this point, and while the lighting system still feels lacking, the models are much less blocky and more detailed, a feeling that extends to the diverse environments the game provides. A clear upgrade, and a big step forward.The diversity of characters and gameplay provides a similar diversity in side content, as well - all of the typical minigames are present for most of the playable characters (Haruka gets shafted pretty hard in this regard, unfortunately, as she has access to comparatively little), and like in 4, each character (except Akiyama) has a fully-fleshed out side story to play through in addition to the main scenario. Unlike 4, these are actually fun! They're also designed so that you can play straight through from start to finish the moment you get access to them, as nothing is gated behind story progression, and that's how I did all of them. In terms of enjoyment, I'd probably rank Kiryu first, then Haruka, Shinada, and Saejima, but all four were interesting and engaging.The story is long and incredibly dense - rather than how 4 felt like it progressed linearly, handing off the story to each subsequent protagonist, 5 feels like it tells four different stories that contain common through-lines and subplots, all pointing to the finale where everything finally comes together. Indeed, the finale of 5 is more robust than any game that comes before it in the modern play order, needing multiple chapters to reconcile the numerous plot threads running throughout each previous part. What I found satisfying about this was seeing supporting characters from each part interacting and crossing over with each other, resulting in new, novel interactions even this far into the game. In terms of both quality and entertainment, I feel like it easily clears 4's story, and sits on par with 3 and Kiwami, even if the sheer scope of it leaves some threads frustratingly underdeveloped. Supposedly, the game's story was written front to back, with little planning as it went along, and this feels clear to me especially when it comes to the climax of the game, but on the whole, I was entertained and engaged from beginning to end.I think Yakuza 5 is another great entry in a series that has had basically no missteps to this point. You can see the quality of the storytelling and the gameplay rise up throughout the Remastered Collection games, as we finally return to the Dragon Engine after getting a long taste of it in Kiwami 2. In that way, Yakuza 5 feels like a reward for getting through the often-frustrating gameplay of 3 and the ridiculous story of 4, where both of those elements are far more stable and entertaining. As Kiryu's story barrels towards its (originally intended) end, Yakuza 5 does him and its world justice, and is 100% worth experiencing first-hand.

_childDocuments_.review: The core idea of Yakuza 5, four parts in four different cities, along with a whole slew of new minigames easily made it the most ambitious game in the series up to that point. In addition to all that, the game received a large overhaul in the areas of lighting and gameplay. It still feels pretty similar to Yakuza 4, but you also start to see the beginnings of 0 - it is more or less a halfway point. The lighting alone really gives the game a face-lift that makes it resemble what would later be 0 more than any of the previous titles. It also includes some new gameplay mechanics in combat: the additions of enemy reinforcements, enemies that run away and crowds that back up as you approach, opening the combat area up a little more. It also introduced Climax Heat Actions and AppStims that newcomers to the franchise may recognize from the Kiwami games (though there the former works more like red heat from Y3-4). A more unfortunate change to the gameplay is that weapons now have requirements to equip them; you increase your weapon ability by using weapons you pick up. Possibly the worst change of all, though, is how they handle Premium Adventure and NG+ in this entry. Unlike every mainline entry before and after, you cannot create clear data in Premium Adventure. This means that if you do NG+, nothing you do in Premium Adventure will matter for it. This idiotic system premiered in Kurohyou: Ryu Ga Gotoku Shinsen for the PSP and went on to be in the original Ishin release (but fixed for the remake). The music in Yakuza 5 is some of the best in the series up to this point with some truly great tracks that hype you up for the action and make the emotional moments even more memorable. The substories as well overall are particularly strong, though, unfortunately, these don't escape the iffy issues that the series sometimes falls into and in my opinion, they are particularly bad here as well being more prolonged than usual such as an entire substory about a mixer where the entire joke is “haha they're ugly aren't they” and another substory where the joke is essentially that they're fat. There's also a substory that's rather copaganda with an ending that's somewhat jarring. Another thing that really stood out to me is the sheer variety - and not only in terms of the four cities. It seemed to me the NPCs had more variety to them, between the random civilians to enemies. There's also quite a few unique locations in the main story and even substories. One negative thing about the game's story is that it has some fairly bad pacing problems. For the most part each individual part is fine but the end of each one is something of a cliffhanger and the plot is really put on hold to introduce each character’s storyline. However, the way the plot is laid out I'm not sure how they could have rectified this other than alternating characters every chapter or two and that could get messy fast with the amount of protagonists in this one. Part 1 starts off with… Kiryu? But why is he a taxi driver in Fukuoka? Why isn't he with Haruka? This game really likes its mysteries and you're hit with multiple right off the bat. Kiryu’s taxi minigames are very fun, especially when you start street racing to some really hype eurobeat. Part 2 is with Saejima and his part is… Decidedly rougher. His part doesn't really open up much at all until chapter 3 with his side story minigame and even then, he doesn't get his substories until chapter 4. The way his story is handled is baffling and really kills all momentum the plot had, unfortunately. The first two chapters are mainly cutscenes and dialogue but if you stick with it there is atleast good payoff on those chapters. Once things open up it becomes very enjoyable. Part 3 is very unique for the franchise - it features Haruka, now turned idol and has two different rhythm games and a multitude of other minigames as part of her career. It portrays some unfortunate truths about the idol industry that can be quite uncomfortable, particularly early on but I do think it’s important that they didn’t try to brush it under the rug. Partway through her part, Akiyama becomes playable, his story intertwining with that of Haruka’s and creating a really lovely dynamic for them. If Kiryu is her father, then Akiyama is like her uncle. New to this game for Akiyama’s moveset as well are some ridiculous juggling mechanics that allows him to do some Devil May Cry-esque float-y attacks. This part has the strongest set of characters in the game, in my opinion.Part 4 features a new protagonist by the name of Tatsuo Shinada who is a broke ex-pro Baseball player turned nightlife journalist. He is a very charming and likable, down to earth guy even to the local bartenders of Kineicho, Nagoya. His moveset is very weapon oriented, with an unbreakable pipe that only does a little bit of damage. He later gets access to a master who will help increase weapon durability, as well. On the whole I enjoyed the story but unfortunately the story crumbles a bit at the end for me. The reveal of the final boss in particular feels like a massive asspull that actively made it worse for me.

_childDocuments_.review: The most ambitious Yakuza story so far drags a bit, but becomes absolutely spectacular by the end.This is the one that people call "the long one" and playing it for just two hours shows one why. Five playable characters, four chapters more than usual, robust side-games, and more substories than any other game before makes an hour of gameplay in Yakuza 5 progress the story much less than any other Yakuza game. That's not always a bad thing, because the side content is excellent and the new cites are a lot of fun to explore. However, it does make the story drag like never before.There are things to like about the story's slow pace. Where Yakuza 0-2 feel almost like movies, and 3 and 4 feel like high-budget tv shows, 5 almost feels like a novel. It explores a wild range of lifestyles in Japan. Working class guys, pop stars, prisoners, celebrities, perverts, loan sharks, farmers and hunters, athletes, strippers, and of course yakuza all get explored, and more than in any other installment. A big theme that works well in the game is how all sorts of people are connected in ways they can't imagine, and the story does well at proving that. However, the story is also a bit too complicated for its own good. It's not usually a problem for me in these games, but in this one, I had trouble remembering certain key characters because their few appearances happened so far before I got to hear about them again. The character writing far outshines the plot. Kiryu feels dynamic and thrilling to play as in 5 after his glorified cameo in Yakuza 4, and while Akiyama and Saejima don't develop too much more, they're still fun for the same reasons that they were fun in 4. Haruka's development is interesting and her rhythm gameplay is a lot of fun. The standout though is Yakuza 5-exclusive Tatsuo Shinada. His story is damn-near literary and (in my opinion) was worthy of its own spinoff title a la Judgment. Where Yakuza 4's exclusive Tanimura was so cliched that it made me wonder if he was plagiarized from eight different movies, Shinada is so dynamic and his story is so fascinating that it made me wonder if he was based on a real person or two.Yakuza 5's gameplay is great. If you're like me and you started with 0, this is where the games catch up with that. The combat (style switching notwithstanding) is Yakuza 0's combat, and the minigames and substories are at the level of that game again. Yakuza 5 is certainly unwieldy and (by my very sentimentally biased standards) not the masterstroke that Yakuza 0 was, but it's an excellent game, and shows the breadth of what RGG Studios is capable of.

_childDocuments_.review: A massive entry in the series that offers a plethora of minigames/activities for the player to engage with. This entry does a great job of tethering some narrative to these activities to make them worthwhile to players who would otherwise skip them if they lacked it. Further, Y5 does a great job of developing its supporting cast, such that these arcs outweigh the otherwise flimsy major conflict of the story. I found the combat to be as enjoyable as it was in 4, i.e. on the easier side with fewer aggravating enemies that would incessantly block. I did take issue with a many of the Heat actions being quite lengthy and pretty silly (e.g. smearing someones face on concrete, Saejima's snowman, Shinada's pretty unimpressive wrestling KOs, and Akiyama's lengthy kicking ones). Visually, 5 is a great improvement on 3 and 4, and I noticed that the cutscenes exhibited more cinematic flourishes with camera movement, foreshadowing just how well the action would flow from cutscene to gameplay in the later entries in the series. In sum, Y5 is a behemoth of an entry, so long as you remember to partake in the aspects of the game that you enjoy, and not make yourself sick by forcing content that doesn't resonate with you, you should have a great time. I myself look forward to having only one protagonist and great focus on one location in the next entry.

_childDocuments_.review: A 106 hours I have spent on Yakuza 5, my second longest time I've taken on fully completing a Yakuza game within the franchise. Will this game be better than the, in my opinion, flop that was Yakuza 4? Or will this game be just as much as a disappointment as its previous installment within the franchise? Let's talk about it.Two years after the events of Yakuza 5, you start this game as the franchise's protagonist, Kazuma Kiryu, who now has moved away from Okinawa and has left the care of the Morning Glory Orphanage in other people's hands. You start your game as him being a taxi driver within Nagasugai, a district in Fukuoka. With word spreading around town that the Tojo Clan are reaching out for allies, due to the Seventh Chairman of the Omi Alliance being ill with terminal cancer, and thereby the truce being on shaky grounds, you get a surprise passenger, namely the Sixth Chairman of the Tojo Clan; Daigo Dojima. Suddenly however with his disappearance, all of the foundations get shaken up, and it's now your job, as the five playable characters, to solve and prevent chaos from happening.One of the biggest positives that comes with Yakuza 5, is its improvement in combat. As opposed to Yakuza 3- where all the enemies blocked too much- and Yakuza 4- where too many enemies had super armor, and used movements that were done in the middle of your combos, and thereby undodgeable- Yakuza 5 is similar to Yakuza 0 in terms of its combat. It's a nice mixture of Yakuza 3 and 4's combat style, and Yakuza 5's balance in terms of the enemies and the bosses. Not to mention the addition of Climax Heat for each character is a nice addition and makes them feel all the more diverse. One of the second pros to me are the new substories that each character (other than Akiyama) has. Kiryu has his taxi driving, Saejima has his hunting animals minigame, Haruka has her story to become a Pop Idol and her Dance Battles, and Shinada has his making amends with his past as a former pro baseball player. All of them feel diverse and fun. There are also some new fun minigames, like Taiko: Drum Master and Tatsuya Noodles. This game also has a ton of diverse minigames to do and complete. Some might add too many.One of the biggest cons that Yakuza 5 has in my opinion, is perhaps that the game has too much to offer. Too many minigames, which some may not appeal to people as others. With two different baseball minigames, the usual shogi, mahjong, air hockey, all of the gambling minigames, Taiko: Drum Master, Gunrheim, two separate fishing minigames- I can go on and on. Long story short, in terms of minigames, there's a ton to do. Some may love that, others may get burnt out on it in terms of completing the games fully. Additionally to that, there are a ton of Masters in this game too to fully do. And one of the Masters can be rather annoying to fight, especially as one of the characters. Those who know, know. Another con that this game has, is the same as Yakuza 4 has. The story is divided into the perspectives of five characters, with one chapter shared by two. Unlike Yakuza 4 however, you can follow the plot easier. Only Part 4 is a part of the game where you kind of forget what's going on in terms of the overarcing plot. And some people don't like the first half of Part 3. I personally did, but some don't.When I look at Yakuza 5, I feel it's a better game than Yakuza 3 and 4. It has more pros than cons by a long shot. I'd even say that this game is more enjoyable than Yakuza Kiwami, which came much later. The additional characters, each with their own original way of fighting, their own original Heat Actions, which some of them are absolutely beautiful. Especially Shinada's Heat Actions to me were my favorite of all the characters. Most of them were unique, fun to pull off and very fun to watch him perform them. I'd say overall I'd give this game a solid 8/10. It is on the same level as Yakuza Kiwami in terms of scoring, but it's a weaker game than Yakuza 0 and Yakuza Kiwami 2, which so far on my list are still my two favorite games in the franchise thus far. I highly recommend people to play this game, and enjoy how much content this game has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: I've left silly reviews for the other Yakuza games, but honestly I think this one deserves a proper one. Yakuza 5 is a great game. You should buy it. I could honestly just leave the review there. but what's the fun in that? In Y5, there are a total of 5 different characters, which is impressive for any singleplayer story game. First, there's the legendary Dragon of Dojima, Kiryu Kazuma, who is of course the main protagonist in every entry before this. He plays great, using a mix of his moves from 3 and 4, along with some new ones. His part really gives you the feels, and helps set up the story really well. Then, you have the "Slayer of Eighteen", Taiga Saejima, once again, another returning character. He feels really flushed out here, like they acknowledged the issues with his moveset in 4, and fixed him up to play better. His involvement in the story is really interesting too, and I think 5 did a great job hyping him up to be an equal to Kiryu. After Saejima, you have Haruka Sawamura, the adopted daughter of Kiryu Kazuma, who's appeared in every entry from 1-4. Her gameplay is much different than the others, which makes sense taking her into account as a character. She only has 2 chapters where you use her alone, which I think helps make that whole part much more welcoming for returning players. As for the second half of part 3, you can play as the man, the myth, the legend. The lifeline of Kamurocho himself, SHUN AKIYAMA!!! (Yes, he is my favorite character). Akiyama controls great here, they even gave him mid-air combos in his combat. His inclusion into the plot also works fine, although for the sake of keeping this review as spoiler free as possible, I won't dive into it. You end up switching between him and Haruka a lot in this part, but I honestly never had an issue with that. Last of all, in part 4 of the story, you play as Tatsuo Shinada, a character who only appears in Y5 and none of the other entries. He's easily the most unique character here, using weapons and throws primarily in his combat. He's a funny guy who lost everything, and I think his plot, albeit relatively self contained from the rest of the story, is still really good, and you get a feel for the guy. I guess in conclusion of this whole review though, if you've finished all the other Yakuza games from 0-4, definitively check out Yakuza 5, as it's amazing, and probably my new favorite game of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is a step up from 4 in pretty much every way. The story, while confusing and complex in the moment, ended up being interesting and well-fleshed out, especially with the way the characters all end up meeting and being interwoven near the end (though I will admit… I needed a hefty recap to keep everything straight in my head, thanks Nisha). As mentioned in my Yakuza 4 review, this game definitely has done the multiple character perspective better than the previous game (though in terms of move-sets every other character still pales in comparison to Kiryu and, from the next game released, Yakuza 0, Majima). However, at the end of the day, this is basically prime Yakuza. We've come out of the (apparent, as I've never played the OG releases) jankiness of 1 and 2, past the awkward early 7th gen transitory period of 3 and light but overall weaker experimentation with multiple characters in 4 and into near perfection, though actual perfection won't be reached until 0, in my opinion. This is also the first game in which I completed all side missions and took on (and beat) Amon. A pretty hard set of bosses but really satisfying (if not a little BS at some points). Overall I’d say that Yakuza 5 was the best game at the time of its release, and if not for Yakuza 0 coming out after it, would likely have remained that way until perhaps Yakuza 7, though I guess we’ll see when we get there.(Guess that’s a bit of a spoiler for my early thoughts on 6 so far, oops.)

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5 is the longest Yakuza game in the series, has biggest minigames ever and in-depth variety of sidestories for its multiple characters. The Tojo/Omi intrigue and central theme of "dream" is executed rather well but it could certainly be better by having more focus on the main story and cutting the last playable character, Shinada, who contirbutes so little to the main story, solely due to him being a regular dude with no connections whatsoever to Yakuza underworld.Shinada felt forced into the main story just so RGG Studio can explore more about the theme of "dream". It doesn't help that his fighting style is very bland compared to others. His only saving grace is his likable personality and a full character arc. Returning characters like Daigo, Majima and Date are also underused in the main story, especially Majima who should have more screentime as he is very important to the overall plot.Set aside the underutilized theme and last playable character's misstep, Yakuza 5 is still a great entry in the series. It has 5 cities from Fukuoka, Sapporo, Osaka, Nagoya and the usual Kamurocho in Tokyo, all rendered beautifully with each cities have their own distinct looks and feel. Each 5 characters have their own story arcs, good character developments, their own side stories which are essentially semi full-fledged games like Kiryu's taxi missions, Saejima's hunting, Haruka's idol life and Shinada's batting game with their own storylines, all are told very well with their own game mechanics to master. Substories are often the most wholesome in the series.Each characters' fighting styles, except Haruka, are very different to one another, resulting in a variety of playstyles. Combat is much faster, smoother with some of the best Heat actions in the series. Haruka's "combat" rely on dance battles and idol concert which are very addictive, fun, and fresh with each songs being played out are often bangers.  Overall though, due to how bloated Yakuza 5 is, it does have shortcomings and it kind of struggles to juggle between each parts of the story resulting in its somewhat lack of focus. But Yakuza 5's characters, gameplay, sidestories, varieties of minigames, multiple cities and each characters' personalities and story arcs end up being some of the series best with many gut-wrenching moments, heartfelt drama and a very good ending.Yakuza 5 does multiple characters' stories much much better than its predecessor, with the game being brave enough to let its characters shine through their own arcs, especially Kiryu and Haruka/Akiyama's parts being the highlight of the game. It feels like a really long story, but it feels very rewarding to know and understand these characters and the dreams they want to protect.

_childDocuments_.review: It always surprises me when this franchise doesn't change much but each time the new game comes out it feels so familiar yet so fresh. But this one has changed a lot, much more than previous games. New mini-games, new gameplay mechanics and activities awaits you!Yakuza 5 mainly is an action game, pretty violent one with some crazy and funny moments in between all the serious drama. But this game tries to be more, a racing game, survival game and rhythm game on top. It's just insane how much content it has, a huge step up from 3&4.Remember how you played as four characters in Yakuza 4? This time there are five characters. While in Yakuza 4 all characters had roughly the same gameplay and the city was the same, this time every character plays differently and you have different cities to explore.The beginning of the game is really chill. You start playing as Kiryu by doing everyday stuff with nothing happening story-wise, you're just living your everyday life of an honest hard working man. But you're bombarded with new activities pretty soon. So after this game you can add more stuff Kiryu is good at like skilled street racer or taxi driver. But you know how it is, he will be dragged down into another story and oh my it's good.There's a new taxi driving mini-game. While it looks really simple from the first sight it's not as simple as it looks. You need to pay attention, talk with passengers, do not brake or accelerate too quickly, use turn signals, stop at traffic lights. While the mini-game is fun the controls are way too sensitive and it's too easy to make a mistake.And there's street racing where you race against other drivers and can even tune your car. Quite fun but but due to the controls I just mentioned it sometimes is frustrating. Nevertheless more gameplay mechanics is always good.Another new mini-game is ramen game. You serve noodles to customers and must boil them to a certain hardness. This one is hard but it's so funny that you can't feel mad.Next character is Saejima, tough as ever having fun with Mad dog. But same as in Yakuza 4 I don't enjoy his chapters, I just don't like his fighting style and there are too many events one after another which are too long. Mainly in the beginning there are only story events in an extremely closed area and there's nothing to do besides the story. It drags little too long. But the story is great. Later on it gets more interesting along with environment changes. Saejima can hunt, there's a map to explore and to find animals. You can set up traps, shoot animals, it's like a survival game within a game. We also see snow and winter for the first time. And finally Saejima gets to explore another city.Haruka lives in Osaka, she's a young lady now and she went to pursue her dream. Haruka's gameplay is very different and a very welcomed change in gameplay, I really enjoyed Haruka's part. First you'll need to dance which is similar to karaoke where you press the buttons on time and is similar to a concert battle mode against rivals. You have idol heat mode. You have four idol abilities – singing, appeal, basic skill and performance. When you get XP these abilities increase so it works as Haruka's leveling system. Haruka can't fight all those strong men obviously so instead of smashing faces her combat alternative is dancing battles. You meet people on the street and challenge them to a battle. It plays as a rhythm game and can be really tough depending on the opponent.And since when Yakuza teaches you english? Well, you'll learn how to speak english properly.Haruka's story is heartwarming and heartbreaking.Then there's Akiyama. His gameplay is the same as usual. He has some new cool moves and I absolutely love his fighting style. He's still a loan shark, lazy guy who loves beer. But soon he becomes a part of the story.And finally Shinada – a writer who writes about adult entertainment. He was a baseball player in the past and now he's just a lazy guy not doing much. Shinada's fighting style relies on weapons a lot and is again different from other characters. He's slower, similar to Saejima in some way – slow powerful attacks.The side stories are probably the worst for this character, it involves baseball so you'll be hitting the ball a lot to finish his stories.The story in general is amazing, it has plot twists, it makes you care about each character and it's long.The transition to combat is dynamic, no black screens anymore, it feels more natural. Combat gameplay hasn't changed much but it definitely is much more enjoyable than Yakuza 4 or Yakuza 3 especially. The moves feel much smoother and it feels like your attacks connect nicely into fluid and visually impressive combos.One interesting new feature is that enemies now can run away from you if they're scared.Avoiding enemies is a bit easier too, often you can see enemies from afar. But it feels like there are more enemies on the street and sometimes getting from one side of the street to another could take 3-5 encounters which sometimes is annoying.Fishing has been slightly improved too and is quite fun. You can fish in river or sea. River fishing is simpler and sea fishing is the same as in previous games.Obviously there are all the other, smaller mini-games, pool, darts, casino, arcade machines and many more, too many to list.Revelations are as funny as always and finally it's enough to just go through the qte's without choosing the right answer which is a relieve.Besides substories there's side stories now, these are tied to each character and are just mini-games tied to that character. So even more side content for you to enjoy.Graphics are improved to the similar level of 0 and Kiwami, pre-rendered cut scenes look much worse than in game graphics which is ridiculous but gameplay looks good. Game is locked to 60fps unfortunately but no biggie, it somehow feel smoother than 3&4. There's decent amount of graphics settings including resolution scaling which makes the game even crispier.Performance is good, playing on 5800x, 2070s, 32gb @3440x1440 on max settings, locked 60fps.Ultrawide support is partial but it's easily fixed with a simple community fix.Sound as always is great. Voice acting is top notch, very believable and emotional. Music is great, pop, jazz, piano, rock tracks and there's always an appropriate track playing depending on what's happening on the screen.This is a wonderful game which could be compared to Yakuza 0. Great story, great cast, insane amount of side content, fun combat, funny, sad and crazy moments. Just buy it already.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm coming back to this review because my old one didn't do this one justice at all.Mechanically, I think Kiwami 2 is my all time favourite. Story wise, It was 3. But holy hell...Yakuza 5...I think became my new favourite of them all.This one is the wackiest of the preceeding titles and has finally ascended into dragon ball territory with how wild the combat has become. But man...the story is really kickass. The plot isn't terribly shocking but it's more then enough to keep you engaged. This is also the first yakuza game I've ever...and I mean EVER, did most of the side quests BEFORE finishing the story.I went through the game at my usual pace, actually teared up from [Redacted]'s phone call to Shinada at the end cause it was so effing heart warming and so very emotional, as much as [redacted]'s death in Yakuza 3 was! only it made me feel really happy instead of total despair x.x Then went on to take on the final boss and oh my god...he had more health bars then I had fingers and I realized...this was gonna be a slog. The fight went on forever and I almost had him beat, but then he stun locked me and killed me before i could heal. But man. [Redacted] Is a real man. Mad respect for the way he started the fight. Anyway, I realized that If I was gonna retry that fight...I'd have to go through that entire slog all over again...and I had to question whether or not I was willing to. I decided, I wanted to beef up Kiryu a bit since i never...EVER...use any trainers to unlock abilities in any yakuza game. But going back to serena meant I'd have to do like EIGHT BOSS BATTLES ALL OVER AGAIN.It was decided. If I'm putting myself through all that again, I'm gonna do it with style and grace. So I went back, took control of every character, did almost every side quest as each of them, completed all their training, nearly maxed them all out. Did all of Food Boi TV's quests then I decided to step back up to the plate. Literally. _childDocuments_.review: This is the most painful review I've written out of all the games in the series. Yakuza 5 is good, but is has a lot holding it back. Not to the same extent as 3, thankfully.With Yakuza 4's wild strategy of having FOUR protagonists, how could Yakuza 5 ever top it? Five protagonists of course! Kiryu, Akiyama, and Saejima return, with two new playable characters filling in for Tanimura. In addition to having so many characters, there are FIVE cities to explore. Like the previous title, the game is divided into parts, and each part has its own character(s) and city it takes place in, with everyone joining together at the end.That's not all, as every character except one has a personal side story to embark on as optional content, usually rewarding you with some cash along with some backstory for some of the NPCs. This idea is expanded upon better in 0, as these side stories are one of my biggest issues with the game. Of course other than the moment the side stories are introduced, they are entirely skippable. But for a completionist, you'll tempted to see them through to the end, having to slog through some of the most repetitive, boring, and half baked content I've seen in these games.That's not the only innovation 5 brought to the table, as this is the first and only game to feature Kiryu's adopted daughter, Haruka, as a playable character. As you might expect, she does not fight, but rather engages in dance battles and gigs as an up and coming idol, which take the form of rhythm games. I have nothing against rhythm games, but when they make you play the same song 5 or 6 times in a row, then introduce a new song to play 5 more times, and then one final song you do a handful of times, it makes her whole chapter feel hamfisted. Her side story consists of repeating the same songs you have to perform in the story, all to make a little extra money you probably don't need since she doesn't have to fight anyone.With that overlooked, 5 starts to look like a very strong entry to the series. The plot is really interesting, right up until the end where it falls apart. I can't describe why I don't like it without spoiling the story, but I feel deep down that the writers simply ran out of ideas and just wrote the first things that popped into their head. It's got the classic Yakuza surprise twists, but in ways that aren't entertaining.Like I stated at the start, it hurts to come down on this game, because it had moments where I felt like I was playing the best game in the series since I played 0. Yakuza has always been transparent about the bulk of inconsequential minigames it has, but in this case I think 5 really went too far with just how much fluff was added.It's a good game, but only if you don't have expectations set too high.I'd also like to add that early in the game, it makes a point that Kiryu and Haruka can both send money to the orphanage via ATM. Doing this has no point, aside from getting an achievement. You can let the orphans starve and there is no mention of it at any point in the game. You can send them a million yen a day and not even get a thank you text message. So no matter how important they make it sound: you do NOT have to do Kiryu's mundane taxi driving job for any reason.

_childDocuments_.review: I am recommending this game simply because if you are going to buy it, you are going to buy it. You have already gone through Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 4, and probably won't stop here. (if you haven't played these two... you will need to because the Yakuza 0-6 story is all related).This is honestly one of the weaker Yakuza games in the series, the story is exceptionally confusing, even for a Yakuza game. I have the entire series' plotline and interactions mapped in my brain like the back of my hand and even I struggled to keep up here. Some important plot points will be mentioned in ONE LINE at the most obscure moments and not brought up again until ten hours later where the game makes a big revelation over it, or pulls a character in who was involved in that one sentence. Act one starts off a bit boring but picks up speed, act two has some... pacing issues to put it lightly (trust me, you will be stuck isolated in a minigame world completely unrelated to the plot for like 5 hours minimum, unable to escape). Act three is fine. And act four feels like an idea for a Yakzua game that was scrapped and jammed into this ones storyline. The finale is great as expected with Yakuza games. Akiyama is a great character but honestly feels shoehorned into the plot, this combined with the endless amount of coincidences makes you suspend your disbelief even higher than you normally would for a Yakuza game.As per usual- combat, substories and minigames are solid. Haruka's ♥♥♥♥ is surprisingly brilliant and overall I still love the game, but not quite as high as the other Yakuza's. Also take a shot each time the word "Dream" is said and you will probably kill your liver.Edit: Forgot to mention the absurd amount of streetfights, in 3 it was super easy to avoid them  but this game is the opposite. Walking down Tenkaichi street will have you enter about 3/4 nigh unavoidable fights with 8 or so blokes each time. Annoying if you are trying to get somewhere specific for sure. Especially save/quit.After replaying the game- the story makes a lot more sense when you know who is betraying who etc. If you headcanon Dojima being involved in the Akiyama/Haruka ♥♥♥♥ but never being named for it, the coincidences feel less obscure. The Shinada act makes a lot more sense overall and the final boss even fits into place, the whole game is around the  delusion.This is a damn good game that is absolutely bursting to the brim with content (it has an unbelievable amount of things to do) and also packs insane attention to detail. I take my hat off to RGG studio here.

_childDocuments_.review: *POSSIBLE SPOILERS*Yakuza 5 is more or less the same deal as most of the other mainline Yakuza games, however it has its' own kinda unique ups and downs. So first the good stuff: 1) Combat is solid and responsive (minus the forever garbage lock on system of the series), there are 5 characters you can play as and 4 of them have extremely distinct fighting styles out of which 3 are good and 1 is pretty meh (1 of the characters doesn't really have fights per se). 2) You get to explore 5 cities which is unheard of in this series and I loved that, all of the cities have their own unique flair and style. And on top of that you also visit couple of other smaller locales (like a mountain hunting ground, a prison etc.) 3) There is lots and lots of extra content, like substories, side missions and activities, crafting, mini-games, dating sim (kinda), arena fights and other things like that. 4) Music in this game is awesome. There are a number of different styles/genres of music included and I enjoyed most of it, especially combat themes for the characters and the climactic battles. 5) I haven't played Y3 and Y4 so Akiyama was a new character for me and I gotta say I loved him and his super slick and fun fighting style.As for the bad stuff: 1) This was the easiest Yakuza I have played yet. The only challenging part of this game was the Amon fights where I died 3 times (I died 4 times total in this game on hard difficulty). And btw the Amon fights, even though were not THAT hard, they were EXTREMELY annoying and awfully crafted, especially Kiryu's and Tatsuo's fights. While on the other hand, the other two were very easy (especially Saejima's fight). 2) Even though there are a lot of side activities to get into, almost all of them are very dull or they become very dull in a short while because most of these side activities tend to be way longer than they have the right to be. And that is basically the whole "thing" with Yakuza 5. 3) The upgrading system is very streamlined and easy to understand, however they decided to block your progress at lvl 20 until you get to the endgame and that part annoyed the living s..t out of me because all the exp you gain after 20 is lost until you get to the end. 4) Kiryu and Saejima are so strong that they completely overshadow the other 2 fighting characters when you have a choice to make. Those two are broken especially Saejima, because he has an ability where his attacks cannot be interrupted in heat mode and as you keep attacking you gain a lot of heat so you are always in heat mode and the dude is completely impossible to stop so that throws out any kind of challenge this game can provide while on the other hand, Kiryu's tiger drop deals so much damage that it is just at cosmic levels of insane. 5) The story starts out being very interesting, however during the second half of the game you will experience constant IQ level drops as the story gets dumber and dumber as if you are falling down a bottomless pit of stupidity and I am not talking about that "over the top anime funny" type of stupidity. 6) Even though this game is not the longest Yakuza game I have played, it really felt like it because it got so boring and needlessly drawn out that I struggled to get to the end. After I finished up the 4th character and I thought I was at the end, the game introduced a fifth character with his own story, side-missions and everything and I wanted to smash my head against my monitor repeatedly because I was already bored to death by the second half of the 3rd character (which is the non-fighting one) and on top of that I hated the 5th guy which was completely based on baseball that I hate (sorry baseball fans :D ). And his fighting style involves a lot around weapons and I hate using weapons in Yakuza so yeah not a happy-fun time for me. 7) This game felt hella wonky and would have definitely benefited from a Kiwami remake in my opinion so I kinda regret playing it in this format.In conclusion, the cons largely outweighed the pros for me with this one, however I still think that Yakuza 5 is better than Kiwami 1 in almost every way but the main problem with Yakuza 5 said in one sentence is: It severely overstays its' welcome. And now I really don't want to play the other remasters (3 ,4) in hopes that they might someday release kiwami versions of them and possibly make them better. So I would only recommend this game for relatively die-hard Yakuza fans who want to experience all of what this series has to offer, otherwise just skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: "Slop 5 Remastered" is a 2019 remaster of an old 2012 Open world Beat Em' Up PS3 game called "Slop 5," which also came out on PC and Xbox in late 2021. follows 5 different characters you can play as: Suzuki, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and Shinada (Kiryu is staying out of this one this time /j) as you experience their daily lives until an incident happens that brings them all at the crossroads in Kamurocho once more to fight off some evil Yakuza with a Vendetta on them. of Slop 5 Remastered remained relatively the same as the older Yakuza games, and the game now features 5 different cities, some of which are genuinely the best looking in the entire series. But sadly, the game doesn't let you explore them due to them being tied to the story, so it's just a whole-ass wasted potential. Kamurocho especially remained empty on side missions, so other than the finale, there's literally nothing to do on this copy-pasted map. But generally, when this game is trying to be Yakuza and not something else, it works really well.Now when we get down to the story, it starts off relatively good. There's this sense of suspense and mystery behind the disappearance of the Tojo clan chairman, which I really liked and wanted to see what's gonna be next until the game showed me a giant middle finger and diverted my attention to some taxi driver submissions, most of which consist of talking to passengers or driving while obeying the traffic rules, which was generally boring. I already wanted to drop the game in the first 5 hours, but the wish of knowing what the hell happened to Daigo kept me going.When you thought the game diverting your attention to the mundane taxi missions, which don't even matter on the grand scheme of things, was already bad enough, the game shows you an even bigger middle finger in Part 2, in which Saejima escapes from prison AGAIN. This would've been fine on its own since we get to know the new cast of characters and his new sworn brother, but what makes my blood boil is what happens after that. As you're already starving to see the story, some epic plot twist, or anything regarding Kiryu’s part, the game diverts your attention AGAIN and becomes a frickin HUNTING SIMULATOR??? WHAT WERE THEY THINKING? Why in the god's name would I wanna hunt a bear in a game about crime dramas and hand on hand combat? And the worst thing is the gunplay in this hunting simulator is not even good; it's shallow, doesn't have an impact, and takes absolutely 0 skill. So why the hell would they add this other than to add more filler to an already bloated game is beyond me.And what is worse is  As you're spiraling down your sanity of wanting to see a great story, the game shows you a middle finger a size of a Millennium tower instead cause F*ck you! You're playing as HARUKA now! My first genuine reaction was WTF, how would she battle enemies? Oh wait what? Dance battle? Oh, that makes sense cause she's an idol now! The entire part which took me around 7 hours to beat consists of playing this terrible project diva knockoff minigame that only has 3 songs that you're gonna have to play at least a dozen times. And memorizing all the patterns to each song makes this whole chapter stale as a crusty Stalin's foot as they force you to play the same songs on repeat, which your mind can't even take it anymore. If only it had more compositions or different patterns every time, it would've been tolerable a bit. Overall this Part, despite being important to the story unlike 2, which could be described in 1 sentence, literally bored me out of my mind, and I don't understand why it would ever be included in a game about Yakuza families.As it introduces a new character into the mix - Tatsuo Shinada, a former baseball player that got banned from the game for suspicion of stealing enemy's signals. And a return to the classic beat 'em up Yakuza formula. This chapter was very enjoyable as it has very charismatic characters, engaging substories, a new city, and much-needed humor. Shinada, despite being piss broke, is very determined in his goal, confronting his demons and finding out the truth about his expulsion. If only every other Part of Slop 5 was like this one this would've been the greatest game in the series in my eyes.Every character in Slop 5 has a unique move set which you can learn and master throughout their respected Parts, I'd even say you'd get way too much time to master them cause even traversing around towns is a pain in the ass since you can't take 2 steps without a random encounter, and it gets really annoying. Learning the combat thoroughly doesn't really make much sense either unless you're planning on doing a legendary difficulty playthrough in which case yeah, you're gonna need that knowledge. Otherwise, most bosses and encounters can be cheesed by using the same move the enemy is weak against, therefore rendering the entire move system useless. surely has one of the most ambitious final bosses in the series if only there was a way to not cheese him by using the same move 300 times. Another thing that disappointed me that all the skills and stats you grinded throughout the game simply don’t matter in the final encounters, especially for Haruka since you don’t even get to perform the songs as her what a shame and what a butt hurt that caused me when I realized I spent hours doing godawful side missions and maxing out the stats mattered to nothing. And the cliffhanger ending didn’t help my scorched butt either as it was reaching the critical temperatures of 100 billion degrees Celsius after realizing that I spent 50 hours on an empty shell of a game that looks huge at first but at its core, it’s a glorified artificially extended with filler and copy-pasted missions slop. was pleasant overall other than a minor glitch that would occasionally randomize audio in the cutscenes.Overall, , therefore, everything more or less feels like a huge filler in this game. Like George R.R Martin once said in Family Guy, “You just took a lot of pills, mashed a bunch of sci-fi and cliché together, and crapped out a 2000-page turd.” Since the game constantly revolves around dreams and family, I can only dream of a better game after beating Slop 5. This will remain as my most unfavorite game and a resemblance of 50+ hours of my life that I'm never getting back. - We've got monsters, Yakuza, Mishima, a lawyer, and special forces… But Kamurocho's still missing something.
