_childDocuments_.review: Verdict:40 hours in, I finally beat the game, and here's my take: This game is quite good. Definitely worth the asking price, as is, while it's still in early access. They're not necessarily doing anything new with this game, but the combination of mechanics from other games is unique and works very well. Story:There's not much to the story, as there aren't really any characters and there's not really any structured story arc, but what's there is pretty cool. I won't spoil anything but you are tasked with protecting one of the last cities on the planet after magic destroyed everything. This city has some of the last surviving mages and they're working on the "last spell" that will destroy magic and heal the land. That's pretty much it. But I like it.Gameplay 1: [City Management] It takes about 12 rounds/waves to win. There are two phases to each round, day-time city management and then the battle at night. The city management or preparation phase is pretty fun. It's a lot like the various tower defense games and city building games out there. First you maintain your heroes; which means leveling them up and choosing their skills and perks, and getting them new weapons and armor. Then you're buying new buildings with the gold you've won in the battles, stuff like an armorer that will keep creating random armor for your heroes. You have a set number of citizens that you can assign to either clear out old buildings and make space, or you can assign them to some of the buildings you've made so they can give you extra stuff (more gold, more defense materials, more armor, etc). Next, you're placing your heroes in stretegic spots and building defensive walls/towers/catapults.Gameplay 2: [Battle]The battles play out in turn-based gameplay where you're moving characters around on a grid based map and attacking with either ranged, melee, or magic. It's pretty similar to FFT, XCOM, and Into the Breach, but the devs have definitely put their own spin on things. The battle mechanics are pretty great, because there is a lot of variety. There's like a dozen or more different enemy types that are randomly thrown at you, and they all have different traits and abilities that have to be dealt with strategically. If you've got a zombie with high dodge, don't attack him with innacurate weapons. If you've got a zombie with high armor (that replenishes every turn), don't use attacks that are bad against armor. And to go along with that enemy variety, there is a ton of variety to choose from with your heroes. You start out with 3, but can buy more at the inn until you've got six. And that team of six can be anything you want. All archers (My favorite), all mellee or mages, a mix of all classes, hybrid characters that play multiple roles, whatever you want. The classes are fairly balanced if you play them right. For instance, what the melee characters may lack in range, they make up for in tankiness. That tankiness makes it to where they can just stand in the middle of damn hoard, stun them all, take zero damage, and keep the baddies off of your walls. Overall thoughts:There are so many different strategies to play with here in how you build your characters, what items/weapons/armors you choose, how you build your city, how you build your walls/defenses, how you do battle... this game has a lot of replayability. You can't really beat the game on your first run, as you have to slowly unlock all of the permanent upgrades (like giving your heroes more starting mana). But that's okay, since it's fun just to get farther and farther into the later rounds and see what kind of crazy monsters and hoards get thrown at you. Once you do eventually beat the game, you can just keep playing new runs with new strategies and new difficulty levels (like enemies have more hp). You can see that once you beat the game, the devs have more planned (like maybe other cities that have to be defended?), but what exists for now is more than enough. It's good as is, and will probably be great over time, as long as the devs stick with it and keep updating. So far it seems like they're very engaged with their fans and are working hard. But seriously, they could quit tomorrow and the game could still be a hit.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game not long after it came to Early Access, hooked by the fact that The Algorithm composed the OST - but I also love turn-based RPGs and roguelikes. This game has a great soundtrack, is a fantastic turn-based RPG and a great roguelike/lite with a pretty vast range of both horizontal and vertical progression.A lot of people (devs included) compare this game to Final Fantasy Tactics, but I've never played FFT so I cannot speak to that. Of the turn-based RPGs I've played, this is probably the least "story focused", not that there isn't a story but imo it takes a backseat in this game.It's a classless RPG, skills and abilities are based on your equipment (mostly weapons, but other equipment can also have abilities tied to them), or in some cases the perks you choose from as your characters level up; you also choose from a number of random primary and secondary attributes to increase on level up (one of each), which vary from common small increases to rare large increases, this includes: damage*, movement points, health, mana, health/mana regen (per day), stun chance, poison damage etc. - you also get limited rerolls on the selections, which might give you another chance to get better or rarer choices for your character.*as a primary attribute you can increase generic damage, and as a secondary attribute you can increase specific damage types (magic, ranged, physical) so you have the ability to increase overall damage, and then also specialise your character into a specific type of damage as well. This is where the classless aspect opens up into combining different weapons and damage types with the attributes and perks you get on level ups to get quite a good range of permutations.You also can choose from a number of mutators called "omens" before you begin a run that alter certain parameters, like more starting HP or getting more resources from scavenging.The aim of the game really is to do a run, earn upgrades that you can use in your next run - such as new weapons and armour, better starting conditions like having more resources or starting with better equipment, more defences and structures you can build and so on, until you can eventually beat the boss wave for each town. There are a lot of things to unlock, and I'll admit since the progression reset recently I've zoomed through quite quickly so far but newer players who still have to learn what the best combinations are might not progress as quickly.With the amount of hours I've put into this game since it came to Early Access, and how far its come since then, I can only recommend it as a very good example of Early Access done right. It can be buggy and I've had my fair share of bugs happen where things just don't work the way they should but I don't think it takes enough away from the core experience to impact my "score" that negatively.I give it an arbitrary 8.212/11.788.

_childDocuments_.review: Easy game for me.  I can see why individuals invest thousands of hours into a specific genre now.  Understanding funnels for character traits, minimizing specializations to enable late game transitioning and alling bosses are important to be successful.   Game expects you to have wide utility coverage to prevent evasion spam or hits a/g 1K armor aka poor Action Point usage.  Blue level up bonuses shouldn't be expected, green level ups are adequate.  Reviews say 2-3hrs per run, for me its 10-20 hrs for a run.  You have to capitalize on specific perks and movement to mitigate dozens of dmg or increase your effective damage value.   There is no one answer to perk selection since it's random and your character customization varies based on first few days creating an eventual full build.  Archetype is similar to late game slay the spire, although I appreciate The Last Spell much more due to it's overall complexity.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence for months about this because of the reviews, but I finally decided and... I love it!! I consider myself somewhat elitist and very picky of the genre, so let me just get out of the way what sours people.You. Will. Lose. A lot. This has nothing to do with skill. Without unlocks and progression from just playing and dying, you'll straight up not be strong enough to win the game. Heck, you won't win the game in the near future (I am at 10 hours and am still not very close.) But each run gets more and more fun. You go from a hopeless, desperate battle to beginning to fight back in earnest. A lot of games throw on unlocks to pad things, or as a lazy way to 'eventually' win through sheer force of numbers, but this feels actually central to playing it, and makes the procedural repeated fights meaningful as you are not trying to win, you are trying to get stronger.The tactical depth is very much there, and managing position, resources, decisions, mana, health, and all of that is *chef's kiss*. Of course, some complaints are still valid.* Dodging is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for enemies. There's no two ways around it. I once fired 3 times at someone about to panic my city and they made a 5% 3 times. I hated this in X-Com and I hate it here. It's bad enough having to gamble on damage range securing a kill without also needing to actually hit. Given you are fighting dozens and dozens of enemies, it WILL happen.* There is not much variation in being optimal constructing your city. If you want to have fun, you'll invest in gold mines and mana regen. It IS fun, I just think this area needs enriched somehow.* Perks are very hit or miss. Ever play Battle Brothers? It's like that but even worse. There's so many mandatory perks, and not much room to take other stuff, of which there's very strong Plan B options, and some are just bad (2% stacking crit per attack until you crit with no control? I'd love to see the metrics on how that is considered strong, chances are I'll waste the crit shooting something with my longbow that was gonna instant die anyway)* The map is repetitive, and some starting perks on your heroes are incredibly crippling. Maybe later I can pay stuff to stop getting sucky ones. I like random starting perks as an idea, but getting short circuit (-3 mana regen per day) sometimes makes me want to just reroll the run, amongst others.Bravo to the devs, most of my criticisms will be fixed, and I know dodge is just A Thing for some designers/gamers, so I'll live with it.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm a major fan of tower defense or anything somewhat resembling it. Since Early Access, The Last Spell has shown a lot of promise in terms of gameplay quality and challenge, but it is definitely not for short sessions, as a single gameplay as a beginner or someone with moderate experience with the game will have you playing one map for at least 3-4 hours or more for later maps. If you enjoy the slight randomization of your character units' boosts and debuffs like "Wise" (More Magic Damage) or something like "Unadorned" (Can't equip trinkets), as well as a big list of perks that are not that random based on their race and other factors, you may enjoy the game for 10-20 hours, depending on your skill level. You'll begin each map with three units, each with their own starter gear and stats; you'll then decide what you want them to be in the later stages. Maybe one of them has the perks for Spike, Armor, Health but their starter is a mage, you can make changes and hope to find the weapons and gear you need with all of the unlockable features and buildings you can find while simply playing and unlocking things with the essence from killing the hoards of undead. It's actually a very enjoyable and interesting game if you, like me, enjoy renaming people anytime you want to change their appearance to someone you know or even yourself to make things more personalized and to connect more with them rather than being pixelated characters on the screen, you know bring some life to these units. Once you've played each level, you'll know how to deal with it relatively easily and then you'll need to learn the higher level difficulties. I've been playing this game since it was in Early Access, and I remember it taking me up to 20 hours to complete the first handful of spells. This is really only and issue for those who played Early Access, but when the full game was released, the save files were removed for anyone who had previously played, so 20 hours of progress with unlocks were reset. I had to go through the spells again with no upgrades, weapons, gear, or anything. It all had to be redone manually, which was irritating, but because I had experience with each level, I knew exactly what I had to do for each boss and where they generally spawned, and even without many of the elements that make the gameplay smoother, it only took 6 hours to get back to where I was before rather than the 20 hours it did throughout all this time. The game is still very challenging and fun, and it really gives you that sense of tension and uncertainty, but once you understand what's going to happen on each map, it's very easy to overpower hoards of monsters with proper setup and gear, where your units have 7-8 action points, 6-8 multi-shots with multiple refreshed, or just a massive AOE that can one-shot everything but bosses. Not to mention how insanely powerful the Dwarven DLC is for the base game. Even though many of the elements are random, if you don't challenge yourself by constantly upping the difficulty to the highest level, there isn't much replayability because you'll just expect the expected.In addition, the randomization process is more streamlined. If you want to force a playstyle, you can pick which items appear and then play solely with those items rather of the many you will unlock over your sessions, making it much easier / more fun depending on your preferences. \So basically, it's a fun game with a variety of different challenging settings, but can get repetitive if you replay older maps on the same difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't felt compelled to review a game in a good while - I really enjoy this game. It is sort of a mix of FF tactics and left for dead if that makes sense?You essentially are controlling a few power heroes with different gear (each weapon enables different abilities, ranged, melee, magic, AOE, etc.). Combat plays out in standard tactics format, with additional weak enemies spawning in from the edge of the map each turn. Presuming to survive the waves, you are then put into a preparation phase where you equip the loot you salvaged from the last run, level up your heroes, and spend resources to upgrade your town. You also unlock many different modifiers for your runs, such as more resources, stronger town defenses, etc.. These are limited though to never give yourself too much of an edge (you can equip more and more the further you progress in the story, but this is a natural progression due to the increased difficulty).The real gem of the game is the progression - this game is HARD, but there is such a wealth of permanent unlock-ables that assist you in subsequent runs. However, as you progress through the story you can almost never rely on the upgrades alone due to the difficulty. It's a wonderful balance of strength through progression, developing your own skills, and just a slight peppering of RNG to keep things fresh without ever feeling like that alone is losing your runs.HIGHLY recommended for anyone that enjoys tactics games, RPGs, tower defenses, or even any games that take royalties from any of those genres.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: For the moment, this game is hard to recommend.I'm a big fan of grid based TRPGs - my favorite game of my childhood being final fantasy tactics, growing up with disgaea and tactics ogre, and various others.  To say the least, it is a varied genre with a lot of appeal.  At first glance, that's how I considered this game.  Perhaps that leads me to my poorer interpretations.Having a trio of randomly generated characters is interesting. In a way, I think of Darkest Dungeon when I play this.  However, due to the generic nature of the maps and how little bearing the maps themselves seem to have on the overall gameplay, I found myself quickly bored.  Skills seem to be determined by which weapon type you have, with a few others you can access through a trait tree.  Everyone has unique quirks - but the dialogue they shout over the match is all generic, as everyone of them says the same thing.  Having played many games that have a variety of unique maps that give their appeal, in addition to the characters, that did leave me bored.On top of that, there feels like very little difference between generated characters, even with that quality, as skills are broadly determined by weapon.  The general variability of skills, due to that, feels lacking - perhaps I am not far enough as of yet, but it is a frequent thought on my mind.  There are things I do like, however.  Enemy phases are quick and they move in unison, reducing the amount of time each round takes - on top of that, there is a turbo button if it is such a concern.  The art style is just what I love to see in a game like this.  The pixel art is a delight, and I enjoy every quality of it.  I like the idea of the grind it presents - but the homogeny in enemy type and maps just leaves me cold.  I played for three hours and frankly feel like I got nowhere in terms of understanding the story or general intent of the game, which is a bit of a frustrating thing for me.  I suppose I do care a lot about a story in a tactical RPG, as my favorites have had stories I love.  That doesn't mean this game is bad.  At the end of the day, I feel like it isn't for me, despite my love of this genre of game.  I will say, I am glad to see a smaller game from a smaller studio with this genre, and I think the rogue-lite elements could be great.  But After playing what felt like the same exact battle, over and over, I just kind of feel.  Bored.People describe this game as hard, and I wouldn't necessarily say that?  I felt prepared going into every night I've done thusfar, but it feels like a game where if you lose, it's because it's a game made to lose, for the sake of getting better options.  But nonetheless.  Your mileage will vary.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. The progression, complexity, challenge, and lure of possibly building a god tier combination(or a killer defensive layout) is never ending and each run feels uniquely distinct. There are so many things to praise from bangin soundtrack to meta progression, yet the vast variety in talent, trait, enemy type, gears, buildings, trap etc  etc is what stood out the most. It does have a steep learning curve but system is very intuitive and challenge curve is linear, perhaps slightly higher on boss night. I've played a lot of roguelite and town/tower defense but the last spell definitely ranks among the top as the devs clearly understood the importance of actually viable build variety and constantly changing challenge that demands planning and adaptation between each wave(night). A hero I've lovingly invested gold and training(shrine thing) and brain wrecking build planning into each day holding a side of town by him/herself heroically against endless tide of deadly enemies never fails to bring tears to my eyes. I strongly recommend this game to anyone with even a passing interest in town/tower defense where hero build is roughly the 70% and defensive layout is the rest with constantly changing unique enemies testing your mettle.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a  of roguelites, I have over 2000 hours in the genre. It takes a lot for me to say a roguelite is unique, and this one is. This combination of RPG, town-building/resource management, tower-defense and roguelite is very special and very fun. I highly recommend it.One big issue which I hope is being worked on - severe lag and crashes, when abilities are cast for the first time. When any ability (including boss/monster/player) ability is used for the first time in a level, it causes very high lag for me which means that the first few nights in a level are terribly laggy, sometimes resulting in crashes. Particularly, I've had the game crash mid-fight with the second boss, which is bad when it takes 3-4 hours of gameplay just to get through every night of the second level to get to that boss. Thankfully the save system is generous and it re-started me on the boss again. My PC is above the required specs for the game so, I hope they get this fixed.Other things that could be improved - the tower defense and Town-builder aspects can really use more depth, I get that these are not the central focus of the game (and I might have not yet unlocked the full scope), but I think more types of defenses could improve the game a lot, and more variety with what you can do in town beyond just "get max workers, get max resources, go brrr", but again, maybe I will discover more as I play more and in that case I will edit this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently, The Last Spell has only one map. And you can play it for 40 hours without getting bored.That's how good it is.It's about the survival of the last bastion of mankind. It's about building and equiping your characters, turn-based combat, base defense and resource management.You'll build production and defensive structures, assign workers to certain tasks (such as gathering gold, healing or crafting items), and level-up, equip and position your characters during the Preparation Phase.Then the night comes, bringing waves of undead to destroy you. And you beat the s**t out of them with melee and ranged weapons, spells, traps and ballistae/catapults.So far, it sounds good. But...The game has a lot more depth than I expected.Customizing your characters is great. When they level up, you get to pick 2 skills from a random list of 5 possible improvements (re-rollable twice) which may contain things ranging from +HP to +Multi-Hits to +Action Points. And any improvement that shows up can have 3 rarities -- common, uncommon and rare -- and give better stats accordingly.You'll also receive 1 perk point per level, expendable on a fairly sized "perk tree" (it's a rectangle, actually). These can be things like "restore 1 mana whenever you land a critical hit" or "+50% reliability when at full health."And that's another point: you have these... "things" like "reliability," "propagation," "opportunity," etc. I won't get into details because that would take too long, but it's another layer of depth to the game.Besides skills and perks, you also get to equip your heroes. They have torso, legs, helmet, two hand and up to two trinket slots. And a maximum of 4 bag ones (with perks), for consumables.Items can be common, uncommon, rare or epic, with the latter being  rare. They can give you all sorts of bonuses, and generally come with a basic armor, dodge or resistance stat. Or damage, in case of weapons, of course.You also have accuracy, daily HP/mana regen, variable move points, critical damage, and so on. There's a bunch of things to tune up.Regarding your base, there's a fair number of production structures to be built, and you have to seriously consider how to spend your resources. Gold is used to build them, hire more heroes and buy items. Materials are used to build defensive structures. And workers allow you to "scrap" ruins or increase the production of your facilities, yielding more items, resources and other stuff.The combat is turn-based, and it works perfectly. You have enough Action and Movement points to give you a much higher than usual degree of freedom. How you position your heroes is also very important, as well as which skills you decide to use and when, since they all have limited per-turn uses. You'll be fighting hundreds of enemies on each wave.The undead can be quick, dodgy units, flying ones that move past your walls, tanky armored skeletons, debuffers, archers, etc. There's a good variety of them (with more to come) and how and when you decide to kill each kind of enemy is quite important.After each night, you'll be rewarded with Taint -- a currency used to unlock new items and upgrades. There's already quite a lot of stuff to unlock in the game.When completing certain "milestones," such as "deal 500 damage in a single ranged attack," you'll unlock different things, on a  list of upgrades. Both lists contain a lot of interesting things. Also, there's no chance whatsoever of beating the game on your first run -- you  at least some of these upgrades to succeed.After beating the game the first time, you'll unlock the tier I Apocalypse difficulty. Tier II after that, and so on.Finally, I didn't spot a single bug in the game.And, BTW, the UI is pretty cool. And the soundtrack as well. The game's whole art style is quite charming.Not really.Other than really minor stuff (such as having to click, twice, to upgrade or repair each section of wall), the only thing that comes to mind is that, as it happens with many other roguelikes, the more types of items you unlock, the lower are the odds of finding any of them. So the more Taint/Milestone upgrades you unlock, the lower your chances of acquiring your favorite items.After 11 runs or so, I never actually had to use weapons I didn't want to for more than a few waves but, theoretically, it could happen. This can end up forcing you to play in a way that you're not very comfortable with. At the same time, it shakes things up, so... it's a neutral thing -- some may like it, some may not. Personally, I'm not a big fan of it, so I'd like to see them at least implementing a re-roll to the shop's daily items, so you get a better chance of finding what you want.Based on my own experience, if you think you'll like The Last Spell, you'll probably  it.The randomness of character traits and level ups, the good amount of different weapons, armors and trinkets, combined with the management side of the game makes playing it a considerably deeper and more interesting experience than I was initially expecting. This is a  thoughtful, well made, fun and fairly priced game. Just go ahead and give these guys your money -- they deserve it.

_childDocuments_.review: Short answer: This is a really cool game for the turn-based tactics genre. The balancing is effective, and the story is equal parts awesome and terrifying. It is difficult, but definitely worth checking out.Long answer:There are definitely parts of the game that just don't really work with the overall horde defense enemy style, but overall the game balances on the edge of tension and victory very well. There's only a few instances where I've had to throw my hands in the air and give up (mostly from rng screwing me over).The story draws a very *explicit* parallel to the MAD doctrine of nuclear defense, and ties it to magic so that there's technically a clean solution (based on text hints, it's not).The only gripe I have with this, is that the roguelike structure does not compliment the game's strengths, and instead pulls out its weaknesses. The story has a lot less of a bite when victory is functionally inevitable (albeit still difficult). And the rng already in the combat gets even swingier when your weapons, characters, and stat boosts are randomized.My average run time so far is ~4 hours each (over 10 runs). That is not very many runs to be fair, but it's still 40 hours of gametime, and the roguelike design structure works best for shorter games (easier to pick up/put down, getting back into a run is quick and smooth, and so on). This is especially true in tactics games, since their strengths are in storytelling, which roguelike design actively breaks up.Overall, it's a good game, it was just *so close* to being great.

_childDocuments_.review: Does a wonderful job rotating small base building elements with tactical gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: of tactical and management game. It gives the player the incredible feeling of a rogue-like game with much choices and no return for the run; it lets the player build its town in his favorite manner, and it tests the built town against waves of enemies. Any mistake is followed immediately by its consequences, and at the end, the victory depends only on the right choices, all along the process. A run lasts for some hours, so it's not a "quick run" game. You need some time to play a run, but you can always stop and continue later, as usual in this kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: The soundtrack is awesome and the game somehow makes the characters feel overpowered while also seeming like the odds are completely against you. I enjoy the strategy requirement behind the nights from preparation to the battles. Planning out your characters and city upgrades feels meaningful and messing up hurts without crippling your run.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: Post Release: This game is truly phenomenal; a labor of love and I can feel it in every aspect of the game. This game was made for me, beautiful pixel art, astounding score, and alll the stat/damage breakdowns make my math mind giddy. Just the breakdown of damage for every action is truly a work of art. While the game is challenging, it is entirely possible to beat the entire game without losing. I have played every major release since elderlicht came out and each time would play all the available content from the bottom up. PLEASE give this game a shot, each run may take a while to complete, but the time will fly by.Original: An incredibly fun game for those who love thinking about efficiency and dealing with big odds; with a gorgeous soundtrack and art style. I have completed the EA content (not gotten all unlockables, just completed a full run) after about 30 hours. (probably 26-28 as i left the game running sometimes) and I am eager to see what is to come. Only flaw that I noticed was the perk system, found myself using a select few perks dependent on the character's skill/proficiency, but the developers have already stated they are working on that.

_childDocuments_.review: A good overall game even in early access.1) You're first game will be a lost one, don't worry about it.2) The "souls" by beating each waves to unlock new weapons, skills, buildings and such, wonderful ! Can't wait to get them all3) You have some "achievements" to unlock other stuffs, read it well and aim for it, it'll help your futur runs !4) The possibility to play again and again, with new heroes build, new tactic, and also all the differents apocalypse (difficulty lvl) which can become tough in the hardest area, you have to master and be a bit lucky sometimes !As for the downs, i'll say the "ending" each time is the same, and when you lose to a wave you don't get any souls to get upgrades so you must finish one to get anything, or get absolutely nothing !

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. It is in early access, but there's already a lot of content, it plays really well, and appears to get better with each update.Thanks to some neat design choices this turn-based game somehow manages to feel  than similar real-time games: - The monsters move in "screen-displayable" groups instead of one by one during the enemy turn, so you get to see e.g. most enemies on the north side move instead of having to wait for each enemy to move and then attack. This makes the game progress quickly without losing readability of what's going on.- The hero attack patterns and possible combos make it enjoyable to try to mow down the enemies as efficiently as possible during each turn, to avoid getting overwhelmed. For example archers can create patterned gaps in the swarm that allow heroes with certain weapons to leap in and damage many enemies at once. Or you can avoid creating the gaps and focus on propagating magic or attacks instead.- Movement can be undone as long as you haven't attacked, avoiding the annoyance of using up movement points going somewhere and realizing the that the attack reach is to short.Most of the time is spent in the battles. The building phases allow setting up walls, stationary defenses and production buildings and such, which allow rather different strategies.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down an amazing game, I'm very excited for what the devs have in store for this as it continues through early access.It's a very fun game that reminds me a lot of XCOM - great fights broken up by some fun resource management in between. I'm continuously surprised by how many weapons and abilities there are, and that most of them feel quite balanced when compared to each other. There's quite a lot of enemy types that different heroes will be better at dealing with than others. The sprite and animation work is beautiful and very satisfying to watch, and alongside with the great music and sound design, means you don't really get tired of playing it for several hours in one go.The only downside I would say is that you do need to grind to complete a run. In a lot of other roguelikes or roguelites, it is maybe possible for you to complete a run when you start the game - and all the upgrades or other weapons you unlock are modifiers that are helpful but not necessary. Not so in The Last Spell. You WILL need to go through several failed runs to gather up the essence to unlock more action points for your heroes, and buildings like the Inn and the Seer are downright necessary to complete a run, which you do not start with.Only other negative comment I have to make is that you will sound like a fool when you say the word "Clawers". There's simply no good way to pronounce it.All in all, this is a wonderful game and I look forward to its full release!
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: Nice little turn based game....love the fact you can pause/save at any point so easy to drop in play a night and jump out.Not sure I'll play it to the end but enjoyed opening the first seal so far (and can always play it later...think it'll become a sometimes game when I want something slowpaced/pausible)Oh and love the music :)

_childDocuments_.review: Release update: As of 1.0 this game is phenomenal, and and absolute steal for its price. The team at Ishtar made the most of Early Access in the best way possible, constantly improving and balancing their game and adding features that enhance the roguelike experience. The full release provides a wonderfully addictive tactical roguelike experience with a slew of ways to approach its challenges. And the soundtrack is banging. Original thoughts: Another indie early access title that puts AAA studio releases to shame. Well done Ishtar games.Game is supposed to be hard, and is somewhat repetitive (like most roguelikes), but so far in 20 hours there is a constant trickle of increased difficulty along with new and interesting tools to combat it with. Only slight downside is that it's a little tedious having to repeat days on subsequent runs that are a walk in the park, but with the slew of new items, buildings, and tools each run, this can be an opportunity to experiment.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sheer brilliance.  The best comparison I can come up with is a turn-based Hades, complete with enthralling music, effects, and replayability.  I finally got through it after 23 attempts, and every  single one was nail-biting!   The shock factor of the ending is on par with the threesome scene from the Witcher 3.  The only thing I'd change is to call this game what it is:  Crack for Nerds.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: This game took way too much of my time, in a good way. Completed Apoc 4 on night 28 after 12 or 13 tries, disgustingly brutal, don't want to do that again. After that I played it again on easy mode Apoc 4 to try out different weapon strategies. I can understand the criticisms of the game, but I also appreciate most of what the developer is trying to do. Those that criticize it for a meaningless grind simply didn't get too far. In Apoc 3 & 4, the decisions you make with town building, or even spending 3-4 points more mana for a skill in the early days can end up affecting your build order and late game strategies. Invest more time into it and you'll get what I mean, esp the Apoc difficulties. The game is not without its flaws but is pretty solid in general.Likes:- disgustingly challenging in normal Apoc 3 & 4- fun variety of strategies up to Apoc 2- so much loot- decent variety of unlocks in the oraculum- dig the art- high replayability up to Apoc 2Dislikes:- unfortunately normal Apoc 3 & 4 really demands a specific set of strategies that include specific weapons, some weapons like the rifle just don't cut it, it good to have 1 rifle for debuffs but any more than that and you lose precious AOE damage output, clearing Apoc 4 without certain weapons like the hand crossbow is almost unthinkable- weapons are not sufficiently balanced for late game- late game really requires RNGsus to smile upon you and most of the time he doesn't, there should be some late game achievements in oraculum to slightly narrow down your level up bonuses- the damn RNG reminds me of XCOM2, esp the part where you miss 3 shots in a row on an 8% evadeOverall I highly recommend the game, even though there's stuff to iron out. I got my money's worth of entertainment out of a game less than 20 bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games of all time. Extremely satisfying grid turn based game with super super fun item/hero progression and build paths. Heroes feel just as fun from level 1 to level 10 which is so difficult to achieve in most SRPGs. Perks, item upgrades, changing items as economy gets better, specific stat growth choices, secondary weapon sets, hero emblems all are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun to play around with. The best way to sell this game is that nearly every single weapon feels super fun and different to use. Complaints are that there is a lack of diversity as the game goes on. Rounds can often take FOREVER as you play higher ascensions and deeper maps, and there's only really like 6-7 items? Once you get used to them and find which specific builds you like to play, there does end up being a dramatic lack of replay-ability which will hopefully be solved by DLC.Another complaint is that econ doesn't feel great in this game, often it feels more like you need everything and it doesn't particularly feel good to not have one type of building. Especially feels bad being pigeon-holed into buying the seer building sometimes. Lastly maps end up feeling really similar in this game. I think there is a lack of theming for enemy characters that makes each map feel distinct. One map could be a rush of a million creeps whereas another could be waves of high health monsters. Instead to an extent the ascensions define the map much more than the map itself.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game even at initial EA launch. Unlocks do not require excessive grind like some have mentioned. However, it is a fast game loop. I personally love it and don't find it repetitive. The more you unlock the more variety and randomness of gear and character traits you can start with. That, combined with the unlock goals, keeps me wanting to come back for more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being in early access, this game is already a lot of fun, has a decent amount of good gameplay time, and really nails the core gameplay mechanics.Weapons and abilities are varied, but all useful, so you'll have very different play experiences each run. It's impossible to win the first few runs (I think?), which makes it feel a bit grindy and repetitive as you earn various unlocks, but that scales up quickly. The combat is quick paced, dynamic, but tactically fulfilling, while the hordes of enemies have the perfect balance of feeling overwhelming but also manageable. If you've ever played Blood Bowl, there's a similar vibe to planning out your character's movements and synergizing abilities. There's also a decent strategic/resource management/base building side to things that forces tough choices on whether to spend limited resources to survive the next wave, or invest in longer term gains.I'll update when the final release hits, but as is, if you like tactical, turn-based combat, and don't mind a bit of grindy repetition, you'll get a lot of mileage out of this game in its current form, and it should only get better with refinement.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Spell

_childDocuments_.review: Theres a few parts of the game that are frustrating, also the UI needs polish (including scaling and QoL)But the game so far feels quite solid for an early access, though hard as nails, the game rewards you for continuing to play it, making each night easyer, feels like a true progression rather than a harsh slog, this is a good direction to take the game (hard, but rewarding).  The feeling of being overwhelmed, but still fighting to the last has such an interesting flair as you strive to just hold out one more day before everything crashes down.

_childDocuments_.review:
War was rampaging all over the land for decades. In a desperate move to end it all, the mages provoked The Cataclysm. Massive balls of pure magic obliterated nearly everything. A strange purple mist propagated everywhere. They say that those who entered the mist were killed, driven mad, or worse

Only a few Havens keep up the fight against the hordes of bloodthirsty monsters that come out at night from this damned mist. A few strained heroes protect the walls night after night, until a handful of mages manage to cast The Last Spell and banish all magic from this accursed world. And maybe save us all. Maybe.

name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan
detailed_description: HEROES COME IN ALL COLORS. Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan is a wholesome, creature capture, 2.5D Adventure-Puzzle-Platformer with over 30 hours of gameplay! It is a family-friendly, openly accessible, RPG-infused adventure in which you must save whimsical creatures by bringing back color to the world you once knew! Rainbow Billy tells a universal coming of age story about dealing with changes in the world and accepting ourselves and the others around us! Sometimes it only takes a conversation, empathy, and a new point of view to make a world of a difference. EXPLORE A WONDROUS, EXPANSIVE WORLD! Play over 30 hours of gameplay with dark caverns on secret islands to hidden coves off in the stormy seas. Explore a rich world filled with 85+ islands and caves, treasure, fish (because every great game has a fishing minigame!), friendship and... danger! BEFRIEND CURIOUS CREATURES! Collect over 60 strange, lovable creatures and help them with their problems in non-violent encounters! Create your own unique team to save the day! SOLVE ENVIRONMENTAL PUZZLES! Each world is filled with clever challenges and secrets that unlock new areas to explore! RECOLOR THE WORLD! Restore color to a monochrome world and help your friends find the courage to be their true selves in a story about empathy and growth.

_childDocuments_.review: offers a different take on the RPG genre, more notably in combat. It's not groundbreaking by any means, but offers a fresh experience that is intriguing and unique to play. With its charming writing, wholesome gameplay, and unique characters, this title delivers a delightful and laid back experience that anyone can enjoy.• A fresh take on combat• Full to the brim with creativity and personality• All 60 creatures are unique with their own personality and dialogue• Short cutscenes look amazing, like an old cartoon show brought to modern standards• The game feels too easy, a difficulty setting would’ve made me appreciate the combat mechanics more• The unique one time gimmicks in battle could’ve been used to add more depth and challenge to the combat• Some minor glitchy textures every now and then• Sometimes the 2D characters look odd in the 3D space follows a boy filled with colour and joy called Billy. After helping his home town set up a fireworks display and then proceeding to watch it, the noise and bright explosions awaken Leviathan, a colourless sleeping dragon, from its slumber. Leviathan thinks that these people live in a fantasy world, full of happiness that refuses to accept any negative emotion, thought or action. He takes it upon himself to curse the world to make Billy see that not everything is sunshine and rainbows, stripping the world and creatures of their colour and happiness. Billy manages to escape his town before his colour is taken from him and is now tasked to defeat Leviathan and bring the world back to its true colours.After Billy manages to escape his hometown, he is free to explore the ocean depths. You’ll travel from island to island and although it's not as open and large as I would’ve hoped, there is still a decent amount of area to cover. Some of these islands are out of your reach due to the limited fuel you have, but you can return to them later on when it's upgraded. The islands have access to usually offer a relatively easy platforming or puzzle section in order to advance. These sections usually don’t take too long to overcome which helps keep the pace of the game and avoids players getting stuck. Once you reach the end of an island you’ll usually come across a colourless creature who becomes hostile towards you, despite your best efforts to talk to them with respect. You then engage in combat with them and this is where the game shines the most. sticks out from the crowd of RPGs due to its unique take on combat. Rather than slaying opponents like most RPGs, you instead need to colour and befriend them by helping with their problems. At the beginning of every battle, the colours needed to befriend the creature are unknown but can be discovered in the talking phase. Talking to your opponent allows you to listen and advise them on their problems, as every creature has an insecurity that they talk about openly to you. This information is critical to deliver the most effective advice with the three dialogue options provided to you, the better advice that you give the more colours that’ll be revealed. Although it's not necessary to reveal colours before matching them, you can take an educated guess and figure it out by the process of elimination if need be. This is usually only beneficial when fighting bosses as they have a lot more colours compared to regular enemies.After the talking phase is over, you’ll be dealt a number of tokens that represent creatures you previously befriended. Each of these have their own set of colours they can attack with and can be placed in any of the lanes provided in the battle. After exhausting your moves, the creatures you’ve placed will then attempt to attack the opponent with their colour. Depending who is in the front lane will determine what minigame you play, the more of them in a single lane, the harder the minigame will be. If you haven’t managed to fill all the colours on your opponent after this phase, then they will attack you and the cycle repeats.As to be expected, there is a lot of variety with the minigames to keep you entertained throughout. From Pong, slot machines, rhythm-based sections, etc. Some creatures have the same minigame as others but slightly modified to make them different, maybe the paddle in Pong is shorter or the speed of the rhythm game is faster. However, I felt the challenge in most of the battles was almost non-existent, either because the minigames were too easy, or the enemy wasn’t threatening enough. The only jumps in difficulty that were significant enough to notice were in the boss battles. Consequently, I felt like I couldn’t appreciate the combat mechanics as much as I would’ve if the game provided more of a challenge. Maybe adding a difficulty setting would benefit this title as I felt like I was playing on easy mode, even when fighting the final boss.After befriending a creature you encountered previously, you’ll be able to visit them inside your boat and level them up. They start at level one with a single colour, but as they level up they’ll be able to use more colours and be a lot more diverse in battle. It's crucial to give your creatures as much variety as possible since you don’t get to pick and choose which ones to take with you (you take them all). Leveling them up requires you to give them certain items that you find whilst exploring the islands. Doing this also unlocks new dialogue where they open up about their insecurities and worries further to you. Each of them have a personality and unique traits that make them stand out from the rest and interesting to talk to. Personally, I’ve never been a fan of reading tons of dialogue, but this game held my attention for longer than I was anticipating. I felt compelled to know more about these creatures I’ve saved due to the charismatic and sometimes amusing writing.Occasionally when fighting an enemy, there will be temporary mechanics for the battle that you won’t experience anywhere else. Some enemies are more fragile and emotional than others, which leads to different things happening in battle. Maybe you're up against someone who is egotistical and refuses to fight famous creatures, maybe they are intimidating and scare off the lane with the most creatures, maybe they are jealous of how good you are at the minigames and force you to do bad to attack them, etc. This forces you to be more strategic in battle and know your team better. It's a shame that none of these mechanics got further from just the one battle, it would’ve been nice to add more layers of depth to the combat and possibly add more challenge.There’s no doubt that buckets of blood, sweat and tears went into creating this game as it oozes personality and creativity from every nook and cranny. From start to finish  provides an enjoyable and charming experience that I won’t forget anytime soon. Each character and creature is loveable and full of personality making them feel alive, the battle mechanics are a breath of fresh air, the story is compelling and wholesome and the art style fits the narrative extremely well. My only gripe is that the game is too easy as I was able to breeze through it with no deaths.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Well, it looks like "My first 3D platformer" for 4-year olds, and it also plays that way... in the first few minutes. Then it evolves into a still cute, but quite interesting RPG (with some easy platforming). A bit like Paper Mario. Very unique, bloodless "combat" (select your fighting creatures and press the correct button at the right time), and quite a lot of content. What starts with collecting a few coins and some firework-crackers soon becomes a search for creatures (and giving you more options in following confrontations), thoughts and coins in a large world. You cruise around on your boat (the Friendship, using Rainbow fuel), befriend (and collect) creatures, and color island after island, thereby removing the evil dragon's curse (who made everything black & white).The game is far too advanced for 4-year olds, and I think it might even be too complicated for older kids. It certainly is not cool enough for teens, so it is best played by older players who are not embrassed playing a cute RPG mixed with easy platforming (like me). It starts easy, but especially the fights do get more difficult after a few islands. Controller works fine, actually I would recommend one.Peaceful, cute RPG game that is far more complex than it might appear on first sight.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: This is gonna be an odd kinda review, because it's an odd kinda game.Happy path:* Make new friends and help them to better understand themselves.* Explore three medium-large areas, meeting people and finding collectibles.* Live your life, and be happy by being kind to others!Cynical path:* Meet people and make them your friends by manipulating them into opening up so you can blow their minds with brainwashing colors!* Tell your new friends whatever they want to hear so they'll join your crew!Moderate path:* Help a badly psychologically-traumatized Billy come to terms with recent events.* Help Billy's Leviathan  come to grips with the consequences of his actions.* Talk strangers you meet into joining your crew, and help each one come to grips with their own unique mental imbalances.Okay?  Hokay.Pros:* Lots to explore and collect.* Combat is many & varied.  Each fight is different, some requiring very unique tactics that you work out on the fly.* Lots of cheerful music that's mixed up enough it doesn't totally grate on your eardrums.* Several kinds of collectibles. (some that I didn't bother to collect)Cons:* Some of the late-game fights were just formulaic.  ("Oh, this one has THREE blocker-minions where the last ones had just two... yay."  *CLICK* "Lemme see what's on TV, I'll come back to this later")* You'll need a controller to play at Hard difficulty - says it supports keyboard controls, and there's options to reduce combat difficulty.   I kept it at "medium" and I routinely screwed up.* There's (currently?) no way to remap discrete keys to controls - there's 3-4 predefined key configs and you can select between them, but that's it.Meh:* Hard to figure the target demographic - the conveyed message and game mechanics are better understood by a teen or an adult, but the music and character design is juvenile and may drive off teens.* Many of the same combat conversation choices show up vs multiple 'enemies' - their responses are unique, though, so this isn't a "con".* Combat is by reflex-based mini-games.* No real penalty for losing a fight - you just get kicked out and can re-attempt.TL;DR: If you're a diehard fan of explore-and-talk games, you're open to diversity, and you have a controller (or don't have any issue w/ your reflexes), 8/10; else, avoid.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Hello friends,Today I will write a review about the game Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan. This a a game that takes place in the world of imagination and with the hero Billy. Can Billy save the world of imagination from the evil Leviathan? They may, but only help from their friends, which you can help all over the imaginary world. First though, you need to solve their problems. Each friend in imaginary world has a issue, whether it be depression, anxiety, worried about their looks, or just overly tired. By solving these issues, you can then use the friends to help quest more and find even more friend in imaginary world. This is the basis of the game, collect friends and solve their problems and then try to fight the black and white leviathan. Anyways, here is my PROS and CONS lists:PROS:- A story about imagination and helping others.- 2d and 3d graphics that look like there right out of a 1950's cartoon.- Collecting friends to help solve issues with the imaginary world.- Mini games to "catching" friends and helping bosses.- Fishing for items to gift to friends.- Collectibles hidden around the world.- Puzzles and power ups.- Secret Areas and post game things to find.- Works with controllers. I used a logitech F310.- Works with Windows 11 OS.CONS:- The cartoony looking graphics may look like the game is for little kids, but there are serious things hidden in the game.- The game is too short.- The story is emotional and may not be for everyone.Recommended game for fun playing, finding friends and collecting hidden things, and emotional storyline. The game has some deep issues so if children play the game, they may not understand the weight of some of the topics the friends mention. There are also many mini games, when catching new friends and when helping bosses. Not for those individuals who want to avoid serious issues in games.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: I was blown away by this game when I tried the demo, but the full game was even better. The best way to describe Rainbow Billy is that it's a mashup of a ton of great things from the action RPG and monster raising genres, but with all the sweet and cutesy kindness you can expect from the title. You get to explore a world for secrets, learning new skills along the way, and every character you recruit has their own backstory accessed by being their friend. These backstories are things everyday people can relate to, from being overworked at a job, to struggling to find motivation for art. The story itself becomes something more when you reach the end and see what it's all been building up to, as well.The mechanics are pretty solid. You choose allies to help you in battle, and the better you do at their attack minigame, the more damage you do. Minigames are varied, and with the large amount of party members avaliable it becomes quite a challenge to memorize them all. You also get to choose dialog options to affect the battle. Choose carefully, as a wrong answer will cost Billy some morale (this game's version of HP).The most important part of a game is that you have fun, and Rainbow Billy delivers this with solid game mechanics, fun visuals, and great characters/story. I highly recommend it, and consider it one of my personal favourite games of 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a lot more than I expected. Very colourful and uplifting, the mini-games were fun, some were quite challenging. Honestly the story was a lot deeper than I expected, and the credits... well. You'll see. All in all, an enjoyable game about a little boy rescuing creatures by restoring the kindness in their hearts. Sounds lame but the individual characters each have good stories for why they are the way that they are, and honestly I could compare a lot of the characters feelings and outlooks on life to myself and those around me. It can definitely touch a heartstring or two. I definitely recommend it for some mildly challenging, not-quite-casual, relaxing game play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful and sweet little game. I'm not quite sure how to begin.It's as if Paper Mario was designed to help adults and children alike to better understand and contextualise the negative aspects of themselves and those around them, but it's blatantly obvious that it benefits children directly, since it puts the characters' flaws into as clear a light as possible. With each character you meet and befriend as part of your small army of goofy pals, you explore a personality you either definitely have encountered before, or will encounter in time, that is if you don't already see their flaws in yourself. Sometimes these explorations of character defects are a bit simplified, but oftentimes the game's commentary on these personalities can be direct and apt. However resistant you are to the game's charm, you'll be thinking "Yup, makes sense" quite often.It goes without saying that the game contains LGBTQ+ themes, and that your main character *might* have a slight crush on another boy, but the game's scope is far beyond just that. Sure, it's part of it, but it's a broad game that covers many aspects of life: bitterness, resentment, mania, the pursuit of happiness, queerness, otherness, bullying, belonging, depression, overworking and exhaustion, duty, masculinity, weakness, conformity, jealousy, people-pleasing, ignorance, elitism, rage, etc. etc. It's a game about people in general.The combat is pretty basic. Some of the minigames used for "attacks" feel imbalanced compared to others, to the point you'll often avoid using certain characters entirely despite their bonuses. The real light of the "combat" is the dialogue, in which you try to intuit which response to a character's behaviour is the most empathetic or appropriate.The cinematics leave something to be desired. They are abruptly short and made shorter by long "Iris" transitions that obscure the cutscene, even if sound is already playing, and the cutscenes themselves can often feel disjointed. In fact, the game's presentation in general can sometimes lack. Without wishing to spoil anything, a few music tracks in the game have lyrics in them. Sometimes, this improves the scene, but it renders the finale somewhat cringeworthy and cloying, to the point that the entire finale feels something of a disappointment. In fact, the end-state of the game also feels somewhat anticlimactic, as though there could have been more to it, but that's salved by the very sweet tale told during the credits. I feel as though this could all be remedied, but perhaps it's a little too late to hope.All in all, I loved it. If a game can ever touch my heart, then it has won a big victory in spite of any and all shortcomings. This game absolutely has the capacity to help people. Maybe try it if you find yourself in a particularly dark or lonely place.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Helping enemies through their insecurities is a charming concept but it soon gets repetitive. 4-6 archetypes stretched out into 40-60 Neopet looking creatures all joining your side after being told to quit pressuring themselves. Combat consists of throwing shapes until they stick with an excruciatingly simple minigame before each and every attack. Open areas are alright. Thought the boat would be more involved. Plays almost like a children’s educational game which is in direct contrast with the wordy dialogue trees and darker themes.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: OK, first up - this is a joy.  It's a fabulous entry in the low-stakes platform genre, with not-too-taxing puzzles and a very forgiving structure (but with a decent difficulty curve and the odd surprise.)  As with a lot of these games, the graphic style is full-on cartoonish but this is all in support of the overall design which is beautifully executed; don't dismiss it just because it appears childish - in a sense, that's kind of the point.Whilst the core game elements are well-trodden - minigames to stand-in for combat, lots of hidden extras that provide bonuses, and an unsubtle plot, it's the story, graphic, art and music design that you should be here for.  Every part of it feels coherent, with fun characters, lots of interaction, and a logical flow that still allows for a bit of non-linear progression.And of course there's the critical core of a story about identity, personality and the lesson that just because other people are different doesn't mean that they are lesser people, and a reminder that "prejudice" literally means "pre-judging" before you know the background story, which all of us still have a natural tendency to do.(Disclaimer: I backed this on Kickstarter many moons ago.)
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Okay. Okay wow. Just beat the main story, found myself at 94% completion due to thorough sidequesting.Pros: > Unique take on a battle system.> Impressively poignant story.> Well-designed cartoon-inspired aestheics and art.> Dozens of interesting and colorful characters to meet and befriend. > You can jump nearly anywhere and onto nearly anything.> You can pet the dog.Cons:> Dialogue options doesn't always let you know what they lead to Billy saying.> Map doesn't show where you are on it.> Cannot manually mark map.> Some cutscenes feel awkward when transitioning back to gameplay.When I got this game, I was expecting a friendly, lighthearted romp that I would be able to watch on Cartoon Network or such.  Which, I guess is kind of the case, with the likes of Steven Universe and such?But to say it's lighthearted isn't the correct impression I would like to leave. Rainbow Billy is an idealistic game where friendship solves everything, yes. But doing so also involves tackling subject matters ranging from mental illness to poverty.While the limitations of the game doesn't allow it to explore these serious subject matters, it treats them with a high degree of respect and understanding--to the degree that I could see myself as having some of the issues present had my life turned out differently in certain ways.In addition, the frame of the game is incredibly intense, though this is something only revealed after the first world.Speaking of, the first world and the story that you see there doesn't hold a candle to what happens in the rest of the game. All in all, I enjoyed my time with the game, despite the awkward way dialogue options are presented during confrontations making me frustrated more than once. ((I remember a choice in Frightfrost where Billy compared a potential friend to his dad--up to this point, he had always praised his dad's sayings and actions, so I had assumed he had a positive opinion on his father... And ended up insulting the potential friend instead.))
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan... I don't know where to start with this game. My initial perception of the game was that it was simply an amazing art-style Pokemon-ish game, but then it went in completely a different direction and I ended up really enjoying myself with the game.So to start off with you start in a happy sunshine setting and then everything gets ruined and turned black and white, you then wonder throughout the world to work on getting the color restored to the world. Along your journey you will meet a bunch of creatures that all have their own mental and physical shortcoming, you then need to help them get over their problems through support and helping them get over or accept their mental issue. I did NOT expect the game to get that deep with the interactions but it sure did.At the end of the game, a whole new light gets shined on exactly what was going on and it was slightly expected but a really good segment non the less. Some of the creatures' occupations and situations might go over a kids head too much for them to understand what's going on, but at the same time the combat gets really difficult later on so I don't think this was intended as a game for small kids to play through by themselves.Now that I mention the combat I guess I can elaborate on that. The game's combat is quite unique, in essence, each creature has attacks that take different shapes on the enemy's "health bar", once you have completely filled it you have won and the creature will join your group. The combat itself is a variety of quick-time button prompts (think GuitarHero), a runaway game where you mustn't touch any object flying at you (think Undertale), and then a more generic slot machine. Each creature's attack mini-game is different when it comes to the general patterns, speed, and difficulty, so you need to learn whose attack mini-game is easier for you and make sure they lead the row they are on to make sure you do maximum damage.The game also has a wide variety of collectibles that you need to fully max out your friendship with the creatures as well as get overall upgrades to gameplay and accessories for your boat buddy. The completionist experience is very rewarding and quite easily achievable if a person puts time into it. With an update, they added the ability to get a rough idea of where you're missing collectibles. The only pain when it comes to collecting everything is that there isn't an indication of what fish you get where, so if you're missing some fish you need to find an online guide or ask the community.Anyways, let me cut to the rating. The game gets a 4.5/5 from me, it was a really charming and fun experience and I would easily recommend the game to people who like turn-based combat, a cute world, or Monster Taming games.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan is a pacifist, pokemon-esque game with visuals inspired by old rubber hose cartoons and/or Cuphead. I would recommend playing with a controller.The game was very fun and easy to play, the game also offers varying difficulty settings to make it easier if need be. I really enjoyed the battle system and the creature collection. For how few levels there are, there are quite a few creatures to befriend. Each of the creatures have two designs, one black and white and one in colour. I like the edgy look of the black and white designs better personally, but the colour designs look alright. You can level up your creatures only twice, but each creature has a backstory that's revealed through levelling up, so there is a bit of content in those two level ups.There were some big issues with the game. The most obvious issue is, that in its current state, it's pretty buggy. There has been an update to fix some bugs, so hopefully the rest of the bugs will get patched out in the future. The collectables can be annoying to find, but future patches have promised to make some quality of life fixes in the future too. My big issue, that cannot be patched out, is that the writing is sometimes a bit on the nose for my taste, but I understand that for what the game's going for, this might be hard to avoid. I found the introductory tutorial level a bit garish and obnoxious, but the rest of the game isn't.The game gives a lot of advice on a lot of topics. I haven't personally experienced many of these things, so I cannot really say whether the advice is good or not. But the game does really push for giving people support and being kind, and support and kindness is generally pretty good advice.Overall, it's a pretty good game. It's very queer and cute. A really nice little creature collector that's pretty easy and fun to play. Will probably been even better after a few more updates though.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: The main issue that a lot of players may have with this game, is that the first part out of the three, feels very boring and easy, and it might make a lot of people quit the game before even giving a proper try. After talking with a developer on my stream while playing Rainbow Billy, he told that the first world was created before the team won a big money reward form a contest and expand it's team to 30 people that it has now. So after the new developers came in there was no going back to the first world and completely redoing it from scratch. They patched it, they made it a little better, but they gave all their focus and energy into making the second and third world something better. And they totally did!This game after the first wordl feels so much better and different. The stories of the buddies you fight became more impactfull, not only as stories and problems, but in the gameplay as well. The level design and puzzles are more clever and intresting. And the game really starts to feel like a true adventure of restoring happiness and color to the world, while helping other people along side Billy, deal with their problems. This game has so much originality, character and love put into it, and it's definitely a unique experience for young and older audiences. Don't let the rough early game get you down and make you quit the game, just keep going and the game just get's better and better! But dont expect a very deep or hard game at any point.Rainbow Billy is a delightful, one of kind a game, that it is not for everyone, but everyone can enjoy something about it. Give this game a try with a friend, or with your child, or a younger sibling. It has a lot of nice messeges about acceptance of your problems and others, and about socializing.Worth the kickstarter wait and i can't wait to see what ManaVoid will do next :D I give this game a 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes a rare gem of a game comes along that is not only entertaining, but also has the power to truly lift spirits. At the heart of this game is a message of walking through the world with kindness, compassion, and empathy, for ourselves and others, and for "learn[ing] to accept the true colors in ALL our hearts." The whimsical, colourful style exudes the joy of stepping into one's authenticity---quite literally---as you play as Billy helping to re-colour the world: Billy collects "friends" (creatures) by understanding and empathizing with them via persuasion (battle) mode, each of whom has different personal issues that they need help processing (e.g., self-image, sense of belonging, anxiety, people-pleasing, anger issues, bitterness, depression, loneliness, ignorance, resentment, bullying, burnout/exhaustion, toxic masculinity, jealousy, otherness, and more). Once they feel understood, these creatures then can help Billy in future trials and bringing other creatures on board the mission (and tugboat!). Some of the creatures touch on heavier topics, but nothing is too dark if playing with kids. I was surprised at how much some of the creatures' issues spoke to my inner kid as well!The narrative pace is relaxing, yet steady and doesn't feel meandering at all. None of the puzzles are overly challenging, but were nonetheless satisfying to complete. I was expecting the mini creature games to become incredibly difficult by the third act, but they never did. I progressed at a leisurely pace, backtracking quite a bit looking for secrets and missed creatures, and still beat the game in 19 hours. You could likely complete 100% achievements in 18-24 hours.Overall, this game was an absolute joy to play. Kudos to the studio team who had the vision to explore concepts of positive psychology as well as processing difficult emotions and accountability in a fun game format. If you are looking for a game that will lift your mood and feel like there really is still good in the world, this game will make you smile end to end.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished this. I'm not going to mislead you with gushing promises of what this game ISN'T. It does not present any particular challenge, beyond the occasional fat-fingered screwing up of a minigame. The characters are not going to embed themselves in your memory when you think back among the pantheon. The music is thoroughly unmemorable, to the point that I played much of the game with various podcasts on in the background.But I will tell you what this game IS, which is, among other things, a source of a near-constant smile on my face for the roughly 14 hours I took to finish it. It bursts with color and, far more importantly, earnestness. Maybe it just speaks to the state of the world right now, but my time with Rainbow Billy ticked many boxes I really need ticked right now:Tranquil. Peaceful. Positive. Kind. Empathetic.No, you'll never be gripping your controller with white-knuckle intensity during this game. But it still might end up being just what you need.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: I would have actually liked if the game was a little bit shorter. I love the concept. The combat was unique, and the characters all have unique personality quirks they are working through.My only gripes: the camera kept auto-fixing itself, which would be fine if this game did not involve platforming. As one who wanted to befriend all of the creatures (FK you in particular Oowoo), I cannot say I will return back to this game anytime soon. I kept getting billy stuck in places all over the maps, and had to spam a lot to get out. I normally like to try to 100% games. This will not be one of them. There is no decent way to track where you have fished before.

_childDocuments_.review: ☑️Innocent, Cute & Wholesome.☑️Story is very enjoyable.☑️Beautiful and colorful visuals.☑️Quirky & lovable characters.☑️Feels like a genuine adventure.❌More people aren't playing it.Billy and the curse of the Leviathan is a story about the LGBTQIA+ community weaved into a wonderful little game. There is no fighting. There is no hate. There are just characters, story & puzzles on the seafaring adventures with your friends, "Friend-Ship", "Rod-Rigo" & all the friends you make along the way who are scared of being who they want to be. Their true self because of society. The game genuinely feels like you're playing Paper Mario and Kirby's Epic Yarn combined into one, while I get a sense of WindWaker from the charting of the ocean and little mini-quests along the way. There really isn't much to say about the game. It's really wonderful, and more people should be playing it. It makes you wanna reach forward and give each character a big hug. Be yourself, there are people who accept you for who you are. You just gotta keep trying.
