_childDocuments_.review: Pet a dog, make friends, get them to feel better about themselves, and hug a dragon. What's not to love? As a journey of mental healing, it addresses very serious topics diluted through a child's innocence. You just KNOW a game is good if it makes you teary-eyed every 15 minutes. It's hard to believe it didn't blow up. Amazing soundtrack, great characters, a decent story and engaging gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan is in essence a turn based creature collection game with slight puzzles and platforming, without actual combat and all about teaching empathy in a way that I haven't seen realized this well anywhere else.The basic premise is that colour got sucked out of the world and it is up to Billy and their friends to find creatures overwhelmed with their struggles and confront them about these. The confrontations consist of finding every creatures colours using the help of ones you've already befriended and then choosing appropriate conversation lines to try and talk them through whatever they're struggling with.These struggles consist of a variety of things like an artist feeling anxious about creating a masterpiece so there's something left of them when they're gone, a prankster just wanting to bring some humour into their surroundings and not understanding the difference between good and bat pranks and then many critters with anxieties about growing up, something on their looks or even whom they're attracted to. After confronting them and making a new friend you'll find them in your boat and will be able to give them gifts and treats and have at least two more conversations with them filling out the character more and even establishing connections to other critters. There's over 60 creatures, all of them come with their own stories and something that I love about this is that already befriended creatures can pop up during a confrontation with someone that's going through something similar, offering Billy to let them talk to this future friend instead and therefore helping out others with their struggles.Despite being a game all about empathy and showing a bit of compassion to fellow beings it never really feels like a depressing drag. There's a lot of silly, lighthearted humour going about between confrontations and while some subjects are heavy, like what our main character Billy turns out struggling with, there's always a return to lightness and hope afterward. Really the people this game will hit the hardest will be us adults because we have lived through a lot of the struggles represented; it may bring a lot of memories back. But I'd still recommend experiencing this anyhow, especially if you have children, since this is actually a good game to play with them as a family, see the choices they'd make and talk a little about the different topics coming up. Because they don't have these life experiences yet it won't be as heavy of an experiences and it's a good way to get them ready for various situations that may crop up in the future.Either way, I highly recommend giving this game a go. It is well realized and the only problems I've encountered with it were some bugs pertaining to the very last boss in the game that were ironed out by a couple restarts. Likely patched out by now.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game - the art style is very cute and the gameplay loop is satisfying and doesn't overstay its welcome. I cannot recommend enough playing on a controller, either. The character designs were delightful and while the puzzles weren't too complex, they still felt satisfying to complete.The game feels fairly juvenile at first glance, and is easily family-friendly, but is best understood by a teen or an adult. I enjoyed it enough to complete all the achievements. It's also pretty easy to tell that a lot of heart and soul was put into this game by the developers, and it feels so very earnest. I quite enjoyed the music throughout the game and how it evolved in the different areas, and despite spending enough time in each area to 100% it, the background music never really felt grating. I experienced a few minor bugs in my playthrough, but nothing that was game-breaking and they were primarily visual.All in all, would highly recommend if you enjoy emotional games that are pretty dialogue-heavy, with turn-based combat and strategy elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy is a wonderful game with a strong heart that got a bit unfairly compared to its influences; while it has its own issues, it is a unique and ambitious effort with very little like it in the indie space.Billy is a shy and quiet kid hanging out in the World of Imagination when all of its wonderful colors are drained by the evil Leviathan and his curse. Billy goes on a journey to retrieve the 3 color cores and bring color back to the land. He’ll make friends along the way, explore the vast seas and solve numerous puzzles to do so, showing bravery and compassion every step of the way. Pretty straight forward, and while the game isn’t subtle there is a little more going on here than just what you see at face value.The game is an interesting mix of puzzle solving platformer and “puzzle” combat. Let’s get this out of the way; yes, it is very much influenced by Paper Mario and Cuphead in art style and sorta gameplay. And I think people were expecting it to simply be a reskin of PM, when it very much does its own thing. Unfortunately it was sorta lose/lose because if it was just PM again, people would call it unoriginal and now that it does its own thing others thought it would be PM again and got something different instead. Can’t win with that kind of attitude.The confrontations, as they are called, are never fights but always opportunities to make a new friend. Each friend you make gives you more options in combat, as you draw your friends from a stack of chips to make rows of friends that unleash specific colors of the heart. Eventually, when you fill the opponent’s heart with all the right colors they join you! Give gifts and talk to all your friends to level them up, giving them passive skills when they lead a row and new colors as they grow and learn more about themselves and their problems. The confrontations are done through minigames such as slot machines, avoiding little buzzsaws or rhythm buttons.When not increasing the size of your party, you can sail the seas and find new islands to explore on your boat, solve puzzles and find collectables on these islands, go fishing or try and locate new friends. I will say, I was honestly surprised with the scope of this game when it came to the areas as despite being a smaller indie title they really put a ton of effort into making unique areas and giving you a ton of reason to explore. I beat the game in around 20 hours which was much more content than I had expected going in.Now, the game sets itself up as almost Saturday morning cartoony - aimed at children, explaining why you shouldn’t bully and how being yourself is happy. So the tone can sometimes be a bit…corny? It’s not subtle because it wants to get its points across but that often leaves some interactions feeling too “made for TV” Which can also be jarring because the game doesn’t just focus on issues kids might go through; all the friends you make range from young to old with problems that can be silly to adults or downright rough for even the toughest of us. Kids who get picked on for being poor, lovers who broke up because they were both mentally unhealthy, someone wanting to be tough but not lose their femininity, a fricking Manta that was in the Marines and has PTSD (like I said, there are friends with some REAL problems in this game). I admire 1. The team’s efforts to address topics that adults often don’t trust children with and 2. Not sugar-coating the reality of a lot of the bad situations or choices one can find oneself in. As a result though, the tone might not work for everyone. I liked what the game was doing enough to look past some of the trite or kiddy dialogue.Art-wise I found a lot to like and a little to not. It emulates an old 20s animation style a la Cuphead (which can be confusing given kids nowadays aren’t nostalgic for that style but adults are, yet the game is targeted at…who? Hard to say). But due to the diverse cast of characters and location it does not take cues from any other game and creates a very solid world out of it. I thought it was a very good looking game, with the designs being more hit than miss. I chalk it up to the choice to not always make an animal friend the “easy” lovable animals. Sure there’s dogs and rabbits, but there’s also snakes and spiders and sharks and all manner of animals. My favorites were actually ones they “cutified” that most people don’t enjoy like all the above. Sometimes the 20s animations style didn’t mesh with what they were going for, making an animal look kinda…awkward, but for the most part the designs come across well. I will readily admit that I liked a lot of the “color-drained” designs better than the filled ones lol. And I will defend Prickle to the death; don’t talk to me or my Aztec Snake son ever again.The music is decent enough, with a number of big vocal tracks at important points in the game. I will say, similarly, the corniness might be a turn off for some of them but they didn’t actively make me dislike them. It’s just not my cup of tea musically (I’m much more in the realm of Skulliwag, who was my other favorite friend. Mash the A button to headbang!).This is wholeheartedly a game worth playing to the end. If you do decide to pick this up, and I recommend it because this game is a vibrant and joyful good time, watch the end credits do NOT skip them. Trust me, it will make you focus on the game in a new light and enhanced my love of the game tremendously.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend that you try this game. It reminds me a lot of Spiritfarer without the crafting. And not nearly as good. Rainbow Billy is an indie adventure game with graphics and gameplay inspired by the Paper Mario series. Throughout the main game, you travel from island to island to return color to them. This usually ends with a battle encounter where Billy must match different colors on the enemy's health bar to win. Once beaten, the color returns to the island, and you recruit your enemy to your party. It's time to head to the next island!I found it engaging to explore the seas for optional islands, which have optional party members and power-ups. The game does have turn-based combat. It doesn't have any grinding, which I liked. The game has some decent music. I liked the background music for the second sea the best. As for the writing, we'll get to that.This game had a lot of missteps that could've been ironed out. The game's art style looks very childish, to the point that it evokes a preschool. The writing definitely has a bias that tells me that the writer(s) are either straight out of college or still in college. A team that's more diverse and has more life experiences could've brought more to the table. For now, the childish visuals and bland story will turn people away.The core gameplay and music show that this game had a lot of potential. It's hampered by its story and visuals. I do recommend that you give this game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly overlooked, Rainbow Billy is a monster-tamer unlike any other in tone, world-building, and battle mechanics. Its stellar writing and commitment to its characters outshines the rough edges you might find in its overworld's presentation.Rather than assembling a team of monsters, in Rainbow Billy, you AMASS a team of monsters. Every monster you find can be recruited, added to your collection, upgraded, and is always readily available in subsequent battles. You don't pick them -  your friends are always here. Sort of like a deck-builder, the monsters show up as a hand of pogs with different attack "shapes" that you can cycle through as you fight. "Battle" and "fight" might be the wrong words here, because the combat in context is all about conversing with the creatures and working through their traumas. As you become closer with them by giving them their favourite gifts, they elaborate on their backstories, work through their insecurities, and learn new attack shapes. There are a surprising number of these. 61, almost all of them with their own island/puzzle to unlock them, and all with their own unique issues and backstories. The amount of text breezes by and was something I actually looked forward to because Rainbow Billy's writing was so well thought-out. I kept being surprised by how many relatable issues the devs could present in a healthy and insightful way, all while being digestible for kids.When I recruited my first buddy, Deedle-Dee the dinosaur, and he started doing a little dance to the recruitment music, I knew this was gonna be a special game. Little did I know that Deedle-Dee would be outclassed in design 20 times over by all my new favourite characters. I really did like every design I saw.Some elements of the overworld did feel a little clunky. While the core loop of exploring islands to find new friends was super fun, there were a lot of clipping issues and wonky level geometry that left things feeling like they could have used a little more time in the oven. While I love the design of Rodrigo, Billy's sentient fishing rod (and functionally their "Kazooie"), his main punching move lacked a lot of impact, and you'll have to do it hundreds of time throughout the game. Nothing to ruin my experience, but a little polish in these areas would go a long way. The game is also very easy. I set the difficulty to hard, but never lost a fight. The later bosses were challenging enough, but the game definitely favours showing off its writing and designs over providing tough enemies.But, as I said, Rainbow Billy shines so brightly in other aspects that it's easy to overlook the small stuff. You won't find a game like Rainbow Billy anywhere else, and if you've been on the fence about it, I'd definitely say that it's worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: A puzzle-platformer with turn-based "combat" that's much more engaging than first impressions let on. The overworld exploration and puzzles are decent, the battle system is consistently engaging with opponents that frequently shake up the basic loop, and the writing helps shine a positive light on a wide range of topics surrounding emotional/mental health. Though it fumbles some of its mechanics and some bugs are still present, it's a good 10-20 hours of your time you won't regret spending.  tells the story of a child named Billy, who lives in a vibrant world of friendship and color until the powerful Leviathan unleashes a curse that drains the color from the world and its inhabitants, sapping them of their positivity to leave only their deepest negative emotions. Billy must travel the world in order to break the curse, and use the power of friendship to help a diverse cast of characters overcome their insecurities and regain their color. Between an art style and premise that feel like they were pulled straight out of a Saturday morning cartoon, it's easy to assume you're in for a painfully simple game--but rest assured that there is much more here than meets the eye.There are two main sides to the gameplay: overworld exploration and turn-based encounters with the creatures you need to recolor. , as every collectible you find can put you a step closer to new character upgrades. Most exploration revolves around light platforming challenges, but there's also a bunch of puzzles scattered around for you to solve as well. , where the objective is to move a ball down a specific path while utilizing or avoiding obstacles in your path--posts to stop your movement, ice to slide the ball off-course, bumpers to move the ball in a different direction, etc. This side of the gameplay was fine, but most of my enjoyment came from the other side: the turn-based encounters.Each turn of an encounter is a two-stage process: you start with a multiple-choice "Talk" system, where picking the right dialogue option can reveal some of your opponent's weaknesses; followed by a "card battler" system to recolor the opponent. --nine times out of ten, the most "correct" choice is just the one that best strokes your opponent's ego, so it's not that engaging outside of a few notable encounters that buck the trend. That said, the actual "battle" is much,  more interesting, and this is where the game really shines for me. The gist is that you have to drop tokens corresponding to specific colors onto a grid, then play one or more minigames in order to actually apply the color--but you must target the opponent with specific colors (revealed through Talking), or your attacks will be nullified. The core gameplay loop in this phase never radically changes, but each encounter makes subtle tweaks to the loop that can affect your usual strategy. Some of these tweaks are recycled with slight changes (like putting obstacles between you and your opponent), but I was surprised by the amount of "one and done" mechanics that didn't just add variety to the gameplay, but tied itself into the creature's personality and story arc in the process. It's far from the hardest game you'll ever play, but you can't just button-mash your way to victory--you have to think carefully about every move you make. Speaking of personalities and story arcs, . A lot of focus is put on the characters, as every successful encounter with a creature has them occupying a space in the overworld that lets you can talk with them further, and you're encouraged to give them gifts so they'll open up to you about their troubles that drained them of their color in the first place. This part of the game touches on a broad range of topics involving various emotional struggles, social insecurities, and mental health issues; and I'm sure many players--myself included--can find someone in this cast of characters whose struggles and road to recovery they can relate to. , focusing heavily on the fact that such traits don't make a person unworthy of acceptance, friendship, or love. Though I wish I could say more about the overarching story, it's better that you experience that for yourself.The last thing I want to touch on is accessibility, because there are a few good and bad points that should be noted before you consider a purchase:, and even though the exploration side of things started to drag in the last few hours of collectible hunting, it was a fun game overall. The quality of the turn-based gameplay and the maturity of its writing were both pleasant surprises given its initially simplistic and childish exterior, and it's a good lesson on why you should never judge a book by its cover.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, just .I'll say honestly that I probably wouldn't have played this game if it wasn't personally recommended to me. Didn't quite look like my type of game - but I really enjoyed it! If you're on the fence, I get that, but give it a chance and you won't regret it.First off, this game is bigger and deeper than it might look. Steam didn't count a bunch of my playtime, I guess because I was in offline mode, but it took me at least 15, maybe 20 hours to play through, with more for collecting the last hidden goodies. There's some bang for your buck!The same is true for the story : while the game is definitely full of sugary sweetness, I was surprised by how deep and dark it can get, while keeping that veneer of sweetness. It touches on all this serious stuff content keeping an optimistic, healthy view of things, and it results in what ended up being a really touching story.To really appreciate all that depth, you will need to read a lot of text - this is a dialogue based game, afterall. But while the enemies have a lot of similarities in their stories and in how you deal with them, there's enough fresh twists, hints at the darker side of the lore, and cheeky jokes to keep it interesting. Once you get to about the 2nd world, the deeper side of the story really kicks off, and by the 3rd, I was really invested.The game play is surprisingly nice, too The main issue to me is the tutorialization for the combat system, which is practically non-existent, but the game does a really good job of building smoothly from a simple base to more and more complicated encounters, so it works out. Though the game branded itself as a creature collector, the battles actually feel a bit more like they're from a deckbuilding game, with added puzzle elements. The end result is a really clever combat system that's nice and easy but still engaging.The gameplay outside of combat is fun too, pretty classic puzzle platformer, with well designed levels and puzzles and with a good amount of variety yet again.The sound and image wraps it all up into a nice cohesive package - the score for this game is honestly fantastic. The art is great too, but in some instances it comes off looking a little "scratchy", which is really a shame as it takes the polish off otherwise really nice art. Its really nice how well everything fits together though : the visual art, writing, music and gameplay all just click together really well, and it really gives the whole thing a certain something.That all being said, the game isn't perfect. There are a few points where the dialogue is a bit repetitive or a bit too sappy, I got my fair share of bugs when I was running around all over the map trying to get all of the last collectibles, and those little issues with the arts assets do remove a sense of polish from the game. That being said, that's mostly what the issues are in this game: polish. There are no big gamebreaking issues, and I say this having 100%ed it less than a week after it came out, so good on the devs for shipping a product that works well from the very start!Overall, I was really impressed by this game. Its not a super challenging, edgy action game, so if that's what you're looking for, this isn't it - but its a great game to unwind with and to put a smile on your face after a rough day! :) Thanks for the smiles Billy!

_childDocuments_.review: The adventures of Rainbow Brilly... sorry, I mean Billy, is one that very few people can't relate to in some way. Whether it be from the semi-nostalgic art style, being a mixture of Paper Mario's style and a lot of classic 2.5D games, or the various mini-games that count as "actions" for you to find, it's hard to deny that this Rainbow has a color for everyone, even if it doesn't seem quite in your spectrum.For the positives of this game, I'd commend it's simple, yet still interactive style of puzzles and encounters or "confrontations" as they're called.  Your objective in almost every fight is to color your opposition's world; and I said opposition instead of opponent because there's not really that many characters that are outright antagonistic as their point. They're trouble souls, just like you, and your way of combating their gray outlook on life is to talk to them and use the support of your other friends and /their/ other friends to help them realize that there's more to life than just one shade.Each "friend" you encounter has one of four mini-games for you to use, with some having unique twists typically revolving around the speed or tempo. These mini-games honestly could be quite irritating to me personally, not because they were bad, but because I was either bad at them, or the hit boxes ... don't quite line up as I expect them to. For example, one of the mini-games involves dodging spinning blades with your icon and moving it around inside a box to do so. But the hit-box for your icon is a bit higher than it is lower, not quite matching up with the size of the icon overall as things can go under you harmlessly, but still hit the top of your head at around the same distance. This isn't a huge negative as they're still playable, but it can take a bit to get used to it~ For the story of the game, it also goes back to the idea of having a little bit in there for everyone, as many of the characters you meet have their own personalities, worries, and connections with other people. While you don't meet everyone mentioned in the game directly, you can befriend and talk to everyone that you fight against to get to understand them better. You aren't forced to forgive them, but still asked to talk. To listen, which also ties into the main game mechanics as choosing the wrong option in some confrontations can actually affect you negatively, reducing your morale. Which is your only actual life source; as long as you see the color of the world and don't [Submit] to the [Darkness] in your opponent's heart, you can overcome them, and help them overcome themselves, too.I don't wish to spoil things for the overall story, but going into it blind makes you question a few of the backstories that some of the characters have. Notably a lot of them seem to deal with bullies and school stuff, so it felt odd there was no real school to be seen in the game... plus all the "bullies" you meet end up being pretty swell guys once you got to really know them. Which is true for reality of course; not everyone is born evil and often has their own reasons for doing what they do, but not everyone is good, either. But still, the story progresses at a decent pace and the overall theme is enjoyable, with bits and pieces of the truth scattered throughout. The "Thoughts" you can find are also amusing stray thoughts that most people have had in their life. Such as "Can Brilly really call it Rainbow Brilly if he's just got Blue in his name?" or something similar. The music is also upbeat and dramatic, making me not regret buying the soundtrack along with it to begin with, and the puzzles you can find on each island are handled well. But this is also where I switch to the negatives, because there's a handful of major ones that I feel need fixing, but none of them are super game breaking...Firstly, there's a lot of notable audio and visual bugs, including movement. The biggest one that affected me was using a grab mechanic to grab a balloon, as I hit something else. This locked me into a "Jumping" state, causing Billy to keep rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling, but nothing stopped it, even if I put my hands up or down. I had to completely reset the game to fix it, which was silly. Another one I had to reset to fix was an audio bug; I "fast traveled" right as I hit a loading screen for another room and the room I was going to played its music over the music of the place I /actually/ traveled to. Overall minor of course, but a silly bug regardless.Other major bugs I'd like to see fixed would be Billy getting stuck on walls often and some places that really should have and should not have invisible walls; a place in Chapter 2 that you go up is very easy to get stuck in, resulting in you having to Fast Travel out of it or reset the game, as Billy loses the ability to jump when he's "sliding" down a wall. The other thing is that there are three thoughts, and no real way to track them outside of what chapter they're in, that I can't seem to find. I hear them, but I don't see them, and there's no notable puzzle in the area, either. It's possible I'm just missing something, but... Having beat the game, with all friends, I'm not really sure what that'd be.But that's overall it for negatives; there's a few visual and audio bugs here and there that should have probably been caught, but nothing game breaking. Just a model that needed smoothed out, or one major character that has their model completely flipped in one fight that I'm surprised wasn't caught~ That said...I'd still recommend this game. While it isn't perfect and its message almost revolves around the /idea/ of nothing being perfect, but good enough anyways, it's still a delightful and cute game that can give a smile to anyone. Hopefully it's a rainbow that can brighten up your day.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy is a lovely adventure game with bright, colorful 2D-3D mixed visuals and, frankly, quite an astonishingly great soundtrack (one of my favorite parts of the game). If the game may appear childish to some at first glance, there is depth to the characters evolving through both hardship and joys, and enough thoughtful material to make one reflect on how they approach their own life.The game manages to subvert a lot of what usually makes other mechanically similar ones. Instead of bashing your way through waves of enemies, you listen and talk to them in an attempt to calm situations and have them accepting to help you go further. The high number of characters and the somewhat Pokemon-like collection aspect to how you interact with them does kind of limit how truly meaningful the relationships may feel: like it could be felt as if you're manipulating/exploiting them, but there is enough kindness and effort put through the dialogues to at least suggest otherwise. In any case, considering this high number of creatures, the general uniqueness of each one is commendable.Mechanics are neat overall. I applaud the way you can easily read recent dialogues, in case you missed something or pressed a button accidentally. The exploration/puzzle part stays strongly in the easy territory until the later areas of the game, yet without being necessarily boring. As for "combats", apart from the relative novelty of fighting with words of encouragement, the mix of strategy, unique effects, and mini-games before each "attack" works surprisingly well. I must admit I found the whole experience either a tad too long or not varied enough, but that's taking into account I chose to do pretty much all of the optional stuff. Still, assuming an unchanging length, having a few more types of mini-games, sometimes special ways to make relationships grow outside of giving gifts and what I assume to be candies, and perhaps more instances of creatures that can be befriended without going through the same fighting ritual might have been nice.Now, the only serious issue I had with the game are the bugs. There are a few which seemed recurrent (limits/walls which are easily glitchable, occasions to softlock oneself), and some which did not (falling indefinitely after getting stuck between two colliders, a thought never ceasing to make sounds after being collected). Those were not too bad in the sense that you can usually just teleport to the start of an island from the menu (something you might want to keep in mind). However, I also encountered two bugs that could potentially have been game-breaking. - During the volcano climb, one puzzle was impossible to solve without me activating V-Sync in the menu, suggesting there's some fps-dependant physics issue with the rolling balls. At least this looks easily solved (on my PC at least).-  In the sanctum of self, right after lighting up the second "ray", I relatively easily reached some island instead of getting right back to the central pyramid, not realising I wasn't supposed to be able to do that. As a result, I was stuck in an area (for some reason, teleportation was also unavailable at that time) until I found some place to jump and blindly fly from, in order to barely reach another island and exploit the easily glitchable surfaces to climb over the "inaccessible" area to somewhere the game considered I had the right to be. At this point, the only thing I can recommend is making sure the teleportation function is available before straying too much from the main path.All in all, regardless of the bugs and minor shortcomings, I truly had some fun with the game and I enjoyed the honest attempt at making a more optimist and kind type of game than what tends to be made in the same genre. The music is amazing, the visuals are nice and cute, and the dialogues are thoughtful and feel truthful. I absolutely recommend it!8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Off we get into the realm of Rainbow Billy and the land of IMAGINATION! What lies ahead and what could this simple title await you? Read on and find out! o0oGame-play : 9/10The world of Rainbow Billy offer a vast variety of game-play to the player. From elements of running around as Billy, environmental puzzles, to speeding along in your boat or just doing strategy battles via mini-games. This game really has it all. Even some true strategy and toughness that you can easily modify if needed. While I would give the 99% of the game-play a solid pass, there is the small learning curb you'll have to master to get the game right. One thing I will bring up here too is the clever aspect of TALKING to your enemies. With this you try and figure out your encounters and some can really test you! I put this all into the Game-play aspect as this make for a HUGE mechanic when interacting with your battles.Another element the game leads into is the Friend aspect when you go into your boat you sail and talk encourages your Friends you meet along your journey. Even something as clever as fishing mini-games are setup into the game with this idea in mind. Even getting to know and talk to your Friends more helps them power them up and do better in battle. Something again Rainbow Billy excels in.Graphics : 10/10Despite how somewhat simple the game might look, there's alot more under the hood when it comes to Rainbow Billy. The worlds to been seen/explored is just so vibrant and charming and the game's style of coloring keeping every world and characters unique and fitting to that realm. Not to mention, the blend of cartoon fun and 50's style of cartoon is quite the unique blend and cute. Also, there's some aspects of the game where you just get lost in the beauty.Controls: 9/10This is where I had some issues. GRANTED, I used a keyboard to play this game the game itself warns at the title screen to play with a controller. But I didn't have that opportunity. The only way around this with learning better how to play with the keyboard was that the keys cannot be rebound. So this ended up having to lower the difficulty for some of the mini-games. Yes, entirely my own fault here. BUT, the controls on the overall are very tight and you feel very in control of Billy and again being able to adjust settings and get a better feel is very welcomed. You'll never feel that you DON'T have control of the game or its cheating you.Sound/Music : 11/10Cannot stress enough how brilliant the music matches this game. Some immense talent went into its track not just general background music, but even songs that are sung and other details I wont' spoil here! Let it be known you can hear an immense level of music from characters and how they react when talking to show their various emotions and even the slight change in vocals/sounds to illustrate the VAST amount of characters/friends you meet. And each character you meet remains unique in their own from even any action sounding like you think it would. I did however has some slight sound issues with some characters not making any of these unique sounds when you talked to them. But its a VERY minor point at best, thankfully.Lastly, there's some truly amazing tracks that follow you in this game. Even ones that  actually build up as you accomplish some tasks that build to your end goal. There's even points where you just want to stop and listen to it and hear an extra accompanying whistle from your boat just to enjoy the moment.Difficulty : 10/10Good solid mix here between the game being quite easy and a good bit of challenge. There is some puzzle elements along good jumping/timing that might take a bit to master. Nothing that I felt was too harsh. By the end of the game, you feel very confident in your skills and how smooth you can play through things. Even better you can switch difficulty as needed to change things up should you need more of that spice in your life. This reaches out greatly towards people of any age grasping onto this game. And sometimes its okay to just have an easier game and just enjoy yourself. I think Rainbow Billy hits that perfect mix.Story : 11/10Keeping this as sweet and simple as it needs to be. You are tasked with finding a way to remove the Curse Of The Leviathan and its as simple as that. The way the story keeps building up with characters, bosses and everything feels so natural. I always felt engaged and the story worked enough to keep in mind everything you needed to keep building Billy up to overtake this Curse and save the land of IMAGINATION. The story did very well to throw some EXTRA things in there you might figure out yourself. *winks*Audience: ???This is a new section for me to include, but I bring this up because  the varying degrees of this game and how it reaches out. It really does reach out towards kids, teens, adults and even the elderly in some ways. The level of commitment (covered more in the Writing section) sticks out. It legit feels this game will stick to you in ways you didn't expect. Might only mention the talk of some issues might go well past younger audiences head. I think there's a level of respect that this game kinda does apply to everyone. I dunno. o-0Writing : 100/10Broke the scoreboard here and in that's the way it needs to be. The writing of this game is something I never would have thought to delight so much. EVERY character and interaction feels so unique, well thought up and just plain engaging to make you stop and read it. There's some really layering to some interactions I dare not spoil and even Friends you meet having to discuss their issues.There is that idea of them covering a larger issue in a simple way, but I think they do to this in the sense open up the discussion and even more the connection of WHY a character is like this. Its nothing MEGA-BRAIN themed, but the there is serious determination put into the fun, silly, wild, whacky, serious, sorrowful weight of each conversation. It even more applies into the battles and I'm going to leave it at that. <3The writing also too has some added creativity with the additional expression work to note the whimsy, the lows and the confusion in way people/character's interact. Along with just the original writing itself, it really helped enhance how engaged you feel talking to someone who feels "lazy" and how llllaaaazzzzyyyy they talk to you. Its top shelf work.Cost : 10/10Even at full price, this game is remarkably worth your coin. I managed to get a 27 hour game-play from start to end out of this title and I felt I could have gotten even more.TLDR : 10/10 - GET THIS GAME. Don't even second guess yourself if you a bit curious about this title and any of it looks a bit appealing to you. You won't soon regret it. *thumbs  up*Overall Score : 10/10 - This game has it all and more. I never thought there would be so much to unpack and enjoy in Rainbow Billy : The Curse of The Leviathan. From everything to its game-play, sound, design, DETAILS, characters, encounters and everything but the kitchen sink, it really is gem. There's even details I haven't mentioned in this long winded review you NEED to experience yourself. You won't regret trying this game out and if you can manage to really get into it, I think you'll feel as close to the world of IMAGINATION and Billy as well. So board the Friend-Ship, grab your Rod-Rigo, and ready up your dearest friends (plus don't forget to pet your beloved Giro). You've got this. I know you do. *salutes*Final Thoughts: One last thing that caught me off guard here was how often I would Screenshot certain lines and dialogue from characters. This is very normal in most Steam games. However, I never expected to be taking so much that by the end of the game I had a whopping 77 Screenshots! For someone like myself who doesn't normally hit that F12/Screenshot button, I was beyond surprised. Bless this game to the rainbow and back. <3

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR at the bottom.I think this is a good game for kids.If you're an adult and still want to try it, play on the Hard difficulty.This is a Turn-based strategy game that makes an attempt at teaching kids empathy, listening skills and how different words may impact a situation completely.Well, I'll still emphasize-It makes the attempt.Most of the conversation can be glossed over and if you're an adult I'll guess you can probably guess the answer that will help you continue forward with a conflict, solving without actually reading any of the interaction.There's not many games like it and I admire the way they decided to handle "Combat" by it not actually being a fight but an interaction which when you handle it the best way, both sides have the best outcomes.The creatures you have these interactions look a bit grotesque in a way until you manage to help them.I personally took it as a metaphor of how negative emotions may make you appear badly to others and these who can see through it or try and understand you will get to see the nice sides of you too.When the conflict is over, they turn into a completely different and adorable version of what you saw and join your team.I'd compare this game to Costume Quest.Both are games that are made for kids with Collectathon elements that may inspire childlike wonder.Though 1 is clearly more violent than the other.The gameplay elements directly have to do with healthy, caring and, emphatic communication.I think the mechanics that involves the conflicts aka "Confrontations" is a way of keeping the game light but obviously it's not a direct 1 to 1 to real life and if you want to learn more about healthy communication this is not the place.But I can totally see this is a more palatable option for kids if you want them to maybe learn about it.TL:DR-The whole concept of the game is kind of like an attempt at teaching healthy communication to kids.Do I recommend? Kind of.Look, it's charming but it's a hard sell.I think the graphics and some of the design choices makes up for it.So I guess!-Get it for your kids before they enter the rebellious stage.If you don't have kids, adopt and buy them the game.If you're an adult and want to try it, play it on the Hard Difficulty which wont change the fact that the game is easy but it's still something.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a really good feeling about this game from the moment I saw it, but had no idea it was going to be so fun, so engaging, so inspirational.This game is a combination of an RPG, a platformer, a monster collector, even a deck builder in a lot of ways, and it blends them all together beautifully. The most important element is that you "defeat" your enemies by talking to them, working out their problems, and supporting them.Over the many critters you help, they cover a wide variety of emotional issues... some might be depressed, others headstrong, others shy, and many something completely different. The dialogue used to help them is masterfully written and throughout the story you really feel like you're making a difference in their lives. You can then level them up by giving items to them, which triggers even more meaningful conversation, and you get to see your newly-made friends develop even further! The protagonist Billy even develops in a lot of ways, reconciling their inner demons.The overworld puzzles and combat system are equally brilliant. In trying to win over a creature, you are given a deck of tokens from the friends you've made and each one has special powers and symbols that may help, and get more, the more you've helped each friend.I would recommend this game to nearly everyone - both kids and adults in need of emotional exploration alike.

_childDocuments_.review: Billy lived a drab existence devoid of purpose or joy until the day a one-eyed dog lead him to a cult. He became a "friend" of the cult (the lowest rank) and was soon fully indoctrinated. This new perspective completely transformed his life. Everything made sense, like the world bursting into color from black and white.With newfound purpose and brotherhood, Billy worked his way up the ranks in the cult until his promotion to "best friend". The game begins with Billy helping the other cultists prepare his advancement ceremony. Then, the grim specter of reality invades, represented by a literal leviathan draining the color from Billy's world. The elders are upset and begin to question Billy's dedication.They decide to send him on a recruitment mission to prove his loyalty. He must gather three ingredients, er... orbs, and recruit several new "friends" on the way. Recruitment takes place on a special confrontation screen where you sweet talk potential recruits and play minigames to apply colored shapes (presumably hallucinogenic drugs, given the game's prismatic theming). Then, you deepen recruits' loyalty using gifts and "gummies", with each level unlocking another shape that recruit may use in a confrontation. Thus can Billy reaffirm his dedication to the cult and restore color to his world.Overall, the game has cute art and animations. The dialog and characters are very wholesome, making this an easy recommendation for children or the young at heart. Older, more jaded gamers may find themselves creatively interpreting the game's saccharine presentation.

_childDocuments_.review: RecommendedIn Rainbow Billy your main goal is to bring color back into the world. Along the way you meet creatures who have been turned by the darkness and you have to recolor them into friends by helping them with their insecurities and anxieties. The dialogue while you are doing this can easily get boring but it's also easy to just click through. The game offers around 10-15 hours of playtime to beat and possibly more if you do everything. Some of the fights you have to meet certain challenges that make the battle more interesting and unique. Your characters also have special abilities once they reach level 2 such as healing you or revealing one of the opponents weaknesses. There are some side collectibles called thoughts that you can find which give you upgrades.The game ultimately is about accepting yourself and learning to accept others. The game is enjoyable and worth the $20.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute game with a very creative and clever combat system, great art and music, and good writing all around. You have to engage with them in dialog to win the combats, and many (though sadly not all) have creative fight gimmicks to contend with too.My main criticism is that as it goes on the game kinda repeats itself a lot with the correct dialog choices for combat, which is not great when dialog is put front and center like this. _childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy is certainly a unique take on the monster taming genre. Each creature is sapient with their own unique personality and insecurities/issue that Billy needs to resolve by coloring and talking to them. If you enjoyed Undertale passive run this will be right up your alley. This game is dialogue heavy, with heavy emphasis on development on the creature you befriend. Your character still get their on major character development arc in the 3rd act.Later the dialogue in the battle option are not so obvious and I'm finding myself picking the wrong option more often.Some creature will have unique line and interaction if you play certain character. Sometime you can call upon character during the talk phase. The interaction can be detrimental or advantageous. Later the dialogue option are not so obvious and I'm finding myself picking the wrong option more often.Upgrading creature will yield more dialogue furthering their character development and story.I highly recommend playing the game at the hardest difficulty to try and engage with all the mechanic, such as passive effects on token. Mini game can range from easy to unfair depending on the the type and how many creature are stacked on the lane. Underneath the bright and cheery surface lays a much darker tone of grief, loss and blame. As the game progress you'll unravel the nature of the world of Imagination and Billy himself.As for criticism, the game plays into the bully angle quiet a lot. It seems to be an endemic issue in the land of imagination. Though this is somewhat made clear why that might be the case in the credit.You get way more money than you actually spend meaningfully. You only need enough money to buy gift. You end up getting plenty fish from trying to get gift from fishing spot that buying fish is mostly pointless. You only need to collect coin in the way and that's enough money for the entire game unless you want the 500 coin achievement.The intro was a time waster, the firework fetch quest at the start didn't feel meaningful, fun or even represent what the game is about. I felt like the game was trying to stall me for the two hour refund period during this. I'm glad I stuck through to play the actual game and thankfully this kind of quest never appears again.SummaryA very sentimental monster taming game where each creature have their own personality and story. Majority of the game is playing Paper Mario esque mini game so that you can match all the shape/color of the opponent, picking the right dialogue choice and playing the right creature. The game mask its darker and mature theme with its bright and cheery aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me 31 hours to complete this game and 100% all of the achievements. Rainbow Billy is an incredibly colorful, vibrant game that keeps your attention, and has a ton of hidden pickups and free-roaming abilities. I love everything about this game honestly, and there wasn't a moment where I lost interest - even while getting the rarer achievements. When it comes down to it, this game is a gorgeous and pleasant masterpiece about how to properly communicate with people with anxiety, depression, and other mental health issues. I left this game realizing that some of the things I've said to comfort my loved ones in the past... weren't exactly what they needed in that moment. I look at this game FAR less as a kiddie game and more as a game that adults can comprehend, and kids would just like to look at. Rainbow Billy really went into that depth of emotional intelligence that I've never seen a game do before. Hats off to the developers, thank you for an amazing experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Cute little game, but upon learning it was a Kickstarter project it makes a lot of sense. That doesn't mean it's bad, just I can see some places where some expansion/tweaking could have been but didn't happen due to financing. The controls could use some tweaks cause it's a bit jank, even though I am using a keyboard instead of the recommended controller. But considering how the jank can come from Billy just interacting with environment (including one memorable moment where I was trying to grab onto a balloon right in front of me, but instead got dragged across the sea to a balloon on an island halfway across the map) I don't know if it would make a difference. The battle system and interacting with the critters once you recruit them gets kind of tedious too: for the latter, you need specific presents and gummi fish to raise friendship, but what presents and fish you get are random so it takes a while, and the battle system takes so long as the game goes on! I've had to fight a critter (think his name is Gort) 3 times because he's got 3 backup fighters and a huge amount of colors to fill. And it doesn't help that so many of your recruitable critters have the same 3 colors, while the colors you actually need may only be on one or two critters, and I have NEVER had to use the hexagon one, and I'm in the last completable level before the final boss! I really think the critter list should have been severely pruned to about half the roster, especially when I have to keep wasting turns trying to find the one critter with the color I need, and also an undo function in battle when you accidentally put out a critter on the wrong color, or goof and draw a new hand when you were just trying to pick a color on a token. But despite my nitpicking, I did enjoy playing it. Just take note of the flaws and wait for a sale to pick this up, because for the 8 bucks I paid for it I'm willing to deal with it, but for the full 20 dollar price tag I'd have been royally miffed.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this game, and I gotta say that it's a real shame this ain't getting more attention as I think this has the potential to be a real gem. On the surface, Rainbow Billy seems like a kids cartoon version of Paper Mario, and in some ways it is, but it's much more than that, I felt. The story starts out a bit cliched with "big bad evil dude doing bad things and our hero and their new friends have to travel the world and collect Mcguffins to stop them" but the more I played the more mature and complex this story became. Almost every character you face/befriend has hidden layers to their persona and many of their issues are surprisingly relatable, whether it's bullying, anxiety, feelings of hopelessness, loss, betrayal, etc. Heck, it's even made clear that no matter how much you help, these issues and shortcomings  will never completely go away...but you don't have to let them stop you from finding joy and meaning in your life. Also, the game has some really great music that I sometimes just stopped and bopped my head to. The boss fights that cap off each area were also a major highlight for me and could get surprisingly intense, especially towards the end. Does this game have flaws? Of course. The "combat" system kinda wore on me after a while, finding the right items to get certain characters Friendship Levels up was sometimes a chore, and I did feel the messages got kinda preachy at times, or just very obvious.Regardless, I still recommend this game. If you manage to look past the cutesy surface, I think you'll find a surprisingly engaging experience with some really good messages to take away and apply in our own lives. Whether you're a kid, a teen, or an adult, I think you'll find a lot to enjoy in Rainbow Billy: Curse of the Leviathan.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: -It looks real pretty (the animated cut-scenes are especially nice)-has a decent soundtrack (a couple of voiced songs as well which was nice surprise)-The game-play is fine; Its sort of a card battler collect-a-thon type of deal with some light puzzles and platforming which was all good and a fishing mini-game thrown in. -Lets you explore the world after completing the main story in order to find items, get achievements etc.Cons:-The combat does get repetitive but I think that is just the nature of these card battle games. In fairness the Devs added combat mini-games to try and alleviate this but these come off more tedious then entertaining in my opinion but its something I suppose. -Wonky camera at times, you don't have any control of the camera for the most part.-The character can easily get stuck into a slide animation. I got stuck a couple of times trying to traverse up mountains and had to restart.- There is far too much dialog for my liking; if you want to upgrade your cards (creatures) then get ready for a lot of reading (or get ready to skip through it) -Froze during the final boss which was kind of immersion breaking. I feel like this might be just bad luck though.Overall I enjoyed it and would recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's safe to say that this was one of the most underappreciated games of 2021. There is a lot to enjoy and the art style is pretty distinct, so it's sort of a wonder why this didn't get more coverage. The gameplay consists of two parts: 3D platforming and turn-based combat. The platforming isn't the best, but then again, this isn't exactly A Hat in Time. A grand majority of the plaforming just consists of solving puzzles, such as pressing buttons and traversing simple platforms. There are a few optional sections that require more complex platforming and are really difficult to do due to the limited platforming mechanics, but since they are rare and not required, it's not that big of a deal.The combat is somewhat similar to the Mario RPG games, which require additional inputs after an attack has been chosen to ensure the attack actually goes through. Normally, I absolutely hate this gameplay gimmick. Most titles that I have tried that implement it just have a quick-time thing, usually with an extremely tight margin of error, and it's really punishing if you whiff. In this game, however, the attacks feature actual minigames which are relatively forgiving, ensuring that you will land perfect hits basically every time. There is a lot more depth to the combat, as well, as the attack type you can use is limited based on which friends you have unlocked. On one hand, unlocking more friends unlocks a wider selection of attack types you can use, but also potentially clogs your attack pool each turn with attacks you might not need. On top of all of this, your friends can give you a buff when played each turn, which adds more variables to think about when forming your strategy. It's a constant balance of making sure you have the most optimal friends in your hand each turn or shuffling them out, if needed. Even though the combat is overall not too difficult, there is a surprising amount of depth built into it.The worst part about the game is possibly the writing. Every enemy you fight has some cringy backstory that is basically some variation of,  Fortunately, it's relatively easy to skip past these pointless sob stories and focus on the rest of the game, instead.Overall, I am having a really fun time with this game. Even though the platforming is not the best, the puzzles are fun and there is a lot to explore. The combat is easy, but contains a lot of depth, making it really fun, as well. There aren't too many massive flaws here and I really think this game deserved WAY more support than it looks like it did, with  Steam reviews as of writing this!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've played this year. This game is phenomenal. Not only does it have an amazing soundtrack and colorful visuals (think Paper Mario esque), but it reaches into your heart and finds those places of darkness that you hide from. It shows you all the warmth and compassion that Billy shows his friends. It shows you that flaws are a part of being true to who you are. This game has representation, emotional growth, humor, strategic game play, puzzles, light platforming, and many collectables. Every character feels unique, with their own flaws and growth. I felt connected to them and was genuinely invested in them. There were moments that almost brought me to tears. (I am admittedly an emotional person, but still.) The base combat(?) is interesting and fun, as are the variations that sometimes crop up.A few technical things. There are several difficulty levels so it is adaptable for many ages and skill levels. There are occasional audio bugs (Thought sounds where there are no Thoughts) but I did not run into that too often before the last area.  The camera can swing a little wildly when you are moving through narrow areas or around corners, and the out of bounds areas can be a little wonky if you accidentally end up in them.I played this game for 35 hours and 100% completed it. I know I will end up playing it again so that I can experiment with different dialogue options and battle choices. It is worth every penny I spent on it. I cannot recommend it highly enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan

_childDocuments_.review: Paper Mario vibes meets Pokemon vibes meets good vibes. It's a delight start to finish, with a comfortable set of mechanics that feel complete without being bloated, and the themes of acceptance and kindness avoid being too on-the-nose with some grounded character vignettes and an overall framing that really pulls together at the very end. Look elsewhere for a challenge, but grab Rainbow Billy if you want to make friends with shark dogs and cat bats and yell at them about how great and valid they are.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where I wish there was a maybe option, the game is colourful and can be fun, but it is also very preachy and slow, there are things to love but it can also feel like a drag at times. The battle system is unique, fun most of the time and tedious at others, some of the dialogue options repeat from fight to fight and feel out of place, some of the story beats are extremely predictable,  and while the message is heart felt, it can feel like the game is trying shove it down your throat at times, every monster has a tragic backstory where either their wife left them or they were bullied as a child, and yes everyone has their own struggles in life, but every encounter, every monster levelling up reveals something about their tragic past, and while it fits thematically with the story it can feel a little forced at times and you may find yourself skipping some of the dialogue because it sometimes becomes wall of text after wall of text. There are also glitches scattered throughout and camera issue that make the game a little annoying at times. I would still recommend this game as it is quite charming and beautiful and again the message is hearfelt I would just have some caveats about it

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, but... man, the pacing just kills it. Slow text speed (that you can skip), slow attack animations from both sides that make battles feel like they take forever, puzzles and platforming that are too slow-paced to be challenging... I was way into this at the start but because the combat never functionally changes, your moveset only ever gets slightly bigger (and only in a notable way in the third and final world), these long battles interrupting the overworld manuevering on an annoyingly regular basis, and the game starts running out of new niche mental anxieties to turn into characters, this turned into a real slog by the end and that's unfortunate because there's a lot of potential and a lot of heart in this game. I think stripping back the number of friends to half of what's here and tweaking battles to be a bit faster would help immensely, though it certainly wouldn't fix a lot of the small flaws - a few platforming mechanics that just straight don't work (the clams! wow!), kinda glitchy platforming and slopes in general, the fishing minigame never going past 5 slots even as some of the later ones get so many moving parts they essentially become games of chance (two moving parts is the max you should expect any player to deal with and even then it's a bit much). The game also expects you to memorize every friend's personality for the fights where certain personalities will cause issues and like... I don't have room in my brain for all of these characters who I generally only even interact with twice, guys.Like, the combat concept at its core is good - nonviolent, talking-and-minigame combat (though two of the minigames - the pong-like and the avoidance challnge - are regularly way harder than the other types and often more punishing too), a lot of emotional drama packed into a very basic system, and there's a nice attempt at a variety of platforming and puzzle challenges, plus the game looks and sounds great, vibrant landscapes and character designs and an all-around solid soundtrack, all the stuff that got me on board in the first place but didn't end up being enough to keep the whole ride entertaining by itself.I do recommend it but the $30 asking price is a bit steep even if I recognize the effort that went into making this - that's a LOT of character designs and a pretty expansive soundtrack with more than a few vocal tracks to boot - I just don't think the game offers enough variety (or, let's be honest, challenge) to be worth its length, which is unfortunate. It's also kind of a case study for why Undertale keeping its similar themes to a more compact, concise length was probably the smarter idea in the long run.

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy on the surface is just a child friendly throwback to cartoons of old, almost like Cuphead in that regard, however it differs in the gameplay and especially the plot. The gameplay goes for what I feel is best described as almost like deck building, except you get all the cards. The gameplay itself is almost like a puzzle RPG, you obtain friends that will aid you in battle, these friends hold specific shapes and colours, you then use those friends to confront enemies who's health is in fact a combination of these same shapes and colours, and ultimately turn them into a friend, with them becoming part of your team. It's quite an innovative way of tackling RPG like gameplay, there are no random encounters, no EXP and levelling, In the over world though it will employ more puzzle like behaviour at times to progress. My only gripe with this is that the over world consists of multiple islands that you sail between, which felt ultimately pointless, they did remedy this somewhat by making the boat your main base where you want to go to upgrade your friends and to redeem secrets you unlocked by finding collectables within the game.The Leviathan has turned the world black and white and it is up to Billy and his friends to return the colour back to the world, at first glance the plot is very surface level, but it becomes increasingly obvious that this is plot that is supposed to be fun for kids, while at the same time teach them about accepting, understanding and respecting other people. I enjoyed this plot, even if sometimes it could be a bit on the nose for what specific things meant. Although if you didn't notice them in the playthrough the credits will put them all into perspective.Musically the game is awesome, at start up the game mentions it's best enjoyed with sound on and I must admit that this is true. Having sound just added a new layer of appreciation. It makes use of Jazz, Rock/Metal, Synth, Pop and even Musical, using the music to tell plot points while you're fighting. This was truly the stand out part for me.Graphically the game looks awesome, reminding of old Steamboat Willy era cartoons throughout with a sprinkling of Paper Mario 2d-ness, although there is quite a jarring difference in quality for the gameplay and the cutscenes. The gameplay itself looks to run so smooth where as the cutscenes looked a lot more rigid and static, which I would have expected it to be the other way round, but it makes sense since the cutscenes are short in length, and aren't used all that much.I would recommend trying Rainbow Billy out, it's uniqueness of the battle system, combined with a great soundtrack and overall handling of subjects is very good, and I would feel it unfortunate if people did not at least give this game a shot

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: Rainbow Billy succeeds at creating an original approach to confrontation in games that relies entirely on being compassionate and understanding through dialogue. Some games such as the Persona series and Undertale touch upon this idea but not as wholeheartedly as this game. The exploration and confrontations are most comparable to the Paper Mario series, with vibrant islands and perspective based secrets. The "combat" involves a combination of timing based puzzles and dialogue that tests your understanding and compassion for the creatures you encounter. The game doesn't hide its childlike imagination and optimism here but rather wears it on its sleeve with pride. When in the game's home base, the "friend-ship" (heheh) you get to chat with your recruited creatures and get to know them better (levelling them up) which feeds nicely into the gameplay loop and the game's themes.Overall Rainbow Billy feels very well thought out and realised. ManaVoid set out to create a game the subverts the expectations of games as blood-filled violence machines and presents the player with an uplifting game about listening to and understanding those around you to improve the world we live in. It is a triumph in what it sets out to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Rainbow Billy is a masterful indie game that pulls from many genres and weaves it all together with love and care.Pros:- The mini(or micro) games are fun, challenging and dynamic.- The puzzles can be difficult, and you might even get stuck on a few- The score is a masterpiece; every song fitting perfectly with the level designs and themes of the story.- The game can be quite challenging later on; befriended allies' minigames ramp up in difficulty at later levels.- Finding "thoughts" scattered about is enjoyable if you are a completionist.- The fishing game is also excellent and scales up in difficulty later on as well.- The characters and especially the bosses are beautiful and aptly themed. A huge cast of colorful ;) characters.Cons:- "Correct" dialog choices can be pretty obvious.Would be nice:- Music should start in loading screen, that way you're immediately drawn into the atmosphere - Mouse should disappear after a few seconds when controller input is detected- Some of the before or "mean" versions of characters are pretty and interesting in their own ruggish way; I don't think their change of heart should change all their natural pupils, for example. - Being picky here but Friend-Ship locked gas should not show up as locked. Having one or two locks visible all the time is weird; it just reminds you that you don't have something. Just add the gas later on without the lock icon.Summary:Rainbow Billy is an adorable, sweet game about compassion and taking care of your friends and being true to yourself. It is a beautiful experience to be enjoyed by all.

_childDocuments_.review: What struck me most was the inherent positive nature the game was entrenched in. Yes, there is a big bad guy who is looking to ruin your day, but the quests toward victory often involved very positive dialogue and character building.Though the "combat mechanics" were relatively easy, they gradually become more challenging, but never tip the scales to feeling difficult. Visually wonderful, engaging, and fluid to explore. A great game to unwind with, without the stresses or pressures of overly difficult platforming.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Gameplay feels great. It's simple but stays fresh throughout the whole game since almost every fight has a unique little thing.Puzzles are fun, reminded me of good old LoZ style dungeons.Story is complex and has a LOT of side content if you want more info on the Lore (every creature has its own background and honestly I wasn't ready for how real some of those are)Length i'm around 30h in and i'm only missing 1 collectable and the final part of the game to 100% it.Cons: Difficulty is a bit easy,i stayed on the default medium for minigames + game and i honestly didn't struggle to clear the game. I did notice there is a hard mode in the options so I guess you could always use that if you wanted a more challenging experience.TLDR:Cute and wholesome game, great for like a weekend playthrough if you just want some positive thoughts and a fun experience. 10/10 would die for Bark

_childDocuments_.review:
Rainbow Billy: The Curse of the Leviathan is a wholesome, creature capture, 2.5D Adventure-Puzzle-Platformer with RPG elements. It is a family-friendly and openly accessible adventure in which you must save whimsical creatures by bringing back color to the world you once knew!

Rainbow Billy tells a universal coming of age story about dealing with changes in the world and accepting ourselves and the others around us! Sometimes it only takes a conversation, empathy, and a new point of view to make a world of a difference. EXPLORE A WONDROUS WORLD!
From dark caverns on secret islands to hidden coves off in the stormy seas, explore a rich world filled with treasure, fish (because every great game has a fishing minigame!), friendship and... danger!
SOLVE ENVIRONMENTAL PUZZLES!
Each world is filled with clever challenges and secrets that unlock new areas to explore!

BEFRIEND CURIOUS CREATURES!
Meet over 60 strange, lovable creatures and help them with their problems in non-violent encounters! Create your own unique team to save the day!

RECOLOR THE WORLD!
Restore color to a monochrome world and help your friends find the courage to be their true selves in a story about empathy and growth.

name: The Complex
detailed_description: 📢 WISHLIST THE ISLE TIDE HOTEL About the Game After a major bio-weapon attack on London, two scientists find themselves in a locked-down laboratory with time, and air, running out. With interactive gameplay, your actions and your relationship with other characters will lead you to one of eight suspenseful endings. Having treated the victims of a chemical attack in the totalitarian state of Kindar, Dr Amy Tenant is a leader in the advancement of Nanocell Technology. Now, in London, news breaks of a blood-vomiting civilian whose identity is far from coincidental. Reunited with an old friend, Amy is trapped in an impenetrable HQ of laboratories—a womb of scientific advancement with a perilous secret. The Complex is written by Lynn Renee Maxcy, part of the Emmy award-winning writing team from The Handmaid’s Tale. The interactive movie stars Michelle Mylett (Letterkenny, Bad Blood), Kate Dickie (Game of Thrones, The Witch) and Al Weaver (Grantchester). Featuring guest acting performance by Twitch streamer and former Xbox UK presenter, Leah Viathan. Relationship Tracking Throughout the game you will interact with characters and — depending on your choices — will either strengthen or weaken your relationship. The relationship scores are calculated from the start right through to the very end and will affect certain scenarios as well as having major consequences in the concluding scenes. Personality Tracking For every decision you make, every interaction, your character’s personality is being tracked. At the end of each playthrough, you are rewarded with a Personality Score and a breakdown to see how you played the game. Discover the five basic dimensions of a personality; openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Which of those will your character play? Features • A completely live action, cinematic interactive sci-fi thriller, filmed in the UK. Directed by Paul Raschid, and written by Lynn Renee Maxcy (The Handmaid's Tale - TV Series). • Multi-optional storytelling with 8 different outcomes. • Real-time Relationship Status Tracking that influences the story as you play. • Real-time Personality Trait Tracking that evolves based on your choices. • Starring Michelle Mylett (Letterkenny, Bad Blood), Kate Dickie (Game of Thrones, The Witch) and Al Weaver (Grantchester) • Guest acting performance by live streamer and presenter, Leah Viathan. • Unlockable features include Skip Scene, Personality Assessment and a Hidden Event. • Featuring a Pause Choices option for improved audience participation during live streams.

short_description: After a major bio-weapon attack on London, two scientists find themselves in a locked-down laboratory with time, and air, running out. The Complex is an interactive sci-fi thriller movie where your decisions lead to one of eight suspenseful endings.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Complex" is a medium-length (about 80 minutes) interactive thriller movie about two scientists and an intern, who try to disentangle a web of corruption while being trapped in a high-security lab. The two scientists have a prior history together and the intern, whose motives are in question, has been infected with deadly nanocells that ravage her body.I found the story interesting and enjoyable, though some parts are a bit far-fetched, and in one of the paths, it needlessly spins into violence that feels tacked-on just to have some action in the movie. The acting was okay - nothing stellar, but it got the job done, and especially the complicated relation of the two main characters was presented very well.The occasional choices were engaging, and the game tracks how well the other characters think of you, which means that the same choice can lead to different outcomes depending on how your previous choices affected your relationship with that character. This is a fresh technique that enhances immersion and replayability. That said, the story is still too linear for my taste - it follows the exact same plot with just a few additions or omissions based on your choices, and around the middle it branches into two different paths, that's it. Rhinotales' "She Sees Red" did a better job in that regard.There are nine different endings, and exploring them is fun because contrary to Wales Interactives's previous games in this genre, this one lets you skip scenes that you have already seen. This turns hunting for achievements and/or different endings into an engaging experience, rather than the tedium of previous titles. Some of the endings feature surprises, and watching all of them gives you a better understanding of the plot, though once again "She Sees Red" showed that this can be done even better.The game does not have any puzzles to speak of, unless you regard "finding a good ending" as one. I didn't miss them since your choices are still interesting and meaningful, they just focus more on handling personal relations and finding the right tone, rather than traditional problem-solving.Altogether, "The Complex" is still not quite where I would like interactive movies to be, but it is a noticeable improvement over the company's previous titles like "Late Shift" and "The Bunker", especially in terms of user-friendliness. It's a bit pricey considering that there's little reason to spend more than 4 hours with it even as a completionist, but filming movies isn't cheap, and I prefer an engaging 4-hour experience over a boring, drawn-out longer one.One final note that wasn't important enough to mention earlier: the game is pretty amateurish in its presentation of medical procedure. The scientists handle the intern's cannula without disinfection, they leave blood spittle on reused equipment (that also does not get disinfected), and if you have some knowledge of these things, be prepared that this game does worse than even a bad TV show in that regard. These are minor details that didn't affect my personal enjoyment, but they are noticeable enough to potentially be an immersion breaker for some players.
