_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: On a pure craftsmanship level, The Complex is a solid entry in the FMV genre. Production values are decent enough to compete with cheap TV shows, the lead actress does a fine job and the side characters a passable one. It would be unfair to expect Oscar level performances here.For me, there was enough story and developing relationships between characters to feel entertained. There's a few minor twists and surprises, and the occasional joke.My main gripe is that the game boasts with having 9 endings. In reality, there are two depending on a choice made fairly late in the game, with a couple of variants depending on who liked you how much. And there is a third ending you can get after a few choices in, which is more a tongue in cheek ending than a serious one.Also there are a few situations where you have to pick one person out of multiple but regardless end up with the same result. This felt very annoying because you waste time replaying for nothing. Thankfully you can skip scenes you've already seen, so the waste of time is limited.I recommend to play it until you found the ending where everybody dies (bonus points for you being about to die soon). And after that just watch a youtube video about the other endings.Nevertheless, for the most part I enjoyed my time with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this after getting 3 of the 9 possible endings. I'm pretty sure I've had my monies worth by now and I'll probably come back to it in the future.Production value is decent though don't expect a big budget extravaganza. Use of the available sets was good and the cinematography was professional enough though some of the cgi was at times bad enough to distract from the effective storytelling. Acting was on point. There are points where some of the decisions seems a little arbitrary but along with the main story effecting decisions there are decisions that can effect relationships with various characters, this can lead to extra scenes or in some cases effect the available paths to one of the 9 endings. FMV games will always be a hard sell for hardcore gamers but this fills the gap between a passive movie watching experience and a hands on gaming experience.To say this is a great game for people who aren't gamers seems a bit negative but I don't mean it that way. This would be a good alternative to netflix and chill.If what I've said so far hasn't put you off so far you should probably give it a go. As FMV games go this is a good one. Wales Interactive also made 'Late Shift' and in my opinion they seem to have taken what they learned from making that to come up with something better.I bought this game on the release date and would strongly recommend that you avoid watching any of the inevitable play-through's and don't waste the experience by following a walk-through. There are enough clues in the story to help you realise what you should and shouldn't be doing and the end of game analysis should give you ideas about other ways to approach the story.If you're at all interested in FMV games this is not going to disappoint. If you don't know what an FMV game is this might not be your cup of tea, Personally I was impressed.

There is SOME tolerably good acting.  Plot is weak, with a particularly bad fail right at the beginning.  Details would be a spoiler but just can't be made to make sense with the later story. _childDocuments_.review: My third foray into the genre of interactive film (the others being  and ), The Complex delivered as expected. If you’ve never “played” an interactive film, it can serve as a good entry point. Otherwise, it really depends on much you enjoy this style.Good cinematography, decent acting and soundtrack, all the trademarks of a high-quality TV production are present. Like many other titles in this genre, one may find The Complex a bit short, but there’s isn’t any way around this, for financial reasons (production cost mainly).In comparison to other titles like this, The Complex offers better UI, settings options, a good array of subtitle languages and, above all, a good skip scene mechanic after you finish your first playthrough. This is essential given that this style usually tries to offer many different endings and paths, so having to rewatch bits you already seen once can be cumbersome.However, I must say that even though the game does offer different endings, some of its variations are very minor, not qualifying as different endings in my opinion. Not only that, but the consequences of your actions throughout the story offer little variance, leaving something to be desired.Even though I still contend that  is the best I’ve played so far in this genre, I still fully enjoyed the experience and would recommend it if you have the inclination for this style.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: My least favorite of the Ultimate FMV bundle. It's not "so bad it's good". It's obvious a lot of work went into this game but for me it fell flat.It has the usual compilation of things we expect in a proper FMV game since maybe Harvester - mediocre to sub-par acting, obvious green screens, cheap looking costumes and sets, drone footage (the crack cocaine of independent movie making in last few years), obvious mistakes that could be solved by using Wikipedia. Funniest one was the  - there was obvious lack of any sort of advisers participating - chemistry student or a medical student would probably make a massive improvement.Much like in the screenplay a chemistry adviser was needed on the set - or maybe not, because there was no chemistry.Don't get me wrong - these are the things I am fine with. But the game commits the cardinal sin of interactive fiction - the choices made did not feel like they had any impact. At that point, you are watching a B movie, not playing a B movie game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those cases where a neutral recommendation would be best...- The story is interesting.- The gameplay is intuitive.- The acting is decent.- One playthrough without skipping is about ~70-80 minutes- "Replayability"The reason I put quotes is the same reason I don't recommend this (at $9). While you do unlock a skip function after finishing the story, there is no "scene select". If you wanted to make all the same choices except the last one, you have to play through the whole thing again. I didn't have the motivation to do that, effectively giving me just over an hour of gameplay for $9.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of fun, very interesting story. My only complaints are that there are a few pretty amateurish scenes, particularly one where the characters are poorly greenscreened into a wide open warehouse-like building. Additionally there are a handful (I can think of 2 or 3) decisions that you can make that don't sound too bad until you actually make the decision - in one case  Some of the acting and dialogue is pretty meh, particularly one character who constantly wise-cracks jokes while near death throughout the early-mid part of the game.I've only played through once and got one of the endings, so I can't really say how much the choices actually matter but for <$10 it's more than worth it. I do love that the game lets you skip through scenes you've already seen on future playthroughs which is weirdly uncommon in these movie-games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: No spoilers except that I reached the Perceptive ending upon my first and only (as of this review) playing of The Citadel.Pro: player gets to think like a believable scientist in a realistic thriller settingCon: there are points in the plot where a choice could have been a great fit but wasn't utilized by the game itselfPro: even though I don't agree with every twist and turn in the game, I think the studio deserves credit for making something which couldn't have been made this well in the pastCon: in the final third of the game, there were two points where I got the impression that the game ignored my choice and did what it wanted to in order to make the plot workPro: Overall, I'm glad I bought and played The ComplexCon: I'm not sure if I want to play it again, but that's because I don't regret any of the decisions I made during my first playthrough.Pro: the sets, costumes, props, acting, etc. were at that Goldilocks zone between labor-of-love versus prohibitively expensive to make. (and between indie student film versus profits-uber-alles megastudios) Con: on three (but only three) moments in the plot where I thought I saw an important clue, only to find out in a couple of scenes that it was probably not a clue but simply a scene which was accidentally written unclearly as to what the player sees.Pro: I was in the mood to watch a science fiction thriller intrigue mystery movie, but I wasn't in the mood to watch a two-hour long movie or any the-first-three-seasons-are-awful-but-the-final-two-seasons-are-so-good series. I was in the mood to play a video game, but I wasn't in the mood to play a game where I had to invest a lot of time learning the controls, grinding, listening to bratty players get mouthy to players who wanted to try out multiplayer, or requiring weeks to earn upgraded armor named Rusted Weak Chestpiece Scraps -2. With The Complex, I got to enjoy an immersive, intelligent movie where I had a say in what sort of dilemmas a protagonist made. It was a worthy after-work one-evening activity for me tonight.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting choose-your-adventure movie. Good acting from the main character, and a surprisingly good visual quality for what I'm sure was a low-budget production. Definitely worth at least two playthroughs to see the different outcomes of your choices. I love the ability to skip scenes you've already watched (a feature that "Late Shift" sorely lacks). First playthrough takes around 80 minutes, and finding the rest of the endings in other playthroughs take about the same amount of total time thanks to the "skip scene" ability.The "relationship tracker" is an interesting feature, since some of the endings depend on how well you treated various characters throughout the movie. * Some of the choices early on referenced specific character names before I had a chance to learn them (especially on the first playthrough). How about adding the character names next to their pictures on the Stats screen so they are easy to reference?* Almost all of the possible endings played off the same two "ultimatum" scenes: . I was pleasantly surprised to find a hidden ending after the ambulance choice on another playthrough. Please add more endings that branch off from mid-game choices, so that not everything is determinant on the same final scenes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, excellent pacing, acting and production. To be very clear here it is story and character first, adding then in interactive elements to nudge the narrative different directions. No character trees, no RPG elements, no 100 hr gameplay, just a very concise and compelling nugget with characters you care about and encouraging you to play through all versions. Well done :)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a FMV based in an alternative near future. You play as Dr. Amy Tenent, a microbiologist and genetic engineer that works for a company, called Kennsington Corp. You've worked for them for 4 years when things really go downhill. An intern at your company suddenly takes sick and you have to leave an important business meeting to deal with it. Then, your ex shows up. Talk about a bad day at work!In this FMV, you will mainly be watching a movie and just making choices as you go through it. The choices determine your relationships with other characters and what ending (there are 9 of them) that you will receive. Your choices do matter in this game. PROS:The movie was well done. The acting was good. The characters were interesting and engaging.Achievements aren't too hard to accomplish (I have 100%) and you can get them pretty quickly, just not on 1 playthrough.After playing once, you can skip scenes that you've already seen in subsequent playthroughs.CONS:Requires multiple playthroughs to accomplish all endings and achievements. Fairly short.Would suggest you get the game when it's on sale as it isn't an extremely long game. However, it is completely worth buying and playing, especially if you like FMV games anyway. It's definitely top tier for its genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I recommend this game for others, there are some slight hitches that are quite annoying.  The story IS engaging and it isn't TERRIBLE acting, though I found myself talking to the characters out loud like I would in a movie I've never seen.  It flows pretty well as far as pausing for making decisions and such.However, at the time of this review, they still haven't fixed the screen jumpiness, though there are unofficial workarounds posted on the forums.  You can't go back an revisit a decision.  So for example, my game ended abruptly because I chose wrong and the game ended with no real ending other than a fade-in of one of the endings.  I couldn't reload to that decision to make it again - instead I have to play through to that point again, which is a HUUUUUGE waste of time.  They claim this is supposed to be like the old "Choose Your Own Adventure" books, and in most cases it is; however, books you can go back to the point of failure and choose again, unlike this game.  Related to going back, the game does NOT have a coherent checkpoint or saving structure.  I had to quit once or twice because life happened and I had to play through about 15-20 mins of game time (and remember my choices) to get back to where I was when I initially quit.  It would have have been a ton wiser to include a SAVE GAME option to pick up exactly where you left off - just like opening to a bookmarked page in a novel.  I give it a Solid 7 out of 10

Sure, but i'd expect her character to be visibly more in charge and a much more driven personality. Alas, blinkey eyes girl more often looks like a deer caught in the headlights.Furthermore in the first 15 minutes all male characters are stereotyped as little more than superficial douchebags while all women seem to be troubled victims by said douchebags, which isn't a great motivation to go on. _childDocuments_.review: Strong points. --------------- I definitely enjoyed the game. The acting was between okay and good. I think the lead actress did her job very well. I'd like to see her other works. The overall production quality of the game is high. Costumes, menu design, etc. = perfect! Weak points. -------------- At times, the story was a bit dumb, though. Characters were slightly difficult to relate to. Most of them were unlikable. My real concern here is that, they didn't conduct themselves in a manner a scientist would have. A bit like that, yeah, but not really. Perhaps you guys could check out some of the early star trek episodes, to see how a science-fiction problem is presented there, and handled by scientists. I think maybe more emphasis on science-fiction, with the science part in bold, would have made the game more intelligent. I'd have loved to hear more information about the subject in question. How to improve it: - put more mystery in it, by focusing more on the science-fiction part- introduce mystery gradually- suspense should increase higher, try to give people chills, make them sweat- introduce suspense more gradually- make it less about drama between people, the focus was almost entirely on that- if there is lab equipment there, then scientists would use it. they'd not focus on relationships with other people, they'd be there to solve a terrifying, bone-chilling problem. they'd do it rationally, effectively. - make it episodic (?) or longer- learning skills takes time. i won't be able to hack into a computer system, just because i'm sitting before it. unless they designed the system, no engineer will be able to just sit down and do whatever they want, immediately. - biolab security design = cool. but dumb. although, if it was the government doing it, it'd be believable. - biolab design = super dumb. i didn't like the escape route. i'd put something more intelligent there. also the vents..... super dumb. - multiple-choices.....    1) "trap choices" = well.... it's good, that there are such paths. not really needed though. does not serve much purpose here.      2) overall choices. could have been better. try reading "Heart of Ice" from Dave Morris, to see how a multiple-choice story should be told. (Heart of Ice is a gamebook = multiple-choice book, one of the best ones) Personal dislikes. ------------------ - didn't like the male lead character- didn't like the role the male lead character played in the story = he was a jackass. a weak character. that's not what men are like, who were forged in a highly competitive environment- didn't like the main kindarian girl, and the role she played in the story = her background was good, but for the most part, she functioned as a distraction in the story. - didn't like it, that people were hired to work in a biolab, without background checksGeneral advice. watch an episode of house md. to see how a little bit of biology / medicine can be introduced into the story, in an entertaining way, such that the show is still about people. people don't understand what the doctors are talking about, but they love the show anyway. watch early star trek to see how problem solving can be introduced into the story. find and read the best multiple-choice books, to see how multiple-choices can be introduced into the story. i don't regret supporting the creators. it was fun. a bit short though. looking forward to your next work.

_childDocuments_.review: The Complex is an interactive movie/FMV game that's about 1.5 hours long, but due to choices it gives and different outcomes, it has some replay value. It takes place in a modern day London and revolves around the use of new biotechnology and how it goes out of control, as well as politics surrounding it. Most of the story takes place inside the lab complex itself, as the main character, Dr Amy Tenant, and her colleague, Dr Rees Wakefield, attempt to find out how the experimental biotech got out and who's responsible. More problems add into the mix, and the two scientists then have to make hard decisions and find a way out of the lab complex alive. It's a nicely-paced and gripping plot with well-developed characters and some interesting twists along the way.The gameplay is mainly about making choices from time to time in some scenes. Some choices have a big impact, although many don't change the outcome much and mostly just alter something in the scenes. There are 8 different endings, although some of them are very much alike. However, it is worth replaying the movie so to experience a few of them. After playing through it once, it then becomes possible to skip scenes we've seen already, so you can go through the scenes much more quickly and jump straight to the choices.There are some statistics given at the end, such as relationship percentage with different characters and personality profile, but these don't play much of a role in the outcomes.Generally the presentation is good. Acting is good, the setting and locations are well-designed, action and special effects are decent. It's closer to being a movie than a game. However, the number of choices that require player input are plenty, and some of them can be a bit tough on a moral level and would make you think afterwards.Overall, this is a nicely-designed and gripping interactive movie. It is more or less linear until the very end, so many of its choices might seem like they have too little of an effect, but it is a good story worth checking out. Whether you're familiar with FMV games or are new to them, The Complex is a solid recommendation.For a more in-depth review, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, The Complex falls well short of expectations.The Bunker and also Late Shift gave me a lot of joy and my expectations for The Complex were accordingly high. Unfortunately, this interactive movie can't meet my expectations in the least.The story seems extremely constructed and I couldn't identify with any of the characters. They have no depth and you get to know, at least up to the moment when I quit the game, extremely little about their motivation or background. That was the case after about 60 minutes. Because the characters are so superficial and some appeared out of place (I can't tell if it's the actors or the dialogue direction) I realized after about 15 to 20 minutes that I didn't care what options I chose and after 60 minutes I was so bored that I didn't care at all how the story ends.If the story hadn't been so boringly staged, with so many logical flaws, it would have had potential. That's a pity, because after Late Shift I was actually sure that I would like The Complex. Late Shift also doesn't offer the most believable story, but at least it is told in an interesting way, so that you wanted to know what effects the decisions you made had. The Complex seems to me as if they tried to cut a script that was planned for 2 hours down to 80-90 minutes and than rigorously cut away everything that connects the different story elements and characters.But not everything is bad about the game/film. I really liked the cinematography, the special effects look good, even if especially some technical, visual gimmicks seem a bit out of place or over the top, and the option to pause during decisions, which is especially interesting for streamers or if you are generally playing with several people, I think is a great idea. But unfortunately this is not enough to hide the dull characters and the weak story.While in Late Shift the impression was still given that decisions made actually affect the story, here the feeling arises that most of the decisions are trivial. Should I use tool A or B to get to C? This is not very interesting if the result is inevitably C. It gives the impression that the decisions almost exclusively affect the graphs in the main menu with the characters' attributes and this is simply not enough. It's possible that these graphs of percentages will affect the final scene, but the path to it seems to be extremely linear.In my opinion, there's nothing to complain about in the technical execution. The decisions to be made fit smoothly into the sequence and are well placed. Without a doubt, this is an interactive movie. Unfortunately it is much too linear to be an interesting interactive movie.Maybe I made the mistake to raise my expectations too high. I was firmly convinced that I will write a positive review - but only until I started playing the game.I know that WI can do better and that's what I hope for the next interactive movie.(This review has been reworked. WI answered to my previous posting.)

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Good FMV quality✅Multiple endings✅Scene skip option for watched scenes➖Low quality CGI➖Some choices are ignored or don’t matter➖Disappointing conclusion(s)Game World: The Complex takes place as a large scientific research center in London called the Kensington Complex. Being that this is a FMV game, there isn’t so much of a game world to traverse, this is a legitimate movie, so the settings are based on real life locations of London, with the fictional government of Kindar portraying the protagonists.Narrative: The story consists of a new technology, nanotech, being introduced. Nanotech is described as a type of cellular technology that inhabits a host's bloodstream to render aid if needed. Within the first 30 minutes, you find that the nanotech has been injected into a person who is now infectiously able to transmit nanotech via blood-to-blood transmission. As a player you often have between 2-4 choices to make at any given time to influence the situation you're in. There were times when the choice I made didn’t matter and another character did the choice I wasn’t going to do anyways, but most of the time the choices you made will determine who lives, dies, and the ending you get. There are 9 endings in total, and with the ability to skip already viewed scenes, it’s a much better experience than Late Shift’s version of having to replay the entire story over from the beginning each time. I would say the only thing that I don’t enjoy about The Complex was the ending. No matter which one I went with, I just didn’t feel like the endings were strong enough. The beginning and middle are intriguing and kept me engaged, but I was disappointed with the end. Length: I 100%’d the game in a little over 3 hours. Mechanics: This is a FMV game, so the mechanics are very simple - you simply choose an option. In Complex, there is another angle where the choices you make also impacts the relationships of other characters and how they view you. So if you treat a character badly, their relationship will decrease which may impact future scenes with that character in a negative way. Makes sense from a logical relationship standpoint, but Complex takes it a step further and adds a visual indication of relationships for each character via the stats menu. Aside from the relationship part, the game is simply choosing an option, so like most FMVs it's mechanically sparse. Difficulty: None, you just choose options. Quality: Quality is FMV. Looks solid, like a HD movie. No issues with the UI either. The only minor thing is all the CGI looks atrociously bad. The drone part in particular was laughable. Performance: I encountered no performance issues or bugs.i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDSound Effects: No complaints with the sound, it was as good as any movie is. Music: Music is sparse, not much music here, but what was present fit with the theme of a near-future type score. There are 9 endings to watch, and thankfully with the skip scene feature, watching them all isn’t as cancerous as Late Shift. Still, once you finish those 9, there is no reason to replay, unless you like rewatching movies. I felt The Complex had a weaker plot than Late Shift, but Complex at least had the basic tools that allowed me to “Explore” as best you can in an FMV game. I enjoyed the first 2/3rds of Complex, but of the 9 endings, even including the “Canon” ending, I think it just wraps up too quickly without a real element of danger. I would recommend this game if you don’t mind FMVs, it's one of the better ones I played. You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: The Complex is an FMV, or essentially, a choose your own adventure film. It follows the story of Amy, a researcher researching the potential of nanocells as a universal panacea. When her nanocells are stolen from her lab, however, she finds herself thrust into the midst of a heist, an international conspiracy, and a bevy of moral dilemmas. Much like any other FMV, the gameplay is less centred around movement or gameplay as such, but rather on making choices and watching their consequences play out. The Complex, specifically, focuses on Amy’s relationship with those around her, and uses those relationships to shape which scenes play and how storybeats play out. While the decision points are ordinarily quicktime events - and I played the game with them as such - there is the option to pause these events and deliberate on the options. I’ll get it out of the way - there is a lot about the plot of the Complex that makes no sense. The science makes no sense. The set-up makes no sense. There are logical skips and jumps that don’t follow from one another, plot threads that go nowhere, and the occasional plot hole that has to be dodged. Storywise, it is not the greatest story ever told, nor does it always make sense. It’s a story that asks for disbelief to not only be suspended, but perhaps airlifted out of the picture entirely for its own safety. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, nor do I think it’s particularly the game’s fault. A certain amount of disjointedness is inevitable when a story has to incorporate a myriad of different choices a player might make at any given time. Indeed, the Complex does a fairly good job of remaining coherent within the understanding that players’ choices might go any number of ways. What is a bit more problematic is the shallowness of the choices presented, or the presentation of a false choice. Part of the game’s mechanics is Amy’s personality and her relationship with those around her. Interestingly, despite the game’s plot being a high stakes action plot, the game itself remains fairly concerned with how Amy relates to those around her, and how her choices relate to them specifically. It’s never particularly clear how any given choice moves these stats, or what a choice actually entails. Seemingly minor choices that make sense in the moment might have outsize consequences, with no indication to the player that they might do so. As an example, the choice of whether or not to undress in front of a male colleague apparently has potentially as large an impact on Amy’s relationship with him as choosing whether or not to save him later. For a game that focuses so heavily on player choice, not making it clear what the impact of that choice is, or even what action stems from it limits how meaningful that choice can actually feel. Similarly, on multiple occasions, I made a choice, only to have the game railroad me into the opposite choice. I would choose to accept a phone call, only for my companion to reject the call. While I again understand there are a limited number of strands the story can follow, presenting a false decision point raises the question of what the distinction in all the other decision points actually is. It makes all subsequent decisions feel less meaningful, as there’s always the lingering suspicion that nothing I choose makes a difference either way.Still, I can’t deny that I had a lovely time with the Complex. As silly as its story might get, and as shallow as the decision points are, it still presents its mishmash of a story well, and immerses the player in the world. The world never felt quite believable, but that didn’t mean it felt meaningless. The Complex fills the same niche as a popcorn action movie - fast fun that flashes by, hoping the viewer doesn’t dig in deeper, but knowing that it doesn’t matter either way.

I managed to get them all but it took me around 40-50 playthroughs, and the last scenes were very elusive. Skipping scenes greatly helps, though, but like I mentioned, this is purely optional and not worth hunting for most players.Overall, I enjoyed this title and can easily recommend it on sale if you’re a fan of the genre. _childDocuments_.review: In "The Complex," you find yourself thrust into a gripping narrative where every choice you make shapes the outcome of the story. Set within a secretive research facility, you take on the role of a protagonist faced with a life-or-death situation. As the tension builds, you must navigate through a maze of moral dilemmas and intense encounters, with the fate of multiple characters hanging in the balance.Your adventure begins when an experimental bio-weapon is unleashed, threatening to cause widespread devastation. As chaos ensues, you must decide how to respond, making choices that will determine the course of events. Along the way, you'll encounter a cast of intriguing characters, each harboring their own secrets and motivations.As you delve deeper into the complex, you'll uncover a web of conspiracies, forcing you to question whom you can trust. Your decisions will not only impact your own survival but also shape the lives of those around you. The game presents you with branching paths, offering multiple possibilities and endings based on the choices you make.A captivating choose-your-own-adventure movie awaits, where your decisions shape the course of the story. As you immerse yourself in the film, you'll find yourself making choices based on your own instincts, allowing you to experience the thrill of living through those exhilarating situations.The Complex is a gripping and atmospheric FMV (Full Motion Video) game that seamlessly blends live-action footage with interactive storytelling. Brace yourself for an intense and alluring experience as you step into the shoes of the protagonist, making choices that will shape the outcome of the game.At the heart of this immersive journey lies the enigmatic Dr. Amy Tenant, portrayed by Michelle Mylet  who brings a seductive magnetism to the character. Her presence is electrifying, creating an air of mystery and sensuality that lingers throughout the game. As you unravel the intricacies of the story, the tension between desire and danger becomes palpable, drawing you deeper into Dr. Tenant's web of secrets.The FMV aspect of the game adds a unique layer of realism and engagement. You'll find yourself immersed in a world where the boundaries between reality and fiction blur, as you navigate through stunningly filmed scenes and interact with live actors. This dynamic approach elevates the storytelling, allowing you to connect with the characters on a more personal level.Throughout your journey, you'll encounter a series of morally challenging choices. These decisions have a significant impact on the storyline, driving the narrative in divergent directions and presenting you with various outcomes. The weight of responsibility hangs in the balance as you grapple with complex moral dilemmas, making every choice a thought-provoking and suspenseful experience.Visually, The Complex is a treat for the eyes. The cinematic production values are evident in every frame, immersing you in a world that is both visually stunning and emotionally charged. From the meticulously crafted sets to the nuanced performances of the actors, the game's attention to detail creates an immersive and captivating experience.The gameplay mechanics of The Complex are designed to keep you on the edge of your seat. As thns.e story unfolds, you'll find yourself engrossed in a web of intrigue and suspense. Your choices not only affect the immediate outcome but also shape the development of the characters and the overall narrative arc. This interactive element adds a layer of agency, immersing you in a world where your decisions truly matter.The Complex is a tantalizing and suspenseful FMV game that pushes the boundaries of interactive storytelling. With its captivating performances, immersive visuals, and morally complex choices, it offers an experience that blurs the lines between gaming and cinema. If you're seeking an atmospheric and engaging journey filled with steamy suspense and thought-provoking decision-making, then The Complex is a must-play."

_childDocuments_.review: Wow this is fantastic.  The quality of the movie you are effectively writing as you go is incredible.  Yes it has 8 endings - one playthrough took me 90 minutes and I cannot wait to "play" it again - but it just is not really a video game, in the best sense.  The acting sucks you in immediately.  Some of the choices are very strong opposites of each other, but there is such a variety.  It is a far more subtle system than the Store page lets on.  The final over-the-moon moment for me was a detailed page at the end (spoiler free if you wanted to share with friends) where it has all of the stats you raised or lowered with your actions, that the engine used to determine what options to give you, and you realize just how many scene *and options* were hidden from you because of those scores. So far, best game of 2023 for me.  And i dont play this genre of games at all.  I only bought it because a friend of mine loves these and I wanted to try it out while on sale before gifting it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty good interactive movie game. Gameplay wise, they did great because they allowed to skip scenes you already saw, and they also gave you the option to pause when there is a decision, which are 2 mandatory things to add in this genre.The story is pretty good, not great, but solid, with a few weird things. Actors are good overall.A few drawbacks:The different endings are a bit disappointing, it's pretty much tied to 2 decisions, which gives you 8 endings, some of them are quite similar.The game is really short, even when trying to find different endings. I played 4 games, then decided it was playthrough time to get the 5 remaining endings: a bit more than 3 hours, which is a bit short for the price, but I understand that this is pretty costly to make.Really enjoyed the moment anyway, need more games like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: The Complex is technically polished, with seamless transitions between scenes and beautiful-looking HD video. _childDocuments_.review: The Complex is essentially an interactive Sci-Fi Original Movie™, and I gotta say as a fan of the melodramatic, low budget camp that implies, it's safe to say I was primed to enjoy this game from the out. It's essentially a sequence of choices, and you watch how the scenes play out. For an FMV game, the acting is better than I was expecting, though that wasn't a high bar, and the story was compelling if brief. I enjoyed the intrigue and wondering where it would go, and with the game having multiple endings it was easy to go back and see what could be done differently once I finished since you can skip scenes you've encountered already. It's not mind blowing or anything, but it's a fun linear romp. The only negative I can say is the endings leave a bit of a sour taste afterwards. But I wouldn't say the spoiled it for me or anything like that. I'd probably pick it up on sale, but it's a good evening's time!

_childDocuments_.review: Another interactive movie. If you hate this genre of gaming this product won't change your mind. Having only played two of these type of games, I am no expert. However I have watched thousands of films. As a film, it would be slightly above average. Maybe a B+ film. Good production, good acting, good story. Since I hate anything having to do with medicine, my opinion may be a bit skewed. But I am a fan of sci-fi, and this movie deals with technology gone wrong, a sci fi trope since Frankenstein. The tech this time is nanotechnology. Like the Borg. The only real game element is choosing what the actor does on screen. There are lots of choices. Some involve people dying. Some involve nothing more than whether to answer a phone. These choices lead to 9 different endings and 196 scenes. My three hours of play allowed me to get 5 endings and over a hundreds scenes. This involved 5 play-throughs. The first one took an hour and a half. About what you would expect from a movie. The last one took 10 minutes thanks to the skipping game mechanic. The five endings are quite different. The extra scenes are not so different. At this point I have lost interest in doing any more runs. I am having to wade through too much repetition to get to anything new. The game needs the chapter system used by Detroit: Become Human. In that game you see every pathway (the result is covered until you reveal it through game play). With this system in place the gamer could skip over having to redo the whole story every play-through. Conclusion: do you like movies? Yes? This is a movie with 9 different endings. May become tedious if played too many times in a row. May be overpriced if more than $10.

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy my playthrough of The Complex, but I wanted to like it so much more. The scenario has promise, but it's let down by a myriad of small mistakes that tar the experience. Let's break out the list:- Characters have flip-flop style mood and relationship swings without any real warning, which makes it hard to know if you're supposed to trust a character that suddenly does an about-turn on their previous attitude towards you.- One character meaninglessly withholds plot elements (even after they start telling you incriminating stuff) until the game needs to move the story forward. Furthermore, they only half-heartedly and cryptically attempt to explain elements of their backstory, which makes it impossible to understand whether they're on your side or not, but they also don't really have any reason to be as cryptic as they are given the point the story's at.- Another character voices their ethical opinion on something in a way that's portrayed as humane and kind, and it's done so in a way that feels very genuine. This same character then later reveals they're basically evil incarnate, but they still believe in their initial position somehow? There's definitely an argument to be made about how detached the character is to the latter ethics situation while the former is much more involved, so, while both  be held by someone, the real issue is that the character's two positions aren't presented coherently enough to allow us to understand how they hold both at the same time.- Another character has almost nothing to do with the organisation and yet is talked to as if they're intimately involved and have major authority over elements in play, which they clearly wouldn't do in the real world.- I wasn't really sold on the protagonist's position in the story. She's presented as someone that's been through tough stuff and now she's a bit callous and dedicated to her work. She clearly has the chops to call the shots and be a leader type. It would make more sense for us to be watching her making decisions, rather than making them for her. With us making the decisions then she suddenly looks all indecisive and unclear, which I don't think would be the case for the kind of character she is. Indecisiveness works in other FMV titles like Late Shift (the protagonist is a relatively young person very much out of their depth) and Five Dates (the protagonist is dating, which is inherently awkward and there aren't necessarily easy, right answers), but it's a really bad look on a character like The Complex's protagonist.- Furthermore, in one of the endings, the protagonist pulls (directly from her rear) a hitherto completely undisclosed major backstory element that you've been given no hint of up to that point and would've massively informed your decision-making throughout the story. And the really bizarre part is this backstory beat only exists BECAUSE of that ending. If you take another ending then that whole element of her backstory simply doesn't exist. What? The whole point of a character's  is that they're fixed  the plot as we see it takes place. Instead, The Complex decided it could just slip a new element in when it feels like and not have it be consistent across endings. Utterly bizarre.- The story as told isn't super clear about what the plot priority is at any given moment. When you start then priority A is a clear and pressing issue, but almost as soon as you get going on A then you're given priority B and A is basically abandoned, despite A being critical. I kept wondering "when're we going to get round to the very urgent A?" The story does provide a weak justification for this, but the timescale doesn't really add up in terms of how critical A is presented as and yet the situation seemingly doesn't get any worse when you're told earlier it will.- You're presented with a few choices that're actually just made for you regardless of what you pick (presumably because the writers couldn't think of a way out of the path it would take you down if you were allowed to take it). Conversely, there were also some moments that felt like obvious opportunities for decisions that were never offered, I'm guessing production limitations cut these moments off at the neck.- There's one scene where a character's dialogue straight up gets cut off mid-sentence by the scene after it.- Pauses between conversation moments in general felt stilted in a lot of places.On an individual basis, none of these are significant, but you're gonna be seeing at least one of these in most scenes and it really jars your playthrough. Overall, an okay FMV game, and I suspect the story and characters were decently developed in pre-production, but it just translated badly into the game.

_childDocuments_.review: If the story is relatively forgettable even in its more ridiculous possible permutations, it’s the dialogue which truly sinks much of the promise; chock full of cringe-worthy attempts at humour that evoke an undeniable “straight-to-video” vibe, and that’s when it’s not busy piling soulless, robotic exposition on top of the player/viewer.My first run through the game took around 75 minutes, while racking up a few repeat runs and discovering most of the available content brought that up to around three hours, though my interest – and, I imagine, that of most players – had tapered off a good while before that. The Complex is desperately lacking the narrative meat necessary to support its promising presentation, so only the most ardent FMV game fans need apply.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: It feels more of a movie than a game, but the interactive aspect makes it more interesting than going to the cinema.The visuals, cinematography and direction are all top-notch - far above any other interactive game I've seen.The game-play however is the weak element.I wasn't able to alter the volume of the music independently of the speech, so using a poor-quality set of headphones I could barely make out the speech over the music.The game doesn't offer a save/load option, so there's no opportunity to start playing, then pause and pick up again along different paths, nor is there any option to fast-forward or roll back, as you would expect with an AVN.Enjoyable, but demands a concerted period of time to sit down and give it justice.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: Playing The Complex is like watching an interactive made-for-TV medical disaster film, with all the lapses in logic that entails. The production values are decent enough, though there aren't very many branching options. Most decisions are binary and only affect which reaction video you see, after which the story continues unchanged. On the plus side, reaching any ending unlocks a skip feature for later playthroughs.Get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: That was good. The story was simplistic, but still engaging due to the good pace, good acting and likable characters. I got the Stalemate ending on my first playthrough, and despite its (obvious) disadvantages for pretty much all of the characters, it punctuated the "greater good" aspect of "my" Amy's philosophy quite well. I will probably replay this again in a few years to see a different side of her, Rees and the other characters. Overall I feel this was a really good FMV with a good length for interactive movies (~80 minutes).
_childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: Don't waste your life / money on this one. As a game, the technical implementation is all right - it doesn't crash, I didn't encounter bugs and was able to complete the game. It's not possible to pause the movie portions and there's no save option so if you want to see all endings, you'll have to replay from the beginning. (You won't want to, trust me.)Movie quality is decent and the music is passable. Some of the sets / props are decent; most are just ok.Now for the negatives:- Incompetent, idiotic writing. Kindergarten plays have more coherent, thought-out stories with fewer cliches. The whole thing is just so, so very stupid, it's really hard to describe it.- There are more plot holes than story.- The "science" is just... moronic. This goes hand-in-hand with the bad writing but as a sci-fi story (heavily focused on science), this is criminally bad.- Acting ranges from mediocre to poor; I'd really prefer not seeing any of these actors in movies in the future. Everyone would be better off if they switched to other professions.I liked the X-Files Game and Gabriel Knight: The Beast Within so it's not the genre (FMV game) that is the problem - this one is just really poorly done.I could keep going but you probably see the pattern already. I played through once and couldn't get myself to try again. Do yourself a favor and avoid it.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't want to be too negative but I'm highly disappointed. First the basic story seemed too corny but I hoped the writer will surprise me with a good twist or something, but no (I mean there is a twist but not something I wouldn't think of).Also it has too many plot holes and I think it's not acceptable for a game where the key element is the story itself.The environment and the costumes are fancy and I can see the budget was big, but that doesn't explain why the acting is so bad. _childDocuments_.name: The Complex

_childDocuments_.review: I did buy this on offer for about £5. After finishing I was told I'd found 1/9 endings and I'd watched about 88 scenes out of about 166. So I see a lot of replay value.Production and editing, I felt I was watching a movie, a box office movie. Sound, visuals, story line, acting and plot second to none. I have seen reviews saying the acting is poor, oh not so at all. Maybe one actor is a bit below par but he's hardly in it. All the main actors and supporting actors are first class. Even the baddies that have small parts were plenty good enough for the story. Clever twists along the way, a very solid and engrossing story. The only problem was, I read too many negative reviews and so I was just looking too closely to the acting trying to see how bad it "supposedly" was. I will be playing this again to get more endings and now I won't be focusing on the acting as that rubbish feedback has been put to rest. REALLY REALLY well done. Yes the interaction is minimal but it changes paths and you know, sometimes it's nice to sit back and watch a really good and clever story and get the chance to influence things along the way.Buy it and enjoy it. IF I'd bought this at full price I would still be happy.Bottom line, I have played for 88 minutes and finished it. I could ask for a refund now but even if it had only one ending, I still wouldn't ask for a refund out of respect and the enjoyment I've had from this product.

_childDocuments_.review: For starters - I played this game on the NVIDIA 465.89 driver with no glitches or crashes. I took about 80 minutes to finish the game, [completed with only 7/20 achievements, might play the other endings to obtain all the other achievements - I have watched the walk throughs for them already though.]The story was intriguing and attractive. I really enjoy the 'Choices Matter' genre of games, and The Complex was one of it. However, After playing and thinking through it, I thought that the storyline would be pretty obvious. However, the cast was really amazing and it allowed the storyline to be followed easily. There weren't much character developments, but I guess you really cant develop a character that much in 90 minutes. I still liked it though! Amy's character was the most prominent, followed by Clare and Rees. I did not really feel like the other characters made that much else of a difference in how I would have made my decisions in the game. I enjoyed the 'Personal Tracking' and 'Relationship Tracking' part of this game quite a little bit. The fact that the different qualities were ranked based on the choices made actually allowed me to understand more about the choices that I make. This was actually a pleasant surprise. One thing that I hoped could have been better was the diversity of endings. This is because I felt that regardless, the collective ending of the game would be the same - and I honestly did not see any other way where the ending could have differed. This created the situation where I really thought - well maybe my choices did not matter after all. That being said, I've read about the Secret Ending which I have not explored

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend The Complex. The story of The Complex does pose some though-provoking questions about the cost of advancing civilization and who should sacrifice for future generations and the ethics of deciding to kill some so that many more will live. There are multiple endings to this game and the first one I got illustrated the complexity of that issue very well. There is a fundamental flaw with these choose-your-own adventure FMV games that keeps me from appreciating them. The flaw is that with so many different choices to make, realistically after only one or two meaningful choices the game would be very different very quickly and its just not plausible to produce a video game like that. So, the choices are not really meaningful at all. The overall game will still fold out essentially the same way with a few details changed. This also affects the overall story because it's so constrained to have to accommodate so many different permutations. The characters were not that great either. They were ok, I guess. Only Rees had any real likability and he was a bit of dufus still. The main protagonist was hot. She seemed way too young to even be a doctor, though, let alone be at the top of her field with years of experience. One major plus for the game (and should be a standard feature for all future interactive-movie games) is after finishing the story for the first time, you can now skip all the scenes you've already seen on subsequent play-throughs. The first time through took me 75 mins to finish. The next two times through took another 75. After a few play throughs, the story can be finished in minutes as it's just a series of clicking choices and seeing what few new scenes that round of choices led to. Overall, The Complex does have some positive aspects to it. This style of game just doesn't do it for me and I don't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: In the last couple of years, Wales Interactive have been gathering experience with FMV (Full Motion Video) games as (co-)developers and publishers. The quality of their games has visibly improved. The Complex, a thriller about a virus - uncannily released while we deal with a real pandemic - looks great and features an engaging story with a coupe of twists that will take you multiple playthroughs to fully grasp. Definitely give this a try if you like FMV, but be aware of the inherent limitations of the genre, such as the condensed story and a rather short play time. Because of the limited number of outcomes, with story branches eventually meeting again at certain points, it might feel like your choices don't always matter all that much. Overall, The Complex is a short but worthwhile interactive experience that shows Wales Interactive at the forefront of the recent resurgence of FMV.

_childDocuments_.review: For the cost of a full-priced movie ticket, you get a choose-your-own-adventure game.  You play as Amelia J. Tenent, played by actress Michelle Mylett.  Your role is as a biomedical engineer, whose developed amazing technology, with a dark side.  Through the game/movie, at the end of about half of the scenes, you get to choose how to respond.  Through this, you build or destroy relationships, which alter the course of the story, and your options available further on.  You can save your current game by exiting, but you cannot roll-back choices, nor restore from any save other than your current, active game.  You can use "S" to show your relationship and personality stats for the current run-through, and you can use TAB to skip any section you have watched before.  There are a few sections that seem to be exactly the same as others, which you cannot skip, but mostly, as you get further on in the achievement list, you can skip most options.  If you hit TAB too many times, you may skip out of a choice you meant to make differently.  I found getting to 55% achievements was pretty easy, and a few more took paying closer attention.  I needed a walk-through for the last two: "Stalemate" and "Not a People Person".  Overall, it took 4.1 hours to get all of the achievements.  If you're on a limited budget, you might find that $12 base price is too high for 4 hours of game-play.  If you consider it more like a movie + choose-your-own-adventure, then it's not too bad.  You can have a small group making decisions at the same time, and enjoying it together.  Once you get through the whole thing though, it's not really something you would go back and re-play.  It is not an overly complicated story.  The acting varies from A- to C- depending on who it is, and which scene.  The writing as a solid B+.  I'm happy I bought it, and I'm happy I got it for 25% off.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're in the mood for some 'Choose Your Own Adventure' style shenanigans, then Wales Interactive are doing a great job of keeping you entertained with their products. I played 'Late Shift' a while back, and had the opportunity to check out The Complex. The subject matter may be a little too close to the bone at the moment (what with the current pandemic affecting the world) but for those still love a good yarn about a potential virus that could wipe out humanity, then you've come to the right place. The best way to experience The Complex would be to get a friend or partner to play it with you - timewise it's about the length of a film (about 80 minutes) and whilst the writing won't be winning any academy awards anytime soon, it's making the moral choices that give you a sense of scope within the narrative. The two main scientists have a prior history together and YOUR choices will dictate how this interactive thriller ends.Usually with these types of FMV style interactive films, the acting can be a little...pants. Interestingly enough, The Complex didn't feel stilted and the actors seemed to bounce off each other, which was surprising and well-met. Some of the choices seemed a little trivial or inconsequential, and other choices seemed redundant or just there to branch other choices together.  The game has a relationship tracker - letting you know how well the other characters think of you, which means that the same choice can lead to different outcomes depending on how your previous choices affected your relationship with that character. I'm not sure if this was superficial dressing or whether this actually had a core impact on the gameplay, but it's  a fresh take that encourages replaying the game again.Pros: - Replayability (9 different endings) - Good storyline, good acting - not as stilted as other FMV type choose your own adventure games - Immersive and engaging world - Best played with a partner to encourage decision arguments and debates!Cons - Do you want to go through this multiple times to find all the endings? - dialogue and writing can be a tad far-fetched at points  - Some decisions seem inconsequential or scripted to lead to a certain linear path Check out my playthrough here:

name: Children of Silentown
detailed_description: During the day the forest is calm and peaceful.                                                                                 It is during the night that you hear the roars...                                                                                                                                    ...of monsters. Accompany Lucy and her friends in this grim, beautifully hand-drawn adventure game by the creators of Little Briar Rose, in collaboration with studio Luna2. Lucy is afraid of the forest, just like any other child: every night, the echoing roars rob her of her sleep. Not even her dreams are a safe place where she could play. People disappearing is nothing uncommon in the village, but this time, Lucy is old enough to investigate on her own. Or so she thinks. Children of Silentown is a point & click adventure game telling a mysterious and endearing story. Explore the town and its dangerous surroundings, meet its quirky inhabitants, solve puzzles and master minigames. Accompany Lucy on her adventure to get to the bottom of what is haunting the strange Silentown... if you dare. Explore Silentown in search of hints, but beware: do not enter the forest. A unique, unsettling 2D art style fitting for a mysterious, dark tale. Music plays a crucial role, and learning how to sing will help Lucy in times of need. Combine items to obtain widely unexpected results! Many quirky characters (and animals!) to interact with. Be nice to them before they disappear. Play minigames with the other children of the village! A very mean cat, programmed to mess with Lucy at any given chance. Curious, original puzzles: use a leash and a pair of shears to break into your mother’s best friend’s house, all in order to steal… a flower?!

name: Eldest Souls
detailed_description: Depths of the Forgotten - FREE EXPANSION Eldest Souls now includes ‘Depths of the Forgotten’: a free, major expansion which introduces a new and perilous region, three new bosses, a selection of special weapons, a weapon customisation system, and an all-new, obliterating ability. Entrenched within the very bowels of existence, far removed from the moon’s pale radiance, rots an ancient abyss: The Forgotten Depths. It is as these unfathomable reaches, that Eksyll caged those that no longer served his abysmal purpose; a general with naught to command; an heir of crippling malcontent; and a King, consumed with the elongation of his own hollow existence. The very world, and all within it, had long forgotten these forlorn souls, until now… Step forth into the void once more, brave warrior. For the deepest depths are calling, and froth with the bitterest vengeance. About the Game Following centuries of servitude, Man finally rebelled against the Old Gods, imprisoning these colossal calamities within the sacred walls of the Citadel. But an evil stirred within... In a final act of vengeance, the Old Gods have unleashed a great Desolation upon the world. Mankind is fading, with but a glimmer of hope remaining. Heavy is the burden that lies on one lone Warrior. Armed with a greatsword… of the purest Obsydian. Challenging Combat Fast-paced and challenging souls-like combat awaits, where every moment counts. Yet fortune favors the bold, and defeating the Old Gods may grant the player powers beyond mortal comprehension. Boss Brutality Eldest Souls focuses on the toughest and most engaging of combat encounters - the Bosses! - with each Old God presenting a new and unique challenge for the player to overcome… with fitting rewards for those who triumph! An Ancient Kingdom As you explore the labyrinthine passages, in search of the Old Gods, you’ll encounter intriguing NPCs, compelling questlines, and a series of dark and ominous mysteries. Slowly uncover the truth behind the Old Gods and their agelong imprisonment... Pixel Perfection Bask in the pixel perfection of the consecrated Citadel, dripping in gorgeous 16-bit attention-to-detail. But don’t gaze too long. This monument of Human triumph has long been forgotten, and something dark has taken root deep within. Your Build. Your Rules. Every encounter with the Old Gods presents its own unique challenge… and rewards. Claim their celestial powers to unlock a vast array of unique Talents and Abilities, ready to customize your own combat style from a multitude of combinations. FEATURES: Battle your way through a series of uniquely challenging combat encounters. Discover a cast of intriguing NPCs and questlines as you explore the ancient Citadel. Unearth the mystery of the Old Gods, before total devastation befalls the World. Bask in the glorious pixel-perfect graphic style, dripping in gorgeous attention-to-detail. Your Build. Your Rules. Customize your own combat style from a multitude of ability combinations.

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the first boss on the first try. Second boss made me so frustrated I started making monkey sounds and rattling my chair after choking at the last 1%. Third boss made me experience all 5 stages of grief (mostly anger). Then I got jumpscared by a giant crow.Pretty good so far, 10/10 would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game however I feel like the Dark souls comparisons are only to the game's detriment. This game is much more 'Titan Souls' with health bars and abilities rather than being any type of souls-like. Has a short, well crafted campaign that is more focused on replayability rather then content and the art style is a visual feast. Would highly recommend for a quiet afternoon however I'll note if you go into this thinking this will be pixel art Dark souls (not that I would blame you with how they've advertised the game) your going to be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Eldest Souls

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game, but it's very unbalanced... The first time i finished the game i didn't even understand half of the bosses' mechanics because with ANY combination of shard or skill you can just face tank 90% af the attacks and use your Dps to heal through anything.So i decided to do another playthrough with base damage and without using any skill or shard (there is even an achievement for that), and i realised that there are a lot of problems with mechanics from each boss.From lingering hitboxes, to windup animations that are the same for 3 different attacks, to attack that don't even have a startup animation, and even rng combination of attacks that make almost impossible if not impossible to not take damage (which there is also an achievement for).It's not at all a bad game, but there are better boss rush game out there.Edit: also anything outside the bossfight is forgettable, and there is not a single dialogue or codex that is worth reading
_childDocuments_.name: Eldest Souls

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps Eldest Souls is not for me. I found the game to be very difficult in ways that were more annoying than genuinely challenging. I might return to complete it one day but after beating the first handful of bosses, I needed a break and never really got back into it. If you're really into 'souls-like, boss-rush' titles or gain a lot of self-fulfillment from challenging experiences, you might enjoy this game more than I did but do yourself a favor and wait for a steep sale. - Player movement feels slow and sluggish. Enemies telegraph their moves well-enough but you're so slow that the RNG of placement for enemy attacks can sometimes make it impossible to dodge or escape an AOE in time. Dashing is overly constrained by limited usages and distance traveled. It's also very easy to get 'stuck' on a boss when you're in close proximity and trying to maneuver around them.- Battles take FOREEEEVVVVERRRRRRRR. The bosses are so beefy relative to the damage you inflict. The basic attack is basically worthless and the fully charged attack is only marginally stronger. Coupled with the nightmare that is your movement speed and considering the absurdly quick manner in which the bosses spam their fast-moving attacks, you'll spend much of a battle desperately trying to get close enough to the boss to land a hit only to chip off 1/50 of it's health bar. - The game has generally uninteresting lore. You discover little notes and talk to a handful of folks that provide small snippets of insight into the world you're playing in but you're not given any meaningful reason to care about what happened to the world or what your objectives are in fixing things. Obscurity works well in the Dark Souls series because of the pretty scenery and focus on tight gameplay but it doesn't work here when the visuals are uninspired and the mechanics feel unrefined.
_childDocuments_.name: Eldest Souls

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good. A must-play for people who like Furi, Soulslikes, or boss rush games. I bought and played this on Xbox right before Elden RIng came out, and I did it again on PC to support the developers.Also, don't listen to the negative reviews of this game. They complain about the combat being too "clunky" and the difficulty being unfair, but this is false. I completed the game and I found all of the bosses to be challenging, but fair. They just heavily punish you for reckless decisions, same thing for combat. Yes, you're only given 3 dodges that recharge slowly, but you're rewarded with a free dodge if you time it perfectly with an enemy attack. This means that rather than mindlessly panic dodging, the player is encouraged and rewarded for analyzing the boss's move set and dodging appropriately.

_childDocuments_.review: Eldest Souls is at its best when you’re dodging attacks with symphonic precision, using your giant sword to spray colorful visual effects across the screen. It’s a game that knows what it excels at, choosing to focus on intense and varied boss encounters that are as tough as they are enjoyable. Although this choice has some unwanted consequences, fans of Souls-like titles are likely to enjoy this boss-rushing journey. I’ll address it right away: when it comes to gameplay, there’s little to see aside from the boss battles. It’s clear that a lot of time went into making them, as they are entertaining to fight and come with many surprises up their sleeve, but the same can’t be said for the world you’re inhabiting. In between the blood-pumping clashes, you can explore the game’s smaller areas. Although the pixel art that forms them is pretty, the sites you’ll visit are mostly forgettable. There’s also little to do in them other than finding items that you can gift to the individuals you meet, granting you some lore exposition. I would’ve loved to see some more unique and inspired locations, and perhaps a proper reason to scour the world. With that out of the way, though, I’m pleased to report that Eldest Souls is damn good. The bosses that you’ll spend most of your time fighting offer exuberant action that will keep you on the edge of your seat as you struggle to keep up with the frantic pace, and their diversity make them complex enough to justify spending hours in battle. There’s no Bed of Chaos or Royal Rat Authority here. Each battle presents a new challenge while still not relying too much on obscure gimmicks. I was often surprised by the number of ways in which a boss could kill me, whether it’s rapid arrows, ice spikes, or a good old thrust. The game also makes use of the top-down perspective by introducing bullet hell-like segments in which dodging is the key to survival. My experience with similar titles did not come to my aid; the game obliterated me more times than I can count. By the second boss, I was sold. A captivating and varied moveset combined with foreboding music that told me just how screwed I was shaped one of the game’s highlights. But it just kept coming. The bosses got harder, my death count rose, and my warrior slowly developed a potent moveset.What makes the fights so enjoyable is how distinctive the bosses are. The first one pits you against a watchdog who’ll charge at you with a rusty sword, damage you from afar by slamming its shield into the ground, and occasionally hop around the arena. Later on, the game throws an icy warrior at you, whose frosty attacks will slow you down if you’re not too careful. No two bosses are the same — at least up until the final one, which disappointed me. It’s a good boss, but I expected something more grandiose for the finale, and it’s too reminiscent of an earlier one. Offing your enemy is so fulfilling, even if they just jarringly disappear upon their demise. Because the action is so fast-paced and the stakes so high, you rarely have time to look at the health bar on the bottom of your screen. Yes, people are busy and pressed for time these days, but I'm sure no one would mind giving the bosses a few seconds to die. Now that I’ve talked about how the bosses will kill you, it’s time for how  will kill the bosses. The lone warrior you play as wields a heavy greatsword, so your attacks will be slow but devastating. Initially, the low amount of stamina might seem too restrictive, but it provides a nice change of pace from other titles — you can’t just dance around the arena. Dodging through attacks will refill it quicklier than playing the waiting game, so you’re encouraged to face your enemy head-on. Some of the battlegrounds are also small, which forces you to grasp the enemies’ movesets. To some, the lack of multiple weapons will be worrying; won’t it limit the replayability? Luckily, the game introduces a unique progression system: upon death, a boss will drop its shard, which can be infused into one of your moves to amplify it. The shards won’t change your attacks fundamentally, but they add a welcome sense of variety.On top of this, you can choose between three play styles: Windslide, focusing on rapid movement; Berserk Slash, which allows you to charge up your fury and unleash it; and Counter, one all about deflecting attacks. Each comes with a skill tree and a special move you can use during battle. The ability to respec your skill points at any moment means that you’re free to experiment, so you don’t have to be a min-maxing god to create a powerful build. If you finish the game and decide it wasn’t challenging enough, the New Game+ mode spices up each boss and even gives them an additional attack. I was surprised when I discovered this, and I’d like to see more developers do the same. You can also replay fights from the main menu, so if you’re in love with one of the later bosses, you don’t have to play through the game again. Earlier, I mentioned the lore. Admittedly, I had trouble getting invested in it. To me, it seemed diffuse, as if concentrating on the stories surrounding the gods rather than the overarching narrative. The introduction cutscene gives a good first impression with an interesting creation myth, but the lore struggled to keep my attention afterwards. Perhaps this can be blamed on the uninspired world design. Dark Souls uses environmental storytelling to make you wonder what transpired in the locations you visit; Eldest Souls doesn’t have that benefit. When I look back on the 11 hours I spent playing Eldest Souls, I remember the exciting boss fights and interesting progression system. The game is far from perfect, but many of its flaws come from the focus on making these fights as good as possible. And when the bad parts of a game aren’t in your face the entire time, they don’t have much of an impact — at least that’s how I feel about the debut title from Fallen Flag Studio, a developer who clearly has a lot of passion for making games. If you’re looking for some boss-fighting fun, go buy this.
