_childDocuments_.review: 3.2h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. Yes (4 achievements, all are missables). No. is a short, puzzle platformer game where you need to jump between platforms to reach the other side of the screen. More stories will be revealed after you solve some puzzles, revealing more clues to what happened.- 28+5 short and simple puzzles- Smooth animations- Dialogues can be cut off if you leave the game in the middle of a dialogueIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650The game boasts beautiful-looking visuals. Both sky and water look shiny with their presentation, and the backgrounds complement them with their beauty. The parallax effect also helps to make the journey more satisfying, showing you variations of the background as you go. Sadly, the same can't be said for the character portraits. The main character looks weird whenever she's smiling and another character looks weird in the portrait. I'd rather see the characters in the small size instead - they look cuter and more compact, especially with their small eye.I don't know whether to say the story is good or bad. It will be revealed little by little as you play, and the main character will piece everything together later on. I didn't manage to know what happened at that time, but the main character was kind enough to let us know what "happened". The ending leaves me thinking for a while though, especially with the extra revelation given near the end. It makes me think back on what happened, connecting the new information that I got with the story that was given. However, the longer I think about it, the more I'm bitter about it. The ending is something that can be considered good or bad from your perspective, and some part of the story doesn't make sense to me. Still, I'm satisfied with the process - I'm just disappointed that the story wasn't as good as I thought it would be.The game is basically a puzzle platformer with a story. You will switch between solving puzzles and reading dialogues from time to time. It helps to make the puzzle solving not repetitive, although there aren't many puzzles in the first place. Judging from the number of hieroglyphs, which are the basis of the puzzles, it's safe to say there are 28+5 puzzles in total with some repetitive ones mixed in them.The puzzles themselves are unique. It still has a puzzle-platformer mechanic as its core, allowing you to jump between platforms to reach the other side. The thing is, most platforms will disappear as you jump, forcing you to find different platforms to land in. A special platform will be available to use to manipulate this mechanic: visible platforms will disappear and invisible platforms will appear if you step on it. You will have to figure out which platform you need to keep and which one you don't to solve the puzzle. Other platforms with different mechanics will also be introduced later on, increasing the difficulty.Although the puzzles can be confusing at first, it doesn't take long before you learn how they work. The puzzles will increase in difficulty as you play, although you can use brute force to solve them. I didn't know how I managed to solve the puzzles most of the time - I just jumped around between platforms until I could finish them. Those who prefer to think before attempting a puzzle might know exactly how to solve it, although those who prefer to try things around like me will just find the puzzle solved by itself. I didn't feel satisfied solving them because of it.The game isn't difficult at all - you just need to jump around the platforms to solve the puzzles, and if it doesn't work out, the game offers an option to skip them. As you can see, the game is very short even if you finished all puzzles without skipping. It only took me 3.2h to finish them all, which also includes the 15 minutes when I idled to get an achievement.Some dialogues will be cut off if you try to leave the game in the middle of a dialogue. I usually try to go to the main menu to reread some dialogues, but it turns out that saving behaves randomly: sometimes you will be able to retrigger the dialogue from the beginning, sometimes the game will save right at the moment you leave, and sometimes the game will start from a few dialogues from where you were in.Despite being a short game,  still manages to leave an impression on me. It took me a while before I could digest everything, and although I was still bitter with some of the facts, they are still good enough. The feeling that I get when I finished the game, combined with the beautiful-looking scenes, really set the mood apart. The game might not be perfect, but it is still better than most games. I could recommend it if you want to enjoy a short, relaxing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this one. I'm going to give it a thumbs up because it successfully kept me hooked with "What the hell is going on?", and the puzzles are well-designed. The 2.5 hour runtime should tell you they're not terribly difficult, but there were a few headscratchers, and they were all intuitive - there weren't any with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ solution no one could have reasonably found out on their own.The reason I'm torn, though... I won't spoil anything, but I will say that the story is the kind that makes you view everything up to that point in a completely different context, which is cool, except the more that I think about it, the less I actually like it. Once I got past the twist, I started to realize the most interesting character in the game actually has nothing to do with anything and is just there for show. And I'm sure someone will say "That's the point!", but unless the point was "Make the player regret seeing this story to its conclusion," then I'd say they whiffed. And if making players regret it *was* the point, then... well, that sucks.It's the difference between story and story-telling. The story-telling is fantastic - like I said, I was hooked. I was super interested in finding out how all of these seemingly unconnected threads came together. But the story - how it all ended up coming together - feels less and less satisfying the more I think about it. I know the old cliche is "It's not about the destination, it's about the journey!", but when the destination retroactively makes the journey less satisfying... I don't know. I will lean thumbs up because, as a narrative-driven puzzle game, it's well made (and also gorgeous). And I imagine everyone's mileage may vary for the ending. It just didn't do it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: It takes a long time for  (maitan69, 2020) to unwind itself. Information is laced into conversations with bewildering confidence in the player’s comprehension, flashbacks and lore dumps used not so much as narrative devices than stage directions. There is no clear audience insert so there is no immediate conduit by which to interpret the futuristic yet ancient world that _Evan’s Remains_ resides within. So when the pieces lock and the curtains are drawn it is almost a relief to realize the degree of abstraction the game is comfortable working in, that the player doesn’t need to understand the significance of SpyMaster or the existence of teleportation and pocket dimensions. This story is both much simpler and more ambiguous than it's set dressing suggests. is a puzzle platformer where-in Dysis, a woman in a sunhat of unknown affiliation, is searching a deserted island for Evan, a man of huge scientific importance who has voluntarily disappeared. Very quickly Dysis encounters Clover who is also exploring the island but in the hopes of discovering a lost relic able to bestow immortality. Seeing the progress Clover has already made, Dysis joins up with him and they begin traversing the island by way of a series of monuments.For most of , it is difficult to tell if the game is building towards anything. It presents as narratively ambitious, frontloading its lore and giving as much if not more time to character interactions as it does puzzle solving. But for all this, the story always feels loose, like it is only as deep as is required to hold a scene together and were a character to ask the wrong question the whole façade would come crumbling down. Then the game starts pulling out bricks itself.It happens that Clover’s quest is an elaborate decoy constructed by Evan to placate Clover’s grief. Clover is terminally ill with an unknown disease, as is his sister, Dysis (distinct from the sunhat Dysis), which is what caused him to come to this island in the first place. He knows he won’t last, but he hopes that finding this relic will let his sister live.Evan knew about Clover’s illness and found the island first, only to discover that the relic wasn’t real. Rather than give up, Evan decided to fake it. He altered the relics, built a new meaning for Clover to interpret, hoping only to bring him some peace before he died. But of course, Clover wanted the relic for his sister, which is how Dysis in a sunhat entered the picture. Dysis is an actor. Her role was to find Clover, befriend him, and eventually convince him that she was his sister and that the island’s magnetic field had slowed time for him while she aged normally. In his desperation, Clover believes her. Then he dies in her arms. OK, still with me?All of  science fiction machinations have been building towards this moment, and it is only at this point that the player sees how all the proper nouns, island lore, and ominous corporate mystery were only ever meant to steer Clover towards believing his sister had survived her illness and found him on this island. It is obscene, it is messy, but it explains a lot. Had the game ended here, it would fit somewhat uncomfortably into our contemporary fascination with “sick-lit,” heartwarming stories about the terminally ill dying after discovering true happiness. I am not entirely ready to say  isn’t guilty of employing the same devices as sick-lit, but it’s the final scene that leaves it somewhere else.After fainting when Clover dies in her arms, Dysis awakes in Clover’s home village as his funeral is taking place. Evan is there, along with another scientist, and they are arguing about if what they did was right. What seemed altruistic before now appears manipulative and ghoulish in the wake of Clover’s death. He died believing a lie, believing his sister had survived and was holding him when she had already died somewhere far away. Evan wanted to help his friend, to save him from his torment, but the only way he could conceive of doing so was betrayal on an island-sized scale.It is a devastating rejection of everything  spends the rest of the game constructing, a twist of an invisible knife. Evan cannot resolve his guilt and uncertainty and neither does the game attempt to justify itself. It simply ends, letting the melancholy and loneliness hang limply in the air. In “Nothing Feels as Real,” Julie Passanante Elman, associate professor at the University of Missouri, writes that sick-lit’s purpose is “offering a good cry as a form of rehabilitative treatment…” We are meant to cry, to empathize with the terminally ill, then to go on living with a newfound vigor and appreciation of our lives. But in doing so we are reducing another life into a moral platitude. employs many of the same tactics as sick-lit, but it doesn’t give its characters the bittersweet ending they’re desperate for. This is undercut tremendously by a tactless post-credits scene immortalizing the game’s Kickstarter backers, but that aside the game’s conclusion is remarkably sad, or at least hopeless. The jointly authored paper “Literary Plastination: From Body’s Objectification to the Ontological Representation of Death…” positions sick-lit within a wider cultural separation of death from the body. The paper posits that as death becomes less present in most people’s lives due to advances in medicine, our mechanisms for navigating the emotional impact of death have similarly deserted us.In place of being able to conceptualize and resolve our response to death, we have disconnected the loss of a person from the death of their body. Sick-lit’s fixation on the death of the body is viewed as tasteless as it violates this refocusing of what death is. It is not the loss of a body, it’s the loss of the person, so why are we spending so much time focusing on how their body is failing them? _Evan’s Remains_ sidesteps this discussion as the mechanics of the illness which kills Clover are purposefully unclear, and his death occurs off-screen. His death is allowed to remain one of personhood, not of bodily failure.But still, the significance is left upon Evan and his wresting of control from Clover by way of his plot.  monologues and collapsed world-building begins to make more sense when recognizing that the game is structured not as a linear narrative but a morality play. Everything is intense and big and driving at the central theme of trust and hopelessness. Evan wants to repay Clover for trusting him when he was homeless and welcoming Evan into his home. But he cannot stop the disease so he resorts to what he is good at, bluffing, reading people, setting a plot in motion. His love of and skill at the game SpyMaster becomes a desperate attempt to give Clover a peaceful death. But it is still, always, a lie.I am not sure if  entirely earns its thematic heft when so much of it is inscrutable, but that it is willing to end its plot in a moment of intense duress is daring enough to elevate its weaker moments. It helps significantly that its sets are gorgeously rendered, pixel art that moves so smoothly as to verge on the unnerving but always immaculately lit and drawn. Landscapes of flowers and alien water pumps add flavor to a world that doesn’t always make use of its beauty but is nevertheless richer for it. _Evan’s Remains_ is untidy, its themes barely cohesive. But if it were not so unusual, if it had simply doubled-down on puzzles and pretty screens, I do not think it would have left half the impression it did.

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains. It is a story based puzzle platformer created by maitan69 and published by Whitethorn Digital. Beautiful pixel art graphics and sweet OST that the game provide are enough to draw our attention. As introduced in the game store, if you can actually experience this game, you will see why this game has been chosen at various game events such as GDC.Evan's Remains is a mystery adventure that merges clever puzzles with visual novel elements. The player have to find a missing genius boy called Evan. A strange letter arrived from him and said that he wants a girl named Dysis to find him. As Dysis, you need to solve this mystery series of puzzles to unravel the entire secret.Gameplay is close to the platformer style, and the story will unfold as the visual novel style, every time the player solves from some puzzles. It starts with easy ones, and new mechanics are added gradually. It is quite challenging, but there seems to be no interaction between the puzzle and the story. Fortunately, there are features to skip the puzzle and focus on the story itself. The UI is a bit rough, but the game experience is neat and nice.Evan's Remains. This is a well-made puzzle platformer game. The total play-through time is about 3-4 hours, and the quality is good compared to the game price. The girl running on the beach and the sun shining warmly at her were my favorite moments in this game. Despite some glitches, this game is well worth trying. Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: While you may believe you're playing a puzzle game with a story, it’s actually the opposite. The plot is the game's main selling feature, and the puzzles are merely there to keep you from reaching the climax too quickly. Because the only reward for solving a challenge is a few lines of cryptic text between characters that delivers very little information about what's truly going on, this style of presentation feels disappointing. Throughout the game, the puzzles use the same mechanics and designs. The goal is to jump from platform to platform to reach the top of the wall. The fact that platforms change makes this a challenge. You have platforms that vanish, change from visible to invisible, transport you to its twin, and so on. It's all quite simple. The opportunity to skip puzzles after a time reinforces the fact that this is a story-driven game.I kept playing in the hopes that the ending would justify everything. No, it doesn't. The conclusion forces you to watch cutscenes and read several minutes of new information, which simply adds to the confusion. It turns out that everything you've done thus far has been reduced to a joke.Pixel art is attractive, and some of the locations are pretty lovely. It's a shame that these aren't visible during gameplay. The section between the puzzles where dialogue takes place always looks the same. It’s just a landscape with a character on each side. Although the background changes in each zone, the location remains devoid of any items.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: ​Very charming puzzle game with a surprisingly good story. You're playing a girl who arrives on a mysterious island, searching for a man who disappeared. On her way she encounters strange monoliths, that contain physics puzzles which reveal hints about a secret artifact  when solved. But after solving a few puzzles, it seems there's something really fishy going on.Most of the puzzles are very easy and can be solved rather quickly. But the story is so good that you'll keep playing to know what happens next. In combination with the lovely pixel art and music, this game is a must play for everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: The mystery that the story builds up falls completely flat in the end, when a bunch of plot twists come out of nowhere, invalidating a bunch of the plot (and leaving plot holes galore). The puzzles are boring. Most can be solved as follows: "Do the only thing possible that doesn't get you back to a state you were already in. Repeat until solved." There's not really much thought necessary to solve them, and the state space is small enough that even if you get stuck you can probably just brute-force them. Maybe two puzzles in the whole game actually felt designed to have even a simple key 'aha' moment.The art for this game is absolutely *beautiful*, as are the sound design and music. (Watch the trailer - you can see for yourself!) Unfortunately, I can't recommend the game based off of that alone. The two main reasons to play the game -- the mystery and the puzzles -- both don't hold up.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains is a puzzle platformer where you play as Dysis, a girl on a random uninhabited island in the Pacific Ocean who is tasked to search for an individual known as Evan. The story is centered around exploring the island and looking for leads toward where Evan is located. While exploring the island, you encounter a variety of monoliths featuring puzzles and an individual who is scrawling a variety of things in his notebook. Telling any more than this would go into spoiler territory, but just know that the story is engaging and full of intrigue while never dragging on too long. The gameplay is pretty basic. You walk to the right, you jump around a bit in order to solve puzzles, and then you continue walking right until you encounter another puzzle or a story point. The whole game works on this "game loop." The puzzles aren't bad, but they just feel really boring, even when later puzzles have a bit more "spice" to them. I attempted completing the puzzles at first, as I wanted to actually experience the gameplay, but I realized that I enjoyed just outright skipping the puzzles and focusing on the story after a certain point. I did this by using an option the game gives you to skip puzzles entirely with no downside. Even if it felt a bit cheap using this option, I can say that I actually enjoyed this game more when I DIDN'T need to interact with the puzzles. It's a shame, but that's how I feel. The graphics are pretty good! The pixel art is lovely, and the environments are well designed. However, at first, I found the portraits of the characters to be a bit jarring, as I think they sort of clash with the look of the main game and look a bit less polished in comparison. Despite this, I saw myself growing accustomed to the look of the portraits, as this game mostly feels like a visual novel with the way it plays due to the dialogue often taking precedence over the gameplay. The music and sound designs are fine; however, they have their issues. The music tends to get a bit monotonous as it constantly loops with periods of silence before it loops the same track again. Of course, different locations have slightly different tracks, but the difference isn't very noticeable. There are also certain flashback scenes that have a really annoying static sound effect that plays every few seconds, so there is that too.Overall, I think Evan's Remains is a good game. The gameplay leaves much to be desired, but the story makes up for the somewhat boring gameplay. I'd say to give this a try if you're fine with the minimal gameplay and want a good story.(P.S. I like how one of the characters legit mention that you can just walk around these puzzle monoliths, which is what you're likely doing when using the "Skip Puzzle" option. Also, the messages in the gameplay after the credits were so heartwarming!)

_childDocuments_.review: 1-3h 1/10 1 No Yes, there is a guide here on steam.   11 on Astats No Yes, I'll explain them below No No No No No difficulty option NoThis is such a beautiful story-based game with additional puzzles. You'll have to complete 1 or 2 puzzles for the achievements, but as for the rest, you can use the skip option if you don't want to do them or can't figure it out. There is also a speed-forward option for the dialogue but I highly recommend that you read it. Evan's Remains is such a well-crafted story that only takes around 2h to complete. I won't tell you anything about the story in this review because the plot can easily be spoiled and it is better for you to experience it for yourself.It has a few easily missed achievements, many are easy enough to find, so to replay the game wouldn't take you long with all those skipping options, however, I'll explain those here for all of you who just want to get them during their first attempt: Wait 15 minutes in a puzzle. For this one, you can do this pretty much on any puzzle really but the easiest time to do it will be during the first one. Play part of the game in Spanish. After you get the chapter achievement: "The Garden," Go back to the main menu and switch the language to Spanish and then continue on with the game. If you are like me and don't miss out on the story, your save file is stored on the following location and is a simple text file: Copy-paste it to a save spot, play through the story in Spanish until you've gotten the achievement, then place this save-file back in after you close the game. That way you don't miss anything from the story. Move to the left directly after the scene with Andre. You'll find a stranger on a pillar, stand next to the pillar and then go back to the main menu, choose to continue in the main menu and you'll be at the start of this puzzle. Once you've completed it, you'll get the achievement. Watch the end of the credits and after that start moving and it will unlock.This may sound like there's a lot of missable achievements but not really, as it isn't that hard to do and again, even if you miss something while playing through it the first time, you can easily replay the game in under an hour with the goal of unlocking these remaining achievements in mind. Give this game a try and I believe you'll discover a truly wonderful story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a simple puzzle platformer that invites comparison to To The Moon (and its whole series).  And this is its downfall - because it completely misunderstands what people like about To The Moon.Sure, that game series twists, and those twists involve mortality and how it is inescapable.  It's also heartfelt, earns its twists, and has comedy and emotion in spades.  I cried at all three of those games.  There is no central 'villain' to the story, merely circumstances that are undefeatable.  Man Vs. Nature or Man Vs. God to bring forth the classical struggles.This game's story was clearly written by someone who played To The Moon (and perhaps Finding Paradise) but did not understand why other people liked it, and perhaps even actively disliked it.  The twists are mean-spirited, they contradict what we learn early from POV characters, and are pulled from nowhere for no reason.  There is a character in this story that is supposed to be considered a super-genius, but they are written like Stephen Moffat writes Sherlock Homes in the BBC miniseries, where "super-genius" means someone who can perfectly predict all actions of all people at all times.  Or, to put it in shorthand, a stupid person's idea of what a smart person is.I got this as part of some humble bundle or other, I think.  I'd have to suggest, even at the price tag of free, don't play this game.  The story is dreadful, the twists are unearned and bad, and the entire mood of the last bit of the game feels resentful that humans genuinely feel emotion at the ending of To The Moon specifically.  This is the anti-To The Moon, in effect.  It's a fairly embarrassing product that isn't even comfortable enough in its twists to not look directly at the camera and explain them to the audience.And there are a variety of very trivial changes one could make to actually make the story feel heartfelt and emotional.  Spoilers below:So no, I would not recommend this at all.  You could change very little about the game and make it great, so this wasn't a 'so close to being good,' but a case of the creator fundamentally not understanding what people like about the games that are their clear influences, resulting in something bad in its own right and woefully inferior to other products.

_childDocuments_.review: Largely a visual novel with some platforming puzzles sandwiched in-between text-based cutscenes. The presentation is great and the puzzles are fun, but the story that should have carried the experience ended up dragging it down due to sudden and rapid overcomplexity. Despite being required to pick a "yes" or "no" rating to publish this review, I can't confidently steer you in either direction.  is a visual novel/puzzle-platformer that tells the story of a girl named Dysis and her mission to track down a missing boy genius named Evan, who claims to be located on a deserted island filled with mysterious monoliths and ancient technology. Along the way, she encounters a young man in search of a hidden artifact somewhere on the island, and the two agree to work together to find what each one is looking for. The ratio of its two genres leans more in favor of the former, meaning , but whether that's a positive or a negative is a matter of opinion. It's another one of those games where I wish Steam would give me a middle ground option, because neither one feels entirely right to me. I can't say I disliked what I played, but it's hard for me to comfortably recommend it as I find it to be a story-driven game that fumbled on the execution of its story.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm unsure if I do or don't like this game.On one hand, it was a fun puzzle game. Sure, the puzzles weren't too hard, but they were at least fun.And the story was getting good and I liked what it was saying about how, even if people know you, they don't care about you. But those who care about you, know you. Was really good.But "The Revelation" sucks.It feels like they wanted to have some big plot twist that was shocking. You don't need a twist like that, and having this girl just be a friend of Evan but not be Dysis would have worked much better. I think it would have been better if Clover had to choose between her sister living, but forced on this island for the rest of her life. Or having her die. Some choice like that would have honestly been so good. But instead, the game kind of left me empty inside with a troublesome message about how "it's okay to lie to people, as long as they are happy". Which I think is just problematic since while, lying isn't a black and white issue, Andre's plan should not have been rewarded. Yes, Evan does comment on it being insane, but it works, so does that mean that it's okay to do so? I just think it's messaging at the end of the game is bad, which really kills it for me. The game's content is just moving from left to right on a horizontal plane, solving a puzzle with only a few variations, then moving from left to right some more. These puzzles are often interrupted by story and dialogue. Often the dialogue would go on forever and forever while I just wanted to solve some puzzles - the game could have definitely benefitted from some better pacing in terms of how the storz was told.That being said, the game is still worth the money. The pixel art is well done, the puzzles are simple, but still difficult enough in the latter half of the game to be at least somewhat challenging. _childDocuments_.review: Evan’s Remains presents itself as an adventure / puzzle platformer game, with a very strong story that will make anyone eager to know its end.This title, produced by just one person, Matías Schmied, started as a project on Kickstarter and after a year sees the light of day.The player wears the skin of Dysis, a girl with a mission to find the young genius Evan who is missing. Rumors indicate that he is located on a desert island. For some strange reason, the company Up-Link decided that Dysis was the only person suitable to end this strange mission.On an apparently deserted island, the player quickly unravels his secrets and discovers that there is really more at stake than just finding this genius.In terms of gameplay Evan’s Remains is a mix of a puzzle with visual novels. The formula is simple, the player finishes a puzzle and is presented with a short cutscene with a story, without voice acting, just small lines of text.The puzzles themselves are simple in the sense that there is no great complexity of actions or movements, but they are sometimes quite challenging. The aim of all puzzles is to overcome the barrier present on the right side of the monitor, since the whole game is presented as a side scroller, therefore from left to right, and thus continue on your way. For this, the player has platforms for different purposes, such as switches that slide platforms up or down and even left to right, or platforms that disappear when the player jumps.No special skills are needed nor are new skills presented as the adventure progresses, it is only necessary to think and try each platform presented in the puzzle. After a few attempts, the feeling of overcoming is quite rewarding and enlightening in the face of a heavy and quite touching story.It turns out that each puzzle is a monolith with a secret message that is unveiled after its completion, not by the player himself, but by his “friend” on this island. Yes, it turns out that this is not an island completely devoid of human contact. There are a lot of twists and turns, and on several occasions, I stuck to what was going on in the small text boxes. There are traces of narrative about family which leads to some exciting and even tragic changes.All the pixelart in the game is incredibly detailed, like Dysis’s hair waving as she jumps or runs, as well as the entire created environment that serves as the backdrop for each new location on the island.Evan’s Remains is a very accessible short puzzle-platformer game that tells a very touching story.Check more recommendations from Exile

_childDocuments_.review: Normally puzzle games do not interest me, and to be quite honest, I'm not even sure why this game caught my attention at all... But after having played it, I can say that it was well worth my time.Evan's Remains has a beautiful and simple design, with a great sound track to go along with. For a puzzle game, the levels did not seem to be too difficult. But then again, I believe the main purpose of this game was to understand a story that develops as you continue to play. Discovering the secrets of this mysterious island was quite entertaining, and the introduction of new characters continued to give more questions than answers.If you're the type of player that likes to achievement hunt, then it is fully possible to 100% this game in a single run, which would take just a few hours; including the options to skip both dialogue cut scenes and certain levels.There are a handful of those who have complained about the numerous cut-scenes that involve quite a bit of reading, which I can understand. However, I feel that part of a good story is reading along and becoming emotionally invested into the plot itself and the characters included. If you find it difficult to enjoy reading lengthy conversations between characters as contributions to a progressing story line, then I do not think this game would be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for March 2022. If you are interested in the game and it's before April 5th, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A solid puzzle game ruined by an overindulgent story. I liked the first fifteen minutes of Evan’s Remains. A girl appears on an uninhabited island and solves some interesting platforming puzzles with a couple of clever tricks.  They were solid puzzles and I was looking forward to more. But over the hour I spent with Evan's Remains, the story kept popping up and rather than hinting at something bigger, the game got stuck in the story, and just had long-winded discussions that weren’t extremely interesting.   The thing is Evan’s Remains has great puzzles and I might return just to play the puzzles, but I’m at the point with the story that I could easily just skip it and read the synopsis online, in fact, I have and I don’t think the story pays off, or at least I’m not willing to sit through all the scenes to let it take me where it wants to go.  Pick this up if you want a melodramatic story, with some minor puzzle gameplay in it.  You can skip the story or the puzzles, but skipping either takes away everything the game is trying to do, and it might be better to play something else.   As much as I enjoyed the clever puzzles, I probably won’t return. _childDocuments_.review: I played through this on stream today and here's my thoughts:-The puzzles are cleverly designed and fun to solve.  None of them are so obtuse that you will be stuck on them forever, but some of them do require you to pause and think for a few moments.  They all succeed in making you feel smart when you solve them.  I kind of wish there was a video explaining the general idea of the puzzles because I don't know if the trailer got that across because its very well done and feels pretty original. -The characters are well written. The moment to moment dialog is believable and there is a genuine emotional moment where I got a little choked up on stream because of it.  I would love to see more done with these characters. -Unfortunately there is A LOT of plot dumps between the various puzzles.  I wish there were about 40% more puzzles inserted to break this up more, even if that doubled the game's cost. Could just be me though...-The ending kind of got out of hand and the morality of the characters at the end confused me.  Maybe I'll make sense of that as it sits with me, but unless there is more story coming with these characters (which is sort of implied), then it sort of hits a sour note at the end. I still recommend it if you want a short experience to play through with great puzzle design.

_childDocuments_.review: This is without a doubt the single absolute worst story I've had a chance to experience in a game and probably any medium in recent memory.Without going into specific spoilers, the entire playthrought you feel like the slow and somewhat cliched story with one-dimensional characters is building up to some interesting conclusion. Well, guess what MF, turns out it actually was building up to an absolute trainwreck of an ending that made it so the other 95% of the game you've just played though made no sense from the logical standpoint and soured the entire experience for me (i actually liked the cute artstyle, the soundtrack and simple puzzles&story to that point) so much that and I'll never be able to look at this game the same way.It was so comically bad in fact, that you can't help but think that some rogue developer added the ending as some sick practical joke in a vendetta against other the rest of the developement team and all future players. The game would've been infinitely better without the final 20 mins of 'story'. If you're planning on playing this yourself I strongly recommend you hard press ALT+F4 the second you  uninstall the game and never look back.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I'm struggling to review this one, although I do feel compelled to because I do have some strong feelings about it that I'd like to convey through a review format. With that in mind, I'll give it a crack here.Evan's Remains is less of a traditional gaming experience, and more of an experiential tone poem of sorts, capable of generating a specific kind of malaise that few have to ever truly grapple with to any extreme degree. Having myself worked through the emotions of loss and dreams-which-could-not-have-been from forces outside of anyone's control, it brought me back immediately to that pit of dread sitting in my stomach that came from just letting myself exist in those moments from the past. It's one of those feelings that's difficult to describe to anyone who hasn't experienced it, but to those who have, it will be intimately familiar and immediately recognizable.This is not a game about puzzle platforming, so don't get it if you're looking for that. In fact, that component is so utterly trivial that it honestly may improve the game in terms of pacing and experience if it was removed entirely in favor of more scripted, interactive scenes. You can skip every single puzzle in the game (literally, there is a "Skip Puzzle" option available for every puzzle in the game and it does not impact any story decisions from what I can tell) and the game will be about 99.9% the same, as well as moving significantly faster. There is no real reward to remembering tiny details, as the story will be spelled out more or less in plain text for you at the end to catch you up on anything you might have missed, and there are no satisfying narrative payoffs for noticing anything ahead of time since any "twists" are generally telegraphed very obviously or almost immediately revealed minutes later. Instead, spend time letting the dialogue and the implications thereof wash over you in an abstract way, and consider the general concepts being played with by what's being done on behalf of and to these characters - what it means for the people involved, what the right or wrong decisions (if any) might be, and if it's the kind of thing you can even fathom being an act of compassion.In the interest of avoiding direct spoilers for the story, I'll merely state that there were two points at which I thought the experience was complete before it continued on. The first one felt like a New Game+ experience at first, which I was pleasantly amused by, until it was completely subverted a short way through. The second one comes after the credits, and should be completely avoided to prevent the atmosphere of the ending from being ruined - seriously, you can simply turn the game off when the credits roll, I would strongly advise doing so.This game is one of those bite-size experiences that I think I'm going to be mulling over in my head for quite some time. As I mentioned before, the recommendation is conditional - I would not advise getting this if you're expecting anything other than 45-60 minutes of decent storytelling with a casual, low pressure, almost incidental platforming puzzle element that can be optionally ignored with no negative consequences to the game itself. If you recognize that this is what this game is, then it's a really lovely little tale that'll possibly leave you wrestling with some emotions that, ugly as they might be, are still worth exploring as part of the infinite complexity of human experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Again, the only good game-related YouTube ad I've ever gotten, which I finally decided to play.It's a nice little game; a puzzle platformer that is pretty simple.You can beat it in about 2 hours, and 100%ing isn't very difficult if you want to do that, however, I would recommend that you do not look at the trailer on Steam. _childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains (2020)An extremely beautiful pixel game where you solve some jumping puzzles. The story is pretty cool, you play as a girl called Dysis who sets off to a mysterious island to find a man named Evan. The puzzles are these where you jump on a platform and it disappears so you need to solve the puzzle by making certain platforms disappear and reappear as you try to make your way over the wall to move on. All puzzles can be skipped if you want to or find one tedious. The game's strong points is certainly the graphics, the story is great and the puzzles can keep you busy for a while. Great game if you love pixel style art games. The game is not very long but I would say it is worth the money for the beautiful graphics alone.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: My Video Review is available here:Is Evan’s Remains the game that is worth investing your money and time in? One can find many positives there - mysterious complex story, relaxing gameplay, puzzle design, gradual learning curve, responsive controls, beautiful graphics and nice music. There are also few negatives that I have found while playing - the puzzles become quite repetitive sooner or later due to simplicity of their design, the adventure lovers might not like frequent puzzle platforming sequences and vice versa, hard to follow for children and absence of dubbing.Pros:- story- relaxing- puzzle design- gradual learning curve- controls- graphics- musicCons:- creeping stereotype- the mix of genres is not for everyone- hard to follow for children- no dubbingIf you are looking for a pure adventure or pure puzzle platformer better look somewhere else. But if you would like to try a puzzle platformer with a strong story you are on the right address here. I personally have enjoyed playing Evan's Remains and I am therefore giving it Thumb Up and VideoGaming Father’s Index 7+ out of 10 - recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect much from this game as I thought it would just be a normal relaxing puzzle platformer and it turned out to be much more.The story telling is amazing and there's a ton of dialogue which makes you think of life and how you perceive it. It's also really sad near the end as the story lets you know more and more about the characters.It's definitely worth the play, even if puzzle platformers aren't your thing as you can just skip them if you wanted to and only want to experience the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles were fun enough that I wanted to replay the game on my Deck a few years after playing it on a different platform, but the story is so insanely stupid it made me dumber just by experiencing it.I actually hate it how they've buried a pretty decent puzzle game underneath such an insanely dumb story. The devs had such hard-ons for plottwists that they wrote twist after twist while not realising that each twist made the story dumber and less believable. Fun puzzles though.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a neutral rating, but since I can't I have to give it a thumbs down.TL:DR The plot feels rushed and unfinished, the puzzles are good and mildly challenging but not worth full price. If its on sale, maybe.Overall this is marketed as puzzle platformer with a mystery. While it does provide puzzles platforming, the plot does not hold up. Without specific spoilers, the game starts with us knowing nothing and learning along with our protagonist Dysis. The plot has some holes from the beginning (some it even joking breaks the 4th wall about) but its not bad. Then at the end it pulls a huge plot twist that just doesn't make sense. The dev's clearly have a lot of ideas and story to share but it almost seems like trying to mash 2-3 different plots into one game. After the final credits you go to a post credit moment that I hoped would continue the plot and answer my remaining questions but it was just to shout out their kickstart backers. To make the plot work it would need like an hour or so more gameplay. Andre/Evan/Vincent/Dysis are all under explained. The only character I feel like I understand and know the backstory of (and don't dislike) is Clover. I feel like I am supposed to like Dysis but I just don't feel like she makes sense. I don't wanna even get into my thoughts on Andre since I don't want to spoil the game. The puzzles are the only real pro, they are fun and the mechanics are good. They keep it interesting, but also stay at about the same difficulty once you get past the first 2 levels. Just keep in mind you will have about 2-5 minutes of story every 3 puzzles or so (though you also can skip dialogue from the menu but it will go through animations at regular speed so it will still take 15-65 seconds per cutscene)So if its on sale or if you just really want to do some cool puzzles but don't care about the story, maybe pick this one up. But for full price or if the story is important to this one, I would skip this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Not saying that the game is bad at all.  I mean, I played through to the end, so it can't be that bad. But it's got a story that makes no sense, so you're basically paying for a badly-written and overwrought visual novel occasionally interrupted by some reasonable-but-uncreative platforming puzzles.  Also, the game is VERY short.  Don't let my 3 hours of play time fool you, this is a 2-hour game that I happened to let sit idle for a while.  I think there are 31 puzzles, most of which are basically the same in terms of approach, and some of which are literally exact repeats.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful piece of art wrapped in a 2d platformer. This game had me second guessing myself right up until the end. Definitely well worth it's price the puzzles are fun and kept me engaged. This game is also heavy on story so if you're just looking for a puzzle game this might not be it for you. The music is beautiful and the visuals are gorgeous, the theme ended up having me left with tears in my eyes. -pretty visuals-gorgeous music-story heavy-varying difficulty of puzzles
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really charming VN puzzle game where you play as a character named Dysis on a distant island. The story is really complex and interesting. You need to read all the dialog to clearly understand the story, however you can skip the puzzles if you struggle. Most of the puzzles are quite easy, but two of them are really difficult. The art style, music and sound effects are really amazing and fit the game so well. The art style is beyond beautiful and you can see the creative thinking that went into the design of the game as well as the puzzles.Overall a lovely game with achievements. It takes about 3 hours to 100% the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and unexpected, I've got to admit. Well done puzzle platformer with a complete story. It is also rather refreshing for that price. Never overstayed it's welcome puzzles can be skipped too. I liked it a lot to the end, charming pixel graphics and music was already enough but also background for characters to make feelings. _childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Even's Remains isn't bad as a game. It's a puzzle platformer, and while it's not the best around, it gets the job done. The puzzles are well designed without being too frustrating, and they can be fun. The graphics are probably the best part, dripping in pixelated goodness, and the music is relaxing and fits what the game is going for. So all that's good.What breaks the game is the story.On the surface, it's about a young woman named Dysis hired to find a boy named Emil on a deserted island, home to some ruins from an ancient civilization. You find a dude named Clover there, who's trying to discover the ruins' secret and save his little sister from a hereditary disease. Simple enough, right?And then you get to the ending and everything goes topsy turvey.Ultimately, the game tries to say that you should do what you can with the time you have because you don't know when it'll be gone. But all it really says is that you should give your friends false hope before they kick the bucket, especially when they're dying of a terminal disease. Which is just... abominable.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: No, I don't recommend it. It's a puzzle game but the levels are incredibly easy, if you get stuck you will solve it accidentally by brute-forcing anyways. I finished the game without skipping a puzzle or spending more than 15 minutes solving one.The story at first seemed okay-ish, it had some mediocre dialogue but was still decent until the ending randomly decides to mess up everything. Seriously, they threw in over 3 plot twists for no real reason.Overall, it feels like a visual novel disguised as a puzzle game - underwhelming. A friend gave me the Steam key, so I didn't lose anything apart from my time.

_childDocuments_.review: is a puzzle-platformer. A short game best played in a single sitting with a story that's both emotionally and intellectually gripping, this is a solid short story in game format for those who'd like to read a character-driven mystery while solving some easy puzzles along the way.You play as a brunette woman tasked with exploring an undiscovered island to search for a man named Evan. Upon this island are strange monoliths, artifacts of some previous civilizations, which comprise some sort of jumping challenges. Solving these, you must continue onward through the increasingly bizarre yet serene landscapes of the island, searching for whatever remains of Evan..., while functionally a puzzle-platformer, is really here to tell its story. The puzzles are interspersed with cutscenes, monologues, and flashbacks at least every 2-3 puzzles, sometimes with only one puzzle in between. The story throughout is a mystery, though over time it also becomes an emotional, character-driven experience. The story does form the foundation of the game, as there is no menu to select puzzles from or anything; it's just a linear run rightward through a series of a couple dozen jumping puzzles.The puzzles themselves are simple and easy. The game introduces roughly three different mechanics to the puzzles over the course of the game, but the basic idea remains: climb to the upper-right using platforms that disappear after jumping on them once. Some of the levels' ease comes from the fact that it's just as simple to solve a puzzle backwards as it is forwards, given that the solution always lies in the upper-right. Furthermore, the game allows players to skip any and all puzzles without penalty, which does save from frustration over the few truly tricky ones and does keep the story moving, but at the cost of making the gameplay feel optional and thin.Overall,  manages a satisfying balance between simple puzzles and a short story. The narrative does end on a somewhat convoluted note with a few nagging questions in spite of its general resolution for things, and the thinness of the puzzles may have warranted some deeper investment in the actual gameplay, but for what this is going for it manages a decent time. Just be sure you're the kind of player who's up for the casual experience that's on offer here.  gets a B+.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains is, in my opinion, a game that is only slightly above average. Evan's Remains is a visual novel interlaced with mostly easy platforming puzzles that feel pretty unique to this game and weaves well into the story. The music is a bit average, nothing worth remembering, the pixel art is pretty impressive, and the story takes quite a few turns, and I'm not sure they're all for the better. Still, I enjoyed what I played of Evan's Remains.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a diamond in the rough as far as I'm concerned. I'm not really a fan of puzzle platformers but I found this one to be really enjoyable. All the puzzles were just the right amount of difficulty for me and there was even a no-stress "skip puzzle" option (of which I only used once).What was more compelling for me was the excellent story. It was fun trying to figure out what was going on and then finally have it all laid bare. Had a bit of an emotional roller coaster there as well and had me pondering it for a while after the final credits rolled. I had a very similar feeling with this game as I did when I finished To the Moon. I definitely want to keep a lookout for more games from this developer.I recently received this in the Humble Choice bundle for March 2022. If you're interesting in seeing my first impressions for this game and others in the bundle then please check out my review video:
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game, this is an artful animated story reader. Yes, there are some puzzles - but they are relatively easy and always skippable with no real repercussions. They are just there to try to get you more involved in the story - and there's a lot of story. Not a bad one, although I've found the end twist quite disappointing. But make no mistake, this is just a visual novel with no choices, no effect on the outcome - practically just an animated book that asks you to go right and press space at the end of each sentence in a dialogue.Does it worth the price? Depends on your budget. Does it worth your time? If you like reading a LOT. Will you be challenged by a satisfying puzzle game with increasing level of difficulty? Definitely not, unless this is your very first game where you have to think.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:Puzzles, visuals, and music are great, story is trash. Shame the devs decided to focus on the story. If the story wasn't so bad or took a back seat I could recommend it. But, as it stands, Evan's Remains is a criminally under cooked puzzle-platformer that thinks it's a story game and wastes over half of the short run-time acting like it. I must stress that every aspect besides the story shines bright, it's just a shame the story had to drag the package down.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: This is labelled as a puzzle platformer, but there's no actual platforming game here and there's a little over an hour's worth of puzzles in what ends up being a three hour game.You need to enjoy the story and the atmosphere to enjoy the game, and it wasn't for me. The puzzles were fine, but I found the story bloat too disruptive to recommend it for them alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles were fun, not too hard, but engaging enough overall. The art was beautiful and the game play was fluid. Unfortunately, I play games for stories, and this story was so disappointing to go through that I felt like I had to not recommend this game. The twist makes no sense and makes the whole first two-thirds of the game make no sense story-wise, and after the big "twist" the last one-third of the game feels like a drag.It felt like the writer was just full of himself and trying to pull a "smarter than everyone else!" type deal. I won't go into spoiler stuff.If you want to play the game for good art and okay puzzles, this is for you. If you're even remotely interested in the story, the thing the game description advertises, I would not recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Too much dialogue, too little platforming.Played for 20 minutes, of which I felt 18 minutes was dialogue skipping and 2 minutes was platforming.Graphics are beautiful, controls are good, puzzles (the few I got to try) was great.If you want to be told a story it might be for you, but it was not for me.A option to skip cutscenes would have been very welcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: It's... okay? It's an unambitious puzzle-platformer grafted onto a visual novel with a hokey and contrived narrative. There's a hint of a thematic relationship between these two parts, which might have elevated the experience and justified the narrative contrivances, but in the end this never pays off. The pleasant pixel art and low-friction puzzles make for an inoffensive way to spend a couple hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Solid puzzles, and never too difficult, but the meat and potatoes for this game are found in the story and setting. There are some moments where the more well-read individuals will pick up on certain cues, and figure out where the story is headed; but that doesn't make it any less enjoyable. The themes that this game explores are extremely poignant, and despite the presentation being a little rough around the edges, the delivery still hits like a shot to the gut.Absolutely worth the asking price; enjoyed every moment of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: This feels rather like a "mixed" game, than "very positive".Yes, the story is good, but only up to a certain point. Before you reach it, you keep going because you want to know what is really going on. You form diverse ideas on what to expect. And then the last 20-30min of this rather short game (completed in ~2.5-3h), are one of the most ridiculous endings I've ever experienced. It feels way too far off.Gameplaywise it is an okay platform puzzler. Rather easy and straight forward. The number of cutscences and dialog increases towards the end, reaching a point, where you just push one button to forward the text. More Puzzles, less cutscences would have been better.Overall a decent game, but because of the ending, I cant recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to rate this game since I played it all the way through in one sitting, which suggests that it was good for its (short) duration. However, at the same time the actual gameplay didn't really build up to anything, just more of the same puzzles. There was even a line in the game itself saying that the difficulty curve is all over the place, which is true – the last puzzle was one of the easiest in the entire game. Also, there's only about 1 hour of puzzles in the game, the rest is dialogue and cutscenes.As for the story, without spoiling anything, if you think you saw what was coming in the end, you probably didn't. That's a good thing in itself, but I think most people won't feel particularly satisfied with the ending, so I'm hesitant to recommend this game for sake of just the story. I also don't think the characters were particularly believable or deep, and especially Vanille seems annoyingly like yet another dreamgirl character written by a man.In summary: if you have this from a bundle or such, it may be worth playing (or, rather, reading since it is more a visual novel than a game), but I would skip buying it at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game from Humble Bundle.-Okay, so... The art is alright, nothing too special. The music is pretty decent. I believe that the option to Skip every single puzzle, makes the game way too easy and shows that it's not taking itself seriously. You quickly realize that solving the puzzles really has nothing to do with the story. It's optional, and you don't really get much out of it. So basically, if you skip every puzzle, you've got a walking simulator with tons of dialogue... Which I don't personally think is worth 5.69 euros. The twist ending is.... Frustrating, to say the least. I saw another review saying that the plot pissed them off, and I honestly have to agree. I'm not entirely sure if I enjoy the idea of such a twisted ending. That, paired with the cheerful graphics and nonchalant  overall theme of the game, just doesn't sit too well with me. The ending leaves you feeling unsatisfied, disgusted and disappointed. Andre is such a psychopath and makes me feel uneasy.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains is short, but it uses it's time to tell a really captivating story. Spending time with these characters, learning who they are and what makes them tick while solving fun puzzles was an absolute blast. The music is really solid, and while I would love to talk about the story, I refuse to spoil it for people. Please play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: i like the puzzles but i really don't care about the characters nor the story. it gives you enough info regarding what you're doing but not really WHY you're doing it. it's got skip puzzle option (i mean why, mc says it's the only fun thing on this island) but it has no skip scene option. skip dialog only fast forwards the dialog but you'll have to endure the animations like walking from here to there in normal speed.really on the fence on this one, so if you can get this for really cheap then go for it. can't say for full price, got this from humble.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: waaaay too much slow slow slow exposition and slow animations and not enough game, there is a fast-forward dialogue option which i exasperatedly resorted to towards the end and it turned out there was only 2 more epic-length cut scenes that probably  explained it all.the graphics are cute, the sound is mostly annoying dialogue bleeps, the puzzles were fun and one or two were a bit tricky,  but they're clearly not the focus of the 'game' which is really the slow ponderous delivery of a text-heavy story that you have no control over.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: There are two sides to Evan’s Remains; the endless dialogue and the puzzles, and I found the latter quite entertaining with a nice progression of difficulty and some truly challenging designs.   The puzzles play out in a 2D side view with lots of ledges, some that toggle other ledges, some that teleport to other ledges, some than springboard, some that are always there, some that move along a path, and others that reset the whole puzzle. Once you land on a platform it will vanish as soon as you jump off which factors into this whole binary on/off pattern of setting up the ledges in just the right way to navigate the design and make it over the tall green wall and continue to the next puzzle or bit of the story. Things start off slowly but the progression of difficulty is continually evolving as new aspects of gameplay and types of puzzle pieces keeping getting added to the mix.The presentation is awesome with what I must confess to be fantastic pixel-art even if my $1000 RTX video card has nothing to do with those mirror-like reflections on the water. The character portrait art is equally as stunning and there are all sorts of nice effects like lighting and subtle animations. It really took me back to my Turbo Grafx-16 and SEGA Genesis days. The music is fantastic and available as a standalone soundtrack for only a dollar.Read Full Review -
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains is one of the games where I wasn't sure if I wanted to play it because when I checked the store I saw some negative reviews about it even though overall the game was rated very good. But I recently learned that I should play games by myself and see if I enjoyed them more than listening to other people whether they have enjoyed them.It has been on my wishlist for quite some time now and thanks to Humble Bundle it finally found its way into my library. Speaking for me, I enjoyed it very much. I am a big fan of puzzle platformers and combining this with a very humane, touching story is all I really need. Admittedly, it starts kinda confusing but over time most of it gets revealed to the player.I'm not sure if that feature was included since the beginning but it also got a skip dialogue and skip puzzle option if you are not interested in the for some people gameplay interrupting story or in the story interrupting puzzles. In my opinion, I found the continuous switching very unique and fit for this game and its way to tell the story.What this game needs is a chapter select once you have beaten the game because I would have loved to go back to specific segments and try to get the missable achievements without having to go through the whole game again.With 2 - 2,5 hours of playtime it's also a game with just the right length in my opinion and looking at the price tag you really can't expect much more. The music didn't really stick with me but it did its job, however the pixel art is amazing and I love the way the hair's flying around in the wind and the water reflecting the beautiful scenery.The puzzles in the beginning are very simple but get harder over time, but at least for me, I didn't feel like I had to skip one of them.Evan's Remains get a recommendation from me, but I would say, just as I did, don't listen to reviews too much and instead try to find out by yourself if you like it or not. I can just say that the controls are tight, the puzzles are fun, the pixel art looks awesome and the story really connected with me and actually makes me want to play it again since I enjoyed some parts of it so much and would like to experience it again.EDIT: One more thing I appreciate is the many localization options, including german, but there were quite a few typos or words too many or words that didn't really fit?
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: It is kind of difficult, to decide between recommend and not, this game. After I finished it, I thought 'It looks beautiful, but it is plain and bad.'. I had to replay it, to unlock the missable achievements, to realize that I actually liked the platforming and puzzles. What happens is, that the ending ruins the whole experience of the game. Throughout the game the story unveils in a cryptic and interesting way, to end up in a long and boring ending that almost makes the game not worth your time. I encourage the developer to keep making games, because the art and animations are beautiful, and the game mechanics were fun.Side note: Worst achievement ever. You have to drink from the developer's head, since this game was clearly made after Dec 9, 2018. (:
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect game to play on this lazy Sunday afternoon. Super casual puzzle platformer with a great story behind it. Gorgeous art and wonderful music. One great feature is that you can choose to skip each puzzle or each story part you encounter. Puzzle too hard? Skip it and continue so you stay immersed in the story. Want to replay just the puzzles? Skip all the story just to get your puzzle solving fix satisfied. While there isn't much replayability, per se (nothing changes from each playthrough), I have the option to go back and enjoy specific pieces without having to be interrupted. The story blew me away so I went back and read all of it again without solving the puzzles for a second time. A great hidden steam gemEdit: I may not have played all of the huge titles that were released in 2020, but looking back this was the best game I played that released in 2020. The story had me hooked and was unmatched.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: does not try to revolutionize anything, but offers an interesting mix of genres in one pixelated package.Here are a few pros and cons:If you're willing to give it a go, make sure to stay clear of any spoiler.Definitely!It's rather cheap, so if you like it enough within the game (and want to further support the makers) why not!Have fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very nice and short puzzle platformer with a great story behind it. The best part about the puzzles is that they require no tutorials. You intuitively learn how to solve the easier ones and just go on from there. Don't expect them to become a massive challenge, though. The controls would benefit from some Coyote Time and a short jump button a la 1001 Spikes, but they're otherwise very precise and you won't get frustrated if you suck at platformers like I do.I was pleasantly surprised by the story (avoid spoilers!) and the artstyle is very nice. Also, BOQUITA, PAPÁ!

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's Remains is a unique puzzle game with an emotional story. The graphics are beautiful and the music is fantastic. Definitely something I look forward to with replayability. There are quite a few curveballs in this and the puzzles were a lot of fun. My only complaint is that I wish there had been more puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: It took me around 3 hours to beat this game, so anyone going in should be aware that it isn't a long game by any stretch. You can replay to get achievements obviously, if that's your thing, so your own mileage may vary. But for me it was a short, narrative top-heavy puzzle platforming experience where the gameplay sometimes felt secondary to the plot.Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed a lot of things about this game. I thought the graphics were nice, the writing was really good in places, the platforming was solid and the puzzles were fun (I just wanted more of them & bigger & more complex). However it is undeniably the story that will keep most people playing til the end because ultimately the plot is the greatest puzzle in the game. As long as you're cool with playing something that feels like a graphic novel with gameplay elements, then you'll enjoy it.So would I recommend this game? Short answer yes with an ; long answer no with a .Pros- Beautiful pixel art graphics- Nice sound design- Intriguing story & characters- Some really emotive writing- Makes you philosophise- Solid platforming- Fun puzzles- ShortCons- Gameplay feels secondary to plot (which is sad cos it IS fun)- Feels repetitive after a while (hence why 'short' is a pro)- No real 'options' menu- Dialogue 'noises' can get irritating-
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: A puzzle platformer. Help Dysis uncover the mystery behind the missing genius and the mysterious island he was said to be on.Gameplay involves moving from monolith to monolith and solving the platforming puzzles that each possess. They involve platforms that do different things when landed on. They provide a decent mental challenge, and the controls are nice and simple. You also have the option to skip any puzzle at no penalty if they end up being too much. The game has really nice art overall, with beautifully drawn backgrounds and nice fluid animations. The nice, relaxing soundtrack coupled with the beautifully depicted waves of the sea make this game soothing to play too!The small cast of characters are likeable, the dialogue and the overall mystery is interesting. The conclusion is satisfying, although I would also have liked to explore other elements of the world more.It's a very enjoyable and engaging game overall, would recommend it to those fond of puzzle platformers and narrative focused games.
_childDocuments_.name: Evan's Remains

_childDocuments_.review: The story is really engaging, high quality right there. The plot, the environment, all the many details, it makes you feel like you're in there, a unique sensation, and then such a good script, all characters felt so natural and alive, it can get you quite emotional.The puzzles were pleasant, its mechanics were not difficult to understand, they were user friendly but also challenging, it gives you a nice feel of satisfaction completing them, and I'm happy none of them managed to stress me. I liked the fact that the difficulty didn't just grow linearly, which is a normal thing in most games, having every once in a while a more simple puzzle was refreshing, that made it more enjoyable and it's something I appreciate a lot.Definitely worth it to play, for the price, it's cheaper than a ticket at the cinema and you get to enjoy a story that I'd say it's even better than most movies.

_childDocuments_.review: Welp. That was an underwhelming game. It's really pretty, the music is super nice, and the puzzle are fun: one would think with such strong starting points, that would be enough for a wonderful experience, and it kinda is. But for some unexplained reason, the creator of the game wrapped it all in a increasingly convoluted story. The mysteries pile up quickly, and the delivery on them comes late and all at once, without being given enough foreshadowing... The pacing is aimless and weird.Doesn't help that most of these mysteries end up really complex and out there without any theme or reason, it's just. It's there. And not explained for really long, which makes it mysterious I guess. The explanations fail to make them more meaningful. Which is kind of a shame, since if there's one theme central to the games, it's that life is precious and purposeful. It could be touching but the unnecessary secrets and plot-twists make the story more and more pointless. It's hard being engaged when the climax finally comes: at that point I was nothing more than a bit tired and grated, while the game was obviously expecting tears from me.I had the same dissonant experience with the characters : very promising, but made weaker and weaker by having their circonstances made more an more uselessly elaborate. Which again, is really damaging to the gaming experience, because it goes out of its way the make them the core of the journey. It was really intriguing at first ! But in the end I was just struggling with a big "meh, oh well".I guess the convoluted aspects of the story would have made sense in a "this is a puzzle game, of course the story would be puzzling" way. And it could have had ! But the story makes those puzzle more and more irrelevant. Again, any meaningful integration they seemed to have in the story is kind of dropped once the big revelations come in, which sure is a choice to make in a puzzle game. Overall I spent most of my gaming time solving things that didn't really made sense solving. Guess I should have spent that time playing detective on the plot. Oh wait, actually I couldn't: it's all-over-the-place and there is no solid cue. Too bad.In the end, the game feels genuine and is really pretty. It just tries to get deep in very tangled and meaningless ways, and loses itself in its plot-twits. It tries to juggle too many themes and stories at once and fails at doing so. It feels like the creator of the game tried to give a super impactful explanation to everything, and forgot to simply tell a story, or at the very least floundered to choose which story was being told.What could have been a rich, emotion packed and story-wise copious game (if handled better); or at least a profound and evocative one (if made much simpler and reduced to the core concepts), ends up nothing more than a bit disheartening and ineffective.(Also I'm aware this review is very critical, no hate on the creator, it is still an impressive work. Props and respect for such a beautiful game made with such a small team. I just think it tries to play really hard on what its biggest flaws ultimately are, and that just... well, it doesn't work.)

_childDocuments_.review: I play puzzle games for the plot, it provides the motivation to go forward.Here, I was acutely feeling every wasted minute.Just how has a child launched a solo expedition to decipher ancient monoliths? Such premises work when that's all it is, we aren't questioning Billy Blaze's grasp of general relativity or Mario's plumbing skills. But when you're working toward a "deep and poignant" -- i.e. stupid -- twist, this is utterly mentally exceptional. It's like if the answer to Life, the Universe, and Everything was "55378008" but you were supposed to feel sad.It gets worse, there's shades of To the Moon, Stein's Gate, Angels and Demons (the book where they blow up the pope with antimatter), the good old cat hair puzzle, and the Sherlock 4chan copypasta (they even do the "Sherlock winks at the screen" bit), with an extra helping of sick sadism. Just read the other reviews, or watch a playthrough.I'm not getting those 0.7 hours back. Let's see if I can get back the money.

_childDocuments_.review: Evan's remains is really two different games rolled into one:1) a visual novel about Dysis coming to an island with a vague mission to find someone named Evan2) jumping block puzzlesIndie games that combine two genres can be a hit or a miss, and most often have one part drag down the other. This game, almost to my own surprise, doesn't do placeholders. That is: the story is genuinely intriging and involving but (thus far) doesn't jump the shark or becomes a mess. It's clearly someone had the entire idea in his head for some time, probably had it proofread and polished, and used it in the game as intended. There's enough to keep you engaged, but no padding.Granted, the way jumping puzzles are crammed in requires some suspension of disbelief ("I just do them because they're fun"), but it provides a nice variation. But more importantly: these aren't just there to entertain the player, but they are genuinely good as well. Not overly complex but not a chore either. They have those great "oh yeah: of COURSE!" moments if you beat them, but probably don't have you searching a walkthrough in frustration.It's a low budget title, but it has charm and it clearly was made with a lot of love and dedication. So...and easy thumbs up (I'd give two, as both aspects deserve it, but ey...that's steam for you).
