_childDocuments_.review: The quick and dirty review is that they tried to emulate Dark Souls, but somehow took all the wrong lessons from the game and didn't seem to actually grasp any of the subtleties of what makes it great.Let's jump into some more details on the game's own merit (rather than as a comparison to other games), but first, a note about myself.  I'm a long-time player and fan of the soulsborne series, having started with Demon's and with around 5k hours of playtime across the full series.  I'm also someone who has an education in game design, for whatever extra nugget of legitimacy that may grant.  I was interested in Mortal Shell from early on, but trepidatious at how little hitstun seemed to play a factor in the early footage presented, and now that I've finally spent a solid amount of time feeling out the game's systems, I've come to the conclusion that it has a few fatal flaws and a whole host of inconveniences.  I also don't own the DLC, as I'm not interested in the alternate game mode.First, and most importantly, the game rewards the wrong things.  This is present in so many facets of the game, but let's focus on combat.  The game presents three defensive options in the form of Harden, Parry, and Dodge.  Harden is an awesome concept, allowing you to defend against a single incoming blow without sacrificing your offensive momentum.  The problem is many enemies are not staggered by it (allowing them to still hit you as a result of multi-attack chains), or even worse, some can outright ignore it and damage you regardless of being Hardened.  It is only situationally reliable, and requires blatant trial and error to find out when it won't work.  Parry is massively powerful if you have Resolve to spend, but requires timing (which seemed a bit inconsistent for me at times, so the window must be rather small) and doesn't work against most enemies' biggest attacks.  Your parrying instrument flashes bright red and makes a brief noise during the startup frames of any unparryable attacks, but you may have trouble noticing that as the ranged weapon on your back completely obscures the visual cue while locked on and the game's ambient music is nonstop violence against the player's ear.  Oh, and if you don't have resolve, a successful parry either puts your opponent into a second of stun or puts you BOTH into a second of stun (giving you no reward for successfully executing it), depending on the attack you successfully parried.  Once again, situational in usefulness, and has the highest skill requirement of use among the three options.  Dodging gives you full invulnerability from everything, costs some stamina, and can be cancelled into a second dodge roll for additional distance coverage.  The stamina cost makes it not a terribly reliable option while using low stamina shells, but if you're using a shell with moderate or better stamina, you'll quickly find that dodging out of the enemy's range is completely risk free and almost always gives you an opportunity to punish with your heavy attack (that has significant forward momentum), which can then safely be dodge cancelled again.  Interestingly, this strategy works against everything I ran up against - whether mobs of any size or bosses - and also has the added benefit of exploiting every single enemy's paper thin AI process.  It isn't even stamina intensive, as there's often enough time between when you dodge away and actually get an opening to punish that your stamina completely refills.  The last half of my playtime was spent doing that exact same sequence of dodge, wait for the end of the attack chain, punish with heavy attack, dodge cancel back and repeat.  It actively sucks the fun out of encounters when they are all addressed the exact same tedious way with no regard for having to learn anything more than "when are the breaks between enemy attack chains".  I learned neat skills, upgraded my shells with new passives, got various bonus riposte effects I could swap between for parries...and yet, the most effective way to play was to actively ignore all of that and just keep using the same old tired pattern that flawlessly worked against every enemy and boss.  Why bother with putting in the effort of learning how to play better when you can use the zero effort, zero skill, universally applicable answer to everything?Second, let's talk about the environment layout and pathing.  The environments are aesthetically distinct between stages, but often lack obvious landmarks for easy mental mapping within a stage, and frequently reinforce the player with a message of "don't bother with exploring" as there's often either nothing to be found, or a secret item that's just a run-of-the-mill junk item that has little value.  The trouble is, they do occasionally (about once or twice per map) have one actually important hidden item nestled in somewhere amidst all the vast emptiness and trash consumables.  It sends very conflicting signals, as if they want you to explore every nook and cranny of their world, but don't believe they should actually reward it 90% of the time.  The other bizarre aspect is that, for most of the game's stage design being on rails, there are shockingly few shortcuts to reward successful navigation through objectives and encounters.  To further stack upon this, enemies can't correctly navigate the stages.  They will frequently get stuck on geometry or simply walk themselves into corners because they're trying to walk a straight line to the player instead of actually recognizing the path they need to traverse to reach you.  This wildly reinforces just running through the stage, ignoring enemies to quickly rush down objectives without expending resources (such as healing items), which once again encourages player behavior of NOT engaging with the game (which loops back into the first point).The final point is the lack of motivation they give the player.  You are presented with a comical quantity of cryptic item and shell lore that seems to relate to various aspects of this bleak and pointless world, but absolutely zero narrative motivation to actually progress through the game content.  The most you get is a giant bird-like prisoner asking you to bring it nectar, so that it might get free.  That is legitimately your sole narrative direction to keep playing for some sort of implied payoff... except the payoff isn't even for you in the first place?  Unlocking the various shells and weapons is only hinted at by a montage of 2-3 visual flashes of environment that you're intended to follow.  There's not any narrative binding any of this, falling into the trap of just expecting the player to keep playing for the world lore snippets (which don't paint a particularly engaging story or offer any motivating drive) or the gameplay loop itself (which, we've already established actively encourages the player to ignore most of the content).  As a result, I found myself not motivated enough to complete the entire game.There are a host of other minor things that could be addressed, such as enemy poise reinforcing the no-skill combat loop, lack of meaningful difference between weapon movesets, reinforced behavior of spending time farming tar/glimpses/mushrooms, having to use items to find out what they do (including items that have outright negative effects), not being able to swap weapons in the field until you've completed an entire leg of the game, or locking the sole quick travel item in a shop that's only accessible after you've fully mastered a shell.  Ultimately though, these are all minor inconsiderations of design and pale in comparison to the big three flaws listed above.

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Shell seems difficult at first until the player discovers how OP the 'Harden' ability is. It's basically a 100% damage protection and 0% stamina use shield that can be used once every few seconds. It breaks after the character gets physically hit, but it can be used at absolutely every moment - even mid-air and during an attack.After realizing the above, the whole game can be cheesed to the point of not receiving any damage, and not even struggling to achieve that. The strategy is always the same - charge your heavy attack, use 'Harden' just before the attack is executed, and wait until an enemy mindlessly hits you. Repeat after the cooldown until the enemy is dead.There are no classic shields, though the player can use the 'Parry' ability. It's another super overpowered, and also upgradable ability, yet its main con is that it doesn't work. The parry windows are inconsistent and seem impossible to learn. Maybe it's a skill issue but still, if I can just use 'Harden' without taking any risk, the choice is simple.Another thing that makes me not recommend Mortal Shell is the weird choice of character customization - there is none. The player can just swap between 4 'shells' that come with different, buyable upgrades, and that's it. The same goes for weapon choice - there are only a few, and they come with only 4 or 5 (can't remember now) possible upgrades.This means that the character 'builds' are predetermined and can be varied only by the weapon choice. Different weapons need different materials to upgrade anyway so there's no need to focus on maximizing a particular one. Also, the aforementioned 'Harden' combat strategy obviously works best with the most powerful single-attack weapon.Finally, Mortal Shell is a very short and small game. There are only 4 main bosses and then thank you, your work is done. I understand it doesn't come with the standard Souls game price - which is pretty high - but come on. If I can't even collect any items (besides the usable ones), what's the point of going through NG+?

_childDocuments_.review: I have to mention that I'm not a big fan of soulsborne-like games, but I got this in a bundle on Fanatical as it seemed interesting enough, and this is why I'm giving it a positive.The game is Ok for the most part, but terrible frustrating due to frequent clunky control and animations that can get you killed by falling off the edges, and the lack of a jump mechanic while having abilities that require you to be either jumping or falling from great heights.A big minus is the fact that the game is broken into two modes, the main "story" mode and a rogue-like mode called Virtuous Cycle, that makes the gameplay more interesting than in the main mode and adds more elements to the story, but more frustrating as it bugs quite easily, forcing you to either quit and resume, or die and start over. Virtuous Cycle can be incredibly cheesable or incredibly hard, depending on what character and weapon you choose. For example, Solomon armed with a couple of moonshine and the Smoldering Mace weapon can one-shot any boss, with the correct upgrades, called "instincts" in the mode.Another minus is the amount of farming you have to do for the achievements, and if you're not calculated in how you do it, it can actually extend your farming time. Two incredibly tedious achievements are the ones in which you have to play the main game as the Foundling, both regular and Obsidian Form, a form that can be one-shot by anything. There is one also for the Virtuous Cycle, but that one is easier since you actually have enough manageable HP.Visually it looks great, even on my mid tier laptop (on which I played CP2077 at medium details), but has its stuttering moments.I would only recommend it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth waiting for a sale.Mortal Shell is a very creative Soulslike, if short. Instead of DS's plethora of mostly-useless weapons, armor and rings, Mortal Shell cuts to the point: You have four weapons to pick from, a modest set of useful consumables, and four "Shells" - bodies you inhabit to fight in. One's an all-rounder, the other three specialize in something.Mortal Shell is much more forgiving than Dark Souls, in a good way. When you hit 0 health you get knocked out of your shell, and if you get back to it without being hit (because your shell-less form dies in one hit to literally anything) you get the shell back and a HP refill. But, get taken to 0 again, and you die. It has a parry mechanic that was infinitely easier to use than in Dark Souls for two reasons: firstly, the parry frames are obvious (the thing you parry with flashes brightly), and secondly, you get warned about unparrayable attacks (the thing you parry with flashes red during the enemy's windup).It's got just enough customization to have depth and let you pick a build, without overwhelming you with options. It does creative things with the areas you have to go through. Because there's no levelling, the game is very nonlinear. It can be a bit rough at the beginning while you find your footing, but it's worth sticking with through to the end for a fun Soulslike experience.

Only negative is the AI, where it quite blind, missing the fact that you are slaughtering their allies 10 meters away from them. In most cases you can easily aggro one enemy from a group, isolate, kill and repeat. That said, the title is worth a try regardless, very solid souls-like!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I really enjoyed this. It is one of the shorter experiences among all the other "souls-like" games but it still manages to provide a solid amount of stuff to fight/find/discover.All the good-Harden feature. This was a nice defense/counter and makes it much easier for those who could never roll or parry in souls like games so here's another chance.-For me I was actually able to become parry god in this game so my guess is its much easier because I cannot parry in dark souls like .-Item familiarity. Because this game takes the dark souls route of world building (minimal dialogue, minimal cutscenes, lore in all the items instead of spoken through someone) I found it much more appealing to read through and look at item descriptions because I can level them up for better effects and new info being unlocked along the way. Not a massive thing but it just felt satisfying.-Bosses. Most of these games do this fairly well and this is no exception although very few. Not bad but not stellar either. The only exception being the final as it can come off as too long and has a really dumb mechanic.Yes/NoThese are both the good and bad things that I can't decide where they belong so that's up to you.-Shells and weapons. Limited build variety as there are no real stats to level only swap around and slightly upgrade. Shell designs are really dope, they each have their own backstory, a unique ability or two and their stats differentiate enough to essentially be classes in a way but no big number upgrades on that front. Weapons keep your typical level up status but not much changes other than damage. Only several weapons in the game and each having 2 special abilities. While they are all unique to one another only like 2 stand out and feel effective or reasonable enough to use, but that might just be me. My example being the Martyr blade, feels like I'm carrying the weight of 1000 suns with that thing and my enemies die of age before it reaches their chest. To add onto this there is no magic, so strength builds all the way baby-DLC. I actually find the DLC a bit challenging yet really entertaining. My one and only issue being that it acts separately from the main game so if you planned playing through the main game and bought the DLC expecting more story, more enemies, more weapons or armor or anything else your wrong. It's a gauntlet, separate from your main game save, of everything you've already seen and done and forcing you to progress through the game in a different manner which like I said I really enjoyed BUT yeah nothing really new new so be careful with that.-Scenery/Locations. Really mixed on this. Very few areas but a shorter game so expected. The environments are unique and cool to be in however one in particular, Seat of Infinity, can feel too expansive with little to no reward for exploration. Just a big open space with a lot of walking room and enemies but not enough reward to match the risk. Other areas were more confined and the length felt much better since I wasn't travelling 3 miles east and fighting groups of enemies along the way to look in the corner and see nothing. Infinity can suck but hey you might like it.The Ugly-Rare but I would come across some bugs every now and then, nothing game breaking. Some enemies would be clipped into the floor, sometimes a bit, sometimes up to their neck. There was a camera bug that kept me zoomed too close to the character and didn't break until I interacted with a tunnel so finding one was a pain.-This is sort of a spoiler so beware I guess but keeping it vague, those who have watched the game or played themselves should know. There is a particular section of the game where it requires you to backtrack an area while resetting it in the process and ONE part of it is very very frustrating but otherwise nothing else has been set up as poorly as this section. Like 30 arrows to the knee and don't think it'll be changed.-Using tunnels. So this can be used to your advantage however most of the time it'll get you without you realizing it. Some areas require a short and sweet journey through some random hole that you come across and will lead you into a new area which is cool and all however you can get your ass beat coming out if it. There is an unnecessary short scene that plays making it so YOU cannot input jack however anything that happens to be chilling by the exit you come out of will aggro and usually smack you upside the head before the scene ends and you're not invincible. While this may not be an issue all the time, when your not using a shell this is literally life or death. The advantage being you can avoid negative status effect ticks while sitting in one assuming its long enough and doesn't automatically send you through, not sure if this still works but usually they don't hurt enough to be a massive concern.While it seems I have more negative stuff to say over positive I feel it might be me being nit-picky.To sum it up yes I think it's a great game. No it's not perfect and lacks in a few areas but it's not a AAA game and is one of the better "souls-like" games I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very obviously looking to scratch an itch for a lot of people. A Dark Souls itch lots and lots of people seem to be developing these days. And game developers all around are noticing these disgustingly hardcore, dark, and soulsy rashes. Mortal shell is very much a "soulslike". Ultimately if you're buying this game you'll mostly know what you're getting yourself into.Fortunately it delivers. It's not long at about 20 hours to finish the base game, though there's NG+ and some roguelike (yet another itchy rash going around) if you're unsatisfied with that. This game has a couple of mechanics which makes it pretty different to a lot of stuff coming out these days, and just for playing around with them it's probably worth picking up if you're into soulslikes. You can inhabit different "shells" which you can find about the place, which have varying unique skill trees and base abilities. There's no stat upgrades, only consumables, skill trees, and weapon upgrades. These shells are dead humans with their stories unlocked through their skill trees, personally i would've found it a bit more interesting if they did something more with you getting to play a part in their story or something...I mean, there's hints of it with some npcs reacting differently depending on which you are, but it's more minor than i'd like. You have a "harden" ability which renders you immovable and invincible, but will break once hit - this is quite a nice addition which adds some strategy to fights as well as a welcome alternative to use parry-averse people. Though, there is a parry ability, which oddly is upgraded and given new abilities for each major area conquered/boss defeated, which seems like an odd choice considering parrying is a pretty divisive ability among gamers. Though in those areas you also find 2 weapon upgrades, which usually give an elemental buff and a magic-ish ability.There's 4 weapons and 4 shells, plus one dlc shell and weapon you can obtain after getting them all (i liked those two the best, they seem pretty OP, though not game-breaking). While the gameplay and abilities are all quite good and unique something about it (and as a general note to this game as a whole)just feels...lacking. It's not quite as in-depth or well thought out or tightly designed as it could have been. This really shows in the level design, which is good in places, but just amounts to dotting various enemies on mostly open stretches of terrain at time. It feels as though this game had a lot of potential to be something more than it is. It's also noticeably buggy at times. It just feels like it needed a bit more time in the oven - though it's still updating so one can hope most of these will be patched.The story, lore, and tone are all dark, fantasy, soulsy as well as cryptic and hard to find/understand. It takes after dark souls but does it less well. Though the story is hardly that important. It accomplishes what it needs to in setting the right tone and feel of consistency. I do quite like the MC and what he is, feels rather unique - basically a ghost instead of a zombie as in most souls games.Graphics, audio, and music are all up to standard and mostly unremarkable. Some of the music i quite enjoy, especially the lute and clockwork lute you can play. Graphics are also quite good, though occasionally enemy characters take up until you're a few meters away to load....which can be annoying.For some reason you can't remap weapon abilities on the controller, which is annoying since they're a combination of two very frequently pressed buttons in combat. Overall, if you're looking for a unique and fun interpretation of the soulslike genre, pick it up. But don't go in expecting this to be your new favourite game. I liked it a lot and enjoyed my time with it, perhaps i'll try the roguelike and a bit of NG+. I'd be interested to see a longer and more polished sequel.

Pros: - Unique Seal parry mechanic- Unique harden mechanic- Great visuals- Combat feels fluid- Interesting NPCs- Photo ModeAnd a bit more to the list.Cons: - Confusing map layouts- Clipping bugs and glitches - Very shortMy biggest complaint about Mortal Shell is that it's short, as a souls veteran and speedrunner, going in blind I finished the game in under 4h, for 30$ that's a bit low on content. If this goes on sale for 10$, this is worth it, it's not a very punishing souls-like, and makes it more fun for casual players.

_childDocuments_.review: First proper souls-like game I got since I don't usually play these types. I had quite a lot of fun. I'll try not to spoil much.TLDR: Its great, a bit clunky sometimes, but still fun none the less. At the time of review, I've finished it and am on a new game plus. Fighting is pretty decent and simple, there's no complicated combos. tho it is a bit clunky at times, just dont forget to lock on your enemies. There are  with different stats and play styles, even  being a very good one and the shell I used the most and finished the game with. This is paired with  with varying damage, reach, speed, and abilities (starter sword being my favorite).  is a pretty neat feature, its a click and hold block that can be done during an attack. It's practically a more safer parry that can be used offensively when done right.  is the usual timing counter that becomes an  with different abilities with enough resolve, tho you'll likely be using the Healing riposte more since  (heals are only from the heal riposte and food). Between Parry and Harden, I found myself using Hardening more since I'm not the best at timing with parry, you can practically play the game with only hardening and dodging. Oh right, there's also a . unfortunately, with new game plus, you'll start taking reduced damage with harden, but by that time, you've likely mastered or at least got the hang of parry. Killing enemies give Tar and a chance of glimpse, the game's currency. they are used for the shop, shell upgrades, and weapon upgrades.The map is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ maze... at first. just explore around and you'll likely know the place pretty quickly (at least from my experience). The main area, Fallgrim, connects to 3 different Temples with their own enemies and each temple will have 1 weapon for you to get and their respective upgrades. Shrine of ash (best to start with this one), Crypt of martyrs, and Seat of infinity(best to do this last). not much to say since its best for you to see them for yourselves. try your best to fight a few enemies at a time, even the simple bastards can kill you quickly, fortunately, most enemies just walks towards you and a low aggro range (depends). Enemies have normal attacks and unparryable attacks, the usual. normal attacks can be negated by harden (and knockbacks the attacker) and be riposte'd by parry. some enemies have very predictable normals and quick hard to parry normals. unparryable are self explanatory, they can still be blocked by harden and be dodged. ranged enemies are quite a pain, especially the temple ones, I tend to kill those first. You can of course run past enemies but you'll lose the chance to get Tar and glimpse to improve your shells and weapons.There's a cat you can pet, and a Frog that will happily listen to your lute.

_childDocuments_.review: I've nearly completed the game in a matter of 8.2 hours. I have sat down and played this game three times, yeah with some decent length sections but still.I really missed the DS series, and it's very reminiscent of that, to which I appreciate. I've got well over 1.2k hours on DS3 alone, across my PS4 and Steam. Beaten it countless times.Mortal Shell is alright, however it's not without it's criticisms though. Yes, there are a lot of quotation marks, and that's on purpose. Good graphics, decent performance, pretty decent sound track. It's honestly really disappointing because I think they had some really good concepts and ideas here, and just didn't live up to the potential.What even is the story? Not really sure, like I get vague concepts and I've tried going around in the world to gather what I can, just doesn't feel evident enough from what I'm getting. Sure, I can and have looked it up and stuff, but I shouldn't have to, especially to this degree. It felt like the devs just wanted to try recreating some DS mechanics with some of their own twists, then half ass threw a "world" around it. There's no motivation, and no immersion.The maps can be beautiful, but they feel cluttered and hectic. Even worse than the over the top environment in Bloodborne. At the same time, there's not really anything to go off of in your environment in order to build a good mental map of the place.Boss rooms are sick, general map can just be a tad much I'd say, even when considering that into the setting it's trying to portray in a given area.Do you like exploring maps to find cool items, areas, encounters and more? Well give up on that in this game, because you *might* be "rewarded" for that twice. So much of the already limited amount of map is just blank, or full with filler.The AI leaves a lot to be desired. The Hadren fights would all break for me, no matter how many times I'd restart them. I ended up just going along with it, and just wailing on a frozen character who might occasionally try to swing while standing in place. General path finding is rather bugged, could use some tuning there. Enemies get stuck on props, or corners, and all sorts of things, and it's a bit ridiculous.The game felt difficult at first, I loved it. There's a little bit of a grind you can do to get your gear upgraded to make things easier. But there's a big issue in this game, in my opinion, and that's that there isn't enough. We're limited to 4 characters with pre-determined stats, with generic variation. You get a "skill tree" with the a limited amount of options, though they do offer a couple cool bonuses/effects/buffs/etc. Maxing out a character really doesn't take long at all, and while that may sound good, it just doesn't feel like you're doing anything with your character, there's no customization. I could understand a lack of customization for narrative purpose, and there "is" to a degree, but I wouldn't say enough to justify it. There are like 3 main bosses, a handful of "mini bosses," and what feels like maybe 10 enemies otherwise. Given the 4 choices of weapons, with no difference in move-sets other than speed, combat got boring very fast. Like I said, I'm writing this at the last boss fight with 8 hours in.Parrying and Riposte are inconsistent af. I gave up on using it, which really disappoints and frustrates me considering it's a way to heal and this game severely holds back healing options. But hey, at least Harden is cool?The game is actually really easy, stupidly easy actually. They try to make up for it by making you thirsty for items that actually do anything at all, like healing. "JuSt DoNt GeT hIt!" Yeah, parry is inconsistent af, and dodging sucks unless you're using Tiel, so there's pretty much just harden. And excuse me, I didn't realize that a pro not hit speed runner was reading my review, nice to meet you.It's frustrating that I held hope and held out for the game, wishing it would pick up, only for it not to. So now I won't be able to return it, lmaoIt's not like what I'm saying hasn't been said before, just look at these other reviews.Also, +1 for letting me pet a cat

_childDocuments_.review: Superb game, please don't listen to the haters. It's incredibly good, and the DLC makes it orders of magnitude better.Some are saying the combat mechanics are badly designed/implemented. They couldn't be more wrong. Yes, combat is deliberately slow. Or rather, slow and deliberate. There's a serious sense of weight, which is entirely intentional and far from "clunky". In terms of speed it's much closer to Dark Souls 1 combat than even the other DS games themselves, without feeling in any way dated.This game is entirely worthy of the title of "soulslike", and, while obviously inspired by Dark Souls (again, particularly the first one), it fully stands on its own two feet and couldn't be further from an empty clone. I expect Elden Ring to have more than one Mortal Shell reference in it ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Shell is too bloody short, way too bloody short. Dark Fantasy? Ascensionism? Other dimensional? yes, now give me more please. The swinging of each weapon rivals that of other (I dare say) "souls-like games". New game plus:10/10. Leveling up:10/10(and very immersive). Movement hasn't reached its full potential but what is there feels weighty and "real". The only major critique left, that isn't "it needs bloody more" is that there are some unpolished sections. Most notable, animations/attacks/abilities of the player character and enemies and the enemy and checkpoint placement. Some a/a/a are really jank. _childDocuments_.review: Attempted playing this game several times but never made in far in. Twice now I've beaten the first boss and progressed into the second area of the game, but that's it. My latest and final attempt lasted only an hour.Each of my attempts at this game has ended quickly due to 3 general issues with the game.The first is that it's extremely janky and unpolished - it feels like an alpha test. All of the cutscenes are awkward and generally feel unfinished. Movement and combat animations are poorly-made and feel "slidey" or "clunky" (for example, your character noticeably slides forward before taking a step when moving). I also encountered several bugs in my short time playing, including a screen-flickering/lag spike issue, a controller vibration issue, and some general audio weirdness that I think qualifies as bugs (though might just be poor design).The second is that the game is boring. You are given absolutely zero direction or motive to progress in the world, so the only thing to do is aimlessly explore for the sake of exploring. The problem is that exploration is awful. The starting zone is a large, maze-like collection of indistinct paths that connect in ways that feel randomly decided, and there is no clear way forward towards any kind of goal. I killed my first boss, but there was nothing of interest after it. Despite exploring what I felt what must have been most of the starting swamp, I never encountered any checkpoints, and when I finally reached what seemed to be a distinct new area, I was immediately killed by the first enemy there with no easy way back. The game also (as far as I'm aware) never gives you a regenerating source of healing, and the healing consumables are hard to come by, so you need to play perfectly for long stretches of time just to get back to where you died. This felt unreasonably punishing in a way that far exceeds the punishing nature of the Souls series that Mortal Shell so heavily draws upon.After 2 failed attempts at killing that first new enemy, I quit for good - even if I did have the willpower to push through the challenge, I didn't have anything interesting me in continuing to play the game. Nothing I had seen so far was impressive or interesting in any way, and the game seemed to be specifically designed to make the player hate it.Side note: despite including settings involving ultrawide and HDR support, the game actually supports neither and is just pretending to. The game "supports" ultrawide by simply cropping the top and bottom of the screen to fit the aspect ratio, drastically reducing your vertical field of view, and HDR support is completely broken by admission from the developer and is not planned to be fixed. Additionally, the only way to play at the proper aspect ratio (16:9) on an ultrawide monitor is to play in windowed mode.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly the first time I write a bad review about a soul-like game...The environment is good, enemies looks awesome. In terms of graphics? It definitely reaches FromSoft level, like I can genuinely say I'm playing dark soul 3. But the core problem is its control and mechanism. If there's one thing that this game proves, it's the fact that control in not only soul-like, but any action-based RPG are very hard to fine-tune. This game's control is nothing but terrible. I was never able to focus on the first enemy when there are more than 3 enemies together, the system will focus on a further away enemy which I can only see half of its body while ignoring the big guy that is right in front of me. If I was put into dying state, I immediately lost focus on the enemy and If I happen to face a poor direction, I'm just screwed. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ control kills me more than the enemy did. Then the core mechanism. This game has the worst way to interact with the world:- There is no spawn point, or break point. You die, you spawn at home- There is no estus flask, and there are essentially no effective healing method beside from parrying- Speaking of parrying, you have to slowly earn them through combat, and when you're out of combat, any unfinished parry status will rewind. This is just dumb. It forces me to keep slashing corpus just to build up parries. - Item usage will only be revealed after certain uses. Another dumb mechanic that makes no sense. - Natural items in the world has a real-time cooldown of spawning. WHY? Just WHY? Grinding in this game is already a lot, and now we have to wait in real time for a mushroom to spawn? Insane. - Traps cannot be disarmed, even if you step on this. This is usually ok if there are only one small area that does this, but the devs just LOVES to put traps on every freaking where, especially in narrow combat area. - The "get harden" mechanic might seems fresh at the beginning, but later on you'll realize it's a really boring mechanic that serves more like a gimmick rather than a core mechanic. All the above summarized into one thing: You made a small mistake in the beginning of your adventure, you're screwed. Might as well use the mask to reset, because there is no estus flask. I'm pretty sure I missed out a lot of the content, but honestly? I don't even bother open this game anymore after the first bear boss. It's just terrible.

_childDocuments_.review: If you thought that Dark Souls was cryptic with its mechanics then you should definitely check out this game. It doesn't explain anything to you besides basic controls like how to attack and harden (this game's equivalent of blocking). Then you are thrown into the world without any guidance. You are somewhat guided towards the hub but it still might not be clear where the entrance is. And when you find the hub, you get one remark to get the "gland" from the "temple". And that's it.You pick up a seal but the game doesn't tell you what it's for. Turns out it's for parrying. But to effectively parry you need one bar of "resolve" (what is resolve? Turns out it's the meter above your health). After that you can riposte an enemy to get some health. But the game does nothing to explain ANY of this to you. That's just one example. (You can also parry when you have no resolve but you can't riposte.)But if you can get past all of that and figure it out, you can actually appreciate some aspects of the game. The combat is quite weighty and slow-paced - you can't just wail on enemies since your stamina is quite limited, so you can only deal a couple of hits before you have to back off.The main mechanic of the game is inhabiting different characters (shells). Each character has different stats (HP, stamina, resolve) and different abilities you can unlock. To unlock them you need two currencies - tar and glimpses. Tar is regular (like souls in Dark Souls) and is dropped upon death. And glimpses are bound to the shell (so when you switch shells, you need to collect new glimpses, which the game obviously did not explain, which in turn caused a short panic and confusion for me).When you start exploring the first area, the swamp, you quickly realize that it's hard to navigate - there are no landmarks or anything to show you where you are currently. So you either roam around until you figure out which paths lead where, or you look up a guide online (and even then it might be hard to understand where you need to go). You also notice that there are crawlspaces that you can get into to get either to another area (like a shortcut) or to a small cave. And those crawlspaces have two transition screens for some reason... Also, you can't go backwards while you are crawling.As you explore, you will find items that you can use. But to know what those items do you need first to use them at least once. That's another mechanic of the game - item familiarity. You use an item - you fill the familiarity bar, and when it's filled, you get an extra effect from using this item. Sounds interesting on paper, but in reality there are no interesting uses of this mechanic. The only one I can think of is a mushroom that first poisons you, but when you fill the familiarity bar, it grants you immunity to poison. But you only need to eat this mushroom two times to fill the bar...You will also find other areas while exploring. These are the "temples" from which you have to get the "gland". At the start of those areas you can get a new weapon, but you have to defeat a tutorial boss that wields this weapon. This is also not explained by the game, so you could be confused about why you were transported to another arena and have to fight the tutorial boss again...Those other areas (temples) are much more linear than the swamp. You have to get to the end, fight a boss, after which you can finally get a gland. But it's not all, because as soon as you get the gland, the temple becomes dark and stronger enemies spawn. And now you have to backtrack all the way to the entrance. And that's not the end, because the swamp also changed - it's covered in fog now, and all the enemies are replaced with one type - jumping monsters. And you have to go to the hub, and give the gland to the prisoner there. After that the swamp turns back to normal. As far as I know, once you pick up the gland, there is no turning back, and of course, the game doesn't warn you about this. So if you run out of healing items, then tough luck...Although one area stands out - the fortress with obsidian-looking stones (there are names of the areas but the game doesn't really tell them to you). It's huge and very open at the start, you can run around freely while looking for switches that you need to progress. It also looks nice since it's not a cave unlike two other areas, the light reflects from the stones which looks nice and atmospheric. It seems like most of the team's effort went into this place.Some other issues that I noticed:1. Enemies can sometimes materialize in front of you out of thin air. They just spawn in front of you and start attacking. It's probably because the game despawns enemies to save resources but doesn't catch up to you when spawning them back in.2. Status effects apply to you immediately instead of having a build-up. So you can get poisoned or set on fire instantly.3. The game loves putting enemies around corners to ambush you. It would be fine if used sparingly. But it happens too often and quickly becomes annoying.But even with all these quirks I still enjoyed the game. The process of figuring out the game mechanics by yourself reminded me of when I played Dark Souls 1 for the very first time. It's not as refined as it was here, but still very similar. And there was also a moment where everything you learned just "clicks" together and you start enjoying it, also like in Dark Souls.The game is very rough, but even then it's worth picking up on sale if you are REALLY prepared to learn everything by yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Shell captures the exploration of adventure that souls games themselves sometimes struggle to manifest! Finding your favorite combination of the five characters and five weapons and investing into perfecting it is very satisfying. The map design is compact and polished, for a great feeling of discovery when first starting out, to a gratifying mastery of after navigating it into memory. The audio design is impressive, with no music aside from the occasional lute playing of some idle enemies in the swamp every ribbit of a frog or groan of a thrall adds to the immersion. To top off the immersive experience the voice acting had no need to go so hard. Each voice which occasionally reads the lore for various upgrades or checkpoints feels like an entity speaking using their entire being, weather that's a deep gutteral rumble of a chained deity or a throaty gurgle from the froggy vendor, or even the soft respite of the "sester" checkpoints the audio design is not something I expected to be a standout here. After 100%ing the base game I checked out the DLC and it's a masterclass on how to use an existing framework to expand into something more. Some roguelike modes additions falter by either missing some crucial element (looking directly at you Remnant 1 DLC for not allowing any pause or checkpoint in runs that are expected to take 5+ hours) or just don't feel as complete but the Virtuous Cycle mixes up everything just enough to make the existing knowledge of the game feel necessary for the fresh experience, without having to remake the whole game just layering a progression system and upgrade system onto randomized enemy spawns and boom 5x replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: From what I'm feeling while playing, I can best describe this game as a smaller, tighter, more demanding soulslike. With five total weapons, no bonfires, healing being only through items, and an unforgiving combat system, it demands patience- or a calculated fierceness.Both of these approaches work. I mainly play Harros, a shell with balanced stats. You can either play defensively, working with your harden (the primary defensive tactic, much like a limited invincibility), dash attacks, and backpedaling, or, if you know your enemy, a hyper-aggressive dodge-and-slash style that keeps you directly in, using the exact same harden to stay on the offense, instead of backing off to regenerate stamina.As for weapon variety- There are five, the Hallowed Sword, a balanced approach weapon, the Martyr's Greatsword, a frosty, slow, heavy hitter that rewards tactical aggression, both of which I have used, and the Hammer & Chisel, Flaming Mace, and Axtana, which I have not, and cannot offer much in the way of review.The game is, however, enthralling in setting and ambiance. Also, you can make a frog buddy and if you feed him cooked rats and play him a song, he'll burp new colors on you. That's pretty cool.

_childDocuments_.review: All of the souls aesthetic, and none of its charm.Giving this a thumbs up despite not enjoying it that much, purely because I don't think it's a bad game. The problem is it draws so heavily from souls games without really studying what makes souls games good.Pros-Aesthetic; the world is beautiful and sets a grim tone -Combat has a nice weight to it -Having shell progression instead of levelling is a nice change -The shell concept is interesting & new (to me)-controls are basically the exact same as dark souls, so take that as you willCons-Short. Completed the game in just under 8 hours including at least an hour of just having the game on without playing.-The game consists of a hub area, and 3 connected pathways that each lead into a temple. The entire game is completing each of these 3 temples then returning to the hub. Unfortunately they're all pretty short, and the game attempts to double the length of them by making the temple foggy after you kill the boss, unlocking new chests for items to find. While a cool idea, it's really not entertaining to just run through the same temple twice in a row.-The areas themselves are beautiful and unique, however while running around each area it all looks the same. It makes it difficult to remember where you are and spot landmarks when each area doesn't have unique locations - something that the souls games does very well making it easy to traverse those maps-Way too easy. Beat all the bosses first try with the same approach, and only the final boss really gives a good challenge.-Lack of enemies considering the game is already small - had there been more enemy variety I would have enjoyed it more. But generally once you clear one room in an area, you've seen all that area has to offer.-One of the best things about souls is the level design - especially dark souls 1. Things feel interconnected without ever feeling random and you truly feel like you're exploring another world. I don't get that feel from this game - generally run straight with side paths giving you extra stuff to find. -You can harden for an infinite amount of time and absorb all the damage from the next attack you receive. This makes combat essentially just jump attack -> harden -> quick attack -> repeat-parry timing feels bad, man-the upgrades for each shell aren't particularly useful or interesting I got this game on sale for 8.24$, so I got just under an hour of play per buck, which I'm happy with. Had I paid full price I would have been disappointed. I realise that this is a smaller indie company, so I can't really fault them for the game being short - but had the level design been more interesting, I would have opted for multiple replays and it would not have bothered me.All in all, solid game for a small studio to fill your dark souls void for a day, but they need to study what makes dark souls so great in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: i want to recommend this game. i really do, but i can't. if i could give it a mixed review, i would but being forced to choose between yes or no, i have to choose no. on the one hand, the atmosphere is excellent and the concept is new and delightful, but at the same time everything is pointless. "progression" doesn't so much come from killing enemies as it comes from finding loot and using them to upgrade your weapons. while you do kind of need to kill enemies to upgrade your shells, the problem is that almost all of the upgrades (aside from hadern's) are inconsequential relative to personal skill. this would be all well and good if not for the fact that it encourages blitzing past all of the enemies to loot the area. combine this with the fact that all of the shell upgrades are very expensive relative to most enemies' rewards and the result is you should't ever kill things unless you are specifically farming for an upgrade that you can't afford just by using the currency items. designing a game such that it encourages the player to not actually engage with the game's content is extremely detrimental to the viability of the game and the predominant reason why i can't suggest this game.add on top of that many mechanics are extremely gimmicky (like those ghoul vampire dudes who jump on you just sortof... appear on you even though they just started their jump) and every encounter just feels like crap. either it's too easy because you mitigated the gimmick, or it's ridiculous because the gimmick got you anyway. this applies to bosses just as readily as it does mobs. the first one i killed was crucix who was the only one of the bosses that actually gave me any trouble for reasons players who've fought him would be aware of but i'm not gonna spoil. after him, every other boss was basically child's play including the final boss. 2 attempts for the ice guy, 1 attempt for the fire guy, and 2 for the last guy and that was only because i ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and not because of the boss.one last major problem is that this game bloats playtime by disallowing fast travel until you have maxed out one of the shells aside from hadern (then you have to buy the damn thing). this problem is exacerbated by felgrim's hold+outskirts functionally acting like a maze. until you learn the frankly very monotonous and samey area, you'll probably be running around like an idiot. once you get into one of the temples, though, it becomes extremely linear. there are, of course, side paths, but they are all either dead ends or seemingly tacked on. compared to the souls series, there is very little map cohesion in the form of opening shortcuts by progressing through the map and, aside from fulgrim tower/outskirts, there isn't very much to actually explore. everything is just a buffer between you and the boss.in short, this game feels kinda like the demon's souls attempt of this franchise. i hope their future games can do better but i can't rightly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Mortal Shell

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Shell is a ruthless, third-person action role-playing game that's heavily inspired by Dark Souls, BUT saying just that is massively underselling since it manages to make it's own unique and interesting spin on the 'souls-like' genre making it at the same time very 'unlike-souls' entry where players get to take on a role of a Foundling who's got an uncanny ability to control different defeated warriors aka "Mortal Shells" and use their unique combat masteries to help us do the bidding of mysterious "Dark Father" who sets us on arduous journey through this shattered world we now inhabit and which is constantly testing not only our awareness and will to survive but also our crumbling sanity.An Indie budget title with art design that's truly excellent, developed by a coalition of seasoned veterans who made such beautiful graphics with attention to details in such high fidelity is with no doubt worth all the praise it can get.. From Falgrim with it's dense and ominous fog covering the tattered forest landscape to each one of the hidden sanctums of devout followers, starting with Crypt of Matryr's caught in winter's snare and her bitter currents whispering between the holy chamber; to the Seat of Infinity with it's indestructible geometry wrought from stark yet pleasantly alien obsidianite. Each and every location we get to discover is a sight to behold. The same can be said about the sound design which truly compliments the whole game and is simply phenomenal. It sets the atmosphere of this crumbling land oozing with murk and filled with rotten brigands, croaking wildlife and all kind of monsters barely clinging to life, quite well. Not a single thing is out of place. Starting with proper enemy audio queues, sounds of surrounding us environment to the sounds of your own armored boots stepping in the mud. Good voice acting isn't something normally expected either from such a small studio but I was pleasantly surprised to have it anyway. Also there's nothing as enjoyable as the magnificently crafted notes of a lute  which in on itself is bloody awesome. Watching life pass on by while you play on a lute.. *chef's kiss* We start the game in our Foundling form, the most vulnerable one, and through process of exploring the world  we get to obtain and inhabit shells, corpses of lost warriors, about which we'll be able to learn more through Sester Genessa and spending Tar obtained from certain objects or simply by killing enemies. That will lead us to learning various abilities they're in possession of, to hone in their unique skill trees. Each shell has her own pros and cons, and it's for the player to decide what kind of playstyle they want to pursue. Furthermore you can easily swap between the shells whenever you want, and no I don't mean running back to Sester Genessa every single bloody time. The game has this items, effigies that can be used to change shells but also weapons. Which comes to my next point. We can choose between five different melee weapons, offering different special skills, and one long range one  that we can use to fight the enemies and the only catch is... yes, we got to find their location first. The game also introduces us to a new type of defensive mechanic, The Hardening. It allows us to turn into stone, preventing enemies from dealing any kind of damage. Weaving this tactic into attacks can sometimes be a bit of a challenge since you can't just spam this ability, it has a cooldown but you can bet your rotting arse you will hear when it's replenished. And when it's active, it might take a second to actually go into effect so you can't use it right as enemy is about to attack you either. You have to be strategic with it's use since this opens a lot of tactical possibilities that are very not 'souls-like'. Yet when Hardening is finally mastered, the combat will just instantly 'click'. At least it did for me. This mechanic takes a turn from a weird substitute of a shield to an interesting tool which skilled players can use to prevent the interruption of a flow of combat and getting their stamina back, whatever to dodge or successfully parry the next attack, which can only be done if you obtain Tarnished Seal and it needs one bar of resolve but the reward for it is extremely valuable since not only you can stun and injure the enemy but also it allows you to regain certain amount of health so you don't have to 'farm' healing items or buy +99 of them to survive. It's all about constantly learning, using and adapting to what you're equipped with in the game instead of rushing straight in while swishing your weapon without no strategy and complaining it didn't work. Take your time to master it all instead of crying about how you're already the master... Combat here is very strategic and deliberate! You must commit your weapon only when an opportunity opens. Last but not least it's worth to mention that essentially we as Foundling inhabiting a Shell, have two lives. If we lose the first one, we're knocked out of our chosen Shell but if we manage to get back to our body and basically put it back on, we come back to life with full health while Foundling form with no shell can be killed in just, one. hit.It's all very mysterious and a bit convoluted, and like with any game like this it's really down to the players own interpretation. Without spoiling too much, I can only say that there's two stories slowly but simultaneously revealed to the player. There's the backstory of the wider world which somewhat explains it's disgusting and decaying state, the histories of the characters we meet and the meaning behind the places we visit and the things we see but at the same time, then there's the story of our main character, The Foundling, who we play as and what drives us to find the three sacred glands. Much like Fromsoftware's games actually working this stuff out is a pretty tall order requiring a combination of item descriptions, quite cryptic npc dialogue and interpretation of the environment including hidden around the world inscriptions and etchings.There was absolutely nothing that impacted my performance or caused glitches. The game run smooth as butter for me. Bugs? I didn't even know there where any until I looked at other people reviews about the game. In my humble opinion, if there where any bugs/glitches they surely had been fixed and when it comes to performance issues, well.. check your system requirements first ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)Mortal Shell is a pretty good entry into 'souls-like' genre. I just can't say it's gonna be a game for everyone because a lot of people will not be able to let go of their surface level criticisms that it's just a DS poor copy instead of judging it as it's own beast. This is a genuinely great game. Yes, it can have it's quirks, a dark twisted world with decent amount of surprises to explore and very enjoyable combat, lute for life™ while also being quite short and pretty hard at times. It's a game that takes us into new and innovative places with a polish that it has absolutely no business having and will do all of that without trying to hold your hand no matter how much you want it. And yet while being all of that it's exciting and more friendly to players than DS, making it a great entry to start of your journey into that particular genre. I had my fun and the game didn't overstay it's welcome, so it's super easy for me to recommend this game. Whatever you want to buy it on a good sale or with it's full price, this is a title worth trying out. | September 23, 2022 | [★★★★★]

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy souls-like games, this might be your cup of tea. However, I feel it might not be for everyone as there is a mechanic uniquely different from other souls-like you have to incorporate. The first boss forces you to learn how to use the mechanics to beat him but at the same time not ridiculously hard. The graphics are really good, enemies, friendly npcs, and bosses are also pretty well designed. My favorites part was learning the new playstyle, trying different shells, and the special skills that can be used to crush enemies. As much as I enjoyed the combat style and design, I still have my pet peeves that this game brings. A few issues were that some parts of the map look very similar to each other making it confusing and difficult to figure out where you are especially in the starting zone. There is fast travel in the game but by the time you can purchase it, you're already more than halfway through the game. There are only a few different weapons to choose from and you only get enough upgrade materials for two max weapons. I also feel like they could made the checkpoints too far apart. I would have to sprint by the all enemies every now and then just to get to the next checkpoint. At least the boss ones were close. Overall, I would rate it a  6/10 as the gameplay is pretty fun but there are some setbacks that hinder the experience. Also, I've seen some people talk about janky controls but I personally have had little to no issues with the way the controls work. The dodging mechanic is slightly different which may throw some people off.

_childDocuments_.review: i want to like this game but i cannot get into it. I really enjoy how the game encourages you to try items that you find. Coming from souls games, i would often have a bunch of consumable items in my inventory at the end of a play-through that i never used, but having the mechanic where you get more efficient by using items really makes me want to experiment with different things which i think is cool for exploration. I also like the hardening mechanic, i think its a really cool gimmick that can change the pace of fights.However, I just cant get past how off the combat feels. Things feel very "floaty" and for whatever reason my actions dont really feel like that have impact. Moreover, some of the enemy animations, like greisha pulling its claw out of the ground dont seem like it would be a damaging move but i find myself getting caught by that when circling its back after its pounce. This might just be something i need to get used to but it doesnt feel like the player deserves to be punished by that move specifically unless it looks more threatening or adds a sound to indicate its an attack as well. Sometimes clunkyness of a game can be forgiven when taking in the world atmosphere, which i think is another miss for Mortal Shell. There are some pretty areas in the game, but it the swamp area you spawn in does not inspire the player to adventure. It almost seems like im playing a procedurely generated map like those found in Warframe where the map is tile based and organized in different orders to give variance. I know this isnt the case for Mortal Shell but i cant help but feel like "ive already been here" when exploring new areas. Maybe the abundance of the color green in the atmosphere is to blame. i dont know. I'll probably end up installing this game a few more times, ill remember how i had fun with the hardening mechanic and how the cat bobs its head when you play the lute for it. However this will probably lead to me making all of these realizations again and beating  a souls-borne game another time to scratch the itch. TLDR: this game has some truly unique features which add new ways to approach souls-like games, but there is just too many things in the game that bug me and don't let me get immersed.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Souls-like stuff, go for it. This is normally the type of game I try to go out of my way to avoid, to prevent broken controllers and an early death via aneurysm. Despite myself, I snagged it during a sale, thanks to the visuals and feel of it from various footage. After really getting (somewhat of) a hang of the combat and finding out what works for me, it was an overall enjoyable experience. Visuals are lovely. Dig the atmosphere and themes. Some animations can be wonky, but those are generally good, too. Sounds are decent, with some pretty good voice acting, throughout.The comments about enemies popping up in front of you as you traverse the map (due to getting optimized-out as you explore and then simulated again kinda late/close-proximity), whipping around 180 degrees (in the air, even) mid-attack, or lunging across the map at you at mach 5 (for enemies/attacks for which it ain't really appropriate) are totally true. Just, beware, lol.Parrying sucks. I suck at parrying, sure; but, the parrying still sucks. Just dodge/roll/harden, instead. The risk of most likely missing a parry is not usually worth the reward of just barely correctly timing one.The game is actually pretty short. I play through games kinda slow. I spent way too much time wandering in circles. There are basically three linear areas that each end in a boss fight, with a swampy area connecting them. The end features one last, big boss fight. Each area contains enemies which are mostly-unique to their respective area. The weapons and shells are kinda meh until you start upgrading them, but you can generally mix and match them to meet your preferences. I'd recommend Eredrim or Tiel, and the Martyr's Blade or Hammer-and-Chisel, personally.I think I'd like to see more of the world - more fleshing-out of things - in potential, future games, as there seems to be a decent bit of lore to it. A nagging thought in the back of my head kept saying that a lot of it just sounds kinda ripped-off of Souls/bourne stuff, though, and I'm kinda unresolved about it. I don't think Souls/etc. should get a monopoly over some concepts, themes, or types of lore/writing/etc.; but, I obviously can't help but be reminded of it, I guess.Again, if souls-like stuff is your thing, maybe you'll dig this game. If not, just pass. Perhaps worth noting: my brother has played the heck out of souls, bloodbourne, etc., and he supposedly uninstalled this shortly after getting his first shell. Take that for what you will. (I think something wonky (enemy/animation-wise) happened that really killed it for him. I get that - I get way more frustrated at dying/etc. for what feels unjustified (bug, glitch, wonky animation, etc.) than when I know that I died because I'm just bad at the game. I just never thought of Souls etc. as being totally free of these very problems, lol.)

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Shell is hard... like mega difficult and frustrating but I love it. This game delivers what I loved most about  the souls games. Getting absolutely rekted time after time after time but you eventually get through the BS and nothing is more rewarding. This game is unique and was definitely made with Dank Souls in mind. The devs did an amazing job at creating a new mechanic that's different but still makes the game feel playable. I like how the focus was placed on leveling the different shells to unlock new abilities etc. I would highly recommend this game even if you haven't played a souls game before its difficult but rewarding and I gotta say I love the world and levels. The enemies are well designed and at some points are rather creepy. Each location is unique and well thought out. Its a well designed open world game that encourages exploration and learning. The boss fights feel good and learning their move sets was simple enough. As for the price I have the feeling that the game is gonna end up being rather short in comparison to other Souls games but with that said I think the price tag of $30 is fair. Recap: Pros: Great souls like game that feels like souls but is different. Has new mechanics and options for different play styles. Fair price for what you get.Great atmosphere, world, locations, enemies, NPCS.Cons: Game can take some time to get used to especially if you are new to this style of game. Can feel a bit confusing and overwhelming at first and will take some time to learn. Didn't feel like I was progressing till about five or so hours in. Keep in mind its a learning experience and patience is a must XD All in all I recommend Mortal Shell. If you are a fan of Dank Souls don't let this gem pass under your radar. Might help kill some time before Elden Ring comes out. LOL Keep it real and stay safe!! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Mortal Shell

_childDocuments_.review: Will give you a lot more to chew on than its small size might indicateVery focused gameplay - not a lot of mechanics, just 3-4 core ones really, but each one is well thought-out and if you enjoy experimenting will give you a decent amount of depth and enjoymentA few minor polish issues that I think stem from this being a smaller studio than a AAA title - Hitboxes and combat are still crisp - Occasionally I have gotten stuck on terrain, but can usually dodge/roll out, worst-case you have a "Homeward Bone" - Lack of telegraphing on some attacks feels a bit unfairSome replayability with multiple Shell + Weapon combination, although I cannot speak on this personally as I have not yet completed the gameThe only thing that has affected my enjoyment is the lack of telegraphing on certain attacks from larger enemies, particularly mid-chain attacks - this has lead to me getting clipped quite a lot when first learning their attack patterns, and feels a bit unfair - will frustrate you if you get KO'd by a weird, un-telegraphed attack.This could have been an attempt by the Developers to encourage a more patient, deliberate style of play, which is a good thing because this took a while for me to get my head around. Credit where it is due, as the rest of the game feels very well thought-out. Problems occur when the next attacks occur before you have a chance to dodge (very fast sometimes!) and unless you know it's about to happen and are anticipating it, you will get hit - the same goes for a few first-in-chain attacks that will really take you off-guard and can force a very passive style of play. There are ways around this but in my opinion they are a departure from the feeling the rest of the gameplay has cultivated.If you like a challenge, get the game, very cool.

_childDocuments_.review: it has great visuals and an interesting combat system, I think the parry is really cool, but after parrying the same mob enemy for the 30th time within an hour of playing, it gets pretty stale. The levels don't have much variety, spamming the same two enemies throughout it, while the environment looks exactly the same no matter where you go, making exploration extremely confusing, and the land marks you do find to orient yourself are uninteresting and seem to be copy and pasted throughout the levels. The bosses had cool designs, were challenging, and I enjoyed fighting them, but the barrier of an overwhelming amount of mobs made the runbacks get old quick. I think if the levels were a bit more condensed and fleshed out, it would have been a much better experience.After playing for only a few hours, I had already unlocked 90% of the weapons and playable classes/characters, and it didn't really feel like I earned them. I mostly played the first class you get, the more beefy but slower class, and I really liked unlocking the skills he had like the kick. However, since the kick required you to use limited resources each time, it felt like a fun mechanic was put behind grinding to access it.The npc's were neat. I liked big frog. All in all, it wasn't terrible, I enjoyed playing it, but I definitely think it could have been way better with a bit more effort put into the level design.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not play long so I'll just stick to my first impressions.The start of the game is unnecessarily frustrating to get into a fun combat flow,  especially the first tutorial character that doesn't seem to get stunned / stubble by the massive 2 handed sword hitting it.  The dodge to avoid incoming attacks does not feel responsive enough and the whole hardening of skin (Parry) honestly feels like a system that was added because the work to add shields / weapon block etc... to the combat system would be far more costly for overall developmentInteractions are inconsistent in the world space, some being hold to interact, some a simple tap with the most annoying part being some interactions auto complete while some others require you to hold the button for approximately 2 to 3 seconds to dismiss the screen while nearby enemies may aggro you during said interaction can come and kill you while you are trying to stop interacting... the last experience I had before turning off the game and leading me here.It's a good looking game and has potential just like Dark Souls 1 did when it first came out. Like DS1 it also seems to suffer from some slight clunky inconsistencies which can be improved upon in sequential titles. Much like From Software has done well with in all of the follow up titles. Assuming sales met expectations it's probably safe to assume there will be another one, I look forward to seeing control, combat, interaction and presentation improvements in the next one.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not exactly a bad game, but I think many things could be better. First, the difficulty is a little too high at the beginning. After that, combat became boring and repetitive after discovering the best strategy is to "harden" in the middle of a heavy attack. Also, it can be hard to navigate the first area due to a lack of landmarks. The second boss I found wasn't enjoyable. He felt like a sponge, and his second phase was the same as the first. The difference was he was a little faster and dealt more damage.At first, the character system seemed unique, but it's really not. You're simply changing classes. You just have to find those classes first. You can re-enter your body after defeat, but that's just the game's version of Second Chance, especially when an upgrade makes all the enemies freeze until you re-enter the body.It's not the worse game I've played, and it's definitely unique compared to other games in this genre, but it's not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Shell is a decent game, overall. But there are quite a few issues with it. The parry mechanic is clunky and sometimes enemies hit me through it. The world-design has some flaws as well; while being incredibly atmospheric and fitting the theme of an unforgiving world very well, it can be very confusing to traverse the environments that are sometimes indistinguishable from others. There will be a lot of backtracking. Enemy variety is very poor and combat with them will be repetitive sometimes. The same can be said about armour (or in this case, Shells) and weapons, as there are only four of them (4 Shells, 4 weapons). But in most cases, the Shells and the weapons are good enough and serve a few playstyles. Just don't expect the level of customisation and gameplay freedom offered by games like Dark Souls or Elden Ring. The swordplay in general feels quite slow in Mortal Shell, but it feels great at most times, making me wonder if it was an intentional design choice. Almost every weapon hits like trucks loaded with obsidian and the heaviest armaments will send enemies flying. Very satisfying. The Hardening mechanic also deserves a mention because it's unique and actually works well for the most part. It works as a sort of blocking mechanic which turns your character into stone and ignores all damage. The best part is that you can pair this with any attack or movement, making for some interesting and powerful moves. Oh, and the combat can be badass and cool asf. As for the narrative and lore, it is interesting and worth keeping track of. But don't expect anything too deep. One of the best facets of this game was its voice acting. Almost every voice I heard was brilliantly performed and I haven't seen that much quality in even certain FromSoft games. In conclusion, I recommend this to patient gamers who are willing to understand that this is the first game developed by Cold Symmetry, and that many flaws are present in the game. It's worth the price but I'd say it's much better to purchase it on sales, as the prices might dip down to less than $5. I hope to see a sequel to this, as I think this does have potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent souls-like. Notice here that I said souls-like. Notice I did not say Dark Souls. If you come in expecting Dark Souls like so many, then you'll be disappointed when you discover it is indeed another product entirely. Don't do that. However if you can not rush headfirst into groups, then you probably won't complain about poor enemy placement. If you can take an hour to figure out the map layout, then you probably wont complain about getting lost. If you can figure out that you are gonna need to learn to use the Harden mechanic because there is no block, then you probably wont complain about a lack of a shield and not being able to block. OR, TL:DR, Git Gud ScrubsTruly a great game. Level design isn't the games strongest area, but the aesthetic and the combat are both excellent, and the enemies and bosses were for the most part fun. The game above all else does an excellent job of really making everything feel weighted, Not in a chunky blocky way but in a hey im swinging a weapon that weighs the same as a large chunk of metal kind of way. A game that looks amazing and tries some different stuff with the formula, turns out its good soup.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great in many ways. I would highly suggest it for the price it is sold as.+Artstyle and graphics are gorgeous when you aren't watching the same dark green screen with a fog. The characters, enemies and especially bosses look amazing.+The Combat is generally satisfying, especially when you pull off a good parry and you get into the rhythm.+Bosses are easily more challenging than most of the Dark Souls bosses, but also really rewarding when defeated. They also have variety. There are no useless bosses or bosses that don't make sense in the game. Just wish there were more of them.+Enemies react meaningfully to attack. A smaller enemy recoils in fear of your height differences- I mean when you kill another enemy, you might see one recoil and even fall backwards as they watch you slaughter their compatriots.+Very few bugs, and maybe only one game breaking bug (I got stuck, unable to make attacks when the boss had 10% hp left after a special attack with the weapon. Using items didn't work either.)-Weapon upgrade requires you to go to NG+6 to get maxed out on the weapons, otherwise you're probably stuck with a single weapon upgraded to a reasonable level for the NG, limiting options for variability. You cannot farm the upgrades from mobs.-Most of the zones are rather monotone, with little of interesting things to see. You will simply look forward to completing the zone, making repeats not as interesting.-All healing items are single use. There is no healing item that gives even the bare minimum that would replenish itself consistently or doing anything to replenish it. You will have to get currency to get healing items or wait for rare spawning mushrooms to replenish themselves after minutes. It can slow the game down to a halt early game. Imagine Dark Souls 2 small life gems being your only healing item, but it does not stack the healed health if you use it several times.One, if not the best "Souls-like" games. Worth the money.Things I would've liked to see a bit more of:>More different types of enemies, more bosses>More things to see, to reward exploration even more. Not even just items, just more things to see. Not just templates of text.>More zones. Especially ones that aren't just green and foggy or typical catacombs>More interesting NPC's. There aren't that many NPC's you can talk to in the game and there are little to no NPC questlines.Bugs encountered (Version 1.10 Virtuous Cycle):>Attacks got bugged with the special attack that gets you airborne, causing you to be unable to attack until you talk to merchant or to Sester. Might cause you to be unable to use the item menu or items that aren't healing items too.
