_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: High school JoJo JRPG with a Stardew-valley social system. Also a murder mystery.I started this series (Beginning with Persona 5 Royal) at the start of quarantine, and it has changed my life. I listen to the music of these games daily, think about the amazing characters, and the life lessons I have gleaned from the stories of P5R and P4G. I started this game thinking that it wouldn't live up to the modern quality of Royal, but I was blown away by how wrong I was.THE CHARACTERS (10/10): Amazing as always. This series lulls you in with characters that look super tropey and stereotypical, and then blows your mind with some seriously deep stuff. I started my journey thinking that karate-Velma (you'll see) was an annoying loudmouth, and I couldn't stand her. I ended the game, a 19 year old nearly-grown man, in tears when I had to leave her behind. If you let go and let yourself become engrossed in the world, these characters feel like true friends. If you are lonely, play this game. Please.THE MUSIC (10/10): It's PERSONA, my guy: of COURSE the music is going to be legendary. And while at first I didn't like the music as much as 5, it grew on me HARD until it came to the point that I couldn't stop tapping my feet during the combat sequences. Absolute banger of a soundtrack.THE GAME (8/10): The game is approaching a decade old, and it does show a little bit (don't hurt me). Persona 5 vastly improves on the dungeon design and combat flow: if you're coming here from Royal, there is no baton-passing, and no showtimes. There is an advantage to this, however: I found myself use stat-buffs, debuffs, and ailments much more than in Persona 5. There is much less emphasis on alpha-striking and nuclear numbers here. Other than that, the combat is as fast-paced and fun as usual. Despite being a JRPG, you actually do need to keep your brain turned on during the fights, because enemies will punch your lights out if you let them have a turn without debilitating them. The weakness system adds a strategic layer that turns every fight into a fun puzzle that feels AMAZING to demolish.FINAL SCORE: 9.3/10This game is outstanding. I've been playing video games sense I was a kid, and I really thought I had seen everything out of them. This series, with only two entries played in less than a year, has become my favorite ever. If you aren't big on JRPG's, it's a toss-up whether you will like it or not, but I have a feeling the story will keep you around. If you are an RPG nut, just get it. This game is easily 90-100 hours long, and will keep you busy for a long time, even if you don't finish it. That being said, if you have a PS4, start with Persona 5 Royal. I think it's a better introduction to the series overall.ADVICE: Yep, I'm putting this here for any newbies, because this game is a bit daunting.Get a nighttime job. You didn't need them in 5, but you need them here. You get additional Social Links, money, and stats, and you don't use the nighttime slot for much anyways.Fuse a Persona of the same Arcana as whatever Social Link you are trying to level up. This will sound like total gibberish to anyone who hasn't played this series, but you'll figure it out if you play. This is a function that I think gets mentioned once and never again: abuse it and you will get to know so many more characters over the course of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILERS AHEADPersona 4, a game that, to me, had quietly aged for a dozen years, beckoned me to its virtual world with the unassuming promise of a simple RPG experience. Little did I know that beneath its unassuming surface lay a narrative of profound depth, characters whose stories were finely etched, and gameplay that would leave an indelible mark. As I delved deeper into the intricate story, explored the intricacies of its characters, and savored the immersive gameplay, I couldn't help but grasp the fervor and adulation showered upon this JRPG gem by its passionate fanbase. Persona 4's fusion of genres is a stroke of genius. It seamlessly combines traditional RPG elements like turn-based combat and dungeon exploration with life simulation and social simulation gameplay. While most RPGs focus solely on the hero's journey and combat, Persona 4 adds a layer of depth by intertwining the player's real-life decisions with the in-game narrative. This blend creates a world where everyday activities like going to school, part-time jobs, and forming friendships are just as important as the main story and battling supernatural “shadows” in the TV World. This unique approach to gameplay challenges the conventions of the RPG genre, making Persona 4 an innovative and refreshing experience. The characters of Persona 4 are the beating heart of the game. Each member of the protagonist's group has their own distinct personality, struggles, and growth arc. From the cheerful and outgoing Chie to the reserved and introspective Yukiko, these characters feel like real people. As players spend time with them, they witness personal development and emotional growth, forging deep connections that go beyond typical RPG party dynamics. The investment players feel in these characters is a testament to the exceptional character writing in the game. Persona 4's central theme of identity and self-discovery is a philosophical underpinning that elevates it above many RPGs. The Midnight Channel, a realm born from hidden desires, serves as a metaphor for the masks people wear to conform to societal expectations. As players uncover the truth about the characters' shadows and confront their own inner demons, they are encouraged to reflect on the complexities of human nature. This introspective aspect adds layers of depth and meaning to the game, prompting players to question their own identities and the personas they present to the world. The emotional storytelling in Persona 4 is a masterclass in narrative design. The game expertly balances moments of humor, warmth, and heart-wrenching sadness. Through its character-driven plot and well-timed revelations, it keeps players emotionally invested throughout the entire journey. The overarching mystery of the murders in Inaba, combined with the intimate exploration of the characters' personal struggles, results in a story that resonates deeply with players, leaving a lasting emotional impact. Shoji Meguro's musical score is a standout feature of Persona 4. The soundtrack doesn't merely accompany the gameplay; it enhances and enriches it. The diverse range of music, from the catchy "Reach Out to the Truth" to the melancholic "I'll Face Myself," mirrors the game's tonal shifts and emotional beats. The music is so iconic that it becomes an inseparable part of the player's journey, invoking nostalgia long after the game is completed. The combat system in Persona 4 is a brilliant blend of strategy and creativity. Players must not only choose the right Personas for battle but also exploit enemy weaknesses for extra turns and powerful All-Out Attacks. The Persona fusion system allows for experimentation and customization, giving players a sense of ownership over their characters' abilities. The complexity and depth of combat make every encounter exciting and rewarding, whether it's a random shadow or a challenging boss fight. Persona 4's multiple endings and New Game+ feature provide players with countless hours of gameplay. The various story outcomes offer a sense of agency and encourage players to explore different choices and character interactions. New Game+ allows players to carry over their hard-earned progress, making subsequent playthroughs feel fresh and unique. This replayability is a testament to the game's depth and the enduring appeal of its world and characters. The time management mechanics in Persona 4 add a layer of realism and immersion. Players must allocate their limited time wisely, deciding whether to study, work, strengthen bonds with friends, or venture into the Midnight Channel. These choices impact character progression and story outcomes, creating a sense of agency and responsibility. It's a clever way to make players feel truly invested in the game world and the lives of its characters. Persona 4's influence on the RPG genre cannot be overstated. Its success not only led to the development of sequels and spin-offs but also inspired other game developers to explore similar narrative-driven, character-focused experiences. This impact has shaped the industry's approach to storytelling in RPGs, emphasizing the importance of relatable characters, emotional depth, and player agency. Persona 4's exceptional qualities, from its unique blend of genres to its profound themes, deep characters, emotional storytelling, iconic soundtrack, engaging combat, replayability, and influence on the RPG genre, make it a standout RPG in gaming history. It transcends the boundaries of the medium, offering players an unforgettable journey of self-discovery and human connection. As we look back on its legacy, it's clear that Persona 4 rightfully claims the title of the best RPG ever created, and its impact on the gaming world will continue to resonate for generations to come.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me about 71hrs to play through until New Years and finish what I assume to be the majority of the game.  There was more time to tighten up all my bonds with my companions and max out all of my Social Links and to eventually fight some big nasty boss but I decided to put the game down and step back.  My knee-jerk reaction is that Persona 4 Golden is one of the best RPGs I've played in the last few years.  I have never played any other Persona game or Shin Megami Tensei game.  I enjoyed the feeling of autonomy you get when controlling your character's actions within the time-blocks.  You essentially get one full school year broken up into after school and night time time-segments to pursue friendships, romantic relationships, folding cranes, translating things, or even part-time jobs like working in a hospital.  And all of your choices contribute to the overall story and make your character unique in his experience and interactions.It felt a little drawn out with how many times we have to dive back into the TV to save people over and over and over again.  And there's 10 floors of randomly generated mobs and hazards with no save points so you have to goho-me and save each time and then restart from the 5th or 6th floor - depending on how far you got.I loved the story!  It's a teenaged-murder mystery that really engages its audience and makes you feel like you're in control of solving the murders.  The music was fantastic and the characters are unique and loveable and really heartwarming.  I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of JRPGs or Final Fantasy RPGs or just turn-based tactical RPGs in general.  The combat was a lot of fun and they make the rock-paper-scissor mechanic go very far.  It gets a little old but it's well-done and entertaining!

But once you get past all that the game becomes extremely addictive and has bundles of charm. (Despite being a murder mystery at heart). From the side characters, random NPC's to the Main Cast everyone is memorable and has something to say. Talking to your unnamed class mates can also get you insight into the game world and they also have little story arcs of their own which can be fun to follow up on. Same with the unnamed townsfolk!The Social Links are memorable and have some good stories. I am not a fan of the culture club drama story line as I find it very melodramatic but at the same time its quite an important one in terms of themes. The Main Cast are endlessly entertaining with great English voice work. The chemistry between them is incredible and really helps make these characters seem like people despite having some typical anime tropes. The story is good but I wouldn't say it is on par with Persona 5's and its usually allot of going over what we already know and sometimes they fail to realise super obvious stuff for the sake of padding. But the characters help remedy that with great dialogue and some genuinely touching and funny moments.The graphics are just a bit above the original PS2 style but with some great HD retouching and the character models look great. The games style really helps make it timeless despite Persona 5 raising the bar in terms of its own style. A nice touch is the fact they use pictures of trees, bushes, farmland from real life so it makes the countryside feel like the countryside which is what they did with the Vita version. TLDRDespite lackuster dungeon design and a story, while never boring, gets a bit padded and often retraces conversations from before, this is a masterpiece of gameplay and character development.10/10Good;CombatSocial LinksCharactersBad;DungeonsSome padding in the story.

name: IXION
detailed_description: NEW GAME FROM THE DEVELOPER About the Game With Earth on the brink of ecosystemic collapse, DOLOS A.E.C. leads efforts to find a new home for the human race. Whether by chance or fate, its prototype space station, the Tiqqun, finds itself cast adrift, a disintegrating ark upon which the remnants of humanity must find sanctuary – and you, Administrator, are at its helm. IXION is a city-builder that requires you to be vigilant, to constantly assess and reassess, to learn and adapt. If you and your crew are to endure, you must confront the perils of space, while at the same time uncovering its secrets and extracting its resources. Danger, however, will come from within as well as without; you’ll need to establish, maintain and develop the Tiqqun’s infrastructure while managing the station’s population, deciding how best to answer their pleas so as to maintain their trust in you and the mission. There are no simple solutions; your actions will have repercussions, now or further down the line. How you deal with those repercussions will be the difference between survival and extinction. A population to manage, survivors to find, cryopods to recover... Maintain your crew's trust in the corporation that started this venture, or face failure and mutiny. Six sectors can be unlocked within the station, each able to house more population, support new jobs, and provide opportunity to monitor the crew with the Data Listening System. Will you bring hope to the people? Who said DOLOS was the only faction to escape the fate of the Earth? Brush up against other pockets of survivors, navigate on from the failures and wrecks of others… IXION will lead the player through gripping chapters of story, where new threats and opportunities are presented, all in aid of reaching the final destination, a new home. DOLOS are famed for their innovative technology, their scientists, but the Tiqqun now finds itself cut off. Find what resources you can, research what you do not have. Find new ways to provide for your settlement, construct new buildings to create what’s needed. Modify the Tiqqun station, improve it, forge ahead in this odyssey. Space is a dangerous place. Hull breaches, overloaded power supplies, electrical fires... It is up to you to manage these risks, deal with emergencies, create backup power solutions, and enable Extra Vehicular Activity… There are whole new stellar maps to explore. Send out probes to reveal what’s hidden, create mining and cargo ships to find resources, commission science expeditions to discover the secrets and threats you’ll find out there in space. Encounter other survivors and bring them into the fold of your mission, objective - survive.

_childDocuments_.review: I have so far finished the first chapter and had a fantastic timeThe good:- Plays smooth and is responsive, had 0 hitches or jank in my playtime so far- Generally looks incredible, lots of care and details put into every building and the whole station- The soundtrack is incredible and I am convinced it would be a big contender for game soundtrack of the year would it have released earlier- The story is very intriguing and I'm looking forward to see where it is going- The tech tree is immense and seems to have huge customization potentialThe bad:- The game definitely needs a few difficulty options (I don't think I've seen any?) since the game so far expects you to provide your own lube as it is going in dry!- Micromanaging can be lots of fun, at some places this goes a little bit far though, especially with resource and population transportation between station sectors which creates artificial bottlenecks and forces duplicate buildings- The tutorial could be a bit more extensive instead of just dropping text on you, but that's a minor complaintThe ugly:- I don't mind getting pushed ahead by a morale debuff for staying too long in a system to keep things moving, but finally pushing on and immediately getting it replaced with the same amount of debuff cause  feels like a cruel jokeIn conclusion:I am shocked that it's currently standing at mixed reviews since I think this game is tough but amazing and I can recommend it wholeheartedly (buy it with the soundtrack!)

_childDocuments_.review: I am only halfway through the game, but I feel that I have seen enough to make an honest review.First of all, I have to praise the amazing atmosphere of the game.The soundtrack is beautiful! So are the graphics and overall feel of the setting, it just all has this great immersion effect of a good sci-fi space game.From a game mechanics perspective, this is best described as Frostpunk in space. It looks quite obvious that the devs were inspired by this other game.For me, the game mechanics work well. There is enough pressure from the "survival" aspect to keep the "city builder" intense and rewarding. The story progression (which is quite interesting by itself) adds a good backdrop to the "city builder" progression and therefore minimizes repetitiveness.I am yet to explore how much replay value there is here.This is a very good game. I read some of the negative reviews and I am aware of the other players critique, but I disagree with most of them.I would say, if you like Space setups for game + city/survival mashups, give this one a ride. I am 95% sure you'll enjoy it enough to recommend it yourself.EDIT: I am towards the end of the first chapter of my second run. I am unable to make any significance progress since I am stuck with 83% research progress on the *project you have to research*, but I have exhausted all of my other science incomes throughout the galaxy. I have to rely on my research lab producing 1 science every 30 cycles... This is a big issue, and should be fixed. I hope the devs do something about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Short answer:  Get the game. Its fun in a Chore kind of way... But it has some LAG issues. not clue why. but green roads, i dont know. If you like this game you will also like Frost Punk. Id get that as its got a nice setting. After a little time with this. I can be more certain of what this is.Its a story driven, management survival (with small margins for error -_- ). ( ran into a one bug nothing would build. Unsure cause.  But delete and rearrange stuff or turn on off power to structures to perhaps fix )Think of juggling some items in the air, and as you progresses you just, juggle more stuff.I think if I can describe the game like this, perhaps its not as deep as I'd like..So this game is shallow i think. But what is there, is at least worth one play-through. Little replay value after that. Because the game is not deep or interesting it seems at first glance.What is here is good specially if new to these games as I am new. But eventually you'll notice as the game applies more pressures, and becomes a chore, the lack of depth becomes more apparent. And is revealed for not being as mentally challenging or interesting as it could have been. Long musings follow:I dont like the simplistic way the game conveys some things to the player with bars and stuff. It works .But I was left with wanting more. More story board cards, more interactions and insights from the Station population. And aspects of the stations technology and schematic structures to learn about to maintain and granularity augment or balance. etc .. What about combat ships ? So maybe its more attrition than depth. Even though there is a good base here.Where is the real world physics?  Real world metrics data variables?? Im asking too much perhaps. But its still a good game for what it is. The Si Fi presentation is what drew me to IXION.Searching for more game play depth and mental management than RTS war games afforded.  I already liked the Sci Fi Space exploration genre.I play'd a good bit of Star Citizen (Roberts Space Industries) by CIG.  But was looking for a brake from a hyper real sim.I'm new to resource management strategy sims. I've typically but rarely play RTS war games like Warno, Command and Conquer 3 andAshes of the singularity escalation. And a all around space flight game mmo, Star Citizen.What I was hoping with this was more logical cause and effect play. Maybe based in real world concepts or physics. Rather than arbitrary levels. Problems I encountered:If nothing builds, try deleting and rearranging. There's tutorials as you go. And how to transfer stuff and people between"Sectors". But its not clear about the controls for it.  Only by process of elimination did I get results. And then after many failed attempts.When changing the sector sliders, a drawn arrow will reveal flow of Resources. Once you see it, means its basically set. Two menu types given for Sector resource logistics :Simple and Advanced. I'm not sure advanced is as advanced as it is. But I didn't really play with it much. Simple menu is basically color coded sliders that whatever falls below said amount is kept, if available and conditions are present then its sent.  To mirrored Stockpiles etc.About dismantle:  (button "house X" icon top right or bottom left ) a structure (Stockpile for example)there needs to be one present to receive the resource type from the Stockpile building you wish to dismantle. If you want to destroy a resource within a stockpile with the Trash Icon, you should first select which resource will replace it, in its structure menu also.And you don't always have to destroy a Stockpiles resource, as the game allows for some overlap of resource storage. A Stockpile can act as a temporary transfer point between two resources as you switch those on and off in its small window.  You also can't transfer resources between Sectors ( sections) of the station without mirroring Stockpile buildings on either side. And you'll soon find  you can build your way into a "soft lock" as some reviewers call it.Meaning little room for correction, when some steps should precede others. Otherwise you will find yourself biting off more than you can chew. Overbuilding or under building as the case may be.   Then when the game on the second map begins throwing out I suppose higher random negative rng events, then you realize there is little opportunity or mechanics present to recover. But according to one reviewer this may not be true.As I didn't complete the game yet. So that can be a negative the other way.  Not being sufficiently consequential enough to warrant the survival aspect or drive to survive?Opening a new sector you'll find not enough resources there to sustain it. As Sector 1 implied. Each new Sector relies heavily on the previous one. The mood of the population is also not adequately conveyed to the player. There are angry icons and happy icons emojis. And some basic numbers to observe. With few actions you can take. There appears to be little nuance to the population. They are either happy, indifferent or prone to be mad. There's arbitrary structures that award 1 stability point for the populations mood. Was able to fit at least two in one sector.So some edge cases to get caught up in.With small margin for mistakes this game affords(( Yet that is also why its entertaining. ))Some will find it boring.Has good replay value if you are willing to accept that you might not understand it the first few or many times.I've only noticed a visual response bug with a button or something. Nothing braking the game yet.Still haven't managed to open two successful Sectors.Graphics: Not Star Citizen level of visuals. The game assets are very rudimentary.Its presented well enough.The Exterior Station is not detailed for the sake of detail. But looks like a space station. Overall compared to other sci fi games the graphics and colorpalette in IXION is dull and drab.  ( ReShade software can at least  be used to color correct it. I might upload a re-Color LUT on NexusMods.)Controls:  are basic point and click and you can rotate buildings with R or scroll wheel.Holding mouse right click to rotate entire camera inside the Station. But outside rotate used middle mouse button hold. You can magnify too.Music: is not "Solar Fields", an reminds me so of The Cycle Frontier - now canceled. Not exactly. I give it a pass. And after a long time sounds repetitive.Sound effects and background ambiance seem average yet okay.Adequate voice actors: except the ships AI voice is not convincing.  In the drawn out way she pronounces words as a kid might interpret a robot.However its tolerable and fits the overall tone the developers set. The character are presented as illustration cards, with subtle digital effect.  Pretty basic and low effort. Nothing interesting.I like the visual story boards that convey what happens in game.But they are few and somewhat Too basic. The art selected for that is questionable. With little variety or depth to convey togame-play or environment, lore or actions.So while its Not perfect. I do find myself returning to it at times.Even with the gameplay problems it has, and lack of Sci Fi polish, I recommend this game to new players.  Because its story driven I imagine the game to be rather short. If you want to scratch that itch of a strategic base management  with a okay Sci Fi setting then its worth. ""IXION"" passively plays off Greek myths its story template. Whenever I see Developers working Greek mythology into games I feel like im being preached at about something. Too many in the entertainment industry like to incorporate it.  Like Ixion is to the wheel, so too the player is to the juggling act the game Devs made..There's is a little bit of that Earth-good people-bad too.  I recommend Frost Punk 1 and 2. Truth:  TheShepherdsChapelChannelYoutube.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice.I did not expect to see so many bad reviews, given that IXION is a finished, content rich game and has a lot of depth and replay value to it despite having a linear story and progression system with almost zero random element to it, which is very hard to achieve imho.Maybe that's exactly why some people find it hard to take the L and try again, they took their time to write a negative review complaining about the difficulty (most of them showing very little understanding to how the game mechanics actually work). But I have to write something to defend the devs here - having an unforgiving and straight forward punishing mechanic does not make IXION a bad game. Instead it had great music, top-notch sound effects, very well optimized and reliable performance. Best of all it has a core mechanic which needs you to take your time to learn and make the right choices, now paired with a rewarding progression system, this is game design at it's best.A tweak I would make to the game that could probably help with this negative review situation would be to make the Events/Quests from your peasants have a progression system. For example to the '-1 from spending too long in the system' modifier that players complain the most, the first one could have been made into a progress bar that you could track, or maybe just add some messages prior to the event itself, like "The people in Sector 1 are getting anxious for not leaving the system for 120 cycles, they start to doubt the mission.", and gradually leads to a -1 Stability Penalty to all sectors, instead of clicking an event and found out somehow all sectors now has this penalty all in a sudden. Which makes players blame the game for screwing them up, instead of trying to improving their strategies to take the challenge. And honestly the game is not that hard once you understand how the stability system works. I think the devs needed to convey the idea that this is a challenge by design, not by some random chances, which a lot of players have misunderstood.I'd like to thank the devs for releasing such a polished and challenging game, it's risky but me and my friends absolutely love it. I hope this game gets the attention and praise it deserves for how well made it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure about buying IXION, seeing the mixed reviews. After a bit of reading about the difficulty curve and  a few YouTube videos about mechanics, I decided to try it anyway. Sometimes you'll get overwhelmed and everything will fall apart.But through all of this, you'll be learning and adapting; each attempt and each reload will bring you closer to success. The pride of completing a chapter feels earned.For a game about humanity venturing out into space with limited resources, I can't think of a more fitting set of emotions that a game would convey.

_childDocuments_.review: No spoilers: I have not yet finished the game (64 hours in), but I've reached Chapter 5, utilized almost all of the technology upgrades, and appear to be in rock-throwing distance of the endgame. I've managed to keep my crew happy for the past 3 chapters with little difficulty, so I think I have a reasonably good handle on the game mechanics. I have read a lot of the comments citing "death-spirals", and those complaints are legitimate to an extent. There will be multiple times where you'll have to restart chapters or load from a previous save (save when you have a risky decision to make) in order to learn from your mistakes. You will make mistakes. Sometimes low-risk decisions go terribly bad, while high-risk decisions can sometimes pay off handsomely (this is not the first video game to utilize this approach). In one instance I used up all my science points upgrading technologies when I discovered I needed to research a new technology to advance the story, and there was none left to be had in the system. Oops. Re-Load. Another time I restarted a chapter thinking I missed something critical. I had not, I just needed to keep going a little further with my current objective, then the way forward presented itself.But the real question is: is the occasional frustration encountered having to backtrack ultimately worth it? I think it is. The game is simply gorgeous to look at. The exterior shots of the Tiqqun, especially in motion, are stunning. You can zoom in to watch your crew members going about their jobs, or zoom out to view the entire solar system to locate available resources and points of interest. The in-game imagery matches the cut-scenes (and your external ship augmentation is visible in the cut-scenes). You'll want to make use of the Ctrl+U keys to turn off the interface occasionally just to grab some screenshots.The audio is also quite atmospheric (although towards the end of the game it gets a little repetitive). The story is compelling and unfolds at a good pace, and draws you forward in the game. There's a limited amount of technobabble, but it's consistent and feels right in the context of the story.Technology upgrades are absolutely necessary to most efficiently utilize very limited building space, so you'll need to be strategic with your research, while carefully managing and balancing food production, population, housing, manufacturing, and stability to keep your ship operational (yes, your crew are a bunch of whiny babies). Other upgrades will allow you to reinforce the initially fragile vessel to make it more capable of meeting the challenges faced later in the game. My only complaint is there's no way to train non-workers to become workers, so you exhaust a lot of resources on crew-members who don't contribute to the ship's operations.Note: do not ignore collecting the cryo-pods. You don't need all of them to complete the game, but you can't ignore them, either. You're going to need additional crew members to combat attrition and supply the workforce for new buildings as you open up additional sectors. And you might need a few colonists for your new home, if you find one.Aside from the aforementioned "Oops" situations, you are presented with all the information you need to manage your ship via a clean and well-designed interface.  You can see ship-wide and sector-specific quantities of all raw and finished resources, population, objectives, sector status and issues you need to address all on the main interior view. Brief tutorial notes pop up when new game mechanics are introduced, so you're dropped right into the main game from the start, there's no secondary sandbox to learn the ropes (which I liked).There's a similar visual style to Frostpunk in the game (as well as the need to manage limited building space), and references to "Frostpunk in Space" are appropriate, but I think that's good thing. Both games are highly immersive, getting you deep into their lore. Ultimately I think most of the complaints about the game being too hard should be taken with a grain of salt. The dead-ends to the story line don't stop you from playing the game, but they serve as a constant reminder that you're operating in a highly unforgiving environment and add atmosphere to the overall story. And at some point you'll probably want to play through those dead-ends just to see what happens.Is it hard? Yes. Is it fun? Yes. Is it worth the investment in money and time? Yes.Overall Score: 8/10.----------------------------------------------------Sixty-eight hours in: I completed the main story line. Saved humanity! Yay!There were a couple of anomalous behaviors: mostly having to do with creating a large number of colonists and the means of transporting them to the planet, but never actually having to do so, when all previous colony tests involved physically moving the colonists via cargo ship to the planetary location. What's up with that?Another odd behavior is a couple of "new projects" that appear: one shows up as a docking bay upgrade, another shows up as a new exterior hull construction object. It's inconsistent with other "new project" behavior, and doesn't quite match the verbal directions provided.I also would have preferred that final climax to be done via a cut-scene as opposed to art panels, but oh well.Do either of those things change my overall score? No. Still 8/10. I enjoyed it immensely. There are a couple of unresolved sub-plots that I might have to return to as well. I think Robert Frost said about the road not taken...

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing when compared the fabulous dream game in my head inspired by their marketing:  1 Part Frostpunk, 1 Part Elite Dangerous, and one Part Tropico, all served with a generous dollop of rogue-like random replay elements.The reality is a solid B game during it's finest moments:  Thoughtful city building, with very light economic elements.  There's some enjoyable dramatic situations, like running out of room,  that builds tension successfully the first time it happens.  The second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh time, it's unrelenting tedium.   Honestly, it seems like this game could have been a strong AA game if it had just had more solid playtesting.   All of the frustrations are incredibly obvious on even a casual run. The soundtrack, courtesy Guillaume David,  is one of the most incredible I heard this year.   It's Brian Eno meets Squarepusher meets Art rock.   It's textured nuance was as listenable the seventh time around.   The art was of consistently good quality, and was what initially caught my eye.  I was disappointed after about an hour of gameplay, as there wasn't quite the feeling of life and vividness I wanted.  (and competitor Frostpunk does so well)I couldn't give this an unqualified recommendation at it's release price point, $40.   If you are a fan of the city building genre, have a weakness for 2001-inspired visuals, and also happen to love ambient music, please go ahead.   I think most gamers will be satisfied when this drops to around $20.   If it's ever on a $10 sale, unqualified buy.I think that there's a strong exoskeleton of a game here, and with about a year of patches and a couple DLC's, I hope that it will emerge into a Frostpunk level contender.

_childDocuments_.review: I have updated the review after finishing the game. I will try to keep this review free of story spoilers.TL;DRThe game is fun and has incredible atmosphere, but it's also rough around the edges. I recommend it IF you really like survival city builders like Frostpunk, don't mind a lot of trial and error, and you can deal with a bit of jank and some bugs, of course.SOME ADVICEEvery element in the science grid has a bunch of upgrades hidden behind it. For example you can unlock upgrades that increase how many science points the science building passively generates, or research better versions of the dormitory that can house more crew members in higher quality buildings. My recommendation is to get your passive science point generation up as fast as you can, because it means science keeps accumulating if you spend time in a chapter after finishing all the story beats there, allowing you to not just gather resources and upgrade your ship, but also keep researching.THE SURVIVAL MECHANICSHonestly, this game is all about preparing. You should take it slow especially in the earlier chapters, and spend some time in each chapter after finishing the main story there to stock up and build up. Once you have a good alloy pipeline and a good food pipeline going, you're pretty much good to go on your fundamentals. And while the waste management mechanics are entirely optional, they are amazing for chip production, which is extremely helpful when chips and silicon are in short supply.For me personally I had the Tiqqun in tip-top shape around the end of Chapter 3, with all sectors unlocked and fully specialized in specific tasks (S1 hull repairs, S2 industry, S3 storage, S4 housing, S5 food, S6 recycling), and expected to be able to breeze through the game from there. And although it was true I didn't have to make any more major modifications to the ship from there on out, the game does like to keep throwing curveballs at you, so you're never too prepared.THE STORYThe story is very interesting, with a bunch of unexpected twists to it. The first one of these you might already know, but I can assure you there are a bunch more ahead as you continue to progress through the game. There is also a layer of lore and spiritualism behind the story of the game that helps to set the stage of a deeper and much more complex universe. I hope the devs will expand on this universe in the future.EXPLORATION EVENTSAs you explore a system, you come across exploration events on its celestial bodies that each tell a short story and reward you with science points, materials, and sometimes even special technologies or other things. Unfortunately it is impossible to tell ahead of time which progression path you should choose for the more dangerous events, and a misstep can easily result in losing crew members and/or ships, which encourages savescumming or just straight up looking up a guide.There is also a kind of very obscure optional storyline that weaves through the entire game and is told through certain exploration events, but it requires a very specific set of steps that are not obvious at all. I only found out about this when it was already too late for me to course correct, and was unable to finish it. This feels like it was probably added for replay value.PROLOGUE & CHAPTER 1 (No story spoilers)Overall I feel like the prologue section of the game should be much longer, since it lets you learn about and experiment with fundamental mechanics in a much more lenient environment. The progression from the prologue to the first chapter is really well done but I feel like suddenly having to start scrounging for iron to keep your hull from degrading and having to deal with cryopods and the resulting population boom are enough to ramp up the challenge in Chapter 1. By also waiting to introduce a bunch of other mechanics that could be taught in the Prologue, the learning curve in Chapter 1 becomes a bit too steep.BUGSSadly the game is also quite buggy still. Interface elements will not update properly sometimes, and at one point after a VOHLE jump my game got stuck on endlessly showing me the prompt to initiate the jump after it was completed, which completely locked down the game after a bit. Other examples include objects in space not properly loading in when the Tiqqun is near them, or showing the wrong model or effects for the stage they are in. Progression triggers don't always work properly either, sometimes triggering too early, too late or not at all. Fortunately I haven't encountered anything as game breaking as the save corruption bug that has already been fixed in a patch.A DIAMOND IN THE ROUGHAll of this aside, the atmosphere and music are done really well, and the story of the game is really interesting. This game is definitely a diamond in the rough of the survival city builder genre, and is a close second behind Frostpunk for my favourite game in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished this game and...  No question there was a steep learning curve.  But once I took the time to actually READ everything presented to me, I realized the fault was mine.  It's worth noting that this game has many realistic factors, like the fact that distances matter between supply and demand buildings.  And the hull needs constant maintenance...  But on the flip side, the amount of resources seems skewed.  What you need to maintain everything feels daunting both at the start and end of the game.  In the first chapter, it seemed impossible to find the resources to build everything.  And while demands ramp up over time, by the final chapter, it seemed impossible to find places to store all of your excess resources.  And science availability seems similarly skewed in the wrong direction.  While you need tons in the start to make everything efficient, you have to pick and choose what to focus on, while at the end I was left with leftover science.  And while the story is great and the chapters seems to increase in difficulty at a perfect rate, the final chapter is just...  almost a free-for-all.  No difficulty, no time limitations, just endless resources and (presumably) a fully functional station that churns out resources faster than you can use them.All that being said...  My play style is my own and your experiences may vary.  I was hesitant about this game at first due to the reviews but in the end, I thoroughly enjoyed it and (99 hours in) I'm willing to give it another run through!  Personally, I think that's WELL worth the money!

_childDocuments_.review: IXION can be described as a narrative-driven survival city builder. But there are two factors that set it apart from other games in its genre. The first factor is the ability to move the "city", given that your "city" is actually a space superstructure in search for a new planet to colonize. The need to manage Power (which depletes as you move) and the distance your ships will need to travel to get to and from resource areas make positioning the "city" an interesting strategical feature. The second factor is its narrative, which draws from sci-fi and cosmic horror to represent an indifferent and, at times, hostile universe. The game is constantly throwing new challenges at you that tie directly into the main narrative, and while there were perhaps one too many bait-and-switches for my liking, my overall experience was very positive. I'll be looking forward to an Endless mode that the developers have already stated to be in the works.

_childDocuments_.review: This may be my new favorite city-builder, science fiction game in a long time. First off, really interesting story overall and you feel invested to find out whats going on which is rare for a game in this subgenre. Second, this game is punishing and I think alot of people who are giving it a hard time are expecting like a cozy-game experience sort of builder. Absolutely not even in the same universe of cozy, this is about survival and being tightly focused on everything you are doing and managing your precious resources. You are engaged and always thinking about how to maximize what you have and what you need to do next. Not a builder where you are constantly pressing 3x speed waiting for something to get built either. Third, its a good balance of intense but logical in how the production of resources work and it feels for the most part balanced. You don't feel locked out of fixing a problem if you mess up if that makes sense. You can turn it around and fix it, your not just "Ok well I have to start over I messed up and there is nothing i can do to stop the ship from imploding." I do have some minor issues but the main one for me is the hull damage part is punishing (which totally makes sense) but maybe a little more punishing then it needs to be. Otherwise, this is a super well made game that I'm really enjoying. I highly recommend this game for science fiction and base/city-builder fans. Word of warning, this is a tough game unpurpose so expect to be frustrated as survival is a big aspect unlike other city builders which can be a more forgiving. It kind of reminds me of Banished back in the day but in space and with a plot.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a mix of Frostpunk city-building in a perilous situation, Stellaris-like writing, and FTL: Faster Than Light-style traveling to new (non-procedurally-generated) systems to outrun catastrophe.Just like Frostpunk, this game absolutely nails atmosphere, and in some ways leapfrogs it. Immaculate vibes, an evocative writing style, beautiful cutscenes, gripping suspense and drama, some fascinating cosmic mysteries to uncover out there in the universe, and superbly-written lore. The UI is gorgeous and the sound design is layered and vibrant. The graphics and planets are gorgeous (though you will probably not see most of them since you have to move your cumbersome station into orbit to get a close-up view).Weakest point, aesthetically? The characters. You meet them once, get a passing hint of their personalities, and never see them again. There's a good explanation for why, but no matter the reason, it still doesn't make for engaging storytelling. This game would have benefited spectacularly from some XCOM-style running commentary from various members of your crew, reacting to each new story development, squabbling over the right direction to take leadership, or explaining some of the more confusing and poorly-delivered story beats. To elaborate on that last bit, the story is excellent and engaging, but often very clumsily-told. Some major reveals happen with zero fanfare. Others never get explained ever. In particular, the big event after you leave the prologue is super visually misleading and you'll likely be left not quite understanding what happened. (Also, the monologue from the first guy you meet in the game, the foreman-looking dude, is hella tangenty and boring.)Difficulty-wise, the game is absolutely unforgiving, way harder than Frostpunk. There's a lot of logistics, pipelines, and infrastructure you need to nail down to getting your space station running smoothly, and you have to optimize the ever living hecc out of everything. Planning the layout to your station is tough as nails, but satisfying to get right—you don't get a lot of space, and the buildings are quite oddly dimensioned. The game also gets harder and harder by way of satcking debuffs that constantly push at whatever sense of safety you manage to eke out—your ship is barely functioning and constantly falling apart, and the station's inhabitants grow more scared and depressed as the story confronts you with setback after setback, so you have to counteract both by shoring up your hull repair pipeline and providing an increasing number of amenities to keep the people satisfied and motivated. Thematically it really nails down the growing sense of desperation, a perfect example of narrative delivered via gameplay. But mechanically? IT'S HARD AS HECK.But it CAN be done. (With the help of some save scumming), I went my entire first playthrough with a net positive Stability (this game's version of Happiness) and never letting the ship disintegrate, even with the constant maluses. The game provides TONS of tools to bolster your citizens' morale and has stacking buffs that make it easier to keep the ship's health high.The most unfair mechanic, imo? Exploration. Like Stellaris's Anomalies, you often stumble on really cool mysteries when exploring with science vessels. But while the mysteries are REALLY cool, the outcomes are hella tough to predict, poorly telegraphed, and the consequences are frustrating. I will admit to save-scuming my way through most of these, but mostly because there's a lot of cool lore and narrative to be uncovered by the successful expeditions.All in all, a solid 4 stars out of 5. Goes right up on the shelf with Frostpunk.

_childDocuments_.review: Played Early Access Games More PolishedImportantly, until you've played it once you don't know how important some things are.I say as someone who's completed the game.1. User Instruction:* "Tutorials" are anything but.  I've seen manuals provide more details than those do.* The tech tree gives a single sentence about what a tech does, and a paragraph of fluff text.  This includes new buildings.  Oh, you wanted to know the size, material, manpower, or electricity cost of a building before researching it?  Too bad.During the game one of the required techs to progress turned out to be an upgrade to the Docking Bay.  This was never stated in any of the dialog and I actually loaded an earlier save assuming it was just another bug.Going along with that, there was no indication that some upgrades do unlock new buildings.  This is important, and I did not realize this until late game!2. Space MagicIf you know anything about space or science then this game will frustrate you with how much it gets wrong.Here's an example. Early on you learn that "Electro Kinetic Propulsion" uses the entirety of the power grid, so batteries are needed.More solar panels do not mean less batteries are needed.  Even  does not reduce battery need.Okay, so then more power means the thing goes faster?  No!  That's a tech upgrade.Heck, the visual is rocket motors, but no fuel is used.There are many cases like this.  They wanted something for gameplay reasons and spent all of 5 minutes coming up with an excuse.That excuse is then put on all the tips and in the UI.Personally one of the most jarring was near the end the logical ships Assistant starts saying things like "I can feel it".What?  It was very jarring.  Like if you asked directions and Google Assistant responded "X is near. I can feel it."Oh, and later on 3. Poor TranslationI hope it's a poor translation, and not the writers using deliberately confusing wording.  Eg, "Repatriate" instead of return."Tiqqun" is pronounced by the Voice Actors as "Tycoon".4. A story that is both too straightforward and too randomThe entire game is a "get to x place" story.  Yet, what happened, why, and even the bad guys are all over the place.There's some cool background possibilities going on, but then they go a completely different direction.At a guess, half of the exploration missions are based on sci-fi movies, because most have no connection to the plot.Like I did every exploration mission, but still have no idea why the ultimate bad guy was so powerful or how things happened.They can't decide between if the games focus is "ecosystemic collapse", crazy religions,, or .There are four different plot threads that are based on made up words, with none of them given the focus needed to explain what is going on.5. Too much micromanagementThis is admittedly partly on me, but here's a simple example that just took my attention for no reason.Early on you find that it costs Alloy to repair the hull.  The more Airlocks active the more points can be repaired, but the more alloy it takes.Importantly, even if the hull is fully repaired all the airlocks still consume the larger amount of Alloy.So, one or two need to be turned off to avoid wasting significant resources.To make things even more complicated, the higher the hull's value the less efficient airlocks are.In practice, this means that if you're willing to sit at ~80% you can turn off an airlock and cut alloy usage in half!The other place it shows up is in power/personnel management with warehouses.  Especially if, like me, someone does not realize how important the tech upgrade for the larger warehouses are.I found myself constantly turning warehouses on and off as they got full.  It was a chore.6. Difficulty spikes* Food production* Trust modifiers* Fires7. BugsOne constant annoyance was the UI not updating immediately.  One of the two main causes seemed to be the lower right hand corner not triggering an update on change. Requiring me to leave the sector and return to see the new status.The other one is there's no indication anything was chosen until at least a tick goes by.  Players like me, who make many actions while paused, will find themselves constantly unpausing the game just to get the UI to update.The main boss killed me the first time because I didn't realize how missile defenses worked.When I reloaded the save, he never attacked me at all.

_childDocuments_.review: After-finish update:DO NOT buy this game for Lore/Story. Its bad. And I dont mean Breaking Bad, I mean "we gave the story to a team of 5 year olds to write" bad. When these 5 year olds are chinchillas. Its illogical, PAINFULLY linear, to the point that one wrong step forces you to reload. Its also absolutely basic, with no massive surprises or whatever. You're not challenged, nothing forces you to think, and the only two emotions this story prongs in people are boredom and dissapointment. Unfortunately, I have to change my review after spending some more time in the game. I was so super hyped for Ixion. Love the concept, love the climate, you can clearly see the passion behind it. Unfortunately, the balance is still far, far off. Working conditions in a sector are optimal, yet the crew decides to go on strike because whatever snowflake reason. Starting a new sector with 40 workers. I build something that puts the sector into overwork - Infirmary blows up 2 seconds after overwork pops on the screen. Hull repairs are tedious instead of challenging. I know they wanted to introduce a "fight for your life" mechanic, but its more of a "tedious chore" one. I will happliy amend my review after more tweaks are done to the balancing, but for now its only fun if you like to torture yourself. First review:Initially Ixion has been called "Frostpunk in space", and after a few hours into it, I have to both agree and disagree. It definitely is fun. But it doesnt give you the "fight for your life everyday" pressure. I'll amend my review after a few dozen hours, ut so far its been worth the money paid for it.

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, IXION is a very complex, very good game, and I enjoyed it for the most part.Even though I'm only 4 hours into a possibly 20-30 hour long game, I feel like I've seen enough to say what I think.This game has a few issues that I just can't wrap my mind around. For example, and * SPOILER ALERT *, if you stay in your system for too long, the game is bugging you to leave and is throwing all kinds of stuff at you to make you leave, including negative stability, which is the "happiness" of the workers. That stability leads to them being sad and mad, which leads to several of them being overworked, angry, and at the end leads to a strike, which in turns annoys even more people, so once a strike starts, its basically a never ending roulette of who will strike next.All that, if you do leave the system, the game throws another joke at you, -1 stability because you left the system. oh, and those are permanent, meaning you're f**ed.But fine, you've dealt with their happiness and can manage to deal with it, I have no idea if this is procedural, but the game sent me to a system, that has virtually no iron, meaning you can't make alloys, and then your suddenly lose all of your hull and you die and lose. I haven't found a way around this yet, still looking.And now to the part of getting enough population, at some point, you find cryopods with people in them, those people are either workers,  or not. if they are not, they can be trained to be colonists at some point in the game, but until then, you're stuck with them taking food and complaining about random stuff. Now, apparently workers are kinda rare, so you deal with hundreds of non-workers and get maybe 100 workers out of 500 cryo-pods, now, as you're currently thinking, "just dont open the cryopods unless really needed" well, I thought so too, until the game screamed at me that the people are very unhappy because the cryopods exist.overall, at the current state of the game, I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: So there's a lot of people giving this game bad reviews due to balancing. Chiefly around the accidents that can occur and the maintenance of your ship, the Tiqqun. I still don't understand why people expect perfect games at launch nowadays and use steam reviews for complaints instead of forums or other direct methods. You don't need to shame every developer to get them to improve their game.Anyway, there are already patches out that reduce the number of accidents occurring. I will admit it was pretty frequent how often people would die even when conditions were 'optimal.' If you want to avoid this keep stability in the positive and never allow extra hours. It's not too hard to do if you plan properly although some events can knock that number down which is fine because it's part of the story and challenge. The Tiqqun also requires a constant supply of alloys for repairs. This isn't as big an issue as some people claim it is but it's still something to keep an eye on. In short: the more sections of your ship you open up and the more jumps the Tiqqun makes, the more alloys you need per tick to keep it from falling apart. Again with preparation such as sector specialisation and research this isn't hard to do. However the trick here is to accept that keeping the Tiqqun at 100% hull is literally impossible and settling for about 50% is fine for most of the game. Again, parts of the story may challenge you by damaging your hull further and again this is fine.Now that's all out of the way I do want to say that this 'sci-fi frostpunk' is a gorgeous game. The soundtrack is made by Guillaume David who also is behind the awesome Mechanicus ost and both soundtracks are a delight to listen to. The visuals of Ixion are splendid with the different systems having interesting locations to explore with the Tiqqun and it's fleet. The cutscenes are really well made genuinely giving me goosebumps at points and the story is also very gripping, enticing you with just enough information to keep you digging for more answers.As for gameplay that hasn't already been covered, this is a story based game so no endless mode or the suchlike which means replay is in refining your approach and overcoming challenges. Autosaves are enabled by default. You'll spend most of your time building up within sections of the Tiqqun to match both the needs of your people/ship and also directing your fleet to locations in the system the Tiqqun occupies. An important part of the game is making sure you get the resources you need from the system before leaving. There are elements of the game which could be better but honestly nothing is broken and unusable. I will admit I haven't finished the story yet but I wanted people to be aware that balancing/fixes are being released and this game is worth trying if you have enjoyed Frostpunk or are interested in trying a story driven survival city builder.tl;dr:- balancing & fixes are happening- story and ost are amazing- Challenging gameplay but rewarding with planning- 8/10 for love of my space washing machine of doom

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult and unforgiving game but it's meant to be! I'm enjoying it so much I've clocked up a lot of hours already.  I don't usually write reviews but there seems to be a lot of negativity about the game because of the difficulty, and the 'mixed' reviews based on the difficulty seem a little unfair. Despite being difficult, Ixion is a very enjoyable game.  It keeps you on your toes.  You can't just amble along like you have all the time in the world but then the premise of the game is such that you wouldn't expect to! If you're looking for a game where time doesn't matter and resources are pretty much unlimited, this isn't the game for you; however, if you like a little jeopardy in your life, you'll probably enjoy it. The difficulty makes any small success all the sweeter but any mistakes have consequences.  The story is interesting and I'm looking forward to seeing how it unfolds in the end.There are a few minor bugs that are mostly just annoying but updates seem to be reasonably regular. Overall, a very enjoyable game.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the futuristic, bleak yet, sliver of hope attitude the game has. Yes, it's a RTS but, it's more than that. The resources scarcity is cool yet, goal orientated.The corporate performance pressure is there along with the colony's opinion on you. It's tough but, you're lead through this story that immerse you into the role really well.10/10 for complexity and cerebral sanctification.8/10 for the amount of story art they provide. The artist/graphics team did a great job. I want more!!*EDIT*: The game is pretty challenging and in my opinion,rightfully so! There's a lot of comments/reviews the game being "tOo DiFfiCuLt". Yes, the game is difficult and I do agree that difficult settings WOULD BE NICE however... the story and concept is you're in space, managing a SPACE STATION and this is done by ONE PERSON (the player). The idea that a single human overseeing a single space station while trying to keep your station integrity up, population morale up, manage resources AND follow through with the space station's purpose (the story plot) is a daunting task (game producers vision: the game).So with all that being said: if you'd like a game that is intentionally hard, mentally difficult AND a great story with some cerebral immersion; this is your game.

_childDocuments_.review: For the people trying to get a nutshell of what Ixion is: it is an extremely complex game, definetly too complex for its own good. It is a game that can be infuriating even if you know how to play it, some of its design choices are trully obnoxious to deal with. It feels cluncky overall, you can see as you play simple ways to improve the flow of the game, but you are stuck with what you bought. At the same time Ixion grips you tight precisely because everything really hard to manage and succeding in doing so is moderately satisfying. Here is the loop: you need a thing done but don't have the resources to make for it, the good part is you can build the building that will bring you said resources, but you ain't got energy to build said building, so you must either increase you energy production or  shutdown other buildings, which you can't afford, at the same time you are not making enough food to feed your people, your running out fo alloys to repair your ship and since you had to shutdown a great deal of you infrastructure there is a massive gridlock going on. So that's that, you want to solve 3 things that pose inmediate danger to your station but resolving them is tremendously hard and complex, there is very little room to make things on the station better, but you must manage to not only survive, but thrive.  Story time: it is really good... up to a certain point. The whole story becomes really odd by the end and it feels poorly resoluted, with a lot of answers missings, and a lot of completely unexplained misteries... Soundtrack: good! you have awe inspiring songs that don't really fit on the overall narrative, absolute bangers that perfectly suit what you are playing and some other that are just good enough, also really good voice acting. Performance: Not the kind of guy that can tell much about this, it runs poorly for me with a pretty high speck pc, but you are not here for the looks. So yes, I recommend this game, if you enjoy it you will end up like me, wondering how  much more this could have been, but gratefull to have spent time on it.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's an avid space buff and currently only on chapter 2 of IXION, I can say that this is an incredibly engrossing game. Even though I've been playing for 12 hours, I've been having an absolute blast exploring the game's many intricacies and uncovering its secrets. Yes, the game's hard but that's the point. The people who aren't recommending this game because of the difficulty are like the people in college who rate the professor horribly because they didn't do the work and got a bad grade. While the developers have released an easier mode, the difficulty in IXION is a deliberate design choice that adds to the game's sense of immersion and realism. Those willing to take on the challenge will find an incredibly rewarding and immersive gaming experience, making IXION a must-play for those who appreciate a game that doesn't hold your hand. What really stands out to me about IXION is the team's passion for science and realism. From the realistic technologies and impressive graphics to the carefully crafted environments, everything feels like it was created with a great deal of care and attention to detail. Watching the station use the warp engine or even just travel across the solar system to another planet is breathtaking. It's clear that the team behind IXION is truly dedicated to creating a game that not only looks amazing, but also feels authentic and grounded in real-world science.But it's not just the attention to detail that makes IXION such an amazing game. The storyline is incredibly engaging, with plenty of unexpected twists and turns that keep me hooked. And even though I'm only on chapter 2, I can already tell that this is a game with a lot of depth and complexity.The gameplay itself is also incredibly well done. The puzzles and challenges are challenging but I've never found myself getting frustrated, I just take a step back and do some risk and resource management. The controls are also intuitive and easy to use. It's the kind of game that really rewards careful exploration and attention to detail, and I've been taking my time to really savor the experience.Lastly the music and sound design are astonishing! There's not much to say except this soundtrack is ******* amazing and it's probably one of the best I've listened to.(The only thing I hope for, and this is just a personal opinion, are more complex AI and a form of realism when it comes to the citizens moving around on board the station. Something along the lines of zoo tycoon/park builder or something like that.)Overall, I would highly recommend IXION to anyone who loves science fiction or space games. It's a truly exceptional game that's definitely worth the investment of time and attention. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ixion is a building game, but not for the faint of heart. It is first and foremost a survival game and a mistake can spiral out of control quickly. I have had to start a new game several times both due to game over and seeing better ways to do things on YouTube to make life easier later on. There are definitely more ways to play this game wrong than there are to play the game right.Game over occurs from one of two things. If your ship’s null drops to zero you are destroyed. Materials are required to keep the hull in repair. How effectively this is accomplished depends on available raw resources, and the tech you’ve acquired to help you. As the game progresses, you have less total hull points to work with, adding to the challenge.The second way to lose is a loss of trust. If you lose the trust of the crew, you are forcibly removed. The level of trust is based on how happy your crew is. There are buildings and polices to combat negative sentiments. Overwork and apathy toward crew requests removes trust, fulfilling needs and wants builds trust. There are also world events that effect your overall trust score, much like the hull mechanic above.The tech tree is extensive. There are multiple tech tiers, each with multiple techs to unlock. And each tech has multiple upgrades for additional benefit.Is the game worth the money? I’s say yes.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very convinced of IXION being a great game back when it only had a demo available on a summer game fest. Now as the owner of the full game, I can confidenty tell you this is the survival game I always dreamed of. To put it simply, Battlestar Galactica meets Frostpunk and ANNO. I always wanted a space ship management game that is not about conquering and destroying another civilization, or even building your own. Most space games are either about combat, or some sort of 4X empire building. None of them are about what the fantasy / premise of Battlestar Galactica offers: your gigantic mothership is out in space, on it's own. You have a limited set of resources: quite literally nothing comes to your aid. Survive. Figure out how to create food from nothing, energy from nothing, maintain crew morale stability, ship integrity, advance in your technologies and expand your options by blindly exploring space, holding onto nothing but hope that you find something useful: an asteroid belt rich with minerals, or ice, a gas giant you can harvest gas from, anything and everything you can crawl your way to across the stars as your dying ship and crew starve for a drop of hope.IXION is the perfect delivery of this. And to my greatest pleasure, it doesn't feel like a cartoony mobile game like some Mars colonization games from bigger publishers: it's dark, rough, feels real and scientific (as much as a game can be) and to my surprise, has a surprisingly strong narrative: there are chapters of a campaign story and random events to deal with, much like in Frostpunk. This is supported by excellent graphics, art style, music, and voiceover. What more you can you wish for? And to think, all of this came from a small indie developer - hats off to you guys.

_childDocuments_.review: There used to be a demo for this game, and that is how I decided to buy it. If the demo was still available, that would help make a decision better than any of these reviews.Then there's the comparisons with Frostpunk: I loved Ixion, and didn't like Frostpunk at all. Many people, maybe expecting Ixion to be a Frostpunk-like, were disappointed. That might give a good hint as well.To me this game reminded more of Northgard, gives me a feeling of a board game, with the complex balance between many difference resources, and having to do magic with a small-ish population where each person, like the viking villager, can do many different trades.As a strategy game, it's better than most in the genre. I got my achievements in a weird order compared to the rest of players, and to me this proves that there are different ways to win. But, more importantly, there are ways to improvise and error-correct and do a comeback, so one doesn't need to go back to a save 50 turns(cycles) ago to save a run. This is rare in this genre, but really important in my opinion: there must be different ways to win (even mine :D).I have played the "intended" experience: the game wasn't too easy, nor too hard. I had to do some save/loads in the last missions. I have not followed a guide, and I don't like games that require guides or save/load almost as a "game mechanic". Definitely not as hard as other games in the genre that are more popular, but, consider that "easy" doesn't necessarily mean "popular". If you have a Hi-Fi system, this is one of those few games that will somehow make use of the absurd amount of money spent on sound equipment. The OST is in FLAC. _childDocuments_.review: I went into this game thinking it was just a regular factory building game and I feel that most of the negative reviews are thinking the same thing. I do agree there are some balancing issues but you can work around that for now. I think it does take a few attempts at a new game to really get a good strategy going. My first run, I made too many early on mistakes. Didn't properly calculate my housing/food requirements, Didn't plan properly for when I opened Sector 2 etc... The second run went much smoother, but I decided to VOHLE jump too soon, thinking there would be significantly more and easier to reach resources in the next star system. I also didn't realize I had a food shortage coming and didn't have the resources/workers to resolve that fast enough. Currently on my 3rd attempt and here's some things I've learned so far:1. Don't be afraid to turn off buildings (including your second EVA Airlock) for a while. Keep your working conditions optimal at all costs. I'll even take negative hull repair for a few minutes to utilize the workers elsewhere, then switch it back. 2. Pause the game and plan/think out your next moves. Things can happen quickly and you need to act/react right away in some cases.3. Food supply shortages will sneak up on you especially if you are waking people up.4. Speaking of waking people up, Don't wake them up too fast to the point where you don't have the infrastructure to support the increased population. That was the critical mistake I made on the 2nd run. You can turn off the cryonics center for a while if you need to. Also, don't collect too many cryonic pods. I strategically tell my cargo ships to grab more. 5. When you are presented with the option to move on to the next part of the story, don't think you have to right away. That was the mistake I made on the first run. If there's still resources to collect, collect them. Still events for your science ships to investigate, do those.  This is a very punishing factory/survival game. But when you think about the story, it probably should be. I'll be honest, I'm not far in the game and I'll probably end up doing more fresh starts, learning from my mistakes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't easy.In fact you will mess up, and that might be the point. It's to show you just how difficult it will be to move beyond Earth. To deal with a dead Earth, with no home to return to.Do I think some more balancing might be required? Or perhaps easier modes so you can scale up to harder modes? Probably.Some major tips: Don't rely on Waste-driven mechanics, especially when it comes to Food. Push towards Water/Crops, and then Waste Driven later. But remember, the only guaranteed food source is insects. So ALWAYS have a back-up plan.Which comes to part 2, plan for when your economy grinds to a halt due to lack of resources, but strive to push as hard as you can to exit the system. Always go for the DOLOS related stuff PRIORITY ONE, and be ready for that moment you need to exit a system.They are not lying when they say you have to make HARD-DECISIONS. Sometimes, you might have to starve your population by moving your mothership during a meal cycle, so you can have full food stores in the next meal cycle. Also, keeping similar things near to one another is a big thing. Try not to have storage units far away from your production centers.Best of Luck Fellow Administrators!

_childDocuments_.review: *Anything below, while worded as objective truth is only my subjective 'Opinion'. Your experience may vary depending on your preferences and past experience with like games.*The setting, aesthetic and vibe are all A+. The Mechanics are interesting and you could spent hours designing and redesigning everything from top to bottom; And unfortunately you'll have to. Unfortunate, because the city planning elements of this game are extraordinarily frustrating, requiring you to have storage for all resources in the sector you build it in, wait for resources to be delivered to buildings, wait for the buildings to be constructed, as well as all the above steps again should you want to remove a building you placed. Both steps again twice if you want to re-build a structure somewhere else.This means that a simple redesign of a sector is all but impossible. You are better off building a new sector and replacing the old one after you have it's replacement. Long story short, the 'City building' aspect of this game can be extraordinary unsatisfying and frustrating, and since it is 85% of the game, I cannot recommend this game in good faith. So while I will personally have to persevere through this extremely annoying and time consuming endeavour as I have already been hooked and want to see where it goes, I do not recommend this exercise in frustration on anyone else, especially if you are used to stronger city builder titles (i.e. Any of the impression games).TL;DR A game with a great aesthetic in both visuals and music, a story more interesting than city builders usually have and a thematic delivery that is excellent. Unfortunately also suffers from deeply faulty city building mechanics, causing at least 50% of your hours played to be excruciatingly frustrating, compounded by a time limit on all your missions.*1*1 Revision 26/07/2023  The aforementioned time limit is pretty much removed around mission 3. The time limit can also be extended or removed through the difficulty settings.The rest of the review still applies, after 15 hours of additional play. In fact, both its strong points and it weak points have only intensified.Enjoying the excellent music, theme and storyline, I do not regret continuing, but have found even more very specific examples as to why this is not a 'good' city builder, and requires any who try it to approach it with extreme patience and a lot of time.
