_childDocuments_.review: Ixion... An amazing game concept that could be soooo much fun.Unfortunately, the game hates you. It hates you SO MUCH. It't like an angry teenager screaming at you in the kitchen how much it hates you because you overworked a sector for 3 seconds. It slams the doors and screams profanities at you because you didn't plan 10 hours ahead and then stuck to the plan with microscopic precision because you missed the timing and don't have enough to build an extra farm, so now everyone riots with NO regards to the fact that their riots may most likely 100% cause everyone to die. This game requires micromanagement of everything and you must perform the most precise (almost scripted) actions to maybe have a chance of making it to the next level. The residents couldn't care less about the situation, (which actually sounds kind of like humans today, so I guess they got that right...) and they will do EVERYTHING in their power to make life in space way worse for everyone. And who came up with the idea of an UNFIXABLE HULL!?? That person needs to be spanked. Who in their right mind flies to space in a massive space station with ZERO welders and no shielding what so ever?? I could accept that the hull might get a breach once in a while due to debris or material degradation, but constantly leaking EVERYWHERE?? Are you f-ing kidding me. Once you removed that part by modding the game a bit, it was actually a really enjoyable game. Anyway, this is not a space colony survival sim, it's an apocalypse simulator, and no one wants to survive. Until they make this game actually playable without dying more often than you do in dark souls, I can't recommend this to anyone but serious masochists.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence about this game for a long time before buying because of the middling reviews. You can and will make mistakes that you can't recover from.  I did.  Several times.  I think I played chapter 1 three or four times before I was happy to move on, and chapter 2 at least twice, by that point I had figured out supply chains, layouts, priorities and was able to roll through the last three chapters relatively quickly. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved the background settings of this game - a station with the mission of saving humanity and finding new homes. However, the gameplay really disappointed me.       The first reason is subjective since I was expecting a game with much higher freedom instead of following the set story. I'd like to be able to jump to numerous different systems, stand in awe in front of natural miracles across the universe and have different challenges wherever I go. But the game is very rigid and does not have a lot of leeway for me to explore, the experience is more like watching a movie rather than writing your own story.       The second reason is that the 'movie', or the story is very dark in a sense that there is no hope in the future - the station is destined to fail in the end. There is no brighter future after the storm, there is no hope for humanity, we are all doomed. Every time you use the VOHLE drive, the hull of the station suffers irreversible damage, indicating that in the future, the journey of this station will come to an end. All the plans you make, all the buildings you put down will be for nothing when the station breaks apart and that is really discouraging.        The third reason is the cumulative debuffs that citizens have. They are a problem not in the sense of gameplay - the game can be hard and the citizens should have requests. But this really hurts the immersive experience that I'm trying to have. Remember, these people on board are the few thousand out of billions of people on earth. They are the smartest, toughest, and most professional astronauts who have the duty of preserving humanity's existence. They should be well trained to any challenges that may appear to them while have a shared dream. Seeing these people crying like little babies and mental breakdowns due to a few extra hours of work is really almost hilarious to me.       Just to add to that immersiveness of the game play, I understand that some survivors may not be able to work on space stations, they might be sportsmen or bankers or whatever before they were frozen, but why is it that you can't have them trained to be workers? Why do they have to become colonists?        Overall, good game with great potentials. But right now I really don't want to recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Up to a point, it's a great game. It's a fun, stressful timed puzzle as you try to arrange buildings to keep everything running and have to rip out pieces to replace them with better pieces, and reorganize sections to make them more efficient and use the space better. In that sense, it's a lot like Frostpunk in how you have to constantly manage an escalating situation and once you slip and fall behind a little it's almost inevitable that you fall behind A LOT and then it's time to start over and do it better.So why wouldn't I recommend it?First, there are too many situations where the challenge is the lack of control or lack of information. You're having trouble getting enough parts to transfer between sectors. Do you need: A) a better warehouse; B) more warehouses; C) to up the numbers on the resource transfer screen; or D) something provided by future tech that you haven't seen yet? I've finished the game, and I still have no idea. Oh no - a giant space storm is killing all of your ships! Boy, it'd be nice to be able to tell them to come back into your service bays and save at least a third of them but no, no, they sit outside and die. Can't even get the crews to come inside, they bravely insist on going down with their miner. Little stupid "why can't I"s abound.Second, the plot takes a nose-dive in the late game. The last chapter is mostly empty, doesn't really provide a challenge, and then gives you an ending that seems disconnected from the rest of the plot. It made me sad that I had put more time into the game.So, overall, it's not terrible, but it's flawed, and flawed in writing and design ways that seem unlikely to be fixable.

_childDocuments_.review: IXION is nearly there - and when it gets there I will update my review (if I remember), but, their attempt to make a survival citybuilder/management game has been blighted by a ludicrous overzealousness that turns difficulty into just feeling like you're not supposed to progress.Everything in this game in regards to blowing ♥♥♥♥ up on your station is WAY over the top. Turning a building back on? Expect it, and others around it, to spontaneously explode. Want to process waste material into useful things - instead of shoving it out the airlock? Expect your grateful survivors to strike. There's a neat little thing in one of the chapters where 'space weather' moves in, with no warning, no ability to mitigate, DESTROYING YOUR ENTIRE FLEET. No mining, no collection, diddly squat.Logistics are a mess, with you unable to set priorities between sectors, and obvious things like 'Oh, the fire station can drive firetrucks across all sectors, right? WRONG. Get ready to build 6 fire stations you incandescent peasant.There are many examples of the Devs trying to funnel player behaviour. Putting an arbitrary (and hidden) time limit on each level so you can't prepare as much as you would like. Having the aforementioned spontaneously exploding buildings also cause massive hull damage. Putting huge penalties on picking up cryo pods and waiting until you can FEED THE OCCUPANTS because OH WAIT everyone will throw a strike because they think you're stopping them seeing their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grandma who it still frozen and NO don't expect her to work - she's only going to moan and whine and strike.I rarely write reviews - but this game needs to show me and other players a little more respect in allowing us to PLAY THEIR GAME the way we would like to - instead of EXPERIENCING THEIR LE ART.Needs MAJOR balance patches, and reworking of logistics and morale systems. Love the storybook, keep getting cuts from the razors you put between the pages.Hull Integrity 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a tough one, but I can't really recommend this as a great gaming experience. The first couple of hours are great; amazing music, great look, engaging story, decent enough tutorial. After that it becomes more of a miss. Constantly moving resources and population between sections. Constantly managing and re-assigning storage. Constant pausing to check up on science probes. Micromanaging which building are activated and which aren't to avoid blackouts. And that's just the straightforward stuff. The game keeps putting pressure on you to move to next sector, but I found it better to stick around. I don't think I'd survive the end-game if I didn't squeeze the most out of everything.There's a workload stat for each sector. If you assign one too many people, the workload goes from Optimal to Extra Hours. That in turn drastically increases accident chance. In reality, if you don't double-check the stats all the time and accidentally turn on the tiniest kiosk for a split second, you end up with two factories exploding, a dozen injured and three more dead. There's a lot of information that is just hard to read. Your population is a sum of workers, non workers and colonists. You're looking at the wrong stat. Food production is just confusing and the output number swings wildly based on whether it's it's time for population to eat. There was a very satisfying time in the mid-game where the research tree was unlocking a lot of building improvements. Bigger, higher capacity, better access. There is no penalty for demolishing and rebuilding, so it was pretty fun to get everything re-arranged and more efficient. But then it was disappointing to see some of the end-game buildings being worse than their middle tiers. Final battery building had much lower energy density than mid tier. Final storage house had the same storage density, which is fair because you eliminate the need to more road access. But then you figure out that two smaller storage units give you diversity of things to store (can't mix) and twice the number of trucks to distribute it.Mining and transport ships are kinda hard to coordinate. There's a lot of them, editing priorities is a lot of clicking and the ships are stupid. You can't assign certain resources to be delivered to a specific sector, so you need to build infrastructure for redistributing stuff after the fact. All ships with the same priority will head for the exact same target. I kept ending up with my mining ships flying in a pack, and five transport ships flying all the way across the galaxy to pick up the same item, then returning all the way to the ship empty-handed, before being able to pick another target...If you want to check it out for the story, which is still good, my advise would be to pick it up on sale and play on easy.

_childDocuments_.review: Ixion: A Stellar Journey Through SpaceFrostpunk meets spaceRating: ★★★★☆Story and SettingIn Ixion, you take on the role of the administrator of the Tiqqun space station, tasked with ensuring the survival of humanity.The game’s narrative is rich and immersive, drawing you into a universe filled with peril and hope. The story unfolds through beautifully crafted cutscenes and in-game events, making you feel the weight of every decision you make.Gameplay MechanicsThe gameplay is both challenging and rewarding. You must manage resources, construct buildings, and maintain the morale of your crew while navigating the dangers of space. The game’s mechanics are intricate, requiring careful planning and strategic thinking. The balance between managing the internal affairs of the Tiqqun and exploring the vastness of space keeps the gameplay dynamic engaging.Visuals and SoundVisually, Ixion is stunning. The graphics are detailed and atmospheric, bringing the cold, dark expanse of space to life. The design of the Tiqqun and its various modules is both functional and aesthetically pleasing. The soundtrack complements the visuals perfectly, with a hauntingly beautiful score that enhances the overall experience.=Comparison to Frostpunk=Setting and Atmosphere:Frostpunk is set in a post-apocalyptic, frozen Earth where you must build and manage a city to survive the extreme cold. The atmosphere is bleak and oppressive, emphasizing the harshness of the environment.Ixion, on the other hand, takes place in the vastness of space, with a focus on exploration and survival in a hostile universe. The atmosphere is equally tense but offers a different kind of isolation and danger.Gameplay Focus:Frostpunk emphasizes moral choices and the well-being of your citizens, often forcing you to make difficult decisions that affect the entire community.Ixion also involves managing the morale of your crew, but it places a greater emphasis on exploration and the technical challenges of maintaining a space station.Visuals and Sound:Both games excel in their visual and auditory presentation. Frostpunk’s icy landscapes and somber music create a chilling atmosphere, while Ixion’s detailed space environments and evocative soundtrack immerse you in the vastness of space.ConclusionIxion is a must-play for fans of city-building and survival games. Its intricate mechanics, compelling narrative, and stunning presentation make it a standout title in the genre. While it shares some similarities with Frostpunk, Ixion offers a unique experience that sets it apart. Whether you’re a fan of space exploration or simply enjoy a good survival challenge, Ixion is sure to captivate and entertain you.

Similar to the 3-box icon of "There isnt any carbon connected to this polymer plant" there should be a more obvious visual indicator when something other than time is needed for an item to complete construction and it isnt going to happen on its own.3) Make an ambient/chill mode that lets you jump to random systems or something to go along with the campaign. _childDocuments_.review: This game is just...awkward, it doesn't feel that difficult as such, it just feels like the game is fighting you every step of the way. Want resources in another sector? Build a stockpile in both sectors using 5 workers each and set up a resource distribution rule. Want colonists from sector 1 to use the airlock in sector 2? Well you can't. Want to spend endless resources constantly patching up the hull? Want to have your science ships destroyed with no possible way of anticipating it? Want your cargo ships to go around the giant space storm of death? Nope.  Just turning 60 cryopods into humans and then sending them down to a planet turned out to be a near impossible fiddly task that took hours. The premise is great but the implementation is poor.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun but wait for a sale.IXION feels similar to a Frostpunk in space with better story telling and production value. After playing the game for a while I can safely say that if you like Frostpunk and sci-fi then you're most likely going to like IXION.Despite the slightly better production value I would say IXION is far less polished than Frostpunk. Things always feel rough around the edges or like they're falling short of reaching their full potential. This goes for graphics, sound, game systems, balance, cinematics, etc.PROS:- Great storytelling and production value thus far. The game looks great and I appreciate all the voice acting- The prologue was engaging. It was a great introduction to the story, characters, and game mechanics.- It's not easy. You can definitely get yourself into a bad situation and have to start the chapter over.- I keep getting put into situations where I have to decide between 2 or 3 things that I really need because my resources are low.CONS:- Encountered many bugs. (Update: I'm sure many have been fixed by now)- Systems aren't quite as complex or in-depth as I would like them. Nearly all systems feel like they fall just short of reaching their potential.- Event rewards are static which I'm going to assume will reduce replay value- Pacing of story, science, resources, and some specific in-game events/things feels a bit off. Things just don't feel like they match up sometimes.- I very strongly dislike being rushed out of chapters

The cinematics and how the game plays generally shows scale absolutely FANTASTICALLY! When I'm observing the Tiqqun, especially from the outside, the soundtrack reinforces the scale of the ship and its epicness - there are just so many wow moments. The Homeworld series comes pretty close. The voice acting is also amazing and I love hearing the dialogue just for its immersion alone.The game's difficulty is extreme. Every wrong decision, indecision or letting things get out of hand, can cause a spiral effect of doom. Nonetheless, I'm a bit of a perfectionist when I enjoy something so I restarted the campaign 2 times after getting to chapter 3. When I finally looked closer at the research tree, things became much, much easier. Here are some tips:  I do have some problems with IXION. (1) It's not very intuitive. For instance, most missions, that are done Frostpunk style, do not explain preliminary choices or final ones. Again and again I would choose an option that would end the expedition by picking the final decision without knowing it was the final decision. This has caused much frustration and some save-scumming.(2) You cannot easily recall all your ships without messing up your priorities, unless you just don't scan.(3) Storage is a major issue. Docking ports wont unload unless there's a storage building and the logistics is pretty simple, so it sometimes requires unnecessary micro-management. (4) the game is in dire need of a blueprint planner.IXION has been an absolute blast, but I must admit, the end was fairly anti-climatic, especially how amazing all the other systems were.  Keep in mind that it is a story driven game. Even though you have quite a bit of freedom, you are still restricted. Nonetheless, I highly recommend IXION, especially to sci-fi space nerds...

_childDocuments_.review: Rate this game a 7 out of 10.  It's a great game but still rough around the edges.  The game is beautiful and it has a great story.  About 29 hours in and I completely failed and need to restart, don't think I've ever failed at a game so irrecoverably before.  There isn't very much in-game help and you need to puzzle out most things on your own.  I don't know if that is the cause of my failure or not.  For example you don't make tech progress unless you find research nodes.  I wasted so many resources on a tech lab and kept it running but it would take 3000 cycles to get one tech improvement.  I didn't know that each tech branch has it's own tech options until about 20 hours into the game.  Progress in tech is very slow & restricted (am I missing something?).  - I spent a full game year in one system but the planets never moved around the sun.  Planets should move.  - You can't change the trajectory of miners & hauler craft.  In chapter 2 there is a death cloud called "space weather".  Like an idiot I put my capitol ship behind this cloud because there were lots of good resources.  I thought my craft would maneuver around it.... but no.... ship after ship got destroyed and things went downhill quick.  - I really really really don't like the hull maintenance, seems like busy work.  Mysterious things affect the hull integrity.  Adds to the unnecessary micro management of the game.  Why does an airlock take up SO much room?  Could fit a fricken battleship through the airlock which are required to repair the hull, in every sector.  Seems excessive.  Hull maintenance is a good game mechanic thing but could much better.  This is my biggest compliant about the game.  I won't play again until this is improved.  Would like to see an graph over time of this to try and learn what things affect it.  The indicator is useless (-89 one cycle, +69 another cycle... WHY?).  As an administrator responsible for the salvation of humanity... I'd want to see trending data on my desk the next morning.  - It's the end of humanity and people bicker about the smallest things at the worst time.  I get that people are demoralized but really.... your people start wining the second you warp into a new system which is when you are trying to repair the hull, look at the new solar system and a bunch of other things.  Can't they wait a day or two to start whining?  Excessive pressure.at the worst time.. please spread it out.  I agree with the mechanic but not the implementation.  For example, complaining about noise and smoke is believable but they ask you to shut off all "factories".  What is considered a "factory"?  I turned off nearly everything (people were starving) and still didn't make those wining bastards happy.  Maybe add a "comfort" or "pollution" indicator per sector?  Some indicator to let an administrator know when they are improving things. A graph maybe?  - When you open a new sector, resources are spread out over a large area.  You need to create a road to each, collect resources and then remove them.  Unnecessary time waster.  Would a loader really just splat resources around a large area like that?  Makes sense at the start of the game as a tutorial but get's old fast.  -  For the quests, there should always be a "leave the area" option unless there is a breakdown of some kind.  Couple of times my spidey-sense went off and I felt that I should leave but there was no option and ruin followed.Ultimately I was forced to quit because of a bug.  I had to help with repairs on another ship.  I selected a craft to move materials around.  I forget why, but I scrapped the designated ship when I was moving docks around.  I couldn't specify a new ship to handle moving materials to help repair another ship so I couldn't complete the major quest and ran out of resources.

_childDocuments_.review: It tries to be Frostpunk in space, but simply lacks many of the key elements that made Frostpunk what it was - time pressure, meaningful grey-area choices, etc.  The atmosphere and story are engaging, but the gameplay ends up being too frustrating to stay engaged with that story.  There is a great game hidden beneath the frustration - hopefully it will receive the updates it needs.#1 issue is the lack of a building move tool.  The level of time and micromanagement required to destruct a building and rebuild it is far too high.  This might be more acceptable if there was any realistic prospect of planning a future-proof design from the beginning - but the buildings are virtually all different sizes, and are extremely large given the sector size - it is simply isn't feasible to not move things around.  It isn't an interesting / challenging gameplay mechanic (since you get 100% refund anyway) - it is just a huge timesink.Which leads into another major issue: pacing.  The game doesn't really provide any urgency / guidance on how long things should be taking.  You could theoretically sit in one of the first couple of chapters collecting resources and building basically indefinitely.  There is a minor penalty for taking too long, but it is extremely minor.  It is very hard to know the right balance of necessary v unnecessary preparation.Resource consumption, availability, and consumption rates feel like they need more tuning.  The demand for alloys to keep up with meaningful population growth is simply staggering.  Even with multiple production buildings, multiple miners and freighters - it takes hours to build up the necessary infrastructure.  This might just come back to pacing - where the player has no idea how prepared they need to be to progress.Some more targeted issues:Accident rate is comically frequent - even with the most lenient working conditions, accidents occur constantly.  Dropping into even a 1 employee worker shortage often causes an accident instantly - and any level of worker shortage seems to shift the outcome from injuries to deaths.Research upgrades feel very inconsistent - some are extremely powerful (probably overpowered  - e.g. many of the housing upgrades drastically increase capacity, plus improving stability), while others are an absolutely pitiful 10% to a meaningless statistic - for the same research cost.The "demands from the crew" mechanic feels very lacking - you can reject the demands for no penalty, and the rewards are often meaningless - adding to an already maxed out Trust score.  With the constant gain/decay, there is little meaningful opportunity for this mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: IXION is an early access city manager set on a giant mobile space station that hues mostly toward a speculative science fiction rather than futurist fantasy. It’s got great graphics, a lot of fun details, and an epic story. IXION has all the makings of a great game.I *really* want to recommend IXION, and one day I probably will. But for now, there are a lot of really problematic details that the devs need to iron out.It’s fun and accurate that you need to mine—and then pick up with cargo ships—Iron and Carbon to make steel and polymers which are used to maintain the ship and build new buildings and ships. But the maintenance system for the hull, for which you need massive quantities of steel, and the cargo storage facilities, which can only store one type of cargo at a time and are a massive waste of space and time for the player, ruin the experience. To add insult to injury, the station is divided into six segments and each segment requires its own storage and source of each material, and transfers between must be made somewhat manually, which makes the micromanagement a sort of endless ledger of shortages and gluts which could be easily fixed through automation. Beyond that, your progress in the game can be hindered by trying to prepare too much and spending all of your science points before you need them to reveal a critical plot point—which is an obviously avoidable gameplay flaw.After three playthroughs, I can’t help but feel that there’s more to the game and that eventually I will love it, but I can’t be bothered to micromanage tiny quantities of steel and iron across the station’s sectors for long enough to find out. The day will come when I’ll recommend this game, but I’d pass on it on until the kinks are ironed out.

_childDocuments_.review: As the current the state stands, the game isn't polished enough to become a fun game for me. There are mainly two complaints I have, Accidents and Resource management, which I hope the developers will take a look at and adjustment their design accordingly.1. Accidents are events that happens when you overwork you workers due to being short staffed, causing injuries to workers and event deaths. This mechanic, however, is pretty broken at the moment since accidents can happen in optimal working conditions, seconds after your sector is short staffed for only a brief time, and randomly no matter what. The devs have already acknowledge this as an issue so this is less of a serious problem as I think they will soon address it later.2. Resources in this game are poorly management by game design. As someone who has played frostpunk and loves the game, I believe that a city survival game should the precise variety of resources to keep the game interesting while also not frustrating. IXION's resources management shortcoming comes at the fact the variety and how they are stored and transferred are a lot of micromanaging and frustration. Having raw and processed resources is fine, but since each stockpile can only take in one resource (4x4), each resource takes a lot of space to stockpile both raw and processed as well as the gaint factory to process the resource. The resource also can't be transferred between sectors without a stockpile existing in both sectors, this means that you'll won't be able to specialize sectors with specific resources and will likely need to have 4 or 5 stockpiles just to have resources moved to other sectors for building a single building or ship.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a qualified recommend: it's good but it's brutal.It's basically 'Frostpunk in space' with an overworld that is quite interesting, a well-written plot, and a theme of survival in the hostile cold darkness of space.  As a genre veteran, I've managed to not die, although it's been close several times.  This is a game that will kick you in the teeth, then watch you carefully as you get to your feet, let you make some progress, and then kick you in the groin.If it has you very powerfully hooked (as it does me) there still comes a point where you have to ask yourself "Am I masochistic enough to continue?"  And you find yourself looking for something a bit less bleak, maybe writing a passive-aggressive review about it.And I have to say, for a game that is determined to smack you into the floor, it's got a fantastic variety of ways to let you get back on your feet.  I particularly appreciate the fact that roads are free, and every building can be recycled with 100% efficiency.  Which is good, because alloys (your main building material) need to be spent continuously in order to keep the ship alive.  Which creates an interesting balancing act where you want to strip every system clean, but there comes a point where it's not helping you anymore.So yeah, if you want to prove to yourself that you're the absolute best survival city-builder out there, then this is a good opportunity to do it.  And at least there's enough autosaves that you can save scum if you feel the need. (I did.)

_childDocuments_.review: Really awesome game, but plagued by poor balance.Like, there's just a constant drain of iron for..reasons? Like I get taking damage while travelling, but you should just be able to fix it and move on with your life. NOPE, all damage is permanent and constantly draining hull integrity. And then there's permanent trust loss from your crew that also continues to drain. And once you've restarted a few times and now know what to expect, you get everything super balanced out, everybody's happy, but then this mission comes up where you spend 200 units of an already very stretched thin resource to save another ship and get rewarded with 250 non-workers which throws the balance of your ship so far off that everyone starves before you can do anything about it. Just feels like the people who wrote the missions didn't like their jobs and put a lot of "♥♥♥♥ you" in to everything they did.There's also some cool scenario's you come across where you get to make a choice of how you handle them, but that choice usually comes with an unfair lack of information and you often only get one choice that nets one resource, but for no reason. Like why can't I survey the debris field AND check out the derelict ship? Is my science ship on some sort of time crunch I don't know about? Does every choice have to come with a GOTCHA?Also, why is everybody on my ship so pissed about keeping people in cryo until we can properly implement them in to population? There's only so many resources available, and it takes time to get things setup for new arrivals.Anyway, a lot of this could be solved with a difficulty slider.I'm going to hold my recommendation for this game, because it's got so much stuff in it that I absolutely love, but has some terribly frustrating gameplay decisions made by the devs that ruin the game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this review, only 61% of reviews are positive which is a shame. Much of the criticism comes from the increased difficulty. _childDocuments_.review: This game requires 4 things:1. Patience2. Alloy3. Food4. Saving (a lot)This is a game that grabs you by the short and curlies, pulls you in close, and says in a deep gravely voice "You are MINE"If you like management and strategy games, this is a game for you. If you have hours to kill, this is a game for you. If you have a lot of  patience, this is a game for you.You cannot just jump in and build, build, build with this game. You must be patient, and build slowly, in order to conquer this game. Your main challenge will be to keep the hull integrity up, and the people fed and happy. Be prepared to start a chapter over a couple of times, in order to make it through with sufficient hull integrity and food on hand.Also, when you are bringing survivors and/or cryopods on board, you must scale up your food and housing to match. It is easy to get distracted by the many other tasks, and suddenly you have 300 homeless and starving people and your trust is tanking. A slight exaggeration, but you get the picture. This is where saving comes in. When things are going well, and all sectors are happy, save. Then, if the defecation hits the oscillator, you can reload the save.Overall, this is a very challenging and fun game. It requires focus, and patience, and saving. Did I mention saving?I really like this game. Once you get the hang of it, and adjust for the learning curve, it is great.

_childDocuments_.review: Ixion successfully combines a range of elements from other games in the sci-fi city builder genre in a story that is at times enjoyably uncomfortable. It has been most commonly compared to Frostpunk in its non-conforming city builder layout style, but also shares elements from games such as Halcyon 6 and Anno 2070. This includes having multiple views from inside the ship, outside the ship and the wider planetary system, with each view having its own mechanics and requirements. The constrained and interconnected build areas promotes a strong focus on space management and production supply chain optimisation, further enhanced by the approach adopted for sectors and associated specialisation. The cut scene cinematics and story appeal to an older gamer (such as myself) that lived on narrative driven single player games and help to build the sense of urgency and peril. As a city builder survival game, the threat of failure is present enough to require some thought, but not so great that it feels like a roguelite. Despite this the game has a decent amount of replayability, due to its comparatively long playthrough duration, especially if you are into supply chain and layout optimisation and min-maxing.At present, the game lacks an endless or sandbox mode disconnected from the story. The platform appears to be well positioned for this to be implemented and I understand this is on the cards. Given the focus on space management, this should be prioritised.The game is under active development with a dynamic Discord community. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: Months later, I'm changing this back to a positive review, as I'm assuming (hoping) they fixed this terrible bug.------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Edit: I am going to need to change my review to a negative now because of one thing.  I encountered a game breaking bug that causes your accidents to not be allowed to be repaired.  When they need to be repaired, they are inoperable and cannot even be dismantled.  So you are left permanently with a dead building and permanent accident - if it is your tech lab as I'm seeing other people have now then you literally cannot progress, with your only option being starting over or hoping you have saves that are even remotely recent and that your auto saves didn't update after the fact (3rd option below if you're desperate) otherwise you are going to lose a HUGE amount of work and playtimeIf you're really desperate, you can go into your LocalLow foldier then go to your Ixion saves, find your save game, open the building.sav file, find the building that has the requestedRepair set to true, and annihilate the entire building from the file.Obviously I'm going to leave the review negative as you shouldn't have to go into the game's files to fix the game.Had it happen again 1 day later, as well as an issue now with the accident flag not being removed for a sector despite no accidents.-----------------------------------------------------------I haven't had this much with a survival colony sim since FrostpunkI took a look at some of the negative reviews and can't say I relate with the resource management as I haven't had an issue with sectors, nor an issue with accidents (they're easily avoided and minimal impact).  The game also gets much more difficult after the first chapter - which I love (I have no idea how people are saying it's too easy)  My only complaint is that the soundtrack is too good and there's no way to loop music in game (joke criticism) - but really it's frustrating that you can't cancel science events, this sucks if you misclick and possibly end up with disasterOtherwise I have nothing but good things to say about this game, I LOVE space so I might be biased for a space exploration colony sim.  The game has so much story for being a colony sim and you feel you're actually advancing toward something.  There's many struggles as with any survival sim but as you overcome you unlock better and better technology to remove the pain points that you had been facing.  This provides really a satisfying gameplay loopFuture Update: 30 hours in everything fell apart, the game gets MUCH harder as you progress (which I love, but it's pain)

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why the reviews might be mixed, but for me, this game has fallen heavily on the recommend side.A strategy city-builder set in the near future, where humanity is able to reach out to the stars to escape a uncertain future on Earth, Ixion gives only a brief introduction to the core mechanics needed to survive; it reminds me very much of strategy games 20 years ago, and I don't think it suffers for it. You learn the game as you learn the scenarios; I think it ties in relatively well with the story of discovery of ever increasingly weird and wonderful background.The main meat of building your station is challenging for a first run through. The game expects you to be demolishing and rebuilding frequently; it's not a static landscape of "Once Built, Forever Here". The expansion into new sectors and the logistics that entails takes some figuring out, but adds an added dimension of population and resource management.The strategic side requires vigilance; you can slip into a death spiral if not paying attention. There are different avenues to pursue in this regard - do you rely on mining or aim for an entirely self-sufficient ship? Have I scouted for sufficient resources near a destination prior to moving? Do I have sufficient battery capacity to traverse a star system and not have essential maintenance buildings shut down? Does my storage system have enough transports to get the food out to the whole station? The game isn't going to tell you this ahead of time, or even that you need to be aware of this. Is that a weakness? Maybe to some, but for me I appreciate the challenge.Behind a positive gameplay experience on the whole is a bucket-load of lore, with allegories to art, greek mythology and ancient history. No name in the game has been chosen without reason, there are a incredible number of cultural easter eggs, and the story is deeply layered and multi-faceted. At first glance, this isn't necessarily readily apparent. As with every other gameplay mechanic, Ixion doesn't draw attention to it, but it's there and obvious if paying attention and not clicking rapidly through everything.Graphics are reasonable, but there is an unreasonable requirement to reduce setting in my eyes. The game will chug in certain parts even with relatively strong hardware. The music is generally tone-sensitive background stuff. Neither outstanding nor offensive. Ixion's biggest strength and weakness is the fact it rarely draws attention to things happening within. For many, that may make it a hard game to get through, but if you enjoy a fusion of strategy and lore discovery, then this game could very well be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Oof, this one hurts.IXION is a great game when it comes to concept and the way the concept is worked out into gameplay.Unfortunately its narrative does something that several other post-apocalyptic city-builders also do, which is that it puts you in a doom spiral where things get progressively worse the further you progress, so instead of getting to feel like you're making progress (re)building a new society after a disaster, instead you're just constantly in danger and forced to grow your 'city' in order to not die.On the lowest difficulty, it's not  to survive if you pay attention, but you do constantly have to pay attention.And that would have been fine if not for one crucial thing: The narrative constantly has you chase things that will supposedly offer a solution to a problem, but that never pan out and often end up introducing an unexpected complication that makes things worse. And that gets real tiresome, real fast. Maybe if there were an occasional success or bright spot in the narrative where things do end up getting a little better, I might have endured the game longer.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished the game at the exact 30 hours mark without much save loading and replaying.This is a very solid game with high production quality and art, overall a very stable, fun and refined experience and well worth the current price tag of 35 euros.A lot of the reviews say that the game is very iffy when it comes to difficulty/balance and can softlock you out of a 15+ hour save and that first held me off from buying the game. You will have problems in this game if this is your first city builder or a logistical game, but if you are at least a bit experienced in the genre the game is not really that hard after you get a grasp on the mechanics, a little bit of thinking and planning ahead goes a long way, one thing I can point out that the game is very unforgiving and consequences of the mistakes made may (and will) follow you throughout your adventure. So if you were afraid of that - don't, the reviews greatly exaggerate the "difficulty problems", hull damage is really not that big of a deal.The game has a bit of a replay potential for 1-3 more playthroughs if you want to try different strategies/outcomes.Highly recommended for city builder/logistics genre enjoyers, this is some quality stuff right here.And please for the love of god start building your docking bays and EVA's from the corner of the sector, you will thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game; with caveats.The game does an exceptional job of setting the tone and telling its story and is worth playing for that alone, but the gameplay style is definitely not for everyone. Ixion is, as other reviews have mentioned, a difficult and very micromanagement-heavy game. Don't even touch the time acceleration; the temptation to speed things up will be your doom. Your station is balanced on a knife's edge and things can go very wrong very fast if you're not paying attention.- Story is good, though more voice acting would have been nice- Music is great and fits the game perfectly; I've been listening to the soundtrack while doing chores around the house!- Gameplay has flaws, but it might just be your cup of teaAn update: I initially wrote this review midway through chapter 2. I've now finished the game, and have a few more thoughts. I ran into a couple more annoying bugs, but they were always resolved easily by saving and reloading. I found myself always running low on resources in the early game, but in the mid to late game, my biggest challenge was figuring out where to put all my resources! I do agree that the balance could use some minor tweaks; primarily to reduce the amount of resources available in the later game to keep the pressure on. However, as it stands, the game is a very solid 8/10 for me. Challenging, enjoyable, and with some very interesting world-building.

_childDocuments_.review: IXION is a fine game. To be honest, I expected a bit more in terms of the writing and polish of the game, but besides that it was great fun and worth its price in my opinion.I'll start with the bugs I experienced because those were the main pain point: there were all related to docking bays, ships stuck waiting for disassembly, not being able to deconstruct a docking bay because a ship assigned to it is stuck in another chapter, and other similar problems. I ended up having two unusable docking bays by the end of the game, that were always powered down and only served to increase the space specialization of the sector.Another thing that could be improved is that there is a mechanic where space weather can destroy your fleet. There are techs to make your ships have 50% better resistance to space weather, but since they normally would be destroyed within 2-3 seconds (at speed X3) of being in bad space weather, that just makes it get to 4-6 seconds, and they get destroyed anyway. The only way to prevent that is to MANUALLY click on EACH resource chunk that is on the other side of space weather and mark it as to be avoided. Of course, once the space weather goes away, or you moved your ship somewhere else, you'll need to manually toggle that off for each of them again. For some reason, late game, clicking the avoid button made my game freeze for 1s, so in the 5th chapter, I ended up spending around 5 minutes just clicking buttons with the game paused to avoid losing my fleet.I came in expecting Homeworld-level writing, and was slightly disappointed from the beginning. I think IXION takes a lot of great ideas from other titles (the storyline with the scientists getting duplicated seems taken from Stellaris for example, but I might be wrong.) but its own original ideas seem too simplistic, too naive, IMO. It seems to me like the kind of story a high school student would imagine, not a science fiction writer.The game is not as challenging as other similar games, since there is no urgency and that the two resource sinks in the game can be acquired in unlimited quantities early on if you focus on it (produce food with electricity which is infinite, produce alloys with waste which is infinite). It tries to make you think there is urgency by giving you a debuff to happiness if you stay too long in a chapter, but anyway each chapter adds onto the unhappiness, so if you can't stay in a chapter because of the unhappiness, you're going to be in an even worse position by rushing things.I really like the sector specialization mechanic though, but I wish it was more complex. Maybe having more than 2 tiers per specialization, and maybe having exactly 6 of them. A "logistics" specialization could be interesting for example, to make drone bays and storage more efficient in a sector, in order to in the late game, have a centralized storage sector.Overall I have mixed feelings about this title, because I have a lot of small complaints about it, but the gameplay, graphics, music and sound design compensate for the shortcomings I described earlier, so all in all I had an okay time with it, and for 30 bucks I think that was good enough. If you get it on sale, I think it's a great deal.

Where the game falls apart is in the later chapters where the only challenges are "Did you save up 600+ Polymer!" or "Did you spend a bunch of Alloys to fill every inch with batteries?". The game attempts to force you to move onto the next chapter but attempt is the right word as you can just ignore the consequences which means you can just have a gigantic stockpiles of every resource to solve the previous problems.There are no real moral choices in the game, the game does not judge you for forced rationing or overworking everyone, there is a cult that seems to be cut content or just forgotten. _childDocuments_.review: Colony Survival games are at their best in the early and mid game. When the hard choices need to be made and you have to weigh up where you are putting your resources to give you the best chance of success. It's hard to make that feeling last for a long time. When everyone has comfortable shelter, plenty of food, there are loads of extra hands to make work easier, and cover any illness or mishaps. Colony sims can ironically get a little stale right at the moment when you move from surviving to thriving. Because that's when the challenge is gone. Ixion didn't make a convincing late game for me. I found the back half of my 27 hour playthrough a real slog, to the point I almost didn't finish. So why the recommendation? The early game is real good. The cushioning of free resources from the tutorial gives way to some careful decision making lest you run dry of alloys or food or power, and your mission falls to ruin. That first 10-12 hours had me hooked. But as you make your way through the midgame, a mixture of gradually building up resource stocks and advancing technology gives you more room to breathe, until you reach a point of near self-sufficiency. You've got it all, and most likely only needed about half the buildable space the game allows. So what then? Well, then the game asks you to get 1000, no 2000 more people. Thematically colonisation is the whole goal, but in practice your cryonic facilities unfreeze 3 people per day. So... you're going to need a lot of them, and I guess all those upgrades to let you unfreeze 5 or even 6 people a day make a bit more sense now. And then you'll dismantle it all and move on to the next thing. because the game keeps throwing a next thing at you, and perhaps it's unfair of me to brush over what comes beyond those early chapters, but I don't want to spoil the story because it's the other reason to recommend this. Just be prepared to spend 1/4 of the time absorbing the narrative and the balance of that time watching your ships strip mine the galaxy to meet the tasks required to get that next story bit. I guess my complaint here is that the mechanics of meeting the game's increasingly grand tasks just aren't as interesting as the opening battles for survival, and they take a massive amount of time even running the game at 3x speed. This would be marvellous as a 16 hour game, but it's just stretched quite thin. Still, you might want that slower pace, and that is really my only complaint here.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I gave this game an honest try, but probably won't bother with it again.The short of it: the colony and resource management side of the game is lots of fun. However, I felt like I kept getting burned for doing side content and not immediately engaging with the "story" missions. I also fell prey to some beginner traps, which really soured my view on the game.As said, I did enjoy the colony management side of things. You have very limited space to place infrastructure and production, and having to shift things around when new needs arose or when tech was researched made for a fun organic puzzle. Really could use a 'visible grid' option, but maybe I missed it. Resources, too, were great to manage. Having to scan for new clusters of vital elements and organising miners and freighters to collect them felt like you were making choices without being micro-manage-y. It was also exhilarating when you start to realise that the system you're in is running out of resources and so you have to start being very discerning of future build choices.The game prides itself in having a story, but it certainly could do better. It starts off pretty strong, with a prologue that also serves as a tutorial. You meet a wide cast of characters and it ends in a quite literal bang. Afterwards, however, it drops off pretty quickly. What I encountered afterwards could be summed up as "your corporate overlords are in another castle." It was always just about getting to the next system, nothing more. Any descriptions of events, places or characters was always surface level, usually just two-three sentences that could be summed up in one. Not really gripping stuff.Finally, there's a difficulty. I won't say this game isn't difficult, as said you do have to keep in mind your dwindling resources, but a lot of the difficulty seems artificial and arbitrary. An example of it being done right is with some of the space weather. There's a patch of space that has a chance of destroying your ships but on the other side are some notable resource nodes. So now you have an engaging choice of risking your ships or leaving those precious resources be. An example of it being done wrong is when your citizens decide that they're just going to be more sad today. I also ran into what I feel are "beginner traps." That is too say, problems that I had no way of knowing that they were going to be a thing. The big one is that I failed to realize that there was an absolutely vital piece of technology that I needed to get right away: the one that allows your research building to actually be useful. Seems like a no-brainer when compared to other games, but in Ixion research is primarily gained from science ships about in the system. Not from your single lab. However! Despite that the game gives you research points like candy, they are limited and you have no way of knowing when that well is going to run dry. And if you didn't do the precious main quests first you can suddenly find yourself locked out of progression. When I ran into this, the communities consensus was, seriously, to edit more science into my save file. This really did not sit well with me, but then again maybe I just suck.Also, if you do get the game, keep a very close eye on your cryo-station. You *will* end up with too many people eating all your food without you realising it if you don't keep that thing monitored and off.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, full disclosure: I've been waiting to play this game since I got my hands on the demo what feels like a year ago now. And this is everything I've ever wanted in a videogame, short of a full-on AAA adaptation of David Weber's Honorverse novels. Spiritually this owes more to something like the Homeworld franchise than it does a game like Cities: Skylines or the Anno series which it more superficially resembles.As it stands right now, Ixion has more than its share of balance issues. Its ridiculously easy to piss off your AI pops and send your game into an unrecoverable death spiral. The devs are aware of the issue and, as of this writing, have already issued an retracted one patch in an attempt to solve the problem. Even then, it definitely feels like there's a way through the overarching narrative that the devs intended the player to choose, and any other choices will lead to a game over. Just as an example, the similarities to Homeworld led me to try and mine out each system, which resulted in my simultaneously having an overabundance of basic resources and severe lack of advanced resources, ultimately leading to production bottlenecks and the destruction of my station.All that being said, this game has kept me up for almost two nights straight, I love it to bits, and I really don't want to stop playing. If you're like me and a fan of the likes of David Weber, Peter F. Hamilton, Iain M. Banks, Ann Leckie, Andy Weir, etc, this game is your MUST BUY of 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed Ixion. If you're familiar with Frostpunk, this is a similar take only the doom you're running from is the cold death of space instead of winter. The two share a lot of concepts down to the circular building area (though Ixion it's the curved interior of a spacecraft). Ixion is its own game though, taking on a stronger narrative story with minor branching based on your decisions as you play. The story presentation reminds me of the Homeworld games in some ways, where each scenario depends on how you did in the previous, just with a management game instead of an RTS as the core gameplay.This is a difficult building and management game. I lost catastrophically a few times and had to redo things from a save. You want to save often, it's easy to make semi-permanent mistakes, especially at the start of the game. It does ease up a little later in the story as you unlock technology but the start is rough. You are generally given just enough time to solve things if you stay on top of everything. I found it fair enough but it is on the stressful side for this kind of game. It also leans a little more on the micromanagement side but I think they've done a good job with balancing it around some core systems.A few mechanics I think could be improved, I didn't like how probe scanning worked. You have to launch so many probes and you have to do it constantly, it can be distracting and feel like busy work. Space weather can require clicking tons of probed down locations to enable/disable ships from visiting them and that's really annoying, I wish you could select a large group at once. It's also possible to starve the station by committing a transport ship to a mission too early, so be careful about accepting an event to transport things before you can produce them.The music, sound, art direction, story are all excellent. Graphics are pretty good but there are some rough spots like some soft UI elements or minor glitches. I don't want to spoil the story at all but there's some unique ideas in it that I really enjoyed. Overall the presentation is great.I had a few technical issues but nothing showstopping. The worst was some tooltips would be drawn off screen at times, so I couldn't read them. It ran well for the majority of the game but once you open up all sectors I started seeing some slowdown. Everything is working fine on Linux and it's playable on the Steam Deck but I think you'll prefer to play with a mouse. The one annoying problem I had is each time I started the game it would pick a very wrong resolution (ultrawide 60Hz for my 16:9 144Hz monitor) but I could just change it to the correct one. Some achievements are currently broken. While I thought I ran into some events that didn't work, I replayed these and realized I just missed some element during the narration and it worked when I was paying better attention.I'd love to see some patches to fix up these issues but I think it is absolutely worth it as is if you enjoy a challenging management game and an original scifi setting.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people talk about the difficulty. It's not to my taste, even with the difficulty editor. But that isn't the main problem.The main problem is that the "city building" part is shallow and bad. You can get to a place where you're self-sufficient(ish) even at normal difficulty pretty easily. But there really isn't a tonne of depth to be had; make sure you have enough housing, enough stability, etc. It's very primitive as far as city building goes. You'd think the confined building space would be the challenge but no; it's really not.Compounding that is the mandatory events that introduce permanent negative effects. I understand the goal is to force you to move along but it basically punishes you for not knowing how to proceed in the most efficient manner from the get go. Actually using the mechanics of the game? Gather resources? You took to long, here is a permanent -1 stability you can't get rid of. There's a late game system where it's a permanent -2 modifier and you have no way of speeding through on your first attempt - you can not POSSIBLY know what needs to be done from the start.But by far the worst is the story. It has an interesting premise. It kind of takes that premise and starts running to a place that by chapter 4, I was genuinely excited! I though I had an idea of where it was going on and I was interested. And then it went the most generic and uninteresting route possible. Also I accidentally skipped the ending cutscene because I assumed the first bit was just the usual "Engines powering up" cutscene and skipped it, but no...missed the whole thing, cut to credits. Did not care to play through 10~ minutes to rewatch.

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many crybabies and people who really don't know what they are talking about in the review section that made me hesitate to try this out. Big mistake.The game is great. It is hard at first, you will reset at least once or twice until you understand how to play and organize stuff efficiently. Is it perfect? No of course not, but it is a great experience and a good challenge for those looking to scratch that survivalist itch.Many people criticize the difficulty and I can understand this. The game does a somewhat poor job of explaining how some of the more complex mechanics work. Also the fact that there are some deadly exploration events where your only choice is to savescum (or read a guide) is a slight turnoff. Despite that, the game is very straightforward: Have enough food to feed your people and have enough alloys to "feed" your ship and use the rest of your resources to scale this up for when your needs increase. People complaining about the ship needing too many alloys... learn to deal with it, that IS the point of the game.Also, there are some odd people who are complaining about the "permanent" -1 stability if you stay in a system for too long. This "permanent" modifier is gone when you jump to a new system. While I admit that the game should communicate this better, the fact that these people actually complained in the reviews means 1 of 3 things: 1)They lied, 2)there is an issue with their IQ, 3)they quit the game and left a review instantly when they saw the -1 "perm" debuff (implying a situation similar to [2]). As for the resource management for the multiple sectors, it is daunting when you first see it, but once you realize how it works everything becomes smooth sailing. Finally the accidents: I dont know how it was at launch, but apparently there was a patch that reduced them. They are annoying and scary when they start happening at first, but if you have an infirmary (or 2 for big sectors) and your people are happy and not overworked then you can just ignore them once your bots can auto repair stuff. The happy part is extremely important... angry sector people will practically kill themselves by smashing their hollow heads on buildings made to keep them alive.The music was fantastic and the jumping cinematic was great. The story was unfortunately just ok. It started out great but the ending (the entire last chapter specifically) was a bit lackluster, especially in contrast to the quite unique second-to-last chapter.All in all, I really enjoyed the game and the puzzle of optimizing and specializing my sector to survive. While there is not much replayability, just a single FULL playthrough is worth the price (esp if you get it on a sale like me)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game and the reviews are ultimately held back by a lot of players who are either unwilling to learn or don't want a challenge. And that's fine, but it's not reflective of the quality of the game. With that said, more thorough review time:The good:- the main story is generally interesting- the game mechanics themselves are generally solid and there's a gradual introduction of new mechanics- it's generally just a very solid city builder/survival builderThe negative:- There is ample space for ux improvements. It's easy to get bogged down in minor details because the ai is intentionally bad. It's a game set in a high tech space colony yet I have to continuously manually give orders for people to not do stupid stuff like. Better control of transfer of resources(not just importing but exporting too) as well as more control over automated population transfer would get rid of a lot of tedious busiwork which isn't hard, it's just repetitive.- The mechanics for trying to push you into the next chapter are not clear(you get a "permanent" penalty for overstaying but the penalty is gone once you move one). But you can basically stick around forever. Which is very forgiving(you can spend a lot of time to get really ready for the next chapter), but it really slows down the pace of the game. Perhaps they can add in an extra difficulty mode which more aggressively forces you to keep movingIf you like management games and city builders this is an excellent choice. It could still use a little extra polish, but it's extremely enjoyable as is. I'd consider it a solid 8/10 game as it is now and a 9 if they could just iron out some of the tedious busywork.If you're afraid to be challenged and want an easy forgiving experience it's probably not the game for you, but you probably figured that out looking at the other reviews. But it really isn't that hard, You'll probably want to restart once, but just give some thought as to what went wrong, why, and what you can do to avoid that happening again. Explore the different mechanics, and don't be afraid to do a bit of experimentation to see what works.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes I recommend but there's one major caveat.Only play custom and turn resource levels up to max. It will more closely resemble reality.I did an annoying amount of math and found that there is at least 750k square feet of buildable space inside the Tiqqun. I did that math based on the approximate size of a human in the thing, estimated each square to be about 8ftx8ft, then counted how many steel mills I could fit in a given sector, multiplied by the number of sectors.Even if a square is 10x10ft or 15x15ft, we aren't talking dyson sphere here.Then, even if the rest of the structure of the Tiqqun was 10x the internal buildable size, there would still be thousands if not millions of years of material to maintain it in just our solar system, let alone a solar system where no one has inhabited it.In most games the rate of trees regrowing is unrealistic, the rate of fish restocking is unrealistic, things like that. Resources regenerate too fast.In this game, resources are unrealistically scarce by default. But you can, fortunately, adjust that.I kinda wish the devs made the resources harder to access instead of just capping the quantity. Use distance or hazards or whatever.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/8/2023 I doubt I'll ever finish the game due to the resource management madness, but the team did complete the difficulty settings that should have been there at launch, so I guess that's a start. We'll see if any other updates come out. I've changed my review from not recommended to recommended because I think some people who couldn't play the game as it was will be able to find settings that allow them to finally finish it. 4/19/2023 I've put in quite a bit more time, though the resource movement around the various sectors is an area in which the devs believe is "working as intended." It's just way too much micro for me at this stage in my life, working and with a family - more like taking on a second job. "Imagine if you had to tell every single worker in Frostpunk where to take their resources." is a comment I read on the Steam forums and I believe it's accurate. If you're in college and you care nothing about your grades or if you're a teenager with no responsibilities at home, no chores, and someone cleans your room for you, then this is your game. The storyline gets 5 stars from me, though. Fix the resource movement and I'll gladly come back, change my review back to "recommended" and finish the game. 2/24/2023 The game is still buggy, but it's coming along and I'm enjoying it while working around the bugs. I'd recommend you buy it in about a month, after the next patch or so. I'm finally having fun with the game. 2/5/2022 Looks like the first of the much needed patches are slated to release about three months after initial launch (probably early March 2023). I've uninstalled the game and plan to check back this summer. The forums are almost dead and it appears as though the game has lost most of the initial audience. I'd look for this during the Steam Summer Sale if you find you're still interested. It's a good one to wishlist. Has incredible potential after bugs fixed and balance issues addressed. The bug reporting thread is almost 80 pages at time of review. Last game update was Dec of 2022. Might take a few months to a year or so to address the issues reported - small dev team. _childDocuments_.review: I seldom review games and I have played many city builders. After completing this title on standard difficulty I am overall mixed on it but leaning to negative.Pros: The music is excellent and the game has an interesting premise. It is overall similar to Frostpunk though there is plenty to set this title apart. Cons:The game has a LOT of fundamental issues. Filled with bugs. an un-intuitive sector logistics system which only adds annoyance to the player. A large amount of the challenge for me was having resources properly transfer between sectors. Key resources would often stockpile on the producing sector while the destination you set them to sits empty. This is a game where all can quickly spiral into failure from a breakdown in your planned logistics.  The story, though starting out compelling, is presented in a fragmented log-style format from points of interest and is not particularly deep. Without spoilers: the ending also severely disappointing both in content and presentation (brief slideshow of painted images with some generic narration)Overall: There is some enjoyment to be had but the design feels overall frustrating. You will reload your saves quite a bit due to game-breaking bugs. The story though initially promising is lack-lustre.

_childDocuments_.review: While IXION can probably benefit from some balancing, polish, and QoL, I disagree with negative reviews that claim these are major dealbreaking issues, especially the balance. IXION is definitely not a relaxing experience or an easy one, but that makes it immersive and intense.The game is constantly throwing difficult dilemmas at you: industrial accidents, sudden heavy expenses, surprise drops in happiness, multiple research possibilities that are mutually unaffordable, or influxes of refugees you need to figure out how to feed and house. If you don't deal with these problems quickly, your situation can certainly spiral out of control. But it's exactly those stakes that make the experience so rewarding. You're being constantly tested and you need to think ahead, keeping resources in reserve to handle the unexpected, and reacting ruthlessly when necessary. This all fits in perfectly with the dark scifi theme of barely keeping the candle of unhelpful humanity burning in a pitiless inhospitable void. When you succeed, even temporarily, you really earned it and it means something.Having been burned on many titles in the past that promised way more than they ever delivered (or intended to deliver), I'm quite happy with the way this game runs and how it's been put together. To top it all off the soundtrack is absolutely banging. This is an easy buy for anyone interested in the management genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another game with a very promising premise and lots of potential that misses the mark.I really wanted to like this game, but very poor game design choices and balancing makes it a hard pass, at least for the time being and until the developer, if the developer, patches things up. Yet, I fear that even with some balancing correction, the underlying issue cannot be resolved.First the good.Art direction, simplicity of UI and cohesive layout, not to mention the sound design and story are top notch. There is a minor annoyance of camera blur that does not seem to turn off even if you turn off motion blur, but it is a minor thing. It is also great at conveying information to you in regards to how things are going, be it your factories output production rate or events in the world. The sensation of having a proper pipeline from mining from space to your stockholds to your factories and people, is a rewarding feeling and the game's greatest accomplishment.Now the bad and oh boy this is going to be comprehensive. Balancing is terrible and that is after the developer fixed the accident balancing. This is unfortunately a game similar to mobile games, where poor game design choices artificially push you to scale things or change things to counter world events. I say this is artificial, because as they occur, nothing makes sense as to why they occur, it is very obvious that a developer sat and said "right, let's decrease the amount of this and increase the amount of that to push the player". This sense of constantly being pushed is worsened by timers, such as bad weather phenomenons and lack of a particular resource occurring.On top of the poor game design choices and bad balancing, you have yet another big issue. All ingame events are pre-fixed, meaning they will always appear the same with the same outcome depending of course on your choices with them.If you add the aforementioned issue with poor game design choices and balancing with pre-fixed events, you end up with a management game that is very linear, meaning that it has the illusion of being open-world with freedom and creativity to go your way, but in actuality, it is a linear dictated path that is so narrow, that you will probably not play it a second time, because the only difference in a second playthrough will be your anticipation of fixed events to come and minor efficiency in meeting them head-on. Nothing else will change.I was expecting the developer to be more open-minded and allow for the player to experiment and set things up how they want, but that is not the case with this game. It is a linear, survival game with artificial timers and pushes, rather than a open-world management game that welcomes creativity and adaption. As such, despite the promise and potential, I cannot recommend a mobile-like game design for a PC audience that has come to expect more.Review will change if the product changes.
