_childDocuments_.review: AN ACCIDENT HAS OCCURRED ON THE TIQQUN.While the game has a compelling story and amazing visuals, its gameplay is unintuitive and easy to break -- and after the gameplay is thus broken, the game just becomes an exercise in tediousness until you're through with the story.  Additionally, I wish more was available for somebody trying to follow the story and its many organizations and characters, such as a codex.More detail follows, mostly me griping about the gameplay, which I'll split into sections.CITY MANAGEMENTMost of the gameplay is city management, which I'm experienced with.  In IXION, the city management suffers badly from unintuitive surprise mechanics.- City layout, for instance, involves no strategy except for keeping your stockpiles close to the buildings that supply and demand from them.  Literally nothing else matters except for the fire station: you can put your housing anywhere, your stability buildings anywhere, your batteries anywhere, your mess halls almost anywhere.  Being mindful of the shapes of buildings is important, but planning for that is an annoyance since you are never told the dimensions of a new building until you research it (so have fun trying to place down that exo-fighting dome).- The accident mechanics are a massive existential threat until you understand that each sector needs two infirmaries (hint: if you're stretched for personnel and/or power you can shut one down until the other suffers an accident) and enough spare workers to step in if 90% of the workers in the sector's biggest building are suddenly injured and unable to work for a week.  Then, the accident mechanics are trivial.  It's that simple.  You have to baby sectors a bit to make sure the working conditions are always "optimal" because as soon as they creep into "Extra Hours" you're going to be dealing with explosions and fires and dead workers all day every day.- Cryopods are like loot boxes, 90% of the time you regret opening them.  The in-game tutorials have a vague line about the cryo center opening worker and non-worker (aka useless) cryopods according to the ratio of people in the sector or something, but I seriously wish I could just mouse over my cryopod stocks and see how many were workers and how many were waste machines, since the cryo center workers seem to know.- City management simply stops being a challenge halfway into Chapter 2, and it's easy to grasp why.  Look at every single guide on the community hub and you'll see the same strategy repeated over and over: Rush Science.  Frostpunk had an issue where the sole bottleneck you had to worry about was how quickly you could research new techs, and once you had that bottleneck under control the game was a cinch.  IXION is very similar: once you've upgraded your tech lab and science ships, you no longer have to seriously worry yourself over which techs to prioritize because you can just research everything.  Once you get upgraded housing you can stop worrying about homelessness and (mostly) stability; once you get the DLS Center you can stop worrying about stability entirely.  Once you get upgraded input efficiency for your steel mills, you can stop worrying about hull repairs (hint: because of the steel mill's tiny input stockpile, input efficiency is crucial to keeping it running nonstop).  Once you get crop farms, you can almost stop worrying about food until you get the mess hall upgrades (then food is never a problem again).  Once you get waste processing set up, you never have to worry about any of your resources ever again except how much space they're taking up on your ship.  Rush Science and your economy snowballs so hard, so fast, that by Chapter 3 the whole thing is kind of boring.- Sector specialization bonuses are extremely important (a few of them anyway, industry specialization is useless) for keeping your economy running on all cylinders, but you won't know this until you actually know what the bonuses are, and you won't know that either until you either fulfill their thresholds or check the Steam Community Hub.  Please list the sector specialization bonuses in game, devs.- Please stop with the "surprise, that's a -1 to stability forever" landmine events.  The DLS is supposed to be a cutting-edge system for telling me everything that my crew is thinking; an early warning would be nice.  Granted, once everybody's in a domotic quarter (or at least "mostly" according to how the stability bonus works; bring on the cell housing) I don't have to care anyway.SPACE EXPLORATIONWhenever you're not in F1 mode watching your crew roam in circles at the hanging edges of roads, you're in F3 mode poring over the star system map.  Surprise mechanics are a bit more understandable here since space is a terrible environment, but there are still a number of issues that could use addressing.- Chapter 2 introduces the player to something called Space Weather, large hazard blobs on the maps you visit.  Chapter 2 has the most egregious instance of this, giving the player two static hazard blobs: one that almost instantly kills any probe and ship that blunders through it, and one that's just colder than the rest of space (somehow) and causes absolutely no issues to anything except the Tiqqun itself when navigating in it.  The only hint you get that the two hazards are so different from each other is that when you are ordering ships or probes on the star map, the former hazard shows a red dotted line for the ships' navigation indicators and the latter hazard shows no such warnings.  This can mislead the player into thinking that half the sector is a no-go zone.  Later chapters have different types of space weather, whose effects are similarly uncommunicated; Chapter 4 in particular has a hazard blob that's completely harmless to ships and probes but sending the Tiqqun through it is a russian roulette situation.  The game could benefit a lot from some indicator/text blob, somewhere, at all, hinting at each hazard blob's effects.- The incredible dumbness of the mining, cargo, and science ships means they have to be babied fairly frequently, in order to make sure they don't sail right through some death blob or something more spoiler-y.  It would be nice if the devs at least took a page out of Dwarf Fortress's book and had resource patches automatically set themselves to "avoid" if they suddenly found themselves in "you will die instantly if you go here" territory.- The nature of expeditions encourages hardcore savescumming.  That is all.STORYThe story is why I kept playing this game after city management became a matter of "where am I going to put all these extra resources that are piling up."  It's a great story, I'll give it that, and I only have a few quibbles.- The game throws a lot of names, and organizations, and concepts, and projects at the player.  Like, a lot.  There's a huge amount to keep track of, and frustratingly, a great proportion of the lore is seen only in expedition flavor text that cannot be re-accessed after the expedition ends.  I like the story a lot, and would deeply appreciate an in-game codex or something instead of having to resort to whatever wikia has sprung up for this game.  Being able to piece together what the hell happened with the BMS and the Piranesi and so forth right in game would be amazing.- The most crucial events in the story seem to depend on having enough resources hoarded up ahead of time.  This is not an issue if you're a compulsive polymer hoarder (and if you looked at the tech tree for more than the thirty seconds necessary to understand that in order to win this game you need to Rush Science), but I can imagine it being a sticking point if you don't like to build stockpiles everywhere and/or you don't like having to reload to a previous save and wait to build up resources before you step on an event tripwire.- The ending sequence and cinematic just felt empty and lifeless, after the amazing prologue.

_childDocuments_.review: So after a fair chunk of play I think this game is great.Less of a city building and more a management resource game it's exactly what I've been looking for while waiting for FP2.The game is not overly difficult but there have been times where I've been close to imploding and have to act fast to save my race from annihilation.I like to play on normal speed on these types of games and it seems to pay off in Ixion as there can be a few moving parts you need to keep an eye on.I've read a few reviews saying that the game can get boring. I haven't found this is as I really enjoy the downtime and just lose the hours navigating from screen to screen exploring, gathering resources and generally just browsing over my people. This to me "IS" fun.So far the story is nice and you I get the feeling that wrong decisions can severely damage your progress. I really enjoy that the game is story driven.All in all I love the expansive feeling you get when looking out across a solar system, it's a really unique vibe.The resource/energy management is really great which is a great twist on just dig/gather/consume.For £26 this game is worth the money if you enjoy exploring, an evolving story and resource management.Been a while since I found a game that literally swallows up the hours.Big fan.

_childDocuments_.review: I have had this on my wish list for awhile but the mixed reviews kept me from getting it at full price.  I waited for a really good discount and am glad I did since I agree with other reviewers in that this game is not worth the full price compared to what is offered in other games.   That being said the 40-50% off gave me the impetus to buy it.  As for the game, it is an interesting type of city builder with a somewhat interesting plot behind it.   Cut scenes leave much to be desired but they get the point across.  It can get very tedious at times and required more micro managing than I thought was necessary which detracted from the play.  It would have been nice to have some sort of agent manage a sector and assign it a specialty.  So it goes.  What drives this game was the story line of trying to save the remnants of humanity that are on your ship.  I wanted to see how it panned out.  The story itself left a lot of loose ends and unanswered questions.   Many times I was thinking to myself "okay so why" in terms of the story.  It needed a lot more polish.So why do I give it a thumbs up?  I like space stations and sci-fi and it was entertaining.  It is worth playing ONLY if you can get a decent sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend you play this game, however there are two components that really killed my enjoyment for this game the longer I played it. Primarily, the entire material transportation system aboard the ship is awful, with things taking forever to go where you want them. The only way to meaningfully increase this is locked away until right at the end of the game, at which point its made redundant.The second is the difficulty. It took me 25 hours to beat chapter 1 to 2, but only 8 hours to beat chapter 3, 4 and 5. The later chapters are made trivial with the sheer quantity of resources the game gives you in chapter 3, that it completely ruined all the tension that was masterfully built up in chapter 1 and 2. The developers have said they are adding difficulty modifiers in an update in the future, and the later chapters did feel more story focused which could be a reason to lower the difficulty, but as of now the difficulty plummets too harshly and it really didnt sit well with me in what is otherwise a very enjoyable but tense experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a really excellent choice if you're looking for a challenging survival city-building game with a fantastic story and love to listen to game-soundtracks.  Pros:  - Story- Soundtrack- Visuals / Gameworld- Interesting point-of-interests to uncover in space- Good design of factories and resource management- Mining / transporting resources is well integrated in the gameflowPro/Con:- The longer you stay in a system, the harder it gets to survive Cons: - Steep learning curve, so tutorials (text/ images) could be better- Hull integrity (always decreasing HP of the space station) has to many dependencies with high penalty points- The building grid is to cluttered, which results in bad building decisions after opening a new sector of the space station You need to understand, that this game is slow to forgive, it is better to load a save than to try to fix gross errors that you have caused yourself by inattention. And that's not bad at all, it's a singleplayer with an exciting story and not a grinding MMO. You play it for yourself to get better every time you make mistakes. I think many of those who gave a negative rating are too vain to admit that they made those mistakes and it is not the game that is too unfair. Sure, decisions and story-parts are cut to force an either/or situation, but the game isn't meant to be a child's playground. Finally, kudos to the soundtrack producer. The soundtrack is one of the greatest things in this game. It brings exactly the mood you expect in such an environment and the motivation to move forward and discover new things. Very well done!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is okie; but having to endlessly manage supplies one by one is tedious. There is no reason the supply page shouldn't have an auto balance setting that distributes materials accordingly. Also, perhaps an intuitive depot would be nice. Instead of needing to hand place and designate every single stockpile. Ixion suffers from the same problem Frostpunk does. Reaching a distorted balance of workers and jobs, as well as conditions can ruin the game fairly quick. The hull and constantly needing alloy is idiotic, especially when the steel mill doesn't produce enough to meet demand. The random starting bundles are just band aid fixes that don't solve anything. I hate how you need to restart from the very beginning every time you F up. The A.I. does jack all, and the research tree sucks. _childDocuments_.review: So.I must say I like the game. The balancing is totaly fine. I personally think its a bit too easy on giving you resources but oh well...  The resource transfer system is well done. It only gets easier the more sectors you open up. With the 3rd sector its kinda routine already. Lets talk about storage space. Saving up resources gets exponentialy easier after you unlock the medium Storage area...Ended up finishing with 2400+ Metal and 1700+ Fe still stored.Was kinda disapointed with the minimal use of polymers. was kinda close too a waste after finishing the solar panels.The punishments and malluses should be harder in my opinion. Because atm everything goes away with a bit of party and a lot of propaganda. The Dog helped too :D.The only timeconstraint you have in the missions is the amount of Iron you can mine in a give System. The Research has kinda annoyed me personally. I realized only on chapter 4 that i can cue it up. But only having 1 project in the cue is kinda nonsensical. I constantly forgot to use it because i was focusing on the macro and micro management. By the End i had reached 999 Research points and everything after that went... somewhere... maybe make that a 4 digit counter? Cuz I still had them when i researched something I didnt drop under 999 but ye... Food gets a bit too easy after you get the farms...Yes I realized that i had a water problem somewhere in chapter 4. Seems like 1 icemelter aint enough for 2 fully upgraded waterfarms... The waste-to-Water Converter helped there. But feeding 5k+ Crew with only those 2 farms was kinda too easy.Of course i needed every upgrade for the "foodcourt" as I call it but still. Too easy.Population issues... Kinda dunno what to say. Maybe Implement some kinda additional line of how many possible workers there are in the sector and how many there are currently. Or show somewhere how many sick workers there are in a sector. They kinda get hurt all the time you know. Kinda was wasting a lot of time trying to micromanage the worker transfers until i realized that the numbers are flactuating because they are only temporary in the hospital. The mallus for staying too long should be more than a one time thing. By Rotation 365 people should realize based on soundclues that 1 Rotation = 1 day. Kinda logical that people will get kinda upset about staying too long without anything happening. I mean i finished the game with 2500+ Rotations. If you rly want to add a feeling of pressure you should add a -1 every year. then you can go and say that was kinda close at the end. I ended the game with a +6 in Trust on most of my sectors and it could have been more if i wanted to. So you should maybe change it around and give a +1 (temporary) every time you start a new chapter. And every year you waste you get -1 (permanent).The game offers decent amount of story and multiple endings. Sadly the initial sequence is the only visualy stunning one in the game. Some of the discoverys are well done and interesting and others are kinda too non-saying for the amount of reading you do. Seeing as you can actually level your ships there should be a reward in form of more interesting discoverys depending on the level of your science ship. Or possibly a more chance based punishment if you pick the wrong option. Would be a boost for the replay-ability of the game IMO. In the future I will hope for more Frostpunk-like DLCs. It would be nice to view the Story from the perspective of the other factions. All around still a totaly solid game. Not a 10/10 must have. But a solid 8/10 worth the Money.Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: (please keep in mind this is my first time playing a game like this)I am stuck between two opinions. The game wants you to only prioritize certain things to the point where it almost feels like railroading. But at the same time, finding the correct most optimal path is the most rewarding feeling from the game. I am also not sure how to feel about "the more you expand, the tougher it gets" deal. The station doesn't really manage itself at all. Every step must be planned with lots of foresight. You need to make sure the sectors of the ship are self sufficient before moving to the next step, and not letting your workers overdo tasks. You constantly have to tweak and move resources. Which some might find annoying, but is satisfying when route your resources efficiently to allow your sectors to work autonomously.I only reached 3 sectors in the game, and juggling those three was already really tough. My only complaint is having failing systems happen quite often even with optimal work hours, I can't imagine multiplying this rate by 6. Also the station seems small, I am unsure why workers have to live in the sector they work. Maybe allowing an upgrade for all populations to move freely would be really good. Another complaint is that certain buildings won't work unless you make rules for it, which the game doesn't explain. So I just wasted a ton of resources and research... This is just a personal one though.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.It's by far not perfect, it needs some rebalancing, and it has some of the standard, annoying, "difficult just for the sake of being difficult" civilization-management mechanics that seem to plague this genre, but I love it.This is going to be a very long-winded review, so there will be a tl;dr at the end.===========================================================What I love:- The soundtrack. I haven't enjoyed a soundtrack this much since Surviving Mars, and Surviving Mars is unironically one of my top ten albums on Spotify.- The theming. This game does a fantastic job of selling the exploration of space post-apocalypse. The cutscene for warping to a new area is the same every time, but I never skip it because its just so damn cool.- The cheesy Corsair peripheral effects. Is it silly? Yeah. But do I love it? Yeah. I get just a little giddy every time I start the game and the "Loading" theme plays out on my keyboard and mouse.- The push for sector specializations. I'm also going to mark this as a con (and talk more about it later), but Im an organization freak. By default I end up making "specialized sectors" in my head in any civilization management game. Being rewarded for doing so is a +1 to me.- No penalties for deconstructing. I feel like this is something that gets overlooked a lot, but getting 100% of your resources back when you deconstruct something is essential to me in any building or settlement-management game. As I get new technology and learn the game, I want to optimize my layout, and I don't want to be punished for doing so.===========================================================What I'm "mid" about:- Transferring resources between sectors. Once you get further in the game and unlock the later tech, this becomes less of an issue, but its still annoying. It's reminiscent of Surviving Mars in its "set stockpile to have x desired amount" mechanic, which is fine, but it seems to punish specialized sectors; which is odd because I just said the game rewards specialized sectors.- The stability system. Population morale is a staple of this genre, and of course this game has it too. The only problem is that in this game it's either really punishing or completely a non-issue. There is no in between. Stay too long in a system? Permanent -1 to morale; oh but you can also enable "extreme propaganda" to get a +1 back with no penalty. Adopt the weird alien dog? Also a permanent +1. Ahhh, but you have too many people on your ship still in cryostasis because you don't want to overload your infrastructure.. temporary penalty scaling with the people still frozen. - The hull health system. Same thing as the stability system. Another mechanic that only exists to make things harder as you get further in the game for no other reason except to balance out your technology upgrades. I understand why it has to exist, but I don't feel happy about it.- Game pace. Like I mentioned in the stability system section, the game punishes you for staying too long in a system, but in reality the penalty is a lie. You will not outpace the penalty, and if you do, you will fail. A lot of people are comparing this game to Frostpunk, and I see why. It feels like Frostpunk, but it's not. You're not actually racing against a clock. The game will tell you that you screwed up by staying in a system too long, but you only get one of these penalties per system. You can take your time as much as you like as long as you're building sustainable infrastructure. The only real timer is how many resource nodes are left in the area, and frankly I've only had to rush to a new system because of that once, and that's because I was doing a lot of new construction. I like this because I can take my time and do what I want, but I also never really feel like I'm in danger, which can be kinda boring.===========================================================What I hate:- The system weather events. There is no upgrading through these. The game gives you technology options to "give your ships better survivability" but its a lie. Your ships will die, and there's nothing you can do about it other than move your entire Ark so that the automatic pathing will avoid the storms. They're also not consistently dynamic. In one system the storms will never move, and in the next they will move every time you resolve a science ship event. Once again: either very punishing or a complete non-issue- The research system and story progression. This is going to be a two-parter. You can soft-lock your game pretty early on if you're not careful. In the early game, research points come almost exclusively from investigating points of interest. There are a set amount of these points per system warp. As you progress through the story, the game will give you new technology nodes that are required to progress, and give no other benefits. Meaning if you spent all your research points on improvements, you can end up in a situation where you either have to spend almost half a year in-game in order to progress.. or load an earlier save. Later on this isn't so much of an issue because you get technology upgrades that give you more technology points passively, but it can be brutal earlier on.- The research system and itself. Some technology upgrades are locked behind arbitrary requirements. Want faster recovery rate in your hospital? You're going to need to research specific tech upgrades on two other buildings. This sort of thing happens again with resource transfer tech, as well as a few other key tech upgrades. It doesn't feel thematic, it feels like artificial time-gating, especially since points of interest are fixed per system.- Sector specializations (the con side). You can't see what sector specializations do until you reach a specific tech tree. You also can't see your progress towards earning new bonuses until you hit another tech tree upgrade. This feels extremely arbitrary, and leads to sector specializations feeling pointless until much later in the game. The industry specialization feels underpowered, and the population specialization feels very hard to meet for an "okay" bonus. Space and agriculture feel fine though.- Science ship encounters. These don't feel rewarding, they push people towards save-scumming, and many of them feel illogical. Land on a gaseous planet with an anomaly? You can either use explosives to reach the anomaly faster, or spend more time and drill towards it. You'd think drilling would be the safe, correct answer, right? Wrong. Now your whole science team is dead. Reload your save, use explosives, and oh look at that, it turned out magically beneficial! Half the time these events reward reading the event text, and the other half of the time they seem.. I'm using this word a lot.. arbitrary. I save scummed the hell out of this game because of these encounters, and no, I don't feel guilty about it.===========================================================tl;dr: I've written a whole essay on this game, but at the end of the day I love it. I think it's fairly priced. It needs some work, but it's a lovable experience. It's not as brutal as Frostpunk but not as casual as Surviving Mars, and has the charm of both. If you're on the fence about it, find it for $20-25 and you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I've read some of the reviews of this game though I'd add my own voice. The game is a survival resource management game, in space - think Frost Punk, but in a move-able space city. It is very, very difficult and when you start playing some of the problems you'll come across will appear to come out of nowhere.  I can appreciate the reviews that say that the game "hates you" - it definitely feels like that at the start.  The system actively punishes you if you make a mistake - One time, i accidentally overworked a sector and that cascaded into a full blown riot over food shortages. You really need to be able to balance population, resource collection, public opinion, material refining, power, water, hull repair and science to be in with a chance and it can be difficult to keep track of everything at once. As you gain time with in game on board the Tiqqun, you start to understand the nuances of the game structure and some of the problems start to vanish. You then realise that the game is only as hard as you make it for yourself. Some key things I learned over my 90+ hours playing were: 1. Don't ever have more jobs than workers, and turn buildings off if you have too. You want to have no accidents! 2. Always be gatherin' resources. 3. Don't be scared to move the Tiqqun. I'd say this game is for experienced resource management game players. Players who are new to genre will may have some problems with managing all of the systems. I'd definitely recommend this game, but be aware its not an easy trip through space.
_childDocuments_.name: IXION

_childDocuments_.review: Really an interesting game, with a good story, and great mechanics. Ixion is very much a management game in a scifi post-apocalyptic setting. Having finished the game several times over the biggest thing is that as you progress optimization is key. Moving from one sector to a second may seem like a lot, but once you get around to finishing the station and zeroing in on specializations is really where Ixion comes into itself.Through all of the chapters and into the finale I never felt like I was done with building my station. "This building could be more effective here" and "Do I really need that in this sector?" became very common thoughts as the Tiqqun meandered its way through the galaxy on its journey. There was always something that could be made more effective and more efficient, so if you love optimization this is totally something to check out.Finally the music and the art really bring things home. If it were just for the gameplay I would already consider this game, but the visuals are stunning and the music is the perfect blend of atmospheric and beautiful.The game is hard. It's not the most forgiving. Choices that you make can have real impacts on how difficult you find things. These aren't negatives in my mind at all, if choices were trivial then they wouldn't matter. There may be a couple of things that you might get tired of hearing, like "An accident has occured" but all in all I would highly recommend picking up Ixion, and it definitely deserves to be rated much higher than it shows.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to the Tiqqun, humanity's latest misguided attempt to colonise the stars. What could go wrong?You are the Administrator, tasked with running this behemoth as it travels through the harshest, most unforgiving environment imaginable: space. You'll suffer a constant stream of problems, manage the fears and expectations of a people who only want solid ground beneath their feet, and hold the hull together with hopes, dreams, and a (relatively) few alloys. This isn't a voyage for the faint of heart. You're not building a shining civilisation of the stars, you're building a bubble with whatever you can find. There will be no help. No rescue.This isn't going to be a casual experience. You're not going to be able to bruteforce you way through. Balance is the key here. Without a keen eye for micromanagement you may struggle, and that's ok. Keep trying and the puzzle will reveal itself in time; and what a beautiful, atmospheric, and challenging puzzle it is.

_childDocuments_.review: TL/DR: Chaotic mess with undescribed building functions and chained "pick one of two bad options"-events. Long version:My absolute favorite: a typical tech needs 30-45 "science". The science lab produces 1 science each 30 "cycles". to get an idea how long a cycle is: i played 4h real time end ended up around cycle #210. So basically this factilities' "No I am not just a button-carrier for the research screen, I produce the 'science' too" is a totally useless feature.So, given the fact that you get new tech mostly because of the research expeditions you send your science ships on - which means that you have to choose wisely, which tech to unlock, you are given the task to "rescue" 500 additional colonists, which need food, housing, stability, work and so on. Just to get an idea how ridiculous it is: you start with buildings you can build, which provide amenities for 15 people each, and food producers which produce food worth for 50 people in a given time.speaking of work: my second favorite is the "cryogenic facility", where people are created out of rescue pods you need to look for by using probes on the map. This building has a selection screen on the bottom, which reads: rows: Sector 1, sector 2, etc...; columns: "Working pop", "non-working pop". All entries are "black square".Since i desperatly needed additional workers in both sectors 1 and 2. (Why? check below) I highlighted the square "sector 1/working pop" which turned white. After waiting until the buildings' bar filled, i checked the population: Non-working pop +1. "Ok", I thought, "maybe i need to highlight the settings other way around..." - flipped "sector 1/working" back to "black square" and "sector 1/non-working" to "white square" (sorry, if it reads stupid, but the whole settings menu of this building is as stupid as you can read here...). *Ding* another non-working pop.Speaking of working and non-working population: Each facility you build requires a certain amount of workers for operation. In the beginning you quicky run into the situation that you need a lot more working people than you have. The game simulates that in a way that it simply increases the workload of your population beyond 100% which severly rises the probability for accidents to happen. What does that mean? In an accident you get your building damaged, so that it does not work for a while (until you clicked on "repair" and waited for your overworked construction robot to fix that bugger) and a random number of people either need to be hospitalized or just plainly die. Oh you don't have a hospital yet? Wave good-bye to these people they will die at the end of the next "cycle". Oh you have a hospital? very nice.... until the accident happens exactly there - or at the food producers or in the food distribution... etc.Thus you get into a nice, dirty spiral of accidents which disables a raising number of your people.But hey! You can prevent that by sending people from your overcroded sector (the one with the cryo facility) to the one which needs additional workers? Yeeeeeeees. But don't think that only by looking at the people overview ("working pop 58, jobs 90") and doing simple math ("send 32 workers to sector 2") you will fix your problem here. Nooooo ... this game is too complex (stupid?) for that, you will end up with something like 72/90 and still buildings exploding due to accidents.Did I mention that your station permanently loses hitpoints and you need to invest a significant amount of your resources into just to keep its hp-bar up? Would not be a problem, but somebody had an accident in the airlock (threw himself out of despair?) So no repairs for you tonight.Did i mention that your stations inhabitants seem to be some morons? "Oh, we accidentally messed up the solar system rendering earth uninhabitable and destroyed humanity. But wait, now we have jumped lightyears away from that mess... WE WILL NEVER BE ABLE TO COME BACK! LETS RIOT OVER THAT!"

_childDocuments_.review: Challenge update: Finally! They patched their gamebreaking bugs and even added custom challenge setup, that's +10. Now I can fully recommend this atmospheric and astonishing game. Patch - 1.0.2.2 Update: I like the enthusiasm of the devs, not gonna lie. Will see what happens next year. Happy festivus for you devs! After reaching the end, honestly I thought it would be a little more "intense". After all those crazy debuffs in every sector, you don't get that feel of satisfaction. Was it worth to even try that hard to maintain and counterfit all those negative permament stats you gain with every level? No, not for me at least. I had a feeling that the end is too empty, not rewarding at all, kinda short on story too. Oh, and want a cherry at the top? Your hull breaks apart from the prologe to the very end. Every.damn.second. More and more with EVERY.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.NEW.SECTOR. (Devs, probably: "Git Gud")Anyway, this game could be recommended but it's too grindy, a lot. _childDocuments_.review: I can’t recommend this one in its current state. Others have commented on the precise issue: gameplay balance. There are mechanics that are impossible to mitigate which do not reinforce the desire to continue playing, which is unfortunate given the scope of work, story, atmosphere, music, etc which are all well done and — unlike other 2022-era games — polished. Management sims can be punishing, and that’s what can make them fun. But fulfillment comes from solving problems that persist throughout the game — solving the problems that are punishing. _childDocuments_.review: I would definitely recommend this game, even though it has lots of room to improve. Here's why.First, the Pros:- The visuals are STUNNING, from the inside of the space station, the buildings and the little people running around, to the outer hull view that let's you see what you are currently orbiting, to the system view, to the cinematics. Seriously, they are spectacular.- The music is incredible, especially the one when you do a Vohle jump. I want to buy the soundtrack.- The story is interesting and immersive. I was quickly very engaged and wanted to find out what would happen next, not just in terms of events in system but also in the next systems.- The voice acting is amazing, and I really enjoyed the writing as well.- The gameplay is very similar to Frostpunk in that you have to manage a number of different resources to keep your doomsday colony from perishing, with one resource in particular more important than the rest (alloys to repair your hull, similar to coal in Frostpunk), all the while maintaining the trust of the population.- The in-game events are cool, although their outcomes tend to be fairly similar, aka you either get some science or you lose some scientists/science ships.Next, the Cons:- There is a LOT of micro-management of resources. I'm constantly having to go between sectors to transfer X resources to make room in other sectors, or changing the resources being stored in sectors based on what resources the cargo ships are bringing in to those specific sectors at that time. It's CONSTANT. This was my biggest frustration, really took a lot of time away from me working on more interesting things in my "colony" like redesigning my sectors to be more space efficient or exploring space.- I bought the game on launch day, and played for a few hours before initially giving up in frustration. It was gruelingly difficult, with accidents caused by overworked workers causing a vicious cycle that was impossible to recover from. I lost maybe 3 times in the first 6 hours due to getting to 0% trust from overwork sectors and deaths. It got MUCH better once they patched the frequency of accidents, and I haven't had any issues since.- Was a bit frustrated by the things (people, resources) not easily moving between sectors. It's entirely a manual process, which on one hand gives you more control, but on the other it's needless control. I'd rather be able to build the station as I see fit, with other types of limitations.- It would be nice to be able to select multiple resources to mark them as "To avoid" rather than having to manually click on each resource then on the checkbox.In summary:If you like colony builders or Frostpunk, then you will love Ixion. While there is a learning curve initially, patches have since really smoothed that out to make the experience less punishing. Not to mention this game came out less than a week ago! I can't wait to see what kind of updates and DLCs they have in store.I would definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves a lot better than the (currently) mixed reviews it's getting. It seems that a lot of people are struggling with the resource management and the downward spirals that can happen if you fall behind. This aspect of the game can be extremely punishing, especially in the early chapters. However, if you take the time to actually master these systems and consider your first attempt(s) to be a training session, then you'll find that the balancing is heavily in the player's favor.For reference, this is what I had to do to get through the game:1. Fail chapter 1 due to downward spiral of resources2. Restart and make it through chapter 13. Attempt chapter 2 twice, fail both times due to resource and stability (crew happiness) issues4. Restart the entire game, breeze through chapters 1 and 2 with my better understanding of the game's systems, have excess resources and stability for basically the entire duration of the gameOnce you get through the first few chapters, you can really outscale the need for resources and stability so that you don't have to worry about that anymore. The game doesn't get boring at this point though, since the later chapters have unrelated challenges to keep things fresh. If you can persevere through the initial difficulties you have with this game, you'll get to enjoy its tense atmosphere and terrifying mysteries. I do have a few complaints about the story and writing, but the atmosphere (especially in the science expeditions where your decisions can lead to horrific consequences) makes up for this in my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: It gets off on a great start, but very soon, it's set up to strain your resources to a near-brakikng point, even at the easiest mode. The game itself forces you to move very fast and eventually become un-prepared, since the inhabitants are a bunch of entitled morons who "don't like hanging around" to gather resources that are vital for the survival of the species. They think they're in LA and that somebody snatched their lunchables. In real extinction-survival conditions, the military would have mass executions.Also, beware. Once you start advancing in your research (which is a maze with the sub-research chaos), all of a sudden, your sectors will go on fire. I opened up a small storage, and the moment the first package arrived, there was an accident and the whole building went aflame.If we ignore the population's apocalyptic idiocy and emotional awareness of an amoeba (=hyper entitlement), the game is really great when it comes to its atmosphere, environment, graphics and music. Those are the areas it excels. Beyond that, the developers really need to work on the psychology parameters of the population. Reason and endurance is the one thing that is lacking from the people in the humanity's last ark.Spoiler alert:Once you perform your 2nd jump, you have a mission to awaken 2,000 people from their cryo status. The process is excruciatingly slow. Meanwhile, the rest of the people will get angry for staying in a system too long (they like traveling, like morons) and they'll burn half the station via accidents. At that point, the game demands the player to effectively manage a world war before jumping to a system that is probably an extinction level event that awaits.My recommendation is the following:Play it a little bit if you enjoy these types of games. The quests and events in outer space are really great. What happens inside a station however, it's like a highschool where all students had truckloads of injected hormones!

_childDocuments_.review: Soooo...  there are some things I like about this game.  But you're interested in what I don't like.TL;DR: as it is right now, I'd call this a $10 - $15 game.  Some bug fixes, a tutorial on how to use the advanced view resource transfer (very important for food distribution), and more content (especially involving game lore) would easily make this game worth $35.1. Camera angles.  a. The 'city view' defaults you to a specific angle that is quite useful.  Fortunately for the player, you are forced back into that angle every time you re-enter city view.  It's fortunate because it's effectively impossible to manually control the angle back to it's default.b. The solar system view defaults you back to close zoom.  Which is annoying, as I keep having to zoom back out.c. The outer hull ship view is pointless.  But since they included it, make sure to play with it a bit as it's decently pretty.  But definitely not worth paying for.2. Storyline.a. Too short.  There are only 5 solar systems you visit.  I'd call this $15 dollars max worth of gameplay.b. Choices don't matter.  Yes, a few of your choices actually do matter, but most of them don't do anything except give different reward values and/or blow up your scout-scientists.  Which is truly sad.  Some of the ♥♥♥♥ your scientists will dig up are shocking and disturbing!  I was expecting this game to lean into the choices.  But instead, most of what you do appears to be ignored.c. There is lore in the game that adds to the craziness your scientists will discover.  But finding the lore doesn't do anything or unlock anything.  Very disappointing.3. Gameplaya. Buildings cannot be grouped.  If I'm trying to budget my power grid and want to turn off my carbon factories, I have to turn off each factory and turn off each warehouse.  This is typically 4 buildings.  And that's not too annoying...the first time.  But when I'm doing it repeatedly, and doing for my processor factories, and my steel factories, and my cryo facilities... it becomes very tedious.b. warehouses are idiots.  You will repeatedly find that your warehouses will stop working because of a delivery between sectors.  This is a bug, as the game explicitly states that delivery between sectors uses a different truck than delivery within the same sector.  Next, add on that the warehouses will often deliver a single item between sectors simply because it wouldn't wait .1 seconds for the next truck to add to the load. c. transports are idiots.  If you watch, you will see your transports go after the same ore deposit.  If there's enough ore, it's fine when multiple transports go after it.  But you will often see multiple transports go after an ore deposit that is nearly empty.  So if 5 transports go after a deposit that will run out with the first ship, the next four transports KEEP FLYING TO THE EMPTY SPOT.  AND THEN THEY GO BACK TO YOUR SHIP EMPTY!!!!   ARGH!d. mining ships are idiots.  There's a weird bug in the game where you can have two or more mining ships go after a deposit, and the mining ships keep trying to position themselves on top of each other.  So the adjust themselves, and wind up on top of each other again...and again...and again...oh, and they're not mining, so this is a massive waste of time.e. paradigm shift.  This is a space ship game.  And you rescue people from other space ships.  And you find that these people are mostly useless?!?  Why are the crews from other space ships mostly worthless?  This makes no sense.  As a game mechanic, this was the biggest trick that forced me to restart my game.  Once I wrapped my head around the understanding that I didn't need to have redundant sectors, and instead had to set my ship up to handle useless refugees, I was able to beat the game fairly easily on normal difficulty.f. AI helper not helping.  What's the point of having an AI assistant if it won't tell me that my missile countermeasures are built in the probe launch facility?  Or that my docking bays that have no free slots to build ships are still able to build shuttles?  For the most part, the AI assistant is helpful.  But there are a few flaws.  Btw, "A probe has completed it's scan" is not useful!  Don't tell me that.  Tell me when a probe is ready to launch instead!4. Cutscenesa. I have two issues with the cutscene you get when you engage your FTL.  First, it's exactly the same every time.  It would have been nice to see the ship fly to different exit points.  Second, the video and the audio look mismatched.  If the audio were to start about half a second later, the deep notes would match with the ship drive animations.  And then extend a half second of video of ship flight to balance out my change at the beginning.b. There is a public address cutscene at the beginning of the game.  But Dolos CEO is annoying.  Which is sad, as I kinda wanted to watch the very end of that cutscene again.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR:  meets  on an atmospheric space adventure with difficulty level out of hand. If you are a fan of ANNO series, give it a shot and if not, stay away, you will suffer.I really struggled if I shall give this game thumbs up or not. It strongly depends on your relationship with ANNO games series. The core game mechanics, which are very much like in ANNO games and which we know and love, combined with some Frostpunk-like events. The twist in this game is unfortunately the ridiculous difficulty (not in a good way like in Souls games).Don’t get me wrong, I don’t mind difficult games (I finished Dark Souls after all). Problem is, that this game is punishing even when you have done everything right. It just swarms you with plenty of problems with no means to solve them. It is this kind of artificial difficulty which annoys me in games. Hey, if you want to make my playing even more hardcore, why don’t you break a few of my fingers? That would make things more difficult for sure.There is constant supply of problems from the very start. To demonstrate, let’s take work force as an example. You expand your crew by finding life pods and from them you can get either workers which run your ship, or freeloaders which do not do anything but consume resources. And there is no way to train them to become workers, no sir. They just sit there, sipping their afternoon tea and watching the poor workers die from overwork, while enjoying the ride…And this for me kills the potentially great game; the constant never-ending micromanaging. And I am not talking about the fine-tuning management which weirdos like me actually enjoy (that is after all what ANNO is about), no. It is the mind-numbing unnecessary hassle between sectors and bad storage management, energy production (which is simply too low). Now after finishing the game, I know how I should have played it and it would be manageable but now is too late. This is due to non-existing tutorial which could help me avoid all of the pit falls.I could go on and on about all the flaws, but at the end of the day, they got the basics right and this is why I gave it the thumbs up. All these problems could be easily fixed and this game could be turned into a gem because the core gameplay is really fun! On top of it, the story is interesting and the atmosphere is great, mainly thanks to very well-chosen music.

_childDocuments_.review: Preliminary review - I do think I'll come back to this eventually. Story is intriguing, composition is good. The thumbsdown is purely on this question: 3.5 hours in, when I decide that it's a bit too fussy in "default" difficulty, do I look forward to starting over? Not today, DOLOS, not today.20 hours in: Having played a lot of early city builders back in the day (Caesar 3?), I wonder if my dislike for his game - and perhaps the entire modern genre - here is the use of a single very long campaign with continuity, rather than a sequence of short scenarios. If something goes wrong, you're going to be living with that permanent penalty forever, and there are many, many surprise penalties in this game. Or maybe it's the capture of so many genres by hardcore players - on Easy ("journey") mode, consulting multiple guides, I'm still playing sufficiently "suboptimally" that I'm going slower than intended and getting the permanent penalties for time trials. Without spoilers it feels like this would be a fifty- or hundred-hour game because there'd be so many unavoidable errors and so much reloading.Well done, but not to my taste.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game and you should play it.  It does, in my opinion, fall in to that "false sense of choice" category of games, where they confused pace-setting with gatekeeping.  Practically speaking, there is no flexibility with respect to how you "build up".  With both the science quantities and the resources being effectively capped (aside from rushing food production and then letting the thing run for a million hours during the prologue, where it will hit a stack overflow and crash) the replayability is limited.  There's no "final chapter decision making" that's going to make me want to replay, and it gets to be a more than minor hassle to remodel sections to try a different build.  That said, the one play-through is a great story and a fantastic variation on the city builder genre.  Remember your old-school Boots of Re and you'll enjoy it immensely.

Get Frostpunk instead.Several annoying user interface issues which are huge time wasters and extremely annoying.  Also it is lacking key binds for several basic commands.  Event choices lack some handling, warnings and feedback.  Mostly they lack consistency with how they are handled and described.  Some events are funny as most are stolen from other stories, movies, tv etc.  However, this means that most are ridiculous, make no sense and have no real way to make good decisions.There is no way to gauge time for storms and anomalies that pop up due to the idea that your ship apparently lacks any sensors to keep an eye on them.  Upgrading them is also impossible.  Lack of explanation is common for games, but it creates multiple exasperating situations in this one.Many game like this give you timetables based on having things like working sensors or... eyes. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, I'm satisfied.  The game delivered on its premise in a lot of ways.  However, I do have some notes:The game runs into the same problem that early versions of Stellaris did with its event system.  There are a lot of explicitly wrong event paths.  With no RNG involved, the optimal play is to have the wiki open at all times.  This is not great for immersion reasons and doesn't offer meaningful choice so much as the opportunity to 'cheat' by reading ahead and getting the optimal path, or not cheat and potentially wreck or seriously disadvantage your playthrough.  This can be solved in the same way that Stellaris solved it - by providing the player with the general information of what that choice will entail, and allowing the user to make an informed choice, with expected consequences.I felt the ending was rushed.  I was really hoping to  I get that it is in literal terms more about the journey than the destination, but still.On the note of the story I think the factions involved could have been characterized more.  It was a little vague a lot of the time who the others you were interacting with were, and it could have been beneficial to have more characters to interact with from other factions as well.Could have used some more music tracks.  The music worked for the game but hearing the same track over and over got pretty old in the endgame.Anyway those issues aren't enough to have me not recommend the game overall, but just some things to consider.  If anything I can tell this was a passion project, and I certainly hope we see more from this universe in time and the game concept can be refined and built upon in additional scenarios.Also some gameplay tips, honestly once you know them the game isn't anywhere near as blistering as some seem to believe:-All your buildings are fully refundable, so feel free to reconfigure to optimize space.-Recycling is key, particularly for sustainable food production-Get DLS buildings up in your sectors as soon as you start experiencing stability issues as they give you a lot of tools to work with.  These let you enact policies in sectors.-There's no meaningful downside to increasing propaganda everywhere, and this can offset food rationing and recycling stability penalties-Take your time, though the game never truly throws anything at you that's unfair to the extent of needing to fill the tech tree to advance-Keep a watchful eye on your worker levels.  When expanding, don't overbuild and put yourself into bad working conditions.  Workers are a resource to be managed like everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: So.... you wanna be a space dude.Well keep waiting as Ixion requires some serious tuning work as if you even have 1 job more than you have workers you'll find EVERYTHING starts exploding, people start dying in accidents and your hull integrity tanks super hard.To succeed at Ixion in the current state you must make 0 mistakes and balance ALL the things on a super fine razors edge. Which I mean I find kinda fun and rewarding but at the same time it can be more infuriating than fun when you see all your work start exploding become Steve got sick and now accidents are endemic.I'd also strongly recommend to Bulwark to consider implementing different difficulty levels which change the availability of rare resources and the incidence rate for negative events (like accidents, explosions and permanent stability drops).Edit ------------------------- Spoilers BelowSo the ending is kinda crap to be frank, "save humanity" becomes "turn into green plant loving aliens". Not so much a humanity ♥♥♥♥ yeah as I was hoping for and more humanity be woke yo.Material and population management needs some work, population management more than resource management. It was ridiculous at points feeding people towards the end of the game as the mess halls only service so many folks so you end up with a large number of them.Chapter 1 = Tutorial landChapter 2 = End of EarthChapter 3 = Jump 1Chapter 4 = Jump 2 with our first challengerChapter 5 = Jump 3 with our first challenger and some woke plant bois.Replayability is more or less non-existent outside of trying to do a bit better on the knife edge micro-management. Sure you could play through the main story again, but it won't change anything. Feels pretty much railroaded from A to B with a high difficulty curve. 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game wasn't what I expected, but it was a lot of great fun. It mixes base building, resource management, and space exploration well. The story is okay with some rough edges, but it keeps it short enough with enough to keep the game going and get you back to base building. You get used to reworking your bases as you progress and expand. It feels like a small amount of space at first, but there is a bit of a shallow limit on resource processing making it more then plenty of space.I really enjoyed it and felt it was worth the money paid, but likely isn't something that I'll put much time in to play again. I think replay value for this is limited to a very small group of people who want to challenge themselves as the game doesn't really give you much reason to play again.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that I do not recommend the game in its . There are a lot of things that IXION excels at and with the right polish and re-balancing this game can easily change this review. I have seen a lot of different Reviews of the game that range from people complaining about the semi poor balancing when it comes to labor management, death spirals and even some logistical nightmares. After spending time with the game this has lead me to one conclusion:In the current state of the game it is a puzzle game. While that is not a bad thing within itself, going in with the mentality of a city builder is a fast way to fall into the many pitfalls with the current state of the game. Efficiency, Planning, adjusting, adapting, these are some of the many things that you constantly have to go through with the game, but in IXION, it becomes your soul focus. If you enjoy a challenge, then go ahead, this game is perfect for you. However if your enjoyment comes from story, building, and exploring, you may find that your not having as much fun as you would want; since most of your time will be spent by the game punishing you for not playing in a certain way. IXION is Linear in that regard which is why IXION is better off being called:

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, but only because it's bugless and well done.As a game its...  Well, there's a tendency after Dark Souls to make everything punishing and brutal, because apparently fun isn't a thing you're supposed to have in games.  This game plays like a failed mission, like the lead up to a mission that finds your frozen corpse floating next to a cryptic message written in someone else's blood.  Yes, the odds should be stacked against you, yes, space is harsh and uncompromising.  And I want the game where I have the tools to succeed against that.  With Ixion, its a matter of how long before your crew murders you - there's a timer, the longer you take to build your base, the pissier your crew gets.  And you don't really have the tools to placate them.-1 because doom.  And another -1 because doom.  And more doom that you had no control over.  Oh, and they're sad, because space is lonely -1.  And you can chose between appeasement, or fixing the hull.  And eventually - for me, it was just past 500 cycles - they decide to give into the despair and you die, they die, humanity dies.Pass.Now, as a game, it's very well done.  I haven't seen any bugs, the graphics are well done, the plot is interesting, if not a little depressing.  Everything is right about this game, it's exactly the sort of game I love to play.  And I hate it.I might - might - go back a third time and turn off all the difficulty just to see how the story turns out, but no further.Buy it if you like self-inflicted pain.  And base builders.

_childDocuments_.review: I binge played IXION for 40+ hours since release, came to pluck in my review and I see "Mixed" with a buncha of negative reviews from <10h dudes crying this game is too hard yet they couldn't even pass the most basic encounters in the game. Accidents they claim to be PUNISHING are very solvable: DO NOT OVERWORK YOUR HUMANS AND THEY WON'T DIE (OSHA approves of this). This game does not deserve the Mixed reviews. There are no difficulty levels as well, had to check if I was playing on "Easy".Great game, enjoyed the visuals, arts, story and the endless stream of microtasks you have to solve on spot fit my soul nicely. Absolutely loved the autobalancing resources feature, spent 15 minutes figuring out how this works and made a self-sustaining station without me having to do anything pretty much.PROS: 0) Looks like Frostpunk and general rules apply in IXION as well.1) T H E W H E E L S T A T I O N: If you are familiar with The Expanse series, you will enjoy your own Nauvoo lol and the views oh my god2) Intense gameplay of micromanaging everything until you make it work like a clock3) Moderately hard game4) It's nice to plan sectors and make them houses-only, food-only etc, resource balancing feature takes care of the rest.5) Immersive OSTBut there are some rough corners of course:1) Accidents. _childDocuments_.review: IXION is the bastard child of Frostpunk and the 4X genre. Which honestly sounds like a great deal for anyone familiar with Frostpunk or Endless Space etc. It is sadly at this time more frustration than fun.It tries to marry the familiar tight-rope act of balancing "Hope and Discontent"  with constant and increasing consumption. However, they missed one of the fundamental lessons of Frostpunk: "It's not arbitrary".This is probably one of the most fundamental faults of the entire game as of now. Everything is or seems arbitrary.Accidents/Fires/Explosions - Meant to partially simulate the "event" system of Frostpunk instead become repeated punishments without recourse. You can't mitigate or prevent these in any way."Events" - Trigger with no inherent logic. For example the event for permanent -10% trust due to "not listening to their needs" triggers regardless of "happiness" and "trust" levels. In my most current save, both were maxed.Research expeditions - Whatever choice you make is irrelevant and the effect, gain or loss, is completely arbitrary. This is obviously not true, but the game does nothing to inform, guide or caution a player on what each choice might mean, or involve or result in. You simply roll the dice. every. time. There are even interesting and I'd argue important lore implications and mini "missions" that are utterly missable and never foreshadowed or hinted at in several locations. Every location is a meaningless list of buttons with no relevant information available to the player (with one exception so far, out of 16 locations). This doesn't just invalidate the players agency, it invalidate the whole mechanic. Why even present a choice when the intentional lack of information makes the act irrelevant.Hull degradation - This is IXIONS version of the worsening temperature logic from Frostpunk. However it sets itself up so poorly and the information about the ship and the story you are served keep you in the dark about it's functionality and importance and even the mechanisms for hours until you have by force of experimentation figured out the ACTUAL way the system works by yourself. The game also flat out lies to you several times and omits critical information for decision-making about this central mechanic.Finally, gameplay system legibility is incredibly confused.The various systems that govern "trust" and "happiness" also interact with at least 3 more subsystems that are explained and displayed separately and with different units of value. Making the quick estimation of your current "state" incredibly annoying and unclear. The "Section" system exacerbates this even further due to some systems only displaying per section when others have a full station indicator. Other "resources" can have per section breakdowns integrated into the tooltip when hovering over the total value, but as "sentiment" values are a product of sever different types of values this doesn't work.Research and Tech tree progression seems at first glance to make sense, the expanding rings take over for the "levels" of Frostpunks research tree, but then again the arbitrary hammer comes whacking. "Sub" research on already researched technology is suddenly a critical factor once you travel beyond the first "chapter". But how to unlock the ones you need is never explained, neither is "tech tiers" explained. Unless you happened to click on an old tech you had already researched you wouldn't even know about "sub" research at all.I could keep writing, but honesly, these are the biggest hurdles right now. If this is fixed the game as it is would be great fun. The flaws this game has can be fixed via better writing and UI tweaks. Meaning, the "game" it self is already there, the ui, the graphics, the modeling, the setting and moderately entertaining story is all great.It just doesn't feel great right now. No one plays Colony/4X games to be punked by "gotcha" mechanics and literal missing information on mechanics and game functions. Fix that and you're pretty much there.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a not a casual city builder game.  It can quickly fall into a death spiral if you do not stay above all the mechanics that can cause negative outcomes (not enough workers, not enough food, hull damage, etc.).  You are in for an optimizing challenge to build the most efficient space station while trying to keep everyone happy and healthy. Those not recommending the game do not enjoy this type of challenge and view it as unfair.  I actually prefer this type of difficulty and the need to restart in order to do better.  I do anticipate that once you have learned how to optimize the game and win there really won't be a challenge upon further playthroughs.  But I feel the current price point is more than fair for the time spent learning and beating the game.  The game is bug free and hard, enjoy it for what it is and stop asking the devs to make it easier.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, yes. This is not the game is all about, but maybe a part of it. This is a city builder after all. More specifically, a fully scripted story-telling city builder set in a (more or less) near future. You have to deal with resources, city planning and a resource management hell. I just loved it. It's set in a little-worn gerne, uses different levels of gameplay inside and outside your space station, and is challenging. The game has some handholding, but to be honest this is not a walk in the park.However the game isn't that difficult if you read the plot and the science tree carefully. Since there are a few city builders coming out at the moment, it's worth mentioning that Ixion's difficulty level is not based on a variety of different resources (there are more than three, though).The downside of Ixion is the low replay value. In my opinion a lot of the difficulty is based on the plot and its scripted triggers. Once you know them, there is only a little to discover.

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to summarize this game is that it's a Space Oddessy.It's a cross between a city builder, a space explorer, and a text-based thriller.The soundtrack is absolutely sublime, and along with the sound effects and voice lines, this is one of the most audio appealing game I've ever played.The gameplay is decent, with challenging encounters that require you to make choices at every exploration point, research node, station, wreck, or planet, and the outcomes fairly reflect the option you chose, rather than a random outcome.The city and resource management aspect is quite fun, well balanced, and interesting enough to be fun on the easy mode and incredibly challenging on the hard difficulty.The plot is well done, even if some of the more hidden secrets are utterly bizarre. If you bother to translate the encrypted text or read the deeper lore, you'll find some disturbing things, which are reflected in the two ending choices, neither of which are appealing in my opinion.TL;DR:Music and SFX are the best in any game I've played, gameplay is fun, plot and choices are fair, endgame is frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: I quit the game without saving after my 12th accident in 30 cycles. It's arbitrary, completely unpreventable, and a mechanic which forces a death spiral (which this game has several of, such as the ability to construct new space ships and some kind of quantum slip drive but not be permanently able to repair your ship causing increasing bleed rates each chapter). Let me give you some quick math. Chapter 1 started, for me, with 199 people. Each accident loses you between 2-5 workers on average, sometimes they die but that doesn't truly matter because you'll wish the ones who didn't did anyways. Accidents can, and do, trigger when you have : No shortage of materials, an abundance of workers meaning optimal working conditions, a nearly perfect hull, no power difficulties. An accident triggers, on average, every 1.5 cycles. Accidents often are explosive, which means they will damage the surrounding buildings, if you build optimally this means two/three accidents per major malfunction, so 4/6-10/15 losses. So let's take the most conservative average, 12 * 5 = 60 that is 30% of my workforce gone. Consider then, that it takes 8-15 cycles for someone to heal from an accident, and each worker you're short of your optimal workload increases the risk and severity of accidents. Hospitals, naturally, need doctors and with 3 accidents filling up a single hospital, you increase your worker shortage by another 20%. Well golly gee, that means that I literally cannot avoid dying.This needs to be fixed it is absolutely insane and makes the game so abhorrently tedious and arbitrary I regret having made it over the 2 hour threshold.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't perfect, but it does deliver. Both story and music are awesome, the concept is hard sci-fi with current available tech (the Tiqqun is a feasible artificial gravity ring), the beginning is also very easy to grasp and gives you an 'emergency dread' that few games are able to replicate. The problem begins right after you start to grow, expand and create new stuff; you notice that the building is more similar to a fine-tuning and fitting pieces than to actually planning. Each sector will begin to cramp up fast and you'll have no choice but to expand to more sectors, which will consume more alloys per cycle, which will demand you more production, which also means more workers and extra working hours... you'll get what I'm talking about. It's a spiral of production that infers in refactoring, rebuilding, and fitting more buildings inside an already cramped space. Sectors can get specializations that boost efficiency of certain buildings and it's kinda crucial to improve and achieve self-sufficiency, but you cannot get proper information about it inside the game so There's too much stress involved in overall progress and you'll also get punished from being still trying to get it right, which you will  and spend a few hours camping in the system trying to prevent your workers from getting blown up in the factories. Don't get me wrong, it's a good game! Nonetheless, it  be a better game.

_childDocuments_.review: When I bought this game I was looking for something to itch the scratch that FrostPunk had left on me, then I started playing this game and was wowed by how great the graphics are, how interesting and immersive the games world is, and then the difficulty hit and I felt like I was dealing with Frost Punks unrelenting older brother. Now having played it for ~18 hours and ran into bug after bug after unplayable bug, I realize I'm really dealing with FrostPunks gilded cousin, Ixion looks appealing, but whatever spaghetti code is supposed to be functioning on this game is just not holding the game together. I could go over all the little bugs I've found, but really I want to talk about the three main bugs that make this game quite literally impossible to play.1.) You lose the ability to click on all buildings? Clicking on a building is the most essential part of a city builder type game, you click on a building, you turn it on or off, you dismantle it, you see its stats, you select the units this building is creating/has deployed. For whatever damned reason, a building will just not be clickable occasionally, and this will affect all buildings to not be clickable. My go to fix for this was to simply save and reload my save so that the game would fix itself, but finally that fix stopped working, so that ends that several hour long campaign.2.) Ships get stuck?So the only way to gather resources in this game is that you have a fleet of small ships which go out and collect resources then come back to your main ship, they dock on your ship, unload their cargo, and then automatically go back out to get more for you. But what happens when a ship randomly just wont dock? The game designers made it so that when a ship is docking you can't try to move it to another dock, or forcefully undock it, so when it gets stuck docking, you might never be able to collect the resources it has, it'll never go back out to collect more and god have mercy on your soul if you don't realize quickly that one of your cargo ships which could be 50% of your fleets total population has just been missing from the game for some time. Eventually I realized you can destroy the ship when it gets stuck docking, and then rebuild the ship afterwards in order to get it 'unstuck' but really? that was like my third work around for bugs in the game already.3.) Population just disappears while migrating?So the game splits your 'city' into 6 sectors. sector 1 might have too many idle workers while sector 2 needs more, the obvious solution is to just send more workers to sector 2 from 1. But what happens when some of those workers you sent just vanish into thin air? Well better send another population migration, but now sector 1 has not enough workers and sector 2 now has just barely enough, and I thought the problem was just me, but eventually I caught on and saw other threads of this issue. The problem was not send 'Only workers' wasn't checked, the game just didn't know how to send  workers to this new location.Honestly what a let down to learn the mechanics of the game, get a little lost in the lore and love the graphics, only to suffer at the hands of what seems to be more and more common these days where a game is just released before being play tested properly. Because all the mechanics, graphics, story, and love from the developers is very evident in the game, but the bugs are just too much to call this a finished game. Maybe give it another half a year from this review and the game might be bug free enough to give it another shot, but as is this game was just frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: The game runs fine on my PCA good city-builder game with an interesting story about space exploration (survivale) & an entertaining parody on big tech companies & billionaire philanthropies. The game looks visually great with some minor “*pushing back glasses* “Well actually…”” parts that are not worth mentioning.The game is more story driven & can be unforgiving. If you expand too slow or too fast it can spiral out of control & you lose. So it’s less a Cities Skyline city-builder & more a Banished or Surviving Mars city-builder. You can however customise the difficulty a lot. How often events happen. How severe the penalties are for low stability. Accident frequency etc. ()The building part can feel frustrating sometimes because making small adjustments to the layout can be time consuming. As far as I can see you can’t move buildings, only deconstruct & rebuild them. You do however get back all the building materials when deconstructing buildings so you never lose materials. Even with that frustration it’s still an enjoyable game. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Love the concept behind the game....Its an never ending fight to make progress.  Chapter three, and 1/2 the map is a thunder storm that moves...   I have the research that allows my ships to better survive in those storms... and Ive lost all of my ships.    My probes cant make it out the door without dying.  Like wtf.  What is the point in the research if it didnt improve anything.  I cant move my ship that far across the map to get out of the storm, because guess what....  you take even more hull damage flying your ship.  And since the storm kills my probes, i cant get anywhere.  With that said, what is the point in having your ships level up if they are so easy to die?  Its virtually impossible to keep them alive long enough.  Not without having to micro manage the star map at the same time as your space station.  Chapter 3-300 permanent hull damage.-60 hull damage a cycle from the 3 vohle jumps.-32 hull from my 4 opened sectors.Plus my crew is constantly taking damage cause im stuck in a storm. Not to mention the periodic downtime for getting struck by lightning and hurting my solar panels.I have 3 working EVA repair bays and am barely netting 1 eva's worth of repair on my hull, at the cost of 12 alloy per cycle.I had 12 cargo ships, 3 miners, and 3 science ships. I have a waste recycling plant pumping out alloy and im barely scraping by.All in all,  Once they fix some of the crap, it will be a really good game.  Just wish I had not left the game running while i was doing other stuff or I would request a refund.EDIT: Since the updates back in May the game has become far more enjoyable.   There is still alot of missing potential in my opinion, but it is a solid game (albiet short).  So I will change my rating to recommend at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: I've got 20 hours.  I've played the game.  It's absolutely frustrating how good they could have made it.The game is definitely good-looking, I really dig the story, the atmosphere, the art, it's the gameplay that tanks it completely.
