_childDocuments_.review: I originally played IXION as a demo and was immediately impressed. The atmosphere and building mechanics were really engaging and I hung on until full release. It wasn't that well received due to lack of difficulty options and bugs, but it's had a ton of work done on it since then. If you enjoyed Frostpunk, you'll probably like this. Personally, the amount of micromanaging and lack of QoL features stopped me from playing past the first chapter.- Looks awesome- Runs well- Voice acted- Nice UI- Send science ships on missions- Tech tree for upgrades- A HUGE number of difficulty settings. Not just hard or easy, but you can change all the metrics of how the game works to suit your playstyle. I don't have the time or patience to replay hours of the game if you fail, so being able to turn off some mechanics was wonderful. Most of the negative reviews are about the difficulty, which has been rectified with the addition of all these difficulty settings.- Interesting story and events to follow- Amazing aesthetic and atmosphere- Building mechanics are annoying. You can't move things, and you rapidly run out of space, so you have to deconstruct, store the materials, add a new building, wait for materials to be delivered, then constructedIt's very easy to misclick while looking for probe locations, which launches it and wastes the resources- I found the food mechanic confusing. Food is measured every 5 days, with 1 insect farm making 1 food per day. Which means every time I gain crew members (all the time) I have to think "number of insect farms * 5 / 10" instead of just looking at a number- There are no buildings that take up 2 tiles, so there's loads of wasted space- In order to transfer resources from one sector to another, you have to have a stockpile in each one. If your ship brings in resources to an airlock in a sector where you don't want those resources, you still have to build a stockpile to hold them, to move them. Which means you need all 11 stockpiles in every sector, even in sectors where you don't want that resource- I dislike there being arbitrarily workers and non-workers on the ship. It just adds another layer of annoyanceIt's one of those games (like Frostpunk) where everything starts against you, and just gets worse. You get penalised for staying in a system too long. You get penalised for moving to a new system. You get permanent hull damage for moving. - Accidents happen all the time even when everything is happy and well staffedMining ships do not avoid hazardous areas, so unless you watch them every 10 seconds, they fly through danger clouds and die

_childDocuments_.review: The easiest comparison to make is to say that Ixion on many levels resembles Frostpunk.  You have a limited circular area to build essentially a city, in a dystopian environment, to protect the remnants of human civilization while managing and processing the limited resources they need to survive.On the other hand, Ixion is a very unique take on the RTS genre story-wise, taking place in a space opera universe at the edge of human society preparing to take a step into space colonization that takes a dark turn.  Unlike many of the city-builder RTS titles that preceded it recently, Ixion is very story-heavy, and I think that definitely works to its advantage.  Your goal isn't just to win the game or save humanity, but it's also to see where things are going and where things went wrong.Like Frostpunk, though I find Ixion in many ways to be the superior game, Ixion is hard.  There isn't a lot of handholding, and part of the early game is simply realizing how important it is to set up the sections of your station well in the beginning, in addition to discovering what resources are more or less important.  This is a game that rewards replaying and re-thinking.Personally, I highly recommend it, but it may not resonate with people who don't enjoy a challenging game.

_childDocuments_.review: A challenging, punishing, unforgiving, ruthless colony survival game. That ends up being so rewarding, satisfying, emotional, and fun once you get into it. The game presents an entirely hopeless situation, and then gives you the tools you need to succeed or fail. Failure is always your choice, its not forced on you, its not RNG. You decide how to, or not to, suffer. Ive seen people complain about the station maintenance being a problem. But you try taking technology we barely understand, warping through what I can only assume is a representation of the 4th dimension, and get out without your ship imploding on itself. Despite all that, regular maintenance has been a concept since we started building mud huts. Just now its required to keep pressurised bulkheads from collapsing and metal plates from corroding in a giant vaccum that doesnt care if you live or die. The story and the visuals are incredible. Every landmark you can fly to is rendered beautifully and creates incredibly tranquil scenes no matter whats happening in your station. Then the music ontop of it all, is masterful. Ive loved every sec What an adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played a lot of base-builders.  Many many.  This one is made by developers who clearly love base building games (and Frostpunk in particular) but fail to understand the different between a challenging game and an INTERESTING challenging game.They have a number of ways to ratchet up the tension and keep you pushing forward, but none of them involve CHOICES.  They aren't "this or this" it's just "deal with this or die".When did I quit, you may ask?  I lost a ship to space weather.  Why, in any possible discussion of how to design a game, would this have been a good idea?  The choice is "babysit your ships at all times or else one of your human-crewed vessels will enter a storm they know will kill them".  There is an upgrade to make ships more survivable, but . . . . what's the point of that mechanic at all?  You can also set certain specific points in the system to be avoided, but how am I supposed to know what Hohmann transfer orbit my ships will take to get between two spots that aren't my home base?  Why could I not just tell my pilots to . . . I dunno . . . . avoid space hurricanes?  If you want space weather to be an INTERESTING challenge, then maybe: make vital and unique resources only available within the storm and give ships a limited timeframe / threshold of damage before they leave.   Make probes an expendable resource to map the storm in limited areas and increase survivability.  Playing "The ground is lava" with ships on the screen that is NOT the primary focus of the game is . . . . I refer back to my earlier statement; a basic misunderstanding of what makes a challenge fun.Same deal with stability.  They tried to make political stability the same as the cold mechanic in Frostpunk, and it just feels "this is hard" instead of "this is challenging".  I'm on the 2nd system and I'm already at -4 Stability: PERMANENT in big ol' letters.  That is punitive, not challenging.  The interesting way to make that mechanic is to make it costly to avoid or lessen those impacts.  Hell, the worldbuilding even says "some people will start to develop DES" and then anytime something bad happens, the WHOLE STATION gets a drop from that new issue.  Why not have that be a sliding scale depending on a number of people who affect it, and have a long and arduous process at the infirmary or psych office to move people back to good.  There's an interesting choice.  How many days can you take people off production lines to invest in your long-term stability?  Can you keep things afloat while you fix workers or do you need to bribe them and keep them on the line?  Instead, we just have a "do this or die" rolling boulder, Indiana Jones style.  Challenging, but not interesting.Tack onto that a fiddly resource management system, fully-scripted events, no way to return to an event later (???  Why?), a weird mechanic where your science ships get science and then have to hang around to "harvest" it (WHY?  So I have to click into the large map 30 seconds after I just did in order to move the ship that I could've just sent new instructions when it finished the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mission?  WHY???) and the "non-worker" mechanic that clearly exists as just another way to siphon resources without providing an interesting CHOICE, and you have . . . Ixion.  The devs clearly wanted to build a challenging game, but forgot the fun.Edit: Well, I kept playing it out of spite (after I went and did a game of Frostpunk in between), but damn if it still isn't just overly fiddly for no good reason.  Having to babysit individual ships, blacklist specific asteroids (can't swipe a box and select those?  Any reason why not?) and god, the research tree is just offensive to me.  Locking useful things besides useless ones, or my personal favorite, the "research this to unlock something in the UI to explain the game" button.  Beware devs that force interaction with parts of the game because they clearly don't trust it enough to be useful on its own.  Oh, and I'm just save-scumming the encounters, too.  No reason not to.  Plus when I make choices in the game portion, there seem to be just no repurcussions.  Nothing narrative, no hits to Trust, nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the complaints about the game being imbalanced are a joke.TLDR: Game is 100% playable and quite enjoyable. The music is godly. The balance may not be perfect, but its not even in the same galaxy as EA or Paradox levels of broken... Its a hardcore colony survival game and it feels it.The Read:This game isn't a simple colony builder (like Cities/Banished/Farthest Frontier/etc) in which you have time, resources, and the space to make cosmetic and unneeded decisions. Its a survival colony builder. EVERY second, decision, and resource counts.Complaints about accidents are more about not wanting to micro manage the repair function (which is fine, but just say that instead of saying their too common) Repairing is easy and requires an inexpensive building (both in resources and space) to 100% resolve. As long as you out repair the total damage, you're fine....Accidents are exceedingly rare if you have enough workers in your districts. Do that, and accidents literally vanish. Its purely a case of 'get good'. Unpopular opinion, i know.As for those complaining about resources being rare or hard to acquire... I have no idea what your talking about... The amount of resources in each zone is nuts. To the point that you absolutely cannot mine them before the deficits start to hit from the stress timers. Its literally not possible. Scan better (again... get good...)Lastly, performance issues. On an 8 year old laptop with a GTX 970 I can play the game just fine on medium. I'm already 2 chapters in and having barely any frame drops with a population of over 900 crew.... I understand each rig is different, but there is no way my 970 and an 8 year old rig out powers someone with 2000's or 3000's gen cards and hardware.... Quit running it on ultra with shadows and RT on max and it *might* stop dropping frames when 1000+ objects start walking around.At the end of the day, I'm extremely pleased with my purchase.The game is fantastic and the music is to die for.If you want a space themed Frostpunk, this is it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is Frostpunk in space, not a chill space station builder, adjust your expectations early and prevent the disappointment of losing the game over and over. Bring your survival instincts, optimization sense and prepare well before jumping into the unknown, or the consequences will be punishing - your space station carries over into the next chapter as you have built it, there is no fresh start.Despite the numerous bugs, glitches, imbalance and some just plain unfinished features that plague the game, the experience itself is captivating and kept me in the chair for hours on end, sometimes just watching the station slowly spinning in space. Soundtrack is amazing, the station itself is detailed and pretty, as is the universe around.Now, for the important facts. - the game doesn't have much replayability. There is just a single story across 5 chapters, but most of the content is in the first three, maybe four chapters Storytelling in the last two chapters shifts, and not in a good way.- the game at a first glance seems a lot more grand than it is, it's being done by a really small studio.- you CANNOT EXPAND your station in any way, unfortunately. The initial torus is all you get, split into 6 sectors that can be slowly unlocked when you need more space.- no endless mode- no difficulty options, yet (confirmed planned update)- very low consequences for random events happening on your station, the whole system from Frostpunk is underutilized- some decisions you make have no consequences later in the story (Cult of the Hull)I recommend the game if you are a BIG fan of space games, otherwise watch the game's updates for fixes and maybe additional content (if any), and decide later. The current story is good for maybe 15-30 hours of gameplay, depending on how much you will rush through it and tinker with optimizing your sector layouts.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Nice StoryNice SettingsNice Music, and ThematicCons:Poorly explained UIFrustrating Resource Management SystemExtremely unbalanced and poorly designed gameI would not recommend this game, as there are many similar style games (although not in this sort of setting), that simply are better, and do the gameplay loop better. Games like Frostpunk work, because there is a scarcity on resources for survival. Ixion doesn't work, because survival resources are abundant, but resources required to progress the story are scarce, and tech (unless you know to get the upgrade) is impossibly slow. This basically means, that you are either forced to wait in a chapter for 3 years afk while you grind out tech and resources, or you have to restart. (Now why does restarting fix this?)Yes, welcome to the environmentalist overlords. The only way to overcome the scarcity of carbon and silicon that you need to progress the game, is (amazingly) Waste management. Unfortunately, waste manager is so overpowered with its infinite resource loop, that it trivializes the whole game.Now, all of this is easily fixable.1. Completely redesign the tech system from the ground up2. Make resources abundant, but 3. Massively increase the negatives of idling, to enforce story progression, and to keep a sense of urgency. Now, instead of randomly running out of carbon to mine in the universe (like really, how is there no carbon to find in our solar system?????????), you will actively be having to make choices as to what you mine and where you mine it to avoid impending doom as you race against the clock.4. Nerf Waste management5. Remove softlocks from the game, and allow for resources to be pushed rather than pulled to your sectors

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; this game needs a bit of polishing but should ABSOLUTELY be more highly rated than "mixed" It is an excellent game that i would HIGHLY recommend to players who like a challenging logistics/ city builder. Plus the space setting is so fracking good. This is an excellent game with an amazing atmosphere and story. The gameplay can be tough to get a handle on at first, but is absolutely manageable. People saying the game is too hard are only half correct; the game is hard but a lot of those people are failing to understand the core mechanics. DONT OVERWORK PEOPLE AT ALL. ALWAYS KEEP YOUR HULL REPAIR GOING WITH MULTIPLE EVA LOCKS. I will say that some things could benefit from more descriptive tool tips, but the mechanics can be understood if you're paying attention and taking your job as the "Administrator" seriously. Shoutout to @Nilaus and @JDplays who both are very skilled and have great tips for new players trying to survive and also for experienced players trying to squeeze every last drop out of each sector and chapter.

_childDocuments_.review: In serious need of balancing.  This is especially true of the stability/morale system which hits you with permanent negative modifiers on a whim, stay in the system for too long? have a permanent -1, leave the system? have a permanent -1, complete the required story objective? have a permanent -1.  The only way to counteract these is to build expensive monuments that take up an enormous amount of space.  Add to that the large permanent downgrade in hull integrity every time you jump.Games can be punishing if they make it clear what it is they want you to do instead.  Ixion seems to punish you for doing what they asked you to do.Just to add to the punishment, new features are brought in with no introduction.  The "tutorial" is limited to a set of text-based manuals you have to go looking for yourself.  I won't be returning unless/until it gets a major update.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid game in the survival builder type. The game play is simple at it's core but fun, and the level of depth for resources, their collection, and management feels good. The game also does an excellent job slow rolling various needs/mechanics/etc organically as the game progresses.I've seen some complaints that the game should be longer, but I thought it was great. It certainly could be, I'd love to see different modes, other campaigns, etc to launch, but I think the core gameplay was fine. I will say that I think the game is good, but has some weird things holding it back from being great. The resource mechanics seem to be just a bit off tuned so that if you know what you're doing you can largely end up ignoring them. Same with Stability, which will rarely if ever be an issue for you as long as you're making sure to place only a couple of the large amount of stability buildings. The lore is off point as well. There's a lot of really cool, weird, sci-fi horrorish stuff going on in missions, and there seems to be some sort of through line, but everything is so vague and oblique and you go so little information that it's really just a guess at the end of the day. Because of that, the science missions which are your main story through the game largely becomes rote task completion and resource collection.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually leave reviews, but with the ratings this game was receiving, I had to leave a note.  If you only read one line of this review, let it be the next one:This is a good game.  It's just mired in opaque mechanics and features that lead people to believe it is far harder than it is.Now, to be a bit more specific- This game is a fun resource management/city builder whose difficulty is pinned in the satisfyingly challenging, yet not hardcore level.  You build and manage massive sectors in a space station as it hurtles through space both trying to survive, and figure out what's going on in the deeper reaches.If you are curious and want to try this game though, you NEED to understand these things that they don't particularly tell you in the tutorial:1. Accidents will happen semi-regularly, but these don't kill.  BAD accidents happen (Very quickly) when your crew is overworked (More jobs than worker members in a sector).  Keep 2 health structures per sector in case of injury overflow.2. You are being timed- kind of.   When you are in a chapter, after a generous amount of cycles (Seemingly somewhere between 120 to 200 cycles each) you will get a 'permanent' debuff to your stability.  What the game doesn't do is warn you when this is going to come about, but more importantly... tell you that this 'permanent' debuff goes away as soon as you jump to the next sector.3. Repairs to your hull happen quicker when it is more damaged.  (This is mentioned in the tutorial, but bares repeating.)  Try to keep your hull over 25% at least, but keeping it at maximum requires multiple airlocks.  That being said, for the first chapter or two you can get by with one if needed, just don't panic.4. The easiest way to manage workerflow is in the DLS technology.  There is a policy that costs -3 stability, but makes it so all people you add to your station are workers- extremely efficient.And those are the main ones; there are lots of little things I'm forgetting, but this is just a review and I'm already yawning on a bit long!  If you enjoy space concepts, Frostpunk, and an engaging if slightly forgiving challenge, then I recommend this game.  And I only recommend fun games.

_childDocuments_.review: Man I really really want to recommend this game because it is so in depth and fun but the problem is after the novelty wears off the game has a bunch of glaring problems. The main issue is that instead of challenging and rewarding the game is impossible (quite literally in this particular sense). Personally, I enjoy city builders and games like this because I like to make something steadily grow to eventually flourish and IXION has such a great concept for this, a space station flying around rebuilding humankind through colonies like a massive ark the last hope of humanity being held together through sheer human ingenuity and spirit! However, the devs seemed to have put a little too much faith in that because the space station that according to the intro was designed to be this ark is made of paper mache. The hull taking damage makes sense as in space even a grain of sand can be a bullet if its travelling fast enough and there is tons of stuff flying around like hail in space but consuming a building material seems a bit strange to me as I feel like it would make more sense for the EVA to use something like a welder to weld or fix any damage to the exterior hull. The second thing that affects station durability is expanding... yeah, opening the blast doors to another section affects the EXTERNAL hull despite the outside being unchanged since nothing was added only accessed. The final part of station durability is that the game pushes you to move the station all the time to keep exploring and searching for habitable planets to set up colonies but the issue with that is that every jump PERMANENTLY damages the hull making the already paper thin hull even MORE rickety and at that point its only a matter of time till its game over so it just feels like a whole exercise in futility because whats the point of having a mobile station to build up in a CITY BUILDER if you cant even move it without everything coming crashing down, it really ruined the entire purpose of the game for me. The other issue with the game in my opinion is that the whole cryopod system makes absolutely no sense. In IXION cryopods are your main source of settlers/crew but they are split between workers and non workers (along with a third called colonists though colonists have to be trained in a special building) but you have no control over which of the two you will get and it seems (atleast in my experience) to be heavily leaning towards non-worker as 7/10 of them were non workers which, as the name implies, arent added to your workforce AKA freeloaders, bums, no hands more mouths, and all in all just not useful when youre trying to keep everyone alive on your flying junk heap. It would make more sense that there are specific TYPES of people such as skilled or not-skilled which would help bump certain building types efficiency up based on how many of said people are in each sector possibly even more so when the section becomes specialized maybe even throw in a debuff for having specialists of a "conflicting" type (like space and waste or agriculture and industry). The main issue is that if you are one of a select few who survived and are flying through space on a degrading lemon of a ship wouldnt you do everything you can to help even if you might not be GOOD at something? Instead of having nonworkers why not train some workers to become colonists and THEN those colonists can laze about until getting to a planet where you can set them down otherwise everyone has to pitch in to live. Now I will say the game does have a lot going FOR it. The story is fantastic and the cut scenes are really well done. I really like the idea of a lone space station flying through the vast sea of stars to try to find a good planet to set up colonies (could even make a sequel game based around one of those colonies) while trying to keep itself flying as best it can and evolving as it explores. The research being done through expeditions was a really fresh and interesting way of doing it. However, despite it all its just not worth the price and I cant recommend it because its just a bunch of really cool ideas poorly executed as it is now but I would like to see some things changed if possible and if that happens I might be able to give it a thumbs up but for now, in my opinion, skip it and play something else.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not understand the negative reviews.  This game is amazing!  I would best describe it as a Frostpunk in Space!  Resource management is extremely challenging and it is very possible that you will fail and have to start over.  Resources will always be scarce, that includes personnel.   All your industry needs personnel, but they in turn need living space and food.  It is a constant fight for balance, a challenge that so far has not stopped.  I really like the exploration portion of the game.   The game does not hold your hand after the initial "tutorial" chapter.  Where you explore, what you explore, and it what order is left up to you.  There is only one story arc true, but I do think there is some replayability to the game.  There are many encounters where you have to make a decision, whatever you choose locks out the other decisions and can sometimes even lead to the loss of resources and lives.  Going back and trying to decisions, new research orders, new building and city layouts has IMHO a huge appeal.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game, great story, music and SPACE. I get the comparison most make with frostpunk, but this has SPaCe and a better story. _childDocuments_.name: IXION

_childDocuments_.review: If you like somewhat more challenging strategy games and SciFy settings, then you will really enjoy this.The look and sound of the game are really good, i especially loved the sound and music design. The story and world are really interesting, but i feel towards the end more of the mysteries of what is going on in the background of your Company and its leaders should be cleared up. There is clearly more going on than meets the eye. Especially in regards to what happend between the proglogue and Chapter 1.In regards to the difficulty many of the negative reviews complain about. The game is stressfull in the beginning.Mostly in chapter 2 if you rushed things in chapter 1. The game tries to lure you into moving on and expanding your station too fast. If you stay in any system as long as resources allow it and only expand you station once it is absolutely necessary, then you will not have much trouble with the game. During the last 2 (of 5) chapters i didnt know where to pile my resources.Staying in one system too long gives you a "permanent" -1 stability, permanent only until you finally continue your journey.Which is annyoing in the beginning but the game gives you more than enough options to deal with it, later on -1 is nothing.After chapter 2 i had basically always +2-4 stability in all sectors despite all the other negatives you will gain over the course of the game. Anything more than +1 Stability is just buffer.As example i saw someone complain about having -2 stability and not knowing how to solve it... while pilling all the crew into the worst kind of housing in the game (+0 Stability) while your basic housing would already give +1 and the first upgrade housing gives +2 and is allround superior housing (less than 50% the space needed, less energy per people) for barely increased cost. While also using policies that give a further -1 Stability.Dont move to the next system too fast. Dont expand the station too fast. And have a very close look at the research options (especially the upgrades for existing tech like the basic quarters)Then you will have no problem with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, quite challenging and very engaging if you play these type of games.There's something I really dislike though: Event results are applied when interacted, this means, even if you lost your ships in an event, it is considered "not yet happened" until you click it.If you interacted before you collected all the science points, you may lose the ships plus the points. But if you don't touch it, you get all the points.This design gives a very strong negative feedback. It's punishing players not for their wrong decisions, but for clicking buttons at wrong timings.EDIT: Also you should really warn players water is not moved when deconstructing fusion stations.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a very good game, the first one in years I bought without some 75-90% discount, and the only one I don't regret buying... Visuals are awesome, the station growing on the outside looked sweet, and all the various designs of buildings and ships were pretty neat.Soundtrack was perfect.Story was intresting, even tho' I didn't really enjoy the end game.That said it has a few things missing or not finished...- Resource logistics within the station were tedious, lacked an option to 'force' resources from one sector to another, instead You need to change quotas on both sectors which may mean other sector resources will start moving... it was the least pleasant part of the game, and it stoped working a few times- Ship Logistics another part where ships frequently flew half full or less while skiping past resources to pick up, and the most infuriating bit, You have to assign a cargo ship to an event with science ship, You can only assign one coz' reasons, so if it needs 4x courses or more, while 5 other ships wait... I had once some glitch with a cargo ship 'eating' 187 colonists, and said colonists simply disappeared, not reaching their destination...- End game, has You colonizing the planet, which is obviously the goal of a colonization mission, but there is no option to pour the colonists down bit by bit, nah You have to get them all trained, You can't pour that human wave out of the station, for reasons... and You can't even pour the excess resources down onto the planet either...- Space station allows for movement of goods, for train construction, for people to be sent from one sector to another, but not for the constructiuon of water pipes... for reasons, most likely it - because it would make things to easy... Deffinetly the visual part was the best, the station idly rotating while orbiting a planet would make for a pretty cool wallpaper - all in all fun game, with very nice graphics and music.

_childDocuments_.review: Released horribly buggy (in a first day patch that made the game completely unplayable from the starting menu) after several months of changing the release date. _childDocuments_.review: Ixion is probably the game that shows the most that steam needs a middle option between dislike and like. the game honestly has almost everything it needs to be fantastic. but having restarted several times and not even leaving sol yet, the few things the game is missing just shows so heavily its hard to keep pushing myself to keep playing. balance wise at least for chapter 1, it feels like there is only 1 way to play, build any other way, you are dead. you cannot get enough steel to have other build paths. it feels like you have to instant start, bull rush steel manufacturing, set up like 3 of those, then bullrush cyrogenics to not have 10 events every 120 seconds and thats not a exaggeration. i think i might even be underselling that. there is so many accidents that punish repair rate for no reason. and you get accidents for not having workers, what do accidents do? kill workers. meaning you need more people, to replace your dying peope, than you can actively replace. so you'd think focus cyrogenics first right? then you run out of steel and die. so you have to play steel first, then cyro, then docks, then eva. at least thats my current working theory so far. maybe that order isnt even right, if its not i do not mechanically understand the game and have no idea how anyone gets past chapter 1 unless they just leave instantly when they can, which would make half the stuff in chapter 1 pointless if thats the intent. but yeah for a rouge lite, so far theres no rng systems every play through i've done has been identical. it feels like you have to play a certain way unless they add more steel to the start of the game. the accident system feels counter intuitive,. i also find myself missing a some sort of culture menu or law system which would spice up gameplay a lot more as well. either way the game is a hard, great game but needs a couple balance passes, i get the game is supposed to be insanely hard, but there is a difference from limiting how you can play, to it being hard to play, and i feel like ixion falls in the former currently.

_childDocuments_.review: While already an incredibly worthwhile and challenging play, I think that with some tweaks here and there and some balancing changes, IXION could be one of my favorite games from this genre.Just know, it's not a city builder. It's a resource management simulator with an engrossing story and an absolutely stellar (pun intended) soundtrack.I would love to see difficulty options for future playthroughs (I've heard they are working on this) and small decoration buildings that cost 1 alloy. It would be nice to add small details to fill in the gaps on the station and make it feel a bit more alive. Although efficiency of space is a key part of this game, I always seem to have a few places where I end up just doubling the roads to fill the gaps. With lower difficulty playthroughs in the future I could see the city building aspect being a very fun part of the game.Overall, highly recommended by me. If you love Frostpunk, Satisfactory, Factorio, etc... you will enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, leaving this review is kind of depressing.I played the demo and absolutely loved it. The game had so much atmosphere. Such a fantastic new setting for a city builder, such heavy narrative focus.Then playing the full version, realising the prologue was fundamentally different to the demo and wondering what else is different. So excited to find out more about where the story will go, what hardships will be endured.But then the quality goes down with every chapter. Fewer voice lines, fewer interesting events, more arbitrary challenges and choices that are basically impossible to get right without using an external wiki.And then, the disappointing ending. The last 6-8 hours of the game were really a pain to get through. Just boringly waiting for stuff to be built, events to complete etc. Plus the endless issues with logistics on your  general it was fairly annoying to try and optimise your "city" as deconstruction would take forever, reconstruction would take forever all due to issues with the logistics system that the game doesn't really give you good tools to solve. Plus, later in the game you get access to a lot of new buildings that you essentially HAVE to build into existing sectors, meaning the game FORCES you to deconstruct stuff and move everything around. Really, a huge pain.I was excited to try and optimise everythinfg but the building experience just sucked too much.Despite how much fun I had with the first 10 hours or so, the game really would have been so much butter would the devs have shortened in by 5h at least and just accepted that they don't have more time/funding to realize their vision. Like this, it ended up being painful. It's clear that this will never change either, so I cannot recommend the game simply because of how frustrated I was for such a large part of playing it, despite loving the basic premise of the story. (if only the ending would have been better...)

_childDocuments_.review: To start, this game does have issues of difficulty at least for those that aren't hardcore management fans.Mainly, there are needless penalties, that when you reload a prior save and avoid it, the same penalty is applied for a different reason. It's already hard enough to get the new sector up and running, even without chaos in the others.That said and done, this game has a clear goal and it is obvious to me that the devs and art team have all communicated greatly and share the same passion.The visual style is truly astounding and the soundtrack equally so.TLDR; Great style but needs difficulty levels to accommodate more players.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this through several times now. It wasn't that the game has a lot of draw to play it more than once I just wanted to knock out a few steam achievements. Research has a different twist. You not only have the usual research tree, but you must also locate science points to research items and upgrades. (Note upgrades are located by clicking on the main item tab in the research tree, I can't be the only one that missed this. I went about 1/3 of my first game without an upgrade lol.) This is usually done with your science ships (imagine that) sending teams to planets and comets. As others have said keeping the crew happy and the ship from falling apart is the biggest challenge. Work your crew too hard and accidents which are frequent become fatal for them, not only this but somehow this reduces their ability to maintain the hull of the ship. Like other similar games it is easy to get in a death spiral. You will mine resources and use them to build things. (Imagine that) Early in the game Iron, which is used to make alloys is your biggest concern along with food you make from insects. (mmm tasty) Later Carbon, which is used to make polymers which in turn makes solar panels and ships. Silicon jumps in as important in the mid game to make electronics, which are needed for most advanced structures and finally Hydrogen to run the one or two nuke plants you will need in the late game. The game is primarily about resource and power management. There is seldom a lack of resources to find, but getting those to the right factory at the right time is the trick. Beware launch bays make great storage locations, but if you fill one up none of the ships assigned to it will unload or load their until some space is made. Lastly there are dead ends, use up all your science points before learning to make a telescoping arm and game over because you need it to move on. Your science teams will die left and right the first time through.(Unless you save a lot.) You usually get 3 options on how your science team should investigate a location. Often the logical choice kills all or part of your team. (What do you expect from devs that think ponytails with receding hairlines is cool) Note a lot of people complain about non-workers, which do nothing, but eat your food and take up space for most of the game. They can be made into colonists needed for colonization research efforts and you will need thousands of them to complete the game. Be ready for things that  seem to make little sense causing your entire crew to be pissed. More people in cryopods than you have people in a sector. Spending too much time in one solar system, knowing one of your colonization tests was less than encouraging etc.Each of the six sectors in your ship can specialize up to two levels in one or more functions, which add bonuses for that sector. You gain this specialization by building specific types of buildings in abundance. Factories give industrial bonuses, Food production structures give agricultural bonuses, Waste management gives both recycling and industry bonuses. Most are easy to obtain second level except population specialization, which seems to require mass amounts of living structures.To accomplish this I had to cover about 90% of a sector in living accommodations. Lastly the game enjoys killing your workers, never set worker levels at the minimum for optimized work load. There will be a factory accident that will injure them pushing the work load up and the next accident will kill workers. The sneakiest trick the game does is overload your infirmaries. You don't get a warning you have too many injured workers for the number of infirmaries in a sector until workers start dying for lack of care. (Many people complain about this workload death cycle, but is possible to play the game through to the end, which I have done twice, without ever going past optimized workload in any sector.) The ending leaves something to be desire. There is no ending accomplishments screen. You never get told how many people died, (unless you lose them in the hundreds during the game) or how many resources you recovered or processed. Graphics are good except for the still pictures of people that send you messages, which look like a third grader drew them. I enjoyed the game and got my moneys worth.
_childDocuments_.name: IXION

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not one to leave reviews on Steam, in fact, I'm pretty sure its my first... spurred on by the unfair thrashing IXION is receiving from some reviewers. I'll keep it short and to the point:-The atmosphere is amazing. Visuals, music, and story telling elements work together to tell a story that balances between hopeful, gritty, and cosmic horror. (Also... psychedelic horror? Is this a thing? I want more.)-Gameplay is fun, immersive, and challenging. Sure, its a bit clunky around the edges, and could do with a couple quality of life updates, like better minion/space ship tasking controls and better population management systems.-Difficulty. This is where its at, where most people bang their heads against the wall. And while I'm really trying not to fall into the classic 'git good'... its hard. The game's chock full of text tutorials, complete with pictures for anything you dont understand. Further into the gameplay (and one or 2 lost games in between) you learn better macro strategies. Move the Tiqqun near your wanted resource asteroids to shorten supply lines. Always be on the look out for iron. Research quantitative upgrades. etc etc. All of this is pretty logical stuff, like solving simple puzzles, only there's a lot of them at the same time.Sure, the hull disintegration mechanic feels unfair at first, but that just means you expand your iron logistics lines. More miners drilling ore for more cargo ship to drag to more foundries to smelt to more EVA locks to use as hull repair. Simple -> more is good. Later into the mid and mid late game, you'll even start pairing back on all that stuff because you researched efficiency upgrades for the smelters and now you are drowning in alloys. Seriously, by the end of the game I couldn't delete stuff because my warehouses couldn't take the alloy out of them without overfilling themselves. Iron asteroids are everywhere in this game: its as simple as moving the Tiqqun and going omnomnomn.If you liked Frostpunk you'll probably love this one... it scratched a massive itch I had for the longest time, and what's more, you're in space! What's not to like?? For everyone else, I'd recommend seeing a few let's play before buying, its a particular kind of strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very addicting survival-base builder game, fun from start to finish.  I have a few complaints that folks should be aware of before picking it up ---Transferring resources between sectors takes time, and can be blocked up by export/import limits, so micro-managing your Resources screen is very important.  It does feel like the kind of thing that should have automation for it (for example, I built out one sector as pure storage, and I frequently had to alter the storage limits on various sectors for resources in order to get different items shipped around)--In the same vein, beware of resource bottlenecks.  My biggest problem throughout the mid- and late-game was trying to actually ensure my "Space" sector was keeping its exports clear so that I could complete events that required resources to ship *out*.  Having resources stuck in the docking bay held up several missions for me.--The game's ending felt a little anticlimactic, if I'm honest.  The penultimate system had a significant and engaging gameplay challenge that required my full attention, and then the last system felt rather underwhelming following that.All that being said I have to emphasize it was a lot of fun, I enjoyed the game from start to finish, absolutely worth the cost of admission.  Basically from the moment I fired the game up I couldn't put it down.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought game, installed, applied update that fixes accidents+triggers. Started game, watched beautiful cinematic, then watched blank black screen with a game menu sprocket top right for 30 minutes. Click game sprocket, twice to get it to bring up a menu, buttons click but don't do anything. Alt-tab, stopped game via Steam Stop button. Restarted Ixion, same result. Verified updated gfx drivers, restarted, same result. Restarted one more time and played with game gfx options, which are locked for some reason. Stopped game via steam for the 4th time, Refunded.***UPDATE***Apparently the patch to fix the "accidents" broke the game for everyone. They fixed it within an hour so I cancelled my refund request.This is another game where we need a "wait and see" recommendation.As you've probably read in other reviews, after you finish the tutorial there are some gameplay elements that feel less than "well thought out". You'll see many reviews referring to "sectors", and unlocking them; but that term is specific to this game and wrong. The term the game was looking for is "Section". You'll need to unlock up to six sections of the ship that are initially blocked off. You'll have to connect roads, provide manpower, and some resources to unlock sections of the ship to build in.The sections (connected by roads) do not share resources or manpower despite you "opening" them up, which is dumb. You can "import and export" resources and manpower through the UI, but the UI for this is terrible and unnecessary because you already have a road connected. There are a couple other annoying details you won't learn until after you've made a few mistakes/destroyed your ship; which also feel unnecessary if the tutorial had mentioned the importance of researching one or two specific  technologies before handing you a crisis you can't manage without the tech. It's not hard, it's just another version of "on rails" strategy. IE: Play the game this way or you will never progress.As others have mentioned, no idea if this is the intended gameplay or just a lack of game testing. I guess we'll find out, because the game potential looks amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Ixion brings a lot to the table both thematically and mechanically, and it delivers on pretty much all of its promises. The mostly hard sci-fi theme (with allowance for FTL) is delightfully rendered both inside and outside the ship with an outstanding eye for detail. I audibly gasped when I realized that, while in a debris field largely composed of human corpses, there are little floating corpses visible in my docking ports from the interior view. Speaking of audio, Guillaume David's (of Mechanicus fame) soundtrack is exquisite and really gives Ixion a musical pulse to accompany its mechanical heartbeat. Similarly, the game asks you to build a finely tuned machine out of components that you won't be at all familiar with when you first play Ixion. While this looks and feels a lot like Frostpunk, I think it actually succeeds at expanding the variety of the "base-building" mechanics comparatively. There's quite a bit of possible research, which allows for a significant amount of leeway in your sector designs. It definitely doesn't include the complex supply chains of Anno, but it gives you significantly more room to build and significantly more variety in resources and structures than Frostpunk. Similarly to Frostpunk, there's a very likely chance you'll fail your first attempt - possibly even several times. This is a game of exploration, but mechanically and metamechanically. Ixion's economy has a tendency to death spiral - once you're critically short on something it becomes very difficult to pull out of that spiral. It's not impossible to fix, but it might well derail a run as penalties for spending your time "not moving forward" pile on. To its credit there are a lot of levers both you and the game pull to slow or stop a death spiral, but it takes careful micromanagement to recover from critical resource shortfalls. For me, that's part of the fun - thinking about how to redesign your sectors to be more efficient or what types of buildings you want to use for food production.Narratively and thematically Ixion nails its goals. The game is frequently bleak and isolating, punctuated by profound loss. It's again impossible to not compare to Frostpunk in that regard. They are more alike than dissimilar, and the solar system map is a pleasant alternative to Frostpunk's expedition map. You'll spend a lot more time on it doing a lot more than just considering where to send your science ships to explore, which is a nice change of pace from base building. You'll need to probe for resources, monitor space weather, and reposition the Tiqqun as necessary. It gives you a solid strategy layer to monitor between base building and the narratives your exploration ships prompt.Ixion is definitely not for everyone. It's arguably less approachable than Frostpunk, but it really nails the same premise with a deeper mechanical system. If you're willing to fail you'll find a striking adventure and an excellent base building game in Ixion.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Ixion is a resource puzzle with city building elements, phenominal presentation, and a tough-as-nails learning curve.While not free of flaws, I'd easily call Ixion my personal Game Of The Year for 2022, easily. It's a very high quality, single player story experience with fantastic visuals, stellar music, and a solid core gameplay loop. Ixion isn't so much a city builder as it is a resource management puzzle. Similar to Frostpunk, there very much is an order of operations when it comes to research and building. The farther along you get, provided you made solid choices early on, allow the resource constraints and pressure to ease off. It's also a game built on trial and error. It expects you to try, fail, and try again. (Tip, keep a catalog of saves around each milestone or major decision, don't rely on the autosaves.)

_childDocuments_.review: What a game. The music, the atmosphere, the S P A C E. So much of this game was just a treat to play. I loved the visuals, the mechanics of exploration and especially the soundtrack. Seeing amazing sights such as the chapter 2 setting and especially the jaw dropping chapter 3 setting made the game that much more memorable. The world building done for each location scattering lore for those willing to read it got me very invested in the world as a whole however that is not to say that I am completely in love with every aspect of the game. It can be a bit frustrating and confusing at times, especially when certain mechanics seem to work against you. Resources, especially your population can lead to frustrating events where you are struggling to acquire workers with more regular citizens being mouths to feed. The story is a bit lacking despite the rich and enthralling world. It is certainly a serviceable story line but it certainly is not the centerpiece of the campaign. The decision system feels somewhat superfluous as they don't necessarily contribute to future events, they are really just a resource expenditure or bonus. Research can be pretty inconsistent as well since you tend to get large science bonuses and end up stuck afterwards and the finale leaves something to be desired with a victory lap type of objective that doesn't really feel all that impact. Overall I would rate the game a solid 8/10 for its stellar world building, soundtrack and overall game play loop and mechanics. It nails the feeling of being truly alone in your journey and the set pieces and secrets scattered throughout are a joy to discover but some frustrating mechanics and a less than stellar story and ending end up taking away some of the excitement of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game, and felt like giving a review because I'm not sure why it's currently on "mixed"A lot of people are citing balance issues and difficulty spikes, but I have to say I'm not currently experiencing any issues. I weirdly thought the game is quite easy. I think its a case of; if you run into problems, they can begin to spiral out of control. The few times I've had accidents or events that caused issues, I'd power down a part of my economy and recover quite fast.Anyways, I'm loving the game. The mix of building internally, externally, managing people and exploring the systems to uncover the story is such a perfect blend of building and narrative. The story is quite interesting and the sector based gameplay, while a bit micromanage-y provides something quite different to most builder games. I think the UI is really top-notch as well, there are lots of options/easy to find menus and tooltips to explain everything. This really might be my game of the year. One drawback though for sure is that it seems fairly linear, there's no sandbox or difficulty options. While I don't mind that really, Frostpunk was the same initially, I think expectation of these types of games means you should have some sort of replayability in there. I hope the game does well enough to get DLC or expansions. I'd actually love to manage multiple ships if I could!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hard sure, but wasn't Frostpunk? Mechanically this game is very similar. You need constant alloys to keep the ship in good shape and as you unlock new sectors and move to new systems your needs will gradually increase. There are other needs too like power, food, crew loyalty, etc. I think the resource management is a little tougher in this game because storage is very limited in the beginning, but you can still stockpile early when you learn some tricks. There isn't any penalty for deconstructing things and rebuilding them so unlike in Frostpunk it seems like the intention here is that you have to occasionally reconfigure sectors to fill the role you need them to or as your tech allows.The vibes in this game are dope though. Sound design, music, graphics, theme, and story are all excellent. I'm having a lot of fun with it. It gets the rec no question.

Unheard of.I understand the challenge the game wants to give and I'm fine with it but its sometimes excessive/tedious. Example (spoiler): Your crew members are upset with staying near earth too long as its sad to see the destroyed Earth. 100% on board with that. But then you get "punished" for leaving the Earth behind... sure I guess. And then you keep a similar cycle going. Also every time you jump, it permanently reduces the hulls structural integrity and the upkeep gets pretty high, very quickly just for using the station. I think its a little weird that by the time I can have a fully upgraded station to admire how nice it looks, its basically a ball of duct tape and bubble gum floating through space.'ve never advocated for an "easy mode" in a game before but I almost feel like I want to because I can see this game has a lot and the potential for a lot more but sometimes I just want to relax, explore, enjoy the work the beautiful game that it is.Don't let the mixed reviews scare you. I enjoy it. I think the challenge I great. Maybe I just think the way I do because it seems like the game adds too much challenge for reasons that seem weird to me. I've lost once so far and just started an entire new run instead of restarting the chapter just to try and do it better again with what I learned.9.5/10 - Would jam out to music and sound of my workers accidentally blowing up the station again

_childDocuments_.review: IXION is a rough gem. Very roughly explained it's a bit like taking Frostpunk and giving it a Sci-Fi theme, but it has significant differences. I see Frostpunk, Cliff Empire, a bit of old Oupost 2 (Taking your base with you, mood management), and a couple of other things in here.The game treats us with a story campaign, colony (station) building, exploration, survival, lots of management (perhaps overly so for some), and some fairly nice visuals; for those wanting to make their station run like clockwork and wanting to perfect things to full efficiency there's definitely something to enjoy that, but for others there's some caution to be had before jumping in.IXION a bit like Frostpunk limits how much you can push forward early on, but less because it's expecting N days to pass or story events to trigger (In some cases, but these happen quickly) and more because your access to resources and especially research points is gradual and limited. Moving through the campaign chapters means your station moving to a new solar system where you need to explore and scavenge. As far as resources go you just have to make a decision early on: Stay long enough on a chapter and suffer a permanent debuff but pick up everything; or be as quick and efficient as possible to grab everything you can and take off to the next chapter. Research however, early on you're heavily limited in finding interest points (some of which give you multi-choice options with different reward/penalty results) which will give you just enough research points to pick up a few specific techs, since your research lab produces points painfully slow until much later.This means that you risk losing the game because you over spent points, or burnt resources ahead of time, or didn't scavenge enough, which is why you either need to have a very logical mindset to be as efficient as possible (where knowing the game ahead of time will clearly help you), or you most likely will inevitably see yourself picking up an earlier save or starting fresh (As I did, though less because of failing and more because I understood the game better and felt I could be more efficient).Taking the time to understand the game is critical, otherwise many things will feel like the game is absolutely disrespecting your time and is sending you into death spirals. Your workers are slightly overworked? Queue the first building accident which sends some to the infirmary (You build one, yes?) and possibly kills 1 or 2 more; which then causes you to be more short staffed and forces you to turn off buildings or the problem just escalates. You didn't built enough quarters? Well people now are getting antsy. Picked up too many cryopods by mistake? Well, people will be unhappy for that and trust may plummet if you're not ready to deal with that. Burned too much alloy? Well, not sure if you can make more in time to patch up that tearing hull breach without bringing down some buildings.When you respect the game's challenging nature you're ready for what it throws at you (some of it), but if you're not ready to understand the game expects you to play it a certain way then it'll feel cumbersome and unfair; which points to what's perhaps another flaw: The game is only a linear campaign with little no randomness it is eventsNot that it can't be satisfying, but it means that aside potentially trying different options at exploration sites to see the result (some of which are negative anyway) you'll see planets in the same places, the same amount of resources in the same spots. It's what allows you to build a strategy but it's also a heads up on why the game is balanced in such a specific way.At the moment there is no free game mode, no random galaxy generators, which hopefully is something the developer would still consider to lengthen the game's life just a bit more, but it's not looking like that was part of the plans. So I give the game a good thumbs up; but caution as the game can be frustrating if you come at it with the wrong mind set.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; A stylish, lovely, and punishing city builder/survival game, with a great core gameplay loop but is lacking in a few areas. Without spoilers, I  this game in its current state. I think the systems are solid, and I trust that the game will be fleshed out more. The game is polished and nearly bug-free, however after completing the game it is hard to believe it is fully realized, and it seems as though many of the choice based story elements were cut or unfinished. If you liked Frostpunk on a city management level however, this is actually more complex in that particular aspect, but as many say the balance is a bit off right now, although if you are okay with reloading a save or two and read the tech tree, you should have an okay time completing the game. The rest of the review will contain minor gameplay and story spoilers, except for sections which are marked by spoilers, which will contain more major story spoilers.One of the problems I have in this game is the lack of voice acting. In the prologue, you talk to several advisors with excellent VA and get a fun and not at all ominous speech from the CEO of the DOLOS. Unfortunately, once you start your journey, all you talk to for the rest of the game are AI robots. Now, this could be intentional, as the game does make clear how lonely your job is, but it does feel like a missed opportunity, and having people to speak with to break up the constant robotic voices would be nice. This, however, may also just be a symptom of a larger problem in the game: the horrific lack of humanity in general, and the disregard of story choices having meaning. Here's an example. After a while into the game, once you , an event pops up informing you that a cult worshiping the hull of the ship as a savior has sprung up, and you are informed that what they are doing does not break DOLOS protocol, and given the option to suppress the cult or let it be. I let it be, and awaited eagerly for problems to arise from this decision. I waited... and waited... but it never popped up again. The only thing it seems to have done is allow me to build a later game temple building that provides stability. Why even add this event? Why don't the cultists ever form a faction against you? Or cause problems? Or even do cosmetic changes like painting murals on the ship walls (as is shown in the event art)? The cult that  isn't even mentioned whenever I . Another plot thread that is sort of pointless, and this is all spoilers, is  There is a building in the game that is basically a surveillance center that is what allows you to change policies and issue propaganda. At one point, I got an event where the people were beginning to worry if the information was being used for malicious purposes, to affect their behavior. I told them it was run by the AI, and that even  was subject to its eye, and... nothing. Not even a response. The event just went away, and I never heard about it again. This, in my opinion, is the biggest problem with the game. The game needs internal politics to keep you intrigued and tell a proper story. As it is right now, the story is basically . There is very little room for personable stories, and no small scale drama, only the big overarching story.The other problem with the game is balance, although not for the same reason others give. I cannot believe people find this game horrifically difficult. Even if you completely ♥♥♥♥ it up, the game has generous saves. Dismantling buildings always gives full resources back, so you can rearrange your build with only a small time investment. In any case, my problem with balance is that the last couple of chapters are really easy to breeze through if you have been holding back to collect resources from previous stages. The final chapter especially just feels like a victory lap rather than a final challenge.I do not understand a few of the points hammered by other reviews of this game. People seem to have a enormous problem with very small nitpicks in the game, instead of looking at the game as a whole. Some of these things aren't even issues. People seem to have a huge problem with the way that repairing the hull works and how you lose maximum hull points each jump, which I simply do not understand. "Why does each jump do permanent damage to the hull?" To make the game more difficult as you get further into the game, as most games do. It increases the upkeep because you are basically spit and duct-taping the decaying superstructure. "Why does expanding into sectors increase the alloy upkeep?" Because you are actively maintaining more space rather than letting it rot. "Why does moving drain upkeep?" Because you are now maintaining engines and slamming into space debris. All the answers I just gave can be dismissed as "copes" by these people for bad game design, however I do not understand this either. People complain about "the drain", but that is just a part of the genre of survival city builder. You don't see people complaining about having to put increasing amounts of coal in the generator in Frostpunk. Such a complaint shows a lack of understanding of the genre, perhaps from people coming in expecting a more standard city building/management game. You are supposed to struggle with managing resources. That’s the difficulty. The current most popular early review is just asking why stability is dropping for seemingly arbitrary reasons, which I think is a fair criticism. I do wish there were more reasonable reasons for lowered stability. However, this this review implies there is nothing you can do to combat these debuffs, which is simply not true. You can invest in mental health centers, parks, propaganda, policing, and more to help with stability. And when it comes to Cryopods, I think people misunderstand what Cryogenics are in the lore of this game. Cryogenics aren't standard. People expect to NOT be frozen, and be able to live once more. Cryogenics are only used in emergency situations to prevent death. So yes, you get a debuff for storing people in ice aboard your ship instead of freeing them from their frozen prison. People seem to want a game with super black and white good and bad options, with an obvious solution. This game prefers trade offs. Sure, you can hold all these people in cryosleep on the ship. You won’t have to feed or house them. But your people may trust you just a little less. Edit: Formatting

_childDocuments_.review: Game plays like frostpunk and cliff empire had a baby, attached a FTL drive and shot it into space.Is it tedious? At times for sure, the word I'd use is daunting.Is it hard? Sure.Will you have to learn through mistakes and death spirals and start again? Absolutely.Will you beat in your first attempt? Uhh, probably not. (its good to set expectations early)The balance may feel iffy at first until you realise that it's just not a city simulator - it's a strategy/logistics game that has you managing several spinning plates simultaneously. Ixion is closer to a puzzle game in a city building disguise than it is to City Skylines or Tropico. There is no putting the speed on max and walking away to make a coffee; neglect in any area will start a doom spiral that may take you an hour of play time to realize has already locked in your fate. The most limited resource isn't food, people, alloys or electronics, it's building space. Pressure ramps up due to a limited population that needs to be supported in the final bastion of human life - that doesn't sound like a walk in the park, and well, it's not. You both have to expand and continually reoptimize the space you consumed already. Buildings have a limited life span, few if any will stay with you to the end. Don't get attached to patterns or symmetry, you've been warned.Game takes place over the span of a decade, so you can't just breed a population to replace all the people that died from mismanagement and neglect. The population you get access to is just as much as resource to be as carefully managed as the rocks and ice that you mine. Time is not on your side, if you're not pausing to make use of each in game day that goes past, you're gonna fail. If you're not keen to ship people off to another area so you can tear it down and rebuild, you're in for a bad time. Too little building materials and food = doomToo much building materials and food = doomToo many houses = doom via wasting precious spaceToo few houses = doom via violent uprisingThe game has no difficulty setting - I like this. You're playing a finely tuned experience that needs as much real time pausing, planning as you spend on max speed waiting for your plans to unfold. When you've bought this amazing game and are struggling, before you come to complain and leave a negative review I have a few tips for you.-Build fewer roads, roads are wasted building space. As I mentioned previously, functionality > prettiness. -Plan your research ahead, research points are a precious resource and you won't be unlocking many upgrades till later on.-Waste is an important resource, make it work for you - stop ejecting it into space (as soon as you can).-Too many cargo ships will doom you, don't plan to mine out a sector. Cargo ships don't have to be active all the time, in fact it is often detrimental if they are.-Be wary of storage, until very late game, having 300+ of whatever resource sitting around is using a lot of building area to sit there and be unproductive. -Specialize your districts, the game only nudges you in that direction rather than grabbing you by the short and curlys and screaming it into your face. You will fail. Buckle up, learn from your mistakes, and throw yourself at it again. This is an excellent game that will test your intelligence and problem solving skills - after the prologue/tutorial, the game will not hold your hand. This game does not deserve the mixed reviews from people upset that they didn't get a trophy for just participating. This is not a pushover game one can blaze through at max speed without pausing to experience the story.Good Luck future Administrators.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been described as "Frostpunk in space" and I think that is true in the best of ways. I've played Frostpunk on PC and Xbox, multiple times through on multiple difficulty levels. The things that keep me coming back are as follows: The art style, the music, the feeling that one mistake will haunt you so you better take your time, but don't take too long or that will haunt you as well. Ixion has all those feelings as well. The music is great and haunting and atmospheric. The gameplay is solid (anyone who complains that it's too hard are the same people who complain that the "Souls" games are too hard) and if you die, learn from it and start again. The story is great so far, I'll be honest I'm savoring the game so I haven't fully beaten it yet. If you want a city builder that demands your full attention and rewards you for it with amazing music, incredible art design, engaging gameplay, and just plain fun...this is a must buy. I'm not sure why they didn't charge $60 for this because it's a full game with tons of replayability and even room for expansions if they so choose.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like IXION. The concept of the game - a colony sim on a space station - is intriguing, and the plot is engaging and easy to get invested in. Nice graphics, good soundtrack, and the gameplay seems solid at first. I got hooked pretty quickly. Unfortunately, the gameplay becomes quite frustrating later on, for a number of reasons. To summarise: Ultimately, it feels like the developers have set you up to fail right from the start. IXION leaves an impression that there's a "correct" approach to take to playing through the game, and deviating from that approach means your playthrough is going to end in failure.I've broken my main issues up into a few categories:: It's incredibly difficult to plan ahead. You have no idea how much space you'll need for buildings you unlock later, and building space is very limited. Trying to reorganise your sectors to accommodate these buildings is time consuming and tedious, and you can't afford to have time consuming problems like that because you're under  time pressure to advance. Crew members start rebelling if you don't progress the mission fast enough, and the space station itself needs constant repairs to not tear itself apart, heavily taxing the finite resources available in each system. Worse again, it's shockingly easy to soft lock yourself by planning "wrong", and you have no way of knowing that you're planning wrong. You may not even find out until hours later. In the first post-tutorial chapter, I went through the research options and began researching the ones I deemed most useful. By the time I discovered that there was a hidden research option I needed to complete for the plot to advance, I had done all the optional space exploration events in the solar system and run out of research points. I had to wait for the tech lab to passively generate more, which is slow, before I could progress. While waiting for this, the crew got angry about me not progressing the mission we were on, which started a death spiral. I had to spend resources on buildings that improve morale, which ate into the resources I needed to maintain the hull, which meant the hull fell into disrepair, which made the crew get angrier, which resulted in them refusing to work, which ultimately resulted in game over. Unbeknownest to me, my run had ended  before I ever saw a game over screen. I tried again, got to the next chapter easily (because I now had the benefit of knowing in advance what was coming) and then failed again in that second chapter because what seemed like sensible planning (building batteries to prevent power outages) ate too much time and resources, causing another spiral. It feels like there's only one correct approach that you need to figure out in advance. is tedious. The space station where most of the gameplay happens is split into six sectors, each requiring its own storage for different resources. You can't ship iron from your docking bay in sector 1 to your steel mills in sector 2, for example. It needs to go through a docking bay in sector 2, or into a storage unit in sector 1 and from there into sector 2. The automation of moving resources between sectors is practically non-existent. If you have too much of a resource in one sector and not enough in another, you need to go into resource management and manually correct it. You'll do this every time you need to adjust how much of each resource is in a sector. Your station also won't automatically use storage bays in other sectors when one fills up. It's annoying discovering that your polymer factory has shut down because the polymer storage bay is full, even though the next sector has an empty polymer storage.Also, you know the constant time pressure I mentioned earlier? The station's hull is steadily deteriorating. As you progress through the game, the rate of degradation gets worse. You're in a constant race to find, mine, ship and process raw iron into alloy to keep the hull repaired. When every building also uses alloy, you'll often find yourself bottlenecked and delayed on building necessary infrastructure. I didn't find this constant race to stay on top of hull repairs fun, especially when the amount of iron in each system is limited.: I'm going to make a comparison to Frostpunk here, as I think that game handled workers far better. If you're not familiar, Frostpunk had three types of people: Engineers, workers, and children. Engineers did specialist jobs like research, workers did non-specialist jobs like mining, children were (mostly) a resource drain.In IXION, you just have workers and non-workers. The non-workers outnumber the workers, and are largely just dead weight. Later you can train non-workers to do colonisation tests on potentially habitable planets, but for the most part they don't do anything. Aside from that not making sense (I could understand non-specialist workers who couldn't defrost cryopods, but you're telling me they can't even be trained to drive a storage bay forklift?), it creates a frustrating experience where most of your crew are just sitting around eating your food. At one point I had about 1,500 crew members, of which only around 600-700 were workers. I don't see any good reason why someone is capable of being trained to establish a test settlement on an alien planet, but that same person is not capable of being trained as a fireman. It just creates a massive resource drain on food and housing stock (and by extension, your limited building space) for the sake of it. 400 specialist workers, 800 non-specialist workers, 300 children? Sure, that'd be a challenge I could work with. 700 workers and 800 non-workers? Frustrating. Sure there are tech tree upgrades that will help alleviate this, like more productive farms, but you have to reach those upgrades first and for all you know you made a fatal mistake three hours ago.: The workers in your station are frustratingly accident prone, with buildings on the station suffering accidents that shut them down and injure workers almost daily. This will happen regularly even in optimal working conditions. If your sectors are overworked (more jobs active than there is workers available) accidents become more common and more severe. As you can't prevent accidents, you need each sector to have a bunch of idle workers to pick up the slack when injuries occur. So in addition to having a majority of the crew being a resource drain, I now also have workers just sitting around idly waiting to fill in at the infirmary when Dr. Smith stabs himself with a needle for the third time this week. There will also be times where you just won't get a chance to react to a problem that will generate an accident, the consequences are occasionally just instant. At one point, I had an accident at my steel mill, injuring 13 workers. I had left a buffer of 20 idle workers in the sector (all I could afford to spare), but 8 of them were already filling in job vacancies from previous accidents. When the steel mill accident occurred, the sector became overworked by a single job, and the game immediately gave me a serious, fatal accident at the tech lab, killing several workers. I got a "helpful" tutorial pop up about how having a sector overworked would result in more serious accidents. We were one job over capacity for a single second but go on.There's more I'd like to talk about, but I've run foul of the character limit on reviews. There are things to like about IXION, and as I said at the start of this review, I really do want to like it. That tutorial chapter hooked me immediately, and if the rest of the game had kept up that standard it would easily be one of my favourite games. Unfortunately, I found the game to be frustrating in its current state and can't recommend it. Other colony sims I've played felt challenging, but fair. IXION doesn't.
